title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS IN AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The following measure seeks to establish a Congressional Commission on Agriculture and Fisheries, or AGRICOM, to perform a comprehensive review, assessment and evaluation of all existing programs, projects, activities and initiatives currently implemented for the development of the Philippine agriculture and fisheries sector across all national agencies and instrumentalities, in pursuit of a more targeted, efficient, efficacious and integrated approach to agricultural development in the Philippines. In line with our country’s perennial national vision and aspirations to elevate agriculture as the primary driver of long-term growth and development in all communities and localities in the country, our government has enacted innumerable laudable policies and legislation in pursuit of this formidable goal. Pieces of legislation adopted into law have, among many things, created a long list of exhaustive and thoughtfully crafted policy frameworks targeting all subsectors of agriculture and fisheries, and have established, in good faith, a running list of advisory and consultative bodies aiming to give a multitude of recommendations from all sides of the issues and challenges faced by our local agriculture and fisheries subsectors. On the part of Congress, two congressional oversight committees on national agriculture and fisheries policy and programs have been created by law: the Congressional Oversight Committee on Agricultural and Fisheries Modernization (COCAFM) established by Republic Act No. 8435 (or the Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act of 1997), and more recently in 2024, the Congressional Oversight Committee on Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage established by Republic Act No. 12022 (or the Anti-Agricultural Sabotage Act). However, it is not the absence of legislation, nor the absence of policies, programs and projects, nor the absence of advisory and consultative bodies for policies and programs relating 1 to agriculture and fisheries that is the source or cause of the problems facing the sector: it is the fact that the frameworks, policies, programs, projects and bodies created by legislation and other national policies are currently being implemented and operationalized in silos. Advisory and consultative bodies currently convened fall under the jurisdictions and report solely to their mother departments, with documents and other pertinent information undisclosed and unavailable to the public even upon request. Some councils do not have regular meetings because of the unavailability of their members, most of whom serve as ex officio members, due to prior commitments or issues with tenure security. Most government instrumentalities convened and mandated by law to perform functions relating to policy implementation, research and development, price stability, capacity building of local players and participants, are paralyzed by conflicting mandates enforced by different agencies and government bodies, conditions which arise from the lack of coordination among the agencies and government bodies ordering the directives. Policies implemented by one agency for an agricultural subsector run contrary to the policies implemented by another for the same subsector. Redundancies in programs and policies due to the disjointed nature of program and policy implementation for the agriculture and fisheries sector continually lead to the double allocation of funds for the same type of program but under different agencies, while other programs and policies of significance suffer low budget allocations or even lack of funding. The list of issues and challenges continues. This country takes its pursuit of developing our agriculture and fisheries sector into its primary pillar of human capital development, sustainable and dignified structural transformation, and economic security on both the national and local levels. The challenges and issues that result from the current lack of an integrated approach to agriculture and fisheries development speak volumes: while a quarter of our nation’s workers work in agriculture, unskilled workers.1 in agriculture and fisheries experience, on average, at least five percent lower monthly wage rates than their counterparts in manufacturing and services,2 labor productivity in agriculture and fisheries continues to decline,3 all the while the sector only produces about nine percent of our country’s gross domestic product and exports from the sector lag behind our neighbors in the ASEAN Region,4 despite the latter (i.e. the countries of Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam) having larger agricultural bases compared to the Philippines. 1 Elementary Occupations (Unskilled Workers) as defined by the Philippine Statistics Authority. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The agriculture and fisheries sector remain a vital yet persistently underperforming pillar of the Philippine economy. Despite our natural resource base and a large rural labor force, the sector’s contribution to national growth continues to lag due to structural weaknesses in governance, policy fragmentation, and underinvestment. In 2024, agriculture contracted by 2.2%, pulling down the country’s overall economic growth to just 5.2%, well below target. In early 2025, the government declared a national “food security emergency” in response to soaring rice prices—an alarming development in a country historically dependent on rice for daily sustenance. While importation and tariff cuts were deployed as immediate measures, they underscore deeper issues: over-reliance on imports, a weakened regulatory framework, and a farm system that continues to underperform despite budgetary support. This situation is not new. Reputable economists and agricultural experts have long pointed to institutional dysfunction at the root of the sector’s woes. The late Dr. Eliseo R. Ponce, a former president of Visayas State University and a former Executive Director of the Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Agricultural Research, conducted a comprehensive review of the agriculture bureaucracy. He identified critical issues such as over-centralization, fragmented mandates, politicized and commodity-skewed budgeting, and the lack of accountability and capacity support for local government units. label: HB 5129
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES, AND FOOD SECURITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS IN AGRICULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The agriculture and fisheries sector in the Philippines is going through a steady decline, as exhibited by the sector's decreasing productivity and competitiveness and diminishing GDP contribution. Current trends, such as the aging population of farmers and fisherfolk due to reduced income and the country’s increased dependence on importation due to lower agricultural yields, do not paint a positive picture for the future of the country’s agricultural and fisheries sector. Particularly concerning is the direct impact of a dying agricultural and fisheries sector on the food security of the Filipino people. As such, timely, well-informed, comprehensive, decisive, and innovative measures must be promptly taken to address the challenges confronting the agricultural and fisheries sector and safeguard the country’s food security now and in the future. This bill proposes the creation of a Congressional Commission on Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food Security, or the AGRICOM, to address the long-standing and intersectional issues plaguing the country’s agricultural and fisheries sector. Among these issues are the fragmented and uncoordinated system of supporting the agriculture sector, the lack of adequate and institutionalized mechanisms of resource- generation, and the disjoined implementation of agricultural laws and policies, thus leading to conflicting mandates, redundant programs, and inefficient budget allocation. The AGRICOM, acting as a central, independent body, shall provide cohesive and comprehensive solutions to the sector's complex and intertwined problems through the following: Conducting a comprehensive review and assessment of all existing agricultural and fisheries programs, policies, and projects across all national agencies in the country; Identifying policy conflicts and program redundancies to formulate a more efficient and integrated framework; Developing targeted, measurable, and_ time-bound policy recommendations aimed at increasing the sector's productivity, competitiveness, and capacity; and Reporting its findings and recommendations to the public with the purpose of fostering transparency and prompting swift action from implementing agencies. The AGRICOM is the government's way of creating a more comprehensive and targeted response to the increasingly complex issues faced by the agriculture and fisheries sector and the consequences of the sector’s decline on national food security, employment, economy, and poverty. The urgency and necessity of taking decisive measures to support the dying sector of agriculture and fisheries cannot be overstated. This bill fully adopts Senator Francis Pangilinan’s SBN 1199 filed under the present 20* Congress. Early passage of this bill is requested. title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES, AND FOOD SECURITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS IN AGRICULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines’ agriculture and fisheries sectors continue to face long-standing problems that limit their growth and stability. Despite numerous laws, programs, and oversight bodies, these efforts remain fragmented, often resulting in overlapping functions, inefficient spending, and weak coordination among agencies. Farmers and fishers — who form nearly a quarter of the nation’s workforce — continue to struggle with low productivity, declining participation, and limited access to support systems that could improve their incomes and competitiveness. These challenges persist because policy direction, implementation, and monitoring are often carried out in isolation. Agencies work within their own mandates with little integration, causing duplication of programs and inconsistencies in strategy. Meanwhile, issues such as climate change, postharvest losses, poor logistics, and lack of access to financing continue to weaken the sector’s performance and the country’s food security. This bill seeks to establish a Congressional Commission on Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food Security (AGRICOM) — a special, independent body that will take a comprehensive look at the entire agriculture and fisheries landscape. The Commission will review existing laws, policies, and programs; assess institutional bottlenecks and overlaps; and recommend concrete, time-bound reforms to make government efforts more cohesive, efficient, and responsive to current realities. AGRICOM will serve as a bridge between policy and implementation. It will bring together experts, legislators, government agencies, and stakeholders from the private sector, academe, and local governments to develop actionable reforms. Its goal is to streamline the bureaucracy, modernize systems, strengthen coordination, and ensure that every peso spent in the sector contributes directly to food security and rural prosperity. By aligning government policies and investments under a unified, evidence-based framework, this measure aims to transform Philippine agriculture and fisheries into dynamic, sustainable, and globally competitive engines of inclusive growth. Immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. label: HB 6689
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE (AGRICOM), TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND AGRI-FOOD SYSTEMS, AND TO RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE, RESPONSIVE, AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS FOR AGRICULTURAL TRANSFORMATION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture and fisheries remain the foundation of national development, ensuring food security, sustaining rural livelihoods, and contributing significantly to inclusive economic growth. These sectors not only provide the country’s staple food and raw materials but also support millions of Filipino farmers, fisherfolk, agri-workers, and rural households who form the backbone of the national economy. Agriculture continues to shape the country’s cultural identity, regional economies, and local food systems, playing a vital role in maintaining social stability, territorial integrity, and community resilience. Yet despite their strategic importance, the sector continues to suffer from long- standing and deeply rooted challenges—stagnant productivity, outdated technologies, inadequate extension systems, weak market linkages, fragmented governance, chronic underinvestment, and the worsening impacts of climate change. These structural issues have resulted in inefficient value chains, high production losses, low rural incomes, and increased dependence on food imports. Global disruptions—from supply chain volatility to geopolitical tensions— further expose the fragility of the Philippines’ agri-food systems. Collectively, these constraints hinder the nation’s capacity to achieve food sovereignty, rural prosperity, and long-term resilience. These persistent challenges have made it clear that agricultural reform cannot be addressed by short-term or piecemeal interventions. There is an urgent need for a unified, science-based, and forward-looking institutional mechanism that can harmonize policies, guide long-term planning, coordinate national and local initiatives, and provide Congress with the analytical rigor needed to legislate transformative reforms. The proposed “Congressional Commission on Agriculture (AGRICOM) Act” responds to this need by establishing an independent, multisectoral, and evidence- informed Congressional Commission mandated to spearhead a comprehensive national review of the agriculture and fisheries sector. The AGRICOM will function as the primary legislative policy advisory body responsible for developing coordinated, inclusive, and future-oriented reforms aimed at making Philippine agriculture more productive, competitive, sustainable, and resilient to climate change. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11060
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES, AND FOOD SECURITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES, RECOMMEND TARGETED POLICY AND INSTITUTIONAL REFORMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture is not merely an economic sector. It is the foundation of the country's food security, rural economy, employment, and national resilience. Yet, despite decades of government programs, subsidies, reforms, and investments, the Philippine agriculture and fisheries sector continues to face a deep and persistent structural crisis. The available government data are difficult to ignore. In 2023, 27.0 percent of Filipino farmers and 27.4 percent of fisherfolk were living below the official poverty threshold, making farmers and fisherfolk among the basic sectors with the highest poverty incidences in the country. While these figures represent an improvement from 2021, when poverty incidence reached 30.0 percent among farmers and 30.6 percent among fisherfolk, the fact remains that more than one in every four farmers and fisherfolk remained poor. This is particularly alarming because agriculture continues to provide livelihoods to a substantial portion of the Filipino workforce. In December 2025, 20.7 percent of all employed Filipinos were working in agriculture, making it the second-largest broad sector of employment after services. Agriculture and forestry alone accounted for 18.8 percent of total employment. Despite employing approximately one-fifth of the country's workers, however, agriculture, forestry, and fishing accounted for only 7.9 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product in 2025. The sector grew by 3.1 percent in 2025 after contracting by 1.5 percent in 2024, but its share of the national economy remained smaller than the 8.0 percent recorded in the previous year. The disparity between agriculture's role in employment and its contribution to national economic output illustrates a fundamental productivity and income problem. Millions of Filipinos depend on agriculture for their livelihood, yet the sector continues to generate comparatively low economic value per worker. The country's food production situation likewise demonstrates the vulnerability of the agricultural sector. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Philippine palay production fell to 6.85 million metric tons, a 5.2 percent decline from the same quarter of 2024. More significantly, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported that this was the lowest fourth-quarter palay production recorded since 2012. The area harvested to palay likewise declined by 4.3 percent during the period. The decline in farm production is accompanied by serious income pressures on producers. From April to June 2025, the seasonally adjusted farmgate price of palay fell by 10.8 percent, from ₱19.45 per kilogram in the first quarter to ₱17.35 per kilogram in the second quarter. By the third quarter, the seasonally adjusted farmgate price had fallen further to ₱16.29 per kilogram, representing another 6.5 percent decline from the preceding quarter. Thus, even when production improves on an annual basis, farmers can remain vulnerable when farmgate prices decline and production costs remain high. Increased output does not automatically translate into improved farmer incomes. The country's dependence on agricultural imports further demonstrates the structural weakness of domestic production. In 2025, the Philippines recorded US$29.63 billion in total agricultural trade, the highest level recorded since the PSA's agricultural trade series began in 1991. However, the country registered an agricultural trade deficit of US$11.12 billion. In other words, the value of agricultural products imported into the Philippines substantially exceeded the value of agricultural products exported by the country. This persistent agricultural trade deficit is particularly concerning for a country whose agricultural sector employs roughly one-fifth of its workforce and whose food security depends on reliable domestic production. The problem is not limited to rice. In the fourth quarter of 2025, the country's overall crop production volume declined by 1.6 percent year-on-year, with palay accounting for a significant part of the decline. Meanwhile, the value of agriculture and fisheries production for the full year of 2025 amounted to approximately ₱1.77 trillion, representing only a 2.6 percent year-on-year increase. Crop production declined by 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter, while palay production value declined by 5.2 percent during the same period. These figures reveal a troubling pattern: the country continues to have a large population dependent on agriculture, but the sector struggles to generate sufficient productivity, income, and economic value for the people who work in it. The crisis is therefore not simply a problem of insufficient production. It is a crisis of productivity, farmer income, competitiveness, market structure, infrastructure, technology adoption, financing, climate resilience, post-harvest systems, and institutional coordination. The persistence of these problems despite the existence of numerous government agencies and programs suggests that the Philippines needs more than another isolated intervention. What is required is a comprehensive assessment of the country's entire agricultural and fisheries system—from production and land use to financing, irrigation, mechanization, research and development, post-harvest facilities, logistics, processing, marketing, trade, and consumer access. There is likewise a need to determine whether government resources are being directed toward programs that produce measurable and sustainable results. The country cannot afford fragmented interventions in which different agencies pursue overlapping objectives without a unified, evidence- based national strategy. It is against this backdrop that this measure proposes the creation of the Congressional Commission on Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Security (AGRICOM). label: SB 1199
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES AND FOOD SECURITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS IN AGRICULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This legislative measure seeks to establish a Congressional Commission on Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Security, or the AGRICOM, to address the long­ standing issues plaguing the Philippines' agricultural sector, which is hindered by a fragmented and uncoordinated system despite numerous existing laws and policies. While there are various oversight committees such as the Congressional Oversight Committee on Agricultural and Fisheries Modernization (COCAFM) and the Congressional Oversight Committee on Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage (COCAAES), the core problem is the disjoined implementation approach. Government agencies operate in "silos", leading to conflicting mandates, redundant programs, and inefficient budget allocation. Despite a quarter of the country's workforce being in agriculture and fisheries, labor continues to decline, and the sector's contribution to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remains low. Our agricultural exports also lag behind our ASEAN neighbors. The persistent issues of post-harvest losses, weak supply chain integration, limited access to credit, and vulnerability to climate-related shocks further hinder the sector's performance. Additionally, the overlapping responsibilities between national agencies and local government units (LGUs), following the devolution of agricultural services, require coordinated action for improvement. The AGRICOM is designed to provide a cohesive solution by acting as a central, independent body that will: (1) Conduct a comprehensive review and assessment of all existing agricultural and fisheries programs and policies, and projects across all national agencies; (2) Identify policy conflicts and program redundancies to create a more efficient and integrated framework; (3) Develop targeted, measurable, and time- bound policy recommendations aimed at increasing productivity, global competitiveness, and capacity building for the sector; and (4) Report its findings and recommendations to the public, fostering transparency and prompting swift action from implementing agencies. The creation of the AGRICOM will help streamline government efforts, assist agencies in balancing their mandates, and ensure that support for the agricultural sector is targeted and effective. This will ultimately address the foundational issues that have long hindered the sector's growth and stability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: SB 1345
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON AGRICULTURE TO REVIEW, ASSESS, EVALUATE, AND RECOMMEND REFORMS IN THE PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURE SECTOR, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution states that "The State shall promote industrialization and full employment based on sound agricultural development." From this constitutional provision, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 8435 otherwise known as the "Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act of 1997" (AFMA). The AFMA emphasized the welfare of small farmers and fisherfolk (SFF) in its push toward agriculture modernization. The AFMA aims to: i. To modernize the agriculture and fisheries sectors by transforming these sectors from a resource-based to a technology-based industry; ii. To enhance profits and incomes in the agriculture and fisheries sectors; iii. To ensure the accessibility, availability, and stable supply of food at all times; IV. To encourage horizontal and vertical integration, consolidation, and expansion of agriculture and fisheries activities; To promote people empowerment by strengthening people's organizations (POs), cooperatives, and nongovernment organizations (NGOs); VI. To pursue a market-driven approach to enhance the comparative advantage of the agriculture and fisheries sectors in the world market; VII. To induce the agriculture and fisheries sectors to ascend continuously on the value-added ladder; VIII. To adopt policies that will promote industry dispersal and rural industrialization; ix. To provide social and economic adjustment measures that increase productivity and improve market efficiency while ensuring the protection and preservation of the environment and equity for SFF Twenty-eight years after its passage, the agricultural and fisheries sector remains hampered by various challenges. According to the 2023 Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES), farmers and fisherfolk continues to record among the highest poverty rates on the 11 basic sectors identified under Republic Act No. 8425 or the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act, with poverty rates of 27.0% and 27.4%, respectively, compared to the national rate of 15.5%. Rice importation continues to increase year on year, with total rice imports reaching 4.68 million metric tons. The share of agriculture in the GDP remains stagnant, with agricultural output contracting by a record 2.2% in 2024. Given these various challenges, it is imperative that the country follows the example of the Education Commission or EdCom and form a high-level Agriculture Commission or AgriCom. This bill aims to create an Agriculture Commission to thoroughly examine the agriculture bureaucracy and recommend institutional reforms to enable the modernization of the sector. For the abovementioned reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. f. title: AN ACT CREATING THE EMERGENCY RESPONSE DEPARTMENT (ERD), APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the countries in the world most vulnerable to disasters and the effects of climate change, and disaster preparedness is everyone’s job to fulfill. While through the years there has been some progress in building disaster mitigation, the two significant changes we have not made are addressing climate change and putting up a specialized department on disaster resilience. In the 2022 World Risk Index, the Philippines ranked first (1st) out of 193 countries in terms of disaster risk.1 Further, according to the 2021 Global Climate Risk Index (CRI), the Philippines ranked seventeenth (17th) in the world as the most affected by climate-related weather catastrophes.2 The study rankings reflect that there is a need to establish a clear chain of command in times of major disasters, a focused and specialized single government agency that functions not only after the occurrence of disasters, but works all-year- round to ensure that effective mechanisms for disaster risk reduction are in place even before a disaster occurs since the effects of climate change and the prevalence of disasters now seem to constitute the “new normal”. Furthermore, one of the major problems that needs to be addressed is the non-compliance with laws such as the National Building Code and Fire Code of the Philippines, the lack of evacuation procedures, the prevalence of illegal logging, the building of structures on rivers and waterways which impede the flow of water, and the non-segregation of garbage in violation of law. The measure seeks to establish a Department that is 1) independent and well-coordinated with other governing institutions, given supervisory functions over the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration and the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, 2) given visitorial powers to ensure 1 https://weltrisikobericht.de/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/WorldRiskReport-2022_Online.pdf; 2 https://cpbrd.congress.gov.ph/2012-06-30-13-06-51/2012-06-30-13-36-50/1291-ff2021-09-global-climate-risk-index -2021 1 that funding and donations to all entities are used actually, directly, 3) equipped with emergency and contingency powers, such as commandeering and calling out the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the Philippine National Police in order to repress lawlessness and maintain peace and order in a disaster-stricken area, and 4) empowered to declare a state of calamity in a locality, in consultation with the local government unit concerned, according to established guidelines and protocols developed by the Department. The proposed legislation establishes the ERD, which shall take over the policy-making, coordination, integration, supervision, monitoring and evaluation functions of the present ad hoc inter-agency council. The proposed department is equipped with bureaus specifically tasked to deal with concerns related to the pillars of disaster risk reduction and management, namely, disaster prevention and mitigation; disaster preparedness; and humanitarian and disaster response. The functions of the bureaus are specified to ensure performance of their critical mandates and roles before, during and after a humanitarian emergency or disaster. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is most urgently and earnestly recommended. Hon. Ricardo “Ading” S. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE "...for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." Galatians 6:7 (KJV) Today is the best time to prepare our nation against calamities and disasters. Today is the best of times to plant the seeds of preparedness. The more that we prepare, the more we are able to cope with disasters. The readiness and resilience of our nation against disasters and calamities lie significantly in our own actions. We must do away with the "ningas cogon" approach to disasters where we work hard only at the beginning but become negligent later on. A sustained perseverance and persistence is required to substantially reduce disaster risk and losses in lives and livelihoods. While through the years there has been some progress in building disaster mitigation, the two significant changes we have not made are addressing climate change and putting up a specialized department on disaster resilience. In the 2021 World Risk Report, the Philippines ranked eighth out of 181 countries in terms of disaster risk. Manila, the country's capital, has also been ranked by the Climate Change Vulnerability Index [CCVI] as the most vulnerable of the world's 20 “high growth cities" to the effects of climate change. Further, according to Berlin-based environmental organization Germanwatch, the Philippines ranked 4th among countries most affected by climate-related weather catastrophes from 2000 to 2019. The country sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, rendering it susceptible to various natural catastrophes. The problem is compounded by gaps in the implementation of laws and regulations. These include, but are not limited to, non- compliance with laws such as the National Building Code and Fire Code of the Philippines, the lack of evacuation procedures, the prevalence of illegal logging, the building of structures on rivers and waterways which impede the flow of water, and the non-segregation of garbage in violation of law. According to the Asian Disaster Preparedness Center, there are different models on disaster management The traditional approach to disaster management has been to regard it as a number of phased sequences of action or a continuum. This can be represented as a cycle. However, more modern models view it as a continuous process, or a sequence of cause and effect, or a system of addressing the underlying causes of disasters towards safer conditions. In many countries around the world, there are specialized agencies at the department level which deal with disasters. There are a few which have a task force model that the President/Prime Minister controls. The present law on disasters. Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010“, revolutionized and pioneered disaster risk reduction and management in the country. Signed into law on May 27,2010, it ordained a National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council with policy-making, coordination, integration, supervision, monitoring and evaluation functions. When the Act was signed into law some three years ago, it was hailed as a landmark legislation which adopts the pillars of disaster risk reduction and management in the country. Today, the Act continues to be relevant in preventing/mitigating, preparing for, and responding to disaster, yet recent experience shows as that our disaster risk reduction management model needs to adapt to our culture and existing circumstances However, legislation should be created, or old legislation revisited, to promote effectivity and efficiency, as well as accountability, responsibility, and transparency. Differences between the national government and local governments as regards structures should be reconciled, where appropriate, and areas for improvement addressed. For instance, in the present law, there must be a mechanism that responds to the eventuality of a total or considerable breakdown of authority resulting from a humanitarian emergency or disaster. This requires response that goes beyond the mandate or capacity of the local government unit concerned. Otherwise, there would be a paralysis in the disaster response system and people affected by the disaster would not be able to receive critical life-saving interventions and relief. In today's world, disasters are a fact of life. Some emergencies may be totally prevented, while others may not be averted. We may not be able to stop disasters, however, we can empower ourselves with knowledge, training/education, equipment/tools, and the right infrastructure to cope with disasters, so many lives would not be lost and there would be less devastation. A window of opportunity exists to sow seeds of preparedness in order to reap resilience to disasters. While we have very good people in the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, it is high time that the government provides for a focused, single-minded, specialized department to upgrade the government's capacity to respond to disasters in an effective and speedy manner. Philippine experience shows that there is a need to establish a clear chain of command in times of major disasters, a focused and specialized single government agency that functions not only after the occurrence of disasters, but works all-year- round to ensure that effective mechanisms for disaster risk reduction are in place even before a disaster occurs since the effects of climate change and the prevalence of disasters now seem to constitute the “new normal". Such specialized Department shall bear laser-like preciseness in focus, give primacy to pre-disaster resilience building, and prioritize life preservation and basic subsistence needs in the communities affected by a disaster. The dignity and value of the human life must be its guidepost and the deterrence of loss of lives is its ultimate mission. label: HB 2912
title: AN ACT CREATING THE EMERGENCY RESPONSE DEPARTMENT (ERD), APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE We are at a crossroads. And whatever decisions we reach and the actions we collectively take today will reverberate through many generations of Filipinos–to our children, our grandchildren, and all those who will come after us. We must step up now. Now is the best time to prepare our nation against calamities and disasters. Now is the best time to plant the seeds of preparedness. Every Filipino has to live with three realities. First, for the third straight year, the Philippines has been ranked the most at-risk country to disasters among 193 countries assessed in the 2024 World Risk Index (WRI) published by the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict and Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft (Alliance Development Works). On a scale of 0 (very low risk) to 100 (very high risk), the Philippines’ score even worsened to 46.91 in 2024 from 46.86 in 2023. Current mean projections of climate up to 2050 suggest the Philippines will become warmer by 1.8 °C to 2.2 °C in 2050, with increasing temperature and decreasing rainfall during the dry season and more extreme rainfall events during the wet season exacerbating both water availability during periods of drought and the intensity of flood events during periods of heavy rainfall. The projected increase in sea level rise of 20 centimeters (cm) by the end of the 21st century will compound water stresses and affect coastal settlements. If we do not act now, there simply will be no tomorrow for our children and future generations of Filipinos. Second, there is a climate emergency affecting the world. From the devastating Super Typhoon Carina to Severe Tropical Storm Kristine to Super Typhoon Pepito, what kind of proof do we still need to show that there is a climate emergency? And third, hazards do not always need to end in disasters. We are far from powerless in the face of this global threat. As United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres pointed out in October 2020, “Bad situations only get worse without good disaster risk governance”. In other words, with good disaster risk governance, we can prevent or at least mitigate the negative impacts of disaster risks. 1 The Philippines, by reason of our geography, is especially affected by various types of hazards. Our country is unfortunately located along the Pacific typhoon belt, in the midst of the Pacific Ring of Fire. Our archipelago of more than 7,600 islands experiences an average of 20 storms and typhoons and about five hundred magnitude 4.0 and above earthquakes in a year. The threat of “The Big One” has loomed over us for the longest time. The Philippines is also susceptible to slow-onset climate hazards such as sea level rise and drought. These events are not just statistics, but are tragedies that destroy lives and devastate communities, leaving scars that defy quantification. Being the country most at risk to disasters is not a death sentence, but a wakeup call and a challenge. We should learn from our neighbors like Japan, which has been able to adapt to the hazards they are facing. While Japan has a higher exposure to extreme natural events than the Philippines, faring third worldwide in terms of exposure respectively compared to the Philippines which ranks fourth, the former fares better than the latter – 24th over-all in the World Risk Index – because of its structural investments in early warning systems and infrastructure and disaster risk management systems. When we bandy our disaster risk reduction and management capabilities, Mother Nature comes in to audit our claims. From 2018 to 2022, disasters and incidents caused by natural hazards resulted in 3,265 deaths, affected 67 million people and caused Php 226 billion worth of damage and losses. In 2023 alone, natural hazards caused Php 24.49 billion in total damages. Whether the government is succeeding in its efforts to reduce and manage disaster risks is measurable in the number of lives lost, houses destroyed, and livelihoods ruined by hazards. Mother Nature’s audit requires not only reflection. It requires action. The Philippines faces increasing risks that exacerbate various types of hazards, resulting in both economic and non-economic loss and damage. Addressing these impacts requires strengthening our disaster risk reduction and management systems to enhance preparedness, response, and recovery in building resilience. While we undeniably made strides in improving our disaster resiliency, current geophysical and climatological risks necessitate a reassessment of our framework. Republic Act 10121 or the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, was enacted into law more than 15 years ago. Since then, our country has undergone multitudes of natural events from which we have learned lessons. Philippine experience shows that there is a need to establish a clear chain of command in times of major disasters, focusing on systematic, synergistic, and sustainable framework for effective and efficient preparation, anticipation, response, and recovery mechanisms to implement immediate emergency response, and establish transformative policy, operational, organization, functional, and resource mobilization interventions to address gaps and needs to stabilise and build resilience of communities over time. 2 Now is the time to double our efforts, and also the time to focus our resources, align our policies, and streamline our institutions. In view of the foregoing, the passage of the bill establishing the Emergency Response Department (ERD) is earnestly sought. This shall be the lead implementing agency of the Philippine Adaptation Master Plan for Disaster Risk Resilience. The ERD shall pursue not only a whole-of-government approach but a whole-of-society approach in facing sudden onset of emergencies. The agency shall ensure that policies will be more than aspirational but will ensure that there is synergy among all government agencies to steer the government towards a more resilient Philippines. label: HB 4116
title: AN ACT CREATING THE EMERGENCY RESPONSE DEPARTMENT (ERD), APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “If one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,’ but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it?” James 2:16 The Philippines, being located within the Pacific Ring of Fire and the typhoon belt, is no stranger to natural hazards and calamities. In recent years, the country has endured countless typhoons, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods, conflagrations, and other hazards, many of which have grown more intense. In 2024 alone, the Philippines endured one of its most active typhoon seasons on record with six tropical cyclones entering the country within just three weeks, affecting over 16 million people with an estimated damage of P15.6 billion1. That same year, the Office of Civil Defense2 reported 225 occurrences of small-scale natural hazards for 2024—the most of which are flash floods or flooding, followed by tornadoes, destructive winds, or strong winds, and fire incidents. The Bureau of Fire Protection also recorded 18,256 fire incidents for 2024, causing nearly P14 billion in property damage and claiming 341 lives3. Beyond natural disasters, the country also confronts various man-made hazards and other humanitarian emergencies, including industrial accidents, environmental degradation, health crises, and public safety threats such as armed conflict and terrorism, which compound the risks faced by vulnerable communities. As a former barangay chairman, I have seen firsthand the realities faced by our local government units before, during, and after disasters and emergencies. I witnessed the struggles of communities left reeling from floods, fires, and typhoons. In those moments, our constituents looked to us for leadership, relief, and protection. The City of Taguig is fortunate to have invested heavily in disaster preparedness and community resilience. Over the years, our city has strengthened its disaster response capabilities, equipped our barangays, and trained personnel to respond quickly when calamities strike. These efforts have helped save lives and reduce losses. Yet, not all local government units are as fortunate. Many barangays and municipalities are left to shoulder responsibilities far greater than their limited resources. This gap is where 1 World Food Programme (2025). 2024 Typhoon Season: WFP Philippines Response Report. Retrieved from https://www.wfp.org/publications/2024-typhoon-season-wfp-philippines-response-report 2 as cited in PSA (2025). Compendium of Philippine Environment Statistics Highlights. Retrieved from https://psa.gov.ph/content/total-225-small-scale-natural-hazard-occurred-philippines-2024 3 https://mb.com.ph/2025/1/5/bfp-nationwide-2024-fire-incidents-up-by-1-823-from-previous-year national government must step in—not to replace local leadership, but to empower and support it by providing adequate resources and better coordination. It is for this reason that a national Emergency Response Department (ERD) is hereby proposed—to ensure that every Filipino community, regardless of size or wealth, has the support it needs in the face of disaster. Under this proposed measure, the ERD shall serve as the lead implementing agency of a national master plan for disaster resilience. It shall institutionalize a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, ensuring that policies are no longer aspirational but operational, and that resources reach people when they need them most. With direct accountability over the four pillars of disaster risk reduction—prevention, response, recovery, and rehabilitation— the ERD will provide a solution-driven mechanism to protect lives and build resilience in every community. The Bible, in James 2:16, captures the essence of meaningful service. It reminds us that words of comfort mean little if not matched with action. Preparedness and response, therefore, must go beyond rhetoric. In times of disaster, sympathy alone cannot rebuild homes, restore livelihoods, or save lives. What our people need is not just compassion, but concrete, immediate, and effective assistance. In view of the foregoing, the passage of the bill is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF CLIMATE RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, situated within the Pacific Ring of Fire and the typhoon belt, faces one of the most complex and overlapping hazard profiles in the world. On average, the country experiences more than twenty typhoons annually, five of which are destructive, in addition to frequent earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, flooding, droughts, and slow-onset climate change effects such as sea level rise and biodiversity loss. According to the World Risk Index 2023, the Philippines ranks as the most at-risk country globally due to the convergence of exposure, vulnerability, and insufficient adaptive capacities1. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 10121 in 2010, which created the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) and advanced the disaster risk reduction paradigm, major institutional gaps persist. Fragmented mandates, weak vertical coordination, limited scientific integration, and persistent underperformance by many local government units (LGUs) continue to undermine national resilience efforts 2. This bill seeks to create the Department of Climate Resilience (DCR) as the lead national agency responsible for policy, planning, coordination, innovation, capacity building, and command in disaster risk reduction, emergency response, climate adaptation, and recovery. The proposed Department shall institutionalize the National Climate Resilience Framework (NCRF), implement 1 Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft & Ruhr University Bochum – Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV). (2023). World Risk Report 2023. 2 Asian Development Bank (ADB). (2021). Philippines: Assessment of Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Institutional Capacity. ADB Technical Assistance Report. risk-informed and equity-sensitive policies, and establish a national system that integrates science, technology, and governance for anticipatory and adaptive resilience. The proposal reflects global lessons and scientific consensus on the need for centralized yet networked governance in climate resilience3. The Department shall anchor its strategy in data- driven planning, localized implementation, interoperable information systems, and sustained financing mechanisms. It will lead the formulation and execution of integrated resilience instruments including the National Risk Register, Local Resilience Performance Index, Digital Twin Technologies, Resilience Bonds, Pre-Disaster Recovery Planning, and a National Climate Resilience Scorecard, among others. These tools align with international frameworks such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030,4 and support national development goals and international obligations under the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 5. Globally, integrated risk governance frameworks—including digital and performance-based systems—have demonstrated significant improvements in situational awareness, anticipatory decision-making, and service delivery 6. The integration of digital twins, interoperable data platforms, and forecast-based action protocols has enabled governments in Asia and Europe to optimize their response architecture and reduce lead time to critical action 7. In the Philippine context, pilot studies show that community-level digital risk tools significantly enhanced hazard mapping, early warning, and evacuation planning capacities in vulnerable rural barangays 8. Scientific literature emphasizes that resilience-building must be adaptive, inclusive, and systems- based9. This bill mandates the creation of functional bureaus and regional support mechanisms capable of providing technical assistance, surge capacity, and accountability enforcement. The Department shall further mainstream resilience procurement, establish Green Resilience Corridors, support Localized Resilience Hubs, and implement Climate Justice and Inclusion Mechanisms to ensure that vulnerable populations are prioritized in planning and response 10. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TERTIARY EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all’. It further requires the State to establish and maintain a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education that is responsive to the needs of the people and society”. At present, post-secondary education is administered separately by the Commission on Higher Education and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority. This bill seeks to establish the Department of Tertiary Education to unify its functions under a single agency, addressing long- standing issues of policy fragmentation, overlapping mandates, and the lack of alignment between academic and technical pathways. The proposed Department will serve as the central agency responsible for the regulation, support, and coordination of all post-secondary education pathways, including universities, colleges, technical-vocational institutions, and non-traditional learning systems. It shall ensure unified standards, promote inclusive access, and align education programs with national workforce and development goals’. By establishing a single authority for tertiary education, the State strengthens quality assurance, institutional efficiency, and the relevance of education in meeting the demands of a rapidly changing economy‘ In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. « . explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives (BAC) has long been recognized as a vital government agency tasked with the development, promotion, and support of agricultural cooperatives in the Philippines. Historically attached to the Department of Agriculture, BAC provided critical services such as credit facilitation, technical assistance, training, and capacity-building programs to empower agricultural cooperatives and improve the welfare of smallholder farmers. Under Republic Act No. 6939, also known as the Cooperative Development Authority Law, the BAC was absorbed into the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), which aimed to consolidate cooperative governance under one umbrella. However, this structural change has limited the CDA’s ability to effectively address the specific needs of agricultural cooperatives, whose operations are closely linked with the broader agricultural policies and programs of the Department of Agriculture. This bill proposes to establish the Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives as a new attached agency under the Department of Agriculture. This establishment will allow BAC to: e Specialize in providing services and support specifically tailored to agricultural cooperatives, including credit programs, capacity building, and technical assistance; e Facilitate stronger coordination with other bureaus and agencies within the Department of Agriculture for more integrated and effective rural and agricultural development initiatives; e Enhance governance, program implementation, and _ service delivery to agricultural cooperatives, ensuring they remain competitive and sustainable; e Contribute significantly to rural development, poverty alleviation, and national food security by empowering agricultural cooperatives. This establishment recognizes the important historical role of BAC and the necessity to restore its mandate within the Department of Agriculture framework to better serve the unique challenges faced by agricultural cooperatives. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Manuel “Ma . explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bureau of Agricultural Cooperative and Industry Development (BACID) is hereby established to address the evolving needs of both cooperative development and the modernization of agriculture in the Philippines. This new agency combines the focus of the previous Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives (BACOD) on cooperative development with an expanded mandate to include the modemization of agriculture, including agro-processing, market access, transportation, and logistics. This expanded mandate aims to empower agricultural cooperatives to actively contribute to the agricultural value chain, ensuring that farmers are adequately supported in value-added activities, ultimately helping to ensure fair pricing, food security, and sustainable agricultural growth. BACID shall likewise promote the clustering of smallholder farms through cooperatives, with the objective of facilitating shared resource utilization, enhancing market access, and improving production efficiency. This approach seeks to strengthen the agricultural sector, promote equitable pricing mechanisms, and contribute to national food security. By establishing BACLD, the government wiil create an agency that not only regulates cooperatives but also drives their growth, market integration, and modernization, which is essential for building a more resilient, inclusive agricultural economy in the Philippines. BACID shall inherit the cooperative development functions of the former Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives (BACOD) but with an expanded mandate to drive agricultural modernization. This includes the clustering of small farms, contract growing, and agro- processing initiatives, which are outside the scope of the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA). While the CDA continues to focus on cooperative regulation and legal compliance, BACID shall focus on cooperative development, market integration, and agricultural modernization. BACID will facilitate the consolidation of small farms through cooperatives and promote contract growing arrangements, creating a more robust agriculiural sector and ensuring fair pricing and food security. Approval of this bill is eamestly sought. Habe ATTY. JAN RURIK D. title: AN ACT ENSURING THE DEVELOPMENT, PROMOTION, AND PROTECTION OF AGRICULTURAL COOPERATIVES, PROVIDING FOR THE CREATION OF THE BUREAU OF AGRICULTURAL COOPERATIVES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Food insecurity and rural poverty continue to weigh heavily on the Philippines. Farmers and fisherfolk—those who put food on our tables—remain among the poorest sectors in society. Many of them still struggle to access credit, technology, and markets that could help raise their incomes and improve their livelihoods. One of the most effective ways to change this reality is through agricultural cooperatives. When farmers and fishers organize, they gain strength in numbers: they can pool resources, buy farm inputs at lower prices, share equipment, and sell their produce collectively to secure better market prices. These cooperatives also become channels for innovation, modern farming practices, and access to government support. However, many agricultural cooperatives remain small, scattered, and under- resourced. They need stronger institutional support to reach their full potential and contribute meaningfully to national food security and rural development. This bill seeks to empower agricultural cooperatives by establishing a Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives under the Department of Agriculture. The Bureau will serve as the lead agency in promoting, regulating, and supporting agricultural cooperatives nationwide. It will provide training, capacity-building, financing, and technical assistance to help these cooperatives modernize, become more resilient, and operate sustainably. The bill also promotes clustering and consolidation among cooperatives to achieve economies of scale, introduces climate-resilient and digital agricultural practices, and creates a Cooperative Climate Resilience Fund to help protect farmers against disasters and climate risks. By strengthening agricultural cooperatives, this measure aims to create a more inclusive and competitive agricultural sector—one that ensures food security, uplifts rural communities, and brings dignity and prosperity to those who feed the nation. Immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. It is a painful irony that those who produce the country’s food are often the ones who experience hunger and deprivation the most. According to the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), cooperatives play a significant role in the Philippine economy. However, many agricultural cooperatives remain fragmented, underfunded, and constrained by limited access to markets, financing, and modern technologies. Studies conducted by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) consistently demonstrate that cooperative members enjoy greater access to credit, improved farming technologies, and wider market opportunities. By enabling small-scale producers to pool resources, purchase inputs collectively, and market their products more effectively, cooperatives help reduce production costs, increase incomes, and improve overall competitiveness. 1 A similar measure has been filed and passed in the Senate and this proposed measure builds upon it and serves as a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives, sharing the common objective of advancing, promoting, and protecting agricultural cooperatives through the establishment of a dedicated bureau. The immediate passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) data (2023) shows that farmers and fisherfolk are the poorest sectors, with poverty incidence estimates at 27.0% and 27.4%, respectively. Agricultural cooperatives are crucial to addressing these issues. Data from the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA) shows that cooperatives are a vital part of the economy, but many agricultural cooperatives struggle with fragmentation and limited resources. Studies from organizations like the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) consistently show that farmers who are members of cooperatives have better access to credit, modern technology, and markets. These organizations enable economies of scale by allowing small-scale farmers to collectively purchase inputs and sell their produce, increasing their income and reducing their costs. This bill aims to strengthen agricultural cooperatives as key partners for national food security and rural development. It seeks to: (a) Provide funding and resources to boost the productivity and sustainability of agricultural cooperatives; (b) Encourage clustering and consolidation to achieve economies of scale, and improve competitiveness of agricultural cooperatives; (c) Promote modern, climate-resilient farming practices and technologies; (d) Enhance access to credit, knowledge, and collective marketing through cooperative networks; and (e) Build the capacity of smallholder farmers through improved extension services and training. It is respectfully acknowledged that a similar measure has been filed by Senator Risa Hontiveros. This bill draws on and complements said measure, sharing the common objective of advancing the development, promotion, and protection of agricultural cooperatives through the creation of a dedicated bureau. Empowering these cooperatives can create a more resilient agricultural sector, reduce poverty, and ensure food self-sufficiency for millions of Filipinos. The immediate passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought. FRANCIS N. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 8485 as amended by RA.10631 by strengthening the provisions of law relating to animal welfare and by likewise creating the Animal Welfare Bureau, attached agency with the Department of Agriculture. For the past years, there has been an increase in the consciousness of the Filipino people on the welfare of animals resulting in a massive surge of establishments catering to animals - from veterinary clinics and hospitals, grooming, pet hotels and pet cafes, pet friendly establishments, among others. The current structure of the Bureau of Animal Industry however, has shown weaknesses in responding to and in addressing the growing welfare issues and concerns affecting the animals. As a regulatory body for animal welfare under RA 8485 as amended, compliance monitoring has become a burden due to lack of dedicated and trained manpower and facilities. Implementation of the law has likewise been severely lacking as a result of the weak cooperation from the LGUS. This Bill aims to strengthen and fortify animal welfare standards, policies, rules and regulation by improving the system of program implementation, monitoring and supervision including adjudication and response to violations. Penalties have also been defined and detailed to deter individuals from violating the law. It is our hope that through the passage of this bill, animal welfare rules and regulations would be more effective as we build a society that not only respects the rights of people but also penalizes the ill-treatment of animals. After all, we serve as the voice for the voiceless animals that plays an important role and contribution to human welfare. label: HB 8398
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure proposes to repeal Republic Act No. 8485, as modified by RA.10631, by strengthening animal welfare requirements in the legislation and establishing the Animal Welfare Bureau, an affiliated agency to the Department of Agriculture. In recent years, there has been an increase in the Filipino people's awareness of animal welfare, resulting in a massive surge of establishments catering to animals, such as veterinary clinics and hospitals, grooming, pet hotels and pet cafes, and pet-friendly establishments, among others. However, the Bureau of Animal Industry's existing organization has exhibited difficulties in reacting to and resolving the mounting welfare issues and concerns impacting animals. This Bill seeks to improve the system of program implementation, monitoring, and supervision, as well as adjudication and response to infractions, in order to reinforce and fortify animal welfare standards, policies, rules, and regulations. Penalties have also been specified and described in depth to dissuade people from breaking the law. If this bill becomes a law, animal welfare rules and regulations will become more effective as we work to develop a society that not only respects people's rights but also penalizes animal cruelty. After all, we are the silent creatures' advocate that has a significant impact on human welfare. On behalf of the people of Parañaque City’s Second District, and for the common good of the Filipino people, the approval of the said measure is earnestly sought. REP. GUS S. label: HB 8677
title: AN ACT CREATING THE ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE TO INSTITUTIONALIZE AND STRENGTHEN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ANIMAL WELFARE AND GOVERN ITS OPERATION AND ITS ENFORCEMENT, REVISING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND APPRORPIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 8485 as amended by Republic Act No.10631 by strengthening the provisions of law relating to animal welfare and by likewise creating the Animal Welfare Bureau, which will be an attached agency to the Department of Agriculture. On 11 July 2023, a Facebook post by a concerned citizen, recounting the tragedy that she has witnessed while in a mall in Quezon City has gone viral. A three-month old puppy was thrown by one of the mall’s security guards off a footbridge causing its tragic death and traumatizing minor children who just a few minutes earlier was adoring and treating the puppy with food. This angered many Filipinos and called for the immediate dismissal of the security guard to which the mall heeded. This also prompted animal welfare NGOs like Animal Kingdom Foundation to file a case against the security guard and also impelled the PNP SOCIA to mandate the inclusion of animal welfare trainings and orientation among all security guards which the latter also committed to heed. This incident is only one of the few cases of animal cruelty and abuse happening that have luckily gone viral enabling citizens to have a united front and appealed for action. Many others, especially those regarded as “strays” are not as lucky. The harsh reality that stray animals experience every single day are not always publicized, leaving them to fend for themselves. In a series of household surveys made in 2017 by the Humane Society International, it was established that dog population is at a minimum of 20% of the human population. With the roaming dog population rising, two pressing issues being faced by the local government units are roaming dog management and rabies control. Sadly, these same dogs which are mostly owned and healthy and vaccinated by the LGUs are the same dogs/cats later on impounded and euthanized resulting to a waste of substantial resources with no clear community impact and solution to issues on animal health and welfare, as well as in reducing stray population issues. This is not to discount the suffering being endured by the dogs and cats in the process, which includes starving the dogs prior to euthanasia in pounds which to date remained to be a major issue time immemorial. The lack of appropriate veterinary care and creation of an adoption and a rehoming program aggravates the said problem. It is for this reason that pet-loving public and animal welfare NGOs and the public see animal pounds as a cruel institution with many asking for pounds to be shut down and closed. There is also the growing movement across the globe to achieve the UN-initiated Sustainability Development Goals necessarily put farm animal health and welfare as part of policy discussion under the Department of Agriculture, Department of Health, Food and Drug Administration, the NGOs and the general public’s growing attitude change towards ethical and responsible sourcing of food. Despite the continuing rise in the consciousness of the Filipino people on the welfare of animals and the aid from kind-hearted Filipinos and different NGOs have been pouring in over the years to protect and promote animal welfare, it is evident that the issue is on the government body who is given the responsibility to promote animal health and welfare, to monitor and investigate, respond and to effectively respond to growing clamor for improved welfare policies and resources. The current structure of the Bureau of Animal Industry has shown weaknesses in responding to and in addressing the growing welfare issues and concerns affecting the animals. As a regulatory body for animal welfare under R.A. No. 8485, as amended, compliance monitoring has become a burden due to lack of dedicated and trained manpower and facilities. Implementation of the law has likewise been severely lacking as a result of the weak cooperation from the LGUS. This Bill aims to strengthen and fortify animal welfare standards, policies, rules and regulation by improving the system of program implementation, monitoring and supervision including adjudication and response to violations. Penalties have also been defined and detailed to deter individuals from violating the law. It is our hope that through the passage of this bill, animal welfare rules and regulations would be more effective as we build a society that respects both the rights of people and animals. After all, it is our duty to be the voice for the innocent voiceless animals. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 10232
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ANIMAL WELFARE STANDARDS IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, THEREBY REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10631, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 8485 as amended by RA No. 10631 and pursues to address the urgent need to strengthen animal welfare standards by strengthening the provisions of the law, by likewise creating the Animal Welfare Bureau, an attached agency with the Department of Agriculture, and imposing stricter penalties for violations, particularly in cases of animal cruelty. The Animal Welfare Act, as amended, serves as the cornerstone of legislation aimed at protecting the welfare of animals in the Philippines. However, in light of evolving societal values and growing awareness of animal rights issues, it has become evident that certain provisions of the Act have proven inadequate in effectively deterring acts of cruelty towards animals and ensuring the proper enforcement of animal welfare standards. In considering the necessity to repeal current animal welfare legislation, it is essential to recognize the profound moral and ethical implications of animal cruelty. Animals, like humans, are sentient beings capable of experiencing pain, suffering, and emotional distress. As such, they deserve to be treated with compassion, dignity, and respect. By allowing acts of cruelty towards animals to go unpunished or inadequately penalized, we not only perpetuate a cycle of violence and injustice but also undermine the fundamental principles of compassion and empathy that are inherent to our humanity. Moreover, strengthening animal welfare standards and imposing stricter penalties for violations are essential components of our duty as legislators to uphold the principles of justice, fairness, and equality under the law. It is incumbent upon us to ensure that the laws of our land reflect the values and aspirations of our society, including our collective commitment to the protection and welfare of animals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RAUL ANGELO “JIL” D. label: HB 1746
title: AN ACT REVISING THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF THE PHILIPPINES AND CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE TO INSTITUTIONALIZE AND STRENGTHEN ITS IMPLEMENTATION, GOVERN ITS OPERATION AND ITS ENFORCEMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 8485, or the Animal Welfare Act of 1998, as amended by Republic Act No. 10631, is a landmark piece of legislation that introduced the foundational legal framework for the protection of animals in the country. However, over two decades since its original enactment, numerous legal, institutional, and practical gaps have emerged in its implementation, signaling the urgent need for a more responsive, comprehensive, and enforceable measure on animal welfare. The existing law does not clearly define key concepts such as what constitutes an “animal,” nor does it provide standards that vary depending on the type or use of the animal. It lacks detailed guidelines for the welfare of animals in different categories—whether kept as pets, raised on farms, used for entertainment, served as working or service animals, or slaughtered for food. This bill aims to revise the Animal Welfare Act to address these longstanding shortcomings and institutionalize a more effective and humane system of animal welfare governance in the country by, first and foremost, creating a full-fledged Animal Welfare Bureau under the Department of Agriculture. This dedicated Bureau will be tasked solely with supervising, regulating, and enforcing animal welfare laws nationwide. This ensures accountability, continuity, and stronger institutional capacity. This bill also seeks to strengthen and modernize the Animal Welfare Act by clearly defining animals to include all sentient non-human beings, whether domesticated or wild, and establishing species- and context-specific welfare standards. It also provides for local enforcement structures and transitional safeguards to ensure continuity from the existing framework. The bill further imposes a clear and categorical prohibition on harmful practices such as dog meat trading and animal fighting, making it unequivocal that these acts are prohibited, regardless of cultural or economic justification. The penalties under RA 8485 are also outdated and inadequate to deter cruelty. This bill updates and scales the penalties to reflect the severity of violations, including elevated sanctions for syndicates and public officers, and reinstates the imposition of maximum penalties for those in positions of responsibility, such as government pound administrators. The framework also introduces administrative adjudication powers for the Bureau, enabling more responsive and streamlined enforcement. Through these reforms, the measure aims to close legal loopholes, professionalize enforcement, and create a more compassionate and coherent system of animal protection in the country. The passage of the bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 2080
title: AN ACT CREATING THE ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE TO INSTITUTIONALIZE AND STRENGTHEN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ANIMAL WELFARE AND GOVERN ITS OPERATION AND ITS ENFORCEMENT, REVISING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 8485 as amended by Republic Act No.10631 by strengthening the provisions of law relating to animal welfare and by likewise creating the Animal Welfare Bureau, which will be an attached agency to the Department of Agriculture. This aims to address several shortcomings in the current system, leading to a more comprehensive and effective approach to animal welfare in our country. Changing attitudes and behaviors towards animals requires sustained public awareness and education efforts. With the roaming dog population rising, two pressing issues being faced by the local government units are roaming dog management and rabies control. Sadly, these same dogs which are mostly owned and healthy and vaccinated by the LGUs are the same dogs/cats later on impounded and euthanized resulting to a waste of substantial resources with no clear community impact and solution to issues on animal health and welfare, as well as in reducing stray population issues. This is not to discount the suffering being endured by the dogs and cats in the process, which includes starving the dogs prior to euthanasia in pounds which to date remained to be a major issue time immemorial. The lack of appropriate veterinary care and creation of an adoption and a rehoming program aggravates the said problem. It is for this reason that pet-loving public and animal welfare NGOs and the public see animal pounds as a cruel institution with many asking for pounds to be shut down and closed. There is also the growing movement across the globe to achieve the UN-initiated Sustainability Development Goals necessarily put farm animal health and welfare as part of policy discussion under the Department of Agriculture, Department of Health, Food and Drug Administration, the NGOs and the general public’s growing attitude change towards ethical and responsible sourcing of food. Despite the continuing rise in the consciousness of the Filipino people on the welfare of animals and the aid from kind-hearted Filipinos and different NGOs have been pouring in over the years to protect and promote animal welfare, it is evident that the issue is on the government body who is given the responsibility to promote animal health and welfare, to monitor and investigate, respond and to effectively respond to growing clamor for improved welfare policies and resources. The current structure of the Bureau of Animal Industry has shown weaknesses in responding to and in addressing the growing welfare issues and concerns affecting the animals. As a regulatory body for animal welfare under R.A. No. 8485, as amended, compliance monitoring has become a burden due to lack of dedicated and trained manpower and facilities. Implementation of the law has likewise been severely lacking as a result of the weak cooperation from the LGUS. This Bill aims to strengthen and fortify animal welfare standards, policies, rules and regulation by improving the system of program implementation, monitoring and supervision including adjudication and response to violations. Penalties have also been defined and detailed to deter individuals from violating the law. It is our hope that through the passage of this bill, animal welfare rules and regulations would be more effective as we build a society that respects both the rights of people and animals. After all, it is our duty to be the voice for the innocent voiceless animals. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR.
