label: HB 8998
title: AN ACT FURTHER STRENGTHENING THE ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING COUNCIL, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING ACT OF 2001,” AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) by amending Republic Act No. 9160 to protect and preserve the integrity of the financial system and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a site for laundering the proceeds from unlawful activities. It provides AMLC with operational independence to function as a Financial Intelligence Unit, specialized in anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing investigation, and acts as the anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism regulator and supervisor of the Philippines. The bill addresses evolving crimes, which the current legal framework has not fully covered, such as cybercrimes, agricultural economic sabotage, and violations of the anti-POGO Act of 2025, among others. The bill likewise addresses the challenges of overseeing digital finance by bringing Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) and virtual assets, such as cryptocurrencies used for payment or investment, under the AMLC to prevent their misuse in financial crimes. It enhances deterrence by increasing fines for law violations and includes a mechanism to raise them by 10% every five years to account for inflation. Additionally, the bill introduces stricter customer due diligence requirements to ensure a more resilient financial system. It grants AMLC the ability to issue administrative freeze orders, allowing forfeiture of assets of “equivalent value” when the original unlawfully acquired property has been concealed, destroyed, or moved outside the country, and ensuring that offenders do not benefit from their crimes by simply hiding the proceeds. Finally, the proposed bill ensures that the Philippines can continue to extend cooperation in transnational investigations and implement financial sanctions related to financing terrorism and proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, consistent with the United Nations Security Council resolutions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 8999
title: AN ACT REDUCING THE VALUE-ADDED TAX (VAT) FROM 12% TO 10% AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A progressive system of taxation requires that the burden of taxation be distributed in a manner that is fair, equitable, and responsive to the economic realities faced by the general public. The Value-Added Tax (VAT), while an efficient and reliable source of government revenue, is inherently regressive in nature, as it applies uniformly to consumption regardless of income level. As a result, lower-income households bear a disproportionately higher burden relative to their capacity to pay. In the context of rising prices of basic goods and services, as well as ongoing economic pressures affecting Filipino families, there is a compelling need to recalibrate consumption-based taxation in order to provide immediate and tangible relief to consumers. A reduction in the VAT rate serves as a direct mechanism to ease the cost of living, stimulate household consumption, and support economic activity. This proposed measure seeks to reduce the VAT rate from twelve percent (12%) to ten percent (10%) across the sale of goods, services, and importation of goods. At the same time, the bill incorporates a built-in fiscal safeguard by authorizing the President, upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Finance and based on objective fiscal indicators determined by the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC), to temporarily revert the VAT rate to twelve percent (12%) when necessary to maintain fiscal stability. By introducing a flexible and data-driven mechanism, the measure strikes a balance between providing immediate economic relief and preserving the government’s capacity to respond to fiscal pressures. It ensures that tax policy remains adaptive to changing economic conditions while maintaining discipline in public finance management. Ultimately, this bill advances the principle that taxation must not only be efficient but also equitable and responsive to the needs of the people. By reducing the VAT rate while safeguarding fiscal stability, the measure promotes inclusive economic growth and supports the welfare of Filipino consumers. 1 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9011
title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER, IRRIGATION, SEWAGE, AND SANITATION RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine government’s responsibility to provide safe, clean, accessible, and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation service to the public is of utmost importance, and it is attainable through well-coordinated, effective, efficient, and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. The Philippine government must take into consideration the rapid population growth, waterborne diseases like diarrhea, leptospirosis, and dengue, agricultural requirements for food and production, water pollution, watershed degradation, climate change, and other related factors that need to be adequately addressed without delay. The proposed measure thus seeks to rationalize the water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation resources management, including water rights, through the creation of the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage, and Sanitation Resource Management. Currently, our national government consists of several agencies which take care of our water: the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), a government agency responsible for the enforcement of the Water Code of the Philippines, under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR); the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), a government-owned and controlled corporation (GOCC) attached to the Department of Public Work and Highways (DPWH) and has regulatory powers over all local water districts (LWDs) and rural waterwork and sanitation associations (RWSAs) nationwide; the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), a GOCC also attached to the DPWH, which is responsible for the water supply and sanitation in Metropolitan Manila and such contiguous areas as may be added to its are of jurisdiction; and the National Irrigation Administration (NIA), a government agency under the Office of the President primarily responsible for irrigation development and management. With the regulation and management of the said water resources currently lodged with various units and agencies of the government, there have been various challenges and confusion in the coordination and implementation of the national policies and plans on water, sewage, sanitation, and irrigation. The fragmentation among water-related agencies has resulted in a backlog in the provision of water supply and sanitation services to the public. The proposed measure shall address the immediate need to create the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage and Sanitation Resource Management, which shall strengthen and coordinate water resource planning and policy- making to ensure sustainable and fair allocation and efficient use of water resources between competing water uses and users, including but not limited to domestic and municipal use, irrigation, power generation, farming, fisheries, commercial, and industrial use. The measure shall also prioritize and pursue the immediate attainment of universal access to safe, adequate, and sustainable water supply and sanitation services for all Filipinos and adopt all necessary measures directed towards the realization of providing a world-class, affordable, and sustainable water supply, sanitation, and sewerage system accessible to every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 9012
title: AN ACT PROVIDING PROTECTION AND INCENTIVES FOR FREELANCE WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Freelancing has emerged as a significant and rapidly expanding sector in the Philippine labor market, driven by the growth of the digital economy and increasing global demand for remote services. While official statistics have yet to classify freelancers as a distinct labor category, available government data demonstrate the scale of non-traditional and independent work arrangements in the country. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the Philippine labor force reached approximately 51.69 million individuals as of December 2025, of whom 49.43 million were employed. A significant portion of this workforce is engaged in self-employment and informal work arrangements, which include freelance and project-based work. In prior labor data, self-employed workers accounted for more than 25% of total employment, representing millions of Filipinos operating outside traditional employer-employee relationships. Further, the Philippine Statistics Authority, through its Decent Work Statistics framework, identifies “stability and security of work” and “access to social protection” as key labor indicators, highlighting persistent gaps affecting workers in non-standard forms of employment. These gaps are particularly pronounced among freelance workers who, by the nature of their engagement, are often excluded from formal labor protections and benefits. The Department of Labor and Employment likewise recognizes employment based on minimal work thresholds under existing statistical definitions, wherein an individual may be considered employed even with limited or irregular work engagement. This underscores the prevalence of precarious and non-standard employment arrangements in the country, within which freelance work is situated. Freelancing has nonetheless become an increasingly viable long-term career pathway for many Filipinos, offering flexible work arrangements, improved work-life balance, and access to global markets. However, despite these advantages, freelance workers remain largely unregulated and continue to face significant structural challenges, including unclear tax policies, limited access to social protection mechanisms such as health insurance and retirement benefits, income instability, and limited legal safeguards. At present, there is no comprehensive legal framework that formally recognizes and protects freelance workers in the Philippines. This policy gap constrains the full development of the sector and leaves a substantial segment of the workforce without adequate institutional support. The proposed “Freelancers Protection Act” seeks to formally recognize freelancing as a legitimate and vital component of the national workforce and to institutionalize mechanisms that will ensure the protection and welfare of Filipino freelance workers. It aims to provide access to social security benefits, establish clear taxation and regulatory guidelines, promote skills development and capacity-building, and enhance the global competitiveness of Filipino freelancers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 9014
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PAYMENT OF HAZARD PAY TO ALL JUDGES OF COURTS IN THE PHILIPPINES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to a fair, independent, and effective judiciary is a cornerstone of any democratic society. Judges serve as the guardians of the rule of law, tasked with resolving disputes, upholding rights, and ensuring that justice is administered without fear or favor. However, the very nature of their duties exposes them to significant risks to their safety and well-being, and these remain largely unaddressed in the current system of compensation and protection. By reason of their profession, members of the judiciary are often placed in situations entailing dangerous, high-stakes cases, including those involving heinous crimes or organized criminal activity. In the course of dispensing justice, judges inevitably encounter disgruntled parties who may resort to threats, harassment, or even violence. Throughout Philippine history, members of the judiciary have been subjected to assaults and even assassination attempts, underscoring the real and present dangers attached to their role. Despite these realities, judges are not accorded hazard pay comparable to other government personnel whose duties similarly expose them to occupational risks or perils to life. Existing policies recognize the necessity of providing additional compensation to public servants operating under hazardous conditions. Yet, the judiciary remains excluded from such benefits, notwithstanding the high-risk classification often attributed to their profession. Therefore, this bill seeks to remove this disparity by granting hazard pay to members of the judiciary. Such compensation acknowledges the inherent dangers of judicial service and affirms the State’s commitment to safeguarding those who dedicate their lives to the administration of justice. Moreover, it aims to strengthen judicial independence by boosting morale and ensuring that judges can perform their duties without undue concern for their personal safety and security. Ultimately, the measure is grounded on the principle that those who uphold the law must themselves be protected by it. By institutionalizing hazard pay for judges, the State reinforces its duty to promote the general welfare, protect its public servants, and preserve the integrity of the justice system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9015
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR STIFFER PENALTIES FOR DRIVING UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF ALCOHOL, DANGEROUS DRUGS AND/OR OTHER SIMILAR SUBSTANCES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10586, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ANTI-DRUNK AND DRUGGED DRIVING ACT OF 2013"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A spate of recent incidents involving drivers under the influence of alcohol or dangerous drugs have occurred in the Province of Cebu. This has raised serious concerns on road safety and have sparked calls to revisit Republic Act No. 10586 or the “Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act of 2013.” Despite the penalties currently being imposed, there seems to be a blatant disregard for the law. This goes to show that there needs to be stricter enforcement and more severe consequences to deter dangerous behavior. The proposed measure reinforces accountability by increasing the penalties for violations of the law. In 2022 alone, the Land Transportation Office (LTO) has recorded around 402 road crash incidents from January to August, some of which have resulted in fatalities, with 353 cases involving intoxicated drivers. Despite repeated warnings to motorists, similar incidents persist. Strengthening the penalties for drunk and drugged driving, including imposing higher fines, longer periods of license suspension, or possibly license revocation, aims to ensure that drivers will feel personally responsible for their behavior on public roads as they operate their vehicles. Driving is a privilege that carries with it the responsibility to protect the lives of others. A motor vehicle which is operated irresponsibly is nothing more than an instrument of harm. For this reason, it shall never be an acceptable excuse for a driver not to be in a proper condition to operate a vehicle. The grant of a driver’s license comes with the commitment to obey traffic rules and regulations and uphold responsible road use. For the foregoing reasons, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9017
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State provides that it shall protect and promote the right to health of all Filipinos and instill health consciousness among them. To this effect, the country’s health system abounds with legislation protecting and providing for the health of the citizens as well as the health care workers. In 1991, Republic Act No. 7160, or the Local Government Code of 1991, was enacted into law, mandating that among the functions of the barangay is to provide health and social welfare services, which include maintenance of barangay health centers and day-care. A few years later, RA 7883 was passed to grant all benefits and incentives for accredited Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) for voluntary health services rendered to the community. These laws, however, currently do not address the disproportional number of BHWs based on the needs of each barangay. To provide better access to health care services, the State must provide an adequate number of full-time health workers to competently deliver these services; the number of which is equitable to the present needs of each barangay. By ensuring that there are enough BHWs in every barangay around the country and by providing these BHWs protection through proper benefits and incentives, each barangay is guaranteed to have health workers who will have the security of tenure and thus perform their duties to the best of their abilities. This bill seeks to improve the overall barangay-level healthcare system by focusing on the welfare of frontliners, the BHWs, who are first in providing immediate medical care for the most marginalized and underprivileged sectors of society. With the designation of barangay health workers, citizens in all corners of the nation will be able to enjoy their right to accessible, affordable, and quality health care. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is urgently sought. REP. label: HB 9019
title: AN ACT PROVIDING GREATER PROTECTION TO LOCAL INDUSTRIES THROUGH THE IMPOSITION OF ANTI-DUMPING DUTY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 301, PART 2, TITLE II, BOOK 1 OF THE TARIFF AND CUSTOMS CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8752
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Pursuant to the mandate of the 1987 Philippine Constitution that the State shall protect local industries against unfair trade practices, this bill addresses the act of dumping, defined as the importation of goods into the Philippines at prices lower than their normal value in the exporting country for domestic consumption. Such practice places local producers at a disadvantage and undermines fair competition. Recent comparative studies on anti-dumping regimes, including an analysis of Indonesia’s legal framework, highlight that dumping remains a persistent global trade concern capable of causing material injury to domestic industries and destabilizing national economies. These studies show that both the Philippines and Indonesia, as developing economies under the WTO system, face similar pressures in balancing trade liberalization with the need to safeguard domestic industries from unfair import surges. They likewise reflect shared juridical challenges such as prolonged investigation processes, evidentiary limitations in proving material injury, and risks of anti-dumping measures being perceived as disguised protectionism, thereby underscoring the need for stronger standards and more transparent procedures. The Indonesian experience further emphasizes that anti-dumping enforcement is most effective when grounded on clear evidentiary rules, improved institutional transparency, and strict causation analysis between dumping and injury. It also highlights a normative dimension of trade protection, where anti-dumping measures are viewed as instruments of substantive justice aimed at preventing economic harm, which is an approach consistent with the Philippines’ constitutional policy of social justice and protection of domestic industries. This measure seeks to address the weaknesses in Republic Act No. 8752, which has been viewed by several sectors as unfavorable to domestic industries. It restores the method for determining the normal value of goods subject to a dumping complaint, a safeguard that was removed when R.A. No. 8752 superseded Republic Act No. 7843. Comparative experience shows that the proper determination of normal value is a critical element in establishing the existence of dumping and ensuring that anti-dumping measures are grounded on objective and verifiable standards. By reinstating this process, the bill ensures a clearer and more reliable basis for 1 Priviet Social Sciences Journal (2026). Legal review of dumping practices in Indonesia: A comparative study of international economic law and Sharia economic law. Available at https://www.journal.privietlab.org/index.php/PSSJ/article/view/1464 evaluating dumping cases. Moreover, the bill removes the requirement for the posting of a surety bond by an affected industry or interested party upon filing a complaint. Considering that the filing of a dumping case already entails significant time and resources, the removal of this requirement prevents the imposition of additional burdens that may discourage legitimate claims. Evidence from other jurisdictions shows that procedural complexity and cost barriers often weaken the capacity of domestic industries to avail of trade remedies, thereby limiting the effectiveness of anti-dumping laws. In addition, the bill amends provisions of the Tariff and Customs Code of the Philippines by removing the authority of the Tariff Commission to withhold the imposition of definitive anti-dumping duties when all legal requirements have been satisfied. While the welfare of consumers and other industries remains important, international practice emphasizes that anti-dumping determinations must primarily rest on the existence of dumping, material injury, and causation, rather than on broader economic considerations that may dilute enforcement. Allowing such external considerations to influence anti-dumping cases may weaken enforcement, as imports sold below normal value may temporarily benefit certain sectors while causing long-term harm to domestic industries. Comparative experience further shows that anti-dumping measures must function as corrective tools to restore fair competition, not as discretionary instruments subject to competing policy preferences. The resolution of a dumping case must therefore be anchored on the existence of the unfair trade act itself. Without these amendments, the current framework may continue to hinder the successful prosecution of valid complaints. Finally, the bill provides that fifty percent (50%) of the duties collected from a successful dumping case shall be returned to the petitioning companies through their respective industry associations. This measure is intended to encourage vigilance among industries in reporting dumping practices, while also contributing to increased government revenue. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully sought. REP. NATHANIEL “ATTY. NAT” M. label: HB 9020
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE LIBMANAN CAVES PROTECTED LANDSCAPE IN THE PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR AS A PROTECTED AREA UNDER THE CATEGORY OF PROTECTED LANDSCAPE, PROVIDING FOR ITS MANAGEMENT AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Investing in forests is an insurance policy for the planet.” Thus said UN Secretary General Ban Ki Moon in his message for the International Day of Forests last 21 March 2016. He stressed that the protection of our forests is fundamental to our vision for a “shared people and planet.” The United Nations Forum on Forests underscores this reality: forests provide 75% of the world’s accessible freshwater, serve as our most efficient carbon capture systems against climate change, and act as a natural shield against landslides and erosion. For the 1.6 billion people who rely on forests for their livelihoods, and for every human who breathes clean air, the conservation of these ecosystems is not a luxury—it is a necessity. The Province of Camarines Sur especially in the Second District where the municipality of Libmanan is located, is known to be endowed with rich biological diversity, a critical watershed for the Bicol River Basin. Located therein is the 19.4-hectare Libmanan Caves National Park (LCNP) which is one of the oldest national parks in the Philippines and the oldest cave system proclaimed as a national park through Presidential Proclamation No. 654 on February 6, 1934. This karst system landscape is composed of stalactites and stalagmites, underwater systems and chambers which took millions of years to develop. This feature of the cave may provide a geological imprint of the history of how caves and probably the Philippine land mass evolved. Furthermore, the cave system and the surrounding areas of the LCNP serve as a critical sanctuary for biodiversity. This site is home to a vast array of endemic species, including 138 plant species—one of which is the Endangared Jade Vine—as well as various mammals, 41 species of birds, and numerous reptiles and invertebrates (35 insects, 11 arachnids, 6 mollusks, and 2 annelids) endemic in the Philippines. Notably, several of these species are found exclusively within the LCNP, and many are currently classified as threatened, vulnerable, or endangered. 10 The national park has the potential to become one of Bicol regions’s important ecotourism sites and haven for biodiversity, ecology, and speleology for researchers and enthusiasts. Furthermore, the LCPL serves as a natural buffer against typhoons while fueling economic growth through sustainable tourism. We are at a crossroads. We can choose to let this landscape succumb to the pressures of time and neglect, or we can choose to be the architects of its preservation. By legislating the Libmanan Caves Protected Landscape, we are not just passing a law; we are signing a pact with nature and securing a clean, sustainable future for our children. To protect our heritage and sustain our common future, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. TERRY L. label: HB 9022
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A THIRTY (30)-DAY GRACE PERIOD FOR THE REPAYMENT OF LOANS AVAILED UNDER THE PUBLIC TRANSPORT MODERNIZATION PROGRAM, FORMERLY KNOWN AS THE PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLE MODERNIZATION PROGRAM, DURING PERIODS OF EXTRAORDINARY OIL PRICE INCREASES, WITHOUT THE IMPOSITION OF PENALTIES, INTEREST, OR OTHER CHARGES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Public Transport Modernization Program {PTMP), formerly known as the Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP), is a key reform aimed at improving the safety, efficiency, and sustainability of the country's public transport system. However, the success of this program is closely tied to the financial capacity of its beneficiaries, such as the public utility drivers, operators, and transport cooperatives, many of whom rely on loans to acquire modernized units. In recent years, the transport sector has been severely affected by persistent and unpredictable increases in oil prices, mostly due to global market volatility and geopolitical tensions. Empirical studies show that fuel price increases significantly elevate operational costs in the transport sector, directly affecting income and livelihood stability. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A UNIFIED TRANSPORT REGISTRY SYSTEM FOR PUBLIC TRANSPORT WORKERS AND OPERATORS, ENSURING INCLUSIVE ELIGIBILITY, STREAMLINED VERIFICATION, AND REGULAR UPDATING OF BENEFICIARY DATABASES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The public transport sector remains a critical pillar of the Philippine economy, ensuring mobility for millions of Filipinos daily. However, the effective delivery of government assistance to transport workers has long been hindered by fragmented, outdated, and difficult-to-access verification systems. These inefficiencies have resulted in delays, exclusion of legitimate beneficiaries, and administrative burdens that undermine the intent of social protection programs. For instance, the Fuel Subsidy Program recently rolled out by the government targeted about 1.43 million beneficiaries from the transport sector. However, only about 201,000 or 14.1% of the public transport workers were able to receive the said government subsidy . 1 A significant portion of transport workers operate within the informal sector, often lacking complete or updated documentation required under traditional verification processes. As a result, many qualified drivers and operators are unable to access timely assistance, particularly during periods of crisis such as fuel price surges or national emergencies. At the same time, overly complex systems increase the risk of duplication, inaccurate records, and the inclusion of ineligible beneficiaries. 1 Janer, R. A., & Janer, R. A. (2026, April 15). title: AN ACT PROMOTING TRADITIONAL FOUNDATIONAL LEARNING IN KINDERGARTEN TO GRADE 6, PROHIBITING LEARNER USE OF PERSONAL DIGITAL DEVICES DURING CLASS HOURS, AND LIMITING SCREEN-BASED INSTRUCTION AS THE DEFAULT MODE OF TEACHING
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The early and middle elementary grades, Kindergarten to Grade 6, are critical years for building and consolidating the foundations of reading comprehension, writing, handwriting fluency, numeracy, study habits, and sustained attention.1 These competencies require focused, repeated, and tactile learning experiences that are best developed through structured, print-based, handwriting-based, and developmentally appropriate instruction especially in the primary grades while progressively strengthening higher-order comprehension and problem-solving through the elementary years.2 While digital tools can support learning when used deliberately, the increasing presence of screens and learner-owned gadgets in the classroom may contribute to distraction and may crowd out time devoted to essential literacy and numeracy skills.3 Excessive or unregulated screen exposure during these formative years risks undermining the development of core competencies and classroom focus.4 1 James, K. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN EXTENDED PRODUCER RESPONSIBILITY (EPR) AND TAKE-BACK SYSTEM FOR HYBRID AND ELECTRIC VEHICLE BATTERIES, PROVIDING FOR THEIR PROPER DISPOSAL, AND REGULATING THE IMPORTATION AND END-OF-LIFE MANAGEMENT THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid adoption of hybrid vehicles has delivered real benefits: lower fuel consumption, reduced tailpipe emissions, and improved air quality outcomes in congested urban centers.1 These gains, however, can be short-lived if policy focuses only on cleaner vehicles on the road while ignoring what happens when these technologies reach end-of-life.2 Hybrid and electric vehicles rely on high-voltage traction batteries with finite service lives, typically degrading after 8-10 years or 150,000-200,000 km.3 As used hybrid vehicles are imported and circulate in the domestic market, the country inevitably inherits the end-of-life problem: failing traction batteries that are discarded, stored indefinitely, or handled by informal channels without clear standards, authorized facilities, or a functioning recycling market.4 Without a lifecycle management system, “green” mobility risks becoming a future toxic waste liability.5 This bill therefore: (a) establishes an EPR and take-back obligation for traction batteries used in hybrid and electric vehicles; (b) requires registration, reporting, and compliance plans for producers, importers, distributors, and assemblers; (c) mandates authorized collection points and environmentally sound interim storage and 1 Changing Transport. label: HB 9027
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR INTERNSHIP PROGRAMS IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS FOR HIGHER EDUCATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many students, an internship is their introduction to the professional world as it offers an opportunity to apply classroom theories, build confidence, and gain practical skills that will shape their future careers. Done well, internships can open doors to lifelong opportunities. However, this is not always the case in the Philippines. Many students report being assigned tasks that have little to do with their course, receiving minimal supervision, or working full-time without any allowance, even when they contribute meaningful work to the host institution.1 With no clear national standards, students become vulnerable to unfair treatment and prevent institutions from maximizing the full learning potential of these programs. Current laws and policies meant to support youth employment also leave a major gap. 1 Nicolas, Honeylet J., Helen G. Manalastas & Robert A. Capalad. “Feedback of Students on Internship Program in an Agricultural Course.” International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education, vol. 11, no. 2 (June 2022): 573-579. DOI 10.11591/ijere.v11i2.21936. Available at https://ijere.iaescore.com/index.php/IJERE/ article/viewFile/21936/13314; Kurt Derhen B. Navales, “Unprotected and Uncompensated Internships: On-the- Job Trainings in the Philippines as a Form of Disguised and Modern-Day Labor Exploitation,” (2020), available at https://www.scribd.com/document/421042756/Navales-Unprotected-and-Uncompensated-Internships-On- The-Job-Trainings-in-the-Philippines-a-Form-of-Disguised-and-Modern-Day-Labor-Exploitation 1 1. Republic Act No. 10869 (JobStart Philippines Act) requires allowances equal to at least 75% of the minimum wage, but it does not apply to college students because the law defines Job Start Trainee as one that has “at least reached high school level; not be employed, studying, or undergoing training at the time of registration”;2 2. Republic Act No. 12063 (Enterprise-Based Education and Training Framework Act) merely provides an avenue for students to undergo technical-vocational internships; and 3. CHED Memorandum Order No. 104, s. 2017 (Student Internship Program in the Philippines) does not require host institutions to provide allowances. These gaps have led to two pressing problems: (1) Students are required to render uncompensated work without proper safeguards; and (2) Pre-licensure internships lack clear protections and standards, even though they are performing essential professional duties. This Bill, the “National Higher Education Internship Act”, responds to the State’s duty to support the development of the youth. It introduces uniform standards that protect students, elevate the quality of training, and strengthen partnerships between HEIs and host institutions. When students are required to perform productive work as part of their education or as a condition for professional licensure, they deserve fair compensation, appropriate supervision, and a safe and supportive learning environment. This is especially crucial for students from low-income families, for whom unpaid internships can be a significant financial burden and a barrier to completing their degree. We believe internships should truly serve their purpose: meaningful learning, real industry exposure, and better employment outcomes for Filipino graduates. In light of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is respectfully requested. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA AGIMAT Partylist 2nd District of Cavite REP. label: HB 9028
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE RE-ENTRY INTO THE WORKFORCE OF PERSONS WHO TOOK A CAREER BREAK, PROVIDING INCENTIVES TO EMPLOYERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution repeatedly affirms the country’s regard for its people: the family, the worker, the women, and many more. This bill seeks to address a pressing social and economic challenge: the difficulty faced by individuals who temporarily leave the workforce due to pregnancy, childbirth, further studies, or caregiving responsibilities for parents, and who later wish to return to gainful employment. Many skilled and experienced workers—particularly women—are forced to interrupt their careers to fulfill essential family duties. Unfortunately, when they attempt to re-enter the workforce, they often encounter barriers such as outdated skills, employer bias, or lack of flexible work arrangements. This results in lost productivity for the economy and diminished opportunities for families. This measure aims to:  Provide incentives to employers who actively recruit and support career re-entry workers.  Establish training and counseling programs to refresh skills and build confidence among returning workers.  Encourage flexible work arrangements to ease the transition back into employment.  Recognize and value caregiving as a vital contribution to society, while ensuring that it does not permanently disadvantage individuals in their careers. Through this measure, the State affirms its commitment to inclusivity, gender equality, and family support. It also strengthens the labor force by tapping into the talents of experienced workers who might otherwise remain sidelined. The government income “lost” through the grant of incentives may be quickly justified by the opportunities given to its people, the multiplier effect of the earned purchasing power, the resources saved by the government from “ayuda” when its people are able to support themselves, among many other reasons. In view of the above cited reasons, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA REP. RAMON JOLO B. label: HB 9029
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE UNIVERSITY OF THE PHILIPPINES NATIONAL CLIMATE RESILIENCE INSTITUTE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is consistently ranked among the most disaster-prone countries in the world, facing recurring typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and public health emergencies. These hazards pose serious threats to the safety of learners, teachers, and education personnel, disrupt the delivery of education, and result in significant damage to school infrastructure. While administrative policies on school-based disaster preparedness are currently in place, there remains no single comprehensive law that institutionalizes and sustains these measures across all educational institutions. This bill seeks to establish a Comprehensive School Disaster Preparedness and Resilience Framework that consolidates and strengthens existing initiatives on disaster risk reduction and management in schools. It mandates the creation of School Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees, the designation of trained coordinators, and the regular conduct of disaster preparedness and emergency drills. It further requires the integration of disaster awareness, climate change adaptation, and hazard mitigation into the school curriculum, thereby fostering a culture of preparedness and resilience among learners. The proposed measure also emphasizes area-specific planning, safe and resilient school infrastructure, early warning systems, continuity of education during emergencies, psychosocial support, and community participation. Through strengthened coordination among schools, local government units, and national agencies, this Act ensures alignment with the national disaster risk reduction and management framework under Republic Act No. 10121. By institutionalizing comprehensive school disaster preparedness, this bill affirms the State’s commitment to safeguarding lives, protecting public investment in education, and ensuring that no learner is deprived of the right to quality education due to disasters. The immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. label: HB 9030
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9513, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE RENEWABLE ENERGY ACT OF 2008
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE: The Philippines continues to face persistent energy challenges marked by high electricity costs, supply tightness during peak demand periods, exposure to volatile global fuel prices, and increasing dependence on imported fossil fuels. The depletion of indigenous energy resources, coupled with growing demand driven by economic expansion, has further strained the country‟s ability to produce a stable, affordable, and secure energy supply. These conditions underscore the urgency of accelerating the development of reliable, indigenous, and sustainable energy sources. Republic Act No. 9513, or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008, was enacted to address these concerns by promoting the development and utilization of renewable energy resources. While the law has facilitated the entry of renewable energy projects, structural gaps and evolving market conditions have limited its full potential to respond to the present energy crisis. There is therefore a need to strengthen the legal and regulatory framework to unlock investments, improve system reliability, and reduce long-term power costs. This bill seeks to amend the Renewable Energy Act to directly address these challenges. 1. Update on key definitions to recognize emerging technologies such as energy storage systems and their integration with renewable energy facilities. This is critical in addressing intermittency issues associated with renewable energy and ensuring a more stable and reliable power supply, particularly during peak demand periods. 2. This measure strengthens the authority of the Department of Energy as the lead agency and streamlines access to land for renewable energy development. By reducing administrative barriers and clarifying access rights, the bill facilitates faster project development timelines, which is essential in addressing immediate supply constraints. 3. This bill modernizes the Feed-in-Tariff system by introducing competitive auction mechanisms. This reform promotes efficiency and price discovery, ensuring that renewable energy projects are developed at least cost, thereby contributing to the reduction of electricity prices for consumers over time. 4. Enhances the Renewable Energy Market framework and strengthens the issuance of Renewable Energy Certificates. 5. Improves the fiscal regime for renewable energy projects by rationalizing incentives, including duty-free importation and real property tax assessment levels. These measures are intended to attract more investments, accelerate capacity additions, and help address supply shortages that contribute to high power costs. 6. Provides clarity and predictability in the government share from renewable energy projects, thereby enhancing investor confidence while ensuring that the State continues to benefit from the development of its energy resources. 7. Removes legal uncertainties by clarifying that renewable energy resources are not subject to constitutional restrictions applicable to natural resources, including nationality requirements and term limits. This is expected to unlock significant foreign and domestic capital, which is critical in scaling up investments needed to address the country‟s energy supply gap. In sum, the proposed amendments are responsive to the country‟s current energy crisis. By accelerating renewable energy development, improving system reliability, reducing dependence on imported fuels, and promoting competitive electricity pricing, the bill provides a comprehensive policy response to ensure long-term energy security and sustainability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND L. label: HB 9033
title: AN ACT INCLUDING GASOLINE AND DIESEL AS PRIME COMMODITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7581, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PRICE ACT," AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10623, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the "Fuel Price Protection Act." SEC. 2. Amendment. - Section 3, Paragraph (8) of Republic Act No. 7581, otherwise known as the "Price Act," as amended by Republic Act No. 10623, is hereby amended to read as follows:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Price Act (Republic Act No. 7581) was enacted to protect consumers against hoarding, profiteering, and cartels, particularly during periods of calamity or emergency. It classifies essential goods into two categories: Basic Necessities and Prime Commodities. While the current law covers a wide range of goods—from rice and salt to plywood and school supplies—it notably excludes one of the most significant drivers of inflation, which is fuel. Gasoline and diesel are the lifeblood of the economy. When fuel prices spike, a domino effect ensues, raising the cost of transporting food, the operation of public utilities, and the manufacturing of nearly every consumer good. Currently, petroleum products are regulated primarily under the Downstream Oil Industry Deregulation Act of 1998 (RA 8479), which favors market-driven pricing. However, this leaves the government with limited tools to intervene when fuel prices become unconscionable or when the public is subjected to "price shocks." By classifying gasoline and diesel as Prime Commodities, this bill grants the government the authority to include fuel in the monitoring list of the Price Coordinating Council, impose price ceilings during emergencies or periods of abnormal price fluctuations, and strictly penalize price manipulation specifically related to fuel products. This amendment is a proactive step toward economic stability and the protection of the Filipino people's purchasing power. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9034
title: AN ACT RECLASSIFYING A 1,151.37-HECTARE PORTION OF TIMBERLAND SITUATED WITHIN THE BUFFER ZONE OF THE MT. MALINDANG RANGE NATURAL PARK IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CONCEPCION, PROVINCE OF MISAMIS OCCIDENTAL, INTO ALIENABLE AND DISPOSABLE LAND Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Reclassification. A parcel of land comprising One Thousand One Hundred Fifty-One and 37/100 (1,151.37) hectares, currently classified as timberland and situated within the buffer zone of the Mt. Malindang Range Natural Park (MMRNP) in the Municipality of Concepcion, Province of Misamis Occidental, is hereby reclassified as alienable and disposable land. SECTION 2. Scope and Distribution. The reclassified area specified in Section 1 is non-contiguous and is distributed across seventeen (17) barangays within the Municipality of Concepcion, with the following area breakdown: 1. Bagong Nayon: 16.41 hectares 2. Capule: 178.62 hectares 3. Guiban: 13.86 hectares 4. Layaan: 36.78 hectares 5. Lingatongan: 3.23 hectares 6. Maligubaan: 192.90 hectares 7. Mantukoy: 47.64 hectares 8. Marugang: 3.56 hectares 9. New Casul: 5.76 hectares 10. Poblacion: 59.33 hectares 11. Pogan: 84.17 hectares
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Concepcion in Misamis Occidental is severely constrained in its economic and infrastructure development because a significant portion of its land is classified as timberland within the Mt. Malindang Range Natural Park (MMRNP) buffer zone. This classification restricts the local government's ability to generate revenue from real property taxes to fund essential social services. On October 14, 2025, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Region X certified that 1,151.37 hectares distributed across seventeen non-contiguous barangays within the MMRNP buffer zone are eligible for reclassification into Alienable and Disposable land. This reclassification will secure land tenure for actual occupants, maximize agricultural productivity, and broaden the local tax base to support the development of schools, hospitals, and government facilities. Article XII, Section 3 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution and Commonwealth Act No. 141, or the Public Land Act, mandate that the reclassification of public lands requires congressional enactment. Consequently, this measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 9304, known as the "Mt. Malindang Range Natural Park Act of 2004," to legally exempt these 1,151.37 hectares from its restrictive classifications while preserving the integrity of the remaining natural park. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought . JASON P. label: HB 9035
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE ADOPTION OF DIGITAL PAYMENTS FOR FINANCIAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE GOVERNMENT AND ALL MERCHANTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to promote social justice, ensure transparency and accountability in public service, and adopt policies that enhance efficiency in government operations. It likewise recognizes the vital role of technology in national development and the duty of the State to promote a more equitable distribution of opportunities and services. In this light, the herein proposed Digital Payments Act seeks to modernize the way government collects revenues and disburses public funds through the institutionalization of safe and efficient digital payments. This measure ensures that public financial transactions are conducted in a manner that is transparent, traceable, and responsive to the needs of the people. Once enacted, the benefits of this bill for our people are immediate and practical. Digital payments eliminate the need to physically line up in government offices, lower transaction costs, and enable payments for taxes, fees, and permits anytime and anywhere. For small businesses and local merchants, the integration of digital payment capability streamlines compliance with local regulations while expanding their access to formal financial services. By empowering local government units to support small and micro-merchants in adopting digital systems, the bill promotes financial inclusion and reduces the risks associated with handling cash. This policy is a necessary step toward building a modern, citizen- centered government. By prioritizing safety, interoperability, and digital literacy, this measure enhances efficiency while reinforcing public accountability. We thus aim to institutionalize routine financial transactions into faster, safer, and more transparent processes, ensuring that government services are delivered with greater convenience, integrity, and reliability for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 9036
title: AN ACT PROVIDING THE MAGNA CARTA FOR TAXPAYERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to enact the Magna Carta for Taxpayers, a policy measure that seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive and enforceable framework of rights and obligations in all dealings between taxpayers and revenue authorities. While existing tax laws provide remedies and procedures, these protections are dispersed and often difficult for ordinary citizens and small businesses to navigate. This measure consolidates and strengthens taxpayer protections to ensure that taxes are assessed and collected fairly, transparently, and responsibly thereby reinforcing public confidence in the tax system. The proposed law enhances taxpayer protection by expressly guaranteeing the right to clear and simplified information, fair and uniform application of tax laws, due process in audits and assessments, protection against baseless or arbitrary assessments, timely resolution of cases, relief from penalties caused by government delay, and respect for privacy and confidentiality. If a small business receives a deficiency tax assessment without a clear explanation or supporting computation, the Magna Carta ensures that the taxpayer can demand a detailed legal and factual basis, present evidence to contest errors, and seek timely resolution. These safeguards promote transparency and accountability in tax administration. Taxes are the lifeblood of the State, indispensable to the government’s ability to function, deliver public services, and promote national development. With this impetus, the power to tax must be exercised with fairness, transparency, and accountability to preserve public trust. By institutionalizing clear and enforceable taxpayer rights alongside defined obligations, the Magna Carta for Taxpayers fosters a culture of mutual responsibility between the State and its citizens. When taxpayers are assured that assessments are grounded in law, procedures are consistently observed, and remedies are accessible, voluntary compliance is strengthened and disputes are minimized thereby securing stable revenues essential to effective governance. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 9037
title: AN ACT IMPOSING EXCISE TAX ON PLASTIC BAGS, THEREBY ADDING NEW SECTIONS 150-C AND 288(H) IN THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Plastic waste remains one of the most pressing environmental challenges facing communities across the country. Despite existing laws regulating solid waste management, the widespread use of single-use plastic bags known as “labo” and “sando” bags continue to strain waste collection systems, clog waterways and pollute our communities. The degradation of our environment due to single-use plastics is clearly seen in our local communities. Local government units (LGUs) bear the primary responsibility for solid waste management and many face fiscal and logistical constraints in fully complying with these national environmental standards. This bill proposes the imposition of an excise tax of Twenty Pesos (₱20.00) per kilogram on plastic bags removed from the place of production or released from the custody of the Bureau of Customs. By imposing an excise tax at the point of production or importation, this bill encourages manufacturers, retailers, and consumers to shift toward more sustainable and reusable alternatives, thereby reducing plastic waste at its source. The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accordance with the rhythm and harmony of nature. In discharging this mandate, this policy measure seeks to curb the proliferation of single-use plastic bags, which significantly contribute to pollution, flooding, and the degradation of terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Moreover, the revenues collected from the excise tax for single-use plastic bags shall be allocated exclusively to local government units (LGUs) for the implementation of their solid waste management plans. These funds may be used for the acquisition of land, construction and operation of sanitary landfill, and other waste management facilities. By providing a sustainable and earmarked funding mechanism, this measure reinforces the partnership between the national government and LGUs, enhances local capacity to protect public health and the environment, and empowers communities to build cleaner, more resilient, and environmentally responsible localities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 9043
title: AN ACT ASSERTING LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT SOVEREIGNTY OVER MUNICIPAL WATERS, STRENGTHENING FISHERIES GOVERNANCE, INSTITUTIONALIZING RESOURCE RENT- BASED FISCAL AUTONOMY, THEREBY ENSURING SUSTAINABLE LOCAL- ECOSYSTEM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine archipelago, with its 36,289 kilometers of coastline, possesses one of the most productive marine ecosystems in the world. However, this natural wealth faces an existential threat. Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA, 2024)1 indicates that the ﬁsheries sector’s contribution to the national GDP remains constrained by chronic overﬁshing and habitat degradation. Scientiﬁc assessments, including the National Stock Assessment Program (NSAP), have consistently shown that more than 80% of major ﬁsh stocks in our municipal waters are currently overexploited. 2 1 Philippine Sta s cs Authority (PSA). (2024). Na onal Accounts of the Philippines: Fisheries Sector Contribu on to GDP. Quezon City, Philippines. 2 Na onal Stock Assessment Program (NSAP). (2023/2024). Technical Reports on the Status of Major Fish Stocks in Philippine Municipal Waters. Bureau of Fisheries and Aqua c Resources (BFAR). i This bill, the "Bantay-Dagat, Yaman-Lokal Act," seeks to operationalize the mandate of Article X, Section 2 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which guarantees genuine and meaningful local autonomy. While the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160) and the Philippine Fisheries Code (Republic Act No. 8550, as amended by Republic Act No. 10654)3 delegate management powers to Local Government Units (LGUs) within the 15-kilometer municipal water zone, practical enforcement is often hampered by bureaucratic friction, overlapping national-local mandates, and a lack of ﬁscal independence for marine conservation. Legal and Constitutional Basis 1. Constitutional Autonomy: Article X, Sections 2 and 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution empower LGUs to manage their resources and create their own sources of revenue.4 2. Statutory Framework: RA 7160 mandates that the LGU is the primary entity for the delivery of basic services and environmental protection. 5 RA 10654 explicitly provides that LGUs have the authority to enact ordinances to protect municipal waters.6 3. International Commitment: As a signatory to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982), the Philippines has an obligation to manage marine resources sustainably. 7 This bill mirrors global best practices in "Community-Based Coastal Resource Management" (CBCRM). 8 The Need for Reform The "tragedy of the commons" continues to plague our municipal waters. Fragmented enforcement, where LGUs lack the budget to sustain Bantay-Dagat operations, has led to rampant Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) ﬁshing. By institutionalizing Resource Rent—the economic surplus derived from the extraction of public aquatic resources—this bill establishes a self-sustaining revenue stream for LGUs. This ensures that the wealth generated by our seas is reinvested directly into protecting those resources. 3 Republic Act No. 8550 (1998). label: HB 9044
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE SECURITY OF TENURE FOR FISHERFOLK AND FISHWORKERS, DEFINING THE EMPLOYER-EMPLOYEE RELATIONSHIP IN THE FISHING INDUSTRY, PROVIDING FOR COMPREHENSIVE EMPLOYMENT BENEFITS, ACCESS TO FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE, AND THE RIGHT TO SELF-ORGANIZATION FOR COOPERATIVE DEVELOPMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, an archipelagic nation, relies heavily on its “blue economy,” with the fisheries sector contributing approximately 1.3% to 1.5% of the National Gross Domestic Product (Philippine Statistics Authority, 2023).1 However, there exists a profound socio- economic paradox: the very individuals who secure the nation’s primary protein source— our fisherfolk and fishworkers—consistently register the highest poverty incidence among all basic sectors at 30.6% (PSA, 2023).2 This systemic impoverishment is not 1 Philippine Sta s cs Authority (2023). Na onal Accounts of the Philippines: Annual Report on Gross Domes c Product by Industrial Origin. Quezon City, Philippines: PSA. (Ci ng the 1.3%–1.5% GDP contribu on of the ﬁsheries sector). 2 Philippine Sta s cs Authority (2023). 2023 Poverty Sta s cs for the Basic Sectors. Quezon City, Philippines: PSA. (Ci ng the 30.6% poverty incidence among ﬁsherfolk). 1 merely a result of environmental factors but is deeply rooted in the legal “gray area” of their employment status. For decades, fisherfolk have been marginalized through misclassification. In both municipal and commercial operations, they are often labeled as “commission-based partners” or “independent contractors.” This nomenclature is a legal fiction designed to circumvent the mandatory obligations of the Labor Code. In reality, these workers operate under a state of total subordination to Fish Traders and Vessel Owners. Judicial Basis: The “Control Test” and Economic Subordination Philippine Jurisprudence is clear on the determination of an employer-employee relationship. Under the “four-fold test” affirmed in landmark cases such as Chavez v. NLRC (G.R. No. 148253) and Pauig v. NLRC, the elements of employment are: (1) selection and engagement; (2) payment of wages; (3) power of dismissal; and (4) the power of control.3 In the fishing industry, Fish Traders exercise absolute control by dictating the timing of voyages, specifying gear requirements, and enforcing exclusivity in the sale of the catch. This level of operational and economic direction is the hallmark of employment. Yet, by denying this status, “Traders” evade their responsibilities to provide social security, medical benefits, and security of tenure. International and Statistical Imperatives The International Labour Organization (ILO) Convention No. 188 (Work in Fishing Convention, 2007)4 identifies the industry as highly susceptible to forced labor and debt bondage. This is largely due to the informal nature of hiring and the “share-based” system, which often operates as a predatory credit mechanism, leaving workers in a perpetual cycle of debt to their traders. 5 Constitutional Mandate Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates the State to afford full protection to labor—local and overseas, organized and unorganized—and guarantee security of tenure and humane conditions of work. The current unregulated state of the fisheries labor market is a direct affront to this constitutional guarantee. 6 3 Chavez v. Na onal Labor Rela ons Commission, G.R. No. 148253 (2005). 4 Interna onal Labour Organiza on (2007). C188 - Work in Fishing Conven on, 2007 (No. 188). Geneva: ILO. 5 Interna onal Labour Organiza on (2014). Report: Caught at Sea - Forced Labour and Traﬃcking in Fisheries. 6 1987 Cons tu on of the Republic of the Philippines. Ar cle XIII, Sec on 3. The “Batas Alon” seeks to bridge the gap between maritime tradition and modern labor rights. By formally recognizing the employer-employee relationship between traders and fisherfolk, this bill ensures that every hand that pulls a net is protected by the Labor Code of the Philippines. It provides a mechanism for financial inclusion, granting fisherfolk the dignity to access formal credit and break the shackles of usurious “advances.” In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9046
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING FISHERFOLK SETTLEMENT AREAS, PROVIDING SECURITY OF TENURE AND PROTECTION AGAINST DISPLACEMENT FOR MUNICIPAL FISHERFOLK, INTEGRATING CLIMATE-RESILIENT COASTAL HOUSING AND LIVELIHOOD SUPPORT, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The municipal fisheries sector is the cornerstone of Philippine food security and coastal resilience, yet it remains among the most vulnerable and marginalized in the archipelago. Despite the critical role of municipal fisherfolk in feeding the nation, data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA, 2021)1 reveals a staggering poverty incidence rate of approximately 30.6% among fisherfolk—a figure significantly higher than the national average. These communities are currently caught in a systemic "triple threat" cycle of resource depletion, climate-induced disasters, and widespread displacement due to coastal reclamation, tourism expansion, and large-scale infrastructure projects. The Necessity and Urgency 1 Philippine Sta s cs Authority (PSA) (2021). Poverty Incidence Among Basic Sectors in the Philippines. i The precipitous decline in fisherfolk productivity underscores the necessity for legislative intervention. Recent reports indicate that the average daily catch per fisher has plummeted from a sustainable 10–20 kg/day in previous decades to a mere 2.5 kg/day due to overfishing and illegal commercial encroachment within municipal waters. 2 Compounding this economic crisis is the physical insecurity of these communities; thousands of families reside in high-risk "coastal danger zones" without legal tenure, leaving them uniquely vulnerable to the intensifying typhoons and rising sea levels associated with the Philippine climate. Displacement, often framed as "development," frequently strips fisherfolk of their proximity to traditional fishing grounds and landing sites. Without the "Kasaganaan sa Baybayin Act," these families remain in a state of perpetual precarity, unable to invest in their homes or livelihoods due to the constant threat of eviction. There is an immediate and urgent need to institutionalize "Fisherfolk Settlement Areas" (FSAs) to provide secure tenure and ensure that coastal development does not come at the expense of our nation's food producers. Constitutional and International Basis This proposed legislation is firmly anchored in both the supreme law of the land and established international human rights and development frameworks:  Constitutional Mandate: The bill draws its authority from Article XIII, Section 7 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which mandates that the State shall protect the rights of subsistence fisherfolk to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources. This Act operationalizes the principle that "those who have less in life should have more in law" by ensuring that coastal land-use policies prioritize the housing and livelihood needs of the municipal fishing sector.  International Alignment: The measure aligns with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Voluntary Guidelines for Securing Sustainable Small-Scale Fisheries (SSF Guidelines), which urge states to ensure tenure security, prohibit forced evictions, and facilitate equitable access to resources to promote sustainable small-scale fishing practices (FAO, 2015).3  Global Sustainability: This Act advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 14 (Life Below Water), which advocates for access for small-scale artisanal fishers to marine resources, and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), which promotes inclusive, resilient, and safe human settlements (United Nations, 2015).4 2 Inquirer.net (2026). The Shrinking Catch: Analysis of Municipal Fishery Produc vity. (Retrieved March 6, 2026). 3 FAO (2015). Voluntary Guidelines for Securing Sustainable Small-Scale Fisheries in the Context of Food Security and Poverty Eradica on. Food and Agriculture Organiza on of the United Na ons. 4 United Na ons (2015). Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. General Assembly Resolu on 70/1. ii Key Legislative Mechanisms To address these challenges, the Kasaganaan sa Baybayin Act introduces several critical innovations: 1. Certificate of Compliance (COC): A mandatory legal requirement for any project— public or private—impacting coastal communities, ensuring that displacement is not arbitrary and that livelihood transition is fully funded. 2. Inter-Agency Committee on Fisherfolk Settlement Areas (IACFSA): An institutional mechanism that ensures national policy coherence across the DA- BFAR, DHSUD, DENR, and other key agencies, with direct participation from the fisherfolk themselves. 3. Climate-Resilience Standards: The bill mandates that all settlements must be designed for climate-adaptation, including elevated structures, coastal green buffer zones (mangroves), and disaster-resilient evacuation infrastructure. Conclusion The "Kasaganaan sa Baybayin Act" is not merely a housing initiative; it is a human rights imperative. By integrating secure land tenure with climate-resilient infrastructure and mandated livelihood protections, the State provides a mechanism for long-term community empowerment. This Act ensures that municipal fisherfolk—the guardians of our marine heritage—are granted the legal protection to remain on their land, secure in their right to continue their traditional livelihoods, and resilient against the existential threats posed by climate change. iii In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9049
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE STOCKPILING OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE OIL RESERVES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL PETROLEUM SECURITY RESERVE AND ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL PETROLEUM SECURITY RESERVE TRUST FUND, MANDATING MINIMUM INVENTORY RESERVES FOR THE PRIVATE SECTOR, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has put a spotlight on the energy vulnerability of the Philippines, particularly in maintaining a consistent and uninterrupted supply of petroleum. Historically, supply crunches and subsequent price spikes have occurred due to conflicts in the Middle East, such as the 1973 Oil Embargo by Arab members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and the 1979 Oil Crisis following the Iranian Revolution. The Philippines, being a net importer of petroleum, must ensure that it has an ample buffer to any future supply disruptions, whether arising from natural or man-made causes, that can cause significant harm to the life of Filipinos and to the national economy. This bill proposes the creation of the National Petroleum Security Reserve, along with legislating mandatory minimum inventory requirements for private industry players to ensure that the country has enough buffer stock of petroleum to sufficiently cushion any future critical supply disruptions. The Reserve shall strictly be used as a mechanism to ensure short-term petroleum supply security during critical supply disruptions; it shall in no way be used as a means for raising revenues for the national government, nor shall it be used as a mechanism to purposely lower price spikes arising from supply shortages. The National Petroleum Security Reserve Trust Fund established under this Act, shall only be strictly used for the purposes of developing and maintaining the operations of the Reserve. As part of responsibility- and risk-sharing, exemptions to the minimum inventory requirements shall be determined on a case-to-case basis, to ensure that market entry is not prohibitive and market competitiveness. These are intentionally woven in to this proposed legislation, lest we make a repeat of the failures and pitfalls of the now defunct Oil Price Stabilization Fund, or the restrictive requirements set forth in Republic Act 8180 otherwise known as the precursor of the current Downstream Oil Deregulation Act. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING THE RIGHT OF PATIENTS TO DESIGNATE A HEALTHCARE AGENT THROUGH A HEALTHCARE PROXY, PROMOTING ADVANCE CARE PLANNING, AND PROVIDING FOR SUPPORTED HEALTHCARE DECISION- MAKING IN THE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM
front_matter: Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City, Metro Manila May 4, 2026 5:34 pm TWENTIETH CONGRESS First Regular Session 9065 HOUSE BILL NO. ______ Introduced by Representative Ryan S. Recto In current medical practice in the Philippines, the determination of who may provide consent on behalf of a patient who lacks decision-making capacity is often guided by the customary application of the “next-of-kin” principle. However, this custom does not have a clear statutory basis under existing laws, including the Family Code and the Civil Code of the Philippines. While informal practices may sometimes accommodate companions or partners, such recognition is inconsistent and dependent on institutional discretion rather than guaranteed rights. At present, the closest reference to “next-of-kin” in the context of healthcare decision-making may be found in the Code of Ethics of the Philippine Medical Association (PMA), which provides that consent may be obtained from the patient’s “next-of-kin or their legally authorized representative.” This gap in the law has led to delays in treatment, ethical uncertainty among healthcare providers, and, in some cases, preventable harm to patients. It disproportionately affects individuals in nontraditional or underserved family arrangements, including unmarried partners, solo parents, and those estranged from their biological families, whose chosen caregivers are frequently excluded from participating in critical medical decisions.

label: HB 9081
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 3 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11210, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED MATERNITY LEAVE LAW”, BY PROVIDING ADDITIONAL MATERNITY LEAVE BENEFITS TO WOMEN DIAGNOSED WITH POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to amend Section 3 of Republic Act No. 11210 to provide additional maternity leave benefits to women diagnosed with postpartum depression, thereby expanding the scope of existing maternity protection to include maternal mental health. Postpartum depression is a serious and often underrecognized public health concern that affects a significant number of women during and after pregnancy. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 10% of pregnant women and 13% of women who have just given birth experience a mental disorder, primarily depression1. In developing countries, the prevalence is even higher, reaching 15.6% during pregnancy and 19.8% after childbirth2. In severe cases, maternal suffering may lead to suicide, and affected mothers may be unable to properly care for themselves and their children, thereby negatively impacting child growth and development Emerging evidence further shows that postpartum depression does not always manifest immediately after childbirth. Studies indicate that depressive symptoms may develop or persist months after delivery, with approximately 7.2% of women experiencing postpartum depressive symptoms as late as nine to ten months postpartum3. Notably, more than half of these women did not exhibit symptoms during the earlier postpartum period, highlighting the delayed and evolving nature of maternal mental health conditions4. 1 World Health Organization. (2023). Perinatal Mental Health. World Health Organization. https://www.who.int/teams/mental-health-and-substance-use/promotion-prevention/maternal-mental-health 2 Ibid. 3 Robbins, C. L. (2023). Timing of Postpartum Depressive Symptoms. Preventing Chronic Disease, 20(20). https://doi.org/10.5888/pcd20.230107 4 Ibid. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 11210, which significantly expanded maternity leave benefits in the Philippines, the current framework primarily addresses physical recovery and immediate postnatal needs. It does not sufficiently account for maternal mental health conditions such as postpartum depression, which may require extended periods of care, treatment, and psychosocial support beyond the standard leave period. This piece of legislation seeks to address these gaps by granting additional maternity leave benefits to women diagnosed with postpartum depression, thereby expanding the scope of existing maternity leave entitlements. Ultimately, this measure ensures that mothers are afforded adequate time and support to recover both physically and mentally, contributing to healthier families and stronger communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Ryan S. Empirical evidence indicates that maternal mental health disorders are a significant and often overlooked public health concern. Studies show that at least 60 percent of Filipino mothers experience clinically significant perinatal depressive symptoms substantially higher than the global average of approximately 25 percent, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO, 2025)1. Despite this high prevalence, the utilization of postnatal care services in the Philippines remains critically low. label: HB 9083
title: AN ACT ABOLISHING THE OPTICAL MEDIA BOARD, REPEALING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT 9239, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “OPTICAL MEDIA ACT OF 2003,” TRANSFERRING ITS POWERS, FUNCTIONS, ASSETS, AND PERSONNEL TO THE INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY OFFICE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Optical Media Board served the purpose for which it was created. It was at the helm of regulating the production and replication of information, sounds, and images stored on optical media. It led raids and acted as a complainant in the prosecution of individuals and syndicates operating in violation of the law. Importantly, it protected the works and rights of our people in the creative industry. Today, the OMB has lost its relevance and effectiveness. It is stuck in a world totally different from our present reality. With the rapid and constant evolution of technology, the exhibition, production, and replication of intellectual and creative works have gone beyond institutional control. They become easily accessible to anyone and can be transferred in seconds, with total disregard for the rights of authors, artists, and producers. We have reached the point where we need to abolish OMB and give it a new life within a different institution. This measure will transfer the powers, functions, and assets of the OMB to the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines. Its personnel will also be transferred upon evaluation of skills and experience or under the existing civil service law. Given the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
