label: HB 9099
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ANTI-DRUNK AND DRUGGED DRIVING ACT OF 2013, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10586, AND PROVIDING STIFFER PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Road safety is a fundamental right, yet the current legal framework under Republic Act No. 10586, otherwise known as the "Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act of 2013," has revealed critical procedural loopholes that allow intoxicated drivers to evade justice. The tragic death of young entrepreneur Kingston Ralph Cheng in Cebu City on February 8, 2026, highlighted a systemic "hiding tactic." By avoiding immediate police contact, suspects allow the alcohol or drugs in their system to dissipate naturally, rendering chemical tests—the primary evidence required by the current law—ineffective. This gap essentially shields hit-and-run behavior and penalizes the victims of road tragedies. Firstly, this bill redefines "driving under the influence of alcohol (DUIA)" as a driver with blood alcohol concentration (BAC) after a breath analyzer test, of above 0.00%, versus the present IRR of RA 10586 which defines DUIA for drivers of private vehicles as drivers with BAC of above 0.05%. It is important to note that the same IRR already provides for DUIA for drivers of motorcycles and public utility vehicles (PUVs) as drivers with BAC of above 0.0%. This bill also proposes that the mandatory alcohol and drug tests be administered within a two hour window from the time of the accident. Moreover, refusal to undergo the mandatory test will amount to a prima facie presumption that the driver was DUI. This bill also defines a "hit and run incident" which shall constitute as an aggravating circumstance to the final penalties given to DUI offenders. In terms of penalties, this bill proposes an increase in fines for all types of violations, from (a) DUI without injury, to (b) DUI with injury and (c) DUI resulting in death. This bill also proposes to lengthen periods for imprisonment for DUI without injury or death to six months (from current three months imprisonment), as an increased preventive measure. For DUI resulting in 1 death or homicide, this bill proposes to increase the penalty to reclusion perpetua (from reclusion temporal per Art. 249 of the Revised Penal Code). Furthermore, this bill proposes the establishment and institutionalization of a dedicated community public reporting channel via the 911 national emergency hotline and/or an official social media platform account for the purpose of reporting DUI incidents. This shall encourage the prevention of DUI accidents, timely reporting of accidents and also providing secondary evidence from the public to ensure that DUI violators are brought justice. Finally, this bill proposes that the Philippine Information Agency (PIA) in coordination with the LTO conduct a continuous educational and informational campaign via social media on the dangers, consequences and penalties for DUI. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RICHARD I. label: HB 9100
title: AN ACT MANDATING GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS AND EMPLOYEES TO EXECUTE AND SUBMIT A WRITTEN PERMISSION TO EXAMINE, INQUIRE OR LOOK INTO ALL THEIR DEPOSITS AND INVESTMENTS THEREBY WAIVING THE BANK SECRECY LAW AS PROVIDED FOR UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NUMBERS 1405 AND 6426
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to require government officials and employees to execute a written waiver authorizing lawful examination of their bank deposits and investments, in connection with duly verified investigations. Grounded on the principle that public office is a public trust, it also seeks to strengthen standards of integrity in government, and to reinforce the obligation of public servants to uphold openness in their financial dealings. The measure is consistent with Republic Act No. 3019, otherwise known as the “Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act”, which seeks to deter graft or corrupt practices committed by public officers and private persons alike. It likewise addresses the legal barriers that may hinder the investigation of unexplained wealth, while strengthening the accountability mechanisms available to the Office of the Ombudsman, subject to appropriate safeguards ensuring confidentiality, due process, and the protection of individual rights. It further recognizes that the effective deterrence of corruption requires not only punitive enforcement, but also structural reforms that institutionalize transparency and reinforce the integrity and capacity of public institutions. Ultimately, the bill advances a meaningful reform that helps foster ethical governance, prevent abuse of public office, and restore public confidence in government. This measure offers a concrete and principled step toward cleaner, more trustworthy governance especially at a time of declining public trust in government officials, public institutions, and the Philippine government as a whole. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9101
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE AND RESPONSIVE CIVIL REGISTRATION AND VITAL STATISTICS SYSTEM, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive, responsive, and modern Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system that ensures the universal, timely, and secure registration of all vital events of Filipinos, both in the country and abroad. It aims to replace fragmented systems with an integrated framework that strengthens legal identity, improves service delivery, and enhances the accuracy and reliability of civil registry data. The measure recognizes civil registration as essential to the protection of rights and access to public services. It seeks to guarantee free and accessible registration of births, deaths, marriages, and related civil status events, with special attention to marginalized and vulnerable sectors, including indigenous peoples, foundlings, children in need of special protection, persons with disabilities, and overseas Filipinos. The bill further promotes the digitization and interconnection of civil registry systems, the establishment of a national database, and stronger coordination among the Philippine Statistics Authority, local government units, and other concerned agencies to improve efficiency, transparency, and data integrity. Ultimately, the measure affirms the State’s commitment to legal identity, data privacy, and inclusive governance by ensuring that every Filipino is properly registered and recognized before the law. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9102
title: AN ACT GRANTING A FIFTY PERCENT (50%) DISCOUNT FROM FUNERAL SERVICES TO INDIGENT FAMILIES AND FREE FUNERAL SERVICES TO EXTREMELY POOR FAMILIES NATIONWIDE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a government-supported burial assistance program to help indigent and extremely poor families cope with the high cost of funeral and burial services. It aims to ensure that every Filipino, regardless of financial capacity, is afforded a dignified and respectful farewell for their departed loved ones. In the Philippines, death is marked by deeply rooted cultural practices that honor the deceased and bring communities together in mourning. Funeral rites serve not only as expressions of grief but also as affirmations of familial and social bonds. However, for many low-income households, these traditions are often overshadowed by the prohibitive costs associated with funeral arrangements and interment. Basic funeral services can cost at least P10,000.00, an amount that is beyond the reach of many indigent families. As a result, some are compelled to seek financial assistance through informal lenders who may charge excessive interest, further worsening their economic situation. In extreme cases, families are unable to secure even the most modest funeral services, depriving their loved ones of a proper and dignified burial. This proposed measure provides a fifty percent (50%) discount on funeral services for indigent families, and free funeral services for those classified as extremely poor. Availment of these benefits shall be subject to standard documentation requirements and a formal funeral agreement involving the bereaved family, accredited service providers, and authorized personnel from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD). By alleviating the financial strain associated with funeral expenses, this bill promotes compassion, dignity, and social equity during times of loss. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9103
title: AN ACT PENALIZING THE ACT OF WAGE THEFT BY AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE ARTICLES 87 AND 116 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to penalize the act of wage theft by strengthening existing provisions of the Labor Code of the Philippines, particularly Articles 87 and 116, in order to ensure that workers receive the full compensation and benefits legally due to them. Despite existing labor protections, wage theft remains a persistent issue affecting workers across various sectors. It manifests in multiple forms, including non-payment or underpayment of wages, denial of overtime pay, withholding of bonuses and benefits, unlawful deductions, and requiring employees to perform off-the-clock work without compensation. These practices undermine the dignity of labor, erode trust in employment relationships, and deprive workers of their rightful livelihood. This measure affirms the State’s commitment to protect workers’ rights by clearly defining wage theft and expanding its coverage to include not only wages but also other earnings and benefits such as overtime pay, tips, holiday pay, and reimbursements. It further strengthens safeguards by prohibiting discriminatory practices in the assignment of overtime work and ensuring equitable access to compensation opportunities. The bill also imposes stricter accountability by providing criminal liability for violators and introducing administrative sanctions, including the suspension and eventual cancellation of business permits for repeat offenders. By institutionalizing comprehensive protections against wage theft, this measure upholds social justice, promotes fair labor standards, and ensures that workers are duly compensated for their labor, both locally and abroad. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9104
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE DISCOUNT ON THE PURCHASE OF GOODS AND SERVICES OF SENIOR CITIZENS AND PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Let each of you look out not only for his own interests, but also for the interests of others. — Philippians 2:4 Republic Act No. 7432, otherwise known as the Senior Citizens Act, and Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, were enacted as social protection measures to help ease the everyday financial burden faced by senior citizens and persons with disabilities. Through mandatory discounts and tax exemptions, these laws seek to make basic goods and essential services more accessible to sectors that are often more vulnerable to rising costs and economic shocks. Social protection is most effective when it is reliable and consistently applied. In daily transactions, however, the benefits granted under these laws are often diluted when goods and services are offered under promotional discounts. Senior citizens and persons with disabilities are frequently informed that the promotional price already replaces the statutory discount, even though the law does not intend for temporary marketing offers to substitute for legally mandated benefits. This practice weakens the protective purpose of existing laws and creates uncertainty at the point of purchase. This bill seeks to address that gap by clearly providing that the discounts and tax exemptions granted under Republic Act No. 7432 and Republic Act No. 7277 shall apply even when goods and services are offered under promotional discounts. It expressly states that promotions extended to the general public cannot be treated as compliance with the discount privileges mandated by law. The measure also clarifies the tax treatment of such discounts to ensure consistent implementation while allowing business establishments to properly account for them in accordance with existing tax laws. At its core, the measure reaffirms the State’s responsibility to uphold meaningful social protection for vulnerable sectors. Preferential treatment for senior citizens and persons with disabilities is a deliberate policy choice grounded in equity and social justice. By removing ambiguity and closing a commonly encountered loophole, this bill strengthens the implementation of existing laws and ensures that the protection they offer is felt in everyday life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. label: HB 9105
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE GROUNDS FOR ANNULMENT OF MARRIAGE AND LEGAL SEPARATION, UNDER ARTICLES 45 AND 55 AND OTHER RELATED PROVISIONS UNDER ARTICLES 46, 48, 55, AND 57 OF EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. 209, OR THE FAMILY CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Preamble is an introductory statement or introductory part of a constitution that usually states the reasons for the intent of the law. The Preamble of the Philippine Constitution for example is a statement that outlines the aspirations of the Filipinos, it aims to establish a government that embodies the ideals and aspirations of the Filipino people. Certainly, marriage in Filipino culture is deeply rooted in tradition, family ties, and community which is why no less than the 1987 Constitution under Article XV Section 1 and 2 states that The State recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation. Accordingly, it shall strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development, and marriage, as an inviolable social institution, is the foundation of the family and shall be protected by the State. Moreover, the Constitution of the Philippines, the highest law of the land regards marriage as an inviolable social institution making the Philippines one of the few, if not the only, nation to do so. For instance, The Italian Constitution although it recognizes the family as a fundamental unit of society, does not explicitly state that the family or marriage is inviolable. Article 29 of the Italian Constitution which states that, The Republic recognises the rights of the family as a natural society founded on marriage and Marriage is based on the moral and legal equality of the spouses within the limits laid down by law to guarantee the unity of the family. Page 1 of 7 Also, in the Spanish Constitution, although it recognizes the family as the basic social institution, it never describes marriage as inviolable. Section 39 of the Spanish Constitution, it is stated that The public authorities ensure social, economic and legal protection of the family. These are the few reasons why in contrast to our jurisdiction, they have many options or avenues to dissolve marriages solemnized under their Family and Marriage Laws. It is noteworthy that in interpreting our 1987 Constitution, the first rule is verba legis (Plain meaning rule) meaning, the words of the Constitution must be given their ordinary meaning except where technical terms are employed. The Constitution is not a lawyer’s document, its language as much as possible should be understood in the sense they have in common use. Words should mean what they mean. The marriage that is enshrined in our Philippine Constitution is unique because of its inviolable character. Hence, the State as mandated by the Constitution must not introduce further means to dissolve a marriage, a key that may unlock and could open up Pandora’s box of problems destroying the foundation of the family that runs counter to the fundamental law. No less than the Family Code has already established modes for the dissolution of marriage. Accordingly, this proposed legislation will still uphold the inviolability of marriage under our Philippine Constitution while also adding new grounds for the dissolution of marriage beyond what is currently available. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. label: HB 9106
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 40, 43(f) AND 60 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001 OR EPIRA”, TO PROHIBIT THE RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSSES FROM CONSUMERS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), was enacted to restructure the electric power industry, promote competition, and ensure transparency in electricity pricing through the unbundling of rates. While EPIRA succeeded in making electricity charges more transparent, it nonetheless allowed the continued recovery of system losses from consumers as a separate line item in their electricity bills. At present, system‑loss charges represent a significant and continuing burden on Filipino consumers. As PIDS notes in “The Philippine Electric Power Industry under EPIRA” (Policy Note 2018‑19), transmission and distribution losses in the Philippines declined from about 17 percent of total power output in 1995 to roughly 9 percent in 2014, indicating that losses are now broadly in the single‑digit range. However, data on electric cooperatives show that the average system‑loss rate hovers around 11–12 percent, with some ECs reaching over 30 percent or even 37 percent, driven by electricity pilferage, aging infrastructure, and operational inefficiencies. These losses are passed on to consumers, effectively requiring households and businesses to shoulder costs that are largely within the control of distribution utilities and electric cooperatives. The financial impact of this practice is substantial. The World Bank Electric Cooperative System Loss Reduction Project (P066532) reveals that for 18 participating electric cooperatives with total annual energy purchases or generation of 2,427 gigawatt‑hours (GWh), a reduction of approximately 3.3 percent in system losses is expected to yield 80 GWh of avoided system losses per year. This corresponds to a non‑trivial volume of electricity that would otherwise be lost in the distribution network, underscoring that even modest percentage‑point reductions in system losses can translate into hundreds of millions of kilowatt‑hours of avoided losses and, in turn, substantial cost‑savings for utilities and consumers over time. Well‑managed utilities, meanwhile, are able to maintain losses within the 5–8 percent range, confirming that much of the loss burden is avoidable and can be reduced through targeted investments and institutional reforms. In this context, the continued practice of passing a system‑loss costs directly to consumers runs counter to the principles of efficiency, accountability, and fairness. While EPIRA introduced transparency, it did not fully address the inequity of charging consumers 1 Philippine Institute for Development Studies (2018). The Philippine electric power industry under EPIRA. Available at https://pidswebs.pids.gov.ph/CDN/PUBLICATIONS/pidspn1819.pdf. for inefficiencies in the distribution system, and the PIDS‑2018‑19 and World Bank‑P066532 data show that those inefficiencies are quantifiable and reducible. This measure seeks to correct that imbalance. Moreover, this bill proposes to amend Sections 40, 43(f), and 60 of Republic Act No. 9136, as well as Section 10 of Republic Act No. 7832, to prohibit the recovery of system losses as a separate charge to consumers. Instead, system losses shall be treated as part of the operating costs of distribution utilities and electric cooperatives, subject to efficiency and loss‑reduction standards to be determined and enforced by the Energy Regulatory Commission, in line with the PIDS‑recommended direction of reducing system losses toward single‑digit levels and the World Bank‑supported emphasis on achieving “significant and sustained energy efficiency improvements” in distribution systems through targeted loss‑reduction programs. By shifting the responsibility for managing system losses back to utilities where it properly belongs, this measure encourages operational discipline, promotes investment in modern and resilient infrastructure, and strengthens accountability mechanisms within the power sector. At the same time, it protects consumers from bearing the financial burden of inefficiencies and losses that can and should be addressed by those tasked with delivering this essential service. Ultimately, this proposed reform advances the State’s commitment to ensure reliable, affordable, and equitable access to electricity for all Filipinos. It reinforces the principle that while consumers must pay for the electricity they use, they should not be made to pay for inefficiencies that can and should be addressed by those tasked with delivering this essential service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. NATHANIEL “ATTY. NAT” M. ODUCADO 1Tahanan Party List REP. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 9107
title: AN ACT AMENDING CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10659, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “SUGARCANE INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT ACT OF 2015,” TO MODERNIZE AND TO FACILITATE COMPETITIVENESS OF THE SUGAR INDUSTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Executive Order No. 18 (s. 1986) established the Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA) to oversee the regulation and orderly development of the sugar industry. Thereafter, Republic Act No. 10659, otherwise known as the Sugarcane Industry Development Act of 2015, instituted programs to enhance productivity, modernize, support farmers, and improve industry competitiveness, thereby laying the foundation for sustained sectoral growth. Despite these legislative milestones, the sugar industry now faces market volatility, rising production costs, climate-related risks, infrastructure constraints, and outdated technical standards. Collectively, these challenges underscore the need to strengthen the operational capacity of existing institutions and programs to ensure the effective delivery of benefits intended under existing law. In response to these continuing challenges, this bill seeks to strengthen and operationalize the mandates of the SRA under Executive Order No. 18 (s. 1986) and Republic Act No. 10659. Specifically, it aims to: ● Improve access for qualified producer organizations to programs, incentives, and support mechanisms; ● Advance modernization in productivity, mechanization, logistics, research, and climate resilience; ● Enhance market transparency and evidence-based planning through reliable industry data. ● Establish standards for the licensing, review, and evaluation of mills, refineries, and covered entities under existing authority; ● Strengthen the implementation capability of the SRA; and ● Improve the utilization of the Sugarcane Industry Development Fund for programs that directly benefit the industry. The proposed amendments are carefully designed to avoid unnecessary regulatory burdens or unwarranted capital replacement requirements. They provide practical tools and balanced 1 mechanisms to more effectively implement existing law, while ensuring due process and appropriate safeguards. Ultimately, by reinforcing institutional capacity, improving transparency, and promoting modernization, this measure equips the sugar industry to address both longstanding and emerging challenges in a coordinated and sustainable manner. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BEVERLEY ROSE A. label: HB 9109
title: AN ACT SEGREGATING PARCELS OF LAND LOCATED AT PIDAWAN, ONGASAN BARANGAY LOAKAN PROPER, BAGUIO CITY FROM MILITARY RESERVATION OF PROCLAMATION 2405 AND CONVERTING THEM INTO ALIENABLE AND DISPOSABLE PUBLIC LAND AND DECLARING THE SAME OPEN FOR THE DISPOSITION TO BONA FIDE QUALIFIED OCCUPANTS AND/OR APPLICANTS UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 730 OR REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10023
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bill seeks to segregate parcels of land containing an approximate area of Two Hundred Seventy-One Thousand Four Hundred (271,400 sq.m.) square meters, located at Pidawan, Ongasan, Barangay Loakan Proper, Baguio City, from Military Reservation under Proclamation No. 2405, subject to private rights and to convert them into alienable and disposable public land and award it directly to actual occupants who are the Heirs of Guesu Dacdacan also known as Guesec Chacchacan, to promote social justice and support the government's housing and urban development goals. The Heirs of Chacchacan had been occupying the said area even before it was proclaimed as military reservation in 1985. In fact, on July 28, 1961, an approved survey plan PSU-186219 in the name of Guesu Dacdacan was issued by the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, now, Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). The approved survey plan was resurveyed which was logged as PSU-CAR-186219 Amd. Furthermore, as early as May 1923, the parcels of land were declared under Declaration of Real Property No. 109 in the name of Guesec Dacdacan which was later changed to Tax Declaration No. 379 under the Heirs of Guesec Dacdacan. When DENR Special Order No. 31, series of 1990 was promulgated to identify and delineate the ancestral lands and domains of indigenous cultural communities within the City of Baguio and the rest of the Cordilleras, the Heirs of Chacchacan applied under this provision for the recognition of their ancestral land claim. An investigation report dated October 15, 1991, was issued by the Office of the Special Task Force on Ancestral Land (STFAL) of DENR-CAR, stating that the ancestors of the Chacchacan are long-time residents of Baguio City and they belong to Ibaloi Tribe. Likewise evidences such as old stonewalls, trees and improvements were found at said place which shows that their ancestors occupied the said land. On January 30, 1992, a resolution was issued by the Office of the Special Task Force on Ancestral Land (STFAL) of DENR-CAR, declaring that their ancestors have clearly established that they have valid ancestral land claims. The STFAL finds that the recognition of ancestral land claim filed by the Heirs of Guesec Chacchacan to be ancestral land under the concept and guidelines contained in the DENR Special Project. With the creation of the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act of 1997 or Republic Act 8371, the application of the Heirs of Guesec Chacchacan was turned over to the National Commission on Indigenous People (NCIP). Up to the present, the application of the Heirs of Chacchacan is still pending before the office of the National Commission on Indigenous People (NCIP). In view thereof, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 9110
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL CREATIVE INDUSTRIES INVESTMENT PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creative industries sector plays a vital role in shaping national identity, preserving cultural heritage, and contributing to economic growth. In the Philippines, creative industries—spanning arts, culture, media, design, and related fields—continue to generate significant artistic and cultural wealth while providing employment and livelihood opportunities for Filipinos. However, despite its potential, the sector remains underdeveloped due to insufficient investment and limited institutional support. Thus, this bill seeks to address these gaps by establishing a comprehensive and coordinated framework for the development and promotion of the country’s creative industries. Central to the measure is the creation of the National Creative Industries Investment Committee (NCIIC), an inter-agency body tasked with formulating and approving a National Creative Industries Investment Program. This program will set clear targets for public spending, private investment, employment generation, and industry output. It will also outline key strategies such as infrastructure development, fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, and initiatives to promote Filipino creative outputs in both domestic and global markets. Recognizing 1 the importance of grassroots development, the bill also mandates national agencies to assist Local Government Units (LGUs) in crafting and implementing local investment plans for the creative industries. By investing in this sector, the State not only strengthens national identity but also drives innovation, inclusive growth, and global competitiveness. Finally, we recognize Rep. Joey Salceda of the 2nd District of Albay for filing a similar bill in the Nineteenth Congresses. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. label: HB 9111
title: AN ACT PROVIDING BENEFITS AND INCENTIVES TO OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS INVESTING IN BUSINESS IN THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) continue to play a vital role in sustaining the Philippine economy through their remittances and sacrifices abroad. In recognition of the State’s duty to protect and promote the welfare of all workers, it is imperative to ensure that OFWs are not only safeguarded from excessive remittance charges but are also adequately supported upon their return to the country. Despite their substantial contributions to national development, many returning OFWs face limited reintegration opportunities and insufficient economic assistance. Recent global disruptions, including the COVID-19 pandemic, underscored the vulnerability of OFWs to sudden job displacement and large- scale repatriation, highlighting the need for sustainable reintegration mechanisms beyond emergency response. This bill seeks to encourage former OFWs to invest and establish enterprises in the Philippines by granting targeted incentives, including initial income tax exemptions, reduced real property taxes, and tax relief on the importation of raw materials, capital equipment, machinery, and spare parts exclusively used in OFW-owned businesses. By promoting entrepreneurship and productive investment, the measure aims to facilitate meaningful reintegration, maximize the productive use of OFWs’ savings, and strengthen national and local economic development. Finally, we would like to recognize former Tarlac, 2nd District Representative Christian Tell Yap for filing a similar measure during the 19 th Congress. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9112
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PHILHEALTH OUTPATIENT COVERAGE ON DIALYSIS AND RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 15, Article II of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people. Furthermore, Section 11, Article XIII mandates the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that will make essential goods, health services, and other social services available to all people at an affordable cost, with priority given to the needs of the underprivileged, sick, elderly, and persons with disabilities. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and End Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) are growing public health concerns in the Philippines. Thousands of Filipino patients depend on life-sustaining dialysis treatments to survive. However, dialysis and kidney transplantation remain among the most expensive medical treatments, requiring continuous therapy and long-term medical management. While the government has expanded health insurance coverage under Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the Universal Health Care Act, many patients still face significant financial burdens in accessing dialysis and renal replacement therapy. The cost of repeated dialysis sessions, transplantation procedures, maintenance immunosuppressive medications, and related medical services continue to place immense financial strain on patients and their families. In addition, access to dialysis services and renal replacement therapy remains uneven across the country. Many hospitals lack adequate dialysis facilities, trained personnel, and coordinated programs for prevention, treatment, and post-transplant rehabilitation. The absence of a unified national framework also limits the effectiveness of existing programs for kidney disease prevention and treatment. This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive system of outpatient coverage for dialysis and renal replacement therapy through PhilHealth. It also establishes mechanisms to strengthen kidney disease prevention, expand dialysis facilities, improve data collection through the Philippine Renal Disease Registry, promote kidney transplantation as the optimal treatment option for eligible patients, and provide rehabilitation support for patients undergoing renal replacement therapy. By strengthening financial protection and expanding access to life-saving renal treatments, this measure aims to ensure that no Filipino suffering from kidney failure is deprived of essential medical care because of financial constraints. This measure was also filed during the 19th Congress and was primarily to the Committee on Health. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. label: HB 9114
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE CREATION OF ECONOMIC AND INVESTMENT PROMOTION OFFICER IN LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local government units (LGUs) play a critical role in promoting economic development, attracting investments, and creating employment opportunities within their respective jurisdictions. With increasing competition among regions and localities for both domestic and foreign investments, local governments must develop the institutional capacity to promote their economic potential effectively and facilitate business development. Under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, as amended, however, the position of an Economic and Investment Promotion Officer is not formally institutionalized within the structure of local government units. In practice, the functions related to economic and investment promotion are often assigned on a temporary or designated basis to existing personnel who have other assignments, resulting in inconsistent implementation of local investment promotion programs across LGUs. Currently, only a limited number of local government units, including Quezon City, Puerto Princesa, Legazpi City, Albay, Negros Occidental, and San Fernando, Bukidnon, have established dedicated economic and investment promotion offices to actively attract investments and stimulate local economic activity. Institutionalizing the position of an Economic and Investment Promotion Officer will strengthen the capacity of LGUs to formulate and implement local investment promotion strategies, develop competitive investment environments, and coordinate effectively with national government agencies and the private sector. This measure therefore seeks to amend the Local Government Code of 1991 to formally establish the position of Economic and Investment Promotion Officer in provincial and city governments and in first- and second-class municipalities, while allowing third to sixth class municipalities the option to create the position depending on their resources and development priorities. By strengthening local economic governance, this bill aims to promote inclusive economic growth, enhance local competitiveness, and encourage sustainable investments in communities across the country. This measure was initially filed during the 18th Congress In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSURANCE OF ALL GOVERNMENT PROPERTIES AND INTEREST WITH THE GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM (GSIS), AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Government properties are constantly exposed to risks such as fire, earthquakes, typhoons, and other natural disasters. When these assets are damaged or lost, the government must allocate significant public funds for repair or replacement, which can disrupt public services and strain national resources. Thus, this bill seeks to establish a comprehensive system for insuring government-owned properties in the Philippines through the creation of an insurance mechanism under the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS). The bill establishes a General Insurance Fund, which will serve as a pool of resources to compensate the government for damage or loss of its properties. The fund will be sourced from premiums paid by government agencies and existing insurance funds. The bill covers a wide range of government assets, including buildings, vehicles, machinery, office equipment, furnishings and properties in transit. It also recognizes the government’s insurable interest in assets owned by its subsidiaries and corporations, including those slated for privatization. 1 Through this bill, it is hoped that the government will strengthen its ability to safeguard its assets by making insurance coverage mandatory, centralized, and professionally managed. By doing so, it helps ensure continuity of public services and reduces the financial burden on taxpayers in times of disaster. Finally, we recognize Rep. Joey Salceda of the 2nd District of Albay for filing a similar bill in the Nineteenth Congresses. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9116
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO WORKERS IN CRITICAL INDUSTRIES DURING A STATE OF CALAMITY OR EMERGENCY OR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 18, Article II of the 1987 Constitution guarantees that the State affirms labor as a primary social economic force and shall protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Additionally, Section 3, Article XIII mandates the State to afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all. The Philippine experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent national states of calamity has highlighted a significant inequity in our labor framework. While "work-from-home" arrangements shielded a segment of the workforce, employees in "critical industries,” ranging from those in healthcare and logistics to sanitation and telecommunications, were required to physically report to the frontlines. These workers do not merely perform their duties; they serve as the nation’s life support system – ensuring that food, medicine, electricity, and communication remain available to the public even as they face increased exposure to health risks, physical hazards, and psychological strain. Currently, hazard pay is generally a matter of management prerogative or specific collective bargaining agreements in the private sector, often leading to inconsistent application. In contrast, public sector health workers are granted hazard pay under Republic Act No. 7305, otherwise known as the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers. Thus, this bill seeks to bridge this gap by institutionalizing a mandatory hazard pay for workers in critical industries in the private sector during a declared state of calamity, emergency, or public health emergency as defined under Republic Act No. 11332, otherwise known as the Mandatory Reporting of Notifiable Diseases and Health Events of Public Health Concern Act. By providing a hazard allowance equivalent to at least twenty-five percent (25%) of their monthly basic salary, the State recognizes the extraordinary risks these workers undertake. Furthermore, this bill ensures inclusivity by extending coverage to third-party service contractors, such as security guards and janitors, who are often the most exposed yet least compensated. This measure is not just a matter of financial compensation; it is a vital act of social justice and a strategic necessity to ensure that our critical infrastructure remains resilient during the nation's most trying times. During the 19th Congress, this bill was principally authored by former Parañaque, 2nd District Representative Gus S. Tambunting. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9117
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ALLOWANCES OF BARANGAY OFFICIALS, GRANTING HONORARIA AND OTHER BENEFITS TO THE BARANGAY WORKERS WHO HAVE SERVED FOR AT LEAST ONE (1) YEAR, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE, THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangays serve as the primary frontliners of governance and public service delivery in communities. Barangay officials and workers play a vital role in maintaining peace and order, implementing national and local government programs, responding to disasters, mediating disputes through the Katarungang Pambarangay system, and ensuring the effective delivery of basic services at the grassroots level. However, under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, as amended, the honoraria of barangay officials remain pegged at a minimum of ₱1,000 per month for the Punong Barangay and ₱600 per month for each Sangguniang Barangay member, Barangay Treasurer, and Barangay Secretary. These amounts were set more than three decades ago and are no longer commensurate with the responsibilities and workload expected from barangay officials. Moreover, barangay tanods, who perform essential functions in maintaining community peace and order and assisting in public safety and emergency response, are not consistently provided with honoraria and benefits despite the critical services they render. This measure seeks to update and rationalize the compensation structure of barangay officials by increasing their minimum honoraria, extending compensation and benefits to barangay workers who have rendered at least one year of service, and recognizing the contributions of barangay tanods through the grant of honoraria and other benefits. By providing a more responsive and reasonable compensation framework, the State acknowledges the indispensable role of barangay officials and workers in grassroots governance while encouraging professionalism, accountability, and sustained public service in local communities. This measure has been filed since the 11th Congress and has been repeatedly referred to the Committee on Local Government. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9118
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING ALL THE PROVINCIAL AND SUB-PROVINCIAL JAILS WITHIN THE JURISDICTION OF THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the Department of Interior and Local Government Act of 1990, the administration of local detention facilities is divided between two authorities: city, municipal, and district jails are managed by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), while provincial and sub-provincial jails are administered by their respective provincial governments. This dual system of jail administration has resulted in disparities in jail management, detention conditions, operational policies, and personnel standards across the country. The absence of a unified authority overseeing all local jails has made it difficult to implement consistent custodial standards, rehabilitation programs, and detention management systems nationwide. Given the BJMP’s mandate and professional expertise in jail administration, integrating provincial and sub-provincial jails into its jurisdiction would enable the establishment of uniform operational standards, improved detention management practices, and enhanced institutional accountability. Thus, this bill seeks to amend Republic Act No. 6975 to integrate all provincial and sub-provincial jails under the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology. Through this reform, the BJMP will be able to implement standardized policies for jail operations, personnel training, inmate welfare, and rehabilitation programs across all local detention facilities. The bill also provides for a transition period to ensure an orderly transfer of functions, personnel, facilities, and resources from provincial governments to the BJMP. By consolidating jail administration under a single professionalized agency, this measure aims to improve detention facility management, strengthen institutional oversight, and promote the welfare and rights of detainees and inmates. This measure has been repeatedly filed since the 14th Congress but has remained pending at the committee level. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9119
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DEPLOYMENT OF LICENSED ALLIED HEALTH PROFESSIONALS TO GEOGRAPHICALLY ISOLATED AND DISADVANTAGED AREAS (GIDAs) AND UNDERSERVED REGIONS AND PROVIDING INCENTIVES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to quality healthcare remains uneven across the Philippines, with geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs) and underserved regions continuing to face significant shortages in health human resources. While government programs have made strides in deploying physicians and nurses, there remains a critical gap in the availability of allied health professionals—such as medical technologists, pharmacists, physical therapists, and other essential practitioners—who play a vital role in diagnostics, treatment support, rehabilitation, and overall patient care. This bill seeks to address this gap through the establishment of a National Allied Health Deployment Program (NAHDP) under the Department of Health (DOH). The program aims to ensure the systematic, equitable, and sustained deployment of licensed allied health professionals to communities that need them most. By aligning deployment with local health system needs and strengthening 1 coordination with local government units and health facilities, the measure intends to improve service delivery and health outcomes in underserved areas. Furthermore, the bill strengthens partnerships with academic institutions, training hospitals, and professional organizations to build a sustainable pipeline of allied health workers. It integrates community-oriented training, supports research and innovation, and establishes a scholarship and return-service program to encourage students—particularly those from underserved areas—to pursue allied health professions and serve their communities. By investing in allied health professionals and ensuring their presence in all regions of the country, especially in GIDAs, the State takes a decisive step toward equitable, accessible, and quality healthcare for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9120
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE PHILIPPINE MAHARLIKA HIGHWAY AS THE NATIONAL FOOD HIGHWAY, PROVIDING AN INTEGRATED SYSTEM FOR THE PROCESSING, STORAGE, TRANSPORT, DISTRIBUTION, AND MONITORING OF FOOD PRODUCTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 21, Article II of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the State shall promote comprehensive rural development and agrarian reform. Furthermore, Section 9, Article XIV provides that the State shall promote the growth and generalized spread of technology and ensure that the benefits of science and technology are used to improve the productivity of the country. The Philippine agricultural sector remains the backbone of the national economy, yet it is burdened by a fragmented and inefficient logistics network. As of 2025, post-harvest losses in the Philippines remain alarmingly high, reaching as much as 33% for mangoes and up to 45% for onions. This is primarily due to inadequate cold storage and the lack of specialized transport corridors. These inefficiencies do not only result in billions of pesos in lost revenue for our farmers but also drive up retail food prices, contributing to the 44% food insecurity rate reported among the population in 2023-2024. By declaring the Philippine Maharlika Highway as the National Food Highway, this bill institutionalizes a strategic, integrated system for the processing, storage, and rapid distribution of agricultural goods. This measure transitions our primary road network from a mere transit route into a "living" logistics ecosystem. It not only prioritizes the movement of perishable goods through the establishment of strategic cold-chain hubs in partnership with the private sector, which is already projected to reach 100,000 pallet positions by 2026, but also ensures that food quality is monitored from farm to table. This bill also creates the National Food Highway Management Board to oversee and implement this Act. Furthermore, this bill introduces the "Philippine Food Loop" concept by integrating the Maharlika Highway with the Western Philippine Nautical Highway. This creates a resilient, multi-modal circuit that ensures the continuous flow of food even when specific regions are hit by typhoons. Designating this highway as a National Food Highway is a critical structural intervention to modernize Filipino agriculture, lower the cost of living, and achieve genuine national food sovereignty. This measure was also filed during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. label: HB 9121
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY AFFAIRS OFFICES (PDAOs) IN ALL LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 40 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10070, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS AN ACT ESTABLISHING INSTITUTIONAL MECHANISM TO ENSURE THE IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS AND SERVICES FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IN EVERY PROVINCE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE More than four decades since the enactment of the country’s first disability legislation, Batas Pambansa Blg. 344, otherwise known as the Accessibility Law, and more than a decade since the Philippines ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), the government has undertaken various legislative and policy initiatives to promote the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities. Among these measures is Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, which recognizes the rights of persons with disabilities to rehabilitation, self-development, self-reliance, and full participation in the mainstream of society. Subsequent laws further strengthened these protections, including Republic Act No. 10524, which promotes employment opportunities for persons with disabilities, and Republic Act No. 10754, which expanded the benefits and privileges of persons with disabilities. In recognition of the need to ensure that programs and services for persons with disabilities are effectively implemented at the local level, Republic Act No. 10070 encouraged local government units (LGUs) to establish Persons with Disability Affairs Offices (PDAOs). These offices are intended to serve as focal points for the implementation of disability-related programs, policy coordination, and the delivery of services to persons with disabilities within their respective jurisdictions. However, more than a decade since the passage of Republic Act No. 10070, compliance among LGUs remains limited. Records from the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) indicate that only a portion of LGUs have established their respective PDAOs, largely because the creation of these offices remains discretionary and subject to the availability of local funds. As a result, many persons with disabilities continue to experience limited access to programs, services, and institutional support at the community level. Moreover, reliable and updated data on persons with disabilities remains insufficient. The lack of a standardized and comprehensive database at the local level hampers effective policy formulation, program implementation, and service delivery. This underscores the need to strengthen institutional mechanisms that will ensure the systematic collection of data and the effective coordination of programs for the disability sector. According to estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately ten percent (10%) of the population lives with some form of disability. In the Philippines, this translates to millions of individuals who require accessible public services, inclusive development programs, and effective representation in local governance. To address these, this measure seeks to strengthen the institutional framework for the protection and promotion of the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities by amending Republic Act No. 7277, as amended by Republic Act No. 10070. Specifically, this bill aims to: 1. Mandate the establishment and operation of Persons with Disability Affairs Offices (PDAOs) in all local government units; 2. Provide clear institutional and funding mechanisms for the establishment and operation of PDAOs; 3. Strengthen the functions, coordination mechanisms, and institutional role of PDAOs in the implementation of disability-related laws and programs; 2 4. Establish a uniform and standardized local database of persons with disabilities linked to a national registry system; 5. Enhance capacity building, policy coordination, and public information efforts for the disability sector; and, 6. Ensure a more responsive and inclusive system of local governance that advances the rights, welfare, and participation of persons with disabilities. By institutionalizing the establishment of Persons with Disability Affairs Offices in all local government units, the State affirms its commitment to inclusive governance and to ensuring that persons with disabilities are empowered, protected, and fully integrated into the nation’s social and economic life. During the 19th Congress, this bill was also filed and was referred to the Committee on Local Government. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. label: HB 9122
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS IN THE PREPARATION AND AUTHORIZATION PROCESS OF THE ANNUAL NATIONAL BUDGET, PROVIDING EFFECTIVELY MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 23, Article II of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall encourage non-governmental, community-based, or sectoral organizations that promote the welfare of the nation. Further, Section 16, Article XIII guarantees the right of the people and their organizations to effective and reasonable participation at all levels of social, political, and economic decision-making, and mandates the State to facilitate the establishment of adequate consultation mechanisms. The national budget is the most concrete expression of the government’s priorities. For decades, however, the budget process has remained largely a "black box" to the average Filipino, with critical decisions made in closed-door sessions or during the highly opaque Bicameral Conference Committee deliberations, leaving the public behind and clueless. While the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has introduced administrative measures like the "Budget Partnership Agreements" (BPAs), these remain executive prerogatives that can be rescinded by changing administrations. To reinforce people’s constitutional right to participate, this bill seeks to institutionalize the participation of Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) in the first two critical stages of the budget cycle: Preparation (at the agency level) and Authorization (at the Congressional level). By providing a formal accreditation process and granting CSOs the right to access budget documents, attend hearings, and even participate in the Bicameral Conference Committee hearings, this measure ensures that people are informed of the decisions of the legislators and that public funds are allocated based on the actual needs of the people rather than purely political considerations. Institutionalizing people's participation does not merely promote transparency; it improves the quality of government spending. CSOs, with their ground-level expertise in sectors like agriculture, health, and education, can provide "alternative budgets" and position papers that highlight inefficiencies and propose more impactful interventions. This bill transforms the Filipino people from mere observers into active partners in nation-building, ensuring that every peso in the national treasury is accounted for and spent for the common good. This measure has been repeatedly filed since the 18th Congress. During the 19th Congress, former Pangasinan, 4th District Representative Christopher V.P. De Venecia principally authored this bill. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9123
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND MECHANISMS FOR THE CREATION, OPERATION, ADMINISTRATION, AND COORDINATION OF SPECIAL AGRICULTURAL GROWTH ZONES IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THIS PURPOSE, THE PHILIPPINE AGRICULTURAL GROWTH ZONE AUTHORITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the policy of the State to ensure that all sectors of the economy and all regions of the country shall be given optimum opportunity to maximize agricultural productivity, promote efficiency and equity and accelerate the modernization of the agriculture and fisheries sectors of the country, by establishing, among others, special agricultural growth zones in selected areas in the countryside, with the active participation of the private sector as enshrined in the 1987 Constitution, to wit: ● Section 20, Article II provides that “The State recognizes the indispensable role of the private sector, encourages private enterprise, and provides incentives to needed investments.” ● Section 8, Article XIII provides that “The State shall provide incentives to landowners to invest the proceeds of the agrarian reform program to promote industrialization, employment, creation, and privatization of public sector enterprises. Financial instruments used as payment for their lands shall be honored as equity in enterprises of their choice.” The State shall promote industrialization and full employment based on sound agricultural development and agrarian reform, through industries that make full and efficient use of human and natural resources, and which are competitive in both domestic and foreign markets. The proposed measure will establish the legal framework and mechanisms for the administration and management of the Special Agricultural Growth Zones (SAGZ) and assist in the preservation of natural resources and biodiversity. It will guarantee the security of ownership, tenure, and income of all farmer-landowners, especially agrarian reform beneficiaries, and ensure that all agricultural, commercial, and industrial arrangements are mutually beneficial. It will modernize the agriculture sector by transforming the special agricultural growth zones into highly developed agro-industrial, commercial, investment, and financial centers, where highly trained workers and efficient services will be available to agribusiness and agriculture-related enterprises. Through the creation of SAGZ, the flow of investors, both foreign and local, would generate employment opportunities and establish backward and forward linkages among industries in and around the agricultural growth zones. Financial and industrial cooperation between the Philippines and industrialized countries in technology-intensive industries will modernize the country’s agricultural sector and improve productivity by leveraging new technological and managerial know-how. Finally, it will open opportunities for people working in the agricultural sector, helping them gain access to modern and developing technologies needed for sustainable agriculture and enabling them to have a competitive advantage in the market. Toward this end, the private sector shall play a major role in establishing special agricultural growth zones by developing and utilizing such areas to spur agricultural development and enhance the productivity of agricultural lands awarded under the agrarian reform program. 2 This measure was also filed and referred to the Committee on Government Enterprises and Privatization during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9124
title: AN ACT CREATING IN THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION THE PLANTILLA POSITIONS OF GUIDANCE COUNSELORS IN EVERY ELEMENTARY SCHOOL AND ADDITIONAL PLANTILLA POSITIONS OF GUIDANCE COUNSELORS FOR HIGH SCHOOL, INCREASING THE SALARIES OF GUIDANCE COUNSELORS AND GUIDANCE-RELATED POSITIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education and to take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Central to "quality education" is the holistic development of the learner - a process that is currently under threat due to a systemic crisis in our mental health support infrastructure. The Department of Education (DepEd) acknowledges that guidance and counseling are indispensable in fostering student resilience and self-discipline. However, the country is currently grappling with a staggering counselor-to- student ratio of 1:14,000, based on 2022 figures. This is a far cry from the internationally recognized standard of 1:250, and even falls short of DepEd’s modest target of 1:500. While the recently enacted Republic Act No. 12080, otherwise known as the Basic Education Mental Health and Well-Being Promotion Act, is a laudable step in institutionalizing mental health services, it fails to address the root cause of the professional exodus: the gap between the qualification and the compensation. Under Republic Act No. 9258, otherwise known as the Guidance and Counseling Act of 2004, a licensed Guidance Counselor must possess a master’s degree. Despite this rigorous requirement, which involves years of post-graduate study and a professional board exam, the entry-level position (Guidance Counselor I) remains pegged at Salary Grade 11. This discrepancy creates a "brain drain" where licensed professionals either opt for private practice, high-paying BPO wellness roles, or migration. Data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) consistently show high vacancy rates for these positions, not because of a lack of graduates, but because the public sector's offer is economically unviable. This bill seeks to bridge this gap by: 1) mandating plantilla positions to ensure every elementary school has a dedicated counselor, moving away from the "designated teacher" stop-gap measure; and, 2) upgrading the salary grades of guidance counselors and increasing the minimum entry level to Salary Grade 16 to acknowledge the Master’s Degree requirement and aligns the position with other specialized technical roles in the government. By offering competitive compensation, the State incentivizes Psychology and Guidance and Counseling graduates to remain in the country and serve in the public school system. Addressing the "mental health pandemic" among the youth, manifested in rising rates of bullying and self-harm as reported by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), requires more than just policy; it requires people. We cannot protect our students with empty offices. 2 Filed since the 17th Congress, this bill is a critical step towards strengthening the Philippine educational system by ensuring that every student has access to professional guidance and counseling services. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9125
title: AN ACT UPGRADING ALL PROVINCIAL AND DISTRICT HOSPITALS BY PROVIDING MODERN MEDICAL EQUIPMENT, AMBULANCE SERVICES, AND ESTABLISHING SPECIALTY UNITS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE At present, many provincial and district hospitals lack adequate medical equipment, infrastructure, and specialized services, resulting in limited capacity to respond to emergencies and address complex medical conditions. Thus, there is a need to address these gaps through an upgrade of hospital facilities, including the provision of modern diagnostic equipment, ambulances, and the establishment of specialty units where it is needed most. The “Universal Health Facilities Enhancement Act” seeks to strengthen the Philippine public health system by modernizing and upgrading provincial and district hospitals across the country. It recognizes the State’s constitutional duty to protect and promote the right to health of all citizens and aims to ensure that quality healthcare services are accessible, efficient, and equitable, especially in underserved and geographically isolated areas. 1 To ensure effective implementation, the bill creates the Hospital Upgrade Commission (HUC), a multi-sectoral body composed of key government agencies, legislative representatives, and local government units. The HUC will be tasked with conducting a nationwide assessment of existing hospital facilities, developing a National Hospital Upgrade Agenda, and overseeing the prioritization, procurement, and implementation of hospital improvements. Overall, this measure seeks to build a more resilient, efficient, and equitable healthcare system by ensuring that all Filipinos—regardless of location—have access to modern, well-equipped, and responsive hospital services. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9126
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ANIMAL WELFARE PROTECTION BY INCREASING THE PENALTIES PRESCRIBED THEREIN, AND BY BANNING THOSE CONVICTED OF ANIMAL CRUELTY FROM OWNING ANY KIND OF ANIMALS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SPECIFIC SECTIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10631, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF 1998
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It has been more than two decades since the enactment of Republic Act No. 8485, or the Animal Welfare Act of 1998, which laid down the foundation for the protection and promotion of animal welfare in the country. It was then further amended by Republic Act No. 101631 in 2012. Unfortunately, there is an apparent disconnect between the intention behind the law, i.e. to deter acts of cruelty, maltreatment and negligence toward animals, and the penalties prescribed therein. Some may argue that the fines, which ranges from P30,000 to P100,000, are merely a slap on the wrist as they fail to effectively discourage repeat offenses. This bill seeks to strengthen our policy on animal welfare protection by providing stricter penalties for animal cruelty. It also introduces an accessory penalty of a perpetual ban on owning any kind of animal for convicted offenders, to prevent recidivism. In relation to the accessory penalty of perpetual ban, this bill also proposes the establishment of a National Animal Offender Registry. This will ease the monitoring of the implementation of this Act. Animal welfare is not just a secondary concern; it is a reflection of our societal values. By enacting these stricter measures, we send a clear message that cruelty will no longer be tolerated and that the law will finally possess the necessary power to champion the lives of those who cannot speak for themselves. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 9130
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FINANCIAL INCLUSION AND MSME CREDIT ACCESS PROGRAM AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Financial inclusion remains a critical driver of inclusive and sustainable economic growth. Data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) 2023 Financial Inclusion Survey reveal that approximately 34% of Filipino adults remain unbanked, while around 60% of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) lack access to formal credit. Only about 25% of transactions are conducted through digital payments, underscoring persistent structural gaps in the country’s financial system. MSMEs, comprising over 99% of all registered businesses in the Philippines, continue to face barriers such as lack of collateral, high borrowing costs, stringent documentary requirements, limited proximity to financial institutions, and inadequate financial literacy. These constraints are more pronounced in rural and underserved communities, where access to formal financial services remains limited. The World Bank estimates that the MSME financing gap in the Philippines exceeds US$220 billion, while the Asian Development Bank notes that enterprises with access to financing are three to five times more likely to expand operations and generate employment. Aligned with the Philippine Development Plan and national financial inclusion strategies, this measure seeks to establish a National Financial Inclusion and MSME Credit Access Program that will: • Expand access to affordable and collateral-free financing; • Strengthen credit risk-sharing mechanisms through a national guarantee fund; • Promote digital financial ecosystems and interoperable payment systems; • Enhance financial literacy and credit readiness among MSMEs; • Establish financial inclusion centers nationwide; and • Develop alternative credit scoring systems and digital financial identities. 1 This proposed measure ensures that entrepreneurs, especially those in rural areas, women-led enterprises, agriculture-based industries, and low-income communities— are empowered with equitable access to capital, enabling them to grow, generate employment, and contribute meaningfully to national development. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAMES “JOJO” ANG JR. label: HB 9132
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure seeks to create the National Education Coordinating Council that shall primarily be tasked with institutionalizing a permanent and high- level mechanism for policy integration, strategic alignment and continuous monitoring across the three pillars of the Philippine education system. The Philippine education sector currently operates under a trifocalized structure where the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) manage their respective sub-sectors independently. While this division of labor was designed to provide specialized focus, the lack of a formal and binding coordination framework has led to significant systemic fragmentation. This disconnect manifests in persistent gaps in the curriculum, misaligned teacher training programs and a widening mismatch between the skills produced by our educational institutions and the actual requirements of the modern labor market. The findings of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) reveal that the country is grappling with a severe learning crisis that requires more than just incremental changes within individual agencies. It demands a unified national strategy that ensures a seamless transition for learners as they move from basic education to higher studies or the workforce. Through the creation of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) under the Office of the President, this piece of legislation elevates education to a primary national security and economic priority. This structure ensures that reforms are not merely departmental but are part of a cohesive National Education and Workforce Development Plan that remains consistent across different administrations. This measure also addresses the administrative inefficiencies that currently plague the sector by directing the harmonization of data systems and the rationalization of overlapping inter-agency bodies. It empowers the Council to streamline resources, optimize the power of the purse through coordinated budget requests and ensure that every educational investment is directed toward a singular vision of Filipino excellence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Ryan S. label: HB 9133
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE BUREAU OF HALAL INDUSTRY, MANDATING THE INCLUSIVITY OF HALAL CERTIFICATIONS IN FOOD, CONSUMER PRODUCTS, HEALTHCARE, AND SERVICES AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The right to free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship without discrimination or preference is the one of the most fundamental of rights enunciated under Section 5, Article III of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Historically, "Halal" has just been narrowly associated with dietary restrictions in the Philippines. However, apart from being a multi-trillion dollar opportunity for the Philippines, Halal industry covers a vast ecosystem including food, non-food products, and life choices that align with Shariah principles. In fact, in the Philippines, the market for the said products is estimated to be worth between ₱40 billion and ₱100 billion annually. Despite this potential, the Philippine Halal sector faces significant hurdles, such as but not limited consumer awareness and a fragmented certification landscape. These inefficiencies have created substantial supply gaps such as, for example, in 2022, the Philippines was forced to import approximately $120 million worth of Halal products to meet local demand. Many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) lack the technical knowledge and financial resources required to navigate current certification processes, which were largely designed for export markets under Republic Act No. 10817 or the Philippine Halal Export Development and Promotion Act of 2016. It is in this regard that a measure mandating Halal inclusivity to mandate the state of its constitutional duty to accommodate the religious practices of its citizens and ensuring that no Filipino is discriminated against in the marketplace or in the provision of healthcare due to their faith. The proposed measure seeks to transform the Philippine Halal industry from a fragmented, export-oriented sector into a unified, inclusive, and mandatory domestic standard. By establishing the Bureau of Halal Industry (BHI) and mandating Halal availability in food establishments, healthcare, and logistics, the proposed Bill intends to ensure religious freedom, achieve economic sovereignty, and standardize the purity of Halal. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z.
