label: HB 9269
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Malnutrition remains a persistent and multifaceted public health challenge in the Philippines, affecting millions of Filipinos—particularly children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable sectors. Despite decades of government intervention under Presidential Decree No. 491, the country continues to face a “triple burden of malnutrition,” characterized by the stunting and wasting, micronutrient deficiencies, and rising rates of overweight and obesity1. Recent data underscore the urgency of strengthening the country’s nutrition governance framework. According to the 2023 Expanded National Nutrition Survey of the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI), 23.6% of Filipino children under five years old are stunted, indicating chronic malnutrition that adversely affects physical and cognitive development2. Meanwhile, 5.6% of children under five suffer from wasting, a life-threatening form of acute malnutrition, while 15.1% are underweight3. In absolute terms, the burden remains substantial. It is estimated that around 630,000 Filipino children are affected by wasting, reflecting the continuing scale of 1 United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Philippines, Health and Nutrition Situation in the Philippines. 2 Department of Science and Technology – Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI), 2023 Expanded National Nutrition Survey (ENNS). 3 Ibid. acute undernutrition in the country4. Malnutrition also contributes significantly to child mortality and long-term productivity losses, with poor nutrition linked to preventable deaths among young children5. Food insecurity further exacerbates the situation. Data show that 31.4% of Filipino households experience moderate to severe food insecurity, limiting access to adequate and nutritious food and reinforcing cycles of malnutrition6. Despite some progress, improvements in nutrition outcomes have been slow and uneven. The persistence of malnutrition is driven by structural factors such as poverty, inequality, limited access to health and nutrition services, and weak coordination among government agencies and local government units. As noted in governance assessments, nutrition indicators in the Philippines have shown minimal improvement over the years, highlighting systemic gaps in implementation7. Presidential Decree No. 491, enacted in 1974, created the National Nutrition Council (NNC) as the country’s primary policy-making and coordinating body on nutrition. While it has contributed significantly to advancing nutrition programs, the increasing complexity, scale, and persistence of malnutrition necessitate a stronger, more empowered, and better-resourced institution. This proposed measure seeks to create the National Nutrition Commission, a restructured and strengthened body that will replace the existing council. The proposed Commission shall serve as the central authority for nutrition governance, with expanded mandates to formulate policies, ensure effective implementation, and enforce accountability across all levels of government. The Commission will be tasked to: • Formulate and implement a comprehensive and integrated national nutrition policy; • Strengthen coordination among national government agencies, local government units, and stakeholders; • Establish robust monitoring and evaluation systems to track outcomes and ensure accountability; 4 Lyle Daryll Casas & Valerie Gilbert Ulep, What Determines the Decline of Wasting in the Philippines, 139 Nutrition 112884 (2025). 5 Louise Maureen Simeon, Price of Malnutrition: Philippines Loses P496 Billion Each Year, Phil. Star (Jan. 30, 2025), https://www.philstar.com/business/2025/01/30/2417987/price-malnutrition-philippines-loses-p496- billion-each-year. 6 Persistent Hunger Affects 3-in-10 Filipino Households—DOST-FNRI, Bus.World (July 11, 2025), https://www.bworldonline.com/health/2025/07/11/685269/persistent-hunger-affects-3-in-10-filipino- households-dost-fnri/ 7 UNICEF Philippines, Raising the Bar: Improving Nutrition Governance in the Philippines. • Mobilize resources and foster partnerships with the private sector, civil society, and international organizations; and • Address both persistent and emerging nutrition challenges through evidence- based and sustainable interventions. By repealing Presidential Decree No. 491 and establishing the National Nutrition Commission, this bill aims to modernize and institutionalize nutrition governance in the Philippines. It seeks to ensure that nutrition policies are effectively implemented, adequately funded, and responsive to the evolving needs of the population. Ultimately, the enactment of this measure is a critical step toward reducing malnutrition, improving health outcomes, enhancing human capital development, and securing a healthier and more productive future for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. PERCIVAL V. CENDAÑA Akbayan Representative JOSE MANUEL TADEO DADAH KIRAM ISMULA “CHEL” I. label: HB 9271
title: AN ACT I N S T I T U T I O N A L I Z I N G D I G I TA L L I T E R A C Y A N D F U T U R E S K I L L S DEVELOPMENT IN THE PHILIPPINE EDUCATION SYSTEM AND FOR ALL FILIPINOS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid acceleration of the digital revolution and the lessons learned from the Covid-19 pandemic have highlighted the immediate need to equip every Filipino with essential Digital Literacy and Future Skills. Digital literacy, defined as the broad set of competencies necessary to use digital media, computers, and information technologies effectively and safely, is no longer a luxury but a fundamental requirement for social inclusion and economic competitiveness. Given the continuous rise globally in time spent online and on social media, international efforts are being accelerated to the development of these digital skill set, coupled with the ability for careful discernment. This legislative measure is, therefore, an important step in preparing the country for the demands of the global digital economy. This Bill, the “Digital Literacy Act of 2025,” aims to institutionalize digital literacy and future skills development to improve the competencies of Filipinos to integrate into, and operate within, a rapidly evolving, technology-driven society. It ensures that no Filipino child misses out on their basic right to education, which increasingly relies on digital technology, while simultaneously upskilling the adult workforce and keeping them relevant for the future of work and their ability to access goods and services digitally. 1 This Bill draws inspiration from significant legislative efforts in both houses of Congress, including House Bill No. 166 (National Digital Skills and AI Readiness Act of 2025) and House Bill No. 4814 (Samar ICT Education and Digital Literacy Act), both filed during the 20th Congress, as well as Senate Bill No. 709 (Social Media Awareness in Schools and Universities Act of 2022) from the previous Congress. The core objective is to ensure that all Filipinos are equipped with the digital literacy and future skills necessary to participate fully, responsibly, and ethically in the global digital economy and information society. Building upon these proposals, this Act adopts and refines the following key measures: a) Including digital literacy and future skills in the curriculum, expanded to include technical-vocational education. b) Integrating basic digital literacy in the National Service Training Program (NSTP) (Note: The term “Social media awareness” is replaced with the b r o a d e r term “digital literacy and future skills” in this measure). c) Establishing Digital Literacy and Future Skills Centers that utilize existing public places, such as libraries, malls, universities and colleges, and cultural centers. To further achieve the aforementioned objective, the following new measures are also proposed: a) Launching a mobile training program (Digital Literacy on Wheels) to reach geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. b) Creating an Inter-Agency Task Force on Digital Literacy and Future Skills. c) Declaring December 2nd of every year as “Digital Literacy Day” (Note: This date aligns with the globally observed World Computer Literacy Day and s i m i l a r national initiatives, such as the Singapore Digital Literacy Day). By strengthening digital competency and ensuring access to future skills training for all, this Bill promotes a more resilient, capable, and united Filipino citizenry. Digital empowerment strengthens the Filipino family and the nation by boosting communication, creating economic opportunities, and helping everyone thrive in the modern world. In light of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is respectfully requested. 2 References: ICDL Asia. (2025). Singapore Digital Literacy Day 2025. label: HB 9273
title: AN ACT PROVIDING POST-HARVEST FACILITIES TO RICE FARMERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State shall recognize the right of farmers, farmworkers, and landowners, as well as cooperatives, and other independent farmers’ organizations to participate in the planning, organization, and management of the program, and shall provide support to agriculture through appropriate technology and research, and adequate financial, production, marketing, and other support services.” Republic Act No. 7900, otherwise known as the “High-Value Crops Development Act of 1995,” recognizes the value of post-harvest facilities for the development of high-value crops. Republic Act No. 8435, otherwise known as the “Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act of 1997,” mandates the creation of an Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Plan (AFMP) with a focus on “food security, poverty alleviation and social equity, income enhancement and profitability, especially for farmers and fisherfolk,” among others. Republic Act No. 10610, otherwise known as the “Agricultural and Fisheries Mechanization (AFMech) Law,” reinforces this by mandating the promotion of “the development and adoption of modern, appropriate, cost-effective and environmentally-safe agricultural and fisheries machinery and equipment to enhance farm productivity and efficiency in order to achieve food security and safety and increase farmers’ income.” However, despite the numerous laws that recognize the need for post-harvest facilities and mandate their construction and development, our country’s agriculture sector continues to face significant challenges on food security, productivity, profitability, and competitiveness, which is attributed to post-harvest losses and exacerbated by the sector’s vulnerability to typhoons and climate events like El Niño and La Niña. According to the Department of Agriculture (DA) in 2024, the Philippines is losing an average of 342,000 metric tons of rice, or the equivalent of P7.89 billion in 1 post-harvest losses annually.1 The country is also losing an average of 151,000 metric tons in corn, equivalent to P2.87 billion annually, in post-harvest losses.2 The DA attributes these losses primarily to the country’s inadequate supply chain infrastructure, with the country still lagging behind agricultural countries in terms of post-harvest facilities.3 As of 2024, the country has a cold storage capacity of 37 cubic meters per 1,000 residents, which is lower than Vietnam’s 116, China’s 132, and the 200 of North American countries. 4 As domestic rice production continues to decline, driven by depressed farmgate prices and ongoing land conversion, and compounded by post-harvest losses, the country’s rice security is put at risk and left vulnerable to price shocks.5 This is especially problematic considering that rice is a staple in every Filipino diet. The country’s vulnerability to post-harvest losses thus poses not just an agricultural profitability and productivity issue, but also a food security issue. As such, this bill seeks to address this nationwide agricultural and food security challenge by mandating the construction of warehouses and rice mills in every rice- producing municipality and city in the Philippines. Initially, every district with at least one rice-producing municipality shall be a mandated beneficiary of at least one warehouse and rice mill. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Ferdinand Beltran, Howard Guintu, Faustino “Bojie” Dy III, Miguel Luis Villafuerte, Vincenzo Luigi Villafuerte, Tsuyoshi Horibata, and Terry Ridon, and Senators Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan and Christopher “Bong” Go. This bill fully adopts Senator Pangilinan’s Senate Bill No. 222. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LEILA M. DE LIMA 1 Manahan, J. (24 June 2024). label: HB 9274
title: AN ACT IMPOSING AN “ULTRA-WEALTH TAX” ON INDIVIDUALS WITH NET ASSETS EXCEEDING ONE BILLION PESOS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE (NIRC) OF 1997 OR REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8424, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to a 2022 World Bank report, the Philippines ranked 15th out of 63 countries in income inequality, having one of the highest income inequality rates in East Asia.1 In the country, the top 1% of income earners contribute 17% of the national income while the bottom 50% capture only 14%.2 According to the 2023 Forbes Philippines’ 50 Richest list, the P3.95 trillion net worth of the country’s 50 richest reported in 2022 increased to P4.44 trillion in 2023, marking a 12.5% increase and reflecting an even widening income gap. The 2022 World Bank report emphasized how income inequality is perpetuated by the intergenerational cycle of poverty.3 For instance, it was found that families with limited financial resources and lower educational backgrounds have significantly less access to antenatal care (ANC) and postnatal care (PNC) compared to the national average, resulting in elevated rates of stunting, underweight, and wasting among them compared to wealthier counterparts.4 At the same time, while students of more affluent households are able to invest heavily on education, with a per capita expenditure on education more than 22 times that of the poorest households, children of lower-income households face reduced enrollment rates and are less likely to be placed in the age- appropriate grades.5 Clearly, the limited access to health care, education, and opportunities for skill development diminishes the opportunities for upward mobility, 1 Ngo, F. (20 September 2023). Income Inequality in the Philippines. The Borgen Project. Retrieved from https://borgenproject.org/income-inequality-in-the-philippines/. 2 Ibid. 3 Ibid. 4 Ibid. 5 Ibid. 1 culminating in the intergenerational transmission of poverty that breeds income inequality. Government interventions are therefore necessary to address the rising gap in inequality brought about by systemic failures, including having a regressive taxation system. The country’s current taxation system include consumption taxes, such as the value-added tax (VAT) and excise taxes, that more significantly impact smaller incomes, thus widening the gap between rich and poor, and the marginalized and the elite.6 At present, a common practice among governments across Asia to reduce public budget deficits is to enforce austerity measures, such as spending cuts, regressive tax increases, or both.7 However, at a time when state provision of healthcare, education, infrastructure, and other basic public goods are crucial to sustain the lives and livelihoods of the people, these anti-people taxes and austerity measures would simply be unacceptable. This bill proposes the imposition of an annual Ultra-Wealth Tax on the country’s billionaires or the ultra-rich whose net taxable assets exceed one billion pesos (P1,000,000,000). The rates of the ultra-wealth tax shall be as follows: 1% for wealth above P1 billion; 2% for wealth above P2 billion; and 3% for wealth above P3 billion. Considering the limited number of billionaires whose net worth significantly exceed the net worth of the bottom 50% Filipino income earners, this proposed ultra-wealth tax shall only target a small number of taxpayers, unlike in the case of consumption taxes that affect a majority of the population, heavily impacting upon the poor. To ensure that the revenues generated from the ultra-wealth taxes are directed to the necessary government programs that benefit the general public, this bill proposes for the exclusive use of the revenues for the following items of public expenditure: public health services nationwide, education, local government support fund, social protection and employment, and housing. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Percival Cendaña, Jose “Chel” Diokno, Dadah Ismula, Kaka Bag-Ao, Antonio Tinio, Sarah Elago, Renee Co, and Raymond Mendoza. This bill adopts several provisions from the aforementioned bills. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. DE LIMA 6 Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development. label: HB 9275
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE BUREAU OF AGRICULTURAL COOPERATIVE AND INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT (BACID) UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, STRENGTHENING AGRICULTURAL AND AGRARIAN REFORM COOPERATIVES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The agricultural sector remains a cornerstone of the Philippine economy, employing a significant portion of the labor force and serving as the backbone of rural livelihoods. Despite its importance, the sector continues to face persistent challenges, including low productivity, fragmented landholdings, limited access to markets and financing, and weak integration into value chains. Agricultural cooperatives have long been recognized as critical instruments in addressing these constraints by enabling smallholder farmers to pool resources, access services, and strengthen their bargaining power. Historically, the Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives (BAC) under the Department of Agriculture (DA) played a vital role in providing technical assistance, credit facilitation, and capacity-building support to agricultural cooperatives. However, with the enactment of Republic Act No. 6939, the functions of the BAC were absorbed into the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), which was mandated to regulate and oversee all cooperatives nationwide. While this consolidation aimed to streamline cooperative governance, it inadvertently constrained the ability of government to adequately address the sector-specific needs of agricultural cooperatives, whose operations are closely intertwined with agricultural production systems, supply chains, and rural development programs. Studies and policy assessments have shown that agricultural cooperatives require specialized support in areas such as value chain integration, post-harvest systems, logistics, and market access, which go beyond regulatory oversight and necessitate close coordination with the DA’s programs and infrastructure support.¹ This bill seeks to address these gaps through the establishment of the Bureau of Agricultural Cooperative and Industry Development (BACID) under the Department of Agriculture. The 1 Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS). Studies on agricultural cooperatives highlight the need for targeted institutional and value chain support beyond regulatory frameworks. proposed Bureau restores and strengthens the developmental mandate of the former BAC while expanding its scope to respond to the evolving demands of modern agriculture. BACID shall serve as the primary government agency responsible for the development, empowerment, and modernization of agricultural and agrarian reform cooperatives. It shall provide targeted interventions, including technical assistance, enterprise development, financing facilitation, and capacity-building programs, tailored specifically to the needs of farmer-based organizations. By situating BACID within the DA, the government ensures stronger institutional alignment and coordination with key agricultural programs, including production support, farm mechanization, post-harvest infrastructure, and market linkage initiatives. Beyond traditional cooperative development, this measure introduces a forward-looking and transformative mandate by integrating agricultural industry development into the Bureau’s functions. BACID shall promote value-added activities such as agro-processing, storage, transportation, logistics, and product branding—critical components that enable farmers to move up the value chain and capture greater economic returns. This approach is consistent with the government’s thrust toward agribusiness development and rural industrialization, as emphasized in national development plans.² Moreover, the bill advances the strategy of farm clustering and consolidation through cooperatives, addressing the long-standing issue of fragmented landholdings that limit productivity and economies of scale. By organizing smallholder farmers into cohesive production units, BACID will facilitate efficient resource utilization, improved access to technology, and stronger market participation. This is aligned with the Department of Agriculture’s farm clustering and consolidation program, which has been identified as a key strategy for enhancing competitiveness in the sector.³ The measure promotes contract growing arrangements and partnerships between cooperatives and agribusinesses to ensure stable markets, predictable incomes, and access to technical and financial support for farmers—mechanisms widely recognized as effective in integrating smallholders into modern value chains.⁴ The proposed legislation clearly delineates the roles of BACID and the CDA. While the CDA retains authority over registration, regulation, and governance, BACID will focus on development, capacity-building, and market integration, ensuring coherence and avoiding overlap. By establishing BACID, the government reinforces its commitment to a resilient and inclusive agricultural sector. The Bureau will empower cooperatives, improve farmer incomes, enhance food security, and support sustainable rural development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. label: HB 9276
title: AN ACT EXCLUDING SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM THE VALUE-ADDED TAX BASE ON ELECTRICITY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 106 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under existing policy, the Value-Added Tax (VAT) is imposed not only on electricity actually delivered to households and businesses but also on system loss charges passed on by distribution utilities. System loss refers to electricity generated but not ultimately delivered to end-users due to line dissipation, technical inefficiencies in transmission and distribution systems, and, in some instances, pilferage or unauthorized connections. In its current application, consumers are effectively made to pay VAT on electricity they never consumed. This contradicts the fundamental principle of VAT as a tax on consumption. By design, VAT is intended to apply only to the value of goods and services actually supplied, delivered, and consumed. However, system loss charges do not represent actual consumption by end-users; rather, they reflect recoverable costs associated with electricity that is lost before it reaches the consumer. Under Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA), system losses are recognized as part of the operational costs of distribution utilities, subject to caps and regulatory review by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). These charges are allowed to be passed on to consumers strictly as a cost- recovery mechanism, not as payment for actual electricity usage. ¹ ² As such, they are fundamentally different in nature from charges for electricity that is metered and consumed. In practice, system loss levels in the Philippines are typically allowed at up to approximately 8.5% for private distribution utilities and 13% for electric cooperatives, subject to regulatory caps.² This means that a portion of every electricity bill represents electricity that was never delivered to the consumer. When VAT is applied to this portion, households effectively pay a 12% tax on 8–13% of non-consumed electricity, translating to an estimated additional burden of around 1% to 1.5% of the total electricity bill. While seemingly modest on a per-bill basis, this accumulates significantly over time, particularly for low- and middle-income households already burdened by high energy costs. The continued inclusion of system loss charges in the VAT base thus expands the scope of VAT beyond consumption and into cost recovery, thereby distorting the tax base. This results in consumers bearing an additional tax burden on inefficiencies and losses that are inherent in the system and beyond their control. International VAT principles, as articulated in guidelines by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, emphasize that VAT should be levied on final consumption and should not apply to amounts that do not correspond to an actual supply consumed by the taxpayer.³ At a time when Filipino households are already facing rising electricity rates, inflationary pressures, and broader economic challenges, the imposition of VAT on system loss charges further aggravates financial strain. A fair and equitable tax system requires that such distortions be corrected. This measure, therefore, proposes to expressly limit the VAT base on electricity to actual metered consumption, and to exclude system loss charges from VAT computation. By clarifying the tax base in this manner, the bill restores consistency with the fundamental nature of VAT, ensures that consumers are taxed only on what they actually consume, and prevents the undue taxation of inefficiencies embedded in the power distribution system. By doing so, the bill promotes fairness, enhances consumer protection, and contributes to easing the cost of living for millions of Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. DALE B. label: HB 9277
title: AN ACT MAINSTREAMING GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE AND NATURE-BASED SOLUTIONS IN NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, ESTABLISHING IMPLEMENTATION AND FINANCING MECHANISMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is among the countries most vulnerable to climate change, experiencing increasingly severe typhoons, flooding, sea-level rise, and coastal erosion, as shown in global climate risk assessments.¹ These hazards place growing strain on public infrastructure and expose the limitations of conventional “gray” infrastructure such as seawalls, drainage systems, and flood control facilities, which are often rigid, costly to maintain, and increasingly insufficient under intensifying climate conditions.² In response, Green Infrastructure (GI) and Nature-based Solutions (NbS) have emerged as globally recognized approaches to climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction. International institutions such as the World Bank, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) recognize that these approaches can complement or outperform traditional infrastructure by enhancing resilience while delivering multiple environmental and socio-economic benefits.³ These systems use natural assets such as mangroves, wetlands, river corridors, watershed forests, and urban green spaces to manage water flows, reduce flooding, and strengthen ecosystem resilience. In the Philippines, these approaches are already being applied in practice and gaining institutional traction. The Asian Development Bank has supported Nature-based Solutions in selected river basin flood risk management programs in the country, demonstrating their technical and economic relevance under local hydrological and climate conditions.⁴ At the local government level, Quezon City has recently expanded its network of flood-mitigating water catchment ponds within designated urban green spaces to temporarily store stormwater and reduce flooding during intense rainfall events, illustrating a practical and scalable form of urban Nature-based Solutions.⁵ These emerging practices reflect a growing shift among national and local stakeholders toward integrating ecological systems into infrastructure planning as a complement or alternative to conventional flood control measures. The constitutional mandate to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology provides the legal foundation for this policy direction. This is reinforced by Oposa v. Factoran, which recognized the doctrine of intergenerational responsibility and affirmed the State’s duty to safeguard the environment for present and future generations, and is further strengthened by Republic Act No. 11995, which institutionalizes ecosystem valuation in national planning and investment. Despite these advances, there remains no unified national framework that treats ecosystems as infrastructure assets or requires systematic evaluation of green, gray, and hybrid options in public investment decisions. This gap has led to underinvestment in natural systems that could improve resilience and reduce long-term costs. This bill therefore seeks to institutionalize Green Infrastructure and Nature-based Solutions as a core national strategy for sustainable development, climate adaptation, and disaster risk reduction. It establishes a national policy framework, strengthens inter-agency coordination through a National Green Infrastructure Council, and introduces sustainable financing mechanisms such as a Green Infrastructure Fund and Payment for Ecosystem Services. These proposed reforms are designed to ensure that environmental assets are no longer treated as incidental public goods but as strategic infrastructure that delivers measurable economic value and risk reduction benefits. By embedding nature-based investments into local and national planning and financing systems, the State is expected to reduce long-term disaster recovery costs, improve the efficiency of public infrastructure spending, and build a more resilient and climate-adaptive development pathway for all levels of governments. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is respectfully sought. DALE B. CORVERA Representative Lone District of Agusan del Norte 1. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ISSUANCE, VALIDITY, AND REGULATION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IDENTIFICATION CARDS, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR ABUSE THEREOF, AND AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Republic Act No. 7277, as amended by Republic Act No. 9442 and Republic Act No. 10754, affirms the State’s commitment to uphold the rights, dignity, and welfare of persons with disabilities (PWDs). Central to this framework is the grant of privileges and support services that enable PWDs to participate fully in society. However, persistent challenges—particularly the misuse and fraudulent issuance of PWD identification cards—have undermined the effective implementation of the law. The lack of standardized issuance, inconsistent validity periods, and weak enforcement mechanisms has led to abuse, ultimately depriving legitimate PWDs of their rightful benefits.¹ This measure seeks to amend Sections 32 and 46 of Republic Act No. 7277 by establishing clear and uniform rules on the issuance, validity, and security of PWD IDs. It introduces differentiated validity periods—ten (10) years for persons with permanent disabilities and one (1) year for those with temporary disabilities, subject to reassessment—ensuring both practicality and accountability. The bill further mandates a uniform ID design prescribed by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) and adopted nationwide by local government units, enhancing recognition and reducing fraud. It also strengthens penal provisions by imposing stricter penalties on individuals who falsify or misuse PWD IDs, as well as on public officials who facilitate such acts. Offenses committed through digital platforms shall likewise be prosecuted under Republic Act No. 10175. To support effective implementation, the measure provides for a strengthened and unified PWD database through coordination among key agencies, aligned with the Community-Based Monitoring System under Republic Act No. 11315, to improve data accuracy, planning, and service delivery.² This proposed legislation builds on prior legislative efforts and addresses the burden of frequent ID renewal, particularly for PWDs with permanent disabilities and limited mobility—an issue compounded by gaps in accessibility despite the mandate of Batas Pambansa Blg. 344.³ The approval of the measure will strengthen safeguards, improve systems, and reinforce accountability to protect the integrity of PWD benefits. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. label: HB 9279
title: AN ACT STREAMLINING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE, REDUCING DOCUMENTARY REQUIREMENTS, AND EXPEDITING PROCESSING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to promote the general welfare and ensure that social services are accessible, responsive, and equitable. This is reinforced by Republic Act No. 11032, or the Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018, which directs government agencies to simplify procedures and eliminate unnecessary regulatory burdens. Despite these mandates, access to government financial assistance remains difficult for many Filipinos, particularly indigent patients and families in crisis. Beneficiaries often spend several hours to an entire day lining up in offices such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development, Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, and public hospitals under the Department of Health. In high-demand facilities, applicants may be required to return multiple times due to inconsistent or repetitive documentary requirements, extending the process to several days. These conditions are consistent with findings of the Commission on Audit, which has repeatedly identified inefficiencies, documentary redundancies, and delays in service delivery.¹ Studies in Philippine public administration likewise highlight duplicative compliance requirements and procedural inconsistencies as systemic barriers.² The World Bank has similarly emphasized that excessive administrative requirements disproportionately burden low-income households by increasing both the time and cost of accessing public services.³ For indigent families, these delays impose real financial burdens. Applicants incur transportation expenses, food costs while waiting, and lost wages from time spent away from work. These indirect costs can significantly reduce the net benefit of assistance, particularly for daily wage earners.⁴ In medical cases, delays may also prolong hospitalization or defer treatment, increasing overall expenses. At the same time, government financial assistance programs administered by agencies such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development, Department of Health, Philippine Health Insurance Corporation, and the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office serve millions of Filipinos annually and involve substantial public resources. However, the process of access has not kept pace with the principles of efficiency and ease of doing business. This bill seeks to address these challenges by establishing a streamlined and expedited framework for accessing government financial assistance. It standardizes documentary requirements, reduces unnecessary submissions, promotes digital access, enforces strict processing timelines, and strengthens coordination with the Anti-Red Tape Authority to ensure compliance. This measure does not create new assistance programs but improves the delivery of existing ones by reducing administrative burdens and ensuring that assistance is delivered in a timely, efficient, and dignified manner. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is respectfully sought. DALE B. CORVERA Representative Lone District of Agusan del Norte 1. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 26 Paternity leave is the period that a father takes off work before, during, and after the delivery in order to support his wife or partner during the earliest stages of childrearing and the mother’s recovery. Research suggests that fathers who take paternity leave, especially those taking two weeks or more immediately after childbirth, are more likely to be involved with their young children.1 Giving new fathers time off work helps to evenly distribute childcare duties and allows women to take care of their health and maintain their careers. Beyond having positive effects for gender equality in the home and at work, paternity leave also greatly improves maternal and infant health, and its multiple advantages echo into the child’s adulthood.2 37 No international standard concerning paternity leave exists. However, the International Labor Organization in 2009 called for governments to develop adequate policies for a better balance of work and family responsibilities, to include paternity and/or parental leave, with incentives for men to use them.3 1 Maternity and paternity at work (Law and practice across the world). International Labor Organization, 2014. 2 State of the World’s Fathers: A MenCare Advocacy Publication. Save the Children (2015). 3 Resolution concerning gender equality at the heart of decent work. 1 1 Republic Act 8187 of the Paternity Leave Act was enacted in 1996, granting seven days leave with full pay to all married male employees in the private and public sectors. Though beneficial, this law limits the vital bond between the expecting parents and their infants, and the period is not long enough for the husband to perform all his obligations. 7 This Bill seeks to grant to male employees a longer paternity leave to give them a longer time to assist their wives and partners and to care for their newborns. Thirty days is about one-third of the total maternity leave of 105 days. 11 This Bill also removes the limit of four deliveries in availing the benefit and extends the benefit to all male employees, regardless of employment status. Furthermore, in recognition of current social realities in which about four million of the population are in “live-in” or common-law relationships,4 the bill proposes to make the benefit available to a male employee who is not married to the woman who gave birth or suffered an abortion or miscarriage, provided that they have no legal impediment to marry each other during their cohabitation and have been living exclusively as husband and wife for at least one year at the time of childbirth, abortion, or miscarriage. 21 For these reasons, passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. 23 24 _____________________________ REP. title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE RECYCLING LABEL, PROVIDING ITS SPECIFICATIONS AND COVERAGE, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 18
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines faces a persistent solid waste management crisis, with plastic packaging constituting a significant portion of improperly disposed waste. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, which established the framework for waste reduction, segregation, recycling, and disposal, implementation gaps remain evident, particularly in waste segregation at source and material recovery efficiency. To address these challenges, Republic Act No. 11898, otherwise known as the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Act of 2022, mandated producers to take responsibility for the recovery and proper management of plastic packaging waste. While this law has created mechanisms for accountability, consumer participation in proper waste segregation remains a critical factor in ensuring the success of EPR schemes and in advancing the country’s transition toward circular economy practices. This bill introduces the Philippine Recycling Labeling Act of 2025, which mandates the standardized labeling of consumer product packaging to provide clear, consistent, and accessible information on recyclability, material composition, disposal instructions, and recycled content. This Act seeks to strengthen waste segregation at source by empowering consumers with accurate disposal guidance, enhance material recovery by aligning consumer practices with the capacity of local solid waste management systems, improve compliance with extended producer responsibility obligations through transparency and traceability of packaging materials, and promote environmental awareness and sustainable consumption through consumer education. Countries with similar labeling systems, such as the European Union, Japan, and South Korea, have demonstrated that standardized recycling information significantly improves recycling rates and consumer compliance. Adopting a similar framework in the Philippines will help harmonize waste management practices, support the goals of RA 9003 and RA 11898, and reduce the volume of residual and mismanaged waste that pollutes the environment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought 46 47 48 49 50 51 ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 9282
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A BILL OF RIGHTS OF AIR PASSENGERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution provides that "The State shall protect consumers from trade malpractice and from substandard or hazardous product." To this end, various consumer protection laws have been enacted so as to realize this constitutionally protected right. In the case of the air transportation industry, this right is encapsulated in the contract of carriage between the airline and the passenger. The passenger is obligated to follow airline policies and other measures related to safe air transport while it is the obligation of the airline as a common carrier to “carry the passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide, using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons, with a due regard for all the circumstances" as stated in Article 1755 of the Civil Code. Despite the protection our laws provide, airline passengers continue to experience various problems such as long queues in check-in counters, delayed or cancelled flights, lost or misplaced baggage, reservation snafus, additional fees and charges and generally poor service. The Department of Transportation and Department of Trade and Industry issued a joint administrative order which provides for the "Bill of Rights of Air Passengers and Airline Obligations". This administrative order is supposed to protect consumers from poor airline services and deceptive practices. However, airline passengers continue to face the same problems as before. Furthermore, it is argued that said administrative order has insufficient penalties and sanctions to airline companies who violate the bill of rights of airline passengers. It has become clear that legislation is urgently needed for a permanent and more comprehensive “bill of rights” for airline passengers. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill earnestly requested. BEVERLEY ROSE A. title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CAPACITY AND CAPABILITY OF DOH REGIONAL HOSPITALS TO PROVIDE REHABILITATIVE SERVICES AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution states that the "State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost." Republic Act 11223 or the Universal Healthcare Act’s objectives are to (a) Progressively realize universal health care in the country through a systemic approach and clear delineation of roles of key agencies and stakeholders towards better performance in the health system; and (b) Ensure that all Filipinos are guaranteed equitable access to quality and affordable health care goods and services, and protected against financial risk. The Philippines has been a leading country in recognizing the rights of persons with disabilities with laws such as Presidential Decree No. 603 (Child and Youth Welfare Code), Republic Act No. 7610 (Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act), and Republic Act No. 7277 (Magna Carta for Disabled Persons) and has also ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2008 and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1990 alongside regional commitments, including the Incheon Strategy “to Make the Right Real” for Persons with Disabilities in Asia and the Pacific. Yet, despite these legal safeguards, health services remain fragmented, underfunded, and inaccessible to many families. This proposed measure aims to provide equitable access to quality and affordable healthcare, specifically, rehabilitative care to individuals with disabling conditions such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, and cerebral palsy, as well as musculoskeletal issues and other physical, cognitive, and communicative conditions as well as children with special needs who face developmental challenges such as Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD),and Down’s Syndrome by enhancing the capacity and capability of regional hospitals to provide rehabilitative medicine services Thus, passage of this bill is earnestly requested. title: AN ACT DECLARING THE VERDE ISLAND PASSAGE MARINE CORRIDOR AS A MARITIME PROTECTED AREA AND AN ECOTOURISM ZONE, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE VERDE ISLAND PASSAGE MANAGEMENT BOARD, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Verde Island Passage is one of the rich biodiversity areas in the country and has been declared the center of center of the world’s marine shore fish diversity by marine scientists. As such, the national government and local government units have taken measures to protect, conserve and sustainably use biological diversity to ensure and secure the well-being of the present and future generations of Filipinos. Then President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, for instance, issued Executive Order No. 578 which established a national policy on biological diversity and created an ad hoc task force to ensure the protection, conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity in the Verde Island Passage Marine Corridor, and formulate a Verde Island Passage Management Plan in consultation with stakeholders, the private sector, civil society and local communities. Local government units, in cooperation with national government agencies, law enforcement, and civil society, signed a memorandum of agreement to create a network for the protection and sustainable management of the Verde Island Passage. Despite these significant steps, the Verde Island Passage remains vulnerable. Human activities such as fishing, shipping, tourism, and navigation still pose a serious threat. Thus, this bill seeks to urgently declare the Verde Island Passage Marine Corridor as a Marine Protected Area and an Ecotourism Zone. The bill also proposes the creation of a management body that shall implement the existing management plan and the policies enunciated in the proposed Act. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this bill is earnestly requested. BEVERLEY ROSE A. label: HB 9285
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING FAIR INVESTIGATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY FOR ROAD CRASHES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Road crash is one of the leading causes of death in the country. It is for this reason that several laws on road safety have been enacted not only to improve road user behavior but also hold erring drivers accountable. However, some groups have been questioning these measures citing bias, particularly on the application and implementation of existing road safety laws. Case in point: Mang Teddy. Mang Teddy was driving his truck when a motorcycle driven by a minor, with no helmet and intoxicated, rammed into his truck. The minor, with his head crushed, died instantly while Mang Teddy was arrested for reckless imprudence resulting to homicide. Although Mang Teddy was eventually released, he was presumed at fault and immediately arrested. Such fault, however, has no presumption in law or existing rules. It has merely been a practice of law enforcers to presume the culpability of a driver of a bigger vehicle. This case of Mang Teddy and other similar cases hit both social media and mainstream media by storm that there has been a tremendous clamor to revisit existing laws, specifically on reckless imprudence. In practice, police officers arrest, detain, and charge drivers who only appear to be at fault but are not factually at fault. Clearly, the problem does not only lie on the law but also on the application of the law. Thus, there is a needed legislation to provide proper evaluation and investigation by police authorities of the circumstances and evidence relative to road crashes in order to ensure that erring drivers/individuals—not innocent drivers—are held accountable. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this bill is earnestly requested. BEVERLEY ROSE A. label: HB 9286
title: AN ACT REQUIRING BROADCAST MEDIA TO ALLOCATE ADEQUATE FREE AIRTIME FOR PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENTS ON VITAL PUBLIC ISSUES AND CONCERNS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 24, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State recognizes the vital role of communication and information in nation-building. Information, after all, is power. Mere recognition of its power, however, is not enough. One can only witness the true power of information when it has been used and applied effectively in nation-building. Instilling discipline, for instance, requires information. A disciplined citizenry presupposes an informed society. One cannot be expected to obey laws, rules, or code of behavior without knowing and understanding what these laws, rules, and code of behavior are. Clearly, the role of communication and information is vital in nation-building. The government is the agency or instrumentality through which the will of the State is formulated, expressed and realized.1 One of the important tasks of the government is to act for the State as parens patriae, or guardian of the rights of the people.2 As guardian of the rights of the people, it is the duty of the government to see to it that the citizens are well-informed of their rights, duties and responsibilities. It is only when people are well-informed of these rights, duties, and responsibilities that they realize the importance of their role and purpose in society. Mass media, on the other hand, is the primary means of communication to reach the vast majority of the general public. The vast reach and influence of media can be seen especially during elections. Political advertisements have been an effective tool in conveying a candidate’s message and in gaining votes and public support. Television, for instance, is considered the most cost effective medium of dissemination.3 Even a slight increase in television exposure can significantly boost a candidate's popularity, name recall and electability.4 If mass media can be used as means to get votes, the more it can be used to inform the public of their rights, their duties, and their responsibilities. Above all, mass media has the duty to inform people. 1 Cruz, I. (2003). Political Law. 2 Ibid. 3 GMA v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 205357, September 2014 4 Ibid. Considering all these, it is vital that we have a law mandating mass media, in particular radio and television broadcasting companies to allocate airtime for public service announcements and infomercials on laws, social welfare, public safety, government processes and other matters of public and national concern to increase awareness and inform the public of their rights, duties and responsibilities. In truth, radio and television broadcasting companies, which are given franchises, do not own the airwaves and frequencies through which they transmit broadcast signals and images. They are merely given the temporary privilege of using them. Since a franchise is a mere privilege, the exercise of the privilege may reasonably be burdened with the performance by the grantee of some form of public service.5 By allocating public service announcements and government infomercials, TV and radio networks are performing some form of public service for the Filipino people. It is time government and mass media work together for the betterment of this country. In view of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly requested. BEVERLEY ROSE A. label: HB 9287
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING THE FORMER PRISONERS’ EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM, PROVIDING FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Prison is meant not only to punish, but also to help people change. Once a person has served their sentence or has been legally released, they should be given a real chance to start over, find work, and live honestly. However, many former prisoners struggle to get jobs because of stigma, lack of connections, and limited opportunities. Without support, these challenges can push them back into crime and make it harder for them to reintegrate into society. The government already recognizes that helping former prisoners rebuild their lives is important for both public safety and the common good. One existing tool is the Public Employment Service Office (PESO), which helps people find jobs, provides training, and offers career guidance. By strengthening and using this system, the government can directly address the barriers that former prisoners face when looking for employment. This bill proposes a Former Prisoners’ Employment Program that will connect qualified individuals to job opportunities through PESO. It will offer job matching, skills training, and support to help them become employable. At the same time, the bill encourages businesses to give former prisoners a fair chance by providing incentives to employers who hire and retain them, while still ensuring that labor standards are followed. 1 | Page Giving former prisoners a fair opportunity to work is not just an act of compassion, it is a practical step toward safer communities and a stronger economy. By helping them become productive members of society, this measure benefits not only the individuals involved but the nation as a whole. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9288
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING ACCESS TO JUSTICE FOR INDIGENOUS CULTURAL COMMUNITIES/INDIGENOUS PEOPLES (ICCs/IPs) BY ESTABLISHING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES JUSTICE DESKS AND SPECIAL CALENDARS IN THE REGULAR COURTS, PROVIDING FOR COORDINATION WITH CUSTOMARY JUSTICE MECHANISMS AND THE NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INDIGENOUS PEOPLES (NCIP), AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Many Indigenous Cultural Communities and Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) still struggle to access justice. Courts are often far from their communities, legal processes can be confusing, and language and cultural differences make it harder for them to be heard. There is also frequent confusion about when to use their own customary laws, go to the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), or ile cases in regular courts. Because of this, disputes are delayed, cases are iled in the wrong place, and the rights of ICCs/IPs are not fully protected. The law already recognizes the right of ICCs/IPs to use their own justice systems and traditions in resolving disputes. It also gives the NCIP authority over certain cases, especially those involving members of the same community, after they have irst tried to settle the matter using their customary practices. However, these rules are not always clearly followed in practice, leading to confusion, repeated cases, and long delays. This bill aims to make justice more accessible and easier to understand for ICCs/IPs. It strengthens coordination between customary justice systems, the NCIP, and regular 1|Page courts to ensure that cases are handled in the proper forum. It also proposes the creation of Indigenous Peoples Justice Desks and special court schedules in areas with large IP populations to provide guidance, reduce delays, and make the legal process more responsive to their culture and needs. By improving coordination and respecting indigenous traditions while upholding national law, this measure helps ensure faster, fairer, and more meaningful justice for ICCs/IPs. It promotes a system that they can trust and participate in. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9289
title: AN ACT GRANTING A MONTHLY SOCIAL PENSION TO INDIGENT PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities (PWDs) remain among the most vulnerable sectors in Philippine society. Despite existing laws that promote their rights and welfare, many PWDs. particularly those who are indigent, continue to face significant economic and social challenges. Limited employment opportunities, mobility constraints, health-related expenses, and barriers to accessing public services often prevent them from attaining financial independence and adequate living conditions. While the government currently provides a social pension for indigent senior citizens, there remains no similar nationwide support mechanism specifically designed for indigent persons with disabilities who are unable to sustain themselves due to physical, sensory, intellectual, or psychosocial limitations. Many of these individuals rely heavily on family members or community support, which is often insufficient to meet their daily subsistence and medical needs. This bill seeks to establish a monthly social pension for indigent persons with disabilities to help alleviate the financial burden associated with their condition and to provide a measure of economic security. The proposed assistance aims to support their basic needs, promote dignity and social inclusion, and strengthen the country’s social protection system for vulnerable populations. By extending financial support to indigent PWDs, the State affirms its commitment to uphold the principles embodied in Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, and to ensure that no Filipino is left behind in the pursuit of inclusive development and social justice. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9290
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROHIBITION AGAINST ILLEGAL WITHHOLDING OF PHILIPPINE PASSPORTS, PARTICULARLY OF OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS, PROVIDING FOR ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A Philippine passport is not just a travel document, it is a lifeline for Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs). It allows them to move freely, seek help from Philippine authorities, leave abusive employers, and return home safely. Yet many OFWs and job applicants still face a common abuse: their passports are taken or withheld by recruiters, agencies, or employers. This practice traps them, limits their freedom, and makes them more vulnerable to exploitation. Our laws already make it clear that a passport belongs to the Philippine government and must never be taken by private individuals or companies. It is illegal to con iscate or use a passport as collateral for a loan or obligation, and such acts can lead to serious penalties. The courts have also recognized that withholding passports is a form of coercion and is often linked to illegal recruitment and even human traf icking. This bill strengthens these existing protections by making it easier to report cases of passport withholding and ensuring faster action to help victims recover their documents. It promotes better coordination among government agencies so that affected workers can quickly get assistance. It also reinforces the rule that passports must never be used as leverage for debt or control, and that those who commit such acts will be held accountable under the law. 1|Page At its core, this measure protects the dignity, freedom, and safety of Filipino workers. A passport should never be used as a tool to control or abuse our citizens. By passing this bill, we take a stronger stand against exploitation and ensure that OFWs are protected wherever they are. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9291
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA FOR PROBATION AND PAROLE WORKERS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Probation and parole workers play a vital role in the Philippine criminal justice system. They help supervise and guide individuals who are serving their sentences in the community, ensuring that they follow the law while working toward rehabilitation and reintegration. Their work promotes public safety and gives second chances to those willing to reform. However, this job often requires them to work in challenging and sometimes risky environments, dealing with complex social and behavioral issues. Despite their important responsibilities, many probation and parole workers face dif iculties such as limited bene its, lack of career growth opportunities, and insuf icient recognition for the risks they take. These challenges can affect their morale and their ability to deliver effective services. There is a clear need to support and protect these workers so they can continue to perform their duties with professionalism and dedication. This bill proposes a Magna Carta for Probation and Parole Workers to address these concerns. It seeks to provide fair compensation, hazard pay, and other bene its, as well as clear opportunities for career development and advancement. It also promotes proper working conditions, protection from harassment, and strong ethical standards to ensure accountability in public service. 1|Page By strengthening the welfare and professional development of probation and parole workers, this measure will improve the quality of community corrections in the country. In turn, it will help reduce reoffending, support rehabilitation, and make communities safer. Supporting these workers means strengthening the justice system as a whole. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9292
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE CENTER FOR DIABETES AND ENDOCRINOLOGY DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND GOVERNANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Diabetes and other endocrine disorders continue to affect millions of Filipinos and place a heavy burden on families and the healthcare system. These illnesses often lead to serious complications such as heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, blindness, and amputations, many of which can be prevented through early diagnosis, proper treatment, and specialized care. While the government has already taken important steps through the National Diabetes Act of 1996, the growing number of cases shows that stronger and more permanent solutions are needed. This bill seeks to establish the Philippine Center for Diabetes and Endocrinology (PCDE), a dedicated national specialty center that will lead the country’s efforts in the prevention, treatment, research, and management of diabetes and endocrine disorders. The PCDE will provide high-quality medical care for patients, especially those with complex and life-threatening conditions, while also serving as a center for advanced training of healthcare workers and research on better treatments and prevention strategies. The proposed measure will also help improve access to specialized healthcare services beyond Metro Manila by supporting regional networks and partnerships with local hospitals and health systems. label: HB 9293
title: AN ACT REGULATING UTILITY POLES AND POLE ATTACHMENTS, ENSURING NONDISCRIMINATORY ACCESS TO POLES AND RELATED SUPPORT STRUCTURES FOR TELECOMMUNICATIONS AND CABLE SERVICES, PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR POLE ATTACHMENT RATES AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Fast and affordable internet, cable, and telecommunications services depend on how quickly and efficiently companies can build their networks. One major problem is access to utility poles, which are needed to carry cables and equipment. In many areas, especially underserved communities, access to these poles is delayed, restricted, or too expensive. When this happens, network expansion slows down, competition is reduced, and consumers end up paying more for poorer service. This bill seeks to solve that problem by creating clear and fair rules for the use of utility poles. It requires pole owners to allow access to all service providers on equal terms, while still ensuring safety and proper engineering standards. It also sets guidelines so that fees for using poles are fair, reasonable, and transparent, protecting both the pole owners and the companies that rely on them to deliver services. To avoid long delays and technical confusion, the bill assigns the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to handle disputes over pole access and pricing. This ensures that issues are resolved quickly by experts, instead of being tied up in lengthy court cases. With clearer rules and faster decisions, companies can expand their networks more efficiently. 1 | Page By improving access to shared infrastructure, this measure will help speed up internet and telecom expansion, encourage fair competition, and bring better, more affordable services to the public. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9294
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE SUSTAINABLE LIVELIHOOD PROGRAM OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SOCIAL WELFARE AND DEVELOPMENT AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Poverty continues to hold many Filipino families back from living stable and secure lives. While government programs like Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) have helped ease daily struggles, many households still lack the means to build lasting sources of income. To truly move families out of poverty, they need more than short- term aid, they need real opportunities to earn, grow, and stand on their own. The Sustainable Livelihood Program (SLP) of the Department of Social Welfare and Development has been helping poor and vulnerable families start small businesses or ind jobs. It works closely with local governments while remaining guided by national priorities. The Supreme Court has af irmed that the national government can carry out programs like SLP, as long as there is proper coordination with local authorities and communities. At the same time, experience shows that programs involving public funds must be handled with great care. Clear rules, transparency, and accountability are essential to make sure assistance truly reaches those in need. Strengthening these safeguards will protect public resources and build trust in the program. This bill aims to make SLP a permanent and stronger program that helps families achieve long-term stability. It will improve how bene iciaries are selected, how 1|Page support is delivered, and how results are measured. By working closely with government agencies, local communities, and partners, this measure seeks to give more Filipinos a fair chance at a better, more secure future. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9295
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING AND PENALIZING THE UNAUTHORIZED PRACTICE OF LAW, THE HOLDING OUT AS A LAWYER, AND OTHER RELATED ACTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The practice of law in the Philippines is reserved only for licensed lawyers because it directly affects people’s rights, property, and freedom. This rule exists to protect the public from unquali ied or dishonest individuals who may give wrong advice or mishandle legal matters. The Supreme Court has emphasized that only those who are properly trained, tested, and regulated should be allowed to provide legal services. However, many people are still being misled by individuals or groups who pretend to be lawyers. Some offer legal advice, prepare documents, or even handle cases, sometimes through social media or online platforms, despite having no authority to do so. This can result in wasted money, invalid ilings, missed deadlines, and serious harm to a person’s legal rights. It also creates problems for courts and government agencies that must deal with improper or unauthorized submissions. This bill seeks to stop these harmful practices by clearly de ining and penalizing the unauthorized practice of law. It covers acts such as pretending to be a lawyer, giving legal advice without a license, preparing or iling legal documents for others, and appearing in legal proceedings without authority. It also punishes those who use fake lawyer credentials or knowingly support and pro it from these illegal activities, while still allowing properly supervised law students to assist under existing rules. By setting clear rules and stronger penalties, this measure aims to protect the public from fraud, ensure that only quali ied professionals provide legal services, and uphold 1|Page the integrity of the justice system. It reinforces trust in the legal profession and helps ensure that every person receives proper and competent legal assistance. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9296
title: AN ACT REGULATING AND ALLOWING THE COMMERCIAL IMPORTATION OF SECOND- HAND OR USED CLOTHING AND RAGS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4653, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 4653, passed in 1966, bans the commercial importation of used clothing and rags in the Philippines. At the time, the law was based on concerns about public health and national dignity. However, despite this long-standing prohibition, the trade in used clothing has continued for decades, often through informal or illegal channels. This has made enforcement difficult, led to lost government revenue, and encouraged smuggling and misdeclaration of goods. Today, the country has more modern systems for trade and customs regulation. Instead of an outright ban that is difficult to enforce, there is now a strong case for a more practical approach, one that regulates the importation of used clothing rather than pushing it underground. A clear and legal framework can help ensure that these goods meet proper health and safety standards, while also allowing the government to monitor and control the trade more effectively. This bill proposes to repeal Republic Act No. 4653 and replace it with a regulated system for the commercial importation of used clothing and rags. It aims to bring this existing market into the formal economy, set sanitary and safety rules, reduce smuggling and illegal activities, and ensure that the correct taxes and duties are collected. By doing so, the government can better protect consumers while also supporting fair and transparent trade. 1 | Page In the end, this measure updates an outdated law to reflect present realities. By shifting from a total ban to a regulated system, the State can improve public health safeguards, strengthen enforcement, and increase revenue, while creating a more transparent and accountable trading environment. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9302
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE CONDONATION OF PENALTIES FOR UNPAID, DEFICIENT, OR LATE SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM, PHILIPPINE HEALTH INSURANCE CORPORATION, AND HOME DEVELOPMENT MUTUAL FUND CONTRIBUTIONS OF HOUSEHOLD EMPLOYERS UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10361, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “DOMESTIC WORKERS ACT” OR “BATAS KASAMBAHAY,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE More than a decade after the enactment of the Batas Kasambahay, many domestic workers are still outside the social protection systems that the law promised them. A 2019 government survey1 revealed that 83% of the 1.4 million registered domestic workers were not covered by any social security benefit, while 2% shouldered the full cost of their entire social benefit contributions without employer’s share.2 The survey further showed that 79.2% were not enrolled in the SSS, 80.7% had no PhilHealth benefits, and 87.6% were not covered by Pag-IBIG benefits.3 This is not new. As early as 2014, the Department of Labor and Employment reported that out of an estimated two million Filipino domestic workers, only around 120,000 were registered with the SSS, 60,000 with PhilHealth, and 25,000 with Pag-IBIG.4 Compliance with the statutory duty of household employers to register, report, and remit contributions for SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG coverage remains inadequate and uneven due to various reasons, including lack of awareness, confusion over procedures, financial difficulty, or the persistent informality of household employment. The proposed Kasambahay CARE (Contribution Amnesty and Relief for Employers) Act seeks to address this compliance gap by establishing a one-time penalty condonation program for household employers with unpaid, deficient, or late contributions to the SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG Fund arising from the employment of kasambahays. By waiving penalties that may otherwise remain uncollected, this measure facilitates the collection of principal contributions, the updating of membership records, 1 DOLE and PSA Survey: 1.4 million kasambahays in the country, 72% on live-out arrangement, NATIONAL WAGES AND PRODUCTIVITY COMMISSION, 17 February 2021, available at https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/dole-and-psa-survey-1-4-million-kasambahays-in-the-country-72-on-live-out-arrangement-2/ 2 Ferdinand Patinio, Only 35K of 1.4M ‘kasambahay’ have written contracts: survey, PHILIPPINE NEWS AGENCY, 02 December 2020, available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1123651 3 Leslie Ann Aquino, 83 percent of domestic helpers do not have SSS, Philhealth and Pag-IBIG benefits -- DOLE, MANILA BULLETIN, 06 December 2020, available at https://mb.com.ph/2020/12/06/83-percent-of-domestic-helpers-do-not-have-sss-philhealth-and-pag-ibig-benefits-dole/ Mayen Jaymalin, DOLE: Many employers not observing Kasambahay Law, PHILIPPINE STAR, 11 August 2015, available at https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2015/08/11/1487143/dole-many-employers-not-observing-kasambahay-law the expansion of coverage, and the strengthening of social protection for domestic workers. It gives household employers a fair and final chance to comply, strengthens the implementation of the Batas Kasambahay, and ensures that the promise of social protection reaches the workers who help keep Filipino homes in order. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9304
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR TRUSTWORTHY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE PHILIPPINES, PROVIDING FOR RISK-BASED REGULATION, SAFETY STANDARDS, AND PUBLIC ACCOUNTABILITY, AND CREATING THE BUREAU OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming economies, governance, and everyday life. It is projected to contribute up to US$15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030, underscoring its potential as a driver of productivity and innovation.¹ However, alongside these opportunities are significant risks, including algorithmic bias, data privacy violations, lack of transparency, and the erosion of human accountability in decision-making.² Globally, governments have begun establishing frameworks to ensure that AI systems are deployed in a manner that is ethical, safe, and aligned with public interest. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has adopted principles emphasizing transparency, accountability, and human-centered values in AI systems.³ Similarly, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization has issued a Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, calling for safeguards that protect human rights, promote fairness, and ensure inclusivity in AI deployment.⁴ The European Union, through its AI regulatory framework, has also introduced a risk-based approach to governance, particularly regulating high-risk AI systems in critical sectors.⁵ In the Philippines, while the Republic Act No. 10173 provides safeguards for personal data, there remains no comprehensive legal framework governing the broader design, deployment, and accountability of AI systems. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in sectors such as healthcare, finance, education, governance, and public safety, the absence of a unified regulatory structure exposes individuals and institutions to risks that current laws do not fully address. This bill seeks to establish the AI Governance Act of the Philippines, creating a comprehensive governance framework that ensures AI systems are developed and deployed in a manner that is ethical, secure, transparent, and inclusive. It proposes the creation of a dedicated regulatory body, the Bureau of Artificial Intelligence Systems (BAIS), to oversee compliance, enforce standards, and guide national AI development. The measure adopts a risk-based regulatory approach, requiring stricter oversight for high-risk AI systems while allowing innovation to flourish through regulatory sandboxes and adaptive governance mechanisms. It establishes a Bill of Rights in Artificial Intelligence to protect individuals from harmful algorithmic outcomes, ensures meaningful human oversight in critical decisions, and mandates transparency, accountability, and fairness in AI deployment. Ultimately, this measure aims to position the Philippines as a responsible and competitive participant in the global AI ecosystem, fostering innovation while safeguarding fundamental rights, democratic values, and public trust. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. CORVERA Representative Lone District of Agusan del Norte 1.
