label: HB 9306
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PRESIDENTIAL BROADCAST SERVICE – BUREAU OF BROADCAST SERVICES AS THE GOVERNMENT LAST-MILE EMERGENCY COMMUNICATIONS LIFELINE, DESIGNATING ITS ESSENTIAL FACILITIES AS CRITICAL EMERGENCY COMMUNICATIONS INFRASTRUCTURE, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL EMERGENCY BROADCAST RESILIENCE PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is among the most disaster-prone countries in the world. Typhoons, earthquakes, floods, storm surges, volcanic eruptions, landslides, public health emergencies, cyber incidents, armed conflict, and other crises regularly test the capacity of government to communicate timely, accurate, and life-saving information to the public. In many emergencies, the first systems to fail or become unreliable are precisely the systems people now depend on most: commercial cellular networks, internet connectivity, cable systems, and television infrastructure. Towers may be damaged. Fiber lines may be cut. Power may be unavailable. Networks may be congested. Remote and geographically isolated communities may be left without reliable access to official information when they need it most. Radio remains one of the most resilient, accessible, and practical means of public communication during disasters. It can reach communities with limited connectivity, can operate with modest receiving equipment, and can continue functioning even when other communications systems are impaired, provided that government broadcast facilities and public radio assets are hardened, powered, connected, and properly integrated into emergency response systems. This bill strengthens the Presidential Broadcast Service – Bureau of Broadcast Services (PBS-BBS), including the Radyo Pilipinas network, as the Government Last- Mile Emergency Communications Lifeline. It designates its essential facilities as Critical Emergency Communications Infrastructure for purposes of this Act and establishes a National Emergency Broadcast Resilience Program to ensure that government broadcast facilities and public radio assets can continue operating before, during, and after disasters, emergencies, crises, and widespread communications disruptions. Legislation is necessary because this measure is not merely an internal administrative adjustment. It establishes a statutory policy, creates an inter-agency coordination framework, provides a basis for recurring appropriations, institutionalizes modernization and resilience planning, protects authorized emergency broadcast operations, and ensures congressional oversight. These objectives require continuity across administrations and coordinated implementation among the Presidential Communications Office, PBS-BBS, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, Office of Civil Defense, Department of Information and Communications Technology, National Telecommunications Commission, Department of Energy, Department of the Interior and Local Government, local government units, and other relevant agencies. The bill is designed to be technically sound, fiscally disciplined, and implementable. It does not diminish the authority of existing agencies, including the spectrum management and regulatory powers of the National Telecommunications Commission. It preserves freedom of speech, expression, and of the press. It protects privacy and sensitive information. It allows flexible and technology-neutral implementation, including the use of leased, managed, shared, satellite, radio, digital, power, and other appropriate systems. It requires lifecycle asset management, maintenance, post-incident reviews, corrective action planning, and congressional review. At its core, the bill treats emergency public communication as a life-saving public service. In a disaster, information is not merely an announcement; it can be the difference between evacuation and exposure, rescue and isolation, calm and panic, survival and loss. A resilient government emergency broadcast system is therefore an essential part of national preparedness, public safety, and continuity of government communications. Immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. label: HB 9308
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PUBLIC OFFICE ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY, MANDATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE DIGITALIZATION AND VERIFICATION OF THE STATEMENTS OF ASSETS, LIABILITIES, AND NET WORTH, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must at all times be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives.” Nowhere can a clearer mandate for transparency and accountability be found other than in Article XI, SECTION 1 of the 1987 Constitution. The filing of the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) has long been enshrined in Philippine law as a cornerstone of public accountability. Under existing rules, government officials and employees are required to annually disclose their financial standing to deter illicit enrichment and promote transparency in public service. SALN declarations, however, remain unverified unless acted upon in the course of an investigation, falling short of its promise to promote greater transparency within the government. Under this proposed legislation, the digitalization of SALN filing and publication shall be mandatory, and cross-agency verification mechanisms shall be established to ensure that high officials cannot hide behind any veil of discretion. By deploying artificial intelligence-assisted analytics and a flagging system, the SALN transforms from a passive disclosure requirement into an active instrument of detection and accountability. Equally important, the bill requires interim disclosure of high-value transactions occurring between annual filing periods, closing a loophole long exploited to obscure the movement of assets. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 9309
title: AN ACT POSTPONING THE NOVEMBER 2026 BARANGAY AND SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN ELECTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12232
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12232 fixed the term of office of barangay officials and members of the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) at four (4) years to promote stability and continuity in grassroots governance. The 1987 Constitution grants Congress the sole authority to define the term duration for barangay officials under Article X, Section 8. While Congress is vested with legislative authority over the scheduling of barangay and SK elections, such authority is not absolute and must be exercised in a manner consistent with the Constitution, particularly the people’s right of suffrage and the periodicity of elections. Jurisprudence, including Abas v. COMELEC and Macalintal v. COMELEC, clarifies that any postponement of elections must be justified by genuine, compelling, and sufficiently weighty state interests, and must not unduly infringe upon the constitutional mandate of regular and periodic elections. Taking cognizance of the state of national energy emergency declared by the President of the Philippines due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, there is a need to postpone the forthcoming Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections. The prevailing socio- economic challenges that have significantly impacted energy supply, inflation, and the cost of essential goods, these conditions strain both government resources and Filipino households. The conduct of the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections under such conditions may impose substantial fiscal pressures on the government and the electorate and may affect the efficient and orderly administration of the electoral process. This bill, therefore, seeks to postpone the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections to May 2027 only as an exceptional and temporary measure, and subject to the standards laid down by the Supreme Court, while ensuring that any extension of terms through hold-over is strictly limited, reasonable, and consistent with constitutional principles. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 9311
title: AN ACT STREAMLINING THE REGISTRATION AND LICENSING OF MINAHANG BAYAN, AND ENSURING ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AND RESPONSIBLE MINING IN THE UTILIZATION OF MINERAL RESOURCES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7076, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PEOPLE’S SMALL-SCALE MINING ACT OF 1991”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to streamline the registration and licensing processes for Minahang Bayan areas and small-scale mining operations. It promotes responsible mineral development, strengthens government regulation, and encourages the formalization of small-scale mining activities. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 7076, otherwise known as the “People’s Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991”. The Philippines is home to vast mineral resources that remain critical to overall national development and industrial growth. The mining sector continues to hold significant economic potential and contributes to exports, local revenues, and rural economic activity, especially in provinces rich with minerals. The Philippine Statistics Authority states that the total monetary value of the country’s Class A gold, copper, nickel, and chromite reserves reached approximately Four hundred and eighty-one billion (P481.45 Billion) in 20241. This is equivalent to 1.69% of the country’s gross domestic product for the same year. Small-scale mining has long formed part of the local economy and identity of mining communities in the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), specifically in the Province of Benguet. It remains a major source of livelihood in seven (7) of Benguet’s thirteen (13) municipalities and continues to support thousands of households dependent on mining for subsistence. The Cordillera region likewise remains one of the country’s most active areas for Minahang Bayan operations. As of 2022, eleven (11) Minahang Bayan sites had already been established in the region, including the four (4) in Benguet, namely the Loacan Itogon Pocket Miners Association, Bagtangan-Goldstar Small Scale Miners Association, Benguet Federation of Small Scale Miners Association Inc., and the Federation of Taneg Indigenous Communities Livelihood Association2. The continuing declaration of Minahang Bayan areas in Benguet reflects the government’s recognition of the need 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. (12 August 2025). Accessed on: 14 May 2026 2 Gasingan, Debbie. (28 February 2022). DENR clears 2 more Minahang Bayan in CAR. Accessed from: https://mirror.pia.gov.ph/news/2022/02/28/denr-clears-2-more-minahang-bayan-in-car. Accessed on: 14 May 2026 to formalize and regulate small-scale mining operations while ensuring environmental protection and worker safety. Despite the enactment of RA No. 7076, many small-scale miners continue to struggle in securing the permits and approvals necessary to operate legally. The process for declaring Minahang Bayan areas and issuing small-scale mining contracts remains slow and costly, particularly for those with limited technical and financial resources. This measure establishes a more efficient framework for the declaration of Minahang Bayan areas by prescribing definite processing periods, standardizing documentary requirements, and clarifying the responsibilities of government agencies involved in the issuance of permits. It likewise strengthens safeguards for environmental protection, occupational safety, indigenous people’s rights, and compliance with mining laws and regulations3 The bill also supports small-scale miners through technical assistance, training programs, and access to lawful and regulated mining opportunities under government supervision. Institutionalizing a more responsive and transparent regulatory framework strengthens not only small-scale mining operations, but also improves environmental stewardship and the protection of mining communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 3 Ragas, Susil. (29 November 2023). label: HB 9312
title: AN ACT PROMOTING LOCAL PARTICIPATION IN THE DEVELOPMENT AND OPERATION OF INDIGENOUS, POTENTIAL, AND RENEWABLE ENERGY RESOURCES, GRANTING QUALIFIED LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, COMMUNITIES, ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, AND DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES THE RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL OVER ENERGY PROJECTS WITHIN THEIR JURISDICTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to promote local participation and equitable benefit-sharing in the development, ownership, and operation of indigenous, potential, and renewable energy resources. It grants qualified local government units (LGUs), communities, electric cooperatives (ECs), and distribution utilities (DUs) the right of first refusal over energy projects located within their jurisdictions. Despite the Philippines' abundant energy resources, many communities continue to experience high electricity costs, inadequate power supply, and limited economic participation in energy projects operating within their localities. While energy investments contribute significantly to national development, the direct benefits to local consumers and communities remain limited. This measure recognizes the vital role of LGUs, ECs, DUs, and organized communities as valuable partners in achieving national energy security. Strengthening local participation in energy development is expected to encourage investments, expand employment opportunities, stimulate local economic activity, and improve public support for responsible energy projects. The bill grants qualified local entities the right of first refusal in the grant, transfer, operation, or sale of covered energy projects, subject to technical, legal, and financial standards. It also provides a priority framework among qualified local parties, encourages joint ventures, and promotes partnerships that can mobilize capital and expertise for long-term energy sustainability. The measure further provides that a reasonable portion of locally generated power shall first be offered to the EC or DU serving the host area. This aims to improve the reliability of supply, stabilize electricity rates, and prioritize the welfare of consumers in areas that host energy facilities. The bill likewise mandates community benefit programs such as local employment preference, scholarships, livelihood assistance, rural electrification support, environmental protection, and infrastructure development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9313
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICE PREMIUM FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS HOSTING CRITICAL WATERSHEDS, PROVIDING FOR THE INCLUSION OF CRITICAL WATERSHED AREAS IN THE COMPUTATION OF THE NATIONAL TAX ALLOTMENT, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish an Environmental Service Premium (ESP) for local government units (LGUs) hosting critical watersheds, recognize ecological services as a basis for fiscal equity, and include critical watershed areas as a factor in the computation of the National Tax Allotment under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as “The Local Government Code of 1991”. It advances a policy framework that compensates environmental stewardship, strengthens climate resilience, and supports sustainable development in communities that bear the responsibility of protecting the country’s vital water resources. Across the country, watershed-hosting LGUs carry the burden of protecting forests, regulating land use, and preventing environmental degradation despite limited fiscal capacity. Watershed areas cover about seventy percent (70%) of the Philippines’ land area and serve as critical sources of water for domestic, agricultural, and industrial use1. At the same time, more than half of key river basins remain unprotected, while only about twenty two percent (22%) of land area enjoys formal protection status, exposing vast watershed areas to deforestation, erosion, flooding, and biodiversity loss2. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources has identified millions of hectares of watershed areas as highly vulnerable to degradation, with consequences that include water shortages, reduced agricultural productivity, and increased disaster risks. Real-world impacts already manifest in major water systems such as the Ipo watershed, which supplies around ninety six percent (96%) of Metro Manila’s water yet has experienced a significant decline in forest cover, weakening its ecological stability3. Despite these, the current fiscal framework under the Local Government Code does not account for 1 Japan International Cooperation Agency. (2022, August 1). JICA-DENR partnership on forestry helps sustain watershed management and efforts of upland communities in PH. JICA Philippines. Accessed from: https://www.jica.go.jp/english/overseas/philippine/information/press/2022/220801_02.html on 27 April 2026. 2 Candano, R. (2024, May 21). Current state of watershed in the Philippines. PCAARRD’s ISP-IS. Accessed from: https://ispweb.pcaarrd.dost.gov.ph/current-state-of-watershed-in-the-philippines/ on 27 April 2026. 3 World Wide Fund for Nature. (N.D.). IPO Watershed. WWF Philippines. Accessed from: https://archive.wwf.org.ph/what-we-do/water/ipo-watershed/ on 27 April 2026. environmental services rendered by LGUs, resulting in a mismatch where communities that protect vital ecosystems receive little to no compensation. This proposed measure institutionalizes an Environmental Service Premium and the integration of watershed areas into the National Tax Allotment formula. It establishes a more equitable fiscal mechanism that recognizes ecological contributions as a measurable basis for resource distribution. It also provides clear criteria for allocation and ensures that funds support watershed rehabilitation, climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and sustainable livelihoods. These reforms align fiscal policy with environmental governance and create stronger incentives for LGUs to actively protect and manage critical ecosystems. This measure responds to an urgent national reality. Watersheds sustain cities, irrigate farms, generate power, and shield communities from floods and droughts, yet the LGUs that protect them often struggle with limited resources and competing demands for development. Every degraded watershed places millions at risk of water scarcity and disaster. Every neglected forest weakens the country’s resilience against climate change. This bill asserts that environmental stewardship deserves recognition, not neglect. It declares that those who protect the nation’s lifelines must no longer stand alone. The passage of this measure affirms a simple but powerful principle: the survival of communities, the security of water, and the future of the nation depend on how decisively we act today. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9314
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PARTIAL TRANSFER OF SUPERVISORY POWERS OVER ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES TO THE COOPERATIVE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, RETAINING THE TECHNICAL AND SPECIALIZED FUNCTIONS OF THE NATIONAL ELECTRIFICATION ADMINISTRATION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 269, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide for the partial transfer of supervision over electric cooperatives registered with the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), where their administrative and corporate oversight is assigned to CDA, while retaining in the National Electrification Administration (NEA) its technical, developmental, and specialized functions. Electric cooperatives continue to play a vital role in delivering electricity services to millions of Filipinos, particularly in rural and underserved communities. Since the enactment of Presidential Decree No. 269, as amended, the NEA has exercised broad supervisory authority over electric cooperatives in support of the State’s rural electrification program. Over time, many electric cooperatives have become duly registered cooperatives under the CDA, thereby placing them under the cooperative principles, governance standards, and regulatory framework established under Republic Act No. 9520, otherwise known as the “Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008”. The existence of overlapping supervision has created regulatory inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and governance ambiguities. As CDA-registered cooperatives, these entities should primarily fall under the CDA with respect to cooperative governance, elections, membership rights, and corporate administration. At the same time, the NEA should continue to exercise its recognized expertise in electrification planning, engineering standards, system development, financial rehabilitation, and other technical matters necessary to ensure reliable electric service. This measure therefore seeks to harmonize the mandates of the CDA and NEA, clarify their respective jurisdictions, strengthen cooperative autonomy, and improve institutional efficiency while preserving the State’s commitment to rural electrification and quality power service delivery. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9315
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING USURIOUS LENDING TO FARMERS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFORE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to protect Filipino farmers from usurious lending practices by imposing a maximum effective interest rate of six percent (6%) per annum on agricultural loans, mandating the restructuring of existing agricultural debts under fair terms, and strengthening the regulatory authority of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) over agricultural credit allocation. Despite their vital role in ensuring food security, many Filipino farmers continue to face limited access to formal credit facilities, forcing them to rely on informal lenders that impose exploitative interest rates that can reach as high as twenty percent (20%) to thirty percent (30%) monthly. The Philippine Statistics Authority confirm that farmers remain among the poorest sectors in 2021, with consistently high poverty incidence compared to other groups1. At the national level, about 18.1% of Filipinos lived below the poverty threshold, reflecting persistent economic vulnerability in rural communities2. Meanwhile, research from the Philippine Institute for Development Studies highlights that access to formal credit remains uneven and insufficient, leaving many farmers dependent on informal and often exploitative lending arrangements4. label: HB 9316
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE TITLING, PROTECTION, AND MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC SCHOOL SITES UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for the titling, protection, and management of public school sites under the Department of Education (DepEd). This secures government ownership, prevents conflicting claims, and supports the uninterrupted delivery of basic education services. As of March 2026, DepEd identified four thousand one hundred seventy eight (44,178) school sites nationwide in need of titling, despite long-standing government occupancy and use. Many of these properties are supported by deeds of donation, deeds of sale, tax declarations, presidential proclamations, or other forms of documentary evidence. Yet, it remains vulnerable to ownership disputes, overlapping claims, and administrative delays. Legal ambiguity regarding land ownership directly impedes national and private infrastructure development. This effectively blocks the construction of essential classrooms, which is not helping the country’s classroom backlog problem of approximately one hundred and sixty five thousand (165,000)1 units. Unresolved property titles also expose critical school sites to protracted court litigations initiated by the heirs of original land donors, which disrupts the continuous delivery of basic education to students. Securing legal ownership over public school sites remains essential to sustain educational infrastructure and protect lands devoted to learning for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 EDCOM 2 Communications. (9 February 2026). label: HB 9317
title: AN ACT TO FURTHER CAPACITATE THE DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENSE AND ITS BUREAUS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for defense administration, military organization, force development, civil defense, and national preparedness. It seeks to enhance the institutional capacity of the Department of National Defense (DND) and its attached bureaus to ensure a more responsive and capable defense establishment, thereby strengthening and modernizing the country’s national defense system.. The Philippines continues to face one of the world’s longest-running communist insurgencies, with the conflict dating back more than five decades and causing tens of thousands of casualties1. Recent developments indicate that while insurgent strength has declined, armed encounters still occur in various regions, including clashes in Northern Samar and other provinces, demonstrating that the threat remains active2. Furthermore, reports indicate that insurgent groups and other armed actors continue to operate in geographically isolated areas, requiring sustained military presence and coordinated government action3. These realities highlight the continuing need for a strong, well-funded, and coordinated national defense system capable of addressing evolving security threats. This proposed measure addresses these gaps through the establishment of a unified national defense framework that strengthens the mandate of the Department of National Defense and improves coordination among security agencies. It provides clear institutional direction in counter-insurgency efforts, ensures adequate and sustained funding support, and mandates periodic review and accountability mechanisms. The bill also rationalizes the roles of various agencies during national emergencies, enabling a more efficient, cohesive, and responsive approach to national security challenges. 1 Alipour, N. This measure responds to a critical national imperative. Security threats, whether internal or external, continue to test the stability of communities and institutions. Every unresolved conflict and every gap in coordination carries real consequences for public safety and national sovereignty. Strengthening the country’s defense system is not merely a matter of policy. It is a necessary step to protect lives, secure peace, and ensure that future generations inherit a nation that is stable, resilient, and capable of defending itself against any threat. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish at least one (1) e-learning center in every city and municipality, expand access to digital learning resources, and strengthen community-based education infrastructure nationwide. It institutionalizes an integrated system of learning spaces and digital technologies to ensure that Filipinos, especially those in underserved and geographically isolated areas, can access quality education, skills training, and lifelong learning opportunities. Despite the increasing use of digital technology in education, many Filipinos still lack adequate access to information and communication technology (ICT). The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) showed that in 2024, only forty-eight percent (48.8%) of households had internet access at home1. PSA further emphasized that despite improvements, millions of households still rely on shared or public connections, which are often unstable and inadequate for sustained educational use2. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies likewise confirms that infrastructure gaps continue to constrain digital learning opportunities across several regions3. These conditions limit access to learning materials and weaken the preparedness of the Filipino youth for an increasingly digital economy. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. (2025, July 21). explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the field offices of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) by upgrading and reclassifying existing plantilla positions, creating additional personnel posts, and rationalizing staffing structures in accordance with the growing demands of election administration. It amends Batas Pambansa Blg. 881, otherwise known as the “Omnibus Election Code of the Philippines”, to modernize the structure and compensation of COMELEC field offices and ensure electoral operations keep pace with needs of voter management and democratic governance. COMELEC field offices face increasing operational pressure amid a rapidly expanding electorate and evolving election demands. COMELEC reported that registered voters for the 2022 national and local elections exceeded 65.7 million nationwide, reflecting a significant increase from previous election cycles1. This translates into heavier workloads for election personnel tasked with voter registration, precinct management, logistics, and enforcement of election laws, often with limited manpower and outdated staffing structures. The continuing rise in voter registration2, including the addition of millions of new registrants even during short registration periods, has further strained field operations. Despite these growing responsibilities, many field offices remain understaffed and inadequately equipped to meet present operational requirements. The absence of adequate technical, administrative, and support personnel has contributed to operational inefficiencies and delays in frontline services during critical electoral processes. These impair the ability of field offices to effectively discharge their mandates and maintain efficient election administration. To address these, the proposed measure establishes a more responsive and professional organizational structure within COMELEC field offices through the 1 Colcol, E. (2021, December 20). An effective and professional electoral workforce remains indispensable to safeguarding the constitutional right of suffrage and ensuring the orderly conduct of elections. This measure affirms the State’s commitment to protecting the sanctity of vote and strengthening the institutions that uphold domestic governance. label: HB 9327
title: AN ACT EXPANDING MENTAL HEALTH COVERAGE UNDER THE PHILIPPINE HEALTH INSURANCE CORPORATION BY ESTABLISHING A MENTAL HEALTH VOUCHER SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution recognizes that the right to health extends beyond physical well-being. It necessarily encompasses mental and psychosocial health, which are equally essential to human dignity, productivity, and overall quality of life. Article XIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that: “The State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost. There shall be priority for the needs of the underprivileged, sick, elderly, disabled, women, and children. The State shall endeavor to provide free medical care to paupers.” The urgency of strengthening mental health systems is evident not only in policy discourse, but in real-life experiences that underscore the consequences of unmet mental health needs. Across the country, there have been reported cases of individuals, including students, parents, and members of vulnerable sectors, who have succumbed to mental health struggles often shaped by complex interplay of financial hardship, social pressures, and emotional distress. These instances serve as a sobering reminder that behind every statistic is a human life marked by potential, relationships, and aspirations. While the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, or the “Mental Health Act,” marked a significant step towards a rights-based approach to mental health care and helped advance efforts to reduce stigma, substantial gaps in access to services persist. For many Filipinos, especially those in low- and middle-income households, the cost of sustained mental health care continues to be prohibitive, often resulting in delayed treatment, interrupted care, or complete non-availment of services. At the same time, the evolving social, economic, and environmental conditions of modern life continue to exert pressures that affect the mental health and well-being of individuals across all sectors of society. These realities underscore the urgent need to strengthen mental health care financing mechanisms and ensure that access to care is not determined by one’s financial capacity. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by expanding mental health coverage under the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) through the establishment of a Mental Health Voucher System (MHVS). The proposed system introduces a targeted, pre-approved subsidy mechanism that enables eligible beneficiaries to access a defined set of mental health services and medications through accredited providers. Under this measure, beneficiaries are entitled to tiered mental health benefit packages corresponding to their clinical needs, with guaranteed minimum coverage for consultations, therapy sessions, medications, and other necessary interventions. It likewise aims to strengthen data-driven governance through integrated monitoring systems and reinforces institutional coordination among the implementing agencies. Ultimately, this measure seeks to reduce the financial barriers that prevent Filipinos from seeking and sustaining mental health care, thereby improving health outcomes, enhancing productivity, and promoting a more responsive and inclusive health care system. Under PhilHealth Circular No. 2023-0018, PhilHealth has taken an important step by launching the “Outpatient Mental Health Benefits Package” which provides 2 coverage for consultations, diagnostics, and psychosocial support for conditions such as depression, psychosis, epilepsy, dementia, and risks of self-harm. However, this program remains an administrative initiative, dependent on annual appropriations and subject to policy shifts. Legislation is therefore essential to institutionalize mental health care as a permanent statutory mandate. By enshrining this program into a law, Congress ensures its continuity beyond administrative discretion, secures stable and predictable funding, and embeds accountability mechanisms. This measure affirms the State’s constitutional duty to guarantee accessible, affordable, and sustainable mental health services, thereby safeguarding the long-term well-being of all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND ALEXANDER A. label: HB 9328
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL PROGRAM FOR UBE OR PURPLE YAM INDUSTRY, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is home to a vast array of unique agricultural products, and ube or purple yam stands as one of the country’s highly sought-after crops. Characterized by its vibrant color and distinct flavor, ube has evolved from a traditional backyard crop into a major commercial commodity with massive domestic demand and rapidly growing international appeal. Driven by social media buzz, global health trends, and rising culinary demand, ube is enjoying an unprecedented international spotlight. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) has reported that export volumes of ube and ube-based products have surged by twenty-four percent (24%) annually, reaching nearly 1.7 million kilos in 2024. However, while the “global purple craze” sweeps international markets and drives retail prices to record highs exceeding P80 per kilo, a concerning disconnect exists domestically granted that the agricultural ube production has drastically declined from a peak of 30,000 metric tons in 2006 to below 13,000 metric tons. The said paradox has been regarded by the experts and economists as due to a heavily fragmented supply chain. Due to resource constraints, a lack of local economies of scale, and isolation from processing facilities, local farmers—most especially indigenous Aeta communities who cultivate ancestral lands—are forced to absorb lower farmgate prices while middlemen and traders extract the bulk of the economic gains. Furthermore, the industry faces severe structural vulnerabilities such as extreme weather events driven by the climate crisis, an unpredictable rainfall pattern, a systemic lack of technical knowledge, and an acute shortage of high-quality, disease-free planting materials. Additionally, as the global demand for ube intensifies, protecting the intellectual property, geographical indications, and brand integrity of genuine Philippine ube against foreign counterfeits has become an urgent economic necessity. To maximize this massive global economic momentum and protect the livelihoods of thousands of marginalized and hard-toiling farmers, it is imperative to institutionalize a National Program for the Ube Industry. The proposed measure seeks to bridge the fragmented supply chain, guarantee a steady supply of high-yielding seedlings through institutionalized seed banks, safeguard the global brand equity of Philippine ube, and establish a climate-resilient roadmap that will secure the country’s position as the premier global source of high-quality purple yam products. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 9329
title: AN ACT MANDATING A “NO-WORK NO-PAY” COMPENSATION SCHEME FOR ALL GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS, EMPLOYEES, AND WORKERS, WHETHER ELECTED OR APPOINTED, INCLUDING MEMBERS OF CONGRESS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution provides: “That public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must at all times be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives” (Sec. 1, Art. XI, Constitution). On the other hand, R.A. No. 6713, otherwise known as the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, mandates that public office is a public trust. Employees are required to serve with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, prioritizing public interest over personal gain. This law declares that it is the policy of the State “to promote a high standard of ethics in public service. Public officials and employees shall at all times be accountable to the people and shall discharge their duties with utmost responsibility, integrity, competence, and loyalty, act with patriotism and justice, lead modest lives, and uphold public interest over personal interest”, enjoining prompt service and an eight-hour workday as a rule. The unequivocal constitutional mandate and R.A. No. 6713 and its policy declaration notwithstanding, it is sad to note the reality that absences and tardiness remain rampant among public officials, employees and workers, both elected and appointed. This is plain dishonesty, disservice and disloyalty to the Filipino people who share in the salaries and benefits of every government official, employee, and worker. Not only human law mandates labor in all honest, loyalty and integrity but more so Divine law. The Holy Writ commands us to work and labor for our sustenance as it declares: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou Page 1 of 8 return” (Genesis 3:19). The same Writ enjoins that we should work in all professionalism, diligence, honesty, integrity and efficiency, declaring in no uncertain words that – “Lying lips are abomination to the Lord: but they that deal truly ae his delight” (Proverbs 12:22). “The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat” (Proverbs 13:4, KJV). “In all labor there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Proverbs 14:23, KJV). “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest” (Ecclesiastes 9:10, KJV). “Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21, KJV). “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Ephesians 4:28, KJV). “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, KJV). “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10, KJV). “For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies” (2 Thessalonians 3:11, KJV). In the light of the foregoing, this bill seeks to institutionalize a “NO-WORK NO- PAY” scheme of compensation for all government officials, employees, and workers, both national and local, whether elected or appointed, including members of Congress, to ensure professionalism, diligence, honesty, integrity and efficiency in public service to promote the general welfare of the people and to enhance national development and progress. The early approval of this bill, therefore, is earnestly requested. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A DISTRICT-LEVEL BLOOD STATION IN THE FIRST DISTRICT OF COTABATO, STRENGTHENING THE LOCAL BLOOD SERVICES NETWORK, PROVIDING FOR ITS MANDATE, GOVERNANCE, QUALITY STANDARDS, HUMAN RESOURCES, FUNDING MECHANISMS, PENALTIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 59 SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the “First District of Cotabato Blood Station Act.” 62 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect and promote the right to health of every Filipino, and to ensure the availability of safe, adequate, accessible, and equitable blood supply for all, particularly those in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs). Consistent with Republic Act No. 7719, as amended,, Executive Order No. 7 series of 2010 on the National Voluntary Blood Services Program, and the Universal Health Care Act (Republic Act No. 11223), the State shall strengthen district-level blood service delivery through complementary facilities that integrate within the national blood services network. Blood services shall at all times be voluntary, non-remunerated, non-commercialized, and governed by the highest standards of safety, quality, transparency, and accountability. The State shall likewise safeguard blood services from political interference, commercial exploitation, and any form of discrimination. 74 SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. As used in this Act: 76 (a) "Blood Station" refers to a DOH-licensed blood service facility authorized to conduct voluntary donor recruitment, blood collection, storage, and distribution of screened blood and blood components received from a licensed blood center, but not to conduct blood testing or component processing. (b) "District-Level Blood Station (DLBS)" refers to the blood station established under this Act within the First District of Cotabato. (c) "Blood Services Network" refers to the integrated system of blood centers, blood stations, hospital blood banks, and blood collection units operating under the technical supervision and regulatory authority of the DOH.

label: HB 9340
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A PHILIPPINE NATIONAL AUTISM CARE PLAN FOR THE SUPPORT OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects communication, behavior, social interaction, and learning. As awareness and diagnosis of autism continue to increase, many Filipino individuals with autism and their families continue to face challenges in accessing early intervention, specialized healthcare, education, employment opportunities, and community support services. The Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the rights of all citizens to quality health services, education, and social development. It likewise recognizes the need to support vulnerable sectors and ensure that persons with disabilities are able to participate fully and meaningfully in society. As such, there is a compelling duty on the part of the government to establish comprehensive and responsive mechanisms that address the unique needs of persons with autism throughout their lives. Despite existing laws protecting persons with disabilities, gaps remain in the coordination and delivery of autism-related programs and services. Many families continue to experience limited access to diagnosis, therapy, specialized education, livelihood opportunities, and long-term support systems. There is likewise a need for stronger inter-agency coordination, research, awareness campaigns, and community-based interventions to ensure a more inclusive and supportive environment for persons with autism. Therefore, this bill seeks to institutionalize a National Autism Care Plan that will strengthen early detection and intervention programs, improve access to healthcare and education, promote protection against discrimination, and establish a comprehensive framework for autism-related policies and services nationwide. Ultimately, this bill aims to empower persons with autism to reach their full potential and become active and productive members of society while ensuring that their dignity, welfare, and rights are fully protected. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9341
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A COMPREHENSIVE AND AFFORDABLE FRAMEWORK FOR EARLY DETECTION AND INTERVENTION SERVICES FOR CHILDREN WITH SPECIAL NEEDS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Early detection and timely intervention are critical in improving the long-term development, learning capacity, and quality of life of children with developmental concerns. Delayed diagnosis often results in missed opportunities for early care and support, which may lead to more severe developmental challenges later in life. However, many Filipino families continue to face difficulties in accessing affordable screening, assessment, therapy, and intervention services, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. Every child deserves the opportunity to grow, learn, and reach their full potential regardless of physical, developmental, or social challenges. There is a need to establish a comprehensive and inclusive framework that ensures accessible and affordable early detection and intervention services for children with special needs. Through strengthened coordination among government agencies, healthcare providers, educational institutions, and local government units, more children can receive timely support and appropriate interventions during their formative years. Therefore, this bill seeks to institutionalize a National Program for Early Detection and Intervention that will strengthen developmental screening and assessment services, improve access to therapeutic and educational interventions, enhance public awareness, and promote the training of qualified professionals in child development and special needs care. Through this bill, we aim to ensure that every Filipino child is given the opportunity to reach their full potential through accessible, responsive, and inclusive early childhood intervention services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. title: AN ACT TO PROVIDE EARLY YOUTH SUICIDE INTERVENTION AND PREVENTION EXPANSION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The mental health and emotional well-being of the youth have become pressing concerns in contemporary society. Increasing numbers of young Filipinos are experiencing anxiety, depression, emotional distress, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts brought about by academic pressure, bullying, family problems, social isolation, and other challenges. These realities highlight the urgent need for stronger and more proactive measures to protect the mental health of the youth. The Constitution recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and mandates the State to promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. As such, the government must establish effective mechanisms that will provide early intervention, accessible mental health support, and community-based prevention programs for vulnerable young individuals. While Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” established a national mental health policy, there remains a need for programs specifically focused on youth suicide prevention. Schools, families, healthcare institutions, and communities must be equipped to recognize warning signs, provide psychosocial support, and encourage young people to seek help without fear of stigma or discrimination. Therefore, this bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive Youth Suicide Prevention Program that will strengthen mental health education, establish early intervention systems, and enhance counseling and peer support mechanisms in schools and communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9343
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE NATIONAL YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH AND DIGITAL WELLBEING PROGRAM, PROVIDING MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS IN SCHOOLS, REGULATING HARMFUL DIGITAL PRACTICES, AND STRENGTHENING EARLY INTERVENTION FOR FILIPINO STUDENTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rapid advancements in digital technology have transformed the way young Filipinos learn, communicate, and interact. While digital platforms provide valuable opportunities for education and connectivity, excessive and unregulated use of social media and online platforms has also contributed to growing concerns involving anxiety, depression, cyberbullying, social isolation, sleep disruption, and other mental health challenges among the youth. The Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people and to instill health consciousness among them. This responsibility includes safeguarding the mental and emotional well-being of children and young people, especially in the face of emerging digital risks that affect their development and overall welfare. While Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” established a national framework for mental health services, there remains a need for stronger school-based mental health programs and initiatives that specifically address the effects of excessive digital exposure on students and young individuals. Therefore, this bill seeks to institutionalize a National Youth Mental Health and Digital Wellbeing Program that will strengthen mental health services in schools, promote responsible digital engagement, establish early intervention and counseling mechanisms, and encourage healthy offline social interaction among the youth. Ultimately, this bill aims to foster a healthier, safer, and more balanced digital environment for Filipino students while promoting emotional resilience, responsible technology use, and accessible mental health support systems. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9344
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR SOLO PARENTS PROGRAM (FASPP), PROVIDING FOOD, MEDICAL, EDUCATIONAL, LIVELIHOOD, AND CASH RELIEF SUPPORT, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Solo parents carry the immense responsibility of raising and supporting their children while often facing economic, emotional, and social challenges on their own. In many cases, they serve as the sole providers of food, education, healthcare, and overall welfare for their families. Despite their resilience and sacrifice, many solo parents continue to struggle with rising living costs, limited employment opportunities, and insufficient access to social support services. The State recognizes the vital role of solo parents in nation-building and affirms its duty to promote their welfare and protect their families. Section 1, Article XV of the 1987 Constitution declares that the family is the foundation of the nation and mandates the State to strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development. Likewise, Article XIII on Social Justice directs the State to prioritize measures that protect vulnerable sectors and reduce social and economic inequalities. Republic Act No. 11861, otherwise known as the “Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act,” strengthened the benefits and privileges accorded to solo parents. However, many solo-parent families, particularly those belonging to low-income households, continue to face difficulties in meeting their daily needs due to inflation, increasing educational expenses, healthcare costs, and other financial burdens. Therefore, this bill seeks to provide more responsive and accessible assistance to solo parents through a comprehensive support program covering food, medical, educational, livelihood, and other essential forms of financial assistance. By institutionalizing targeted interventions for qualified solo parents, the State can help ease their financial burdens and enable them to provide a more secure and stable future for their children. Ultimately, this bill aims to uphold the dignity and welfare of solo parents by ensuring that they are not left behind in the country’s social protection framework. Through this measure, the State reaffirms its commitment to inclusive growth, family welfare, and the holistic development of Filipino children. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9345
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE WALANG GUTOM PROGRAM AS A FOOD STAMP INITIATIVE TO COMBAT INVOLUNTARY HUNGER, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution guarantees every Filipino the right to adequate food and mandates the State to uplift the living standards of the poor. Yet despite existing poverty alleviation and social protection programs, many Filipino families continue to experience involuntary hunger brought about by food insecurity, unemployment, inflation, and economic vulnerability. Addressing hunger remains essential not only to national development, but also to the country’s commitment to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 2 or “Zero Hunger,” which aims to end hunger, achieve food security, improve nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture. Millions of households struggle daily to provide sufficient and nutritious food for their families, particularly children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, and pregnant or lactating women. Hunger and malnutrition not only threaten physical health and development, but also impair educational outcomes, productivity, and overall quality of life. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has demonstrated that targeted food assistance programs can help address hunger among the country’s most vulnerable sectors. By providing food credits that may only be used to purchase nutritious food items through accredited merchants, the program promotes healthier food consumption while ensuring accountability and accessibility in the delivery of assistance. Therefore, this bill seeks to institutionalize the Walang Gutom Program as a permanent national food assistance initiative that will strengthen the State’s efforts to combat involuntary hunger and improve food security among low-income households. Through a more responsive and sustainable system of food assistance, the program aims to protect vulnerable families from the long-term effects of hunger and undernutrition. Ultimately, this bill affirms that access to adequate food is a basic human right and that no Filipino family should be left to suffer from hunger in a country capable of providing for its people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9346
title: AN ACT CREATING ONE (1) ADDITIONAL BRANCH OF FAMILY COURT IN THE FIFTH JUDICIAL REGION TO BE STATIONED IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF GUBAT, PROVINCE OF SORSOGON, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The family is recognized under the Constitution as the foundation of the nation. As such, the State has the duty to protect and strengthen the family as a basic social institution, especially in matters involving children, domestic relations, adoption, violence against women and children, custody, support, and other cases affecting the welfare of Filipino families. In the Province of Sorsogon, residents from the Municipality of Gubat and neighboring towns are constrained to travel considerable distances in order to access Family Courts located in other areas of the judicial region. This situation poses financial and logistical burdens, particularly on women, children, and senior citizens – litigants who are the usual parties in family-related cases. The current number of Family Courts serving the area remains insufficient to adequately address the growing volume of family-related cases in the Province of Sorsogon. This situation contributes to court congestion, delays in the disposition of cases, and difficulties for litigants seeking timely judicial relief. Establishing a Family Court in the municipality will help decongest existing court dockets, improve access to justice, and ensure the timely resolution of sensitive family-related matters. Therefore, this measure seeks to create a new branch of the Family Court to be stationed in the Municipality of Gubat, Province of Sorsogon, pursuant to Republic Act No. 8369, otherwise known as the “Family Courts Act of 1997.” Through this measure, the State reaffirms its commitment to protecting the welfare of Filipino families and ensuring that justice remains accessible, responsive, and compassionate to the needs of the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MANUEL “WOWO” L. FORTES, JR. label: HB 9347
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SENIOR CITIZEN RESIDENTIAL CARE HOMES IN EVERY REGION OF THE PHILIPPINES, PROVIDING FOR THEIR FUNCTIONS, FUNDING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 11, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and make essential social services available to all people at affordable cost, with priority for the elderly, among others. Likewise, Republic Act No. 7876 declares it a policy of the State to provide adequate social services and improve the quality of life of senior citizens. The law further provides for the establishment of senior citizens centers to promote the welfare and well-being of elderly persons. Despite existing laws, many senior citizens remain abandoned, neglected, homeless, or without adequate family support. A significant number of elderly Filipinos suffer from lack of shelter, medical care, nutrition, and emotional support, thereby exposing them to abuse, exploitation, and serious health risks. This proposed measure seeks to establish at least one Senior Citizen Residential Care Home in every region of the country to serve as a safe haven for indigent, abandoned, neglected, homeless, and vulnerable senior citizens. These centers shall provide residential care, medical and psychosocial services, nutrition, recreation, and other interventions necessary to ensure a dignified and humane quality of life for the elderly. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 34 35 36 HON. JULIENNE “JAM” L. label: HB 9349
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF RESIDENTIAL UTILITY CONSUMERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Do not have two differing weights in your bag—one heavy, one light. Do not have two differing measures in your house—one large, one small. You must have accurate and honest weights and measures, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you. - Deuteronomy 25:13–15 The 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates consumer protection through explicit provisions promoting welfare, safety, and fair trade practices. Meanwhile, Article XIII, Section 12 directs the State to recognize consumers' right to health and safety, quality standards, information, choice, representation, redress, education, and a healthy environment. Finally, Article XVI, Section 9 requires the State to protect consumers from trade malpractices and substandard or hazardous products. These constitutional guarantees are given statutory effect under Republic Act No. 7394, as amended, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines. The law provides for the protection of consumers against hazards to health and safety, deceptive and unfair sales acts and practices, and other forms of abuse in the marketplace. It also sets standards on product quality, warranties, and labeling, and provides remedies such as refund or replacement at no additional cost. In the context of residential utilities, consumer protection remains limited in scope. The clearest existing example is the Magna Carta for Residential Electricity Consumers issued by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) under ERC Resolution No. 10, Series of 2004, as amended. However, this applies only to residential electricity customers under approved rate schedules. To date, there is still no single and comprehensive charter of rights for household consumers across essential utility services. This gap is significant because electricity, water, and internet services are indispensable to the daily lives of Filipino households. These services are closely tied to the fulfillment of basic needs and to the welfare and well-being of families. Electricity is necessary for lighting, food storage, communication, and other essential household activities. Water is vital for sanitation, hygiene, health, and everyday domestic use. Internet access has likewise become increasingly important for communication, learning, access to information, online transactions, and participation in daily life. However, many Filipino households still encounter obstacles in obtaining reliable utility services. They struggle with high expenses, frequent service disruptions, subpar quality, and ineffective complaint systems. Most consumers are either unaware of their rights or vulnerable to utility providers who function with minimal oversight and accountability. This bill seeks to address these issues by empowering residential consumers through the creation of a Magna Carta that provides a clear and comprehensive framework governing the rights and duties of residential utility consumers and the obligations of utility providers. It introduces mechanisms for complaint resolution, defines service quality standards, and enhances regulatory supervision of electricity, water, and internet providers. Through this measure, the bill reinforces the State’s duty to safeguard public welfare by guaranteeing fair access to essential utilities, fostering accountability and transparency, and preventing unjust and exploitative practices. By reaffirming the State’s responsibility to safeguard the well-being of its people, this measure goes beyond a legal framework; it represents a commitment to honor God by defending the rights of every Filipino, strengthening communities through access to essential, high-quality services, and advancing the nation by embedding principles of equity, accountability, and empowerment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. label: HB 9350
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING THE RIGHT OF PATIENTS TO DESIGNATE A HEALTHCARE AGENT THROUGH A HEALTHCARE PROXY, PROMOTING ADVANCE CARE PLANNING, AND PROVIDING FOR SUPPORTED HEALTHCARE DECISION-MAKING IN THE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE AN ACT RECOGNIZING THE RIGHT OF PATIENTS TO DESIGNATE A HEALTHCARE AGENT THROUGH A HEALTHCARE PROXY, PROMOTING ADVANCE CARE PLANNING, AND PROVIDING FOR SUPPORTED HEALTHCARE DECISION-MAKING IN THE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM The protection of human dignity in the medical setting is now widely understood to extend beyond the provision of competent care to the preservation of the patient’s voice across the threshold of incapacity. The 1987 Constitution affirms this understanding in successive provisions: Article II, Section 11, in which the State accords paramount value to the dignity of every human person and guarantees full respect for human rights; and Article XIII, Section 11, which directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that gives priority to the underprivileged, the sick, the elderly, persons with disabilities, women, and children. These provisions are not merely programmatic. They presuppose a legal architecture under which the patient’s prior expression of will continues to operate at the moment its operation is most consequential, that is, when the patient is no longer in a position to articulate it. The international instruments to which the Philippines is a party are to the same effect. Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, Articles 3 and 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the United Nations Principles for Older Persons, taken together, locate the State’s obligation in the removal of legal and structural barriers that prevent individuals from exercising meaningful agency over the care they receive. The substantive concern is not the availability of treatment in the abstract but the conditions under which the individual’s autonomy survives the contingencies of clinical practice. Measured against these commitments, the framework presently in force discloses a structural inadequacy. Article 199, in relation to Article 194, of Executive Order No. 209, series of 1987, otherwise known as the Family Code of the Philippines, establishes a fixed hierarchy of relatives, namely, the legally married spouse, descendants in the nearest degree, ascendants in the nearest degree, and brothers and sisters, in that order, which has in practice become the operative framework applied in healthcare settings to determine who may consent to medical procedures and make decisions on behalf of an incapacitated patient. The hierarchy was, at the time of its adoption, broadly consonant with the prevailing configuration of the Filipino household. It rests, however, on an empirical premise that is no longer sustainable: that legal proximity and practical proximity describe the same constellation of persons. Where the two diverge, and they now diverge as a matter of course, the regime substitutes the determinations of a legally recognized but practically absent relative for the considered judgements of those most familiar with, and most trusted by, the patient. The displacement is not incidental to the regime. It is its predictable operation. The empirical record sustains this assessment. As of 2020, more than fifty-seven per cent of children in the Philippines were born to unmarried parents1, and approximately fifteen per cent of the population subsists in common-law partnerships2, proportions that do not capture the full range of contemporary domestic arrangements. The World Health Organization, in its 2024 country profile, identifies fifteen million solo parents in the Philippines, ninety-five per cent of whom are women.3 The Social Weather Stations Survey of 2023 reports that seven per cent of Filipino families have at least one member engaged in overseas employment4, with the attendant consequence that geographically separated households are routinely unable to discharge the decision-making functions the law presupposes in them. Successive studies of the Philippine Institute for Development Studies further establish that extended and multi-generational households have grown from twenty-five per cent of the total in 1990 to twenty-nine per cent in 2020.5 The aggregate picture is one in which care and companionship within Filipino households are increasingly distributed among persons whose relationships the Family Code’s hierarchy does not, and cannot, recognize. The consequences are most acute in emergencies involving incapacitated patients. The person most familiar with the patient’s condition, most present in their daily life, and most trusted to act in their interest may have no legal standing, while a legally recognized but practically absent relative may be vested with full decision-making authority by default. The costs of this configuration are borne, in the first instance, by patients themselves, in the form of delays to treatment, conflicts among parties, and outcomes that do not reflect their actual wishes; and, in the second instance, by healthcare providers, who are compelled to adjudicate competing claims in the absence of a clear legal framework. Neither cost can be characterized as incidental. Both are the systematic outputs of a regime that privileges legal form over the substantive autonomy of the patient. The need for a national legislative response is further evidenced by the action that local governments have already taken within the limits of their own jurisdictions. Quezon City, San Juan City, Iloilo City, and Dasmariñas have each enacted Right to Care ordinances, Parañaque City has endorsed a comparable measure now awaiting local executive approval, and the Province of Cavite has enacted the first province-wide Right to Care ordinance in the country. label: HB 9351
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY–ILIGAN CITY HINTERLAND ROAD IN BARANGAY ROGONGON, ILIGAN CITY A NATIONAL ROAD, PROVIDING FOR ITS CONTINUED DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes that infrastructure is a critical instrument for regional integration and equitable access to opportunities. Strategic road networks, particularly those that connect urban centers to hinterland communities, play a vital role in unlocking economic potential and ensuring that development reaches even the most geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. The Cagayan de Oro City–Iligan City Hinterland Road in Barangay Rogongon is envisioned as a crucial corridor linking Iligan City to upland barangays and connecting it further toward Cagayan de Oro City. A feasibility study has already been conducted, affirming its viability and strategic importance to regional connectivity and upland development. Traversing agricultural production areas and remote communities, the road is intended to facilitate the movement of goods, services, and people. Access across this terrain has long been constrained by distance and inadequate infrastructure. While road opening and initial concreting works have commenced at the regional level by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), substantial portions of the alignment remain incomplete and underdeveloped. This condition limits continuity, constrains mobility, and prevents the road from fully serving as both an economic driver for upland communities and a strategic inter-city linkage. For upland communities, improved road access directly translates to better market integration and increased access to essential services such as healthcare, education, and government programs. For the broader region, the road strengthens connectivity between Iligan City and Cagayan de Oro City, enhancing trade flows, supporting logistics, and contributing to a more resilient and interconnected Northern Mindanao corridor. Declaring the Cagayan de Oro City–Iligan City Hinterland Road a national road and ensuring its full construction and completion require sustained national support. This will enable the DPWH to undertake comprehensive infrastructure development, including the continued opening, upgrading, and long-term maintenance, in accordance with national standards. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9352
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE ILIGAN CITY CIRCUMFERENTIAL ROAD (C3) EXTENSION, FROM GREEN GOLD GAS CROSSING IN BARANGAY PUGAAN TO RUNAY BRIDGE IN BARANGAY DIGKILAAN, TRAVERSING BARANGAYS PUGAAN, MANDULOG, LANIPAO, AND DIGKILAAN, ILIGAN CITY, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes that an efficient and integrated road network is essential to urban mobility, economic activity, and the orderly expansion of growing cities. Circumferential roads play a critical role in distributing traffic, reducing congestion along primary corridors, and improving connectivity across urban and peri-urban areas. The Iligan City Circumferential Road (C3) Extension, traversing Barangays Pugaan, Mandulog, Lanipao, and Digkilaan, serves as a vital continuation of the City’s circumferential network. Extending from the Green Gold Gas Crossing in Barangay Pugaan to Runay Bridge in Barangay Digkilaan, the road strengthens linkages across multiple growth areas and supports access to both residential and production zones. A feasibility study has already been conducted, affirming its viability and strategic importance. The road has likewise been validated for conversion into a national road, recognizing its significance in completing the circumferential road system of Iligan City. However, it remains under local jurisdiction, which constrains sustained development, maintenance, and integration into the broader national road network. Converting the Iligan City Circumferential Road (C3) Extension into a national road will enable the Department of Public Works and Highways to undertake comprehensive improvement and long-term maintenance. This will ensure that the road meets national standards and fully functions as a critical component of the city’s transport network. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9354
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE ILIGAN CITY COASTAL BYPASS ROAD, FROM ST. PETER’S IN BARANGAY STA. FELOMINA TO PALM COURT IN BARANGAY TOMAS CABILI, ILIGAN CITY A NATIONAL ROAD, PROVIDING FOR ITS CONTINUED DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes that forward-looking infrastructure planning is essential to managing urban growth, sustaining economic activity, and ensuring long-term mobility. Bypass roads are critical components of such planning, as they redirect through-traffic away from congested urban centers, improve traffic flow, and support the efficient movement of goods and services. The Iligan City Coastal Bypass Road is envisioned as a strategic coastal corridor that will serve as an alternate route to the City’s existing road network. A feasibility study has already been conducted, affirming its viability and importance to the city’s long-term transport and infrastructure development. Following its original alignment from St. Peter’s in Barangay Sta. Filomena to Palm Court in Barangay Tomas Cabili, the road is designed to ease congestion along primary urban corridors and enhance connectivity across key coastal areas. While portions of the alignment have been constructed, the road remains incomplete and is not yet open to traffic. This condition continues to constrain its intended function as a bypass route and limits its contribution to overall traffic decongestion and network efficiency. Establishing the Iligan City Coastal Bypass Road as a national road will ensure sustained funding, coordinated implementation, and adherence to national standards. This will enable the Department of Public Works and Highways to undertake its phased construction and completion as a vital component of the City’s transport network. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT DECLARING THE ILIGAN CITY–CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY ALTERNATE ROAD (DIGKILAAN–BULUA SECTION) A NATIONAL ROAD, PROVIDING FOR ITS CONTINUED DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes that infrastructure is a critical instrument for regional integration and equitable access to opportunities. Road networks that provide alternative corridors between major urban centers are essential in strengthening connectivity, improving mobility, and ensuring the efficient movement of goods and services across regions. The Iligan City–Cagayan de Oro City Alternate Road, particularly the Digkilaan–Bulua Section, serves as a vital link between Iligan City and the Municipality of Opol in Misamis Oriental. A feasibility study has already been conducted, affirming its viability and strategic importance. Beginning at the Barangay Hall of Digkilaan and extending toward Limuda Integrated School in Barangay Mainit, Opol, the road establishes a strategic inter-city and inter- provincial connection. Road opening and concreting works are being undertaken by both the regional office of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the Iligan City District Engineering Office. However, key segments remain incomplete, limiting continuity and preventing the road from fully functioning as a reliable alternate corridor. Once completed, the road will enhance mobility between Iligan City and Cagayan de Oro City, decongest existing routes, and strengthen transport resilience across Northern Mindanao. It will also improve access to essential services and facilitate trade and logistics. Declaring the Iligan City–Cagayan de Oro City Alternate Road a national road and ensuring its full construction and completion require sustained national support. This will enable the DPWH to implement comprehensive infrastructure works in accordance with national standards. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
