label: HB 9422
title: AN ACT SIMPLIFYING THE DOCUMENTARY REQUIREMENTS FOR ACCESSING GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to simplify and standardize the documentary requirements for availing government financial assistance in order to ensure the timely, efficient, and dignified delivery of aid to individuals and families in need. Despite the State’s mandate to promote social justice and provide responsive social protection, existing systems for availing government assistance remain inconsistent across implementing agencies. Programs under the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Department of Health (DOH), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), and the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) often impose overlapping requirements which result in delays that undermine the urgency of assistance, particularly in medical emergencies, burial needs, and other crisis situations. The need for reform is underscored by recent developments illustrating the human cost of administrative inefficiencies in aid distribution. A reported incident on 19 April 2026 in Quezon City, involving a motorcycle taxi rider who died while waiting in line for a fuel subsidy payout, highlights the urgency of streamlining government assistance systems to prevent avoidable hardship and ensure that support reaches beneficiaries in a timely manner.[1] While Republic Act No. 9485, otherwise known as the “Anti-Red Tape Act of 2007”, as amended, mandates the simplification of procedure and reduction of bureaucratic inefficiencies in government services, the absence of a uniform standard for documentary requirements allow administrative discretion to persist, creating barriers for indigent and vulnerable beneficiaries who are least equipped to comply with complex processes. 1. Villanueva, G. (2026, April 19). Motorcycle taxi rider dies while lining up for cash aid in QC. Inquirer. Accessed from: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2214879/motorcycle-taxi-rider-while- in-line-for-cash-aid-at-qc. Accessed on: 26 April 2026. This measure therefore establishes a standardized and minimal set of documentary requirements, mandates expedited processing timelines, and strengthens coordination among implementing agencies to ensure efficient and humane delivery of public assistance. It reinforces the State’s duty to ensure that social protection mechanisms are accessible, responsive, and compassionate for those in need. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9423
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FREE ANNUAL MEDICAL CHECK-UP FOR FILIPINOS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide all Filipinos access to a free annual medical check-up as a fundamental preventive health intervention that promotes early detection, timely management of disease, and improved overall health outcomes. In the Philippines, many illnesses go undiagnosed until they reach advanced and more costly stages, often due to financial barriers and inadequate access to routine screening. This measure advances a more preventive, accessible, and people-centered approach to health care. It covers annual medical check-ups, including essential laboratory tests such as blood sugar and cholesterol screening, and provides for the expansion of diagnostic services subject to available resources. It strengthens access to basic preventive services, enables early identification of health risks and chronic conditions, reduces avoidable complications, lowers long-term treatment costs, and eases pressure on the health system. The bill gives stronger effect to the preventive and promotive principles of Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act”, by institutionalizing regular health monitoring and prioritizing early intervention over costly, late-stage treatment. It reflects a policy direction grounded in evidence-based governance and the long-standing consensus among health professionals that prevention is both more humane and more efficient than cure. Countless families continue to face financial catastrophe due to medical expenses, while preventable diseases persist as a major public health concern. Ensuring universal access to routine, preventive care is therefore a necessary intervention that strengthens individual well-being, promotes health equity, and enhances the overall resilience of the health system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9424
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL PATIENT NAVIGATION AND REFERRAL SYSTEM TO STRENGTHEN HEALTH CARE DELIVERY AND DELIVERY SYSTEMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a nationally integrated patient navigation and referral mechanism that enhances coordination among health facilities, improves access to health care, and optimizes the use of limited available health resources in the country, consistent with Republic Act No. 11223 or the “Universal Health Care (UHC) Act”. However, despite the gains under the UHC Act, many Filipinos, particularly the poor, those in remote communities, and patients requiring urgent or specialized care, continue to face serious barriers in navigating the health system, securing referrals, accessing available facilities, and obtaining financial assistance. Through improved referral pathways, real-time coordination, and stronger linkages across provider networks, the measure seeks to decongest health facilities, reduce delays in treatment, improve continuity of care, and enhance the responsiveness of the health system, especially during emergencies and for underserved populations. Equally important, the measure reinforces the implementation of UHC Act by strengthening the role of primary care, supporting efficient health systems management, and integrating patient assistance with financial protection mechanisms. In a healthcare system where access often depends on a patient’s ability to navigate complex and disconnected institutions, this bill offers a practical and compassionate reform that places the patient at the center of care and advances a more equitable, coordinated, and resilient health system. In view of the foregoing, the approval of the proposed bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9425
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE FORMULATION AND INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF A COMPREHENSIVE INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT MASTERPLAN, ESTABLISHING THE MASTERPLAN FOR INFRASTRUCTURE AND NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a long-term, integrated framework for infrastructure planning and development in the Philippines through the Comprehensive Infrastructure Development Master Plan (CIDMP) and the creation of the Masterplan for Infrastructure and National Development (MIND) Council. The measure provides a thirty (30)-year roadmap that ensures that infrastructure development is strategic, continuous, and aligned with long-term economic and regional development needs. It likewise acknowledges that infrastructure is a critical driver of inclusive economic growth, job creation, and improved quality of life. To this end, it institutionalizes a whole-of-government and multi-stakeholder approach to planning and implementation, bringing together key executive departments, local government units, and industry experts under the MIND Council. Establishing a clear, long-term national blueprint is essential to ensure that public resources are used wisely, that development gains are sustained across administrations, and that no region is left behind. The State must ensure that every peso spent translates into meaningful infrastructure that benefits the Filipino people through decisive and coordinated government action. All for the collective goal of a more systematic, resolute, and competitive public service that secures long-term progress for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9426
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE ANTI-STUNTING ACTION PLAN COUNCIL IN THE PHILIPPINES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish the Anti-Stunting Action Plan Council as a high-level, multi-sectoral mechanism to strengthen and institutionalize the country’s response to stunting, one of the most persistent and consequential public health and development challenges facing the Philippines. The measure responds to the need for a more integrated and strategic approach by aligning and strengthening efforts across relevant government agencies and stakeholders. It advances a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach that links nutrition, maternal and child health, food security, sanitation, education, and social protection, recognizing that stunting is a complex societal challenge that demands a unified and coordinated response rather than fragmented interventions. This proposed measure further seeks to address the root causes of stunting through sustained, evidence-based, and convergent interventions, with particular focus on nutritionally vulnerable children and high-poverty communities. Ultimately, it aims to safeguard every child’s right to proper nutrition, healthy development, and a fair opportunity to develop and reach their full potential. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9427
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1096, THE NATIONAL BUILDING CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AS AMENDED, BY MANDATING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONWIDE INSPECTION OF BUILDINGS AND IMPOSING STIFFER PENALTIES AGAINST BUILDING OFFICIALS WHO VIOLATE THE PERTINENT PROVISIONS OF THE SAID CODE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate a comprehensive nationwide inspection of all buildings and to strengthen Presidential Decree No. 1096, otherwise known as the “National Building Code of the Philippines”, by imposing stricter penalties on officials who violate the provisions highlighted on this measure. In light of the country’s heightened vulnerability to natural hazards such as earthquakes, typhoons, and fire-related incidents, there is an urgent need to ensure that all structures comply with established safety and engineering standards to safeguard lives, property, and public welfare. This proposed measure introduces stiffer penalties including imprisonment, perpetual disqualification from public office, and revocation of professional licenses for officials found guilty of false or fraudulent issuance of permits and certifications. It reinforces accountability, deter negligence or misconduct, and ensures that regulatory authority is exercised with integrity and that public safety is not compromised by corruption or abuse of discretion. Overall, the measure advances the State’s duty to protect life and promote resilient, safe, and disaster-prepared communities by ensuring strict compliance with building safety standards and strengthening enforcement mechanisms under the Code. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9428
title: AN ACT PROVIDING COMPASSIONATE AND RIGHT OF ACCESS TO MEDICAL CANNABIS, EXPANDING RESEARCH INTO ITS MEDICINAL PROPERTIES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to legalize and regulate the compassionate medical use of cannabis in the Philippines to provide safe and accessible treatment options for patients suffering from debilitating conditions. The use of plant-based remedies has long been embedded in medical practice, with herbs such as lagundi and ginger commonly utilized in the country. Similarly, cannabis—particularly its component cannabidiol (CBD)—has been recognized in various cultures for its therapeutic potential. Recent global developments show a growing shift toward the regulated use of medical cannabis, supported by studies indicating its effectiveness in managing conditions such as epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain. In the Philippines, health authorities have acknowledged its potential benefits. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) supports its use in pharmaceutical form, while the Department of Health (DOH) recognizes the need for proper regulation to ensure safety and efficacy. Accordingly, this measure proposes a strict regulatory framework governing the medical use of cannabis, ensuring that it is prescribed, dispensed, and monitored under appropriate medical and government supervision. It aims to expand access to alternative treatment while preventing misuse and safeguarding public health. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9429
title: AN ACT TO CREATE A HEALTHY FOOD MARKETING ENVIRONMENT BY REQUIRING FRONT-OF-PACKAGE WARNING LABELS FOR FOOD HIGH IN FAT, SODIUM, OR SUGAR AND REGULATING THE MARKETING OF SUCH FOOD TO CHILDREN
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to foster a healthier food environment by enabling consumers to make informed food choices and protecting children from the pervasive marketing of unhealthy food and beverage products. Amid the growing incidence of obesity and diet-related noncommunicable diseases, particularly among the young, there is a compelling need for stronger safeguards that address the commercial and environmental drivers of poor nutrition. The measure adopts a preventive and rights-based approach to public health by recognizing that food environments significantly affect nutrition outcomes and that children deserve heightened protection from manipulative marketing practices. It strengthens transparency and accountability in the food industry, mobilizes coordinated government action, and advances the State’s duty to protect the right to health and promote the welfare of children through evidence-based nutrition policy. Unhealthy diets are increasingly driving the burden of disease and generating avoidable social and economic costs. This measure therefore offers a timely and necessary policy response to promote healthier communities and ensure improved health outcomes for both present and future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9437
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION AND WELFARE OF ANIMALS, REPEALING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10631, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF 1998”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the welfare of all terrestrial, aquatic and marine animals in the Philippines by supervising and regulating the establishment and operations of all facilities utilized for breeding, maintaining, keeping, treating or training of all animals either as objects of trade or as household pets. 1 Thirteen years have passed since the amendment to the Republic Act No. 8485 has been enacted, and still, nefarious animal abuse, cruelty, maltreatment, neglect, and abandonment continue to sprawl on the streets in broad daylight and even in the privacy of some dwellings. This can be gleaned from the records of the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) and the Compassion and Responsibility for Animals (CARA) Welfare Philippines where over 7,000 cases of animal cruelty between 2010 and 2017 and 3,000 in the year 2020 were reported.2 On April 8, 2026, A video of a group of high school students allegedly abusing stray cats in Concepcion, Tarlac has gone viral and has raised alarm among netizens, local officials, and animal welfare groups. In the video, two boys can be seen putting the cats inside a sack and then appearing to shake them. A girl can also be seen repeatedly kicking the sack, while one of the boys was hitting the cat with a slipper.3 On May 3, 2026, authorities are investigating the death of thirteen dogs in San Miguel, Iloilo whose caretakers believe were poisoned. The family who took care of the dogs found a blue substance mixed into the animals’ food when they found the dogs dead on April 29, 2026. The investigator said it is possible that the culprit may just be a resident in the area because 1 An Act Amending Certain Sections of Republic Act No. 8485, Otherwise Known as “The Animal Welfare Act of 1998” - https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/58330 2 Caring for Animals is a Humanist Value - https://hapihumanist.org/2023/12/29/caring-for-animals-is-a-humanist-value/# 3 https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/regions/2026/4/8/tarlac-cat-abuse-video-by-minors-stirs-concern-1720 the police have received complaints that many who pass by the area are afraid of the dogs wandering around.4 This is animal cruelty. And this has to stop. With all this news, it is alarming to see that the problem lies deeper than the loud barks and the stigma. This is already a gradual decline of our ethical standards and values as a nation. With the passage of this bill, stricter penalties will be enforced against the perpetrators of animal cruelty. Information drives for the humane and ethical treatments of animals will be widely disseminated to our schools, workplaces, and down to our barangays and municipalities. The success of a nation is manifested not just by its wealth and power. But more importantly, when its citizenry beams with kindness for those who cannot defend themselves. In championing the lives of the defenseless and the voiceless, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. JANICE V. label: HB 9438
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF 24/7 PUBLIC LIBRARIES OR LEARNING HUBS IN ALL CITIES AND CLUSTERED MUNICIPALITIES IN THE COUNTRY TO PROVIDE SAFE, SUSTAINABLE, AND ACCESSIBLE PUBLIC STUDY SPACES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: Section 1. Short Title.- This Act shall be known as the “24/7 Public Libraries or Learning Hubs Act”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to ensure that such education is accessible to all. Public libraries and study hubs support the education of our learners through free, equitable access to information and technology, and safe learning environments, regardless of their socioeconomic status. Despite the passage of Republic Act No. 7743, or “An Act Providing for the Establishment of Congressional, City and Municipal Libraries and Barangay Reading Centers Throughout the Philippines, Appropriating the Necessary Funds Therefor and for Other Purposes,” that mandates the establishment of congressional, city, and municipal libraries, as well as barangay reading centers throughout the Philippines, implementation remains significantly behind schedule. Data from the National Library of the Philippines (NLP) reveals a severe implementation gap: a 2023 study reported that public libraries constitute only 3% of the ideally prescribed statutory target1. Subsequent reporting highlights that out of 44,000 local government units, only 1,721 maintained NLP affiliation in 20242, a number that rose only slightly to 1,754 by February 20263. These figures fall considerably short of what would be expected given the country's population and geographic distribution. Furthermore, many of these existing facilities operate during limited hours, with some failing to offer extended evening or 24/7 access for learners who rely on library resources after working or attending school during the day. 1 4 libraries for the people-and why we need more of them, Erin Alcala, Nathalie Grace Adalid, intquirer.net, December 9, 2024, https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2013392/4-libraries-for-the-people-and-why-we-need-more-of-them (last accessed 3 April 2026) 2 Why our reading crisis is a public library crisis, Arnold Almacen, 5 July 2025, Rappler, https://www.rappler.com/life-and-style/arts-culture/why-reading-public-library-crisis/ (last accessed 3 April 2026) 3 Statistical Number of Affiliated Public Libraries, National Library of the Philippines, https://web.nlp.gov.ph/directory-2/ (last accessed 3 April 2026) 1 The lack of 24/7 public libraries or learning hubs forces students and young professionals to rely on commercial venues like coffee shops and fast-food chains, incurring unnecessary costs to access safe and conducive environments for study and work. A 2018 study on extended library hours in the Philippines4 reveals that the main reason library users study during extended library hours is the lack of availability during the day making nighttime the most practical period for their study and research work. Furthermore, respondents recommended extending library operating hours to 24 hours a day, seven days a week. This measure seeks to address the challenges faced by many Filipino learners and young professionals: the lack of access to free, well-equipped, and safe learning hubs at any time of day. The proposed establishment of 24/7 public libraries or learning hubs constitutes a strategic initiative designed to significantly enhance educational accessibility and efficacy, alleviating the financial constraints and scheduling conflicts learners face. Furthermore, this bill envisions 24/7 public libraries or learning hubs as safe and secure, creating the perfect environment for focused study or research. By providing this reliable infrastructure, we can make education fairer for everyone, use resources more effectively, and help learners achieve better results through consistent, barrier-free access to quality learning spaces. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. JANICE V. DEGAMO Representative, 3rd District, Negros Oriental 4 Mariano, ABC, & Janio, RV ( 2018). label: HB 9439
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE RESILIENCY AND ADAPTABILITY OF FARMERS TO ADVERSE WEATHER AND CLIMATE EVENTS BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE USE OF CROP CLIMATE CALENDARS, EQUIPPING FARMERS FOR CLIMATE SENSITIVE DECISION-MAKING, AND PROVIDING ACCESS TO LOCALIZED WEATHER AND CLIMATE INFORMATION Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: Section 1. Short Title.- This Act shall be known as the “Climate Resilience in Agriculture Act”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change impacts, regularly confronting intensified typhoons, shifting rainfall patterns, and extreme weather temperatures. According to the Philippine Atmospheric Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration or PAGASA, more tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) than anywhere else in the world, with an average of twenty tropical cyclones passing through the PAR annually. Extreme weather events like super typhoons are expected to become more frequent and stronger, while temperatures are projected to rise further.1 As one of the sectors most severely impacted, agriculture suffers annual losses from flooded farmlands and destroyed crops, directly threatening livelihoods and the country’s food security. One of the ways by which we can mitigate the effects of climate change is by institutionalizing the use of crop climate calendars. While traditional crop calendars, which are available at the local agriculturists' offices, are widely available, it only provides standard planting and harvesting dates but lack critical data on local weather and climate conditions. title: AN ACT CREATING A COMMUNITY ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES OFFICE (CENRO) IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BADIAN, PROVINCE OF CEBU, TO CATER TO ENVIRONMENTAL AND NATURAL RESOURCES MATTERS IN THE 7TH DISTRICT OF CEBU, PROVIDING FOR ITS MANDATE, POWERS, FUNCTIONS, ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, APPROPRIATIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Seventh District of Cebu is rich in natural resources, coastal areas, forests, rivers, and tourism sites that provide livelihood and economic opportunities to its people. However, the district continues to face growing environmental problems such as improper waste disposal, pollution, coastal and watershed degradation, climate change, and environmental hazards. At present, local government units in the district have limited manpower, technical support, and resources to effectively address these environmental concerns. Existing environmental offices and agencies also cover large areas, making it difficult to provide immediate and focused attention to the specific needs of the Seventh District. The creation of a Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) in the Municipality of Badian seeks to strengthen environmental protection and management in the district. The proposed office will help improve the enforcement of environmental laws, coordination among local government units and national agencies, protection of natural resources, solid waste management, climate change adaptation, and disaster risk reduction efforts. This measure will also support sustainable tourism, protect the livelihood of local communities, preserve natural resources for future generations, and promote a cleaner, safer, and healthier environment for the people of the Seventh District of Cebu. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICIA C. label: HB 9441
title: AN ACT RENAMING THE LAPU-LAPU CITY DISTRICT HOSPITAL IN THE CITY OF LAPU-LAPU TO LAPU-LAPU CITY HOSPITAL (LLCH)
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The enactment of Batas Pambansa Blg. 838 on 27 April 1984 changed the name of the Opon District Hospital in Lapu-Lapu City to Lapu-Lapu City District Hospital. More than four decades after, it is but timely and necessary to rename the Lapu-Lapu City District Hospital to Lapu-Lapu City Hospital to reflect its present role as the City’s primary public hospital. The continued use of the term “District Hospital” no longer reflects the hospital’s actual city-wide service coverage and referral role. Omitting this term will also help eliminate confusion in emergency referrals, patient transfers, procurement documentation, and inter- agency records, such as the Department of Health (DOH) licensing and PhilHealth contracting. Renaming the Lapu-Lapu City District Hospital to Lapu-Lapu City Hospital will more accurately reflect its present function, mandate, and level of service as the principal public hospital of the city, consistent with its existing and/or targeted DOH hospital licensing classification, bed capacity, service capability, and role as a city-wide referral and service facility. The hospital has continuously expanded its scope of services, facilities, and capabilities, and now serving not only a district but the entire City of Lapu-Lapu. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. Junard “Ahong” Q. label: HB 9442
title: AN ACT RENAMING THE STA. ROSA COMMUNITY HOSPITAL LOCATED IN OLANGO ISLAND, LAPU-LAPU CITY TO LAPU-LAPU CITY HOSPITAL-OLANGO (LLCH- O)
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to rename the Sta. Rosa Community Hospital located in Barangay Talima, Olango Island, Lapu-Lapu City, to Lapu-Lapu City Hospital-Olango (LLCH-O). Established more than 44 years ago by virtue of Batas Pambansa Blg. 134 enacted on 12 September 1981, the Sta. Rosa Community Hospital serves as the City-owned health facility that caters to the residents of Olango and the City of Lapu-Lapu. Renaming the hospital to LLCH-O will reflect this present role, provide a unified and updated hospital identity, and ultimately contribute to the fulfilment of the City’s expanded health services delivery. Moreover, this move will reduce the risk of misrouting in emergency referrals and inter-facility transfers, ensure consistency in Department of Health licensing, PhilHealth accreditation and claims, procurement, and official records. Renaming it will likewise eliminate confusion with similarly named hospitals in the country, including those in the province of Laguna. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. Junard “Ahong” Q. label: HB 9443
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING OPEN DATA GOVERNANCE AND DISASTER RESILIENCE THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF OPEN DATA PHILIPPINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The foundation of a strong democracy is a well-informed citizenry. The right of the people to information on matters of public concern is enshrined in Section 7, Article III of the 1987 Constitution. Aside from access to official records and documents, access to government research data used as bases for policy development is also afforded to citizens. Moreover, the State is also mandated to provide the policy environment for the full development of Filipino capability and the emergence of communication structures suitable to the needs and aspirations of the nation and the balanced flow of information (Article XVI, Section 10, 1987 Constitution). Unfortunately, these constitutional provisions have not been realized to their full extent albeit the existence of technological platforms that has revolutionized access to information around the world. In 2011, progress has been made when the Philippines became a founding member of the Open Government Partnership (OGP), a multilateral initiative that aims to secure concrete commitments to promote transparency, empower citizens, fight corruption, and harness new technologies to strengthen governance. Afterwards, an ad-hoc task force composed of the Office of the Presidential Spokesperson (OPS), Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and the Presidential Communications Development and Strategic Planning Office (PCDSPO) was formed to develop data.gov.ph (now gov.ph/data) resulting into the enactment of Joint Memorandum Circular (JMC) No. 2014-01, which was subsequently supplemented by JMC No. 2015-01 on the strength of Section 24 of the 2015 General Appropriations Act. Thus, “Open Data Philippines” was born. Thereafter, Republic Act No. 10844 or the “Department of Information and Communications Technology [DICT] Act of 2015” was passed. The DICT is mandated to harmonize and coordinate all national ICT plans and initiatives to ensure knowledge, resource, and information sharing, database building, and agency networking linkages among government agencies, consistent with E-Government objectives in particular, and national objectives in general.1 This fresh mandate paved way to the recalibration of the Philippine open data strategy as well as the involvement of other pertinent government agencies such as the Philippine Statistics Authority, National Archive of the Philippines, National Privacy Commission, and the Civil Service Commission.2 This bill, the first of its kind in the Philippine legislature, intends to legislate this outstanding initiative in order to encompass the whole government structure. It seeks to adopt a policy of openness with regard to all datasets created, collected, processed, disseminated, or disposed through the use of public funds to the extent permitted by applicable laws and subject to legally mandated restrictions. Its primary aim is to democratize data by cultivating a culture of information-sharing among government institutions and the public in order to strengthen evidence-based policymaking, enhance citizen participation, and improve government transparency, accountability, and effectiveness. Importantly, the bill also recognizes the crucial role of open data in disaster resilience. The Philippines, being one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world, requires timely, accurate, and interoperable datasets to strengthen disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and emergency response. By mandating the disclosure and real-time availability of disaster-related datasets—such as hazard maps, climate and weather forecasts, infrastructure inventories, and social protection data—this bill empowers local governments, communities, and citizens to take proactive measures that save lives and protect livelihoods. Open data becomes not only a tool for transparency, but also a lifeline for resilience, ensuring that information serves as a foundation for safer, stronger, and more prepared communities. The bill further provides for the creation of the Open Data Policy Board and a counterpart Open Data Bureau that shall ensure the effective and efficient implementation of this measure. A detailed set of principles and specific criteria for datasets to be considered open are likewise provided. With a growing technology-savvy citizenry and the ever-improving technological infrastructure, the government must be able to catch up and institutionalize data-driven governance. More importantly, it must harness the power of open data to strengthen disaster resilience, empower communities, and safeguard lives. Rep. KAREN HOPE F. title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2010,” BY INSTITUTIONALIZING A MANDATORY ANNUAL COMMUNITY-LEVEL EVACUATION DRILL AND READINESS PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State, in fulfillment of its constitutional duty to protect life and property, must continuously strengthen its capacity to anticipate, prepare for, and respond to disasters. This commitment is aligned with Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, as well as the Climate Change Act of 2009, as amended by Republic Act No. 10174. These laws underscore the urgency of addressing the root causes of vulnerability, mitigating the impacts of natural hazards, and mainstreaming climate change adaptation in local and national governance. Yet, despite this legal framework, recent events have demonstrated that community-level preparedness, particularly at the barangay level, remains inadequate in the face of increasingly severe and frequent climate-induced disasters. In November 2025, Typhoon Tino (international name “Kalmaegi”) and Super Typhoon Uwan (international name “Fung-Wong”) struck the Philippines only days apart, revealing significant gaps in evacuation readiness and local disaster response. Combined fatalities reached close to 300 people, with reports documenting up to 297 deaths across affected regions1. Cebu Province suffered one of the worst impacts, with Typhoon Tino alone claiming an estimated 150 fatalities, while 451 individuals sustained injuries. According to a report from the Office of Civil Defense (OCD), several communities also reported missing persons as authorities struggled to conduct search-and-rescue operations under rapidly deteriorating conditions. The destruction extended beyond loss of life. Hundreds of thousands were displaced by widespread flooding, landslides, and structural damage throughout the Visayas and Luzon. Evacuation centers were quickly overwhelmed, and humanitarian 1 Peralta-Malonzo. “Typhoon Tino Death Toll Rises to 269.” SunStar, https://www.sunstar.com.ph/cebu/typhoon-tino-death-toll-rises-to-269 agencies reported urgent needs for water, sanitation, food, temporary shelter, and medical assistance. These events underscored how sudden, high-intensity disasters can strain both local and national capacities. Economic losses further illustrate the magnitude of the crisis. Initial assessments on the amount of losses to agriculture and infrastructure in Negros Occidental jumped to P1.98 billion2, while Cebu City reported at least ₱41 million3 in agricultural losses alone. Tens of thousands of farmers were affected, placing additional pressure on local economies. These figures are expected to rise as post-disaster evaluations continue. The dual devastation caused by Tino in Central Visayas and Uwan in Northern and Eastern provinces in Luzon highlights the increasing likelihood of multiple destructive weather events occurring in close succession. Climate research group Greenpeace Philippines have warned that rising sea temperatures and intensifying rainfall patterns are consistent with accelerating climate change4. These trends reaffirm the need for proactive, localized disaster preparedness rather than reactive, last-minute response. Given these realities, it is imperative to adopt more systematic and institutionalized mechanisms for preparing communities for disasters. Annual, community-level evacuation drills have proven effective in minimizing casualties during sudden-onset events. Regular rehearsals enable households, barangay volunteers, schools, and local responders to identify evacuation routes, assist vulnerable individuals, and execute coordinated responses with greater precision. Barangays with practiced protocols consistently report fewer casualties and faster mobilization during real emergencies. Institutionalizing drills also prepares communities for the increasing likelihood of consecutive disasters. The back-to-back arrival of Tino and Uwan demonstrated how rapidly hazard events can overwhelm government resources. By strengthening barangay-level preparedness through trained evacuation teams, standardized protocols, and coordinated drills, communities become less dependent on overstretched national response units. Economically, preparedness is far more cost-efficient than post-disaster reconstruction. The millions of pesos in agricultural and infrastructure losses recorded 2 Talabong, Rambo. “Tino Damage to Negros’ Agriculture, Infrastructure Jumps to P1.98 Billion.” The Philippine Star, 16 Nov. 2025, https://www.philstar.com/nation/2025/11/16/2487498/tino-damage-negros-agriculture-infrastructure-jumps-p198-billion 3 “Losses to Tino Hit Agri in Cebu City Reach P47M.” GMA Regional TV, https://www.gmanetwork.com/regionaltv/news/111335/losses-to-tino-hit-agri-in-cebu-city-reach-p47m/story/ 4 “Uwan (Fung-Wong) Damages Surged by 30 Percent Due to Climate Change — Report.” Greenpeace Philippines, https://www.greenpeace.org/philippines/press/68725/uwan-fung-wong-damages-surged-30-percent-due-to-climate-change-report/ this month alone underscore how early evacuation and asset protection can significantly reduce damages. Investments in preparedness such as training, drill implementation, hazard communication tools, and basic equipment, are minimal compared to the financial burden of rebuilding devastated communities and restoring livelihoods. This proposed measure institutionalizes annual community evacuation drills in all barangays and requires LGUs to include these drills in their local DRRM plans. It strengthens planning, enhances responder training, establishes monitoring mechanisms through the NDRRMC, and ensures funding support through national and local DRRM allocations. It also promotes widespread public education on early warning systems and hazard-specific evacuation procedures. By empowering barangays, the measure ensures that disaster preparedness is systematic, consistent, and measurable. Ultimately, this bill seeks to reduce loss of life, protect livelihoods, enhance community resilience, and align the country’s disaster risk reduction agenda with national policies and

label: HB 9445
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11223, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “UNIVERSAL HEALTH CARE ACT,” BY INSTITUTIONALIZING TELEHEALTH SERVICES, ESTABLISHING RURAL TELEHEALTH CENTERS, AND PROVIDING COMMUNITY-BASED TRAINING PROGRAMS FOR INDIGENOUS AND RURAL HEALTH WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health and ensure access to essential health services for all. Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution expressly provides that “the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them,” while Article XIII, Section 11 requires the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and make health services available to all at affordable cost, prioritizing the underprivileged. Despite these mandates, many Filipinos from Unserved and Underserved areas (UUAs), Geographically Isolated and Disadvantaged Areas (GIDAs) and Indigenous Peoples communities, continue to face systemic barriers to healthcare access. According to the Department of Health (DOH)1, as of 2024, there are over 7,193 areas all over the country that remain partially or severely underserved, with large clusters of UUAs found in Mindanao, the Cordillera, Eastern Visayas, and remote island provinces. Families in these areas often travel several hours, or in some cases days, by boat, habal-habal, or on foot to reach the nearest primary care facility. These barriers contribute to delayed diagnoses, preventable maternal deaths, untreated chronic illnesses, and widening inequities in health outcomes—challenges consistently acknowledged in national health assessments. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the immense potential of telehealth and digital medicine to bridge these gaps. DOH documented a surge of 100,000 patients a month 1 DEPARTMENT MEMORANDUM No. 2024-0459: Dissemination of the 2024 List of Underserved and Unserved Areas." Department of Health, 20 Nov. 2024. in the first quarter of 20212, demonstrating the ability of remote medicine to extend care despite physical distance, lockdowns, or workforce shortages. Telehealth has since proven essential for primary care, specialist referrals, mental health counseling, follow-up care, and health education. It was confirmed by the National Institute of Health of the University of the Philippines-Manila that there was at least a 50% increase in the use of telemedicine services in 2020 from pre-pandemic levels in urban areas3. However, not so much has been recorded from rural areas due to the lack of access. This bill seeks to strengthen the Universal Health Care Act by institutionalizing telehealth services, establishing Rural Telehealth Centers (RTCs), and integrating them into local Service Delivery Networks. It mandates the DOH and LGUs to ensure referral linkages, operational standards, and digital infrastructure support. Crucially, the bill also establishes a Community Telehealth Development Program in partnership with the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), TESDA, and the Indigenous Peoples Health Program. This program will train Katutubo Health Workers (KHWs)4, Barangay Health Workers, midwives, and community telehealth aides in telemedicine operations, culturally appropriate primary care, emergency teletriage, and digital health literacy, ensuring that IP communities and UUAs receive safe, respectful, and effective healthcare within their cultural context. Ultimately, this bill reinforces UHC by ensuring that digital health solutions become permanent, standardized, and accessible components of the national health system. In view of the foregoing, and with the urgent need to ensure that no Filipino, regardless of geography, ethnicity, or economic class, is denied timely and quality medical care, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9446
title: AN ACT MODERNIZING THE DEFINITION OF RAPE, STRENGTHENING PROTECTION AGAINST SEXUAL VIOLENCE, AND RATIONALIZING PENALTIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the declared policy of the State to value the dignity of every human person, guarantee full respect for human rights, and ensure the protection of its citizens, especially women and children, from all forms of violence and sexual exploitation. While the Philippines has made significant strides through landmark legislation, notably the Anti-Rape Law of 1997 (Republic Act No. 8353) and the subsequent increase in the age of statutory rape through Republic Act No. 11648 (2022), interpretive gaps and outdated provisions in the Revised Penal Code (RPC) and related statutes continue to undermine the effective prosecution of sexual offenses. This measure is urgently needed to address these deficiencies by placing the victim’s right to bodily autonomy and consent at the core of the law. The primary challenge lies in the prevailing definition of rape under Article 266-A of the RPC, which, despite R.A. No. 8353, still largely focuses on the presence of force, threat, or intimidation, rather than the absence of freely given, conscious, and voluntary consent. As noted by organizations like the Philippine Commission on Women1, this force-centric approach often creates an undue burden on victims to prove resistance, which may be physiologically impossible due to "tonic immobility" or psychological trauma. Beyond the principle of consent, this bill addresses two critical structural deficiencies: the lack of clarity on the consummation threshold and the need for legal harmonization. A key issue in rape prosecution is the precise point at which the crime is consummated, distinguishing it from the lesser crime of attempted rape. The Supreme Court addressed this critical ambiguity in the landmark case People v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo2. The Court definitively clarified the minimum anatomical requirement, establishing that rape through penile penetration 1 Philippine Commission on Women. “Amending the Anti-Rape Law.” Philippine Commission on Women, 18 March 2020, https://pcw.gov.ph/amending-the-anti-rape-law/. 2 Supreme Court of the Philippines. “PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. EFREN AGAO Y AÑONUEVO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.” G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022, https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68651. is consummated as soon as the penis "penetrates the cleft of the labia majora... in even the slightest degree." This "slight penetration" rule ensures that minimal contact, which may not cause severe injury but nonetheless constitutes an invasion of bodily integrity, is sufficient to constitute the more serious crime of consummated rape, thereby preventing the under-punishment of offenders. This measure specifically codifies this slight penetration rule into Article 266-A to ensure that the legal standard is explicit, clear, and uniformly applied by courts, thereby resolving ambiguities between consummated and attempted acts and rationalizing their respective penalties. It also codifies a statutory presumption of lack of consent, rationalizes penalties for consummated and attempted rape, and provides for gender-neutral application. Furthermore, the law on sexual harassment has evolved through Republic Act No. 7877 (1995) and the comprehensive Safe Spaces Act (Republic Act No. 11313, 2019), which covers streets, public spaces, and the online sphere. To maintain a cohesive legal structure, the complementary offense of Acts of Lasciviousness, Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code must also be modernized. This bill amends Article 336 to align its application with the principle of lack of consent and ensures a gender-neutral application across all relevant provisions, reflecting the reality that sexual violence affects all persons, regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation. In light of these persistent gaps and in compliance with the State's declared policy to guarantee full respect for human rights, this bill seeks to modernize Articles 266-A to 266-D of the Revised Penal Code and amend Article 336. By centering the definition of rape on consent and rationalizing the related penalties and provisions, this measure establishes a more robust, clear, and rights-based legal framework for prosecuting sexual violence in the Philippines. label: HB 9447
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING HEALTH- AND POLICY-BASED RESPONSES TO VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND CHILDREN BY MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN PROTECTION UNITS AND DESKS NATIONWIDE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Violence against women and children (VAWC) remains one of the most pressing public health, development, and human rights concerns in the Philippines. Despite the enactment of a comprehensive legal framework that includes Republic Act (RA) No. 7610 or the “Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act,” RA No. 9262 or the “Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004 (Anti-VAWC),” RA No. 9775 or the “Anti-Child Pornography Act of 2009,” and most recently, RA No. 11930 or the “Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (OSAEC) and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (CSAEM) Act,” violence against women and children persists at alarming levels. According to the Philippine Commission on Women, 8,055 cases1 were reported under Anti-VAWC alone. A report2 from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) and national child-protection reporting systems further reveal that tens of thousands of cases of violence against children are recorded yearly, reflecting both the magnitude of abuse and the gaps in protection and prevention. These figures are consistent with the findings of the Philippine National Police (PNP) and the Council for the Welfare of Children, which highlight the urgent need to strengthen frontline responses. Qualitative studies and operational reports further confirm the persistence of systemic barriers. Many hospitals and police stations remain without standardized Women and Children Protection Units (WCPUs) or Women and Children Protection Desks (WCPDs). In some cases, existing desks are understaffed, or manned by personnel without specialized training. Medical personnel in hospitals lack uniform protocols for forensic and psychosocial care, weakening the preservation of evidence and increasing the risk of re-traumatizing victims. Survivors in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs) are further deprived of immediate assistance due to the absence of accessible protection mechanisms. This bill ensures that existing laws on violence against women and children are translated into concrete and adequately funded frontline services by mandating the 1 Philippine Commission on Women. “2024 18-Day Campaign to End Violence Against Women.” Philippine Commission on Women, 2024, https://pcw.gov.ph/2024-18-day-campaign-to-end-violence-against-women/ 2 Philippine Statistics Authority. Violence Against Women 2024 Fact Sheet on Women and Men. Philippine Statistics Authority, 2024, https://psa.gov.ph/sites/default/files/phdsd/Violence%20Against%20Women%202024%20Fact%20Sheet%20on%20Women%2 0and%20Men.pdf establishment of Women and Children Protection Units in all government hospitals and Women and Children Protection Desks in every police station nationwide. It also provides for Mobile Protection Teams in geographically isolated areas, standardized protocols for medical, forensic, and psychosocial care, dedicated funding with accountability mechanisms, and continuous capacity-building programs for frontline personnel to guarantee survivor-centered and evidence-based responses. The benefits of this measure are clear. Survivors will gain faster, more survivor-centered responses, with immediate medical, legal, and psychosocial support. Higher reporting rates and improved data collection will enable government agencies to strengthen policy planning and resource allocation. Prosecution rates are expected to improve through standardized forensic and chain-of-custody procedures, while mobile teams and mandated units will ensure equitable access to services across both urban centers and remote areas. This measure likewise includes critical safeguards: minimum staffing standards per WCPU and WCPD, 24/7 operations or rapid-response systems, mandatory training and certification, and child-friendly protocols such as private interview rooms and trauma-informed processes. Furthermore, it acknowledges the evolving nature of abuse by including cyber- and OSAEC-related modules in training, and by requiring institutional cooperation with internet service providers and digital platforms in the enforcement of RA 11930 and RA 9775. The Constitution mandates the State to value the dignity of every person and to guarantee full respect for human rights. By strengthening health- and policy-based responses to VAWC and mandating institutionalized frontline services nationwide, this bill fulfills that constitutional duty and ensures that women and children across the country are not left behind in the fight against violence and abuse. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. Rep. KAREN HOPE F. label: HB 9448
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN’S PERSONAL DATA IN DIGITAL AND ONLINE ENVIRONMENTS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10173, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “DATA PRIVACY ACT OF 2012”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid expansion of digital platforms has fundamentally reshaped how Filipino children learn, communicate, and participate in society. While online spaces offer educational and social benefits, they also expose children to serious risks such as online sexual exploitation, cyberbullying, harmful content, algorithmic manipulation, and the misuse of personal data. Recent international developments, including Australia’s decision to restrict social media access for children under sixteen1, underscore the growing global consensus that stronger state action is necessary to protect minors in digital environments. In the Philippines, existing laws recognize the special protection owed to children, including Republic Act No. 7610 or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation, and Discrimination Act, and Republic Act No. 11930 or the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (Anti-OSAEC) Act. However, these laws were enacted before the widespread dominance of algorithm-driven platforms, immersive digital environments, and large-scale data profiling of minors. There remains a regulatory gap in imposing affirmative, child-specific duties on digital platforms operating in the country. Children today are growing up in a digital environment where online platforms, social media applications, games, educational tools, and content-sharing services play an increasingly central role in their daily lives. Filipino children are among the most active internet users in Southeast Asia. According to UNICEF2, Filipino children spend 1 “Australia Bans Social Media for Children Under 16.” The New York Times, 9 Dec. 2025, www.nytimes.com/2025/12/09/world/asia/australia-social-media-ban-under-16.html 2 UNICEF Philippines. Executive Summary: Protecting Children Online in the Philippines. United Nations Children’s Fund, 2021, https://www.unicef.org/philippines/media/2616/file/UNIPH-2021-PKO-Executive-Summary.pdf an average of two hours per day online, often beginning as early as age nine. This suggests the need for younger children – including those at primary school - to be taught the technical skills, and digital citizenship, that may be required to ensure that they stay safe online. Recent global research underscores the scale of the problem. A 2023 report by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) found that digital platforms routinely collect extensive data on minors, including location data, browsing behavior, biometric identifiers, and inferred psychological traits, often without meaningful parental awareness or consent. In the Philippine context, online harms affecting children are rapidly increasing. Data from the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group shows a sharp rise in online sexual exploitation of children, identity misuse, and data-driven grooming cases since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Department of Justice has likewise noted that social media platforms and messaging services are frequently used to collect, store, and disseminate children’s personal information without adequate safeguards. These risks are exacerbated by algorithm-driven content systems that amplify harmful material and normalize intrusive data collection practices. While the Republic Act No. 10173, also known as the Data Privacy Act of 2012, establishes a general framework for the protection of personal information, it does not contain explicit provisions addressing the unique vulnerabilities of children in digital and online environments. The Act treats children’s data largely the same as adult data, relying on general consent and security standards that are insufficient in the context of algorithmic profiling, targeted advertising, and large-scale data processing by global technology platforms. In contrast, international best practices now recognize children as a distinct category of data subjects requiring heightened protection. For example, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)3 mandates enhanced safeguards for children, including limits on profiling, stricter consent requirements, and child-specific transparency obligations. The United Kingdom’s Age Appropriate Design Code4 further requires platforms to design systems with the best interests of the child as a primary consideration. These measures reflect a growing global consensus that child data protection must be proactive, preventive, and embedded in system design. 3 European Union. General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): Summary. EUR-Lex, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/general-data-protection-regulation-gdpr.html 4 Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Age-Appropriate Design: A Code of Practice for Online Services – Executive Summary. ICO, https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/childrens-information/childrens-code-guidance-and-resources/a ge-appropriate-design-a-code-of-practice-for-online-services/executive-summary/ Amending the Data Privacy Act to explicitly integrate child-specific data protection standards will align Philippine law with these international norms while strengthening accountability for digital platforms operating in the country. By imposing heightened duties of care, requiring child-focused data protection impact assessments, restricting harmful data practices such as behavioral profiling and targeted advertising, and empowering the National Privacy Commission to enforce child-centered standards, the proposed amendment seeks to close critical regulatory gaps. Ultimately, protecting children’s personal data is not merely a privacy issue but a matter of child welfare, digital safety, and human rights. In an era where data-driven technologies increasingly shape children’s experiences, opportunities, and vulnerabilities, the State has a duty to ensure that the legal framework evolves accordingly. label: HB 9449
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE MALICIOUS USE OF SYNTHETIC MEDIA AND DEEPFAKES, PROVIDING CIVIL REMEDIES AND CRIMINAL PENALTIES THEREFOR, ESTABLISHING CONTENT-NEUTRAL PLATFORM OBLIGATIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has enabled the creation of highly realistic synthetic audio, image, and video content, commonly referred to as “deepfakes.” While these technologies have legitimate artistic, educational, and commercial uses, they have also been weaponized to destroy reputations, deceive voters, exploit women, defraud the public, and erode trust in institutions. The danger is no longer speculative. The World Economic Forum has identified AI-generated misinformation and disinformation as among the most severe short-term global risks to democratic processes and public trust1. In the Philippine context, where digital media consumption is among the highest in the world, the societal impact of malicious synthetic media is particularly acute. Non-consensual explicit deepfakes, in particular, have inflicted grave emotional and psychological harm, disproportionately targeting women and private individuals who lack the means to defend themselves2. Empirical research demonstrates that manipulated media significantly undermines public confidence in institutions and can distort political discourse3. A single fabricated video can influence elections, incite public unrest, or permanently stain a person’s name. These harms are not theoretical, they are documented, measurable, and escalating. Yet despite these risks, legislative responses must be carefully calibrated to ensure that the cure does not become more dangerous than the disease. Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution provides that “no law shall be passed abridging the freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press.” The Supreme Court has consistently held that prior restraint, or any government action that suppresses speech before it is published, bears a heavy presumption against constitutional validity. In Chavez v. Gonzales 1 World Economic Forum, Global Risks Report 2024 (2024), identifying AI-generated misinformation and disinformation as a top global risk 2 Henry Ajder et al., The State of Deepfakes: Landscape, Threats, and Impact (Deeptrace Labs, 2019); see also Citron, D. (2019). “Sexual Privacy.” Yale Law Journal, 128:1870. 3 Chesney, R., & Citron, D. (2019). “Deepfakes and the New Disinformation War.” Foreign Affairs, 98(1), 147–155; see also Vaccari, C., & Chadwick, A. (2020). “Deepfakes and Disinformation: Exploring the Impact of Synthetic Political Video on Deception, Uncertainty, and Trust in News.” Social Media + Society, 6(1). (2008)4, the Court struck down governmental warnings that effectively suppressed media publication. It emphasized that even well-meaning government warnings can unlawfully impose a chilling effect on free expression. Any regulation of synthetic media must therefore avoid blanket bans, speech licensing systems, or mandatory registration schemes that operate as prior restraint. This bill does not regulate opinion, criticism, satire, or dissent. It regulates harmful conduct. It punishes only the malicious use of synthetic media - that is, when a person intentionally uses fabricated digital content to deceive, defraud, defame, harass, threaten, or sexually exploit another. By focusing on demonstrable harm and culpable intent, the measure avoids unconstitutional overbreadth and vagueness. The Supreme Court has long required precision in speech regulation to prevent chilling effects, and this bill adheres to that standard by narrowly defining prohibited acts. For public officials and public figures, the bill adopts the constitutional standard of “actual malice,” as recognized in New York Times v. Sullivan5. This means that no public official may recover unless it is shown that the malicious deepfake was created with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard for the truth. This safeguard ensures that political debate remains robust, that satire remains protected, and that citizens remain free to criticize those in power without fear. Rather than impose government censorship before speech occurs, the bill adopts a measured and constitutional approach. It requires social media platforms to act upon verified reports of malicious deepfakes after publication, through a clear notice-and-takedown directed at platforms. By imposing post-publication remedial obligations rather than pre-publication censorship, the measure respects constitutional boundaries while providing victims with meaningful recourse. The State’s interest here is substantial: protecting citizens from fraud, exploitation, and identity abuse. The bill also prioritizes civil remedies over broad criminal sanctions. Legal scholarship and comparative legislation indicate that civil liability frameworks are less intrusive to speech while still deterring harmful conduct.6 Victims are given the right to seek damages in court. Criminal sanctions are reserved only for clearly unprotected acts such as fraud, identity theft, and sexual exploitation. This balanced framework recognizes that while speech is protected, deception and abuse are not. Ultimately, this measure recognizes that freedom of expression is not absolute. Our freedom does not include the right to weaponize falsehood to destroy another person’s dignity or to undermine public institutions. The Constitution protects speech, but not fraud, identity theft, 4 Chavez v. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, 15 February 2008, 545 SCRA 441. 5 New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964). 6 Citron, D. (2014). Hate Crimes in Cyberspace. Harvard University Press; see also U.S. Congress, “DEFIANCE Act of 2024” (civil remedies for non-consensual intimate deepfakes). or malicious deception. It does not protect calculated digital impersonation designed to cause harm. As technology evolves, so too must the law, provided that it remains faithful to constitutional principles. This bill therefore seeks to protect individuals, preserve democratic integrity, and promote responsible innovation, while simultaneously safeguarding the fundamental freedo

label: HB 9450
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE USE OF THE LEGAL ASSISTANCE FUND AND THE AGARANG KALINGA AT SAKLOLO PARA SA MGA OFWs NA NANGANGAILANGAN (AKSYON) FUND, ESTABLISHING A GLOBAL NETWORK OF RETAINED LEGAL COUNSELS AND A 24/7 LEGAL CRISIS HOTLINE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 26 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8042, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MIGRANT WORKERS AND OVERSEAS FILIPINOS ACT OF 1995,” AS AMENDED, AND SECTION 14 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11641, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “DEPARTMENT OF MIGRANT WORKERS ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution expressly enshrines the State’s commitment to afford full protection to labor, both local and overseas. In fulfilling this mandate, the Philippine government has long institutionalized mechanisms for legal and consular support through the Legal Assistance Fund (LAF) and the Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo para sa mga OFWs na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund. However, despite these mechanisms, the delivery of justice is often hindered by bureaucratic limitations, funding inflexibility, and procurement laws that delay the hiring of foreign legal representation during critical times of crisis. Currently, Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) frequently face legal and judicial challenges abroad. These range from investigation and detention to arrest and indictment, and are often without the benefit of immediate legal assistance. As emphasized in our own Constitutional tenets, any person under investigation for the commission of an offense has the fundamental right to be informed of their right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel. When our OFWs are subjected to foreign custodial investigations, the lack of immediate, culturally sensitive, and language-appropriate legal counsel puts them at a severe systemic disadvantage. Funding flexibility alone is inherently reactive. What is currently lacking in our legal assistance framework is a proactive and systemic first-response mechanism. This proposed measure, the "Overseas Filipino Protection and Legal Assistance Enhancement Act," adopts the vital funding expansions proposed in existing measures, while introducing two unique, groundbreaking provisions: 1. The Establishment of a Global Network of Retained Foreign Legal Counsels. Instead of scrambling to procure foreign lawyers only after an OFW is arrested, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) shall be mandated to pre-vet and retain a standing network of foreign law firms in countries with high OFW populations. 2. A 24/7 Overseas Legal Crisis Hotline. A dedicated, round-the-clock hotline manned by Philippine legal officers who can provide immediate, preliminary legal advice (such as the translation of their right against self-incrimination) while the retained foreign counsel is being dispatched. By marrying expanded financial flexibility with a proactive network of pre-retained legal defenders, this Act ensures that the Philippine government's promise of protection is not just a constitutional ideal, but a highly operational, real-time reality for our modern-day heroes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. KAREN HOPE F. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING AN EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES SYSTEM (EMSS), CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL EMSS COUNCIL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 SECTION 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the “Emergency Medical Services System (EMSS) Act”. 31 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. - It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people. Pursuant to this policy, the government shall institutionalize a comprehensive, accessible, integrated and standardized system of emergency medical services and provide an environment that will maximize the capability and potential of emergency medical services personnel. 37 SEC. 3. Objectives. - This Act has the following objectives: a. To create a national Emergency Medical Services System Council; b. To develop and institutionalize an emergency medical services system at the national, regional and local levels of government; c. To encourage and promote the active participation of the private sector in the provision of emergency medical services; d. To establish a national standard for an emergency medical services including, but not limited to, accreditation of EMS institutions and/or training of EMS personnel, establishing standards for design, accreditation and regulation of emergency medical vehicles;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Access to timely and effective emergency medical services is essential in saving lives during accidents, disasters, and other medical emergencies. However, many communities in the Philippines continue to face challenges such as delayed emergency response, lack of trained personnel, inadequate ambulance services, and the absence of a unified and standardized emergency medical system. These gaps place countless Filipinos, particularly those in underserved and geographically isolated areas, at greater risk during emergencies. 29 According to the World Health Organization (WHO), organized emergency care systems significantly reduce preventable deaths and disabilities caused by trauma, cardiac arrest, stroke, and other life-threatening conditions. Meanwhile, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has recognized the importance of strengthening emergency response systems, including the nationwide implementation of the 911 emergency hotline. 36 This measure seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive and integrated Emergency Medical Services System (EMSS) in the country through the creation of the Emergency Medical Services Systems Council (EMSSC), establishment of national standards for emergency medical services, strengthening of emergency response and ambulance systems, and professionalization of EMS personnel. It also strengthens the unified and free nationwide 911 emergency hotline to improve coordination and accessibility of emergency services. 44 By institutionalizing a standardized and responsive emergency medical services system, this proposed measure aims to enhance public safety, improve access to life- saving emergency care, and strengthen the country’s overall disaster and health emergency preparedness. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. JERNIE JETT V. label: HB 9454
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF LOCAL HOUSING BOARDS IN ALL LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face a housing challenge. Although estimates vary, studies consistently indicate that the number of informal settler families (ISFs) has long exceeded one million and continues to rise annually. The UN-Habitat estimated that the country had 3.7 million ISFs in 2022.1 In Metro Manila alone, 596,308 ISFs occupied 3,447.93 hectares of land in 2024.2 This persistent challenge is been compounded by the housing backlog and limited access to affordable housing. As of December 2022, the country’s unmet housing needs had reached 6.66 million units.3 A 2022 study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) found that low-income households cannot afford housing at 30% of their income.4 Moreover, the PIDS study underscored that housing policies and projects catering to the poor are more evident in LGUs with functioning Local Housing Boards (LHBs), particularly those that uphold more responsive representation, transparency, and openness in addressing the housing needs of the marginalized families. The study recommended that, to be fully functional and effective, LHBs must be provided financial support through a socialized housing fund. It further emphasized the need for LHBs to be involved not only in addressing informal settlements, but in the broader decision-making process for city-wide shelter and land use planning. The 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes the invaluable role of the private sector in public governance. It encourages the participation of non-governmental, community-based, and sectoral organizations, while emphasizing the State’s duty to facilitate adequate consultation mechanisms.5 Consistent with the cited studies, policy recommendations, and constitutional principles, this bill seeks to institutionalize LHBs in all local government units (LGUs) to ensure a coordinated, responsive, and inclusive approach to housing. By defining their composition, powers, and funding mechanisms, the measure empowers LGUs to plan, regulate, and implement housing programs and services consistent with national and local development frameworks, while safeguarding the rights of informal settler families and strengthening multi-stakeholder participation in the housing sector. 1 Given the necessity of this Bill, its enactment is highly sought. label: HB 9455
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2003, the Optical Media Board (OMB) was created under Republic Act No. 9239 to regulate the manufacturing, distribution, sale, and use of optical media such as compact discs (“CD”), and digital video discs (“DVD”), and to combat piracy through administrative licensing and criminal enforcement mechanisms. As years passed, the use of optical media has sharply declined as consumers and businesses moved to digital downloads, streaming, cloud storage, and online platforms for accessing and distributing copyrighted works. As the OMB’s statutory mandate is limited only to the regulation of optical media, its core regulatory function no longer matches the realities of how copyrighted works are created, distributed, and infringed in the digital age. As a result, the OMB’s original mandate has lost its relevance, leading to institutional redundancy and an inefficient allocation of public funds. At the same time, the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) serves as the country’s primary agency for protecting intellectual property rights and already possesses the specialized digital infrastructure, legal frameworks, and technical expertise required to dismantle modern, web-based piracy operations effectively. Clearly, the OMB’s core functions, such as licensing optical media manufacturers and replicators, monitoring the optical media industry, investigating piracy, and filing administrative and criminal cases, are now subsumed by IPOPHL’s comprehensive copyright and IP enforcement mandate. In other words, the OMB’s regulatory and enforcement activities are redundant because they overlap with IPOPHL’s existing authority and capacity to address copyright infringement across all media, including optical media, when they still exist In view of the foregoing, the bill provides the legal mechanism to abolish the OMB, transfer all its functions to IPOPHL, and ensure a smooth transition that preserves enforcement continuity while eliminating an obsolete and redundant agency. Furthermore, this bill ensures that affected OMB personnel are equally protected through fair absorption mechanisms, separation packages, or retirement benefits. 1 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Many Filipinos seeking medical, burial, and other forms of government financial assistance are often burdened by lengthy procedures and excessive documentary requirements. In times of illness, emergencies, or financial distress, applicants are frequently required to secure multiple certifications and documents from different offices, resulting in delays that further aggravate their hardship. 27 While government agencies provide various forms of assistance to vulnerable individuals and families, the absence of a standardized and simplified process has made access to aid difficult, especially for indigent patients, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, and those living in far-flung communities. Long queues, repetitive submission of documents, and bureaucratic inefficiencies continue to hinder the timely delivery of assistance. 34 This proposed measure seeks to simplify and standardize the documentary requirements for accessing government financial assistance programs by limiting the required documents to the most essential records necessary for verification and processing. It also mandates government agencies to streamline processing periods, establish digital or online application systems whenever practicable, and publicly post clear guidelines and requirements to improve transparency and accessibility. 41 Furthermore, the bill strengthens coordination with the Anti-Red Tape Authority (ARTA) to ensure compliance with Republic Act No. 11032 or the “Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018,” and to address complaints involving delays and unnecessary requirements. 46 By reducing red tape and simplifying access to financial assistance, this measure aims to provide quicker, more responsive, and more compassionate government service to Filipinos in need.
