label: HB 9694
title: AN ACT FURTHER EXTENDING THE PERIOD OF AVAILMENT OF ESTATE TAX AMNESTY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11213, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TAX AMNESTY ACT”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to further extend the period for the availment of the Estate Tax Amnesty provided under Republic Act No. 11213, otherwise known as the “Tax Amnesty Act”, as amended. It expands its coverage to estates of decedents who died on or before December 31, 2024, and extends the availment period until December 31, 2028, allowing installment payments under certain conditions. Many Filipino families remain unable to settle estate obligations due to financial difficulties and procedural challenges. This leaves numerous inherited properties untitled, unregistered, or informally transferred among heirs. This likewise prevents families from fully utilizing inherited assets and limits government revenue collection. This proposed measure seeks to address these concerns by granting taxpayers additional time to avail of the Estate Tax Amnesty and by allowing installment payments to ease the financial burden on heirs and beneficiaries. The bill aims to encourage greater compliance with tax laws, facilitate the transfer and registration of inherited properties, and promote broader economic participation through the formalization of property ownership. The Estate Tax Amnesty program has proven to be a practical and compassionate mechanism for helping Filipino families secure legal ownership of inherited properties. Extending its availment affirms State’s commitment to accessible, fair, and responsive tax policies. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9695
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A REGULAR CAMPUS OF THE CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BAGGAO, PROVINCE OF CAGAYAN AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a regular campus of the Cagayan State University (CSU) in the Municipality of Baggao, Province of Cagayan. Access to quality and affordable higher education remains a vital instrument for social mobility, economic development, and poverty reduction. In the Province of Cagayan, particularly in the Municipality of Baggao and its neighboring localities, many deserving students continue to face challenges in pursuing tertiary education due to geographical distance, transportation costs, and the limited availability of higher educational institutions within their reach. As the premier state university in the province, the Cagayan State University (CSU) has played a significant role in providing accessible and quality education to the people of Cagayan. However, the growing demand for higher education opportunities necessitates the expansion of CSU's presence in underserved areas to ensure that more students can benefit from its academic programs, research initiatives, and extension services. The Municipality of Baggao is one of the largest municipalities in the province in terms of both land area and population. The establishment of a regular CSU campus in the municipality will bring higher education closer to students and their families, reduce educational expenses, promote greater enrollment and completion rates, and contribute to local socioeconomic development. It will likewise help produce a highly skilled, productive, and globally competitive workforce capable of supporting regional and national development goals. The proposed campus shall offer degree programs, technical and professional courses, research activities, and extension services responsive to the educational, economic, and developmental needs of the municipality and the province. It shall further support the government's commitment to inclusive growth and the equitable distribution of educational opportunities, particularly in rural and geographically isolated communities. Moreover, CSU has already conducted a favorable feasibility study on the establishment of a CSU campus in Baggao, Cagayan, and initial funding has been allocated under the 2025 General Appropriations Act for the proposed campus infrastructure on the property donated to CSU for the establishment of CSU – Baggao Campus. These developments demonstrate the viability of the said establishment and the strong support it has garnered from stakeholders and the local community. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JOSEPH “JOJO” L. label: HB 9696
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE NURSING LAW TOWARDS A QUALITY HEALTH CARE SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9173 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE NURSING ACT OF 2002
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution, Article XIII, Section 3, mandates the State to ensure humane conditions of work, a living wage, and participation of workers in policy and decision- making processes affecting their rights and benefits. This constitutional guarantee underscores the State’s obligation to address long-standing inequities affecting the nursing workforce in the country. The Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) Board of Nursing recognizes nursing as one of the backbone professions of the Philippine healthcare system. Nurses play a pivotal and transformative role in the delivery of health services, particularly in the context of Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act, where they serve as frontline providers in achieving accessible and equitable healthcare for all Filipinos. Despite their critical contribution, Filipino nurses continue to face persistent and systemic challenges, including insufficient compensation, unsafe and overburdened working conditions, limited opportunities for professional advancement, and the underutilization of their competencies. These long-standing concerns have contributed to the continued migration of nurses seeking better opportunities abroad, driven by the need for fair compensation, career growth, and safer work environments. This sustained outflow of nursing professionals has resulted in a significant shortage of nurses in the country, thereby weakening the overall capacity of the healthcare system and hindering the full and effective implementation of the Universal Health Care Act. The shortage is particularly felt in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, where access to quality healthcare remains a persistent challenge. While the Philippines is globally recognized for producing highly skilled, competent, and compassionate nurses, the country has not fully maximized the potential of its nursing workforce to address persistent gaps in healthcare delivery. There is a growing need to strengthen the profession by expanding clinical roles, enhancing training pathways, and enabling nurses to practice to the full extent of their education and competencies under a clear and unified regulatory framework. International experience shows that countries which have strengthened and expanded advanced nursing roles have achieved significant improvements in healthcare access, quality, and efficiency, including reduced hospital congestion, improved chronic disease management, enhanced patient education, and better continuity of care, particularly in underserved areas. Global evidence further highlights that strengthening nursing roles is a key strategy in achieving Universal Health Coverage and reinforcing primary healthcare systems. label: HB 9707
title: AN ACT REPEALING PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1620 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “GRANTING TO THE INTERNATIONAL RICE RESEARCH INSTITUTE (IRRI) THE STATUS, PREROGATIVES, PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES OF AN INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A world without the International Rice Research Institute is a world free from monopoly of rice crop varieties and from diseases and deaths brought by IRRI’s agro-chemicals. IRRI’s existence in the Philippines is more than half a century but failed to contribute in attaining food security in the country. This concrete situation pushed Filipino peasantry, agriculturists and scientists, food security advocates and people’s organizations to press the government for agricultural programs and policies based on genuine rural development, free from foreign monopoly control and sincere in achieving food security for the people. The IRRI was established in 1959 by virtue of a Memorandum of Understanding between the government of the Republic of the Philippines and both the Ford and Rockefeller foundations. The institute was envisioned to be the world’s prime mover in rice science and technology purportedly to reduce food-insecurity-related poverty in the Philippines as well as in the rest of the rice-producing countries in the underdeveloped regions. Fifty-seven years hence, however, according to the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), a nationwide peasant organization, the IRRI cannot at all claim its positive 1 contribution to the food security of the country or of other poor and agricultural countries. IRRI’s research, which they claim improves rice and even corn production, have not led to any significant development in the country’s agricultural productivity. In fact, the state of Philippine agriculture has consistently worsened to the point that the very host country of IRRI, fell to becoming the world’s biggest net importer of rice in 2008, and being the third last year, following China and Nigeria. One of the highlighted cases of extreme starvation and production difficulties was experienced by more than 6,000 farmers and Lumad people from Kidapawan and other parts of North Cotabato in Mindanao, who protested demanding food on April 1, 2016. While this was predominantly driven by the extreme drought, they also suffered abuses such as displacement and militarization that hampered their agricultural cultivation and exacerbated their access to food. Worsening was the government neglect, amidst the many reports of hunger, the local and national government failed to address the situation, through immediate food relief and assistance. The farmers’ actions were replied with a bloody dispersal by the Philippine National Police known as the Kidapawan Carnage that left two farmers dead, more than a hundred injured and seventy eight detained, including elderly and pregnant women. If the IRRI actually accomplished anything, it was the institutionalization of a rice production system that is highly dependent on agro-chemical products such as pesticide, promoted by its transnational corporation (TNC) partners. IRRI’s science and technology mandate has long been geared almost solely toward the constant development and dissemination of hybrid, genetically engineered crops to complement and perpetuate the use of the said harmful chemicals promoted by predatory TNCs such as Monsanto, Syngenta, Bayer, Dow AgroSciences and BASF among others. For over five decades now, IRRI has indeed been an instrument of monopoly capital's onslaught upon the agriculture of the Philippines and of other Third World nations. The introduction of IRRI's high-yielding varieties of rice and corn grains during the now infamous Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s led to an unprecedented use of and dependence to agro-chemicals that eventually harmed the natural ecosystem in the rice fields. Scientific tests have in fact proven how genetically modified (GMO) crop varieties produce particular types of toxins and allergens that not only prompt allergic reactions but could also cause damage to vital human organs. On April 8, 2015, Bill Gates, the 2017 Forbes richest billionaire, donated USD 10.3 million dollars to the IRRI through the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) intended for various research on genetically modified Golden Rice, a genetically manipulated variety that contains beta carotene. According to Masipag, a network of farmer’s groups, scientists and non-government organizations in the 2 Philippines, the funding will be used for high technology solutions like chemical farming and GMOs that would create further trouble among poor peasant families and consumers. Moreover, the IRRI is enjoying its immunity to the point of blatant disregard of its workers who were exposed to harmful and dangerous agro-chemical products and outright violations of labor rights. According to the Brotherhood of IRRI Support Services Group (BISSIG), a labor organization in IRRI, has been abusing its international status through its seemingly endless list of violations of its workers’ rights to organize, to collectively bargain and negotiate, and to hold strikes. In 1979, President Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 1620 declared the IRRI as an international organization, with all the privileges and immunities that came with the granting of such status. The IRRI thus has been able to justify its anti-labor practices. It has intermittently carried out mass lay-offs in 1989, 1993 and 1996. It has implemented a questionable retrenchment program that has warranted the unfair dismissal of regular employees. The institute has also engaged in union busting which included the harassment of union leaders and members. These workers have failed in their various attempts to seek redress from the courts given IRRI’s immunity from suit which it enjoys under Presidential Decree No. 1620. The same immunity has also been invoked to bar the workers from claiming compensation for having been afflicted with illnesses due to exposure to toxic chemicals and to inhuman working conditions. label: HB 9708
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING THE PARTICIPATORY GUARANTEE SYSTEM (PGS) AS A FORM FOR CERTIFICATION FOR LABELLING ORGANIC PRODUCTS AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT 10068, ALSO KNOWN AS THE ORGANIC AGRICULTURE ACT OF 2010, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The enactment of R.A. 10068, also known as the Organic Agriculture Act of 2010, is considered a boost to the local organic market. While it is still in its initial stages of implementation, there is a need to fine-tune the Act in order to further promote organic agriculture and truly empower our local farmers. However, criticism towards the seemingly exclusive rights given to private certifying bodies inhibits the growth of organic agriculture as it deters small farmers from going organic. The high cost to get certified, in order to carry the “organic” label discriminates against our small farmers and indigenous peoples who have long traditions of raising and producing organic goods. Denying them to label what is essentially an organic product as such is also detrimental to their livelihood. Local government units (LGU) should be given a bigger role in the promotion of organic agriculture. An increasing number of LGUs recognize the health, economic and environmental value of organic farming, and have likewise issued ordinances in support of organic agriculture. These local initiatives should be considered by national government agencies before they allow crops or agricultural methods that may affect the organic nature of farming in the localities where they intend to operate or test. 1 This Bill recognizes the Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) in the certification and labeling of organic products and encourages the appropriate agencies to develop and strengthen such alternative certification mechanisms. It likewise ensures the protection of indigenous organic resources against cross contamination of engineered crops. For decades, the lack of sustainable alternatives and genuine support from the national government have turned generations of Filipino farmers slaves to the land, instead of stewards of it. This is due to the fact that landlords, big agro-corporations and government policies have been used to tie farmers to usurious practices and products, further pushing peasants to poverty. Sustainable agricultural methods, such as organic farming, are a welcome alternative to the import-based and toxic farming methods which are destroying our natural resources. This Bill was first filed by Bayan Muna Representative Teddy Casiño in 2011 during the 15th Congress. It was refiled by the Makabayan Bloc in the succeeding Congresses. In view of the foregoing, immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. REP. SARAH JANE I. ELAGO Gabriela Women’s Party REP. ANTONIO L. TINIO REP. RENEE LOUISE M. label: HB 9709
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DISTRIBUTION, SALE, AND USE OF GLYPHOSATE IN THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Glyphosate or N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine is a broad-spectrum herbicide developed and commercially introduced by Monsanto in 1974 under the brand name Roundup. It is believed to inhibit protein synthesis in weeds leading to death. It persists in some soils for up to three years and can bio-accumulate. It is used in plantations, parks, gardens and orchards. The global production of glyphosate reached 1.1 million tons in 2012 causing tremendous pressure to disperse Roundup Ready (RR) crops. RR crops increased glyphosate use from just 25-30 million lbs in 1995 to 180-185 million lbs in 2007. In 2016, Environmental Sciences Europe reports that 18.9 billion pounds (8.6 billion kilograms) of glyphosate have been used globally. A growing body of independent scientific evidence suggests that glyphosate is harmful to humans. Use of glyphosate formulations was found to induce DNA damage and has been associated with increased risk of (i) cancer especially non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma; (ii) neurobehavioral disorders in children; (iii) birth defects and other diseases. In the laboratory, glyphosate formulations were found to (i) inhibit the production of steroid hormones e.g. progesterone; (ii) cause cell death and necrosis in various human cell cultures at fairly low levels; (iii) induce congenital craniofacial malformations on frog and chicken embryos; and (iv) be highly toxic to frogs. Continuous use of glyphosate disrupts soil microbial communities, and makes RR 1 crops more susceptible to disease, deficient in key nutrients, and less productive than conventional crops. Glyphosate increases the severity of sudden death syndrome—a serious plant disease caused by Fusarium—in RR soybeans. Low level glyphosate spray has caused reduced leaf concentrations of calcium, manganese and magnesium as well as reduced seed concentrations of calcium, magnesium, iron and manganese in non-transgenic soybeans. Intensive glyphosate use led to the emergence of glyphosate-resistant (GR) weeds; that resistance is now recorded in 35 weed species in 27 countries. Such widespread use also contaminated the environment with glyphosate residues being detected in food, drinking water, wine, beer, and in RR cotton products. The extent of human exposure is confirmed by the presence of glyphosate in human urine and breast milk. In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate as a probable human carcinogen. During the Monsanto Tribunal on October 2016 in the Hague (Netherlands), Dr. Peter Clausing a toxicologist, debunked the arguments used by the authorities to dismiss the significant finding of glyphosate-induced malignant lymphoma in mouse carcinogenicity bioassays that led to the reclassification of glyphosate as non-carcinogen. In that tribunal, Dr Clausing declared: “In 2017 the European Chemicals Agency has to decide whether it accepts the compelling evidence for glyphosate’s carcinogenicity and declares it a carcinogen. This would be an overdue acknowledgement of the reality.” Such declaration resulted in national bans and restrictions, and voluntary action by local authorities and retailers to curb glyphosate use. Sri Lanka was the first country to ban it completely, although the ban has recently been relaxed to allow use in tea plantations; Italy has banned pre-harvest use, and all use in public places and those frequented by children and the elderly; France is phasing out the use of pesticides in towns and public areas; and the European Union has extended approval for glyphosate for only 18 months instead of the usual 15 years. Glyphosate is included in Pesticide Action Network‘s (PAN) List of Highly Hazardous Pesticides targeted for global phase-out. The PAN monographs detail glyphosate’s adverse effects on humans, ecosystem functioning, pollination services, biological controls, soil fertility and crop health. PAN has strongly urged governments to adopt agroecological approaches to pest/weed management. Dr Rosemary Mason’s open letter to European Chemicals Agency Executive Director Geert Dancet described the devastating effects of agrochemicals and how corporate power works to encourage scientific fraud and subvert public watchdogs and policy-making institutions to get toxic agrochemicals, especially glyphosate, onto the market and ensure they remain there. Revelations in Dr Mason’s letter include (i) US Environmental Protection Agency’s collusion with Monsanto in changing glyphosate’s classification from Group C /probable carcinogen to Group E/evidence of non-carcinogenicity for humans; (ii) Monsanto’s sealed secret studies showing glyphosate’s carcinogenicity since the 1970s; (iii) Glyphosate’s possible link with 2 increased incidence of cataracts and interstitial damage, and a range of diseases e.g. brain tumors, cancers, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer’s and dementia; (iv) Glyphosate’s adverse effects on bumblebees, butterflies, moths, bush crickets, spiders, dragonflies, ladybirds, solitary bees, hoverflies, bats, beetles, shield bugs and many other small creatures that have all but disappeared in glyphosate-ridden areas. Mason posed the question “Why are you all protecting the pesticides industry?” to the various agencies responsible for protecting health and the environment, and recapped: “Monsanto has been lying to you for the sake of money. CEO Hugh Grant and the US EPA knew that glyphosate caused all of these problems. The corporation concealed the carcinogenic effects of PCBs on humans and animals for seven years. They have no plans to protect you and your families from the tsunami of sickness that is affecting us all...” The same question may be posed by us and the people to this Assembly if this bill is not passed the soonest possible time. Furthermore, a very recent study entitled Community Pesticide Action Monitoring in Mindanao, Philippines conducted by Dr. Romeo F. Quijano, President of the Pesticide Action Network Philippin

label: HB 9710
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DISTRIBUTION, SALE AND USE OF PARAQUAT IN THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The number of global cases of pesticide poisoning is estimated to be over one million each year. Tens of thousands of the cases result in death. A significant portion of these cases can be attributed to the use of Paraquat, which is the substance with the most victims in various countries (ECCHR, 2011). Paraquat is one of the world’s largest selling weedkillers and is registered and used in about 100 countries. It has been a subject of controversy for several decades, especially regarding the safety of farmers and agricultural workers in developing countries. Both intentional and unintentional poisonings with paraquat, mainly among agricultural workers, farmers and inhabitants of rural areas, have led to serious concern among national health authorities, workers’ unions and non-governmental organisations. Acutely toxic pesticides are used in many countries under inadequate conditions and cause ill health and deaths, both among agricultural workers and the general public. The injuries suffered often cause chronic health problems, and are sometimes fatal (ECCHR, 2011) Paraquat (1,1’-dimethyl-4,4’-bipyridinium dichloride) is a fast-acting, non-selective contact herbicide that causes rapid drying of plant leaves. It is used to control weeds and grasses in more than 100 different crops, including bananas and oil palms. It is used in the Philippines, particularly in Mindanao, where the work conditions (hot/humid climate, lack of protective clothing, leaking/clogged equipment, 1 continuous use, lack of washing facilities, lack of training/awareness, and lack of medical facilities) make its use particularly hazardous. The product was first sold in 1961 and it is the most toxic herbicide used today, about 28 times more acutely toxic than glyphosate, the most widely used herbicide globally. From the time when it was first marketed until today, accidental and suicidal ingestion of paraquat has caused an innumerable loss of lives. Paraquat is often mistakenly ingested because containers for drinking water and storage or mixing of paraquat are confused, and paraquat has been found available in stores in re-packed containers without proper labelling. An oral ingestion of a mouthful of a 20% paraquat solution is likely to cause death, and depending on the constitution of a person, 10 ml are enough to be fatal. Fatal poisoning at the workplace occurs mostly when paraquat absorption through skin is increased after prolonged contact with undiluted or diluted paraquat solution. Spray mist deposited in the nose may be swallowed and sprayed in the air can be ingested when workers breathe through the mouth. The level of exposure to paraquat that workers may experience when handling paraquat is high enough to lead to absorption of an amount that can result in acute poisoning. The symptoms of poisonings are often delayed. Damage to the lungs, for example, may not be evident until several days after absorption. Since there is no antidote against paraquat poisoning, the outcome can be fatal and in these cases death mostly results from respiratory failure (ECCHR, 2011). The use of paraquat raises safety concerns on both human health and environment on a global scale. Paraquat is a neurotoxic herbicide and has been linked to increased incidence of Parkinson’s disease. It is a potential endocrine disruptor, teratogen, genotoxin and carcinogen. Paraquat causes multiple organ failure as it damages the lungs, heart, kidneys, adrenal glands, central nervous system, liver, muscles, spleen, skin and eyes. The Permanent People’s Tribunal on Agrochemical Transnational Corporations (PAN International, 2016) in its 2011 assembly reported that sprayers have died after sucking clogged spray nozzles or after applying pesticides with a leaky knapsack sprayer, or from splashes of concentrate on their bodies. Sprayers often suffer skin damage, burns, eye injuries/blindness, nail damage/loss, nose bleeds and respiratory problems. Changes in wind direction result in sprayers’ exposure through inhalation and contact with skin and eye. The Tribunal also found that agricultural equipment are either left unwashed or are washed in streams and rivers due to inadequate washing facilities, contaminating the water source. Some sprayers also bring home their equipment endangering household members. There are incidents of paraquat poisoning that have been recorded in the Philippines. Dr. Norma Pacalso of the Benguet Provincial Health Office said there is an increase in monitored cases of poisoning in the province. She said from 39 cases in 2011, it rose to 48 in 2012. In 2013, twenty one (21) cases have already been recorded. 2 In 2010, the Department of Health conducted a study on the paraquat exposure among farmers in Agusan del Sur and its summary findings were disturbing as follows: ● Integumentary changes (chronic irritant dermatitis) that could be compatible with chronic paraquat exposure were seen in 21.4 %; nail changes were seen in 69.6% ● 30.3% had abnormal spirometry findings ● Urine paraquat was detected in 90% of workers, although less than detectable limit in 43% ● Although majority of workers use PPE, the item used may not provide enough protection against paraquat Paraquat is marketed by Syngenta, with an approximate market share of 75%, under the brand name Gramoxone in formulations ranging from 24%-36% active ingredients. Other companies produce it under the trade names Crisquat, Dexuron, Totacol, Cyclone, Gramixel, Pathclear, and many others. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies it as moderately hazardous (Class II) but the Pesticide Action Network (PAN) considers it as highly hazardous (Class I) due to its acute toxicity, delayed effects and lack of antidote. The US Environment Protection Agency classifies paraquat as highly toxic by inhalation. Its use has been unauthorized in Norway since 1981 and in Syngenta’s home-base Switzerland starting December 1989. Six European Union countries banned para

title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE USE OF PRODUCTS CONTAINING GENETICALLY MODIFIED ORGANISMS (GMO) ON FOOD AND AGRICULTURE IN THE COUNTRY, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Genetically modified organisms (GMO) technology, particularly on food, has been introduced globally by giant agro-chemical transnational corporations (agro-chem TNCs) and international institutions such as the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI). GMO proponents claim that its uses range from biological and medical research, production of pharmaceutical drugs, experimental medicine and agriculture. Living organisms such as microbes, plants, animals and crops are being tweaked using genetically modified (GM) and genetically engineered (GE) technology. From research and development funding to distribution and sales profit, the role of transnational and multinational corporations has been apparent in the proliferation of GMO crops and products. The Convention on Biological Diversity defined “biotechnology” as “technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives thereof, to make or modify products or processes for specific use.” The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety meanwhile defines “modern biotechnology” as (a) in vitro nucleic acid techniques, including recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and direct injection of nucleic acid into cells or organelles, or (b) fusion of cells beyond the taxonomic family, that overcome natural physiological reproductive or recombination barriers and are not techniques used in traditional breeding and selection. An example of this is genetic engineering which is the direct manipulation of an organism's genome using biotechnology. GMO crop (genetically modified food crops) proponents in the country have always invoked adequate food production and the fight against poverty, hunger and malnutrition as the ultimate goals for the introduction of such technology. But it is not the real solution. Filipino farmers and scientists across the country assert that GMO in Philippine agriculture is not a solution but in fact, a serious problem. The national farmers organization, Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP, Peasant Movement of the Philippines), and the Resist Agrochemical TNCs Network (RESIST), an alliance of farmers, scientists, and consumer groups, are firm on their position that GMO crops have no positive contribution in local agricultural production and in the eradication of hunger and poverty. Fundamentally, rice productivity does not depend on the variety of rice but on a comprehensive system which includes, among others, infrastructure that is supposed to facilitate the growth and development of the Philippine rice industry and agriculture in general. In the current state of such a system, the presence of GMO in Philippine agriculture is beyond the range of acceptable options. False claims that GMO crops would solve or even contribute to solving poverty, hunger and malnutrition in the country are all superficial, given the lingering problems in Philippine agriculture, one major aspect of which is the continuing failure of the state to implement genuinely redistributive agrarian reform. Hunger is brought about by extreme poverty, and in the countryside, farmers are extremely poor due to landlessness and lack of support from the government. Without resolving landlessness, hunger and its consequence, malnutrition, would not be thoroughly addressed. Amplifying yield production does not lead to the upliftment of the socio-economic status of the poor farmers as production is generally controlled by the local landowning class and its foreign big business partners. Moreover, production yield increase is price tagged with the extensive utilization of agro-chemical inputs. This translates into huge profits for the transnational corporations who provide these inputs in addition to providing the seeds to begin with. Fortunately, the Filipino people are aware of the uncertainties of the GMO products, as several local government units have approved resolutions that prohibit such products in their localities: a. In Bohol, Resolution 2003-235 was unanimously passed by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan declaring the province free of GMO to protect the ecological balance of the province and health safety of Boholanos from the adverse effects of GMOs. The resolution was followed by Provincial Ordinance 2003-010, known as the “Safeguards against GMOs,” which enumerated the conditions against the entry of Genetically Modified (GM) plants, animals and microorganisms into the province. b. The provinces of Mindoro Oriental and Marinduque, both parts of the “Organic Haven Islands” of MIMAROPA, have institutionalized their respective Provincial Environmental Codes and Administrative Orders banning the entry of GMOs in their areas. c. In 2007, Negros Occidental passed Provincial Ordinance 2007-007 or “The Safeguard Against Living Genetically-Modified Organisms” in line with the province’s goal of becoming the “Organic Food Bowl of Asia.” Along with Negros Oriental, Negros Occidental signed a memorandum of agreement committing to a 10% organic island-wide production by the year 2010 and to the banning of GMOs. d. Some towns in Iloilo have expressed their apprehension with the ongoing field testing in their areas and have called for the suspension of the production of BT (Bacillus thuringiensis) eggplant, a genetically modified crop. e. In Davao City, a city resolution was passed in 2011 banning BT eggplant. Sectors are also clamoring to declare Davao City as a GMO-free zone. Aside from LGUs banning GMO crops in their localities, people’s organizations and non-government organizations have sustained their opposition to GMO crops, such as the KMP and its regional chapters and affiliate organizations, RESIST, Magsasaka at Siyentipiko para sa Pag-unlad ng Agrikultura (MASIPAG, Farmer-Scientist Partnership for Development). label: HB 9712
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROVISION OF A FIFTEEN THOUSAND PESOS (P15,000.00) PRODUCTION SUBSIDY TO THE FILIPINOS EMPLOYED IN THE FISHERIES AND AQUACULTURE SECTOR, TO STRENGTHEN PRODUCTION, SUPPORT SECTORAL RECOVERY, AND ADVANCE NATIONAL ECONOMIC RESILIENCE AMID ECONOMIC CRISES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Among the country’s basic sectors, fisherfolk are among the poorest of the poor. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the incidence of poverty remains higher among fisherfolk. From 2018 to 2023, the number of poor fisherfolk increased from 287,070 to 353,190. Subsequent interventions involving fisherfolk were largely limited to broad categories such as assistance to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and measures to ensure supply chain continuity. In practice, fisherfolk were subsumed under a small allocation of credit facilities—₱1 billion shared among approximately 40,000 small farmers and fishers—primarily in the form of concessional loans. This approach contrasts sharply with direct subsidies provided to other sectors, such as rice farmers. Furthermore, policies focused on market access and supply chains primarily benefit intermediaries and traders, rather than addressing the production challenges faced by small fisherfolk. Notably, no substantial production subsidies were provided for the fisheries sector. This omission reflects a failure to uphold the principles enshrined in Republic Act No. 8425, including access to basic services, asset reform, sustainable resource development, and participatory governance. Despite repeated warnings from international bodies and calls from fisherfolk organizations such as Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas (PAMALAKAYA), the lack of targeted support has exacerbated the sector’s marginalization and vulnerability. Compounding these challenges is the recent surge in global oil prices, which has significantly increased operational costs for fisherfolk. By early February, a typical fisher using 10 liters of diesel per trip faced an additional ₱1,760 in monthly expenses (based on 16 fishing days), increasing costs from ₱7,200 to ₱8,960. By March, this increase reached approximately ₱3,800 per month. As a result, some fisherfolk have reportedly ceased operations due to the risk of financial losses. Given these conditions, there is an urgent need to provide production subsidies for small fisherfolk, alongside social amelioration for fish workers. In response, the proposed measure seeks to provide P15,000 in production subsidy to fisherfolk. This support aims to stimulate small-scale fishery production, contribute to national food security, and facilitate economic recovery, while mitigating the disproportionate impact of the crisis on already impoverished and vulnerable fisherfolk households. The urgent passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. SARAH JANE I. ELAGO Gabriela Women’s Party REP. RENEE LOUISE M. CO REP. ANTONIO L. label: HB 9713
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE MAGNA CARTA FOR PUBLIC DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKERS Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the "Magna Carta for Public Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Workers.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect and promote the right to life, health, safety, and socioeconomic security of every person as enshrined in Article II, Sections 4, 15, and 18 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. The State therefore affirms its duty to uphold, protect, and promote the rights, welfare, and well-being of all Public Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Workers who, as frontliners in the delivery of essential public service, are tasked with safeguarding lives, property, and the environment from the adverse effects of disasters and other emergencies. In recognition of their indispensable role as agents of resilience, humanitarian response, and sustainable development, the State shall ensure that appropriate measures are instituted to guarantee their protection, security, and professional advancement. Towards this end, this Act aims to: A. Promote and improve socioeconomic and psychology well-being of Public DRRM Workers, through the improvement of working conditions, environment, and terms of employment; B. Promote the continuous development of the skills, competencies, and capabilities of Public DRRM Workers to ensure their responsiveness and preparedness in the effective delivery of disaster risk reduction and management services and program; and
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has been considered as one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world1 not merely because of man-made sources of disasters but also because of its geographical location that makes it vulnerable to potential natural hazard, which causes heavy human casualties, damage to properties and infrastructures, and decline of human welfare such as health status and livelihoods. Considering its significant and catastrophic impact, it has been a long-standing battle cry of the country’s Public Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Workers to urge the government to institutionalize the rights and welfare of our disaster responders who risk their lives during calamities and disasters. In addressing the gaps in the welfare and safety of our DRRM workers, a Magna Carta for Public Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Workers is necessary to streamline the benefits accorded to them. These include, among others, mandatory hazard and subsistence allowances for workers deployed in low- to high-risk operations; the provision of medical, mental health, and psychological examinations; the inclusion of insurance and health coverage for work- related injuries, illnesses, and disabilities; and the standardization of a career progression framework to ensure the continuity of DRRM operations in the country. In recognition of the crucial role and bravery of our disaster responders, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 9715
title: AN ACT DECLARING AUGUST 30 OF EVERY YEAR AS A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF MANDAUE, PROVINCE OF CEBU, IN COMMEMORATION OF ITS CHARTER ANNIVERSARY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to declare August 30 of every year as a special non-working holiday in the City of Mandaue in the Province of Cebu in commemoration of its Charter Anniversary. On June 21, 1969, Republic Act No. 5519 otherwise known as the “Charter of the City of Mandaue”, was signed into law by President Ferdinand Emmanuel Edralin Marcos, Sr. Presidential Proclamation No. 586 series of 1969, signed on August 6, 1969, designated August 30, 1969 as the date of formal organization of the government of the City of Mandaue. Since then, every year, the Mandauehanons have celebrated the Mandaue City Charter Day on August 30. Mandaue City has a total land area of 34.87 square kilometers (13.46 sq mi) and is composed of 27 barangays. According to the 2024 census, the city is home to 364, 482 Mandauehanons. As of 1991, Mandaue City was recognized as a Highly Urbanized City (HUC) and is a thriving first income class city known as the industrial heartland of Cebu. In 2019, Mandaue City separated from the sixth legislative district of Cebu and since 2022, it is represented under its Lone District. 1|Page Every year, upon the request of the City Government of Mandaue, the Office of the President declares August 30 a special non-working day in the city to allow its people to celebrate and participate in its annual celebrations. Fifty-Seven (57) years after the enactment of Republic Act No. 5519, it is high time that Mandaue City’s Charter Anniversary be declared a special non-working holiday through legislation. In doing so, the people of Mandaue City will automatically be given an opportunity to recognize the men and women who has contributed to the city’s progress and development as well as encourage the full participation of Mandauehanons in the annual cultural celebration while ruminating on its historic founding in 1969. For the foregoing reasons, the passage of this proposed legislative measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A BUSINESS PERMIT AND LICENSING OFFICE IN EVERY CITY OR MUNICIPALITY IN THE COUNTRY AND MAKING THE POSITION OF A BUSINESS PERMIT AND LICENSING OFFICER MANDATORY IN EVERY CITY OR MUNICIPALITY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 171, 175, 176, 177, 178, 179, 180, 181, 183, 194, 195, 196, 280, 316, 443, AND 454, AND ADDING SECTION 490-A TO REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11032, or the Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018, was enacted to streamline government procedures, reduce red tape, and improve the delivery of public services. Despite this, challenges persist at the local level, particularly in the processing of business permits and licenses, where fragmented functions and overlapping responsibilities continue to delay transactions and discourage business formation. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Business Permit and Licensing Office (BPLO) in every city and municipality, consolidating the processing of permits, enforcement of tax ordinances, and regulation of business activities under a single office. It also transfers specific revenue-related and enforcement functions from the local treasurer to the Business Permit and Licensing Officer to ensure a more efficient, accountable, and business-friendly system. By strengthening local business permitting systems and clarifying institutional responsibilities, this measure aims to improve ease of doing business at the local level, enhance revenue generation, and promote a more conducive environment for investment and economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought KENNETH T. label: HB 9717
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE BILL OF RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS OF TAXPAYERS, CREATING THE OFFICE OF THE NATIONAL TAXPAYER ADVOCATE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE While recent reforms such as Republic Act No. 11976 or the Ease of Paying Taxes Act have simplified tax compliance, there remains a significant imbalance between the powers of tax authorities and the protection of taxpayer rights. Reports of harassment, abuse of discretion, and lack of accessible remedies continue to undermine public trust in revenue agencies such as the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) and the Bureau of Customs (BOC). Existing laws, including Republic Act No. 6713, provide general standards for public officials but do not sufficiently guarantee enforceable rights and remedies for taxpayers. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Taxpayer Bill of Rights and Obligations (TBORO) that clearly defines the fundamental rights and duties of taxpayers in their interactions with tax authorities. It aims to ensure transparency, fairness, due process, and accountability in tax administration, while also promoting voluntary compliance through better taxpayer awareness and protection. The measure likewise proposes the creation of an independent Office of the National Taxpayer Advocate, mandated to assist taxpayers in resolving disputes, address complaints, and safeguard taxpayer rights against abuse, inefficiency, or inaction by revenue agencies. By strengthening taxpayer protection mechanisms, this bill seeks to foster greater public trust, improve compliance, and ultimately enhance revenue collection. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9718
title: AN ACT PRESCRIBING MANDATORY GUIDELINES ON THE ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION OF LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Within the last few years, the demand for tertiary education in the country has steadily increased. From 26.63% in 2018, it has increased to 49.9% in 2024, reflecting a 23% percent increase in just six years. To respond to this growing demand, more local universities and colleges (LUCs) have been opened, increasing from 95 in 2011 to 174 in 2024. The expansion of LUCs has enabled thousands of Filipino students to access higher education and complete their studies, particularly those from underserved communities. However, despite their critical role, LUCs remain structurally vulnerable due to their dependence on local government units. Their operations, funding, and policy direction are largely influenced by the priorities of local chief executives and the Sanggunian, making them highly susceptible to political transitions. This dynamic undermines institutional stability. Funding allocations and scholarship programs are often subject to shifting political interests, resulting in inconsistent support for students and academic programs. The absence of long-term planning and institutional safeguards has contributed to persistent challenges, including limited research capacity, inadequate infrastructure, gaps in faculty development, and weak quality assurance and evaluation systems. 1 Local universities and colleges serve as vital instruments for democratizing access to higher education. They provide affordable and community-based learning opportunities, helping bridge educational disparities across regions. LUCs also contribute to local development by producing a skilled workforce attuned to the specific needs of their communities. This measure seeks to strengthen the institutional capacity, governance, and sustainability of LUCs by establishing clear standards, ensuring stable and adequate funding mechanisms, and promoting merit-based and transparent systems for scholarships and administration. It aims to insulate LUCs from undue political interference, enhance quality assurance mechanisms, and support long-term development through faculty training, infrastructure investment, and research support. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9719
title: AN ACT RENAMING THE LITERACY COORDINATING COUNCIL TO THE NATIONAL LITERACY COUNCIL, STRENGTHENING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, STREAMLINING ITS MEMBERSHIP STRUCTURE, PROVIDING ITS LOCAL SUPPORT MECHANISMS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7165, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Literacy Coordinating Council (LCC) was established under Republic Act No. 7165 in 1991 to lead the country’s efforts in eradicating illiteracy, and was later strengthened by Republic Act No. 10122 in 2010 to expand its coordination and partnership functions. Despite these measures, universal literacy remains unmet. Based on the 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS), 93.1% of Filipinos aged 10 to 64 are basically literate, leaving about 5.87 million unable to read, write, or perform basic computations. More notably, only 70.8% are functionally literate, meaning around 24.8 million Filipinos lack higher-order comprehension and critical thinking skills. These gaps highlight persistent challenges in literacy and education outcomes, underscoring the need for stronger coordination and more responsive institutional mechanisms. This bill seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 7165 and transform the LCC into the National Literacy Council, with strengthened powers, a streamlined structure, and better alignment with Republic Act No. 11510 (Alternative Learning System Act) and Republic Act No. 11315 (Community-Based Monitoring System Act). It transfers the Council’s secretariat to the Bureau of Alternative Education and designates Local School Boards as local literacy bodies to strengthen community-level implementation. 1 The measure also mandates a three-year national literacy roadmap, with clear targets and data-driven strategies, to be mirrored at the local level. By improving coordination, strengthening local support, and institutionalizing long-term planning, this measure aims to accelerate the achievement of universal literacy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9720
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL EDUCATION COUNCIL, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The education system in the Philippines has undergone numerous reforms throughout its long history, reflecting continuing efforts to improve access, governance, and outcomes. Among the most significant of these was the 1991 Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM), which recommended the restructuring of the system to enhance efficiency and accountability. This led to the tri-focalization of education in 1994, establishing separate agencies for basic education, higher education, and technical-vocational training. While this structure enabled each sub-sector to focus on its respective mandate, it also resulted in fragmentation, coordination gaps, and inconsistencies in policies and programs. Recognizing these challenges, subsequent reforms sought to establish mechanisms for alignment, including the creation of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) in 2000. However, these efforts were not sustained, leaving the system without a permanent and institutionalized body to ensure coherence across all levels of education. As a result, the Philippine education system continues to face issues in coordination, efficiency, and overall performance. The absence of a central coordinating mechanism has limited the alignment of programs with national development goals and constrained long-term, strategic planning. 1 This bill seeks to address these gaps by establishing a National Education Council that will serve as the central body for coordination, planning, monitoring, and evaluation across the three education sub-sectors. It aims to align policies and programs, promote long-term strategic direction, and strengthen collaboration among government agencies, local government units, the private sector, and other key stakeholders. By institutionalizing a unified and permanent coordinating mechanism, this measure seeks to reduce fragmentation, improve governance, and enhance the overall effectiveness of the Philippine education system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9721
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL POLICY AND FRAMEWORK FOR ENERGY ADVOCACY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), restructured the power sector into a competitive but regulated industry and established the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to ensure consumer protection and fair market operations. While the ERC performs a critical balancing role in rate-setting and regulation, there remains a clear gap in the representation of end-users in its proceedings. This bill seeks to address this gap by creating an Energy Advocate Office (EAO), led by an Energy Advocate, to serve as the independent representative of consumers in all rate-setting, rule-making, and other energy- related proceedings before government, judicial, and quasi-judicial bodies. By institutionalizing consumer representation, the measure aims to strengthen regulatory oversight, promote fairness in decision-making, and help ensure more reasonable electricity rates. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9722
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NURSING HOME FOR HOMELESS AND ABANDONED SENIOR CITIZENS IN EVERY CITY OR MUNICIPALITY IN THE PHILIPPINES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino culture has long upheld the value of caring for the elderly within the family. However, cases of abandonment and neglect of senior citizens are increasing due to financial constraints, family conflicts, and the inability of caregivers to provide adequate support. Some local government units have taken steps to address this gap. In Valenzuela City, facilities such as Bahay Kalinga and Bahay Kanlungan Tahanan nina Lolo at Lola provide shelter, healthcare, and daily support for homeless and abandoned senior citizens. Despite these efforts, such facilities remain limited, leaving many elderly Filipinos without proper care and protection. Aligned with the State’s duty to protect the welfare of senior citizens, this bill seeks to institutionalize a nationwide framework for the establishment of nursing homes for homeless and abandoned elderly in every city and municipality. These facilities shall be constructed by local government units and operated and maintained by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) in coordination with LGUs. This measure complements Republic Act No. 7876, or the “Senior Citizens Center Act,” by ensuring that vulnerable elderly individuals not only have access to community programs, but also to residential care when family support is no longer available. 1 By strengthening institutional support and expanding access to care facilities, this bill aims to uphold the dignity and welfare of senior citizens, particularly those most in need. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9723
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A NEW SEPARATION, RETIREMENT, AND PENSION SYSTEM FOR THE MILITARY AND THE UNIFORMED PERSONNEL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The necessity for reform in the system of benefits for the military and uniformed personnel has never been more urgent in light of the unexpected spending brought about by the ongoing war in Gulf area. The reality of the budgetary burden should of course not turn a blind eye on our Constitutional duty to ensure professionalism in the service and adequate remuneration and benefits of its members. Reformation in the system of benefits is an appropriate response in recognition of the invaluable role of the military and uniformed personnel in protecting the nation and its citizens from various threats. This bill intends to find a balance between the existing ballooning financial burden of meeting the benefits to uniformed personnel and ensuring provision on adequate remuneration and benefits to them. It is after all the State’s constitutional duty to, from time to time, review the pensions and other benefits due to retirees of both the government and the private sectors. Accordingly, this bill primarily intends to establish a Uniformed Personnel Trust Fund Committee in order to establish a system of contributions that would ensure the continuity of the benefits. The immediate passage of this bill is most earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9724
title: AN ACT REDUCING THE MINIMUM SERVICE REQUIREMENT FOR RETIREMENT BENEFITS UNDER THE GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997 FROM FIFTEEN (15) YEARS TO TEN (10) YEARS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1146, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Across countries, retirement planning reflects a common goal: to preserve one’s standard of living after leaving the workforce. It enables retirees to be self-sufficient, ensuring that they have enough resources to maintain their daily needs and maintain financial security. In the Philippines, government workers receive retirement benefits through the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), while self-employed individuals, informal sector workers, Overseas Filipino Workers, Non-Working Spouses, and private-sector employees receive them through the Social Security System (SSS). Currently, eligibility for retirement benefits under the Government Service Insurance System Act of 1997 depends largely on age and years of service – a member must be at least sixty (60) years old, have rendered a minimum of fifteen (15) years of government service, and must not be receiving a monthly disability pension. This framework effectively requires individuals planning to retire at age 60 to enter government service no later than age 45 and to maintain continuous, qualifying service thereafter. In reality, this pathway is not easily attainable. Many Filipinos spend years securing eligibility through the civil service system and obtaining stable government employment. 1 As of September 2025, the Government Service Insurance System reports over 2.77 million members and pensioners, yet only a fraction of active members are likely to complete the 15-year requirement and qualify for retirement benefits. In contrast, the Social Security System adopts a more flexible, contribution-based approach. A member needs at least 120 monthly contributions (equivalent to 10 years) to qualify for a monthly pension, with no requirement of continuous employment. Those who fall short receive a lump sum benefit instead. This allows workers with interrupted or non-linear career paths to still qualify for retirement support. Given these differences, there is a compelling basis to revisit the current GSIS framework. This bill proposes to reduce the minimum service requirement from fifteen (15) to ten (10) years, aligning it more closely with SSS standards and making retirement benefits more accessible to government workers. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is respectfully sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9725
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MODERNIZATION, CAPACITY BUILDING, AND ORGANIZATIONAL STRENGTHENING OF THE NATIONAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION (NBI), APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In recent years, the Philippines has uncovered the presence of transnational organized crimes within its borders, ranging from illegal gambling and large-scale scams to cybercrime and human trafficking. These operations persisted for years despite existing enforcement structures, underscoring gaps in detection, intelligence-sharing, and investigative capacity. While the Philippine National Police is primarily responsible for maintaining peace and order at the local level, the National Bureau of Investigation is mandated to investigate complex, transnational, and high- profile crimes, including graft and corruption, cybercrime, and human trafficking. However, the rapidly evolving nature of these threats—driven by digital platforms, encrypted communications, and cross-border syndicates— demands a corresponding upgrade in the NBI’s technological, forensic, and intelligence capabilities. At present, constraints in funding, equipment, and personnel limit the NBI’s ability to fully perform its mandate. Many of its investigative processes remain constrained by outdated tools, insufficient forensic infrastructure, and limited access to advanced cybercrime technologies. Moreover, the increasing 1 volume and sophistication of cases require highly specialized training, inter- agency coordination, and sustained investment in modern investigative systems. This bill seeks to address these gaps by providing dedicated modernization funding for the NBI and strengthening its institutional structure. It aims to support the acquisition of advanced forensic equipment, enhancement of cybercrime and intelligence capabilities, development of modern digital investigative systems, and expansion of specialized services within the Bureau. It likewise promotes improved personnel welfare and professional development, as well as a more sustainable funding mechanism through authorized retention of service-related revenues, ensuring the long- term operational efficiency of the agency. By investing in the institutional strength of the NBI, the State affirms its commitment to upholding the rule of law, protecting national security, and ensuring that justice is swift, effective, and responsive to emerging threats. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9726
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF THE OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Out-of-school youth (OSY) remain one of the most vulnerable yet underutilized sectors in Philippine society. Despite existing programs under the Alternative Learning System (ALS), Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET), and various social protection mechanisms, significant gaps persist in coordination, accessibility, and long-term reintegration. Many OSYs continue to face systemic barriers such as poverty, lack of access to education, unemployment, social exclusion, and exposure to exploitation and abuse. Current interventions are largely fragmented across agencies, resulting in duplication of efforts, inefficient delivery of services, and limited measurable outcomes. More importantly, there is no comprehensive rights-based framework that explicitly recognizes OSYs as a distinct sector entitled to targeted protection, opportunities, and government support. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth, anchored on human rights, substantive equality, and inclusive development. It establishes a unified policy framework that consolidates government efforts and mandates a whole-of-government and multi-stakeholder approach toward the empowerment of OSYs. The bill provides for the recognition and protection of the rights of OSYs, including protection from discrimination, violence, and exploitation; guaranteed access to education through ALS, TVET, and pathways to formal tertiary education; expanded employment, entrepreneurship, and livelihood opportunities through coordinated programs of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), Technical 1 Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and Department of Trade and Industry (DTI); comprehensive social protection measures, including health, insurance, and social services; special interventions for OSYs in especially difficult circumstances; strengthened institutional mechanisms, including a national database, localized profiling, and coordinated implementation across national and local government units; and clear accountability measures and penalties for violations of the rights of OSYs. By investing in the development of OSYs, the State not only fulfills its constitutional mandate to promote social justice and human dignity, but also unlocks a critical segment of the population that can significantly contribute to national development. This measure ensures that no young Filipino is left behind—not by circumstance, not by system failure, and not by lack of opportunity. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9727
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7638 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY ACT OF 1992
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The energy industry is one of the most highly technical and specialized sectors, where expertise is developed through extensive knowledge, experience, and industry exposure. As the principal agency responsible for the formulation and implementation of the country’s energy policies, the Department of Energy (DOE) requires leadership that possesses not only competence and integrity, but also a deep understanding of the complexities of the energy sector. At present, existing law imposes restrictions that may disqualify otherwise qualified individuals from appointment as Secretary of the DOE solely on the basis of prior affiliations with energy industry participants. While safeguards against conflicts of interest remain essential, such restrictions may unnecessarily limit the pool of competent and experienced professionals capable of leading the Department. This measure seeks to remove the prohibitive provision while strengthening transparency and accountability mechanisms. To prevent conflicts of interest, the bill mandates the public disclosure of prior industry involvement, the divestment of any financial interests in energy-related entities, and the termination of any employment, consultancy, directorship, or 1 other connections with energy industry participants upon assumption of office. By allowing highly qualified and experienced professionals to serve in the DOE, subject to strict conflict-of-interest safeguards, this bill aims to strengthen the country’s energy governance and policy implementation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 9728
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE NET-METERING PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9513, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE RENEWABLE ENERGY ACT OF 2008
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9513, otherwise known as the Renewable Energy Act of 2008, declares it a policy of the State to promote the development and utilization of renewable energy systems through fiscal and non-fiscal incentives. One of the key mechanisms under the law is the net-metering program, which allows qualified end-users to install renewable energy systems, generate their own electricity, and export excess power to the grid. Through this program, consumers become “prosumers,” enabling them to reduce electricity costs, protect themselves from energy price volatility, and contribute to cleaner and more sustainable energy generation. Despite its benefits, the net-metering program remains underutilized. As of 31 December 2024, only 15,605 qualified end-users nationwide participate in the program, with a significant concentration in Luzon and very limited participation in Mindanao. This may be attributed to the existing 100- kilowatt cap, which restricts participation by larger electricity consumers, as well as the cumbersome and fragmented permitting and application process. This measure seeks to strengthen and expand the net-metering program by removing the rigid 100-kW cap and authorizing the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to determine appropriate capacity limits based on grid 1 stability and consumer welfare considerations. The bill likewise mandates the streamlining and rationalization of permitting and documentary requirements, including those imposed by local government units, consistent with the timelines under the Energy Virtual One Stop Shop Act. label: HB 9737
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE KATARUNGANG PAMBARANGAY SYSTEM BY PROVIDING NATIONAL AND LOCAL SUPPORT MECHANISMS FOR THE LUPON NG TAGAPAMAYAPA, INSTITUTIONALIZING TRAINING-BASED INCENTIVES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Katarungang Pambarangay system under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, particularly under Title I, book III (Sections 399-422), serves as the State’s primary mechanism for community-based dispute resolution. It promotes the amicable settlement of disputes at the barangay level, thereby decongesting court dockets, reducing litigation costs, and preserving social harmony within communities. At the core of this system is the Lupon ng Tagapamayapa, constituted pursuant to Section 399 of the Local Government Code, and vested with mediation and conciliation functions under Sections 40 to 404 thereof. Lupon members, who are appointed by the Punong Barangay, perform quasi-judicial dispute resolution functions without compensation, motivated largely by civic and community service. While the law recognizes the importance of the Lupon, existing provisions on support mechanisms remain largely decentralized and discretionary, resulting in uneven implementation across local government units. Although Section 393 (d) of the Local Government Code authorizes the grant of allowances, honoraria, and other emoluments to barangay officials and personnel subject to budgetary limitations, there is no uniform national framework specifically addressing the welfare, training, and incentives of Lupon members. Further, while the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has issued administrative guidelines to strengthen KP implementation, including training programs and performance monitoring, these remain policy- based and not statutorily institutionalized, resulting in gaps in capacity- building, standardization, and sustainability. This measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a national support framework for Lupon members, providing a carefully structured, non- salaried honorarium that respects the fiscal autonomy of local government units and avoids the creation of an employer-employee relationship, and linking incentives to training, certification, and performance standards. It likewise strengthens capacity-building mechanisms and ensures the professionalization of Lupon service while preserving its community-based and voluntary character. In strengthening the Katarungang Pambarangay system, this measure affirms the State’s commitment to accessible, efficient, and culturally responsive justice at the barangay level. This measure does not convert Lupon members into government employees, nor does it create Plantilla positions. Instead, it streghthens an existing Despite their crucial role, Lupon members often receive uneven and inadequate support, with incentives varying widely depending on local government income classification. This disparity affects morale, capacity, and the overall effectiveness of barangay-based dispute resolution, particularly in low-income and geographically isolated communities. This measure seeks to strengthen the Katarungang Pambarangay system by providing a nationally supported, fiscally responsible framework for Lupon assistance. It establishes a nationally funded, minimum honorarium, subject to training and certification, and authorizes tiered incentives tied to capacity- building and performance. It preserves the voluntary and non-salaried nature of Lupon service, avoids the creation of Plantilla positions, and respects fiscal autonomy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 9738
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FAIR DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES IN DIGITAL AND TRADITIONAL LENDING, STRENGTHENING REGULATION OF ONLINE LENDING PLATFORMS, ESTABLISHING A VERIFIED COLLECTION IDENTITY SYSTEM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid expansion of online lending applications (OLAs) in the Philippines has significantly transformed access to credit, particularly among underserved and financially vulnerable sectors. Recent industry data indicate that millions of Filipinos have availed themselves of digital lending services, driven largely by ease of access, minimal documentation requirements, and immediate fund disbursement. However, this rapid growth has also been accompanied by a surge in complaints involving abusive, deceptive, and predatory debt collection practices. Records from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the National Privacy Commission (NPC) show a significant number of grievances involving harassment, threats, and unauthorized disclosure of personal data by online lending entities and their agents. In several reported cases, borrowers have been subjected to repeated threatening messages, public shaming, and the dissemination of personal information to third parties, in clear violation of existing laws and regulations. The SEC, through SEC Memorandum Circular No. 18, Series of 2019, has expressly prohibited unfair debt collection practices, including the use of threats, insults, and disclosure of borrower information to unauthorized persons. Despite these regulatory measures, enforcement remains challenging due to the increasing use of anonymized communication channels, such as unregistered mobile numbers, email accounts, and social media platforms, which allow abusive actors to evade identification and accountability. While existing statutes such as the Lending Company Regulation Act of 2007, the Data Privacy Act of 2012, and the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 provide mechanisms to regulate lending practices, protect personal data, and penalize cyber-related offenses, these laws do not sufficiently address the unique and evolving challenges posed by digital lending platforms—particularly the traceability and accountability of collection agents operating in online environments. This measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a comprehensive regulatory framework governing online lending and digital debt collection practices. It introduces a Verified Collection Identity System (VCIS), which requires all lending entities and their agents to register and utilize traceable and verifiable communication channels in the course of collection activities. This system aims to eliminate anonymity in debt collection and ensure that all collection-related communications can be properly attributed and regulated. The bill further strengthens protections for borrowers by codifying prohibited collection practices, enhancing transparency requirements, and providing clear mechanisms for enforcement and redress. It likewise aligns penalties with existing penal laws, including applicable provisions of the Revised Penal Code, the Data Privacy Act, and the Cybercrime Prevention Act, thereby ensuring that violations committed through digital means are met with appropriate civil, administrative, and criminal sanctions. Ultimately, this proposed legislation affirms the State’s policy to protect consumers from abusive and unethical lending practices, safeguard the right to privacy, and promote fairness, accountability, and transparency in the digital financial sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D.
