title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROVISION OF COMPREHENSIVE RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) TO PATIENTS WITH END STAGE RENAL DISEASE IN NATIONAL, REGIONAL, AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT HOSPITALS, INCREASING FOR THE PURPOSE THE PHILHEALTH PACKAGE RATE FOR MEMBERS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Renal diseases are the fourth leading cause of death among Filipinos, according to the 2019 Global Burden of Disease, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study. 1 Meanwhile, according to the National Kidney and Transplant Institute, one Filipino develops chronic kidney disease (CKD) every 40 minutes, equivalent to 36 Filipinos getting the renal disease in a single day. In 2021, there are more than 7 million Filipinos with CKD.2 Moreover, one Filipino dies from kidney failure every hour.3 The number of patients undergoing dialysis is increasing every year. From 4,000 dialysis patients in 2004 recorded by the Department of Health (DOH), the number rose 1 Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation: Philippines profile. University of Washington, 2021. http://www.healthdata.org/philippines. 2 De Villa, Kathleen. “Chronic kidney disease: 1 Filipino develops it every 40 minutes,” Inquirer.net, 25 July 2022, https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1616181/chronic-kidney-disease-1-filipino-develops-it- every-40-minutes 3 “UP webinar takes on the challenges of kidney disease and dialysis in a time of COVID,” University of the Philippines, 1 December 2020, https://up.edu.ph/up-webinar-takes-on-the-challenges-of- kidney-disease-and-dialysis-in-a-time-of-covid/. 1 to 23,000 by 2013. For two-to-three times dialysis sessions a week, a patient has to spend ₱25,000 to ₱46,000 a month or ₱300,000 to ₱552,000 a year. On top of this, maintenance medication also costs about ₱20,000 a month.4 With an average monthly income of patients with CKD at only ₱4,838.16, most of them could not afford treatment, according to a 2013 research. In 2015, some 691,489 claims were filed by PhilHealth for hemodialysis, the most among procedures covered by the agency. The total benefits paid were ₱4.67 billion. Yet, patients with PhilHealth coverage can only claim half of the cost of their treatment. According to the National Kidney and Transplant Institute (NKTI), only 15% of the partially-subsidized patients are PhilHealth members.5 Because of the high cost of hemodialysis, poor patients had to beg around for funds to pay for their treatment. Many of them regularly solicit funds at the offices of the Members of Congress, Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, and offices of political parties and charitable organizations. Poor kidney patients survive, either at the cost of being in deep debt or after begging around. Dialysis services are inadequate especially in regions and far flung areas. Even NKTI, the government’s specialty health facility for kidney transplant and kidney- related diseases, was only able to serve, out of the total 2,694 outpatients served in January 2015, 27% or 723 service patients and 1,971 or 73% were pay patients. The NKTI said that with limited income and resources, it can hardly afford to expand its services. While there are regional or provincial hospitals with dialysis facilities, most are presumably just like in NKTI, where there is no free treatment for renal diseases. In 2015, during the 16th Congress, the House of Representatives approved House Bill 5956 mandating the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation to increase the coverage for dialysis treatment to ninety (90) sessions per year. PhilHealth accordingly issued Circular 024-2015 (August 27, 2015) that increased the dialysis sessions covered by PhilHealth from 45 to 90 sessions per year and pegged hemodialysis cost to ₱2,600 per session from the previous ₱4,000 per session. In 2024, PhilHealth further expanded the coverage for dialysis treatment to 156 sessions per year. The new hemodialysis package includes facilities and dialysis machine use, drugs and medicine (0.9 sodium chloride, heparin, bicarbonate or acetate hemodialysis solution, e cart drugs), supplies and others (fistula kits, blood tubing, dialyzer [low flux], syringe, and gauze), and professional fee. However, the new package no longer includes the injection of epoetin alfa or beta previously included in the old PhilHealth’s case rate for hemodialysis. 4 “The worsening problem of renal diseases,” Council for Health and Development, 16 June 2015, https://web.archive.org/web/20190816111852/http://www. chdphilippines.org/2015/06/the- worsening-problem-of-renal-diseases. 5 Ibid. 2 Patients complained of increased out-of-pocket expenses in the form of co-pay mechanisms and injections and laboratory procedures which they now have to shoulder. According to the Hemodialysis Patient Organization, the co-pay charge per session was increased by ₱350-P550 per hemodialysis session. Injection of epoetin drug costs ₱1,200-2,400 per session, bringing the cash-out of patients to ₱1,500 to ₱3,000 per hemodialysis session. In 2016, the monthly cash-out of patients can run as high as P13,752 to P19,054. The amount does not even include the laboratory procedure expenses. According to NKTI,6 the hospital has to charge co-pay, otherwise, it would incur losses as a result of the reduction of PhilHealth benefits. In response to the clamor of dialysis patients, Bayan Muna Party-List Representatives filed House Resolution 1761 to investigate the plight of peritoneal dialysis patients during the 16th Congress, and a similar HR 244 during the 17th Congress. HR 244 became one of the measures consolidated into House Bill 9156 or the Comprehensive Renal Replacement Therapy Act which was passed on third reading. During the 18th Congress, Bayan Muna Representatives Carlos Isagani T. Zarate, Ferdinand R. Gaite and Eufemia C. Cullamat, ACT Teachers Party-List Representative France L. Castro, Gabriela Women’s Party Representative Arlene D. Brosas and Kabataan Party-List Representative Sarah Jane I. Elago filed HB 251 as one of their priority legislations. This Bill was again passed on Third Reading as HB 6803. Accessibility and affordability of dialysis treatment and renal transplantation may spell the difference between life and death for many end stage renal disease patients, especially the indigents. label: HB 9745
title: AN ACT DEFINING STRATEGIC LAWSUITS AGAINST PUBLIC PARTICIPATION, PROHIBITING THE FILING THEREOF, PROVIDING MEASURES FOR ITS DISMISSAL, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 23 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 26 The past several years have witnessed the proliferation of a special kind of harassment suit called Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPP) as a powerful mechanism for stifling the cognate rights of freedom of speech, expression, or of the press, and the right of the people peaceably to assemble and petition the government for redress of grievances. 32 SLAPP defies simple definition. They are initiated by influential entities like corporations, government officials, politicians, landlords, or employers against community residents, indigenous peoples, environmentalists, members of the press, peasants, workers, students, or even against ordinary citizens to prevent them from fully exercising their right to participate in matters of public concern. 38 The term SLAPP was coined in the 1980s by University of Denver professors Penelope Canan and George W. Pring. It was originally defined as “a lawsuit involving communications made to petition for a governmental action or outcome, which resulted in a baseless suit filed against individuals or non-governmental organizations, on a substantive issue of some public interest or social significance.” It has since been defined more broadly to include suits arising from speech on any public issue. 45 1 Essentially, SLAPPs are designed and intended to intimidate and silence certain public constituencies by burdening them with the cost of a legal defense until they abandon their advocacies and concerns. Winning the lawsuit is not necessarily the intent of the plaintiff or complainant. Their goals are accomplished if the defendant, respondent or accused succumbs to fear, intimidation, mounting legal costs or simple exhaustion and thereby abandons the public advocacy. 7 According to New York Supreme Court Judge J. Nicholas Colabella, “Short of a gun to the head, a greater threat to First Amendment expression can scarcely be imagined.” 11 SLAPPs are cloaked as claims or accusations for multi-million libel suits, slander, grave coercion, nuisance, illegal assembly, direct assault, resistance and disobedience, and injunction, to name a few. 15 In the Philippines, for instance, a notable SLAPP case involves the charges against fifteen (15) individuals in connection with the evacuation of some 700 Lumads to a church sanctuary in Davao City. The Lumads left their homes because of alleged human rights violations and militarization in their communities. The Haran 15, as they are collectively called, are composed of human rights workers, church people, prominent members of indigenous peoples and socio-civic groups, who were charged with kidnapping and illegal detention. The case was eventually dismissed by the Department of Justice after finding no probable cause for the commission of the accused crime. 25 For all the diversity of SLAPPs, however, their unifying features make them a dangerous force: they are brought not in pursuit of justice but rather to ensnare their targets in costly litigation that distracts them from the controversy at hand, and to deter them and others from engaging in their rights of speech and petition on issues of public concern. 31 Hence, the poor and the marginalized sectors, who have become the usual victims of SLAPPs, find it difficult to continue their work or pursue their livelihood, engage in social and participative actions, and assert their civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights as they are being burdened, restrained, threatened, or distressed by SLAPPs. 37 The inequality of wealth and resources between the rich and the poor, the abuse of power and processes, the lack of independence and impartiality of prosecutors and judges, among other reasons, bring about these SLAPPs. 41 In other jurisdictions, particularly in Canada, Europe, and twenty-six (26) States and one (1) territory of the United States, to name a few, the disturbing increase in SLAPPs has led said jurisdictions to either enact anti-SLAPP legislations or promulgate rules against SLAPPs. 2 1 Hence, this proposed measure is being filed as a concrete step to address the societal problems caused by SLAPPs in the Philippines, particularly the achievement of the following purposes: 5 a. Promote and protect the constitutional rights of freedom of speech, expression, and of the press, and the right of the people peaceably to assembly, and petition the government for redress of grievances; b. Encourage and strengthen the participation of individuals in matters of public concern; c. Prevent any abuse of the judicial process that shall curtail such participation; d. Prohibit the filing of SLAPPs; e. Establish the speedy dismissal of SLAPPs; f. Award damages, litigation costs, attorney’s fees, and other relief to the defendant, respondent, or accused, as the case may be, upon the final and executory dismissal of SLAPPs; and g. Provide the defendant, respondent, or accused, as the case may be, the right to recover separate damages, litigations costs, attorney’s fees, and other relief by filing a SLAPPBack action against the complainant of a SLAPP upon the final and executory dismissal of such SLAPP. 21 This Bill was first filed in February 2009, authored by Bayan Muna Party-List Reps. Satur Ocampo and Teodoro Casiño, aiming to prohibit the filing of harassment cases against persons involved in “public interest advocacies.” It was refiled by Bayan Muna Partylist representatives Neri Colmenares and Carlos Isagani Zarate in the 16th Congress in recognition of the need for the protection against legal harassment of people in the environment, human rights and other socio-civic advocacies. It was refiled by the Makabayan Bloc in the succeeding Congresses. 29 It is in this light that the approval of this proposed measure is earnestly sought. 31 32 REP. ANTONIO L. title: AN ACT EXEMPTING JOURNALISTS FROM ACTING AS ANTI-DRUG OPERATIONS WITNESSES AND AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT 10640, ENTITLED “AN ACT TO FURTHER STRENGTHEN THE ANTI- CAMPAIGN DRUG OF THE CAMPAIGN GOVERNMENTTO OF THE GOVERNMENT," FURTHER STRENGTHEN AMENDING THE FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 21 OF REPUBLIC ANTI-DRUG ACT 9165, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “COMPREHENSIVE DANGEROUS DRUGS ACT OF 2002” 26 27
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 29 In the past years, the Philippine National Police has increased its reliance on journalists to act as witnesses to the inventory of contraband and other items seized during anti-drug operations. This practice, however, has always been met with resistance by both individual journalists and media groups from all over the country. 34 The practice was first made a legal requirement under Section 21 (1) of Republic Act 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002, which mandates: 37 The apprehending team having initial custody and control of the drugs shall, immediately after seizure and confiscation, physically inventory and photograph the same in the presence of the accused or the person/s from whom such items were confiscated and/or seized, or his/her representative or counsel, a representative from the media and the Department of Justice (DOJ), and any elected public official who shall be required to sign the copies of the inventory and be given a copy thereof… 45 Although this provision has since been amended by Republic Act 10640 (July 15, 2014) and media witnesses were made merely optional, journalists throughout the country report that law enforcement units continue to require them to sign on as 1 witnesses, often as a condition for being allowed to cover anti-drug operations. Worse, there are reports that they are made to sign even if they did not actually witness the operation or the inventory of seized items. 4 Journalists who decline find their sources or the normal channels of information no longer accessible. 7 Aside from the obvious coercion and attempts to control information of vital interest to the public, the media’s opposition to this practice also stems from the fact that it unnecessarily places journalists at risk of retaliation from crime syndicates, on the one hand, and exposes them to prosecution for perjury and other offenses in the event of irregularities in the conduct of anti-drug operations, on the other. 13 To end this dangerous and unfair practice, it is imperative that this Congress, in the exercise of its mandate to take every conceivable step to protect journalists from harm as well as to help ensure that their reportage remain objective and factual, pass in the most expeditious manner an amendment to laws that engender such situations. 18 For these reasons, the passage of this Bill is most urgently sought. label: HB 9749
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MANDATORY APPOINTMENT OF A MUNICIPAL VETERINARIAN OFFICER, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991'' 24 25
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 27 The Philippines is an agricultural country, with the livelihood of the majority of its population directly dependent on farming. Farming generally includes, through both backyard and commercial operations, the raising and production of farm animals such as cattle, carabao, goat, hog, chicken and duck. 32 From 2001 to 2013, according to the Bureau of Agricultural Statistics (BAS), the country’s average annual production of carabao was at 137.68 metric thousand tons, while cattle was at 250.98 thousand metric tons. For the same period, average annual production of hog was at 1,826.65 thousand metric tons, goat was at 76.13 thousand metric tons, chicken was at 1,285.40 thousand metric tons, and duck was at 43.24 thousand metric tons. 39 In 2024, according to data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, the country’s production of carabao was at 129.76 thousand metric tons, while cattle was at 233.33 thousand metric tons. Production of hog was at 1,708.79 thousand metric tons, goat was at 67.43 thousand metric tons, chicken was at 2,080.25 thousand metric tons, and duck was at 26.96 thousand metric tons. 45 1 Based on the October 2024 national livestock and poultry data of the Philippine Statistics Office, the number of farm animals in both backyard and commercial farms are as follows: 49 Type of Semi- Smallhold Commercial Total Animals Commercial Carabao 2,650,842 16,141 3,403 2,670,386 Cattle 2,181,203 338,648 58,387 2,578,238 Goat 3,776,453 12,221 12,427 3,801,101 Duck 6,481,953 254,263 2,360,212 9,096,428 Hog 9,629,567 4,447,876 358,979 14,436,422 By number of heads 51 Chicken Type No. of heads Broilers 79,426,043 Layers 48,638,960 Native/improved 82,753,055 Gamefowl 9,804,126 Total 220,622,184 By number of heads 53 Most animal raising and production farms are found in rural or far-flung areas in the country where there is, unfortunately, despite the consistently high rate of livestock and poultry production, a pervasive dearth of veterinary services. This can be largely attributable to the fact that the law, particularly Republic Act No. 7160 or The Local Government Code of 1991, specifies that only provincial and city governments are mandatorily required to appoint a veterinarian officer, leaving a great number of municipalities for the most part deprived of access to much-needed public veterinary support and assistance. 62 Animal raisers, especially those engaged in backyard operations and are poor, usually cannot afford the services of private veterinarians. They are often made to wait for the provincial or city veterinarian to visit their area, a very rare occasion, in fact, which comes at no certain time. 67 Backyard animal raisers are, thus, practically left to themselves in treating animal diseases. They employ traditional forms and ways that do not necessarily guarantee either a quick fix or the prevention of such diseases from being transmitted to other animals or, worse, to people. There are obviously animal diseases, such as cat scratch disease, mad cow disease, and brucellosis, among others, that need the immediate attention and professional expertise of duly licensed veterinarians. 74 Moreover, failure to properly treat animal diseases naturally jeopardizes the supply of livestock and poultry products in the market, to the detriment of the public and the economy. 78 2 Thus, this Bill, filed previously in the 15th, 16th and 17th congresses by former Anakpawis representatives Rafael Mariano, Fernando Hicap, and Ariel Casilao respectively, is here being refiled with the intent of amending certain provisions of Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991 in order to prescribe the mandatory appointment of veterinarian officers not only in provincial and city governments but also in municipal units. 85 This legislative measure seeks to decisively address the proliferation of contagious and harmful animal diseases in the countryside and the immediate delivery of public veterinary services to far-flung villages where the raising and production of farm animals is concentrated. 90 This measure also aims to expand certain functions and duties of a veterinarian officer in order to more adequately and regularly serve the veterinary needs of remote communities. 94 In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this Bill is urgently sought. 96 REP. label: HB 9750
title: AN ACT WITHHOLDING OPERATIONAL FUNDS OF UNITS OF THE ARMED FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES AND THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE IMPLICATED IN GROSS HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS 23 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 26 Under the Arroyo administration, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) gained international notoriety for its alleged involvement in a significant number of extrajudicial killings and involuntary disappearances of citizens, many of whom were activists opposed to the administration's policies and programs. Such gross violations drew the attention not only of human rights organizations such as Amnesty International (AI) and Human Rights Watch (HRW), but also the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Summary and Extrajudicial Killings, Philip Alston, and even the United States Senate Defense Committee led by Sen. Barbara Boxer. All acknowledged a link between human rights violations and the AFP's counterinsurgency program, then known as Oplan Bantay Laya. Many noted that the so-called “climate of impunity” enabled perpetrators to commit violations on such a scale. 38 The passage of the years and changing of administrations saw only the worsening of the human rights climate in the country. The HRW noted that, under the Aquino administration, “several key institutions, including law enforcement agencies and the justice system, remain weak and the military and police commit human rights violations with impunity” (Human Rights Watch World Report 2011). Until now, only a few military and police personnel have been criminally charged, least of all convicted, for human rights violations. 46 1 Duterte—who made no secret of his contempt for human rights and human rights defenders with statements such as “I don’t care about human rights”—has been repeatedly scored for systemic violations of the people’s rights, state terror, violence, and repression under his reign by the United Nations and local and international rights monitors. Under his administration’s bloody anti-illegal drugs campaign, thousands of civilians, including minors, were killed by state forces, particularly by members of the Philippine National Police (PNP). Worse, only three policemen were convicted by local courts for murdering Kian delos Santos, a minor. The majority of perpetrators and masterminds behind the anti-people war on drugs campaign still remain at large without any case filed against them. 11 Furthermore, laws passed during President Duterte’s term, such as the Anti- Terrorism Act, the establishment of the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict, and red-tagging as a state policy, only foreshadow the country becoming a killing field in the coming years—a figurative one, with the death of human rights protection, and a literal killing field, with state agents and paramilitaries emboldened to threaten, harass, then kill citizens. 18 The government should use every tool at its disposal to promote respect for human rights and end impunity, particularly within the ranks of the military and the police. The national budget is one such tool. Experience shows that the release or non- release of funds can be a powerful instrument for promoting reforms and modifying behavior in the ranks of government. This Bill proposes the introduction of a “no impunity provision” in our laws, one that would link the release of operational funds of units of the AFP and the PNP to their compliance with human rights standards. 26 Such a provision will encourage the AFP and PNP chain of command to ensure that their units uphold and respect human rights at all times in the discharge of their duties, even during counterinsurgency operations. Furthermore, it will encourage AFP commanders and PNP chiefs to promptly identify perpetrators and make sure that the proper charges are filed. It also underscores the responsibility of the Secretary of National Defense and the Secretary of Interior Local Government in ensuring that charges are filed against individual perpetrators. For its part, the Commission on Human Rights is given the role of vetting complaints and weeding out spurious allegations. 36 The proposed amendment draws some inspiration from the Leahy Law in the United States, a provision in US foreign aid appropriations legislation introduced by Senator Patrick Leahy that prohibits the granting of US military aid to foreign security forces units with a known track record of gross human rights violations. 41 42 43 44 45 46 2 Approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. 2 REP. label: HB 9751
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE OBSERVANCE OF 23 NOVEMBER OF EVERY YEAR AS NATIONAL CONSCIOUSNESS DAY TO END IMPUNITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 23 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 26 November 23 is the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists as proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 2013 in commemoration of the assassination of two French journalists in Mali on that same day and year. 31 In the Philippines, November 23 is remembered as one of the grimmest incidents where 58 men and women were massacred in Ampatuan town of Maguindanao province in 2009. It is also the worst attack on press freedom in Philippine history because 32 of the victims were media practitioners. Marking it as a National Consciousness Day to End Impunity will remind us that as long as high crimes remain unpunished, the fight against injustice in the country should continue to broaden and persist. 38 The Philippines has been tagged this year by international media groups as one of the most dangerous places for journalists being ranked poorly or is placed among the worst worldwide for unsolved journalist murders. Key witnesses end up dead or forever fear for their lives like the ones in the Maguindanao case who were murdered, with one of them even dismembered and mutilated. 44 1 It took a decade for the Philippines to hand a verdict to the perpetrators of the Maguindanao massacre. In 19 December 2019, Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 221 convicted masterminds Andal Jr. and Zaldy Ampatuan and 26 accomplices, including police officials, of murder, and sentenced them to reclusion perpetua without parole. Meanwhile 15 were convicted as accessories and 56 other people, including Sajid Islam Ampatuan were acquitted.1 7 However, the case was still classified ongoing/unresolved by the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). While there are 58 victims, only 57 murder convictions were handed down in the landmark verdict, excluding photojournalist Reynaldo "Bebot" Momay, who the court recognised as a victim even if his body was not found.2 Moreover, the families of the victims are yet to receive the damages as there are still no resolutions of the appeals on the case.3 Furthermore, nearly 80 other suspects are still at large. 15 Impunity exists whenever perpetrators of a crime are not prosecuted or are not held accountable because of their power or influence in society. Families of the victims of extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and other human rights violations point to state security forces but to no avail. 20 The term “impunity” has attained prominence and common usage during the previous administrations. Former President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s nine-year term suffered from corruption issues, electoral fraud and worsening poverty of its citizens, thus the discontent of the populace over her leadership, and increasing calls for her ouster. As a response to this growing dissent, the human rights situation under Arroyo turned to worse. Determined to stay in power, the administration institutionalized a campaign to repress forces critical of the administration through military and police force. A systematized human rights violation then took place and the result: 1,206 victims of extrajudicial killings and 206 victims of enforced disappearance perpetrated against activists and critics from among workers, peasants, women, indigenous people, students, lawyers, church people, and media practitioners. 32 Until now, no commitments were fulfilled to hold accountable high officials for the massive corruption and fraud under the previous administrations, and also for the gross human rights violations that will in turn serve justice to the people especially the 1 Witchel, Elisabeth. “Ten years for justice in Maguindanao case is too long: We can do better.” Committee to Protect Journalist, 19 December 2019. https://cpj.org/2019/12/ten-years-justice- maguindanao-massacre-impunity-journalists/ 2 “Joint Statement: Ampatuan massacre to remain ‘unresolved.’” International Federation of Journalists, 25 September 2020. https://www.ifj.org/media-centre/news/detail/category/press- releases/article/joint-statement-ampatuan-massacre-to-remain-unresolved.html 3 Buan, Lian. “Maguindanao massacre appeals slow moving, 15 cops may be freed.” Rappler, 23 November 2021. https://www.rappler.com/nation/maguindanao-massacre-appeals-slow-moving-cops- may-be-freed/ 2 victims. Further, killings and enforced disappearance in the context of suppression of civil and political rights has already reached 422 cases for extrajudicial killings and 21 for enforced disappearances under the administration of President Rodrigo Duterte as of July 2016 to June 2022, according to human rights organization Karapatan.4 These killings are on top of the tens of thousands of people killed under the flagship anti-drug policy of the Duterte government. Men, women, pregnant, and children are among the victims of extrajudicial killings under the drug war. 8 In fact, there is a clear lack of intention to investigate the extrajudicial killings under Duterte’s bloody drug war. According to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) in January 2025, only 52 cases were referred to them. Of this number, only 13 were recommended to be prosecuted, seven are still under investigation and 32 were provisionally closed. The families of the victims have already resorted to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in pursuit of justice. However instead of supporting the aggrieved families, President Marcos Jr. refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation “unless permitted by former President Duterte.”5 He also continually ignores the call to rejoin the ICC.6 18 The police continue to refuse or stall investigations, the military persists in making blanket denials and arrest warrants against alleged perpetrators have not been executed. The climate of impunity persists. 22 The killings have continued⁠—and, have in fact worsened—under the present administration. label: HB 9752
title: AN ACT CREATING PROGRAMS FOR INCARCERATED PARENTS AND THEIR CHILDREN 22 23
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 25 Persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) are forced to leave their children during the time that they are in detention or commitment. As a result, most of the children of those in Philippine jails and detention facilities are deprived of much of the basic needs for their physical, mental, moral, and psychological growth and development. Our country lacks mechanisms and facilities for detained and committed parents to still enjoy their parental rights, and for the needs of their children to be attended to. Prison walls and jail bars must never negate the best interests of the child, even as their mother or father is still innocent in the eyes of the law, and even when the latter is already sentenced. 34 This need to care for incarcerated parents and their children is made more obvious and dire in the case of mothers, especially those who are expecting or nursing, and solo parents who oftentimes have no relatives to whom the rearing of their children could be entrusted. 39 The Philippine government has obligations under several international law instruments on the rights of the child, women’s rights, and cruel and inhumane punishment to name a few, to prevent the suffering of parents in jail and their children. Take the cases of Reina Mae Nasino and baby River, and Amanda Echanis and baby Randall Emmanuel. Both mothers are political prisoners arrested amid the raging times 1 of COVID-19 pandemic. Until now, Echanis is still suffering under fabricated charges. Meanwhile, in July 2023, the Manila Regional Trial Court Branch 47 dismissed the case of Nasino and her companions due to lack of evidence. However, her acquittal is years late since baby River passed away in 2020. Brought by the insufficient prenatal and post-natal care and the stress caused to Nasino throughout her pregnancy and childbirth, baby River contracted pneumonia then died at three months old. The court and elements of the Philippine National Police denied Nasino the right to mourn her daughter in peace, granting her just a total of six hours to go to her daughter’s wake and making her attend the funeral in handcuffs, closely surrounded by a score of police officers. A case has also been filed in the Ombudsman in relation to the “hijacking” of baby River’s remains by police forces. 12 Echanis, herself a child of incarcerated parents when both her parents became political prisoners in the 1990s, was recently arrested with her newborn son, Randall Emmanuel. As planted arms and explosives assured a non-bailable—yet trumped-up— charge against her, she is now faced with the choice of nursing her newborn in detention or being separated from him, totally unable to nurse him. 18 It should be noted, however, that Echanis herself was allowed to stay with her mother, Linda Lacaba Echanis, and also her father, slain Anakpawis leader and National Democratic Front of the Philippines peace consultant Randall Echanis, when both were arrested in August 1990. Government and custodial authorities consented for humanitarian reasons to Amanda’s confinement at Camp Crame in the political prisoner’s wing so that Linda could continue breastfeeding Amanda who was 1 year and 10 months old, which was still short of the two-year minimum period set by WHO guidelines for breastfeeding for survival. Both Linda and Amanda stayed in Camp Crame until Linda was released after six months. In effect, this establishes a humanitarian as well as instructive precedence for the protection of babies of incarcerated mothers. 30 “Just and humanitarian considerations” should be enough to accord these mothers, and other parents in jail, and their children the rights to a family, and the love and nurturing of a family. However, current institutions do not. 34 This proposed bill aims to establish mechanisms that shall assist imprisoned parents, especially mothers and solo parents, in the performance of their parental and child-rearing obligations particularly during the early and formative years of the child. 38 This Bill was originally filed in the 18th Congress by Senator Maria Lourdes Nancy S. Binay, as well as Representative Myra Salvador-Tambunting, Representative Manuel Cabochan and the Party-List Representatives of the Makabayang Koalisyon ng mga Mamamayan (Makabayan). 43 44 2 Approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9753
title: AN ACT REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT 11506, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “AN ACT GRANTING SAN MIGUEL AEROCITY INC. A FRANCHISE TO CONSTRUCT, DEVELOP, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, AND MAINTAIN A DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BULAKAN, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, AND TO CONSTRUCT, DEVELOP, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, AND MAINTAIN AN ADJACENT AIRPORT CITY” 27 28
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 30 The New Manila International Airport Project or the “Aerotropolis” was an unsolicited proposal of the San Miguel Aerocity, Inc presented by San Miguel Corporation (SMC) President Ramon Ang to the Duterte administration in February 2017. It was never a public policy but a profit-oriented brainchild of the private sector, particularly from one of the richest oligarchs in the country. The SMC is neither a scientific institution, nor a champion of democratic governance in the country. In fact, its history is tainted with its immoral involvement with the multi-billion-peso coconut levy fund scam during the Marcos dictatorship. 39 The issue of additional airport for Greater Metro Manila was raised in May 2011 by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to the Aquino administration. It claimed that there is an urgent need for a new gateway airport as the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) was already almost saturated. In October 2013, it identified Sangley Point in Cavite and Laguna Bay as potential sites based on cost and 1 viability. It excluded the Manila Bay area of Bulacan province. 2 In June 2014, the JICA recommended Sangley Point to be the project site and began its feasibility study. In August 2015, the then-Department of Transportation and Communication (DOTC) received the New Manila Sangley Airport feasibility study report from JICA. 7 According to the report, the Obando site along Manila Bay has several disadvantages such as risk of flooding, limited possibility of urban development and expected high cost for stabilization of sub-surface soils. Furthermore, the development of NMIA in this site could cause significant obstruction against discharge from the river in case of heavy rain, resulting in a high risk of flooding. The JICA noted that there is no significant advantage offsetting these disadvantages. 14 The SMC’s Aerotropolis Project is just around 4 kilometers away from the JICA- studied Obando site, and the marine environment and the geological characteristics are comparable. As early as 2015, there were overwhelming literature and scientific studies that demolished the feasibility of constructing an airport at the Manila Bay area of Bulacan province 20 In August 2019, the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Development of the University of the Philippines Diliman campus (OVCRD UP Diliman) and National Institute of Geological Science (NIGS) published its study entitled “Articulating geomorphology and geohazards in the coastal development issues of communities along the northern coasts of Manila Bay, Philippines.” The study focused on the impact on Barangay Taliptip, the ground zero of the Aerotropolis Project. 27 It concluded that: 29 “Most sitios of Brgy. Taliptip are built upon shallow tidal flats of the tidal- dominated Pampanga delta system. Four major geohazards were identified: earthquake, tidal and fluvial flooding, storm surge, and subsidence. These geohazards are commonly present and consistent with the geology, geomorphology, and hydrometeorological setting of the area. The first three hazards corroborated with anecdotes of residents while subsidence, though unreported, remains a threat based on earlier studies.” 37 It also cited as potential impact of the aerotropolis project: 39 “Construction of the Bulacan Aerotropolis will bring both permanent and temporary changes to the immediate vicinity and nearby areas. Thus, it is important to consider potential effects in all stages of development (i.e., construction and operational stage) to the social, physical, and environmental resources of the area. 45 One of the immediate and obvious effects would be the alteration of the physical 2 environment. Loss and reclamation of land, changes in river and drainage pathways, and removal of natural flora and fauna, consequently, influence the sediment and water transport pathways. If the risk is unmitigated, these could lead to flooding and siltation in nearby areas.” 5 It added, 7 “Pollution is another problem that should be taken into consideration. Air and noise pollution are unavoidable during construction and operation. label: HB 9754
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE USE OF THE BICYCLE AS A REGULAR MODE OF TRANSPORTATION, DEFINING THE RIGHTS OF BICYCLE RIDERS, ESTABLISHING APPROPRIATE INFRASTRUCTURE AND FACILITIES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 25 26
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 28 The pandemic has brought to the fore a major weakness in the country’s system of mass transportation. Various studies found that 72% of Filipinos found it difficult to go to work when the COVID-19 pandemic hit and the lockdowns were implemented and even afterwards—and majority of them are ordinary workers and employees in the private and public sectors. These are those who do not own cars or even motorcycles, who cannot afford to ride in taxis or book ride-hailing services. Due to the long-time stoppage of the operations of buses, jeepney, FX vans, and the MRT and LRT, 87% of Filipinos in 2020 have hoped that the government would accord the public transportation system a higher priority, rather than private vehicles. 38 According to the Move as One Coalition and UP School of Urban and Regional Planning, 70% of road users in Metro Manila rely on public transportation but they are only able to use 22% of the road space. On the other hand, nearly a third of private vehicles (30%)—just a small minority—of those on the road use private vehicles, and they are given rein over almost 80% of the road space. It is estimated that there is not much difference in other parts of the country. 45 1 Otherwise put, majority of Filipinos are commuters, but they are crammed into a very small portion of the roads. No wonder, sardinas-like public utility jeepneys, buses, and vans as well as the MRT and LRT trains are common. Lines or clusters of people waiting for rides, oftentimes spilling over into the roads, are the average sight everyday. 6 Move as One continued with a forecast: Even if all projects under the ambitious and much-touted Build, Build, Build Program were completed, there will be a “transport supply shortage” come 2030. Therefore, there is an urgent need for “sustainable mobility”—and one of the first measures towards that is laying down policies, mechanisms, and infrastructure for a safe, healthful, budget-friendly, and fast mode of transportation: bicycling. 13 Many have discovered and rediscovered bicycling in the past few years. In just the education sector, many teachers and education support personnel “padyak their way to school,” deliver modules, and do their various tasks. But they do not feel that the appropriate recognition is accorded to cyclists and the bicycle as road users just like everyone else, especially private vehicles. In fact, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority is finding ways to either narrow or remove the bicycle lanes, or share it with motorcycles. As their complaint goes, “Tao din kami, pwedeng gumamit ng kalsada. Gulong din kami, may karapatang umarangkada nang ligtas sa daan.” 22 This Bill aims to introduce the Philippine Bicycle Act to serve as the “unang padyak,” the first ride towards a more mass-based system of transportation, in which the respect and recognition to cyclists and the protection for their rights can be seen not just in words but also in the policies, even in the infrastructure or the physical components of the system. May this proposal give way for policies from the concerned agencies, as well as other laws for safe cycling. 29 We aim, beginning with the Philippine Bicycle Act, to get more bikes out in the streets, to make the roads safer for cyclists, and to promote a more health-friendly, environment-friendly, and sustainable mode of transport. 33 This Bill is borne out of consolidated proposals in the 18th Congress for the above mentioned objectives, and incorporated various inputs from bicycling advocates such as Move As One. Among the salient provisions are the institutionalization of the bicycle as a regular mode of transportation, the establishment of protected bike lanes in all primary and secondary roads for the exclusive use of cyclists, a “hierarchy of road users,” and the introduction of the rights of cyclists, such as the right to own and use bicycles, parity of rights with drivers of motorized vehicles, and the right to be protected from street harassment. 42 Also incorporated is the proposal of ACT Teachers and the Makabayan bloc in the bill for Minimum Overtaking of Cyclists Distance Act which obliges all drivers of motor vehicles to maintain a minimum overtaking distance of 1.5 meter from cyclists. This particular bill was approved on third reading during the 17th Congress. 2 1 Also sought to be mandated is a Bike to Work Program and Bike Awareness Program under the Department of Transportation, and the granting of incentives such as tax reliefs and benefits, including a ₱2,500 tax deduction for employees using bicycles, and the observance of the World Car-Free Day and National Car-Free Day. 6 The Committee on Transportation gave this Bill a green light during the 18 th Congress. Hopefully, this 20th Congress will set the wheels in motion for safer cycling, make it less expensive and prohibitive for the ordinary Filipino, and raise the status of cyclists as road users equal to all other road users. Approval of this Bill is therefore earnestly sought. 12 REP. ANTONIO L. TINIO ACT Teachers Party-list REP. SARAH JANE I. ELAGO REP. RENEE LOUISE M. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF A MEMORIAL FOR THE VICTIMS OF SUPERTYPHOON YOLANDA IN TACLOBAN CITY, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 23 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 26 November 1, 2013. Super Typhoon Yolanda was one of the worst natural disasters to strike the country in recent memory. The death toll was apocalyptic in magnitude and the damage to property was biblical in proportion. Conservative reports from the National Risk Reduction Management Council (NDRRMC) tallied 6,300 dead, 28,688 injured, and 1,062 still missing.1 However, survivors’ group People’s Surge placed the number of casualties up to 19,000 people, citing the uncounted dead in the far-flung areas of Eastern Visayas. The total cost of damages reached some ₱95.5 billion. 35 Days prior to Yolanda’s landfall, the Philippine Atmospheric Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) already gave warnings that a supertyphoon was about to enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) that could generate storm surges of up to 17 feet high. President Benigno Aquino III addressed the country, confidently saying that all preparations are already in place and that the 1 “Final Report re: Effects of Typhoon “Yolanda” (Haiyan).” National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, November 2013. https://ndrrmc.gov.ph/attachments/article/1329/FINAL_REPORT_re_Effects_of_Typhoon_YOLAN DA_(HAIYAN)_06-09NOV2013.pdf 1 country is ready for the onslaught of the supertyphoon, which came in with an estimated packed winds of up to 280 kph and gustiness up to 315 kph.2 3 But the aftermath of the disaster manifested the lack of comprehension of the warnings released by PAGASA, from the local government units to the highest office in the Executive Department. 7 The response was dismal, there was a clear lack of body bags, and the dead were left lying on the streets for days. Authorities had a difficult time identifying bodies. Worst, the people were left almost entirely to their own devices on fleeing, taking shelter, and surviving, even for days afterward. 12 Additionally, reconstruction efforts have been abysmal. According to the National Economic Development Authority (NEDA), the government allocation for Yolanda relief, reconstruction and rehabilitation amounted to approximately ₱144.4 billion as of June 2016. While 71% of this has been released, only 53.4% were disbursed according to the submissions of the government agencies. The overall weighted accomplishment or physical completion of projects funded by these releases was only 40%, while 27.7% are ongoing and 33% have not yet been started.3 20 Independent think-tank IBON Foundation noted that agencies tasked to facilitate survivors’ fundamental needs, such as housing, food, livelihood, and water received rehabilitation funds, had very low overall weighted accomplishment. The National Housing Authority (NHA) received the largest allocation amounting to ₱39.2 billion but the Department of Budget Management (DBM) reported that its overall weighted accomplishment was only 12.3%, with 45% ongoing and 42.6% not yet started, three years after the disaster struck. The overall weighted accomplishment of the Department of Agriculture (DA), which received ₱1.5 billion, was only 14.1%, with 11.6% ongoing and 74.3% not yet started. The overall weighted accomplishment of the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), which received ₱737 million, was only 2.9%, with 2.5% ongoing and 94.6% not yet started.4 32 Additionally, IBON Foundation noted, on the fourth-year anniversary of Yolanda, that only 25% percent or 50,891 of the 205,128 houses for the victims have been built. Of the completed units, only 27 percent are occupied.5 36 The poor preparedness, the lack of response and relief, and the abysmal reconstruction efforts by the government resulted in the massive death toll and 2 Sabillo, Kristine Angeli. “Aquino: PH ready to face supertyphoon ‘Yolanda.’” Inquirer.net, November 2013. https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/522661/aquino-ph-ready-to-face-supertyphoon-yolanda 3 “Use funds to hasten Yolanda rehab, Duterte gov’t urged.” IBON, November 2016. https://www.ibon.org/use-funds-to-hasten-yolanda-rehab-duterte-govt-urged/ 4 Ibid 5 “Only 25% of houses for Yolanda survivors completed after four years — research.” CNN, November 2017. https://www.cnnphilippines.com/news/2017/11/9/Yolanda-houses-survivors- incomplete-after-four-years.html 2 continuing injustice for the survivors. A memorial in Tacloban City will serve as a marker in memory of the victims including the many unidentified dead buried in mass graves, and as a reminder to our leaders and the people to work towards a disaster- resilient nation. 5 This Bill was first filed during the 16th Congress by Bayan Muna Rep. Neri Colmenares as House Bill 4100. The Makabayan Bloc refiled this Bill in the succeeding Congresses. 9 In this regard, the immediate approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. 11 REP. ANTONIO L. label: HB 9756
title: AN ACT REPEALING THE AUTOMATIC APPROPRIATION FOR DEBT SERVICE BY AMENDING SECTION 31 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1177 AND SECTION 26, CHAPTER 4, BOOK VI OF EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. 292, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ADMINISTRATIVE CODE OF 1987” WHICH REITERATES IN TOTO SECTION 31 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1177 26 27
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 29 This Bill amends Section 31 of Presidential Decree No. 1177, otherwise known as the “Budget Reform Decree of 1977,” issued during the martial law period which provides for automatic appropriation for public debt service. It likewise amends Section 26, Chapter 4, Book VI of Executive Order No. 292, otherwise known as the “Administrative Code Of 1987,” which reiterates in toto Section 31 of PD 1177. These laws provide for a no-questions-asked priority for debt servicing, a policy implemented during martial law and throughout the post-EDSA 1 administrations, thereby limiting the budget available for education as well as other social services. 38 The effective repeal of automatic appropriation for debt service remedies a long- standing defect in the government’s policies on the budget—the indiscriminate payment of all public debts including indefensible loans, regardless of the grave diversion of finances from basic services. It affirms and asserts the obligation of the State under Article II, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution to “promote a just [social order]…through policies that provide adequate social services.” 45 1 The Bill’s passage will pave the way for a more rational and humane budgetary process. It will bring, annually, hundreds of billions of pesos within greater control of the people, rather than being paid for debt servicing. The excesses of past administrations—from the Marcos Sr. dictatorship until the Marcos Jr. administration— will no longer hold the country hostage, and only legitimate loans, not onerous and fraudulent debts, will be serviced. The government can begin to prioritize badly needed social services. 8 Since 1986, cumulative debt servicing has been consuming almost a third of the annual national government budget. Meanwhile, the country’s public schools, universities and colleges perennially suffer from decrepit facilities, teachers, textbook and classroom shortages. Government hospitals are being closed, public health services are a pittance, and vital medicines and treatments, especially for the poor, have become inaccessible. Public provision for social goods and services are steadily being crippled, with increasing reliance on the private sector, to the detriment of vulnerable sectors such as the poor, senior citizens, and persons with disabilities. 17 The need to repeal the law on automatic appropriation for debt servicing has become more urgent as the public debt has become an albatross for the nation. The country’s debt is bloated by revenue losses from trade liberalization, overly generous fiscal incentives for foreign investors, and the guarantee of profits as the government assumes contingent liabilities. Debt-to-GDP ratio is still high at 65.2% as of March 2026.1 The government’s continued dependence on borrowing means that the debt service burden is getting heavier and heavier. 25 The large share of debt servicing in the national budget has exacerbated the government’s worsening neglect of social services since 1997. Education, health and social welfare budgets remain insufficient while a large share of the people’s taxes is allocated for debt payment. In 2026, debt servicing amounted to ₱2.006 trillion, of which ₱950 billion is for interest payment and ₱1.056 trillion is for payment for principal amortization of foreign and domestic debts. The amount for debt servicing is higher than the 2026 allotment for the Department of Education, which is ₱961.32 billion, and the Department of Health with ₱297.86 billion. 34 From ₱5.95 trillion in June 2016, the national government outstanding debt doubled to ₱12.79 trillion in June 2022. According to the Department of Finance, the Duterte administration has added ₱6.84 trillion in debt due to the pandemic, surpassing the combined borrowings of all previous administrations from Marcos Sr.’s ₱365 billion; C. Aquino’s ₱372 billion; Ramos’ ₱681 billion; Estrada’s ₱766 billion; Arroyo’s ₱2.40 trillion; and B. Aquino’s ₱1.37 trillion.2 As of March 2026, the total 1 “National Government Debt.” Bureau of Treasury, 7 May 2026. Retrieved from https://www.treasury.gov.ph/?page_id=12407. label: HB 9757
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE SELLING AND/OR BUYING OF ADMISSION TICKETS THROUGH UNAUTHORIZED SALES CHANNELS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In recent years, the Filipino public, particularly the youth, women, and the working class, has been increasingly subjected to the predatory practices of ticket scalping. Concerts, fan meetings, cultural and sports events, and other forms of entertainment are vital avenues for social expression, community building, and relief from the daily struggle. However, the commodification of these events has given rise to parasitic entities and individuals who exploit high demand by hoarding tickets through deceptive means, only to resell them at unconscionable and exorbitant prices. The rise of digital technology has further aggravated this exploitation. The use of automated bots and sophisticated software allows unscrupulous entities to bypass security measures and purchase limits, effectively hijacking the inventory of tickets before the general public can access them. Such practices are not merely "market-driven" transactions; they are a form of economic sabotage that disenfranchises the masses and concentrates access to culture in the hands of the few who can afford inflated rates. This bill seeks to penalize ticket scalping acts and protect the interests of the consuming public. By setting clear definitions and prohibitions, the State asserts its role in regulating the market to prevent the exploitation of the people's desire for recreation and cultural participation. The salient features of this Bill include: ● Defines and penalizes the act of reselling tickets at a markup higher than ten percent (10%) of the face value, ensuring that tickets remain accessible to the intended audience. ● Criminalizes the use of software, scripts, or any deceptive technology designed to bypass purchase limits and security controls on ticketing platforms, thereby leveling the playing field for all consumers. ● Mandates event organizers and ticketing entities to implement internal policies, signages, and reporting mechanisms to prevent scalping within their systems. ● Provides for graduated fines and imprisonment for violators, with specific provisions for corporate accountability, to serve as a strong deterrent against large-scale scalping operations. ● Provides exemptions for private, non-commercial, and occasional resales at or below face value, ensuring that the law targets predatory hoarders rather than ordinary citizens. Through this measure, we take a decisive step toward curbing scalping practices that turn culture and entertainment into tools of exploitation. We must ensure that access to these events is determined by fair opportunity. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. SARAH JANE I. label: HB 9764
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO WORKERS IN CRITICAL INDUSTRIES DURING A STATE OF CALAMITY OR EMERGENCY OR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social and economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights and welfare of workers. During the COVID-19 pandemic and other national emergencies, workers in critical industries continued to report for duty despite heightened risks to their health, safety, and well-being. These workers ensured the uninterrupted delivery of essential services such as healthcare, food supply, transportation, utilities, telecommunications, sanitation, and public safety. While some public sector workers are granted hazard pay under existing laws, many employees in the private sector who face similar risks do not receive the same protection and compensation. This disparity highlights the need for a clear and uniform policy that recognizes the sacrifices of workers who remain on the frontlines during times of crisis. This bill seeks to institutionalize the grant of hazard pay equivalent to at least twenty-five percent (25%) of the monthly basic salary of workers in critical industries during a declared state of calamity, emergency, or public health emergency. It likewise extends such benefit to workers engaged through service contractors who perform essential frontline functions. By providing adequate compensation for extraordinary risks, this measure promotes social justice, protects workers' welfare, and helps ensure the continuous operation of vital services during national emergencies. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. label: HB 9765
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SAFEGUARDS FOR THE USE OF SOCIAL MEDIA BY MINORS, PROMOTING A SAFE AND AGE APPROPRIATE DIGITAL ENVIRONMENT, AND PROTECTING ADDICTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish clear safeguards on the use of social media by minors to ensure a safe, responsible, and age-appropriate digital environment. While recognizing the growing role of social media in education, communication, and social interaction, the measure also addresses the increasing risks faced by young users, including exposure to harmful content, cyber exploitation, privacy breaches, and excessive screen use that may negatively affect their well-being. To protect minors, the bill introduces age-based access guidelines, requiring parental or guardian consent for users aged thirteen (13) to seventeen (17), along with access to safer, age-appropriate platform versions with enhanced privacy and limited features. It also mandates social media providers to implement reliable age verification systems, strengthen identity authentication processes, and provide effective parental control and content filtering tools. Ultimately, this measure upholds the State’s duty to safeguard the welfare of children while promoting responsible digital engagement and empowering parents to actively guide their children’s online activities in a safer digital space. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. label: HB 9766
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF PRIVATE HEALTH WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Despite reported economic gains, many Filipinos continue to experience poverty and limited access to quality health services. The country’s health system remains strained due to long-standing issues such as inadequate funding, workforce shortages, and persistent neglect. Health workers, who are vital in delivering essential services and responding to public health needs, continue to face low wages, heavy workloads, and insecure employment. Many receive compensation that is insufficient to meet the rising cost of living, particularly in the private sector where pay and benefits are significantly lower than in government service. Contractualization further worsens the situation, as many health workers are employed under non-regular arrangements with limited job security and minimal benefits. This has contributed to the continued migration of nurses and other health professionals seeking better opportunities abroad, resulting in staffing shortages in local health facilities. Although public health workers are covered by the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers, those in private institutions are excluded from similar protections, creating inequality within the sector despite performing the same duties and facing similar risks. This bill seeks to address these gaps by promoting the welfare, security, and fair treatment of private health workers and reducing disparities between public and private health sectors, in order to strengthen the country’s healthcare system and encourage health professionals to remain and serve in the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. label: HB 9767
title: AN ACT FURTHER PROMOTING THE GENERAL WELFARE, AND ENHANCING THE STATUTORY BENEFITS AND INCENTIVES OF PUBLIC HEALTH WORKERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7305, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE MAGNA CARTA OF PUBLIC HEALTH WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the Magna Carta for Public Health Workers by updating its long-overdue provisions. While the law was enacted to improve the welfare, working conditions, and benefits of health workers, the fixed monetary allowances have remained unchanged for decades despite rising costs of living and economic challenges. To address this gap, the measure proposes the increase of mandated benefits such as hazard pay, night shift differential, subsistence, and laundry allowances. It also expands the definition of public health workers to include those serving in health-related offices, SUCs, GOCCs, and LGUs, ensuring broader coverage and recognition of their roles. Ultimately, the bill aims to provide fairer compensation and better support for around 150,000 public health workers, reinforcing the State’s commitment to a stronger and more sustainable public health system. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. label: HB 9768
title: AN ACT PROVIDING PROTECTION AND INCENTIVES TO FREELANCE WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The nature of work has significantly evolved in recent years due to technological advancements and changing employment preferences, particularly among younger Filipinos. This shift has contributed to the rapid growth of the freelance sector, with the Philippines ranking among the countries with the highest number of freelancers per capita. A significant share of these freelancers are engaged in creative and digital industries, and many are women. Despite their growing role in the economy, freelance workers remain largely outside the coverage of existing labor protections. Common concerns include the lack of written contracts, delayed or non-payment of fees, unclear work arrangements, and limited remedies in cases of dispute or abuse. These gaps expose freelancers to unfair practices and leave them with little to no protection against exploitation. This bill seeks to address these issues by establishing a clear legal framework that recognizes and protects freelance workers. It requires written contracts to ensure transparency in work scope, compensation, and conditions; mandates fair payment practices including a minimum down payment upon engagement; and provides for applicable benefits such as hazard pay and night shift differentials. It also imposes penalties for abusive practices and strengthens access to justice by authorizing the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to handle complaints through mediation and conciliation. In addition, the measure provides support mechanisms such as tax assistance through relevant government programs and the establishment of help desks in revenue offices. It likewise requires DOLE to conduct information campaigns and submit regular reports to ensure proper implementation. Ultimately, this bill recognizes the evolving nature of work and seeks to extend basic rights and protections to freelance workers, ensuring fairness, security, and dignity in their profession. label: HB 9769
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS OF THE FUTURE IN TECHNOLOGY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid advancement of digital technology has transformed the way knowledge is created, accessed, and shared. In the education sector, these innovations present a critical opportunity to improve learning outcomes, enhance teaching effectiveness, and expand access to quality education for all Filipino learners, regardless of social and economic circumstances. This measure recognizes the constitutional mandate of the State to give the highest priority to education and responds to the growing need to integrate information and communications technology (ICT) into public basic education. The experiences during national health emergencies have further underscored the importance of having an accessible and reliable complementary mode of learning that ensures the continuity of education in times of disruption. Accordingly, this Act seeks to establish a comprehensive and coordinated framework for the integration of digital technology and innovation in public education through the formulation and implementation of a PSOFT Road Map. It aims to harness innovative teaching and learning tools, promote access to digitized educational resources, and regulate the effective and responsible use of digital technology in public schools to enhance the overall learning experience of students and teachers. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought to advance inclusive, resilient, and future-ready public education through digital transformation. HON. RICARDO S. label: HB 9770
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR PROTECTION OF THE REMITTANCES OF OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to the latest data of the Philippine Statistics Authority, the number of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), or Filipino workers who worked abroad, in 2024 was estimated at 2.19 million, an increase of 1.5 percent from the previous year’s estimated number of 2.16 million. Overseas Contract Workers (OCWs), or Filipino workers with existing work contracts, comprised majority or 97.9 percent of the total OFWs during the period1 Many Filipinos seek employment opportunities abroad in pursuit of better economic prospects and to provide a more secure future for their families. These Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) make significant sacrifices by working outside their home country to support their loved ones in the Philippines. Through their remittances, OFWs contribute substantially to the nation's economy, playing a vital role in sustaining household incomes and promoting economic growth. It is the responsibility of the State to protect their rights, safeguard their welfare, and ensure that they are able to fully benefit from their hard work. The bill seeks to strengthen and protect the rights of the Overseas Filipino Worker (OFWs) in relation to their transfer of foreign funds in accordance with the government’s mandate. RICARDO S. label: HB 9773
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE DISCOUNT ON THE PURCHASE OF GOODS AND SERVICES OF SENIOR CITIZENS AND PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9994, otherwise known as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, and Republic Act No. 10754 or known as An Act Expanding the Benefits and Privileges of Persons with Disability (PWD) grant senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs) a twenty percent (20%) discount and exemption from the value-added tax (VAT) on selected goods and services, including medicines, medical and dental services, professional healthcare fees, transportation, and other essential expenditures. Despite these existing benefits, many senior citizens and PWDs continue to face economic difficulties brought about by rising costs of living, limited sources of income, and increased expenses associated with healthcare and daily necessities. As vulnerable sectors of society, they require greater support to help ease their financial burdens and improve their quality of life. This proposed measure seeks to enhance the benefits currently being given to senior citizens and PWDs by ensuring that the twenty percent (20%) discount and VAT exemption are granted in addition to any promotional discounts, special offers, or price reductions provided by business establishments. Through this measure, the State reaffirms its commitment to promoting the welfare of senior citizens and PWDs and recognizing their valuable contributions to society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RICARDO S. CRUZ JR. In 2022, only 353,000 of the estimated 1.9 million PWDs were employed1, while just 38.2 percent of the 2.538 million qualified senior citizens had gainful employment.2 This situation reflects the need for greater access to employment opportunities for these sectors. The Constitution recognizes labor as a vital social and economic force and directs the State to uphold the welfare of all workers. In line with this policy, there is a need to expand employment opportunities for senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs), many of whom continue to face barriers to gainful employment despite their skills and capabilities. By providing greater access to employment and support services, the State can promote economic independence, social inclusion, and equal opportunities for these sectors while recognizing their valuable contributions to society and national development. This proposed measure seeks to strengthen existing Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs) by enhancing their capacity to provide targeted employment assistance, job matching, skills development, and other support services for senior citizens and PWDs. By expanding access to employment opportunities, the measure 1 Guillen et al. label: HB 9775
title: AN ACT PROMOTING CRITICAL MEDIA AND INFORMATION LITERACY IN THE PHILIPPINES AND PRESCRIBING ITS ENHANCED INCLUSION IN THE EDUCATIONAL SYSTEM AND CURRICULUM IN THE PHILIPPINES, FOR SUCH OTHER PURPOSES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The way Filipinos consume information has completely changed. While the rise of social media and digital platforms has made it easier to connect, it has also opened the floodgates for misinformation, fake news, and deliberate online manipulation. In the Philippines, where digital media consumption is among the highest in the world, our citizens -- especially the youth -- are constantly exposed to distorted narratives that weaken public trust and cloud public discourse. In this environment, simply knowing how to navigate the internet is no longer enough. Digital literacy must go beyond operating a smartphone; our students need the critical thinking skills to analyze, verify, and question the information on their screens before they hit "share." While the Department of Education currently includes Media and Information Literacy (MIL) in the Senior High School curriculum, a single subject late in a student’s academic life is no longer sufficient to counter the scale of modern digital threats. We need a more comprehensive and systemic approach that starts earlier and runs deeper. This bill seeks to institutionalize and enhance the integration of critical media and information literacy across the Philippine educational system. It aims to update our curriculum to match evolving technology, provide educators with specialized training and resources, and fund community-level programs to reach the non-formal education sector. Protecting our information ecosystem is a matter of national resilience and civic empowerment. By equipping the next generation with the tools to discern fact from fiction, we foster a society grounded in truth, accountability, and critical thinking. In view of the urgent need to secure our digital space and protect our youth, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. CRUZ, JR. label: HB 9776
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The vital role of public school teachers in nation-building cannot be overstated. As the backbone of the country’s public education system, they are tasked not only with the intellectual development of the youth but also with various civic duties that extend well beyond the classroom. However, the demanding nature of their profession often takes a severe toll on their physical and mental well-being. Under Republic Act No. 4670, otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Public School Teachers, educators are explicitly entitled to free annual medical examinations. Despite this statutory mandate, full implementation remains a challenge due to persistent budgetary constraints. Consequently, many public school teachers are forced to shoulder the costs of routine checkups, diagnostic laboratory procedures, and maintenance medications out of their own personal funds. This financial burden is counterproductive to the state's goal of maintaining a robust and highly motivated teaching force. When teachers suffer from unaddressed health issues, the quality of instruction and the overall stability of the classroom environment are inevitably compromised. To bridge this gap, this legislative measure proposes the institutionalization of a dedicated Medical Examination and Treatment Allowance for all public school teachers. By providing a direct and reliable financial subsidy specifically for healthcare, this bill ensures that our educators can proactively manage their health, access timely medical interventions, and alleviate the financial strain associated with medical upkeep. Providing institutional healthcare support to our teachers is a matter of administrative necessity and social justice. It is an essential investment in the very custodians of our educational system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought RICARDO S. CRUZ, JR. label: HB 9777
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Road safety remains a critical concern in the Philippines, with a significant number of accidents attributed to mechanical failures of buses, trucks, and other heavy vehicles. These vehicles, by their very nature, carry large numbers of passengers or heavy loads, and when they malfunction on the road, the consequences are often severe and far-reaching. This proposed measure seeks to mandate monthly preventive maintenance and quarterly inspections of buses, trucks, and other heavy vehicles. The objective is to institutionalize regular and systematic checks to detect mechanical issues early, thereby reducing the risk of accidents caused by vehicle failure. Such inspections will not only protect passengers and drivers but also safeguard other motorists and pedestrians who share the road. By requiring transport operators to comply with strict maintenance and inspection schedules, the State affirms its commitment to ensuring public safety, promoting accountability in the transport sector, and fostering a culture of responsibility in road use. This measure complements existing traffic regulations by addressing the root cause of many accidents -- mechanical neglect -- thus strengthening the overall framework for road safety. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. CRUZ, JR. label: HB 9778
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR ADDITIONAL MATERNITY LEAVE TO WOMEN WITH POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION, EXPANDING FOR THIS PURPOSE THE COVERAGE OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11210 AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11210, otherwise known as the "105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law," was enacted to provide working mothers with sufficient time to recover from childbirth and to nurture their newborns. However, the law does not expressly address the needs of women who suffer from postpartum depression, a condition that significantly affects maternal health and family well-being. Postpartum depression is a recognized medical condition that may impair a mother’s ability to care for herself and her child. Extending maternity leave for women diagnosed with this condition is a necessary measure to safeguard their health, promote recovery, and ensure the welfare of their families. This measure seeks to expand the coverage of RA 11210 by granting additional maternity leave to mothers who are medically certified to be experiencing postpartum depression. By institutionalizing this support, the State affirms its commitment to protecting maternal health, strengthening family relations, and fostering a healthier society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. CRUZ, JR. label: HB 9779
title: AN ACT PROVIDING SICK LEAVE BENEFITS OF FIFTEEN DAYS WITH PAY PER YEAR TO ALL PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The teaching profession is among the most demanding vocations in the country. Public school teachers devote long hours to lesson preparation, classroom instruction, and administrative responsibilities, often at the expense of their own health and well-being. In recent years, more and more cases have shown that teachers are experiencing stress, burnout, and illness brought about by heavy workloads, overcrowded classrooms, and the emotional demands of guiding students. Despite their indispensable role in shaping the nation’s future, teachers are not sufficiently provided with paid sick leave benefits that would allow them to recover without financial strain. This proposed measure seeks to grant all public school teachers fifteen (15) days of sick leave with pay per year. Such provision recognizes the reality that teachers, like all workers, are vulnerable to illness and must be afforded adequate time to recuperate. By institutionalizing this benefit, the State affirms its commitment to safeguarding the welfare of educators. Healthy teachers are better equipped to deliver quality instruction, maintain classroom productivity, and contribute to the overall advancement of the education system. Ensuring their well-being is not only a matter of fairness but also an investment in the future of Filipino learners and the nation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. CRUZ, JR.
