label: HB 9780
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE CONDUCT OF PERIODIC INSPECTION AND MAINTENANCE OF NATIONAL GOVERNMENT INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS, AND ALLOWING THE DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS AND HIGHWAYS ACCESS TO THE SITES OR LOCATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A well-planned and well-built infrastructure system is vital for national development and economic transformation.1 Every year, the government allocates funding for the construction of roads, bridges, public buildings, and other vital structures. These projects are intended to provide high-quality, safe, reliable, and resilient infrastructure facilities and services that are directly responsive to the everyday needs of the Filipino people. However, construction is only the first step. The true value of any infrastructure project is found in its longevity and usability. It is necessary to ensure that these public investments do not prematurely deteriorate, and instead remain as long-term assets. One strategy to optimize the use of public funds in relation to these national infrastructure projects is for the government to analyze the life cycle and utilization of said assets.2 Central to this strategy is the implementation of systematic inspections to accurately identify which projects require maintenance, preventive repairs, or more extensive rehabilitation. On the ground, however, a critical issue hinders these essential upkeep efforts. The Department of Public Works and Highways face difficulties when trying to access the 1 https://pdp.depdev.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Chapter-12.pdf 2 https://pdp.depdev.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Chapter-12.pdf 1 sites of existing infrastructure projects, primarily due to land ownership disputes and conflicting or unclear titles and authorities. This problem is especially seen in older public works implemented years ago. Over time, properties may have changed hands or authority over the sites may have become muddled by the involvement of private developers, homeowners’ associations, or other private entities. Consequently, structures fall into disrepair because the government is denied entry or access to perform inspections and maintenance works. While Republic Act No. 12289 or the Accelerated and Reformed Right-of-Way (ARROW) Act was recently enacted to hasten the acquisition of properties for national government infrastructure projects, this does not answer the issue of access to existing infrastructure projects and their rehabilitation or maintenance. This measure bridges this gap by requiring the Department of Public Works and Highways to conduct regular and periodic inspections of all national government infrastructure projects. The inspections shall be conducted every five to ten years after completion, as determined by the DPWH, based on the project type. Based on the inspection findings, the DPWH shall undertake the necessary maintenance, repair, or rehabilitation measures for these projects. In line with this, the owner or lawful possessor of the site or location of the national government infrastructure projects is mandated to allow access to the national government for the conduct of the regular and periodic inspections and the maintenance, repair, and rehabilitation of said government projects. By institutionalizing this framework, we elevate the standard for national infrastructure projects and ensure that we do not treat these as disposable commodities, but as long-term investments for our nation’s development. Ultimately, we want to safeguard billions in public investments so that taxpayers get their full money’s worth out of these projects for years to come. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 9781
title: AN ACT SEPARATING THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL OF MASVILLE NATIONAL HIGH SCHOOL IN BARANGAY BF HOMES, CITY OF PARAÑAQUE FROM MASVILLE NATIONAL HIGH SCHOOL CONVERTING IT INTO AN INDEPENDENT SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL TO BE KNOWN AS THE MASVILLE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Over the years, Parañaque City has experienced sustained population growth driven by residential expansion and urban development. This increase has inevitably translated into greater demand for public education, particularly at the secondary level. As enrollment continues to grow, ensuring that students receive quality instruction and adequate support services requires a more responsive institutional arrangement. This measure seeks to separate the Senior High School Department of Masville National High School in Barangay BF Homes, Parañaque City and convert it into an independent institution to be known as the Masville Senior High School. Barangay BF Homes remains one of the city's largest residential communities, serving thousands of families whose children rely on public schools for their education. As of School Year 2025-2026, Masville National High School serves approximately 500 senior high school students sharing only ten (10) classrooms. The sheer size of the student population presents operational and administrative challenges that can affect the quality of instruction, student support services, and school management. Separating the Masville National High School Senior High School department will help decongest existing facilities, improve the allocation of educational resources, and create a learning environment better suited to preparing students for higher education, employment, and entrepreneurship. It will likewise allow the school to focus exclusively on the unique academic, technical-vocational, sports, and arts education needs of senior high school learners. The establishment of the Masville Senior High School is a necessary investment in the future of Parañaque's youth. As enrollment continues to grow, our educational institutions must grow with it. Every learner deserves a school system that is equipped to provide the enabling conditions where dreams of young people may be nurtured. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 9785
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE PENALTIES FOR THE REFUSAL OF HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL CLINICS TO ADMINISTER APPROPRIATE INITIAL MEDICAL TREATMENT AND SUPPORT IN EMERGENCY OR SERIOUS CASES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BILANG 702, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ANTI-HOSPITAL DEPOSIT LAW”, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to fortify the enforcement of Batas Pambansa (BP) 702, otherwise known as the “Anti-Hospital Deposit Law”. It imposes stronger penalties to hospitals, medical clinics, and officials who deny or fail to deliver the necessary initial medical treatment and support in emergency or serious cases due to the non-payment of deposits or advance payments. The amendments priorly provided in BP 702 advocates for financially incapacitated individuals and families who are refused to be given urgent medical care and treatment. However, in spite of these additional holds, reports of requiring deposits persist resulting in non-accommodation of patients and families even in emergency situations. Further amendments to this Act, as provided in this bill, seek to decisively deter hospitals and medical practitioners from refusing to provide immediate medical assistance to patients and their families by imposing stiffer penalties for violations. Moreover, repeated offenses may warrant the revocation of the health facility’s license to operate, without prejudice to the imposition of other administrative, civil, or professional sanctions. This bill is anchored on the firm conviction that the State must uphold and protect the people’s constitutional right to accessible and adequate healthcare. No individual must be denied or deprived of urgent medical attention. Our healthcare institutions must not operate solely for financial gain; at the heart of every health facility lies the fundamental duty to serve the people and provide compassionate, humane, and proper medical care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9796
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FIVE-YEAR VALIDITY PERIOD OF THE PROFESSIONAL IDENTIFICATION CARDS OF ALL PROFESSIONAL UNDER THE PROFESSIONAL REGULATION COMMISSION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide a five-year validity period for all Professional Identification Cards (PICs) issued by the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC), subject to compliance with all legal and mandatory requirements for renewal, including the Continuing Professional Development (CPD) requirements under Republic Act No. 10912. At present, professionals are required to renew their PRC identification cards every three years, resulting in additional financial costs, administrative burdens, and inconvenience for millions of Filipino professionals. Frequent renewals often lead to long queues, processing delays, scheduling difficulties, and unnecessary expenses, particularly for professionals residing in far-flung areas or those working overseas. This proposed measure seeks to address these concerns by extending the validity of Professional Identification Cards from three years to five years while retaining all existing legal and regulatory safeguards for renewal. The bill likewise directs the PRC to strengthen its digital systems and administrative processes to ensure more efficient and accessible public service delivery. Providing a longer validity period for PRC identification cards promotes convenience, efficiency, and ease of doing business for Filipino professionals without compromising regulatory standards. At a time when the country continues to pursue digitalization and streamlined government services, the State must adopt practical and responsive policies that reduce unnecessary burdens on the public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9799
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF CHILDREN
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution recognizes the duty of the State to protect every child from abuse, neglect, exploitation, and all conditions harmful to their growth and development. This proposed Magna Carta of Children seeks to strengthen that commitment by ensuring that all Filipino children, especially those who are poor, vulnerable, neglected, or abused, receive the care, protection, and opportunities they deserve. It builds on existing child-protection laws and provides a stronger and more uni ied system for safeguarding children’s rights. The Magna Carta of Children is envisioned as a comprehensive law that clearly de ines and protects the rights of every child. Instead of scattered and overlapping laws, it creates a single framework that promotes the child’s best interests, dignity, safety, and overall well-being. It recognizes children not only as individuals needing protection, but also as rights-holders whose voices and welfare must be respected in all matters affecting them. This measure also strengthens the Philippines’ commitment to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC). Guided by the principles of non- discrimination, survival and development, protection, and participation, the proposed law ensures that every child has the right to grow in a safe, supportive, and nurturing environment. It also recognizes the important role of parents and families, while requiring the government to provide support and intervene when children are at risk. 1|Page Finally, the Magna Carta of Children seeks to improve coordination among government agencies, local government units, schools, and child-serving institutions to ensure effective delivery of programs and services for children. By harmonizing existing child-related laws and policies, this measure aims to build a stronger protective environment where every Filipino child can learn, grow, and reach their full potential. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. title: AN ACT RATIONALIZING THE BARANGAY NEWLY-ELECTED OFFICIALS (BNEO) PROGRAM BY LIMITING MANDATORY PARTICIPATION TO FIRST-TIME ELECTED AND NEWLY APPOINTED BARANGAY OFFICIALS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The barangay is the government unit closest to the people and serves as the primary frontline provider of public services in every community. To perform their duties effectively, barangay of icials must be equipped with the necessary knowledge and skills in governance, planning, inancial management, and accountability. For this purpose, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) requires participation in the Barangay Newly-Elected Of icials (BNEO) Program, which provides basic orientation and training for barangay of icials. While the BNEO Program remains an important tool for capacity-building, requiring all elected of icials to repeatedly attend the same basic orientation, even those who have previously served and completed similar trainings, results in unnecessary and duplicative expenditures. These costs, which are borne by barangay funds, could otherwise be used to support essential programs, projects, and services that directly bene it local communities. This bill seeks to rationalize the implementation of the BNEO Program by limiting mandatory participation in the Basic Orientation Course to irst-time elected barangay of icials and newly appointed of icials who have not previously served in an elective barangay position. It likewise directs the DILG to recognize prior completion 1|Page of substantially similar training programs to prevent repetitive training requirements, unless additional or updated learning is necessary. By focusing resources on of icials who genuinely need foundational training, this measure promotes more ef icient use of public funds, avoids unnecessary expenses, and strengthens the professionalization of barangay governance. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9801
title: AN ACT MODERNIZING THE BUREAU OF IMMIGRATION BY DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, FURTHER PROFESSIONALIZING ITS ORGANIZATION, UPGRADING THE COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS OF ITS OFFICIALS AND EMPLOYEES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Immigration Act of 1940 has become outdated and no longer meets the demands of modern immigration management. Over the years, its gaps have been addressed through various administrative issuances, resulting in inconsistent policies, conflicting interpretations, and confusion among the public. These weaknesses have also created opportunities for inefficiency and corruption, affecting public trust and the country's reputation. This bill seeks to modernize the Bureau of Immigration by strengthening its organization, enhancing its institutional capacity, and professionalizing its workforce. It establishes a Board of Commissioners with policy-making and quasi-judicial functions, and harmonizes existing immigration rules to promote transparency, consistency, and predictability in the implementation of immigration laws. The measure also creates an Immigration Trust Fund to ensure sustainable financing for the modernization of facilities, equipment, and services, as well as the training, development, and welfare of Bureau personnel. 1 | Page This proposal builds upon similar measures filed and approved on Third Reading during the Nineteenth Congress, reflecting broad recognition of the need for immigration reform. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9802
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE AUTHORIZED CAMPAIGN EXPENSES OF CANDIDATES AND POLITICAL PARTIES, AND INDEXING THE SAME TO INFLATION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 13 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7166, ENTITLED, “AN ACT PROVIDING FOR SYNCHRONIZED NATIONAL AND LOCAL ELECTIONS AND FOR OTHER ELECTORAL REFORMS, AUTHORIZING APPROPRIATIONS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Free and fair elections are the foundation of democracy. Our laws on campaign spending were created to give candidates a fair chance to reach voters and prevent elections from being dominated by money and political in luence. However, the campaign spending limits set by law in 1991 have remained unchanged for more than three decades, despite the rising costs of transportation, communication, printing, media, and other lawful campaign activities. What may have been reasonable in 1991 is no longer realistic today. Because these limits no longer re lect present economic conditions, candidates may struggle to conduct legitimate campaigns within the outdated ceilings. This can encourage underreporting, weaken transparency, and push campaign activities into informal or unregulated channels. Instead of strengthening accountability, unrealistic limits may unintentionally undermine public trust in the electoral process. This bill seeks to update the allowable campaign spending limits and provide a fair system for adjusting them over time based on in lation and of icial economic data. The measure does not remove spending controls; rather, it ensures that the law remains 1|Page practical, enforceable, and responsive to current realities while still protecting equal opportunity among candidates and preventing excessive in luence by wealth and political machinery. The measure also continues to encourage transparency by maintaining existing rules that exempt properly reported campaign contributions from donor’s tax. Ultimately, this bill aims to strengthen clean, honest, and accountable elections by ensuring that campaign inance laws remain fair, realistic, and effective for both candidates and the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9803
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING YOUTH DEVELOPMENT AND CHILD WELFARE PROGRAMS, ENHANCING SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AND COMMUNITY-BASED INTERVENTION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every child deserves the chance to grow up safe, healthy, educated, and hopeful. Yet many Filipino children continue to suffer from poverty, hunger, neglect, violence, and lack of support. Too often, children who stop attending school or struggle at home are only noticed when they are already in serious trouble. This bill seeks to strengthen youth development and child welfare programs so that children receive help early, before they fall deeper into crisis. Although existing laws already protect children, many communities still lack enough counselors, social workers, nutrition programs, and support services. As a result, many young people become disconnected from school, exposed to abuse, or pushed toward conflict with the law. This measure strengthens coordination among schools, barangays, local governments, and national agencies to ensure that children are guided, supported, and protected rather than neglected or punished. The bill promotes practical and compassionate solutions such as school attendance monitoring, feeding and nutrition programs, counseling services, and community- based intervention for children at risk. By helping children stay in school, addressing family and mental health concerns early, and providing stronger support systems, this measure gives every child a better chance to succeed and build a brighter future. 1 | Page In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AT SOUTHERN LEYTE STATE UNIVERSITY – HINUNANGAN CAMPUS A HIGHLY-SPECIALIZED RESEARCH INSTITUTE TO BE KNOWN AS THE DISASTER RESILIENCE FOR ECO-EFFICIENT AGRICULTURE MANAGEMENT INSTITUTE (DREAM INSTITUTE), DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, FUNCTIONS, ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Southern Leyte possesses immense ecological, agricultural, and tourism-linked assets that place it in a strategic position to pursue an integrated Tourism-Environment- Agriculture (TEA) Nexus of development. As an agriculture-based province with important upland, watershed, spring, riverine, coastal, and biodiversity-rich ecosystems, Southern Leyte requires a specialized institutional mechanism capable of generating baseline scienti ic data, translating such knowledge into resilient production and livelihood systems, protecting biodiversity and ecosystem integrity, and supporting disaster- and climate-responsive decision-making. Southern Leyte State University – Hinunangan Campus has already established three Board-approved research centers that respond to portions of this challenge: the Soil and Water Research Institute (SWaRI), the Smallholder Horticulture and Agroforestry Research & Extension (SHARE) Center, and the Biodiversity Conservation and Management Institute (BioCon). However, these centers presently operate with a limited personnel complement and a fragmented institutional arrangement, making it dif icult to fully respond to the increasing demands of climate adaptation, environmental protection, agricultural resilience, biodiversity conservation, community-based development, and policy support in the Province of Southern Leyte. 1|Page To address this need, this bill seeks to establish a uni ied and highly specialized institute to be known as the Disaster Resilience for Eco-ef icient Agriculture Management Institute (DREAM Institute) at Southern Leyte State University – Hinunangan Campus. The proposed DREAM Institute shall consolidate and elevate the functions of SWaRI, SHARE, and BioCon into one integrated institutional framework, with SWaRI serving as the Foundation Room, SHARE as the Production and Livelihood Room, and BioCon as the Shield and coordinating lead. Under this framework, the Institute shall adopt the following key systems and platforms: WADE (Wilderness Areas Diversity Enhancement) as the ecological restoration framework institutionalizing the principle “One Man, One Tree Can Make a Forest” through native tree stewardship, habitat restoration, ecological buffering, and integration of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS); the League of Wildlife Conservancy (LWS) as the Institute’s social engine for volunteerism, stewardship, citizen science, and community mobilization; Das-ay Link Platform as the nervous system of the Institute, serving as the central data, validation, and decision-support platform for baseline data from SWaRI, government institutions, validated and veri iable IKS, and future operational outputs from DREAM LABS, DREAM FARMS, DREAM BIOSECURE, and DREAM WATERSHIELDS; ACCESS (Adaptive Climate Change Education Support Services) as the trend-based adaptive learning and support stream arising from Das-ay Link; and RADAR (Resilience Against Disaster and Agricultural Risks) as the shock-based resilience and response stream likewise arising from Das- ay Link. The creation of the DREAM Institute through congressional legislation will provide Southern Leyte State University – Hinunangan Campus with a stronger, more coherent, and more functionally relevant platform for soil and water science, biodiversity conservation, ecological restoration, climate adaptation, risk reduction, resilient agriculture, community extension, and sustainability governance in Southern Leyte and the broader region. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 9811
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE PERSONNEL ECONOMIC RELIEF ALLOWANCE (PERA) GRANTED TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES, PROVIDING FOR AN AUTOMATIC INFLATION ADJUSTMENT MECHANISM, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Personnel Economic Relief Allowance (PERA) is a cost-of-living allowance granted to government employees to help cushion the effects of inflation and rising prices of basic goods and services. PERA was first granted in 1991 through DBM Budget Circular No. 4 dated June 28, 1991, which authorized a monthly allowance of Five Hundred Pesos (₱500.00) for qualified government employees. The allowance was intended to augment government compensation and mitigate the adverse effects of inflation and increases in fuel and commodity prices on public sector workers. Recognizing the continuing erosion of purchasing power caused by rising prices, the government subsequently expanded and enhanced the benefit. In 2009, through Senate and House of Representatives Joint Resolution No. 4, s. 2009, the Personnel Economic Relief Allowance was consolidated with the Additional Compensation (ADCOM) and increased to the current amount of Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) per month, in recognition of the rising cost of living and the need to provide additional economic relief to government personnel. However, the PERA has remained unchanged since 2009. During the intervening years, inflation has steadily increased the cost of food, transportation, housing, utilities, healthcare, education, and other basic necessities. As a result, the real value and purchasing power of the allowance have significantly diminished, undermining its original purpose as a meaningful source of economic relief for government employees. Had the allowance been adjusted to keep pace with inflation, its present value would be substantially higher than the current monthly rate. The prolonged absence of any adjustment has effectively reduced the level of assistance provided by the government to its employees despite the continued rise in the cost of living. This measure seeks to restore the value of the Personnel Economic Relief Allowance by increasing the monthly PERA from Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) to Four Thousand Pesos (₱4,000.00) and establishing an automatic annual adjustment mechanism based on the official inflation rate published by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). By linking future adjustments to inflation, the measure ensures that the allowance remains responsive to economic conditions and continues to provide meaningful relief to government personnel. The proposed increase and indexation mechanism embody the State's commitment to promoting the welfare of government employees and preserving their purchasing power in the face of rising prices and changing economic circumstances. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 51 52 53 HON. JULIENNE “JAM” L. label: HB 9813
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE BUGUEY EXTENSION CAMPUS OF THE CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BUGUEY, PROVINCE OF CAGAYAN, INTO A REGULAR CAMPUS OF THE CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY, TO BE KNOWN AS THE “CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY – BUGUEY CAMPUS”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the existing Buguey Extension Campus of the Cagayan State University (CSU) in the Municipality of Buguey, Province of Cagayan, into a regular campus of the University, to be known as the Cagayan State University – Buguey Campus. The 1987 Constitution recognizes the vital role of education in national development and mandates the State to establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education responsive to the needs of the people and society. Consistent with this constitutional mandate, the government must continue to expand access to quality higher education, particularly in underserved and developing communities. Buguey is a coastal municipality that serves as a strategic center for agriculture, fisheries, trade, and other economic activities in the northeastern part of the Province of Cagayan. As the municipality and its neighboring localities continue to grow, so does the demand for accessible, affordable, and quality tertiary education. However, many students and aspiring professionals continue to face financial and logistical challenges in pursuing higher education, particularly when they are compelled to enroll in campuses located far from their communities. The CSU - Buguey Extension Campus has played a significant role in broadening access to higher education in the municipality and nearby areas. It has provided educational opportunities to countless students and produced graduates who contribute meaningfully to local and national development. Nonetheless, its status as an extension campus limits its capacity to expand academic programs, strengthen institutional operations, and access the resources necessary to effectively address the growing educational needs of the region. The conversion of the Buguey Extension Campus into a regular campus will enhance the University's capacity to deliver quality instruction, research, and extension services. It will enable the campus to accommodate more students, expand its academic offerings, improve infrastructure and learning facilities, strengthen its faculty and personnel complement, and provide adequate student support services. These developments are essential to sustaining academic excellence and fostering institutional growth. Moreover, the establishment of the CSU – Buguey Campus as a regular campus will promote greater access to higher education for students from Buguey and neighboring municipalities. It will help reduce educational disparities, support local human resource development, and contribute to inclusive socio-economic growth in the Province of Cagayan. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JOSEPH “JOJO” L. label: HB 9814
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE CALAYAN EXTENSION CAMPUS OF THE CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CALAYAN, PROVINCE OF CAGAYAN, INTO A REGULAR CAMPUS OF THE CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY, TO BE KNOWN AS THE “CAGAYAN STATE UNIVERSITY – CALAYAN CAMPUS”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the existing Calayan Extension Campus of the Cagayan State University (CSU) in the Municipality of Calayan, Province of Cagayan, into a regular campus of the University, to be known as the Cagayan State University – Calayan Campus. The Constitution recognizes the vital role of education in national development and mandates the State to establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education responsive to the needs of the people and society. The Municipality of Calayan, situated in the northernmost part of the Province of Cagayan, is composed of several island barangays and remains geographically isolated from the mainland. Access to and from the municipality is largely dependent on sea transportation, making travel difficult, costly, and often affected by weather conditions. Consequently, many students from Calayan and neighboring island communities face significant barriers in pursuing higher education due to distance, limited accessibility, and financial constraints. Recognizing these challenges, the local government, in partnership with Cagayan State University, facilitated the establishment of the CSU – Calayan Extension Campus to bring tertiary education closer to the residents of the municipality. Since its establishment, the extension campus has played a crucial role in expanding access to higher education and producing graduates who contribute to the social and economic development of the locality. However, its status as an extension campus limits its capacity to broaden its academic programs, strengthen institutional operations, and access the resources necessary to effectively respond to the increasing educational demands of the community. The growing need for accessible and quality higher education in the municipality underscores the importance of elevating the campus to regular campus status. The conversion of the CSU – Calayan Extension Campus into a regular campus will strengthen the University's presence in this geographically isolated area and enhance its capability to deliver quality instruction, research, other education services. It will enable the campus to expand its academic offerings, improve its facilities and infrastructure, and provide the faculty, personnel, and support services necessary to sustain quality higher education and accommodate a larger student population. Moreover, the establishment of a regular CSU campus in Calayan will promote equitable access to higher education, particularly for students from geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. It will help reduce educational disparities, foster inclusive socio-economic growth, and contribute significantly to the long-term development of the Municipality of Calayan, the Province of Cagayan, and the nation as a whole. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JOSEPH “JOJO” L. label: HB 9815
title: AN ACT GRANTING A FRANCHISE TO THE NEGROS ORIENTAL II ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE INC. (NORECO II) TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE CITIES OF DUMAGUETE, TANJAY, AND BAYAWAN, AND THE MUNICIPALITIES OF PAMPLONA, AMLAN, SAN JOSE, SIBULAN, VALENCIA, BACONG, DAUIN, ZAMBOANGUITA, SIATON, STA. CATALINA, AND BASAY, PROVINCE OF NEGROS ORIENTAL Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Republic of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Nature and Scope of Franchise. - Subject to the provisions of the Constitution and applicable laws, rules and regulations, there is hereby granted NEGROS ORIENTAL II ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. (NORECO II), hereunder referred to as the Grantee, its successors or assigns a franchise to construct, install, establish, operate, own, manage and maintain in the public interest and commercial purposes, a distribution system for the conveyance of electric power to the end-users in the Cities of Dumaguete, Tanjay, and Bayawan, and the Municipalities of Pamplona, Amlan, San Jose, Sibulan, Valencia, Bacong, Dauin, Zamboanguita, Siaton, Santa Catalina, and Basay, all in the Province of Negros Oriental As used in this Act, distribution system refers to the system of wires and associated facilities including sub-transmission lines belonging to a franchised distribution utility extending between the delivery point on the national transmission system or generating facility and the metering point/facility of the end-users. SECTION 2. Manner of Operations of Facilities. - All electric distribution facilities, lines and systems for electric services installed, owned, operated, managed or maintained by the Grantee
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Reliable and adequate electric power is indispensable to the social and economic development of every community. It powers homes, schools, hospitals, government offices, agricultural activities, commercial establishments, and industries that drive growth and improve the quality of life of our people. In Negros Oriental, the continued availability of electric service has been made possible in large part through the efforts of the Negros Oriental II Electric Cooperative (NORECO II), which has served as the primary electric distribution utility in its franchise area for nearly five decades. Since its incorporation with the National Electrification Administration in 1977, NORECO II has played a vital role in advancing the government's rural electrification program and in bringing the benefits of modern energy to communities across southern and central Negros Oriental. Through sustained investments in distribution facilities and service infrastructure, the Cooperative has successfully energized all 272 barangays within its coverage area, ensuring that households, educational institutions, healthcare facilities, businesses, and government establishments have access to electricity necessary for daily operations and long-term development. At present, NORECO II serves more than 183,000 member-consumer-owners in the Cities of Dumaguete, Tanjay, and Bayawan, and in the Municipalities of Pamplona, Amlan, San Jose, Sibulan, Valencia, Bacong, Dauin, Zamboanguita, Siaton, Santa Catalina, and Basay. As a non- stock and non-profit electric cooperative, it operates not for the benefit of private shareholders but for its member-consumer-owners. Any surplus generated from its operations is reinvested into the improvement of its distribution system, expansion of services, enhancement of reliability, and implementation of programs that directly benefit the communities it serves. The eventual expiration of its legislative franchise necessitates the grant of a new franchise to ensure the uninterrupted delivery of electric distribution services within its service area. A renewed franchise will provide the legal authority required for the Cooperative to continue operating, maintaining, and upgrading its facilities while pursuing critical investments in system modernization, substation development, renewable energy integration, digital transformation, and disaster-resilient infrastructure. These initiatives are essential in meeting the growing energy requirements of a developing province and in responding to the increasing expectations of consumers for efficient, reliable, and affordable electric service. More importantly, the renewal of NORECO II's franchise is a measure that protects the public interest. The continuity of electric service is fundamental to economic productivity, public safety, education, healthcare, communications, investment generation, and overall countryside development. Ensuring that NORECO II remains capable of fulfilling its mandate will help sustain the gains achieved through decades of electrification and support the province's long- term development goals. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA ISABEL L. label: HB 9816
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution affirms the State’s duty to afford full protection to labor and to ensure just and humane conditions of work, including the right of workers to receive a fair and living wage. Central to this guarantee is the ability of workers to know, verify, and, when necessary, contest how their wages are computed and paid. Without clear and accessible documentation of earnings and deductions, these rights are rendered difficult to enforce in practice. Under the Labor Code of the Philippines and related issuances of the Department of Labor and Employment, employers are required to pay wages properly and ensure transparency in deductions. However, the obligation to issue itemized pay statements or payslips is not explicitly provided in the statute itself, but instead inferred from implementing rules and reinforced through administrative advisories. This gap in statutory clarity has resulted in uneven compliance across industries and employment arrangements, particularly in subcontracted, small and medium enterprise, and non-standard or emerging forms of work. In practice, many workers do not regularly receive payslips. This creates a serious enforcement gap. Without documentary proof of wages received, workers are placed at a significant disadvantage in asserting claims for underpayment, non-payment of statutory benefits, or illegal deductions. Existing enforcement mechanisms, which are largely complaint-driven and inspection-dependent, often require workers to substantiate claims without access to basic Page 1 of 8 payroll records. As a result, wage-related violations, including wage theft and disguised deductions, may persist with limited accountability. This bill addresses these gaps by making the issuance of itemized payslips an explicit statutory obligation and, more importantly, by positioning payslips as a core enforcement and transparency mechanism in labor standards compliance. The measure strengthens enforcement by integrating payslip compliance into the visitorial and enforcement powers of the Department of Labor and Employment under Article 128 of the Labor Code. It ensures that compliance is subject to routine and complaint-based inspections and treated as a labor standards violation when not observed. To address evidentiary barriers faced by workers, the bill establishes a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee in cases where the employer fails to issue payslips, thereby aligning legal procedure with the realities of workplace documentation and strengthening workers’ ability to assert their claims. Recognizing the recurring nature of wage opacity, the bill imposes graduated administrative penalties per affected employee and per pay period, ensuring that non-compliance is not treated as a one-time infraction but as a continuing violation warranting proportionate sanctions. This deterrence framework is designed to promote sustained compliance rather than episodic correction. The measure likewise addresses enforcement gaps in contracting and subcontracting arrangements by imposing joint and solidary liability, ensuring that wage transparency obligations cannot be evaded through layered employment structures. It also clarifies coverage of non-standard work arrangements, without altering existing legal tests for determining employer-employee relationships. At the same time, the bill adopts a practical and modern compliance framework by allowing the issuance of electronic payslips, subject to accessibility, verifiability, and record-keeping requirements. This ensures that the measure remains feasible for employers, including small enterprises, while safeguarding workers’ access to their wage records. In sum, this measure does not merely restate existing policy. It closes a clear statutory gap, strengthens enforcement through integration with existing powers, introduces evidentiary tools that make labor rights actionable, and establishes a proportionate deterrence system against wage opacity and abuse. Page 2 of 8 By transforming payslips from a procedural formality into a central instrument of wage transparency, accountability, and worker protection, this bill advances the State’s commitment to social justice and the dignity of labor. In solidarity with the working class, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ELIJAH R. title: AN ACT CREATING THE SOLAR HOME SYSTEM FINANCING FOR SOCIAL HOUSING PROGRAM, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR 98 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 100 Section 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Solar Home System Financing for Social Housing Program Act.” 103 Section 2. Declaration of Policy. – The State recognizes its constitutional duty to make decent housing with basic services available at affordable cost to underprivileged and homeless citizens in urban centers and resettlement areas. Electricity is indispensable to health, education, safety, and economic participation. 108 Informal settler families (ISFs) displaced by government infrastructure projects, urban renewal programs, or disaster risk reduction measures are disproportionately excluded from grid electricity. Connection costs and occupancy-based service requirements make grid power inaccessible to most resettlement communities, negating the material benefits of resettlement. 114
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 Energy is a key component of progress for a society. It is an essential tool for nation-building and an effective weapon against poverty. In the Philippines, while access to electricity has expanded across most of the country, it unfortunately remains inaccessible for many, especially those who need it most. 27 The data is uncontestable. Despite an electrification level of 91.1% as of mid-2023, approximately 2.45 million Filipino households remain without power. The majority of them are in remote and off-grid areas,1 including in-city and off-city resettlement sites occupied by Informal Settler Families (ISFs). The lack of reliable and affordable electricity in resettlement sites also compromises the government’s program because ISFs find it difficult, if not impossible, to remain in homes where there is no access to basic service such as electricity. 35 Millions of Filipino households, especially resettlement sites, remain in the dark because of two primary reasons. First, private utility companies require at least 90% occupancy of subdivisions before connection to the grid is allowed.2 Second, alternatives 1 Department of Energy, Phil., 2023–2032 National Total Electrification Roadmap (2023), accessed at https://legacy.doe.gov.ph/sites/default/files/pdf/electric_power/2023-2032-NTER-2023-2032-Annexes.pdf. 2 Ballesteros and Egana, Efficiency and Effectiveness Review of the National Housing Authority (NHA) Resettlement Program, PIDS Discussion Paper No. 2013-28, at 13 (Phil. It can, whenever applicable, exist independently from grid connection, and effectively bypass the dependence of households on private public utility companies as providers of access to electricity. 47 Unfortunately, while solar technology offers a solution, the next barrier is the cost which is prohibitive. Currently, solar energy loans reach up to PhP 500,000.3 ISFs cannot afford this. The remedy then is to spread out the obligation into manageable tranches and include them as part of existing housing loans offered by the government, subject to reasonable and favorable terms for the target beneficiaries. 53 By aligning new initiatives with – and enhancing – existing government programs, the problem of households (especially ISFs) deprived of access to affordable electricity could finally be solved. label: HB 9818
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE MINIMUM SALARY GRADE LEVEL OF NURSES FROM SALARY GRADE 15 TO 19, AMENDING SEC. 32 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9173, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS "THE PHILIPPINE NURSING ACT OF 2002"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Nurses play a vital role in the delivery of healthcare services and are indispensable to the promotion, protection, and restoration of the health of the Filipino people. As frontline healthcare professionals, they perform critical functions in hospitals, health centers, schools, communities, and other healthcare settings, often under demanding and high-risk conditions. Despite their invaluable contribution to the healthcare system, many Filipino nurses continue to face inadequate compensation, prompting many to seek employment opportunities abroad or leave the profession altogether. This continuing exodus has contributed to shortages in the nursing workforce, placing additional strain on the country's healthcare system and affecting the quality and accessibility of healthcare services. While Republic Act No. 9173, otherwise known as the "Philippine Nursing Act of 2002," and subsequent issuances improved the compensation of government nurses, there remains a need to further enhance their salaries in recognition of their professional qualifications, responsibilities, and indispensable role in safeguarding public health. This bill seeks to upgrade the minimum salary grade level of nurses in government service from Salary Grade 15 to Salary Grade 19. By providing more competitive compensation, the measure aims to strengthen the recruitment and retention of nurses in the public sector, improve morale and productivity, and ensure a more stable and responsive healthcare workforce for the benefit of all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 9819
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE HEMODIALYSIS, PERITONEAL DIALYSIS, AND OTHER RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPIES FOR SENIOR CITIZENS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the right of every Filipino to health and adopts an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. Senior citizens, who are among the most vulnerable sectors of society, are particularly susceptible to chronic kidney disease and other renal illnesses that require regular dialysis treatments for survival. Despite existing government health programs, many senior citizens continue to face significant financial burdens arising from the costs of hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, renal replacement therapies, related laboratory procedures, medicines, and supplies. For elderly patients who rely mainly on limited pensions or family support, the continuing expenses associated with dialysis often result in delayed treatment, financial hardship, and reduced quality of life. This measure seeks to guarantee full coverage of medically necessary hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and other Department of Health-approved renal replacement therapies for all senior citizens through PhilHealth-accredited health facilities, thereby ensuring that no elderly Filipino is deprived of life- sustaining treatment due to financial constraints. By strengthening health protection for senior citizens and promoting equitable access to essential healthcare services, this bill advances the constitutional mandate to protect and promote the right to health of the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 9820
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE AND NUTRITIOUS SCHOOL MEALS TO ALL PUBLIC-SCHOOL CHILDREN TO PROMOTE HEALTH, LEARNING, AND INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Good nutrition is fundamental to learning, health, and human development. Yet many Filipino children continue to suffer from hunger, undernutrition, and micronutrient deficiencies that adversely affect their physical growth, cognitive development, school attendance, academic performance, and long-term productivity. Studies consistently show that children who come to school hungry are less able to concentrate, participate in classroom activities, and achieve their full learning potential. Malnutrition remains a significant barrier to educational attainment and contributes to poor health outcomes, increased absenteeism, and reduced economic productivity later in life. While existing school feeding initiatives have benefited millions of learners, their coverage remains limited and uneven. There is a need to institutionalize a comprehensive, sustainable, and adequately funded national school meals program that ensures all public-school learners have access to safe, nutritious, and age-appropriate meals throughout the school year. This measure seeks to establish a Universal Free School Meals Program covering learners in the public basic education system, strengthen nutrition interventions in schools, promote healthier learning environments, improve attendance and educational outcomes, and support the government's broader efforts to combat hunger and malnutrition. The measure likewise promotes the procurement of food from local farmers, fisherfolk, and cooperatives, thereby supporting local agriculture and rural livelihoods while enhancing food security. By investing in the nutrition of Filipino learners today, the State invests in a healthier, more productive, and more competitive future generation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 9821
title: AN ACT PRESCRIBING A JUST AND HUMANE CODE OF CONDUCT FOR THE RESETTLEMENT OF UNDERPRIVILEGED AND HOMELESS CITIZENS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Part of the objectives of enacting Republic Act No. 7279 or the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992 (UDHA) was the provision of secure, safe, adequate, decent, and affordable housing for the urban poor, especially for informal settler families (ISFs). Although the UDHA intended to limit the displacement of the urban poor and provide safeguards in cases of resettlement, experiences of ISFs over the years show a distortion in the implementation of the existing framework to circumvent the requirements under the law. In 2008, the United Nations Committee on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (UN CESCR) expressed its deep concern for the large-scale forced evictions of urban families: “The Committee regrets that most of its previous recommendations relating to the prevention of illegal forced evictions (E/C.12/1995/7, paras. 31 and 32) have not been acted upon by the State party, and remains deeply concerned about the large- scale forced eviction of urban families carried out for the purpose of urban renewal and beautification, which has reportedly affected over 1.2 million people in the period between 1995 and 2008. It is also concerned about the lack of effective consultation of, and legal redress for, persons affected by forced evictions, and the inadequate measures to provide sufficient compensation or adequate relocation sites to families who have been forcibly removed from their properties.”1 Eight years later, the UN CESCR urged the Philippines to amend the UDHA and adopt a legal framework “to be followed in the case of evictions in line with international standards[.]”2 Over three decades have passed since the enactment of the UDHA, yet there is still no legal framework for housing and resettlement that adequately addresses the needs of ISFs and the urban poor that is consistent with our constitutional mandates and core international instruments. The proposed bill seeks to address the gaps in the UDHA by: a) strictly prohibiting unjust evictions of ISFs and demolitions of the structures they live in; b) imposing additional requirements before, during, and after any eviction or demolition of ISFs, such as social preparation, adequate resettlement, spaces for children to play and interact in relocation sites, and adequate and genuine consultation; and c) designating the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor (PCUP) as the central coordinating body and clearing house for evictions and demolitions. The ISFs and the urban poor have experienced many of the worst injustices in our country. At the center of these injustices are children who are forcibly displaced from their homes and suffer abusive and inhumane practices in the conduct of eviction and demolition. No less than Section 10 of Article III of the Constitution mandates that “[u]urban or rural poor dwellers shall not be evicted nor their dwelling demolished, except in accordance with law and in a just and humane manner.” In light of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 9822
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A COMPREHENSIVE AND AFFORDABLE FRAMEWORK FOR EARLY DETECTION AND INTERVENTION SERVICES FOR CHILDREN WITH SPECIAL NEEDS”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every child deserves the opportunity to reach his or her full potential. Yet many Filipino children with developmental delays, disabilities, and other special needs remain undiagnosed or receive intervention only after critical developmental milestones have been missed, particularly in underserved and geographically isolated communities. While Republic Act No. 11650 or the Inclusive Education Act strengthened the State's commitment to inclusive learning, gaps remain in the early detection, assessment, referral, and intervention systems needed to support children with special needs. Families continue to face barriers such as limited access to specialists, high therapy costs, and inadequate community-based support services. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive and affordable framework for the early detection and intervention of children with special needs through accessible screening, assessment, intervention, parent support, workforce development, and stronger coordination among health, education, and social welfare agencies. It also strengthens community-based support systems, enhances Special Education (SPED) Centers, and promotes accountability through monitoring and oversight mechanisms. By ensuring timely intervention and support, the State can help children with special needs achieve better developmental, educational, and social outcomes, while ensuring that no child is left behind. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 9823
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE FREE DIGITAL PROVISION OF TEXTBOOKS USED IN BASIC EDUCATION, ENCOURAGING OPEN EDUCATIONAL RESOURCES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to quality education is a constitutional right and a vital foundation of national development. Yet many Filipino learners continue to face difficulties in obtaining timely and affordable access to textbooks and other essential learning materials. In an increasingly digital world, educational resources must be made more accessible, inclusive, and responsive to the needs of learners. This bill requires that all textbooks and instructional materials submitted for approval, adoption, or procurement by the Department of Education (DepEd) be accompanied by a digital copy that may be made available free of charge to learners, teachers, and schools through DepEd-authorized platforms. Compliance with this requirement shall be a condition for DepEd approval and procurement. The measure likewise promotes the development and use of Open Educational Resources (OER), which are freely accessible and openly licensed educational materials that may be used, adapted, and shared to expand learning opportunities. By ensuring the free digital availability of approved learning resources, this measure will reduce costs for families, expand access to quality educational materials, support flexible learning modalities, and help build a more inclusive, resilient, and future-ready basic education system. The measure respects and preserves the intellectual property rights of authors and publishers while advancing the State's responsibility to make education more accessible to all. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. ERIC L. label: HB 9824
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE MEDICAL ACCESS OF OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS (OFWs) AND THEIR FAMILIES BY STRENGTHENING THE OFW HOSPITAL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR’”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) make invaluable contributions to the Philippine economy through their hard work and sacrifice abroad. In recognition of their vital role in nation-building, it is imperative that the government ensure accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare services for OFWs and their families. While the establishment of the OFW Hospital in San Fernando, Pampanga marked a significant step in addressing the healthcare needs of migrant workers, there remains a need to expand access to specialized healthcare services in other parts of the country and to institutionalize financial protection for OFWs seeking medical treatment. This measure strengthens the OFW Hospital, authorizes the establishment or designation of Regional OFW Hospitals to bring healthcare services closer to OFWs and their dependents, and institutionalizes a zero-billing policy to ensure that qualified OFWs and their dependents receive medically necessary treatment without financial burden, subject to existing laws and available government assistance programs. By enhancing healthcare access and support mechanisms for OFWs and their families, this bill affirms the State’s commitment to safeguarding the welfare of the nation’s modern-day heroes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 9826
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE BENGUET HIGHLAND FARMERS ASSISTANCE PROGRAM, PROVIDING DIRECT SUBSIDIES, CLIMATE RESILIENCE SUPPORT, POSTHARVEST ASSISTANCE, AND MARKET DEVELOPMENT INTERVENTIONS FOR FARMERS IN THE PROVINCE OF BENGUET, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Benguet Highland Farmers Assistance Program to amend existing agricultural support frameworks under the Department of Agriculture (DA). This creates a dedicated, institutionalized mechanism for direct subsidies, climate resilience interventions, postharvest support, and market development assistance for farmers in the Province of Benguet. The measure recognizes the absence of an active funding mechanism under the Agricultural Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (ACEF), which under Republic Act No. 10848 was set for termination upon the lapse of its collection period in 2022, thereby necessitating a new statutory program anchored on annual national appropriations to ensure continuity of agricultural support services for highland farmers. The Province of Benguet remains one of the country’s primary vegetable-producing provinces, supplying a significant portion of highland vegetables consumed in Metro Manila and other urban centers. However, despite its critical role in national food security, Benguet farmers continue to experience severe market volatility and income instability. In 2026, multiple reports documented that cabbage farmgate prices in Benguet dropped to as low as Three pesos (P3.00) to Ten pesos (P10.00) per kilogram, far below production costs. This forces farmers to either sell at a loss or leave crops unharvested. The same reports show that production costs reach approximately Eighteen pesos (P18.00) to Twenty pesos (P20.00) per kilogram, creating persistent negative margins for farmers amid weak demand and oversupply conditions. GMA News further reported that many farmers have been forced to abandon harvesting altogether due to rising fuel and transport costs, which make delivery to trading centers financially unsustainable1,2. Complementary coverage also shows instances where vegetables are either sold at extremely low 1 Lema, K. and Portugal, A. (2026, April 7). Benguet farmers let crops rot due to oversupply. GMA News Online. Accessed from: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/regions/983309/benguet-farmers-let-crops-rot-due-to-oversu pply/story/. Accessed in: June 4, 2026. prices or given away due to lack of buyers in trading posts3. These conditions are further worsened by the rising of fuel and fertilizer costs, climate-related disruptions, and structural inefficiencies in the agricultural supply chain, all of which continue to place Benguet farmers in a cycle of production losses despite their critical contribution to the national food supply. The proposed measure provides a comprehensive package of interventions, including direct input subsidies, fuel assistance, climate-resilient farming technologies, postharvest infrastructure, agricultural insurance support, and market development initiatives. Unlike fragmented and project-based interventions, the bill establishes a unified program under the DA to ensure coordinated planning, implementation, and monitoring of agricultural assistance. It also strengthens accountability mechanisms through annual reporting to Congress, guaranteeing that government support translates into measurable improvements in farm productivity, income stability, and sectoral resilience. This measure responds to a persistent and painful reality: the very farmers who sustain the nation’s food supply remain among its most economically vulnerable. Every season of price collapse, every field left unharvested, and every farmer forced to sell below cost reflects a deeper structural failure that cannot be ignored. Benguet farmers continue to feed millions, yet many struggle to feed their own families with dignity. This bill seeks to break that cycle of vulnerability and neglect. It carries the urgency of a sector that cannot wait for another harvest cycle of loss, and it calls for immediate and sustained government action to ensure that those who cultivate the nation’s food are finally given the support they have long deserved. label: HB 9827
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE TAX-EXEMPT THRESHOLD FOR PERSONAL INCOME TAX AND THE TAX-EXEMPT CEILING FOR DE MINIMIS BENEFITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24 AND SECTION 32 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8424, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997”, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to increase the tax-exempt threshold for personal income tax from Two hundred fifty thousand pesos (P250,000.00) to Five hundred thousand pesos (P500,000.00). It also seeks to raise the tax-exempt ceiling for the thirteenth (13th) month pay and other benefits from Ninety thousand pesos (P90,000.00) to Two hundred thousand pesos (P200,000.00). The 1987 Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social and economic force and mandates the protection of workers’ rights, and the promotion of their welfare. Republic Act No. 10963, otherwise known as the “Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law”, restructured individual income taxes to provide relief to taxpayers. However, persistent inflation and the continued increase in the prices of basic goods and services have substantially diminished the purchasing power of Filipino households since its implementation. As a result, the current tax-exempt thresholds no longer provide the same level of relief originally intended under the law. The existing tax-exempt income threshold and tax-exempt ceiling for employee benefits have become inadequate because of increasing cost of living, thus reducing the real value of workers’ earnings and take home pay. The proposed measure allows workers to retain a greater portion of their earnings, provides additional financial relief to low- and middle- income families, and supports domestic consumption and economic activity. This bill advances social equity and the welfare of every Filipino worker in the country who earnestly works hard to provide for the daily subsistence of their families. Ensuring that the tax system remains fair, responsive, and attuned to the realities faced by the labor sector reaffirms the State’s commitment to protecting the welfare of labor amid evolving economic conditions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9828
title: AN ACT PENALIZING FRAUD AGAINST OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to penalize fraudulent acts committed against Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs). This includes investment scams, false sales, hidden charges, coercive financial practices, and financial account scamming. OFWs sustain families, communities, and the national economy through their labor and remittances. However, their distance from the country, reliance on digital transactions, and limited access to immediate legal remedies expose them to fraudulent aches that target their savings, income, and financial accounts. These factors not only cause personal financial loss, but also undermine the welfare of families who depend on OFW remittances for education, health care, housing, and daily subsistence. Fraud committed against OFWs require a more specific legal response because perpetrators often exploit their distinct circumstances as migrant workers. This bill strengthens protection for overseas workers and their dependents by expressly defining prohibited fraudulent acts, imposing higher penalties, and allowing restitution for financial losses suffered by the victims. The proposed measure affirms the State’s duty to protect migrant workers not only from labor-related abuse, but also from financial exploitation that deprives them of the fruits of their work abroad. It establishes a clear deterrent against persons and entities that prey on OFWs through deceit, misrepresentation, coercion, or abuse of financial accounts. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9829
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE PRODUCTION, IMPORTATION, SALE, DISTRIBUTION, PROVISION, USE, RECOVERY, COLLECTION, RECYCLING, AND DISPOSAL OF SINGLE-USE PLASTIC PRODUCTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for national plastic waste management across the country. It aims to regulate the production, importation, sale, distribution, provision, use, recovery, collection, recycling, and disposal of single-use plastic products. Plastic remains a primary driver of environmental degradation in the Philippines, with hundreds of thousands of tonnes of plastic entering marine ecosystems annually from coastal urban centers. This volume translates to billions of single-use plastics such as plastic drinking bottles, bottle caps, food wrappers, straws, shopping bags, and other polystyrene containers discarded every year. Accelerated economic growth and shifting consumer consumption patterns compound this issue, and creates an unsustainable trajectory of solid waste generation that outpaces current containment capacities. This bill seeks to regulate the production, importation, sale, distribution, recycling, and disposal of single-used plastics. It also aligns with international frameworks, specifically supporting the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Paris Agreement on climate change mitigation. Transitioning industries toward localized, sustainable alternatives protects public health, safeguards marine resources, and reinforces the climate resilience of vulnerable coastal communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9830
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FREE FINANCIAL EDUCATION TO OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND THEIR FAMILIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive and accessible financial education program for Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) and their families. This promotes financial security, informed decision-making, and the productive use of remittances. OFWs continue to play a vital role in the Philippine economy through the remittances they send to support their families and contribute to national development. Despite these contributions, many OFWs and their households remain vulnerable to excessive debt, fraudulent investment schemes, and financial mismanagement. Financial literacy is essential to ensure that the earnings of OFWs translate into sustainable economic gains for themselves and their families. Equipping them with practical knowledge on budgeting, savings, investments, credit management, insurance, and consumer protection strengthens their capacity to build financial resilience and prepare for future uncertainties. This measure integrates mandatory and regularly updated financial education into the migration cycle by incorporating such training into Pre-Departure Orientation Seminars (PDOS) and Post-Arrival Training Seminars (PATS). It likewise extends financial education services to the families of OFWs through online and community-based platforms, recognizing their invaluable role in managing remittances and household finances. The bill further strengthens public awareness against online scams, fraudulent schemes, predatory lending practices, and other financial threats that target OFWs and their dependents. Consistent with the State’s constitutional duty to protect labor and promote the welfare of Filipino workers overseas, this measure empowers OFWs and their families with the knowledge and skills necessary to achieve long-term financial stability and maximize the benefits of overseas employment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9831
title: AN ACT GRANTING BENEFITS AND PRIVILEGES TO INDIGENT OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant benefits and privileges to indigent Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) who have returned to the Philippines after years of employment abroad and who remain economically vulnerable despite their significant contributions to the country’s national development. The migration of Filipino labor serves as a primary pillar of national macroeconomic stability. The remittances of our OFWs sustain millions of Filipino families and provide a stable source of foreign exchange that supports economic growth. Their sacrifices have earned them recognition as modern-day heroes, often requiring years of separation from their families in pursuit of better opportunities for their loved ones and the nation. Despite these contributions, many returning OFWs face significant reintegration challenges. Limited employment opportunities, inadequate savings, rising cost of living, and restricted access to affordable healthcare often leave them in financially precarious situations. These were particularly evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, when thousands of repatriated OFWs struggled to secure sustainable sources of income upon their return. This proposed measure grants qualified indigent OFWs discount and privileges on essential goods and services. This includes medicines, medical and dental care, transportation, utilities, lodging, burial services, and government programs. It likewise provides access to livelihood, housing, training, and other forms of assistance intended to promote their welfare and improve their quality of life. The State has a responsibility not only to protect Filipino workers while they are employed overseas but also to support them when they return home. Reintegration assistance should extend beyond employment facilitation and livelihood programs to include measures that help address the immediate social and economic needs of vulnerable returning workers. Those who have devoted years of their lives to supporting their families and contributing to the country’s prosperity deserve the opportunity to return to a homeland that values their sacrifice and enables them to rebuild their lives with dignity, hope, and security. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9837
title: AN ACT GRANTING A TEN-DAY BEREAVEMENT LEAVE WITH FULL PAY TO ALL EMPLOYEES IN THE PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a mandatory bereavement leave benefit of ten (10) days with full pay for employees both in the public and private sector who suffer the loss of an immediate family member. The measure likewise guarantees the non-diminution of existing benefits and protects employees from dismissal, demotion, or other adverse employment actions arising from the availment of bereavement leave. The death of a loved one is among the most difficult experiences a person can endure. Beyond the emotional and psychological toll of grief, family members are often burdened with funeral arrangements, legal and financial obligations, and the responsibility of supporting relatives during a period of mourning. Despite these realities, there is currently no comprehensive national law granting bereavement leave to all employees, leaving many workers dependent on employer discretion or forcing them to use vacation or sick leave credits during times of personal loss. Studies have shown that bereavement can significantly affect an individual's mental health, emotional well-being, and work performance1. The American Psychological Association recognizes grief as a major life stressor that can impair concentration, productivity, and overall functioning, particularly in the period immediately following a loss2. Providing adequate time for mourning and family obligations can help employees cope with grief and facilitate their eventual return to work in a healthier and more productive manner. This measure grants employees a reasonable period of paid leave to grieve, attend to funeral arrangements, and support their families without fear of losing income or employment. The bill promotes compassion in the workplace while recognizing the importance of family solidarity and employee well-being. 1 Lundorff et al. (2017). Prevalence of Prolonged Grief Disorder in Adult Bereavement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Affective Disorders. Accessed on 6 June 2026. 2 American Psychological Association (2023). Grief: Coping with the Loss of Your Loved One. American Psychological Association. Accessed on 6 June 2026. The Filipino family remains the foundation of society, and public policy must reflect the realities faced by workers during times of profound personal loss. Granting bereavement leave is a human and compassionate measure that affirms the dignity of labor, strengthens family support systems, and recognizes that employees should not be forced to choose between their livelihood and their need to mourn. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9838
title: AN ACT MANDATING PUBLIC TELECOMMUNICATIONS ENTITIES AND INTERNET SERVICE PROVIDERS TO INSTITUTE AN AUTOMATIC REFUND MECHANISM FOR SERVICE OUTAGES AND DISRUPTIONS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate all Public Telecommunications Entities (PTEs) and Internet Service Providers (ISPs) operating in the Philippines to institute an automatic refund or bill adjustment mechanism. This is in favor of subscribers who have experienced service outages or interruptions for an aggregate period of twenty-four (24) hours or more within a billing month. The Philippines faces a persistent and well-documented crisis in internet reliability. In 2024, Opensignal ranked the country among the lowest-performing nations in the world on this metric1. A separate Opensignal study likewise placed the Philippines alongside India, Colombia, and Mexico as one of the lowest-scoring countries globally for broadband reliability2. This is particularly damaging given that more than one and a half (1.5) million Filipinos work remotely and the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) sector, which employs 1.82 million and contributes to roughly nine percent (9%) of the country’s GDP, depends entirely on stable Internet connectivity3. Aside from this, ordinary consumers feel this too through dropped calls during online meetings, failed digital payments, and sudden data loss. Under existing regulations, subscribers bear the burden of seeking compensation for service interruptions. This bill eliminates that transfer of burden to the consumers by mandating for refunds to be automatic and provider-initiated. Reliable internet connectivity is no longer a luxury but an essential infrastructure in a competitive economy.
