label: HB 9839
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSTALLATION OF CLOSED-CIRCUIT TELEVISION SYSTEMS AT GOVERNMENT TRANSACTION COUNTERS AND THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PUBLIC SERVICE HOTLINES, STRENGTHENING TRANSPARENCY, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND RESPONSIVENESS IN GOVERNMENT SERVICE DELIVERY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6713, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CODE OF CONDUCT AND ETHICAL STANDARDS FOR PUBLIC OFFICIALS AND EMPLOYEES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to require the installation of Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) systems in government service counters and public areas. It strengthens Republic Act No. 6713, otherwise known as the “Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees,”, and also establishes accessible public service hotlines for reporting misconduct, unethical behavior, and violations committed by public officials and employees. Public office is a public trust. Government agencies are expected to deliver services with integrity, accountability, transparency, and professionalism. However, complaints involving discourteous conduct, inefficiency, abuse of authority, solicitation of favors, and other forms of misconduct continue to erode public confidence in government institutions. In many instances, the absence of effective monitoring mechanisms and accessible reporting channels discourages citizens from reporting wrongdoing and seeking redress. This bill institutionalizes the use of CCTV monitoring systems in government offices and establishes confidential reporting hotlines to promote greater accountability, improve service delivery, and strengthen public trust in government. It likewise ensures that all recorded footage and reports are handled in accordance with applicable privacy and data protection laws while supporting the effective enforcement of ethical standards in the public sector. Integrity, transparency, and accountability are fundamental pillars of good governance. The adoption of modern mechanisms to enhance oversight and encourage public participation in reporting misconduct will help significantly in upholding the highest standards of ethical conduct in public service and in ensuring that government remains responsive to the people it serves. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9840
title: AN ACT PROCLAIMING THE RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS OF PATIENTS, PROVIDING A GRIEVANCE MECHANISM THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive Magna Carta of Patients’ Rights and Obligations, together with an accessible and structured grievance mechanism, in order to strengthen the delivery of humane, ethical, and quality healthcare in the Philippines. While significant strides have been made in expanding access to health services, there remains a need to clearly define and uniformly uphold the rights of patients as well as their corresponding responsibilities within the healthcare system. This measure affirms the fundamental principle that every patient is entitled to dignity, informed choice, privacy, and equitable access to care, while likewise recognizing that effective healthcare delivery requires mutual respect, accountability, and cooperation between patients and healthcare providers. At the same time, the bill establishes a clear and progressive grievance redress mechanism to ensure that complaints arising from alleged violations of patient rights are addressed promptly, fairly, and without undue adversarial burden. The measure promotes accessible dispute resolution while helping preserve trust in the doctor-patient relationship through a structured system of hospital-based and community-level mediation, with escalation to professional and ethical review bodies when necessary. It also reinforces the shared obligations of patients to provide accurate information, comply with medical advice, and respect healthcare institutions and personnel, thereby fostering a culture of responsibility alongside rights. Overall, the measure aims to strengthen the integrity of the healthcare system, enhance patient trust, and promote ethical medical practice through clearly defined rights, duties, and remedies. It gives full effect to the State’s constitutional mandate to protect health and uphold human dignity in all healthcare settings. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 9842
title: AN ACT PROFESSIONALIZING PARALEGAL PRACTICE IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THIS PURPOSE A PROFESSIONAL REGULATORY BOARD OF PARALEGALS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Paralegals perform an indispensable role in the legal industry and provide essential support to lawyers. This allows lawyers to provide services in the most effective and efficient way possible. Their contributions to case preparation and other legal work are vital to the development and success of a case. Despite the rising demand and increasing complexity of legal cases, there are no laws or regulations establishing standards for paralegals. The growing number of paralegals emphasize the need to establish a framework to advance the professionalization of the field. Multiple jurisdictions have opted to regulate the practice of paralegals. In Ontario, Canada, paralegals are required to be graduates of a paralegal education program and pass a licensure examination.1 In California, the roles of paralegals are defined by law, including the limitations of their profession. Their qualifications are also provided by law, as well as the requirement that they undergo mandatory continuing legal education.2 This measure seeks to promote competence within the paralegal profession. It creates the Professional Regulatory Board for Paralegals and defines the paralegal practice. It mandates that all aspiring paralegals pass a licensure examination and avail of continuing professional education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of the bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9843
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RECOGNITION, QUALITY ASSURANCE, STACKABILITY, AND PORTABILITY OF MICROCREDENTIALS AND SHORT COURSES, STRENGTHENING WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT, PROVIDING FLEXIBLE LEARNING PATHWAYS IN HIGHER EDUCATION AND PROTECTION FOR EMPLOYED STUDENTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid pace of technological change, evolving labor market demands, and the increasing prevalence of non-traditional forms of employment have fundamentally transformed how Filipinos learn, work, and acquire skills. Today, a growing number of learners are simultaneously employed, self-employed, or engaged in livelihood activities while pursuing education and training. However, the existing education framework remains largely structured around long-duration, full-time programs that often require learners to step away from employment, resulting in lost income and limited access for working individuals. This situation poses a significant challenge to inclusive human capital development and workforce resilience. Many Filipinos—particularly employed students, freelancers, contractual workers, and those in the informal sector— require learning opportunities that are flexible, practical, affordable, and responsive to real-world skills needs. There is therefore an urgent need for a legal and policy framework that recognizes alternative learning pathways without undermining academic quality and integrity. This proposed measure, entitled the “Abot-Kayang Pangarap Act,” seeks to address this gap by formally recognizing microcredentials and short courses as legitimate and integral components of the Philippine education and training ecosystem. These credentials provide competency-based, outcomes-focused learning opportunities that may be completed over shorter periods, delivered through flexible modalities, and aligned with industry and workforce requirements. The bill establishes a National Microcredential and Short Course Quality Assurance and Credential Framework to ensure credibility, comparability, and public trust in such credentials. It mandates harmonized standards among the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Department of Education (DepEd), while respecting institutional autonomy and existing mandates. Central to this measure is the promotion of stackability, portability, credit equivalency, and Recognition of Prior Learning, allowing learners to accumulate microcredentials and short courses toward formal academic qualifications without unnecessary repetition of learning already demonstrated. The bill further authorizes CHED to promulgate outcomes-based rules governing academic credit conversion and articulation, guided by transparency, academic integrity, and international best practices. Recognizing the realities faced by working learners, the Act provides protections and reasonable accommodations for employed students and encourages employer support for employee upskilling, consistent with labor laws and management prerogatives. It also establishes a secure Digital Credential Registry to safeguard credential integrity, enable verification, and promote learner mobility. Ultimately, the Abot-Kayang Pangarap Act affirms the State’s commitment to lifelong learning, inclusive access to education, and workforce development by ensuring that opportunities for skills acquisition and professional growth remain attainable, flexible, and responsive to national development priorities—so that education remains within reach for all Filipinos, regardless of employment status or economic circumstance. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 9844
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COHERENT EDUCATION-TO- EMPLOYMENT FRAMEWORK BY ALIGNING THE QUALITY ASSURANCE SYSTEMS OF THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION, THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, AND THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT WITH LABOR MARKET NEEDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed Comprehensive Education-to-Employment Alignment Act establishes a coherent national framework that deliberately aligns education and workforce development as a shared responsibility central to national progress, social mobility, and human dignity. While the country has made significant investments in higher education and technical-vocational training, persistent skills mismatches, underemployment, and uneven regional workforce outcomes indicate the need for a more integrated and evidence-based system. This measure institutionalizes an Education-to-Employment Framework that ensures learning standards, curricula, quality assurance, accreditation, and program delivery are intentionally oriented toward productive, decent, and sustainable employment, without reducing education to short-term labor market matching. It affirms that education quality must be measured not only by academic rigor, but also by its capacity to prepare individuals for meaningful work, adaptability, citizenship, innovation, and inclusive growth—while fully respecting academic freedom, institutional autonomy, and diverse educational missions. The Act mandates structured and continuing coordination among the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to ensure policy coherence and operational alignment across the education-to-employment continuum. Through harmonized quality assurance reforms, differentiated accreditation pathways, curriculum-to- occupation mapping, tracer studies, employer feedback integration, and regular National Education-to-Employment Gap Assessments, the measure embeds workforce relevance into program design, review, and evaluation. At the same time, it safeguards due process, learner protection, and developmental—not punitive—approaches to program rationalization. Labor market intelligence, industry participation, and interoperable data systems will serve as strategic planning tools to anticipate skills mismatches, respond to technological and sectoral change, and strengthen school-to-work transition mechanisms nationwide. Ultimately, the bill strengthens accountability and transparency by integrating education-to-employment outcome indicators into quality assurance systems and requiring the submission of an Annual Education-to-Employment Alignment Report to Congress. It provides for capacity-building, technical assistance, and institutional support to enable higher education institutions and training providers to undertake meaningful reform. By modernizing accreditation, promoting regional labor market alignment, enabling rapid curriculum adjustment in high-mismatch sectors, and prioritizing inclusive and equitable workforce participation, this Act advances a responsive, future-ready, and socially accountable education and training system. The passage of this measure is therefore earnestly sought to ensure that the nation’s education investments translate into dignified employment, sustained productivity, and long-term national development. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9845
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE HIGHER EDUCATION-INDUSTRY PARTNERSHIP FRAMEWORK, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE TRIPARTITE COUNCIL FOR TERTIARY EDUCATION, AND STRENGTHENING STRUCTURED COLLABORATION BETWEEN HIGHER EDUCATION AND INDUSTRY FOR WORKFORCE RELEVANCE, INNOVATION, AND NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive and coherent framework for sustained collaboration between higher education institutions and industry in the Philippines, in recognition of their shared responsibility in developing a skilled, adaptive, and competitive Filipino workforce. Despite existing policies and programs on education, training, qualifications, and workforce development, persistent challenges remain, including graduate unemployment and underemployment, job–skills mismatch, uneven regional development, and weak linkages between learning, research, innovation, and productive economic activity. These challenges underscore the need for a more systematic, structured, and institutionalized mechanism to align higher education outcomes with labor market needs and national development priorities. The proposed measure establishes the Higher Education-Industry Partnership Framework (IHEPF) as a national coordination and governance architecture to guide regular engagement, joint planning, labor market and skills intelligence exchange, and shared accountability among higher education institutions, industry partners, and relevant government agencies. The Framework is expressly designed to function as a coordination and facilitation mechanism only and does not confer regulatory, supervisory, or enforcement powers, nor does it interfere with academic freedom, institutional autonomy, or existing quality assurance and accreditation systems. To support the implementation and continuous refinement of the Framework, the bill creates a Tripartite Council for Tertiary Education (TCTE) composed of representatives from government, higher education, and industry. The Council shall serve as the principal national advisory, coordinating, and intelligence body, tasked with monitoring labor market and skills trends, generating and analyzing workforce and innovation intelligence, and recommending policy measures to strengthen higher education–industry alignment. The Council is consultative in nature and does not supplant or diminish the statutory mandates of existing agencies such as CHED, TESDA, DOLE, DepEd, and DTI. The bill further provides for an Annual General Assembly to serve as a national convergence platform for dialogue, assessment, and collective learning among stakeholders, as well as the possible creation of Regional and Sectoral Advisory Boards to ensure that local and sector-specific contexts, priorities, and labor market conditions are adequately reflected in national policy discussions. Recognizing institutional diversity and autonomy, the measure encourages—but does not mandate—higher education institutions to establish Higher Education–Industry Partnership Units to manage and coordinate engagement with industry partners in a transparent, ethical, and systematic manner. Overall, this bill seeks to strengthen the relevance, responsiveness, and future-readiness of the Philippine tertiary education system by fostering structured, inclusive, and sustained partnerships with industry, while fully respecting academic freedom, institutional autonomy, and existing legal mandates. In doing so, it aims to enhance graduate employability, innovation capacity, and national competitiveness in support of inclusive and sustainable development. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE, COHERENT, AND SUSTAINABLE FACULTY DEVELOPMENT AND RESEARCH FRAMEWORK FOR PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION, PROVIDING FOR FACULTY SCHOLARSHIPS AND RESEARCH GRANTS, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE A FACULTY DEVELOPMENT AND RESEARCH FUND, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Higher education is a cornerstone of national development, playing a central role in building human capital, advancing innovation, promoting social mobility, and enhancing global competitiveness. At the heart of a strong higher education system are its faculty members—teachers, researchers, mentors, and academic leaders whose qualifications, competencies, and scholarly productivity directly influence instructional quality, student achievement, and the creation and application of knowledge. Despite sustained efforts to reform the higher education sector, faculty development and research in the Philippines continue to face persistent and structural challenges. Existing scholarship, research, and capacity-building initiatives have often been fragmented, short-term, and dependent on changing administrative priorities. The absence of a unified, statutory, and long-term framework has contributed to uneven faculty qualifications across regions and institution types, underdeveloped institutional research systems, limited graduate supervision capacity, and weak alignment between higher education outputs and national development objectives. Significant disparities remain between well-resourced institutions and those located in geographically isolated, disadvantaged, or emerging areas. Many higher education institutions (HEIs) experience difficulty in meeting faculty qualification standards, sustaining graduate programs, or developing a critical mass of research-active faculty. These constraints adversely affect teaching quality, restrict innovation, weaken graduate education, and diminish the contribution of higher education to economic growth, social progress, and evidence-based policymaking. This proposed measure, entitled the “Philippine Higher Education Faculty Development and Research Act,” seeks to address these challenges by establishing a comprehensive, coherent, and sustainable national framework for faculty development and research. It explicitly affirms faculty development and research as core, integral, and continuing functions of higher education, alongside instruction and extension. The bill mandates the formulation of a National Faculty Development and Research Framework to be led by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), providing a unified policy direction for faculty development, research capacity strengthening, and graduate education enhancement. The framework adopts a developmental, differentiated, and equity-sensitive approach that respects institutional autonomy while recognizing variations in institutional mandates, typologies, stages of development, and regional contexts. The measure institutionalizes a broad range of faculty development and research interventions, including graduate and post-graduate studies, teaching and learning innovations, research capability-building, academic leadership development, industry and community immersion, and mentoring and peer- learning systems. It likewise strengthens the higher education research ecosystem through competitive research initiatives, support for early-career researchers, strengthened research ethics and governance, enhanced graduate research supervision, and mechanisms for research dissemination and utilization. The bill further reinforces governance and accountability by establishing a permanent Faculty Development and Research Service within CHED, institutionalizing systematic monitoring and evaluation, requiring regular 2 reporting to Congress, and creating a National Higher Education Research Repository to promote transparency, accessibility, and knowledge sharing. Ultimately, this measure provides a long-overdue statutory foundation to professionalize, sustain, and equalize faculty development and research across Philippine higher education, ensuring that improvements in teaching quality, research capacity, and academic leadership translate into meaningful and lasting contributions to national development. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9847
title: AN ACT ALLOWING, UNDER EXCEPTIONAL CONDITIONS, THE APPOINTMENT AND GRANT OF ACADEMIC TENURE TO QUALIFIED FOREIGN NATIONALS IN TEACHING AND RESEARCH POSITIONS IN STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed Foreign Academic Faculty Tenure Act affirms as a controlling constitutional principle that government service is primarily reserved to Filipino citizens, a rule rooted in national sovereignty, democratic accountability, and public trust. At the same time, it recognizes that public higher education plays a strategic role in scientific advancement, economic productivity, and national development. This measure therefore establishes a narrowly tailored and strictly exceptional framework under which foreign nationals may be appointed to tenured teaching or research positions in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs), only when their expertise is demonstrably unavailable or insufficient within the Filipino academic community. The bill underscores that SUCs exist principally to cultivate Filipino human capital and leadership, and that any engagement of foreign faculty must be instrumental, time-bound, and capacity-building in nature—never a substitute for sustained investment in Filipino faculty development. To safeguard constitutional fidelity, the Act limits its application exclusively to teaching and research roles within SUCs and expressly excludes all administrative, executive, managerial, governance, and policy-determining positions, which shall at all times remain reserved to Filipino citizens. It clarifies that such academic posts, by their professional and non-sovereign character, are not deemed public offices for purposes of the citizenship requirement, while preserving the public character of SUCs and compliance with all other laws. Foreign appointments are permitted only upon a rigorous showing of exceptional necessity and internationally distinguished merit, subject to approval, periodic renewal-of-necessity review, non-displacement safeguards, and strict prohibitions against administrative authority. The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is vested with primary oversight, regulatory, and enforcement authority, in coordination with the Civil Service Commission, to ensure uniform standards, transparency, and constitutional compliance, including the imposition of graduated sanctions for violations. Ultimately, this bill seeks to reconcile the constitutional primacy of Filipino citizenship in public service with the strategic need, in rare and clearly justified circumstances, to access globally distinguished expertise for the advancement of national academic standards and priority disciplines. It institutionalizes stringent tests of necessity, continuing qualification review, knowledge-transfer commitments, and a five-year sunset review to prevent dependency and ensure that any foreign engagement directly strengthens Filipino faculty capability and institutional self-sufficiency. By embedding strict safeguards, accountability mechanisms, and legislative oversight, the measure ensures that foreign academic tenure remains exceptional, limited, and aligned with the long-term objective of building a self-reliant, world-class Filipino higher education system. The passage of this Act is thus earnestly sought to uphold constitutional principles while prudently advancing national academic excellence. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 9848
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE INTERNATIONALIZATION CAPACITY OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL INTERNATIONALIZATION FRAMEWORK, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE AN INTERNATIONALIZATION SUPPORT FUND, STRENGTHENING EDUCATION EXPORT THROUGH INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Higher education has become an increasingly important driver of economic competitiveness, innovation, workforce development, and international cooperation in an interconnected global environment. Around the world, countries have adopted comprehensive internationalization strategies to strengthen the quality of their higher education systems, expand academic and research collaboration, attract international students and scholars, and position education as a strategic export sector that contributes to national development. The Philippines possesses significant strengths that can support a more globally engaged and internationally competitive higher education sector. The country's widespread use of English, strong academic traditions, growing research capabilities, cultural openness, and strategic location within the Asia- Pacific region provide substantial opportunities for Philippine higher education institutions to participate more actively in international academic networks, transnational education initiatives, and global knowledge economies. Despite these advantages, internationalization efforts across Philippine higher education institutions remain uneven, fragmented, and largely dependent on individual institutional initiatives. There is currently no comprehensive statutory framework that provides sustained national direction, dedicated financing, and coordinated institutional support for higher education internationalization and education export. At the same time, international education has emerged as a major economic sector in many countries, generating significant investments, employment opportunities, research collaboration, and foreign exchange earnings. The Philippines is well-positioned to participate in this growing global market. However, maximizing these opportunities requires deliberate public policy interventions that strengthen institutional capacities, improve international visibility, expand academic mobility, promote transnational education, and ensure that international engagement contributes directly to quality enhancement and national development objectives. This measure seeks to institutionalize a National Internationalization Framework for Higher Education to provide strategic direction and continuity to the country's internationalization efforts. It promotes a whole-of-sector approach that integrates international, intercultural, and global dimensions into instruction, research, extension, governance, and student development while safeguarding academic freedom, institutional autonomy, and national interest. Ultimately, this proposed legislation recognizes that higher education internationalization is not merely an academic undertaking but a strategic national investment that can enhance educational quality, strengthen research and innovation, improve workforce competitiveness, expand opportunities for Filipino learners and educators, and contribute to long-term economic growth and global engagement . In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. (ESAMELCO) A FRANCHISE TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE CITY OF BORONGAN, AND MUNICIPALITIES OF MAYDOLONG, BALANGKAYAN, LLORENTE, SAN JULIAN, SULAT, GUIUAN, MERCEDES, SALCEDO, LAWAAN, BALANGIGA, GIPORLOS, QUINAPONDAN, GENERAL MACARTHUR, HERNANI, TAFT, CAN- AVID, DOLORES, ORAS, MASLOG, JIPAPAD, SAN POLICARPO, AND ARTECHE, ALL IN THE PROVINCE OF EASTERN SAMAR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant a congressional franchise to Eastern Samar Electric Cooperative, Inc. (ESAMELCO) to continuously provide an electric power distribution system to the people of City of Borongan, and Municipalities of Maydolong, Balangkayan, Llorente, San Julian, Sulat, Guiuan, Mercedes, Salcedo, Lawaan, Balangiga, Giporlos, Quinapondan, General MacArthur, Hernani, Taft, Can-avid, Dolores, Oras, Maslog, Jipapad, San Policarpo, and Arteche, all in the Province of Eastern Samar including any other municipality that may hereafter be created, reconstituted, or otherwise added to the Province. Furthermore, it lays down the standards and conditions that the franchise grantee must attain and fulfill in order to implement an effective partnership between the government and the distribution utility as its implementing partner for total electrification. ESAMELCO has been in operation from 1981 up to the present as a service-oriented, non-stock, and non-profit cooperative. Pursuant to the provisions of Presidential Decree No. 269, ESAMELCO was registered on December 9, 1977. On September 9, 1981, the National Electrification Administration (NEA) issued Certificate of Franchise No. 081 to ESAMELCO, granting it a 50-year franchise to operate. The franchise is set to expire on September 9, 2031. As the sole franchise holder for electric distribution in the coverage area, ESAMELCO has been providing excellent service to the 22 municipalities and 1 city of the province, achieving 95.85% electrification level, based on the potential household connections as of September 30, 2025. Over the years, the cooperative has demonstrated its technical, financial, and institutional capability to carry out its mandate, evidenced by its efforts in reducing system loss, minimizing power outages, and maintaining high collection efficiency. It is worth noting that the cooperative has garnered NEA’s performance rating of AAA, from 2016 to 2022, A for 2023, and AA for 2024. Granting this franchise will ensure the continuous supply of electricity to the people of Eastern Samar. It will also allow ESAMELCO to sustain its mission of playing a vital role in the socio-economic development of its coverage area by providing an affordable, dependable, efficient and reliable electric service to its member- consumer-owners. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO C. LIBANAN CHRISTOPHER SHEEN P. label: HB 9851
title: AN ACT DEFINING THE CRIME OF SUBORNATION OF PERJURY, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE ACT NO. 3815, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED PENAL CODE,” AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The administration of justice depends on the truthfulness of testimony and evidence presented before courts, quasi-judicial bodies, and other tribunals. When witnesses are induced, coerced, or persuaded to give false testimony or execute false affidavits, the integrity of judicial proceedings is undermined, innocent persons may be wrongfully prosecuted or convicted, and public confidence in the legal system is eroded. In Hondrade v. Office of the Ombudsman (Visayas),1 the Supreme Court discussed the offense of subornation of perjury and defined it as the act of knowingly and willfully procuring another person to swear falsely. The Court explained that subornation of perjury is presently treated as perjury, with the 1 G.R. No. 226526, 7 December 2021. offender punished as a principal by inducement under the provisions of the Revised Penal Code. There is currently no distinct felony that specifically punishes subornation of perjury under the Revised Penal Code. This legislative gap fails to adequately recognize the unique and grave nature of inducing another person to commit perjury. The individual who orchestrates, procures, or pressures another to provide false testimony is the principal architect of the deception and poses a direct threat to the administration of justice. By expressly defining and penalizing subornation of perjury as a separate crime, the State strengthens its ability to deter witness manipulation, protect the integrity of judicial proceedings, and hold accountable those who seek to corrupt the truth-finding process. The need for stronger accountability is even more compelling when the offender is a public officer. Public officials occupy positions of authority and influence and are expected to uphold the law and safeguard the fair administration of justice. When a public officer uses the powers or prestige of public office to induce another to testify falsely, the resulting harm extends beyond a particular case and undermines public trust in government institutions. For this reason, the bill imposes a higher penalty when subornation of perjury is committed by a public officer. This is consistent with Article XI, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, which declares that: "Public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must at all times be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives." By clearly defining and penalizing subornation of perjury, this bill seeks to safeguard the integrity of judicial proceedings, promote truth and accountability, and strengthen public confidence in the administration of justice. label: HB 9852
title: AN ACT MODIFYING THE BOUNDARY OF THE TICAO-BURIAS PASS PROTECTED SEASCAPE (TBPPS), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 4 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11038, THE “EXPANDED NATIONAL INTEGRATED PROTECTED AREAS SYSTEM (E-NIPAS) ACT OF 2018”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11038, otherwise known as the “Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System (E-NIPAS) Act of 2018”, which amended Republic Act No. 7586 or the “National Integrated Protected Areas System Act of 1992, aims to strengthen environmental conservation efforts in our country, particularly in ecologically important areas. Under the E-NIPAS, the Ticao-Burias Pass Protected Seascape (TBPPS) was declared a protected area under the classification of national park. The TBPPS covers a marine ecosystem spanning 413,745 hectares across four provinces in the Bicol Region: Albay, Masbate (specifically Ticao and Burias Islands in the First District), and Sorsogon (collectively known as the ALMASOR), and Camarines Sur. It is home to the whale shark, manta ray, and dugong, and has diverse ecosystems including mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and coral reefs. While the E-NIPAS has benefits for an island-province rich in biodiversity like Masbate, it also poses some challenges. The law prescribes an easement of forty (40) meters within which human activities are restricted. Entrepreneurs who intend to build or continue their small businesses are required to obtain a permit that often takes considerable time to process. Government infrastructure projects in coastal and marine areas within the protected zone cannot be implemented even if such projects will ease up transportation in the area. In the long term, these restrictions will adversely affect local tourism and economic growth. Moreover, the TBPPS encompasses built-up areas, like barangay sites and townships, where residents have established their homes and lived for decades prior to the passage of the E-NIPAS in 2018. Strict enforcement of the E-NIPAS law among those who reside within the 40-meter easement, particularly the imposition of fine, demolition, or eviction, could result not only in the displacement of these settlers but also in long and arduous legal disputes. In view of the foregoing, this bill seeks to modify the territorial boundary of the Ticao-Burias Pass Protected Seascape (TBPPS) in order to rectify the erroneous inclusion of alienable and disposable (A&D) lands and private properties within the protected area. The immediate passage of this bill is most respectfully requested. REP. ANTONIO T. KHO REP. ELISA T. label: HB 9853
title: AN ACT PRIORITIZING THE PAVING AND SOLAR-LIGHTING OF CRITICAL ARTERIAL ROADS CONNECTING AGRICULTURAL ZONES TO COMMERCIAL MARKETS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture remains the backbone of the Philippine economy, yet our farmers consistently face crippling challenges in transporting their produce from farm to market. Post-harvest losses in the Philippines reach up to 15% to 30% for high- value crops, largely due to delays and damage caused by unpaved, uneven, and poorly lit local roads. When farmers cannot transport perishable goods efficiently, food prices spike in urban centers while farmgate prices drop, trapping agricultural workers in a cycle of poverty and threatening national food security. Furthermore, the lack of adequate street lighting along these rural transit corridors forces farmers to transport goods only during peak daytime hours, exposing crops to extreme heat and contributing to daytime traffic congestion. This bill, the "Agri-Market Infrastructure and Solar Lighting Act," seeks to mandate the prioritization of paving and solar-lighting critical arterial roads that directly connect agricultural zones to commercial markets. By aggressively paving these arterial roads, we reduce travel time, minimize product bruising, and lower vehicle maintenance costs for transport groups. By integrating solar-powered street lighting, we empower farmers to safely transport their harvests during the cooler nighttime and pre-dawn hours. This not only preserves the freshness of the produce but also promotes the use of sustainable, off-grid renewable energy that does not strain the national power grid or local municipal budgets. Securing our food supply chain begins with securing the roads our farmers travel. Hence, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9854
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD SYSTEM TO ENSURE CONTINUITY OF CARE, IMPROVE MEDICAL EFFICIENCY, AND PROMOTE UNIVERSAL HEALTH ACCESS FOR ALL FILIPINOS Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The right to health is a fundamental constitutional guarantee. Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly declares that the State shall protect and promote the people's right to health and instill health consciousness among them. This mandate was significantly advanced with the enactment of Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act, which aims to realize universal health coverage for all Filipinos progressively. The UHC Act's full implementation is hindered by a fragmented health information infrastructure. Patient records are often filed in various hospitals and health units, forcing patients to carry physical copies of their medical history. In emergencies, the lack of immediate access to this information can result in diagnostic errors, delayed treatment, and preventable complications. Furthermore, the absence of a unified system results in redundant medical tests, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and a lack of real-time, accurate public health data necessary for proactive government epidemiologic interventions. This bill seeks to address these gaps by establishing the National Electronic Health Record System (NEHRS). The NEHRS will serve as a secure, centralized, and interoperable digital platform that aggregates a patient’s medical history across all healthcare providers nationwide. The modernization of our healthcare system through digital integration is no longer a luxury; it is an urgent public health necessity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9855
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL GOVERNMENT INITIATIVE FOR INNOVATIVE ORAL HEALTH CARE, THEREBY AMPLIFYING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 1082, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “AN ACT STRENGTHENING HEALTH AND DENTAL SERVICES IN THE RURAL AREAS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR” Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The state of oral health in the Philippines presents a silent but pervasive public health crisis. Decades of data indicate that dental caries (tooth decay) and periodontal diseases affect the vast majority of Filipinos. According to recent epidemiological assessments, roughly 70% to 80% of Filipinos suffer from dental cavities, while a significant portion of our school-aged children experience chronic oral discomfort that directly impacts their school attendance, nutrition, and overall development. Republic Act No. 1082, enacted in 1954, was a landmark piece of legislation that sought to strengthen dental health services in rural areas by creating rural health units and deploying dental infrastructure. While RA 1082 laid the groundwork for public health dentistry, its framework is now over seventy years old. It predates modern advancements in preventive dentistry, teledentistry, biometric health tracking, and minimally invasive oral care technologies. Furthermore, our current public healthcare system remains heavily reactive— focusing on extractions and emergency interventions rather than proactive preservation. For marginalized communities, visual and physical access to a dentist remains a luxury due to geographical isolation and economic barriers. This Bill, aptly titled the "National Initiative for Innovative Oral Health Care Act," seeks to fundamentally overhaul and modernize our national oral health strategy. It amends and strengthens the spirit of RA 1082 by integrating cutting- edge innovation into the public dental sector. By modernizing our infrastructure and shifting our philosophy from "extraction to preservation," this measure will significantly reduce the economic and physical burden of oral diseases on the Filipino workforce and youth. In view of the foregoing urgent public health considerations, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9856
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PROTECTED BICYCLE LANES AND PEDESTRIAN WALKWAYS IN HIGHLY URBANIZING PROVINCIAL CENTERS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid economic growth of provincial centers across the Philippines has brought unparalleled opportunities, but it has also imported a severe urban crisis: traffic congestion, vehicular pollution, and the marginalization of the commuting public. As cities outside Metro Manila—such as component cities, provincial capitals, and first-class municipalities—continue to urbanize, their road networks are increasingly designed exclusively for motorized vehicles, leaving pedestrians and cyclists highly vulnerable. Active transport—specifically walking and cycling—is the most fundamental, equitable, and sustainable mode of mobility. However, the lack of dedicated and protected infrastructure forces cyclists to share lanes with speeding motor vehicles, leading to fatal accidents, while pedestrians are relegated to narrow, obstructed, or non-existent sidewalks. This bill, the "Provincial Active Transport Infrastructure Act," seeks to mandate the establishment of protected bicycle lanes and safe, accessible pedestrian walkways in all highly urbanizing provincial centers. It shifts the paradigm of urban planning from moving cars to moving people. By requiring physical separation for cyclists and clear, elevated pathways for pedestrians, this measure will: 1. Protect lives by significantly reducing road crash fatalities involving vulnerable road users. 2. Promote public health by encouraging physical activity and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. 3. Ensure inclusive mobility by providing a free, safe, and efficient transport alternative for the majority of Filipinos who do not own private vehicles. To prevent our provincial centers from repeating the car-centric mistakes of the past, the State must institutionalize active transport infrastructure now, before these growing cities become entirely gridlocked. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9857
title: AN ACT PROMOTING MENTAL HEALTH AND WELL-BEING IN THE WORKPLACE, INSTITUTING MEASURES TO PREVENT BURNOUT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The modern workplace has changed significantly, blurring the lines between professional and personal life. While technology boosts productivity, it also fosters an "always-on" culture in high-pressure environments, leading to widespread workplace burnout across industries. Burnout, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), is an occupational phenomenon stemming from unmanageable chronic workplace stress. It involves feelings of energy depletion, mental distance from work, and decreased professional efficacy. Burnout reflects a systemic organizational failure that significantly affects an employee's psychological, emotional, and physical well- being. The economic costs of unmanaged workplace stress are staggering, resulting in decreased productivity, high employee turnover, absenteeism, and rising healthcare expenditures. Conversely, a workplace that actively promotes mental health fosters innovation, engagement, and sustainable economic growth. While existing laws, such as Republic Act No. 11036 (The Mental Health Act), lay down the national framework for mental health care, there is an urgent need for specialized, enforceable legislation that directly addresses the unique structural stressors of the employment sector. By establishing clear guidelines, providing institutional support, and protecting the fundamental right of every worker to a safe and healthy working environment, this measure seeks to transform workplace culture from one of endurance to one of holistic well-being. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE State universities and colleges (SUCs) serve as vital institutions in advancing equitable access to quality higher education and in developing the country's human capital. They are instrumental in reducing educational disparities and promoting inclusive growth through the delivery of instruction, research and development, extension services, and technology-driven programs responsive to the needs of society.1 Human capital development remains a fundamental pillar of sustainable economic growth and national competitiveness. As the Philippines strives toward greater economic progress and adaptation to an increasingly knowledge-driven and technology-oriented global landscape, the need for a highly skilled, innovative, and productive workforce becomes even more imperative. Knowledge and technological advancement are key drivers of economic transformation, making investments in higher education essential for long-term national development.2 The Technological University of the Philippines–Cavite Campus has played an important role in providing quality technological education and skills development 1 Flores, H. Through its academic offerings and technical training programs, the institution has contributed significantly to the development of competent graduates equipped to meet the demands of industry and the labor market. However, with the increasing demand for accessible higher education and the growing need for professionals in engineering, industrial technology, applied sciences, and related fields, there is a compelling necessity to strengthen the institutional capacity and autonomy of the campus. Converting the Technological University of the Philippines–Cavite Campus into a regular campus of the Technological University of the Philippines, to be known as the Technological University of the Philippines–Cavite (TUP-Cavite), will enhance its capability to broaden academic offerings, improve institutional governance, expand research initiatives, and upgrade facilities and support services for students and faculty. label: HB 9859
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE GRANT OF STUDENT LOAD DISCOUNT PRIVILEGE ON MOBILE AND INTERNET SERVICES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Article 28 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) provides that, “States Parties recognize the right of the child to education, and with a view to achieving this right progressively and on the basis of equal opportunity.” These emphasize not only the right to quality education but also the necessity of actively making it accessible on an equal basis to all. In today’s digital age, equal access to quality education is inextricably linked to digital connectivity or access to internet services. This reality was affirmed and acutely felt during the COVID-19 pandemic when schools had to shift their teaching modality to online arrangement, permanently expanding learning space even in the present post-pandemic setting. Even as most schools and classes in the primary, secondary, and tertiary education levels have returned to the face-to-face class modality, the digital tools, resources, and platforms used during the pandemic have remained integral to the delivery of education. However, the increasingly significant role of digital accessibility in education and learning has created a new barrier to access to quality education in the country. In the Philippines, the deepening digital divide exacerbates deep-rooted injustices in the education sector that leave students from underprivileged families and communities behind as they struggle to keep up with various learning expenses not covered by existing public education, scholarship, and learning subsidy programs. 1 Among these learning expenses is the access to mobile and internet services that allow students to make use of online tools, resources, and platforms to enhance their learning experience and school performance. This bill seeks to provide a 20% discount on mobile load, text, call, and internet services to all Filipino students currently enrolled in a duly authorized elementary, secondary, technical-vocational, or higher education institution, excluding post- graduate degree courses. This bill seeks to bridge the digital accessibility gap and address the emerging hindrance to equally accessible, quality education by easing the financial burden on Filipino students for whom internet access is now a basic educational necessity. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Walfredo “Arman” Dimaguila, Jesus “Bong” Suntay, Antolin Oreta III, and Javier Benitez, and Senators Bam Aquino, JV Ejercito, and Mark Villar. This bill fully adopts Senator Bam Aquino’s Senate Bill No. 126. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. The seismic event was the strongest earthquake to strike the Philippines and was considered one of the most destructive since 19762. The earthquake triggered over 130 aftershocks and generated tsunami warnings across multiple Asian nations3. As of June 10, the Office of the Civil Defense (OCD) reported that the official casualty count rose to 45 confirmed deaths, with about 630 persons injured and 17 reported missing4. label: HB 9861
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE UNIVERSITY OF EASTERN PHILIPPINES AS THE NATIONAL UNIVERSITY FOR SUSTAINABILITY STUDIES AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFORE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The University of Eastern Philippines has long served as a vital institution for higher education, research, and community development in Northern Samar and the wider Visayas region. As the first state university in the Visayas, UEP has carried the responsibility of providing accessible and quality tertiary education while addressing the socio-economic needs of its region. Its continuing work in instruction, research, extension, and production reflects its commitment to producing competent graduates and responsive programs that contribute to local and national development. This bill seeks to declare the University of Eastern Philippines as the National University for Sustainability Studies. The measure recognizes the University’s existing mandate and strengthens its role in integrating sustainability, innovation, green entrepreneurship, and environmental stewardship into higher education. This is especially relevant as the country continues to face challenges brought by climate change, environmental degradation, resource limitations, and the need for inclusive and sustainable economic growth. The proposed designation is not merely symbolic. It gives UEP a clearer national direction to lead in sustainability studies through academic programs, research initiatives, technology development, policy support, and community-based extension services. By strengthening UEP’s institutional mandate, this bill will help develop professionals, researchers, entrepreneurs, and community leaders equipped with the knowledge and skills necessary to respond to environmental and development challenges. It will also support the broader national policy of promoting quality education, ecological protection, innovation, and sustainable development. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO C. LIBANAN CHRISTOPHER SHEEN P. label: HB 9862
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON ROAD MOBILITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF MOBILITY IN THE PHILIPPINES AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mobility is essential to the daily lives of Filipinos. Integrated, accessible, and efficient transportation options are indispensable in enabling citizens to reach places of employment, education, commerce, health and community services, leisure (including public open spaces and parks), and cultural activities. Conversely, the absence of adequate transport options restricts access to opportunities and undermines social and economic participation. Mobility outcomes, however, are not determined by transport services alone. They are fundamentally shaped by land-use patterns and the design of the built environment, which influence travel demand, distances, accessibility, safety and the viability of public and active transport. Despite this, conventional transport planning – which has historically prioritized faster transportation, particularly car-based transportation – has often been pursued by the Philippine government at the expense of other modes of transportation, particularly, public transport, walking and cycling. This approach has reflected a focus on transport inputs, such as vehicle movement and capacity of roads to allow vehicle movement, rather than mobility outcomes, including accessibility, safety, efficiency, and equity in the movement of people. For instance, in Metro Manila, while only an estimated 12% of the population owns private cars, a disproportionately large share of road space is allocated to car-centric movement.1 Meanwhile, vehicle sales continue to rise. In 2025, total vehicle sales reached 491,395 units, representing a 3.7% increase from the 473,842 units recorded in 2024, according to joint data released by the Chamber of Automotive Manufacturers of the Philippines, Inc. (CAMPI) and the Truck Manufacturers Association (TMA).2 This car-dependent model also reinforces the country’s heavy reliance on diesel and gasoline, which makes transport systems vulnerable to the volatility of fuel prices and supply disruptions, as seen in the 2026 fuel crisis as a result of the Iran war. The resulting structural imbalance in road space allocation, when combined with dispersed land-use patterns, long travel distances, and built environments that do not support walking, cycling, and public transport access, have contributed to worsening traffic congestion, inequitable mobility outcomes, unsafe conditions for vulnerable road users, especially children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, pedestrians, and cyclists, including heat-related illnesses and risks. The consequences of these structural imbalances are reflected in road safety outcomes. Road crashes remain among the leading causes of mortality in the Philippines,3 and cost the country an estimated USD 11 billion in 2021, equivalent to roughly 3% of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in addition to healthcare expenditure of 5.9% of GDP in the same year.4 These challenges are encountered across the various government agencies involved in transport planning, infrastructure development, traffic management, environmental protection, housing, and land-use regulation — functions which collectively shape the built environment within which mobility occurs. These agencies include, but are not limited to, the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA), Land Transportation Office (LTO), Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD), Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DepDev), Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, and other concerned entities. Gaps in coordination among these agencies, overlapping or unclear mandates, and inconsistent standards governing infrastructure, roads, and the hierarchy of road users remain persistent challenges. These constraints hinder the development of a coherent, integrated, and people- centered mobility system in the Philippines. Recognizing that mobility challenges are systemic and rooted not only in transport operations but also in infrastructure planning, land-use decisions, environmental 1 Gatarin, et al. (2024). label: HB 9863
title: AN ACT REQUIRING FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS TO DISPLAY THE CALORIE CONTENT OF FOOD AND BEVERAGE ITEMS OFFERED FOR SALE, PROMOTING INFORMED CONSUMER CHOICE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The increasing prevalence of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and other diet-related illnesses has become a significant public health concern in the Philippines. These conditions impose substantial burdens on individuals, families, and the healthcare system. One contributing factor is the lack of readily available nutritional information at the point of purchase, which limits consumers' ability to make informed dietary decisions. In today's fast-paced environment, a growing number of Filipinos rely on meals prepared by restaurants, fast-food chains, cafés, and other food establishments. However, consumers are often unaware of the calorie content of the food and beverages they consume. Without access to such information, it becomes difficult for individuals to manage their dietary intake and make choices consistent with their health goals. Providing calorie information on menus and menu boards empowers consumers to make healthier choices, promotes transparency in the food service industry, and increases public awareness of nutritional intake. Experiences in various jurisdictions have shown that menu calorie labeling can positively influence consumer behavior and encourage food establishments to offer healthier menu options. By making calorie information readily accessible, consumers are better equipped to balance their food choices and adopt healthier lifestyles. This proposed measure seeks to require food establishments to display the calorie content of standard food and beverage items in a clear, accurate, and accessible manner. The bill aims to strengthen consumer rights by ensuring that essential nutritional information is available before purchasing decisions are made, thereby enabling consumers to make informed choices regarding their health and well-being. The measure likewise recognizes the vital role of the Department of Health (DOH) in promoting public health and preventing nutrition-related diseases through evidence-based policies, nutrition education, and regulatory oversight. As the lead implementing agency, the DOH shall establish standards and guidelines to ensure the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of calorie information disclosed by food establishments. The bill also acknowledges the important role of the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) in protecting consumer welfare and ensuring that consumers receive accurate, transparent, and accessible information about the products and services they purchase. Through its participation in the implementation of this measure, the DTI shall help promote consumer awareness and support compliance with calorie disclosure requirements as part of its mandate to uphold consumer rights. Moreover, Local Government Units (LGUs) are essential partners in the effective implementation and enforcement of this Act. As front-line regulatory bodies responsible for business permitting, licensing, and local inspections, LGUs are strategically positioned to monitor compliance by food establishments and assist in ensuring the successful implementation of calorie disclosure requirements within their respective jurisdictions. Through the collaborative efforts of the DOH, DTI, LGUs, food establishments, and consumers, this measure seeks to foster a culture of informed food choices, encourage healthier eating habits, improve transparency in the food service industry, and contribute to the prevention of obesity and other nutrition-related diseases among Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 61 62 63 64 HON. JULIENNE “JAM” L. label: HB 9867
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING ORGAN DONATION AND TRANSPLANTATION ACTIVITIES IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL ORGAN DONATION AND TRANSPLANTATION COMMISSION, DEFINING ITS POWERS, FUNCTIONS, AND ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The increasing burden of end-stage organ failure and chronic diseases requiring transplantation continues to pose a major public health challenge in the Philippines. Thousands of Filipinos suffer annually from kidney failure, end-stage liver disease, serious lung and heart disease, and other life-threatening illnesses for which organ transplantation remains the most effective and often the only definitive treatment. Despite advances in transplantation medicine and surgery, the country continues to face significant challenges in organ donation and transplantation, including very low organ donation rates, inadequate registration systems, fragmented coordination among hospitals and transplant centers, inequitable access to transplantation services, limited public awareness, and insufficient regulatory oversight. While Republic Act No. 7170 or the “Organ Donation Act of 1991” provides the legal basis for organ donation after death, there remains a need to institutionalize a comprehensive, cohesive, integrated, ethical, and sustainable national organ donation and transplantation system, as in several countries that have had successful national organ donation programs. The World Health Assembly, the World Health Organization and the Declaration of Istanbul have repeatedly called upon member states to strengthen governance mechanisms for organ donation and transplantation by promoting voluntary and unpaid donation, equitable allocation systems, transparency, traceability, patient safety, and safeguards against organ trafficking and transplant commercialism. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize organ donation and transplantation activities nationwide through the establishment of the National Organ Donation and Transplantation Commission (NODTC), which shall serve as the primary policy-making, coordinating, regulatory, and oversight body for organ donation and transplantation in the Philippines. For brevity, the word organ shall refer to tissues as well. label: HB 9868
title: AN ACT RECLASSIFYING QUALIFIED THEFT OF COCONUTS AND FISH AS SIMPLE THEFT UNDER ARTICLE 308, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE ARTICLE 310 OF ACT NO. 3815, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED PENAL CODE,” AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Criminal laws must be founded on principles of fairness, reasonableness, and proportionality. Persons who commit similar acts causing similar harm should generally be subject to similar penalties. Yet, under Article 310 of the Revised Penal Code, the theft of coconuts from the premises of a plantation and fish taken from a fishpond or fishery are classified as qualified theft and punished two degrees higher than ordinary theft, regardless of whether the value of the coconuts and fish are minimal. These distinctions create an arbitrary disparity in the treatment of offenders and is difficult to justify under present conditions. The consequences of this disparity were illustrated in the case of Pedro Amarille, a farmer from Maribojoc, Bohol. In 2011, he was convicted of qualified theft and sentenced to six (6) years of imprisonment for taking 200 coconut fruits valued at only P2,000.00. After years of litigation, the Supreme Court ultimately acquitted him in 2023.1 In his separate concurring opinion on the same case, Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen took the opportunity to manifest that: “Singling out theft of coconuts as a qualified theft has become anachronistic and amounts to a violation of the equal protection of the laws. It is discriminatory not only against other food products, but also against the poor.”2 The special treatment accorded to coconut theft has a specific historical context. In the 1950 case of People vs. Isnain,3 the Supreme Court explained that the reason for a heavier penalty on the theft of coconuts was “to encourage and protect the development of the coconut industry as one of the sources of our national economy. Unlike rice and sugar cane farms where the range of vision is unobstructed, coconut groves cannot be efficiently watched because of the nature of the growth of coconut trees; and without a special measure to protect this kind of property, it will be, as it has been in the past the favorite resort of thieves.” While the coconut industry remains an important contributor to the country's economy, the conditions that justified this exceptional treatment more than seven decades ago have substantially changed. Advances in technology, transportation, and farm security now 1 Amarille vs. People, G.R. No. 256022, 7 August 2023. 2 J. Leonen, Separate Concurring Opinion, Amarille vs. People, G.R. No. 256022, 7 August 2023. 3 G.R. No. L-2857, 28 February 1950. provide more effective means of preventing and detecting theft in farms and plantations. More fundamentally, there is no substantial distinction that justifies granting coconuts greater protection than other agricultural products. As Justice Leonen further explained: “[T]here is no substantial distinction as to why the coconut industry is given more protection from thieves, while other fruits, cereals, or forest or farm products are not. The nature of growth of coconut trees does not make for real differences, as some people still resort to stealing coconuts, as in Gaviola. Hence, there is no reasonable classification between coconuts and other fruits, cereals, or forest or farm products so as to justify the imposition of a higher penalty for the theft of coconuts compared to other food or farm products.4 The same observation applies with equal force to fish taken from fishponds or fisheries. Like coconuts, fish receive special treatment under Article 310 solely because of the nature of the property involved, even though theft of other agricultural products, produce, or aquaculture resources may cause comparable economic harm. There is no substantial distinction that warrants punishing the theft of fish from a fishpond two degrees more severely than the theft of similarly valued property. Indeed, modern advances in farm management, aquaculture practices, surveillance technology, and law enforcement have significantly improved the ability of owners to protect plantations and fisheries from theft. At the same time, the penalties for qualified theft have become increasingly 4 Separate Concurring Opinion, Amarille vs. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 256022, (7 August 2023). disproportionate in cases involving low-value coconuts or fish, producing outcomes that are difficult to reconcile with the principles of fairness and proportionality that underpin the criminal justice system. Moreover, Article 310 already protects particularly blameworthy forms of theft, such as those committed by domestic servants, with grave abuse of confidence, or during calamities and civil disturbances. Those qualifying circumstances relate to the manner in which the crime is committed or the heightened culpability of the offender. By contrast, singling out coconuts and fish based solely on the type of property taken creates an outdated classification that no longer serves a compelling public purpose. This bill therefore seeks to remove the classification of theft of coconut and fish as qualified theft and instead punish these acts under the general provisions on simple theft. Offenders will remain criminally liable, but the applicable penalties will be determined in accordance with the ordinary rules governing theft rather than an obsolete statutory exception. By doing so, the measure promotes a more equitable, rational, and proportionate criminal justice system while continuing to hold offenders accountable for unlawful conduct. Finally, the bill removes the reference to large cattle in Article 310. This amendment is intended to harmonize the Revised Penal Code with existing law, as theft involving large cattle is already governed by Presidential Decree No. 533, otherwise known as the Anti-Cattle Rustling Law of 1974, which superseded the corresponding provision in Article 310. By eliminating outdated distinctions that no longer serve a compelling public purpose, this bill advances the constitutional principles of equal protection, fairness, and proportionality in the administration of criminal laws. JOSE

label: HB 9869
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMMUNITY TOOLBOX IN BARANGAY BAGBAG, DISTRICT V OF QUEZON CITY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay Bagbag, located in District V of Quezon City, is a densely populated and rapidly developing community where many households rely on incremental home improvement, informal repairs, and small-scale livelihood activities to sustain their daily needs. Despite this, access to basic tools for carpentry, plumbing, sewing, and minor construction remains limited due to financial constraints. For many residents, the cost of purchasing tools competes with essential household expenditures such as food, education, and healthcare. At the same time, a significant number of residents possess the skills necessary for basic repairs and productive activities, but are constrained by the lack of access to appropriate equipment. This measure seeks to establish a Community Toolbox in Barangay Bagbag, which will serve as a shared facility where residents may borrow essential tools for home maintenance, small construction, and livelihood-related activities. By institutionalizing a tool-sharing system at the barangay level, the measure promotes: 1. Economic Relief – reducing the need for households to purchase costly tools for occasional use; 2. Livelihood Support – enabling residents to engage in small-scale repair services and income-generating activities; 3. Disaster Preparedness and Resilience – ensuring communities have access to the tools necessary for immediate repairs during emergencies; 4. Environmental Sustainability – encouraging shared use of resources and reducing unnecessary consumption; and 5. Community Cohesion – fostering cooperation and shared responsibility among residents. The establishment of a Community Toolbox aligns with the State’s policy to empower local government units and strengthen community-based initiatives that improve quality of life at the grassroots level. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMMUNITY TOOLBOX IN BARANGAY BAGBAG, DISTRICT V OF QUEZON CITY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay Bagbag, located in District V of Quezon City, is a densely populated and rapidly developing community where many households rely on incremental home improvement, informal repairs, and small-scale livelihood activities to sustain their daily needs. Despite this, access to basic tools for carpentry, plumbing, sewing, and minor construction remains limited due to financial constraints. For many residents, the cost of purchasing tools competes with essential household expenditures such as food, education, and healthcare. At the same time, a significant number of residents possess the skills necessary for basic repairs and productive activities, but are constrained by the lack of access to appropriate equipment. This measure seeks to establish a Community Toolbox in Barangay Bagbag, which will serve as a shared facility where residents may borrow essential tools for home maintenance, small construction, and livelihood-related activities. By institutionalizing a tool-sharing system at the barangay level, the measure promotes: 1. Economic Relief – reducing the need for households to purchase costly tools for occasional use;

label: HB 9870
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMMUNITY TOOLBOX IN BARANGAY CAPRI, DISTRICT V OF QUEZON CITY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay Capri, located in District V of Quezon City, is a densely populated and rapidly developing community where many households rely on incremental home improvement, informal repairs, and small-scale livelihood activities to sustain their daily needs. Despite this, access to basic tools for carpentry, plumbing, sewing, and minor construction remains limited due to financial constraints. For many residents, the cost of purchasing tools competes with essential household expenditures such as food, education, and healthcare. At the same time, a significant number of residents possess the skills necessary for basic repairs and productive activities, but are constrained by the lack of access to appropriate equipment. This measure seeks to establish a Community Toolbox in Barangay Capri, which will serve as a shared facility where residents may borrow essential tools for home maintenance, small construction, and livelihood-related activities. By institutionalizing a tool-sharing system at the barangay level, the measure promotes: 1. Economic Relief – reducing the need for households to purchase costly tools for occasional use; 2. label: HB 9879
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMMUNITY TOOLBOX IN BARANGAY SAN AGUSTIN, DISTRICT V OF QUEZON CITY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay San Agustin, located in District V of Quezon City, is a densely populated and rapidly developing community where many households rely on incremental home improvement, informal repairs, and small-scale livelihood activities to sustain their daily needs. Despite this, access to basic tools for carpentry, plumbing, sewing, and minor construction remains limited due to financial constraints. For many residents, the cost of purchasing tools competes with essential household expenditures such as food, education, and healthcare. At the same time, a significant number of residents possess the skills necessary for basic repairs and productive activities, but are constrained by the lack of access to appropriate equipment. This measure seeks to establish a Community Toolbox in Barangay San Agustin, which will serve as a shared facility where residents may borrow essential tools for home maintenance, small construction, and livelihood- related activities. By institutionalizing a tool-sharing system at the barangay level, the measure promotes: 1. Economic Relief – reducing the need for households to purchase costly tools for occasional use; 2. Livelihood Support – enabling residents to engage in small-scale repair services and income-generating activities; 3. Disaster Preparedness and Resilience – ensuring communities have access to the tools necessary for immediate repairs during emergencies; 4. Environmental Sustainability – encouraging shared use of resources and reducing unnecessary consumption; and 5. Community Cohesion – fostering cooperation and shared responsibility among residents. The establishment of a Community Toolbox aligns with the State’s policy to empower local government units and strengthen community-based initiatives that improve quality of life at the grassroots level. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D.
