title: AN ACT RENEWING AND GRANTING TO THE NEGROS ORIENTAL II ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE (NORECO II) A FRANCHISE TO ESTABLISH, OPERATE, MANAGE, AND EXPAND ELECTRIC POWER DISTRIBUTION FACILITIES FOR THE DELIVERY OF ELECTRICITY TO END USERS IN THE CITIES OF DUMAGUETE, TANJAY, AND BAYAWAN, AND IN THE MUNICIPALITIES OF PAMPLONA, AMLAN, SAN JOSE, SIBULAN, VALENCIA, BACONG, DAUIN, ZAMBOANGUITA, SIATON, STA. CATALINA, AND BASAY IN THE PROVINCE OF NEGROS ORIENTAL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to reliable, affordable, and continuous electric power is essential to the growth, safety, and welfare of communities. In Negros Oriental, the Negros Oriental II Electric Cooperative (NORECO II) has long served as a vital distribution utility for households, businesses, public institutions, and communities in its coverage area. Electric power is no longer merely a household necessity. It is the backbone of education, healthcare, public safety, commerce, local governance, tourism, agriculture, and disaster preparedness. For communities in Dumaguete, Tanjay, Bayawan, and the municipalities of Pamplona, Amlan, San Jose, Sibulan, Valencia, Bacong, Dauin, Zamboanguita, Siaton, Sta. Catalina, and Basay, dependable power distribution is indispensable to continued development and economic opportunity. This bill seeks to grant NORECO II a congressional franchise to establish, operate, manage, own, maintain, and expand electric power distribution facilities for the delivery of electricity to end-users within its service area in the Province of Negros Oriental. The grant of this franchise shall be subject to the Constitution, existing laws, rules and regulations, and the regulatory authority of the Energy Regulatory Commission and other appropriate government agencies. In view of the urgent need to ensure a stable and accountable power distribution system for the people of Negros Oriental, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 9884
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR VOLUNTARY GSIS CONTRIBUTIONS BY PROVINCIAL, MUNICIPAL, CITY, AND BARANGAY ELECTIVE OFFICIALS TO COMPLETE THE MINIMUM SERVICE REQUIREMENT FOR RETIREMENT, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under the Government Service Insurance Act, entitlement to a lifetime retirement pension from the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) requires at least fifteen years of service, and the duty to contribute ends upon separation from the service.1 This requirement does not fit the structure of elective office. Local elective officials at the provincial, municipal, and barangay levels may serve only three consecutive terms, a total of nine years, before a mandatory interruption. These officials form the backbone of local governance, often serving their communities across multiple offices and multiple levels of government without ever accumulating the uninterrupted service that the current law rewards. Completing the fifteen year requirement converts an official who would otherwise receive only a refund into the holder of a lifetime pension. To ensure that this imposes no cost on the public and no strain on the fund, the bill requires that the voluntary contribution be set at the amount actuarially determined by the GSIS to fully fund the additional benefit, borne entirely by the official, with no government share charged to any public appropriation. This measure gives them a fair and fully self funded opportunity to earn the security that the law already extends to those in continuous service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 9885
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MONTHLY SOCIAL PENSION FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our Constitution directs the State to give priority to the needs of the underprivileged, the sick, the elderly, the disabled, women, and children within an integrated approach to health and social development.1 The Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, as amended, affirms the same commitment.2 Yet while the State already extends a monthly social pension to indigent senior citizens under Republic Act No. 11916, no equivalent, predictable, and universal cash support exists for persons with disability. Disability imposes recurring costs that ordinary income does not capture, among them maintenance medicines, assistive devices, rehabilitation, caregiver support, and specialized transportation. These costs are borne by every person with a disability, regardless of economic status. For those without income, the twenty percent discount under existing law offers little relief because a discount helps only those who already have money to spend. For those with limited income, the additional burden of disability-related expenses erodes what little they earn. The result is a structural gap in the social protection system that falls across the full spectrum of persons with disability. By converting scattered and discretionary assistance into an enforceable and universal statutory entitlement, this measure affirms the dignity, inclusion, and full participation of all persons with disability in national life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 9888
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING AND PROTECTING THE LAND OWNERSHIP OF DEPED SCHOOL SITES AND MANDATING THE EXPEDITED ISSUANCE OF TITLES FOR REAL PROPERTIES USED AS PUBLIC SCHOOL SITES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. In fulfillment of this constitutional duty, the State, through the Department of Education (DepEd), must ensure that public schools are supported by secure, legally recognized, and sustainable school sites capable of accommodating present and future educational needs. However, a significant obstacle to the effective delivery of public education is the absence of clear land tenure and registered ownership over thousands of public school sites nationwide. Approximately sixty-nine percent (69%), or 32,424 public schools, remain untitled in the name of the DepEd. Of these, 6,045 schools, representing nineteen percent (19%) of untitled schools, are classified as congested, with elementary schools constituting the majority of such institutions. The lack of registered titles prevents or delays the implementation of government-funded infrastructures projects due to documentary, legal, and audit requirements governing the expenditure of public funds. It likewise exposes public schools to ownership disputes, adverse claims, risks of dispossession or eviction, and restrictions on the construction, expansion, and improvement of educational facilities. The foregoing circumstances exacerbate the national shortage of more than 165,000 classrooms, compelling many schools to adopt double or triple shifting arrangements that adversely affect the quality of instruction and welfare of learners and educators alike. Without secure land titles, the government’s capacity to address classroom congestion and undertake timely infrastructure development remains significantly constrained. label: HB 9889
title: AN ACT MODIFYING THE BOUNDARY OF THE TICAO-BURIAS PASS PROTECTED SEASCAPE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 4 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11038, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED NATIONAL INTEGRATED PROTECTED AREAS SYSTEM ACT OF 2018”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature. Pursuant to this constitutional duty, Republic Act No. 11038, otherwise known as the “Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act of 2018” or the E-NIPAS Act, was enacted to strengthen the protection, conservation, and sustainable management of the country’s ecologically significant areas. Among the protected areas declared under the E-NIPAS Act is the Ticao-Burias Pass Protected Seascape, or TBPPS, a marine ecosystem of national importance spanning portions of Masbate, Albay, Sorsogon, and Camarines Sur. As part of the country’s protected-area system, the TBPPS represents the State’s commitment to preserve biodiversity, protect critical habitats, and ensure the responsible use of natural resources for present and future generations. The Province of Sorsogon fully recognizes the importance of the TBPPS. For many years, Sorsogon has been at the forefront of marine conservation, coastal protection, and nature-based tourism. The municipalities of Pilar, Donsol, Magallanes, and Castilla, among others, are directly linked to the life, livelihood, and ecological integrity of the Ticao-Burias Pass. These coastal communities depend on the Ticao- Burias Pass for fishing, tourism, transportation, small enterprises, and local economic activity. However, implementation of the E-NIPAS Act has raised serious concerns where long-established barangay sites, town centers, residential communities, private properties, alienable and disposable lands, and areas devoted to public use appear to have been included within the protected area. These areas are not pristine or 1 uninhabited conservation zones, but existing communities where families have long lived, built homes, sustained livelihoods, and established lawful possession or ownership prior to the passage of the E-NIPAS Act. The strict application of protected- area restrictions and coastal easement rules may therefore cause uncertainty, delay essential public infrastructure, burden small enterprises, and expose residents to hardship, displacement, and avoidable disputes. This concern is particularly felt in Sorsogon’s coastal municipalities, where marine conservation must be balanced with access to livelihood, transport, tourism, and basic public services. This bill, therefore, seeks to amend the territorial coverage of the Ticao-Burias Pass Protected Seascape under Republic Act No. 11038, in order to correct the inclusion of alienable and disposable lands, titled or privately owned properties, existing barangay settlements, town sites, and areas already devoted to lawful public use. The measure does not seek to diminish the State’s commitment to environmental protection. Rather, the proposed amendment is a practical and balanced response to the realities of Sorsogon’s coastal municipalities. It preserves the ecological integrity of the Ticao-Burias Pass, while ensuring that residents, fisherfolk, small businesses, and local governments are not unnecessarily burdened by an overly broad or imprecise protected-area boundary. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 8187, otherwise known as the Paternity Leave Act of 1996, was a landmark social legislation that institutionalized paid paternity leave for married male employees in both the private and public sectors.1 Enacted to promote shared parental responsibility and support maternal recovery, the law grants a qualified employee seven (7) days of 1 Republic Act No. 8187 (1996). paid leave for the first four (4) deliveries of his legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting.2 Although progressive at the time of its enactment, R.A. No. 8187 has not kept pace with evolving labor standards, changing family structures, and contemporary understandings of gender equality in childcare.3 While existing laws such as the 105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law have strengthened protections for mothers, women continue to bear the disproportionate burden of child-rearing and unpaid domestic work. Evidence shows that childcare in the Philippines remains deeply gendered. According to data cited by the Philippine Commission on Women and national studies, Filipino women spend nearly 11 hours daily on unpaid care and domestic work, significantly limiting their access to education, employment, and economic opportunities.4 At the same time, research supported by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies shows that married women are three to four times more likely than men to cite housework as the primary reason for not participating in the labor force, highlighting how entrenched care responsibilities constrain women’s economic participation.5 This imbalance fails to reflect the realities of modern parenting and undermines the State’s policies on family solidarity, child development, and gender equality. Nearly three decades since its enactment, R.A. No. 8187 has not kept pace with evolving labor standards, changing family 2 Ibid. Article II, Section 14 mandates that the State “shall ensure the fundamental equality before the law of women and men,” which extends to the duty to care for children. Article XV, Section 1 recognizes the Filipino family as “the foundation of the nation” and directs the State to strengthen its solidarity and promote its total development, including responsible parenthood. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE REGULATION AND SAFETY STANDARDS OF LOCAL OFF-CAMPUS EDUCATIONAL ACTIVITIES OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 SECTION 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the “Local Off-Campus Activities Safety Act”. 31 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. - It is declared the policy of the State to establish, maintain and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people. It is likewise the policy of the State to protect, foster and promote the right of all citizens to affordable quality education at all levels. Consistent with these policies, the State recognizes the authority of basic and higher education institutions to adopt learning delivery strategies that integrate relevant off- campus educational activities with regular classroom instructional programs to broaden and supplement the learning opportunity.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 The 1987 Constitution enshrines a myriad of policies that guide the State in promoting the welfare and development of the Filipino people. Among these are the duties of the State to inculcate in the youth patriotism and nationalism, encourage their involvement in public and civic affairs, foster appreciation of the nation's history and cultural heritage, preserve and enrich the Filipino national culture, and promote the nation’s historical and cultural heritage and resources as well as artistic creations. 28 Consistent with these constitutional mandates, educational institutions have long utilized off-campus educational activities as an important complement to classroom instruction. 32 However, recent accidents and the tragic loss of young and promising lives during off- campus non-curricular activities remind us that no educational opportunity should come at the cost of a learner's life. These unfortunate incidents have exposed the limitations of existing guidelines, which remain largely administrative in nature, and clearly show the lack of a comprehensive, uniform, and enforceable framework for risk assessment, supervision, and accountability applicable to all off-campus educational activities. 39 This proposed measure seeks to establish a risk-based framework governing off- campus educational activities by public and private educational institutions. It introduces the need for accreditation for service or venue providers, mandatory risk assessments, minimum supervisor-to-learner ratios, comprehensive parental disclosure requirements, weather-related restrictions, and the imposition of criminal liability for supervisors and other heavier penalties for responsible entities who disregard learner safety. 47 Through these safeguards, the bill seeks to strike a balance between promoting meaningful off-classroom learning and ensuring that every reasonable precaution is taken to protect the life and welfare of learners. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. JERNIE JETT V. label: HB 9898
title: AN ACT IMPOSING HIGHER PENALTIES FOR THE DETENTION OF PATIENTS AND/OR THE BODIES OF THE DECEASED PATIENTS (CADAVERS) IN HOSPITALS, MEDICAL CLINICS, OR ANY OTHER SIMILAR FACILITIES DUE TO NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9439 AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Health care services in the Philippines are indeed very expensive despite continuous efforts of the government to augment the financial and medical needs of individuals needing such assistance. Many Filipinos, especially those belonging to the indigent sector are burdened by the huge amount of hospital bills and medical expenses that they could obviously not afford to settle but have no other choice but to bear in the hope that they could extend the lives of their sick relatives. In 2007, Republic Act No.9439 or “An Act Prohibiting the Detention of Patients in Hospitals and Medical Clinics on Grounds of Nonpayment of Hospital Bills or Medical Expenses” was enacted to prohibit the detention of patients (including those who may have died) for nonpayment, and to allow financially incapable patients to leave upon the execution of a promissory note secured by either a mortgage or by a guarantee of a co-maker. However, even with the existence of such law, many hospitals, medical clinics and similar facilities still practice detention of patients and cadavers/bodies of deceased patients because of unsettled payment of hospital bills and medical expenses. Also, while there is a penalty imposed for violation of said law, such amount is rather insignificant especially for hospitals owned by corporations. Hence, this proposed legislation seeks to impose higher penalties for violation of said law, including imprisonment, if necessary, to finally curb this inhumane practice. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 9899
title: AN ACT IMPOSING CRIMINAL PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS OF OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AND HEALTH STANDARDS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11058 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “AN ACT STRENGTHENING COMPLIANCE WITH OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY AND HEALTH STANDARDS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Occupational accidents, injuries and deaths are tragic reflections of how safety and health standards here in the country are often taken for granted and the welfare of workers is sacrificed in the favor of economic gains. The 1987 Philippine Constitution declares labor as a primary social economic force, and mandates the State to protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Pursuant to this, Republic Act No. 11058, otherwise known as “An Act Strengthening Compliance with Occupational Safety and Health Standards and Providing Penalties for Violations Thereof” was enacted to strengthen compliance with occupational safety and health standards, and to provide penalties for violation thereof, including the imposition of administrative fines for willful non- compliance with occupational and health standards (OSH) and compliance orders. Under the law and its implementing rules, daily administrative fines may be imposed until correction of the violation, and separate administrative fines may likewise be imposed for violations that expose or result in death, serious injury, or serious illness, and for obstruction, misrepresentation, or retaliation; these are expressly without prejudice to the filing of criminal or civil cases in the regular courts, as applicable. However, despite these measures, serious workplace hazards and willful disregard of OSH requirements persist, particularly in high-risk industries. While administrative fines are essential to ensure immediate correction and compliance, the State likewise has a strong interest to define and penalize grave and willful violations that expose workers to grave and imminent danger or result in injury or death so as to strengthen deterrence and accountability. The 2021/2022 Integrated Survey on Labor and Employment covering establishments employing at least 20 workers showed that there was a decline in work-related accidents by 36.3% or 3,322 establishment out of 36,342 in 2021 as compared to the 10.9% or 4,186 out of 38,305 recorded in 2019.1 The same survey also noted that the total occurrences of occupational accidents have decreased by 32.4% or 27,636 cases from the 2019 record of 40,892. Despite these, workplace risks remain significant and compliance gaps continue to exist. Many establishments, employers, contractors and sub-contractors still remain lax in terms of compliance to occupational safety and health standards. In fact, according to the Department of Labor and Employment’s (DOLE) Bureau of Working Conditions (BWC) 52 out of 95 or 55% of the constructions projects that it inspected covering the period of August 1 to 15, 2023 in Metro Manila were found to have violated basic occupational safety and health standards. 2 Among the top violations were lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) for workers that include safety shoes, helmets, harnesses, gloves, and goggles. If there were PPE, these were found to be inadequate or incorrectly used.3 There were also no designated OSHS personnel such as safety officers and first aiders, no safety and health committee, no mandatory OSHS training for workers and no copy of the construction safety and health program in the workplace. It is high time that the government adopt measures that criminalize grave and willful violations of occupational safety and health standards to reinforce compliance and protect the welfare of the worker. Hence, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. label: HB 9902
title: AN ACT DECLARING APRIL 20 OF EVERY YEAR AS "ARAW NG SAMAL,” A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SAMAL, PROVINCE OF BATAAN, IN COMMEMORATION OF ITS FOUNDING ANNIVERSARY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Samal, the second oldest town in the Province of Bataan, was founded by Dominican friars on 20 April 1641, and placed under the spiritual patronage of St. Catherine of Sienna. Rich in history and culture, Samal is recognized as the pioneer of the capiz shell industry along the surrounding coastlines, the birthplace of the province's wooden shoe ("bakya") making industry, and the site of the country's first pulp mills. Over the centuries, Samal has gracefully evolved from a quaint coastal settlement into a progressive municipality. Driven by the remarkable resilience and industriousness of its people, the town has sustained its thriving agricultural and fishing sectors, ensuring food security and economic vitality. Commemorating its foundation day serves not only as a tribute to this colorful past but also as a celebration of the community's continuous growth and achievements. Every year, the people of Samal proudly commemorate their foundation day. Recognizing the profound historical significance of this date, the Sangguniang Bayan of Samal passed Resolution No. 26-103, advocating for the legislative enactment of April 20th of every year as a special non-working holiday in the municipality. Declaring April 20 as a special non-working holiday will allow the people of Samal to fully participate in meaningful civic, cultural, and commemorative festivities. It provides the working population and students the opportunity to honor their ancestors and strengthen their sense of community without the constraints of work or school. Furthermore, institutionalizing this celebration will promote local tourism, attract visitors, and contribute to the economic growth and cultural development of the municipality. In view of the foregoing, and to give due recognition to the socio-historical importance of Samal's founding, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. title: AN ACT PROHIBITING ALL PUBLIC TELECOMMUNICATIONS ENTITIES AND INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATIONS TECHNOLOGY PROVIDERS FROM IMPOSING AN EXPIRATION PERIOD ON THE VALIDITY OF PREPAID LOAD CREDITS AND THEIR FORFEITURE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It hardly needs statistical proof to recognize that nearly every Filipino has, at some point in their lives, maintained a prepaid mobile phone subscription, and most continue to be subscribers of such services today. Before the broad availability of the internet, Filipinos were able to become a collective, interconnected people largely through mobile phone subscriptions. In fact, the mobile phone subscription industry remains one of the most pervasive in the country. In the 2024 Annual Report of the National Telecommunications Office (NTC),1 the subscriber base for mobile prepaid users among the three (3) largest telecommunications industry players was reported as follows: PLDT with 56,731,489 subscribers, Globe with 57,714,593 subscribers, and the newest entrant, DITO, already reaching 28,227,421 subscribers. For all of these consumers, the current regulatory framework permits telecommunication companies to enforce expiration dates on prepaid load credits, resulting in the forced forfeiture of billions of pesos in consumer assets annually. This regime originated in Joint Memorandum Circular No. 05-12-2017, issued jointly by the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), Department of 1 National Telecommunications Commission. (03 May 2026). Annual Report 2024: Shaping a Digital Future Through Innovation. National Telecommunications Commission. Retrieved from https://ntc.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2026/ANNUAL_REPORT/FY_2024_Annual_Report.pdf 1 Information and Communications Technology (DICT), and Department of Trade and Industry (DTI). The Joint Circular imposed a uniform one-year validity period for all prepaid loads regardless of the amount. Under this policy, consumers who purchase load in advance must either use their credits or forfeit them, a result contrary to basic consumer expectations that money spent should remain spendable until used. That policy is unfair and inequitable, as it forces consumers to use up their data or credit allowances prematurely to avoid forfeiting them to service providers. Consequently, the unilateral expiration of privately owned prepaid credits constitutes a clear injustice, particularly given that the mechanism places the consumer at a severe structural disadvantage. Thus, this proposed measure. This bill prohibits all public telecommunications entities and providers from imposing expiration periods on prepaid load credits purchased by active subscribers. The bill makes unlawful three specific acts: (1) imposition of any expiration period on unused prepaid load credits; (2) forfeiture of such credits on active accounts, except for mobile number portability purposes; and (3) refusal to refund forfeited credits without valid cause. To address legitimate operational concerns, the bill includes a narrowly tailored provision for dormant accounts, those inactive for a minimum period of one (1) year. Such accounts may be deducted ₱1 per day of inactivity until credits are fully consumed, allowing carriers to reclaim dormant numbers for reallocation while preserving the vast majority of consumer assets. Subscribers must receive notification of these daily deductions. The telecommunications industry, as vital as its contribution is to the national economy, must be enjoined in protecting consumer rights. In the hopes of maintaining social justice, even every peso that avails us of the ability to communicate in this day and age must be safeguarded. The State may then intervene when the common good requires, when the general welfare demands, precisely as this legislation does, safeguarding the assets of millions of Filipino consumers and supporting the digital economy's expansion into underserved populations. In the 20th Congress, Senators Sherwin “Win” T. Gatchalian and Jinggoy Estrada filed similar measures as SBN 1095 and SBN 382, respectively. This version fully adopts Senate President Gatchalian’s SBN 1095. The prompt passing of this measure is respectfully urged. LEILA M. label: HB 9904
title: AN ACT GRANTING A MATERNITY BENEFIT TO WOMEN WORKERS IN THE INFORMAL ECONOMY, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11210, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State shall protect working women by providing safe and healthful working conditions, taking into account their maternal functions, and such facilities and opportunities that will enhance their welfare and enable them to realize their full potential in the service of the nation.” Republic Act No. 11210, otherwise known as the “105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law,” is among the landmark laws affirming the State’s commitment to strengthen the protection of working mothers and their children. Republic Act No. 11210 significantly expanded the maternity benefits among Filipino working mothers. The law provides them with ample time to recover their health and overall well-being, while allowing them to focus on childcare before returning to work. However, the existing law fails to cover women working in the informal economy who are non-members of the Social Security System (SSS). According to 2021 data from the Philippine Legislators' Committee on Population and Development (PLCPD), “more than 70% of Filipino workers were informally employed, with women disproportionately represented in this sector.”1 They include “street vendors, domestic helpers, and micro-entrepreneurs,” among others, who often don’t have access to fair wages, benefits, and job security, including SSS membership.2 1 Philippine Legislators' Committee on Population and Development. (07 March 2025). Lifting the women who lift us: Accelerating action for Filipino women in all sectors. Retrieved from https://www.plcpd.org.ph/lifting-the-women-who-lift-us-accelerating-action-for-filipino-women-in-all- sectors/. 2 Ibid. 1 This bill seeks to expand the coverage of maternity benefits to women workers in the informal economy by providing a one-time direct maternity cash benefit per delivery equivalent to the prevailing daily minimum wage rate in the mother’s region of residence multiplied by forty-four (44) days. The cash benefit distribution will be administered by the Department of Social Work and Development (DSWD). This bill therefore, seeks to further strengthen the State’s Constitutional mandate to ensure that the rights to health and decent working conditions of all working women in the country are upheld and promoted. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Brian Yamsuan, Ferdinand Martin Romualdez, Yedda Romualdez, Andrew Romualdez, Dadah Ismula, Jose Manuel Diokno, Percival Cendaña, and Kaka Bag-ao in the House of Representatives, and Senator Risa Hontiveros in the Senate. This bill fully adopts Senator Hontiveros’s Senate Bill No. 1597. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 9905
title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING TWO BILLION PESOS FOR THE DEMOLITION OF THE BURNED DOWN HALL OF JUSTICE AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF A NEW AND MODERN HALL OF JUSTICE IN CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Hall of Justice Building in Cagayan de Oro City used to be a grand building. However, time and neglect had rendered it very dilapidated and in dire need of repairs and renovations. A big fire last January 30, 2015 completely burned the building. The City government was able to provide a temporary location for all court transactions. Despite this, there is a need to have a permanent world class and modern Hall of Justice for Cagayan de Oro City. This new Hall of Justice Building can still be located in the old location. In view of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly requested. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. RODRIGUEZ, JR. label: HB 9907
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10175, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CYBERCRIME PREVENTION ACT OF 2012,” TO CRIMINALIZE THE UNAUTHORIZED AND MALICIOUS USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS FOR IDENTITY THEFT, ONLINE FRAUD, COMPUTER-RELATED FORGERY, AND OTHER COMPUTER-RELATED OFFENSES, PROVIDING SAFEGUARDS FOR LEGITIMATE USES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid advancement and widespread accessibility of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies have transformed the digital landscape, creating unprecedented opportunities for innovation, economic growth, and public service. However, the same technologies have also introduced new avenues for cybercrime, particularly through the creation of highly realistic synthetic identities, deepfakes, voice cloning, automated impersonation schemes, and other AI-generated content capable of deceiving individuals, businesses, and government institutions. Republic Act No. 10175, otherwise known as the "Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012," penalizes computer-related identity theft, fraud, forgery, and related cyber offenses. Nevertheless, the law was enacted before the emergence of modern generative artificial intelligence systems, and does not expressly address the unique risks posed by AI-enabled criminal activities. Recent developments have demonstrated how AI can be exploited to impersonate individuals through fabricated images, cloned voices, manipulated videos, and synthetic digital identities. Such technologies have been used to facilitate financial scams, phishing schemes, identity theft, reputational attacks, misinformation campaigns, and other fraudulent activities. The increasing sophistication of these tools has made it more difficult for victims, law enforcement authorities, and the public to distinguish authentic content from fabricated material. The absence of explicit statutory provisions governing AI-assisted cybercrime creates uncertainty in enforcement and may limit the ability of authorities to effectively investigate and prosecute offenders who use emerging technologies as instruments of criminal activity. While existing provisions of Republic Act No. 10175 may apply in certain instances, there is a compelling need to clearly define and penalize the unauthorized use of artificial intelligence systems for identity theft, online fraud, computer-related forgery, and other cyber offenses. This proposed measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 10175 by: (1) Defining artificial intelligence systems, synthetic identities, and deepfakes for purposes of criminal liability; (2) Criminalizing the unauthorized use of AI technologies to impersonate, deceive, or misrepresent the identity of natural or juridical persons; (3) Penalizing AI-assisted computer-related fraud and computer-related forgery; (4) Establishing the malicious deployment of AI systems for cybercriminal purposes as a punishable offense; (5) Treating the use of artificial intelligence as a qualifying circumstance that warrants higher penalties when employed in the commission of cybercrimes; and (6) Strengthening the capacity of law enforcement agencies to address emerging forms of technology-facilitated criminal conduct. This bill does not seek to hinder legitimate research, innovation, or beneficial uses of artificial intelligence. Rather, it aims to promote the responsible and ethical use of AI technologies while safeguarding individuals, businesses, and public institutions from deception, fraud, and other harms arising from the malicious exploitation of these tools. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERNESTO “ERNIX” M. DIONISIO, JR. label: HB 9913
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 272 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991," TO EXPAND THE ALLOWABLE USES OF THE SPECIAL EDUCATION FUND, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.1 At the local level, this commitment is manifested through Section 272 of the Local Government Code of 1991 (“LGC”). Section 272 allocates one percent of real property tax collections to the Special Education Fund (“SEF”). When the LGC was enacted the enumeration of allowable SEF expenditures corresponded to the education programs that existed at that time. More than three decades have passed, and numerous new education programs, not included in the previous list, have come into existence. Local school boards are now expected to implement Early Childhood Care and Development (“ECCD”), the Alternative Learning System (“ALS”), and inclusive education for learners with disabilities – programs that Section 272 does not authorize the SEF to fund. This mismatch has produced a detrimental fiscal consequence. The Second Congressional Commission on Education documented approximately fifteen billion pesos in unspent SEF collections in 2022 alone, which could have been used to address the education crisis.2 In the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment, the Philippines placed among the five lowest-performing countries out of 81 participants. Only 16 percent of Filipino students reached minimum proficiency in mathematics, 24 percent in reading, and 23 percent in science.3 As of the end of School Year 2024 to 2025, the Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment revealed that 48.76 percent of learners in Grades 1 to 3 are still not reading at their respective grade levels.4 This bill, by expanding the enumerated programs for which SEF Fund can be used for, seeks to prevent billions of pesos worth of fiscal firepower to remain unutilized when it could have been used to help solve the education crisis. Aligned with the wisdom of this initiative, the executive branch already responded through DILG-DepEd-DBM-DOF Joint Circular No. 1, series of 2025, expanding allowable SEF uses to cover all three programs. By including said expansion 1 art. XIV, § 2(1), 1987 Constitution. 2 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), “Fixing the Foundations: A Matter of National Survival,” Year Two Report (January 27, 2025); EDCOM analysis of DOF-BLGF data, 2018–2022. OECD, PISA 2022 Results: Country Note - Philippines (December 2023), accessed at https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2022-results-volume-i-and-ii-country-notes_ed6fbcc5- en/philippines_a0882a2d-en.html 4 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), “Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reforms,” Final Report (January 2026), citing Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment (CRLA), End of School Year, SY 2024– 2025 p 22. within a legislative framework, this bill erases any legal doubt that may persist despite the executive department institutionalizing the expansion of the programs allowed to be funded by the SEF Fund. This bill amends Section 272 of the Local Government Code to permanently authorize SEF expenditures on ECCD, the ALS, and inclusive education for learners with disabilities. The sole purpose is to align the statute with the education system it was always meant to support. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. _____________________________________ _____________________________________ REP. SANCHO FERNANDO “ANDO” REP. label: HB 9916
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE DENTAL, VISION, AND HEARING ASSISTIVE DEVICES, INCLUDING DENTURES, PRESCRIPTION GLASSES, AND HEARING AIDS TO SENIOR CITIZENS AND INDIGENTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a special benefit package that shall provide senior citizens and indigents free dental, vision, and hearing assistive devices. Untreated vision impairment, hearing loss, and oral health conditions are common medical issues that are most oftentimes overlooked. These conditions drastically reduce productivity and compromise the quality of life of our elderly and economically disadvantaged citizens. Essential medical devices remain painfully out of reach due to prohibitive cots: dentures can cost up to Forty thousand pesos (Php 40,000.00) per arch, prescription eyeglasses typically ranges from One thousand five hundred pesos to more than Five thousand pesos (Php 5,000.00) per pair, and hearing aids may cost up to over Two hundred fifty thousand pesos (Php 250,000.00) per ear. Senior citizens commonly experience age-related deterioration in eyesight, hearing, and oral health, while indigent individuals frequently forego treatment because of financial constraints. The absence of appropriate assistive devices contribute to preventable disability and a lower quality of life. The proposed measure implements a special benefit package that will fully cover the cost of assistive devices such as dentures, prescription eyeglasses, and hearing aids for qualified beneficiaries. It likewise ensures that recipients undergo proper medical, dental, or ophthalmologic evaluation to guarantee appropriate diagnosis and prescription. This vital piece of legislation strengthens the State’s commitment to protect the welfare, dignity, and well-being of senior citizens and indigent Filipinos. The provision of these necessary healthcare devices restores their autonomy and empowers them to participate actively in community life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9917
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE UNIVERSAL DIGITALIZATION OF ACADEMIC RECORDS AND PROVIDING FREE ACCESS TO EMPLOYMENT DOCUMENTS, STRENGTHENING THE TRANSITION OF FRESH GRADUATES ENTERING THE WORKFORCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate the free issuance of essential employment documents and the digitalization of academic records systems in all higher education institutions (HEIs). It aims to facilitate a seamless transition for Filipino graduates from college to the workforce and remove unnecessary financial and administrative barriers that delay employment opportunities for newly graduated Filipinos. For many fresh graduates, the path to employment is stalled at the very beginning due to high costs of documentation and processing charged by HEIs. While Republic Act No. 11261, otherwise known as the “First Time Jobseekers Assistance Act”, covers for the waiving of fees for government clearances, it does not comprehensively cover the costs and processing challenges associated with academic records required by employers. As labor market conditions become increasingly competitive, there is a need to ensure that fresh graduates can promptly access the documents necessary to pursue employment opportunities. This measure mandates all HEIs, both public and private, to provide fresh graduates with free copies of their transcripts, diplomas, and certificates of graduation. It likewise establishes a Digital Academic Records System to facilitate a more efficient and secure processing of academic records. The youth represents one of the nation’s greatest assets and a driving force of economic growth and national development. It is a constitutional imperative for the State to protect their social well-being and promote full employment. Through the provisions stipulated in this Act, the State helps unlock opportunities, strengthen productivity, and support inclusive economic progress. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9918
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSTALLATION OF CLOSED-CIRCUIT TELEVISION SYSTEMS IN BARANGAY POSTS AND OTHER SPECIFIC LOCATIONS UNDER THE JURISDICTION OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS TO ENHANCE PUBLIC SAFETY AND SECURITY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate the installation and maintenance of closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems in barangay posts and other locations under the jurisdiction of local government units (LGUs). It seeks to strengthen public safety, support law enforcement, and improve security at the community level. As the primary units of local governance, barangays bear the responsibility of maintaining peace and order, and ensuring the safety of their constituents. label: HB 9919
title: AN ACT MANDATING LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS TO USE A BODY-WORN CAMERA DURING LAW ENFORCEMENT OPERATIONS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate the use of body-worn cameras by law enforcement officers during the conduct of official operations in order to promote transparency, preserve evidence, and strengthen accountability and public confidence in law enforcement institutions. Law enforcement operations often involve the exercise of coercive authority, the restriction of individual liberties, and direct interactions between law enforcement officers and the public. In the absence of reliable documentation, disputes regarding the conduct of operations may arise, thus resulting in allegations of abuse, questions on the propriety of police actions, and difficulties in establishing accountability. The use of body-worn cameras provides an objective record of law enforcement activities and assists in the accurate determination of facts during criminal, administrative, and judicial proceedings. Recorded footage may protect civilians from misconduct and safeguard law enforcement officers from false and unfounded complaints. This bill therefore provides for the standards in the activation, use, storage, retention, disclosure, and custody of recorded footages. The measure further provides safeguards to protect privacy rights and privileged communications, regulates access to recordings, and authorizes the use of redaction technology when necessary to protect sensitive information. The institutionalization of body-worn cameras promotes accountability in law enforcement operations, strengthens public confidence in law enforcement institutions, and reinforces the State’s commitment to the protection of human rights and the rule of law. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9920
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING LOCAL CLEAN-UP TEAMS AND INCREASING THE FINES AND PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize local clean-up teams in every city and municipality in the country to immediately respond to incidents of illegal dumping and littering. It strengthens Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000”, and also increases the fines and penalties imposed under the Act. Despite the enactment of the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, improper waste disposal and littering continue to degrade waterways, public spaces, and communities. Rapid shifts in lifestyle and heightened consumerism have led to an increase in plastic wastes and vastly outpaces garbage collection capacities. This has led to clogged drainage systems, polluted rivers and esteros, and the accumulation of solid waste which contribute to flooding and public health risks. This measure establishes local clean-up teams that shall undertake waste removal, site rehabilitation, and preventive interventions in coordination with local solid waste management authorities. It likewise allows offenders sentenced to community service to participate in clean-up activities under the supervision of local government units, reinforcing accountability, and encouraging reform and civic responsibility. Effective solid waste management depends not only on regulation and enforcement but also on active community participation. This measure promotes the spirit of volunteerism and reinforces the Filipino value of kapwa through collective action in maintaining clean surroundings, protecting public health, and promoting environmental stewardship at the local level. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9921
title: AN ACT DECLARING A ONE-TIME, ONE-MONTH TAX HOLIDAY, EXEMPTING COMPENSATION INCOME FROM INCOME TAX, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to declare a one-time, one-month tax holiday on compensation income by exempting salaries and wages from income tax for individual taxpayers. Filipino workers and employees consistently contribute a substantial share of government revenues through income taxation. Amid increasing economic pressures and growing public demand for responsive fiscal policies, the State must provide meaningful and immediate relief to taxpayers whose earnings sustain public services and national development. The temporary exemption from income tax will increase the take-home pay of employees and strengthen the purchasing power of households. It likewise promotes economic activity by allowing workers to retain a greater portion of their earned income. The bill safeguards the full enjoyment of the tax relief by prohibiting the diminution of compensation, allowances, and benefits during the tax holiday period. It also preserves mandatory contributions to the Government Service Insurance System, Social Security System, PhilHealth and PAG-IBIG Fund to ensure the continued protection of employees’ social security and welfare benefits. A compassionate government must remain agile enough to return wealth to its citizens when circumstances demand it. This one-month tax holiday is an extraordinary economic lifeline that restores public trust in governance by proving that the State is responsive to the economic welfare of its people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9922
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE RIGHTS OF PIECE-RATE WORKERS, PROVIDING FOR STRICTER REPORTORIAL REQUIREMENTS AND PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THERETO, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to ensure the fair and lawful implementation of piece-rate compensation systems. It requires approved production standards, enhances regulatory oversight, and imposes penalties for violations of labor laws affecting piece-rate employees, commonly known as “pakyawan”workers. While Article 101 of Presidential Decree No. 442, otherwise known as “The Labor Code of the Philippines”, recognizes result-based compensation schemes, the absence of an updated framework leaves “pakyawan” workers highly susceptible to economic exploitation. Many businesses bypass traditional payroll tracking mechanisms and this oftentimes result in the underpayment of wages and the denial of mandatory statutory benefits like holiday pay and service incentive leaves. This measure transitions piece-rate adjustments from an optional company practice into a strictly regulated administrative process. It requires employers to duly adopt Piece-Rate Orders duly approved by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board supported by valid Time and Motion Studies, maintain transparent compensation records, and comply with mandatory reportorial requirements. This ensures that baseline productivity quotas reflect humanly attainable metrics that mathematically correspond to the current minimum wage. The vital piece of legislation safeguards the rights of piece-rate workers and transforms state labor policies from passive guidelines into an active, self-executing shield for the working class. It ensures that piece-rate workers receive fair wages, lawful benefits, and adequate protection from exploitative labor practices. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9923
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING TRANSPORTATION NETWORK COMPANIES AND DRIVERS, PRESCRIBING REQUIREMENTS, GUIDELINES AND STANDARDS FOR THEIR OPERATION, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a clear legal framework for the regulation, operation and standardization of Transportation Network Companies (TNCs) and Transportation Network Drivers (TNDs) in the Philippines. Digital ride-hailing platforms have become an integral component of the country’s transportation system and have since provided commuters with additional mobility options and has since created livelihood opportunities for thousands of drivers. Despite its rapid expansion, these platforms continue to operate under ambiguous frameworks that compromise consumer protection, complicate driver accountability, and distort market competition within the broader public transport sector. The proposed measure recognizes transportation network services as a legitimate mode of public transportation and defines the respective rights, duties, and liabilities of TNCs and TNDs. It requires the registration and regulation of transportation network companies, establishes minimum qualifications for drivers and vehicles, mandates insurance coverages, and prescribes standards for passenger safety, data privacy, and fare transparency. This vital piece of legislation prevents monopolies from happening through the restriction of corporate-owned fleets and digital operations to authentic, peer-to-peer ride sharing and fosters an environment of safe and technologically advanced transit options for millions of commuting Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9924
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA OF COMMUTERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a Magna Carta of Commuters that establishes mobility as a basic human need and guarantees the commuting public safe, reliable, and affordable transport infrastructures. It mandates an inclusive public transportation network that prioritizes commuter welfare. Millions of Filipinos depend on public transportation to access employment, education, healthcare, and other essential services. Yet many commuters continue to endure long travel times, inadequate transport services, unsafe facilities, and insufficient transport information. These inefficiencies reduce productivity and diminish the quality of life of the riding public. The proposed measure establishes minimum standards for public transportation services, mobility infrastructure, and commuter welfare. It promotes integrated transport systems, efficient service interconnectivity, and transport services that respond to the mobility requirements of communities. It likewise advances active transport through the development of safe sidewalks, bicycle lanes, pedestrian facilities, and other infrastructure that support walking and cycling. The bill further strengthens commuter protection by requiring real-time transport information, improved road safety measures, accessibility for persons with disabilities and greater accountability among transport service providers and government agencies. It also creates the National Transport Data and Planning Center to ensure data transparency and establishes the dedicated Office of Commuter Affairs at both national and local levels. An efficient and sustainable transport network services as the backbone of a resilient economy. The enactment of a Magna Carta of Commuters shall uphold the rights of the riding public, improve mobility outcomes, and promote a transportation system that is safe, inclusive, and responsive to the needs of the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9925
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PUBLIC CREMATORIUMS IN CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES, PROVIDING FREE CREMATION SERVICES TO INDIGENT FAMILIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 17 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to mandate the establishment of public crematoriums in all cities and municipalities across the Philippines. It amends Section 17 of Republic Act (RA) No. 7160, otherwise known as the “Local Government Code of 1991”, to include public crematoriums among the basic facilities and services that local government units must provide. This provides for a dignified, affordable and accessible alternative to traditional burial services while ensuring free cremation services for indigent families. Public cemeteries throughout the country are currently experiencing congestion, while the rising cost of funeral and burial services places financial burden on many Filipino families. Although cremation has emerged as a practical and space-efficient alternative, its use remains largely dependent on private facilities whose services are often beyond the means of low-income households. The absence of government-operated and maintained crematoriums limits affordable options and compels many families to incur debts during periods of bereavement. This measure strengthens the capacity of cities and municipalities to deliver essential funeral services, improve land use management, and promote public health and social welfare. To safeguard public health and environmental integrity, all public crematoriums shall comply with the requirements of Presidential Decree No. 856, otherwise known as the “Code on Sanitation of the Philippines”, and RA No. 8749, otherwise known as the “Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999”. This bill offers a sustainable solution to urban congestion and alleviates the financial distress of bereaved Filipino families. It ensures that even in death, all citizens are afforded dignity without placing an economic burden on those they leave behind. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9926
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SAFEGUARDS FOR THE USE OF SOCIAL MEDIA BY MINORS, PROMOTING A SAFE AND AGE APPROPRIATE DIGITAL ENVIRONMENT, AND PROTECTING MINORS FROM DIGITAL ADDICTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish safeguards governing the use of social media by minors and aims to promote a safe and age-appropriate digital environment and to protect children from the harmful effects of online exposure and digital addiction. The increasing use of social media among children and adolescents has expanded opportunities for learning and access to information. At the same time, unrestricted access to digital platforms has exposed minors to online exploitation, harmful content, cyberbullying and excessive screen time that may adversely affect their mental development and holistic well-being. Despite existing laws protecting children from abuse and exploitation, no comprehensive framework currently exists to regulate minors’ access to social media or to recommend obligations for digital platform providers. The absence of clear standards has limited the ability of parents, schools, and government agencies to address the risks associated with unsupervised online activity. This proposed measure establishes age-based access restrictions for social media platforms. Minors aged thirteen (13) to seventeen (17) may access social media only upon verified parental or guardian consent, and through age-appropriate services with enhanced privacy protections. Children below the age of thirteen (13) years old shall generally be prohibited from maintaining social media accounts, except for educational purposes. The enactment of this vital piece of legislation strengthens the protection of minors in digital spaces and promotes responsible social media use while preserving the ability of young people to access information and communicate in an appropriate and safe online environment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9927
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE UNLAWFUL LENDING, BORROWING, OR FRAUDULENT USE OF LICENSES, PERMITS, AND OTHER CONCESSIONS GRANTED BY THE STATE, PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to penalize the unlawful lending, borrowing, and fraudulent use of licenses. This upholds the integrity of licenses, permits, and other government-issued concessions. Licenses and permits are privileges granted by the State only to persons or entities that satisfy the qualifications and standards prescribed by the law. These privileges are issued to ensure competence, accountability, and compliance with regulatory requirements in activities that affect the public interest. Despite existing regulations, the practice of license lending, fronting, and other unauthorized use of government-issued privileges persists. Some individuals and entities allow others to use their licenses or permits to circumvent legal requirements, while others misrepresent or fraudulently use such privileges to conduct transactions without lawful authority. These practices undermine regulatory systems, distort fair competition, and expose the public to significant data and identity theft risks. They facilitate fraud and erode public trust in government institutions, particularly when public officials knowingly issue or facilitate the issuance of licences to unqualified persons or entities. This measure affirms the non-transferable nature of licenses, permits, and other government-issued privileges, except when otherwise provided by the law. It also provides corresponding administrative and criminal sanctions and establishes liability for public officials who issue or facilitate the issuance of such privileges in violation of existing laws. This bill advances the integrity of government regulatory processes and reinforces transparency, accountability, and public confidence in the administration of State-issued privileges. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9928
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE CHARTER OF THE OVERSEAS FILIPINO BANK, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish the charter of the Overseas Filipino Bank (OFB) as a government financial institution mandated to provide accessible, secure, and responsive banking services to overseas Filipinos and their families. It also seeks to promote financial inclusion and support their economic welfare and reintegration. Overseas Filipinos continue to play a vital role in sustaining the Philippine economy through remittances, investments, and other intangible contributions to national development. Despite their significant contributions, many overseas Filipinos still have limited access to affordable banking services, credit facilities, and investment products suited to their circumstances. The absence of a dedicated financial institution limits the government’s capacity to deliver targeted financial programs and responsive banking services to our overseas Filipinos. This measure provides for the capitalization, governance, and operational framework of the and authorizes the Bank to develop financial products and services, facilitate affordable remittance transactions, expand access to credit and investment opportunities, and support programs on reintegration, financial literacy, and welfare assistance. The bill likewise ensures the prudent, transparent, and accountable operations of the OFB in accordance with existing banking laws and regulations of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. The establishment of the Overseas Filipino Bank affirms the State’s commitment to protect the financial interests of overseas Filipinos, reduce the cost of financial transactions, expand economic opportunities, and promote our modern day heroes’ long-term economic security. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 9930
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE CREATION OF PLANTILLA POSITIONS FOR SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICERS IN ALL PUBLIC ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution guarantees every Filipino learner the right to quality education. This guarantee, however, cannot be fully realized unless schools are safe, secure, and conducive environments for learning. The increasing incidence of violence and security threats in and around educational institutions underscores the urgent need to strengthen security measures in public schools nationwide. Recent events have exposed the vulnerabilities that continue to exist within educational settings. On 22 June 2026, a shooting incident at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City claimed the lives of three students and injured several others when two students allegedly brought firearms onto school grounds and opened fire during class hours. Likewise, a separate stabbing incident in a school in General Trias City, Cavite, involved a Grade 8 student who allegedly attacked several Grade 5 pupils using a kitchen knife, injuring at least seven learners. Together, these incidents demonstrate that violence in schools is no longer a remote possibility but a real and emerging risk affecting the safety and psychological well-being of learners. Many public schools currently rely on limited security arrangements, including contractual guards whose deployment varies depending on local resources and budget availability. Numerous schools, particularly in rural and underserved areas, have no dedicated security personnel at all. This measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a permanent school security framework through the creation of plantilla positions for School Security Officers (SSOs) under the Department of Education. These SSOs shall be career government employees who are properly trained, adequately compensated, and fully integrated into the school system. Their presence will help ensure consistent monitoring of school premises, access control, and coordination with law enforcement and local government authorities. A secure school environment enables learners to focus on their studies, teachers to perform their duties effectively, and parents to have confidence that their children are protected while in school. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 45 46 47 HON. JULIENNE “JAM” L. label: HB 9932
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING THE INTERTWINED ROLE OF PARENTS IN CHILD-REARING BY EXPANDING THE PATERNITY LEAVE BENEFITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8187, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PATERNITY LEAVE ACT OF 1996" Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 8187, otherwise known as the "Paternity Leave Act of 1996," was enacted nearly three decades ago to recognize the vital role of fathers in providing support to their spouses during the period of recovery and the care of their newborns. It granted a modest seven (7) days of paid leave, restricted strictly to married male employees and limited only to the first four (4) deliveries. Since then, our understanding of shared parental responsibilities has evolved significantly. The enactment of Republic Act No. 11210, or the "105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law," highlighted the state's commitment to maternal and child health, but it also underscored the wide disparity in parental leave allocations. While a mother may voluntarily transfer up to seven (7) days of her leave to the father, the standalone benefit allocated directly to fathers remains structurally insufficient at just one week. Early infant care and the postpartum recovery of a mother require active, sustained partnership. Studies consistently demonstrate that increased paternal involvement during the neonatal stage leads to better developmental outcomes for the child, reduces the incidence of postpartum depression in mothers, and fosters stronger family units. Furthermore, our laws must adapt to the shifting realities of Filipino households by expanding protections to cover long-term cohabiting partners without the benefit of marriage, ensuring that no child or father is penalized based on civil status. This Bill seeks to amend Republic Act No. 8187 by increasing the paid paternity leave to fifteen (15) working days, removing the four-delivery cap, and extending eligibility to common-law spouses. By investing in our fathers, we strengthen the foundational core of our society—the Filipino family. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. label: HB 9933
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE USE OF AEROPONICS, HYDROPONICS, AND AQUAPONICS FOR THE PRODUCTION OF HIGH-VALUE FISH, CROPS, AND VEGETABLES, PROVIDING INCENTIVES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture is facing unprecedented challenges. Rapid urbanization, land degradation, climate change, and unpredictable weather patterns are continuously shrinking arable land and threatening food security. Traditional farming methods, while foundational, are becoming increasingly vulnerable to these environmental pressures. To safeguard food sovereignty and boost economic productivity, we must transition toward climate-resilient, space-efficient, and technology-driven agricultural practices. Aeroponics (growing plants in an air/mist environment), hydroponics (growing plants in a nutrient-rich water solution), and aquaponics (a symbiotic system combining aquaculture and hydroponics) represent the frontier of modern sustainable farming. These methods provide key advantages over traditional farming, using up to 90% less water with closed-loop systems. They reduce the need for arable land, making vertical and urban farming feasible. Closed environments lower risks of soil-borne pests and diseases, minimizing chemical pesticide use. Additionally, they enable continuous cultivation of high-value crops, vegetables, and fish, regardless of weather conditions. This Bill aims to establish a national program promoting aeroponics, hydroponics, and aquaponics in rural and urban areas. By investing in these technologies, offering incentives to agri-tech entrepreneurs, and creating community farming hubs, it seeks to boost the income of fishers and farmers, ensure a steady supply of high-value vegetables and fish, and promote climate- smart agriculture. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9934
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006," AS AMENDED, LOWERING THE AGE OF CRIMINAL LIABILITY, REMOVING CRIMINAL EXEMPTIONS FOR HEINOUS CRIMES AND MASS VIOLENCE COMMITTED WITHIN ACADEMIC INSTITUTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The state’s duty to protect its citizens is paramount, yet a deeply concerning trend is challenging the peace of our local communities. Schools and public spaces— traditionally reserved as safe havens for learning and youth development—have increasingly become the stages for unexpected, lethal acts of violence carried out by minors. Most recently, on June 22, 2026, the entire nation was shocked by a horrifying mass shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City. In that incident, two heavily armed teenagers—aged 14 and 15—opened fire inside active classrooms with a Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol and a .38 caliber revolver, killing three innocent students and wounding several others. This tragic event does not stand alone; it follows a string of violent student-on-student offenses nationwide, including a severe multi-victim knife attack just a week prior in Cavite. While Republic Act No. 9344, otherwise known as the "Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006," was originally enacted with the noble intent of protecting the rights and rehabilitation of minors, the evolving landscape of juvenile delinquency requires a firm reassessment. Present-day minors have unprecedented access to sophisticated weapons, criminal networks, and modern communication. When a 14-year-old or 15-year-old demonstrates the tactical capacity to load, reload, and deploy military-grade firearms inside a crowded classroom, treating them with absolute exemption from criminal prosecution creates a dangerous legal vacuum. It deprives victims' families of meaningful justice and fosters an environment of impunity. This Bill introduces two critical, targeted updates to the law: 1. Lowering the Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility (MACR): It lowers the baseline from 15 to 12 years of age, but ensures safeguards by mandating a strict legal determination of discernment (the capacity to distinguish right from wrong and understand its consequences). 2. Absolute Exclusion for Heinous and Gun-Related Mass Violences: It declares that any minor, from age 12 up to below 18, who commits an act of mass murder, severe gun violence, or heinous offenses inside or near educational institutions, shall automatically be excluded from absolute exemption. Instead, they will be subjected to the standard, specialized prosecution under a modernized family court system, while maintaining high-security rehabilitation under specialized youth facilities (Bahay Pag- asa). We must strike a vital balance: we must remain dedicated to reforming troubled youth, but we can no longer allow the law to act as an unyielding shield for those who commit horrific acts of violence against their peers. In view of the urgent need to secure our schools and restore public safety, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 9935
title: AN ACT DECLARING VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND CHILDREN AS AN AUTOMATIC GROUND FOR MARRIAGE DISSOLUTION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. 209, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE FAMILY CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9262, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANTI-VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN ACT OF 2004
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure seeks to uphold the State’s constitutional duty to defend and protect its citizens, particularly women and children, from violence and abuse that destroy the very foundation of familial harmony. As a necessary consequence of an abusive and traumatic marriage, this bill shifts the focus entirely toward protecting the victim-survivor considering how there is absolutely no reason for them to remain legally bound to a union that has turned violent. According to data gathered by the World Health Organization (WHO) in the years 2000 to 2023, 25.8% of women (roughly 682 million), from the ages 15 to 49, have suffered from physical or sexual intimate partner violence at least once in their lifetime. Even with the legal safeguards under Republic Act (R.A.) No. 9262, otherwise known as the "Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004", violence against women appears to be one of the country’s most pervasive social problems that rattles and disturbs familial relationships. This piece of legislation inserts a new Article into Executive Order No. 209, otherwise known as the Family Code of the Philippines, explicitly mandating that when a spouse is convicted by final judgment of any of the crimes of violence enumerated under Section 5 of R.A. No. 9262, the marriage contracted by the offending spouse shall be automatically dissolved. Furthermore, it mandates that the convicted husband's entire share in the conjugal partnership or community property will be forfeited in favor of his wife and children. The bill also inserts a new section into the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004 that mandates the dissolution of a marriage upon the conviction of the accused. The resulting dissolution of the marriage will legally carry the exact same effects as a formal annulment under the Family Code of the Philippines. This measure does not attempt to diminish the sanctity of marriage, but rather it recognizes that the country has the duty to protect the lives of its citizens by providing these victims of abuse a way out, especially for those trapped in abusive marital unions. In this way, the State actively prioritizes the safety, dignity and recovery of the survivor over the preservation of an abusive partnership. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Ryan S.
