label: HB 9986
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A UNIFORM FRAMEWORK FOR INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY IN THE PREVENTION OF, RESPONSE TO, AND INVESTIGATION OF REPORTABLE INSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT, PRESCRIBING THE DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF COVERED INSTITUTIONS, PROVIDING PROTECTION FOR COMPLAINANTS, VICTIMS, WITNESSES, AND WHISTLEBLOWERS, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR INSTITUTIONAL VIOLATIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Institutions occupy a position of trust and authority. Schools educate students, employers supervise employees, athletic organizations train athletes, government agencies exercise public authority, and numerous other institutions direct, train, supervise, and protect individuals under their care. The effective performance of these functions necessarily requires the exercise of discipline, supervision, leadership, and accountability. Although Philippine law penalizes various offenses, including homicide and physical injuries under the Revised Penal Code (Act No. 3815), coercion and threats under the same Code, sexual offenses under Republic Act No. 8353 (The Anti-Rape Law of 1997), as amended, and Republic Act No. 11648, hazing under Republic Act No. 11053 (Anti-Hazing Act of 2018), bullying in educational institutions under Republic Act No. 10627 (Anti-Bullying Act of 2013), sexual harassment under Republic Act No. 7877 (Anti-Sexual Harassment Act of 1995) and Republic Act No. 11313 (Safe Spaces Act), and unsafe working conditions under Republic Act No. 11058 (An Act Strengthening Compliance with Occupational Safety and Health Standards), these laws principally define and penalize specific unlawful acts or regulate particular sectors. However, no general law presently establishes uniform statutory obligations applicable across institutions to ensure the timely receipt, reporting, preservation of evidence, investigation, documentation, and appropriate institutional response to allegations of serious misconduct. As a result, institutional responses often vary significantly, resulting in delayed investigations, inadequate protection for complainants and witnesses, loss or destruction of evidence, inconsistent accountability measures, and diminished public confidence in institutional governance. This bill seeks to fill that legislative gap by establishing minimum standards of institutional accountability applicable to both public and private institutions. It imposes affirmative duties upon covered institutions to receive and investigate reports of serious institutional misconduct, preserve relevant evidence, protect complainants, victims, witnesses, and whistleblowers from retaliation, implement appropriate interim protective measures, maintain accountability mechanisms, and cooperate with competent authorities whenever required by law. This measure does not create new crimes for conduct already punishable under existing laws, nor does it diminish the authority of institutions to impose lawful and reasonable disciplinary, supervisory, academic, athletic, military, employment, or training measures. Rather, it establishes a uniform governance framework governing how institutions are expected to prevent, receive, investigate, document, and respond to serious misconduct occurring within their respective jurisdictions. By strengthening institutional accountability while preserving legitimate institutional authority, this measure seeks to promote transparency, integrity, public trust, and the protection of every person under the care or supervision of a covered institution. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAN “ATTY. JP” D. label: HB 9987
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SMART IRRIGATION WATER SHARING PROGRAM TO PROMOTE EQUITABLE, EFFICIENT, AND CLIMATE-RESILIENT ALLOCATION OF IRRIGATION WATER, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture remains one of the most water-dependent sectors of the Philippine economy. However, recurring droughts, prolonged dry seasons, and the increasing impacts of climate change continue to threaten agricultural productivity and the livelihoods of millions of Filipino farmers. While irrigation infrastructure has expanded over the years, challenges in the allocation and management of available water remain. During periods of water shortage, farmers located at the tail-end portions of irrigation systems often receive insufficient water, resulting in reduced crop yields, lower incomes, and increased vulnerability to food insecurity. These inefficiencies become more pronounced during El Niño events and other climate-related disruptions, when available water resources must be managed more carefully and equitably. Advances in monitoring and information technology now provide practical tools that can improve irrigation management. Real-time monitoring of water availability and distribution can help irrigation authorities make more informed decisions, minimize wastage, and ensure a fairer allocation of water resources among farmers. By modernizing irrigation management and adopting data-driven water allocation systems, the government can improve agricultural resilience while maximizing the benefits of existing irrigation infrastructure. This bill seeks to establish a National Smart Irrigation Water Sharing Program that promotes the efficient, equitable, and climate-resilient allocation of irrigation water. It aims to ensure that all farmers, including those located at the tail-end portions of irrigation systems, receive fair access to irrigation water, particularly during periods of drought and water scarcity. In strengthening irrigation management and promoting the efficient use of water resources, this measure contributes to the broader goals of food security, agricultural productivity, and climate resilience. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9988
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PHILHEALTH MEMBERS BY MAXIMIZING HOSPITAL BENEFITS, ENHANCING BILLING TRANSPARENCY, AND REDUCING OUT-OF-POCKET HEALTHCARE EXPENSES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution declares that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. Consistent with this policy, the enactment of the Universal Health Care Act and the continued expansion of PhilHealth benefits have significantly improved access to healthcare services for millions of Filipinos. Despite these reforms, many Filipino workers and their families continue to incur substantial out-of-pocket hospital expenses. Even after PhilHealth benefits are applied, patients are often billed additional amounts for medicines, diagnostic procedures, medical supplies, and other hospital charges. As a result, many households are forced to deplete their savings, incur debt, or postpone necessary treatment despite years of mandatory PhilHealth contributions. The challenge today is no longer merely expanding membership but ensuring that existing benefits are fully utilized and effectively translated into meaningful financial protection. Workers who faithfully contribute to PhilHealth should receive the maximum benefits available under the law, while hospitals should adopt transparent and patient-centered billing practices that minimize unnecessary financial burdens. This measure seeks to strengthen the existing healthcare framework by requiring the automatic maximization of PhilHealth benefits, improving transparency in hospital billing, and establishing mechanisms to reduce out-of-pocket expenses for qualified PhilHealth members and their dependents in accordance with existing laws and available government financing. In doing so, the bill reinforces the objective of universal health care that no Filipino should suffer financial hardship because of illness and that every contribution to the national health insurance system should provide genuine and meaningful protection. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9989
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RECOVERY OF PUBLIC FUNDS OBTAINED THROUGH FRAUD, IMPOSING CIVIL LIABILITY FOR FALSE CLAIMS, AND STRENGTHENING ACCOUNTABILITY IN GOVERNMENT PROJECTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every Filipino deserves to see their taxes build sturdy bridges and safe communities, not vanish into the pockets of crooked officials. The Philippine False Claims Act delivers on this by shifting the focus from slow criminal trials to the swift recovery of stolen public funds. While current laws like Republic Act No. 3019 require the standard of "proof beyond a reasonable doubt," this Act introduces a civil framework designed to recover taxpayer money quickly. By lowering the evidentiary threshold, the State can aggressively reclaim funds lost to ghost projects, substandard infrastructure, and fraudulent schemes that hinder national development. The Act holds any entity liable for submitting fraudulent claims, and ensures a powerful deterrent through a "treble damages" provision, which holds perpetrators accountable by requiring them to pay heavy civil penalties plus three times the government's total loss.Further, it introduces a "qui tam" mechanism, which turns ordinary citizens into partners in justice by rewarding whistleblowers with a portion of the recovered assets— effectively creating an environment where corruption has nowhere to hide. In essence, this Act enforces public accountability by providing a swift tool to recover losses, deter fraud, and ensure that public funds directly serve the public good. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9990
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PHILIPPINE IDENTIFICATION SYSTEM BY INCLUDING THE JOB, OCCUPATION, OR PROFESSION OF A CITIZEN IN THE PHILIPPINE IDENTIFICATION CARD, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 8 AND 13 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11055, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PHILIPPINE IDENTIFICATION SYSTEM ACT" Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Identification System (PhilSys), enacted under Republic Act No. 11055, established a central identification platform for all citizens and resident aliens. However, systemic gaps in government aid delivery demand that we maximize the national ID’s utility by including a vital piece of information: an individual's job, occupation, or profession. This proposed measure mandates the inclusion of an individual's job, occupation, or profession into both the PhilSys Registry and the physical PhilID card to eliminate ghost beneficiaries and prevent the manipulation of state assistance programs.Further, this amendment is highly relevant and urgent given the recurring challenges in the distribution of government welfare assistance. Past emergency relief operations have exposed weaknesses in the government's ability to identify qualified beneficiaries. Efforts to provide targeted financial aid (ayuda) to legitimate recipients were often compromised by ghost claimants, forged credentials, and unlawful double-dipping, while unauthorized individuals took advantage of the lack of a centralized and verified occupational database. Through this Act, the State strengthens identity verification by integrating a citizen's occupation into the national ID system. Beyond securing ayuda, it cuts financial red tape and provides real-time labor data for better economic planning,while fully complying with the Data Privacy Act of 2012. Given these distinct benefits to administrative efficiency, transparency and public welfare, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9991
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 49 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000," BY INCREASING THE PENALTIES FOR LITTERING, DUMPING, AND IMPROPER DISPOSAL OF WASTE MATTER, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE When Republic Act No. 9003, also known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, was passed over twenty years ago, it set the standard for proper waste management to keep our communities clean. However, its original penalties (a fine of ₱300 to ₱1,000 or 1 to 15 days of community service) are outdated and no longer stop people from littering. Today, minor nominal fines are easily dismissed as a negligible cost of non-compliance, while short community service windows fail to inspire genuine behavioral change. Consequently, this persistent littering cumulatively obstructs our drainage systems and waterways, directly causing severe street flooding and leaving local governments to exhaust valuable resources on emergency cleanups. This measure scales the penalties to a range of ₱1,000 to ₱10,000 and extends the alternative community service to 15 to 30 days. This ensures a meaningful reformative impact on offenders while simultaneously rendering meaningful civic service to support the Local Government Units (LGUs) in community cleanup efforts and environmental restoration. In view of this urgency, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9992
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE PUBLIC PARADING AND PRESENTATION OF UNCONVICTED ARRESTED SUSPECTS TO THE MEDIA, PRESERVING THE CONSTITUTIONAL PRESUMPTION OF INNOCENCE, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly guarantees that in all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed innocent until the contrary is proved (Article III, Section 14(2)). This constitutional shield protects individuals from the power of the State until guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt in court. Yet, law enforcement agencies routinely parade unarraigned suspects before media cameras in handcuffs and detention vests. This practice inflicts irreversible public humiliation, damages reputations, and creates a trial by publicity that prejudices the administration of justice. Even if a suspect is later cleared or acquitted, the public vindication rarely undoes the initial televised damage. While reporting on crime is necessary, it must not turn unconvicted citizens into a public spectacle. This Act explicitly prohibits law enforcement from showcasing arrested suspects to the media and public. This measure protects the constitutional rights and human dignity of individuals under custody by imposing strict criminal, civil, and administrative penalties for violations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9993
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING WORKER PROTECTION IN FLEXIBLE WORK SETUPS BY MANDATING A UTILITY AND CONNECTIVITY ALLOWANCE FOR TELECOMMUTING EMPLOYEES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11165, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TELECOMMUTING ACT,” AND PROVIDING TAX INCENTIVES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11165, or the Telecommuting Act, recognizes telecommuting as an alternative work arrangement and encourages the use of technology to promote efficiency and productivity in the workplace. In recent years, many employers have adopted telecommuting and hybrid work arrangements as part of their regular operations. While these arrangements allow businesses to reduce office-related expenses and provide employees with greater flexibility, they have also resulted in the transfer of certain work-related costs from employers to employees. Workers who perform their duties from home often shoulder additional expenses for electricity, internet connectivity, and other utilities necessary to carry out their work. For many employees, particularly those in low- and middle-income households, these additional expenses represent a significant financial burden. Although telecommuting enables employees to save on transportation and commuting costs, the increased consumption of electricity and the need for reliable internet access often offset such savings. At present, there is no clear statutory framework requiring the equitable sharing of these work-related expenses. This measure seeks to address this gap by requiring employers that adopt telecommuting or hybrid work arrangements to provide a reasonable utility and connectivity allowance to covered employees. To support business compliance and encourage the continued adoption of flexible work arrangements, the bill likewise allows the full amount of such allowances to be claimed as deductible business expenses for tax purposes. By promoting a fairer allocation of work-related costs, this measure seeks to protect employee welfare while supporting productivity, business continuity, and modern workplace practices. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9994
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE AGRICULTURAL DEBT MANAGEMENT CORPORATION (ADMC) TO PROVIDE FOR THE DEBT REHABILITATION AND ASSET PROTECTION OF SMALL FARMERS AND FISHERFOLK, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine agricultural sector, the backbone of our nation’s food security, remains shackled by a persistent and debilitating cycle of indebtedness. While the New Agrarian Emancipation Act (RA 11953) provided landmark relief by condoning debts related to agrarian reform land awards, it addressed only one facet of the crisis. It left a significant portion of the farming population—specifically smallholder farmers with private-sector and commercial bank obligations—without a lifeline. Currently, distressed agricultural loans prevent farmers from accessing formal credit markets, rendering them "un-bankable." This financial exclusion forces producers into the hands of informal lenders and predatory interests, often leading to "pawning" or the outright loss of agricultural lands. Without a dedicated mechanism to resolve these non-performing loans, the sector cannot modernize or achieve the productivity levels required for national food security. Through the establishment of the Agricultural Debt Management Corporation (ADMC), this measure introduces a strategic, long-term solution to debt restructuring, ensuring that our agricultural producers can transition from financial distress toward sustainable productivity. The ADMC aims to restore the creditworthiness of small farmers through proactive loan negotiations and rehabilitation, allowing their reentry into the formal banking system under sustainable terms. Likewise, the ADMC seeks to safeguard national food security through the management of non-performing assets to prevent the loss of productive lands to premature conversion or land grabbing. Lastly, this measure secures the future of Philippine agriculture by keeping land in the hands of those who till it. It empowers our farmers and creates the stable financial foundation required to build a truly resilient agricultural economy for the benefit of all Filipinos. In light of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9995
title: AN ACT MANDATING ABSOLUTE PRICE TRANSPARENCY IN COMMERCIAL AVIATION TICKETING, PROHIBITING THE IMPOSITION OF HIDDEN FEES AND SURCHARGES, AND PROVIDING STRICT PENALTIES FOR DECEPTIVE DRIP-PRICING PRACTICES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In recent years, the cost of air travel has become a major financial strain for millions of Filipinos, including our Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), MSME entrepreneurs, and middle-class families. While competition among commercial airlines has supposedly democratized air travel through advertised "low-cost" base fares, consumers are systematically subjected to a deceptive practice known as "drip pricing" or the accumulation of "junk fees." Under current airline booking systems, consumers are enticed by low advertised ticket prices, only to discover a cascade of mandatory hidden charges added sequentially throughout the digital checkout process. These surprise surcharges—ranging from arbitrary web administration fees, mandatory booking system fees, hidden fuel adjustments, and pre-checked optional add-ons like insurance or seat selection traps—frequently double or triple the final cost of the ticket. This deceptive pricing model actively distorts market competition and violates the fundamental rights of consumers to clear, honest, and upfront information. This measure, the "All-In Airline Ticket Price Transparency Act," is an original, standalone bill designed to protect the purchasing power of Filipino travelers. It mandates that any domestic or international airline operating within the Philippines must display an "All-In" price—inclusive of all taxes, surcharges, and non-optional fees at the very first point of consumer interaction. By eliminating predatory hidden costs and forcing absolute price transparency, this bill restores integrity to the aviation consumer market, protects hard-working citizens from predatory corporate pricing, and fosters a fairer domestic travel industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9996
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE SCOPE OF INSIDER TRADING LIABILITY, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE SECTIONS 3.8 AND 27 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8799, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE SECURITIES REGULATION CODE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The integrity of the Philippine capital market relies entirely on public trust and investor confidence. For the market to thrive, investors must believe that everyone is playing by the same rules. At present, Sections 3.8 and 27 of Republic Act No. 8799, otherwise known as the Securities Regulation Code (SRC), define an "insider" to include individuals with a direct relationship to the company such as directors, officers, controlling shareholders, or individuals who obtain material non-public information directly from these sources. However, this narrow definition leaves a dangerous regulatory blind spot. It cannot punish third-party bad actors who steal confidential, market-moving data from their own employers or clients to trade stocks, simply because they have no direct relationship with the company being traded. This loophole undermines market integrity and is insufficient to protect the investing public—a legal deficiency that international jurisdictions successfully addressed through the Misappropriation Theory. This Act adopts the Misappropriation Theory which anchors liability on the breach of a duty of loyalty and confidentiality owed to the source of the information, rather than to the corporation whose shares are being traded. By expanding the definition of an insider to include anyone who misappropriates material non-public information in breach of a duty of trust or confidence, this Act ensures that no one can legally profit from stolen secrets, and more importantly, safeguards the Philippine capital market for all investors. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9997
title: AN ACT TO ESTABLISH THE MAGNA CARTA FOR BARANGAYS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Strong communities require strong barangays. As the government's most immediate and accessible unit, the barangay is entrusted with responsibilities that extend far beyond local administration. It serves as the first responder during emergencies, the primary venue for community dispute resolution, the frontline implementer of national and local programs, and the closest provider of basic public services to the Filipino people. In recent years, however, the functions assigned to barangays have significantly expanded while the institutional support available to barangay officials and personnel has not evolved at the same pace. They are expected to undertake responsibilities in public health, disaster risk reduction, peace and order, social welfare, environmental protection, and community development, often despite limited resources and inadequate compensation and benefits. This disparity affects not only the welfare of barangay officials but also the efficiency and quality of services delivered to local communities. The Constitution recognizes the importance of local autonomy and the role of local government units in national development. Consistent with this policy, strengthening the country's smallest political unit is essential to building more responsive, accountable, and effective governance. Investing in barangays is ultimately an investment in better public service, stronger citizen participation, and sustainable community development. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive Magna Carta for Barangays by institutionalizing mechanisms that enhance the welfare, protection, and capacity of barangay officials and personnel while ensuring that barangays are better equipped to discharge the functions entrusted to them by law. The objective is not merely to provide additional benefits but to reinforce the institutional foundation upon which grassroots governance depends. The necessity of such legislation has long been acknowledged, as similar measures have been introduced in previous Congresses seeking to establish a Magna Carta for Barangays or to improve the rights and benefits of barangay officials. The repeated filing of these measures demonstrates a continuing recognition that existing legal and institutional frameworks remain inadequate to address the evolving demands placed upon barangays. Their enactment, however, has yet to be realized. For these reasons, the passage of this bill is both timely and imperative in order to strengthen local governance, improve the delivery of public services, and advance the constitutional policy of genuine local autonomy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9998
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A WAGE GUARANTEE FUND TO PROTECT WORKERS' CLAIMS IN THE EVENT OF EMPLOYER INSOLVENCY, OCCUPATIONAL BANKRUPTCY, OR CORPORATE LIQUIDATION, CREATING THE WAGE GUARANTEE FUND ADMINISTRATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Article 110 of the Labor Code and the Financial Insolvency and Rehabilitation Act (FIRA), workers are classified as preferred creditors when a company goes bankrupt. However, this preference is often an empty promise. Corporate liquidation takes years, and by the time assets are sold, the proceeds are consistently exhausted by taxes, administrative fees, and banks. Displaced workers are left empty-handed despite their statutory preference. This Act aims to address this by establishing the Wage Guarantee Fund. Instead of making workers wait out grueling liquidation proceedings, a centralized, employer-contributed fund will immediately pay out their backwages and separation pay. The State will then assume and recover the workers' claims from the company to shield the workforce from sudden destitution during prolonged bankruptcy proceedings. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 9999
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING FOUNDATIONAL LITERACY AND NUMERACY THROUGH THE INTEGRATION OF DAILY MENTAL WELLNESS AND FOCUS ACTIVITIES IN BASIC EDUCATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to the World Bank's Learning Poverty estimates, approximately nine out of ten Filipino children aged ten are unable to read and understand a simple text appropriate for their age, highlighting a serious challenge in foundational learning.1 At the same time, educational and health experts point out that modern youth face unprecedented mental health pressures. Today, teachers in face-to-face classrooms are constantly dealing with a noticeable spike in student anxiety, stress, and attention issues, which directly ruins a student's focus and ability to learn. The Philippines continues to confront a dual challenge of learning loss and declining student well-being. National and international assessments have demonstrated significant gaps in foundational literacy and numeracy, while educators increasingly report difficulties in learner engagement, concentration, and emotional regulation. These factors are interrelated and directly affect classroom performance and long-term educational outcomes. International experience demonstrates that strengthening academic instruction alone is insufficient to address learning recovery. Educational systems in jurisdictions such as Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Australia have increasingly integrated evidence-based social-emotional and classroom wellness strategies into daily instruction to improve learners' focus, resilience, and readiness to learn. Studies likewise show that structured social-emotional learning interventions are associated with improvements in academic achievement, classroom behavior, and student well-being. Recognizing these developments, this measure establishes a National Classroom Wellness and Learning Recovery Program under the Department of Education. Rather than creating another academic subject or extending instructional hours, the Program institutionalizes practical, evidence-based classroom strategies that may be integrated into existing teaching practices while simultaneously strengthening foundational literacy and numeracy. By combining learning recovery with learner well-being, the proposed measure seeks to improve educational outcomes, reduce learning gaps, and promote the holistic development of every Filipino learner. 1 Cagaanan, J.S. (2025). When schooling does not translate to learning: localizing the World Bank’s Learning Poverty Framework for SDG 4. Langkit Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities, 14(2), 93-110. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. Jan “Atty. JP” D. label: HB 10001
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE MANDATORY ORIENTATION OF ALL PUBLIC SCHOOL FACULTY AND STAFF ON EMERGENCY OPERATIONS PLAN AND CRISIS RESPONSE TRAININGS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every so often, the Department of Education in coordination with the local government units, the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office, the Bureau of Fire Protection and the Philippine National Police conduct simulation exercises and drills in schools to promote awareness among faculty, staff and students on how they should response to specific situations and disasters. On June 8, 2026, on the first day of school, General Santos was hit by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake. While the earthquake damaged a lot of establishments and infrastructures, the children and school personnel were able to assemble on the school grounds and were safe, which may be attributed to the earthquake drills regularly conducted in schools. Meantime, another crisis situation happened on June 22, 2026 at San Jose National High School in Tacloban, Leyte where a school shooting claimed the lives of three (3) students and injured many others. The incident left many students and school personnel traumatized and were at a lost on how to manage the crisis at that time. This may be an indication of the lack of proper knowledge on how to deal with this specific situation, This proposed measure seeks to prepare school faculty and staff, so that they may be able to prevent casualties, stabilize the situation and provide support and guidance to students in case similar incidents happen in the future. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10002
title: AN ACT IMPOSING PENALTIES ON PERSONS WHO FAIL TO SECURE THEIR FIREARMS FROM BEING ACCESSED BY MINORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The mass school shooting incident involving minors in San Jose National High School in Tacloban, Leyte that left three (3) students dead and twenty (20) others wounded, raised alarms on the dangers posed by minors gaining access to firearms, including risks arising from the irresponsible handling and failure of gun owners to secure their firearms. Reports confirmed that the weapons used by the perpetrators were allegedly registered to the aunt of one of the suspects who happens to be a police officer, while the other was registered under a security agency. Nevertheless, the responsibility of safekeeping such firearms rests on the owner or to whom such weapon was issued. This responsibility is consistent with the State policy to maintain peace and order and protect the people against violence through comprehensive regulation of firearms and ammunition under Republic Act No. 10591. In another incident, a 13-year old student was allegedly shot by a fellow seventh grader at a private school in Barangay Macasandig in Cagayan De Oro in 2020.1 The student allegedly brought a 9mm pistol for a school activity. It was also reported that prior to the incident, the same student brought a hand grenade to school. These incidents underscore the need for clearer statutory duties on safe storage and for penalties when a firearm possessor’s unsafe storage enables minors to gain access. 1 CDO dad pushes probe on 'accidental' school shooting. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1092671 These call for the need to require stricter compliance to protocols on proper storage and handling of firearms and ammunition to ensure that minors who may likely to inflict injuries whether accidentally or intentionally to others or to themselves may not be able to gain access to such firearms. While Republic Act No. 10591 provides a comprehensive licensing and regulatory framework, there remains a need to specifically penalize unsafe storage practices that expose minors to ready access to firearms, and to provide calibrated penalties when such access results in harm. Hence, this proposed bill seeks to impose penalties to gun owners who neglect safety protocols and fail to secure their firearms. It likewise strengthens the State’s protective mantle over children by operationalizing responsible gun ownership through minimum safe-storage standards and accountability mechanisms, consistent with the public safety rationale of firearm regulation. It is also consistent with the principle that administrative agencies may be given reasonable latitude to craft implementing rules within sufficient legislative standards CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10004
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE LEGAL ASSISTANCE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED, PARTICULARLY BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9994, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED SENIOR CITIZENS ACT OF 2010”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the family has the duty to care for its elderly members but the State may also do so through just programs of social security. At present, Republic Act No. 7432, as amended, particularly by R.A No. 9994 otherwise known as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, grants senior citizens discounts and privileges on select good and services, but does not expressly include legal assistance. Senior citizens, while no longer at the prime of their lives, continue to face legal issues involving their persons, properties, and rights. They may be parties to civil, criminal, administrative, and quasi-judicial proceedings, and may require counsel to prevent or address harassment suits, property disputes, and abuses. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize free legal assistance for all senior citizens, delivered through government legal assistance offices and coordinated legal aid mechanisms, consistent with the Supreme Court’s Rules on Unified Legal Aid Service (ULAS) and the Supreme Court’s exclusive rule-making power over pleading, practice and procedure, and legal assistance. It likewise recognizes existing incentives for pro bono legal aid, including MCLE crediting and other incentives under ULAS, and tax incentives under Republic Act No. 9999, where applicable and subject to existing laws and Supreme Court rules. In view of the foregoing , the passage of this proposed bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10005
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE IMPOSITION OR COLLECTION OF PARTICIPATION FEES IN MOTOR VEHICLE COMPREHENSIVE INSURANCE CLAIMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A motor vehicle comprehensive insurance policy protects vehicle owners against financial loss from damage to or loss of the insured vehicle due to accidents, theft, fire, and natural disasters, subject to the terms and conditions of the policy. In practice, many motor vehicle comprehensive insurance policies require the insured to pay a “participation fee” or “deductible” for every claim, which may range from Two Thousand Pesos (P2,000.00) to Five Thousand Pesos (P5,000.00) or higher depending on the policy. While risk-sharing mechanisms may be used in insurance pricing, participation fees may operate to unduly reduce the actual benefit received by the insured, particularly where the loss was caused by another motor vehicle. This bill seeks to protect consumers by prohibiting the imposition and collection of participation fees (deductibles) in motor vehicle comprehensive insurance, ensuring transparency, fairness, and the availability of prompt indemnification, while recognizing the regulatory authority of the Insurance Commissioner. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10006
title: AN ACT DIRECTING LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES TO ESTABLISH OR EXPAND SOCIAL WORK DEGREE PROGRAMS, IN COORDINATION WITH THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION, TO AUGMENT THE NUMBER OF REGISTERED SOCIAL WORKERS FOR THE DELIVERY OF PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT AND OTHER SOCIAL SERVICES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. To this end, the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Commission of Higher Education (CHED) have exerted efforts to improve the quality of education, providing adequate seminars and making education accessible especially to indigent students through the establishment of Local Universities and Colleges (LUCs), which are established and undertaken by the Local Government Units (LGUs) under Republic Act No. 10931, LUCs refer to CHED- accredited public higher education institutions established by LGUs through an enabling ordinance, financially supported by the LGU concerned, and compliant with CHED policies, standards, and guidelines. In fact, starting School Year 2018 to 2019, students of 78 local universities across the country no longer have to pay tuition fees since the CHED decided to include 78 LUCs covered by Republic ACT No. 10931 otherwise known as the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act. Meanwhile, the Philippines encounters a lot of disasters yearly and social services are in demand. Many registered social workers are required to provide psychosocial support and interventions for victims of disasters and abuse. Although, there are quite a number of social workers already employed in government offices, there is still undeniably a great need for them. The standard worker–beneficiary ratio for individual casework is 1:25 children for placement; 1:20 children in need of special protection and persons in crisis needing casework; 1:15 children in conflict with the law; 1:60 children for independent living, education purposes, temporary residential care due to circumstances at home; 1:25 disadvantaged women / internally displaced person (IDPs); 1:15 women with dependents; 1:25 senior citizens; and 1:15 persons with disabilities.1Clearly, it can easily be noted how overloaded the social workers are just by the standard ratio of worker to beneficiary. This proposed measure aims to augment the number of social workers in the country by directing LUCs to establish or expand CHED-recognized social work degree programs, and by ensuring that eligible students may avail of free tuition and other school fees under RA No.10931. Recent events, like school-based violence, natural disasters like earthquakes and strong typhoons with flooding have left so many traumatized. Hence, there is a need for social workers to provide interventions and support to affected families and individuals. It is time that the State invests in providing free education to students who are willing to be the government’s partners in implementing social services efficiently and with utmost dedication. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. 1 WORKER-BENEFCIARY RATIO. label: HB 10007
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE RIGHT OF FARMERS, FISHERFOLK, COOPERATIVES, AND INDEPENDENT REPAIR PROVIDERS TO REPAIR FARM MACHINERY AND AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT, REQUIRING ACCESS TO REPAIR INFORMATION, TOOLS, AND SPARE PARTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to ensure that farmers, fisherfolk, cooperatives, and agricultural enterprises are not only provided with agricultural and fisheries machinery, but are also given access to the necessary repair manuals, service information, diagnostic tools, and basic technical guidance needed to properly operate, maintain, and repair such equipment. At present, the lack of accessible manuals and repair information often forces farmers to hire the services of mechanics even for basic troubleshooting or minor repairs, resulting in additional costs and delays in farm operations. With the availability of proper manuals, repair guides, and technical orientation, farmers and fisherfolk will be better equipped to maintain their machinery, reduce unnecessary expenses, and prevent avoidable downtime. In this regard, the role of the Department of Agriculture should not be limited to the distribution of machinery and equipment, but must also include education, training, and capacity-building to ensure that beneficiaries can fully and effectively use the machinery provided to them. Farmers, fisherfolk, cooperatives, and agricultural enterprises rely on tractors, harvesters, irrigation equipment, dryers, cold storage units, sensors, and other machinery to sustain production, reduce losses, and support food security. According to the Philippine Institute for Development Studies and International Rice Research Institute (PIDS–IRRI), agricultural mechanization must be evaluated not only in terms of production, but also in relation to employment, income distribution, and the public and private support needed for an effective mechanization strategy. The study likewise recognized that mechanization policy should be responsive to the needs of rural communities and small farmers. A study by Elepaño et al. shows that the level of agricultural mechanization in the Philippines remains relatively low, with many farm operations still performed manually. They also emphasized that small and medium-scale farmers may benefit from machinery pooling, custom hiring services, and cooperative arrangements that allow them to use farm machines without individually owning costly equipment. According to a study by Severino, cooperatives can help promote mechanization among smallholding farms through information dissemination, education, training, and shared machinery services. However, the study also identified financial barriers, preference for manual labor, lack of appropriate technology, and weaknesses in cooperative operations as continuing challenges to mechanization adoption. While Republic Act No. 10601, or the Agricultural and Fisheries Mechanization Law, already promotes mechanization through standards, testing, registration, after-sales service, warranty requirements, repair service centers, and related support programs, access to machinery alone is not sufficient. Farmers and fisherfolk must also be able to keep such machinery operational. When basic repairs are delayed because manuals, diagnostic tools, spare parts, firmware support, or service information are unavailable, agricultural users face higher costs, avoidable downtime, and possible crop or post-harvest losses. This bill complements Republic Act No. 10601 by addressing a specific post-acquisition concern: the right of equipment owners and independent repair providers to lawfully diagnose, maintain, and repair agricultural and fisheries machinery. It requires fair and reasonable access to repair manuals, diagnostic tools, wiring diagrams, calibration procedures, error codes, service bulletins, firmware tools necessary for lawful repair, and spare parts. At the same time, the bill protects safety, intellectual property, data privacy, equipment integrity, and lawful restrictions against tampering with emissions, security, or safety systems. By improving access to repair information, tools, and spare parts, this measure seeks to reduce repair costs, extend the useful life of agricultural and fisheries machinery, minimize production losses, and strengthen rural repair enterprises that support farmers, fisherfolk, cooperatives, and agricultural communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10008
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING ANIMAL RESCUE, EVACUATION, TEMPORARY SHELTER, AND WELFARE PROTOCOLS INTO DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT PLANS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Pets, livestock, poultry, working animals, and other domesticated animals are often placed at risk during typhoons, floods, fires, earthquakes, volcanic activity, and other disasters because evacuation and response plans do not always provide for animal transport, temporary shelter, feeding, veterinary care, identification, and reunification. In many communities, families delay or refuse evacuation because they cannot leave their animals behind, while farmers and fisherfolk may suffer serious livelihood losses when livestock, poultry, or working animals are injured, abandoned, or lost. This measure recognizes that animal welfare is closely connected to public health, evacuation compliance, livelihood protection, food security, and community recovery. Companion animals provide emotional support and household security, while livestock, poultry, and working animals are livelihood assets that help families recover after disasters. A disaster response system that completely ignores animals may unintentionally place both people and animals in greater danger. Consistent with Republic Act No. 8485, otherwise known as the “Animal Welfare Act of 1998,” as amended by Republic Act No. 10631, this bill seeks to ensure that humane treatment, protection against cruelty and neglect, disease prevention, and responsible animal handling are observed before, during, and after disasters and emergency displacement. This bill institutionalizes animal-inclusive disaster risk reduction and management by requiring local government units to include animal rescue, evacuation, temporary shelter, veterinary support, identification, and reunification protocols in their disaster plans. It also strengthens coordination among the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), the Office of Civil Defense, the Department of Agriculture (DA), the Bureau of Animal Industry, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), local government units, veterinarians, animal welfare organizations, farmers’ and fisherfolk groups, rescue groups, and the private sector. At the same time, this bill expressly provides that the protection of human life and safety shall remain the paramount consideration in all animal rescue and shelter operations. Animal rescue must be humane and practical, but it must never require rescuers, public officers, volunteers, evacuees, or animal owners to expose themselves to serious and immediate danger. By integrating animals into disaster preparedness, response, and recovery planning, this measure promotes humane governance, reduces abandonment and avoidable animal suffering, protects livelihoods, supports public health, and helps build more resilient Filipino communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10009
title: AN ACT PROTECTING CONSUMERS FROM UNFAIR ONLINE SUBSCRIPTION RENEWAL AND CANCELLATION PRACTICES, REQUIRING SIMPLE ONLINE CANCELLATION, CLEAR PRE-RENEWAL NOTICE, AND SAFEGUARDS AGAINST DARK PATTERNS IN RECURRING DIGITAL BILLING
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of digital payments, e-commerce, and online services in the Philippines has changed the way Filipino consumers subscribe to goods and services. Today, subscriptions are no longer limited to traditional utilities or memberships. They now include streaming platforms, mobile applications, cloud storage, gaming accounts, online publications, and other recurring digital services. This development is consistent with the country’s movement toward a cashless economy. According to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), digital payments accounted for 57.4% of total monthly retail payment volume and 59.0% of total retail payment value in 2024. This means that more Filipino consumers are now exposed to recurring online charges, automatic renewals, saved payment methods, and subscription-based billing arrangements. The Philippine digital economy has likewise become a major part of national economic activity. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that the country’s digital economy reached PhP 2.25 trillion in 2024, equivalent to 8.5% of gross domestic product. The Philippines was also reported as one of the fastest-growing internet economies in Southeast Asia, with its digital economy growing from US$26 billion to US$31 billion in 2024. However, the increase in online transactions has also resulted in new forms of consumer risk. In 2023, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) reportedly received 28,824 consumer complaints, with 42% related to online transactions. Many of these complaints involved deceptive, unfair, and unconscionable sales acts and practices, as well as misleading or fraudulent sales promotions. The Department of Trade and Industry has already recognized the need for stronger digital consumer protection. In 2024, the DTI launched the eReport System for Online Consumer Complaints through the eGovPH app, pursuant to Republic Act No. 11967 or the Internet Transactions Act of 2023. This system was designed to help consumers report e-commerce concerns and strengthen consumer protection in the digital age. While existing laws already protect Filipino consumers against unfair and deceptive practices, there is still no clear and specific statutory rule requiring online subscription cancellation to be as easy as subscription enrollment. Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, protects consumers against deceptive, unfair, and unconscionable sales acts and practices. Republic Act No. 11967, or the Internet Transactions Act of 2023, governs certain business-to-consumer internet transactions involving parties in the Philippines or platforms availing of the Philippine market. Despite these protections, Filipino consumers may still face practical difficulties when cancelling subscriptions, such as hidden cancellation buttons, unclear renewal terms, forced customer service calls, difficult refund procedures, or continued charges after attempted cancellation. These practices may not always be adequately addressed by general consumer protection rules, especially when the service provider is a foreign digital platform, mobile app, software provider, or online media service consumed in the Philippines. The need for a specific subscription cancellation law is further supported by the government’s recognition that foreign digital services are now part of the Philippine consumer market. In 2024, the Philippines enacted a law imposing value-added tax on non-resident digital service providers, including streaming services and online platforms consumed in the Philippines. This shows that digital services used by Filipino consumers are now sufficiently significant to require clearer regulatory treatment, not only for taxation but also for consumer protection. This proposed measure therefore seeks to fill a specific gap in Philippine consumer protection law. It establishes a simple fairness standard: if a consumer can subscribe online, the consumer must also be able to cancel online through a simple, accessible, and transparent process. The bill also seeks to prevent unfair automatic renewal practices, require clear notice before recurring charges, protect consumers from hidden or burdensome cancellation procedures, and ensure proper redress for continued billing after cancellation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10010
title: AN ACT PROTECTING CHILDREN WHO APPEAR IN MONETIZED ONLINE CONTENT BY SAFEGUARDING THEIR EARNINGS, PRIVACY, EDUCATION, HEALTH, AND RIGHT TO REMOVE EXPLOITATIVE CONTENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino children are growing up in a world where childhood moments can be recorded, uploaded, shared, and monetized in a matter of minutes. A child’s first words, school routine, birthday, medical condition, family conflict, or even moments of embarrassment may now become part of a public online identity before the child is old enough to understand what privacy, consent, or permanent digital exposure means. This reality is especially important in the Philippines, where online and social media use is deeply embedded in daily life. DataReportal’s Digital 2026: The Philippines reported that the country had around 98 million internet users and 95.8 million social media user identities as of late 2025, equivalent to 83.8% and 81.9% of the population, respectively. The same report also shows that children and minors make up a significant portion of the Philippine population, with those aged 0 to 17 comprising roughly one-third of the country. The rise of family vlogs, livestream selling, short-form videos, sponsored posts, and “kidfluencer” content has created new income opportunities for families. However, it has also created a legal gap: when a child becomes the main reason why a video earns views, sponsorships, advertisements, gifts, or platform revenue, there is still no clear guarantee that the child will receive a fair share of those earnings. In some cases, the child is effectively working, but without the protections usually attached to child labor, entertainment work, trust accounts, working-hour limits, or independent oversight. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that there were 861,000 working children aged 5 to 17 in 2024, and 509,000 of them were engaged in child labor. Existing Philippine labor standards already recognize that children require special protection when work affects their health, education, rest, or development. Yet online child influencing is harder to detect because it often happens inside the home, under the control of parents or guardians, and appears to the public as ordinary family content rather than work. The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has likewise recognized that while existing child labor laws cover child entertainers, they do not yet squarely include online child influencers. This measure also responds to the privacy risks faced by children online. UNICEF Philippines reported through a 2025 U-Report poll that 85.56% of children and youth respondents had encountered unsafe content or behavior online, while only 2.99% reported such incidents to authorities or hotlines. The 2022 Disrupting Harm in the Philippines study by UNICEF Office of Research, INTERPOL, and ECPAT International reported that 20% of internet-using children aged 12 to 17 experienced online sexual abuse and exploitation in 2021. UNICEF also cited the 2019 Philippine Kids Online Survey, which found that more than half of Filipino children surveyed could access the internet without supervision. While Republic Act No. 11930, or the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (OSAEC) and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (CSAEM) Act, strongly addresses online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, not every harmful use of a child’s image is sexual in nature. Some harms involve overexposure, humiliation, excessive monetization, disclosure of home or school location, publication of medical or educational information, or the long-term loss of control over a child’s identity. RA 11930 itself recognizes the need to protect children from online abuse and exploitation committed through information and communications technology. Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012, already requires transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality in the processing of personal information. However, child influencer content presents a unique problem because a parent or guardian may be the one collecting, posting, monetizing, and controlling the child’s personal data. Republic Act No. 7610 or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act also declares it a State policy to protect children from abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, discrimination, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. This bill builds on these laws by addressing a specific modern form of child exposure and economic exploitation that existing statutes do not fully regulate. Comparative developments abroad show that governments are beginning to treat child influencer work as a real labor and privacy issue. Recent laws and proposals in jurisdictions such as Illinois, California, Minnesota, and Utah require trust accounts, record-keeping, and in some cases content removal rights for children featured in monetized online content. Research on “sharenting” and child influencers also warns that repeated posting of children may affect their privacy, media habits, and future sense of control over their own image. The proposed Child Influencer Earnings and Privacy Protection Act seeks to ensure that a child is not treated merely as content, branding material, or a source of family income. It provides safeguards so that when a child’s name, image, likeness, voice, daily life, or personal story is used for monetized online content, a fair portion of the earnings shall be preserved for the child in a protected account. It also requires transparency in accounting, reasonable limits on content production, protection of schooling and rest, and safeguards against the disclosure of sensitive personal information. The bill further recognizes the child’s right to dignity and future autonomy by providing a mechanism for removal or takedown requests involving content that exposes, humiliates, endangers, or unduly commercializes the child. It also promotes coordination among appropriate agencies such as the Department of Labor and Employment, Department of Social Welfare and Development, Council for the Welfare of Childre

label: HB 10011
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF WORKERS IN THE INFORMAL ECONOMY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), through PSA Board Resolution No. 18, Series of 2025, approved and adopted the definition of the “informal sector” as comprising “economic units whose production is mainly intended for the market for the purpose of generating income and profit, but which are not formally recognized as producers of goods and services separate from the own-use production activities of the owner-operators’ households (informal household unincorporated market enterprises).” Based on the May 2026 Labor Force Survey, 36.2% of the country's total working population or 17.8 million are informal sector workers. We cannot discount the significance of the informal sector's contribution to the Philippine economy. Yet, the informal sector is unseen in government programs, services, and social protection, and struggling at the margins of Philippine society, vulnerable and exposed to the vagaries of poverty and inequality. They are the faceless unaccounted informal sector workers or workers in an informal employment arrangement. They are the self-employed, home workers, industrial workers, ambulant vendors, small transport operators, small and landless farmers, artisanal fisherfolk, intermittent non-corporate construction workers, waste pickers and recyclers, petty retailers, barter traders, small-scale miners, and quarry workers, entertainers, beauticians, laundry persons, hairdressers, on-call domestic helpers, barkers, cargo-handlers, farmers, fisherfolks, and all other livelihood that fall under the definition of PSA Board Resolution No. 18. At various government instrumentalities, they are the forever job order workers, the barangay health workers, barangay tanod, barangay nutrition scholars, barangay daycare workers, and volunteers during disasters. They are the informal economy workers in the public sector. They are not covered by the Labor or Civil Service Code. They live in substandard conditions and are vulnerable to exploitation, working long hours at meager wages, without benefits, and under deplorable working conditions. They have limited access to productive resources, justice, and preventive programs for work-related diseases and risks and are underrepresented in policy-making bodies relevant to their issues and welfare. They lack contributory social protection such as those provided by the Social Security System (SSS), Philippine Health Insurance 1 Corporation (PhilHealth), and affordable housing programs such as through the Pag-IBIG Fund. At most, they do not even qualify to tax based social protection programs. There have been several attempts to enact the Magna Carta for Workers in the Informal Sectors. Therefore, it is high time that the 20th Congress will finish the work to provide rights and benefits to workers in the informal economies, provide them with affordable social protection and security in the workplace, among others. label: HB 10017
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL WOMEN’S MACHINERY REDEFINING ITS POWERS, FUNCTIONS, AND STRUCTURE, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 14, Article II of the 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall recognize the vital role of women in nation-building and ensure fundamental equality before the law of women and men. Guided by this constitutional mandate, the Philippines has progressively built a robust legal and policy framework to advance gender equality and women's empowerment, anchored on landmark legislation such as Republic Act No. 71921, Republic Act No. 97102, Republic Act No. 113133, alongside its commitments under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), and the Beijing Platform for Action. The Philippine Commission on Women (PCW) serves as the government’s primary policy- making and coordinating body on women’s rights, gender equality, and women’s empowerment. As the national machinery for gender equality, the Commission leads national policy development, coordinates government-wide implementation of gender equality programs, and serves as the central institution responsible for advancing the State’s commitments to women’s rights and empowerment. Yet, despite the significant expansion of its mandate over the past five decades, the Commission’s institutional structure, powers, and resources have remained largely unchanged. The result is a growing misalignment between the State’s expanding gender equality commitments and the institutional capacity required to effectively implement them. When the Commission was established in 1975 through Presidential Decree No. 633, its functions were primarily centered on policy advocacy, coordination, information generation, and promoting women’s participation in development. During this period, the regulatory and organizational framework for gender-related rights was far more restricted, characterized by fewer systems for accountability and a more limited scope of government responsibilities. 1 Women in Development and Nation-Building Act. 2 The Magna Carta of Women. 3 Safe Spaces Act. In 2025, the nation marked the 50th anniversary of the creation of the PCW. This milestone presents an important opportunity not merely to commemorate the Commission’s historic contributions, but to modernize and strengthen the country’s national gender equality machinery so that it remains capable of responding effectively to present realities and future challenges confronting Filipino women. Five decades after PCW’s creation, the institutional environment surrounding gender equality governance has evolved significantly, requiring a stronger and more empowered Commission. The enactment of Republic Act No. 9710 or the Magna Carta of Women fundamentally transformed gender equality from a policy objective into a legally enforceable obligation of the State. As a result, the Commission’s responsibilities expanded significantly, requiring it to ensure that government institutions nationwide integrate women’s rights standards into laws, policies, programs, and public institutions in ways that did not exist when the Commission’s current structure was originally conceived. Equally important, the challenges confronting Filipino women have become increasingly complex and urgent. Despite significant progress in women’s rights and participation, women continue to face persistent discrimination arising from gender-based violence, trafficking, economic inequality, workplace discrimination, unequal care responsibilities, digital exclusion, online harassment, conflict-related vulnerabilities, and intersecting forms of discrimination affecting women from marginalized sectors. Likewise concerning is the persistence of misogyny and gender-based discrimination in public discourse itself. In recent years, the country has witnessed repeated instances of misogynistic remarks, sexist rhetoric, degrading public statements, and harmful gender stereotypes being perpetuated by public officials and other public figures. Left unaddressed, these acts erode the State’s constitutional commitment to uphold the dignity of women and guarantee substantive equality in both law and practice. The PCW, despite being the government’s lead agency for promoting and protecting gender equality, currently lacks sufficient statutory authority to independently initiate formal fact-finding inquiries, examine systemic or recurring acts of gender-based discrimination affecting women in public life, gather relevant information and documentation, and issue formal recommendations to appropriate government agencies or policymakers for responsive action. As a result, the PCW is often left unable to act decisively in situations where public conduct, institutional behavior, or emerging patterns of discrimination demand immediate intervention, policy response, or accountability measures. This widening institutional gap can no longer be ignored. This measure seeks to comprehensively strengthen and modernize the PCW by aligning its institutional powers and organizational structure with the scale of its present-day responsibilities. Specifically, this bill seeks to: ● Reposition the Commission under the Office of the President, restoring its policy advisory and coordinating role at the highest level of government, recognizing that gender equality is a cross-cutting national development concern requiring whole-of-government coordination and stronger institutional accountability; ● Strengthen the Commission’s policy leadership, oversight, research, and coordination functions to enable government to respond more effectively to emerging and increasingly complex gender equality challenges; ● Authorize the Commission to undertake fact-finding and policy inquiries on systemic, recurring, or emerging patterns of discrimination, exclusion, or institutional barriers affecting women, including gaps in the implementation of laws, policies, programs, and services, and to issue formal findings and recommendations to appropriate government agenci

label: HB 10032
title: AN ACT EXPANDING PHILHEALTH COVERAGE FOR AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, STRENGTHENING BENEFIT PACKAGES FOR DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition requiring sustained, multidisciplinary, and often intensive interventions across the life course. While the State has taken an important step through the establishment of the Z Benefit Package for Children with Developmental Disabilities under PhilHealth Circular No. 2017-0029, coverage remains limited in scope, duration, and financial adequacy. At present, PhilHealth benefits for autism are largely confined to early diagnosis and a capped number of therapy sessions, leaving families to shoulder the long-term cost of occupational therapy, speech therapy, behavioral interventions, assistive services, and mental health support. Moreover, coverage is largely restricted to children, with minimal support for adolescents and adults with autism who continue to require services for independent living, employment readiness, and social integration. While the proposed “Autism Care Act of 2025” establishes a comprehensive national program and mandates PhilHealth inclusion, there remains a critical need to define, expand, and institutionalize specific benefit packages within PhilHealth to ensure meaningful financial risk protection for persons with autism and their families. This bill seeks to strengthen the National Health Insurance Program by: • Expanding PhilHealth benefit packages for autism across the life span; • Increasing coverage for diagnostic, therapeutic, behavioral, and assistive interventions; • Institutionalizing outpatient, community-based, and long-term care coverage; • Ensuring provider accreditation, quality standards, and nationwide accessibility; and • Establishing sustainable financing mechanisms for autism-related services. This measure complements, operationalizes, and reinforces existing and proposed policies without duplication, ensuring that the State’s commitment to universal health care fully includes persons with autism. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 10033
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MAGNA CARTA FOR BARANGAY VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN (VAWC) DESKS AND OFFICERS, INSTITUTIONALIZING THEIR MANDATE, NATIONAL STANDARDS, QUALIFICATIONS, COMPENSATION, BENEFITS, PROTECTION, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND FUNDING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Violence against women and their children (VAWC) continues to persist in communities across the country, often hidden within homes and underreported due to fear, stigma, economic dependence, and lack of accessible support systems. While landmark laws such as Republic Act No. 9262, otherwise known as the “Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004,” and Republic Act No. 9710, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta of Women,” provide comprehensive legal protections, the effectiveness of these laws largely depends on responsive and functional mechanisms at the barangay level. Barangay Violence Against Women and Their Children (VAWC) Desks serve as the first point of contact for victim-survivors seeking immediate assistance, protection, referral, and access to justice. However, many barangays continue to face challenges in maintaining fully functional VAWC Desks due to inadequate staffing, lack of training, inconsistent funding, absence of national operational standards, and insufficient institutional support. In many instances, VAWC Desk Officers are designated without adequate preparation, compensation, or security of tenure, resulting in weak case management, poor continuity of services, and diminished trust from victim-survivors. This measure seeks to institutionalize and professionalize Barangay VAWC Desks and Officers by establishing mandatory national standards for operations, qualifications, training, compensation, benefits, accountability, and protection mechanisms. It also formally adopts the Barangay VAW Desk Handbook as the official operational standard for barangay-level VAWC response and strengthens monitoring and oversight systems to ensure effective implementation nationwide. Through this measure, every barangay shall become a safe, accessible, gender- responsive, and survivor-centered space where women and children may seek immediate protection, assistance, and justice. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. label: HB 10035
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE ALICIA SPORTS ACADEMY AND TRAINING CENTER IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF ALICIA, PROVINCE OF ZAMBOANGA SIBUGAY AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports play a fundamental role in nation building by fostering unity, cultivating national pride, promoting physical and mental health, driving economic development and promoting social development among the youth. Sports provide opportunities for young Filipinos to discover and develop their talents while fostering values that contribute to responsible citizenship and community engagement. The Province of Zamboanga Sibugay has produced talented athletes who have excelled in various local, regional and national competitions. However, the absence of a dedicated sports academy and training center limits opportunities for systematic athlete development, coaching enhancement, sports science support and the provision of adequate training facilities. The Municipality of Alicia, strategically located within the First Legislative District of Zamboanga Sibugay and accessible to neighboring municipalities, is well-positioned to serve as a hub for sports development in the province. Establishing a sports academy and training center in Alicia will help identify, nurture and develop promising athletes while providing a venue for training camps, sports competitions, coaching clinics and youth development programs. The proposed Alicia Sports Academy and Training Center shall serve as a center for excellence in sports development, training and education. It shall promote grassroots sports programs, enhance athletic performance through modern training methodologies, and contribute to the overall development of sports in Zamboanga Sibugay and nearby provinces. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MARLO C.
