label: HB 10135
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF PATIENTS AGAINST HOSPITAL DETENTION ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES AND PROVIDING STIFFER PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT 9439 ENTITLED “AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DETENTION OF PATIENTS IN HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL CLINICS ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Enshrined in the 1987 Constitution is the people's right to health, a right grounded in the State's commitment to upholding the dignity of every person and guaranteeing full respect for human rights.1 The primacy of such right is further articulated in Article XIII, Section 11, which commands the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development, ensuring that affordable health care is available to all people at all levels of society. Pursuant to this Constitutional mandate, Congress has passed several legislations that endeavor to curtail hospital practices that are prejudicial in nature. One such law is Republic Act No. 9439, otherwise known as "An Act Prohibiting the Detention of Patients in Hospitals and Medical Clinics on Grounds of Nonpayment of Hospital Bills or Medical Expenses". R.A. 9439 declares as unlawful the detention of patients in hospitals when they are unable to pay the full value of their medical bills. However, to this day, complaints against hospitals on allegations of hospital detention continue to persist.2 Reports indicate that some health care institutions 1 Art. II, Sec. 11, 1987 CONST. 2 Crisostomo, S. (5 December 2019). DOH probes 77 illegal detention complaints vs hospitals. The Philippine Star. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2019/12/05/1974390/doh-probes- 1 continue to employ practices that effectively prevent patients or their relatives from leaving the hospital or obtaining the documents necessary for their discharge, despite the law's clear prohibition.3 More stringent measures are thus necessary. This amendatory bill seeks to strengthen the safeguards of RA 9439 by expressly prohibiting the detention not only of patients, but also of their relatives, representatives, carers, and newborn children. It also expands the prohibition by stating that even outstanding professional fees shall not constitute a lawful ground for detention. Lastly, the measure exempts indigent senior citizens from the requirement of executing a promissory note upon proper endorsement by the hospital's social service office. Nevertheless, this bill, in recognizing the legitimate interests of health care providers in securing payment, broadens the acceptable forms of security for unpaid obligations. In addition to promissory notes, it authorizes the use of deeds of assignment covering benefits from the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) or the Social Security System (SSS), as well as guarantee letters issued by the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO), the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), or the Department of Health (DOH). Ultimately, by providing more safeguards and imposing more effective sanctions for violations, this bill emphasizes what seems to be forgotten by many: the right to health is not a privilege reserved only to those who can afford it, but it is a right of every Filipino irrespective of status and capacity. In the 20th Congress, a similar bill was filed by Senators Risa Hontiveros, Jinggoy Estrada, and Erwin Tulfo as Senate Bill No. 1511, Representatives Dadah Kiram Ismula, Jose Manuel Diokno, Percival Cendana, and Kaka Bag-ao as House Bill No. 6832, and Representative Arlyn Ayon as House Bill No. 7476. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LEILA M. DE LIMA 77-illegal-detention-complaints-vs-hospitals; Tupas, E. (4 April 2024). Private hospital accused of illegal detention. label: HB 10136
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR MEDICAL PAROLE TO QUALIFIED PERSONS DEPRIVED OF LIBERTY (PDL) AND SETTING RULES ON THE GRANT THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State values the dignity of every human person and guarantees full respect for human rights.” Although imprisonment serves the legitimate purpose of punishment, deterrence, and rehabilitation, it does not justify the unnecessary deprivation of basic rights and inhumane conditions for persons deprived of liberty (PDLs), especially those suffering from terminal illnesses or an incapacity that renders them incapable of managing their own affairs. At present, the deplorable conditions within our prisons are undeniable. Approximately 70% of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) jails are reportedly congested.1 Congestion rate is at 500%, where 200,000 people are held in facilities that can only accommodate 41,000.2 This leads to malnutrition and limited access to adequate and proper healthcare among PDLs. Such reality is evidenced by an increasing mortality rate among PDLs, 2.5 times higher than the general population.3 More people are unnecessarily dying within our prisons. In light of these realities backed by statistics, this bill seeks to institutionalize granting parole based on medical humanitarian grounds. 1 Consignado, D., Penales, R.- vhee K., Puhawan, N. L., Diason, C., Corcolon, K., & Quintana, M. L. (2026). Health Status of Persons Deprived of Liberty in a Jail Facility in the Philippines. Journal of Interdisciplinary Perspectives, 4(5), 60–69. https://doi.org/10.69569/jip.2026.068. 2 Lacuesta J. V. E. (2026). Accessibility and Availability of Healthcare Services in Jail Facilities among Persons Deprived of Liberty (PDL) in Dumaguete City, Philippines. Acta medica Philippina, 60(5), 17– 25. https://doi.org/10.47895/amp.vi0.11884. 3 Baron, G. (20 August 2025). Tuberculosis tops causes of death among PDLs — expert. Daily Tribune. Retrieved from https://tribune.net.ph/2025/08/20/tuberculosis-tops-causes-of-death-among- pdls-expert. 1 A medical parole refers to the conditional release of a prisoner from a correctional institution, provided they are suffering from a terminal illness or a permanent or irreversible incapacity. A medical parole not only allows for more humane treatment for medically suffering PDLs, but also rationalizes the correctional practice by allowing the conditional release of PDLs who are no longer capable of serving their sentences within the correctional facilities due to their medical conditions. Under this bill, qualified PDLs shall serve out their sentences under the care of their families and shall be allowed to seek better medical care outside correctional facilities. Furthermore, the bill institutionalizes the mandate of the Board of Pardons and Parole (BPP) to grant medical parole to PDLs, providing for the standardized guidelines and requirements for its grant. Finally, the bill specifically requires that the grant of medical parole presupposes that the conditional release of a PDL shall not constitute a threat to public order and safety, and clearly provides for a mechanism for citizens and interested parties to oppose any application. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Javier Benitez, Eric Yap, and Edvic Yap, and Senator Erwin Tulfo. This bill fully adopts this Representation’s Senate Bill No. 1146 in the 18th Congress. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 10137
title: AN ACT PROVIDING PRE-EMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE TO INDIGENTS BY IMPLEMENTING A SCHEME FOR CHARGING AND GRANTING DISCOUNT ON FEES IN SECURING PRE-EMPLOYMENT CERTIFICATIONS AND CLEARANCES FROM GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reiterates the gradual decrease in the country’s unemployment rate with a hit-low record of 3.8% in 2024. The decrease in unemployment rate means an increase in the anticipated employment opportunities. In anticipation of this economic progression, the implementation of programs that support unemployed individuals becomes all the more critical. Before gaining employment, job applicants are typically required by potential employers to submit various certifications and clearances that confirm their identity and background. However, for those with little to no income, obtaining these documents poses a significant barrier, as they come with associated costs. This bill aims to extend pre-employment assistance to indigent individuals by establishing a mechanism for waiving fees for required certifications and clearances. Specifically, it mandates the issuance of these documents free of charge upon first request, and provides a 20% discount on subsequent issuances from government agencies. Through this initiative, financial burden on underprivileged Filipinos striving to secure employment are gradually, if not significantly, eased at the head start. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10138
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FURTHER OPPORTUNITIES FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AS EMPLOYEES IN PRIVATE ENTITIES BY GRANTING INCREASED INCENTIVES TO PRIVATE ENTITIES THAT EMPLOY SENIOR CITIZENS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN PROVISION OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9994, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE EXPANDED SENIOR CITIZEN ACT OF 2010
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is currently undergoing a demographic shift marked by a steadily aging population. According to the Commission on Population and Development, as of 2018, there are approximately 8.7 million Filipinos aged 60 and above–accounting for 8.2% of the country’s total population. Alarming as well is the data from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), which reports that nearly 1.3 million elderly Filipinos are living in poverty. The issue is further exacerbated by the limited social protection coverage of the aging population. The World Social Protection Report 2017–2019 reveals that only 39.8% of individuals beyond the statutory pensionable age in the Philippines receive some form of old-age pension—whether contributory, noncontributory, or a combination of both. This leaves a significant portion of the elderly population vulnerable and financially insecure. One of the critical barriers faced by senior citizens is age-based discrimination in employment. Despite their desire and capacity to remain economically active, many seniors are denied opportunities solely based on their age. In fact, studies show that up to 70% of Filipino senior citizens still prefer to work, driven by the insufficiency of their pensions and retirement savings to meet their daily needs and support their families. Beyond economic necessity, senior citizens bring a wealth of experience, discipline, and institutional knowledge acquired over decades of work. Their contributions, if harnessed properly, can greatly benefit industries, strengthen intergenerational workplaces, and promote inclusive economic growth. This proposed measure seeks to expand employment opportunities for senior citizens by encouraging both government agencies and private enterprises to hire qualified elderly workers. It likewise proposes to provide incentives to entities that employ senior citizens, while ensuring that job placements are appropriately matched to the skills and capacities of the elderly. Ultimately, this bill aims to shift the societal perception of aging—from one of dependency to one of productivity—while addressing the financial insecurity of senior citizens and maximizing their continued contribution to national development. In view of the foregoing, the approval of the bill is earnestly sought. HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10139
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY DISTRICT OFFICE IN THE CITY OF DAVAO AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7796, or the Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994, underscores the State’s responsibility to deliver “relevant, accessible, high-quality, and efficient technical education and skills development” in support of producing a competitive and skilled Filipino workforce aligned with the nation’s development goals. In pursuit of this mandate, this measure proposes the establishment of a TESDA Central Office in Davao City. As one of the most populous and economically significant cities in Mindanao, Davao City serves as a strategic location for a central administrative hub that will oversee and coordinate the implementation of technical-vocational education and training (TVET) programs across the region. Currently, the absence of a central TESDA administrative presence in the city poses limitations in terms of efficient program delivery, inter-agency coordination, and accessibility for constituents in the southern Philippines. A Central Office would address these gaps by serving as the primary command center for policy execution, monitoring and evaluation, and resource allocation for regional and district offices within Davao Region and nearby provinces. More importantly, the proposed TESDA Central Office will expand access to quality training programs for marginalized sectors—including low-income families, out-of-school youth, persons with disabilities, and indigenous peoples—who are often left behind in economic growth. By equipping them with market-relevant technical skills and industry-based certifications, the office will enable them to become self-reliant, competitive, and productive members of society. Beyond individual empowerment, the presence of a TESDA Central Office in Davao City will strengthen the region’s human capital, support local industries, and foster inclusive development in Mindanao—helping bridge the socio-economic gap between urban centers and underserved communities. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10140
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE INCLUSION OF FINANCIAL LITERACY AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP AS SEPARATE CORE SUBJECTS IN THE JUNIOR AND SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL CURRICULA OF THE K-12 PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10679, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “YOUTH ENTREPRENEURSHIP ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Financial literacy and entrepreneurship are increasingly recognized as indispensable life skills in this fast-paced society, serving as cornerstones for economic empowerment, poverty reduction, and long-term national development. In the Philippines, millions remain vulnerable to economic shocks and financial mismanagement. Hence, it becomes of primordial importance to equip citizens with the knowledge to make sound financial decisions and develop income-generating activities. Despite the proliferation of digital financial technologies, which is fueled by the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid expansion of cashless transactions, the Philippines continues to face alarmingly low levels of financial literacy. According to the World Bank, only 25% of Filipino adults possess basic financial knowledge, a finding echoed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). This gap is especially concerning given the growing complexity of financial products and the rising prevalence of digital lending, online scams, and unsustainable consumer debt. To address this gap, this bill proposes the inclusion of Financial Literacy and Entrepreneurship as core subjects in the junior and senior high school curricula of both public and private schools. The proposed measure aims to institutionalize financial education as part of the formal learning system—embedding it early in the educational journey, at a time when lifelong habits and skills are formed. This measure builds upon Section 4 of Republic Act No. 10922, or the Economic and Financial Literacy Week Act, which mandates the promotion of financial literacy among Filipinos. It aligns with the need to overhaul curriculum priorities and focus on foundational and future-ready skills to improve educational outcomes and relevance. When young Filipinos are empowered to start micro-businesses, manage capital responsibly, and contribute to household or community income, they become agents of inevitable economic progress in the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10145
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A FREE CHILDCARE CENTER IN BARANGAY SAN BARTOLOME, QUEZON CITY, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes its constitutional duty to defend and strengthen the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. As such, the government enacted into law the Republic Act 6972, otherwise known as the Barangay-Level Total Development and Protection of Children Act as well as signed the ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1990. While these laws support the welfare of children, there is currently a gap in existing legislation that needs to be filled as regards the well-being of the parents of infants and toddlers who are struggling to find a balance between caring for their children while pursuing their respective careers. It has been the primary goal of existing barangay daycare centers to prepare the children for formal schooling. With said primary goal in mind, existing barangay daycare centers have since only accommodated children between the ages of three years and four years and eleven months, despite being intended for all children below the age of five. As a result of placing a minimum age to avail of the services of the designated barangay daycare centers, the parents of children below the age of three are forced to request help from their family members, if not hire domestic helpers to care for their child, while those who are not as fortunate are forced to stay at home and neglect their careers. Recent World Bank and International Labor Organization estimates show that female labor force participation in the country remains at around 49% as of 2024-2025, reflecting minimal improvement over the past decades. Despite gains in education, a persistent gender gap of over 20 percentage points compared to men continues to characterize the Philippine labor market. A large proportion of women are held back from gainful employment opportunities due to responsibilities to their respective families, more particularly, the caring of their children between the time they are born until two years of age1. For women who cannot afford the cost of early childhood care, the most convenient option is to forego any economic opportunities to care of their infants and toddlers. As the disparity in women’s participation in the labor sector has been a constant hurdle in the State’s goal of achieving gender equality, the present bill seeks to address this gap by providing a free childcare center to women and parents or guardians who are solo-parents, indigent, temporarily displaced, and/or are looking for job opportunities in Brgy. San Bartolome, Quezon City. By establishing such infrastructure, infants and toddlers are given the care they are entitled to while giving their parents a fair chance to advance their respective careers. It is the hope of this bill that the Philippines will eventually close the gender disparities in the country by providing full support to childcaring services. It is the intention of this bill to afford safe and nurturing spaces for infants and toddlers in our District, while giving the parents peace of mind as they work for a brighter future for their children. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is urgently sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS Fifth District, Quezon City 1 Investing in Women. As such, the government enacted into law the Republic Act 6972, otherwise known as the Barangay-Level Total Development and Protection of Children Act, as well as signed the ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1990. While these laws support the welfare of children, there is currently a gap in existing legislation that needs to be filled as regards the well-being of the parents of infants and toddlers who are struggling to find a balance between caring for their children while pursuing their respective careers. It has been the primary goal of existing barangay daycare centers to prepare the children for formal schooling. With said primary goal in mind, existing barangay daycare centers have since only accommodated children between the ages of three years to four years and eleven months, despite being intended for all children below the age of five. As a result of placing a minimum age to avail of the services of the designated barangay daycare centers, the parents of children below the age of three are forced to request help from their family members, if not hire domestic helpers to care for their child, while those who are not as fortunate are forced to stay at home and neglect their careers. Recent World Bank and International Labor Organization estimates show that female labor force participation in the country remains at around 49% as of 2024-2025, reflecting minimal improvement over the past decades. Despite gains in education, a persistent gender gap of over 20 percentage points compared to men continues to characterize the Philippine labor market. A large proportion of women are held back from gainful employment opportunities due to responsibilities to their respective families, more particularly, the caring of their children between the time they are born until two years of age1. For women who cannot afford the cost of early childhood care, the most convenient option is to forego any economic opportunities to care for their infants and toddlers. Nagkaisang Nayon, Quezon City. By establishing such infrastructure, infants and toddlers are given the care they are entitled to while giving their parents a fair chance to advance their respective careers. It is the intention of this bill to afford safe and nurturing spaces for infants and toddlers in our District, while giving the parents peace of mind as they work for a brighter future for their children. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is urgently sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS Fifth District, Quezon City 1 Investing in Women. For women who cannot afford the cost of early childhood care, the most convenient option is to forego any economic opportunities to care for their infants and toddlers. As the disparity in women’s participation in the labor sector has been a constant hurdle in the State’s goal of achieving gender equality, the present bill seeks to address this gap by providing a free childcare center to women and parents or guardians who are solo-parents, indigent, temporarily displaced, and/or are looking for job opportunities in Brgy. Santa Monica, Quezon City. By establishing such infrastructure, infants and toddlers are given the care they are entitled to while giving their parents a fair chance to advance their respective careers. It is the hope of this bill that the Philippines will eventually close the gender disparities in the country by providing full support to childcaring services. It is the intention of this bill to afford safe and nurturing spaces for infants and toddlers in our District, while giving the parents peace of mind as they work for a brighter future for their children. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is urgently sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS Fifth District, Quezon City 1 Investing in Women. label: HB 10159
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE PRACTICE OF MICROBIOLOGY IN THE PHILIPPINES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Microorganisms provide a multitude of benefits to humans. They are utilized in the production of food and condiments, such as bread, cheese, beer, and soy sauce. Pharmaceuticals also use microorganisms in the production of antibiotics, vaccines, vitamins and hormones such as insulin. Environmental clean-up, as well as cultivating biogas and bioethanol require the use of microorganisms. Utilizing such microscopic organisms has proven beneficial due to their sustainability. Microorganisms also recycle elements such as carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur in both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Furthermore, microorganisms serve as sources of nutrients at the base of the ecological food chains. In addition, microscopic organisms are employed in scientific research and technology. The underlying foundation of microbiology sets the stage for modern biotechnology, which includes genetic engineering, and cell and tissue culture. On the other hand, there are also evident downsides in using microorganisms. These include the spoilage of food and processed goods and postharvest losses. In addition, microbes serve as the cause of multiple diseases humans acquire, such as HIV and cholera, as well as food poisoning; in livestock, such as foot and mouth disease; and various other crop diseases. Hence, it is crucial to enact a proper regulation in the handling of microorganism as this requires adequate skills and prior educational background to utilize it to its full potential efficiently. Background knowledge on the fundamentals of microbes is essential for quality control of processed food and manufactured goods, in controlling environmental pollution and in repairing degraded soils. This will also aid in alleviating epidemics among humans, animals, and crops, as well as to produce microbial-based goods and services efficiently. This can be ensured by providing academic preparation and training in universities and colleges. However, due to existing differences in philosophical beliefs, facilities, and resources, these courses may differ from institution to institution. With the crucial role played by microbiologists, this bill seeks to regulate the profession and overall practice of microbiology. The COVID-19 pandemic further emphasizes the microbiologists’ role in responding to public health emergencies. The regulation and standardization of the practice of microbiology in the country will safeguard the Filipinos’ health for the present and the future. It will ensure high quality delivery of technical services in the monitoring, surveillance, prevention and control of future epidemics. In synergy and convergence with other professions regulated by the Professional Regulation Commission where microbiology is an essential component of their practice, Doctors of Medicine, Doctors of Veterinary Medicine, Medical Technologists, Agriculturists, Pharmacists and Food Technologists, among others, shall continue to practice microbiology without registering under this Act. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10160
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE SALE OF ELECTRICITY FOR RESIDENTIAL, AGRICULTURAL, COMMERCIAL, INDUSTRIAL, AND OTHER END- USER CONSUMPTION FROM VALUE-ADDED TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 108 AND 109 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 20 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 23 SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the "Electricity VAT Relief Act." 26 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect consumers from rising electricity costs, promote affordable and reliable access to electric power, support economic productivity, and enhance the competitiveness of Philippine industries. 31 Recognizing electricity as an essential public necessity indispensable to households, education, healthcare, agriculture, commerce, and national development, the State shall remove the burden of value-added tax on electricity consumption in order to reduce the cost of living and improve the purchasing power of Filipino consumers. 36 SECTION 3. Section 108(A) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended, is hereby further amended to read as follows: 39 “SEC. 108. Value-Added Tax on the Sale of Services, Including Digital Services, and the Use or Lease of Properties. — 42 “(A) Rate and Base of Tax. — There shall be levied, assessed, and collected a value-added tax equivalent to twelve percent (12%) of the gross sales derived from the sale or exchange of services, including digital services, and the use or lease of properties.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 14 Electricity is no longer a luxury. It is a basic necessity that powers every Filipino home, every classroom, every hospital, every small business, every farm, and every workplace. Yet every month, Filipino consumers continue to pay a twelve percent (12%) Value-Added Tax (VAT) on their electricity consumption—a tax imposed on an essential service that no household or enterprise can reasonably do without. 20 At a time when families are struggling with rising prices of food, transportation, housing, education, and healthcare, the answer should not always be another subsidy funded by taxpayers. The more sustainable and equitable solution is to allow Filipinos to keep more of what they rightfully earn. Every peso that government chooses not to collect from essential consumption is a peso that remains in the pockets of hardworking families to spend on their children's education, better nutrition, healthcare, savings, or investment. Rather than taxing citizens on nearly every aspect of daily life and later redistributing assistance through various government programs, public policy should first recognize that the fruits of one's labor belong primarily to the worker and his or her family. 31 The removal of VAT on electricity is one of the most direct and meaningful forms of tax relief that Congress can provide. Unlike subsidies that benefit only selected sectors, a VAT exemption on electricity benefits every Filipino consumer. It immediately reduces monthly electric bills, lowers operating costs for businesses, eases the burden on farmers and manufacturers, and enhances the competitiveness of Philippine industries. Lower electricity costs likewise help moderate inflation by reducing production and distribution expenses across the economy. 39 This measure likewise promotes transparency and efficiency in governance. A twelve percent (12%) reduction in the VAT component of electricity bills is immediate, automatic, and requires no application, qualification, or government intervention. Consumers receive the benefit directly through lower monthly bills without additional bureaucracy or administrative expense. 45 1 This bill embodies a simple but important principle: government should tax only to the extent necessary to provide essential public services and should avoid imposing unnecessary burdens on basic necessities. Allowing Filipinos to retain more of the value of their hard work strengthens families, stimulates economic activity, encourages investment, and ultimately contributes to sustainable national growth. 6 For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 8 9 10 11 12 REP. label: HB 10162
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A FREE MEDICINE ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR THE POOR, ESTABLISHING ACCESS SITES IN ALL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES OF THE COUNTRY, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The World Health Organization has observed that the major causes of death in low-income countries can be treated effectively with simple essential medicines. However, the medicines are often not available, not accessible or not affordable. Recent evidence indicates that limited access to affordable and essential medicines remains a persistent challenge in the Philippine health system. A Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) assessment found that only 2 in 10 hospitals have a complete set of essential medicines, forcing many patients to procure medicines outside health facilities at their own expense.1 The Department of Health (DOH) has an ongoing free medicine program for indigents called Medical Assistance Program (MAP), a program intended to provide medical assistance to patients seeking consultation, rehabilitation, examination, or otherwise confined in government hospitals. On the other hand, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) also provide medical assistance to indigent patients in its Assistance to Indiviuals in Crisis Situations (AICS).2 1 Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS), Assessment of the Service Capability and Readiness of Philippine Hospitals to Provide High-Quality Health Care (2021) 2 DSWD Memorandum Circular No. 14, series of 2016. While the government has expanded access through programs such as PhilHealth’s outpatient medicine benefits (e.g., the YAKAP Program), availability remains uneven, and facilities are required to maintain sufficient stocks of covered medicines to ensure continuity of care. This bill seeks to improve Filipinos’ access to essential medicines by institutionalizing a free medicine assistance program for the poor and marginalized, and by establishing accessible distribution sites in all cities and municipalities nationwide. Through these measures, it aims to enhance survival rates among underserved populations suffering from treatable conditions, thereby contributing to improved overall public health outcomes in the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10163
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE INCLUSION OF THE CONTINUING DRIVER’S EDUCATION PROGRAM IN THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL CURRICULUM AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Road and vehicular-related accidents remain among the leading causes of death globally. According to the World Health Organization’s Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023, road traffic crashes claim approximately 1.19 million lives each year worldwide and are the leading cause of death among individuals aged 5 to 29 years. In the Philippines, road traffic injuries continue to pose a significant public health concern. Recent data indicate that road traffic deaths reached 11,096 in 2021, with a mortality rate of about 9.7 deaths per 100,000 population, reflecting the persistent and growing risks posed by vehicular accidents nationwide. Studies show that most traffic-related accidents and vehicular incidents are attributable to human error and negligence (i.e. overspeeding, using a cellphone while driving, drunk driving, overtaking and wrong turning, etc.) However, most of these incidents can be prevented through appropriate intervention such as the proper education and continuing training of our road users on road safety and traffic regulations. This bill seeks to include a comprehensive continuing driver's education program in the Senior High School (SHS) to develop our students' knowledge on traffic rules and regulations as well as on the safe operation of motor vehicles pursuant to international road and traffic safety standards. The program further seeks to enable students to assess their skills and behavior on the road and instill in them the sense of responsibility that comes from acquiring the correct knowledge on driving motor vehicles to ensure their safety as well as of other road users. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10164
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROVISION OF CHILD-FRIENDLY FACILITIES IN EVERY DINE-IN RESTAURANT IN THE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State provides that it shall defend the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. The country additionally is a signatory to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, signifying its commitment to upholding the rights and welfare of children, including their right to be nurtured in an environment that fosters understanding, tolerance, and peace and enables growth and development. In recognition of the importance of ensuring that children dining out with their families have access to child-friendly spaces that cater to their needs as well as promote a positive and enjoyable atmosphere for all patrons, this bill proposes that food establishments such as restaurants, cafes, diners, and similar establishments must provide child-friendly facilities as a part of their establishments. Specifically, the proposed “Child-friendly Restaurants Act” mandates proportional child-friendly seating in food establishments and baby-changing facilities in restrooms. By mandating the provision of child-friendly facilities in food establishments, this legislation encourages businesses to prioritize their youngest patrons and support the well-being of dining parents and families with young children, thereby creating inclusive and welcoming environments while helping the food establishments boost their economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10165
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR INTERNS’ RIGHTS AND WELFARE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Internships serve as a critical transition from education to employment, equipping students and young graduates with practical skills, workplace experience, and professional discipline. In both public and private sectors, interns contribute to organizational operations while gaining competencies essential for future employment. However, despite their growing role, many interns remain inadequately protected and are exposed to exploitative practices such as unpaid labor, excessive working hours, lack of supervision, and unsafe working conditions. While existing policies—such as the Labor Code of the Philippines, Republic Act No. 11058 or the Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) Law, and relevant guidelines issued by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA)—provide general labor and training standards, there remains no comprehensive framework specifically addressing the rights and welfare of interns. This measure seeks to fill this gap by establishing a National Framework for Interns’ Rights and Welfare. It sets minimum standards for internship programs, including fair and reasonable compensation or allowances, safe and healthy working conditions consistent with RA 11058, reasonable working hours, access to mentorship and structured learning aligned with CHED and TESDA requirements, and protection against abuse, discrimination, and exploitation. It further strengthens coordination among educational institutions, employers, and government agencies to ensure that internships remain primarily educational, developmental, and compliant with labor and safety regulations. By institutionalizing these safeguards, the State upholds its constitutional mandate to protect labor, promote decent work, and invest in a competent, skilled, and globally competitive Filipino workforce. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10166
title: AN ACT ALLOWING THE ADOPTION OF ALTERNATIVE WORK ARRANGEMENTS IN ENTERPRISES REGISTERED WITH INVESTMENT PROMOTION AGENCIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 309 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights of workers while promoting full employment, productivity, and the participation of private enterprises in national development. As digital technologies continue to reshape the workplace, employment policies must likewise evolve to encourage innovation, improve competitiveness, and provide flexible work arrangements that benefit both employers and employees without compromising labor standards. Republic Act No. 11534, otherwise known as the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises (CREATE) Act, provides fiscal incentives to registered business enterprises operating within economic zones and freeports. However, its requirement that registered activities be conducted exclusively within these designated areas has created uncertainty regarding the adoption of alternative work arrangements such as telecommuting, hybrid work, compressed workweeks, and other flexible work schemes. Although temporary administrative measures were adopted during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, the absence of a clear statutory framework continues to create regulatory uncertainty for investors and enterprises seeking to modernize their operations while maintaining their incentive eligibility. The rapid advancement of digital infrastructure and information technology has demonstrated that many business processes, particularly in information technology, business process outsourcing, research and development, engineering, finance, and other knowledge-based industries, can be performed efficiently outside traditional office settings. Allowing registered enterprises to adopt alternative work arrangements enhances operational resilience, reduces business costs, improves employee productivity and work-life balance, expands employment opportunities for persons in geographically distant areas, and strengthens the Philippines' competitiveness as an investment destination in an increasingly digital global economy. This measure seeks to amend Section 309 of the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended by the CREATE Act, by expressly allowing registered business enterprises under Investment Promotion Agencies to adopt telecommuting, work- 1 from-home, hybrid work, flexible work arrangements, compressed workweeks, and other lawful alternative work arrangements without forfeiting their entitlement to fiscal incentives. At the same time, the bill ensures that such arrangements remain voluntary, mutually agreed upon, and fully compliant with Republic Act No. 11165, otherwise known as the Telecommuting Act, as well as existing labor laws, occupational safety standards, data privacy requirements, cybersecurity safeguards, and other statutory rights afforded to workers. The proposed measure likewise empowers Investment Promotion Agencies to issue reasonable implementation and monitoring guidelines that balance regulatory oversight with operational flexibility. By institutionalizing alternative work arrangements within the country's investment incentives framework, the bill promotes business continuity, encourages technological innovation, attracts higher-value investments, supports environmental sustainability through reduced commuting, and enables Philippine enterprises to remain competitive in the rapidly evolving global digital economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 10167
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 5(3) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9225, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CITIZEN RETENTION AND RE-ACQUISITION ACT OF 2003”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as a fundamental instrument for national development and mandates the State to promote quality education, advance science and technology, and ensure that institutions of higher learning remain centers of excellence, innovation, and public service. In an increasingly interconnected world, the ability of Philippine higher education institutions to attract and retain globally competitive Filipino scholars has become essential to strengthening the country's academic and research capabilities. Republic Act No. 9225, otherwise known as the Citizenship Retention and Re- acquisition Act of 2003, allows natural-born Filipinos who have reacquired Philippine citizenship to enjoy full civil and political rights. However, Section 5(3) of the law requires dual citizens appointed to public office to renounce their oath of allegiance to a foreign state before assuming office. While this requirement is appropriate for positions involving the exercise of sovereign governmental powers, its application to faculty members, researchers, and academic administrators in public higher education institutions has inadvertently discouraged many highly qualified Filipino professionals abroad from serving in the country's state universities and colleges. Philippine public higher education institutions increasingly compete for world- class educators, scientists, researchers, and academic leaders whose expertise has been developed through international education, research, and professional experience. Many of these individuals have acquired foreign citizenship while maintaining strong ties to the Philippines and have subsequently reacquired their Philippine citizenship under Republic Act No. 9225. Requiring them to renounce their foreign allegiance as a condition for academic service often creates legal, professional, and personal barriers that discourage their return, resulting in the loss of valuable expertise that could otherwise strengthen the country's research, innovation, and human capital development. This measure seeks to amend Section 5(3) of Republic Act No. 9225 by exempting faculty members, researchers, and administrators of public higher education institutions from the requirement of renouncing their foreign oath of 1 allegiance. The proposed amendment recognizes that these positions primarily advance education, research, and knowledge generation rather than the exercise of sovereign political authority. At the same time, these individuals remain bound by their oath of allegiance to the Republic of the Philippines, the Constitution, and all applicable laws governing public service. By removing an unnecessary barrier to academic engagement, this measure will encourage more highly qualified Filipino scholars, scientists, innovators, and academic leaders abroad to contribute their knowledge and experience to Philippine higher education. Their participation will strengthen research collaboration, improve instructional quality, expand international partnerships, enhance technology transfer, and ultimately contribute to the country's scientific, economic, and social development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 10168
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A SUSTAINABLE HOUSING PROGRAM FOR TENURED PERSONNEL OF STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, PROVIDING CAMPUS AND OFF-CAMPUS HOUSING ASSISTANCE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as a vital instrument for national development and mandates the State to protect and promote the welfare of teachers and other public servants who dedicate their lives to advancing knowledge, research, and public service. State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) serve as the backbone of the country's public higher education system, producing skilled professionals, generating research, and extending vital services to communities. Ensuring the well- being of their personnel is therefore indispensable to maintaining the quality, stability, and continuity of public higher education. Despite their indispensable role, many teaching and non-teaching personnel of SUCs continue to face significant challenges in securing affordable and decent housing, particularly those assigned to universities located in highly urbanized areas or geographically distant campuses. Rising property values, increasing rental costs, and limited access to affordable financing have placed homeownership beyond the reach of many government employees. In many instances, long commuting hours not only impose financial burdens but also reduce productivity, diminish work-life balance, and affect the quality of instruction, research, extension work, and administrative services. This measure seeks to institutionalize a sustainable housing assistance program for tenured personnel of State Universities and Colleges through a balanced approach that combines affordable campus housing with expanded access to off-campus housing opportunities. The proposed measure authorizes SUCs, subject to the availability of resources, to establish affordable in-campus housing while also strengthening partnerships with government housing agencies and financial institutions to facilitate socialized housing, rental assistance, housing loans, financial literacy programs, and other forms of housing support. The bill likewise requires every SUC to develop a long-term Housing Development Program tailored to its institutional needs and capacities. Recognizing the diversity of circumstances among SUCs nationwide, the bill adopts a flexible and fiscally responsible framework by allowing each institution, 1 through its Board of Regents, to establish transparent criteria for housing eligibility, occupancy, and prioritization based on objective standards such as years of service, housing need, operational necessity, and financial capacity. It also encourages the use of public-private partnerships and other innovative financing mechanisms to expand housing opportunities without placing undue pressure on limited government resources. Providing secure and affordable housing for SUC personnel is an investment in the country's educational future. Stable housing contributes to higher employee morale, improved recruitment and retention of highly qualified faculty and staff, stronger institutional performance, and ultimately better educational outcomes for Filipino students. By helping ensure that those who educate future generations enjoy decent living conditions, the State likewise strengthens the quality, accessibility, and sustainability of public higher education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 10169
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL METROLOGY INSTITUTE (PNMI), STRENGTHENING THE NATIONAL MEASUREMENT SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Accurate and internationally traceable measurements form the foundation of scientific research, industrial productivity, consumer protection, public health, environmental monitoring, trade facilitation, and technological innovation. Virtually every sector of the economy depends upon reliable measurement systems to ensure product quality, regulatory compliance, manufacturing precision, and international market acceptance. As global trade and advanced technologies become increasingly dependent on measurement accuracy, a strong and internationally recognized national metrology institution has become indispensable for national development. While the Philippines has made significant progress in developing its national measurement capabilities through the National Metrology Division of the Department of Science and Technology–Industrial Technology Development Institute (DOST-ITDI), the country's expanding industrial, scientific, and technological requirements demand a more robust, permanent, and internationally credible institutional framework. Strengthening the National Measurement System will improve the country's competitiveness, facilitate exports, support innovation, enhance consumer confidence, and ensure compliance with international standards and mutual recognition arrangements. This measure seeks to establish the Philippine National Metrology Institute (PNMI) by transforming the existing National Metrology Division into a dedicated national institution responsible for maintaining national measurement standards, providing calibration and technical services, conducting metrology research, developing human capital, and representing the Philippines in regional and international metrology organizations. The bill likewise strengthens governance through the creation of a Governing Board, institutionalizes regional metrology laboratories, establishes a National Metrology Training Center, and provides a long- term Capacity Enhancement Plan to ensure sustained development of the country's measurement infrastructure. The proposed legislation likewise promotes stronger coordination among government agencies, industry, academe, and international partners, while supporting 1 research, innovation, education, and workforce development in measurement science. By reinforcing the National Quality Infrastructure, the measure enhances the country's ability to compete in global markets, improve manufacturing capability, strengthen regulatory systems, and safeguard public welfare through accurate and reliable measurements. Establishing the Philippine National Metrology Institute is a strategic investment in the country's scientific and technological future. It lays the foundation for a modern, innovation-driven economy supported by internationally recognized measurement standards that advance industrial development, public confidence, and sustainable national growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 10170
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE NATIONAL REGISTRY OF WORKERS, ESTABLISHING THE EMPLOYMENT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SYSTEM FOR THE PURPOSE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution affirms that labor is a primary social economic force. Regarded as the cornerstone of national development, the spirit of labor shall afford workers with full protection of their rights and interests. However, while such comprehensive protection remains to be the mandate of the state, such should still be taken in cognizance with the rights of the employers. The aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic eventually led to initiatives by the government to institutionalize the transition of the government to e-governance which is applicable to all government offices and agencies including local government units and government-owned or controlled corporations. This is also simultaneous with the intent of Republic Act No. 11967 or the Internet Transactions Act (ITA) of 2023 which further regulated e-commerce by protecting both online consumers and merchants, ensuring secure internet transactions, and promoting the growth of digital commerce. Hence, it becomes of primordial importance to enunciate a middle ground in terms of digital innovation, both on the part of the private entities whose majority are employers and the employees whose rights are enforced by the government. At present, the Department of Labor and Employment quarterly monitors its labor force through the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA’s) Labor Force Survey. This is in addition to Department of Labor and Employment’s (DOLE’s) Labor Advisory No. 03 Series of 25 2024 which required all private establishments to submit an annual report on the verified itemized listing of their labor component, specifying the names of their rank-and-file employees, including learners, apprentices, and workers with disabilities who were hired under the terms prescribed in the employment contracts, and their corresponding salaries and wages through registration in the Department of Labor and Employment's Online Compliance Portal. DOLE has also been incorporating digital reforms, one of which is the Management Information System (MIS) which includes real-time reporting of inspection results which can generate various reports on compliance, violations, and other labor-related data of employers. It is in this regard that this measure seeks to establish a centralized information system which would cater to all labor-related information, primarily to the regional and field offices and attached agencies of DOLE. Granted, however, that the proposed measure will not be in contrary with laws regarding protection of personal privacy, national security, records retention, access for persons with disabilities, and other relevant laws. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10171
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL PROGRAM FOR THE PREVENTION, EARLY DETECTION, AND MANAGEMENT OF CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD), MANDATING PRIMARY CARE SCREENING, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) has quietly escalated into a massive national public health crisis and currently ranks among the top ten leading causes of death in the Philippines, with National Kidney and Transplant Institute (NKTI) data revealing that one Filipino develops kidney failure every hour. Recent health figures indicate that approximately 11.2% of the population, or an estimated 12.94 million Filipinos, live with some form of kidney damage. Crucially, data from the Philippine Renal Disease Registry (PRDR) highlights that this crisis disproportionately impacts the national workforce, as 57.44% of diagnosed patients are between the ages of 20 and 59, alongside an equally critical upward trend in kidney cases among young children. For years, the government's approach has been to step in only when the kidneys have already failed. While expanding PhilHealth subsidies for dialysis and kidney transplants has been a lifesaver for thousands, this approach is financially unsustainable. Dialysis and long-term treatments push Filipino families into severe financial distress and place a heavy, long-term drain on our public health funds. The tragedy is that kidney disease can be stopped if caught early. The main causes of kidney failure in the country are high blood pressure (33.07% of cases), diabetes complications (30.04%), and chronic kidney inflammation (12.20%). If we catch these issues in their early stages, simple lifestyle shifts and proper medical care can stop the kidneys from getting worse. Since early kidney disease does not cause pain, millions of our citizens have no idea their health is at risk until it is too late. To confront this challenge, health awareness out of the hospitals shall be brought directly to where Filipinos spend their daily lives. The behavioral risk factors driving chronic kidney disease, including high-sodium diets, excessive sugar intake, and the misuse of nephrotoxic painkillers, are rooted in daily life at home, work, and local markets. Consequently, health promotion campaigns must transition out of clinical environments and meet citizens within their daily environments Maximizing public awareness through a practical and everyday approach, the proposed measure mandates the strategic deployment of clear health reminders directly within key public and commercial spaces. Specifically, it integrates simple signage at supermarket shelves and checkout lines to guide consumers toward low-sodium choices, utilizes culturally sensitive posters in public wet markets (palengkes) to educate shoppers on hidden salts in local food preparation, and leverages daily commutes by displaying accessible health tips inside public utility vehicles (PUVs) and major transit terminals to reach millions of working-class Filipinos. 1 Through a comprehensive approach that prioritizes early screening in primary care and deploys pervasive public health education across community spaces, the proposed Bill aims to halt the progression of chronic kidney disease before it reaches the stage of debilitating, capital-intensive treatments. Implementing this proactive framework represents both a sound fiscal strategy that will conserve billions in healthcare resources and a vital humanitarian mandate to protect the lives of millions of Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 10172
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSTITUTIONALIZATION, DEVELOPMENT, TRAINING, ORGANIZATION AND ADMINISTRATION OF BASIC RESERVE OFFICERS TRAINING CORPS (ROTC) IN GRADES 11 AND 12 IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7077, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "CITIZEN ARMED FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES RESERVIST ACT", AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 4, Article II of the 1987 Constitution provides: “The prime duty of the Government is to serve and protect the people. The Government may call upon the people to defend the State and, in the fulfillment thereof, all citizens may be required, under conditions provided by law, to render personal, military or civil service.” As emphasized in the aforementioned Constitutional provision, the defense of the State is a shared responsibility of both the government and the citizenry. Republic Act No. 7077, also known as the Armed Forces of the Philippines Reservist Act, institutionalized mandatory military training for students enrolled in colleges, universities, and similar educational institutions through the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) as a requisite for earning a baccalaureate degree. However, with the passage of Republic Act No. 9163, or the National Service Training Program (NSTP) Act of 2001, ROTC became optional for male college students. Consequently, there has been a notable decline in ROTC enrollment, as more students have chosen the alternative NSTP components: the Civic Welfare Training Service (CWTS) and the Literacy Training Service (LTS). Statistics show that there are only 59,637 graduates from both basic and advanced training of the ROTC in 2015-2016, while it reached a low of 46,936 in 2017-2018.1 These figures highlight the growing concern of the AFP regarding the sustainability of reserve manpower and the government's ability to respond effectively to national security threats and emergencies such as the recent Marawi City siege and the continued harassment of Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea. 1 Philippine News Agency. label: HB 10189
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MODERN HOSPITAL NETWORK LICENSING SYSTEM, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4226, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “HOSPITAL LICENSURE ACT”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide a regulatory framework that recognizes integrated healthcare delivery networks, digital health technologies, interoperability, and coordinated healthcare services. It repeals Republic Act (RA) No. 4226, otherwise known as the “Hospital Licensure Act”, and establishes a modern Hospital Network Licensing System.. It also ensures that healthcare institutions deliver safe, efficient, resilient, and patient-centered services consistent with the country's evolving healthcare needs. RA No. 4226 was enacted more than six (6) decades ago, long before the emergence of electronic health records, telemedicine, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and integrated healthcare networks. Today, healthcare delivery has become increasingly interconnected, requiring hospitals and healthcare facilities to coordinate patient referrals, share health information securely, and respond collectively to public health emergencies. The experience of the COVID-19 pandemic further exposed the need for stronger hospital coordination, interoperable information systems, and more adaptive regulatory mechanisms capable of responding to rapidly evolving healthcare challenges.1 This measure adopts interoperability and digital health standards for hospital networks, strengthens patient safety and quality assurance mechanisms, enhances emergency preparedness, and encourages innovation while safeguarding data privacy and cybersecurity. Shifting from a facility-based licensing approach to a modern network-based regulatory framework, the bill improves the continuity of care, optimizes healthcare resources, and strengthens the overall resilience of the Philippine health system. Modernizing hospital systems is essential to achieving a responsive and future-ready healthcare system capable of delivering quality services to every 1 World Health Organization (2020). This measure reaffirms the State's commitment to universal access to quality healthcare and strengthens the country's preparedness for future public health challenges. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10190
title: AN ACT EXPANDING MENTAL HEALTH COVERAGE UNDER THE PHILIPPINE HEALTH INSURANCE CORPORATION BY ESTABLISHING A MENTAL HEALTH VOUCHER SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Mental Health Voucher System under the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) that provides financial assistance for psychiatric consultations, psychotherapy, medications, diagnostic services, and rehabilitation. It strengthens the implementation of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act”, by making mental health care more accessible, affordable, and continuous for all Filipinos. Mental health conditions continue to impose a significant burden on Filipino individuals and families. According to Acta Medica Philippina, approximately 3.6 million Filipinos are living with mental, neurological, or substance use disorders, while depression and anxiety remain among the leading causes of disability worldwide.1 Despite the enactment of the Mental Health Act, many Filipinos still struggle to access treatment due to the high cost of psychiatric consultations, psychotherapy, medications, and the limited availability of mental health professionals, particularly in underserved communities. While PhilHealth has introduced mental health benefit packages, coverage remains limited and often insufficient to support long-term treatment and continuity of care. Many patients discontinue therapy or medication because of financial constraints, resulting in worsening conditions, avoidable hospitalizations, reduced productivity, and diminished quality of life.2 Expanding financial protection for mental health services is therefore essential to ensuring that seeking treatment does not become an economic burden. This measure establishes a Mental Health Voucher System that enables qualified PhilHealth members and their dependents to receive tiered benefit packages based on clinical need. It provides subsidies for consultations, psychotherapy, medications, diagnostic procedures, and rehabilitation services while 1 Mina, W. (2024, October 31). Navigating the Stream: Empowering Filipinos In Their Mental Health Journey. Acta Medica Philippina 58(19):5–6. doi: 10.47895/amp.v58i19.11983 2 World Health Organization. (2022). World Mental Health Report: Transforming Mental Health for All. World Health Organization. Accessed via https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240049338. Accessed on 06 July 2026. strengthening program monitoring, accountability, and data management to ensure efficient and sustainable implementation. Mental health is an essential component of universal health care. Investing in timely and affordable mental health services not only improves individual well-being but also strengthens families, workplaces, communities, and the nation’s productivity. This measure advances the State’s constitutional duty to protect the health of every Filipino and ensures that no one is deprived of treatment because of financial difficulty. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10191
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MANDATORY IMMUNIZATION PROGRAM, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10152, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MANDATORY INFANTS AND CHILDREN HEALTH IMMUNIZATION ACT OF 2011”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive National Immunization Program. It repeals Republic Act No. 10152, otherwise known as the “Mandatory Infants and Children Health Immunization Act of 2011”, and ensures that the population is equitably protected from vaccine-preventable diseases. Immunization remains one of the most effective and cost-efficient public health interventions, preventing an estimated three and a half (3.5) to five (5) million deaths globally every year.1 Despite this, routine immunization coverage in the Philippines has yet to fully recover from the decline experienced in recent years, leaving many children and vulnerable populations at risk of vaccine-preventable diseases. A published study in 2024 reported continued measles outbreaks in several regions, highlighting persistent immunity gaps and the need for a comprehensive immunization program and public cooperation.2 The existing law primarily focuses on infants and children which no longer adequately reflects current public health priorities. Today, vaccines are recommended not only for children but also for adolescents, pregnant women, adults, senior citizens, and high-risk populations. Moreover, emerging infectious diseases and evolving scientific evidence require a responsive immunization system supported by independent technical experts, sustained public education, stronger vaccine delivery systems, and broader financial protection for vaccine recipients. This measure institutionalizes an evidence-based, sustainable, and accessible National Immunization Program that covers all life stages. It strengthens vaccine governance through the creation of a National Immunization Technical and Advisory Group (NITAG), to provide evidence-based recommendations, thereby strengthening school- and community-based vaccination programs and expanding public education and health worker training. It likewise integrates immunization 1 World Health Organization (2026, June 30). Vaccines and Immunization. Accessed via www.who.int/health -topics/vaccines-and-immunization#tab=tab_1. Accessed on 6 July 2026. 2 Cordero, D. (2024, February 12). Another measles outbreak in the Philippines? The essentiality of a successful vaccination program and public cooperation. Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics, 20(1). doi.org/10.1080/ 21645515.2024.2312605 services into the benefits provided by the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth). Through these reforms, the bill seeks to improve vaccine coverage, strengthen disease prevention, and safeguard the health of every Filipino. Protecting the health of the people is among the State's foremost responsibilities. A stronger and more responsive immunization program will save lives, reduce healthcare costs, prevent future outbreaks, and reinforce the country's capacity to respond to emerging public health threats. Investing in immunization is an investment in a healthier, more resilient, and more productive nation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. title: AN ACT MANDATING A SMOKE–FREE AND VAPE–FREE ENVIRONMENT IN ALL PUBLIC PLACES AND WORKPLACES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9211, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TOBACCO REGULATION ACT OF 2003” AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11900, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “VAPORIZED NICOTINE AND NON-NICOTINE PRODUCTS REGULATION ACT”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen tobacco and vape control in the Philippines. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9211, otherwise known as the “Tobacco Regulation Act of 2003”, and RA No. 11900, otherwise known as the “Vaporized Nicotine and Non-Nicotine Products Regulation Act”, thereby mandating a smoke-free and vape-free environment in all public places and workplaces in the country. In 2025, Tobacco Atlas reported that ninety five thousand and five hundred seventy-four (95,574) Filipinos die from smoking in the Philippines annually from more than sixteen (16) million adult smokers.1 Meanwhile, in 2021, the World Health Organization reported that more than one million (1.21 million students) are e-cigarette and vape. This represents fourteen percent (14.1%) of the Filipino youth and highlights the prevalence of these nicotine-infused products among the youth in the country.2 These trends underscore the need for stronger regulation and more effective enforcement to protect public health. This measure mandates the creation of local Smoke-Free and Vape-Free Task Forces, establishes a licensing system for tobacco and vape retailers, strengthens enforcement mechanisms and penalties, and provides safeguards against tobacco industry interference in policymaking. It likewise promotes community participation, accountability, and support for affected workers through livelihood assistance and incentives for compliance. Protecting Filipinos from the harmful effects of tobacco smoke and vape emissions is a fundamental public health responsibility. This measure safeguards the health of present and future generations while fulfilling the State's constitutional duty to protect the right to health of every Filipino. 1 Tobacco Atlas (2025). explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish the National Nutrition Commission, thereby repealing Presidential Decree No. 491, otherwise known as the “Nutrition Act of the Philippines,” which created the National Nutrition Council. It strengthens the Commission’s powers and functions as the country’s primary policymaking, coordinating, and monitoring body on nutrition and food security. The 2025 Updating Survey released by the Department of Science and Technology Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI) reported that more than twenty five percent (25.3%) of Filipino children under five (5) years of age are stunted. This represents a 1.7% increase from 2023.1 At the same time, the country faces a growing burden of overweight and obesity among both children and adults, highlighting the need to address the double burden of malnutrition through stronger nutrition governance and coordinated interventions.2 This measure mandates the formulation of a ten-year Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition aligned with the Philippine Development Plan and reinforces a whole-of-government and -society approach to addressing malnutrition. It provides the Commission an enhanced authority to formulate national nutrition policies, coordinate government interventions, strengthen nutrition surveillance, mobilize resources, and monitor the implementation of nutrition programs. label: HB 10194
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE ALLOCATION AND UTILIZATION OF CONFIDENTIAL AND INTELLIGENCE FUNDS IMPOSING PENALTIES FOR MISUSE AND MISAPPROPRIATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Confidential and intelligence funds (CIFs), by their very nature, are granted exceptional treatment in the national budget process due to their sensitive purpose in advancing national security, law enforcement, and public order. Historically, their release has required either presidential approval or specific authorization under the General Appropriations Act (GAA), which governs their legal basis. As defined in the GAA, confidential expenses refer to surveillance activities in civilian government agencies that are intended to support their mandates. However, in the absence of a comprehensive statutory framework, CIF utilization has become a growing source of concern—particularly as the public rightfully demands greater transparency and accountability over the use of public funds. At present, CIFs are governed primarily by Joint Circular No. 2015-01, issued by the Commission on Audit (COA), the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and other oversight bodies. While this circular outlines general guidelines for the release, utilization, and audit of these funds, it remains limited in scope and enforceability. Compared to the rigorous standards applied to regular public funds, the liquidation and documentation requirements for CIFs are notably lax, leaving them vulnerable to misuse. Previous inquiries by the House Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability have revealed troubling practices in the handling of CIFs. These include the allocation of confidential funds to civilian agencies with no mandate related to national security or public safety, utilization of funds for activities outside the agency’s core programs, and disbursements without sufficient supporting documentation. Instances were also uncovered where rewards were paid to unidentified individuals, or information was purchased without any proof of utility or impact on agency operations. In some cases, there were no formal agreements or certifications verifying inter-agency coordination or success of operations, despite substantial disbursements. During the 2024 budget hearings, it became evident that confidential funds in some civilian agencies were being used not for security purposes, but to augment regular administrative functions which is contrary to the intent and legal basis of such funds. These revelations reinforce the urgent need to re-examine how CIFs are granted and monitored, and to close the regulatory gaps that allow for potential abuse under the veil of confidentiality. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize stricter requirements and clearer guidelines in the granting, utilization, and liquidation of confidential and intelligence funds. While recognizing their legitimate role in protecting national security, it also affirms the duty of the government to ensure that all public funds are used judiciously, efficiently, and lawfully. Through this Act, Congress aims to restore the integrity of confidential funds by embedding transparency and accountability into law, and by upholding the public’s right to demand responsible stewardship of taxpayer money. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10195
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING TRANSPARENCY, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND EFFICIENCY IN THIRD-PARTY PROVIDER CONTRACTING FOR PHILHEALTH AND DOH PROGRAMS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The increasing reliance of the Department of Health (DOH) and the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) on third-party service providers for critical health system functions underscores the need for stronger governance, transparency, and accountability in health service contracting. This bill seeks to reform and institutionalize a comprehensive framework for health service procurement and contracting to ensure that public funds are used efficiently, transparently, and in accordance with the principles of good governance and universal health care. It strengthens procurement safeguards by mandating competitive bidding, performance-based contracting, conflict-of- interest controls, and risk-based oversight mechanisms. The measure establishes a Health Procurement and Contract Oversight Committee to provide independent review of high-value contracts and introduces a centralized digital transparency and analytics platform to ensure full public visibility of procurement activities and contract performance. It further professionalizes procurement practice through mandatory certification and training programs and strengthens whistleblower protections and anti-corruption safeguards to deter fraud, collusion, and misuse of public funds. By aligning procurement processes with modern governance standards and data-driven oversight systems, this Act aims to significantly improve the integrity, efficiency, and effectiveness of health service delivery in the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A.
