label: HB 10236
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE CYBERSECURITY OPERATIONS CENTER FOR THE PROTECTION OF PNP CRITICAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine National Police (PNP) increasingly relies on digital systems, interconnected networks, electronic databases, and online frontline services in performing its law-enforcement and public-safety functions. While these technologies have improved the delivery of police services, they have also exposed the organization to cyberattacks, unauthorized access, data breaches, malware, service disruptions, and other forms of cyber intrusion. A successful attack against PNP systems may interrupt essential police operations, compromise sensitive and special personal information, impair the delivery of public services, and weaken public confidence in law-enforcement institutions. The reported breach involving the PNP Firearms and Explosives Office illustrates the serious consequences that may arise when systems containing sensitive government and citizen information are not adequately protected. Cybersecurity within the PNP can no longer be treated solely as a routine information technology function. It is an essential component of operational readiness, data protection, public safety, and national security. The protection of PNP Critical Information Infrastructure must therefore be supported by a permanent, specialized, and coordinated institutional capability. This measure seeks to establish the PNP Cybersecurity Operations Center, or PNP CSOC, as the primary operational and technical unit of the PNP responsible for cybersecurity operations, cyber threat intelligence, and incident response for the protection of PNP Critical Information Infrastructure. It is consistent with the declared policy of the State to strengthen the cybersecurity posture of law-enforcement agencies and ensure the security, integrity, confidentiality, and availability of PNP systems and online frontline services. The PNP CSOC will provide a centralized mechanism for continuously monitoring cyber threats, identifying vulnerabilities and emerging attack methods, analyzing cybercrime trends that may affect PNP systems, and coordinating timely responses to significant cybersecurity incidents. Instead of relying on fragmented or purely reactive measures, the Center will allow the PNP to adopt a unified and proactive approach to the protection of its digital assets and critical systems. The Center will also provide specialized technical and digital forensic support to PNP units investigating cybercrime offenses that directly affect, or originate from attacks against, PNP Critical Information Infrastructure. This includes the proper identification, collection, examination, preservation, and handling of digital evidence necessary to support investigations and prosecutions. In addition, the PNP CSOC will gather, analyze, and disseminate actionable cyber threat intelligence; develop cybersecurity, incident-response, and digital-forensics training programs for PNP personnel; conduct research and development; recommend appropriate cybersecurity policies to the Chief PNP; and contribute to public-awareness initiatives on the protection of personal information when using PNP online services. It will likewise coordinate with the Department of Information and Communications Technology and other relevant national and international government and law-enforcement institutions involved in cybersecurity and the protection of government-owned critical infrastructure. The mandate of the PNP CSOC is deliberately focused on the protection of PNP Critical Information Infrastructure. It is not intended to replace or duplicate the general mandates of existing cybersecurity and cybercrime agencies. Rather, it will strengthen the PNP’s internal capability while enabling more effective coordination with other government institutions whenever a cyber incident affects PNP systems, networks, databases, or digital services. To ensure effective leadership and accountability, the Center will be headed by a Director with the rank of Police Brigadier General or higher and will be composed of highly skilled and specialized personnel, including cybersecurity analysts, cybercrime investigators, and digital forensic examiners. Its detailed organizational structure, staffing pattern, and regional presence will be determined by the Chief PNP, in consultation with the National Police Commission and subject to the availability of funds. The measure further directs the PNP to provide the Center with the technologies, tools, secure infrastructure, digital forensic laboratories, and incident-response capabilities necessary to perform its functions. Because the Center will handle sensitive cybersecurity and investigative information, the bill requires the strictest confidentiality and the adoption of safeguards against unauthorized access, use, disclosure, or compromise. Funding for the establishment, continuous operation, and enhancement of the PNP CSOC shall be included in the annual General Appropriations Act and the regular budget of the PNP. The Chief PNP, in coordination with the National Police Commission and the Department of Information and Communications Technology, shall promulgate the necessary implementing rules and regulations within ninety days from the effectivity of the proposed law. The establishment of the PNP Cybersecurity Operations Center will institutionalize a dedicated, professional, and unified cybersecurity capability within the Philippine National Police. It will strengthen the protection of PNP Critical Information Infrastructure, safeguard sensitive government and citizen data, improve the resilience and continuity of police operations, and enhance the PNP’s capacity to prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to cyber threats. As law enforcement becomes increasingly dependent on digital technologies, the PNP must be equipped not only to police the physical domain but also to protect the digital systems upon which its operations and public services depend. label: HB 10237
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE SERVICE INCENTIVE LEAVE OF EMPLOYEES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE, ARTICLE 95 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed measure seeks to amend Article 95 of Presidential Decree (“P.D.” No. 442, otherwise known as the Labor Code of the Philippines, by increasing the Service Incentive Leave (“SIL”) from five (5) days to ten (10) days with pay, in recognition of the evolving demands of the modern workplace and the State’s constitutional duty to protect labor. Under Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution of the Philippines, the State is mandated to afford full protection to labor, promote humane working conditions, and ensure the well-being of workers. However, the current statutory minimum of five (5) days SIL has remained unchanged for decades, despite significant shifts in labor conditions, increased work intensity, and growing awareness of the importance of employee health and work-life balance SIL, a mandatory benefit for employees with at least one year of service, provides essential paid leave for rest and personal contingencies.The Philippine Supreme Court has reinforced SIL as a mandatory benefit that must be provided or converted to cash if unused.1,2 The proposed increase to ten (10) days is grounded on both policy and empirical considerations. Studies across jurisdictions show that adequate rest periods significantly improve employee productivity, reduce burnout, and enhance overall well-being. The World Health Organization has classified burnout as an occupational phenomenon linked to chronic workplace stress, 3 while research literature demonstrates that paid 1 Auto Bus Transp. Sys., Inc. v. Bautista, G.R. No. 156367, 491 Phil. 353 (2005). 2 JPL Mktg. Promotions v. Ct. App., G.R. No. 151966, 501 Phil. 366 (2005). 3 World Health Organization. (2019, May 28). Burn-out an "occupational phenomenon": International Classification of Diseases. https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational- phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases leave contributes to improved job satisfaction and mental health.4 Moreover, international labor standards and practices in many countries provide for longer paid leave periods, typically ranging from ten (10) to twenty (20) days annually, indicating that the Philippine standard is relatively low.5 Aligning the country’s labor policies with these benchmarks will not only strengthen worker protections but also improve competitiveness by fostering a healthier, more productive workforce. From an economic perspective, increasing the SIL is not merely a cost imposition on employers but a strategic investment in human capital. Evidence shows that employees who are given sufficient rest are less likely to incur absenteeism, more likely to remain in their jobs, and generally perform better.6 Thus, enhanced leave benefits reduce turnover costs and increase organizational efficiency. This is consistent with the State’s policy of promoting both labor welfare and industrial productivity. This proposed measure complements the objectives of the Republic Act No. 11058, which mandates the provision of safe and healthy working conditions, and the Republic Act No. 11036, which recognizes the importance of mental health in the workplace. By expanding leave benefits, the State reinforces these policies and provides workers with the time they need to recover from physical and psychological stress. Furthermore, the bill retains important safeguards for employers by maintaining existing exemptions, such as for establishments with fewer than ten (10) employees and those already providing equal or superior leave benefits. This ensures that the measure remains balanced, taking into account both labor protection and business viability. At the same time, the non-diminution clause embedded in labor law principles is preserved, ensuring that employees continue to enjoy benefits already granted to them. Increasing the Service Incentive Leave to ten (10) days is a necessary and timely reform that responds to contemporary labor realities. It upholds the constitutional mandate to protect labor, aligns domestic policy with international standards, promotes worker health and productivity, and ensures a more humane and equitable workplace. By strengthening this fundamental labor benefit, the State affirms its commitment to the dignity, welfare, and overall well-being of Filipino workers. 4 Westover, J. H. (2014). The impact of paid leave on employee job satisfaction and motivation. Journal of Applied Business and Economics, 16(3), 21–32. 5 International Labour Organization. (2022). Working Time and Work-Life Balance Around the World. ILO Publications. 6 Deery, S., & Jago, L. (2015). Revisiting talent management, work-life balance and retention strategies. International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management, 27(3), 453–472. https://doi.org/10.1108/IJCHM-12-2013-0538 This bill has been approved by the House of Representatives in the 19th Congress and was transmitted to the Senate for its consideration and approval. However, due to lack of material time, this proposed measure was not enacted into law. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is most earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10238
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE USE OF ANIMAL TESTING FOR COSMETIC PURPOSES, REGULATING THE MANUFACTURE, IMPORTATION, DISTRIBUTION, AND SALE OF COSMETICS IN RELATION THERETO, PROMOTING THE USE OF ALTERNATIVE METHODS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines stands at a critical juncture in aligning its regulatory framework with evolving global standards on animal welfare, scientific innovation, and consumer protection. While Republic Act (“R.A.”) No. 8485 (1998), otherwise known as the Animal Welfare Act of 1998, as amended, provides a general framework for the humane treatment of animals, it does not expressly prohibit the use of animals in cosmetic testing, an area that has increasingly drawn ethical, scientific, and economic scrutiny. Cosmetic testing on animals involves subjecting them to procedures that may cause pain, distress, or lasting harm, often for products that are non-essential to human health. Advances in science have rendered such practices largely unnecessary. Today, validated alternative methods, ranging from in vitro testing to computational models, offer more reliable, human-relevant, and cost-efficient means of ensuring product safety.1 The continued reliance on animal testing for cosmetics is therefore no longer justified on either scientific or ethical grounds. Globally, a decisive shift has taken place. The European Union has implemented a comprehensive ban on animal testing for cosmetics and the marketing of animal-tested 1 Krewski, D., Acosta, D., Jr, Andersen, M., Anderson, H., Bailar, J. C., 3rd, Boekelheide, K., Brent, R., Charnley, G., Cheung, V. G., Green, S., Jr, Kelsey, K. T., Kerkvliet, N. I., Li, A. A., McCray, L., Meyer, O., Patterson, R. D., Pennie, W., Scala, R. A., Solomon, G. M., Stephens, M., … Zeise, L. (2010). Toxicity testing in the 21st century: a vision and a strategy. Journal of toxicology and environmental health. Part B, Critical reviews, 13(2-4), 51–138. https://doi.org/10.1080/10937404.2010.483176 cosmetic products. 2 Similar measures have been adopted by jurisdictions such as India, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, among others. These reforms demonstrate that prohibiting cosmetic animal testing is not only feasible but also compatible with robust industry growth and innovation. In fact, global markets are increasingly favoring cruelty- free products, creating both reputational and commercial advantages for compliant industries.3 In the Philippines, the absence of a clear legal prohibition creates regulatory ambiguity and disadvantages local manufacturers in accessing international markets that require cruelty-free certification. Consumers, both domestic and global, are becoming more conscious of ethical sourcing and production practices. A national policy that decisively addresses cosmetic animal testing will therefore enhance consumer confidence, strengthen export competitiveness, and encourage the domestic industry to transition toward modern, science-based testing approaches. This proposed measure seeks to fill the existing legal gap by prohibiting cosmetic testing on animals within the country, as well as the manufacture, importation, and sale of cosmetic products that rely on such testing. It likewise provides a clear regulatory framework for enforcement, allows narrowly defined exceptions when strictly necessary for public health and safety, and promotes the development and adoption of validated alternative methods consistent with international standards such as those recognized by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Importantly, the bill adopts a balanced and pragmatic approach by providing a reasonable transition period for industry compliance, recognizing the need for adjustment while ensuring that reform is both effective and sustainable. The long-term benefits, such as reduced testing costs, improved scientific outcomes, enhanced global market access, and strengthened ethical standards, clearly outweigh the short-term adjustments required. This measure affirms the Philippines’ commitment to humane and responsible innovation. It aligns national policy with global best practices, supports the 2 European Commission. “Cosmetics – Animal Testing.” Available at: https://ec.europa.eu/growth/sectors/cosmetics/animal-testing_en 3 Market Reports World, “Cruelty-Free Cosmetics Market Size, Share, Growth, and Industry Analysis , By Type (Cream, Gel, Liquid, Powder, Others), By Application (Supermarket/Hypermarket, Specialty Retailers, Convenience Stores, Online Store, Others), Regional Insights and Forecast to 2033,” last updated 30 March 2026, accessed 16 April 2026. modernization of the cosmetics industry, and upholds the principle that animal welfare must not be compromised for non-essential purposes. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10239
title: AN ACT REQUIRING PUBLIC ESTABLISHMENTS TO PROVIDE FREE MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS IN PUBLIC RESTROOMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Menstrual health is a fundamental aspect of public health, gender equality, and human dignity. Yet, for millions of Filipinos, access to basic menstrual products remains inconsistent, unaffordable, or stigmatized. Public establishments such as malls, transport terminals, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and government facilities serve as essential spaces where individuals spend significant time daily. However, most public restrooms fail to provide even the most basic menstrual necessities, placing women, girls, and menstruating individuals in vulnerable, uncomfortable, and sometimes unsafe situations. This lack of access contributes to period poverty, a condition linked to school absenteeism, reduced workplace productivity, and adverse health outcomes. International experience demonstrates that providing free menstrual products in public spaces improves hygiene, supports participation in economic and social life, and reduces stigma.1 In the Philippines, menstrual health challenges are already visible in school and sanitation data. UNICEF reported in 2024 that access to sanitary pads in schools improved from 60% in 2017 to 83% in 2020, but access to single-sex toilets remained at 1 Hennegan, J., Brooks, D. J., Schwab, K. J., & Melendez-Torres, G. J. (2023). Menstrual health and hygiene as a public health issue. Frontiers in Global Women’s Health, 4, Article 1152115. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10372806/ only 66% in 2020, up from 49% in 2017. 2 UNICEF’s Philippines country profile likewise noted that only 74% of schools had access to a basic sanitation service and only 61% had a basic hygiene service.3 In 2021, 82.5% of schools reported provision of emergency sanitary pads and information on proper disposal, which means nearly one in five schools still did not report such provision. 4 Research studies further shows that schoolgirls’ menstrual experiences are compounded by inadequate access to clean water, clean and private toilets, and hygiene and menstrual materials in schools, and that these obstacles can lead girls to skip school and show lower classroom engagement.5 Countries and jurisdictions such as Scotland, New Zealand, and several U.S. states have enacted similar policies, recognizing menstrual products as essential items comparable to toilet paper and soap. In the Philippine context, Republic Act (“R.A”) No. 9710 (2009), or the “Magna Carta of Women” and R.A.. 11313, otherwise known as the Safe Spaces Act, affirm the State’s obligation to promote gender-responsive facilities and environments. This measure operationalizes those commitments by ensuring that public establishments provide accessible menstrual products as part of standard sanitation services. By mandating the provision of free menstrual products in public restrooms, this bill advances public health, gender equity, and dignity for all, while imposing a reasonable and socially responsible obligation on establishments that already provide sanitation services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is most earnestly requested. JAVIER MIGUEL L. BENITEZ 2 UNICEF Philippines. Public establishments such as malls, transport terminals, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and government facilities serve as essential spaces where individuals spend significant time daily. However, most public restrooms fail to provide even the most basic menstrual necessities, placing women, girls, and menstruating individuals in vulnerable, uncomfortable, and sometimes unsafe situations. This lack of access contributes to period poverty, a condition linked to school absenteeism, reduced workplace productivity, and adverse health outcomes. label: HB 10240
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 15, 16, AND 17 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1570, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE AERONAUTICAL ENGINEERING DECREE OF 1978, TO MODERNIZE LICENSURE EXAMINATION STANDARDS, INCREASE EXAMINATION FREQUENCY, PROMOTE COMPETENCY-BASED AND CLUSTERED TESTING, AND ENCOURAGE CURRICULUM MODERNIZATION IN RESPONSE TO INDUSTRY NEEDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Presidential Decree (“PD”) No. 1570 (1987), or the Philippine Aeronautical Engineering Decree of 1978, governs the licensure and regulation of aeronautical engineers in the country. However, several of its provisions, particularly those relating to licensure examination frequency, subject structure, and passing standard, have remained unchanged for decades despite significant developments in the aviation industry and the evolving regulatory practices of the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC). As a result, the current framework has created inconsistencies with other engineering professions and may constrain the timely entry and preparation of qualified aeronautical engineers.1 Recent research examining the implementation of PD No. 1570 highlights these structural gaps, noting that the once-a-year examination schedule, relatively rigid subject coverage, and higher passing threshold compared to other engineering disciplines pose challenges for examinees and may no longer be fully responsive to present industry conditions.2 These concerns are particularly relevant as the Philippines continues to position itself as a competitive player in the global aviation industry, including through developments such as the Clark Aviation Hub and the expansion of Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) operations. This bill seeks to address these concerns by introducing targeted amendments to Sections 15, 16, and 17 of PD No. 1570. It provides for at least twice-yearly licensure examinations and the adoption of modern examination modalities, and establishes a competency-based and clustered examination framework while adjusting the passing standard to a 70% general weighted average. These reforms are designed to improve accessibility, align licensure standards with current industry practices, and promote a more responsive and equitable system for aspiring aeronautical engineers. 1 Bangonon, J. et al. (2026). Reforming the Aeronautical Engineering Law: A Legislative Proposal on Licensure Examination Standards and Frequency for Enhanced Engineering Management and Public Safety. SSRN Electronic Journal. doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6058336 (date last accessed: April 9, 2026). 2 Ibid. By modernizing key aspects of the licensure framework, this measure aims to strengthen the pipeline of competent professionals, support the growth of the aviation industry, and ensure that regulatory standards remain aligned with both national development goals and the overarching requirement of public safety. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10241
title: AN ACT FURTHER AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY,” AS AMENDED, TO PROVIDE FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7277 (1992), otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, recognizes the rights of Persons with Disabilities (“PWDs”) and guarantees their access to programs, services, and privileges that promote their welfare, inclusion, and participation in society. These benefits are largely accessed through the PWD Identification Card (“IDC”) issued by local government units. However, under existing practice, PWD-IDCs are subject to periodic renewal regardless of whether the disability is temporary or permanent. Currently, the PWD-IDC issued to the PWD shall be valid for five (5) years.1 For persons with permanent disabilities, this requirement often results in unnecessary expenses, repeated medical certification, and additional administrative procedures despite the lifelong and irreversible nature of their condition. The burden is particularly felt by individuals with mobility limitations, those residing in remote areas, and indigent PWDs who rely on uninterrupted access to statutory benefits and assistance programs. This bill seeks to establish a clear statutory definition of “permanent disability” and provide lifetime validity for PWD-IDCs issued to qualified individuals. The measure requires that permanent disability be certified by the municipal or city health office and verified by the Local Social Welfare and Development Office (LSWDO) to ensure the integrity of the system. By eliminating repetitive renewal requirements for conditions that are medically determined to be irreversible, the bill reduces bureaucratic barriers while preserving appropriate safeguards against misuse. The measure likewise promotes more efficient public service delivery by allowing local government units to focus their resources on identifying, registering, and assisting unserved and underserved members of the PWD sector rather than processing repetitive renewals. As of 2025, the National Council for Disability Affairs (NCDA) reported more than 2.5 million Filipinos who are registered as PWDs nationwide,2 a figure that remains 1 National Council on Disability Affairs (NFDA), Administrative Order No. 001, s. 2021. https://ncda.gov.ph/disability-laws/administrative-orders/ncda-administrative-order-no-001-series-of-2021/ (date last accessed: June 18, 2026). 2 Cabalza, D. (2025). Registered PWDs in PH now at 2.5M. INQUIRER.net. https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2072065/registered-pwds-in-ph-now-at-2-5m (date last accessed: June 18, 2026). 1 significantly lower than global disability prevalence estimates. Simplifying procedures for persons with permanent disabilities can help improve access to government services, encourage registration, and ensure the continuous enjoyment of benefits guaranteed under the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10242
title: AN ACT REQUIRING BUSINESSES TO SUBMIT JOB VACANCY INFORMATION TO THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT SERVICE OFFICE (PESO) UPON RENEWAL OF BUSINESS PERMITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11032, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EASE OF DOING BUSINESS AND EFFICIENT GOVERNMENT SERVICE DELIVERY ACT OF 2018,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution declares as a primary goal of the State the promotion of full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all. 1 While the country has enacted significant reforms to streamline government transactions through the Republic Act (“R.A”) No. 11032 (2018), otherwise known as the Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018, regulatory modernization can further be leveraged not only to reduce red tape but also to strengthen employment facilitation systems at the local level. Local government units already process thousands of business permit renewals annually. This routine interaction between enterprises and government presents a strategic opportunity to gather real-time labor market information that can significantly improve job matching. At present, many Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs), established under R.A. 10691, or the Public Employment Service Office Act of 2015, rely largely on voluntary reporting of vacancies. As a result, jobseekers often face fragmented access to employment information, while businesses struggle to reach qualified local applicants. This bill proposes a minimal, non-burdensome disclosure mechanism requiring businesses renewing their permits to indicate whether they have current or projected job openings. The requirement is purely informational and facilitative. It does not condition permit approval on hiring outcomes, does not impose penalties for non-hiring, and does not introduce additional fees. Instead, it integrates employment reporting into an already 1 1987 Philippine Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 9. existing administrative process, ensuring that regulatory efficiency and labor market development operate in tandem. By electronically transmitting vacancy information to PESOs, the measure strengthens local employment ecosystems, enhances workforce analytics, and supports evidence-based planning. It enables faster job matching, reduces friction between employers and jobseekers, and promotes inclusive economic growth, particularly for first-time workers, displaced employees, and underemployed sectors. This proposal aligns with the State’s commitments to employment generation, digital governance, and public service modernization. It transforms a routine compliance procedure into a proactive employment linkage mechanism without undermining the principles of ease of doing business. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10243
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A SCHOLARSHIP AND RETURN SERVICE PROGRAM FOR STUDENTS PURSUING A BACHELOR’S DEGREE IN OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY, PHYSICAL THERAPY, AND SPEECH AND LANGUAGE THERAPY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State affirms its commitment to ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare services for all Filipinos. However, there remains a significant shortage of rehabilitation and allied health professionals, particularly occupational therapists, physical therapists, and speech-language therapists, across the country, especially in underserved and rural areas. This gap limits access to essential services for persons with disabilities, children with developmental needs, the elderly, and patients recovering from illness or injury. The demand for rehabilitation services continues to grow due to population aging, rising incidence of non-communicable diseases, and increasing awareness of developmental and speech-related conditions. Yet, the supply of qualified therapists remains insufficient and unevenly distributed, with most professionals concentrated in urban centers. As a result, many public hospitals, schools, and community-based facilities lack the necessary personnel to deliver these critical services. This proposed measure seeks to address this gap by establishing a Scholarship and Return Service Program for students pursuing degrees in Occupational Therapy, Physical Therapy, and Speech-Language Pathology. The program provides comprehensive financial support to qualified students and, in return, requires them to render service in public institutions and priority areas after licensure. By linking education support with mandatory return service, the measure ensures that public investment in human capital directly translates into improved access to healthcare services. It also promotes a more equitable distribution of professionals by prioritizing deployment in underserved communities, where the need is greatest. Furthermore, the bill supports the long-term development of the country’s healthcare workforce by encouraging more students to pursue careers in rehabilitation and allied health. It reduces financial barriers to education while providing a clear pathway to employment and public service. This measure strengthens the healthcare system by addressing both the supply and distribution of essential health professionals. It ensures that Filipinos, regardless of location or socio-economic status, have access to rehabilitation services necessary for improved quality of life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10244
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PROGRAM FOR THE USE OF PUBLIC AND PARTICIPATING PRIVATE SPACES FOR ART EXHIBITS OF LOCAL ARTISTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the vital role of arts and culture in nation-building, identity formation, and inclusive development. The promotion of Filipino creativity is not only a constitutional mandate but also a strategic investment in the country’s cultural and creative industries. However, despite the abundance of talent across the country, many Filipino artists, particularly those in the regions and those at the early stages of their careers, continue to face significant barriers in accessing platforms where they can publicly exhibit their work. One of the most persistent challenges confronting local artists is the high cost and limited availability of exhibition spaces. Traditional galleries are often concentrated in urban centers and may be financially inaccessible to emerging artists. As a result, many are deprived of opportunities to showcase their work, connect with audiences, and participate meaningfully in the creative economy. This lack of access not only constrains artistic development but also limits the public’s exposure to diverse forms of Filipino expression. At the same time, numerous public spaces across the country, such as parks, plazas, government buildings, and other communal areas, remain underutilized or are not fully optimized for cultural engagement. These spaces present an opportunity to bring art closer to the people by transforming them into accessible venues for artistic expression and appreciation. By integrating art into everyday public environments, the State can foster a more vibrant, inclusive, and participatory cultural landscape. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by allowing the free use of available public spaces for art exhibits of local artists. Through the coordinated efforts of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts and the Department of Tourism, in partnership with local government units, the program will establish regional and local platforms where artists can exhibit their works without the burden of prohibitive costs. In doing so, the bill democratizes access to artistic spaces and ensures that opportunities for creative expression are not limited by geography or financial capacity. Beyond supporting artists, this measure advances broader social and economic objectives. Public art enriches communities by making culture more visible and accessible, fostering a deeper sense of identity, pride, and shared heritage among Filipinos. It transforms public spaces into dynamic cultural hubs that encourage engagement, dialogue, and creativity. Moreover, by enhancing the cultural character of localities, art exhibitions in public spaces can contribute to tourism development and stimulate local economic activity, benefiting small businesses and surrounding communities. The measure is likewise timely and necessary in light of the ongoing recovery of the creative sector. Many artists continue to experience limited income opportunities and reduced exposure following disruptions in recent years. Providing accessible venues for exhibitions serves as a practical and immediate intervention to help revitalize artistic livelihoods and sustain creative production across the country. Ultimately, this bill represents a low-cost yet high-impact approach to cultural development. By maximizing existing public infrastructure, it creates opportunities for artistic expression, strengthens the creative economy, and promotes inclusive access to culture for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10245
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11901, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE AGRICULTURE, FISHERIES AND RURAL DEVELOPMENT FINANCING ENHANCEMENT ACT OF 2022, TO STRENGTHEN SMALLHOLDER AGRICULTURAL VALUE CHAIN FINANCING AND MARKET LINKAGES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture remains a critical pillar of the Philippine economy, yet small farmers and fisherfolk continue to face persistent structural constraints. Despite existing financing mandates under Republic Act No. 11901, known as the The Agriculture, Fisheries And Rural Development Financing Enhancement Act Of 2022, many rural producers still lack access to affordable, appropriate, and well-integrated financial services. Credit is often extended as stand-alone lending, disconnected from markets, postharvest systems, insurance, and other support necessary for sustainable income generation. Recent data underscore the urgency of reform. Farmers and fisherfolk remain among the poorest sectors in the country, with poverty incidence rates significantly higher than the national average.1 At the same time, Philippine agriculture continues to face productivity challenges, climate risks, and supply chain inefficiencies, all of which weaken the ability of borrowers to repay loans and discourage financial institutions from deeper engagement in the sector. This measure seeks to address these gaps by strengthening smallholder agricultural value chain financing (AVCF) within the framework of RA 11901. Rather than creating a new system, the bill operationalizes what the law already envisions: financing that is linked to the full agricultural cycle—from input supply and production to aggregation, processing, and market access. International experience demonstrates that this approach is more effective than traditional credit models. The Food and Agriculture Organization notes that value chain 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, Poverty Incidence Among Basic Sectors, 2023. financing improves access to credit by tying lending to actual market relationships, reducing risks for both lenders and borrowers.2 Similarly, studies by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies highlight that agricultural finance yields better outcomes when linked to technology adoption, market participation, and coordinated value chain support rather than isolated lending.3 The proposed amendments are likewise consistent with developments across ASEAN. Regional frameworks recognize that smallholder farmers must be integrated into value chains involving cooperatives, agribusinesses, financial institutions, and institutional buyers. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has explicitly emphasized responsible and inclusive agricultural investment that connects smallholders to markets and supply chains.4 In practice, several ASEAN countries have already moved in this direction. Vietnam has supported value chain-based financing arrangements linked to export- oriented agricultural sectors such as rice and coffee, enabling farmers to access credit backed by supply contracts and market demand.5 Indonesia has expanded agricultural financing programs that incorporate cooperatives, off-takers, and agribusiness firms, improving credit access through structured market linkages. 6 Thailand, through its specialized agricultural bank, has long combined credit with marketing support, cooperative strengthening, and value chain development.7 These experiences show that integrating finance with markets and support services improves both productivity and repayment performance. This bill builds on these lessons by clarifying definitions, expanding eligible financing activities, promoting market linkage arrangements, strengthening reporting requirements, and supporting capacity-building for farmers’ organizations, cooperatives, and rural financial institutions. It also encourages the use of digital payments, insurance, 2 Food and Agriculture Organization, “Agricultural Value Chain Finance,” FAO, accessed 2026. 3 Charlotte Bayudan-Dacuycuy and Marife Ballesteros, Sustainable Value Chain Financing for Smallholder Agricultural Production in the Philippines (Quezon City: Philippine Institute for Development Studies, 2022). 4 Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN Guidelines on Promoting Responsible Investment in Food, Agriculture and Forestry (Jakarta: ASEAN Secretariat, 2018). 5 World Bank, Vietnam Sustainable Agriculture Transformation Project (VnSAT): Implementation Completion and Results Report (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2023), 23–24, noting coffee credit-line financing, preferential rates, and supply/offtake contracts for coffee value chains. 6 World Bank, Indonesia Agriculture Value Chain Development Project (ICARE): Project Appraisal Document (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2022), 14–15, discussing Indonesia’s agribusiness-led value chains and the role of private actors as processors, buyers, input providers, logistics providers, and financiers. 7 Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives, “About BAAC,” accessed May 2, 2026; Witsanu Attavanich, “Case Study of Bank for Agricultural Cooperatives (BAAC) Rice Value Chain Implementation,” FFTC Agricultural Policy Platform, July 3, 2018. credit information systems, and investments in postharvest and logistics infrastructure, all of which are essential to modern agricultural value chains. By embedding value chain financing more explicitly within RA 11901, the measure aims to ensure that agricultural credit is not only counted for compliance, but actually works for smallholders. The ultimate goal is to improve access to finance, stabilize farmgate prices, reduce risks, strengthen repayment capacity, and increase rural incomes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10246
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A DEFORESTATION-FREE GOVERNMENT PROCUREMENT POLICY, ESTABLISHING STANDARDS AND VERIFICATION MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution imposes upon the State the duty to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.1 This constitutional command is not abstract. In Oposa v. Factoran, the Supreme Court recognized that the protection of the country’s forests is inseparable from the principle of intergenerational responsibility, and that every generation bears a duty to preserve the environment for those yet to come.2 In the Philippines, deforestation remains a serious environmental, climate, and governance concern. The Climate Change Commission has reported that from 2001 to 2022, the country lost approximately 1.42 million hectares of tree cover, while the country’s total forest cover as of 2022 was estimated at 7.22 million hectares, or only 24.07% of the country’s land mass. 3 This is particularly alarming for a country recognized as one of the world’s megadiverse countries, with exceptional levels of endemism and biodiversity that depend heavily on healthy forest ecosystems. 4 Globally, deforestation is also closely linked to commodity supply chains, with the Food and Agriculture 1 1987 PHIL. CONST. Art. II, Sec. 16. 2 Oposa v. Factoran, G.R. No. 101083, 224 SCRA 792, July 30, 1993. 3 Climate Change Commission, “Keeping up with deforestations,” Mar. 21, 2024. https://climate.gov.ph/news/851 (last accessed May 29, 2026). 4 Philippine Clearing House Mechanism, “Biodiversity,” Biodiversity Management Bureau, Department of Environment and Natural Resources. https://www.philchm.ph/status-of-philippine-biodiversity-2/ (last accessed May 29, 2026). Organization of the United Nations reporting that agricultural expansion drives almost ninety percent of global deforestation.5 The Philippines already has laws protecting forests, protected areas, wildlife habitats, ancestral domains, and climate resilience. However, while these laws regulate forest protection and environmental management, they do not yet establish a specific, uniform, and enforceable rule that would prevent the government itself from purchasing goods whose supply chains are linked to deforestation, illegal logging, unlawful forest conversion, or degradation of protected and ecologically sensitive areas. This gap is especially important because the Government is a major consumer of paper, furniture, timber, wood-based construction materials, fixtures, and other products that may carry forest-risk inputs. Existing policy already recognizes the role of public procurement in environmental protection. Executive Order No. 301, series of 2004, directed government agencies to establish Green Procurement Programs and include environmental criteria in public tenders whenever practicable.6 More recently, Republic Act No. 12009, or the New Government Procurement Act, institutionalized Sustainable Public Procurement and Green Public Procurement, requiring procuring entities to integrate environmentally relevant criteria into procurement design and specifications, and directing the Government Procurement Policy Board (“GPPB”) to implement green procurement in phases.7 This bill builds on that framework. It does not create a parallel procurement regime. Rather, it supplies a clear deforestation-free standard for covered products within the existing procurement system. This proposed measure institutionalizes a Deforestation-Free Government Procurement Policy. It requires public agencies to procure covered forest-risk products only when these are certified or verified as deforestation-free. The bill is designed to be practical and implementable. It adopts a phased approach, beginning with products where government demand and verification systems are most feasible, such as paper, pulp, timber, plywood, lumber, furniture, fixtures, and wood-based construction materials. It allows risk-based verification, recognizes equivalent certifications and government documents, provides exceptions for emergencies and temporary market unavailability, and requires simplified compliance pathways for small producers, cooperatives, community-based forest management organizations, MSMEs, and Indigenous Peoples’ enterprises. The measure also aligns the Philippines with emerging global best practices. The European Union, for example, has adopted a deforestation-free products regulation requiring covered commodities and products to be deforestation-free and produced in accordance with the laws of the country of production before being placed on or exported from the EU market.8 The Philippines does not need to copy foreign models wholesale. Instead, this bill adapts the core principle to Philippine realities: fragmented land records, smallholder production, island-based supply chains, community-based forest management, public procurement capacity gaps, and the need to protect both the environment and local livelihoods. label: HB 10247
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL PROGRAM FOR MALUNGGAY INDUSTRY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Malunggay, or Moringa oleifera, is one of the Philippines’ most abundant and nutritionally dense plants. Long a staple of Filipino households and traditional medicine, it has in recent years attracted significant international attention as a superfood, valued for its exceptional concentration of vitamins, minerals, and amino acids, as well as its established and potential medicinal properties. Its applications extend well beyond food and nutrition, encompassing pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, cosmetic, agricultural, and biofuel uses, making it a plant of extraordinary commercial and developmental versatility. The global moringa market has been expanding steadily, with increasing demand from health-conscious consumers in North America, Europe, and Asia creating meaningful export opportunities for producing countries. The Philippines, with its favorable climate and the widespread cultivation of malunggay across the archipelago, is uniquely positioned to capitalize on this growing global demand. Yet the country has not fully harnessed malunggay’s economic potential, owing to the absence of a coordinated national program that integrates productivity improvement, research and development, processing, standardization, and market promotion under a unified policy framework. The malunggay industry remains largely informal and fragmented, with smallholder farmers lacking access to technical support, appropriate agricultural inputs, processing facilities, and market linkages. This bill seeks to address that gap by establishing a National Program for Malunggay Industry Development supported by a dedicated inter-agency committee, a five-year framework for development, and a comprehensive industry roadmap. The proposed bill creates a Malunggay Industry Development Committee chaired by the Secretary of Agriculture, with the Secretary of Science and Technology as Vice- Chairperson, and composed of the Secretaries of Trade and Industry, Health, Interior and Local Government, and Education, together with representatives from state universities and colleges, farmers’ groups, and the private sector. The Committee is tasked to formulate a five-year Malunggay Framework for Development, validated and updated annually, which shall guide the harmonized implementation of policies and programs across four strategic pillars: productivity improvement, research and development, market promotion and development, and extension services. The Committee shall likewise prepare a Malunggay Industry Roadmap in consultation with all industry players, to be updated every five years. Under the Framework, productivity improvement programs shall include the identification of optimal malunggay species and variants, the establishment of suitable planting areas, the creation of communal fields for marginalized communities, and the initiation of alternative livelihood projects. Research and development efforts shall focus on validating and maximizing malunggay’s nutritional and medicinal properties, supporting the development of science-based standards and technical regulations, surveying international market potential, and exploring malunggay’s applications in biofuel, animal feed, and agricultural inputs. The DA, DOST, and concerned state universities and colleges are directed to identify appropriate species for product development and establish processing facilities in suitable planting areas, while the DA shall determine proper agricultural practices and ensure conformity with applicable food safety and industry standards. The Department of Finance, in collaboration with the Land Bank, the Development Bank of the Philippines, and other financial institutions, shall provide financing modalities for malunggay-based industries, and concerned agencies shall prioritize the development and harmonization of Philippine National Standards for malunggay products across primary, processed, and non-food industrial categories. The establishment of a national malunggay industry program represents a strategic investment in one of the country’s most promising and underutilized agricultural assets. By providing a coordinated policy framework, institutional support, research backing, and market development assistance, this bill will unlock the full economic potential of malunggay for Filipino farmers, entrepreneurs, and communities, while contributing to national food security, public health, and export competitiveness. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10248
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL TRADITIONAL ARTS APPRENTICESHIP AND SUCCESSION PROGRAM FOR CULTURAL MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs), PROVIDING FUNDING THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has a strong cultural and creative base, and traditional cultural expression remains one of the living foundations of that economy. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the country’s creative economy reached PhP 1.94 trillion in 2024, accounting for 7.3 percent of GDP, while creative industries employed 7.51 million Filipinos.1 Republic Act No. 11904, or the Philippine Creative Industries Development Act, likewise declares it a policy of the State to promote and support the development of Philippine creative industries by strengthening the capacities of creative firms, artists, artisans, creators, workers, and indigenous cultural communities. 2 Nevertheless, many heritage-based enterprises are under pressure not only from market competition, but from a more basic threat: the weakening of intergenerational skills transfer. A recent Philippine case study on cultural MSMEs found that many traditional enterprises face difficulties in attracting younger generations, maintaining a skilled workforce, and planning for succession, even when market demand and cultural value remain present. The same study emphasized that the decline of artisanal skills and the absence of formal training pathways are among the major constraints on the long- term sustainability of weaving, embroidery, food traditions, and other heritage-based enterprises.3 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, “Philippine Creative Economy Expands by 8.7 Percent in 2024, Accounted for 7.3 Percent of Gross Domestic Product,” press release, March 20, 2025. 2 Republic of the Philippines, Republic Act No. 11904, Philippine Creative Industries Development Act, July 27, 2022. 3 June Ann J. Casimiro, Karenina B. Romualdo, and Via Shane R. Santiago, Innovation Strategies in Traditional Cultural Expressions MSMEs in the Philippines: A Case Study, PIDS Discussion Paper Series No. 2024-48 (Quezon City: Philippine Institute for Development Studies, December 2024). This proposed measure responds directly to that structural gap. The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 seeks to reinvigorate job creation, reduce poverty, strengthen MSMEs, expand domestic production, foster regional industrialization, strengthen academe-industry linkages, and improve access to science, technology, and innovation. A national traditional arts apprenticeship and succession program advances these goals in a concrete and place-based way: it creates livelihood opportunities, supports labor-intensive community enterprises, strengthens local supplier bases, and preserves skills that are both culturally significant and economically productive. 45 This proposal, moreover, is consistent with global safeguarding practice. UNESCO has long emphasized that traditional craftsmanship depends on transmission from generation to generation, and that one proven way of reinforcing such systems is to support instruction and apprenticeship. 6 UNESCO-supported programs in Uzbekistan, for example, have combined traditional craftsmanship training with design and entrepreneurship in order to improve craft quality, develop creativity, and create sustainable income opportunities rooted in heritage.7 Other countries have likewise adopted practical apprenticeship models for heritage skills. In Scotland, the government reported support for a traditional skills programme and a Historic Skills Investment Plan to increase the number of apprentices developing the skills needed to conserve and manage the historic environment. 8 In the United States, the National Park Service runs the Traditional Trades Advancement Program, under which participants receive immersive, hands-on training alongside experienced practitioners in trades such as masonry, carpentry, monuments, and woodcrafting to preserve cultural resources and build career pathways.9 These examples show that heritage apprenticeship is not merely a cultural project; it is also a workforce, enterprise, and local development strategy. For young Filipinos, this bill creates paid pathways into skilled work and entrepreneurship. For master artisans, it recognizes teaching and transmission as valuable labor deserving public support. For families and communities, it helps sustain 4 National Economic and Development Authority, Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 Primer (Pasig City: NEDA, 2022). 5 National Economic and Development Authority, Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028, Chapter 6: Revitalize Industry (Pasig City: NEDA, 2022). 6 UNESCO, “Traditional Craftsmanship,” Intangible Cultural Heritage, accessed April 23, 2026. 7 UNESCO, “National Training in Traditional Craftsmanship, Design and Entrepreneurship for Safeguarding Intangible Cultural Heritage in Uzbekistan,” April 4, 2024. 8 Scottish Government, Programme for Government 2019 to 2020, “Improving Outcomes Through Our Public Services,” September 3, 2019. 9 U.S. National Park Service, “Traditional Trades Advancement Program,” Historic Preservation Training Center, accessed April 21, 2026. cultural MSMEs, local employment, and regional identity. For the State, it offers a practical way to align heritage protection with economic development. International labor research also shows that apprenticeship systems rooted in enterprises can be cost- effective because training already occurs where tools, materials, and production knowledge exist, while apprentices gain practical skills, work discipline, client exposure, and employability.10 This bill therefore seeks to establish a National Traditional Arts Apprenticeship and Succession Program for cultural MSMEs, with paid apprentice slots, master-artisan teaching grants, school-to-enterprise pathways, LGU-supported community training centers, and enterprise succession support. In doing so, it affirms a simple but urgent principle: that the survival of Filipino traditional arts requires not only recognition, but deliberate investment in the next generation who will practice, sustain, and build livelihoods fro

label: HB 10249
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING RISK-INFORMED RELOCATION AND RESILIENT HUMAN SETTLEMENTS PLANNING IN DISASTER-PRONE AREAS, PROVIDING STANDARDS FOR SAFE RELOCATION SITES AND RESETTLEMENT PROGRAMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines remains one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world, facing recurring typhoons, floods, landslides, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and climate-related hazards that repeatedly displace communities and destroy livelihoods. In 2024 alone, the country recorded around nine million disaster displacements, while millions more remain vulnerable to repeated exposure due to unsafe housing and settlements.1 Over the past decade, nearly 43 million disaster displacements were recorded in the Philippines, among the highest in Southeast Asia.^2 2 Despite continued government relocation efforts, many resettlement sites suffer from inadequate infrastructure, poor access to livelihoods, insufficient public services, and exposure to new environmental risks. As a result, some affected families return to danger zones out of economic necessity. This measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a more comprehensive, risk-informed, and climate-resilient framework for relocation and settlement planning. The bill recognizes that relocation is not merely a housing concern but also a matter of public safety, poverty reduction, and sustainable development. By requiring hazard assessments, proper site selection, access to utilities and social services, and stronger inter-agency coordination, the measure aims to ensure that relocated families are transferred to safe, livable, and sustainable communities. ASEAN neighbors have likewise adopted similar approaches. Viet Nam has implemented planned relocation programs in flood-prone areas of the Mekong Delta as 1 Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, 2025 Global Report on Internal Displacement (Geneva: IDMC, 2025). 2 Asian Development Bank, “Disasters Trigger More Displacements than Conflicts, Says New ADB-IDMC Report,” October 15, 2024. part of its climate adaptation strategy, while Indonesia has undertaken permanent relocation programs following major volcanic disasters.^3 3 These experiences demonstrate the growing regional recognition that resilient and well-planned relocation policies are essential to protecting vulnerable communities from increasing climate and disaster risks. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. BENITEZ 3 Jane McAdam Chun, Planned Relocations in the Mekong Delta (Brookings Institution, 2015); Reuters, “Indonesia to Permanently Relocate Thousands of Residents after Mount Lewotobi Laki-laki Eruptions,” November 6, 2024. label: HB 10250
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INCLUSION OF INDIGENOUS ROOT CROPS INTO THE NATIONAL FEEDING PROGRAM FOR UNDERNOURISHED CHILDREN IN PUBLIC DAY CARE, KINDERGARTEN AND ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11037, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MASUSTANSYANG PAGKAIN PARA SA BATANG PILIPINO ACT,” PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Malnutrition among Filipino children has long been one of the most persistent challenges to the Philippine public health system. Through Republic Act No. 11037, or the “Masustansyang Pagkain Para sa Batang Pilipino Act,” the government established the National Feeding Program, which addresses this concern by providing fortified meals to undernourished children in public day care centers and elementary schools. However, one category of nutrient-dense food has remained conspicuously absent from its implementing menus: indigenous root crops. The Philippines is home to a rich diversity of indigenous root crops such as kamote, gabi, ube, and kamoteng kahoy, which have long served as traditional sources of carbohydrates, dietary fiber, vitamins, and minerals. These crops are climate-resilient, adaptable to a wide range of growing conditions, and cultivated by thousands of smallholder farmers across the country. Despite their nutritional and economic value, indigenous root crops remain underutilized in government feeding programs, representing a missed opportunity to strengthen the nutritional content of the program's menus while supporting local agriculture. This measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 11037 by mandating the inclusion of indigenous root crops and root crop-based products in the cycle menus of the National Feeding Program, subject to regional availability and cultural appropriateness. The bill further promotes the cultivation of indigenous root crops through the Gulayan sa Paaralan Program and encourages the prioritization of accredited root crop farmers’ cooperatives and enterprises in the procurement of feeding program requirements. By linking child nutrition initiatives with local agricultural development, this proposed measure advances the objectives of food security, sustainable agriculture, rural economic development, and improved nutrition outcomes for Filipino children. This bill introduces a specific, evidence-based, culturally grounded mandate that the law’s current text does not contain—one that draws on a food source already familiar to, and grown by, Filipino communities nationwide. The passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. label: HB 10251
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING FISCAL INCENTIVES FOR THE ACQUISITION AND INSTALLATION OF SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9513, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "RENEWABLE ENERGY ACT OF 2008," THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution declares that all natural resources are owned by the State and that their exploration, development, and utilization shall be under its full control and supervision for the benefit of the Filipino people. Complementing this mandate, Article II, Section 16 directs the State to protect and advance the people's right to a balanced and healthful ecology. These constitutional principles underscore the duty of government to harness the country's abundant renewable energy resources in a manner that promotes economic development, environmental sustainability, and the general welfare of the people. The Philippines is among the countries most richly endowed with solar energy. Its tropical location provides abundant sunlight throughout the year, making solar power one of the nation's most accessible and inexhaustible natural resources. At the same time, the country continues to face rising electricity demand driven by economic growth, urbanization, industrial expansion, and digital transformation. Despite significant advances in renewable energy technology, many Filipino households and businesses remain dependent on increasingly costly and volatile sources of electricity, resulting in higher living costs and reduced business competitiveness. Unlike conventional power generation, solar energy possesses a uniquely democratic character. The sun shines on every home, farm, school, business, and public building regardless of location or income. Rooftops that once served only as shelter can become productive assets capable of generating clean and affordable electricity. Properly harnessed, solar energy enables ordinary consumers to reduce their electricity expenses, improve their energy security, and participate directly in the country's transition toward a more sustainable energy future. The principal obstacle to widespread solar adoption is no longer the technology itself, but its upfront cost. While solar energy systems generate substantial savings over their operational life, the initial investment remains beyond the financial reach of many Filipino families, farmers, micro, small, and medium enterprises, and institutions. Consequently, the benefits of solar energy have largely been confined to those with sufficient capital to absorb the initial expense. This measure seeks to democratize access to solar energy by reducing these financial barriers through a comprehensive package of fiscal incentives. It establishes a Solar Investment Tax Credit, additional income tax deductions, exemptions from Value-Added Tax and Real Property Tax for qualified installations, duty-free importation of eligible solar equipment, and incentives to encourage domestic manufacturing of solar technologies. These measures are intended to make solar energy ownership more affordable while stimulating investments, creating employment, strengthening local manufacturing, and expanding the country's renewable energy industry. More importantly, this bill recognizes that fiscal incentives are not merely tax expenditures but strategic investments in the nation's long-term economic and energy future. Every solar installation reduces pressure on the electric grid, lowers dependence on imported fossil fuels, strengthens energy resilience, and contributes to a cleaner environment. The resulting savings for consumers, increased private investment, and broader economic activity have the potential to generate benefits that substantially outweigh the foregone revenues from the incentives provided under this Act. Throughout history, transformative technologies have reshaped societies only after they became accessible to ordinary citizens. Electricity, telecommunications, and digital technologies accelerated economic development because public policy encouraged their widespread adoption. Solar energy presents a similar opportunity. By lowering the cost of adoption through well-designed fiscal incentives, government can accelerate the transition toward a future where clean, affordable, and reliable electricity is within the reach of every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 10252
title: AN ACT DECLARING JULY 7 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CUENCA, PROVINCE OF BATANGAS, TO COMMEMORATE THE LIFE, HEROISM, AND LEGACY OF REVOLUTIONARY LEADER COLONEL PEDRO PASIA, TO BE KNOWN AS "COL. PEDRO PASIA DAY"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Colonel Pedro Pasia was one of Cuenca, Batangas' most distinguished sons and a revolutionary leader who rendered exemplary service during the Philippine struggle for independence. His courage, patriotism, and leadership significantly contributed to the revolutionary movement and remain an enduring source of pride and inspiration for the people of Cuenca. Recognizing his invaluable contribution to Philippine history, the National Government previously declared July 7, 1971 a special public holiday in the Municipality of Cuenca through Proclamation No. 874 (1971) in commemoration of his heroism. More recently, the Sangguniang Bayan of Cuenca enacted a local ordinance institutionalizing the annual observance of "Col. Pedro Pasia Day" and adopted Resolution No. 2026-213 requesting the enactment of a national law declaring July 7 of every year as a permanent local special holiday. It is fitting that the State permanently recognize Colonel Pedro Pasia's legacy by enacting legislation declaring July 7 of every year a special working holiday in the Municipality of Cuenca. Such recognition will strengthen historical awareness, promote patriotism among future generations, and preserve the municipality's rich revolutionary heritage. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 10253
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL LEAVE BENEFITS TO PARENTS AND LEGAL GUARDIANS OF CHILDREN WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution declares that the family is the foundation of the nation. It likewise mandates the State to strengthen the family's solidarity and actively promote its total development. In fulfillment of this Constitutional principle, government measures must not only protect the rights of children with disabilities but also empower the families who bear the primary responsibility for their care, development, and well-being. Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, as amended, affirms the State's commitment to the rehabilitation, self-development, self-reliance, and integration of persons with disabilities into mainstream society. These laws emphasize that the realization of the rights of children with disabilities is not the sole responsibility of the government, but of the family, the community and the society as a while. However, while the law recognizes the indispensable role of families, it does not provide sufficient employment support to parents and legal guardians who must regularly accompany their children to medical consultations, therapy sessions, rehabilitation programs, educational assessments, and other interventions essential to their development. Raising a child with disability requires extraordinary time, commitment, and financial resources. Parents and legal guardians often face the difficult choice between fulfilling their employment obligations and attending to the specialized needs of their children. Frequent medical appointments, rehabilitation therapies, individualized educational planning, and government transactions related to disability services commonly require the physical presence of a parent or primary caregiver. In the absence of dedicated leave benefits, many caregivers are compelled to exhaust their existing leave credits, forego income, or even risk their employment in order to fulfill these responsibilities. Recognizing these realities, this measure seeks to institutionalize a ten (10)-day paid Caregiver's Leave for qualified parents and legal guardians of children with disabilities in both the public and private sectors. The proposed leave shall be separate from existing leave privileges and may be availed of to accompany the child during medical treatment, rehabilitation, therapy, educational interventions, and other analogous circumstances requiring the caregiver's presence. The proposed Caregiver's Leave is an investment in the welfare and development of children with disabilities with their families. By enabling parents and legal guardians to actively participate in their children's care without jeopardizing their employment, the State reinforces the constitutional recognition of the family as the primary institution responsible for nurturing every Filipino child while advancing the objectives of inclusion, equal opportunity, and social justice. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KING GEORGE LEANDRO ANTONIO V. label: HB 10254
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE CAREER PROGRESSION AND SPECIALIZATION PROGRAM AND CREDIT ACCUMULATION AND TRANSFER SYSTEM (CPSP- CATS), ESTABLISHING THE CPSP-CATS COMMITTEE AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Filipino professional workforce plays a critical role in nation-building, economic growth, public service delivery, and global competitiveness. As industries become increasingly specialized and technology-driven, professionals are expected not only to maintain competence in their respective fields but also to continuously develop advanced skills, specialized expertise, and interdisciplinary competencies. However, while the country's regulatory framework provides mechanisms for licensure and continuing professional development, there remains no comprehensive and institutionalized system that recognizes career progression, specialization pathways, and transferable professional qualifications across regulated professions. The increasing complexity of professional practice demands a more responsive framework that recognizes diverse career trajectories and promotes lifelong learning. Many professions now require structured post-licensure training, specialization programs, and competency-based qualifications that are not adequately captured under existing professional regulatory mechanisms. Without a unified system for recognizing and transferring professional competencies and qualifications, opportunities for career advancement, professional mobility, and international recognition remain limited. This measure seeks to institutionalize the Career Progression and Specialization Program and Credit Accumulation and Transfer System (CPSP-CATS) for all regulated professions under the Professional Regulation Commission. The proposed legislation establishes an integrated framework for career progression, specialization, competency assessment, and credit recognition that aligns professional qualifications with the Philippine Qualifications Framework and internationally accepted standards of professional practice. The bill empowers the Professional Regulation Commission and the Professional Regulatory Boards to formulate profession-specific career progression pathways, accredit specialty societies and training institutions, establish professional practice standards, and implement mechanisms for recognizing accumulated professional learning and competencies. It likewise creates the necessary institutional 1 mechanisms—including the CPSP-CATS Program Management Committee, profession-specific CPSP-CATS Committees, Technical Working Groups, and dedicated secretariat support—to ensure effective and transparent implementation of the program. Furthermore, the proposed measure strengthens collaboration among government agencies, professional organizations, academic institutions, and industry stakeholders to ensure that professional qualifications remain responsive to evolving labor market demands and technological developments. By facilitating the transfer and recognition of professional competencies and qualifications, the bill promotes lifelong learning, enhances professional mobility, and supports both domestic and international competitiveness of Filipino professionals. Institutionalizing career progression and specialization pathways will not only benefit individual professionals but will also contribute to higher standards of professional practice, improved public service delivery, and greater confidence in the competence and integrity of Philippine professionals across all sectors. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 10255
title: AN ACT AMENDING PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 2010, ОTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CHARTER OF BENGUET STATE UNIVERSITY”, TO PROVIDE FOR A COMPREHENSIVE DUTY AND TAX EXEMPTION ON REVENUES AND ASSETS ACTUALLY, DIRECTLY, AND EXCLUSIVELY USED FOR INSTRUCTION, RESEARCH, EXTENSION, PRODUCTION, OR IN FURTHERANCE THEREOF, AND FOR THE RETROACTIVE APPLICATION THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution provides that all revenues and assets of non-stock, non-profit educational institutions, directly, and exclusively used for educational purposes shall be exempt from taxes and duties. This constitutional policy recognizes the vital role of educational institutions in nation-building and seeks to ensure that resources intended for instructions, research, extension, and related educational functions are devoted to the advancement of learning and public service. Created under Presidential Decree No. 2010, Benguet State University (BSU) serves as the premier state university in the Cordillera Region, providing quality education, conducting research, undertaking extension services, and promoting innovation and sustainable development for the benefit of the Region and the nation. While its Charter grants certain tax exemptions, the scope of such exemptions has not been expressly expanded to comprehensively cover all revenues and income generated from university assets and lawful income- generating activities that are devoted to its educational mandate. At present, Benguet State University is confronted with tax assessments imposed by the Bureau of Internal Revenue on revenues generated from the utilization of its assets and income-generating activities, including rental income. Under the existing legal framework and prevailing jurisprudence, the University’s claim for exemption from such taxes remains subject to limitations that constrain its ability to fully maximize resources intended for its core functions of instructions, research, extension, production, and public service. The revenues generated by the University from its lawful undertakings are not intended for private gain but are reinvested in the improvement of academic programs, research initiatives, extension services, institutional development, and other activities that directly support the University’s educational mission. The imposition of taxes on these revenues diminishes resources that would otherwise be utilized to enhance the delivery of quality education and public service. Considering that the issue pertains to the scope and extent of the tax exemptions granted under the University’s Charter and related laws, a legislative amendment appears to be the most appropriate and enduring remedy. The proposed amendment expressly extends exemption from all forms of taxes, duties, fees, and charges on revenues and assets of Benguet State University that are actually, directly, and exclusively used for instruction, research, extension, production, and other activities in furtherance of its educational purposes. It likewise provides for the retroactive application of such exemption to qualified assessments, claims, and obligations, thereby ensuring consistency with the constitutional policy favoring educational institutions. By providing legal clarity and minimizing future disputes concerning tax treatment of university revenues and assets, this measure will strengthen the fiscal autonomy of Benguet State University and enable it to devote a greater portion of its resources to educational excellence, research and innovation, community development, and public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G.
