label: HB 10256
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11192, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CORDILLERA STATE INSTITUTE OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION ACT” RENAMING THE INSTITUTE AS THE CORDILLERA STATE POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE (CSPI), GRANTING IT GREATER INSTITUTIONAL AND FISCAL AUTONOMY, ESTABLISHING A BOARD OF TRUSTEES, AND PROVIDING FOR THE COLLECTION OF FEES AND OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute Charter Amendments Act”. SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to strengthen public higher education institutions by promoting academic excellence, institutional autonomy, fiscal sustainability, research and innovation, and industry-responsive technical and professional education. Towards this end, the Cordillera State Institute of Technical Education shall be recognized and strengthened as the Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute. SEC. 3. Renaming of the Institute and Establishment of the Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute (CSPI). The Cordillera State Institute of Technical Education (CSITE) created under Republic Act No 11192 is hereby renamed and established as the Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute (CSPI), hereinafter referred to as the Institute. All references to the Cordillera State Institute of Technical Education in Republic Act No 11192 and other laws, executive issuances, rules and regulations shall hereafter refer to the Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11192 consolidated the public technical-vocational institutions of the Cordillera Administrative Region into the Cordillera State Institute of Technical Education (CSITE). While this integration was a significant administrative achievement, the resulting institute continues to operate under structural limitations that prevent it from fully meeting the region’s need for high- level, industry-responsive technical education. The present organizational and governance structure of the Institute is inadequate to meet the increasing demands of higher education, research, innovation, and industry-responsive skills development. This measure then seeks to amend Republic Act No 11192 to incorporate critical reforms that will transform the institute into a true polytechnic institution, to be known as the Cordillera State Polytechnic Institute (CSPI). The bill likewise grants the Institute greater institutional and fiscal autonomy, establishes a Board of Trustees as its highest policymaking body, and authorizes the collection and retention of reasonable fees and other lawful income to strengthen its financial sustainability and improve the delivery of academic and support services These reforms are intended to empower the Institute to pursue excellence in technical, technological, professional, and applied higher education, research extension, and innovation while ensuring accountability, transparency, and responsiveness to the educational and developmental priorities of the Cordillera Region and the nation. It is a deliberate and necessary shift in institutional identity, academic scope, and societal aspiration. A polytechnic institute is distinguished by its comprehensive and multi- disciplinary approach to technical education. It moves beyond a singular focus on isolated trade skills toward the integration of theoretical knowledge with high- level practical application across a broad spectrum of technologies, including engineering technology, applied sciences, and industrial arts. The CSPI will offer a seamless continuum of programs, from foundational skills training to advanced technical diplomas, and foster an environment of applied research, innovation, and technology incubation. The institute will not only produce skilled workers, but technologist, supervisors, and innovators who can drive the region’s economic development and attract higher-value industries, hence, ensuring the Cordillera workforce to possess analytical capability, practical mastery, and creative problem-solving required by the contemporary labor market. To operationalize and sustain this enhanced institutional identity, this measure provides for a genuine fiscal autonomy. The present financial management of the Institute being directly supervised and controlled by TESDA hampers the timely maintenance of advanced polytechnic facilities, the acquisition of modern industrial-grade equipment, and the swift implementation of curricular improvements that require immediate funding. By establishing CSPI as a corporate body with a dedicated revolving fund, it will be liberated from this restrictive financial framework and empowered to retain and deploy its income directly toward strategic institutional priorities, responding rapidly to industry demands without wholly dependent on the annual national budget cycle. Furthermore, the creation of an autonomous Board of Trustees composed of multi-sectoral stakeholders replaces the exclusive supervision of the TESDA. This governance body will bring together representatives from government, industry, labor, and the local community to ensure that the Institute’s strategic direction is deeply rooted in the socioeconomic realities and development priorities of the Cordillera Region. Moreover, the bill establishes an unequivocal statutory basis for the assessment and collection of reasonable fees for all program offerings. This will provide a steady supplementary resource stream that will directly support the continuous upgrading of curriculum, the professional development of its faculty- trainers, and the provision of scholarships for the youth of the Cordillera, particularly those from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, ensuring that access to high quality polytechnic education remains equitable. This measure also addresses a critical gap in the current educational architecture of the region by providing a clear statutory mandate for CSPI to develop and implement ladderized diploma to degree programs. Under the trifocalized education system, the articulation between technical-vocational education and higher education has long been hampered by the absence of enforceable mechanisms that require higher education institutions to recognize and credit TVET qualifications. The Philippine Qualifications Framework and the Ladderized Education Act provide the policy foundation for seamless progression between TESDA and CHED qualifications, yet the implementation of credit transfer arrangements remain largely dependent on the willingness of individual institutions. By explicitly mandating CSPI to integrate its TESDA- registered diploma programs with CHED-recognized baccalaureate degree offerings, this bill creates a tangible, institution-based model for ladderization. This provision established CSPI as a singular institution where a student may enter a technical-vocational track, earn a TESDA diploma, and progress toward a full baccalaureate degree within the same system, with the institute seeking the appropriate recognition from each trifocal agency for its respective programs. This approach does not disturb the trifocalized structure but instead operationalizes it within a single, coherent institution, providing the youth of the Cordillera with clear, accessible, and structured pathways for upward educational and social mobility. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. DOMOGAN Republic of the Philippines HOUSE

label: HB 10258
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING REGULATION IN THE ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 6, 43, 45 AND 71 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), restructured the electric power industry by dividing it into four (4) sectors—generation, transmission, distribution, and supply—and by adopting a regulatory framework intended to promote competition, market development, consumer protection, and the penalization of market power abuse. 1 EPIRA likewise declared that the generation sector, while a “business affected with public interest,” “shall not be considered a public utility operation,” and that entities engaged in power generation and supply of electricity “shall not be required to secure a national franchise.”2 The Supreme Court has acknowledged that this legislative classification produces concrete legal consequences, including the removal of power generation from the ambit of local franchise taxes that may be imposed only on businesses “enjoying a franchise.”3 At the same time, jurisprudence addressing constitutional challenges to EPIRA’s design recognizes that EPIRA continues to treat the generation and supply sectors as businesses affected with public interest and subjects industry participants to rules against market power abuse, cartelization, and other anti-competitive or discriminatory behavior.4 While EPIRA contains safeguards against harmful monopoly and market power abuse, including ERC authority to monitor and take measures against cartelization and other anti-competitive conduct, continued sector experience has underscored the need for stronger structural safeguards, transparency requirements, 1 Sec. 4 of RA 9136. 2 Id. At Sec 6. 3 G.R. No. 180654, National Power Corporation v. Provincial Government of Bataan, et al, March 6, 2017 4 G.R. No. 210245Colmenares, et al. v. Energy Regulatory Commission, et al. August 3, 2021 Page 1 of 14 and more effective enforcement tools to protect consumers from abuse and to promote fair competition. Further, EPIRA’s design places policy formulation and rulemaking within the Department of Energy (DOE) while the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) enforces the implementing framework within its delegated regulatory and quasi- judicial powers; administrative issuances must remain germane to EPIRA’s objectives and cannot contradict the statute. Accordingly, this bill seeks to: (1) strengthen the legal framework governing the generation sector by treating generation as a public utility operation while implementing a workable authorization regime, and by enhancing transparency and enforcement against market power abuse; (2) strengthen safeguards against structural self-dealing and cross-ownership between generation and distribution, and prohibit prohibited affiliate supply arrangements subject to due process and a clear transition; (3) reinforce ERC powers and disclosure requirements in relation to pass-through items and consumer protection, including clearer accountability for system losses; and (4) provide transitory provisions to ensure uninterrupted service and orderly compliance. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. label: HB 10259
title: AN ACT RESTRICTING SOCIAL MEDIA ACCESS TO CHILDREN FIFTEEN (15) YEARS OLD AND BELOW, MANDATING AGE VERIFICATION MECHANISMS FOR SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR NON-COMPLIANCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid expansion of social media use among children has raised significant and well-documented concerns regarding exposure to harmful and inappropriate content, cyberbullying, exploitation risks, mental health impacts, data privacy violations, and the effects of algorithm-driven and engagement-based platform design that may contribute to addictive use patterns. Current platform incentives are largely directed toward maximizing user engagement and time spent on platforms, which may not necessarily align with the developmental needs and welfare of children. International policy developments, including Australia’s Online Safety Amendment (social media Minimum Age) Bill 2024, reflect a growing recognition of the need for a systems-based regulatory approach that places responsibility on social media service providers to implement safeguards against underage access, rather than relying solely on user or parental compliance. This measure seeks to establish a minimum age requirement for social media account access and to mandate that Covered Social Media Service Providers implement reasonable and proportionate age assurance measures to prevent access by children fifteen (15) years of age and below. This bill does not intend to restrict access to digital learning platforms, educational technologies, or private messaging services, but rather to regulate access to social media platforms that facilitate public or semi-public user-generated content and algorithm- driven content distribution. In line with Article II, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates the State to protect the youth and promote their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being, this measure establishes regulatory accountability on social media service providers operating within the Philippines for ensuring safer digital environments for children. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10260
title: AN ACT STANDARDIZING THE FEES FOR THE ISSUANCE, REPRODUCTION, AND CERTIFICATION OF COURT DOCUMENTS, AND GRANTING FEE EXEMPTION TO INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to court documents is a core function of court administration, ensuring that records of judicial proceedings are properly issued, reproduced, and certified in a manner that is consistent, reliable, and accessible to requesting parties. These documents form part of the official record of the judiciary and are routinely required for legal, administrative, and documentary purposes, including compliance with court processes and other lawful transactions. In practice, however, the absence of a uniform and clearly regulated fee structure for the issuance, reproduction, and certification of court documents has resulted in variation in charges across different courts and offices. This lack of standardization may lead to administrative inconsistency, uncertainty in public service delivery, and inefficiencies in the processing of requests for court records. This measure seeks to address these concerns by establishing a standardized and reasonable fee structure applicable to all courts within the Philippine judicial system, thereby promoting uniformity in the delivery of court document services and ensuring predictable and transparent administrative procedures. The bill likewise incorporates a defined exemption mechanism for Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs), consistent with Republic Act No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act of 1997. This exemption is intended as an administrative accommodation within court document services, implemented through a clear verification process, without altering existing rules on judicial proceedings or court jurisdiction. By institutionalizing standardized fees alongside a clearly defined exemption framework, this measure strengthens administrative consistency within the judiciary, improves the efficiency of court record services, and clarifies the parameters for the issuance, reproduction, and certification of judicial documents. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10261
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES FROM FEES IN THE PROCUREMENT OF OFFICIAL SCHOOL DOCUMENTS FROM ALL EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Equal access to opportunities is a fundamental component of social justice and inclusive development. However, for many Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs), access to higher education, employment, professional licensure, scholarships, and government assistance is often constrained not only by geographic and socioeconomic disadvantages, but also by the financial costs associated with securing official school documents required for such opportunities. Official academic records, including transcripts of records, certificates, diplomas, and other school-issued credentials, are essential documentary requirements for educational advancement, employment, and participation in public and private sector opportunities. Although these documents are administrative in nature, the corresponding issuance and processing fees may impose an additional and avoidable burden on Indigenous Peoples, particularly those from geographically isolated, disadvantaged, and underserved communities. Consistent with the State’s constitutional mandate to promote social justice and protect the rights and welfare of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples under Republic Act No. 8371, otherwise known as the “Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act of 1997” (IPRA), this measure seeks to remove financial barriers by exempting Indigenous Peoples from the payment of fees in the procurement of official school documents from all educational institutions, whether public or private. This exemption recognizes that access to essential academic credentials should not be hindered by economic constraints, and affirms the State’s obligation to ensure equal opportunity in education, employment, and public service participation. By institutionalizing this policy, the State strengthens inclusive development and enhances the capacity of Indigenous Peoples to fully participate in national social and economic life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10262
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A FUEL SUBSIDY OR GASOLINE ALLOWANCE FOR PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLE (PUV) DRIVERS AND OPERATORS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public Utility Vehicle (PUV) drivers and operators serve as the backbone of the country's transportation system, providing millions of Filipinos with accessible and affordable mobility every day. Their services are indispensable to economic productivity, commerce, education, healthcare access, and the overall functioning of communities throughout the nation. Despite their critical role, PUV drivers and operators remain among the sectors most vulnerable to fluctuations in fuel prices. Sudden and sustained increases in the cost of petroleum products significantly reduce their daily earnings, increase operational expenses, and threaten the viability of public transportation services. In many instances, transport operators are unable to immediately adjust fares to reflect rising fuel costs, resulting in diminished income for drivers and financial strain on transport operators. While the government has periodically implemented fuel subsidy programs to mitigate the effects of fuel price increases, such interventions are often temporary, reactive, and dependent on available appropriations. The absence of a permanent and institutionalized mechanism leaves transport workers uncertain about the availability of assistance during periods of economic instability and prolonged fuel price surges. There is therefore a compelling need to establish a sustainable and predictable fuel subsidy program that provides timely assistance to qualified PUV drivers and operators. Such a program will help safeguard their livelihoods, maintain the continuity of public transportation services, and protect commuters from the adverse effects of transport disruptions. Moreover, institutionalizing fuel assistance will contribute to economic resilience by ensuring that public transportation remains operational and accessible despite fluctuations in global energy markets. This proposed measure seeks to establish a Permanent Public Utility Vehicle (PUV) Fuel Subsidy Program that will provide targeted, data-driven, and digitally administered fuel assistance to eligible beneficiaries. The program shall utilize modern payment systems, transparent beneficiary databases, and clear eligibility criteria to ensure the efficient, accountable, and equitable distribution of government support. It also aims to strengthen coordination among relevant government agencies to enhance monitoring, evaluation, and program effectiveness. By providing a reliable safety net for PUV drivers and operators, this measure promotes transportation stability, protects the welfare of transport workers, supports economic activity, and advances the State's commitment to a responsive and inclusive public transportation system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10263
title: AN ACT PROMOTING DIGITAL, MEDIA, AND INFORMATION LITERACY AMONG FILIPINOS, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DIGITAL LITERACY PROGRAM, STRENGTHENING RESPONSIBLE DIGITAL CITIZENSHIP, INTEGRATING DIGITAL LITERACY IN EDUCATION AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT INITIATIVES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The digital age has fundamentally transformed the way Filipinos learn, communicate, conduct business, access government services, and participate in society. With the widespread availability of the internet, social media platforms, digital applications, and emerging technologies, digital tools have become an integral part of daily life. From education and employment to commerce and civic engagement, digital technologies now serve as essential instruments for personal and national development. However, the increasing reliance on digital platforms also highlights the growing need for digital literacy among all Filipinos. While access to technology continues to expand, many individuals still lack the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate the digital environment safely, responsibly, and effectively. The ability to use digital devices is no longer sufficient; citizens must also possess the capacity to critically evaluate information, protect their privacy and security, communicate respectfully online, understand their rights and responsibilities in digital spaces, and utilize technology in a productive and ethical manner. As more Filipinos engage in online activities, the consequences of irresponsible internet use become increasingly apparent. The careless sharing of unverified information, exposure to online scams and fraudulent schemes, cyberbullying, identity theft, privacy violations, and other harmful online practices underscore the need for greater awareness and education. Every internet user bears a corresponding responsibility to exercise good judgment, respect others, safeguard personal information, and contribute positively to online communities. Digital literacy is therefore not merely a technical skill but a fundamental life competency. It empowers individuals to become responsible digital citizens capable of making informed decisions, engaging constructively in online discourse, utilizing technology for learning and economic opportunities, and adapting to the demands of an increasingly digital society. It also strengthens national competitiveness by preparing the workforce for the digital economy and fostering innovation, entrepreneurship, and lifelong learning. Recognizing the vital role of digital literacy in nation-building, this measure seeks to establish a comprehensive national framework that promotes digital, media, and information literacy among Filipinos. It aims to cultivate responsible digital citizenship, encourage safe and ethical internet use, strengthen digital competencies across all sectors, and ensure that every Filipino is equipped to participate meaningfully and responsibly in the digital world. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10268
title: AN ACT REQUIRING ALL EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS TO PROCESS AND RELEASE SCHOOL RECORDS, TRANSCRIPTS OF RECORDS, DIPLOMAS, CERTIFICATIONS, AND OTHER ACADEMIC DOCUMENTS WITHIN THREE (3) WORKING DAYS FROM RECEIPT OF A COMPLETE REQUEST, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR NON-COMPLIANCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The timely issuance of academic records and credentials is essential to the educational, professional, and economic advancement of students and graduates. Documents such as transcripts of records, diplomas, certificates of graduation, certifications of enrollment, and other school records serve as indispensable requirements for employment, professional licensure examinations, scholarship applications, transfer to other educational institutions, overseas opportunities, and various government transactions. Despite advances in digital technology and records management systems, many educational institutions continue to subject students and graduates to prolonged and often unnecessary waiting periods before releasing these documents. While some schools are capable of processing requests within a matter of days, others require several weeks or even months before the requested records are made available. Such delays have become a recurring concern among students, graduates, and employers alike. In an era where information technology enables the rapid retrieval, verification, and transmission of records, lengthy processing periods can no longer be justified as a matter of routine administrative practice. The continued reliance on outdated procedures unnecessarily burdens students and graduates who are often faced with strict deadlines for employment, admissions, scholarships, board examinations, and other opportunities. In many instances, delayed issuance of academic documents has resulted in missed job opportunities, forfeited scholarships, deferred enrollment, and other avoidable setbacks. The growing digitalization of educational records, coupled with the government's ongoing efforts to improve bureaucratic efficiency and public service delivery, makes it both reasonable and necessary to establish a uniform standard for the processing of school documents. Educational institutions must be encouraged to modernize their records management systems and adopt procedures that prioritize efficiency, transparency, and responsiveness to the needs of students and graduates. This measure seeks to require all educational institutions to process and release academic documents within three (3) working days from receipt of a complete request, with a target of two (2) working days for institutions possessing digitized records. It further promotes online processing, transparency in service standards, accountability mechanisms, and appropriate sanctions for unreasonable delays. By ensuring prompt access to academic credentials, this bill upholds the rights of students and graduates, strengthens public trust in educational institutions, and aligns the education sector with modern standards of efficient public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10269
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THREATENING, HARASSING, COERCIVE, AND ABUSIVE DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES BY ONLINE LENDING APPLICATIONS, DIGITAL CREDIT PROVIDERS, FINANCING COMPANIES, LENDING COMPANIES, AND OTHER SIMILAR ENTITIES, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid advancement of digital technology has transformed the financial services landscape in the Philippines. Through smartphones, mobile applications, digital wallets, and online platforms, millions of Filipinos now enjoy unprecedented access to financial products and services, including loans, credit facilities, and cash advances. These technological developments have significantly expanded financial inclusion, particularly among individuals who have traditionally been underserved by conventional banking institutions. In recent years, however, the country has witnessed the proliferation of online lending applications and digital credit platforms that offer instant loans with minimal documentary requirements. While many of these platforms operate lawfully and provide valuable financial assistance to consumers, numerous reports have emerged concerning abusive, coercive, and unethical debt collection practices employed by certain lending applications and their agents. Borrowers have reported receiving threatening, intimidating, harassing, and humiliating messages through text messages, social media platforms, electronic mail, mobile applications, and other digital communication channels. Some collection agents have resorted to threats of imprisonment, public shaming, disclosure of personal information, unauthorized contact with family members, friends, employers, and colleagues, and the use of offensive, degrading, or coercive language in an effort to compel payment. The increasing sophistication of technology has likewise enabled certain entities to automate these abusive practices through mass messaging systems, artificial intelligence-powered communication tools, caller identification spoofing, and other technological means that amplify harassment and intimidation. These practices not only undermine the dignity and privacy of borrowers but also erode public confidence in the country's digital financial ecosystem. While existing laws provide certain protections against privacy violations and unfair business practices, there remains a need for a comprehensive legal framework specifically prohibiting the use of threats, intimidation, harassment, coercion, and digital abuse in the collection of debts by online lending applications, digital credit providers, and other similar entities. The State recognizes the right of lenders to collect legitimate obligations and to employ lawful means to recover debts. However, debt collection must be conducted in a manner that respects the dignity, privacy, rights, and welfare of borrowers. Financial innovation must not come at the expense of fundamental rights and protections guaranteed under the Constitution and laws of the Republic. This measure seeks to establish clear standards for ethical digital debt collection practices, prohibit abusive collection methods, provide effective remedies for aggrieved borrowers, strengthen regulatory oversight, and impose appropriate penalties upon violators. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10270
title: AN ACT CRIMINALIZING MALICIOUS AI-GENERATED IMPERSONATION, NON- CONSENSUAL DEEPFAKE SEXUAL CONTENT, ELECTION DISINFORMATION AND AI-ENABLED FRAUD; PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most transformative technologies of the modern era. Among its many applications is the ability to generate highly realistic synthetic content, commonly known as "deepfakes," which can mimic a person's face, voice, likeness, mannerisms, and speech with remarkable accuracy. While these technologies have legitimate uses in education, entertainment, accessibility, research, and innovation, they also present significant risks when employed for malicious and deceptive purposes. In recent years, the rapid proliferation of deepfake technologies has enabled the creation of fabricated videos, audio recordings, images, and other forms of synthetic media capable of misleading the public, damaging reputations, facilitating fraud, manipulating elections, and violating individual privacy and dignity. The accessibility of AI-powered content generation tools has made it increasingly difficult for ordinary citizens to distinguish authentic content from fabricated material. Of particular concern is the growing use of deepfakes to impersonate individuals without their consent. Criminal actors have utilized AI -generated voice cloning and video manipulation to deceive victims into transferring funds, divulging confidential information, or performing actions under false pretenses. Public officials, private citizens, business leaders, and ordinary Filipinos alike have become vulnerable to identity-based deception and fraud. The emergence of AI-generated election disinformation likewise poses a direct threat to democratic institutions. Fabricated speeches, manipulated campaign materials, and false representations of candidates or public officials may undermine informed public discourse, distort electoral processes, and erode public trust in democratic governance. Equally alarming is the increasing prevalence of non-consensual deepfake pornography. Individuals, particularly women and minors, have become targets of digitally manipulated explicit content created and distributed without their knowledge or consent. Such acts constitute grave violations of privacy, dignity, and personal security, often causing severe emotional, psychological, social, and economic harm. Existing laws on cybercrime, identity theft, fraud, privacy, and obscenity provide certain remedies but were enacted before the emergence of advanced generative AI technologies. There remains a need for a comprehensive legal framework specifically addressing malicious AI-generated impersonation, election- related deception, non-consensual deepfake sexual content, and AI-enabled fraud while preserving constitutional rights to free speech, artistic expression, satire, journalism, research, and innovation. This measure seeks to establish clear prohibitions against harmful uses of AI - generated synthetic media, impose appropriate penalties upon offenders, protect victims, strengthen public trust in digital information, and promote the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence in the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 10271
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF LILOY, PROVINCE OF ZAMBOANGA DEL NORTE, A SEPARATE SCHOOLS DIVISION OFFICE FOR THE THIRD DISTRICT OF ZAMBOANGA DEL NORTE, TO BE KNOWN AS THE ZAMBOANGA DEL NORTE- SCHOOLS DIVISION OFFICE II, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure seeks to establish a separate Schools Division Office for all basic education schools in the 3rd Legislative District of Zamboanga del Norte, to be located in the Municipality of Liloy, Province of Zamboanga del Norte. Schools division offices are the primary support structure in school operations. As such, they exercise direct administrative supervision over schools and align their functions and activities toward addressing the urgent problems at the school level. At present, the Schools Division Office of Zamboanga del Norte, which has jurisdiction over the basic education schools in the 3rd District of Zamboanga del Norte, is located in Dipolog City. However, the distance from Dipolog City to Leon B. Postigo, the northernmost municipality under the 3rd District of Zamboanga del Norte, is approximately 105.8 kilometers, with average travel time of 2 hours and 25 minutes. On the other hand, the distance from Dipolog City to Sibuco, the southernmost municipality of the district, is approximately 283.7 kilometers, with average travel time of 6 hours and 24 minutes. Not only is this great distance and long travel physically taxing on teachers and principals who file documents and report to the Division Office, it also wastes a lot of their valuable time which would have otherwise been used for preparing their lessons, checking their students’ works, and doing necessary works. Moreover, the Schools Division Office of Zamboanga del Norte has jurisdiction over 753 schools, 8,609 teachers, and 1,893 non-teaching employees. Ideally, a Schools Division should only comprise of 800 to 1000 teachers. This huge number of personnel under the existing Divisions Office creates difficulty in communication of immediate standard actions and memoranda. If this bill will be enacted, the existing Schools Division Office of Zamboanga del Norte will be divided into two. The Zamboanga del Norte- Schools Division Office I will retain supervision over the schools in the 1st and 2nd Legislative Districts of Zamboanga del Norte, with 414 schools, 4,659 teachers, and 119,245 enrollees. On the other hand, the proposed Zamboanga del Norte- Schools Division Office II will have supervision over the schools in the 3rd Legislative District of Zamboanga del Norte, with 336 schools, 3,950 teachers, and 108,355 enrollees. While still above the ideal composition of only 800-1000 teachers, the division of the existing Schools Division Office of Zamboanga del Norte will make it easier to manage and provide technical assistance to the teachers and personnel of the Department of Education in Zamboanga del Norte. It is also noteworthy that this proposal to create a separate Schools Division Office in the Third District of Zamboanga del Norte came from the existing Schools Division Office of Zamboanga del Norte itself. Thus, establishing a separate schools division office for the schools in the 3rd District of Zamboanga del Norte will not only help the teachers and principals, but will also improve the Department of Education’s desire to provide efficient, effective, and responsive services to the constituents. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ADRIAN MICHAEL A. label: HB 10273
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE PASS-THROUGH AND RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure was consistently filed by this Representation during the 15th, 16th, and 17th Congresses but was not enacted into law. The elimination of system losses has since become a policy priority of the current administration, as articulated by His Excellency, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., in his State of the Nation Address (SONA). It is without doubt that this proposal should now come into reality. Unburden the general public from shouldering the costs of losses it had nothing to do with, this is the intention of this proposal by completely removing the recoverable systems loss allowed to be charged by private electric distribution utilities and restrict recoverable composition of system losses into losses due to design fault and technical loss. Republic Act No. 7832 otherwise known as an “Act Penalizing the Pilferage of Electricity and Theft of Electric Power Transmission Lines/Material, Rationalizing system losses by phasing out pilferage losses as a component thereof, and for other purposes” was enacted in 8 December 1994. R.A. No. 7832 rationalizes the recoverable system losses of electric distributors by authorizing private utilities and rural electric cooperatives to pass on to consumers their respective system losses subject only to the ceiling rate. Subsequently, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 9136 otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, which authorized the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to determine the just and reasonable caps on the imposition of systems loss. Presently, private distribution utilities and rural electric cooperatives are allowed to pass on as much as maximum of 8.5% of the total kilowatt-hours purchased and generated, and maximum of 13% of the total kilowatt-hours purchased and generated, respectively, of their total system losses to the consumers. Systems losses may be non-technical (i.e. loss of electricity due to pilferage) or technical (i.e. loss of electricity in the form of heat due to design fault, administration inefficiencies as well as the electric consumption of the distributors for their operation). It comprises not less than five percent (5%) of the monthly electric bill and is likewise subject to the 12% Value-Added Tax (VAT). In spite of all these measures, electricity prices in the Philippines keep rising, so much so that in Southeast Asia, residential electricity costs in the Philippines are the highest. Unfortunately, instead of protecting the consumers against continuous increase of electricity prices, this provision of the EPIRA law is being taken advantage of by the big companies in the power industry in the guise of systems loss. These kinds of abuses are exactly the evil things sought to be prevented by this proposed measure. It was enshrined in the 1987 Philippine Constitution that the State shall free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services. Hence, legislators are duty bound to help the consuming public. In view thereof, the passage of this measure is earnestly urged. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10274
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING SENIOR CITIZENS COMMUNITY CENTERS AND ENHANCING THE REGULATORY AUTHORITY OF THE NATIONAL COMMISSION OF SENIOR CITIZENS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11350, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “NATIONAL COMMISSION OF SENIOR CITIZENS ACT” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Senior Citizens Community Centers Strengthening Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to uphold the dignity, well-being, and active participation of senior citizens by ensuring their access to quality, safe, accessible, and adequately equipped Senior Citizens Community Centers (SCCCs). The State likewise recognizes the need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for the establishment, operation, regulation, and monitoring of such centers through the National Commission of Senior Citizens (NCSC), in partnership with local government units (LGUs) and other government agencies. SEC. 3. Coverage. This Act shall apply to all cities and municipalities, government agencies, and other entities involved in the establishment, operation, management, and funding of Senior Citizens Community Centers. SEC. 4. Mandatory Establishment of Senior Citizens Community Centers (SCCC). – Every city and municipality shall establish and maintain at least one (1) fully functional Senior Citizens Community Center compliant with the standards prescribed by the NCSC.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7876, otherwise known as the Senior Citizens Center Act of the Philippines recognizes the important role of community-based centers in promoting the welfare, health, social participation, and productivity of senior citizens. These centers are intended to serve as venues for recreational, educational, health, livelihood, and other support services for older persons. Despite the clear intent of the law, many cities and municipalities still do not have operational Senior Citizens Community Centers, while others lack adequate facilities, personnel, programs, and resources. The absence of uniform standards and effective oversight has resulted in uneven implementation across local government units, thereby limiting the access of senior citizens to services that are essential to their well-being and active aging. With the enactment of Republic Act No. 11350 creating the National Commission of Senior Citizens (NCSC), the government now has a dedicated institution tasked with promoting and protecting the rights and welfare of older persons. However, the NCSC requires stronger regulatory authority and clearer mechanisms to ensure the proper establishment, operation, and maintenance of Senior Citizens Community Centers nationwide. This bill seeks to address these gaps by mandating the establishment of at least one (1) fully operational Senior Citizens Community Center in every city and municipality and by strengthening the oversight, regulatory and enforcement powers of the NCSC over these centers. This measure authorizes the NCSC to prescribe binding minimum standards, conduct announced and unannounced compliance audits, issue compliance directives, and impose administrative sanctions after due notice and hearing. The bill likewise creates a dedicated Senior Citizens Community Center Program Office under the NCSC to provide technical assistance, manage nationwide implementation, and maintain a comprehensive monitoring system. To support local government units, particularly low-income, geographically isolated, and disadvantaged municipalities, the measure establishes a Senior Citizens Community Center Development Fund that will provide performance- based financial assistance for the construction, rehabilitation, modernization, and operation of community centers. Furthermore, the bill institutionalizes monitoring, reporting, and accountability mechanisms, including referrals to the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the Commission on Audit (COA), and the Office of the Ombudsman in cases of persistent non-compliance or misuse of public funds. By strengthening community-based support systems for older persons, this measure advances the constitutional mandate to give priority to the needs of the elderly and promotes a society where senior citizens can live with dignity, security, participation, and improved quality of life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 10275
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ANNUAL INCOME TAX EXEMPTION THRESHOLD OF INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO ONE MILLION PESOS (P1,000,000.00) THROUGH A PHASED AND INDEXED TAX RELIEF SCHEDULE, INCREASING THE TAX- EXEMPT CEILING FOR THIRTEENTH MONTH PAY AND OTHER BENEFITS, STRENGTHENING TAX ADMINISTRATION TO PRESERVE REVENUE ADEQUACY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 24 AND 32 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every Filipino worker knows the value of honest labor. Each peso earned represents time away from family, daily sacrifice, and the hope of building a better life. Yet for many middle-income earners, the present tax system takes a significant portion of their income even before they are able to meet the basic needs of their households. The current individual income tax structure exempts only the first Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (PhP 250,000.00) of annual taxable income. This threshold was introduced under the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law, which took effect in 2018. While this reform provided much-needed relief at the time, the real value of the PhP 250,000.00 exemption has since been substantially eroded by inflation. Using the 2018-based Consumer Price Index as reference, the purchasing power of the peso has fallen to approximately Seventy-Five Centavos (PhP 0.75) as of the latest available 2026 data. In practical terms, the same basket of goods and services that could be purchased for PhP 250,000.00 in 2018 would require approximately PhP 333,000.00 today. Conversely, the present PhP 250,000.00 tax- free threshold now carries only about PhP 187,500.00 in 2018 purchasing power. Thus, without any legislative adjustment, inflation has effectively reduced the real value of the tax exemption by about Twenty-Five Percent (25%). This means that the tax system has become heavier on workers not because Congress imposed a new tax, but because the tax-free threshold has remained fixed while the cost of living has continued to rise. Food, fuel, transportation, rent, utilities, education, and health care have become more expensive, while the amount of income protected from taxation has stayed the same. This situation has created an unfair burden on the working and middle class. Many workers receive salary increases only to find that their additional income is reduced by taxes and inflation. This phenomenon, commonly known as bracket creep, weakens the purchasing power of Filipino families and undermines the purpose of wage increases and promotions. This bill seeks to provide meaningful and structural tax relief by increasing the annual tax-free income threshold of individual taxpayers to One Million Pesos (PhP 1,000,000.00) through a phased and fiscally responsible schedule. Under this measure, the tax-free threshold shall be increased as follows: PhP 400,000.00 beginning taxable year 2026; 1 PhP 800,000.00 beginning taxable year 2027; and PhP 1,000,000.00 beginning taxable year 2028 and thereafter. This measure is inspired by the principle that ordinary Filipinos should be allowed to keep more of what they earn. Thus, the proposed Act is aptly titled "Tax- Free First Million Act." It reflects the simple but powerful idea that the fruits of honest work should first serve the needs of Filipino families. The bill likewise increases the tax-exempt ceiling for thirteenth month pay and other benefits from Ninety Thousand Pesos (PhP 90,000.00) to One Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (PhP 150,000.00), thereby allowing employees to enjoy more of the benefits intended for them. To prevent the same inequity from recurring in the future, this measure provides for periodic inflation-based adjustment of income tax thresholds and relevant exemptions. This ensures that the tax system remains responsive to actual economic conditions and does not silently impose a higher burden on workers merely because of inflation. At the same time, the bill recognizes the need to preserve government revenues for essential public services. Accordingly, it directs the Department of Finance and the Bureau of Internal Revenue to implement a Tax Relief and Revenue Integrity Plan focused on digitalization, risk-based audits, improved collection efficiency, taxpayer assistance, enforcement against tax evasion, and stronger compliance from high-risk and high-capacity taxpayers. This bill does not seek to weaken the revenue base of the State. Rather, it seeks to make the tax system fairer by giving relief to compliant workers and ordinary income earners while strengthening enforcement against non-compliance. By increasing take-home pay, protecting family income, and promoting a more equitable tax system, this measure will help improve household welfare, stimulate domestic consumption, encourage savings, and restore fairness for millions of Filipino taxpayers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JOSE MANUEL F. label: HB 10277
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING AN AUTOMATIC REGIONAL MINIMUM WAGE ADJUSTMENT MECHANISM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PERTINENT PROVISIONS OF THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Minimum wage earners across the country continue to lose purchasing power every time inflation outpaces the slow, petition-based wage-setting process of the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards. Workers and their families often wait a year or longer for a wage order, by which time the increase granted has already been eroded by rising prices. This bill proposes an automatic, formula-based adjustment of the regional minimum wage tied to the official inflation rate, removing the need for a new petition each time prices rise. The mechanism retains the tripartite boards' authority to set the base wage and to adjust the formula for extraordinary circumstances, but ensures that workers are not left waiting indefinitely for relief that is already overdue. This measure is intended to protect the take-home pay of minimum wage workers without waiting for Congress or the boards to act on every price spike. Respectfully submitted, REP. ALEXANDER T. label: HB 10278
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE STABILIZATION OF PRICES OF RICE AND OTHER BASIC FOOD COMMODITIES, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FOOD PRICE BUFFER FUND, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sudden spikes in the price of rice and other basic food commodities hit poor and low-income Filipino families the hardest, since food accounts for the largest share of their household budget. Existing buffer-stocking programs are often underfunded and activated too late to prevent price shocks from reaching consumers. This bill creates a standing National Food Price Buffer Fund, sourced from a fixed share of tariff collections on imported agricultural products, to allow the National Food Authority and the Department of Agriculture to pre-position buffer stocks of rice and other staples and release them immediately when retail prices breach a defined threshold. The measure aims to blunt the impact of price spikes before they reach the dinner table, rather than reacting only after public outcry. Respectfully submitted, REP. ALEXANDER T. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FUEL SUBSIDY PROGRAM FOR PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLE DRIVERS AND OPERATORS DURING PERIODS OF SUSTAINED HIGH FUEL PRICES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public utility jeepney, tricycle, and bus drivers absorb the full shock of global oil price increases, often being forced to choose between raising fares — which burdens commuters — or absorbing losses that push them deeper into debt. This bill institutionalizes a fuel subsidy program that activates automatically once pump prices breach a defined threshold, rather than depending on ad hoc, one-time cash aid announced after public protests. It builds on the experience of prior fuel subsidy programs by making the trigger, amount, and distribution mechanism permanent and predictable. Respectfully submitted, REP. ALEXANDER T. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino farmers frequently sell their harvest at prices below the actual cost of production, squeezed between high input costs and the market power of traders and middlemen. Meanwhile, government support often arrives as in-kind assistance that fails to address farmers' most urgent need: cash to cover the gap between production cost and market price. This bill guarantees a minimum farmgate price for staple crops and provides a direct, unconditional cash subsidy to registered farmers whenever prevailing market prices fall below the guaranteed floor, ensuring farming remains a viable livelihood. label: HB 10287
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE USE OF PERSONAL ELECTRONIC DEVICES IN KINDERGARTEN TO SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION SCHOOLS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The widespread use of personal electronic devices, particularly smartphones, has transformed the way learners communicate, access information, and participate in education. While these technologies provide valuable educational opportunities when used appropriately, their unrestricted use during school hours has increasingly contributed to classroom distractions, reduced student engagement, academic dishonesty, cyberbullying, and other adverse effects on learners' well-being. According to the UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report 2023,1 excessive or inappropriate smartphone use during school hours can distract learners, reduce classroom engagement, adversely affect academic performance, and diminish meaningful face-to-face interaction among students. Recognizing these concerns, several countries have adopted policies regulating the use of personal electronic devices in schools while allowing appropriate exceptions for educational, medical, accessibility, and emergency purposes. In France, legislation prohibits students in primary and lower secondary schools from using mobile phones during school hours, except when required for educational instruction or disability-related needs. The French government recognizes that unrestricted mobile phone use disrupts learning, impairs students' attention and concentration, encourages incivility and cyberbullying, and undermines the quality of social interaction essential to students' development. Other countries, including Italy, the Netherlands, Australia, Hungary, Chile, China, and Brazil have likewise adopted varying forms of regulation on students' use of mobile phones in schools. These demonstrate that reasonable regulation of personal electronic devices in educational institutions is neither new nor prohibitive, but a practical measure to foster a more focused learning environment. This proposed measure does not prohibit students from possessing personal electronic devices. Rather, it establishes reasonable limitations on their use during instructional hours while expressly permitting their use for teacher-authorized educational activities, medical monitoring or treatment, assistive technology for learners with disabilities or special educational needs, emergencies, official school activities, and other circumstances authorized by school authorities in accordance with rules to be promulgated by the Department of Education (DepEd). By promoting responsible technology use and minimizing unnecessary classroom distractions, this measure seeks to strengthen the quality of basic education, improve student concentration and academic performance, encourage positive social interaction, and create a safe learning environment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ROLANDO M. label: HB 10288
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING LAW ENFORCEMENT AGAINST ILLICIT TRADE IN TOBACCO PRODUCTS AND RELATED PRODUCTS AS A MATTER OF PUBLIC ORDER, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The illicit importation, manufacture, sale, distribution, and possession of cigarettes and other covered products have evolved beyond a revenue and regulatory concern and now constitute a serious public order issue with implications for community safety and the integrity of law enforcement. The persistence and expansion of illicit tobacco trade undermine the rule of law, weaken State authority, and enable organized criminal activity that threatens public safety, economic stability, and respect for lawful commerce. Illicit tobacco trade has increasingly been linked to organized and transnational criminal networks that exploit porous borders, enforcement gaps, and weak inter-agency coordination. These networks operate with a high degree of sophistication, employing dummy importers, front businesses, fraudulent documentation, and transshipment schemes that frustrate detection and prosecution. The scale and coordination of these activities demonstrate that smuggling is no longer sporadic or opportunistic, but a systemic criminal enterprise that erodes the State’s capacity to maintain public order. The impact of illicit tobacco trade on governance and public order is extensive. Smuggling operations deprive the government of substantial tax revenues, distort legitimate markets, and heighten corruption risks within enforcement and regulatory institutions. More critically, the normalization of large-scale illicit trade weakens public confidence in the State’s ability to enforce the law, entrenches illegal distribution networks in communities, and creates enabling conditions for other offenses associated with organized crime, including money laundering and trafficking in prohibited goods. Illicit cigarettes, being untaxed and unregulated, are widely distributed through informal channels that frequently evade oversight by authorities and local government units. These channels facilitate unrestricted access to tobacco products, including among minors, and contribute to disorderly and unlawful commercial activity in public spaces and online markets. The persistence of illegal tobacco markets in communities undermines local peace and order, strains policing and inspection resources, and diverts enforcement attention from other serious crimes. Despite existing provisions under the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended, and Republic Act No. 10863, otherwise known as the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act, current enforcement mechanisms have proven insufficient to deter large- scale and organized smuggling and illicit distribution. Criminal syndicates often treat existing penalties as part of the cost of doing business and continue operations with relative impunity, while enforcement agencies face operational constraints in monitoring production and distribution channels, including online platforms. The absence of stronger, technology-enabled controls and clearer accountability across the supply chain reduces the State’s ability to rapidly disrupt illicit networks and preserve public order. Moreover, considering that the applicability of the Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Law (RA No. 12022) is contingent upon a threshold amount of at least ₱10 million, smuggling groups have adapted by deliberately fragmenting shipments and distribution into smaller quantities to evade liability under the said law. This evolving practice highlights the need for strengthened legal measures to further enhance enforcement and prosecution. This proposed measure seeks to address these deficiencies by affirming the State’s policy of treating illicit trade in covered products not only as a regulatory offense, but as a serious crime that undermines public order and the rule of law. It strengthens enforcement tools and accountability mechanisms—particularly against illicit distribution networks and unlawful online sales—to enable earlier detection, quicker interdiction, and more effective investigation and prosecution of illicit tobacco activities. By aligning compliance mechanisms and penalties with the true scale of harm inflicted on society, the bill aims to dismantle organized criminal networks, deter corruption and repeat offenses, and protect communities from the destabilizing effects of illicit trade. Ultimately, this measure underscores the State’s commitment to effective law enforcement, protection of public order, and preservation of the integrity of the country’s fiscal, economic, and regulatory systems. It recognizes that safeguarding public revenue, promoting public health, and maintaining peace and order are inseparable objectives that must be advanced through a unified, technology-enabled, and enforceable legal framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ROLANDO M. VALERIANO JOEL R. label: HB 10289
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 144, 145 AND 263-A OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8424, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This legislative measure proposes the establishment of a uniform excise tax rate for all vapor products, irrespective of nicotine formulation. The initiative seeks to rectify structural deficiencies in the current excise tax regime under Section 144(c) of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), which imposes different rates—₱60.20 per milliliter for nicotine salt solutions and ₱69.46 per 10 milliliters (equivalent to ₱6.95 per milliliter) for freebase nicotine solutions. Such disparity has created regulatory loopholes and incentivized tax avoidance, contributing to substantial revenue loss. Illicit trade in vapor products is likewise rampant due to misdeclaration and smuggling. Euromonitor estimates illicit trade of vapor products at 84%. Cognizant of the above issues, the proposed bill introduces a simplified and harmonized excise tax structure. By adopting a single rate across all vapor product types, the measure eliminates classification ambiguities, enhances compliance, and fosters equitable treatment among industry stakeholders. In support of standardization and regulatory clarity, the bill also prescribes specific container or packaging capacities for vapor products: 1ml, 2 ml, 3ml, 5 ml, and 10 ml. This provision aims to streamline tax administration, prevent misdeclaration of product volumes, and facilitate accurate assessment and monitoring. By limiting packaging to defined sizes, the measure reduces opportunities for manipulation and underreporting, thereby reinforcing compliance and enabling more effective enforcement of excise tax laws. The reform is expected to improve collection efficiency and enhance revenues. label: HB 10310
title: AN ACT PROVIDING PROTECTION AND INCENTIVES TO FREELANCE WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social and economic force. Under this mandate, the State must protect workers and ensure safe working conditions. However, our current laws have not kept up with the rapid rise of the digital economy. In 2019, the Philippines ranked sixth globally in freelance growth, with earnings rising by 35 percent.1 During the pandemic in 2020, freelance revenues skyrocketed by 208 percent.2 Today, Filipino freelancers are key players in the global remote work market. They bring valuable foreign currency into our local communities and boost domestic spending. Despite these big contributions, freelancers still work in a legal gray area. They are classified as independent contractors rather than regular employees. This leaves freelancers highly vulnerable to unfair treatment as they may be forced to work without the basic safety nets that traditional employees enjoy. One major issue is that many freelancers work without a written contract. Without a formal agreement, they have no legal proof of their agreed rates, deadlines, or deliverables. This often leads to severe financial abuse. Freelancers frequently face unpaid labor, late payments, or sudden pay cuts. Many also work night shifts or do dangerous tasks without receiving extra pay or hazard compensation. The Freelance Workers Protection Act aims to fix these issues. First, the bill requires a written contract before any work starts. This contract must clearly state the work scope, pay rates, and payment schedules. Second, the bill sets strict deadlines for payments so workers get paid on time. Third, it introduces hazard pay and night shift differentials for freelancers. label: HB 10311
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE COLLECTION OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136 AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 19, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall regulate or prohibit monopolies when the public interest so requires. This constitutional mandate recognizes that industries operating as natural monopolies must be subject to greater regulatory oversight to ensure that the public is protected from unreasonable rates, unfair business practices, and the abuse of market power. Electric distribution utilities (DUs) are natural monopolies. Within their respective franchise areas, consumers have no meaningful choice of electricity provider and cannot transfer to another distribution utility in response to poor service or excessive charges. This unique market structure imposes upon distribution utilities a corresponding obligation to operate efficiently, responsibly, and in the best interest of the consuming public. For decades, however, electricity consumers have been required to pay system loss charges, amounts collected to recover electricity that was generated or purchased but was never delivered to, or consumed by, end-users. These charges are reflected as a separate item in consumers' monthly electricity bills and effectively require paying customers to shoulder losses incurred within the distribution system. System loss generally consists of two categories. 1. Technical losses refer to the energy naturally dissipated during the transmission and distribution of electricity due to electrical resistance in power lines, transformers, and other distribution equipment. While some level of technical loss is inevitable, excessive losses often result from aging infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, delayed investments, or inefficient network design. 2. Non-technical losses, on the other hand, arise from electricity pilferage, meter tampering, illegal connections, inaccurate metering, billing errors, uncollected accounts, and other operational inefficiencies. Under existing laws, including Republic Act No. 7832, otherwise known as the Anti-Electricity and Electric Transmission Lines/Materials Pilferage Act of 1994, and Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), distribution utilities are permitted to recover a portion of these system losses from consumers, subject to caps prescribed by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). While these laws recognize that certain technical losses may occur in the normal operation of an electrical distribution network, allowing utilities to recover both technical and non-technical losses from consumers creates a policy imbalance. It effectively transfers to captive consumers costs that should ordinarily be borne by the distribution utility as part of its responsibility to operate an efficient, secure, and well-maintained distribution system. In effect, consumers are made to pay not only for the electricity they actually use, but also for losses arising from outdated infrastructure, inadequate system investments, operational inefficiencies, electricity theft, billing inaccuracies, and weak enforcement measures against illegal connections. This diminishes the incentive for distribution utilities to modernize their networks, strengthen anti- pilferage programs, improve operational efficiency, and invest in technologies that minimize system losses. This bill seeks to restore fairness and accountability by prohibiting the imposition and collection of system loss charges, whether technical or non-technical, from end-use electricity consumers. Under the proposed measure, system losses shall be treated as ordinary costs of doing business and shall be absorbed by the distribution utilities themselves. Like other regulated enterprises operating under exclusive franchises, distribution utilities must bear the financial consequences of operational inefficiencies and should continuously invest in modern technologies, infrastructure upgrades, preventive maintenance, and loss-reduction programs to improve service quality and operational performance. Ultimately, this measure upholds the constitutional policy of protecting the public from unreasonable charges imposed by monopoly utilities. It strengthens consumer protection, promotes greater operational efficiency within the power distribution sector, and encourages sustained investment in modern, reliable, and resilient electricity distribution systems In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10313
title: AN ACT ENSURING THE WELFARE AND PROTECTION OF BUSINESS PROCESS OUTSOURCING (BPO) WORKERS AND THE RECOGNITION OF THEIR RIGHTS AS PROVIDED FOR IN THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE One of the most significant and successful consequences of economic globalization is the relocation of business operations to developing economies through outsourcing. Foremost among these is the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) sector, which enables global enterprises to delegate critical tasks such as customer relations, information technology (IT) support, and administrative functions to countries with highly cost-efficient and competent labor markets 1. The Philippines has positioned itself as a premier global hub for the BPO industry, leveraging its highly skilled, adaptable, and English-proficient workforce. The economic impact of this sector is profound; according to a report by the World Trade Organization (WTO), the BPO industry contributed 7.3% to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP)2. As the sector projects sustained growth, it remains a primary pillar of the Philippine economy and a vital source of employment for millions of Filipinos. However, the rapid expansion of the industry has exposed BPO workers to severe and systemic challenges. Due to the nature of global operations, workers frequently endure irregular night-shift schedules, inadequate rest periods, high-stress environments, and substandard occupational health and safety conditions. These demanding circumstances compromise their physical health, mental well-being, and overall quality of life. Consistent with the constitutional mandate to protect workers' rights and promote their welfare, this bill seeks to establish the "Magna Carta for BPO Workers." This legislative measure aims to institutionalize critical safeguards, mandate humane working conditions, enforce fair labor standards, and protect BPO professionals from exploitation and unsafe work practices. 1 Ladaran, H. label: HB 10314
title: AN ACT TO LOWER THE PRICE OF ELECTRICITY BY EXEMPTING ITS SALE BY GENERATION, TRANSMISSION AND DISTRIBUTION COMPANIES AND ELECTRICITY COOPERATIVES, AND SYSTEMS LOSSES FROM THE IMPOSITION OF VALUE ADDED TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE, SECTIONS 108 AND 109 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9337, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The high cost of electricity in the Philippines remains a constant burden to Filipino households and businesses, contributing significantly to the rising cost of living and the overall cost of doing business in the country. This situation has been exacerbated by the ongoing conflict in the middle east. A major component of electricity pricing is the imposition of the Value Added Tax (VAT) on the sale of electricity by generation, transmission, and distribution companies, as well as electric cooperatives. Under the current system, VAT is imposed on each stage of the power supply chain, from generation, transmission, to distribution, resulting in compounded tax costs that are ultimately passed on to consumers. Another contributing factor to high electricity bills is the “system loss” charge, which represents the difference between the electricity supplied to the distribution system and the electricity actually delivered to end-users. These losses arise from both technical inefficiencies and non-technical factors such as pilferage. Despite not being directly consumed by households, this system loss component is currently included in electricity billing and remains subject to the Value-Added Tax (VAT). The US State Department reported in its 2022 Investment Climate Statement, that: “Poor infrastructure, high power costs, slow broadband connections, regulatory inconsistencies, and corruption are major disincentives to investment. The Philippines’ complex, slow, and sometimes corrupt judicial system inhibits the timely and fair resolution of commercial disputes. Traffic in major cities and congestion in the ports remain barriers to doing business.”1 This bill seeks to amend Sections 108(A) and 109(1) of the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended by Republic Act No. 9337, to exempt the sale of electricity from VAT. By removing the VAT on electricity, we aim to provide immediate relief to Filipino households and ease financial pressures on businesses, particularly micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Moreover, by removing VAT on system loss charge, we can address the growing public concern over electricity pricing structures. Lowering electricity costs will not only improve the purchasing power of Filipino families but also enhance the competitiveness of local industries, encourage job creation, and promote inclusive economic growth. This measure forms part of a broader agenda to bring down the cost of living and ensure that economic development is felt by all. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BEVERLEY ROSE A. DIMACUHA 1 United States Department of State. (n.d.). Investment Climate Statement. label: HB 10327
title: AN ACT REPEALING BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 36, ENTITLED “AN ACT IMPOSING AN ENERGY TAX ON ELECTRIC POWER CONSUMPTION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to repeal Batas Pambansa Blg. 36, entitled “An Act Imposing an Energy Tax on Electric Power Consumption, and For Other Purposes”. It recognizes that electricity should no longer be burdened by an outdated tax that adds to the cost of every Filipino household’s monthly electric bill. When BP Blg. 36 was enacted in 1979, the country faced economic and energy challenges that justified the imposition of an energy tax. More than four (4) decades later, the circumstances that gave rise to BP Blg. 36 have changed. Electricity has become an indispensable necessity that powers homes, supports education, enables livelihoods, and allows families to access essential services. Currently, Filipino consumers already shoulder numerous charges in their monthly electricity bills, which include generation, transmission, distribution, system loss, universal charges, and other government-imposed taxes and fees. The continued collection of an additional energy tax only increases the financial burden on households that are already struggling with rising prices and the increasing cost of living. The government must ensure that taxes remain responsive to present-day realities and do not unnecessarily burden the public. Repealing this outdated tax shall help reduce electricity costs, provide meaningful relief to Filipino families, and allow households to devote more of their income to food, education, healthcare, and other basic necessities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE SYSTEM LOSS CHARGE BILLED TO RESIDENTIAL END-USER CONSUMERS BY DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES OR ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES FROM THE COVERAGE OF THE VALUE-ADDED TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 109 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8424, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997”, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to exempt the System Loss Charge billed by distribution utilities and electric cooperatives to residential end-user consumers from the coverage of the Value-Added Tax (VAT). It aims to reduce electricity costs and provide financial relief to Filipino households. Electricity is an essential service that powers homes, supports livelihoods, and drives economic activity. For many families, every peso spent on electricity is a peso taken away from other basic necessities like food, education, and healthcare. However, Filipino consumers continue to pay among the highest electricity rates in Southeast Asia1. Apart from the cost of electricity consumed, consumers also shoulder the System Loss Charge which represents electricity losses incurred during transmission and distribution. This charge is also subjected to the twelve percent (12%) VAT which further increases the financial burden on consumers. Removing the VAT on the Systems Loss Charge provides meaningful relief to residential consumers and helps make electricity more affordable. It likewife affirms the State’s commitment to protect consumer welfare and ensure access to reliable and reasonably priced electricity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 TALAVERA, Sheldeen Joy (2026).
