label: HB 10329
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PROTECTION OF THE RIGHTS AND WELFARE OF FILIPINO VIRTUAL ASSISTANTS (VAs) AND ONLINE FREELANCERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many Filipinos who lost their jobs or sought alternative sources of income during the COVID-19 pandemic, online freelancing and virtual assistance emerged as indispensable livelihood alternatives. This accelerated the shift toward remote work and the digital economy. What began as a crisis response has evolved into one of the country's fastest-growing sectors, employing thousands while enabling work from home. Globally, Filipino virtual assistants and digital freelancers are widely valued for their skills, adaptability, and work ethic. They execute a broad spectrum of services, ranging from administrative and customer support to advanced software development, digital marketing, and project management. As these professionals acquire specialized competencies, they are able to negotiate competitive compensation and establish sustainable careers in the international digital marketplace. Beyond creating employment opportunities, this sector has made a significant contribution to the Philippine economy. By servicing international clientele, digital workers generate a steady influx of foreign exchange, which fortifies our currency reserves and stimulates local consumption. Despite these valuable contributions, virtual assistants and online freelance workers lack adequate legal protection. Because most engagements occur through online platforms or direct contracts with foreign clients, workers face unfair terms, delayed or non-payment of compensation, excessive hours, sudden terminations, and exposure to scams. Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution requires the State to “afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all.” In keeping with this mandate, the State should recognize the contributions of virtual assistants and online freelancers by promoting fair labor practices and providing safeguards that protect their rights and welfare. They execute a broad spectrum of services, ranging from administrative and customer support to advanced software development, digital marketing, and project management. As these professionals acquire specialized competencies, they are able to negotiate competitive compensation and establish sustainable careers in the international digital marketplace. Beyond creating employment opportunities, this sector has made a significant contribution to the Philippine economy. label: HB 10331
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY (TESDA) TRAINING AND ASSESSMENT CENTER IN BARANGAY FAIRVIEW, QUEZON CITY, TO BE KNOWN AS THE BARANGAY FAIRVIEW, QUEZON CITY TESDA TRAINING AND ASSESSMENT CENTER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the Constitution provides that “the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” The Constitution further mandates that the State establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society. Access to education is the foundation of the human capital of any country. It shall be made inclusive and afforded to all Filipinos to enhance, cultivate, and formalize their skills to be utilized for their livelihood and for their locality’s economic growth. One of the major strengths of the Fifth District of Quezon City is its youthful and reliable working population. This human capital currently dominates the demographic profile of the area and is equally deserving of vast opportunities such as livelihood and skills and competencies training. Through a Training Center under the tutelage of the Technical Education Skill Development Authority (TESDA), we aim to utilize the growing potential of the District’s youth and working population for economic development. This bill seeks to establish a Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) Training and Assessment Center in Brgy. Fairview, Quezon City. This measure will ensure that residents and most especially out-of-school youths in the area and nearby localities are provided access to technical and vocational education for employment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10357
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DIRECT OR INDIRECT RECOVERY OF DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES, INCLUDING ANY VALUE-ADDED TAX ATTRIBUTABLE THERETO, FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, AS AMENDED, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential public service that powers homes, schools, hospitals, businesses, industries, and government institutions. Reliable electricity at a just and reasonable cost is indispensable to economic development, social welfare, and the daily life of every Filipino. Electricity consumers, however, continue to be charged for “system losses” — electricity lost before it reaches the end-user. These losses may arise from the technical characteristics of transmission and distribution networks or from non- technical causes such as electricity pilferage, illegal connections, defective metering, inadequate maintenance, and operational inefficiency. At its core, this measure asks a simple question: Should consumers bear the cost of electricity that never reaches them, or should that remain a business risk of the entities that own and operate the distribution system? This bill adopts the latter policy, consistent with the principle that financial responsibility should follow operational control. Consumers cannot design distribution networks, replace aging facilities, upgrade transformers, maintain meters, prevent electricity theft, or determine the capital and operational investments of electric utilities. These matters remain within the responsibility and control of distribution utilities. This concern stems from House Resolution No. 976, introduced by Representatives Robert Nazal and Paolo Henry Marcoleta, which called for a congressional inquiry by the Energy Regulatory Commission and the Commission on Audit into Meralco's electricity rates, pass-through charges, and rate methodologies to evaluate if system-loss charges are necessary and transparent. While House Resolution No. 976 offers oversight, this bill provides substantive reform. It ensures that electricity lost before delivery is no longer automatically billed to consumers who cannot prevent these losses. State-franchised distribution utilities and electric cooperatives are obligated to maintain efficient systems, modernize infrastructure, and reduce technical and non- technical losses. Passing these costs to consumers weakens utility accountability for operational risks. Article XII of the 1987 Constitution subjects public utilities to State regulation in the public interest. Congress may therefore determine which costs may lawfully form part of regulated electricity rates and which costs must be absorbed as operating expenses and business risks of the regulated entity. This measure prohibits the charging, billing, collection, or recovery of technical and non-technical system losses from electricity end-users. It treats such losses as operating expenses and business risks of the concerned electric power industry participant and withdraws the authority of the Energy Regulatory Commission to approve their direct or indirect recovery through tariffs, riders, adjustment mechanisms, surcharges, or other rate components. Ang konsumer ay dapat magbayad para sa kuryenteng aktuwal na naihatid sa kaniya — hindi para sa kuryenteng nawala dahil sa pagnanakaw, kakulangan sa pagpapanatili, o kahinaan ng sistema. The entities that control the system must bear responsibility for improving it. This measure advances consumer protection, strengthens accountability, and creates a direct incentive for electric utilities and other industry participants to invest in efficient, secure, and reliable power systems. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 10358
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In line with Section 15, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, this proposed measure is anchored on two equally important state interests. First, it promotes the health and well-being of the population through the prevention, early detection, and treatment of diseases such as bloodborne viral hepatitis, which remains a significant public health concern and a leading cause of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. Second, it protects the rights of Filipinos living with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C, who continue to face stigma, discrimination, and even loss of livelihood on account of their health status, despite the existence of a safe vaccine and treatment modalities for both diseases. It ensures that persons living with these illnesses are able to live with dignity, free from fear, shame, or exclusion, and are treated not as carriers of disease but as Filipinos entitled to the same respect, opportunities, and protection under the law as everyone else. To reconcile these two interests, the bill promotes voluntary and confidential testing as the standard approach to hepatitis diagnosis, while expressly prohibiting mandatory and routine screening as a pre-condition for employment, admission to school, or access to services. It likewise defines the limited and specific instances in which compulsory testing may still be allowed, such as for offenders charged under the Anti- Rape Law, blood and organ donation, and the surveillance of health workers who perform exposure-prone procedures, subject to safeguards against misuse of results. By striking this balance between public health protection and the safeguarding of individual rights, this measure aims to encourage more Filipinos to come forward for testing without fear of discrimination, thereby improving early detection, expanding access to treatment, and ultimately reducing the incidence of liver disease attributable to Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. PERCIVAL V. CENDAÑA Akbayan Representative JOSE MANUEL TADEO DADAH KIRAM ISMULA “CHEL” I. label: HB 10359
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING HEALTHCARE INSURANCE NON-DENIAL AND INCLUSIVE MEDICAL ASSISTANCE FOR ALL WELFARE AND ACCESS NEEDS ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 15 of the Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. Article XIII, Sections 11 and 12 further mandate the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and make essential health services available to all people at affordable cost. The National Health Insurance Program administered by the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) serves as a principal mechanism for providing financial risk protection to Filipino families. Recent reforms, including the implementation of expanded outpatient emergency care benefits, have significantly improved healthcare coverage. However, experience has shown that certain members continue to encounter situations where medically necessary healthcare services are rendered but PhilHealth benefits are unavailable, reduced, delayed, or uncertain due to technical classifications, admission status, duration of confinement, or hospital capacity limitations. These situations include, but are not limited to, the following situations, namely: patients who are formally admitted but discharged within twenty- four (24) hours; patients who incur expenses in emergency departments but do not fall within a specific benefit package; patients advised for admission but unable to obtain hospital beds; patients who remain in emergency departments while awaiting admission due to overcrowding; patients transferred between healthcare facilities because of capacity constraints; and families of deceased patients whose benefit entitlement becomes uncertain due to unresolved classification issues. The circumstances mentioned above arise through no fault of the patient and often result in financial hardship, precisely when families are most vulnerable. No member should be deprived of financial protection because a healthcare facility lacks available beds, because a transfer becomes necessary, or because a medical encounter falls between existing administrative classifications. 1 This measure seeks to ensure continuity of PhilHealth protection by directing the development of mechanisms that address benefit gaps, establish coverage continuity throughout a patient's course of treatment, and promote the liberal resolution of classification ambiguities in favor of qualified members, consistent with the objectives of the National Health Insurance Program and the Universal Health Care Act. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAMES “JOJO” ANG JR. label: HB 10360
title: AN ACT PROVIDING AN INCREASE AND AUTOMATIC ADJUSTMENT MECHANISM IN THE PERSONNEL ECONOMIC RELIEF ALLOWANCE (PERA) GRANTED TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Personnel Economic Relief Allowance (PERA) is a benefit given to government employees in the Philippines to provide relief against the effects of inflation and the increasing cost of living. Despite its purpose, the PERA has remained fixed at Two Thousand Pesos (Php 2,000.00) per month since 2010. Over the years, however, inflation has eroded the purchasing power of Filipinos. Two Thousand Pesos (Php 2,000.00) today has the purchasing power equivalent only to approximately One Thousand One Hundred to One Thousand Two Hundred Pesos (Php 1,100.00 - 1,200.00) in 2010 prices. Recognizing the substantial increase in the prices of basic goods and essential services over the past fifteen (15) years, there is a critical need to increase the PERA to Five Thousand Pesos (Php 5,000.00) per month. The adjustment reflects the true purpose of the benefit by ensuring that meaningful relief is provided to government employees to meet their daily needs. Nonetheless, a one-time increase in the amount of PERA is insufficient. Without a mechanism for periodic adjustment, the value of the benefit would once again diminish over time due to inflation. Eventually, this will necessitate another legislative amendment, a process which inevitably takes time. Thus, the measure proposes that the PERA be automatically adjusted annually equivalent to the increase in the annual inflation rate. The proposed measure is expected to benefit approximately two million government employees nationwide, and by extension, their families who depend on their income. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. YSABEL MARIA J. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) comprise the vast majority of the business establishments nationwide. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, there were 1,076,122 MSMEs operating in the country as of 2021, which accounted for 99.58% of all business establishments.1 The sector contributes approximately 40% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), and generates around 6.4 Million jobs for Filipinos.2 Despite being a significant economic force, many MSMEs continue to face significant hurdles which push them to shutter after a year of operation.3 High costs of doing business, complicated registration and licensing requirements, limited access to affordable credit institutions, and other operational constraints are among the issues which prevent these businesses from continuing their operations and expanding.4 In recognition of their indispensable contribution to national development, this measure seeks to strengthen the Magna Carta for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises through the introduction of reforms which include, among others: - Regulating the fees charged for the issuance of permits, licenses, certifications, and other similar documents; - Increasing the share of MSMEs in the total procurement value of goods and services supplied to the government from ten percent (10%) to twenty percent (20%); - Requiring an allocation of dedicated free commercial spaces for MSMEs; 1 2021 Updating of List of Establishments, Philippine Statistics Authority 2 Austria, R. M. (2026, February 20). The rise of the Philippine MSMEs. Manila Bulletin. https://mb.com.ph/2026/02/21/the-rise-of- the-philippine-msmes 3 Micro, small, and medium enterprises. By addressing these persistent issues, the measure aims to foster a more conducive business environment which will allow MSMEs to operate sustainably, and achieve long-term growth and expansion. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. YSABEL MARIA J. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE GOVERNANCE, ESTABLISHING AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BILL OF RIGHTS, CREATING AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MULTI-STAKEHOLDER ADVISORY COUNCIL, PROMOTING LITERACY, INSTITUTIONAL READINESS, RESPONSIBLE INNOVATION, AND WORKER PROTECTION, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial Intelligence (AI) is no longer a future technology. It is already reshaping economies, labor markets, education systems, public governance, media, finance, healthcare, communications, and everyday life at an unprecedented speed. In the Philippines, AI systems are now widely used in schools, offices, call centers, banks, hospitals, online platforms, content creation, transportation, customer service, and government operations. The rapid expansion of AI in the country is already measurable. The Philippine AI Report 2025 found that more than ninety-two percent (92%) of surveyed Philippine organizations have adopted AI in some capacity, i while more than half (54%) have already used generative AI tools for over a year. Executive-level AI adoption and deployment continue to accelerate across industries. Meanwhile, studies indicate that Filipinos are among the most active users of generative AI tools globally.1 The Philippine AI market itself is projected to expand rapidly in the coming years. Industry studies estimate that the Philippine generative AI market may grow from approximately USD 292 million in 2025 to more than USD 1.2 billion by 2034, driven by the country’s highly digital population, expanding internet access, and increasing demand for automation in business process outsourcing, finance, education, and creative industries. 2 Despite the speed and scale of AI adoption, the Philippines still has no comprehensive national law governing the responsible development, deployment, accountability, oversight, and regulation of AI systems. Existing laws such as the Data Privacy Act of 2012, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, and the Philippine Innovation Act address only certain aspects of AI-related concerns. At present, there is no unified national framework that establishes safeguards against harmful AI systems, protects workers from AI-driven displacement, guarantees transparency in automated decision-making, promotes AI literacy, establishes accountability standards, or creates institutional mechanisms for AI governance. This legal and regulatory gap leaves the public vulnerable to the risks of unregulated AI deployment. AI technologies create enormous opportunities for economic growth, innovation, scientific advancement, improved public services, and increased 1 Tim Santos & Pia Besmonte Ligot-Gordon, The Philippine AI Report 2025 2 (2025), https://philippineaireport.com/ 2 IMARC Group, Philippines Generative AI Market 2026 Worth USD 1,242.67 Million by 2034, OPENPR (May 20, 2025), https://www.imarcgroup.com/philippines-generative-ai-market ii productivity. Global studies estimate that AI adoption could increase global economic output by as much as fifteen percent (15%) over the next decade.3 However, the same technologies also create serious and urgent risks that directly affect democratic institutions, labor rights, public trust, human rights, and national development.AI systems are now capable of generating highly realistic deepfakes, synthetic media, fabricated audio and video, deceptive impersonations, and large-scale automated disinformation. These technologies can be weaponized to manipulate public opinion, undermine elections, spread fraud, damage reputations, and erode trust in democratic institutions and public information. AI systems may also produce discriminatory or biased outcomes in hiring, lending, education, healthcare, policing, insurance, and access to gove1rnment services. Automated systems often operate without transparency, making it difficult for individuals to understand, question, or challenge decisions that significantly affect their lives. At the same time, AI-driven automation is expected to significantly disrupt labor markets worldwide. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates that approximately forty percent (40%) of jobs globally may be affected by AI technologies. In advanced economies, the figure may reach sixty percent (60%).4 Experts have warned that AI may disproportionately affect younger workers, entry-level employment, and vulnerable sectors of 3 PricewaterhouseCoopers, AI Adoption Could Boost Global GDP by an Additional 15 Percentage Points by 2035, (Apr. 29, 2025), https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2025/ai- adoption-could-boost-global-gdp-by-an-additional-15-percentage.html 4 Kristalina Georgieva, AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let’s Make Sure It Benefits Humanity, international Monetary Fund (Jan. 14, 2024), https://www.imf.org/en/blogs/articles/2024/01/14/ai-will-transform-the-global-economy-lets-make- sure-it-benefits-humanity iii the workforce if governments fail to establish proactive labor transition policies and worker protections.5 These risks are especially significant for the Philippines because of the country’s large service sector, including business process outsourcing (BPO), clerical work, administrative support services, online content work, and other industries that may undergo major transformation due to automation and generative AI technologies.6 Without clear national policies, the Philippines risks being technologically unprepared, economically vulnerable, and institutionally incapable of addressing the profound social and economic consequences of AI-driven transformation. The absence of governance standards also creates uncertainty for businesses, educational institutions, innovators, workers, investors, and government agencies seeking responsible pathways for AI adoption. Without clear safeguards and accountability mechanisms, public trust in AI technologies may weaken, while irresponsible or harmful AI deployment may proliferate unchecked. label: HB 10366
title: AN ACT PROTECTING CONSUMERS FROM UNFAIR, DECEPTIVE, AND ABUSIVE ONLINE LENDING PRACTICES, ESTABLISHING THE VICTIM COMPENSATION BOARD FOR ONLINE LENDING ABUSES FOR THE PURPOSE, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of digital technology has created a new market for money lending in the Philippines. Through mobile applications, websites, and digital installment platforms, Filipinos gain easy access to emergency funds as needed. With just a phone or mobile device and genuine identification, any Filipino can loan from recognized online lending platforms. For many Filipinos in need, online lending has become an accessible and convenient source of funds. The online lending market is not entirely unregulated. Existing laws already provide an important baseline framework for the operation of lending businesses and the protection of borrowers. Republic Act No. 3765, or the Truth in Lending Act, requires creditors to disclose all charges and costs of the loan, including interest rates, charges, and the total amount payable. This information is given to enable borrowers to make informed financial decisions. Republic Act No. 9474, or the Lending Company Regulation Act of 2007, governs the establishment and operation of lending companies and requires their registration and supervision by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Republic Act No. 11765, or the Financial Products and Services Consumer Protection Act, imposes standards of fair dealing, transparency, responsible pricing, and consumer protection in the offering of financial i products and services. Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012, regulates the collection, processing, storage, use, disclosure, and protection of personal information or sensitive personal information, including borrower information obtained through digital lending platforms. However, the digital lending market still remains vulnerable to abuse. Despite the existing laws and other regulations, predatory practices continue to persist on a disturbing scale.1 These include threats, the use of obscene or abusive language, public shaming, the dissemination of personal information, fabricated legal notices, and the use of borrowers' contact lists or private data to intimidate family members, friends, co-workers, and employers.2 Borrowers remain exposed to excessive and unconscionable interest rates, deceptive pricing structures, hidden service charges, and loan designs that trap them in cycles of rollover and over-indebtedness. The continued proliferation of unregistered online lending applications further aggravates the problem. According to the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center, from January to February 2026 alone, more than ₱8 million has already been lost from the pockets of citizens due to abusive and fraudulent online lending applications.3 In light of these troubling circumstances, the law must evolve to address the realities of modern credit delivery. It is no longer sufficient to regulate electronic transactions and to require only formal disclosures. The State must also ensure that digital loan or lending products are fair in structure, transparent in cost, proportionate in their collection and use of personal information, and humane in enforcement. Further, individuals most affected by abusive online lending practices are frequently those with limited financial resources and financial literacy. Among them are domestic workers, construction workers, vendors, and drivers. Given their limited access to legal and financial information, it is imperative that 1 Department of Information and Communications Technology, National Privacy Commission & Securities and Exchange Commission, Public Advisory on Online Lending Platforms (Mar. 2026), https://privacy.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/DICT-NPC-SEC-Public-Advisory-on-Online- Lending-Platforms.pdf 2 Mary Joy Salcedo, Around 300 complaints filed vs abusive online lending apps — PAOCC, INQUIRER.net (Sept. 10, 2025, 4:46 PM), https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2107335/around-300- complaints-filed-vs-abusive-online-lending-apps-paocc 3 Andrea Taguines, Gov’t Cracks Down on Unregistered Online Lending Apps as More Filipinos Fall Victim to Modus, ABS-CBN News (Feb. 27, 2026, 7:07 PM), https://www.abs- cbn.com/news/business/2026/2/27/gov-t-cracks-down-on-unregistered-online-lending-apps-1907 ii loan agreements and disclosures be provided in a language familiar to them and expressed in plain, clear, and understandable terms. Hence, the Anti-Online Lending Abuse Act which seeks to: (1) define and protect the rights of borrowers of online lending platforms; (2) define the duties and responsibilities of online lending platforms; (3) limit the charges and total repayment amounts in online lending; (4) enumerate the prohibited acts in online lending and debt collection; and (5) establish a Victim Compensation Board for Online Lending Abuses. label: HB 10376
title: AN ACT POSTPONING THE SYNCHRONIZED BARANGAY AND SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN ELECTIONS TO NOVEMBER 2028, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12232, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12232 was enacted into law to fix the term of office of Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials at four (4) years, providing greater stability and continuity in grassroots governance. Under Section 2 of RA 12232, the next regular Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) are scheduled to be held in November 2026. This bill proposes resetting the next synchronized BSKE to the second Monday of November 2028 to address acute, compounding global and domestic crises. Crucially, the country faces severe economic headwinds driven by escalating Middle East geopolitical tensions. As a heavy net importer of oil, the Philippines is vulnerable to global fuel price spikes, supply chain disruptions, and heightened domestic inflation. At the same time, agricultural production and domestic food security are threatened by the possible devastating impacts of Super El Niño, which has been predicted to induce droughts, crop damage, and losses in rural livelihoods across the archipelago. Holding a standalone local election in November 2026—just eighteen months after the May 2025 national polls and right before preparations begin for the May 2028 elections—places unnecessary strain on government resources during a critical time for our economy. Moving the election date to November 2028 directly serves the public interest. First, it ensures stability by allowing national and local agencies to keep their full focus on economic recovery, disaster response, and inflation control without constant political interruptions. Second, holding the election six months after the May 2028 national polls gives the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) enough time to use fully tested and secure voting technology smoothly while preventing voter fatigue. Finally, aligning the election timeline optimizes state resources and administrative capacity, ensuring that public machinery remains concentrated on protecting vulnerable households, stabilizing essential prices, and restoring agricultural resilience. By balancing the duty to hold regular elections with the urgent need for national economic stability, this bill protects both election integrity and public welfare. In view of these compelling state interests and urgent national economic priorities, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JANETTE L. GARIN HON. JUDE A. ACIDRE HON. label: HB 10381
title: AN ACT AMENDING CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NUMBER 8550, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NUMBER 10654, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE FISHERIES CODE OF 1998
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines' fisheries and aquaculture sector constitutes a critical pillar of our national economy, livelihood, and food security. According to the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources , in the first quarter of 2026 alone, fisheries production reached approximately 856.29 thousand metric tons, valued at roughly PHP 78.58 billion. The sector likewise contributed an estimated 9.6% to the Gross Value Added (GVA) in Agriculture, Forestry, and Fishing. Notwithstanding its economic contribution, the sector faces compounding and systemic threats that undermine both fisherfolk livelihoods and the nation’s long-term food security. Overfishing, driven by excessive fishing efforts , have resulted in the steady decline of major fish stocks. This is further exacerbated by the impacts of climate change, which not only disrupt marine ecosystems but also pose a grave challenge to our municipal fisherfolk, who often lack the resources and seaworthy vessels needed to safely and productively fish in increasingly unpredictable conditions. Given these challenges, there is an urgent need to revisit Republic Act No. 8550, as amended by Republic Act No. 10654, otherwise known as The Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998. The law, while providing a foundational framework for the conservation, management, and sustainable use of fisheries and aquatic resources, has shown outdated enforcement mechanisms and adaptive capacity in responding to the effects of climate change and shifting socioeconomic realities. 1 This bill introduces amendments such as the adoption of the Ecosystem Approach to Fisheries Management (EAFM) which institutionalizes a science based, holistic management framework that accounts for ecological interactions, habitat integrity, and human dimensions of fisheries. It likewise expands the scope of municipal fisherfolk registration to include persons engaged in fisheries culture activities, thereby addressing a longstanding regulatory gap that has excluded aquaculture practitioners from formal recognition, entitlement to municipal water rights, and access to government support programs. This bill seeks to ensure that the Philippine fisheries regulatory framework remains responsive, scientifically grounded, and equitably administered in the face of mounting environmental and socioeconomic challenges. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. title: AN ACT MANDATING AN ACCIDENT AND LIFE INSURANCE COVERAGE FOR CONSTRUCTION WORKERS Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: Section 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the “ Construction Workers Insurance Act of 2026”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 3, Article XIII, of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that "The State shall afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all." This provision establishes the State's obligation to ensure the welfare and security of its workforce, particularly those engaged in hazardous occupations. As of December 2025, approximately 480 million workers are employed in the construction industry according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)1. Due to the precarious nature of their work such as working at heights, operating heavy machinery, digging deep foundations, and manually handling heavy materials such as steel bars and concrete pipes, construction workers face significantly risks of workplace injuries and fatalities. Despite existing occupational health and safety standards, workplace incidents remain alarmingly2 prevalent3. This measure seeks to establish mandatory accident and life insurance coverage for all construction workers across the Philippines. The bill ensures that in the event of work-related injury, disability, or death, affected workers and their beneficiaries receive timely financial assistance to support them during this difficult period. We recognize the fundamental importance of ensuring the safety of those who build our homes and construct our vital infrastructure. label: HB 10383
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ELECTORAL PROCESS BY EXPANDING THE CIRCUMSTANCES TO BE CONSIDERED A NUISANCE CANDIDATE AND MAKING IT AN ELECTION OFFENSE, IMPOSING ADMINISTRATIVE SANCTIONS AND CRIMINAL PENALTIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Elections, as the cornerstone of the democratic process, serve as the fundamental mechanism through which citizens exercise their sovereignty and hold leaders accountable. It relies on the informed choices of the electorate, ensuring that government power derives solely from the genuine consent of the people. However the integrity and sanctity of the election process is often threatened by nuisance candidates. Section 69 of the Omnibus Election Code defines Nuisance Candidate as an individual who files his or her certificate of candidacy (COC) to put the election process in mockery or disrepute or to cause confusion among voters by the similarity of the names of the registered candidates or by other circumstances or acts which clearly demonstrates that the candidate has no bona fide intention to run for the office for which the COC has been filed. Notwithstanding this safeguard, nuisance candidates lacking bona fide intent persist in exploiting the electoral process by adopting names similar or substantially identical to those of registered officials and incumbents to cause voter confusion. Additionally, some political actors resort to coercion, threats, and inducement to secure the filing of nuisance candidates, thereby subverting the democratic process. Furthermore, bad faith actors leverage their own names or resources to monetize and abuse the system. Collectively, these practices distort election results, causes voter confusion, and undermine public confidence in the integrity of democratic institutions. 1 This bill aims to expand the definition of a nuisance candidate and penalize both the malicious filing itself and the individuals who coerce, threaten, or induce such actions. These measures are essential to uphold the people's right to suffrage and ensure the integrity of our democracy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 10384
title: AN ACT PROMOTING ACCESSIBLE GOVERNMENT COMMUNICATION AND TRANSPARENCY BY REQUIRING THE USE OF PLAIN LANGUAGE AND LOCAL LANGUAGE TRANSLATION OR DIALECT IN ALL GOVERNMENT ISSUED PUBLIC DOCUMENTS, ADVISORIES, AND OTHER SIMILAR DOCUMENTS INTENDED FOR PUBLIC DISSEMINATION Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: Section 1. Short Title. - This Act shall be known as the “ Accessible Government Communications Through Plain Language Act of 2026”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Language is the fundamental medium through which we communicate, interact, and forge a common national identity. The Philippines, being an archipelagic nation, is home to many distinct languages and dialects spoken throughout the country. While regions may differ in language, our common Filipino identity and our commitment to the country remains undivided. The 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes the people's right to information, particularly on matters of public concern. Language also serves as an important tool for instruction on public services, for transparency in government actions, and for accountability in holding institutions answerable to the citizens they serve. However, this right can only be meaningfully exercised when the information is communicated in a language the people understand. Despite this Constitutional guarantee, numerous government documents remain inaccessible due to overly technical, formal, or otherwise complicated language. This makes it difficult for the public to understand and take part in government processes and public affairs, leaving many unable to access important information and basic public services. This bill seeks to address this communication gap by mandating all government offices, including Government-Owned and Controlled Corporations (GOCCs), to employ plain language or appropriate local language translations or dialect in all communications intended for the public. It likewise aims to ensure universal accessibility of government information, promote transparency in public transactions, and enable the citizenry to make informed decisions regarding matters of public concern. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 10386
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A DIGITALIZED OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS (OFW) WELFARE AND MONITORING SYSTEM, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the protection of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) throughout their overseas employment. It establishes the Digitalized Overseas Filipino Workers Welfare and Monitoring System (DOWMS) under the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) to ensure timely government intervention and improved delivery of welfare services. The growing number of OFWs has increased the demand for a more responsive and integrated system for government service delivery. Dispersed records across multiple agencies impede efficient monitoring, delay the verification of information, and constrain the government’s ability to provide timely assistance during emergencies. The proposed measure establishes a centralized digital platform that consolidates OFW records and streamlines access to government welfare services. It also facilitates real time reporting of emergencies and labor-related grievances, strengthens repatriation and reintegration efforts, and generates reliable data to support evidence-based policymaking and improve government programs for migrant workers. It likewise ensures that all personal information collected and processed is in accordance with Republic Act No. 10173, otherwise known as the “Data Privacy Act of 2012”. This vital piece of legislation recognizes that protecting OFWs requires not only responsive policies but also modern public institutions equipped to deliver timely, accessible, and responsive services. As our modern day heroes continue to contribute to the country’s national development through their work and sacrifices abroad, the State shall likewise adopt digital systems that will safeguard their rights and welfare wherever they may be. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10405
title: AN ACT PROTECTING ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS BY PROHIBITING THE PASS-ON OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES, STRENGTHENING THE ACCOUNTABILITY OF DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES FOR SYSTEM LOSSES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001 OR EPIRA," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “...panahon na para tanggalin na natin ang system loss na pinapasa sa consumer… Hindi naman kasalanan ng consumer kung bakit nagkaroon ng system loss… therefore, we, the people, request – no, we demand for the immediate amendment of the EPIRA, and to prohibit charging system loss against consumers including the value-added tax thereon…” -President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr., SONA 2026 Republic Act (RA) No. 9136, otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), was enacted to ensure a quality, reliable, secure, and affordable supply of electricity through reforms in the electric power industry. Distribution utilities are currently allowed, as part of their framework, to recover a portion of their system losses subject to prescribed caps set by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). System losses are the difference between the electricity purchased by a distribution utility and the electricity actually delivered and billed to consumers. These losses include both technical losses, which naturally occur during transmission and distribution, and non-technical losses arising from electricity pilferage, illegal connections, meter tampering, fraud, billing errors, and operational inefficiencies.1 Moreover, EPIRA, RA No. 7832 (Anti- Electricity and Electric Transmission Lines/Materials Pilferage Act of 1994, and ERC guidelines regulate the recovery of system loss. Notwithstanding the regulatory caps imposed by ERC on recoverable system losses, Filipino consumers continue to bear the financial burden of electricity they neither received nor consumed. The current framework effectively transfers to consumers costs arising from circumstances largely beyond their control.2 1 https://www.rappler.com/business/explainer-what-system-loss-affect-power-bill/ 2 https://bworldonline.com/corporate/2022/03/16/436190/napocor-seeks-erc-nod-to-use- p335m-for-watersheds/ President Ferdinand “Bongbong” R. Marcos Jr., in his 2026 State of the Nation Address (SONA), urged Congress to amend the EPIRA to remove system loss charges from consumers' electricity bills. He emphasized that consumers should not be made to pay for electricity that never reached their homes or businesses. Sharing the same vision with the President, this Representation believes that this measure shall address the plight of our constituents in carrying the burden of the system loss. This bill seeks to amend the EPIRA to prohibit the recovery of system loss charges from end-users, strengthen the accountability of distribution utilities, intensify anti-electricity pilferage measures, and reinforce the regulatory powers of the ERC to ensure greater efficiency, transparency, and consumer protection. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10408
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING MINIMUM SAFETY STANDARDS FOR SCHOOL- SPONSORED ACTIVITIES, STRENGTHENING STUDENT SAFETY, RISK MANAGEMENT, EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS, INCIDENT REPORTING, CORRECTIVE ACTION MECHANISMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The safety and welfare of students participating in school-sponsored activities are matters of paramount public concern. Educational tours, athletic competitions, leadership camps, community immersion programs, field-based learning activities, and other experiential learning opportunities play a vital role in student development. These activities promote leadership, teamwork, resilience, civic engagement, and practical learning beyond the classroom. Recent incidents involving student injuries and fatalities have highlighted the need to strengthen safety planning, emergency preparedness, risk management, and institutional accountability. While the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) have adopted regulations governing certain activities, there remains a need for a comprehensive statutory framework establishing minimum national standards applicable to school-sponsored activities involving elevated risks. This measure adopts a prevention-oriented approach. It does not create new criminal offenses, alter existing standards of civil liability, or establish duplicative approval systems. Instead, it seeks to strengthen student safety through risk assessment requirements, emergency preparedness measures, transportation safety standards, accident coverage mechanisms, incident reporting systems, corrective action plans, and continuous safety improvement processes. The bill also harmonizes existing DepEd and CHED regulations, preserves existing legal remedies, protects whistleblowers, and establishes evidence-based oversight mechanisms to identify recurring risks and prevent future tragedies. By encouraging proactive safety management while preserving the educational value of experiential learning activities, this measure seeks to reduce preventable injuries and deaths and ensure that students may participate in educational activities under safer conditions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. label: HB 10424
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ALL BARANGAY OFFICIALS, INCLUDING BARANGAY TANODS, MEMBERS OF THE LUPON TAGAPAMAYAPA, BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS, AND BARANGAY DAY CARE WORKERS, A LUMP SUM RETIREMENT PAY EQUIVALENT TO ONE (1) YEAR HONORARIUM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 393 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay officials and community workers serve as the first line of public service, delivering essential government programs and responding directly to the needs of their constituents. As frontliners in governance, they perform vital functions in maintaining peace and order, promoting public health, resolving community disputes, implementing social services, and ensuring the effective delivery of government programs at the grassroots level. Despite their invaluable contributions, many of them retire after years of dedicated service without receiving any form of retirement benefit or financial security. While the Local Government Code of 1991 provides honoraria, allowances, and other benefits for barangay officials, it does not grant retirement pay to barangay officials, barangay tanods, members of the Lupong Tagapamayapa, barangay health workers, and barangay day care workers. As a result, many individuals who have devoted years of service to their communities are left without adequate recognition and financial assistance upon retirement. Therefore, this measure seeks to amend Section 393 of Republic Act No. 7160 by granting qualified barangay officials and community workers a lump sum retirement pay equivalent to one (1) year of honorarium, subject to the conditions provided by law. It likewise establishes a Barangay Retirement Fund to ensure the sustainable funding and efficient administration of retirement benefits for eligible beneficiaries. By providing retirement benefits to barangay officials and community workers, this bill recognizes their invaluable service, promotes their financial security after retirement, and strengthens morale among those who dedicate themselves to public service at the grassroots level. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. label: HB 10425
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF PROVINCIAL/CITY/MUNICIPAL ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES OFFICER AMENDING SECTION 484 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The increasing frequency of floods, landslides, forest degradation, and other environmental challenges highlights the need to strengthen environmental governance at the local level. Local government units (LGUs) play a vital role in protecting and managing forests, watersheds, coastal resources, and other natural assets. However, many LGUs still lack dedicated Environment and Natural Resources Officers (ENROs), as their appointment under the Local Government Code of 1991 remains optional. This results in many LGUs either having no designated ENRO or assigning environmental responsibilities to personnel who lack the technical expertise or security of tenure necessary to ensure continuity in environmental management programs. Therefore, this measure seeks to amend Section 484 of Republic Act No. 7160 by making the appointment of Provincial, City, and Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Officers mandatory and establishing the position as regular and permanent. Institutionalizing these positions will strengthen the capacity of LGUs to implement environmental protection, watershed rehabilitation, biodiversity conservation, climate change adaptation, and disaster risk reduction programs. By ensuring that every local government has a qualified and permanent Environment and Natural Resources Officer, this bill seeks to improve policy continuity, strengthen environmental law enforcement, enhance disaster risk reduction and climate resilience, and promote the responsible stewardship of the country's natural resources for the benefit of present and future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. label: HB 10426
title: AN ACT DECLARING SEPTEMBER 29 OF EVERY YEAR AS A SPECIAL NONWORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF IROSIN, PROVINCE OF SORSOGON, IN CELEBRATION OF THE PARAY FESTIVAL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Irosin is widely recognized as the agricultural heart of the Province of Sorsogon, with rice farming serving as one of the primary sources of livelihood for its people. The abundance of its fertile lands and the dedication of its farmers have significantly contributed to the municipality's economy, local food security, and agricultural heritage. In recognition of these contributions, the Municipality annually celebrates the Paray Festival every 29th of September as its official cultural and agricultural festival. The Paray Festival has become a meaningful expression of the identity, unity, and resilience of the people of Irosin. Through agricultural exhibitions, cultural presentations, trade fairs, and various community activities, the festival pays tribute to the hardworking farmers of the municipality while showcasing Irosin's rich traditions and promoting tourism, local enterprise, and community pride. The annual celebration has become an important occasion for preserving the municipality's cultural heritage and strengthening solidarity among its residents. Therefore, this measure seeks to declare September 29 of every year as a special nonworking holiday in the Municipality of Irosin, Province of Sorsogon, in celebration of the Paray Festival. Declaring the day as a special nonworking holiday will enable residents, particularly farmers, workers, students, and families, to fully participate in the festivities, honor the municipality's agricultural heritage, and reinforce the shared values and traditions that define the community. The measure likewise recognizes the invaluable contribution of Irosin's farmers to the municipality's growth and development. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10427
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF THE OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Out-of-school youth comprise a significant sector of the country's young population. Many are unable to complete their education due to poverty, family responsibilities, unemployment, health concerns, natural disasters, or other socio-economic challenges. Without adequate opportunities for education, skills development, and employment, they remain vulnerable to poverty, discrimination, exploitation, and social exclusion. While the government has implemented various programs such as the Alternative Learning System, Technical-Vocational Education and Training, and livelihood initiatives, these interventions remain fragmented and insufficient to comprehensively address the diverse needs of out-of-school youth. Therefore, this bill seeks to establish the Magna Carta for the Out-of-School Youth, recognizing out-of-school youth as an important sector in nation-building and providing them with comprehensive protection, education, skills training, employment assistance, social services, and other programs necessary to improve their quality of life. The bill likewise strengthens the responsibilities of government agencies and local government units in promoting social inclusion, protecting the rights of out-of-school youth, and creating pathways for them to return to school, acquire technical and vocational skills, secure decent employment, or pursue entrepreneurial opportunities. Ultimately, this bill affirms that every young Filipino deserves an equal opportunity to learn, develop, and succeed regardless of educational or economic circumstances, ensuring that no youth is left behind in the country's pursuit of inclusive and sustainable development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. label: HB 10428
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF STUDENT ATHLETES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Student-athletes embody the ideals of excellence, discipline, teamwork, and perseverance. As they strive to excel both in the classroom and in athletic competition, they contribute not only to the development of Philippine sports but also to the formation of responsible, well-rounded citizens. However, many student-athletes continue to face challenges in balancing their academic responsibilities with the rigorous demands of training and competition, while remaining vulnerable to discrimination, exploitation, inadequate health protection, unsafe training and competition environments, and limited institutional support. Although Republic Act No. 10676, otherwise known as the "Student-Athletes Protection Act," provides safeguards against the commercialization of student-athletes and regulates residency requirements, there remains a need for a more comprehensive legal framework that fully recognizes and protects their rights, welfare, safety, and holistic development. Therefore, this measure seeks to establish the Magna Carta for Student-Athletes, guaranteeing their rights to quality education, safe and healthy training and competition environments, proper medical care, scholarship protection, freedom from discrimination and abuse, and meaningful participation in decisions affecting their welfare. It likewise defines the responsibilities of schools, athletic associations, and government agencies in ensuring that student-athletes receive adequate academic, physical, emotional, and medical support while pursuing excellence in sports. By requiring access to qualified healthcare professionals, safe facilities and equipment, emergency medical assistance, and protection from violence, exploitation, and performance-enhancing drugs, this bill promotes the safety and well-being of every student-athlete throughout their athletic journey. By strengthening institutional support and promoting a balanced approach to education and athletic development, this bill seeks to empower student-athletes to realize their full potential without compromising their academic aspirations, health, safety, and well-being. Ultimately, this bill aims to uphold the rights and welfare of every Filipino student-athlete and foster an environment where academic achievement and athletic excellence complement one another in building a healthier, safer, more disciplined, and globally competitive generation of Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. label: HB 10429
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING REGIONAL YOUTH LEADERSHIP AND NATION- BUILDING TRAINING CENTERS FOR STUDENT LEADERS IN ALL REGIONS OF THE COUNTRY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The youth are among the nation's greatest assets and play a vital role in shaping the country's future. Developing responsible, ethical, and service-oriented young leaders is essential to strengthening democratic institutions, promoting civic participation, and fostering a culture of volunteerism, good governance, and nation-building. However, opportunities for structured leadership development remain uneven across the country, particularly for young people in underserved and geographically isolated communities. Although schools, youth organizations, and government agencies implement various leadership and civic engagement programs, there remains a need for a more accessible and institutionalized system that provides sustained leadership education and practical training for young Filipinos. Therefore, this bill seeks to establish Regional Youth Leadership and Nation-Building Training Centers in all regions of the country. These centers shall provide leadership development, civic education, governance awareness, volunteerism, public service training, and community engagement opportunities for student leaders, youth leaders, and other qualified young Filipinos. By expanding access to quality leadership training and strengthening youth participation in governance and community development, this bill seeks to empower Filipino youth to become catalysts of positive change, innovation, and inclusive development in their respective communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. label: HB 10440
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE INCOME TAX EXEMPTION CEILING FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO FIVE HUNDRED THOUSAND PESOS (PHP 500,000.00) ANNUALLY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) and (b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 28, Article VI of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that the rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and the Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. While taxation remains indispensable to funding government programs and public services, it must not impose an undue burden on workers whose purchasing power has steadily declined due to inflation. In line with this, Republic Act No. 10963, also known as the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law, has significantly reduced the tax burden on individual taxpayers by exempting annual taxable income not exceeding Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (Php 250,000.00) from income tax. At the time of its enactment, this threshold provided meaningful tax relief for low- and middle-income earners. However, persistent inflation, rising consumer prices, and increasing costs of basic necessities—including food, transportation, housing, education, healthcare, and utilities—have substantially eroded the real value of the existing exemption threshold. In recent years, inflation has consistently diminished the purchasing power of Filipino households, compelling workers to devote a greater proportion of their income to essential expenditures. As a consequence, many taxpayers whose nominal incomes have increased merely to keep pace with inflation are nevertheless subjected to higher income tax liabilities despite experiencing little or no corresponding improvement in their real standard of living. This phenomenon undermines the objective of maintaining a fair and progressive tax system. This measure seeks to increase the annual income tax exemption threshold from Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (Php 250,000.00) to Five Hundred Thousand Pesos (Php 500,000.00). By adjusting the exemption to better reflect current economic realities, the proposed measure aims to preserve the purchasing power of Filipino workers, provide meaningful tax relief to low- and middle-income earners, and allow households to allocate a greater portion of their income toward essential goods, education, healthcare, housing, savings, and productive investments. By modernizing the income tax exemption threshold, this bill reaffirms the State's commitment to a just, progressive, and responsive tax system that protects the welfare of Filipino workers while promoting inclusive economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. PERCIVAL V. CENDAÑA Akbayan Representative JOSE MANUEL TADEO DADAH KIRAM ISMULA “CHEL” I. label: HB 10441
title: AN ACT PREVENTING, MITIGATING, AND RESPONDING TO RISKS AFFECTING CHILDREN AND OTHER TOURISTS WHILE ON VACATION, ENGAGING IN LEISURE, OR PARTICIPATING IN ANY OTHER ACTIVITIES RELATED TO THE TOURISM INDUSTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tourism in the Philippines is both a showcase of the nation’s natural wealth and a vital engine of economic progress. With its extensive coastlines, rich marine ecosystems, and world‑class destinations, the country has consistently drawn international acclaim. In 2023, the Philippines was recognized at the World Travel Awards as the World’s Leading Dive Destination and World’s Leading Beach Destination. That same year, the industry contributed ₱2.09 trillion or 8.6 percent of the gross domestic product 1. These achievements highlight the sector’s importance not only to national revenue but also to local communities whose livelihoods depend on tourism. However, the enjoyment of these attractions is not without risk. Visitors, especially children, remain vulnerable to accidents and health hazards such as drowning, jellyfish stings, animal bites, spinal injuries, and infectious diseases. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that in 2021, accidental drowning or submersion claimed 3,604 lives, with children aged 1 to 14 comprising 1,056 of the fatalities. Drowning was the second leading cause of death among children aged 5 to 9 that year. Recent tragedies illustrate the urgency of stronger safeguards. On October 30, 2023, six‑year‑old Sandy O. Garovillas died after a box jellyfish sting at a resort where 1 Philippine News Agency. (2024). Focus on tourism brings record-high figures for PH. Retrieved from https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1229430 trained responders and adequate medical supplies were absent 2. Emergency care was delayed due to difficulties in contacting services and the distance to health facilities, leaving passers‑by, a foreign medical student and a U.S. Army medic, to administer first aid. Pharmacies and hospitals nearby also lacked the equipment needed to treat the sting, despite the Philippines being identified by experts as “ground zero” for lethal jellyfish encounters. A similar incident occurred on June 8, 2021, when a seven‑year‑old girl died and two others were injured after contact with a box jellyfish in Camarines Sur 3. Tourism must therefore be pursued hand‑in‑hand with safety. Protecting visitors is essential to sustaining the industry’s growth and ensuring that the Philippines remains a trusted destination. Establishing emergency response systems, equipping local facilities, and deploying trained lifeguards and first responders are practical measures that can save lives and prevent injuries. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize mechanisms that will prevent, mitigate, and respond to risks affecting children and other visitors in tourist areas. It mandates the availability of life‑saving equipment, medicines, and medical services in destinations across the country, thereby strengthening both public safety and the resilience of the tourism sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. DADAH KIRAM ISMULA Akbayan Representative JOSE MANUEL TADEO PERCIVAL V. CENDAÑA “CHEL” I. label: HB 10443
title: AN ACT REMOVING THE BURDEN OF SYSTEM LOSS COSTS FROM CONSUMER ELECTRICITY BILLS, PROHIBITING FOR THE PURPOSE DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES FROM IMPOSING SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES ON CONSUMERS AND REMOVING VALUE ADDED TAX ON THE SALE OF ELECTRICITY THAT BECOMES SYSTEM LOSS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is a basic necessity, yet its high cost continues to burden Filipino families and businesses. The government must prioritize making electricity more affordable. During his fifth State of the Nation Address on July 27, 2026, President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. called for the immediate amendment of the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) and the prohibition of charging system losses to consumers, including the VAT imposed thereon. System loss refers to the difference between the electricity delivered to a distribution system and the electricity ultimately delivered to consumers. These losses may be technical, arising from the physical delivery of electricity, or non-technical, resulting from theft, pilferage, meter tampering, and other unlawful activities. Under existing law, distribution utilities (DUs) may recover allowable system losses from consumers through a system loss charge. In effect, consumers pay for electricity they did not use, including losses caused by inefficiencies and illegal activities. For a MERALCO consumer using 200 kWh per month, the system loss charge averaged ₱148.95 monthly from August 2025 to July 2026, or about ₱1,787.38 annually, exclusive of VAT. The charge also increased from ₱0.64 per kWh in January 2025 to ₱0.88 in July 2026, a 37.6% increase. 1 This bill seeks to provide immediate relief by prohibiting DUs from imposing or recovering system loss costs from end-users, whether technical or non-technical. Any system loss costs illegally collected shall be promptly refunded to consumers. It likewise exempts from VAT the electricity corresponding to system losses. The measure also strengthens accountability. The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) shall strictly enforce the prohibition and continue monitoring the system loss performance of DUs. Meanwhile, the National Electrification Administration (NEA) shall strengthen its institutional, financial, and technical support to electric cooperatives in reducing system losses. DUs may not use the prohibition on system loss recovery as justification for reducing service quality, delaying necessary maintenance or investments, or refusing service to qualified consumers. Violations shall be subject to administrative fines and, when warranted, suspension or revocation of authority to operate. Consumers should pay only for the electricity they actually use. This measure seeks to make electricity bills fairer, provide immediate financial relief to Filipino families, and strengthen accountability in the power sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 10444
title: AN ACT TO ENSURE THE ACCESSIBILITY OF WEBSITES, DIGITAL PLATFORMS, MOBILE APPLICATIONS, AND ELECTRONIC SERVICES FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, persons with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to full participation in an increasingly digital society. According to the National Council for Disability Affairs (NCDA), as of July 2026, about three (3) million Filipinos are registered as persons with disabilities — 1,072,692 with physical disability, 459,759 with speech impairment, 415,547 with psychosocial disability, and 315,642 with visual disability.1 The consequences of this gap are measurable. In 2020, the Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation (DARE) Index, compiled by the Global Initiative for Inclusive ICTs (G3ict), scored the Philippines 53 out of 100, reflecting comparatively strong legal commitments but weak institutional capacity and outcomes. The country registered only 18 of a possible 50 points across ten (10) measured areas of ICT accessibility, and to date, no agency holds an exclusive mandate over accessible ICTs2. This exclusion runs against the highest law of the land. Article XIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that "[t]he Congress shall give highest priority to the enactment of measures that protect and enhance the right of all the people to human dignity, reduce social, economic, and political inequalities, and remove cultural inequities by equitably diffusing wealth and political power for the common good." Section 13 of the same Article goes further, mandating that the State establish a special agency for persons with disabilities to support their rehabilitation, self- development, self-reliance, and integration into the mainstream of society. 1 Data from National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) as of 06 July 2026. Retrieved from: https://ncda.gov.ph/ 2 G3ict (2020). Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation Index. Retrieved from: https://g3ict.org/country- profile/philippines 1 The Philippines has also undertaken this commitment internationally. It ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) on April 15, 2008, and Article 9 thereof obligates the State to ensure that persons with disabilities have access, on an equal basis with others, to information and communications technologies (ICT) and other services open to the public. Domestically, this constitutional and treaty-level commitment is carried through Republic Act No. 7277, the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, as amended, which mandates that persons with disabilities be afforded equal opportunity in education, employment, and access to public facilities and services 3. It is further operationalized through a series of administrative issuances, chief among them are the 2010 ICTO-NCDA Joint Memorandum Circular on web accessibility4 and DICT Memorandum Circular No. 004, Series of 20175, which adopted the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0 as the technical standard for government websites. DICT M.C No. 004, in particular, requires the use of alternative text for non-text content, captions and transcripts for multimedia, and descriptive links and headings; mandates regular accessibility audits against WCAG 2.0; and requires each government agency to stand up its own web accessibility compliance team. These issuances have laid meaningful technical groundwork, but they remain administrative circulars rather than statute. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0 was developed through the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) process, in cooperation with individuals, organizations, and governments worldwide, to provide a single, shared standard for web content accessibility6. WCAG explains how to make web "content", natural information such as text, images, and sound; the code or markup defining structure and presentation; and dynamic content, multimedia, mobile applications, and AI-driven web interfaces, accessible to persons with disabilities7. WCAG rests on four principles: content must be (1) perceivable, presentable to users through means they can sense; (2) operable, not requiring interaction a user cannot perform; (3) understandable, with information and interface operation that users can comprehend; and (4) robust, interpretable reliably across a wide range of user agents, including assistive technologies, even as those technologies evolve8. Thus, this proposed measure. 3 Chapter 6, Sections 25-28 4 Dated 29 June 2010 5 Dated 12 May 2017 6 Henry, S.L (26 May 2026). WCAG 2 Overview. It adopts WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the minimum enforceable standard for all covered entities— national and local government agencies, government-owned or -controlled corporations (GOCCs), and private establishments offering goods and services to the public through digital means, including banks, e-commerce platforms, educational institutions, healthcare providers, and telecommunications and broadcast companies. It requires covered entities to integrate accessibility into the full lifecycle of digital products and services, from procurement through maintenance; establishes graduated compliance periods calibrated to entity size; and creates a coordinated enforcement framework led by the DICT, in partnership with the NCDA, combining administrative penalties and criminal liability for willful non-compliance. title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE REHABILITATION, SELF-DEVELOPMENT AND SELF- RELIANCE OF DISABLED PERSONS AND THEIR INTEGRATION INTO THE MAINSTREAM OF SOCIETY AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES,” TO MANDATE THE RIGHT TO ACCESS TO INFORMATION AND THE RIGHT TO DIGITAL ACCESSIBILITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he Congress shall give highest priority to the enactment of measures that protect and enhance the right of all the people to human dignity, reduce social, economic, and political inequalities, and remove cultural inequities by equitably diffusing wealth and political power for the common good.” Additionally, Section 13 of the same Article mandates that the State establish a special agency for persons with disabilities to support their rehabilitation, self-development, self-reliance, and integration into the mainstream of society. Since its enactment in 1992, Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Disabled Persons,” has provided the primary framework for advancing the rights and welfare of over 2.5 million Filipino persons with disabilities. 1 However, significant social and technological transformations over the past decades have resulted in the emergence of new barriers for persons with disabilities. With government services, banking, commerce, and everyday transactions shifting to the digital space, the existing law must be amended not just to guarantee barrier-free physical environments, but also accessibility and non-discrimination in the new digital environment. The bill modernizes the RA 7277 by guaranteeing the right to access to information and the right to digital accessibility. The bill further specifies mechanisms 1 Cabalza, D. (20 June 2025). Registered PWDs in PH now at 2.5M. INQUIRER.net. https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2072065/registered-pwds-in-ph-now-at-2-5m. 1 and provisions, specifically on banking and financial institutions, to ensure an environment for persons with disabilities that is free from barriers and free from discrimination. Finally, to align national legislation with modern human rights standards, the bill updates the statutory definition of persons with disabilities and replaces the term “disabled persons” in Republic Act No. 7277 with the more appropriate, person-first, widely acceptable, and empowering term “persons with disabilities. This bill was crafted after consultations with multiple stakeholders in various persons with disabilities groups, sectors, and advocacy networks. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 10446
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FREE ANNUAL MEDICAL CHECK-UP FOR FILIPINOS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Advancements in modern medicine have allowed for most diseases to be treated, but the adage “prevention is better than a cure”, still rings true. To produce the best prognosis possible, early diagnosis is key. However, despite a drop in unemployment and underemployment, the average nominal living wage is still well below the family living wage (FLW) for a family of five1, thus forcing Filipinos to deprioritize health in their necessary expenses. It is an unfortunate reality that a lot of people opt to skip medical check-ups, even in situations where they are sorely needed. Despite holding health as a top priority, health and medical affordance remain a point of anxiety for most Filipinos. A 2025 study shows that despite the clear importance given to health by most; many families still either need an HMO or to go into debt to afford medical assistance2. This figure makes sense: when one earns just enough to provide for their family’s basic needs, getting a medical check-up, despite its clear preventative and proactive benefits, would give way for other pressing needs. It is to help Filipinos from having to make these hard decisions that the present measure aims to mandate the State to provide free annual medical check-up to all Filipinos, so that cost no longer has to be a point of consideration. Through this, it is our hope that diagnosable diseases will be detected at the earliest possible time, thereby reducing the number of Filipinos who fall victim to preventable conditions, raise their quality of life, and in the long-run, ease the burden on the country’s healthcare system. 1 IBON Foundation, “Filipino workers struggling despite reported drop in unemployment, underemployment,” January 08, 2025, available at https://www.ibon.org/filipino-workers-struggling-nov-2024-lfs/ 2 Smart Parenting, “Study Shows 64% of Filipino Families Cannot Afford a P10,000 Hospital Bill,” November 28, 2025, available at https://www.smartparenting.com.ph/life/news/filipino-families-hospital-bill-study-a6837-20251128-dy n?utm_source=Facebook-SP&utm_medium=Ownshare-Photo&utm_campaign=20260504-fbnp-life-filip ino-families-hospital-bill-study-a6837-20251128-dyn-fbold-commentsectionlink Thus, it is for the foregoing reasons that the passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
