title: AN ACT MANDATING GOVERNMENT INSTITUTIONS AND FOOD SERVICE ESTABLISHMENTS TO PURCHASE THE AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE OF LOCAL FARMERS OR PRODUCERS FOR THEIR FOOD PREPARATION AND PRODUCTION Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Pagkaing Pilipino Act of 2026.” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared a policy of the State to ensure local food security and spur the development of the Filipino agriculture industry. As such, the government must give priority to the produce of local farmers and producers in terms of the purchases of government institutions and food service establishments intended for food preparation and production. SECTION 3. Mandatory Purchase. - Government Institution and Food Service Establishments, such as hotels, restaurants, and catering services, shall prioritize the purchase of local agricultural produce of local farmers for their food preparation and production. Moreover, the produce of local farmers within the territorial jurisdiction of the local government unit (LGU) wherein the government institution and food service establishment is located shall take precedence over produce outside their respective LGUs to lower transportation or other hauling costs in the delivery of such produce. Nothing in this Act shall be construed as prohibiting the government institution and food service establishment to purchase local produce in different political subdivisions, provided that the requirement herein set forth is complied by the food service establishment. SECTION 4. Exceptions. - Section 3 of this Act shall not be applicable in any of the following cases where the local produce is: a) No longer fit for human consumption;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local farmers and agricultural producers are often at the mercy of seasonal calamities, economic crises, pressure from middlemen, and other pain points in the agricultural supply and value chain. As such, these important producers are often confronted with having to sell their harvest at below-market prices or to throw it away altogether, resulting in large-scale food loss. Most of such losses happen post-harvest, where the lack of post-harvesting facilities and handling result in losses up to fifty percent (50%) for crops such as rice, wheat, and cereal grains which makes up a staggering seventy percent (70%) of all calories consumed in the country1. These figures indicate that roughly forty percent (40%) of all food being produced are going to waste, with around twenty percent (20%) of all carrots, bananas, cabbage, calamansi, eggplant, mangoes, sweet potatoes, rice and tomatoes going to waste2. With such a pressing need to divert food loss, support farmers and producers, and strengthen food security, a clear mandate is needed to allow government institutions and food service establishments to prioritize the purchase of locally grown harvest and produce. The Philippines, with its growing population and aging harvest and food chain infrastructure, is especially vulnerable to worsening climate impacts and unpredictable economic swings. By prioritizing the purchase of food from local suppliers and growers, the country is not only empowering its own agricultural workers; helping food security; and contribute towards our Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)3, an important action point under the Paris Agreement and an active agenda of the Climate Change Commission (CCC), the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), and the country’s National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP). It is for these pressing needs that the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 The Global Foodbanking Network, “Agricultural Recovery: Rise Against Hunger Philippines,” available at https://www.foodbanking.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2025-GFN-RAHP-Case-Study-v2.pdf 2 ibid 3 Climate Change Commission, Department of Environment and Natural Resources, “Implementation Plan for the Republic of the Philippines Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 2020–2030,” available at https://www.climate.gov.ph/public/ckfinder/userfiles/files/Knowledge/The%20Philippines'%20NDC%20 Implementation%20Plan%20-%20072024.pdf ALFRED C. title: AN ACT TO REDUCE FOOD WASTE BY REQUIRING EDIBLE FOOD SURPLUS TO BE DONATED TO FOOD BANKS AND CHARITIES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Anti Food Waste Act of 2026” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – The State recognizes the universal right to access safe and edible food. It is the purview of the State to provide the necessary conditions not only for the survival of its citizens, but of their safety and comfort, and this begins at the assurance that every Filipino has food on their table. The high number of food waste is both a tragedy and a solution. This Act intends to divert such waste, which may by all standards, still fit for human consumption and be given to those that live in hunger. Towards this end, the State shall adopt a system to promote, facilitate, and ensure the reduction of food waste through redistribution, diversion, and repurposing. SECTION 3. Definitions. – For purposes of this Act, the following terms shall mean: (a) Food waste is defined as food removed from the human food supply chain, including all the crop and livestock human-edible food that, directly or indirectly, completely exit the human food supply chain by being discarded, incinerated or otherwise, and do not reenter in any other utilization (such as animal feed, industrial use, etc.), up to, and excluding, the retail level. Losses that occur during storage, transport and processing, also of imported quantities, are therefore all included;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to food remains an urgent issue for a large percentage of the Philippine population. As recently as March 2026, a Social Weather Station (SWS) survey1 showed that almost a quarter of the country’s population experienced involuntary hunger (23.2%), of which 5.5% experienced severe hunger. Such issues arise from the precarious state of the nation’s food security and the inadequate access to safe, reliable, and nutritious food sources. Tackling food waste goes hand-in-hand with helping alleviate food insecurity in the country and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. As part of global and national actions to end hunger and curb carbon pollution, an Act that mandates food establishments to donate edible food surplus can help tackle the twin problems of food security and reduced emissions. Although the Philippines is making progress in fulfilling its commitments to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), more rigorous legislation is needed to sustain this progress and divert food waste towards food banks. Child stunting, for instance, remains prevalent, with as many as 23.6 of the population experiencing stunting due to malnutrition2. The ongoing 2026 fuel crisis brought on by the conflict in West Asia is also having negative impacts on the nation’s inflation, which has detrimental 1 Isabelle Pechay (2026), “SWS: Hunger among Filipino families rises to 23.2% in March 2026,” Inquirer, May 13, 2026, available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2227801/sws-hunger-among-filipino-families-rises-to-23-2-in-march-2026 2 World Food Programme, “Philippines Country Brief,” available at https://docs.wfp.org/api/documents/WFP-0000174216/download/ effects on the price of food, groceries, and other necessities. As Super El-Niño is expected this year, it may compound the issue of food insecurity further3. There is a very pressing need to establish clear guidelines for determining what food surplus is safe to eat, enforcing donations to curb food wastage, protecting good samaritans from damage liabilities, and empowering LGUs to distribute food surplus to their constituents. This bill aims to establish just such a framework and invite transformative, sustainable change by filling in the policy gaps. This is only the first step towards solving a long-term, systemic issue4. There is enough food for everyone if everyone has equal access to it. This bill effectively aims to tackle the pressure points that prevent a large percentage of the population from accessing safe and nutritious food. By mandating food establishments to donate their excess edible food and distributing it to the marginalized via food banks, we can slowly solve malnutrition, childhood stunting, and hunger in our Philippine islands. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10449
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING GOVERNMENT AID AND SUPPORT FOR MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs) Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE MSMEs or Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises are the backbone of the Philippine economy. Despite being often unrecognized and under-supported, they remain key drivers of sustainable growth, generating employment and contributing greatly in the country’s export earnings. Latest data from a Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) report from 2024 showed that MSMEs made up over 99.6% of all the enterprises in the country1. As each new business evolves and progresses, they serve as “the engine of net employment growth” while also enhancing the overall quality of jobs that Filipinos can be employed in. Despite most of them (90.6%) being micro enterprises or those having less than ten (10) employees or assets less than P3 million, they still employ more than half of the Philippine workforce. By 2024, MSMEs employed 66.6% of the total employment in the Philippines or around six and a quarter million people. MSMEs also account for up to 45% of the country’s GDP and contribute to 25% of our total exports revenue.2 These astounding numbers stem from the nature of their role in the economy and society. In a study by Dano-Luna, Francisco, and Canare,3 they said that “[o]n the one hand, [MSMEs] contribute in maintaining the social-political stability in a country enabling the attainment of inclusive and sustainable national development. On the other hand, [they] have the potential 1 Department of Trade and Industry, “2024 Philippine MSME Statistics,” available at https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-knowledge-hub/dti-statistics 2 Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise Development (MSMED) Council, “Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise Development Plan 2023-2028,” available at https://dtiwebfiles.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/BSMED/MSMED+Plan+2023-2028/MSMED+Pla n+2023-2028_approved+07Nov2024.v2.pdf 3 Maribel Dano-Luna, Jamil Paolo Franciso, and Tristan Canare (2018), Drivers of Philippine SME Competitiveness: Results of the 2018 SME Survey, AIM RSN PCC Working Paper 2018-03, pp.8-9, available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/329584820. to link to large foreign firms and global value chains effectively contributing to regional and global development.” Meanwhile, a study by Miranda and Miranda4, supported the view of Dano-Luna et al. and added that “they are vital to dispersing new industries to the countryside and stimulating employment. They are likely to be labor intensive, thus providing jobs wherever they are established. In this sense, they bring about more balanced agro-industrial growth and equity in income distribution.” With all these contributions and more, MSMEs deserve more support and protection from the government. Their decline would be a significant blow in the employment of our fellow Filipinos and in our economy as a whole, while their continued empowerment and growth will strengthen our economic dynamics. As we have seen in the past few years, such as during the COVID-19 Pandemic, the United States tariffs under the Trump Administration, and the more recent oil crisis brought on by the Iran-American Conflict in West Asia, MSMEs are particularly vulnerable to developments brought about by crises, economic shocks, and geopolitics. While there is an increase in pushing for a more robust MSME sector, it is prudent to institutionalize the aid and support for MSMEs so that we can ensure their survival and sustainability. It is for these reasons that the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. title: AN ACT PROMOTING RURAL FINANCIAL INCLUSION AND DIGITAL LITERACY Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Rural Financial Inclusion and Digital Literacy Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to promote financial empowerment and reduce financial vulnerabilities among its citizens by taking proactive measures in developing technological capacities of various financial institutions in the rural areas to improve access to financial services. Toward this end, the State shall promote financial inclusion and literacy programs that contribute in establishing a financial system to benefit all Filipinos, regardless of socio-economic status, to accelerate economic growth and development especially in rural and provincial areas. SEC. 3. Financial Inclusion and Digital Literacy Program. – A proactive Financial Inclusion and Digital Literacy Program, hereinafter referred to as The Program, is hereby established to promote the engagement with financial service institutions such as rural banks, lending companies, insurance and pre-need companies, and health maintenance organizations (HMOs) in rural areas. The Program includes the conduct of nationwide seminars and workshops, development of modules, training on organizational development and financial management on credit worthiness, loan acquisition and repayment, and wide dissemination of information and education campaign (IEC) materials that are tailored to different sectors. The Program shall also contain a basic understanding of concepts of financial inclusion, and may include technical application to provide the public
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Despite the growing relevance of financial technology mechanisms in the Philippines, there remains a huge gap in reaching financial inclusivity in our country, especially in rural areas. Financial awareness and literacy remains a huge aspect when rolling out such technology. While general awareness of financial technology and its platforms is steadily increasing nationwide, awareness of the responsibilities of financial service providers and of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) consumer assistance mechanisms remains limited, especially among rural, older, and lower-income sectors1. Moreover, even if people are aware of new technological options, Filipinos hesitate to share personal information with such platforms due to perceived cybersecurity risks. Other issues, such as access to basic financial products and fragmented financial and business institutions, continue to challenge the inclusion of Filipinos in innovative digital finance. Growing access to digital financing and other financial access points denote an increasing awareness and accessibility of financial institutions for the general population. For instance, access is high for ATMs, pawnshops, and money-service agents such as e-money agents and cash-in/cash-out transaction providers. This is particularly felt in rural and underserved areas and further reinforces the importance of a multi-modal approach that combines physical presence and digital platforms. 1 Financial Inclusion Office, “Consumer Finance and Inclusion Survey,” Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2025, available at https://www.bsp.gov.ph/Inclusive%20Finance/Financial%20Inclusion%20Reports%20and%20Publications/2025/20 25CFISreport.pdf However, access alone is inefficient. There is a need for sustained efforts to deepen understanding, as well as utilization, of such financial platforms. The proposed bill seeks to address these problems. It is the responsibility of the State to bring about financial inclusivity, especially for those living in rural and underdeveloped areas through mechanisms that ensure equitable access to financial technology. It addresses issues of financial awareness, trust, inclusion, and access. This bill aims to empower Filipinos to be more financially stable and capable to pursue personal and economic development. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval is highly recommended. ALFRED C. label: HB 10451
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ANNUAL INCOME TAX EXEMPTION THRESHOLD FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO THREE HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (₱350,000.00), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) AND SECTION 24(A)(2)(b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure seeks to increase the annual income tax exemption threshold for individual taxpayers from ₱250,000.00 to ₱350,000.00, thereby expanding the number of workers who may retain a greater portion of their earnings. The succeeding tax computations and base tax amounts shall likewise be correspondingly adjusted to preserve the continuity and progressivity of the individual income tax system. Article VI, Section 28(1) of the 1987 Constitution states that “The rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable. The Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation.” This constitutional mandate requires the tax system to distribute the burden of taxation fairly and equitably and recognizes the responsibility of Congress to maintain a progressive system that takes into account taxpayers' capacity to pay and prevailing economic conditions. Congress has long recognized the need to protect workers earning at or near subsistence levels from income taxation. Under Republic Act No. 9504 (An Act Amending the NIRC), approved on June 17, 2008, minimum wage earners were expressly exempted from the payment of income tax on their taxable income. The law likewise exempted the holiday pay, overtime pay, night shift differential pay, and hazard pay received by minimum wage earners from income tax. Thus, the statutory income tax exemption for minimum wage earners has been part of Philippine tax policy for approximately eighteen (18) years. The policy reflects the legislative recognition that workers receiving minimum wages should be allowed to retain their income for their basic needs rather than have a portion thereof reduced by income tax. Thereafter, Republic Act No. 10963, otherwise known as the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law, further expanded this income tax relief. Under Section 24 of the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended by the TRAIN Law, individual taxpayers with annual taxable income not exceeding Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (₱250,000.00) became subject to a zero percent (0%) income tax rate beginning January 1, 2018. Although the rates applicable to the succeeding income brackets were subsequently reduced beginning January 1, 2023, the ₱250,000 tax- exempt threshold has remained unchanged. More than eight (8) years have passed since the ₱250,000 threshold took effect. During this period, the prices of goods and services have substantially increased, diminishing the purchasing power of workers' income and reducing the real economic value of the tax relief originally granted in 2018. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), in its “Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index (2018=100): June 2026,” released on July 7, 2026, the country's headline inflation rate stood at 6.4 percent in June 2026, from 6.8 percent in May 2026. The PSA further reported that the average inflation rate for the period January to June 2026 was 4.8 percent. The PSA identified food and non-alcoholic beverages, housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, and transportation as the three largest contributors to the country's June 2026 headline inflation. These are expenditures that directly affect the everyday budgets of Filipino workers and their families. The effect of rising prices is even more pronounced among lower-income households. According to the PSA's “Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index for the Bottom 30% Income Households (2018=100): June 2026,” inflation for households belonging to the bottom thirty percent (30%) income group stood at 8.0 percent in June 2026, while their average inflation rate for January to June 2026 was 5.5 percent. The foregoing figures demonstrate that inflation imposes a proportionately heavier burden on Filipinos with fewer financial resources, as a larger share of their income is devoted to food, transportation, housing, utilities, and other necessities. The deterioration in purchasing power is likewise evident from the Consumer Price Index. Based on PSA data for June 2026, using 2018 as the base year of 100, the national CPI reached approximately 135.4. In practical terms, the same basket of goods and services valued at ₱100.00 in the 2018 base year would cost approximately ₱135.40 in June 2026. The PSA explains that the purchasing power of one peso relative to the 2018 base year is approximately ₱0.74. This means that the ₱250,000 tax-exempt threshold fixed when the TRAIN Law took effect in 2018 no longer possesses the same real purchasing value today. Accordingly, raising the annual tax-exempt threshold to ₱350,000.00 is a reasonable and measured adjustment to account for the erosion in purchasing power since the TRAIN Law took effect. It does not merely create a new tax privilege; rather, it seeks to restore and preserve the real value of the income tax relief previously granted by Congress. A Filipino worker earning ₱350,000.00 in annual taxable income today does not enjoy the same purchasing capacity that the nominal amount would have represented several years ago. An increasing portion of household income is being absorbed by food, housing, electricity, transportation, healthcare, education, and other essential expenses. Increasing the threshold will provide meaningful tax relief, improve workers' disposable income, help preserve household purchasing power, and ensure that the individual income tax system remains responsive to inflation and present economic realities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10452
title: AN ACT PROVIDING OPPORTUNITIES FOR RETURNING OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKER NURSES TO TRAIN LOCAL NURSES, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL NURSE MENTORSHIP AND TRAINING PROGRAM, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a National Nurse Mentorship and Training Program that mobilizes the expertise of returning Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) nurses to strengthen the competencies of locally practicing nurses, enhance nursing education and clinical training, and improve the quality of healthcare services throughout the country. The Philippines remains one of the world’s leading sources of nurses, supplying healthcare professionals to countries facing workforce shortages. According to the World Health Organization (WHO)1, the global shortage of health and care workers is projected to reach approximately 11 million by 2030, driving sustained international demand for Filipino nurses. While overseas employment provides better compensation and professional advancement, it also contributes to persistent shortages of experienced nurses in Philippine healthcare facilities, particularly in government hospitals and underserved communities. This continuing migration has placed additional pressure on the country’s health system and underscores the need to maximize the value of the nursing workforce that returns home. Returning OFW nurses possess advanced clinical competencies, specialized training, and extensive experience acquired from highly developed healthcare systems. Many have worked in specialized fields such as critical care, emergency medicine, oncology, geriatrics, maternal and child health, mental health, and infection prevention. They also bring practical knowledge on modern healthcare technologies, patient safety systems, interdisciplinary collaboration, and evidence-based nursing practices. Despite the significant value of these competencies, the country has yet to institutionalize a mechanism that systematically facilitates their transfer to the local nursing workforce. This measure addresses that gap through a structured mentorship and skills 1 World Health Organization. (N.D.) Health workforce. Accessed from: https://www.who.int/health-topics/health-workforce. Accessed in July 7, 2026. transfer program under the Department of Health, in coordination with the Professional Regulation Commission–Board of Nursing, the Commission on Higher Education, and the Department of Migrant Workers. The program enables returning OFW nurses to serve as accredited mentors in hospitals, rural health units, community health centers, and nursing schools, creating sustained opportunities for professional development, continuing education, and capacity building across both clinical and academic settings. The bill also recognizes mentorship as a professional contribution deserving institutional support. It grants Continuing Professional Development (CPD) credits to participating nurses while providing appropriate incentives to accredited mentors, including honoraria, tax incentives, and eligibility for government-supported postgraduate education and specialized training. These measures encourage participation, promote professional excellence, and reinforce the value of knowledge sharing within the nursing profession. Beyond workforce development, the proposed measure transforms overseas nursing experience into a strategic national resource. Rather than allowing internationally acquired expertise to remain untapped, the bill promotes its reintegration into the Philippine healthcare system, strengthens institutional capacity, raises standards of patient care, and supports the long-term development of a resilient and globally competitive nursing profession. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10453
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FOR NURSES, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize Continuing Professional Development (CPD) support for Filipino nurses through employer-assisted learning programs, government-funded training opportunities, accessible online CPD resources, and incentives for healthcare institutions that invest in nursing workforce development. The measure recognizes that continuous professional growth is essential in maintaining competent nursing practice, improving healthcare delivery, and strengthening the country’s capacity to respond to evolving health challenges. The implementation of mandatory CPD requirements under Republic Act No. 10912, otherwise known as the “Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016”, ensures that professionals continuously update their knowledge and skills. However, many nurses continue to face barriers that limit their ability to participate in CPD activities. According to Lim-Saco, F. and Guino-o, T., 20241 in their study published in the Silliman Journal identified registration costs, work schedules, and transportation constraints as among the major challenges affecting nurses’ participation in professional development programs. Similarly, the study of Palma, J., et. al., 20202 among hospital nurses in the Philippines found that while nurses recognize the importance of CPD, financial constraints, limited availability of programs, and time-related factors remain significant barriers to participation. These challenges create a gap between the expectation for continuous professional advancement and the actual capacity of nurses to access relevant learning opportunities. The proposed measure addresses these policy gaps through a comprehensive support framework for nursing professional development. It addresses the financial burden of CPD compliance through mandatory employer assistance, including paid 1 Lim-Saco, F. ., & Guino-o, T. A. . (2024). Assessment of Needs and Barriers to Continuing Professional Development among Nurses. Silliman Journal, 65(1). Retrieved from https://su-journal.su.edu.ph/index.php/sj/article/view/538. Accessed in July 12, 2026. 2 Palma, J. A. F. S., Oducado, R. M. F., & Palma, B. S. (2020). Continuing professional development: Awareness, attitude, facilitators, and barriers among nurses in the Philippines. Nursing Practice Today, 7(3), 198-207.DOI 10.18502/npt.v7i3.3348. Retrieved from https://repository.wvsu.edu.ph/handle/20.500.14353/80 . Accessed in July 12, 2026. professional development leave and partial subsidy for required training programs. It expands access to specialized skills development through a government-supported scholarship and grant mechanism that enables nurses to pursue advanced certifications and strengthens the pool of nurse educators and trainers. It also responds to geographic and accessibility barriers through free online CPD platforms that allow nurses, including those in underserved areas, to participate in accredited learning activities. Furthermore, it encourages private sector participation through tax incentives and streamlines hospital-based CPD initiatives to increase the availability of affordable and relevant professional development opportunities. Nurses remain the backbone of the Philippine healthcare system, carrying the responsibility of caring for patients in hospitals, communities, and emergency situations while continuously adapting to new medical technologies and changing health needs. However, a healthcare system cannot demand excellence from its workforce without providing meaningful opportunities for growth and advancement. Supporting nurses in their pursuit of lifelong learning is not merely a professional obligation; it is an investment in safer patient care, stronger healthcare institutions, and a more resilient nation. The country’s nurses have long served as a source of pride and strength, and this measure ensures that they receive the support necessary to continue serving with competence, confidence, and dedication. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10454
title: AN ACT GRANTING RISK WELFARE BENEFITS TO NURSE EDUCATORS ENGAGED IN CLINICAL OR COMMUNITY-BASED RELATED LEARNING EXPERIENCES IN THE PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize the grant of risk welfare benefits to nurse educators assigned to supervise nursing students during clinical and community-based Related Learning Experiences (RLEs) in public and private institutions. The measure recognizes the occupational risks inherent in clinical instruction and establishes a mandatory risk welfare benefit to strengthen the recruitment, retention, and professional welfare of nurse educators, thereby supporting the country's health workforce development and the implementation of universal health care. The Philippines continues to face significant challenges in building and sustaining an adequate nursing workforce. World Health Organization (WHO)1 identifies sustained investment in nursing education, faculty capacity, workforce retention, and decent working conditions as essential to achieving universal health coverage and resilient health systems. The report further emphasizes that strengthening the nursing workforce requires not only increasing the number of practicing nurses but also ensuring the availability and protection of qualified nurse educators who prepare future generations of healthcare professionals. Despite their indispensable role, nurse educators remain outside the statutory coverage of the hazard pay and related benefits provided under Republic Act No. 7305, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta of Public Health Workers”. While supervising students in hospitals, rural health units, laboratories, and community health facilities, nurse educators are routinely exposed to infectious diseases, biological agents, hazardous substances, workplace violence, ergonomic hazards, and other occupational risks substantially similar to those encountered by frontline nurses. The absence of a comparable statutory benefit creates an inequitable situation that fails to recognize the risks assumed by those responsible for educating and training the country's future nursing workforce. The proposed measure addresses this policy gap through requiring 1 World Health Organization. (2025, May 12). State of the World's Nursing Report 2025. Accessed from: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240110236/. Accessed in July 10. 2026. employers to provide risk welfare benefits based on the actual monthly hours of clinical or community-based exposure. The graduated schedule of benefits is patterned after the exposure-based hazard pay framework under the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers and adapted to the clinical supervision workload of nurse educators. The corresponding workday classifications are converted into equivalent monthly hours of clinical exposure to reflect the workload of nurse educators supervising Related Learning Experiences. The bill likewise establishes standards for the certification of exposure hours, prescribes employer responsibility for the payment of benefits, and provides mechanisms for compliance monitoring, complaint resolution, and enforcement to ensure the effective implementation of the measure. Nurse educators carry the responsibility of preparing every generation of Filipino nurses who will serve in hospitals, communities, and healthcare institutions across the country and around the world. They perform this duty while confronting many of the same occupational hazards faced by frontline healthcare workers, yet the law has long denied them the protection and recognition afforded to others exposed to similar risks. Such disparity can no longer be ignored. Extending risk welfare benefits to nurse educators is a matter of fairness, dignity, and sound public policy. Investing in those who educate and train the nation's future nurses strengthens the nursing profession, secures the country's healthcare workforce, and protects the quality of care that every Filipino deserves. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10455
title: AN ACT GRANTING COMPREHENSIVE DUTY AND TAX EXEMPTIONS TO BENGUET STATE UNIVERSITY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 2010, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE CHARTER OF BENGUET STATE UNIVERSITY, AND FOR THE RETROACTIVE APPLICATION THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant comprehensive duty and tax exemptions on revenues and assets that are actually, directly, and exclusively used in furtherance of the Benguet State University’s (BSU) educational mandate. It strengthens Presidential Decree No. 2010, otherwise known as the “Charter of Benguet State University”, and establishes the legal basis for the retroactive application of such exemptions. As a state university, BSU is mandated to provide quality higher education, advance research, and promote extension services and agribusiness. However, revenues generated from the utilization of its assets and income-generating activities, including the rental income, have been subjected to tax assessments due to the absence of an explicit and comprehensive tax exemption under its Charter. This limits resources intended for the University’s academic and public service functions. This measure clearly defines the scope of BSU’s duty and tax exemptions. It recognizes that the University’s revenues and assets are not maintained for private gain but are continuously reinvested in its operations and services. It shall also reduce recurring disputes over tax liabilities and allow BSU to devote more of its resources to the students and communities that it serves. This vital piece of legislation reaffirms the State’s commitment to accessible and quality public higher education, and recognizes the vital role of state universities in regional and national development. It likewise places BSU on a more equitable footing with other state universities whose charters expressly provide comparable tax privileges. Greater fiscal flexibility shall strengthen BSU’s capacity to serve and contribute to development of the province of Benguet and the Cordillera region. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is respectfully sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10456
title: AN ACT GRANTING A RURAL HEALTH SERVICE INCENTIVE ALLOWANCE TO LICENSED PHYSICIANS AND NURSES ASSIGNED TO RURAL HEALTH UNITS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Rural Health Service Incentive Allowance for physicians and nurses assigned to Rural Health Units (RHUs). It aims to strengthen the recruitment and retention of healthcare professionals in rural, remote, underserved, and geographically isolated communities and recognizes the critical role of frontline healthcare workers in delivering essential health services and provides additional support to encourage qualified professionals to continue serving communities where healthcare needs are greatest. Access to quality healthcare remains a continuing challenge for many Filipinos living outside major urban centers. Rural communities often face difficulties in attracting and retaining physicians and nurses due to limited resources, challenging working environments, professional isolation, and the demands of providing comprehensive health services with constrained facilities and personnel. These challenges affect the capacity of RHUs to deliver preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and public health programs that serve as the foundation of the country's primary healthcare system. The Department of Health has consistently recognized the need to address healthcare workforce shortages and improve the distribution of health professionals, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. The implementation of Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act”, highlights the importance of strengthening primary care networks and making sure the availability of capable healthcare providers at the community level. However, financial and professional incentives remain necessary to sustain the deployment of physicians and nurses in areas where healthcare services are difficult to deliver. Despite their vital contributions, many physicians and nurses assigned to RHUs perform demanding responsibilities under conditions that differ significantly from those experienced in better-resourced healthcare facilities. They serve as the first point of contact for communities, respond to public health emergencies, manage a wide range of medical concerns, and provide continuous healthcare services despite geographic and operational challenges. Providing a dedicated incentive allowance recognizes their commitment and addresses the factors that contribute to workforce attrition in rural areas. The proposed measure aims to address policy gaps in rural healthcare workforce development through a dedicated incentive mechanism that responds to the challenges of recruiting and retaining physicians and nurses in underserved communities. It provides a uniform and institutionalized support system for healthcare professionals assigned to Rural Health Units, recognizing that existing benefits do not fully address the unique demands of rural service. It also establishes clear implementation, monitoring, and accountability mechanisms to ensure that the intended beneficiaries receive the benefit in accordance with existing budgeting, accounting, and auditing rules. Through these interventions, the measure strengthens the sustainability of rural healthcare delivery and ensures that communities, regardless of location, continue to receive essential health services from adequately supported healthcare professionals. Investing in rural healthcare workers means investing in the lives and well-being of millions of Filipinos who depend on community-based healthcare services. Physicians and nurses assigned to rural areas stand at the frontlines of public health, bringing medical care to communities where distance, limited resources, and difficult working conditions often stand between patients and the services they need. Their commitment ensures that even the most remote communities are not left behind in the pursuit of universal healthcare. Providing them with meaningful support is not merely an additional benefit but a necessary recognition of their sacrifices and a strategic investment in a stronger, more equitable, and more responsive healthcare system for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 10465
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DIRECT OR INDIRECT RECOVERY OF DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, REDUCING AND EVENTUALLY PHASING OUT THE CAP OF RECOVERABLE SYSTEM LOSSES OF RURAL ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, EXEMPTING SYSTEM LOSSES FROM THE VALUE-ADDED TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, AS AMENDED, REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” SECTION 109 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In his State of the Nation Address (SONA), the President issued an urgent and unequivocal directive to lower the country's power rates, declaring: "At kung pagbawas ng presyo ang usapan, sa aking palagay ay panahon na para tanggalin na natin ang system loss na pinapasa sa consumer.” Emphasizing that ordinary Filipinos are not at fault for these inefficiencies, the President noted that it is unjust to make them pay for it, ultimately demanding the immediate amendment of the EPIRA to prohibit the charging of system losses and the corresponding Value-Added Tax (VAT) against consumers. Answering this urgent presidential mandate, this measure addresses the cost of electricity in the Philippines, which remains a significant consideration for both household budgets and the global competitiveness of local industries. As the nation seeks sustainable ways to lower energy costs, a reevaluation of the components that make up the monthly electricity bill, specifically the charging of system losses and its VAT, is necessary and long overdue. System losses refer to the power lost during the transmission and distribution of electricity due to technical and non-technical factors. Under the current legal framework—specifically Section 10 of Republic Act No. 7832 and Section 43(f) of Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA)—distribution utilities and rural electric cooperatives are authorized to recover a certain percentage of these losses from consumers. However, standard economic principles generally dictate that operational losses—whether due to technical inefficiencies, infrastructure wear and tear, or pilferage—should be absorbed by an enterprise as part of its standard operational risks. Shifting the financial burden of system losses entirely to consumers diminishes the natural financial incentive for distribution utilities to continuously invest in modernizing their grid infrastructure and improving operational efficiency. Furthermore, applying a consumption tax (VAT) on electricity that was lost before reaching the end-user requires legislative correction. To align the power sector with best business practices and lower electricity rates for the public, this measure introduces a comprehensive framework to restructure the treatment of system losses: 1. For Private Distribution Utilities: It mandates the abolition of the system loss charges. Private utilities are expected to absorb these operational risks as overhead, which will inherently incentivize immediate upgrades to their infrastructure and the adoption of better loss-mitigation technologies. 2. For Rural Electric Cooperatives (RECs): Recognizing the distinct financial structures of RECs and the critical importance of continuous rural electrification, this bill institutes an accelerated transition. It initially reduces their recoverable system loss cap to a maximum of five percent (5%), with a scheduled phase-out to zero percent (0%) within one (1) year. 3. VAT Exemption: While the system loss charges is slated for abolition, this bill explicitly amends the National Internal Revenue Code to exempt any such charge from VAT. This is a dual strategy: it provides immediate tax relief to consumers in REC franchise areas during the one-year phase-out period, and it establishes a legal safeguard in the tax code against any future attempts to tax embedded operational losses. 4. Prohibition on Indirect Recovery: To ensure the intent of this policy is realized, the bill tasks the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to strictly monitor and prevent the indirect recovery of system losses through adjustments to other bill components or new administrative fees. By internalizing these operational risks, this legislation aims to protect the consuming public, systematically lower energy costs, and foster a more efficient, modern, and reliable power distribution sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. label: HB 10466
title: AN ACT DECLARING EVERY 10TH OF FEBRUARY OF EACH YEAR AS NATIONAL SAFER INTERNET DAY IN THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to rank among the most active internet users in the world. As of 2025, there are approximately 87 to 89 million internet users in the country, representing over 75% of the population, with Filipinos spending an average of 8 to 9 hours online daily, among the highest globally. This reflects a significant increase from earlier estimates of 76.7 million users and over 10 hours of daily usage. The rapid expansion of internet access has greatly improved connectivity, enabling advancements in education, commerce, communication, and public services. Increasing broadband penetration, mobile connectivity, and digital infrastructure continue to drive the country’s digital transformation. However, the growing digital landscape has also intensified cybersecurity risks. Recent data from the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and global cybersecurity firms indicate that the Philippines experiences millions of cyber threat attempts annually, including phishing, online scams, identity theft, and cyber-enabled exploitation. Notably, the country remains among those with the highest reported cases of online sexual exploitation of children (OSEC), underscoring the urgent need for stronger public awareness and digital safety measures. In addition, reports from organizations such as We Are Social, DataReportal, and Kaspersky highlight that Filipino users are among the most vulnerable to social engineering attacks due to high social media usage and digital engagement. These evolving threats affect not only individuals but also institutions, making cybersecurity a growing national concern. Given these developments, there is a pressing need to strengthen public awareness and promote responsible digital behavior. Educating citizens— especially children and young people—on safe internet use is a critical first step in reducing exposure to online risks. This bill seeks to declare the 10th of February of each year as National Safer Internet Day in the Philippines. By institutionalizing this annual observance, the State aims to promote awareness, encourage responsible online behavior, and foster a culture of cybersecurity and digital responsibility among all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10467
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A RURAL EMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rural poverty and underemployment remain persistent challenges in the Philippines, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. Despite sustained economic growth in recent years, disparities between urban and rural communities continue to widen, with rural households facing limited access to stable employment opportunities, productive assets, and essential services. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the country’s poverty incidence among families stood at 13.2% in 2023, with significantly higher rates recorded in rural areas. Moreover, underemployment remains a pressing concern, with the PSA reporting an underemployment rate of approximately 12.9% as of early 2026, reflecting the continued prevalence of informal, seasonal, and low-quality jobs—especially in agriculture-dependent communities. While existing programs such as the Department of Labor and Employment’s Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) have provided short-term relief, there remains a need for a more targeted, community-based employment intervention focused specifically on rural households. Many of these families rely heavily on irregular income sources, making them particularly vulnerable to economic shocks, climate-related disruptions, and fluctuations in agricultural productivity This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize the Rural Employment Assistance Program (REAP), to be implemented by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) in coordination with local government units. The Program aims to provide temporary but meaningful employment opportunities to qualified members of poor households in rural areas, while simultaneously supporting the development and rehabilitation of essential community assets. Through REAP, beneficiaries shall be engaged in labor-intensive, community-based projects such as the rehabilitation of irrigation systems, construction of farm-to-market roads, establishment of post-harvest facilities, and environmental protection initiatives including mangrove and tree planting. These activities not only provide immediate income support but also contribute to long-term rural development, improved agricultural productivity, and climate resilience. The measure likewise ensures that program beneficiaries receive compensation equivalent to the prevailing regional minimum wage and are afforded access to basic social protection mechanisms, including PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, and Social Security System (SSS) coverage. By linking employment assistance with social protection, the bill promotes both immediate relief and longer-term financial security for vulnerable households. Ultimately, this proposed legislation aligns with the State’s policy to promote full employment, reduce poverty, and improve the quality of life for all Filipinos. It reinforces the government’s commitment to inclusive growth by ensuring that rural communities are not left behind in the country’s development trajectory. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10468
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING JOB PLACEMENT OFFICES IN PUBLIC SECONDARY, TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL, AND HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS TO PROVIDE CAREER SERVICES TO THE YOUTH, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The transition from school to work is a critical stage in the lives of young Filipinos. Yet for many, entering the labor market remains difficult because they lack timely information about employment opportunities, adequate career guidance, and a clear understanding of how their education and skills correspond to actual labor-market demand. The proposed “Trabaho Center in Schools Act” seeks to address this gap by establishing Job Placement Offices or “Trabaho Centers” in public secondary, technical-vocational, and higher education institutions. The need for stronger school-to-work mechanisms is underscored by the country's youth employment situation. Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) show that young people continue to experience substantially greater difficulty finding work than the population as a whole. In the 2024 Annual Estimates of the Labor Force Survey, unemployment among Filipinos aged 15–24 remained considerably higher than the national unemployment rate. The concentration of unemployment among younger workers reflects the particular challenges faced by new entrants to the labor market, including limited work experience, skills mismatches, and inadequate access to employment information.1 The problem extends beyond unemployment. The International Labour Organization (ILO) has emphasized that young people who are not in employment, education, or training (NEET) face heightened risks of prolonged 1 Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), 2024 Annual Estimates of Labor Force Survey (LFS), particularly statistics on employment, unemployment, and labor force participation among young Filipinos aged 15–24. Philippine Statistics Authority, 2025, https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/labor-force-survey. disengagement from the labor market and weaker future employment prospects. The ILO has consequently called for policies that facilitate school- to-work transitions, strengthen career guidance, improve access to labor- market information, and ensure that education and training systems respond to evolving labor-market needs.2 These concerns are particularly relevant in the Philippines, where the transition from education to productive employment must keep pace with technological change and the changing requirements of industries. The proposed legislation responds directly to these challenges. It requires Trabaho Centers to provide career advocacy, assessment, coaching, job matching, employment information, and linkages with employers and training providers. It also integrates the National Career Assessment Examination (NCAE) and the Department of Labor and Employment's Skills Registry System (SRS) into career facilitation, while requiring coordination with Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs), local governments, industry, non-government organizations, and other relevant institutions. Importantly, the measure does not merely seek to help young people find any job. It aims to help students make informed career choices based on their aptitudes, preferences, and the actual needs of local and future labor markets. A more effective school-to-work transition can contribute to reducing youth unemployment and inactivity, improving skills matching, and ensuring that investments in education translate into productive and meaningful employment. Establishing Trabaho Centers is therefore an investment not only in the employability of young Filipinos, but also in a labor force better prepared to meet the country's evolving economic needs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10469
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE AMOUNT OF TAXABLE INCOME EXEMPT FROM INCOME TAX AND ADJUSTING THE GRADUATED INCOME TAX RATES ON INDIVIDUALS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8424, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997", AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article VI, Section 28 of the Constitution mandates that taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and that Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. On 2018, Republic Act No. 10963 or the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law significantly eased the tax burden on Filipino workers by exempting from income tax individuals earning up to PHP250,000 annually. The tax schedule may have been a relief at the time, but persistent inflation and the rising cost of basic necessities have substantially eroded the purchasing power of Filipino households. As a result, the current tax-exempt threshold finds itself incongruent to present-day economic realities. While the costs of food, transportation, housing, healthcare, and other basic necessities kept rising, wage increases have barely served only to keep pace with inflation rather than improve workers' real purchasing power. In April 2026, the inflation rate in the country reached a staggering 7.2%, driven largely by compounding oil shocks that seem to persist due to conflicts outside the country’s control and surging food and transport prices. Consequently, many low- and middle- income earners continue to pay taxes on income that are increasingly consumed by these very daily living expenses, despite experiencing little to no meaningful improvement in their actual financial capacity. This representation then holds the view that there is an urgent need to realign the country's individual income tax schedule to ensure that it remains equitable, progressive, and responsive to the rising cost of living. This bill seeks to restore the fairness and progressivity of the individual income tax system by amending the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended, increasing the tax-exempt annual income threshold from PHP250,000 to PHP350,000 and correspondingly adjusting the graduated income tax schedule. The proposed amendment will allow Filipino workers to retain more of their hard-earned income, strengthen household purchasing power, and stimulate domestic consumption. At a time when Filipino families continue to face elevated living costs, tax policy must adapt to economic realities. Increasing the income tax exemption threshold is simply a prudent, equitable, and timely reform that promotes tax fairness, protects the purchasing power of workers, and affirms the State's commitment to a progressive tax system that taxes citizens according to their true capacity to pay. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 2 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10469 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma. label: HB 10470
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSSES FROM THE CONSUMERS, THEREBY AMENDING SECTION 43(f) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001, AND SECTION 10 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANTI- ELECTRICITY AND ELECTRIC TRANSMISSION LINES/MATERIALS PILFERAGE ACT OF 1994 9 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 12 SECTION 1. Section 43(f) of Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, is hereby amended to read as follows: 15 “Section 43. Functions of the ERC. - Xxx
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino consumers continue to pay among the highest electricity rates in Southeast Asia. Despite efforts to improve the country's power sector, consumers remain liable for charges that do not correspond to the electricity they actually consume. Under Section 10 of Republic Act No. 7832, distribution utilities and electric cooperatives are allowed to recover a prescribed level of distribution system losses from consumers through electricity rates. Section 43(f) of Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), authorizes the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to establish the methodology for determining recoverable system loss charges. Pursuant to this authority, the ERC through its Resolution No. 20, s. 2017, currently allows private distribution utilities to recover up to 5.5% system losses, while electric cooperatives may recover 8.25% to 12%, depending on their classification. The rationale behind allowing the recovery of system losses is to recognize that a certain amount of electricity is inevitably lost in the process of delivering power from generation facilities to end- users. As such, distribution utilities are currently allowed to pass a portion of these losses to consumers through electricity rates. In effect, consumers pay not only for the electricity they actually use but also for electricity that did not even reach them. This then raises the fundamental question of whether consumers should bear expenses arising from operational risks and inefficiencies beyond their control. System losses consist of both technical losses, which occur during the transmission and distribution of electricity, and non-technical losses resulting from electricity pilferage, unauthorized connections, and other operational inefficiencies. Although technical losses may be inevitable to some extent, this representation argues that requiring consumers to pay for system losses effectively transfers to them the financial consequences of circumstances that are entirely beyond their control and even beyond their responsibility. It weakens the incentive for distribution entities to modernize their infrastructure and improve operational efficiency to reduce technical losses and intensify efforts to prevent electricity theft and unauthorized connections. As a matter of fairness and sound regulatory policy, the costs arising from operational risks and inefficiencies should be borne by the entities responsible for managing the distribution system they themselves design and operate, rather than by consumers who merely purchase and pay for the electricity that is actually delivered to them. This bill seeks to prohibit the recovery of all system losses from consumers by amending Section 43(f) of Republic Act No. 9136 and Section 10 of Republic Act No. 7832. Instead, distribution utilities and electric cooperatives shall bear these losses as part of their operational responsibility, while the ERC shall strengthen efficiency standards and technical loss reduction targets to promote accountability, operational excellence, and more equitable electricity pricing. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 2 1 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10470 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma. label: HB 10471
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE FILIPINO FAMILY SERVICE CENTER (FFSC) IN ALL LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, PROVIDING AN INTEGRATED, ONE-STOP, FAMILY-CENTERED DELIVERY OF HEALTH, SOCIAL PROTECTION, EDUCATION, LIVELIHOOD, AND CIVIL REGISTRATION SERVICES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to essential public services remains uneven across the country, particularly at the level of local government units (LGUs), which serve as the primary frontline providers of social, health, and community-based services. Data from national agencies, including the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), demonstrate both the scale of service delivery efforts and the continuing gaps in access that necessitate institutional reform. On one hand, DSWD data show that millions of Filipinos rely on government programs, with over 4.5 million beneficiaries served under major livelihood interventions, and hundreds of thousands of individuals accessing social services annually. However, ongoing beneficiary identification and validation efforts indicate that many eligible individuals remain unreached or underserved, reflecting persistent barriers to access. At the local level, DILG data highlight structural disparities in service delivery capacity among LGUs. As of 2023, only 28.75% of LGUs (493 out of 1,714) passed the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG), with the majority falling short in key service-related areas such as social protection, disaster preparedness, and financial administration. This indicates that a significant number of LGUs face systemic challenges that directly affect the availability, quality, and accessibility of public services. Moreover, while efforts toward digitalization are underway, access remains uneven. Only about 16.9% of barangays (approximately 7,083) have access to digital service systems such as the Barangay Information Management System (BIMS), despite over 65% being oriented on such systems. This gap shows that a large proportion of communities still rely on manual and fragmented processes, resulting in inefficiencies, delays, and limited reach. At the same time, high compliance rates in transparency measures—such as 97.7% of barangays complying with the Full Disclosure Policy—demonstrate that LGUs are capable of meeting governance standards when systems are clear, supported, and institutionalized. This suggests that with the appropriate legal framework and coordinated support, improvements in service accessibility are achievable. Taken together, these data reveal a critical gap: while government programs are in place and continue to expand, access to these services remains inconsistent due to uneven local capacity, limited digital infrastructure, and fragmented delivery systems. The proposed Pamilyang Matatag – Bagong Bayan ng Mamamayan (PM- BBM) Act is intended to directly address these gaps by strengthening local service delivery systems through streamlining processes and expanding both physical and digital access points to ensure that services reach all intended beneficiaries.” Guided by the vision of “Pamilyang Pilipino, Konektado sa Lahat ng Serbisyo,” the measure institutionalizes a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to public service. By institutionalizing reforms that enhance efficiency, inclusivity, and responsiveness, the measure aims to ensure that all individuals—particularly those in underserved and remote communities—can fully benefit from government programs and services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10472
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL PREVENTIVE HEALTH PROMOTION FUND, STRENGTHENING POPULATION-BASED PREVENTIVE HEALTH PROGRAMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes that the health of the Filipino people is a fundamental right and a cornerstone of national development. While significant strides have been made through the enactment of Republic Act No. 11223, the Philippine health system continues to face persistent challenges arising from the growing burden of preventable diseases and the insufficient prioritization of preventive health interventions. Recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) underscore the urgency of strengthening preventive health care. As of 2025, the leading causes of death in the Philippines remain non-communicable diseases, with ischemic heart diseases accounting for 19.7% of total deaths, followed by neoplasms at 11.4%, and cerebrovascular diseases at 9.8%. Diabetes mellitus likewise ranks among the top causes of mortality. These conditions are largely preventable and manageable through early detection, sustained health promotion, and timely intervention. Complementing these findings, the Department of Health (DOH), through its National Objectives for Health 2023–2028, highlights the continuing burden of preventable health risks, including a premature mortality rate attributable to non-communicable diseases at 4.6 per 1,000 population, as well as persistent public health concerns such as child stunting at 27% and maternal mortality at 144 per 100,000 live births. These indicators demonstrate that despite existing programs, significant gaps remain in prevention, early intervention, and health promotion across the life course. The predominance of preventable diseases has resulted in increasing health care costs, overburdened hospitals, and avoidable loss of life. The current health financing structure continues to favor curative and hospital-based services, while investments in population-based preventive programs remain fragmented and insufficiently funded. Although preventive services are recognized under the Universal Health Care framework, there is no dedicated and sustained funding mechanism that ensures the systematic implementation of large-scale health promotion and disease prevention programs nationwide. International and local evidence consistently demonstrates that investing in preventive health care yields substantial social and economic benefits. Prevention reduces the incidence and severity of disease, lowers long-term health expenditures, improves productivity, and enhances overall quality of life. Strengthening preventive health programs is therefore essential not only for improving health outcomes but also for ensuring the sustainability of the country’s health system. This measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a National Preventive Health Promotion Fund that will provide a stable and dedicated source of financing for population-based preventive health programs. The proposed Fund will support nationwide health promotion campaigns, community-based screening and early detection initiatives, lifestyle modification programs, and other evidence-based interventions aimed at reducing health risks and preventing disease. It likewise strengthens the capacity of local government units and community health systems to deliver preventive services effectively and equitably. Importantly, this bill is designed to complement, and not duplicate, the provisions of Republic Act No. 11223. While the Universal Health Care Act provides the overarching framework for health system governance and service delivery, this measure focuses specifically on ensuring that preventive health programs are adequately financed, implemented, and sustained at the population level. By institutionalizing this proposed measure, the “Preventive Measures in Healthcare Act”, a dedicated preventive health fund, the State takes a decisive step toward shifting the health system from a predominantly curative model to one that prioritizes prevention and wellness. Such a shift is critical to reducing the burden of disease, improving the health of all Filipinos, and securing a more resilient and sustainable health care system for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10473
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING AND PENALIZING GREENWASHING AND DECEPTIVE SUSTAINABILITY CLAIMS, INTEGRATING CONSUMER PROTECTIONS INTO THE CONSUMER ACT OF THE PHILIPPINES, MANDATING TRANSPARENT DISCLOSURES IN CORPORATE OPERATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology, while Article XVI, Section 9 directs the State to protect consumers from trade malpractices and hazardous or substandard products. These constitutional principles recognize that environmental stewardship and consumer protection are essential to sustainable national development. In recent years, however, a growing practice known as greenwashing has emerged as a serious threat to both objectives. Greenwashing refers to the use of false, exaggerated, or unsubstantiated environmental claims in promoting products, services, or business operations. Labels such as "eco-friendly," "green," "carbon neutral," "net zero," or similar representations are often used without credible scientific basis or independent verification, misleading consumers and creating an unfair advantage over businesses that genuinely invest in sustainable practices. The international community has recognized greenwashing as a significant barrier to effective climate action and fair competition. In 2022, the United Nations High-Level Expert Group on the Net-Zero Emissions Commitments of Non-State Entities1 warned that misleading environmental claims erode public trust, misdirect investments, and delay meaningful climate action. Likewise, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)2 has identified greenwashing as a market failure that weakens environmental governance and distorts competition. The European Commission likewise found that more than half of the environmental claims it 1 United Nations. High-Level Expert Group on the Net-Zero Emissions Commitments of Non-State Entities. United Nations, https://www.un.org/en/climatechange/high-level-expert-group. 2 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Protecting and Empowering Consumers in the Green Transition. OECD Publishing, 2024, https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/protecting-and-empowering-consumers-in-the-green-transition_12f28e4f-en.html. reviewed were vague, misleading, or unfounded, with many lacking any supporting evidence. The Philippines is not immune to these risks. As more Filipino consumers choose products and services based on environmental considerations, businesses have increasingly incorporated sustainability claims into advertising, packaging, and corporate communications. While many enterprises have made genuine commitments to responsible environmental practices, others exploit the absence of clear legal standards by making environmental representations that cannot be independently substantiated. Although Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, prohibits deceptive sales practices, it does not specifically regulate environmental marketing claims or establish standards for substantiating such representations. Existing environmental laws likewise focus primarily on pollution control and natural resource management rather than the truthfulness of sustainability claims made in the marketplace. Consequently, consumers remain vulnerable to deceptive environmental marketing, while responsible businesses face unfair competition from those that merely project the appearance of sustainability. The consequences extend beyond consumer deception. Greenwashing weakens market incentives for innovation, discourages legitimate investments in cleaner technologies, and undermines the country's transition toward a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. More importantly, it affects Filipino families and future generations. The Philippines remains among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, while children and economically vulnerable communities continue to bear its greatest consequences. Every misleading environmental claim delays meaningful action toward sustainability and diverts consumer support away from businesses that genuinely reduce environmental harm. This proposed Anti-Greenwashing and Consumer Truth Act seeks to establish the country's first comprehensive legal framework against deceptive environmental marketing. The measure defines prohibited greenwashing practices; requires that environmental claims be supported by competent, credible, and verifiable scientific evidence; prohibits deceptive environmental labels and self-created certifications; regulates the use of claims such as "carbon neutral," "net zero," and similar representations unless independently substantiated; and strengthens enforcement under the Consumer Act of the Philippines. The bill likewise promotes transparency and accountability by requiring businesses making environmental claims to maintain adequate supporting documentation and authorizing the appropriate regulatory agencies to investigate, verify, and penalize deceptive environmental marketing practices. In doing so, the measure protects consumers, encourages responsible corporate conduct, rewards businesses that undertake genuine sustainability initiatives, and promotes a fair and competitive marketplace where honesty earns public trust. By institutionalizing standards for truthful environmental marketing and strengthening consumer protection, this measure advances the constitutional duty of the State to safeguard both the people's right to a balanced and healthful ecology and their right to fair and honest commercial practices. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. KAREN HOPE F.
