label: HB 10528
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE COMMUNITY-DRIVEN DEVELOPMENT APPROACH AS A NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR INCLUSIVE GROWTH AND SOCIAL PROTECTION, MANDATING ALL NATIONAL GOVERNMENT AGENCIES AND DEPARTMENTS INCLUDING THEIR ATTACHED AGENCIES, OFFICES, AND BUREAUS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND OTHER GOVERNMENT INSTRUMENTALITIES TO IMPLEMENT THEIR COMMUNITY-BASED PROGRAMS, ACTIVITIES, AND PROJECTS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Community-Driven Development Institutionalization Act.” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policies. – The 1987 Constitution establishes the right of the people and their organizations to effective and reasonable participation at all levels of social, political, and economic decision-making shall not be abridged. The State shall, by law, facilitate the establishment of adequate consultation mechanisms (Article XIII, Section 16). Towards this end, and in the pursuit of inclusive growth, social protection, community empowerment, and poverty reduction, the State shall enact programs that provide capacities and opportunities for community members – particularly the poor, vulnerable, and disadvantaged – to effectively participate in the design, planning, budgeting, and implementation of community identified programs, plans, and projects. CHAPTER I. GENERAL PROVISIONS SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. – For the purpose of this Act, the following terms are defined, as follows: a. “Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plan (ADSDPP)” refers to a long-term plan that embodies the goals and objectives, policies and strategies, as well as programs, and projects of Indigenous Cultural Communities (ICCs)/Indigenous Peoples (IPs) for the sustainable development
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to the World Bank, “Community-driven development (CDD) programs operate on the principles of transparency, participation, accountability, and enhanced local capacity. Experience has shown that when given clear and transparent rules, access to information, and appropriate technical and financial support, poor communities can effectively organize to identify community priorities and address local problems by working in partnership with local governments and other institutions to build small-scale infrastructure and deliver basic services.”1 With community-driven development programs, poverty can be reduced and sustainable development can be attained because the government services reach those in the far-flung areas, and those people groups which are most vulnerable. This is of great development importance in the Philippines, where geographic realities often present challenges to service delivery, hurdles to efficiency, and push ageing infrastructure to its limits. With this, we can take the first step towards spreading development throughout the country, allowing us to decentralize development and ensure that there is no concentration of socio-economic and political development in the metropolitan areas and ensure that holistic progress is achieved even in the countryside. Hence, it is for these reasons that this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to increase the privilege discount granted to senior citizens from twenty percent (20%) to twenty five percent (25%). On April 23, 1992, Republic Act (RA) No. 7432 was enacted granting benefits and special privileges to senior citizens in recognition of their contributions to nation building. RA 7432 was later amended by RA 9257 and RA 9994, expanding the benefits and privileges to senior citizens. Although the benefits under the latter law have been extended to other services and establishments, the twenty percent (20%) discount remains the same. Consistent with worldwide trends on population demographics, the Philippines is also expected to face an ageing population in the coming decades.1 This will have far-reaching impacts on policy, infrastructure, and distribution of social benefits. Thus, as early as now, it is crucial for the nation to prepare our national infrastructure for the upcoming demographic shift. While a growing older segment of the population presents its own unique challenges, adaptation of a “silver economy” hinges on a senior population that are fit, healthy, and strong2. On the long run, tackling this demographic shift will depend on how equipped the country’s senior population will be. Thus, there is a need to update this benefit to keep on pace with the continuing rise in the cost of living, current inflation rates, and the positive increase in lifespan of Filipinos, 1 Raine Musñgi (2026), “As more Pinoys get older, experts say PH should see aging as opportunity, not burden.” ABS-CBN News, 06 June 2026, available at https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/business/2026/6/6/as-more-pinoys-get-older-ph-should-see-aging-as-boon-not-bane- experts-0800 2 Virgilio C. Galvez (2025), “Pinoys living longer but most are unwell,” Manila Standard, 25 October 2025, available at https://manilastandard.net/good-life/314659892/pinoys-living-longer-but-most-are-unwell.html which necessitates upgraded assistance to our senior citizens3. Amidst these challenges, the 20% discount is insufficient to meet the daily needs of senior citizens. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly recommended. ALFRED C. title: AN ACT TO PROMOTE INCLUSIVE BUSINESS TO SUPPORT AND ACCELERATE INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT AT THE NATIONAL AND LOCAL LEVELS THROUGH PRIVATE SECTOR INVOLVEMENT Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Inclusive Business Act of 2026.” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to create enabling policy and economic environments for inclusive business models to thrive and become the standard for doing business in the Philippines. Section 9 and 20, Article II of the 1987 Constitution provide that it is the policy of “[t]he State to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services, promote full employment, a rising standard of living, and an improved quality of life for all;” and “[t]he State recognizes the indispensable role of the private sector, encourages private enterprise, and provides incentives to needed investments.” Furthermore, the State commits to the Philippine Development Plan, to develop Inclusive Business as one of the strategies to expand economic opportunities for the population, and the national plans, such as the zero + 10-point Socio-Economic Agenda, to promote rural and value chain development, and AmbisyonNatin 2040 in making growth more inclusive and poverty-reducing. Moreover, pursuant to international agreements and instruments, including the Sustainable Development Goals, the State is one in promoting sustained, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all women and men, and promoting inclusive and sustainable industrialization. A strong Inclusive Business sector can significantly and systematically contribute to the achievement of the country’s sustainable development goals, and the reduction of poverty on a significant, systemic, and massive scale.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The bill seeks to create an enabling environment for government and businesses to adopt inclusive business models in their entire operations, focusing on key processes in their supply chains, especially processes that seek to increase the participation and benefit of women small scale producers. The Philippines is pushing for widespread adoption of Inclusive Business (IB) investments, particularly the inclusion of small community enterprises into the formal economy. Leveraging relevant discussions by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development in 2005, and the G20 and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), the Philippines has proactively advanced and is leading multi-partite discussions in setting policy direction toward the adoption of the IB agenda. As a starting framework, we consider the definition provided by the G20 Framework on IB: “A private sector approach to providing goods, services and livelihoods on a commercially viable basis, either at scale or scalable, to people at the base of the pyramid by making them part of the value chain of companies’ core business as suppliers, distributors, retailers or customers.” The Base of the Pyramid (BOP) approach adapts an encompassing approach that includes those living in the base of the economic pyramid. In essence, this ‘base’ makes up the largest group of the population, both in the Philippines and abroad, consisting of those that survive on $8 USD or less1. An Inclusive Business (IB) approach tackles precisely this, taking into careful consideration of where the base of the pyramid fit into economic plans. In a previous study, at least 300 million of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) population still live at the Base of the Pyramid (BOP), with actual poverty incidence varying in terms of local definition variations2. In the Philippines, where more than a quarter of the population self-report as ‘poor,’ IBs 1 International Finance Group, “Inclusive Business at the Base of the Pyramid,” World Bank Group, available at https://www.ifc.org/en/what-we-do/sector-expertise/gender/inclusive-business 2 https://www.adb.org/sites/default/files/project-documents/46240/46240-001-tacr-en_0.pdf. models may still provide an opportunity for poverty reduction through the deliberate engagement of businesses in levelling economic opportunities. A turn towards strengthening the country’s IB pathway would also yield greater dividends as the country continues to face challenges from the oil crisis brought about by the US-Iran Conflict, along with the long-standing effects of the previous COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, businesses stand to gain from women’s progress in this regard. Closing the gender gap in the global economy could increase global GDP by $28 trillion by 2025. If women had equal access to agricultural resources, agricultural output in developing countries would increase by an average of 4%, reducing the number of undernourished people by as much as 17%. Companies with diverse workforces are: 22% more productive, have 27% higher profitability and 39% higher customer satisfaction. President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. has also clearly articulated the administration’s focus on an “inclusive and future-ready” direction for the country’s economic growth, and for the Asia Pacific Region in general3 IB is differentiated from Social Enterprise (SE), wherein the first pertains to large scale corporations and seeks to refocus the traditional business model to integrate low-income communities in its business operations and as part of its value chain, through employment, distribution, retail, supply, as customers, or through development of the community. IB often partners with small community enterprises and/or producer communities in a transactional way. The integration of the poor in the IB value chain will positively impact the country’s economic development. On the other hand, SE is focused on the social value output of the business, and in turn can be part of the value chain of an IB Project, as either a distributor, retailer, or supplier. Further, as the 2017 ASEAN Chair, the Philippines developed the first IB policy to provide fiscal incentives to companies that integrate Micro-Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in their supply chain and promote the use of efficient and automated systems and operations. Through the initiatives of Philippine Business for Social Progress, Philippine Business for the Environment, Makati Business Club, and Asian Development Bank, the Asian Inclusive Business Awards was launched and recognized and awarded the Inclusive Business model of Generika.4 Coffee for Peace was also a finalist for its work teaching coffee planting and processing skills to communities in Mindanao affected by armed conflict, illegal logging, and mining. Over the years, the Philippines has shown leadership globally in setting the policy direction of Inclusive Business. Through the Board of Investments (BOI), it created the Inclusive Business Program Management Office (IB PMO) to pilot Inclusive Business models in the agribusiness and tourism sectors, which are the preferred areas for the 2017-2019 Incentives Priorities Plan (IPP 3 Alexis Romero, “President Marcos pushes for inclusive, future-ready APEC,” Inquirer, 1 November 2025, available at https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/11/01/2484061/president-marcos-pushes-inclusive-future-ready-apec 4 Generika provided low-cost generic medicine in rural communities that have little to no access to basic health infrastructure. The generic pharmaceutical products were estimated to cost 85% less than their branded counterparts. Generika also provides free in-store medical consultations for such rural communities. The issues raised for writing a new law include the perceived narrow scope of IB PMO, such that the IB program does not have the authority to call on the other agencies to enable it to effectively pursue and create an enabling policy env

explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Waste Workers are at the forefront of waste management systems. Across the Philippines, they are performing difficult, often invisible labor that puts their health at great risk, all the while facing systemic problems that prevent them from fully enjoying the benefits of work. Waste management, through the barangay, municipal, and city-levels, are an important, often unseen, facet of humane and civilized life. Its effective execution allows for communities that enjoy safe, hygienic, and resilient environments. Proper waste management is a cornerstone of environmental protection. As the increase in consumption of single-use plastics demonstrates, the world is now facing a global plastic crisis.1 In island communities for instance, geographic challenges, along with ageing or non-existent infrastructure prevent proper waste management leading to waste leakage into our oceans. This has far-reaching impacts on our marine biodiversity, the livelihoods of our island and coastal communities, and the overall survival of our biodiversity. In such instances it is with the cooperation of the community and the labor of Waste Workers that make the crucial difference. Why then is this crucial, yet invisible sector so often forgotten? In communities throughout the country, Waste Workers perform the tasks that allow for society to function. They both safeguard public health and help protect the environment. In both formal and informal sectors, Waste Workers perform such tasks despite detrimental effects on their own health, the lack of medical access, little to no labor protection, unsure job security, lack of social protection, as well as stigma, to name a few. 1 Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (Philippines), “REGULATING SINGLE-USE PLASTICS IN THE PHILIPPINES OPPORTUNITIES TO MOVE FORWARD,” 2020, available at https://www.no-burn.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Philippine-Policy-Brief-on-SUPs-Ban-1.pdf The Philippines, at this crucial moment, has already enacted multiple laws that advance waste management. Republic Act No. 6969, also known as the Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act of 1990, Republic Act No. 9003 Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, and Republic Act No. 11898 or the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Law are all legislation aiming to improve and institutionalize waste management in the country. In addition to the aforementioned, this proposed Act aims to introduce protections for Waste Workers that shall improve, extend, and widen the inclusivity and encompassing nature of waste sector legislation. Given all these, a comprehensive law, a Magna Carta for Waste Workers that aims to address all such issues, integrate them into formal labor structures, and protect their welfare while promoting inclusivity, is sorely needed. There is a great need to institutionalize the sector of Waste Workers, to give them the benefits that are rightfully theirs, and to recognize the importance of the role they play to keep our communities and environments safe, healthy, and resilient. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE At the time of the most recent study rankings, the Philippines ranked 43 out of 146 in Economic Complexity, according to the Harvard Growth Lab’s Complexity Rankings and Growth Predictions.1 Economic complexity refers to the composition of a country’s productive output and reflects its structures that hold and combine knowledge.2 This metric primarily looks at the diversity and uniqueness of what a country can produce—that the more diverse and more unique a country’s products are, the more robust is its economy. While Economic Complexity is often seen as an indicator of the economic level of the country3, according to The Atlas of Economic Complexity, the Philippines is more complex than expected for its income level.4 We are projected to further rise in ranking in the coming years. It is important for us to take advantage of our momentum in the current global economy, especially to equip our economy to face the shocks of the compounding issues of climate change, the US- Iran conflict and the oil crisis that followed, geopolitical tensions, and other economic hurdles. As the diversity and uniqueness of what we can produce relies on so many aspects of our economy such as manpower, infrastructure, technology and innovations, investments, and public fiscal management and government procurement, we need a harmonized strategy in order to maximize our economic potential, both in the public and the private sector. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 Growth Lab. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR SAFE, SECURE, RESILIENT, AND SUPPORTIVE EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS, INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL-BASED VIOLENCE PREVENTION, THREAT ASSESSMENT, EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS, CRISIS RESPONSE, RECOVERY, MENTAL HEALTH EARLY INTERVENTION, AND CONFIDENTIAL SAFETY REPORTING MECHANISMS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools must be places of learning, development, and security. Yet verified data show that bullying remains a serious concern. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's Programme for International Student Assessment 2022 country note for the Philippines, 43% of participating girls and 53% of participating boys reported experiencing acts of bullying at least a few times a month. The Department of Education recorded 2,500 bullying cases in the National Capital Region in School Year 2024–2025, up from 2,268 the previous school year. These are reported incidents only, but they demonstrate the continuing need for stronger prevention, reporting, response, and accountability systems. While Republic Act No. 10627 (Anti-Bullying Act of 2013) mandates school anti- bullying policies, disciplinary measures, and law enforcement referrals, it lacks a unified national framework for broader safety threats across basic, higher, and technical-vocational institutions. School safety demands a proactive approach encompassing prevention, threat assessment, emergency medical response, prompt parental notification, evidence preservation, mental health support, recovery, and inter-agency coordination. Institutional delays or lack of accountability are unacceptable when student safety is compromised. Constitutional mandates under Article II, Section 13 (youth well-being), Article XIV, Sections 1 and 4 (quality education and institutional regulation), and Article XV, Section 3 (child protection) provide clear grounds for legislation. Reinforced by RA No. 10121 (disaster reduction), RA No. 11036 (mental health), and RA No. 12080 (school mental health), this measure consolidates these duties into one framework. The principal justifications and effects of the measure are as follows: 1. Establishes a unified National Safe Schools Framework covering prevention, protection, preparedness, response, and recovery across public and private basic, higher, and technical-vocational education institutions, jointly formulated by DepEd, CHED, and TESDA. 2. Requires covered schools to conduct annual safety risk assessments and maintain an updated School Safety and Emergency Preparedness Plan addressing crisis management, medical response, inclusive arrangements, and learning continuity. 3. Mandates behavior-based, multidisciplinary Threat Assessment and Intervention Teams; assessments do not determine liability, and protective traits or lawful conduct cannot solely define dangerousness. 4. Creates confidential reporting channels, bars retaliation against good- faith whistleblowers, and prevents penalties based strictly on unverified anonymous claims. 5. Compels immediate protection, medical checks, evidence tracking, victim care, and child-sensitive probes for serious violence, requiring parent notification within fifteen minutes of school awareness. 6. Prohibits leaving injured learners unattended or unassessed, requires formal medical transfer, mandates screening for hidden head trauma, and explicitly bans using token corrective activities as the sole institutional remedy. 7. Prohibits tampering with relevant incident records under legal notice, and subjects severe violations—including fatalities, weapon use, and cover-ups—to external reviews by education authorities. Victims and their parents or guardians must be informed of available referral mechanisms, consulted on safety measures, informed of the general status of the investigation subject to privacy and due-process limitations, and allowed to submit evidence and concerns, with reasonable accommodation for learners with disabilities or special educational needs. Implementation will be coordinated through a National Safe Schools Council and supported by a Safe Schools Innovation and Assistance Fund. A school cannot provide quality education when warning signs are ignored, parents are informed too late, injured learners are not immediately assessed, or serious violence is reduced to nominal discipline. Ang ligtas na paaralan ay institusyong handang umiwas sa panganib, tumugon agad, at managot sa bawat batang ipinagkatiwala rito. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A FREE ANNUAL COMPREHENSIVE GERIATRIC HEALTH ASSESSMENT PROGRAM FOR INDIGENT SENIOR CITIZENS, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LIBRENG ‘EXECUTIVE CHECK-UP’ PARA SA INDIGENT SENIOR CITIZENS ACT,” PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 11, Article XIII of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that the state shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that makes essential goods, health, and other social services available to all people at affordable cost, with the priority for the needs of the underprivileged, the sick, the elderly, women, and children. In our culture, our elders are traditionally revered as the pillars of the family and keepers of cultural wisdom. But despite our high regard for our senior citizens, the reality is that a large number of senior citizens are living below the poverty line and are vulnerable to chronic and debilitating illnesses such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer. In 2025, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) recorded1 around 4 million indigent senior citizens as beneficiaries under its Social Pension Program. The government has established various social protection measures, which include the RA No. 9994 or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, the Universal Health Care Act, and PhilHealth coverage for Senior Citizens. However, many indigent senior citizens still seek medical attention only after illnesses have progressed to advanced stages. In these trying times, treatment has become more costly, more invasive, and less likely to achieve favorable outcomes. This pattern does not only diminish the quality of life of our senior citizens but also puts a substantive financial burden on their families. Currently, most indigent seniors only visit a hospital when a disease has reached an advanced, painful, and often terminal stage. By providing these comprehensive 1 “4.1 M indigent seniors receive DSWD’s social pension in 2025”, DSWD, January 14, 2026, accessed here: https://www.dswd.gov.ph/4-1m-indigent-seniors-receive-dswds-social-pension-in- 2025/ Page 1 of 8 screenings free of charge, it will potentially increase the chances of successful management, preserve the quality of life for the elderly, and spare them from preventable suffering. Furthermore, providing free comprehensive screenings is a highly cost-effective strategy for the Philippine public healthcare system. Critics might argue that funding executive check-ups for millions of poor seniors would strain the national budget. However, we can view this as an investment. Treating advanced-stage illnesses, stroke rehabilitation, and prolonged intensive care hospitalizations place a massive financial burden on public tertiary hospitals. By investing a modest amount in early diagnostics, the government can save billions of pesos in long-term tertiary treatment costs, allowing public health resources to be distributed more efficiently. While Republic Act No. 9994 provides discounts on medicines and medical services, these deductions are often meaningless to indigent seniors who have zero disposable income. For someone choosing between a meal and a diagnostic test, survival will always take precedence over prevention. Free “executive check-ups” bridge this economic divide, ensuring that quality healthcare is a right enjoyed by all, rather than a luxury reserved for the affluent. By establishing a unified, zero-cost framework for senior citizens with an annual comprehensive geriatric health assessment, and integrating the mandates of the Department of Health (DOH), PhilHealth, and local government units (LGUs), this measure will bridge systemic healthcare gaps, mitigate out-of-pocket medical expenses, and safeguard the dignity and well-being of Filipino senior citizens. A nation that cares for its elderly reflects its moral character. Indigent senior citizens have spent their youth contributing to the country’s economy, raising the next generation of workers, and paying indirect taxes. In their twilight years, they deserve to live with dignity, free from the constant fear of a sudden, catastrophic medical debt. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10547
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE MAGNA CARTA OF PATIENTS' RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES, STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF PATIENTS, PROMOTING PATIENT-CENTERED HEALTH CARE, PRESCRIBING THE DUTIES AND ACCOUNTABILITIES OF HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS AND HEALTH FACILITIES, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 15, Article II and Sections 11 to 13, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution mandate the State to protect and promote the right to health and adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to making quality health care accessible and affordable for all Filipinos. This constitutional policy is reinforced by Republic Act (RA) No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act, which guarantees every Filipino equitable access to quality, people-centered, and financially protective health care. Despite these legal guarantees, many patients still endure limitations in accessing and navigating the health care system. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the country's current health expenditure reached Php 1.87 trillion in 2025, with households shouldering nearly 41% (Php 714.63 billion)1 of total health spending through out-of- pocket payments. Beyond financial burdens, patients often encounter inadequate disclosure of medical information, lack of transparency in hospital billing, limited awareness of available government medical assistance, difficulties in accessing medical records, concerns over the confidentiality of health information, and the absence of an accessible and effective mechanism for addressing grievances. While existing laws, including the Anti-Hospital Deposit Law ( RA No. 10932), the Anti-Hospital Detention Law (RA No. 9439), the Data Privacy Act (RA No. 10173), the Universal Health Care Act, and various Department of Health (DOH) issuances, provide important safeguards, these protections remain dispersed across different statutes and regulations. The absence of a 1 “Government Contributes 46.5 Percent to the Country’s Current Health Spending in 2025” Retrieved from: https://psa.gov.ph/content/government-contributes-465-percent- countrys-current-health-spending-2025 comprehensive legal framework has resulted in inconsistent implementation and limited public awareness of patients' rights and corresponding responsibilities. This bill seeks to establish a Magna Carta of Patients' Rights and Responsibilities to consolidate these protections into a single, comprehensive, and enforceable statute. It guarantees the rights of patients to dignity, quality health care, informed consent, access to medical information and records, privacy and confidentiality, transparent billing, information on available financial assistance, protection against unlawful hospital detention, and accessible grievance mechanisms. At the same time, it recognizes the responsibilities of patients in promoting mutual respect, accountability, and effective partnerships with health care providers. Furthermore, this bill aims to strengthen institutional accountability by requiring health facilities to adopt transparent and patient-centered practices, establish effective grievance mechanisms, and ensure compliance with standards that uphold patient safety, dignity, and quality of care. This proposed measure reinforces the constitutional right to health, advances the objectives of the UHC Act, and promotes a health care system that is more transparent, accountable, compassionate, and responsive to the needs of every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10548
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM THE IMPOSITION OF VALUE-ADDED TAXES (VAT) ON THE ELECTRICAL BILLINGS OF RESIDENTIAL HOUSEHOLDS WITH 400KWH OR LESS TOTAL MONTHLY CONSUMPTION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide relief to Filipino households by exempting from value-added tax (VAT) the electricity billings of residential consumers whose total monthly consumption does not exceed four hundred kilowatt-hours (400 kWh). Electricity is a basic household need. Reducing the taxes charged on electricity can help qualified families lower their monthly bills and keep more of their income for food, education, healthcare, transportation, and other essential expenses. The need for relief has become more pronounced amid elevated electricity costs. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) likewise reported that housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels accounted for 11.9% of total household final consumption expenditure in the first quarter of 2026. Moreover, a December 2025 study of the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) recognized electricity subsidies as instruments for improving affordability and protecting consumers, while stressing the need for assistance to be designed efficiently and equitably. Section 108 of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), as amended, generally imposes 12% VAT on services, including electricity supplied by generation, transmission, and distribution entities, including electric cooperatives. The proposed measure seeks to provide targeted VAT relief to qualified residential households based on their monthly electricity consumption, helping reduce household power costs. According to a 2011 study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS), a family of five in the National Capital Region earning the minimum wage consumed around 100 to 150 kilowatt- hours (kWh) of electricity per month, with electricity expenses accounting for a significant share of household income. Since this estimate is based on 2011 conditions, actual household electricity needs today may be higher due to greater dependence on electricity, wider use of household appliances and electronic devices, and increased cooling needs during hotter weather. More recent data show that electricity use has become more widespread among Filipino households, while PIDS research has also found that weather variability affects household energy consumption. While the existing Lifeline Rate Subsidy provides discounts to marginalized low-income households, many middle-income families facing rising electricity costs receive no comparable relief. Expanding the VAT exemption on electricity bills to cover these households would make the policy more inclusive and help ease the financial burden on a broader segment of Filipino consumers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. label: HB 10549
title: AN ACT GRANTING SECURITY OF TENURE UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES WHOSE NATURE OF APPOINTMENT IS EITHER TEMPORARY OR CONTRACTUAL AND WHO HAVE RENDERED A TOTAL OF TEN (10) YEARS OF EFFICIENT SERVICE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Contractual arrangements in government, more commonly known as job order (JO) and contract of service (COS), often sit outside the standard framework of Plantilla (regular) positions in the civil service. The term “contractual” is used casually across the broad extent of government employment, but legally it can mean different things; however, this proposed measure is directed at the long overdue correction of the usual practice of ignoring, to a large extent, the plight of non-plantilla personnel who have continuously served for more than five (5) or even 10 (10) years as contractual or casual employees. In the interest of social justice, and to recognize their potentials and contributions, this bill seeks to grant civil service eligibility to non-plantilla personnel, and as such, passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 10555
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11350, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “NATIONAL COMMISSION OF SENIOR CITIZENS ACT”, PROVIDING FOR ITS ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, EFFICIENT TRANSITION AND OPERATIONALIZATION, AND MAXIMIZING ITS FUNCTIONALITY FOR THE BENEFIT OF SENIOR CITIZENS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to amend Republic Act (RA) No. 11350, otherwise known as the “National Commission of Senior Citizens Act”, providing for its efficient transition from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) through a more coherent organizational structure, establishing clear mechanisms for its effective operationalization and clarifying institutional arrangements to ensure maximum functionality. RA 11350 or the National Commission of Senior Citizens Act was passed as a response to the decades-long clamor from the elderly sector that there finally be a primary government agency focused on their rights, interests and welfare. While RA 7432 providing for the benefits and privileges of senior citizens was twice amended, first by RA 9257 and then by the prevailing RA 9994, there was a need for a law establishing organizational structures and institutional arrangements that will support mechanisms operationalizing elderly programs and services. Unfortunately, since the RA 11350’s passage in 2019, the efficient transition from the DSWD to the NCSC has not happened. Moreover, even with the appointment of Commissioners starting in 2020, the NCSC continues to face challenges in assuming the full responsibilities and functions of the NCSC pertaining to the senior citizens’ sector. It is for this reason that the law needs to be amended to provide more guidance and clearer directions on the law’s original intention, thereby ensuring that the elderly sector does not suffer the consequences of an inefficient and non-functional body. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly recommended. label: HB 10565
title: AN ACT GRANTING BENEFITS TO NON-REGULAR EMPLOYEES OF THE GOVERNMENT, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution guarantees the promotion of a just and dynamic social order free from poverty through policies that promote full employment geared towards a rising standard of living and an improved quality of life for all. It also recognizes temporary employees of the government as part of the Civil Service, and the same shall also be accorded the protection as may be provided for by law. At present, non-regular employees (i.e., job order and contract of services personnel) are not covered by Civil Service law, rules and regulations, and are only covered by Commission on Audit (COA) rules. Since the services they render are not covered by civil service regulations, most, if not all, of the non-regular employees in the government do not enjoy an employee-employer relationship and are excluded from being covered by the Labor Code and the benefits therein. These reasons, in effect, put the non-regular personnel in limbo – an arena where they are more vulnerable to exploitation. As the largest employer in the country, the government should take the lead in ensuring that its employees are well taken care of and protected from possible exploitation. The State must acknowledge the rights and welfare of its workers and institute better benefits and programs for them. This bill seeks to promote and uphold decent work and labor rights and address the needs of the non-regular employees in the government for more work benefits. As we envision the progressive realization of security of tenure for all government workers, this bill ought to give noble workers of the country what is due to their hard work. Consequently, we hope to encourage more bright and young minds to continue to work for and with the government. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 10566
title: AN ACT JUMPSTARTING OPPORTUNITIES FOR BUSINESSES AND ENSURING EMPLOYABILITY OF THE PHILIPPINE WORKFORCE THROUGH EXPANDED COMPETENCY-BASED LEARNING AND SKILLS TRAINING, TO DRIVE INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT AND SUSTAINABLE GROWTH, AND ESTABLISHING FOR THIS PURPOSE A NATIONAL FUTURE SKILLS COUNCIL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine labor market is undergoing rapid transformation driven by digitalization, automation, and the transition toward a more innovation- led and sustainable economy. These structural shifts are reshaping the demand for skills across industries, requiring workers and enterprises alike to continuously adapt to emerging technologies and evolving business models. Recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) indicate that as of April 2026, the country’s unemployment rate stood at 4.1 percent, equivalent to approximately 2.1 million unemployed Filipinos.1 While this reflects an improvement in overall employment conditions, underemployment remains a persistent challenge at 11.7 percent, signaling the continued mismatch between available jobs and the skills of the workforce. At the same time, the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has emphasized that many industries—particularly in information technology, manufacturing, logistics, and renewable energy—are facing growing demand for higher-order cognitive, technical, and digital skills. The World Bank (2023) similarly notes that the Philippines risks widening skills gaps if reskilling and upskilling systems are not strengthened to meet the 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, Labor Force Survey. April 2026 demands of the digital economy. Technological advancement continues to accelerate labor market disruption. According to the International Labour Organization2, a significant share of jobs in Southeast Asia remains susceptible to automation, particularly in routine and manual occupations. Conversely, there is increasing demand for non-routine cognitive skills, digital competencies, and socio-emotional skills. This shift underscores the urgency of developing a workforce that is adaptable, future-ready, and globally competitive. The Philippines has taken steps to promote innovation and workforce development through Republic Act No. 11293, or the “Philippine Innovation Act,” which recognizes innovation as a key driver of inclusive growth. It emphasizes the importance of strengthening linkages among education, training, and industry. However, gaps remain in aligning skills development systems with real-time labor market needs, as well as in institutionalizing a coordinated national framework for future skills planning. Furthermore, Republic Act No. 10771, or the “Philippine Green Jobs Act of 2016,” highlights the importance of developing a workforce capable of supporting environmentally sustainable industries. The transition to a green economy will require new competencies in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, climate adaptation, and circular economy practices. The Asian Development Bank (2024) estimates that green transformation could generate substantial employment opportunities in the Philippines, provided that the workforce is equipped with the necessary skills. In this context, there is a clear need to harmonize policies and programs across government agencies, educational institutions, and industry stakeholders to address skills mismatches and prepare the Filipino workforce for future demands. A coordinated, forward-looking approach to skills development is essential to ensure that economic growth remains inclusive and that no sector is left behind. The proposed “Jobs Next Act” seeks to address these challenges by promoting competency-based learning, strengthening lifelong learning systems, and incentivizing upskilling and reskilling across the workforce. Central to the measure is the establishment of a National Future Skills Council that will serve as a strategic body to anticipate emerging skills needs, align education and training systems with industry demand, and guide national workforce development planning. 2 International Labor Organization. 2023 By integrating global skills trends with domestic priorities, the measure aims to enhance the employability, productivity, and resilience of Filipino workers. It also seeks to support enterprises—particularly micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs)—in adapting to technological change and remaining competitive in an increasingly dynamic global economy. Ultimately, skills development is a cornerstone of inclusive and sustainable growth. Investing in human capital will enable the Philippines to fully harness the opportunities presented by digitalization, innovation, and the green transition, while safeguarding workers against displacement and inequality. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A LABOR EMPOWERMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM, AMENDING PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State affirms labor as a primary social and economic force and is committed to promoting full, productive, and freely chosen employment. Central to long-term development planning is the national vision articulated in AmBisyon Natin 2040, which reflects the aspirations of Filipinos for a stable, comfortable and stable life, including access to quality employment opportunities within the country. Despite sustained economic recovery in recent years, structural challenges in the labor market persist. Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) show that as of April 2026, the unemployment rate stood at approximately 4.3%, equivalent to around 2.2 million unemployed Filipinos. Meanwhile, underemployment—defined as employed persons seeking additional hours of work or better employment – remained elevated at about 11.7%, indicating continued job quality concerns1. A critical issue underlying these figures is the persistent mismatch between available jobs and the skills of the workforce. Employers continue to report difficulty in filling positions due to gaps in technical competencies, digital 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, Labor Force Survey. April 2026 skills, and job readiness, while many jobseekers face prolonged periods of unemployment or precarious employment. This mismatch disproportionately affects young workers, displaced employees, and those transitioning between jobs. To address these gaps, this bill proposes the establishment of a Labor Employment Assistance Program, a targeted intervention designed to support workers during periods of job transition. The program aims to : (1) provide temporary income support to displaced or transitioning workers at a level not lower than the applicable minimum wage ; (2) offer skills upgrading, retooling, and job-matching services aligned with industry demand; and (3) facilitate faster reintegration of workers into the labor market through coordinated public employment services. By institutionalizing a responsive and integrated support mechanism, the proposed measure seeks to reduce frictional unemployment, improve job matching efficiency, and enhance the overall employability of Filipino workers. Ultimately, it strengthens the country’s human capital and ensures that economic growth translates into meaningful and inclusive employment opportunities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10568
title: AN ACT GRANTING EMPLOYEES THREE DAYS PAID LEAVE TO ATTEND SCHOOL-RELATED ACTIVITIES OF THEIR CHILDREN
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that “the State recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation. Accordingly, it shall strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development.” The Child and Youth Welfare Code further decrees that parents should give their child “affection, companionship and understanding, and extend him the benefits of moral guidance, self-discipline and religious instruction,” as may be necessary for the formation of their child’s character. In recognition of the importance of the parents’ active involvement in their children’s lives and in the educational system, this bill proposes to grant employees three days of paid leave to attend to their children’s school-related activities that are in conflict with their work schedule. In the thrust of developing a strong and proud nation, the State must reinforce the values and spirit of the most basic unit of the Filipino society: the family. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10569
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR SECURITY OF TENURE FOR ALL JOB ORDER AND CONTRACT OF SERVICE WORKERS OF THE GOVERNMENT WHO HAVE RENDERED THE PRESCRIBED YEARS OF SERVICE IN THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT AGENCIES AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Government remains one of the largest employers in the country. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), total employment in the public administration and defense sector alone reached approximately 2.1 million workers as of 2023, reflecting the continued expansion of the public workforce. Meanwhile, data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) indicate that funded positions in the national government have steadily increased, exceeding 1.9 million authorized positions in recent years.1 Despite this, a significant portion of the government workforce remains under non-regular employment arrangements. The Civil Service Commission (CSC) has consistently reported that hundreds of thousands of workers in government are engaged under Job Order (JO) and Contract of Service (COS) arrangements. Based on DBM and CSC estimates, JO and COS workers in government agencies have ranged from approximately 600,000 to 700,000 in 1 Department of Budget and Management Budget Expenditures and Sources of Financing, Fiscal Year 2024 recent years, accounting for roughly 25% to 30% of the total government workforce.2 This persistent reliance on contractual and short-term workers has led to the characterization of the government as one of the largest “endo employers,” mirroring the very labor practices it seeks to regulate in the private sector. While efforts to address contractualization have been initiated in previous administrations—including policy pronouncements and executive issuances promoting security of tenure—the absence of a comprehensive legislative solution continues to leave many government workers in precarious employment conditions. The 1987 Constitution explicitly guarantees full protection to labor, promotes full employment, and ensures equal work opportunities regardless of status. It mandates the State to uphold the rights of workers to security of tenure, humane conditions of work, and a living wage. These constitutional guarantees must extend equally to all workers in government, regardless of employment classification. Under the current framework, JO and COS workers are engaged for short- term periods, typically not exceeding six months per contract, and are excluded from the coverage of the Civil Service Law, rules, and regulations. They are not entitled to standard benefits such as leave credits, retirement benefits, and other social protections enjoyed by regular government employees. Moreover, their service is not considered government service for purposes of tenure and career progression, and no employer-employee relationship is recognized. This bill seeks to address these longstanding inequities by promoting the regularization of qualified Job Order and Contract of Service workers in government. It aims to uphold the constitutional mandate of security of tenure, ensure fair and humane working conditions, and set an example for the private sector by institutionalizing just labor practices within the public sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10570
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ORGANIZATION OF COOPERATIVES FOR FRY GATHERERS, SMALL SCALE FISHERMEN AND FISHFARMERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Recent developments have highlighted the continuing constraints of the local fisheries sector in meeting the growing demand of an increasing population. In 2024, fish and other seafood products remained among the key contributors to food inflation, reflecting persistent supply-side challenges.1 On the production side, the sector continues to rely heavily on millions of small-scale fisherfolk dispersed across coastal communities. According to the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), municipal or small-scale fisheries account for a significant share of total fisheries employment, yet these fisherfolk remain among the poorest sectors in the country. Recent data show that poverty incidence among fisherfolk remains among the highest across basic sectors, estimated at around 30% or more in recent years.2 Despite their vital role in ensuring food security, many small-scale fishermen, fry gatherers, and fish farmers continue to operate under constrained conditions. Limited access to modern fishing gear, reliance on non-motorized or aging bancas, and inadequate post-harvest facilities—such as cold storage and ice plants—restrict both the volume and value of their catch. Moreover, climate 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. 2024 2 Philippine Statistics Authority. 2023 variability and extreme weather events further exacerbate their vulnerability, often disrupting fishing activities and affecting household incomes. At the same time, while the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA) reports a growing number of registered cooperatives nationwide, participation of fisherfolk in well-organized, adequately supported cooperatives remains limited, particularly in remote coastal areas. This gap reduces their ability to pool resources, access financing, improve bargaining power, and establish stable market linkages. Empowering these marginalized fisherfolk must therefore be a priority of the national government. This bill seeks to promote and support the organization and strengthening of cooperatives among fry gatherers, small-scale fishermen, and fish farmers. Through cooperative structures, members can consolidate resources, access credit and government support, and invest in essential assets such as motorized bancas, improved fishing gear, and post-harvest facilities. By fostering stronger cooperatives, the State can help enhance productivity, reduce post-harvest losses, stabilize incomes, and improve the overall resilience of the fisheries sector. Ultimately, this measure aims to contribute to food security, inclusive economic growth, and poverty reduction in coastal communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10571
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR INCENTIVES FOR NEW GRADUATES OF COLLEGES, UNIVERSITIES, AND ACCREDITED INSTITUTIONS OFFERING TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL COURSES OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “BILL OF RIGHTS FOR NEW GRADUATES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The expectations for new graduates in most Filipino families have long been clear: to secure stable employment, earn a decent income, and begin contributing meaningfully to their households and communities soon after completing their studies in college, university, or accredited vocational institutions. In reality, however, many fresh graduates continue to face significant challenges in entering the workforce and obtaining fair and competitive compensation. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the country’s unemployment rate as of 2024 averaged around 4.3%, equivalent to approximately 2.2 million unemployed Filipinos aged 15 years and over. Notably, a substantial portion of the unemployed still comes from the youth sector, with individuals aged 15–24 and 25–34 comprising a significant share of those without jobs. College graduates likewise continue to account for a meaningful percentage of the unemployed, underscoring the persistent gap between educational attainment and employment opportunities (PSA Labor Force Survey, 2024). This reflects the continuing reality faced by many young Filipinos: despite completing their education and preparing themselves for productive careers, a considerable number struggle to find immediate employment or secure work that matches their qualifications and expectations. The State recognizes its responsibility to enable the youth to fulfill their vital role in nation-building. Consistent with this mandate, this bill seeks to provide new graduates with greater access to employment opportunities, improve their chances of securing decent and meaningful work, and ensure that they receive fair and competitive compensation. In doing so, it aims to empower them to become active contributors to the country’s economic growth and long-term development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10573
title: AN ACT GRANTING THE NORTHERN SAMAR ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. (NORSAMELCO) A FRANCHISE TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE MUNICIPALITIES OF CATARMAN, BOBON, SAN JOSE, ROSARIO, LOPE DE VEGA, MONDRAGON, SILVINO LOBOS, SAN ROQUE, BIRI, LAVEZARES, ALLEN, VICTORIA, SAN ISIDRO, CAPUL, SAN ANTONIO, SAN VICENTE, PAMBUJAN, CATUBIG, LAS NAVAS, LAOANG, PALAPAG, MAPANAS, GAMAY, AND LAPINIG IN THE PROVINCE OF NORTHERN SAMAR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Northern Samar Electric Cooperative, Inc. (NORSAMELCO) is the sole electric distribution utility serving the municipalities of Catarman, Bobon, San Jose, Rosario, Lope de Vega, Mondragon, Silvino Lobos, San Roque, Biri, Lavezares, Allen, Victoria, San Isidro, Capul, San Antonio, San Vicente, Pambujan, Catubig, Las Navas, Laoang, Palapag, Mapanas, Gamay, and Lapinig in the Province of Northern Samar. For decades, it has played a crucial role in energizing households, supporting local industries, and enabling socio‑economic development across the province. Electric cooperatives such as NORSAMELCO are indispensable partners of government in achieving total electrification, especially in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs). In Northern Samar—an island province with numerous remote and hard‑to‑reach communities—the availability of reliable and affordable electricity is essential to improving public services, stimulating commerce, and enhancing the quality of life of its residents. This bill seeks to grant NORSAMELCO a legislative franchise to construct, install, establish, operate, own, manage, and maintain distribution systems for the conveyance of electric power to end‑users within its coverage area. The franchise provides the legal framework necessary for the cooperative to continue its operations, comply with regulatory requirements, and undertake system improvements consistent with the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) and other applicable laws. The proposed franchise also incorporates safeguards to protect consumer welfare, promote transparency in rate‑setting, ensure open and non‑discriminatory access to the distribution system, and uphold the authority of the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE). It likewise affirms the government’s reserved rights during emergencies, mandates reportorial compliance, and subjects the franchise to amendment or repeal when public interest so requires. Granting this franchise will allow NORSAMELCO to sustain and expand its electrification efforts, modernize its facilities, and deliver more efficient, reliable, and affordable electric service to the people of Northern Samar. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 10574
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A CHILD ONLINE SAFETY AND AGE-APPROPRIATE DIGITAL ACCESS FRAMEWORK, PRESCRIBING OBLIGATIONS FOR DIGITAL PLATFORM PROVIDERS, STRENGTHENING PRIVACY, PARENTAL SUPPORT, DIGITAL CITIZENSHIP, AND DUE PROCESS, PROVIDING PENALTIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being of the youth. As children increasingly communicate, learn, play, and participate in public life through digital services, this constitutional duty must extend to the online environment. Social media platforms, interactive gaming services, and other networked digital environments offer substantial educational, creative, and social benefits. At the same time, their design and operation may expose children to online sexual exploitation, online grooming (whereby offenders gain a child’s trust through digital communications for the purpose of sexual exploitation, abuse, coercion, or other harm), cyberbullying, privacy violations, harmful content, commercial profiling, contact with unknown adults, and features that encourage excessive or compulsive engagement. Recent events have further intensified public concern over the possible influence of violent digital content on minors. In the tragic school shooting in Tacloban City, Leyte, authorities confirmed that one of the two (2) suspects had previously engaged with a violent video game identified as GoreBox. According to the Police Regional Office Eastern Visayas (PRO 8), in a statement reported on June 23, 2026, the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game prior to the incident. He further described the game as involving shooting mechanics and firearms- based gameplay, and characterized its content as relatively violent. Existing laws punish many forms of online abuse and exploitation but mostly after they occur. A complementary preventive framework is therefore very much needed, and one that establishes age-appropriate access, requires providers to assess and reduce foreseeable risks to children, strengthens parental and educational support, and provides effective but proportionate government oversight. 1 This measure establishes sixteen (16) years as the general minimum age for independently maintaining an account on social media and interactive gaming services, specifically determined in the resulting IRR. It permits only the operation of narrowly defined age-appropriate access arrangements that comply with strict child-safety, privacy, and parental-control requirements. It also provides enhanced protections for all child users, including those aged sixteen (16) and seventeen (17). On the international front, there is a clear trend toward strengthening protections for minors in digital spaces by means of age-based restrictions. In Australia, the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age Act 2024) took effect in December 2025, setting a minimum age of sixteen (16) for access to specified social media platforms. Indonesia has also begun implementing restrictions barring users under sixteen (16) from major social media and online platforms, becoming one of the first countries in the region to adopt such a framework. In Europe, countries such as France, Spain, Greece, and Slovenia have introduced or are advancing proposals to establish minimum age thresholds ranging from fifteen (15) to sixteen (16) years, indicating ongoing policy efforts to limit early exposure to online risks. In Germany and Denmark, similar measures remain under legislative discussion or policy consideration, while Malaysia has likewise expressed regulatory intent toward adopting a minimum age requirement for social media access. Our national statistical data further shows the urgency of such regulatory action. Based on the 2024 National Information and Communications Technology Household Survey conducted by the Philippine Statistics Authority in partnership with the Department of Information and Communications Technology, approximately two-thirds (⅔) of children aged ten (10) to sixteen (16) have accessed the internet within a recent three-month period. This bill similarly recognizes that age checks may themselves create privacy risks, hence it adopts the principle of age assurance rather than prescribing a rigid list of identification or biometric technologies. Any method used must be necessary, proportionate, accessible, data- minimizing, and subject to standards developed with the National Privacy Commission. The commercial use, profiling, or unnecessary retention of age-assurance information is expressly prohibited. The bill further requires child-safety-by-design measures, accessible reporting systems, reasonable controls against circumvention, independent risk assessments, and special protections relating to direct messaging, location sharing, targeted advertising, recommender systems, livestreaming, and other high-risk features. To ensure enforceability, the measure establishes graduated penalties and clarifies the application of the law to foreign providers offering services in the Philippines. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10575
title: AN ACT MANDATING LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS TO USE BODY-WORN CAMERAS DURING LAW ENFORCEMENT OPERATIONS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution declares that the maintenance of peace and order and the promotion of the general welfare are essential for the enjoyment by all the people of the blessings of democracy.1 Integral to this peace and order is the trust between law enforcement and the people they serve. One initiative that can strengthen this trust is the use of body-worn cameras (BWCs). Both locally and abroad, the use of BWCs has become accepted as an effective tool for keeping both citizens and officers safe and for increasing transparency and accountability. Studies on the use of body-worn cameras in various places in the country show its effects in reducing crime rates, promoting transparency in law enforcement, and ultimately strengthening public trust.2 BWCs allow documentation of interactions between law enforcement and civilians, and make police actions subject to scrutiny and review, thus enhancing the credibility of law enforcement operations.3 Just recently in the 2nd District of Paranaque, BWCs were effectively used in the arrest of 1 CONST. Article II, Section 5. 2 Clarito, M. A. & Lagumen, H. A. (2025). Cameras on Duty: Exploring the Impact of Body-Worn Cameras on Law Enforcement Practices and Accountability. International Journal of Multidisciplinary: Applied Business and Education Research, 6(9), 4795-4809. https://doi.org/10.11594/ijmaber.06.09.40. Available at https://ejournals.ph/article.php?id=30956 3 Retiza, L.G.M., Caballero, N.S., & De La Cruz, W.O. (2025). Cops behind the lenses: Lived experiences of police officers wearing body-worn cameras during police operations. The Research Probe, 5(2), 56-72. https://doi.org/10.53378/trp.194 1 a suspect for violations of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002.4 In fact, the use of BWCs is recognized by various government bodies. The Supreme Court has recognized that recordings from BWCs can deter the excessive use of force in the execution of warrants and can help trial courts in resolving issues relevant to criminal cases. The PNP has also issued Memorandum Circular No. 2018-009 or the Operational Guidelines and Policies on the Use of Body-Worn Cameras. Meanwhile, to balance the use of BWCs with the right to privacy, the National Privacy Commission has issued Guidelines On The Processing Of Personal Data Collected Using Body- Worn Cameras. Significantly, mandating the use of BWCs is not just about upholding the community’s peace or guarding civilian rights. It is also about protecting the law enforcement officers themselves in case of baseless accusations and malicious suits. We can make use of the momentum that BWCs are gaining in the country today to push this measure forward. Just this May 2026, the PNP is reportedly preparing to receive body-worn cameras worth PHP800 million for deployment under the Unified 911 emergency response system.5 However, while some stations have already been equipped with BWCs, proper use and implementation has not been consistent due to lack of funding, technical difficulties, and inadequate training in its use. This bill seeks to institutionalize the use of body-worn cameras during law enforcement operations, provide guidelines on when recording should be activated and terminated, and instances when BWC use is prohibited. It also provides for rules on storage, custody, retention, access, and disclosure of the recordings, with the view of balancing the people’s right to privacy. Significantly, it provides for consistent and yearly funding for the continued implementation of BWC-use through the General Appropriations Act. With this measure, we are one step closer to a safer and more orderly community. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 10576
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE OSPITAL NG PARAÑAQUE - DISTRICT TWO IN THE CITY OF PARAÑAQUE INTO A LEVEL II GENERAL HOSPITAL, INCREASING ITS BED CAPACITY FROM 70 TO 100 BEDS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Health is a fundamental right of every Filipino guaranteed by the 1987 Constitution. Article II, Section 15 provides: “The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill consciousness among them. Further, Article XIII, Section 11 further mandates the State to “adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health, and other services available to all the people at affordable cost. There shall be priority for the needs of the underprivileged, sick, elderly, disabled, women, and children.” Despite this clear constitutional mandate, access to affordable, quality health and medical services remains a challenge for many Filipinos. In the Second District of Parañaque alone, the District Hospital, which serves more than 420,000 residents,1 lacks specialized services, such as Pediatrics, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, and Surgery, as well as an Intensive Care Unit and enhanced diagnostics facilities. As a result, patients requiring complex or critical care are often referred to hospitals in neighboring cities. To address this need, this bill seeks to upgrade the Ospital ng Parañaque District 2 in the City of Parañaque from a Level I to a Level II health facility and increase its bed capacity to one (100). The proposed upgrade will expand access to specialized medical services, reduce the need for patients to seek treatment outside the city, and strengthen the district’s local health system. It will also foster the development of a more capable healthcare workforce by creating opportunities for specialized training and improving the quality of patient care. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 10577
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE INCOME TAX EXEMPTION CEILING FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO FOUR HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND (P450,000.00) ANNUALLY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(A) AND (b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution mandates that Congress evolve a progressive system of taxation.1 Pursuant to this, Congress enacted the National Internal Revenue Code, which provides for income tax rates that increase as the person’s taxable income increases. Currently, the law provides that individuals with an annual taxable income of P250,000 and below are exempt from income tax.2 As such, those earning around P20,800 a month do not have to pay income tax. In 2017, when the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law was passed providing for the current tax exemption ceiling, the ceiling covered those in the low income and lower-middle income sectors.3 However, over the years, the range of family income belonging to the different economic classes have also changed. Some who were previously classified as being part of the middle middle- income class in 2017 eventually belonged to the lower-middle income class in 2021.4 The purchasing 1 1987 CONST., Art. VI, Sec. 28. 2 Tax Code, Sec. 24(A)(2). 3 Albert, Santos, Vizmanos. (2018). Defining and Profiling the Middle Class. Philippine Institute for Development Studies – Policy Notes No. 2018-18. Available at https://pidswebs.pids.gov.ph/CDN/PUBLICATIONS/pidspn1818.pdf. 4 Albert, Briones, and Rivera. (2024). New Wealth Creation for Expanding and Transforming the Middle-Class in the Philippines. Philippine Institute for Development Studies. Available https://pidswebs.pids.gov.ph/CDN/document/22DPRMKickOff_Albert.pdf. 1 power of the Philippine peso has also depreciated. What previously cost P1,000 in 2018 would cost over PhP1,300 for the same goods today.5 In addition, the effects of inflation, while felt by all Filipinos, are harder to bear for low- income families who spend the majority of their income on food, transportation, and other basic necessities.6 As the prices of goods and services increase, lower-income households experience a decline in purchasing power and an inability to meet the increasing costs. Notably, there have also been inflation spikes since the passage of the TRAIN Law, particularly in the years 2018 and 2022.7 This demonstrates that the current tax exemption ceiling no longer protects those most vulnerable to income poverty, particularly the low income and lower-middle income class.8 Specifically, lower-middle income families face the risk of falling into poverty due to unforeseen and sudden economic shocks, such as a family member losing employment or medical emergencies. This measure aims to make our tax law more responsive to the changing economic times and the value of the Philippine Peso by increasing the tax exemption ceiling for individual taxpayers from P250,000 to P450,000. This would cover individuals earning P37,500 each month, as opposed to exempting only those earning around P20,800 a month. Under this revised ceiling, those earning P450,000 a year can save up to P32,500 annually or over P2,700 a month. This higher take-home pay for ordinary Filipinos would significantly ease their burden, allow for greater spending on food and basic necessities, and ultimately support the most vulnerable sectors of our society. label: HB 10578
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING MICRO AND SMALL ENTERPRISES FROM MINIMUM CORPORATE INCOME TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 27(E)(1) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro and small-sized enterprises (MSEs) are part of the backbone of our country’s economy.1 They generate employment opportunities, encourage local growth and development, and contribute to poverty reduction and the country’s gross domestic product. In 2023, there were more than 1.2 million MSE establishments in the country, making up over 99% of the total number of establishments. Moreover, these enterprises generated over 5.4 million jobs, accounting for over 60% of the country’s total employment.2 However, MSEs remain vulnerable to economic and environmental circumstances. Difficulties in accessing affordable financing options and the burden of taxation often push MSEs into precarious financial positions. Under the current National Internal Revenue Code, domestic corporations, including MSEs, are taxed at either (a) 20% or 25% of their taxable income (i.e. gross income less allowable deductions); or (b) the minimum corporate income tax (MCIT) of 2% of their gross income beginning with its fourth taxable year, whichever is higher. In practice, MCIT creates an economic burden for struggling small businesses, because 1 MSMEs: Pillars of Inclusive Growth and Resilience in the Philippine Economy. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Research Academy. Available at https://www.bsp.gov.ph/Inclusive%20Finance/EFLP/EFLP_MSMEs_01a.pdf. 2 Cacnio, Faith. (2025). MSMEs: Pillars of Inclusive Growth and Resilience in the Philippine Economy. Available at https://www.bsp.gov.ph/Inclusive%20Finance/EFLP/EFLP_MSMEs_01a.pdf. 1 it is calculated on gross income, without the benefit of allowable deductions. This means that even with very minimum revenue or with the MSE barely breaking even, it will still need to pay income tax. Under this proposed measure, MSEs will be exempt from MCIT, thus easing their financial burden. Therefore, if the MSE is struggling and has zero taxable income for a certain year, it will no longer be subjected to corporate income tax. This measure aims to provide the necessary relief to MSEs, help them get the most out of their revenue, which they can use to improve their daily operations, hire more employees, and expand their business, and ultimately achieve long-term stability. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 10581
title: AN ACT PROMOTING AND STRENGTHENING THE MAGNA CARTA OF PUBLIC HEALTH WORKERS BY ENHANCING THEIR STATUTORY BENEFITS AND INCENTIVES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7305
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The country’s public health workers remain at the forefront of delivering essential healthcare services, safeguarding public health, and responding to medical emergencies. Their unwavering dedication, particularly during public health crisis, underscores the indispensable role they play in ensuring the health and well-being of every Filipino. Republic Act No. 7305, otherwise known as “The Magna Carta for Public Health Workers” was enacted into law thirty-four (34) years ago to promote and improve the social and economic well-being of health workers, their living and working conditions and terms of employment. Hence, the law mandated among other things the payment of benefits and allowances including night shift differential, hazard, subsistence, laundry, to name a few. Despite the protections afforded under the law, many of its statutory benefits and incentives have become inadequate due to inflation, increasing demands of healthcare service, and the evolving challenges faced by the country’s healthcare workforce. This measure seeks to ensure that the public health workers’ statutory benefits and incentives are responsive to present-day realities. It aims to improve compensation package, reinforce incentives for retention and professional 1|Page development, and provide greater recognition and support to those who dedicate their lives to public service in the healthcare sector. The measure likewise expands the definition of health workers to include those deployed outside of traditional health facilities, such as those reporting in health offices, State Universities and Colleges, and Universities, Government- Owned and - Controlled Corporations, Local Government Units, among others. In our pursuit to address the gaps in our public health system and to strengthen the delivery of healthcare services, it is paramount that we ensure that our health workers are not only paid a living wage but that the benefits we provide are likewise sufficient to sustain their living conditions. In view of the foregoing, we urge the swift passage of this measure.
