label: HB 10582
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 43 (f), 45, AND 47 (f) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ‘ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001 OR EPIRA’, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) of 2001, is one of the most important structural reforms in the Philippine electric power industry, with the declared policy of promoting free and fair competition, ensuring transparent and reasonable electricity prices, and protecting the public interest in the provision of power and related services. More than two decades after its enactment, however, captive customers of distribution utilities continue to face opaque and potentially excessive generation charges, particularly under automatic pass‑through mechanisms and complex power supply agreements whose cost structures are difficult for consumers and policymakers to scrutinize. Experience has likewise shown that the existing framework on cross‑ownership and market power abuse does not sufficiently prevent large distribution utilities and their affiliated generation companies from entering into arrangements that allow undue control over supply, pricing, and market behavior to the prejudice of consumers and other industry participants. In Mindanao, the potential privatization of the Agus and Pulangui Hydroelectric Power Complexes would expose strategic, predominantly renewable assets to commercial pressures that may compromise long‑term affordability, public control, and regional equity. These gaps and risks constrain the full realization of EPIRA’s intent and undermine the protection of captive market end‑users. Thus, this bill proposes to amend Sections 43(f), 45, and 47(f) of EPIRA to strengthen consumer protection, deter market power abuse, and preserve strategic public assets, while remaining faithful to the law’s pro‑market and pro‑consumer objectives. First, the amendment to Section 43(f) expressly empowers the ERC, with respect to the generation component recoverable from captive markets, to review, regulate, benchmark, confirm, adjust, or disallow generation rates and corresponding recoverable generation costs, including those reflected in automatic adjustment mechanisms and other pass‑through charges, ensuring that only prudent and reasonable costs are charged to end‑users. Second, the amendment to Section 45 tightens safeguards against cross‑ownership and market power abuse by lowering the allowable share of installed generating capacity per grid and clarifying the limits on bilateral supply that distribution utilities may source from affiliated generation firms, calibrated by demand level. Third, the amendment to Section 47(f) permanently excludes the Agus and Pulangui Hydroelectric Power Complexes from privatization and any form of transfer to private entities, vesting their ownership, operation, and control in the National Power Corporation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. SERGIO C. DAGOOC REP. PRESLEY C. title: AN ACT POSTPONING THE NOVEMBER 2, 2026 BARANGAY AND SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN ELECTIONS, SETTING THE SAME ON THE LAST MONDAY OF MAY 2027, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9164, AS AMENDED, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The postponement and rescheduling of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections is not without legislative precedent. The authority to adjust an election date, however, is not absolute. Because elections involve the people’s fundamental right to choose their representatives, any postponement must satisfy the constitutional standards laid down by the Supreme Court in Macalintal v. Commission on Elections, G.R. Nos. 263590 and 263673. In Macalintal, the SC declared Republic Act No. 11935 unconstitutional insofar as it postponed the December 2022 BSKE to October 2023. It ruled that the postponement of elections must be supported by important, substantial, or compelling reasons and must be reasonably tailored to advance a legitimate governmental interest without unnecessarily impairing the people’s right of suffrage. The Court found the reasons invoked for R.A. No. 11935 insufficient. Among the justifications offered were election fatigue following the May 2022 national and local elections, the desire to allow incumbent barangay officials to continue their projects, and the intended use of the election budget for other government programs. The postponement was therefore considered arbitrary and constitutionally infirm. The present measure is fundamentally different. It is not based on political convenience, election fatigue, the desire to prolong incumbency, or the intention to generate government savings. Neither does it seek to realign or divert COMELEC funds to unrelated government programs. It responds instead to extraordinary and intervening events that have materially affected the financial, logistical, physical, and operational conditions under which the November 2, 2026 BSKE must be conducted. The country is presently confronting an international energy crisis arising from the conflict in the Middle East, which has caused significant instability in global petroleum supply. These developments were not reasonably foreseeable when the appropriations and operational assumptions for the 2026 elections were prepared. The Philippines is particularly vulnerable to disruptions in the global oil market because it relies heavily on imported petroleum. As global supply has tightened, domestic fuel prices have become highly volatile. The resulting surge in fuel costs has significantly increased the cost of transportation, power, logistics, and other essential services and supplies, leaving no dependable cost baseline upon which election contracts and logistical preparations may be based. The seriousness of the situation was recognized by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., who declared a national energy emergency and authorized a unified package of government interventions for livelihoods, industry, food, and transportation. The declaration confirms that the crisis is not merely speculative or temporary, but a matter requiring coordinated and extraordinary governmental action. And it is ongoing with no clear end in sight. These extraordinary consequences directly affect election administration. The conduct of the BSKE requires the nationwide movement of ballots, election forms, equipment, communications systems, security personnel, teachers, and other members of the Electoral Boards. It also requires food, accommodation, electricity, generators, transportation, rentals, training, and emergency logistical support, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. Inflation has further altered the assumptions under which the election budget was prepared. In June 2026, national headline inflation stood at 6.4 percent. Transport costs increased by 12.8 percent; housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels by 8.0 percent; food and non-alcoholic beverages by 5.2 percent; and restaurants and accommodation services by 7.0 percent. These sectors correspond directly to the principal operating requirements of a nationwide election, with emphasis on the reliability, cost, and accessibility of electricity, the dependence of many of our power plants on petroleum and coal, and the recent disruptions to the Philippine grid causing outage on a national scale. Add to that, COMELEC Chairman George Garcia was quoted publicly saying that that the actual cost of BSKE is around Php 19 billion, and this was before considering the effects of the ongoing energy crisis. These difficulties are compounded by successive high magnitude earthquakes, ranging from 6.9 to 7.8, that have hit the country, resulting in damage and temporary closures while schools, roads, electricity, water, and communications systems were inspected and repaired. Schools are indispensable to Philippine elections. Their continuing rehabilitation creates genuine uncertainty regarding the safety, availability, accessibility, and readiness of voting centers by November 2026. The proposed postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections will additionally allow the Commission on Elections and other concerned agencies to devote sufficient attention and resources to the first regular Bangsamoro Parliamentary Election on 14 September 2026. This election is both historic and complex. It marks the transition from an appointed interim government to a democratically elected Bangsamoro Parliament and represents a major milestone in the implementation of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the continuing peace process. The newly elected Bangsamoro Government is expected to assume office on 30 October 2026. Barely a month and a half after the parliamentary election, the BSKE is scheduled on 2 November 2026, with all barangays in BARMM also participating. The postponement will provide COMELEC, teachers, security forces, and support agencies sufficient operational flexibility to manage these major electoral exercises effectively and ensure that the historic Bangsamoro transition receives the administrative attention it deserves. title: AN ACT REMOVING THE BURDEN OF SYSTEM LOSS COSTS FROM CONSUMER ELECTRICITY BILLS, PROHIBITING FOR THE PURPOSE DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES FROM IMPOSING SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES ON CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 43 (F) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” PROVIDING MEASURES FOR THE REDUCTION OF SYSTEM LOSSES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential public service indispensable to daily life, human dignity, economic productivity, and national development. Households, schools, hospitals, and businesses depend on electricity. This is why power costs are particularly burdensome for ordinary Filipinos. Unfortunately, in recent years, consumer electricity bills skyrocketed in the country. As of June 2026, the Department of Energy reported that the Philippines recorded the highest average electricity rates in Southeast Asia at P12.43 per kilowatt-hour, surpassing Singapore by less than a centavo.1 This is in no small part due to system loss charges. Based on Meralco’s 2025 1 BusinessWorld, DoE says Philippine electricity rates highest in Southeast Asia in June (July 21, 2026), https://bworldonline.com/top-stories/2026/07/21/764693/doe-says-philippine-electricity- rates-highest-in-southeast-asia-in-june/. i bill breakdown, system loss accounted for about 5% of an average customer’s bill.2 Between August 2025 and July 2026, the average monthly system loss charge for a 200-kWh consumer stood at ₱148.95, forcing an average family to pay ₱1,787.38 over twelve months for unconsumed power.3 Under existing laws, specifically Section 10 of Republic Act No. 7832 or the “Anti-Electricity and Electric Transmission Lines/Materials Pilferage Act of 1994”4 and Section 43(f) of the EPIRA Act of 2001,5 distribution utilities and electric cooperatives are permitted to recover system losses from consumers, subject to the caps prescribed by the Energy Regulatory Commission. System loss refers to the difference between the energy delivered to the distribution system and energy delivered to the users of the distribution system, the amount of which is eventually measured and billed to the consumers.6 It encompasses both technical losses (physical dissipation of energy through lines and transformers) and non-technical losses (electricity theft, illegal connections, meter tampering, and administrative errors).7 While certain technical losses may be expected in the operation of an electric distribution system, the financial consequences of such losses form part of the ordinary cost and risk of operating a public utility. Like businesses in other industries, distribution utilities are expected to manage these risks by maintaining efficient infrastructure, investing in modern technologies, reducing technical losses, and preventing electricity theft. 2 Lance Spencer Yu, EXPLAINER: What is system loss, and how does it affect your power bill? Rappler (July 28, 2026), https://www.rappler.com/business/explainer-what-system-loss-affect- power-bill. 3 Wilnard Bacelonia, More senators move to strip system loss, VAT from power bills, Philippine News Agency (July 29, 2026), https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1280550. 4 Anti-Electricity and Electric Transmission Lines/Materials Pilferage Act of 1994, Republic Act No. 7832, § 10. 5 Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, Republic Act No. 9136, § 43(f). 6 Energy Regulatory Commission, Resolution Clarifying the System Loss Cap Structure and Performance Standards for Distribution Utilities, ERC Res. No. 10, Ser. of 2018. 7 Supra, note 2. ii Consumers, who have no control over the operation of the distribution system, should not be required to bear these costs. The existing pass-through mechanism weakens incentives for utilities to minimize system losses. If losses are simply recovered from consumers, utilities have no pressure to modernize aging infrastructure, improve operational efficiency, and strengthen anti-pilferage measures. As a result, honest paying households, including those in the lower income brackets, are forced to subsidize these inefficiencies answer for stolen electricity. This measure addresses these concerns by prohibiting the recovery or pass-through of system losses to consumers while preserving the right of distribution utilities to recover losses directly from persons responsible for electricity pilferage, theft, meter tampering, fraud, vandalism, and other unlawful acts through the remedies available under existing laws. The bill likewise directs the Department of Energy, the National Electrification Administration, and the Energy Regulatory Commission to assist electric cooperatives through modernization programs, technical assistance, capacity-building, and access to financing, particularly for those serving geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, to ensure that the transition away from system loss charges does not compromise the reliability of their electric services. The proposed measure is consistent with the Constitution, which directs the State to promote a just and dynamic social order that will improve the quality of life of all the people8 and protect consumers against unfair business practices.9 It is likewise consistent with the principle that public utilities, as holders of State-granted franchises, must provide safe, 8 Const. (1987), Art. II, Section 9. 9 Const. (1987), Art. XVI, Section 9. iii adequate, efficient, and reasonably priced services.10 The ordinary costs and risks of operating a public utility, including the responsibility to minimize system losses, should be borne by the utility itself and not shifted to consumers. Hence, this bill, which seeks to: (1) prohibit the recovery or pass- through of system losses to electricity consumers; (2) strengthen the accountability of distribution utilities in managing system losses; (3) preserve the right of utilities to recover losses from the persons legally responsible therefor; (4) provide technical and financial assistance to electric cooperatives in reducing system losses; and (5) promote a more efficient, accountable, and consumer-oriented electric power industry. label: HB 10586
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES OPERATING IN PROVINCES AND CITIES HOSTING GEOTHERMAL ENERGY RESOURCES OR GEOTHERMAL POWER GENERATION FACILITIES, INCLUDING PROVINCES ADJACENT TO HIGHLY URBANIZED CITIES AND INDEPENDENT COMPONENT CITIES HOSTING SUCH RESOURCES OR FACILITIES, TO DIRECTLY PURCHASE ELECTRICITY FROM QUALIFIED GEOTHERMAL POWER PRODUCERS, EXEMPTING SUCH PURCHASES FROM THE COMPETITIVE SELECTION PROCESS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 23 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Provinces and local communities that host geothermal resources make a continuing and substantial contribution to the country’s energy security. They provide the land, infrastructure, workforce, and local environment that allow indigenous geothermal energy to be explored, developed, generated, and transmitted to consumers throughout the country. Yet the presence of a geothermal power facility within or near a locality does not automatically result in lower electricity rates for the families, schools, hospitals, farms, and businesses in the host and surrounding communities. The Constitution recognizes that local governments and their inhabitants must receive an equitable share in the benefits derived from the utilization and development of national wealth within their respective areas. This principle is reflected in the Local Government Code, which provides that a significant portion of the proceeds derived from hydrothermal, geothermal, and other sources of energy shall be applied to lowering the cost of electricity in the locality where such energy source is located. The same principle must apply when the geothermal resource or facility is located within a highly urbanized city or independent component city. Although these cities are politically and administratively independent from the provinces around them, their geothermal resources and power facilities form part of a wider geographic, economic, environmental, and energy ecosystem. The neighboring provinces and their communities may provide the workforce, transport routes, watersheds, transmission corridors, public infrastructure, and other resources necessary for the continued operation of the geothermal facility. They may likewise experience the environmental, social, and economic consequences of geothermal development. For this reason, the benefits granted under this measure should also extend to the province within which a highly urbanized city or independent component city is geographically situated, as well as to provinces whose territorial boundaries are directly adjacent to such host city. Political boundaries should not prevent surrounding communities from receiving a fair and measurable share in the benefits arising from geothermal resources located within their immediate geographic area. Under Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the “Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001” or EPIRA, distribution utilities are required to supply electricity to their captive markets in the least-cost manner. In implementing this obligation, distribution utilities are generally required to procure their long-term power requirements through a Competitive Selection Process. Competition remains an important consumer-protection mechanism. However, the Competitive Selection Process may become impracticable when a distribution utility seeks to purchase electricity from a particular geothermal power producer located within its own host province, or within a highly urbanized city or independent component city adjacent to the province, and the intended transaction is designed specifically to reduce or stabilize electricity costs for host and neighboring communities. 2 The law must therefore provide a carefully defined exception. Distribution utilities, including electric cooperatives, operating in geothermal host provinces, geothermal host cities, and qualified adjacent provinces should be permitted to negotiate directly with geothermal power producers operating within the relevant host locality. Such agreements should be exempt from the Competitive Selection Process while remaining subject to the full review and approval of the Energy Regulatory Commission. The proposed measure preserves the fundamental principle of least-cost electricity. It requires the Energy Regulatory Commission to determine whether the resulting generation rate is just, reasonable, prudent, and beneficial to consumers. It likewise establishes safeguards against excessive pricing, overcontracting, self-dealing, market abuse, imprudent costs, and anti- competitive conduct. All savings, discounts, rebates, and other economic benefits arising from direct geothermal power procurement must be fully and transparently passed on to electricity consumers. By allowing host and adjacent provinces to source power directly from geothermal resources located within their immediate geographic area, this measure gives concrete meaning to the constitutional principle that the people who host, sustain, and are directly affected by the development of national wealth must be among its primary beneficiaries. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 10593
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10591, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “COMPREHENSIVE FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION REGULATION ACT,” BY REQUIRING THE SAFE STORAGE OF FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION, PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS BY MINORS, IMPOSING LIABILITY FOR CHILD FIREARM ACCESS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Recent incidents involving the access of minors to irearms demonstrate the need for more speci ic and enforceable safe-storage requirements. Republic Act No. 10591 presently provides for the licensing and regulation of irearms, requires applicants to pass a gun safety seminar, and authorizes the suspension, cancellation, or revocation of a irearm license for, among other grounds, the loss of a irearm through negligence. However, the law does not expressly establish a detailed statutory duty requiring irearm owners and custodians to secure irearms and ammunition against access by minors. Nor does it provide a speci ic offense for knowingly or negligently permitting a minor to obtain unauthorized access to a irearm. The State has a legitimate interest in preventing irearm-related injury and death. Firearm ownership and possession are statutory privileges subject to the conditions imposed by law, and not constitutional property rights. This measure therefore proposes mandatory safe-storage requirements, a child- irearm-access offense, administrative sanctions, reporting duties, and a rebuttable presumption of negligence in appropriate civil and criminal proceedings. The 1|Page proposed law preserves due process by requiring proof of knowledge or negligence and a causal connection between the storage violation and the resulting harm. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PLANNING, DEVELOPMENT, CONSTRUCTION AND MAINTENANCE OF THE PANAON ISLAND CIRCUMFERENTIAL ROAD IN THE PROVINCE OF SOUTHERN LEYTE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Panaon Island, home to the municipalities of Liloan, San Francisco, San Ricardo, and Pintuyan in the Province of Southern Leyte, has immense potential for economic growth, tourism, agriculture, and isheries. Yet, despite its strategic location along the Maharlika Highway, many communities on the island continue to struggle with poor road connectivity. Families, farmers, isherfolk, students, workers, and patients often have to travel long and dif icult routes just to reach neighboring towns or access markets, schools, hospitals, and other essential services. This lack of reliable transportation slows economic progress, increases the cost of doing business, and limits opportunities for thousands of residents. This bill seeks to address these longstanding challenges by directing the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) to plan, construct, and maintain the Panaon Island Circumferential Road. The project will connect the municipalities of Liloan, San Francisco, San Ricardo, and Pintuyan through a safer and more ef icient road network, making travel faster, reducing transportation costs, improving the delivery of goods and services, strengthening disaster response, and opening more opportunities for trade, tourism, and investment. The road alignment will be determined only after the necessary engineering, environmental, and right-of-way studies and consultations have been completed, ensuring that the project is safe, sustainable, and responsive to the needs of local communities. 1|Page For many years, the people of Panaon Island have dreamed of a road that will truly connect their communities and bring development closer to their homes. This measure, which has been consistently iled and approved in previous Congresses, re lects the continuing urgency of that dream and the government's commitment to inclusive and balanced regional development. By investing in this vital infrastructure, the State invests in the future of the people of Panaon Island, creating better opportunities, improving access to essential services, and building a more connected and prosperous Southern Leyte. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL SECURITY PERSONNEL IN ALL PUBLIC ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS, MANDATING THE CREATION AND ALLOCATION OF PLANTILLA POSITIONS THEREFOR, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools must be places where children are able to learn, grow, and develop without fearing for their safety. The responsibility of the State to provide quality education necessarily carries with it the responsibility to provide an environment in which learners, teachers, and school personnel are adequately protected. The Department of Education has long recognized the importance of security personnel in schools. Previous DepEd issuances have expressly recognized security guards and watchmen assigned to elementary, secondary, and vocational schools. DepEd has likewise previously directed the establishment of security units in schools using existing personnel and resources. However, the security requirements of today's schools demand a more institutionalized and sustainable approach. Public elementary and secondary schools differ considerably in learner population, campus size, number of access points, operating schedules, location, and exposure to security risks. A large public high school with thousands of learners, several buildings, and multiple entrances necessarily presents different security requirements from those of a small elementary school. For this reason, a uniform requirement of merely one security guard for every school may neither be adequate nor an efficient use of government resources. School security should not depend solely on temporary arrangements, existing personnel being asked to assume additional functions, or security measures adopted only after a serious incident occurs. Security is not ancillary to education. A child cannot meaningfully exercise the right to education if the environment in which that education is delivered is not safe. This measure therefore seeks to institutionalize dedicated security personnel in all public elementary and secondary schools by mandating DepEd, in coordination with the Department of Budget and Management, to create and allocate permanent plantilla positions for qualified school security personnel. Rather than imposing an inflexible one-size-fits-all staffing ratio, the bill requires the establishment of staffing standards based on learner population, campus size and configuration, entrances and exits, operating shifts, location, documented incidents, and assessed security risks. Schools facing greater security requirements shall be prioritized during the initial implementation of the program. The measure likewise recognizes that protecting children requires more than guarding a gate. School security personnel must understand the environment in which they serve. Accordingly, the bill requires appropriate training in child protection, emergency and crisis response, threat identification, first aid, disaster preparedness, de-escalation, and coordination with law enforcement and emergency authorities. The objective is not to turn our schools into fortresses. It is to ensure that when parents entrust their children to our public schools each morning, the State has taken reasonable and institutional measures to keep them safe until they return home. A secure school is fundamental to a functioning education system. The presence of trained, accountable, and adequately deployed security personnel must therefore be treated not merely as an administrative option, but as an integral component of providing safe and accessible public education. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 10596
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE SYSTEM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10630, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Humihinga pa ba?” Those were the first words uttered by the mother of Chris Lorenz Fabian when she arrived at his school in Tacloban. By then, she already knew that her son had been shot. What she did not yet know was whether he was still alive. A mother who knew her son as someone who would not fight back even when he was bullied, even though he was physically capable of defending himself, was suddenly confronted with a reality no parent should ever have to face. Chris Lorenz Fabian, Ayessa Nicole Dazo, and Joyancee Separa lost their lives in the school shooting in Tacloban, a tragedy that shocked not only the families of the victims but our whole nation. In the days that followed, the tragedy drew widespread public attention. Public officials, members of the media, and concerned citizens reached out to the grieving families. But amidst that attention, Christopher's mother acknowledged a reality she had already come to accept: today, their story is at the height of public attention and a lot of people are reaching out; but when the public moves on, she knows that attention will fade, and people will eventually forget. The families, however, will not. Long after the headlines disappear, they will continue to live with the empty seats at their tables, the unanswered questions, and the permanent absence of their children. It is in this context that this measure is proposed. No law can bring Chris Lorenz, Ayessa Nicole, and Joyancee back. No amendment to our criminal laws can undo what happened inside that school. But the deaths of these victims must compel us to examine whether our laws adequately respond when children commit acts involving the gravest forms of violence. Republic Act No. 9344, otherwise known as the “Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006,” as amended by Republic Act No. 10630, established a juvenile justice system founded on restorative justice, diversion, intervention, and rehabilitation. These principles remain essential. Children in conflict with the law must continue to be treated in a manner that recognizes their age, capacity for change, dignity, and potential for rehabilitation. But compassion and rehabilitation cannot mean the absence of accountability. The State has a fundamental duty to protect children, including children in conflict with the law. It has an equally solemn duty to protect other children, families, and communities from violence, to recognize the suffering of victims, and to ensure that the justice system provides an appropriate response to the gravity of an offense. This measure therefore seeks to strengthen and recalibrate the juvenile justice framework while preserving its fundamental child-appropriate safeguards. It provides that children twelve (12) years of age or under at the time of the commission of an offense shall remain exempt from criminal liability and shall instead undergo appropriate intervention. Children above twelve (12) but below eighteen (18) years of age may be held criminally liable, subject to child-appropriate proceedings, with diversion, restorative justice, intervention, and rehabilitation continuing to be prioritized whenever legally permissible. The bill likewise provides a more appropriate framework for heinous crimes. Where a child above twelve (12) but below eighteen (18) years of age commits such an offense, special rules on custody and disposition shall apply. For persons found guilty by final judgment of heinous crimes committed while minors, transfer to the appropriate regular penal facility shall be mandatory upon reaching eighteen (18) years of age, subject to appropriate transition measures and continued access to rehabilitation programs. The measure also recognizes that responsibility cannot rest solely upon the child when adults knowingly contribute to juvenile offending. It accordingly imposes liability upon parents, guardians, or persons exercising parental authority who knowingly encourage, direct, compel, profit from, or induce a child to commit an offense; whose gross negligence or willful failure to exercise reasonable supervision substantially contributes to the commission of an offense; or who unlawfully assist a child in evading lawful custody or proceedings. Safeguards are retained to ensure that no parent or guardian is punished merely by reason of parenthood and that liability must be established beyond reasonable doubt. This bill does not seek to abandon rehabilitation as the foundation of juvenile justice. Neither does it proceed from the belief that every child who commits an offense is beyond reform. Rather, it recognizes that rehabilitation and accountability need not be opposing principles. A justice system can believe in the capacity of a child to change while still recognizing the gravity of the harm inflicted upon another human being. Most importantly, this measure asks that we remember the people behind the cases that eventually disappear from our headlines. Chris' mother understands that the attention surrounding their tragedy will not last forever. She also understands that changing the law will never return the lives that were taken. But their deaths need not be without consequence or meaning. If this tragedy can compel us to examine the gaps in our laws, strengthen accountability for the most serious offenses, better protect our children and communities, and prevent another family from asking whether their child is still breathing, then the lives lost will have left behind something more enduring than a headline. We cannot bring them back. But we can remember them through action, and we can give meaning to their loss by ensuring that what happened to them is not simply forgotten when the public attention fades. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 10597
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ENHANCED PROTECTION, SECURITY, AND BENEFITS FOR MEDIA WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A free and independent press is one of the pillars of a democratic society. Every day, media workers risk their safety to bring timely and truthful information to the Filipino people. They report from disaster areas, con lict zones, crime scenes, and other dangerous situations so that the public remains informed. Yet despite the vital role they play, many media workers continue to face low and delayed pay, insecure employment, lack of bene its, unsafe working conditions, and inadequate protection for themselves and their families. While existing labor laws provide important safeguards, many media workers remain unprotected because they are hired under short-term contracts, freelance arrangements, or other informal work setups that deny them the bene its and security they rightfully deserve. This bill seeks to ensure that media workers are treated fairly by requiring written contracts, guaranteeing at least the minimum wage and mandatory bene its for employees, providing social security coverage, and promoting safe and decent working conditions. It also requires employers to provide hazard pay, insurance, safety equipment, and emergency support for media workers assigned to dangerous areas, while recognizing their right to refuse assignments that pose an imminent and serious threat to their lives. At the same time, the measure irmly upholds the constitutional guarantee of press freedom. It does not regulate or interfere with editorial decisions, nor does it impose 1|Page liability simply because news is published or broadcast. Instead, it protects media workers from harassment, discrimination, and retaliation while encouraging cooperation among government, media organizations, employers, and workers through a News Media Tripartite Council that will recommend industry standards, safety measures, and better workplace practices without controlling media content. Protecting media workers means protecting the public's right to know. When journalists and other media professionals are given fair treatment, decent working conditions, and adequate protection, they are better able to perform their duty of delivering accurate, timely, and responsible news. By promoting both the welfare of media workers and the independence of the press, this measure strengthens democracy and serves the best interests of every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 10598
title: AN ACT GRANTING A FRANCHISE TO CLAVERIA ELECTRIC SERVICE (CES) TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE, AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CLAVERIA, PROVINCE OF MASBATE”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is a fundamental driver of socio-economic progress. In rural and developing areas, the continuous, efficient, and dependable delivery of electric power remains a cornerstone for uplifting the quality of life of every Filipino household and business. The Municipality of Claveria, located in the Province of Masbate, is a rapidly developing community with unique geographical demands and expanding commercial operations. To sustain its economic momentum and meet the growing power requirements of its residents, there is an urgent necessity to optimize and reinforce its local power infrastructure. Access to affordable, safe, and stable electricity is paramount to driving micro-industries, improving local healthcare systems, and enhancing educational frameworks within the municipality. This legislative measure seeks to grant Claveria Electric Service (CES), the specialized electric utility operated directly by the Local Government Unit (LGU) of Claveria, a formal legislative franchise to acquire, establish, operate, and maintain, for commercial purposes and in the public interest, a distribution system for the conveyance of electric power to end users in the Municipality of Claveria. Under this framework, the National Power Corporation (NAPOCOR) shall continue to serve as the source of electric power generation, while the CES shall be responsible for the distribution of electricity to the end users. As the existing LGU-operated electric utility, CES has demonstrated the technical expertise, institutional capacity, and operational capability necessary to establish, operate, and maintain a reliable and efficient distribution system responsive to the municipality's present and future energy requirements. By granting this statutory franchise, Congress empowers a dedicated distribution utility to bridge the gap between generation and consumption, modernize the grid, drastically minimize power outages, and optimize retail electricity rates. This initiative directly reinforces the national policy mandated by the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) of 2001 to ensure total electrification, promote consumer welfare, and foster local development through robust public utilities. The support of the Members of Congress for the prompt and timely passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTONIO T. label: HB 10599
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PAMBANSANG AGAPAY SA PAMILYA AT MALILIIT NA NEGOSYO (PAMANA) PROGRAM, PROVIDING A DIRECT ANNUAL SUBSIDY TO MINIMUM WAGE EARNERS AND THEIR FAMILIES THROUGH DIGITAL WALLETS FOR EXCLUSIVE USE IN LOCAL MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Millions of Filipino minimum wage earners continue to grapple with the rising cost of basic goods, while micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) which account for 99.5% of all business establishments and employ the majority of the Filipino workforce — struggle with thin margins and limited consumer demand. This measure addresses both problems with a single intervention: a direct, regular, and digitally delivered subsidy to minimum wage earners and their families that can only be spent in registered local MSMEs. Unlike traditional cash assistance programs that are one-time, leakage-prone, and often captured by intermediaries, this bill guarantees that (1) assistance reaches families directly through their digital wallets, (2) the benefit is spread throughout the year through monthly disbursements and a daily spending limit, encouraging use for daily essentials rather than lump-sum consumption, and (3) every peso of public assistance circulates within local communities, stimulating neighborhood economies rather than large retail chains. This measure is designed to complement, not duplicate, existing social protection programs. Families already receiving assistance under the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) or its successor conditional cash transfer program remain covered by that program and are excluded from this Act, ensuring that public funds reach a distinct population: minimum wage earners who work full-time yet remain financially strained, and who are typically ineligible for 4Ps but still without a dedicated income supplement. The measure likewise accelerates financial inclusion and digitalization among both households and small businesses, consistent with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 10600
title: AN ACT CREATING A FAMILY COURT IN THE PROVINCE OF EASTERN SAMAR, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The family is the foundation of Philippine society, and the State has the constitutional duty to protect its sanctity and strengthen its role as the basic autonomous social institution. In recognition of this mandate, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 8369, otherwise known as the Family Courts Act of 1997, to establish specialized courts that exclusively hear and decide cases involving children and family relations. Section 3 of the law expressly provides that there shall be established a Family Court in every province and city in the country. Despite this clear legislative policy, the Province of Eastern Samar has yet to be provided with a dedicated Family Court. Consequently, cases involving child abuse, domestic violence, adoption, guardianship, custody, juvenile offenders, support, and other family-related matters continue to be handled by regular Regional Trial Courts, adding to their already congested dockets and resulting in delays in the resolution of cases that require prompt, specialized, and child-sensitive adjudication. The establishment of a Family Court in Eastern Samar will strengthen the administration of justice by ensuring that family and child-related cases are heard by judges and court personnel with the specialized training, expertise, and sensitivity required under the law. It will likewise promote the speedy disposition of cases, reduce docket congestion in existing Regional Trial Courts, enhance the protection of children's rights, and improve access to justice for families throughout the province. This measure seeks to fulfill the intent of Republic Act No. 8369 by finally establishing a Family Court in the Province of Eastern Samar, thereby ensuring that its residents enjoy the same level of judicial protection and specialized legal services envisioned by the Family Courts Act of 1997. label: HB 10601
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE IMPOSITION OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES ON ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, STRENGTHENING ACCOUNTABILITY OF ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY PARTICIPANTS IN REDUCING SYSTEM LOSSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is a basic necessity and an essential public service that every Filipino household depends on. Yet, for decades, Filipino consumers have been burdened by persistently high electricity rates. According to the Department of Energy (DOE), the Philippines now has the highest electricity rates in Southeast Asia.1 This longstanding problem is rooted in the neoliberal framework established by the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) of 2001, which privatized the power industry and transferred control to private corporations. As a result, among the inequitable charges imposed on consumers is the system loss charge. System loss refers to the difference between the electricity purchased by a distribution utility and the electricity actually delivered and billed to the end-users. It consists of technical losses, which arise from the inherent limitations of electrical equipment and transmission lines, and non-technical losses, which result from illegal connections, electricity theft, meter tampering, billing errors, and other unauthorized activities. Under the current regulatory framework, these losses are passed on to consumers, provided they remain within the allowable caps prescribed by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). Consequently, Filipino consumers are compelled to pay for electricity they neither consumed nor benefited from. This effectively shifts to the public the costs of a distribution utility’s operational inefficiencies and its failure to prevent pilferage and other avoidable losses. 1 https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea The DOE estimates that consumers could save approximately five to ten percent (5% – 10%) on their electricity bills, depending on a utility’s system loss rate,2 if system loss charges were removed. This bill therefore seeks to prohibit the collection of system loss charges from electricity consumers and instead require distribution utilities to absorb all costs arising from system losses. This proposed measure will provide immediate relief to Filipino families, workers, and small business owners who already reserve a significant portion of their income to electricity expenses. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. SARAH JANE I. ELAGO Gabriela Women’s Party REP. RENEE LOUISE M. CO REP. ANTONIO L. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE PROFESSIONAL COMPENSATION SYSTEM IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING THE PROFESSIONAL WAGE BOARD AS AN ATTACHED AGENCY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT WITH QUASI-JUDICIAL POWERS, ESTABLISHING THE PROFESSIONAL WAGE COUNCIL AS ITS CONSULTATIVE ARM, CREATING REGIONAL PROFESSIONAL WAGE OFFICES, ALIGNING MINIMUM PROFESSIONAL COMPENSATION WITH THE SALARY STANDARDIZATION LAW, COVERING ALL GOVERNMENT AND PRIVATE EMPLOYERS, PROVIDING FOR PERMANENT FUNDING, PRESCRIBING MINIMUM PROFESSIONAL COMPENSATION STANDARDS, DEFINING AND PENALIZING PROHIBITED ACTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines produces some of the most highly trained licensed professionals in Asia — nurses, engineers, architects, pharmacists, physicians, accountants, teachers, and hundreds of others — yet systematically fails to retain them because domestic compensation does not reflect the investment, expertise, and public responsibility they carry. No existing law establishes minimum compensation standards specifically calibrated to licensed professional practice. The Labor Code and regional minimum wage system were designed for ordinary workers and are structurally ill-suited to capture the unique attributes of professional labor: mandatory years of education, state-administered licensure, continuing professional development obligations, personal and public liability, and the direct bearing of professional services on public health, safety, infrastructure, justice, and national development. This Act proposes a permanent systemic solution through two complementary institutions: the Professional Wage Board (PWB), an attached agency of the Department of Labor and Employment with quasi-judicial authority to issue and enforce binding Professional Wage Orders; and the Professional Wage Council (PWC), a broad multi-sector consultative body that conducts stakeholder consultations and endorses draft wage orders to the Board. This two-tier architecture separates the political legitimacy of the consultation process from the legal authority of the wage- setting institution. 1 A defining feature of this Act is its alignment with the existing Salary Standardization Law (SSL). Rather than inventing compensation benchmarks from scratch, the Board shall use the SSL salary grade equivalents for each covered profession in government service as the statutory minimum floor for both government and private sector employment. This approach leverages a proven, legislatively validated, and regularly updated compensation framework and ensures parity between public and private professional compensation. Private employers may not pay less than the SSL- equivalent rate for a given profession; the Board may set higher rates when brain drain data and market conditions warrant. This Act expressly covers all employers — every national government agency, local government unit, state university and college, government-owned and controlled corporation, government financial institution, private corporation, partnership, sole proprietorship, cooperative, foundation, and international organization operating in the Philippines — without distinction. For government employers, a dedicated budget alignment provision ensures appropriation compliance within one budget cycle. For private employers, graduated administrative sanctions, criminal penalties with imprisonment, civil liability, and a whistleblower reward program provide credible enforcement. The Chairpersonship is open to any seasoned licensed professional with demonstrated leadership — pharmacists, nurses, engineers, and all other licensed professionals qualify alongside lawyers and economists. The Board is organized around the PRC's four professional clusters, with two seats per cluster. The Selection Committee is composed of the heads of the Civil Service Commission, Professional Regulation Commission, NEDA, and DOLE — or their designated alternates of at least Undersecretary rank — ensuring credible, practical, and expedient screening without overburdening already busy officials. Approval of this measure is urgently sought. REP. ISIDRO T. label: HB 10615
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE SPECIAL AREA FOR AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT (SAAD) PROGRAM UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed measure, entitled “An Act Institutionalizing the Special Area for Agricultural Development (SAAD) Program under the Department of Agriculture, Providing Funds Therefor, and for Other Purposes,” seeks to institutionalize the Special Area for Agricultural Development (SAAD) Program as a continuing area-based poverty- reduction and rural-development program of the Department of Agriculture (DA). The agriculture and fisheries sectors remain vital to inclusive economic growth, food security, and rural development. However, many farmers and fisherfolk, particularly those in poor, remote, and vulnerable communities, continue to face limited access to productive assets, technology, extension services, financing, infrastructure, and markets. The Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act of 1997 recognizes the need to improve the income of small farmers and fisherfolk through equitable access to assets, resources, and support services, higher-value production, processing, agribusiness, and agro-industrialization. It likewise promotes the organization of cooperatives, farmers' and fisherfolk's associations, and other people's organizations to strengthen their participation and enhance their capacity to benefit from economies of scale. The SAAD Program complements these statutory objectives by directing focused interventions to priority communities and beneficiary sectors. The measure likewise supports the area-based and integrated development approach embodied in the Strategic Agriculture and Fisheries Development Zones (SAFDZ) framework under Republic Act No. 8435. Under that law, the identification and development of SAFDZs take into account agricultural and fisheries potential, infrastructure and market location, the presence of small farmers and fisherfolk, and the need for integrated planning for production, processing, marketing, human resource development, and environmental protection. The proposed SAAD framework adopts a complementary targeting approach based on poverty incidence, agricultural and fisheries potential, vulnerability, and access to essential support services. The SAAD Program is intended to reduce rural poverty and improve food security by providing targeted and sustainable interventions, including social preparation, community organizing, food production and livelihood assistance, enterprise development, capacity-building, technology transfer, market linkage, and institutional strengthening. These interventions are designed to increase productivity and household income while helping farmers and fisherfolk establish viable community-based enterprises and strengthen their cooperatives and organizations. The measure likewise promotes convergence among the Department of Agriculture, other national government agencies, local government units, state universities and colleges, civil society organizations, development partners, and the private sector. Such coordination is consistent with the policy of strengthening farmers' and fisherfolk's enterprise development through a comprehensive approach that consolidates government support and promotes entrepreneurship in agricultural and fishing communities, consistent with Republic Act No. 11321, otherwise known as the "Sagip Saka Act." To promote transparency and accountability, the bill requires objective identification of Target Areas, transparent beneficiary selection, community participation, monitoring and evaluation, public reporting, and the establishment of grievance and feedback mechanisms. These safeguards are intended to ensure that Program assistance reaches qualified marginalized farmers and fisherfolk and is utilized solely for its authorized purposes. The institutionalization of the SAAD Program will provide a stable statutory framework for sustained government assistance to poor and underserved agricultural and fishing communities. It will enable the Department of Agriculture to implement coordinated, measurable, and accountable interventions that contribute to inclusive agricultural growth, rural prosperity, poverty reduction, and national food security. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONIO T. KHO ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP First District, Masbate Second District, Masbate WILTON T. label: HB 10625
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING QUALIFIED OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS (OFWs) FROM THE COVERAGE OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10912, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT ACT OF 2016 5 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 8 SECTION 1. Section 3 of Republic Act No. 10912 is hereby amended to read as follows: "Sec. 3. Definition of Terms. – The following terms shall be defined under this Act: xxx (X) QUALIFIED OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS (OFWS) REFERS TO FILIPINO PROFESSIONALS WHO ARE ENGAGED IN THE PRACTICE OF THEIR PROFESSION EXCLUSIVELY OUTSIDE THE PHILIPPINES WITH A SERVICE CONTRACT OF AT LEAST THREE (3) YEARS OR HAS BEEN PRACTICING THEIR PROFESSION OUTSIDE OF THE PHILIPPINES FOR A PERIOD OF THREE (3) CONSECUTIVE YEARS." xxx
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10912, otherwise known as the Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Act of 2016, was enacted to institutionalize lifelong learning among Filipino professionals and ensure that they remain competent, globally competitive, and responsive to the ever-evolving demands of their respective professions. The law recognizes that continuing professional education is essential to safeguarding public welfare and maintaining the integrity of regulated professions. Nearly a decade after its enactment, however, experience has demonstrated that the mandatory application of the law does not sufficiently account for the unique circumstances of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), particularly those who continuously practice their professions exclusively outside the Philippines. The Philippines continues to be one of the world's leading sources of highly skilled professionals. A substantial number of Filipino professionals continue to build long-term careers overseas. These Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) include licensed nurses, engineers, architects, physicians, accountants, teachers, physical therapists, and other professionals who are already subject to stringent licensing, accreditation, continuing education, competency assessment, and professional development requirements imposed by foreign governments, professional regulatory authorities, employers, and internationally recognized institutions. In many jurisdictions, compliance with these requirements is mandatory to retain the legal authority to practice. Despite continuously maintaining their professional competence abroad, these Filipino professionals are likewise required under Republic Act No. 10912 to earn Philippine Continuing Professional Development (CPD) credit units solely for the renewal of their Professional Identification Cards (PICs). For many OFWs, compliance entails considerable financial cost, logistical difficulty, and administrative inconvenience. Accredited CPD providers are often inaccessible from their countries of employment, while attending seminars in the Philippines frequently requires taking leave from work, incurring travel expenses, or disrupting existing contractual obligations. Consequently, professionals who are already complying with rigorous foreign continuing education systems are effectively required to satisfy duplicative regulatory requirements that do not necessarily enhance their competence beyond what has already been demonstrated in their respective jurisdictions. This measure then seeks to rationalize the implementation of Republic Act No. 10912 by exempting qualified Overseas Filipino Workers from the mandatory CPD requirement for the renewal of their PICs. This bill does not diminish the value of Continuing Professional Development. Rather, it recognizes that qualified Overseas Filipino Workers are already engaged in continuous professional learning under internationally recognized regulatory systems. By eliminating unnecessary duplication while preserving safeguards for professionals who practice in the Philippines, the measure promotes a more responsive, practical, and equitable implementation of the CPD Act. It likewise serves as a meaningful recognition of the invaluable contributions of Overseas Filipino Workers, whose professional expertise not only enhances the global reputation of the Filipino workforce but also sustains millions of Filipino families through remittances and significantly contributes to the country's economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 2 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10625 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma. label: HB 10626
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A SENIOR CITIZENS' WELFARE DESK IN EVERY BARANGAY 3 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 6 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as "Senior Citizens' Welfare Desk Act." Sec. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the duty of the State to give full support to the improvement of the total well-being of the elderly and their full participation in society, considering that senior citizens are integral part of Philippine society. The government must implement community-based programs that reach to the grassroots level and provide easy accessibility for our elderly to ensure genuine protection of their rights and welfare. Sec. 3. Senior Citizens' Welfare Desk. – There shall hereby be established in every barangay a Senior Citizens' Welfare Desk through which all senior citizens may lodge complaints, make inquiries, or ask for any form of assistance and aid, on issues concerning them, including but not limited to the following: a) Violations of their benefits and privileges under existing laws, ordinances, rules and regulations; b) Cases of abuse, discrimination or maltreatment; c) Abandonment and withdrawal of support from their family or relatives; and d) Grievances and complaints, in general. The barangay official/s assigned to the Welfare Desk shall assist the senior citizen in referring, bringing up or presenting his/her case, complaint or issue to the proper government office or to the Lupong Tagapamayapa, if warranted. Each Welfare Desk shall set up a system for the proper monitoring and following up of the cases, complaints or issues received by them and shall regularly provide feedback and updates to the senior citizen concerned. Sec. 4. Training of Welfare Desk Officials. – The corresponding Office of Senior Citizens Affairs of the city or municipality shall provide the necessary and regular training and guidance to the barangay officials assigned to their respective Welfare Desks on the handling and responding to complaints and grievances, procedures for referral to different government offices, and information dissemination on the various rights and benefits of senior citizens. Sec. 5. Implementing Rules and Regulations. – Within sixty (60) days from the effectivity of this Act, the National Commission on Senior Citizens in consultation with the Department of Interior and Local Government and other relevant government agencies and stakeholders, shall issue the necessary rules and regulations to implement the provisions of this Act.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is undergoing a profound demographic transition. Improvements in healthcare, nutrition, and living conditions have steadily increased life expectancy, resulting in a rapidly expanding senior citizen population. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), there were approximately 11.42 million Filipinos aged 60 years and above in 2024, accounting for 10.2% of the country's household population. This marks a substantial increase from 9.22 million senior citizens, or 8.5% of the household population, in 2020, reflecting the steady growth of the country's elderly population. As the nation ages, the demand for accessible, responsive, and community-based government services for senior citizens likewise continues to grow. The Constitution mandates the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health and social welfare by recognizing the invaluable contributions of older persons to nation- building. Currently, Republic Act No. 9994, otherwise known as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010 does exactly that by granting Filipino senior citizens a broad range of privileges, discounts, and protections. However, despite these legal safeguards, many elderly Filipinos continue to experience difficulty in accessing government services and enforcing their rights. Numerous senior citizens, especially those living in rural communities and urban poor areas, remain unaware of the full extent of the benefits available to them or encounter significant obstacles in reporting violations of their rights. Complaints involving denial of statutory discounts and privileges, elder abuse, neglect, abandonment, financial exploitation, and family neglect often go unreported because of limited mobility, lack of legal knowledge, fear of retaliation, or the absence of an accessible government office where they may seek immediate assistance. At present, while every local government unit is mandated to establish an Office for Senior Citizens Affairs (OSCA), these offices are generally located at the city or municipal level. For many elderly citizens, especially those with mobility limitations or chronic illnesses, traveling to these offices entails considerable financial cost, physical hardship, and logistical difficulty. As a result, many grievances remain unresolved, and government interventions often come too late. This measure therefore seeks to establish a Senior Citizens' Welfare Desk in every barangay to serve as the first point of contact for elderly Filipinos seeking assistance, filing complaints, reporting abuse or neglect, obtaining information on their rights and benefits, and securing referrals to the appropriate government agencies or the Lupong Tagapamayapa when necessary. Barangays already serve as the government's frontline institutions and are uniquely positioned to provide immediate, community-based assistance. Existing laws have already recognized the effectiveness of specialized barangay mechanisms, such as the Violence Against Women (VAW) Desk, in ensuring that vulnerable sectors receive prompt attention, proper referrals, and continuous monitoring of their cases. A similar institutional mechanism dedicated to senior citizens would strengthen grassroots governance and make government services more responsive to the realities faced by the country's aging population. By bringing government services closer to where senior citizens live, this measure promotes accessibility, strengthens local governance, encourages early intervention in cases involving elder abuse and neglect, and reinforces the State's constitutional obligation to protect the dignity, welfare, and well-being of older persons. More importantly, it affirms that as Filipinos age, they should not face additional barriers in accessing the protection, assistance, and respect that they have earned through a lifetime of contributing to the Filipino people and the Philippine society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 13 14 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10626 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma. label: HB 10627
title: AN ACT DECLARING SEPTEMBER 4 OF EVERY YEAR AS A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF PINAMUNGAJAN, PROVINCE OF CEBU, TO BE KNOWN AS "MUNICIPALITY OF PINAMUNGAJAN CHARTER DAY”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Pinamungajan, one of the oldest municipalities in the Province of Cebu, possesses a rich historical, cultural, and socio-economic heritage that has significantly contributed to the development of the province and the region. For generations, the people of Pinamungajan have celebrated their founding anniversary on the 4th of September, tracing their roots to the town's separation from its matrix, the Municipality of Barili. To institutionalize this deeply held tradition, the local government sought the expertise of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) to verify its origins. In a letter dated March 31, 2026, NHCP Chairman Regalado Trota Jose, Jr. officially confirmed that Pinamungajan was established on September 4, 1850, under the patronage of Santa Mónica. This affirmation is heavily corroborated by archival sources, specifically Felipe Redondo y Sendino's Breve Reseña de lo que fue y de lo que es la Diócesis de Cebú en las Islas Filipinas. Anchored on this official historical confirmation, the Sangguniang Bayan of Pinamungajan enacted Ordinance No. 041-2026, recognizing 4 September 1850 as the municipality's official founding day and declaring September 4 of every year as the official Founding Anniversary of the Municipality of Pinamungajan. This legislative enactment reflects the collective recognition of the local community of its historical identity and its commitment to preserving and promoting its cultural heritage for future generations. Complementing this ordinance, the Sangguniang Bayan likewise adopted Resolution No. 091, Series of 2026, respectfully requesting the filing of a bill in Congress declaring September 4 as Pinamungajan Charter Day and a special non-working holiday within the municipality. The initiative was further endorsed by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Cebu through Resolution No. 1597-2026, recognizing the historical, cultural, and educational significance of the proposed measure and expressing the Province's full support for its enactment into law. The formal declaration of September 4 as "Pinamungajan Charter Day" will serve as a fitting tribute to the municipality's enduring legacy. It provides a dedicated opportunity for residents, educational institutions, and government entities to reflect on their shared history, honor the achievements of their forebears, and strengthen community solidarity for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. KAREN HOPE F. label: HB 10629
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE SYSTEM LOSS COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLED TO RESIDENTIAL HOUSEHOLD CONSUMERS FROM THE VALUE-ADDED TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 109 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, PROVIDING SAFEGUARDS TO ENSURE THAT THE BENEFITS THEREOF ARE FULLY PASSED ON TO CONSUMERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity rates in the Philippines remain among the highest in Southeast Asia, imposing a substantial financial burden on Filipino households. Apart from the cost of electricity actually consumed, consumers are billed for various regulated charges, including the system loss charge, which represents the cost of recovering electricity lost during transmission and distribution due to technical losses and other causes recognized under Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the "Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001." Although system loss is a regulatory cost recovery mechanism authorized under existing law, it does not represent electricity actually consumed by residential customers. Nevertheless, the amount collected for system loss forms part of the electricity bill and is presently subjected to the Value-Added Tax (VAT), thereby increasing the financial burden borne by consumers. It is the policy of the State to protect consumers and promote equitable taxation. While VAT is generally imposed on the sale of goods and services, Congress may, in the exercise of its constitutional power to grant tax exemptions, exempt specific transactions or components thereof whenever public interest so requires. Considering the continuing increase in electricity costs, it is imperative to provide targeted tax relief to residential household consumers by exempting the system loss component from VAT. This measure likewise ensures that the tax relief granted under this Act directly benefits consumers by requiring the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to prevent distribution utilities and electric cooperatives from recovering the exempted VAT through other regulated charges or billing adjustments. To promote transparency and accountability, electricity bills shall separately reflect the system loss charge and the corresponding VAT savings resulting from this Act. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10630
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ANNUAL INCOME TAX-EXEMPT THRESHOLD OF INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO THREE HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (₱350,000), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(A) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article VI, Section 28 (1) of the 1987 Constitution provides that the rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and that Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. While taxes are indispensable in funding essential government services, the tax system must likewise ensure that the burden of taxation remains equitable, reasonable and responsive to prevailing economic conditions. Under Republic Act No. 10963, otherwise known as the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law, individuals earning not more than Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (₱250,000.00) annually are exempt from income tax. However, since the enactment of the law in 2017, inflation has significantly diminished the real value of this threshold, causing many workers whose salaries merely kept pace with inflation to become subject to higher taxes despite experiencing no real increase in purchasing power. Increasing the tax-exempt threshold to Three Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (₱350,000.00) will provide immediate and meaningful tax relief to millions of Filipino workers, allowing them to retain a larger portion of their earnings to meet the rising costs of food, transportation, electricity, housing, healthcare, and education. The measure is likewise expected to stimulate domestic consumption, strengthen household finances, improve productivity, and support sustained economic growth through increased consumer spending. To ensure that the law remains responsive to changing economic conditions, this measure likewise provides for a periodic review of the exemption threshold based on cumulative inflation, changes in the cost of living, and the purchasing power of the peso. This measure is likewise consistent with the government's policy direction of providing tax relief to Filipino workers by increasing the income tax exemption threshold to Three Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (PhP 350,000.00). In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10631
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CONSUMER PROTECTION AND TRANSPARENCY IN THE RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSSES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 43(F) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001," AND SECTION 10 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), restructured the Philippine electric power industry by promoting competition, private sector participation, and independent regulation. Pursuant to Section 43(f) thereof, the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) is authorized to determine the recoverable system loss of distribution utilities. To implement this authority, the ERC adopted Resolution No. 20, Series of 2017, establishing utility-specific Distribution System Loss (DSL) Caps based on engineering, operational, and geographic considerations. During the deliberations of previous legislative proposals, the Technical Working Group of the House Committee on Energy likewise recognized that recoverable system losses should continue to be determined through performance-based and utility- specific standards rather than rigid statutory percentages. Notwithstanding these reforms, consumers continue to question the recovery of system losses arising from electricity pilferage, illegal connections, meter tampering, fraud, administrative inefficiency, negligence, and other avoidable causes beyond their control. This measure strengthens the existing regulatory framework by clarifying the statutory principles governing the recoverability of technical and non- technical system losses, reaffirming the authority of the Energy Regulatory Commission to establish utility-specific performance benchmarks, and enhancing transparency and accountability in the recovery of system losses. The bill does not dismantle the regulatory framework established under EPIRA. Rather, it builds upon existing law and regulatory policy by ensuring that consumers are charged only for efficient technical losses determined by the ERC while encouraging distribution utilities to continuously improve operational efficiency. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10647
title: AN ACT RESTRUCTURING THE INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATES OF CITIZENS AND RESIDENT ALIENS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution mandates that the rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and that Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. Individual income taxes should therefore reflect prevailing economic realities and ensure that the tax burden imposed on Filipino workers remains fair, reasonable, and responsive to rising costs of living. Persistent inflation and increasing household expenses have gradually diminished the value of tax reductions. As wages rise merely to keep pace with inflation, many workers are pushed into higher tax brackets without a corresponding increase in their real purchasing power. This measure seeks to reduce the minimum taxable income threshold to Three Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (Php 350,000.00). This adjustment aims to ensure that low- and middle-income earners are not unduly burdened by income taxation and that the tax system remains responsive to current economic conditions. By lowering the minimum threshold, this proposal seeks to provide meaningful tax relief, increase take home pay, strengthen the purchasing power of Filipino families, and stimulate domestic consumption. In turn, increased consumer 1|P ag e spending is expected to support business growth, generate employment, and contribute to sustained economic development while preserving the progressive character of the country’s tax system. The proposal likewise promotes a more equitable distribution of the tax burden by ensuring that taxation better reflects taxpayer’s actual capacity to pay. In view of the foregoing, we urge the swift passage of this measure.
