label: HB 10648
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PAMBANSANG AGAPAY SA PAMILYA AT MALILIIT NA NEGOSYO (PAMANA) PROGRAM, PROVIDING A DIRECT ANNUAL SUBSIDY TO MINIMUM WAGE EARNERS AND THEIR FAMILIES THROUGH DIGITAL WALLETS FOR EXCLUSIVE USE IN LOCAL MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Millions of Filipino minimum wage earners continue to grapple with the rising cost of basic goods, while micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) which account for 99.5% of all business establishments and employ the majority of the Filipino workforce struggle with thin margins and limited consumer demand. This measure addresses both problems with a single intervention: a direct, regular, and digitally delivered subsidy to minimum wage earners and their families that can only be spent in registered local MSMEs. Unlike traditional cash assistance programs that are one-time, leakage-prone, and often captured by intermediaries, this bill guarantees that (1) assistance reaches families directly through their digital wallets, (2) the benefit is spread throughout the year through monthly disbursements and a daily spending limit, encouraging use for daily essentials rather than lump-sum consumption, and (3) every peso of public assistance circulates within local communities, stimulating neighborhood economies rather than large retail chains. This measure is designed to complement, not duplicate, existing social protection programs. Families already receiving assistance under the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) or its successor conditional cash transfer program remain covered by that program and are excluded from this Act, ensuring that public funds reach a distinct population: minimum wage earners who work full-time yet remain financially strained, and who are typically ineligible for 4Ps but still without a dedicated income supplement. The measure likewise accelerates financial inclusion and digitalization among both households and small businesses, consistent with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. REP. JUDE A. ACIDRE REP. ZIAUR-RAHMAN A. ADIONG REP. JOEL R. CHUA REP. JANETTE L. GARIN 2 REP. JEFFERSON F. KHONGHUN REP. label: HB 10655
title: AN ACT REGULATING GAMBLING-RELATED ADVERTISEMENTS, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With the widespread use and growing number of social media users across all ages, more Filipinos are active online, paving the way for the gambling industry to penetrate and expand its presence on digital gaming platforms right before the fingertips of Filipino online users. With gross gaming revenues reaching P396,138,802,763.57 for Fiscal Year 2025, the Philippine gambling industry is seeing record-breaking growth.1 Although this growth can help boost the economy, it poses a serious risk to those who engage in gambling online down to their households. According to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR), the number of Filipino electronic gaming players reached 32.117 million in 20252, representing an almost 200 percent increase from the 8.2 million recorded players in 2024. The growing accessibility of online gambling platforms has been accompanied by an increase in advertisements, sponsorships, marketing, and other forms of consumer communication, which have become more widespread and targeted. The increasing participation in online gambling has raised concerns regarding its impact on gamblers’ mental health, physical well-being, socio-economic stability, and even to their duties and responsibilities in their households. The growing visibility and accessibility of gambling-related advertisements and services have contributed to issues such as the participation of minors and the underage, excessive, compulsive, and irresponsible gambling behavior, financial distress, and other gambling-related harms affecting minors and vulnerable sectors of society. 1 Gonzales, A. L. (2026, April 16). PH gaming revenues reach P396.1-B in 2025. Accessed last 31 July 2026 from: https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1273085 2 Ager, M. (2025, August 14). 32 million adult Filipinos are gamblers, Pagcor records show. Accessed last 31 July 2026 from: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2095743/32-million-adult-filipinos-are-gamblers-pagcor-records-show 1 Recognizing these growing concerns, the bill seeks to regulate gambling advertisements by prohibiting promotional activities such as celebrity endorsements, sponsorships, and other forms of gambling-related consumer communications. It also requires authorized gambling advertisements to include responsible gambling advisories and imposes appropriate administrative and criminal penalties for violations to ensure effective implementation. Similar to the provisions of Republic Act No. 9211, or the Tobacco Regulation Act of 2003, this measure aims to create a more responsible gaming environment by protecting minors and vulnerable individuals, promoting informed consumer decisions, and safeguarding public interest. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill, which is a counterpart measure of Senate Bill 2347, is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 10656
title: AN ACT FIXING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF BARANGAY OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN TO FIVE (5) YEARS, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12232 OR “AN ACT SETTING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF THE BARANGAY OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Barangay, as the frontline institutions of public service, play critical roles in implementing various government programs, maintaining peace and order, resolving disputes, responding to disasters and calamities, and delivering basic services at the community level. As such, the effective delivery of these essential public services depends significantly on the stability and capacity of barangay governments and their officials. Consistent with Article X, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution, which authorizes Congress to determine by law the term of office of barangay officials, this counterpart measure also filed in the Senate likewise seeks to enhance the stability and consistency of public service at the barangay level by providing for a five (5)-year term for barangay officials and members of the Sangguniang Kabataan. The proposed extension would promote continuity in governance, provide sufficient time for the planning and implementation of long-term community development initiatives, reduce disruptions caused by frequent electoral exercises, and enable local officials to focus more effectively on public service rather th an on electoral cycles. Ultimately, this measure aims to strengthen governance in the barangay level and enable them to fully realize their mandates under the Local Government Code of 1991 as the primary planning and implementing units for government policies, plans, programs, projects, and activities in the community. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly requested. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. title: AN ACT RESTORING THE FULL TAX CREDIT TREATMENT OF MANDATORY DISCOUNTS GRANTED TO SENIOR CITIZENS AND PERSONS WITH DISABILITY, PROVIDING FOR THE UTILIZATION AND REFUND OF SUCH TAX CREDITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 204 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, SECTION 4 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NOS. 9257 AND 9994, AND SECTION 32 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10754, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 24 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 27 SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Social Benefits Fiscal Responsibility Act.” 30 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is hereby declared the policy of the State to preserve and fully protect the mandatory discounts and privileges granted by law to senior citizens and persons with disability, while ensuring a fair, transparent, and sustainable allocation of the fiscal cost of such benefits. 35 The State recognizes that private establishments required by law to grant such discounts perform a public function in the implementation of social legislation. As a matter of fiscal policy, the National Government shall assume the cost of the statutory discounts actually and finally borne by such establishments through a full tax credit, subject to reasonable safeguards against duplicate claims, overstatement, and fraud. 41 The State shall further ensure that the tax-credit mechanism operates equitably for establishments of different sizes by allowing the utilization, carryover, and, where authorized under this Act, refund of verified unutilized credits, with simplified compliance for micro and small taxpayers and appropriate reporting and verification requirements for medium and large taxpayers.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 14 The Constitution directs the State to promote social justice and to protect senior citizens and persons with disability through measures that recognize their particular needs and circumstances. Congress has given concrete expression to this policy through the mandatory discounts and privileges provided under Republic Act No. 7432, as amended, for senior citizens, and Republic Act No. 7277, as amended, for persons with disability. 21 When Republic Act No. 7432 was enacted in 1992, Congress required private establishments to grant the statutory senior citizen discount but allowed them to claim the cost of the discount as a tax credit. The Supreme Court subsequently confirmed that the credit contemplated by the original law was not a mere deduction from gross income. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Central Luzon Drug Corporation, G.R. No. 159647, April 15, 2005, the Court held that a tax credit operates after the tax is computed and reduces the taxpayer's liability directly, while a tax deduction merely reduces the income upon which the tax is computed. 30 The policy changed with Republic Act No. 9257 and was retained under Republic Act No. 9994. Instead of a full tax credit, establishments granting senior citizen discounts were allowed to claim the discount only as a deduction from gross income. Republic Act No. 10754 adopted the same tax-deduction treatment for the statutory discounts granted to persons with disability. The difference is substantial. A peso of tax credit reduces tax liability by a peso; a peso of deduction produces tax relief only to the extent of the applicable tax rate. The unrecovered portion of the statutory discount is therefore borne by the private establishment. 39 The Supreme Court has sustained the validity of the tax-deduction scheme as an exercise of the State's police power. Carlos Superdrug Corporation v. Department of Social Welfare and Development, G.R. No. 166494, June 29, 2007; Manila Memorial Park, Inc. v. Secretary of the Department of Social Welfare and Development, G.R. No. 175356, December 3, 2013. This measure does not proceed from the premise that the present arrangement is unconstitutional. Rather, it makes a deliberate legislative judgment that what the State may validly require private establishments to bear need not remain the most equitable or sustainable way of financing a public social benefit. 1 Senior citizen and PWD discounts are benefits created by law for a public purpose. Private establishments are indispensable partners in delivering those benefits at the point of sale, but the ultimate fiscal responsibility for a government-mandated social benefit should rest with the Government. Restoring the full tax credit treatment does not reduce, condition, or diminish the discount received by the beneficiary. It changes only the manner by which the cost of that benefit is allocated after the transaction has been completed. 8 The measure is intentionally limited to the mandatory discounts granted under the senior citizen and PWD laws. It does not automatically alter the tax treatment of student fare discounts, athlete incentives, solo parent privileges, or other statutory benefits. Any extension of the same policy to other social discounts should be separately considered by Congress together with the corresponding fiscal impact. The bill also addresses the practical difficulties that attended the earlier tax-credit regime. The credit is limited to the statutory discount actually and finally borne by the claimant. Where the underlying transaction is VAT-exempt, the credit is computed on the VAT-exclusive selling price and does not include VAT that was never imposed or collected. Any rebate, reimbursement, subsidy, cost-sharing payment, or similar recovery received or receivable with respect to the same discount is deducted from the amount creditable. The same discount may not be claimed twice as a deduction, credit, refund, or other tax incentive. 22 Recognizing that the value of a tax credit depends upon the establishment's capacity to use it, this measure also provides a meaningful mechanism for unutilized credits. The credit may be applied against national internal revenue taxes for which the establishment is directly liable, excluding withholding taxes. Micro and small taxpayers may elect a cash refund of any verified unutilized balance after the taxable year in which the credit arose. Medium and large taxpayers may carry the credit forward and, if it remains unutilized after the prescribed period, may likewise seek a refund. This ensures that the promise of full reimbursement does not benefit only establishments with large and immediate tax liabilities. 32 A full tax credit necessarily entails a greater fiscal cost to the National Government than a deduction. For this reason, the bill couples reimbursement with clear substantiation, anti-duplication safeguards, electronic reporting for larger taxpayers, simplified compliance for smaller establishments, and annual reporting by the Department of Finance and the Bureau of Internal Revenue to Congress on the amount of discounts granted, credits claimed, credits utilized, refunds paid, and the resulting revenue impact. Fiscal responsibility requires both fair allocation of the cost and transparent accounting of that cost. 41 This measure therefore restores the central policy of the original Republic Act No. 7432 while adapting its implementation to the present tax system: senior citizens and persons with disability continue to receive the full benefits guaranteed by law; private establishments continue to deliver those benefits; and the National Government assumes, through a verifiable tax-credit and refund mechanism, the cost of the statutory discounts actually and finally borne by the establishments. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 5 REP. label: HB 10658
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE MEDICAL ASSISTANCE TO INDIGENT AND FINANCIALLY INCAPACITATED PATIENTS (MAIFIP) PROGRAM, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 18 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 21 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIP) Act." 24 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the declared policy of the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. The State shall also improve the adequate delivery of health care services to the people and ensure its availability and accessibility. 29 SECTION 3. Medical Assistance to Indigent Patients (MAIFIP) Program. – The Department of Health (DOH) shall establish a “Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) Program” which shall provide medical assistance to support clinically-indicated needs prescribed by a physician or health professional for indigent and financially incapacitated in-patients and out-patients. This assistance applies to expenses exceeding the applicable PhilHealth benefit packages, case rates, or other available funding sources. 37 The MAIFIP Program shall continue to be available and accessible in all DOH central and regional offices, BARMM Ministry of Health, specialty hospitals, DOH hospitals and treatment and rehabilitation centers, including hospitals under the Department of National Defense (DND) and the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG), State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) hospitals and Department of Justice (DOJ) infirmaries, local government unit (LGU) hospitals, and other partner government and privately-owned hospitals and health facilities. 45
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 14 Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution declares that “the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.” Consistent with this constitutional mandate, Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act,” seeks to ensure that every Filipino has access to a comprehensive range of quality and cost-effective promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative health services without suffering financial hardship, with particular attention to those who are least able to afford the cost of medical care. 23 Despite continuing reforms in health financing, increased PhilHealth expenditures, and the availability of other sources of medical assistance, many Filipinos still face serious financial barriers when illness strikes. For indigent and financially incapacitated patients, even clinically necessary treatment may remain beyond reach when hospital charges, medicines, diagnostic procedures, medical supplies, and other prescribed interventions exceed the amounts covered by PhilHealth benefit packages, case rates, or other available funding sources. 31 The Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) Program has become an important means of addressing this gap. It provides assistance for clinically indicated needs prescribed by a physician or other qualified health professional for both in-patients and out-patients who are unable to fully shoulder the cost of their medical care. In practical terms, the program serves as an essential final layer of financial protection for patients whose remaining hospital and medical expenses cannot otherwise be met. At present, however, the continued operation of such assistance should not rest solely on administrative arrangements, annual budgetary provisions, or changing implementation practices. A program upon which vulnerable patients increasingly depend deserves a clear, stable, and permanent legal framework. 43 1 This measure therefore seeks to institutionalize the MAIFIP Program by establishing in law its purpose, coverage, basic processes, and standards for implementation. Institutionalization will provide continuity in the delivery of assistance, greater predictability for patients and health facilities, and clearer accountability among the agencies and institutions tasked with administering the program. 6 More importantly, placing the program on a statutory footing will help ensure that access to medical assistance is governed by an orderly and transparent process rather than by uncertainty as to whether assistance will be available, what expenses may be covered, or how applications will be processed. A patient already burdened by illness should not also have to navigate an unclear or inconsistent system merely to secure assistance for medically necessary care. 13 The measure is intended to complement, rather than replace, PhilHealth and other existing sources of health financing. MAIFIP assistance shall apply to clinically indicated expenses that remain after the application of applicable PhilHealth benefits, case rates, and other available funding sources. In this manner, the program serves as a necessary safety net within the broader framework of Universal Health Care. 20 Institutionalizing MAIFIP is ultimately about ensuring continuity, consistency, and dignity in the delivery of medical assistance. It affirms that when public policy recognizes the need to assist indigent and financially incapacitated patients, the process for extending that assistance should likewise be dependable, accessible, and firmly established in law. 26 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 28 29 30 31 REP. title: AN ACT PROVIDING BROADER AND SUSTAINING TAX RELIEF TO INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS AND SMALL ENTERPRISES, REDUCING INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATES, INCREASING AND INDEXING THE TAX-EXEMPT INCOME THRESHOLD, REDUCING THE INCOME TAX OF QUALIFIED SELF-EMPLOYED INDIVIDUALS AND PROFESSIONALS, PROVIDING INCOME TAX AND MINIMUM CORPORATE INCOME TAX RELIEF TO QUALIFIED SMALL DOMESTIC CORPORATIONS, GRANTING A ONE- TIME AMNESTY ON CERTAIN NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE TAX LIABILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 24 AND 27 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Sustaining Economic Relief through Broader Income-tax Savings and Yield Opportunities (SERBISYO) Act.” 32 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is hereby declared the policy of the State to maintain a fair, progressive, reasonable, and sustainable system of taxation that raises revenues necessary for government while recognizing the right of taxpayers to retain a reasonable and meaningful share of the income generated by their labor, profession, enterprise, and investment. 38 The State recognizes that income retained by taxpayers contributes directly to household welfare, consumption, savings, investment, entrepreneurship, employment, and economic growth. Tax policy shall therefore protect the purchasing power of Filipino workers and families and prevent inflation from increasing their effective tax burden solely through nominal increases in income. 44
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 14 The power to tax is indispensable to government, but taxation must remain fair, progressive, and responsive to the actual capacity of citizens and enterprises to pay. Government requires revenue to provide public services, build infrastructure, maintain peace and order, educate the young, protect public health, and support those who need assistance. At the same time, every peso collected in taxes is a peso first earned by a Filipino worker, professional, entrepreneur, or business. 21 Tax policy must therefore strike a sensible balance. Government should collect what is reasonably necessary to perform its functions while allowing Filipinos to retain a greater share of the value of their work. 25 The individual income tax system presently exempts the first Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (₱250,000.00) of taxable income. While this represented substantial relief when the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion Act was enacted, the value of that exemption has steadily been eroded by inflation. Food, electricity, transportation, housing, education, healthcare, and other necessities cost considerably more today. A worker may receive salary adjustments merely to keep pace with these increases and yet become liable for greater income taxes even though his or her real purchasing power has barely improved. 34 This phenomenon, commonly referred to as bracket creep, effectively allows inflation to increase the tax burden without Congress imposing a new tax. A tax system intended to be progressive should not treat a nominal increase in income as an increase in economic capacity when that increase merely compensates for a higher cost of living. 39 This measure therefore raises the annual tax-exempt income threshold to Four Hundred Thousand Pesos (₱400,000.00), recalibrates the succeeding income brackets, and reduces the applicable marginal income tax rates. The lowest taxable rate is reduced to eight percent (8%), while the succeeding rates are likewise lowered. The highest marginal rate is reduced to thirty percent (30%). The purpose is straightforward: Filipino taxpayers should be allowed to retain more of the income they earn. 1 The measure also addresses the recurring erosion of tax relief by providing for automatic adjustment of the exemption threshold and income brackets based on inflation. Once Congress determines the amount of income that should reasonably remain untaxed, inflation should not silently diminish that protection year after year. Self-employed individuals, professionals, freelancers, and sole proprietors deserve comparable relief. The optional eight percent (8%) income tax applicable to qualified self-employed individuals and professionals is therefore reduced to six percent (6%), with the first Four Hundred Thousand Pesos (₱400,000.00) likewise excluded from its application where allowed under the National Internal Revenue Code. 10 The same principle applies to enterprises. Micro and small businesses create employment, sustain communities, and provide much of the economic activity outside the country's largest corporations. Yet the minimum corporate income tax may require a corporation to pay tax based on gross income even when its actual taxable profit is minimal. A minimum tax designed as an anti-avoidance safeguard should not become an additional burden upon legitimate small enterprises struggling to remain viable. 17 Accordingly, qualified small domestic corporations are exempted from the minimum corporate income tax. The preferential regular corporate income tax applicable to qualified small domestic corporations is likewise reduced from twenty percent (20%) to fifteen percent (15%), giving these enterprises additional capital for wages, expansion, equipment, and employment. 23 This bill also recognizes that a tax system must provide a practical means for taxpayers with unresolved liabilities to return to compliance. Outstanding tax liabilities that remain disputed, uncollected, or buried under accumulated interest and penalties do not necessarily translate into actual government revenue. A properly structured tax amnesty can convert these dormant liabilities into immediate collections, reduce litigation and administrative costs, improve taxpayer records, and bring taxpayers back into the formal system. 31 A one-time general tax amnesty is therefore provided for qualified national internal revenue tax liabilities for taxable year 2025 and prior years. The rates are deliberately reasonable to encourage genuine participation, while safeguards exclude unlawfully acquired wealth, taxes collected from third persons but deliberately not remitted to government, money laundering, and other unlawful activities. 37 Separate and simplified mechanisms are provided for delinquent accounts, disputed assessments, and estate taxes. Once a taxpayer has truthfully complied with the requirements and fully paid the applicable amnesty tax, the Government must likewise honor its side of the bargain. The amnesty must provide genuine finality rather than merely opening another avenue for subsequent assessment or investigation. 43 2 Ultimately, meaningful tax relief need not always take the form of another government subsidy or assistance program. There are circumstances when the simplest and most immediate form of economic relief is for government to collect less and allow citizens to keep more of what they have earned. Money retained by taxpayers supports household consumption, savings, investment, entrepreneurship, and economic activity without requiring an application, qualification process, appropriation, or administrative distribution mechanism. 8 The Sustaining Economic Relief through Broader Income-tax Savings and Yield Opportunities (SERBISYO) Act seeks to place this principle at the center of tax policy: raise necessary revenues fairly, protect the value of work, give small enterprises room to grow, and make compliance easier for taxpayers willing to fulfill their ob

label: HB 10660
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING DIGITAL EDUCATION ACCESS AND INSTITUTIONALIZING TEACHER DIGITAL SKILLS TRAINING IN PUBLIC SCHOOLS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid integration of digital technologies into education has transformed the way learning is delivered, accessed, and supported. In the Philippines, however, significant gaps remain in digital access among learners in public elementary and secondary schools. Many students continue to face difficulties due to unreliable internet connectivity, limited access to digital learning devices, and the absence of accessible school-based or community-based facilities for digital learning. At the same time, public school teachers require sustained training and institutional support to effectively use digital platforms, blended learning methods, and emerging educational technologies. Digital education is no longer merely supplementary to classroom instruction. It has become an essential component of a modern, inclusive, and resilient basic education system. Beyond access to devices and connectivity, learners and teachers must also be equipped with the skills to locate, evaluate, cite, and responsibly use credible, authoritative, and scholarly digital resources. In an online environment where information is abundant but not always reliable, digital research literacy is necessary to promote academic integrity, evidence-based learning, and responsible use of technology. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize government support for digital education in public elementary and secondary schools by expanding access to reliable internet connectivity, appropriate digital learning devices, and digital learning hubs, with priority given to learners from low-income households and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. It likewise strengthens teacher capacity through continuous and accredited digital skills training, including training on digital pedagogy, online and blended instruction, cybersecurity, data privacy, and the responsible use of emerging technologies. The bill further promotes access to academic digital resources, including credible academic websites, digital libraries, open-access journals, peer-reviewed publications, government research portals, and other reliable sources of research materials appropriate to the basic education curriculum. It also integrates digital research literacy into learning activities and teacher training programs, ensuring that both learners and teachers are guided in proper citation, attribution, paraphrasing, academic integrity, and the ethical use of digital research materials. Furthermore, the bill mandates the establishment of national digital education standards for basic education to ensure quality, consistency, accessibility, data security, child online safety, and responsible technology use. It authorizes partnerships with telecommunications companies, technology providers, public libraries, state universities and colleges, research institutions, academic publishers, civil society organizations, and other stakeholders to maximize resources and accelerate implementation. Regular reporting to Congress and audit by the Commission on Audit are likewise provided to ensure transparency, accountability, and measurable outcomes. By strengthening digital education access, institutionalizing teacher digital skills training, and promoting digital research literacy, this measure seeks to build a more equitable, future-ready, and resilient public basic education system that prepares Filipino learners and teachers for the demands of an increasingly digital and knowledge-based society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JOYCE F. label: HB 10661
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE DISCLOSURE OF NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION IN MENUS OF FOOD SERVICE ESTABLISHMENTS TO PROMOTE HEALTHY DIETARY CHOICES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A growing body of evidence shows that the Philippines faces a dual burden of malnutrition, where undernutrition persists alongside a rapidly increasing prevalence of overweight, obesity, and diet-related noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). Several studies note that rising prevalence of obesity and related chronic diseases alongside persistent undernutrition presents a complex public health challenge. This evolving nutritional landscape calls for urgent and comprehensive policy action. During this year’s World Obesity Day, the National Nutrition Council (NNC), UNICEF, and World Health Organization urged stronger policies to prevent childhood overweight and obesity and to promote healthier food environments. These calls reflect a growing global consensus that structural interventions—particularly those improving food information transparency—are essential in addressing obesity and diet-related risks. Obesity, now recognized as a chronic and relapsing disease, is strongly linked to diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other long-term conditions. Its prevalence has tripled in recent decades, with nearly one (1) in ten (10) children and almost four (4) in ten (10) adults in the Philippines classified as overweight or obese, levels considered high by global standards. This trend is further driven by unhealthy dietary patterns, increased consumption of calorie-dense foods, and limited access to clear nutritional information. Cardiovascular diseases remain among the leading causes of death among Filipinos, largely due to unhealthy diets and sedentary lifestyles. Excess calorie intake— particularly from meals consumed outside the home—significantly contributes to weight gain. Public health research shows that when calorie intake exceeds recommended levels based on Body Mass Index (BMI), the risk of obesity and related diseases increases substantially. Despite these realities, a critical gap persists while prepackaged food products are required to disclose nutritional information, meals sold in food service establishments are not subject to similar transparency standards. As a result, consumers are often left to estimate the nutritional content of their meals, placing both health-conscious individuals and the general public at risk of excessive intake of calories, sodium, and unhealthy fats. Misleading or unclear nutrition claims further worsen the problem, making it difficult for families to identify healthier options. Health advocates consistently emphasize that inadequate labeling contributes to poor dietary decisions, underscoring the need for stronger policies that promote transparency, informed decision-making, and healthier consumption patterns. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by mandating the disclosure of calorie content and nutritional information in menus of food service establishments. By requiring such information to be clearly displayed at the point of food selection, this bill empowers consumers to make informed choices, promotes greater awareness of dietary intake, and encourages healthier eating habits. Providing nutritional information at the point of purchase has been shown to: 1. Enable consumers to make more informed and healthier food choices; 2. Promote greater public awareness of proper nutrition; 3. Support individuals managing chronic conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease; and 4. Encourage food establishments to improve the nutritional quality of their offerings. This measure is firmly anchored on Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JOYCE F. label: HB 10662
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PASSENGER SAFETY IN AIR AND SEA TRAVEL BY MANDATING ONBOARD EMERGENCY MEDICAL KITS, LIFE-SAVING MEDICINES, AUTOMATED EXTERNAL DEFIBRILLATORS, AND OTHER EMERGENCY MEDICAL EQUIPMENT, AND PRESCRIBING STANDARDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Severe allergic reactions can become life-threatening within minutes if not treated immediately. The timely administration of epinephrine remains the standard and most effective intervention to prevent fatal outcomes. However, allergic reactions are only one of several medical emergencies that may occur while passengers are in transit. In the context of air and sea travel, the ability to respond to such emergencies is inherently constrained. Passengers may be at cruising altitude or traveling across open waters, where immediate access to hospitals, ambulances, or medical professionals is not available. In these situations, emergency response must begin onboard, especially for time-critical conditions such as anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, respiratory distress, asthma attacks, seizures, diabetic emergencies, fainting, trauma-related injuries, and other sudden medical episodes. This concern is especially relevant in the Philippines, an archipelagic country composed of more than 7,600 islands, where mobility relies heavily on air and maritime transport. Data from the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) indicate that Philippine airports handle over 50 million passengers annually, while the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) reports that more than 30 million passengers travel by sea each year, particularly along inter-island routes. These figures highlight the magnitude of passengers potentially exposed to in-transit medical emergencies. Despite this, the availability of emergency medical kits, life-saving medicines, automated external defibrillators, oxygen and breathing support devices, trauma care supplies, and trained crew is not uniformly required across air and sea passenger transport. This gap in onboard medical preparedness limits the capacity of operators to respond effectively during the first critical minutes of a medical emergency. This bill seeks to address this gap by requiring air carriers and passenger ship operators to maintain onboard emergency medical kits, life-saving emergency medicines, emergency injectable allergy medication such as epinephrine, automated external defibrillators, oxygen and breathing support devices, trauma care supplies, and other emergency medical equipment. It further ensures that trained crew are available to recognize common medical emergencies, operate emergency equipment, administer or assist in the use of emergency medicines, and coordinate with ground or shore-based medical facilities. The measure mandates the Department of Health (DOH), in coordination with the Department of Transportation (DOTr), CAAP, and MARINA, to establish clear standards for minimum contents, quantities, storage, handling, maintenance, training, reporting, and compliance monitoring. This allows the law to remain flexible and responsive to evolving medical and transport safety standards. By institutionalizing onboard medical readiness, this measure strengthens emergency response capability, enhances passenger safety, and upholds the State’s duty to protect the health and welfare of the traveling public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JOYCE F. label: HB 10663
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE COVERAGE OF THE MALASAKIT PROGRAM TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT-CONTROLLED AND SUPERVISED HOSPITALS AND HEALTH FACILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11463, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MALASAKIT CENTERS ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution recognizes the right of the people to health and mandates the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development, making essential health and social services available to all Filipinos at affordable cost. This constitutional duty is especially important for indigent and financially incapacitated patients who often face difficulty in securing timely medical care due to the high cost of hospitalization, medicines, diagnostics, and other health-related expenses. With the enactment of the Local Government Code of 1991, significant powers, responsibilities, and functions were devolved to local government units. Among the major services devolved were health services previously administered by the Department of Health. As a result, the operation and supervision of many provincial, district, city, and municipal hospitals, as well as rural health units and other local health facilities, were transferred to local government units. This framework brought health services closer to communities, but it also resulted in a public health system where not all government health facilities are directly controlled or supervised by the DOH. In 2019, Republic Act No. 11463, otherwise known as the Malasakit Centers Act, institutionalized Malasakit Centers as one-stop shops for medical and financial assistance in DOH hospitals and the Philippine General Hospital. The law brought together key government agencies such as the DOH, Department of Social Welfare and Development, Philippine Health Insurance Corporation, and Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office to streamline the processing of assistance for indigent and financially incapacitated patients. Through this mechanism, patients are given a more accessible, coordinated, and compassionate means of securing support for their medical needs. However, despite the gains of the Malasakit Program, its mandatory establishment remains limited to DOH hospitals and the PGH. This creates a gap in access for patients who seek care in LGU-controlled and supervised hospitals or health facilities, especially in provinces, cities, and municipalities where such facilities are often the nearest or most accessible points of care. In many communities, district hospitals, rural health units, infirmaries, and similar local health facilities serve as the first and sometimes only available health service providers. Patients in these facilities should not be placed at a disadvantage merely because the facility they access is under local, rather than national, supervision. This proposed measure seeks to address this gap by expanding the coverage of the Malasakit Program to LGU-controlled and supervised hospitals or health facilities. It recognizes the realities of devolved health service delivery and strengthens the connection between national medical assistance programs and local health facilities. By allowing these facilities to adopt, implement, or provide access to the Malasakit Program through centers, help desks, satellite desks, referral systems, digital platforms, or other mechanisms prescribed by the DOH, the bill ensures that assistance reaches patients more efficiently and equitably. The measure is consistent with the objectives of Universal Health Care, which calls for an integrated and people-centered health system. Expanding the Malasakit Program to local health facilities will improve coordination, reduce delays, assist patients in navigating documentary requirements, and lessen the financial burden on vulnerable families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JOYCE F. label: HB 10664
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE EQUITABLE, TRANSPARENT, AND INCLUSIVE DISTRIBUTION OF PHILHEALTH BENEFIT SHARES AMONG PERSONNEL OF PUBLIC HEALTH INSTITUTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution mandates the State to protect life, liberty, and property under Article II, Section 5, and to promote social justice in all phases of national development under Article XIII. It likewise upholds the protection of workers and the equitable distribution of benefits, principles that extend to all personnel in public health institutions who collectively sustain the delivery of essential healthcare services to the Filipino people. With the implementation of the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act (Republic Act No. 11223), the Philippine health financing system has shifted toward pooled PhilHealth reimbursements, global budgeting, and facility-level financial autonomy through mechanisms such as Special Health Funds. While intended to improve efficiency and service delivery, Commission on Audit (COA) observations on Department of Health (DOH) hospitals, together with DOH administrative issuances, indicate that the utilization of PhilHealth-derived revenues and related personnel benefit shares is largely implemented at the institutional level, where hospital management exercises significant discretion in distribution. Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) research on UHC implementation further notes that decentralization of hospital financial management has contributed to uneven and inconsistent application of incentive and benefit-sharing systems across health facilities. As a result, concerns have been raised regarding unequal distribution, lack of standardized formulas, delayed releases, and limited participation of non-medical, non-clinical, and non-permanent personnel, including job order and contract of service workers who nonetheless play essential roles in hospital operations. In practice, disparities exist both across and within hospital systems, particularly between tertiary and lower-level facilities and between plantilla and non-permanent personnel. World Health Organization (WHO) health workforce studies and PIDS policy research consistently show that income-derived incentive systems tend to favor clinical and higher-ranked personnel, while non-clinical workers such as administrative staff, utility personnel, and support service workers often receive lower shares or are excluded depending on institutional policy. The Civil Service Commission (CSC) likewise recognizes that job order and contract of service personnel are not automatically covered by standard government incentive schemes unless explicitly included in agency guidelines, reinforcing structural inequities in benefit access. Delays in the release of PhilHealth Benefit Share allocations are also frequently reported. COA audit findings on hospital income utilization note that administrative processing requirements, pooling mechanisms under the UHC framework, and the absence of uniform statutory timelines contribute to delayed distribution of benefits to personnel. These delays adversely affect workforce morale, financial predictability, and perceptions of fairness in public health institutions. These systemic issues are compounded by the growing reliance of public hospitals on PhilHealth reimbursements as a major source of operational funding. However, in the absence of a uniform statutory framework, implementation remains fragmented, institution-dependent, and vulnerable to discretion-driven variations, resulting in inconsistent treatment of similarly situated personnel across facilities and weakening equity in public sector compensation systems. In light of these conditions, there is a compelling need to institutionalize a standardized, transparent, and inclusive framework for the distribution of PhilHealth Benefit Shares. The proposed bill seeks to ensure that all personnel, regardless of employment status, are fairly included in benefit-sharing mechanisms, while establishing safeguards against delay, diversion, and discriminatory allocation. The bill further strengthens governance by mandating uniform distribution rules, timely release of benefits, transparency and public reporting requirements, protection against retaliation for whistleblowers, and enhanced inter-agency coordination among the Department of Health (DOH), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), Department of Budget and Management (DBM), Civil Service Commission (CSC), and Commission on Audit (COA). In doing so, it promotes fairness, strengthens workforce morale and retention, and ensures that public health financing translates into equitable benefits for all who contribute to healthcare delivery. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JOYCE F. label: HB 10665
title: AN ACT GRANTING ADDITIONAL INCOME TAX EXEMPTION FOR GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEE BONUSES AND INCENTIVE BENEFITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SEC. 32(B)(7)(e) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution mandates the State to promote social justice, afford full protection to labor, and pursue a progressive system of taxation. These principles require that tax policy remain fair, responsive, and sensitive to the real economic conditions of workers, including those in government service. Republic Act No. 10963, or the TRAIN Law, amended the National Internal Revenue Code and retained the tax-exempt ceiling of Ninety Thousand Pesos (₱90,000.00) for benefits covered under the tax category of 13th month pay and other benefits. For government employees, this generally includes the Year-End Bonus and other similar benefits, such as productivity incentives, cash gift, and other authorized bonuses or incentives. While the ₱90,000.00 ceiling provided relief when enacted, it has become increasingly outdated. Since the implementation of TRAIN in 2018, inflation has eroded the purchasing power of the peso. Based on accumulated inflation from 2018 to 2025, the amount of ₱90,000.00 in 2018 would need to be approximately ₱121,500.00 in 2025 to preserve the same purchasing power. In effect, the real value of the existing ceiling has substantially declined. This decline has been worsened by recent increases in the prices of fuel, food, transport, utilities, and other basic goods. In 2022, diesel prices rose from a monthly average of at least ₱51per liter at the start of the year to more than ₱84 per liter in June, contributing to higher transport, logistics, and commodity costs. More recently, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported that inflation reached 7.2% in April 2026, driven mainly by food and non-alcoholic beverages, transport, and housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels. Government employees are directly affected by these rising costs. However, several of their common benefits, including the Year-End Bonus, Mid-Year Bonus, Cash Gift, Productivity Enhancement Incentive, Service Recognition Incentive, and similar authorized incentives, may be aggregated under the same ₱90,000.00 ceiling. Once the combined amount exceeds the ceiling, the excess becomes taxable compensation income, reducing the intended value of benefits meant to provide relief, recognize service, and support productivity. The proposed additional exemption is also fiscally measured. Based on Civil Service Commission data, the government had about 2.1 million career and non-career personnel as of June 2025. If all such personnel were to fully utilize the proposed additional ₱50,000.00 exemption, the maximum tax base excluded from taxable income would be approximately ₱105 billion. Applying the current graduated individual income tax rates, the indicative annual revenue foregone may range from about ₱15.7 billion at a 15% marginal tax rate to ₱26.2 billion at a 25% marginal tax rate, or up to ₱31.5 billion at a 30% marginal tax rate. The actual fiscal impact is expected to be lower, as not all government employees receive benefits exceeding the existing ₱90,000.00 ceiling, not all are in taxable brackets, and not all would fully utilize the additional exemption. This bill therefore seeks to grant additional tax relief by providing a separate and modest tax-exempt ceiling for covered government employee bonuses and incentive benefits. While the measure may result in an estimated annual revenue foregone of approximately ₱21 billion, this amount represents direct relief returned to public servants by allowing them to retain a greater portion of benefits already authorized and appropriated for them. The proposal does not create a new compensation item or require a separate cash outlay, but simply maximizes the real value of existing incentives intended to recognize service, support productivity, and ease the burden of rising household expenses. By preserving the value of government employee incentives, this measure supports the welfare of public servants, strengthens morale in the bureaucracy, and promotes a fairer tax treatment of benefits granted in recognition of government service. The modest reduction in tax collection is outweighed by the immediate and tangible relief to government employees and their families, especially amid inflation, reduced purchasing power, and the continuing rise in the prices of basic goods In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10666
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING PROVINCIAL SOIL LABORATORY FACILITIES IN ALL PROVINCES, ENHANCING SOIL HEALTH MANAGEMENT AND AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTIVITY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agricultural productivity and long-term food security in the Philippines depend heavily on the proper management of soil resources. However, soil degradation, inefficient fertilizer use, and the absence of accessible, science-based soil diagnostics continue to constrain farm productivity and increase production costs. Data from the Department of Agriculture indicate that fertilizer use efficiency in many areas remains low, with only 30% to 50% of applied nutrients effectively utilized by crops, while the rest is lost to the environment. The Food and Agriculture Organization identifies poor nutrient management as a major contributor to declining soil fertility and stagnating yields in developing countries. At present, many Filipino farmers rely on generalized fertilizer recommendations and basic Soil Test Kits (STK), which fail to capture site-specific soil conditions. The limited availability of comprehensive soil laboratory services—especially in rural and geographically isolated areas—prevents farmers from adopting science-based nutrient management practices. As a result, inefficient “blanket” fertilizer application persists, leading to input wastage, lower yields, and long-term soil degradation. This bill addresses these gaps by establishing Provincial Soil Laboratory Facilities nationwide under the Department of Agriculture, through the Bureau of Soils and Water Management. These facilities will provide accessible and comprehensive soil testing, advanced analysis, and technical advisory services to farmers and local government units. Unlike conventional soil test kits, these laboratories will support advanced diagnostics, enabling farmers to make informed, site-specific decisions. The measure also institutionalizes a Site-Specific Nutrient Management (SSNM) framework, ensuring that fertilizer use is guided by laboratory data and local field conditions. Studies supported by the International Rice Research Institute show that SSNM can increase yields by 5% to 20% while reducing fertilizer use by up to 20%, demonstrating improved efficiency and productivity. International experience reinforces the value of soil testing systems. In India, the Soil Health Card Program has reached over 220 million farmers, which improved fertilizer efficiency and reducing input costs. China and Vietnam have similarly achieved higher yields and better nutrient use efficiency through large-scale soil testing and site-specific nutrient management programs. The FAO further estimates that improved soil management can increase crop productivity by up to 58% in degraded lands. By promoting science-based fertilizer optimization, this measure aims to reduce input waste, lower costs, improve yields, and minimize environmental impacts. It will strengthen soil health monitoring, support data-driven agricultural planning, and enhance climate-resilient and sustainable farming systems. This proposed legislation empowers Filipino farmers with the knowledge and tools needed to increase productivity while preserving soil resources for future generations. In doing so, it advances the State’s commitment to food security, rural development, and sustainable agriculture. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 15, 19, 29, 30, AND 31 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Real property taxation is a vital and stable source of local government revenue. To ensure that property assessments remain fair, transparent, and reflective of prevailing market conditions, Republic Act No. 12001, otherwise known as the “Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act” (RPVARA), established a systematic and evidence-based framework for real property valuation. This measure does not seek to repeal or weaken the RPVARA. Rather, it recognizes that its successful implementation must consider prevailing economic conditions and the readiness of implementing institutions. The continuing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have contributed to global market uncertainties and volatility in fuel and commodity prices. At the same time, the Philippines has recently endured successive typhoons, flooding, earthquakes, and other natural calamities that have disrupted livelihoods, damaged property, and strained the financial capacity of many Filipino families and local government units (LGUs). Under these circumstances, a measured transition in the implementation of RPVARA is both prudent and necessary. Beyond mitigating the immediate financial impact on taxpayers, it will provide local government units (LGUs) sufficient time to complete the technical, institutional, and administrative requirements necessary to implement the law effectively and uniformly. Preparing a Schedule of Market Values (SMV), which serves as the foundation of the valuation system under RPVARA, is a highly technical undertaking requiring extensive data gathering, validation of property transactions, market analysis, stakeholder consultations, and compliance with national valuation standards. Although the RPVARA has already taken effect, several implementing mechanisms were issued later than anticipated, while consultations with LGUs reveal varying levels of preparedness in terms of technical expertise, staffing, market data, digital infrastructure, and institutional capacity. These circumstances warrant additional time to ensure the proper implementation of the law. The readiness of LGUs is particularly important because approved SMVs affect not only real property taxation but also various taxes, fees, and charges under existing laws. Premature implementation may result in inconsistent valuations, administrative disputes, and unintended financial burdens on taxpayers, including senior citizens and other property owners who rely on fixed or limited incomes. Accordingly, this measure aims to provide a reasonable transition period by postponing the tax-impacting implementation of approved SMVs, while allowing their preparation, updating, review, validation, calibration, harmonization, approval, and publication to continue in accordance with the law. This approach preserves the objectives of RPVARA while ensuring that its implementation proceeds on a sound, uniform, and equitable basis. By providing LGUs sufficient time to prepare and by mitigating the immediate impact of updated property valuations on taxpayers, especially senior citizens, this measure seeks to strengthen the implementation of RPVARA while promoting a transparent, credible, equitable, and sustainable real property valuation system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RODOLFO “OMPONG” M. label: HB 10670
title: AN ACT ENHANCING DECENTRALIZED GOVERNANCE AND SERVICE DELIVERY IN BASIC EDUCATION, AUTHORIZING THE CREATION AND RATIONALIZATION OF SCHOOLS DIVISION OFFICES, AND AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9155, ОТHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "GOVERNANCE OF BASIC EDUCATION ACT OF 2001
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Effective education delivery is crucial across all schools in the Philippines, as it equips students who will contribute to the country’s growth and development. Since the enactment of Republic Act No. 9155, or the Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001, the realities faced by the Department of Education (DepEd) in decentralizing the administration of the country’s basic education system have significantly changed. Learner populations have grown, the number of schools has expanded, and the complexity of delivering quality education across diverse geographic contexts has increased and there is a need for innovative reforms and adaptive strategies to keep up with the evolving needs of schools and students across the country. According to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), several Schools Division Offices (SDOs) now manage more than 1,300 schools, making it increasingly difficult for division offices to effectively oversee schools, support educators, and implement initiatives at the local level. Moreover, the disparity in workload among SDOs remains one of the most pressing concerns. Under these conditions, the management of divisions face increasing administrative burdens, which may undermine DepEd’s capacity to provide timely and effective support to schools. This bill seeks to address these gaps by authorizing the rationalization and creation of Schools Division Offices to ensure that the delivery of basic education services remains responsive and equitable, as strengthening these Schools Division Offices is important to ensure that national policies provide meaningful support to schools and educators. 1 By allowing school divisions to have a more organized and flexible structure, this measure aims to provide administrative, technical, and management support closer to our educational institutions. Moreover, the bill authorizes the Secretary of Education, in coordination with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), to create additional school divisions and reorganize, combine, adjust, or divide existing divisions and districts, when necessary, based on the number of learners, schools served, geographic conditions, workload requirements, or other factors affecting the delivery of education. This new system and scheme also ensure that every province and city will have a minimum of one school division, giving DepEd the freedom to modify organizational structures in accordance with objective standards and changes in needs. Improving learning outcomes for Filipino students is ultimately the goal of better division-level governance. Students gain the most when teachers are better prepared, school administrators receive more support, and educational services are provided more effectively. Most importantly, these improvements can lead to better learning outcomes, ensuring that every Filipino student receives quality education through a more responsive educational structure. In light of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 10671
title: AN ACT GRANTING BENEFITS TO CASUAL PERSONNEL, JOB ORDER AND CONTRACT OF SERVICE WORKERS ENGAGED BY THE GOVERNMENT, WHETHER DIRECTLY OR THROUGH THIRD-PARTY SERVICE PROVIDERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Based on the Civil Service Commission’s (CSC) Inventory of Government Human Resources (IGHR), non-regular personnel constitute a significant portion of the Philippine public sector workforce. As of the 2025 data, there are approximately 919,868 Job Order (JO) and Contract of Service (COS) workers nationwide, representing about 30.5% of the total government workforce. Among these, JO workers account for 629,862 personnel, while COS workers comprise 290,006 personnel. Likewise, Casual employees, who hold temporary civil service appointments under the Non-Career Service category, comprise another segment of non-regular government workers. They number 119,476, representing approximately 53.0% of the Non-Career Service workforce. Combined, JO, COS, and Casual personnel account for approximately 35% of the government workforce, highlighting their significant contribution to the delivery of public services. However, despite these, workers continue to face persistent challenges arising from their employment classification and limited access to benefits.1 Under existing Civil Service Commission (CSC) policies, JO and COS workers lack security of tenure due to the absence of an employer-employee relationship under civil service laws. Their continued employment depends on contract renewal, project requirements, available funding, and changes in administration, while casual employees remain vulnerable due to temporary appointments and budget limitations. These workers also experience significant disparities in compensation and benefits compared to regular government employees, as JO, Casual, and COS 1 Civil Service Commission. (2025). Inventory of government human resource: As of June 30, 2025. https://www.csc.gov.ph/phocadownload/userupload/irmo/ighr/2025/IGHR%20REPORT%20AS%20OF%20JU NE%2030%202025.pdf 1 personnel are generally excluded from various employment benefits and privileges. Moreover, their service is not credited for retirement or salary progression purposes. Considering these circumstances, this bill seeks to provide financial security, health protection, and employment benefits to qualified JO, Casual, and COS employees in the government who have rendered continuous and essential services. It aims to address the lack of benefits experienced by many non-regular government workers who perform critical functions but remain excluded from privileges such as health insurance, government contributions, bonuses, and leave entitlements. Furthermore, this bill provides qualified workers with protection against unlawful termination intended to evade the payment of these benefits and requires contractors and service providers to comply with the benefits mandated under this Act. By granting these benefits and providing protection against unjust termination, this bill upholds the welfare, dignity, and rights of government workers while recognizing their vital contributions to public service delivery. It also prevents the improper use of contractual arrangements by ensuring that government agencies and service contractors provide appropriate benefits to qualified workers. In light of the foregoing, support for this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 10672
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE PRACTICE OF PLUMBING ENGINEERING IN THE PHILIPPINES, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 1378, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PLUMBING LAW"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public plumbing provides a clean and safe water supply while ensuring proper wastewater management and drainage systems that protect public health and safety. Our systems of plumbing are concealed beneath the concrete slabs of contemporary buildings and are essential to maintaining modern society's sanitation and safety. This makes plumbing design and installation important and must be carried out by individuals with sufficient technical and academic training in compliance with widely recognized engineering standards and procedures. Unfortunately, the law regulating the profession has remained the same despite the major developments in plumbing systems, particularly in the materials used and technologies implemented. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 1378, otherwise known as the Plumbing Law in 1955, the legal framework governing the practice of master plumbing has remained unchanged for the past 7 decades. One clear proof of this obsolescence is that the existing law still considers plumbing a "trade" despite the current era of high-rise buildings and rapid urbanization. If remained out-of-date, this will result in an unconscious threat to public health, proper hygiene, and the overall quality of life in many communities. To address these challenges, this measure seeks to modernize the regulation of the plumbing profession by updating the legal framework to reflect current engineering practices, technological advancements, and internationally recognized standards. It strengthens professional qualifications, promotes continuing competence, and recognizes the increasingly specialized and engineering-oriented nature of plumbing practice. 1 Through these reforms, the bill aims to ensure that the profession remains capable of meeting the country's growing infrastructure needs while upholding the highest standards of public health, safety, and environmental sustainability. In light of the foregoing, support for this bill, which is a counterpart measure of Senate Bill 494, is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 10673
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RULES ON SYSTEM LOSS CAP FOR ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In our system of electricity distribution, system loss refers to the electrical energy lost between the point of generation and its delivery to end-users. These losses may be technical, arising from the physical condition, design, and operation of transmission and distribution facilities, or non-technical, resulting from electricity theft, illegal connections, meter tampering, and inaccurate billing or measurement. System loss remains a serious national concern because a portion of its cost is passed on to consumers, contributing to already high electricity rates. Persistent losses also reduce the efficiency and reliability of power distribution, waste energy that could otherwise serve households and businesses, and require additional generation to compensate for electricity that never reaches paying consumers. While the recovery of system losses is necessary to ensure the continued operation and financial viability of distribution utilities and electric cooperatives, consumers should not be burdened with unlimited charges arising from losses that are largely beyond their control or awareness. This bill excludes transmission losses from recoverable system losses and prohibits their recovery from end-users. The bill also sets a maximum recoverable system loss limit of 5% for private distribution utilities and establishes a tiered cap for electric cooperatives based on operational conditions. In light of the foregoing, support for this bill, which is a counterpart measure of Senate Bill 495 is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 10674
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE INCOME TAX EXEMPTION CEILING FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO FOUR HUNDRED EIGHTY THOUSAND PESOS (P𝟒𝟖𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎) ANNUALLY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) AND (b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 5 of the Philippine Constitution enshrines the principle that the maintenance of a just and dynamic social order shall guarantee the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services and promote a rising standard of living. Over the years, the continuous escalation of the cost of living—driven by inflationary pressures on basic commodities, utility fees, housing, and healthcare expenses—has significantly eroded the purchasing power of the Filipino workforce. While the enactment of Republic Act No. 10963 (otherwise known as the TRAIN Law) provided commendable relief by restructuring personal income taxes, the economic landscape has drastically shifted. The current tax-exemption ceiling of Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (P250,000) annually, established years ago, no longer reflects the economic realities faced by ordinary wage earners and middle-class families today. An obvious mismatch currently exists between fixed personal exemption thresholds and contemporary living costs, forcing low- and middle-income earners to shoulder heavy tax burdens that eat deeply into funds required for basic survival and family welfare. Raising the tax exemption ceiling to Four Hundred Eighty Thousand Pesos (P480,000) annually corrects this imbalance. It ensures that the working class is granted genuine fiscal breathing room, directly injecting much-needed liquidity into households, stimulating domestic consumption, and fostering a fairer, more equitable progressive tax system. Furthermore, this adjustment aligns the 8% preferential tax option for self- employed individuals and professionals under Section 24(A)(2)(b) with the updated baseline, protecting small-scale entrepreneurs and independent practitioners from premature taxation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 10675
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MANDATORY APPOINTMENT OF A MUNICIPAL VETERINARIAN OFFICER, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the "Local Government Code of 1991," decentralized key public services to local government units (LGUs) to foster local autonomy and self-reliance. However, under Section 443(a) and Section 489(a) of the Code, the appointment of a Veterinarian Officer is mandated only for provincial and city governments, leaving the position merely optional for municipal governments. This statutory limitation creates a significant coverage gap in rural and agricultural communities. Most backyard livestock raisers, small-scale poultry farmers, and pet owners reside in municipalities where access to licensed veterinary professionals is severely lacking. As a result, animal diseases are frequently untreated, unmonitored, or managed using traditional methods that fail to prevent contagion. The absence of dedicated municipal veterinarians exposes local livestock industries to devastating outbreaks of transmissible and zoonotic diseases—such as African Swine Fever (ASF), Avian Influenza (Bird Flu), Rabies, and Foot-and- Mouth Disease (FMD). These diseases cause immense economic loss to farming families, threaten national food security, and present serious public health risks to human populations. This bill seeks to amend Sections 443 and 489 of Republic Act No. 7160 to make the appointment of a Municipal Veterinarian Officer mandatory across all municipalities in the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 10676
title: AN ACT EXCLUDING SYSTEM LOSS FROM VALUE-ADDED TAXES (VAT) IN THE SALE OF ELECTRICITY TO RESIDENTIAL HOUSEHOLD CONSUMERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every month, Filipino families open their electricity bills and pay for power they might not even use. Buried within the sum billed for “kilowatt-hours consumed” is a charge for electricity that was lost in the wires — dissipated as heat, siphoned off through pilferage, or otherwise unaccounted for before it ever reached a household meter. This is the System Loss Charge, and under current practice, it is taxed as though it were a service rendered to the consumer. The Value-Added Tax (VAT) is, by design, a tax on consumption. Sections 105 to 108 of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC) of 1997, as amended, impose VAT on the sale, barter, or exchange of goods and services actually rendered or delivered. On the other hand, system loss, by definition, is the difference between the electricity entering a power network and the amount eventually measured and billed to customers1. In other words, it is electricity generated, purchased, or transmitted but never delivered to the end-user. Therefore, to impose VAT on this component is to tax a transaction that, from the standpoint of the residential household consumer, never took place. Thus, this proposed measure. This bill seeks to exempt the system loss component charged to residential household consumers from the value-added tax by amending Article 109 of the NIRC, 1 Yu, L.S (28 July 2026). EXPLAINER: What is system loss, and how does it affect your power bill? Retrieved from: https://www.rappler.com/business/explainer-what-system-loss-affect-power-bill/ 1 as amended. In addition, to ensure that the benefit inures to the households for whose protection this measure is introduced, this bill directs the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to ensure that the resulting reduction in tax liability is not recovered from consumers through distribution wheeling charges or other pass-through mechanisms. This provision effectively closes the door on any circumvention of the exemption's intent through rate reclassification. By removing the tax burden on electricity which never reaches the Filipino household, this measure restores basic fairness to utility billing. This very injustice is what this bill seeks to rectify.
