label: HB 10677
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE IMPOSITION AND RECOVERY OF NON-TECHNICAL SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 43(F) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an important commodity. It is a basic necessity that sustains households, hospitals, schools, and industries alike. Precisely because of its indispensable character, Republic Act No. 11659 classifies the distribution of electricity as a public utility business affected with public interest1, subject to the State’s power to regulate rates and charges to protect the consuming public from abuse. This protective mandate becomes even more cogent amid the reality that, as of June 2026, the Philippines recorded the highest average electricity rate in Southeast Asia at ₱12.43 per kilowatt-hour, driven by rising fuel costs and persistent supply constraints.2 Worse, there is a perennial issue that an average Filipino consumer’s electricity bill does not reflect a just and reasonable pricing, but that it instead includes charges for certain losses (including pilferages) in the distribution or delivery of electricity which are caused by the fault, negligence, or criminal acts of others. It was against this backdrop that President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr., in his 2026 State of the Nation Address, called on Congress to act: 1 Section 4 2Lelis,B. (21 July 2026). DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA. The Philippine Star. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates- now-highest-sea 1 “Panahon na para tanggalin na natin ang systems loss na pinapasa sa konsyumer… Hindi naman kasalanan ng konsyumer kung bakit nagkaroon ng systems loss. Kaya hindi naman tama na kailangan sila pa ang pagbabayarin dito… Therefore, we, their people, request — no, we demand the immediate amendment of the EPIRA and to prohibit charging systems loss against consumers, including the value-added tax thereon.” This bill answers that call, but does so with the precision that sound policy demands. The system loss charge, which makes up roughly five percent (5%) of a consumer’s electricity bill,3 is composed of two distinct components under the 2017 Edition of the Philippine Distribution Code: Technical Loss, which is the loss inherent and unavoidable in the physical transmission and distribution of electricity through wires, transformers, and other equipment; and Non-Technical Loss, which consists of energy lost due to pilferage, meter tampering, erroneous meter reading, and other causes attributable to human action, whether intentional or negligent. 4 In other words, Technical Loss is a scientific inevitability; no amount of vigilance by the consumer or the distribution utility (DU) can reduce it to zero5. Non-Technical Loss, by contrast, is preventable. It is the direct consequence of pilferage committed by third parties, defective or tampered metering, and administrative or billing error, none of which the paying consumer has any control over, and none of which the consumer should be made to shoulder. Yet under the present framework, Section 43(f) of Republic Act No. 9136, or the “Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001” (EPIRA), empowers the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) only to set caps on the recoverable rate of system losses caps that, under ERC Resolution No. 10, Series of 2018, are computed by combining Technical Loss and Non-Technical Loss, whichever is lower than the prescribed cap, in addition to actual sub-transmission and substation losses.6 Thus, for as long as a DU’s combined losses remain within the ERC-approved cap, it may continue to pass on to consumers the cost of energy stolen by pilferers, lost to tampered meters, or misrecorded through billing error. This setup, however administratively convenient, offends basic notions of fairness and cost-causation. 3Santos, T. G. (05 May 2026). Hontiveros: Cut systems loss VAT in power bills. Philippine Daily Inquirer. Retrieved from https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2223376/hontiveros-cut-systems-loss-vat-in-power-bills 4Philippine Distribution Code, 2017 Edition, (Dec. 2017) 5 Gulla, V (05 August 2026). DOE, ERC favor 'phased' removal of non-technical system loss charge from electricity bills. Retrieved from: https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/business/2026/8/5/doe-erc-favor- phased-removal-of-non-technical-system-loss-charge-1904 6ERC Resolution No. 10, Series of 2018, Retrieved from https://erc.gov.ph/Files/Render/issuance/18964 2 This bill therefore seeks to amend Section 43(f) of the EPIRA to expressly confine the ERC’s rate-setting and cap-setting authority to Technical Loss alone, and to categorically prohibit distribution utilities from imposing, charging, or recovering any cost attributable to Non-Technical Loss from their consumers, whether through the System Loss Rate or any other charge, fee, or cross-subsidy mechanism. The cost of Non-Technical Loss shall instead be borne by the DU as an ordinary cost of doing business. Consequently, this scheme can create a direct financial incentive for distribution utilities to invest in anti-pilferage measures, meter security, and collection efficiency, without prejudice to their right to pursue civil and criminal remedies against persons liable for pilferage or tampering under Republic Act No. 7832, or the “Anti- Electricity and Electric Transmission Lines/Materials Pilferage Act of 1994.” To ensure faithful implementation, the bill requires distribution utilities to segregate and report their Technical and Non-Technical Losses to the ERC with corresponding administrative penalties imposed on distribution utilities and responsible officials who fail to comply. Ultimately, this bill gives concrete legislative form to the President’s directive: that no Filipino consumer should be made to pay for electricity that was stolen, mismeasured, or lost to another’s fault. When the very lifeline that powers every Filipino home is priced fairly, only then can the promise of affordable and reliable electricity be truly fulfilled. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LEILA M. DE LIMA 3 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPR

title: AN ACT INCREASING THE INCOME TAX EXEMPTION CEILING FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO THREE HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (₱350,000) ANNUALLY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) and (b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates that taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and that Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation.1 This bill gives effect to that constitutional command by updating the individual income tax schedule under Section 24(A)(2) of the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended, to reflect present economic realities and to protect low- and middle-income earners from tax burdens that have become heavier in real terms. Under the Republic Act (“R.A.”) No. 10963 (2017), or the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion Act, the first ₱250,000 of annual taxable income was effectively placed under a zero-percent rate, while the personal income tax schedule was further reduced beginning January 1, 2023 for individuals earning ₱8,000,000 and below.2 These reforms were intended to increase disposable income and make the tax system more progressive. However, the ₱250,000 zero-rate threshold has remained fixed despite the cumulative rise in the cost of living. As of April 2026, the Philippine Statistics 1 1987 Philippine Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 28(1) 2 TRAIN Law to Further Reduce Personal Income Taxes in 2023 Onwards, Dep’t of Fin. (Dec. 28, 2022), https://www.dof.gov.ph/train-law-to-further-reduce-personal-income-taxes-in-2023-onwards/. Authority reported headline inflation at 7.2%, with food and non-alcoholic beverages, transport, and housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels among the top contributors to overall inflation.3 As of July 202, inflation has eased to 6.2%, the third straight monthly decline since the April peak. Average inflation has run at 5% this year, above target, and the threshold has been frozen since 2018. The effect is felt most sharply by workers and small earners whose income growth does not necessarily translate to real purchasing power. PSA data show that in 2023, the average annual income of Filipino families was ₱353,230.00, while average annual family expenditure reached ₱258,050.00.4 At the same time, minimum wage rates remain calibrated regionally, with the National Capital Region’s current daily minimum wage ranging from ₱755.00 to ₱780.00, while Western Visayas rates range from ₱520.00 to ₱550.00.5 These figures show that many Filipino workers and families continue to operate within narrow margins, where additional take-home pay directly supports food, transportation, utilities, education, rent, medicines, and other basic household needs. This bill therefore proposes to increase the income tax exemption ceiling from ₱250,000 to ₱350,000 annually, and correspondingly recalibrates the graduated tax brackets. The measure also updates the optional eight percent tax regime for qualified purely self-employed individuals and professionals by allowing the eight percent tax to apply only to gross sales or receipts and other non-operating income in excess of ₱350,000, instead of ₱250,000. This preserves parity between compensation earners and qualified self-employed individuals, while maintaining the simplified tax option for small professionals and micro-entrepreneurs whose gross receipts remain below the VAT threshold. The bill does not abolish personal income taxation. It merely restores fairness at the point where income becomes taxable, ensuring that subsistence and modest earnings 3 Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index (2018=100), Philippine Statistics Authority (May 5, 2026), https://psa.gov.ph/price-indices/cpi-ir/node/1684083369. 4 Philippine Statistics Authority. Family Income and Expenditure Survey: 2023. https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/income-expenditure/fies 5 National Wages and Productivity Commission, DOLE. Current Daily Minimum Wage Rates. https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/ncr/ 1 are not prematurely absorbed by tax liability. Higher-income taxpayers remain subject to graduated rates, preserving the progressive structure of the tax system. By increasing disposable income for workers, professionals, and small earners, the measure can help strengthen household consumption, improve voluntary compliance, and reinforce the principle that taxation must be based on real ability to pay. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 10679
title: AN ACT TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF NATURE IN THE PHILIPPINES, INTEGRATING ECOSYSTEM INTEGRITY STANDARDS INTO THE NATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Rights of Nature Act of 2026 seeks to strengthen environmental protection by recognizing natural ecosystems as holders of legally enforceable rights to exist, regenerate, and maintain their ecological integrity. It establishes a unified framework that complements existing environmental laws by integrating ecosystem integrity standards into environmental permitting, land-use planning, and development decision-making. The measure requires government agencies and covered industries to adopt science-based ecological safeguards, promotes accountability for environmental harm, and provides legal mechanisms for the protection and restoration of ecosystems. It likewise ensures that these rights complement existing human rights, indigenous peoples' rights, property rights, and sustainable livelihoods. Ultimately, the bill aims to promote sustainable development by balancing economic growth with the long-term protection and resilience of the country's natural ecosystems for present and future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10680
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL MEDICINE SECURITY FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING LOCAL PHARMACEUTICAL MANUFACTURING AS A STRATEGIC INVESTMENT, ENSURING THE QUALITY, SAFETY, AND AFFORDABILITY OF MEDICINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerability of the Philippine healthcare system to disruptions in global pharmaceutical supply chains. During the initial wave of the pandemic, border closures, export restrictions, and logistical bottlenecks significantly constrained the country’s ability to import essential medicines, placing public health at risk. While existing laws promote access to affordable medicines (e.g. Cheaper Medicines Act), the current regulatory framework relies heavily on administrative issuances of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to safeguard medicine quality and ensure supply continuity. At the same time, domestic pharmaceutical manufacturers incur substantial fixed costs to comply with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, while import-dependent products may enter the market with uneven quality oversight. This imbalance undermines medicine security, public trust, and long-term industrial resilience. Local pharmaceutical manufacturing occupies a distinct and strategic role in the national health system. Unlike purely distribution-based or import-based models, local manufacturing directly supports medicine security by maintaining domestic production capacity, enabling closer regulatory oversight, sustaining technical and skilled employment, and strengthening the country’s ability to respond to public health emergencies and external supply disruptions. For this reason, local pharmaceutical manufacturing should be recognized not merely as an ordinary commercial activity, but as a strategic capability necessary to safeguard public health and national resilience. This bill seeks to establish a statutory medicine security Framework that balances access, availability, affordability, safety, and quality, while strengthening local pharmaceutical manufacturing as a strategic component of national health security. It does not prohibit imports nor confer automatic incentives. The bill also does not discriminate between multinational and local industry players in the market. Instead, it ensures that all medicines, whether locally produced or imported, are subject to equivalent, science-based quality standards. The measure aligns fully with the CREATE Act, the CREATE MORE Act, and the Strategic Investment Priority Plan by recognizing pharmaceutical manufacturing as a strategic investment activity subject to existing incentive regimes. It further strengthens regulatory enforcement through statutory FDA-BOC coordination, risk-based traceability, and enhanced oversight of online pharmaceutical sales. Ultimately, this bill aims to protect Filipino patients, promote fair competition, and ensure that the availability of affordable medicines is never achieved at the expense of quality, safety, and national resilience. Immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. EMIGDIO P. label: HB 10682
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL PROGRAM FOR NUTRITION-SENSITIVE AGRICULTURE, LOCAL FOOD SECURITY, AND STUNTING REDUCTION, STRENGTHENING LINKAGES BETWEEN LOCAL FOOD PRODUCTION AND NUTRITION PROGRAMS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Stunting remains among the most pressing human capital development concerns in the Philippines. The 2025 Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI) Updating Survey reported that 25.3 percent of Filipino children aged zero to 59 months suffer from stunting, reflecting an increase from the 23.6 percent prevalence recorded in 2023. These figures highlight the persistent challenge of chronic malnutrition and inadequate nutrition among young children. The current prevalence level continues to fall within the range classified by the World Health Organization as a high public health concern, emphasizing the need for stronger and more integrated interventions to address the root causes of stunting 1 • Moreover, stunting rates also remain significantly higher among poor households, rural communities, food-insecure households, and geographically isolated areas. Moreover, children from the poorest income quintile experience nearly three times the prevalence of stunting compared with children from the wealthiest households2 • While Republic Act No. 11148 or the "Kalusugan at Nutrisyon ng Mag-Nanay Act" and Republic Act No. 11037 or the "Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act" provide critical nutrition interventions, malnutrition cannot be solved though feeding programs alone. The root causes include food insecurity, limited access to nutrient-dense foods, low agricultural productivity, inadequate dietary diversity, and weak linkages between local food production and nutrition programs. 1 https://apmargin.org/child-stunting-philippines-2025/ 2 https://www.unicef.org/philippines/reports/raising-bar Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10682 HOUSE BILL NO. ------ Introduced by REPRESENTATIVE AUDREY KAY T. label: HB 10688
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE STOCKPILING OF STRATEGIC AND CRITICAL DRUGS AND MEDICINES, VACCINES, DEVICES, AND MATERIALS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE HEALTH PROCUREMENT AND STOCKPILING BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 2025 report of the Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB), an independent monitoring and advocacy body that assesses the world's ability to protect itself from health emergencies, warns that the international community remains dangerously unprepared for the next major pandemic even five years after COVID-191. Titled "The New Face of Pandemic Preparedness," the report finds that the world continues to face a volatile, uncertain, and complex threat landscape, from the persistent circulation of H5N1 avian influenza in animal populations to the recurrence of monkeypox, and calls on governments to care for their populations, measure their true state of readiness, and cooperate across borders and sectors before, and not after, the next crisis strikes. The lessons of the COVID-19 decade remain instructive. The pandemic disrupted the global and local production and distribution of pharmaceuticals and medical devices, as well as the supply of raw materials, active pharmaceutical ingredients, excipients, packaging materials, and finished medical products, after major supplier countries were themselves overwhelmed by the outbreak. Several countries responded by imposing export restrictions on medicines, vaccines, and medical equipment to protect their own domestic supply, leaving countries without independent stockpiles or manufacturing capacity, such as the Philippines, dangerously exposed. This experience prompted the adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025, which obligates state parties, including the Philippines, to strengthen national 1 Global Preparedness Monitoring Board, “The New Face of Pandemic Preparedness: 2025 Report,” October 13, 2025, available at: https://gpmb.org/reports/m/item/the-new-face-of- pandemic-preparedness-2025-report capacities for the equitable and timely access to health products during public health emergencies.2 As one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world by virtue of its geography, the Philippines cannot afford to treat pandemic and emergency preparedness as an afterthought. Recurring outbreaks of dengue and other endemic diseases, the continuing threat of emerging and re-emerging pathogens, and the country's vulnerability to typhoons, earthquakes, and other calamities that regularly disrupt supply chains and health service delivery all underscore the need for a standing, well-funded mechanism to secure the country's supply of critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials ahead of the next emergency, rather than scrambling to procure them once it has already begun. This bill seeks to protect public health by addressing the country's continuing vulnerability to shortages of critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials in times of public health emergencies. It mandates the systematic procurement and stockpiling of critical and strategic pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and raw materials, and creates the Health Procurement and Stockpiling Bureau under the Department of Health to institutionalize this function beyond the life of any single administration or crisis. It is hoped that through this measure, the recurring problem of inadequate access to strategic and critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials in times of national need may finally be addressed in a lasting and institutional manner. In view of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10689
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MODERNIZATION OF THE PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE CAPABILITIES, ESTABLISHING FOR THIS PURPOSE THE CENTER FOR DISEASE PREVENTION AND CONTROL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 2025 report of the Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB), "The New Face of Pandemic Preparedness," warns that the world remains dangerously exposed to the next major health emergency, citing the persistent circulation of H5N1 avian influenza, recurring mpox outbreaks, and a volatile, uncertain, and complex threat landscape that demands sustained institutional readiness rather than crisis-driven improvisation.1 The Board's central recommendation, that countries care for their populations, measure their true state of preparedness, and cooperate across sectors and borders, presupposes the existence of a standing institution mandated to do precisely that. The Philippines, to date, still has none. The COVID-19 pandemic of the early 2020s laid bare this structural gap. Deficiencies in disease surveillance, delays in outbreak detection and response, fragmented data systems, and the absence of a single body empowered to translate scientific evidence into swift, coordinated policy all hampered the country's response at the moment it mattered most. More than five years on, these functions remain scattered across various bureaus and offices of the Department of Health, each operating with limited resources and no unified mandate to manage infectious disease threats comprehensively. This fragmentation continues to produce delays, inconsistencies, and duplicated effort in ordinary times, and becomes acutely dangerous in times of crisis. This gap is not unique to the Philippines, but most of its regional neighbors have long since closed it. The United States, China, Africa, and the European Union all maintain dedicated centers for disease control and prevention that serve as the technical authority for outbreak detection, laboratory coordination, and emergency response. The Philippines' continued reliance on an ad hoc, multi-agency structure leaves the country without a clear national counterpart for coordinating with these bodies and with international mechanisms such as the International Health Regulations, even as the 1 Global Preparedness Monitoring Board, “The New Face of Pandemic Preparedness: 2025 Report,” October 13, 2025, available at: https://gpmb.org/reports/m/item/the-new-face-of- pandemic-preparedness-2025-report World Health Assembly's adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement in May 2025 places new obligations on state parties to strengthen precisely this kind of national capacity.2 Recognizing this urgent need, the House of Representatives has already approved on third and final reading a measure creating the Philippine Centers for Disease Prevention and Control, one of the priority measures identified by the Marcos administration. This bill seeks to carry that effort forward by establishing the Philippine CDC as the country's lead technical agency for the prevention and control of communicable diseases, mandated to lead a science-based, whole-of-government, and whole-of-society response to health threats, whether the sudden emergence of a novel pathogen or the everyday, ongoing burden of tuberculosis, HIV, dengue, and noncommunicable disease. By consolidating expertise, streamlining decision-making, and institutionalizing preparedness as a permanent function of government rather than a temporary crisis response, the Philippine CDC will strengthen the country's capacity to protect lives, safeguard livelihoods, and secure its long-term development against future health threats. In view of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10690
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DIRECT OR INDIRECT RECOVERY OF DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES, INCLUDING ANY VALUE-ADDED TAX ATTRIBUTABLE THERETO, FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, GIVING PRIORITY TO THE MODERNIZATION OF DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS IN RURAL AND PROVINCIAL AREAS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832, AS AMENDED, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rising prices continue to strain Filipino households. Headline inflation rose to 6.2 percent in July 2026, down only slightly from 6.4 percent in the preceding month.1 Such inflation rates are carried over to costs related to housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels. Electricity is a large part of this burden by design: as of 2026, Philippine residential electricity rates were already among the highest in Southeast Asia, surpassing even Singapore.2 For households already stretched thin, a meaningful share of that bill has nothing to do with the electricity they consumed. That share is the System Loss Charge. Under Republic Act No. 7832 (1994) and Republic Act No. 9136, the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, distribution utilities and electric cooperatives are allowed to pass on to consumers the cost of electricity lost within their own networks, whether through outdated equipment, poor maintenance, or theft. Private utilities may currently recover as much as 8.5 percent of total kilowatt-hours purchased and generated, while electric cooperatives, which serve the overwhelming majority of rural and provincial consumers, may recover up to 13 percent, nearly half again as much. In practice, this means the very consumers who already contend with less reliable service, older infrastructure, and fewer alternatives than their counterparts in Metro Manila are also the ones most exposed to paying for electricity that never reached their homes. System loss typically makes up not less than five percent of a household's monthly bill, and, as currently treated, is subject to the 12 percent value-added tax on top of that. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, “Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index (2018=100): July 2026,” August 5, 2026, available at: https://psa.gov.ph/price-indices/cpi-ir 2 Brix Lelis, “DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA,” PhilStar Global, July 21, 2026, available at: https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe- philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea” This is not a new concern, nor is it one this representation raises for the first time. Versions of this measure have been filed in before, and the elimination of system loss charges has since been raised as a policy priority by the current administration, with President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. declaring it as a top priority legislation, going as far as explicitly demanding Congress amend EPIRA to stop both the system loss charge and its VAT from being passed to consumers. At its core, this measure asks a simple question: should consumers bear the cost of electricity that never reaches them, or should that remain a business risk of the entities that own and operate the distribution system? Consumers do not design distribution networks, choose feeder conditions, replace aging transformers, or prevent electricity theft. These are matters entirely within the control of distribution utilities and electric cooperatives, and Article XII of the 1987 Constitution subjects public utilities precisely to this kind of State regulation in the public interest. Congress may determine which costs may lawfully form part of a regulated electricity rate, and which must instead be absorbed as an ordinary cost of doing business by the entity that controls the system. This bill takes the more direct path. Rather than merely narrowing the tax base, as prior proposals have done by exempting the System Loss Charge from value-added tax while leaving the underlying charge intact, this measure prohibits the recovery of distribution system loss from consumers altogether, whether technical or non-technical in origin. Once that recovery is prohibited, no taxable consumer charge exists for value-added tax to attach to in the first place; the VAT problem is resolved as a direct consequence of removing the charge itself, not through a separate carve- out in the tax code. This bill accordingly amends Republic Act No. 7832 and Republic Act No. 9136 to bar distribution utilities and electric cooperatives from billing, collecting, or otherwise recovering system loss costs, in any form and under any name, from electricity end-users, while preserving their ability to recover the legitimate, audited cost of modernizing and maintaining their networks, with particular support extended to electric cooperatives serving geographically isolated, disaster-prone, and underserved provincial communities. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10691
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A MULTIMODAL LEARNING FRAMEWORK THROUGH THE PROVISION OF UNIVERSAL INTERNET ACCESS TO ENSURE THE CONTINUITY OF EDUCATION DURING PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCIES, NATURAL DISASTERS, AND OTHER CLIMATE-RELATED DISRUPTIONS, MOBILIZING THE NATIONAL TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION FOR THE PURPOSE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution is explicit that the State must protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. The extraordinary disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic in the early 2020s first forced the country to reckon with the fragility of its traditional, classroom-bound model of instruction. Nearly six years on, however, the more pressing threat to continuous learning is no longer a single pandemic, but a recurring pattern of climate-driven disruption that has become a permanent feature of the school calendar. According to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), disasters forces frequent face-to-face class suspensions nationwide between, disrupting school days leading to substantial loss of schooling time to typhoons, flooding, and extreme heat.1 Some localities have fared far worse. Just this year, the Department of Education has begun drafting an executive framework for automatic class suspensions once the heat index reaches 40°C or hazard thresholds for typhoons and poor air quality are met, an acknowledgment that disruption is no longer the exception but the expectation.2 Unlike the pandemic, these disruptions are typically localized and short-lived, but the response to them remains improvised. When classes are suspended, the fallback is routinely for schools to shift to what DepEd terms an Alternative Delivery Mode, yet whether this materializes as an online class, a printed module, or an outright loss of instructional time still depends almost entirely on whether a school or student has reliable internet access. 1 EDCOM2: The Second Congressional Commission on Education, “Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reform (2026-2035),” 2026, available at: https://edcom2.gov.ph/ 2 Jan Escosio, “DepEd leads consultations on class suspension, resumption rules,” July 29, 2026, Inquirer, available at: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2273856/deped-leads- consultations-on-class-suspension-resumption-rules That dependency remains the weakest link in the chain. As of 2024, only 48.8 percent of Filipino households had stable broadband access3, meaning generally available internet for use by all members of the household at any time, regardless of whether it is actually used, still far behind regional peers such as Vietnam and Thailand, and internet penetration among the poorest households remains a fraction of that among the wealthiest. While more than 78% of public schools nationwide now have internet connectivity, this still leaves out 12,000 schools nationwide, mostly in Geographically Isolated and Disadvantaged Areas (GIDAs), without internet connection.4 Government efforts to close this gap, including the National Fiber Backbone and the Department of Education's push to connect all public schools by the end of 2025, are meaningful but partial, and they leave open the question of what happens the moment those connections go down, whether from a typhoon, a fiber cut, or a simple lack of coverage in a remote barangay. Hence the need for this Act. Rather than treating connectivity as a stopgap measure for a single crisis, it seeks to institutionalize a standing, multimodal learning framework that allows instruction to continue seamlessly across online, offline, and blended formats whenever physical schooling becomes unsafe or impossible, whether due to a public health emergency, a typhoon, extreme heat, or any other climate-related hazard. It shall mobilize the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to identify priority areas for the establishment of reliable cyber infrastructure and to work with the Department of Education toward the goal of universal, comprehensive, and reliable internet connectivity for all learners, so that the continuity of education no longer depends on how quickly the weather clears. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10692
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE VIROLOGY AND VACCINE INSTITUTE OF THE PHILIPPINES BY MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL AND PROVINCIAL SATELLITE LABORATORIES AND OUTREACH PROGRAMS TO EXPAND ACCESS TO VIROLOGY RESEARCH, DIAGNOSTIC, AND GENOME SEQUENCING CAPACITY IN RURAL AND PROVINCIAL AREAS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12290, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12290, signed into law on September 12, 2025, created the Virology and Vaccine Institute of the Philippines (VIP) to serve as the country's lead institution for virology research, vaccine development, and diagnostic innovation. It was, and remains, a necessary response to the inadequacies during the COVID-19 pandemic, which exposed the country's ability to detect and understand emerging pathogens. However, the Institute's promise will only be felt nationwide if its capacity reaches beyond the capital region, and as presently structured, there is no guarantee that it will. The pandemic made painfully clear what provincial and rural communities have long known: that the country's scientific infrastructure for pathogen detection has always been concentrated in Metro Manila. Genome sequencing capacity, in particular, was housed almost exclusively at the Philippine Genome Center in UP Diliman and the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine in Muntinlupa, forcing provinces to ship samples to the capital and absorb the resulting delays before results could inform local response. The Department of Health itself acknowledged this bottleneck, moving in 2021 and 2022 to establish satellite genome sequencing laboratories in the Visayas and Mindanao to ease the transportation burden on regional health workers. That expansion was a step forward, but it remains partial. Many provinces, particularly those in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, still have no meaningful local access to genome sequencing or virology diagnostic capacity, and must rely on a small number of hub facilities far from where outbreaks actually begin. The VIP, as currently mandated, does not explicitly address this imbalance. Its flagship facility, still under construction, is planned for a five- hectare site in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac. While the site sits outside Metro Manila proper, it remains firmly within the Luzon corridor already best served by existing scientific infrastructure, offering little direct benefit to provinces in the Visayas, Mindanao, and other far-flung regions that were hit hardest by diagnostic delays during the pandemic. Left as is, the country risks building a second generation of centralized capacity that repeats the very gap it was created to close. This bill seeks to correct that by amending Republic Act No. 12290 to explicitly mandate the VIP to establish regional and provincial satellite laboratories and outreach programs, prioritizing regions and provinces currently underserved by existing virology and genomic surveillance infrastructure. It directs the Institute to partner with state universities and colleges, provincial and regional hospitals, and local government units outside Metro Manila to build local diagnostic and research capacity, train local scientists and health workers, and ensure that when the next outbreak begins in a rural municipality rather than the capital, the country's response does not depend on how quickly a sample can reach Manila. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10694
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING LOCAL FISCAL AUTONOMY THROUGH AN ADDITIONAL FIVE PERCENT (5%) SHARE IN ALL NATIONAL TAXES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to Article 2 of the Local Government Code of 1991, the State shall establish a more responsive and accountable local government structure through a system of decentralization, whereby local government units (LGUs) are granted greater powers, authority, responsibilities, and resources. This policy recognizes that empowering LGUs enables them to respond more effectively to the needs of their respective communities and deliver public services more efficiently. However, despite the enactment of the Local Government Code more than three decades ago, significant challenges remain in the devolution of functions and responsibilities from the national government to LGUs. While the Supreme Court's ruling in the Mandanas-Garcia case substantially increased the National Tax Allotment (NTA) of LGUs by expanding the basis for its computation, the decision did not address the long-standing structural inequities in the distribution of national transfers Municipalities remain particularly disadvantaged. Despite serving around 60 percent of the country's population and delivering critical services such as healthcare, agriculture, local infrastructure, disaster response, and social welfare, municipalities receive only thirty-four percent (34%) of the NTA. In 2023, cities generated and spent approximately P10,966 per capita on average, compared to only P3,186 per capita for municipalities, reflecting a substantial disparity in fiscal capacity. However, fiscal inequality likewise exists within LGU categories. Among cities, the proportion with Annual Regular Income (ARI) per capita below the national average increased from 45.65% in 2015 to 59.73% in 2024, indicating that revenue growth has become increasingly concentrated among a small number of fiscally stronger cities. Similar disparities are evident among provinces and other LGUs. 1 This bill seeks to strengthen local fiscal autonomy by granting LGUs an additional five percent (5%) share in all national taxes, to be phased in at one percentage point (1%) annually. Recognizing the fiscal constraints faced by municipalities, seventy percent (70%) of the additional allocation shall be distributed to municipalities, while ten percent (10%) each shall accrue to provinces, cities, and barangays. The bill further introduces an Income Classification Equalization Factor to provide greater support to lower-income LGUs. By enhancing municipal fiscal space, this measure is expected to improve local development outcomes, reduce reliance on congressional insertions for basic infrastructure, and enable LGUs to better fulfill their devolved functions under the LGC and the Mandanas–Garcia framework. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. YSABEL MARIA J. label: HB 10695
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION AND UTILIZATION OF SELF-GENERATING FACILITY ZERO-EXPORT SOLAR SYSTEMS AND MICRO-SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR OWN USE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The increasing cost of electricity, coupled with rapid advancements in solar and energy storage technologies, underscores a need for a clear policy that will promote the adoption of own-use distributed energy systems. Self-Generating Facility Zero-Export Solar Systems (SGF ZESS), Micro-Solar Systems (MSS), and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) enable consumers to generate and/or store electricity for their own consumption, thereby enhancing energy security, improving consumer resilience, reducing electricity costs, and supporting the country's transition to a cleaner and more sustainable energy future. For consumers, these technologies help reduce electricity costs, improve resilience during power interruptions, and lessen dependence on the grid. The wider adoption of these technologies can also help reduce pressure on the distribution system, contributing to a more reliable, resilient, and efficient power sector. At present, however, Republic Act 9136 or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA), does not expressly distinguish own-use distributed energy systems from commercial power generation. This regulatory gap has created uncertainty regarding the legal treatment of end-users who install and operate such systems solely for their own consumption, resulting in the imposition of regulatory and administrative requirements intended for generation companies. This creates an unnecessary burden that discourages the adoption of these technologies. 1 This draft bill seeks to establish a clear policy that governs own-use energy systems. It clarifies that end-users who install and operate SGF ZESS, MSS, BESS, and similar technologies solely for their own consumption shall not be considered generation companies or be subject to regulatory requirements applicable to commercial power generators. It likewise removes unnecessary administrative barriers, strengthens consumer protection, promotes uniform safety standards, and enhances inter-agency coordination to facilitate the responsible deployment of these systems. Additionally, this draft measure empowers consumers to generate and store their own electricity, enabling them to better manage electricity costs, improve resilience against power interruptions, and contribute to a more reliable, secure, and sustainable electric power system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 10696
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE INCOME TAX EXEMPTION CEILING FOR INDIVIDUAL TAXPAYERS TO THREE HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (P350,000) ANNUALLY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24(A)(2)(a) and (b) OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2018, when Republic Act No. 10963 or the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law was passed, the personal income tax exemption was set at Two Hundred FIfty Thousand Pesos (Php250,000.00). Over the past eight years cumulative inflation significantly eroded the purchasing power of Filipinos. As a result, One Hundred Pesos (Php100.00) in 2018 would only be able to buy an equivalent of Seventy-Four Pesos (Php74.00) to Seventy-Eight Pesos (Php78.00) worth of goods and services now. Thus, almost a decade after the passage of the law, it is now imperative to review whether the personal income tax exemption remains responsive to the needs of the majority of Filipinos. This proposed measure seeks to increase the personal tax exemption to Three Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (Php350,000.00). President Ferdinand “Bongbong” R. Marcos Jr. has emphasized the urgency of enacting this measure in his 2026 State of the Nation Address (SONA). The proposal is expected to benefit at least 3.13 Million Filipino workers, including an additional 1.3 Million workers who will no longer be mandated to pay personal income tax. The Department of Finance estimates that this will increase the number of tax-exempt Filipino workers from at least 5.1 Million to 6.3 Million.1 Amid heightened global economic uncertainties arising from international geopolitical tensions, this legislative proposal seeks to provide tangible relief to millions of Filipino families by allowing them to retain a larger part of their wages and increasing their disposable income. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. YSABEL MARIA J. label: HB 10697
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution commands the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education. Fulfilling this mandate requires more than the effective performance of individual education agencies. It demands a coherent governance framework that enables the entire education sector to pursue common priorities, align resources, and sustain reforms across administrations. The present trifocalized system assigns distinct mandates to the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA). While this structure allows each agency to focus on its respective sector, the challenges confronting Philippine education increasingly cut across institutional boundaries. Learner progression, teacher and education workforce requirements, skills development, labor market responsiveness, data interoperability, scholarship policy, and the transition of learners from basic education to higher education, technical-vocational education and training, and employment all require sustained coordination among several agencies of government. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) has underscored the need for seamless and integrated delivery of education and for stronger coordination across the education system. In response to this governance gap, Administrative Order No. 36, series of 2025, established the Education and Workforce Development Group as a central coordinating mechanism for education and workforce development. The gains from such coordination, however, should not depend solely on an administrative issuance or on the priorities of a particular administration. A permanent statutory mechanism is necessary to provide institutional continuity, clear accountability, and sustained policy alignment. This bill therefore seeks to create the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) under the Office of the President as the primary mechanism for directing, coordinating, and monitoring education and workforce development reforms across the Executive Branch. Chaired by the President, the Council will bring together the principal agencies responsible for education, skills development, science and technology, labor and employment, budgeting, and national development planning. The proposed Council is tasked to align agency policies, plans, programs, and budgets with the National Education and Workforce Development Plan; coordinate and monitor priority reforms; develop a comprehensive human resource development plan for the education sector; improve labor market information to better guide learners and institutions; establish an interoperable learner data system; rationalize overlapping inter-agency mechanisms; and institute a results-based monitoring and evaluation framework. It will likewise provide a regular venue for ensuring that major education reforms are implemented coherently and that responsible agencies remain accountable for agreed targets and outcomes. By institutionalizing a permanent apex coordinating body, this measure seeks to address fragmentation without diminishing the statutory mandates of the country's education agencies. Rather, it provides the mechanism through which their respective mandates may operate as parts of a single, coherent education and workforce development system. This will help ensure continuity of reforms, more efficient use of public resources, and policies that respond to the needs of Filipino learners and the evolving demands of the economy. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. 2 FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10698
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE POSSESSION AND OPERATION OF UNMANNED SYSTEMS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Unmanned systems, commonly known as drones, have become increasingly accessible and are now widely used for recreational, commercial, agricultural, scientific, media, and government purposes. Their rapid advancement has significantly contributed to innovation, improved efficiency, and economic development across various sectors. However, the proliferation of drone technology has also brought about serious concerns relating to public safety, national security, privacy, aviation safety, and the protection of critical infrastructure. Incidents involving unauthorized drone operations near airports, military installations, government facilities, densely populated areas, and public events have highlighted the need for a comprehensive legal framework governing their possession and operation. At present, while existing regulations issued by the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) provide operational guidelines for unmanned aircraft, there remains no comprehensive legislation that establishes uniform standards for the registration, possession, operation, accountability, and enforcement mechanisms applicable to unmanned systems. Likewise, there is a need to strengthen coordination among concerned government agencies in monitoring, regulating, and addressing violations involving drone operations. This proposed measure seeks to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the possession and operation of unmanned systems. It aims to ensure that drones are utilized responsibly while safeguarding public safety, protecting individual privacy, preserving national security, and promoting the orderly integration of unmanned systems into Philippine airspace. The bill likewise provides appropriate penalties for unlawful possession and operation, unauthorized surveillance, interference with lawful activities, and other prohibited acts, while recognizing the legitimate use of drones for commercial, educational, research, humanitarian, agriculture, disaster response, and other lawful purposes. By striking a balance between technological innovation and public welfare, this measure promotes the responsible development of the unmanned systems industry while ensuring that emerging technologies are utilized in a manner consistent with the Constitution, existing laws, and the best interests of the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 10699
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 73 AND 75 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS "AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE UNDER A RE-ORGANIZED DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES," AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8551, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS, THE "PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE REFORM AND REORGANIZATION ACT OF 1998," AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine National Police (PNP) stands at the forefront of maintaining peace and order and enforcing the laws of the land. In the faithful performance of these duties, PNP personnel are constantly exposed to dangerous situations that place their lives, safety, and well-being at risk. It is therefore imperative that the State provide them with a retirement and disability benefits system that is fair, responsive, and commensurate with the sacrifices they make in the service of the Filipino people. Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the “Department of the Interior and Local Government Act of 1990”, as amended by Republic Act No. 8551 or the “Philippine National Police Reform and Reorganization Act of 1998”, prescribes the retirement and disability benefits of uniformed personnel of the Philippine National Police. While these provisions have served their purpose for many years, changing economic conditions, increasing cost of living, and the evolving demands placed upon law enforcement personnel necessitate a review and updating of the existing law. This proposed measure seeks to amend Sections 73 of RA No. 6975, as amended, to strengthen the retirement and disability benefits accorded to PNP personnel by increasing the retirement pay of disabled personnel to ninety percent (90%) of the most updated salary corresponding to the rank held at the time of retirement. It likewise amends Section 75 by granting retiring PNP personnel, including non-officer personnel, the option to receive in advance and in lump sum their retirement pay corresponding to the first three years, to be released within six months from effectivity of their retirement. These proposed amendments reaffirm the State’s policy of promoting the welfare of those who have faithfully served in the Philippine National Police. By enhancing retirement benefits, the measure recognizes the sacrifices made by both police officers and non-officer personnel and ensures that they retire with greater financial security and dignity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 10700
title: AN ACT PROMOTING AND INSTITUTIONALIZING THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE NEO- ETHNIC PHILIPPINE TEXTILE AND HANDLOOM WEAVING INDUSTRY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine textile industry is one of the country's industries with significant potential for growth. Neo-ethnic textiles not only promote and preserve our culture but also support local weavers and artisans whose craftsmanship has been passed down through generations. The intricate designs, vibrant colors, and indigenous patterns found in Philippine textiles reflect the richness of our history and embody the unique identity of the Filipino people. In the Philippines, native textiles have become an integral part of many aspects of our lives. They are prominently featured in academic regalia, where their beautiful patterns and colors represent the identity and traditions of our educational institutions. Likewise, more Filipinos are incorporating neo-ethnic textiles into formal attire and other occasions, demonstrating a growing appreciation for clothing made from indigenous materials and native fabrics. This increasing demand highlights the vast opportunities for the Philippine clothing and textile industry to flourish while preserving our cultural heritage. This bill seeks to promote and institutionalize the development of the neo-ethnic Philippine textile and handloom weaving industry by providing the necessary support for local weavers, encouraging innovation, and creating greater market opportunities for Philippine-made textiles. By strengthening this industry, the State not only preserves an important part of the nation's cultural heritage but also generates sustainable livelihoods and contributes to inclusive economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. YSABEL MARIA J. label: HB 10704
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to promote the responsible and wider adoption of behind-the-meter electricity generation and energy storage systems by simplifying regulatory requirements, removing unnecessary restrictions, and establishing clear and uniform procedures for their installation and, when necessary, interconnection with the distribution system. Reliable, affordable, and sustainable electricity is essential to the daily lives of Filipino families, the growth of businesses, and the continued development of our communities. Today, consumers have greater access to technologies such as rooftop solar panels, battery energy storage systems, and other distributed energy resources that allow them to generate and store electricity primarily for their own use. These technologies can reduce electricity expenses, improve the reliability of power supply, and lessen dependence on the electric grid. However, consumers continue to encounter unnecessary procedures, regulatory requirements, and restrictions before they can install and operate these systems, even when such systems are intended solely for their own use and do not affect the public electricity network. Subjecting consumer-owned systems to requirements designed for commercial power producers may impose disproportionate burdens, discourage investment, and prevent households and businesses from taking advantage of technologies that can contribute to greater energy efficiency and resilience. Through this measure, consumers who generate or store electricity solely for their own should not necessarily be subjected to regulations intended for commercial power producers. Where interconnection with the distribution system is necessary, this measure seeks to establish clear, transparent, predictable, and uniform procedures that protect the safety and reliability of the electric power system without creating unreasonable barriers to adoption. The measure is consistent with the energy priorities articulated by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. in his 2026 State of the Nation Address, particularly the need to ensure reliable and affordable electricity and strengthen the country's energy security. Enabling consumers to generate and store electricity for their own use can complement the government's efforts to develop a more resilient, sustainable, and secure energy sector. By removing unnecessary regulatory obstacles while preserving appropriate safety, technical, and regulatory standards, this bill empowers Filipino consumers to take a more active role in meeting their own energy needs. It promotes consumer choice, encourages investment in modern and cleaner energy technologies, supports energy security, and contributes to a more reliable and resilient electric power sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JESUS “Jess” R. label: HB 10708
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MODERNIZATION AND CAPABILITY ENHANCEMENT OF THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Peace and order are indispensable foundations of a stable, secure, and progressive nation. Article 2, Section 5 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes the State's duty to maintain peace and order, protect life, liberty, and property, and promote the general welfare.1 As the country's primary law enforcement agency, the Philippine National Police (PNP) plays a vital role in fulfilling these constitutional responsibilities through the effective enforcement of the law, prevention of crime, and protection of the Filipino people. As it is written in Proverbs 21:15, “When justice is done, it brings joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.” The pursuit of justice requires more than the dedication and courage of police officers. It likewise demands that the State provide its law enforcement institutions with the necessary resources, modern technology, and institutional support to effectively respond to the increasingly complex and evolving security environment while upholding the rule of law and respecting human rights. In recent years, criminal activities have become more sophisticated, driven by rapid technological advancements, the expansion of cyber-enabled crimes, transnational criminal networks, terrorism, and other emerging threats to national security.2 At the same time, many police units continue to face limitations in infrastructure, communications systems, mobility assets, forensic capabilities, and other mission- critical equipment that are essential for effective law enforcement and public safety operations. While the PNP has continuously undertaken capability enhancement initiatives, these efforts have largely relied on periodic appropriations and fragmented procurement programs, such as the Capability Enhancement Program funded in Fiscal Year (FY) 2025. 3 For instance, a Department of the Interior and Local Government accomplishment report shows that from July 2022 to May 2024 alone, the PNP secured over five billion pesos worth of firearms, vehicles, and communication and 1 The 1987 Philippine Constitution 2 United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute. (2026, January) The New Criminal Code: Deciphering Threats in Cyberspace. 3 Guzman, J. (2026, April 6). PNP ensured new equipment, assets to enhance operational capability and mobility. Retrieved from: https://pia.gov.ph/news/pnp-ensures-new-equipment-assets-to-enhance- operational-capability-mobility/ on July 1, 2026 investigation equipment under this same Capability Enhancement Program,4 a scale of acquisition that illustrates both the magnitude of the PNP's continuing modernization needs and the piecemeal, year-to-year character of the funding mechanisms that currently support them. However, the absence of a comprehensive, long-term modernization framework has limited the systematic development of police infrastructure, operational capabilities, and technological advancements, thereby affecting the PNP's capacity to effectively respond to evolving public safety and security challenges. This bill seeks to institutionalize the PNP Modernization and Capability Enhancement Program by establishing a comprehensive and sustained framework for the modernization of police infrastructure, facilities, communications and information technology systems, mobility assets, investigative and forensic capabilities, and other mission-essential equipment. It likewise promotes transparent and strategic procurement mechanisms, strengthens coordination with relevant government agencies, encourages local industry participation and technology transfer, and ensures that modernization efforts remain responsive to evolving national security requirements and international best practices. By providing the PNP with modern capabilities and adequate resources, this measure seeks to build a highly capable, professional, technology-driven, and community- oriented police organization that can more effectively protect the Filipino people, uphold the rule of law, preserve public order, and contribute to national peace, security, and sustainable development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. BOCOBO 4 Philippine News Agency (2025). label: HB 10709
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROPERTY RIGHTS OF PERSONS WHO HAVE ACTUALLY CONTRIBUTED TO THE ACQUISITION OF PROPERTY DURING COHABITATION NOT GOVERNED BY ARTICLE 147 OF THE FAMILY CODE, AMENDING ARTICLE 148 OF EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. 209, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “FAMILY CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the landmark case of Jennifer C. Josef v. Evalyn G. Ursua (G.R. No. 267469, February 5, 2025), the Supreme Court clarified that same-sex cohabitants are not governed by Article 147 of the Family Code because they are not legally capacitated to marry each other. Nevertheless, their property relations may be governed by Article 148, provided that actual contribution to the acquisition of property is established. The Court further held that documentary acknowledgments of contribution constitute competent evidence of ownership and that a party who has expressly recognized another's proprietary interest may be estopped from subsequently denying such interest. While the decision significantly advances the protection of equitable property rights, its application remains dependent upon judicial interpretation on a case-by-case basis. There is currently no express statutory provision recognizing documentary acknowledgments of contribution or establishing clear evidentiary standards for cohabiting persons whose unions are not covered by Article 147. This measure seeks to codify the doctrine established by the Supreme Court by expressly recognizing that any person who has actually contributed money, property, or industry to the acquisition, improvement, preservation, or amortization of property during cohabitation may establish co-ownership through competent evidence, regardless of the legal nature of the parties' relationship, consistent with Article 148 of the Family Code. It must be clarified that this measure neither alters the existing laws on marriage nor creates a new form of civil union. It merely protects legitimate property rights founded upon actual contribution and equity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10710
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE MAINTENANCE MEDICATION, VITAMINS, AND SUPPLEMENTS FOR SENIOR CITIZENS 4 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 7 Section 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Lingap Gamot at Resistensya Pack Para sa Nakatatandang Pinoy Act." Sec. 2. Declaration of Policy. – The State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development, which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health, and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost, giving priority to the needs of the underprivileged, sick, elderly, persons with disabilities, women, and children. It is hereby declared the policy of the State to promote and protect the health and well-being of senior citizens by providing free medical care and support to ensure their continued and meaningful participation and contribution in society. Sec. 3. Free Maintenance Medications, Vitamins, and Supplements. – The government shall provide free maintenance medications, vitamins, and supplements to all senior citizens, as defined under Republic Act No. 9994, otherwise known as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010. Sec. 4. Eligibility and Registration. – To qualify for the free monthly maintenance medications, vitamins, and supplements, a senior citizen must: a) be a registered senior citizen with the Office of Senior Citizens Affairs (OSCA); b) be enlisted in the target client list of the barangay health center where they reside; c) be assigned to a primary healthcare provider; and d) have a valid prescription issued within the last three (3) months. Sec. 5. Access to Maintenance Medications, Vitamins, and Supplements. – The free maintenance medications, vitamins, and supplements shall be accessed through barangay health centers, Botika ng Bayan, and/or deputized and accredited pharmacies: Provided, That access to and delivery of these items for the oldest-old, frail, and bedridden senior citizens shall be done directly by designated barangay health workers. Sec. 6. PhilHealth GAMOT for Senior Citizens. – Maintenance medications, vitamins, and supplements needed by senior citizens but not readily available shall be covered under, and in addition to, PhilHealth's current Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT) package.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The need for sustained pharmaceutical support has become even more pressing as the country's elderly population continues to expand. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), there were approximately 11.42 million Filipinos aged 60 years and above in 2024, accounting for 10.2% of the country's household population, up from 9.22 million or 8.5% in 2020. This growing segment of the population underscores the urgent need for stronger and more accessible health interventions specifically designed to address the evolving needs of Filipino senior citizens. Chronic non-communicable diseases remain the leading causes of illness and death among older Filipinos. According to the Department of Health, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory diseases, and hypertension account for a substantial share of morbidity and mortality in the country, with older persons disproportionately affected. These conditions require uninterrupted maintenance medications to prevent complications such as stroke, heart attack, kidney failure, blindness, and disability. However, many senior citizens, especially those from low-income households, are unable to consistently purchase their prescribed medicines because of financial constraints. According to the 2023 National Health Accounts, household out-of-pocket spending continues to account for 44.3% of the country's current health expenditures, indicating that many Filipino families still bear the primary burden of healthcare costs. This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive government program that provides free maintenance medications, vitamins, and supplements to all qualified senior citizens through barangay health centers, Botika ng Bayan, accredited pharmacies, and direct delivery by barangay health workers for frail, oldest-old, and bedridden beneficiaries. It likewise strengthens existing health financing mechanisms by expanding the coverage of PhilHealth's Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT) package to include medicines that may not be readily available through regular government channels. By integrating medicine provision with primary healthcare services and local government implementation, the measure promotes better treatment adherence, disease prevention, and healthier aging among Filipino senior citizens. Ensuring that senior citizens receive their prescribed maintenance is a long-term investment in public health, social protection, and human dignity. By reducing preventable complications, avoidable hospital admissions, and catastrophic healthcare expenses among elderly Filipinos, the proposed measure advances the State's constitutional duty to protect the health of its people and uphold the welfare of one of the nation's most vulnerable sectors. The immediate passage of this bill is, therefore, earnestly sought. 1 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10710 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma. Victoria Co-Pilar AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE MAINTENANCE MEDICATION, VITAMINS, AND SUPPLEMENTS FOR SENIOR CITIZENS 4

label: HB 10711
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL GROUND FOR CHANGE OF FIRST NAME, THEREBY AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE SECTION 4 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9048 4 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 7 Section 1. Section 4 of RA 9048 is hereby amended to read as follows: “Section 4. Grounds for Change of First Name or Nickname. – The petition for change of first name or nickname may be allowed in any of the following cases: 11 (1) Xxx (4) THE PETITIONER EXERCISES THE RIGHT TO PERSONAL AUTONOMY, PROVIDED THAT SUCH CHANGE SHALL BE ALLOWED ONLY ONCE AND IS NOT MADE FOR FRAUDULENT OR MALICIOUS PURPOSES. 16 Sec. 2. Separability Clause. – If any part, section, or provision of this Act is held invalid or unconstitutional, the remaining provisions not affected shall remain in full force and effect.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A person's name is a fundamental aspect of identity, dignity, and individuality. The principles of individual liberty and self-expression are among the hallmarks of our great vibrant democracy. Every person is afforded the freedom to define and express one’s identity, so long as the exercise of such freedom does not prejudice the rights of others or the public interest. When we think of our first names, it is more than a mere entry in the civil registry; it is the name by which a person is identified in everything that matters. In school, employment, financial transactions, government records, and everyday social interactions, we are known by our first names. It is our very mark in society. Over the course of one's life, an individual may come to identify more closely with a different first name that better reflects one's identity rather than the name by which one has long been known. Consistent with these principles, Republic Act No. 9048 authorized the administrative change of first name under specified circumstances, sparing thousands of Filipinos from costly and time-consuming judicial proceedings. Nevertheless, the law remains narrowly drawn, as it limits the administrative change of a first name to only three specific statutory grounds: the first name is embarrassing or impractical; the petitioner has long and consistently used another first name; or the change will prevent confusion. As a result, individuals who seek to adopt a first name solely as an exercise of personal autonomy remain without an appropriate administrative remedy. This limitation fails to reflect the evolving recognition that personal identity encompasses an individual's reasonable freedom to determine how one wishes to be known and identified as. As society becomes more dynamic and individuals place greater importance on self- identification, the law should likewise evolve to accommodate legitimate requests that do not prejudice public order or the rights of third persons. This bill therefore proposes to amend Section 4 of Republic Act No. 9048 by recognizing the exercise of personal autonomy as an additional ground for the administrative change of a first name. To safeguard the integrity of the civil registry, the proposed ground is subject to clear limitations: the change may be availed of only once and only when it is not sought for any fraudulent, malicious, or unlawful purpose. These safeguards preserve the State's interest in preventing identity fraud while affording individuals reasonable latitude in determining the name by which they wish to be known. Recognizing personal autonomy in matters of one's first name is consistent with the constitutional values of human dignity, liberty, and the free development of personality. Identity is not merely an administrative concern; it is a fundamental expression of personhood that deserves reasonable legal recognition. Or simply because for a lot of people: to be known matters. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session 10711 HOUSE BILL NO. _________ Introduced by Representative Ma.
