label: HB 10712
title: AN ACT INCREASING BY FIFTY PERCENT (50%) THE EXCISE TAX ON SWEETENED BEVERAGES, IMPOSING AN EXCISE TAX ON REFINED SUGAR, AND AMENDING SECTION 150-B OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the people’s right to health and directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. Consistent with this policy, Section 150-B of the National Internal Revenue Code imposes an excise tax on sweetened beverages. In carrying out this constitutional policy, legislation should go beyond regulating conduct. It should also help people understand the reasons behind public health measures and encourage them to make informed choices. This finds a fitting parallel in 1 Corinthians 2:13 (KJV), which speaks of …speaking, teaching, and comparing…” These interconnected acts suggest a process of learning, comprehension, and appreciation, and right application. Applied to public health, it is not enough for people to simply know the risks of excessive sugar consumption. They should understand those risks, appreciate their consequences, and be able to use that knowledge in making healthier choices. At present, the law imposes ₱6.00 per liter on beverages using caloric or non- caloric sweeteners, or a combination of both, and ₱12.00 per liter on beverages using high-fructose corn syrup. Beverages using purely coconut sap sugar or purely steviol glycosides are exempt.1 This bill increases these rates by fifty percent (50%), from ₱6.00 to ₱9.00 per liter and from ₱12.00 to ₱18.00 per liter, respectively. Except for the rate adjustments, it retains the existing coverage, definitions, exemptions, labeling requirements, 1 BIR Ruling No. 343-2021, September 30, 2021, Sec. 150-B of the NIRC as amended. Page 1 of 10 payment rules, penalties, and regulatory safeguards for sweetened beverages. 2 The bill also imposes a new excise tax of ₱5.00 per kilogram on refined sugar produced in the Philippines for domestic consumption and on imported refined sugar released for domestic consumption. For this purpose, refined sugar is principally identified by a polarimeter reading of 99.5° or higher. Color, production process, refinery status, laboratory results, and Sugar Regulatory Administration documentation may be used as supporting evidence under the implementing rules. Existing classifications likewise recognize sugar with a polarimeter reading of 99.5° or higher and/or a color of 800 ICU or less as refined sugar.3 The refined-sugar tax applies to sugar as the product subject to tax. Its subsequent use as an ingredient does not result in a second tax under the same provision. A finished beverage remains subject to the sweetened-beverage tax if it independently falls within Section 150-B. Exports and qualified uses under bond shall be treated as tax suspensions. The tax shall become due upon diversion to domestic consumption or failure to account for the sugar. The Bureau of Internal Revenue, Bureau of Customs, and Sugar Regulatory Administration shall harmonize classification, testing, documentation, bonded transfers, and enforcement procedures. Before the refined-sugar excise tax takes effect, the Department of Finance, in consultation with the concerned agencies, shall submit to Congress a study on its projected revenue, price, health, industry, and enforcement effects, including its impact on consumers, small businesses, sugarcane farmers, smuggling, and the domestic sugar industry. Congress shall review the tax and its implementation three (3) years after effectivity and determine whether the rate and regulatory framework should be retained, amended, or repealed. Revenues from the existing sweetened-beverage excise tax shall continue to be governed by Section 288-A of the National Internal Revenue Code. Fifty percent (50%) of such revenues shall remain earmarked for PhilHealth, medical assistance, and the Health Facilities Enhancement Program. This statutory allocation shall not be altered, reduced, transferred, or repurposed.4 Revenues from the new refined-sugar excise tax shall accrue to the General Fund and shall be subject to appropriation through the annual General Appropriations Act. 2 Id. 3 Secretary of Finance, et al. v. Muñez, et al. G.R. No. 212687, July 20, 2022. 4 Pimentel III, et al. v. House of Representatives, et al. G.R. No. 274778/275405/276233, December 3, 2025. Page 2 of 10 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. label: HB 10713
title: AN ACT FIXING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF BARANGAY OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN TO FIVE (5) YEARS, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12232 OR “AN ACT SETTING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF THE BARANGAY OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay governments, as the frontline units of government, play a vital role in implementing national and local programs, maintaining peace and order, resolving community disputes, responding to disasters and emergencies, and delivering basic services at the grassroots. The effective discharge of these responsibilities depends largely on the stability, continuity, and institutional capacity of barangay governments and their officials. This measure seeks to strengthen governance at the barangay level by extending the term of office of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials from four (4) years to five (5) years and by resetting the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections from the first Monday of November 2026 to the first Monday of November 2028. The proposed five-year term will provide barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials with adequate time to plan, implement, and complete development programs and projects, ensure continuity in governance, reduce disruptions caused by frequent electoral exercises, and allow local officials to focus more on public service than on recurring election cycles. Correspondingly, postponing the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections to November 2028 is necessary to harmonize the election schedule with the proposed five-year term of office and to ensure an orderly transition to the new electoral cycle. This will promote stability in local governance, avoid disruptions in the implementation of ongoing community programs, and enable barangay governments to sustain development initiatives that require longer periods for planning and execution. Ultimately, this measure reinforces the role of barangays, as envisioned under the Local Government Code of 1991, as the primary planning and implementing units of government policies, plans, programs, projects, and activities within their communities, as well as forums where the collective views of the people are expressed, consensus is built, and local disputes are amicably resolved. By providing greater continuity in leadership and a more stable governance framework, this measure seeks to strengthen grassroots institutions and improve the delivery of public services to every Filipino community. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JANETTE L. GARIN HON. DAVID “JAY-JAY” C. SUAREZ HON. FRANCISCO PAOLO P. ORTEGA V HON. JEFFERSON F. label: HB 10714
title: AN ACT FIXING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF BARANGAY AND SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN OFFICIALS TO FIVE (5) YEARS AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12232 OR “AN ACT SETTING THE TERM OF OFFICE OF THE BARANGAY OFFICIALS AND MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The barangay, as the basic political unit of the Philippines, plays a vital role in delivering essential government services, implementing community development programs, and ensuring effective grassroots governance. As frontline public servants, barangay officials require sufficient time to fully implement their programs and address the evolving needs of their constituents. The existing four-year (4) term of office of barangay officials may not always provide adequate time to complete long-term projects and sustain development initiatives. Extending the term of office of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials to five (5) years will provide greater continuity, stability, and effectiveness in local governance while maintaining democratic accountability through regular elections. To facilitate an orderly transition to a five-year electoral cycle, this measure seeks to postpone the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections to November 2028 as a one-time transitional measure. This will allow the electoral calendar to be aligned with the proposed five-year term of office and ensure uninterrupted delivery of public services through a holdover arrangement for incumbent officials until their successors are elected and qualified. Recognizing the need to balance continuity of leadership with accountability and leadership renewal, this measure likewise provides for nationwide consultations among barangay officials, local government units, government agencies, and other stakeholders to establish an appropriate framework on term limitations for elective barangay officials. Through this reform, the State strengthens grassroots governance by empowering barangay leaders with sufficient time to pursue sustainable community development while preserving the democratic principles of accountability, participation, and responsive leadership. label: HB 10719
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FRESH FILIPINO GRADUATES OF PHILIPPINE TERTIARY EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, UNIVERSITIES, COLLEGES AND OTHER TRAINING INSTITUTIONS, OF A ONE-TIME CASH GRANT OF FIVE THOUSAND PESOS (PHP 5,000)
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The transition from educational institutions to the workforce is a critical milestone for fresh graduates and young adults. However, immediate access to employment opportunities is rarely guaranteed upon graduation. Beyond a competitive job market, fresh graduates face immediate financial hurdles, such as the incidental and necessary expenses incurred while searching for work, including transportation, communication, printing, and attire. These are costs that many graduates simply cannot afford. Under Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities. Article II, Section 13 recognizes the vital role of youth in nation-building. This mandates the State to enact policies that will protect their interest and welfare while fostering their potential. While Republic Act No. 11261 or the “First Time Jobseekers Assistance Act” exempts first-time jobseekers from paying fees and charges for government-issued pre-employment documents, there are still financial burdens for job seeking fresh graduates during employment search. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), in June 2026, the unemployment rate in the country increased at 4.9%, with an estimated 2.59 millions unemployed Filipinos.1 Among the 592,000 youth aged 15-24 seeking jobs for the first time, only 310,000 landed gainful employment, leaving 282,000 young job seekers without job. To address the same, this bill seeks to establish a one-time grant of five thousand pesos (PHP 5,000) to qualified Fresh Filipino graduates. The grant aims to provide assistance for the necessary and incidental expenses of the job seeking fresh graduates, complementing the existing benefits under RA 11261. By easing the financial strain on our job seeking fresh graduates, this legislative measure provide a fair starting point for young filipinos as they transition into productive members of the workforce. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 10720
title: AN ACT RESTRUCTURING THE INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATES OF RESIDENT CITIZENS AND RESIDENT ALIENS, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 24 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The prevailing economic conditions that our country faces have compelled us to reconsider restructuring the current tax schedule, as it exacerbates the financial burdens carried by Filipinos. It is imperative to enact measures to provide immediate economic relief to low- to middle-income earners, as well as self- employed professionals. This proposed bill seeks to amend the individual tax schedule by increasing the non-taxable annual income threshold from P250,000 to P350,000. While this adjustment may result in a short-term reduction in direct income tax collections, expanding the take-home pay of our low- to middle income earners directly strengthens their purchasing power. Beyond cushioning households against the rising costs of basic goods and services, this expanded exemption will give vital liquidity into local commerce and stimulate broader macroeconomic growth. Further, the possible fiscal impact is balanced by the fact that the increase of the disposable income of the low- and middle-income families leads to a proportionate increase in spending on basic commodities. This, in effect, directly increase market activity. The restructuring of the individual tax rates schedule aligns with the constitutional mandate to establish a progressive system of taxation, while effectively responding to the economic and societal realities. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. It serves as a natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, and other hazards, while sustaining water resources, biodiversity, livelihoods, and climate resilience. label: HB 10732
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE STOCKPILING OF STRATEGIC AND CRITICAL DRUGS AND MEDICINES, VACCINES, DEVICES, AND MATERIALS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE HEALTH PROCUREMENT AND STOCKPILING BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In May 2026, the Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB) issued its final report regarding the global preparedness in the face of health emergencies. As the body created by the World Health Organization ten years ago to drive reforms to make the world safer, its last report stated that local preparedness has been outpaced by emerging trends. It further stated that momentum towards equitable access to vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics, and countermeasures have begun to reverse. The conclusions of the GPMB were not only brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, but also by the confluence of all the other health emergencies experienced by the world since then. According to the 2025 World Risk Index Report conducted by by Germany’s Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft and Ruhr University Bochum, the Philippines ranked first in the list of disaster-prone countries in the world. This, along with report of the GPMB, highlights the need for a continuous supply of essential and critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials to effectively and swiftly address public health emergencies. label: HB 10733
title: AN ACT TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT THE RIGHTS OF NATURE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 16, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that the State shall “protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.” For decades, environmental legislation in the Philippines has operated primarily under a human-centered framework—treating nature as mere property, a repository of natural resources, or an object to be exploited for economic advancement, provided that regulatory minimums are met. However, the escalating global climate crisis, biodiversity loss, deforestation, marine degradation, and severe weather disturbances demonstrate the clear limitations of this traditional approach. This bill introduces a transformative legal framework: the legal recognition of the Rights of Nature. By conferring legal personality upon natural ecosystems and processes, this proposed measure shifts our jurisprudence from viewing nature as property to recognizing it as a rights- bearing entity possessing the inherent right to exist, persist, regenerate, and be restored. Recognizing the rights of nature does not oppose human development; rather, it guarantees that human activities, economic growth, and technological innovation remain in dynamic balance with the carrying capacity of the Earth. Protecting nature's right to regenerate is, in truth, the ultimate defense of human rights and the well-being of future generations of Filipinos. In view of the urgency of safeguarding our natural heritage and securing an ecologically sustainable future for the nation, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SERGIO C. DAGOOC PRESLEY C. label: HB 10734
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES OPERATING IN PROVINCES AND CITIES HOSTING GEOTHERMAL ENERGY RESOURCES OR GEOTHERMAL POWER GENERATION FACILITIES, INCLUDING PROVINCES ADJACENT TO HIGHLY URBANIZED CITIES AND INDEPENDENT COMPONENT CITIES HOSTING SUCH RESOURCES OR FACILITIES, TO DIRECTLY PURCHASE ELECTRICITY FROM QUALIFIED GEOTHERMAL POWER PRODUCERS, EXEMPTING SUCH PURCHASES FROM THE COMPETITIVE SELECTION PROCESS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 23 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Provinces and local communities that host geothermal resources make a continuing and substantial contribution to the country’s energy security. They provide the land, infrastructure, workforce, and local environment that allow indigenous geothermal energy to be explored, developed, generated, and transmitted to consumers throughout the country. Yet the presence of a geothermal power facility within or near a locality does not automatically result in lower electricity rates for the families, schools, hospitals, farms, and businesses in the host and surrounding communities. The Constitution recognizes that local governments and their inhabitants must receive an equitable share in the benefits derived from the utilization and development of national wealth within their respective areas. This principle is reflected in the Local Government Code, which provides that a significant portion of the proceeds derived from hydrothermal, geothermal, and other sources of energy shall be applied to lowering the cost of electricity in the locality where such energy source is located. The same principle must apply when the geothermal resource or facility is located within a highly urbanized city or independent component city. Although these cities are politically and administratively independent from the provinces around them, their geothermal resources and power facilities form part of a wider geographic, economic, environmental, and energy ecosystem. The neighboring provinces and their communities may provide the workforce, transport routes, watersheds, transmission corridors, public infrastructure, and other resources necessary for the continued operation of the geothermal facility. They may likewise experience the environmental, social, and economic consequences of geothermal development. For this reason, the benefits granted under this measure should also extend to the province within which a highly urbanized city or independent component city is geographically situated, as well as to provinces whose territorial boundaries are directly adjacent to such host city. Political boundaries should not prevent surrounding communities from receiving a fair and measurable share in the benefits arising from geothermal resources located within their immediate geographic area. Under Republic Act No. 9136, otherwise known as the “Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001” or EPIRA, distribution utilities are required to supply electricity to their captive markets in the least-cost manner. In implementing this obligation, distribution utilities are generally required to procure their long-term power requirements through a Competitive Selection Process. Competition remains an important consumer-protection mechanism. However, the Competitive Selection Process may become impracticable when a distribution utility seeks to purchase electricity from a particular geothermal power producer located within its own host province, or within a highly urbanized city or independent component city adjacent to the province, and the intended transaction is designed specifically to reduce or stabilize electricity costs for host and neighboring communities. 2 The law must therefore provide a carefully defined exception. Distribution utilities, including electric cooperatives, operating in geothermal host provinces, geothermal host cities, and qualified adjacent provinces should be permitted to negotiate directly with geothermal power producers operating within the relevant host locality. Such agreements should be exempt from the Competitive Selection Process while remaining subject to the full review and approval of the Energy Regulatory Commission. The proposed measure preserves the fundamental principle of least-cost electricity. It requires the Energy Regulatory Commission to determine whether the resulting generation rate is just, reasonable, prudent, and beneficial to consumers. It likewise establishes safeguards against excessive pricing, overcontracting, self-dealing, market abuse, imprudent costs, and anti- competitive conduct. All savings, discounts, rebates, and other economic benefits arising from direct geothermal power procurement must be fully and transparently passed on to electricity consumers. By allowing host and adjacent provinces to source power directly from geothermal resources located within their immediate geographic area, this measure gives concrete meaning to the constitutional principle that the people who host, sustain, and are directly affected by the development of national wealth must be among its primary beneficiaries. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. label: HB 10735
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PAMBANSANG AGAPAY SA PAMILYA AT MALILIIT NA NEGOSYO (PAMANA) PROGRAM, PROVIDING A DIRECT ANNUAL SUBSIDY TO MINIMUM WAGE EARNERS AND THEIR FAMILIES THROUGH DIGITAL WALLETS FOR EXCLUSIVE USE IN LOCAL MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Millions of Filipino minimum wage earners continue to grapple with the rising cost of basic goods, while micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) which account for 99.5% of all business establishments and employ the majority of the Filipino workforce — struggle with thin margins and limited consumer demand. This measure addresses both problems with a single intervention: a direct, regular, and digitally delivered subsidy to minimum wage earners and their families that can only be spent in registered local MSMEs. Unlike traditional cash assistance programs that are one-time, leakage-prone, and often captured by intermediaries, this bill guarantees that (1) assistance reaches families directly through their digital wallets, (2) the benefit is spread throughout the year through monthly disbursements and a daily spending limit, encouraging use for daily essentials rather than lump-sum consumption, and (3) every peso of public assistance circulates within local communities, stimulating neighborhood economies rather than large retail chains. This measure is designed to complement, not duplicate, existing social protection programs. Families already receiving assistance under the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) or its successor conditional cash transfer program remain covered by that program and are excluded from this Act, ensuring that public funds reach a distinct population: minimum wage earners who work full-time yet remain financially strained, and who are typically ineligible for 4Ps but still without a dedicated income supplement. The measure likewise accelerates financial inclusion and digitalization among both households and small businesses, consistent with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. title: AN ACT PROMOTING BEHIND-THE-METER SOLAR ENERGY GENERATION AND BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS FOR OWN-USE, ESTABLISHING A STREAMLINED REGULATORY, SAFETY, AND CONSUMER PROTECTION FRAMEWORK, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 21 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Republic of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The Philippines continues to face the challenge of ensuring an electricity supply that is affordable, reliable, secure, and resilient. Advances in solar photovoltaic generation and battery energy storage technologies now provide households, businesses, health facilities, educational institutions, government establishments, and other electricity end-users with greater opportunities to generate and store electricity primarily for their own use. 22 Behind-the-meter (BTM) solar generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS) can enable consumers to reduce their dependence on electricity purchased from the distribution system, manage peak electricity consumption, improve energy resilience, and make greater use of electricity generated within their premises. Battery storage is particularly valuable because it allows electricity generated or purchased during periods of lower demand to be stored for use during periods of higher demand or interruptions in grid supply. 31 However, the adoption of these technologies should not be hindered by unnecessary or disproportionate regulatory requirements. At the same time, simplification must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards to protect consumers, electrical workers, distribution utilities, and the reliability and safety of the electric power system. 37 The Sariling Kuryente Act therefore establishes a proportionate and risk- based framework for BTM solar generation and BESS. It provides simplified regulatory treatment for standardized, low-risk systems and streamlines procedures for qualified zero-export systems, while preserving necessary technical, electrical, structural, fire, environmental, and distribution-system safety requirements. 6 The measure also strengthens consumer protection by requiring covered solar and storage equipment to comply with applicable Philippine National Standards and conformity-assessment requirements. It requires the installation and commissioning of covered systems to be undertaken by duly accredited installers and establishes appropriate accountability requirements, including mandatory liability insurance or other financial security, to protect consumers from unsafe installations, defective workmanship, and unqualified or unscrupulous service providers. 15 The bill further protects the ability of end-users to install BTM generation and energy storage systems on property they own or exclusively control, while allowing reasonable restrictions necessary for structural safety, public safety, and the protection of common property. 20 The bill also prioritizes energy storage as a means of increasing self- consumption, reducing peak demand, and supporting distribution-system reliability and resilience. It likewise recognizes the need to account for the adoption of BTM systems in electricity planning while preventing unreasonable cost shifting to consumers who do not have such systems. It also authorizes the development of appropriate financing programs, incentives, and targeted financial assistance for qualified end-users adopting BESS and integrated solar-plus-storage systems, with priority given to measures that support energy storage, reduce or shift peak demand, improve electricity reliability and resilience, and assist low-income or underserved consumers, subject to the availability of funds and applicable laws. 32 By reducing unnecessary regulatory barriers while maintaining appropriate safety, technical, environmental, and consumer-protection safeguards, the Sariling Kuryente Act seeks to make consumer-owned solar generation and energy storage simpler, faster, safer, and more accountable. 37 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 39 40 41 REP. label: HB 10747
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR YOUTH DEVELOPMENT AND EMPOWERMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a young nation. Around 32.4 million Filipinos aged 15 to 30—nearly three out of every ten Filipinos—are part of our youth population. They are students, workers, farmers, entrepreneurs, athletes, artists, volunteers, community leaders, and dreamers who are already shaping the country we will inherit. But being young in the Philippines should not mean being left to figure everything out alone. In January 2026, 14.0% of young Filipinos aged 15 to 24 were not in education, employment, or training, an increase from 11.7% a year earlier. Youth labor-force participation and employment also declined during the same period. These numbers are more than statistics. They represent young people who may be struggling to find a school, a job, a livelihood, a safe space, or simply a clear next step. Government already has many programs for the youth. We have scholarships, skills training, employment assistance, entrepreneurship programs, health services, sports programs, and opportunities for civic participation. The problem is that these opportunities are often scattered across different agencies and difficult to navigate. This bill seeks to change that. The Philippine Youth Development and Empowerment Act creates a stronger national framework that connects existing government programs and brings opportunities closer to where young people actually live. Most importantly, every barangay shall have a Youth Development Hub, managed by the Sangguniang Kabataan in partnership with the Barangay Government. Municipalities, cities, and provinces shall likewise have Youth Centers where young people can access information, referrals, training, leadership activities, employment and entrepreneurship opportunities, digital resources, sports, culture, and other development programs. Because youth development should not depend on where a young person was born. A young person in a far-flung barangay deserves the same chance as a young person in the city. The bill also creates the Department of Youth Development and Empowerment as the national institution responsible for bringing government efforts together—not to replace DepEd, CHED, TESDA, DOLE, DSWD, DTI, DA, DOH, and other agencies, but to make sure that their programs reach young people in a coordinated and meaningful way. The bill is built on a simple belief: When we invest in the youth, we are not spending for tomorrow. We are building today. Every scholarship can change a family's future. Every job opportunity can restore a young person's confidence. Every youth-led project can transform a community. Every safe space can give a young person a reason to stay, grow, and lead. The Filipino youth do not need another promise that someday they will have a place in nation-building. They need that place now. This measure seeks to give them the opportunities, spaces, support, and voice they deserve. Because the future of the Philippines should not merely be something that the youth inherit. It should be something they are empowered to build. The passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10748
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RIGHTS, PROTECTION, DEVELOPMENT, AND EMPOWERMENT OF OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH, PROVIDING FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE AND OPPORTUNITIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Filipino youth deserve a second chance—not because they have failed, but because circumstances should never be allowed to define the limits of their future. The Philippine Statistics Authority's recent data continue to show the challenge of keeping young Filipinos connected to education and productive economic activity. In July 2025, 15.9% of Filipinos aged 15 to 24 were not in education, employment, or training (NEET), higher than the 13.9% recorded a year earlier. While NEET is not exactly synonymous with out-of-school youth, it reflects a serious disconnection between young people and the pathways that lead to learning, work, and economic participation. At the same time, government already has important programs for second-chance education, particularly the Alternative Learning System under Republic Act No. 11510. What is still needed is a stronger framework that connects education with the other realities of an OSY's life: skills, work, livelihood, health, social protection, digital access, and reintegration. This is the purpose of this bill. The proposed Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth Act recognizes OSYs as rights- holders and partners in nation-building. It provides a framework for ensuring that young Filipinos outside the formal education system are not excluded from opportunities available to their peers. The measure is patterned in substance after the policy direction of Senator Raffy T. Tulfo's Senate Bill No. 2064, which was filed in the 20th Congress on April 21, 2026, and carries the same short title and broad objective of providing a Magna Carta for OSYs. It likewise builds upon the earlier SBN 2059 filed by Senator Tulfo in the 19th Congress, which proposed rights protection, education, technical-vocational training, entrepreneurship, employment, social protection, and assistance for OSYs in especially difficult circumstances. The proposed House measure, however, seeks to make the framework more coordinated and implementation-oriented. It does not create parallel education, health, labor, social-welfare, or technical-vocational systems. DepEd remains responsible for basic education and ALS; TESDA for technical-vocational education and training; DOLE for employment and labor programs; DSWD for social protection and welfare; and other agencies retain their respective statutory mandates. Instead, the bill establishes mechanisms for access, referral, convergence, and accountability. It also brings the Magna Carta closer to the community through an OSY Development Hub in every barangay, using existing public facilities whenever possible. A young person should not have to travel to a national office simply to ask: “Saan ako puwedeng mag-aral ulit? Saan ako puwedeng mag-training? May trabaho ba para sa akin? May livelihood program ba? Sino ang puwedeng tumulong sa akin?” Government should have an answer. The bill further recognizes that not every OSY will take the same path. Some may return to school. Others may pursue ALS, TESDA training, employment, entrepreneurship, agriculture, digital work, or other productive opportunities. The State's role is not to force one path upon them, but to ensure that there is a path available. This is why the measure promotes skills recognition, employment and apprenticeship pathways, entrepreneurship, digital inclusion, health and wellness, social protection, and access to essential government documents. The bill also gives special attention to OSYs facing poverty, disability, displacement, geographic isolation, family responsibilities, homelessness, conflict, or other difficult circumstances. Most importantly, this measure seeks to change the way society sees out-of-school youth. Being out of school is a circumstance—not a permanent identity. A young person who left school may still become a skilled worker, entrepreneur, farmer, professional, artist, community leader, or public servant. What matters is whether we give that young person the opportunity to begin again. The State should not merely ask why a young Filipino dropped out. We should ask what we can do to help that young Filipino move forward. The Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth Act answers that call by providing rights, opportunities, protection, and pathways to reintegration. No young Filipino should be told that because they once left school, they have already been left behind. There is always another path. There should always be another chance. The passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. At the same time, government already has important programs for second-chance education, particularly the Alternative Learning System under Republic Act No. 11510. What is still needed is a stronger framework that connects education with the other realities of an OSY's life: skills, work, livelihood, health, social protection, digital access, and reintegration. This is the purpose of this bill. The proposed Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth Act recognizes OSYs as rights- holders and partners in nation-building. label: HB 10749
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A TWENTY-YEAR SPORTS EXCELLENCE ROADMAP TO STRENGTHEN GRASSROOTS SPORTS, DEVELOP WORLD-CLASS FILIPINO ATHLETES, AND PROVIDE A SUSTAINABLE PATHWAY FOR SPORTS EXCELLENCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports can change a young person's life. For many Filipino children and young people, the barangay court, school field, public gymnasium, or community sports program is where confidence begins. It is where discipline is learned, friendships are built, talent is discovered, and dreams of representing the country first take shape. But talent alone is not enough. A Filipino athlete may have the ability to compete with the best in the world, yet lose the opportunity because there is no proper coach, inadequate equipment, limited competition exposure, insufficient nutrition, lack of sports science, or no clear pathway from grassroots competition to elite training. The Philippines therefore needs to stop treating sports development as a collection of short- term programs and start treating it as a long-term national investment. The Roadmap for Sports Excellence Act establishes a clear national pathway: Barangay → Municipality/City → Province → National Development → International Competition. It begins where Filipino talent is first discovered—the community. The bill strengthens grassroots sports by requiring every barangay, subject to available resources and existing facilities, to maintain or designate an appropriate space for sports and physical activity. It also establishes or designates Sports Development Centers at the municipal, city, and provincial levels to serve as venues for training, talent identification, competition, coaching, and athlete assessment. At the national level, the bill strengthens Sports Excellence Centers and creates a coordinated system for athlete development, sports science, sports medicine, nutrition, mental wellness, coaching, competition exposure, and education. Most importantly, the measure recognizes that an athlete is not just a medal-producing machine. Behind every medal is a young person who needs education, health care, mental wellness, protection from abuse, financial guidance, and a future beyond sports. For this reason, the bill provides for student-athlete protection, athlete scholarships and support, safeguarding mechanisms, and a post-career transition program. The measure also recognizes that sports excellence must be inclusive. A child's chance to become an athlete should not depend on whether he or she was born in Metro Manila or in a remote barangay. Young women, persons with disabilities, Indigenous youth, economically disadvantaged athletes, and other underserved groups must have meaningful access to sports opportunities. The proposed Twenty-Year Sports Excellence Roadmap will therefore provide government with something that Philippine sports has long needed: continuity. Athlete development takes years. Coaches take years to develop. Sports facilities require long-term planning. International competitiveness cannot be built within a single administration or a single competition cycle. The country needs a system that survives changes in leadership and remains focused on measurable outcomes. The goal is not simply to produce more medals. The goal is to build a country where every talented Filipino child has a chance to be discovered, developed, supported, and given the opportunity to compete at the highest level. A champion does not begin on the international stage. A champion begins in a barangay. This measure seeks to build the pathway from that barangay court to the world stage. The passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10751
title: AN ACT CREATING AN AGRICULTURAL PENSION PROGRAM TO PROVIDE SOCIAL SECURITY AND PENSION BENEFITS TO FARMERS AND FISHERFOLK
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sa bawat butil ng kanin na ating kinokonsumo, sa bawat isda o yamang dagat na ating nilalasap, may magsasakang tinitiis ang matinding init ng araw at may mangingisdang hinaharap ang mapanganib na alon ng dagat… Ngunit sa kabalintunaan, ang mga magsasaka at mangingisda ang mga sektor na nanatiling pinakaduha sa Pilipinas. Filipino farmers and fisherfolk hold the primary role in ensuring national food security in the country. They are the most indispensable yet most vulnerable sectors of the Philippine economy. Through their hard work, they feed millions of Filipino families every day despite unstable incomes, high production costs, climate-related disasters, and limited social protection. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) research showed that farmers and fisherfolk consistently have the highest poverty incidence among all basic sectors in the country. It further reported that in 2021, the poverty incidence among fisherfolk stood at 30.6%, higher than the national poverty incidence.1 This means that nearly one (1) in every three (3) Filipino farmers and fisherfolk continues to live below the poverty threshold despite their vital contribution to the country’s food supply. Critical sources of livelihood and employment still come from the sectors of agriculture and fishing. Around 22.36% of total employment in the Philippines in 2023 was generated by agriculture-related work, proving the continued dependence of millions of Filipino families on this sector for survival.2 The fisheries sector alone directly and indirectly supports the livelihoods of approximately 2.29 million Filipinos, including those engaged in capture 1Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), Fisherfolks and Farmers Remain to Have the Highest Poverty Incidences Among the Basic Sectors in 2021 (2023). 2 World Bank/ILO Data, Employment in Agriculture (% of Total Employment), Philippines (2023). fisheries, aquaculture, processing, transport, and related industries. 3 The latest records further reported that there are already more than 2.29 million registered fisherfolk in the country. 4 Filipino farmers and fisherfolk remain economically insecure, especially the elderly ones, despite their indispensable role in the country. Most agricultural workers belong to the informal sector and often lack adequate retirement savings, pension security, insurance protection, and stable access to social security benefits. Many continue to work even in old age because retirement is simply unaffordable and not an option. Studies and government reports indicate that the average Filipino farmer is now in their mid-50s, an indication of an urgent demographic concern over the sustainability of food production and the declining interest of younger generations in agriculture.5 Without a comprehensive and dedicated pension mechanism for agricultural workers, not only perpetuates poverty but also discourages younger Filipinos from entering the agriculture and fisheries sectors. Without institutional support, farming and fishing become occupations associated with poverty. This proposed measure seeks to address this longstanding inequity through the establishment of the Farmers and Fisherfolk Social Security and Pension Program, a comprehensive pension and social protection system designed to provide income security and retirement protection to farmers and fisherfolk through access to sickness, maternity, disability, retirement, death, and funeral benefits under the Social Security System (SSS), in coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) and the Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation (PCIC). Recognizing that poverty among farming and fishing households is often intergenerational, this bill further introduces an educational scholarship component for children of registered farmers and fisherfolk. Through this bill, the State empowers the next generation to break cycles of poverty while still honoring and uplifting families whose labor sustains the nation. Higit sa lahat, ang panukalang batas na ito ang nagpapamulat sa isang simpleng katotohanan: Na ang mga taong naghihirap at nagbabanat ng buto upang may makain ang ating bayan ay nararapat lamang na hindi magutom, maabuso at makalimutan. Napapanahon na upang magkaroon ng isang komprehensibo at matibay na social protection mechanism para sa ating mga magsasaka at mangingisda na malaki ang sakripisyo para sa ating bansa. Similar bills were filed such as in the 18th Congress authored by Rep. Florencio Gabriel “Bem” Noel, in the previous Congress authored by Rep. Patrick Michael Vargas, and in the Congress, filed by Rep. Nathaniel Oducado Given the considerations mentioned, this Representation respectfully seeks the passage of this proposed measure. JC M. label: HB 10752
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL AUTISM CARE PLAN, ESTABLISHING A SUB- COMMITTEE ON AUTISM UNDER THE NATIONAL COUNCIL ON DISABILITY AFFAIRS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism, or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), is a lifelong, complex neurodevelopmental condition caused by differences in how the human brain functions1. Social communications and interaction challenges, as well as restricted and repetitive behaviors, are primarily seen in persons with ASD2. The Philippines still does not have an official and available registry of autism prevalence. Recent estimates indicate that approximately one (1) in every one hundred (100) Filipinos may be on the autism spectrum, translating to roughly 1.2 million Filipinos living with autism, including an estimated 350,000 Filipino children with ASD3. Despite these rising numbers, autism care in the Philippines is still inaccessible and expensive to most Filipino families. Support systems are very much inadequate and unevenly distributed in the country. For many low-income households, especially those in underserved and geographically isolated communities, access to developmental specialists, diagnostic services, and intervention programs is out of financial reach. In 2022, it was cited that the Philippines has 99 board-certified developmental-behavioral paediatricians, of whom more than half (52%) are situated in the National Capital Region4. These compel families from provinces to shoulder significant transportation and accommodation expenses merely to access consultations and therapy. The financial burden associated with autism care is substantial and, in many cases, heartbreaking to household stability. The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) jointly conducted a study that concluded that raising a child with a disability requires expenditures approximately forty percent (40%) to eighty percent (80%) higher than raising a typically developing child. Moreover, poverty rates among households caring for children with disabilities are fifty percent (50%) higher compared to other households. The same study also showed that only one (1) out of five (5) children with disabilities possesses a Persons with Disability (PWD) identification card, limiting access to vital government 1 Definition from web (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/about/index.html) 2 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/ 3 Autism Society Philippines prevalence estimate (1 in 100 Filipinos with autism), as cited in Philippine policy materials andautism awareness publications; see also Capitol Medical Center, “National Autism Consciousness Week.” 4 Challenges in Philippine Developmental Paediatric Care. Rafael L G Valenzuela, Julian E D Mendoza, Ourlad Alzeus G Tantengco, Eric D B Ornos. 18 June 2022. Retrieved from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jpc.16055 1 assistance and concessions. More alarmingly, forty-three percent (43%) of disability subsidies are received by the richest income quintile, while the poorest quintile receives less than six percent (6%), underscoring persistent inequities in access to social protection5. According to a Philippine study published in Acta Medica Philippina, the average cost of interventions, such as therapy, education, medication, and developmental monitoring, is about Php38,868 during the first year of care, or about twenty-one percent (21%) of the monthly expenses of a household earning Php15,000. The total cost of diagnostic evaluations for autism ranges from Php1,356 to Php44,634. The same study further revealed that approximately forty-two percent (42%) of diagnosed children received no intervention after diagnosis, largely due to financial and accessibility barriers6. Hindi lamang ito mga numero o datos. Ito ay ang nakapanglulumong realidad ng mga magulang at primary caregivers na isinasakripisyo ang kanilang oras at panahon para lamang alagaan ang kanilang mga mahal sa buhay na may ASD. Ang kabawasan, lalo na ang kawalan ng oras, sa paghahanapbuhay ang s’yang nagpapalugmok sa kanila sa kahirapan. And despite the passage of landmark legislation such as Republic Act No. 7277 or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, Republic Act No. 11223 or the Universal Health Care Act, Republic Act No. 11036 or the Mental Health Act, and Republic Act No. 11650 or the Inclusive Education Act, there is still no comprehensive and coordinated national framework specifically devoted to autism care across the life course, from early childhood through adulthood. Sa pamamagitan ng pagbabalangkas at pagtatag ng National Autism Care Plan at pagsaayos ng isang dedicated inter-agency and multi-sectoral mechanism sa ilalim ng National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA), ang panukalang batas na ito ay hindi lamang tutugon sa mga isyu sa kalusugan… ito ay may hangaring solusyunan ang mga isyu sa kahirapan, panlipunang proteksyon at inklusyong pang-ekonomiya. By investing in early intervention, strengthening inclusive educational systems, expanding access to therapies, and creating networks for skills training, livelihood, and employment, the State empowers persons with autism to become more independent, self-reliant, and productive members of society. Equally important, this measure enables parents and caregivers to remain economically productive while reducing the long-term financial burden borne by families and local communities. The heart of this proposed legislation affirms the State’s obligation to ensure that access to autism care is not determined by geography or financial capacity, but made available to every Filipino family in need. The National Autism Care Plan advances the welfare of neurodivergent Filipinos while contributing to broader national goals of inclusive growth, family resilience, and poverty reduction. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10753
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE SERVICE INCENTIVE LEAVE (SIL) OF EMPLOYEES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE ARTICLE 95 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes labor as a primary socio-economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights and promote the welfare of Filipino workers. Consistent with this constitutional duty, Article 95 of the Labor Code grants employees who have rendered at least one (1) year of service an annual Service Incentive Leave (SIL) of five (5) days with pay.1 Yet despite decades of economic change, rising costs of living, and evolving family realities, this minimum benefit has never changed. This proposed measure seeks to increase the SIL entitlement from five (5) days to ten (10) days with pay, recognizing that Filipino workers deserve not only protection in the workplace but also meaningful opportunities to care for their health, fulfil family responsibilities, and spend time with their loved ones. Today, millions of Filipinos endure the difficult reality of working far from home. While employment opportunities are still concentrated in urban centers such as Metro Manila, Region IV- A (CALABARZON), and Region III (Central Luzon), many workers come from provinces and leave behind their spouses, children, and elderly parents in search of better opportunities. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) recorded approximately 48.5 million employed Filipinos in 2025 2. More than 6.3 million workers are recorded in the National Capital Region (NCR), underscoring Metro Manila’s continued role as the country’s primary employment hub. “Rest days,” or taking time off, are considered a luxury for many workers, especially minimum- wage earners and rank-and-file employees. The existing five (5) days of SIL are indeed often insufficient to address illness, emergencies, caregiving responsibilities, government transactions, and much-needed family time. Most of the time, these workers are left with no choice but to accept meager wages rather than return home to their loved ones. Moreover, additional leave days have a meaningful impact on those who come from Bicol, Visayas, Mindanao, or any distant province. A chance for them to go home opens several doors for their 1 Book Three – Conditions of Employment, P.D. 442, Labor Code Title I – Working Conditions and Rest Periods. https://library.laborlaw.ph/p-d-442-labor-code-book-3/ 2 https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/labor-force-survey family: it means being present at a child’s graduation, celebrating a birthday, caring for an aging mother, or simply spending precious time with family members whom they only see a few times each year. This proposed increase in Service Incentive Leave also comes at a time when Filipino households continue to struggle with inflation and rising living costs. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported sustained inflationary pressures in recent years, reaching 7.2 percent in April 2026 from 4.1 percent in March 20263. This resulted in increased household spending on food, transportation, healthcare, and utilities. These economic burdens disproportionately affect workers who live paycheck to paycheck. PSA data also showed that the average annual income of Filipino families in 2023 was PhP353.23 thousand4. Because of this, they always choose to give up their personal or family needs instead of taking a leave. Furthermore, adequate rest and work-life balance are essential to maintaining productivity and preventing workplace burnout. International labor standards recognize paid leave as an important component of decent work, contributing to improved physical and mental well-being, higher morale, greater employee retention, and better overall productivity5. Workers who are given reasonable opportunities to rest and reconnect with family are ultimately more motivated, healthier, and more productive members of the workforce6. Increasing Service Incentive Leave from five (5) days to ten (10) days is neither excessive nor unreasonable. Rather, it is a practical and compassionate reform that reflects the realities faced by Filipino workers today. It recognizes that workers are not machines, but individuals carrying responsibilities both in the workplace and at home. This bill tells us a simple truth-- labor policies must strengthen the family by giving workers enough time to be with their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10754
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE TEACHING OF THE WEST PHILIPPINE SEA, THE 2016 SOUTH CHINA SEA ARBITRAL AWARD, AND THE PHILIPPINES' MARITIME RIGHTS AND ENTITLEMENTS AS PART OF THE PHILIPPINE HISTORY CURRICULUM IN BASIC EDUCATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2026, the Philippines commemorates the tenth anniversary of the landmark 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, a historic legal victory that reaffirmed the country's maritime rights under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The Award clarified the legal status of maritime features in the South China Sea and declared that China's expansive “nine-dash line” claim has no legal basis under international law. It is a defining milestone in the pursuit of a rules-based international order, providing a final and legally binding resolution to disputes over maritime entitlements. As emphasized by the National Maritime Council (NMC), the 2016 Arbitral Award remains the Philippines' strongest legal foundation for defending its rights in the West Philippine Sea. The Council described the Award as "not merely a legal victory" but "a beacon that guides our national policy and collective action in protecting our maritime rights and ensuring that the West Philippine Sea remains a source of peace, stability, and prosperity for present and future generations of Filipinos." The Council likewise stressed that the Award is final and legally binding between the Philippines and China and continues to guide the country's maritime policy and diplomacy while promoting the peaceful settlement of disputes.1 Beyond its legal significance, the West Philippine Sea is an integral part of the nation's history, identity, security, and economic future. It sustains the livelihoods of Filipino fisherfolk, serves as a vital maritime corridor for trade and commerce, and contains valuable marine and natural resources essential to national development. As such, every Filipino should possess a clear understanding of the historical, legal, and geopolitical issues surrounding the West Philippine Sea. Recent government efforts have shown that increasing public awareness, especially among the youth, helps foster a better understanding of the 1 Esguerra, D. J. (2026, July 12). 10 years on, PH arbitral win remains anchor for WPS rights. Philippine News Agency. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1279257 country's maritime rights and national interests. This highlights the importance of introducing these topics in the basic education curriculum.2 Recognizing that an informed citizenry is essential to safeguarding the country's maritime rights, the present administration launched a transparency initiative to systematically document and publicize developments and unlawful activities in the West Philippine Sea. By exposing coercive actions at sea and grounding the Philippines' position in international law, the initiative has strengthened public awareness, reinforced domestic support, and garnered greater international solidarity behind the country's rules-based position.3 While the transparency initiative keeps the public informed of current developments, public awareness must be sustained through formal education. Institutionalizing the study of the West Philippine Sea and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award in the Philippine History curriculum ensures that Filipino students acquire, as early as primary and secondary education, a factual and evidence-based understanding of the country's maritime history, legal rights, and national interests. In this way, the measure transforms public awareness into enduring civic education and equips future generations to appreciate and uphold the Philippines' sovereignty, sovereign rights, and maritime entitlements through peaceful and lawful means. Despite its significance, discussions on the West Philippine Sea and the 2016 Arbitral Award remain limited in the basic education curriculum. There is therefore a compelling need to institutionalize the teaching of these subjects to ensure that future generations are equipped with knowledge grounded in Philippine history, the Constitution, and international law. This measure seeks to integrate the study of the West Philippine Sea, the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, and the Philippines' maritime rights and entitlements into the Philippine History curriculum in primary and secondary education. This bill seeks to ensure that every Filipino student understands the substance of this victory. It aims to cultivate historical awareness, civic consciousness, patriotism, and respect for the rule of law while encouraging students to appreciate the importance of safeguarding the country's sovereignty, sovereign rights, and maritime interests through peaceful and lawful means. By educating the youth on these matters, the State fulfills its constitutional duty to develop informed, patriotic, and responsible citizens who understand the nation's rights and responsibilities in the international community. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. MA. ALANA SAMANTHA TALIÑO SANTOS Representative, 3rd District of Cotabato 2 Javier, M. J. F. (2025, March 12). Youths embrace Philippine sovereignty in West Philippine Sea. Philippine Information Agency. https://pia.gov.ph/news/youths-embrace-philippine-sovereignty-in-west-philippine-sea/ 3 Ibarra, E. J. label: HB 10755
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL BLOCKCHAIN-BASED LAND REGISTRATION AND PROPERTY RECORDS SYSTEM TO MODERNIZE AND DIGITIZE PROPERTY INFORMATION MANAGEMENT, STRENGTHEN PROPERTY RIGHTS, AND PROMOTE TRANSPARENCY, SECURITY, AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN LAND ADMINISTRATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to rely on fragmented and largely paper-based systems maintained by various national government agencies and local government units. Land records are often dispersed across multiple repositories, resulting in inconsistent information, delayed verification processes, costly reconciliation of records, and administrative inefficiencies. The loss, destruction, deterioration, or unavailability of land records due to natural disasters, accidents, and the passage of time has likewise led to lengthy and expensive title reconstitution proceedings that burden both property owners and government institutions. Land ownership remains one of the most important foundations of economic security, social stability, and wealth creation for Filipino families. Secure and reliable land records are essential to protecting property rights, facilitating investments, improving access to credit, supporting infrastructure development, enhancing local revenue generation, and promoting sustainable economic growth. The lack of an integrated and secure property information system also creates vulnerabilities to fraud, unauthorized alterations, duplicate records, and conflicting claims over land ownership. These challenges undermine public confidence in land administration, increase transaction costs, discourage investments, and impede the efficient delivery of government services. Recent advances in digital governance and blockchain technology provide an opportunity to modernize the country’s land registration and property records management systems. Blockchain technology enables the creation of immutable and verifiable digital audit trails that can significantly strengthen the integrity, security, traceability, and authenticity of land records. By recording and verifying transactions through tamper-resistant digital mechanisms, blockchain technology can reduce opportunities for fraud, facilitate faster verification of ownership records, and improve institutional accountability. The establishment of a National Blockchain-Based Land Registration and Property Records System will enable the integration, digitization, and verification of land and property information across relevant government agencies. The system will support more efficient land administration, facilitate the reconstruction and verification of lost or damaged records, improve disaster resilience, enhance transparency in property transactions, and provide citizens with more accessible and reliable land information services. Moreover, secure and trustworthy land records are critical to strengthening property rights and improving the country’s investment climate. A modernized land registration system can reduce transaction costs, accelerate property-related processes, improve tax administration, support financial inclusion through easier access to collateralized credit, and contribute to the overall ease of doing business in the Philippines. This measure seeks to establish a secure, interoperable, and future-ready framework for land registration and property records management through the strategic use of blockchain technology and digital information systems. By modernizing the country’s land administration infrastructure, the State can better protect property rights, improve governance, strengthen public trust, and support long-term national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10756
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR DISABLED PERSONS”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A government identification card ought to make it easier for a citizen to access their rights, not require them to repeatedly prove that they deserve them. For persons with permanent disabilities, the current requirement to periodically renew a Persons with Disability (PWD) Identification Card can turn a necessary government service into an unnecessary and repetitive burden. A person whose blindness, deafness, loss of a limb, or other disability has been medically established as permanent should not have to repeatedly secure certifications, undergo administrative procedures, travel to government offices, and spend time and money simply to prove once again what is already known to be permanent. For many persons with disabilities, every renewal may mean additional transportation expenses, physical exertion, time away from work or livelihood, dependence on companions, and navigating government facilities and procedures that may themselves present accessibility barriers. A process intended to facilitate access to benefits and privileges can, in practice, become another barrier to accessing them. This is why the law must distinguish between disabilities that are permanent and those that are temporary. The appropriate policy, therefore, is not to subject everyone to the same renewal requirement, but to establish a system proportionate to the nature of the disability. This bill seeks to establish that distinction between permanent and temporary disabilities. It grants lifetime validity to PWD Identification Cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities, upon certification by the appropriate Municipal or City Health Office, while retaining a two-year validity period and medical reassessment requirement for persons with temporary disabilities. These PWD Identification Cards shall conform to the universal design prescribed by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) and adopted by local government units, and shall be issued free of charge. At its core, this measure advances a simple principle: government should not make persons with permanent disabilities repeatedly prove what the government has already certified as permanent. Instead, public systems should adapt to the realities of persons with disabilities by removing unnecessary administrative barriers while maintaining reasonable safeguards against fraud, misuse, and inaccurate records. These proposed reforms also affirm the Philippines’ obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), particularly its commitment to eliminate barriers that prevent persons with disabilities from exercising their rights and participating fully and equally in society. Accessibility must extend beyond physical spaces to include identification systems, government procedures, and administrative requirements that directly affect the daily lives of persons with disabilities. By establishing lifetime validity for PWD Identification Cards of persons with permanent disabilities, maintaining appropriate reassessment for temporary disabilities, requiring universal design, and ensuring that the cards are provided free of charge, this bill seeks to make the PWD identification system more accessible, equitable, efficient, and humane. The proposed legislation will reduce unnecessary paperwork, repeated medical certification, transportation costs, and time spent on renewal procedures, while allowing local government units to focus their administrative and medical resources on cases that genuinely require assessment or reassessment. Most importantly, this measure recognizes that government systems should respond to the realities of persons with disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10757
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR OPTIONAL EARLY RETIREMENT FOR GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES WITH DISABILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities continue to make invaluable contributions to the Philippine civil service despite facing barriers and additional disability-related costs throughout their careers. Many government employees with disabilities devote decades of public service while managing expenses for rehabilitation, medicines, assistive devices, accessible transportation, personal assistance, and other support necessary to perform their duties and participate fully in society. While the Government Service Insurance System provides retirement benefits to qualified government employees, existing retirement laws do not recognize the distinct circumstances faced by persons with disabilities who often experience greater physical, financial, and health- related demands over the course of their employment. As more persons with disabilities enter and remain in government service through inclusive employment policies, there is a corresponding need to ensure that the country’s retirement system likewise becomes more responsive to their circumstances. This proposed measure seeks to provide qualified government employees with disabilities the option of early retirement upon reaching fifty-five (55) years of age and rendering at least ten (10) years of government service. The measure is entirely voluntary and does not compel retirement. Rather, it provides an additional retirement option for those who, after years of dedicated public service, choose to retire earlier in recognition of the unique circumstances associated with disability. The bill likewise reflects the Philippines’ commitment under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), which calls upon States Parties to adopt appropriate measures that promote equality, inclusion, and social protection for persons with disabilities. By recognizing disability-responsive retirement as a reasonable and equitable social protection measure, the State affirms that equality sometimes requires policies that respond to different circumstances rather than treating everyone identically. This proposed legislation honors the dedication and sacrifices of government employees with disabilities by providing them greater flexibility and security as they transition from public service. It strengthens the government’s commitment to inclusive employment, responsive social protection, and the dignity and well-being of persons with disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10758
title: AN ACT EXTENDING THE SIX PERCENT REAL PROPERTY TAX CAPPING PERIOD AND THE TAX AMNESTY PERIOD TO FOUR YEARS UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT", AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 29 AND 30 THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12001, also known as the Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RPVARA), was borne out of the need to optimize the government’s real property tax collection. Aside from promoting a nationally consistent real property valuation based on international standards and the market value as single base for tax assessment, it also mandates the development and maintenance of a comprehensive, up-to-date electronic database of real property transactions. Notably, it improves revenue generation at the local level, further enhancing local government units’ capacity to pursue projects and programs which are responsive to the needs of their constituents. The transition period, however, provided in the RPVARA may be too short. Concerns have been raised regarding the need to further study its impacts beyond property valuation, such as its possible effects on housing affordability, economic competitiveness, and property ownership, to name a few. With the transition period having already lapsed, the policy status quo could do more harm than good. Under the directive of President Marcos Jr. in his fourth Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (LEDAC) to ease the financial burden of the public, including private property owners and businesses, this measure proposes to extend the six percent real property tax capping period and the tax amnesty period to four years, to avoid the abrupt additional property costs and allow for smoother and gradual transition to the new valuation system. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10759
title: AN ACT PROMOTING AND SAFEGUARDING THE INSTALLATION AND OPERATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS FOR PERSONAL CONSUMPTION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Sariling Kuryente Act”. SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to ensure the reliable, secure, affordable and environmentally sustainable supply of electricity, to accelerate the development of renewable energy resources, and to protect the interest of the consuming public. SEC. 3. Definitions. — For purposes of this Act: (a) “Behind-the-meter system” refers to a generation facility, an energy storage facility, or both, located on the premises of an end-user and connected on the end-user’s side of the metering point. (b) “Distribution utility” refers to any electric distribution utility as defined in Republic Act No. 9136, including electric cooperatives. (c) “Export-limiting device” refers to equipment, certified under standards recognized by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), that prevents the flow of electricity from a behind-the-meter system into the distribution system, including reverse-power relays, zero-export controllers and equivalent means. (d) “Non-exporting system” refers to a behind-the-meter system equipped with a certified export-limiting device.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cumulative net-metered capacity stood at 157 megawatts as of May 2025, the yield of twelve years of the programme. Independent analysis of market generation data suggests that roughly 600 megawatts of rooftop solar were added in the twelve months to April 2026 alone. Households are now installing generation faster than the approval system can process it, and the greater part of that capacity sits outside the statutory scheme altogether. The framework no longer describes the industry it governs. This bill closes that gap through a single classification rule, drawn from the Electric Power Industry Reform Act, which ties regulatory obligation to sale into the market: an end-user who generates power for personal consumption is not a generation company. The operative architecture follows from that premise. Qualified non-exporting systems require no prior approval and no certificate of compliance. Distribution utilities may not demand technical studies, meter replacement, agreements or added charges. Notification follows installation rather than preceding it. And homeowners' associations, developers and property managers may not prohibit installations on property the end-user owns or exclusively controls. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 10760
title: AN ACT IMPOSING SAFETY-BY-DESIGN AND AGE ASSURANCE DUTIES ON SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM PROVIDERS WITH RESPECT TO CHILD USERS, ESTABLISHING A MINIMUM AGE FOR SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS, PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Social Media Safety for Children Act”. SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual and social well-being of the youth, and to defend the right of children to special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation and other conditions prejudicial to their development. SEC. 3. Definitions. — For purposes of this Act: (a) “Child” or “minor” refers to a person below eighteen (18) years of age.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7610, Republic Act No. 10175, and Republic Act No. 11930 penalize the abuse and exploitation of children online after it has occurred. No existing Philippine statute regulates the conditions that produce the encounter. A platform is under no legal obligation to determine whether its user is a child, to apply protective default settings to that child's account, or to withhold engagement-maximizing recommendation systems from a minor. This bill addresses that specific gap and does not extend beyond it. This bill imposes safety-by-design obligations on every account a platform knows or ought reasonably to know belongs to a minor, independently of the minimum age requirement. The obligations therefore apply to children who evade the age requirement, and to children who migrate to smaller services with weaker moderation and no Philippine presence. It places the obligation and the penalty on the covered platform. No penalty attaches to a child or to a parent, and parental consent cannot be used to waive the minimum age. This conforms the bill to Republic Act No. 9344, which prohibits the imposition of penalties on minors for status offences, and follows the Australian scheme in force since 10 December 2025. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD.
