title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE AND RESPONSIVE CIVIL REGISTRATION AND VITAL STATISTICS SYSTEM, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive, responsive, and modern Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system that will ensure the universal, timely, and secure registration of vital events involving Filipinos, whether in the country or abroad. It aims to address fragmented civil registration processes by creating an integrated framework that strengthens legal identity, improves public service delivery, and ensures the accuracy and reliability of civil registry records. The measure recognizes civil registration as an important component of protecting individual rights and facilitating access to essential government services. It seeks to ensure that the registration of births, deaths, marriages, and other civil status events remains free, accessible, and responsive, particularly for marginalized and vulnerable groups such as indigenous peoples, foundlings, children in need of special protection, persons with disabilities, and overseas Filipinos. The bill also supports the modernization and digitization of civil registration through the interconnection of existing systems and the development of a national database. It promotes closer coordination among the Philippine Statistics Authority, local government units, and other concerned government agencies to streamline processes, reduce delays, strengthen data management, and improve the integrity of civil registry information. Ultimately, the measure seeks to strengthen the country's civil registration system while upholding the principles of legal identity, data privacy, accessibility, and inclusive governance. By ensuring that every Filipino is properly registered and recognized before the law, the State can help provide individuals with more reliable access to public services, legal protections, and other opportunities that depend on official civil registry records. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10851
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING, INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE STRATEGY FOR PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, disasters are not rare events, they are a constant reality. Typhoons, floods, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions strike with such frequency that they have become part of the daily lives of our people. Each storm that destroys homes, each tremor that shakes our land, is a reminder that our nation sits at the center of one of the most dangerous regions in the world. The 2025 World Risk Index confirms a difficult reality: the Philippines remains the most disaster‑prone country in the world, holding this position for four consecutive years. This is not just a number on a report—it reflects the daily struggles of millions of Filipinos who live under constant threat from typhoons, earthquakes, floods, and other natural hazards that place lives, livelihoods, and communities at risk. This ranking is a reminder of the urgent need to strengthen disaster preparedness, improve infrastructure, and invest in climate resilience. At the same time, it highlights the courage and resilience of the Filipino people, who continue to rebuild and rise after each calamity. Their strength must be matched by decisive action from government, civil society, and international partners to protect communities, uphold dignity, and secure a safer future for generations to come. The Climate Change Commission estimates that disasters cost our economy around 200 billion pesos annually. Since 1990, more than 565 natural disasters have struck the Philippines, claiming nearly 70,000 lives and causing damages worth $23 billion. These numbers show the heavy burden disasters place on our people and our economy. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, marked a significant advancement in national policy. It redefined disaster management from a reactive framework to a proactive system centered on preparedness and risk reduction. Nevertheless, despite these institutional reforms, the economic consequences of disasters remain substantial and continue to challenge financial resilience. This proposed measure seeks to strengthen our resilience by creating a Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council. The Council will develop a framework to ensure quick, reliable, and well- coordinated financing for disaster-related repair, reconstruction, and rehabilitation of government- owned infrastructure. It will use both insurance and non-insurance mechanisms to guarantee that funds are available when urgently needed. The bill also establishes a National Public Asset Insurance Consortium, led by the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) and composed of insurance and reinsurance companies offering public asset coverage. This Consortium will craft a national disaster risk insurance strategy, ensure faster claims processing, and support rapid recovery of damaged public assets. By protecting critical infrastructure and ensuring timely financial support, this measure will help communities recover faster, reduce economic losses, and limit the long-term impact of disasters on our people. It is a step toward building a stronger, safer, and more resilient Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10852
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE GRANT OF EMERGENCY LEAVE TO EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS DIRECTLY AFFECTED BY CALAMITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is no stranger to calamities. The country experiences an average of twenty (20) typhoons annually, in addition to recurring floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. Although Filipinos have demonstrated remarkable resilience in the face of these events, workers who are directly affected by calamities should be afforded sufficient time to attend to their safety, recover from damages and losses, and address urgent personal and family concerns without the added burden of reporting for work. Hence, this proposed bill seeks to institutionalize the grant of five (5) days of emergency leave to employees in both the public and private sectors who are directly affected by calamities. It aims to provide workers with a reasonable period within which to recover from the effects of a disaster, attend to their basic needs and restore their homes and livelihoods, without fear of losing their employment or suffering further financial hardship. It is also consistent with the existing government policies and issuances recognizing the need to protect employees affected by natural disasters and similar occurrences. These include Civil Service Commission Memorandum Circular No. 2, Series of 2012 entitled Special Emergency Leave to Government Employees Affected by Natural Disasters, Memorandum Circular No. 16, Series of 2012 or the Supplemental Guidelines in the Grant of Special Emergency Leave and Labor Advisory No. 17, Series of 2022 on the Suspension of Work in the Private Sector by reason of Weather Disturbances and Similar Occurrences issued by the Department of Labor and Employment. This legislative measure is likewise proposed in furtherance of the constitutional duty of the State to afford full protection to labor and promote their welfare. It is a positive stance to ensuring that Filipinos are able to recover from calamities despite continuing threats these pose to their livelihood, property, financial resources, and, in some cases, the lives of their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10853
title: AN ACT REMOVING SYSTEMS LOSSES AS A SEPARATE COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLS, EMPOWERING THE ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION TO DETERMINE THE COSTS THAT MAY BE RECOVERED AS PART OF DISTRIBUTION SERVICE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential daily need for every Filipino family and a key driver of our local economy. However, for years, consumers have been forced to shoulder high electricity bills—partly because of "system loss charges." Electric companies are allowed to pass the cost of lost electricity straight to consumers, whether the loss is from aging power lines, poor equipment, administrative errors, or power theft. Given that the distribution utilities can easily pass these costs to the public, these companies have little reason to modernize their equipment, fix operational issues, or stop power theft. The burden falls entirely on the paying consumer. This bill, the "System Loss Charge Abolition Act" amends Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA) to fix this unfair arrangement. Under this measure the power companies can no longer list system loss as a separate pass-through fee on monthly bills, shall strictly direct the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to strictly ban utilities from recovering costs caused by power theft, poor maintenance, inefficiency, or administrative mistakes and provides a transition period up to three years (3) years to give utilities time to fix their systems without disrupting power service. By forcing distribution utilities to take full responsibility for their own technical and operational losses, this bill will make power rates fair, hold power companies accountable, and shall give relief to everyday electricity consumers. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 10854
title: AN ACT CREATING THE METROPOLITAN CEBU INTEGRATED WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT BOARD, PRESCRIBING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water scarcity in Metropolitan Cebu has reached critical levels, threatening public health, economic productivity, and long-term urban resilience. Rapid population growth, uneven infrastructure development, and fragmented resource management have strained the region’s ability to ensure safe, sufficient, and sustainable water access for its residents, leaving a governance gap in one of the country’s most densely populated and economically vital corridors. Despite various efforts at the national and local levels, the absence of a unified, science-based, and locally responsive governance framework has hindered the development of long-term solutions. Jurisdictional overlaps, limited coordination among stakeholders, and the lack of integrated planning mechanisms have contributed to inefficiencies in water resource management and infrastructure investment. This bill proposes the creation of the Metropolitan Cebu Integrated Water Resources Management Board. It is a multi-sectoral, inter-local body mandated to plan, coordinate, and implement strategic water resource initiatives across key cities and municipalities in the region. The Board shall be empowered to identify and harness viable water sources, promote conservation technologies, and facilitate infrastructure development through data-driven and climate-resilient approaches. By institutionalizing this Board, the measure aims to bridge existing governance gaps, foster collaboration among local governments and stakeholders, and ensure that water resource planning is aligned with the region’s development goals and climate adaptation needs. It affirms the constitutional right to water and reinforces the State’s duty to promote equitable, transparent, and sustainable resource management. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. EDUARDO R. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING FAIR DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES BY DEBT COLLECTORS AND PENALIZING VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With almost everything within reach of our fingertips because of the internet, several unsuspecting debtors became vulnerable to debt-shaming and harassment by debt collectors or debt collection agencies. As of August 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) has revoked the primary registration of 2,084 lending companies and ordered the closure of 81 online lending applications for their non-compliance with Republic Act 9474 or the Lending Company Regulation Act for using threats, obscene language, false representation and maliciously using personal information in their debt collection practices.1 The number of online lenders involved in this kind of debt collection practice is quite alarming, especially considering that there is a lack of a law that penalizes said practice. label: HB 10856
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ENHANCED PROTECTION, SECURITY, AND SAFETY BENEFITS FOR MEDIA PERSONNEL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Media personnel play an essential role in keeping the public informed and holding democratic institutions accountable. Despite this immense responsibility, journalists, newsroom staff, and field personnel often work under hazardous conditions, economic instability, and a lack of adequate social safety nets. The proposed bill, entitled the "Media Personnel Welfare Act," intends to address these systemic challenges by establishing clear social, economic, and safety protections for all media personnel in the private sector, including freelancers and regular employees. Specifically, the measure provides a guaranteed minimum compensation and benefits by enforcing compliance with standard labor laws, minimum wage rates, mandatory coverage under the SSS, Pag-IBIG, PhilHealth, and retirement benefits, mandates a minimum hazard pay of ₱500.00 per day for personnel assigned in dangerous, distressed, or emergency areas, alongside compulsory provision of basic protective gear such as bulletproof vests, helmets, and medical equipment. Further, entitles workers to compulsory coverage including ₱200,000 for death benefits, up to ₱200,000 for disability benefits, and up to ₱100,000 for medical insurance, grants automatic regular status to media personnel after six (6) months of service- whether continuous or cumulative—to curb unfair employment practices and finally, establishes the News Media Tripartite Council under the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to serve as a platform for policy alignment, dispute resolution, and stakeholder dialogue. 1 By improving working conditions and ensuring fair compensation, this legislation seeks to build a safer and more secure environment for a responsible and sustainable media. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 10857
title: AN ACT GRANTING POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION LEAVE TO QUALIFIED FEMALE WORKERS AND SUPPORT LEAVE TO THEIR QUALIFIED PARTNERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, female workers are entitled to one hundred five (105) days of paid maternity leave for childbirth, regardless of the manner of delivery, under Republic Act No. 11210, otherwise known as the “105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law.” A qualified solo mother is entitled to an additional fifteen (15) days of paid maternity leave, while a female worker may opt to extend her maternity leave for an additional thirty (30) days without pay, subject to the conditions provided by law. In cases of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy, a female worker is entitled to sixty (60) days of paid maternity leave. Under R.A No. 8187, otherwise known as the “Paternity Leave Act of 1996,” a qualified married male employee is entitled to seven (7) days of paid paternity leave for the first four (4) deliveries of his legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting. Republic Act No. 11210 likewise permits a female worker to allocate up to seven (7) days of her maternity leave credits to the child’s father or, in the circumstances specified by law, to a qualified alternate caregiver. The allocated benefit is separate from and in addition to the benefit under Republic Act No. 8187. Although maternity leave provides a period of rest, recovery, and recuperation in connection with childbirth, Republic Act No. 11210 does not expressly establish a separate leave benefit specifically for female workers who are clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression. Postpartum depression is a serious mental-health condition that may affect a woman’s ability to care for herself and her child and may require professional treatment, counseling, medical monitoring, and family support. Its symptoms may arise after childbirth and may persist beyond the period ordinarily needed for physical recovery. According to an online medical article, postpartum conditions may include postpartum blues, also known as “baby blues”, postpartum depression, and postpartum psychosis.1 Postpartum blues are common and generally begin within the first few days of delivery, but their symptoms may subside within a week or two weeks. Postpartum depression is more intense and severe than the baby blues as it can start within one week of delivery and last several months. The article describes postpartum psychosis as an extremely severe form of postpartum depression that requires emergency medical attention. Its symptoms generally develop quickly and intensely, lasting for many weeks or months.2 This proposed legislation seeks to grant thirty (30) days of paid postpartum depression leave to qualified female workers who are clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression. It likewise seeks to grant seven (7) days of paid support leave to the child’s father or the female worker’s qualified partner so that the latter may provide care and support during the female worker’s treatment or recovery. The benefits under this bill shall be separate from and in addition to the maternity leave benefits under Republic Act No. 11210, the paternity leave benefit under Republic Act No. 8187, and any maternity leave credits allocated under Republic Act No. 11210. They shall not be deducted from the female worker’s existing maternity leave credits or from any other leave benefit to which the worker is entitled under law, a collective bargaining agreement, an employment contract, or an established company policy, when the latter is more beneficial. Postpartum depression is a serious concern that affects the behavior, livelihood, and well- being of women after birth, as well as that of their newborns and families. Granting a separate leave benefit will enable qualified female workers to obtain appropriate treatment and additional time for medically necessary recovery, while allowing their qualified partners to provide essential care and support. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. Under R.A No. 8187, otherwise known as the “Paternity Leave Act of 1996,” a qualified married male employee is entitled to seven (7) days of paid paternity leave for the first four (4) deliveries of his legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting. Republic Act No. 11210 likewise permits a female worker to allocate up to seven (7) days of her maternity leave credits to the child’s father or, in the circumstances specified by law, to a qualified alternate caregiver. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed General Appropriations Bill (GAB) for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 translates the National Expenditure Program (NEP) into the annual spending authority of the National Government. It is anchored on the theme: "People-Centered Growth for an Inclusive and Resilient Future" Consistent with this theme, the proposed appropriations direct public resources toward expanding access to quality education and healthcare, strengthening social protection, creating quality employment and sustainable livelihoods, improving food and energy security, accelerating development of strategic and climate-resilient infrastructure, and reinforcing responsive, transparent and accountable public institutions. The measure carries forward the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 and Ambisyon Natin 2040 through investments in human capital, social protection, food and energy security, strategic infrastructure, digital transformation, climate resilience, peace and security, and capable institutions. The FY 2027 proposal was prepared amid slower economic growth, inflationary pressure, geopolitical conflict, volatile fuel prices, climate-related risks, and constrained fiscal space. These conditions require a budget that protects essential government services, sustains productive investment, responds to immediate vulnerabilities, and preserves the country's capacity to finance development over the medium term. Constitutional Mandate and the Power of the Purse The 1987 Constitution vests in Congress the power of the purse. Through appropriations legislation, Congress determines the purposes for which public funds may be spent, the amounts that may be made available, and the conditions governing their use. This authority is inseparable from legislative oversight and ensures that public money is applied only to lawful, necessary, efficient, and accountable ends. i Article VI, Section 24 provides: "All appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills, shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments." Article VI, Section 29(1) further declares: "No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law." Article VII, Section 22 states: "The President shall submit to the Congress within thirty days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriations bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing, including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures." Constitutional Timeline for the FY 2027 Budget On July 27, 2026, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. delivered his fifth State of the Nation Address, formally opening the Second Regular Session of the Twentieth Congress and setting the Administration's policy direction for FY 2027. On August 11, 2026, the President submitted the proposed FY 2027 National Budget to Congress, together with the President's Budget Message, the National Expenditure Program, and the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing, in compliance with Article VII, Section 22 of the Constitution. The submission commenced the House review through the Committee on Appropriations, which examines agency requirements, performance, implementation capacity, policy coherence, and changes from the FY 2026 General Appropriations Act, and recommends the allocations and safeguards needed to address national and local priorities. Fiscal Context, Strategy, and Directions The FY 2027 budget seeks to support economic recovery and transformation while advancing fiscal consolidation. Under the macroeconomic assumptions adopted for the budget, real gross domestic product is projected to grow by 5.0 to 6.0 percent in 2027, following an adjusted growth outlook of 3.5 to 4.5 percent for 2026. The macroeconomic assumptions for FY 2027 include an inflation forecast of 4.0 to 5.0 percent, a foreign exchange rate of ₱60.00 to ₱62.00 per US dollar, and a Dubai crude oil price of US$70.00 to US$90.00 per barrel. Goods exports are projected to grow by 4.0 percent, while goods imports are projected to increase by 5.0 percent. Financing-related assumptions place the 364-day Treasury Bill Rate at 5.0 to 6.0 percent, and the six-month Secured Overnight Financing Rate at 3.0 to 4.0 percent. Collectively, these parameters provide general planning references for estimating revenues, financing requirements, operating costs, procurement requirements, and the resource needs of government programs and projects. label: HB 10862
title: AN ACT REMOVING SYSTEMS LOSS AS A SEPARATE COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 25 AND 43 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It has been more than 25 years since the passage of Republic Act No. 9136 or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA). While this measure restructured the energy sector in the country to ensure reliable electric supply, crucial amendments thereto are said to be long overdue to be responsive to the realities faced by Filipino households. One of the main burdens of the Filipino Household is the rising electricity costs, with the Philippines recorded to have the highest electricity rates in Southeast Asia1. One of the significant factor to this burden is the practice of on system loss charges to end-users. Under Section 43(f) of EPIRA, distribution utilities (DUs) and electric cooperatives (ECs) are legally allowed to pass system loss charges directly onto end-users. While Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) enforces a recoverable system loss cap for private DUs at 5.5% to 6.5%, other ECs, particularly those operating across Mindanao and rural provinces, are permitted pass-through caps of up to 12.0% to 12.5%. This disparity places an unequal financial strain on households in rural areas and Mindanao, where consumers pay significantly higher bills to cover operational inefficiencies, technical line losses, and non-technical losses like power pilferage and theft. 1 Lelis, Brix. "DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA." The Philippine Star, 21 Jul. 2026, https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea. Accessed 16 Aug. 2026. Because these losses fall squarely within the operational control of distributors, current policy unfairly socializes business failures by shifting the cost onto captive consumers who receive no benefit from energy they never consumed. To address this, this measure seeks to reform the system loss pass-through framework to protect end-users and mandate true utility accountability. Through the removal of the system loss pass-through charges, we protect consumer interest and encouraging DUs and ECs to protecting the interest of the Filipino consumers by ensuring that they no longer pay for “ghost electricity” due to technical and non- technical system losses, and (2) encourage the DUs and ECs to improve operations through investment of modern infrastructures and efficient technologies to minimize or eliminate operational losses and inefficiencies. By requiring DUs and ECs to absorb operational inefficiencies rather than passing them on to end-users, this bill restores fairness to power pricing and safeguards the welfare of the Filipino households. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 10863
title: AN ACT EXCLUDING SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM VALUE-ADDED TAX ON ELECTRICITY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The high cost of electricity remains one of the most pressing economic burdens on Filipino households. The imposition of the 12% Value-Added Tax (VAT) on the "system loss" component of electric bills is a major factor that adds to this monthly financial strain. Under the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), as amended, and existing Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) guidelines, the 12% VAT is computed on the gross bill, which is composed of generation, transmission, distribution, and system loss charges. System loss represents electricity lost during distribution due to technical line resistance or non-technical factors such as illegal hookups, theft, and metering errors. Consequently, consumers are not only paying for "ghost electricity" that they never consumed, but they are also paying a 12% VAT on top of those operational losses. The imposition of VAT on system loss fundamentally distorts the principle of Value-Added Tax, which is intended to tax actual consumption of goods or services. Paying VAT on power lost in transit or stolen by third parties forces end-users to shoulder a tax on an operational inefficiency. This tax, unfortunately, hits rural communities and Mindanao hardest. While private distribution utilities have ERC system loss caps between 5.5% and 6.5%, electric cooperatives operating in provinces and Mindanao carry caps of up to 12.0% to 12.5%. As a result, provincial households pay a disproportionately higher tax penalty simply because the system loss charge base in their electric bill is nearly double. To address this, this measure seeks to amend the NIRC and energy regulations to expressly exclude system loss charges from the computation of the 12% VAT on the sale of electricity. This ensures that the Filipino consumers only pay taxes on the actual electricity delivered to and consumed by their households. Together with the other proposed complementary legislative measures addressing system losses charges, this bill provides a direct and practical measure towards economic relief and tax fairness. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 10864
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools are meant to be one of the safest places for our children. This is where they learn, make friends, form their character, and develop skills they will need later in life. However, recent events in the country have shattered this expectation, turning our learning institutions into places of fear and anxiety. We do not have to look far for an example. Just last year, in the 2nd District of Parañaque, a Grade 8 student was fatally stabbed by a classmate inside Moonwalk National High School. Initial reports revealed that the conflict may have stemmed from a piece of makeup that was not lent by one student.1 Since the opening of School Year 2026-2027, there have already been multiple incidents of school-based violence, including two tragic school shootings in Tacloban– which killed 3 students and injured more than 202 – and Zamboanga–which killed 2 students including the perpetrator who took his own life.3 These incidents do not just 1 Macababbad, EJ; Tupas, Emmanuel. Available at https://www.philstar.com/nation/2025/03/28/2431568/grade-8-student-killed-classmate-over-makeup- kit. 2 Gabieta, Joey. (2026). School shooting kills 3 students in Tacloban. Inquirer.net. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2250793/school-shooting-kills-3-students-in-tacloban. 3 Sigales, Jason; Agonoy, Leah. (2026). Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting: 2 students dead. Inquirer.net. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2287724/ateneo-de-zamboanga-shooting-2-students-dead. 1 affect our students. Last year, a teacher in Lanao del Sur was shot and killed by a student over a failing grade.4 These alarming incidents demonstrate the need for a comprehensive measure to ensure our children’s safety in school. This need is further supported by the findings of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), which noted that bullying and aggression often remain unreported because learners fear retaliation or do not know where or how to seek assistance5. Data from the Programme for International Student Assessment or PISA likewise show that bullying remains a significant concern among learners.6 To help address these incidents of school-based violence, this proposed measure seeks to establish, maintain, and periodically update a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework, which will prescribe the standards for school safety plans, school safety infrastructure and security measures, violence prevention and anti-bullying mechanisms, learner well-being and mental health promotion, and emergency preparedness. This measure also provides policies for a safe school culture, zero-tolerance against violence, and anti-bullying. This bill also specifies and clarifies the responsibilities of school heads, school counselors and counselor associates, learner formation officers, and school safety officers. In addition, it seeks to promote the meaningful participation of parents, guardians, and families in the improvement of school safety programs. It likewise prescribes safety infrastructure and equipment, such as CCTV cameras in strategic areas, appropriate screening equipment, visitor management systems, the presence of appropriate security personnel, and emergency equipment. Further, in recognition of the prevalence of technology in children’s lives, this measure also mandates schools to adopt policies and programs that promote safe, responsible and age-appropriate use of digital technologies, including measures to protect learners from cyberbullying. Finally, it requires schools to establish protocols for reporting, assessment, interventions, and immediate response to school safety concerns. No child should enter a classroom in fear. With this measure, we hope to ensure that our educational institutions are safe and remain conducive environments for learning. 4 Bravo, Drema. (2025). label: HB 10865
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE AGRICULTURE INFORMATION SYSTEM IN ALL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, at its core, an agricultural economy, yet the persistent paradox of its farm sector is not scarcity, but supply mismatch. The bountiful harvests of our farmers often go to rot or are sold at a loss, while nearby markets face shortages and higher prices for the very same commodities. This chronic disruption is a traceable crisis that recurs due to failure of information and coordination between production and demand. As a country with agricultural yields, it is highly necessary that we bank on the strengths of our existing industries. It is also shown during times of emergency and crisis that there exists a gap in the information system involving our farming sectors. This pattern has repeated with striking regularity in recent years. In Benguet, in one instance, the country’s so-called “Salad Bowl” that supplies nearly 80% of the upland vegetables sold in Metro Manila, cabbage farmers have seen farmgate prices collapse to as low as P4 to P10 per kilo, forcing many to either sell at a loss or abandon their harvest altogether, even as prices in the end-market remain multiple times higher.1 Likewise, in Nueva Ecija and Rizal provinces, tomato farmers faced a similar collapse in early 2025, with farmgate prices falling to P4 to P5 per kilo, prompting Department of Science and Technology – Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic, and Natural Resources Research and Development (DOST- PCAARRD) and Sen. Kiko Pangilinan to launch multiple initiatives, such as “Operation Sagip-Kamatis-an” to rescue the unsold produce and calling on local government units to procure the excess for feeding programs.2 As one farmer- 1 Carby Rose Basina, “Benguet farmers struggle with low vegetable prices, oppose planned carrot imports,” GMA News Online, 25 May 2026, available at: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/988714/benguet- farmers-struggle-with-low-vegetable-prices-oppose-planned-carrot-imports/story/ 2 Clarizel Joy Jamille Gomez, “Tomato Price Volatility in Luzon: Challenges for Farmers, Consumers, and the Need for Market Stability,” DOST-PCAARD’s ISP-IS, 4 April 2025, available at: advocate group put it plainly: “There is actually market demand. It’s just not reaching it. So, it looks like overproduction.”3 The government has not been without initiatives to address this gap. The Department of Agriculture (DA) currently maintains several digital platforms, among them the Registry System for Basic Sectors in Agriculture (RSBSA), the e-Kadiwa e-commerce platform, and the Bantay-Presyo price-monitoring application. These are valuable, but largely function as centralized, top-down tools; none of them is mandated to operate as real-time, two-way local matching system at the city, municipal, and barangay level where oversupply and undersupply typically originate, and where the earliest, most actionable information exists. The gap that this bill seeks to address is precisely that last- mile layer, the absence of a legally mandated, LGU-anchored information system that captures hyperlocal production data as it is harvested, and connects, in real time, to buyers and to the national platforms/registries that already exist. It was recently shown that a lot of farming communities are forced to throw away their crops due to the supposed oversupply. However, upon careful investigation, it shows that there exists demand in several areas in the country which are not taken account of because of this information gap. Such gaps have become more urgent to close now that the National Government has significantly scaled up its investment in agricultural infrastructure. For example, the 2026 National Budget substantially increased funding for farm-to-market roads, precisely to move produce out of the farms and into markets faster. Roads without a matching information system to tell farmers where the demand is, and buyers where the supply is, will only get produce to market faster without ensuring that it goes to where it is needed. 4 Physical infrastructure and information infrastructure must be developed together. It is for these reasons that this bill seeks to reestablish, in an updated and strengthened form, the Agriculture Information System, built to interoperate with existing national platforms rather than duplicate them, while accessible to farmers who lack reliable internet access through SMS and community kiosks and not just a web application, and backed by a funding mechanism that does not leave under-resources municipalities, communities, and farmer groups to shoulder an unfunded mandate alone. Hence, it is for these reasons that this bill is earnestly sought. https://ispweb.pcaarrd.dost.gov.ph/tomato-price-volatility-in-luzon-challenges-for-farmers-consumers-and-the- need-for-market-stability/ 3 Ibid. 4 Audrey De Jesus, “Harvesting pork, not rural development: The 2026 agriculture budget examined,” Ibon Foundation, 18 January 2026, available at: https://www.ibon.org/tl/pork-not-rural-devt-2026-agri-budget/ ALFRED C. label: HB 10866
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ENFORCEMENT OF MANDATORY SEGREGATION-AT-SOURCE OF SOLID WASTES AT THE BARANGAY LEVEL, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, or the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000,” already requires households and establishments to segregate solid waste at source under Section 21 of the law. More than two decades since its passage, however, segregation-at-source often remains the weakest-enforced link in the country’s solid waste management chain. Barangays, which are on the frontline of collection, generally have no clear, standardized mechanism to refuse uncollected, unsegregated waste, to inspect compliance, or to impose graduated, due-process-compliant penalties on repeat violators. This absence of a workable enforcement mechanism at the barangay level has allowed segregation-at-source to remain, in practice, optional in many communities, undermining the entire downstream chain of materials recovery, composting, and waste diversion that later legislation and local ordinances have tried to strengthen. This bill amends Republic Act No. 9003 by inserting a new section, Section 22, that gives barangays a clear, standardized, and due-process-compliant enforcement toolkit: (1) a designated Barangay Segregation Enforcement Team; (2) authority to refuse collection of unsegregated waste; (3) a graduated schedule of warnings and fines for households and establishments; (4) authority to conduct spot inspections; and (5) a self-sustaining Barangay Solid Waste Management Enforcement Fund sourced from the fines themselves, primarily for information campaigns and segregation materials rather than punitive revenue- raising. By giving barangays real, low-cost enforcement tools instead of merely repeating the mandate to segregate, this measure aims to close the compliance gap that has persisted since RA 9003 took effect. It is our view, that given the precarious situation in which the country finds itself in vis-à-vis solid waste and environmental waste-leakage, tackling segregation-at-source provides a solid step towards the right direction. It is high time that we move on from the old mantra of “tapat ko, linis ko,” and into a new adage: I will keep my community, and therefore the country, clean. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10867
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DISCLOSURE OF FOOD ALLERGENS IN PRODUCTS OFFERED BY FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State, under Article II, Section 15 of the Constitution, is mandated to protect and promote the right to health of the people. In line with this, the Department of Health issued Administrative Order No. 2014-0030 requiring prepackaged food products to list their ingredients, including allergens, to safeguard consumers. However, this protection remains incomplete, as food served in restaurants, cafeterias, and other establishments is not subject to the same mandatory disclosure, leaving millions of Filipinos vulnerable to accidental allergic reactions. Food allergies pose a serious and recurring public health concern. Even the smallest serving of an allergen can trigger severe reactions ranging from swollen tissues, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and painful blisters to difficulty breathing, coma, and even death. Studies in the Philippines confirm that food allergies affect a growing number of children and adults, with many cases going unreported due to limited awareness and lack of disclosure mechanisms. These risks are magnified in provinces and rural communities where access to emergency medical care is limited, making prevention through transparency all the more critical. This bill seeks to institutionalize the duty of food establishments to automatically disclose allergy-causing ingredients in their menu items. By complementing the existing requirement for prepackaged foods, this measure ensures that consumers are protected not only in grocery aisles but also in everyday dining settings. It recognizes that diligence must be shared: while customers have the responsibility to inquire, establishments must carry the equal responsibility to inform. This measure embodies humane regulation as it seeks to protect vulnerable groups like children, the elderly, and those in marginalized communities, by reducing preventable health risks. It also strengthens trust between consumers and establishments, fostering a safer and more inclusive dining culture across the country. The institutionalization of allergen disclosure is a simple yet powerful step toward health equity. It ensures that every Filipino, regardless of where they live or what they can afford to eat, enjoys a safer and more dignified dining experience. It is for these reasons that the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10868
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR COMPENSATION FOR STAY-AT-HOME SPOUSES AND HOMEMAKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under current conventions in economics, work that is not remunerated does not count as productive labor. Unfortunately, this category would include the work done by housewives, stay-at-home mothers, or homemakers who care for dependents, both young and elderly, in their household. Cooking breakfast, washing and preparing the clothes for the day, cleaning the home, balancing the household budget are only some of the many things our mothers, sisters, and many more do that require not only the fullest dedication, time, and a wide variety of skills. And yet, society in its current form, often dismisses or undervalues the labor of home- making. But imagine a tomorrow, where suddenly, housewives and homemakers cease to do the work they usually do. The most likely result would be that the lives of everyday Filipinos as we know it would become commensurately more difficult. Those considered in the productive economy would feel the extra burden of having to pick up the labor gap that ensues, becoming less productive in their professional jobs in the process. It is then worth considering, that if full-time housework is indeed inconsequential, how come that it would be impossible to maintain a productive economy without it? It is thus imperative upon the State to recognize the “invisible labor” done by stay-at-home women, mothers, wives, and homemakers as a valuable part of our economy. In line with the Constitutional imperatives to promote a just and dynamic social order, to value the dignity of every human person, and to recognize the role of women in nation-building, housewives and homemakers should be given the equivalent of a wage. With this, the State takes a step not only to provide a means for families with only one breadwinner to lift themselves out of poverty, but also take a step to recognize the vital role that women and homemakers perform from the onset of one’s life to the twilight of their years. It is for these foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10869
title: AN ACT PROVIDING MENSTRUAL HEALTH PRIVILEGE TO EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall recognize the role of women in nation-building1 and shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.2 Furthermore, the Constitution also provides that the State shall protect working women by providing safe and healthful working conditions, taking into account their maternal functions, and such facilities and opportunities that will enhance their welfare and enable them to realize their full potential in the service of the nation.3 Menstruation is the recurring discharge of blood and tissue from the inner lining of the uterus as part of the menstrual cycle. Menstruation is usually experienced by individuals with a uterus, including cisgender women and transgender men. Some individuals may experience pain and discomfort during menstruation due to dysmenorrhea, the severe and frequent cramps during the menstruation period. It was reported that more than half of women who menstruate have some pain for 1 to 2 days each month4, affecting between 45 and 95% of all women5. 1 1987 CONST. Art. II, Sec. 14. The State recognizes the role of women in nation-building, and shall ensure the fundamental equality before the law of women and men. 2 1987 CONST. Art. II, Sec. 15. The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. 3 1987 CONST. Art. XIII, Sec. 14. 4 National Nutrition Council. (October 28, 2021). Why do women experience Dysmenorrhea?. URL: https://nnc.gov.ph/regional-offices/mindanao/region-ix-zamboanga-peninsula/6274-why-do- women-experience-dysmenorrhea 5 Stella Iacovides, Ingrid Avidon, Fiona C. Baker (September 07, 2015). What we know about primary dysmenorrhea today: a critical review. Available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26346058/ The pain during menstruation is normal, but for some individuals, the pain and discomfort may be severe enough to interfere with their normal activities.6 The pain may be due to hormonal activity during the menstrual cycle or may be an associated phenomenon of an underlying medical condition. In light of the constitutional mandate and the factual backdrop surrounding menstrual health, this bill proposes that a menstrual health privilege be made available to employees in the public and private sectors who experience pain and discomfort during menstruation. The menstrual health privilege shall be in the form of either a two-day paid leave or an option for a work-from-home arrangement during their menstruation period, if applicable to the nature of their duties and responsibilities. The option for a two-day paid leave, distinct and separate from the legally mandated sickness benefit under existing laws, is made available to allow the employee to recuperate in extreme and severe cases of painful menstruation. On the other hand, the option for a work-from-home arrangement is made available to allow the employee to maintain productivity in less-severe cases of painful menstruation. The menstrual health privilege aims to promote the general well-being of employees who suffer from painful and burdensome menstruation and alleviate the distress that they experience. The menstrual health privilege proposed by this bill should not be seen as a special treatment for a particular class of employees. Menstruation and its associated pain and discomfort are both health issues and medical concerns. It is high time that we recognize the plight of employees who experience these realities and give them our support as they go through this recurring struggle. Based on the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. DELOS SANTOS Representative, Ang Probinsyano Party-List 6 Ibid. label: HB 10870
title: AN ACT PRESCRIBING AN ACTIVE MONITORING AND URGENT RESPONSE MECHANISM BY THE GOVERNMENT TO PREVENT THE KILLING, RAPE, AND OTHER ABUSES COMMITTED AGAINST OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the height of tragedy when Overseas Filipino Workers travel to foreign lands in search of opportunities, seeking to help uplift the lives of their family and countrymen, just to be met with grisly, violent deaths in the hands of a stranger. Joanna Demafelis, Jeanelyn Villavende, and Constancia Dayag are just Filipinos whose lives were untimely snuffed out. More saddening is the fact that we are not at all helpless to provide our OFWs the necessary protections. We have had the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration (POEA), the Overseas Labor Office, Filipino Resource Center, and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), most of which, exempting the OWWA, are now under the Department Of Migrant Workers (DMW), and all mandated to serve and protect our OFWs. With their combined wealth of experience, resources, and connections inaction is unacceptable. And yet there are cases, such that of Jeanelyn Villavende, where complaints from OFWs regarding their safety are not promptly acted upon. This is even more timely, as areas of the globe with high concentrations of OFWs continue to grapple with warfare, geopolitical tensions, and other such economic uncertainties, leading to the further precarious situations our OFWs sometime find themselves in. This is the gap that this bill seeks to address. It provides active monitoring and urgent response mechanism to address incidents and emergencies endangering the life, limb, and liberty of our OFWs and to instill that consciousness among our frontline government agencies and stakeholders, under pain of administrative and criminal penalty. This way, prevent future cases of OFWs being abused, raped or killed may be prevented. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10871
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT AND INTEGRATION OF SOLAR-POWERED COLD-CHAIN FACILITIES IN THE PHILIPPINE FISHERIES SECTOR, PROVIDING SUPPORT MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the world’s top fish-producing countries, and the fisheries sector remains a primary source of food and livelihood for millions of Filipinos, particularly small-scale and municipal fisherfolk in coastal communities nationwide. Yet a significant share of the sector’s harvest never reaches the market at full value, this is mostly due to post-harvest losses, which include spoilage, quality degradation, and reduced shelf life, among others. Post- harvest losses remain a persistent problem, driven in large part by the absence of reliable and affordable cold-chain infrastructure at the point of landing, and throughout the seafood supply chain. Many municipal fishing communities are in areas that lack proper infrastructure or suffer from energy insecurity. As a result, fishers and fish processors in these areas often lack access to ice, chilling, or cold storage facilities capable of preserving the quality of their catch between capture and market. This translates directly into lost income for fisherfolk, reduced product value, lower exportability, and food that never reaches the consumers’ tables. At the same time, the falling cost of solar photovoltaic technology has made solar powered cold-chain equipment increasingly viable in remote, under-served, off-grid, or energy insecure areas, such as island communities and remote coastal towns. Solar-powered cold-chain facilities offer a practical, low-emission, and increasingly cost-competitive solution, one that does not require waiting for grid extension and that insulates fishing communities from fuel price volatility associated with diesel-powered generators commonly used for the same purpose today. This Act seeks to harness that opportunity by mandating the establishment and integration of solar-powered cold-chain facilities in priority fishing communities. This measure is expected to generate significant knock-on benefits, such as higher and more stable incomes for municipal fisherfolk, improved food security, greater climate and energy resilience in coastal communities, and the growth of a local industry centered around renewable energy and cold-chain equipment manufacturing, installation, and servicing. Through this Act, we aim to advance the country' s renewable energy goals, its fisheries development goals, and safeguard a way of life that has been thriving for generations. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10872
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE USE AND UTILIZATION OF SOLAR ENERGY IN NATIONAL HOSPITALS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT HOSPITALS, STATE AND UNIVERSITY HOSPITALS, AND OTHER GOVERNMENT-OWNED AND -CONTROLLED HOSPITALS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Reliable electricity is not a convenience for hospitals, it is a matter of life and death. Ventilators, incubators, blood banks, operating rooms, dialysis machines, and cold-chain storage for vaccines and medicines all depend on an uninterrupted power supply. Yet many of our public hospitals, particularly those in far-flung and off-grid areas, continue to grapple with unstable, intermittent, or altogether absent electricity service. During typhoons, earthquakes, and other calamities and public health emergencies, precisely when hospitals are needed most, power interruptions place patients' lives at risk and compromise the delivery of essential health services. At the same time, public hospitals that do enjoy stable grid access shoulder some of the highest and most continuous electricity demands among government facilities, placing a significant and recurring burden on public funds that could otherwise be channeled toward direct patient care, medical supplies, and health workforce needs. Solar energy offers a practical, sustainable, and increasingly cost-effective solution to both dependence on costly and often unreliable conventional electricity sources, lower long-term operating costs, and, when paired with appropriate energy storage, provide a critical layer of resilience that keeps essential hospital services running through outages, calamities, and emergencies. This is consistent with the policy already established under Republic Act No. 9513, or the "Renewable Energy Act of 2008," which promotes the development and utilization of renewable energy to strengthen the country's energy security and reduce its dependence on fossil fuels. This bill mandates the installation, integration, and maintenance of solar energy systems in national hospitals, local government unit hospitals, state and university hospitals, and other government-owned and controlled hospitals. To ensure that this mandate is achievable rather than aspirational, the bill provides for a phased implementation: covered hospitals are required to achieve solar energy generation capability equivalent to at least twenty percent (20%) of their annual electricity demand within one (1) year from the law's effectivity, and at least fifty percent (50%) within three (3) years, subject to standards and guidelines to be jointly established by the Department of Health (DOH) and the Department of Energy (DOE), in coordination with other relevant agencies. The bill likewise directs covered hospitals to integrate energy storage and backup capabilities where technically and financially feasible, so that critical hospital facilities and services remain powered during grid outages and emergencies. In recognition of the role of local industry in nation-building, the bill gives priority to local businesses in the contracting and purchase of solar energy systems from accredited solar photovoltaic installers, while ensuring that all procurement remains fully compliant with existing bidding and procurement laws and is conducted with transparency. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10873
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING DISCRIMINATION OF TEACHERS WHO ARE UNWED MOTHERS, SINGLE PARENTS, AND/OR MEMBERS OF THE LGBT COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Teachers play a vital role in shaping the minds, character, and future of the Filipino people. Their competence and commitment to the teaching profession should be the standards by which their qualifications and performance are assessed, and not their civil status, family circumstances, gender identity, or sexual orientation. Despite the importance of their profession, teachers and applicants for teaching positions may face discrimination on the basis of being an unwed mother, a single parent, or a member of the LGBTQIA+ community, and other such non-heteronormative identifiers. Such discriminatory practices may deprive otherwise qualified individuals of employment opportunities, livelihood, salaries, and benefits solely because of circumstances that do not diminish their ability to perform their duties as educators. This measure seeks to uphold the right of teachers and applicants for teaching positions to equal employment opportunities by expressly prohibiting discrimination on these grounds. It likewise establishes appropriate penalties and institutional accountability to ensure that schools maintain fair, inclusive, and non-discriminatory workplaces. By protecting teachers from discrimination, this measure seeks to foster a more equitable educational system where professional competence, integrity, and dedication determine one's opportunity to serve as an educator, not personal circumstances or identity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10874
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE ANNUAL MEDICAL CHECK-UP FOR ALL FILIPINOS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Annual health examinations are important for the early detection and management of silent medical conditions. However, data shows 40% of Filipinos undergo annual medical checkups.1 Among the primary reasons behind this low rate are the high cost attributed to consultation and diagnostic tests, and prioritization of basic needs over healthcare concerns. We must shift our perspective from a reactive mindset, that is “If it is not broken, don’t fix it”, to a preventive and proactive health care. By prioritizing early intervention, we optimize the window of opportunity to treat and manage diseases before symptoms manifest, which will result to saving more lives at a much lower healthcare costs. Under Article XIII of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State is mandated to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. While we took a big step towards this mandate with the enactment of Republic Act No. 11223 or the Universal Health Care Act in 2018, there should be a continuous efforts to expand and enhance the range of healthcare services being offered to the Filipino people. 1 "New Study Reveals Only 40% of Filipinos Get Yearly Checkups, an issue that can be addressed by UHC law – Atty. As such, this measures seeks to provide all Filipinos access to free annual health examinations, aside from the benefits granted under the Universal Health Care Act. The annual health examination shall includes consultation, physical examination, routine laboratory or diagnostic examinations, complete blood count (CBC), lipid profile, fasting blood sugar (FBS), chest x-ray, among others. The saying “health is wealth” applies not only to individual but to the nation as a whole. Maintaining a healthy population is a good foundation of a robust economy, efficient and effective workforce, and high national productivity. The expansion and strengthening of our healthcare services is an essential investment in our human capital. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With the instability and uncertainties surrounding the electricity generation in the country, Filipinos are increasingly turning to renewable energy sources such as solar power. The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC) reported a surge on rooftop solar adoption in the Philippines, with roughly 600 megawatts (MW) added in the last 12 months leading to April 2026, amid rising power costs and the high cost of living. Behind-the-meter (BTM) energy storage, such as rooftop solar panels and storage systems, offers significant benefits to consumers and the power grid alike. By generating clean, fuel-free energy directly at the point of use, these systems immediately protect households from volatile retail power rates, provide critical back-up electricity during recurring grid blackouts, and reduce overall peak demand on distribution grid. However, everyday Filipino consumers face severe hurdles in adopting these solutions. Case in point: the installation of BTM systems continues being hindered by technology costs, administrative red tape, excessive local government unit (LGU) permit and clearance requirements, among other obstacles. As such, this measure seeks to simplify the regulatory requirements for the installation of behind-the-meter electricity generation and battery storage systems, intended solely for personal use. Through the removal of the existing administrative restrictions, this bill aims to promote public access to these technologies for electricity generation, and to making clean power simple, easy and affordable for Filipinos Households. Through this, the mainstreaming of renewable energy across the country will be accelerated. This measure will expand Filipinos access to alternative renewable energy and directly alleviate the concerns over the rising electricity expenses. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 The dignity of persons with disabilities should include the right to be recognized without having to repeatedly prove their condition. In other words, a permanent disability does not become temporary simply because an identification card has an expiration date. 26 This proposed measure therefore seeks to grant lifetime validity to PWD identification cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities. This proposal recognizes that once the permanence of a disability has been properly established, repeated renewal only adds a burden to our brothers and sisters with disabilities. 31 Likewise, this proposed measure also distinguishes between permanent and temporary disabilities to ensure that PWD benefits remain available to those who qualify, while preventing abuse of PWD privileges. 35 Ultimately, this bill seeks to make the recognition of disability simpler, more accessible, and more humane. Behind every PWD identification card is a person who may already face challenges that require physical, mental, and emotional strength every day. It is now the responsibility of the State to ensure that its laws and systems do not add to these burdens but instead provide an effective support to our brothers and sisters with disabilities. 42 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 44 45 46 REP. label: HB 10882
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE JUSTICE, PROTECTION, AND SUPPORT SYSTEM FOR VICTIMS AND SURVIVORS OF VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN, PROVIDING FOR EXPEDITED PROTECTION AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE MECHANISMS, INTEGRATED SURVIVOR SERVICES, CHILD-SENSITIVE AND TECHNOLOGY-RESPONSIVE PROCEDURES, INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Violence against women and their children remains a serious concern that requires not only strong laws, but also an effective, accessible, and coordinated justice and protection system. The Philippines has enacted significant legislation addressing violence against women and children which provide important legal remedies and protections. However, the existence of legal remedies does not by itself guarantee meaningful access to justice. Victims and survivors may still encounter delays in obtaining protection, difficulty navigating multiple government agencies, inadequate access to legal and psychosocial services, geographic barriers, lack of specialized personnel, repeated interviews and disclosures, insufficient coordination among service providers, and limited access to assistance outside regular government operating 1 hours. These difficulties can be particularly severe for women and children in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, persons with disabilities, persons with limited financial resources, and victims who lack access to reliable transportation, technology, or legal assistance. The urgency of strengthening the justice and protection system is heightened by the changing nature of violence. Abuse may now extend beyond physical spaces into digital environments through online harassment, cyberstalking, threats, unauthorized dissemination of intimate material, technology-assisted coercion, and other forms of technology-facilitated violence. Children are likewise increasingly exposed to online sexual abuse and exploitation, requiring close coordination between traditional child-protection mechanisms and digital investigation and response systems. The proposed measure therefore seeks to strengthen the implementation of existing laws without diminishing or duplicating their substantive protections. Rather than creating an entirely separate judicial system, the bill strengthens the existing Family Court and VAWC framework by allowing the Supreme Court, consistent with its constitutional authority, to establish specialized dockets, calendars, or other appropriate mechanisms for the expeditious handling of VAWC- related proceedings. The bill further establishes mechanisms for expedited protection-order processing and emergency response. In situations involving imminent or continuing danger, victims and survivors should not be required to navigate multiple agencies independently before receiving appropriate assistance. The proposed emergency response mechanism seeks to facilitate coordinated law-enforcement intervention, protection-order assistance, emergency medical and psychosocial services, shelter, transportation, and legal assistance. The measure also establishes integrated Survivor Support Desks and Survivor Support Coordinators to help victims and survivors navigate available legal, medical, psychological, social welfare, shelter, and other government services. This approach seeks to reduce unnecessary duplication, prevent victims from repeatedly recounting traumatic experiences, and improve continuity of assistance from the initial report through the resolution of the case. Every victim and survivor should be able to seek protection without having to overcome unnecessary institutional barriers. Through this measure, the State affirms that protection from violence is not merely a statutory promise but a responsibility 2 that must be supported by functioning institutions, trained personnel, accessible services, accountable agencies, and sustained public investment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10883
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAM, PROVIDING ACCESS TO MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES FOR PREGNANT AND POSTPARTUM WOMEN, INTEGRATING MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH INTO PUBLIC HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Pregnancy and the postpartum period are significant stages in a woman’s life that involve profound physical, emotional, psychological, and social changes. While motherhood is often associated with joy and fulfillment, many women experience mental health challenges during this period, including depression, anxiety disorders, trauma-related conditions, and other mental health concerns. If left undetected and untreated, these conditions may adversely affect the health, safety, and quality of life of mothers, their children, and their families. Maternal mental health conditions remain an underrecognized public health concern due to various barriers, including stigma, lack of awareness, limited access to mental health professionals, inadequate screening and referral systems, and financial constraints. Many women experiencing symptoms do not seek care because they fear judgment, discrimination, or misunderstanding of their condition. As a result, opportunities for early detection, intervention, and recovery are often missed. 1 Thus, this bill seeks to establish a National Maternal Mental Health Program that integrates maternal mental health services into existing maternal, newborn, child, and primary healthcare systems. It provides for routine and evidence-based screening during pregnancy and the postpartum period, standardized referral pathways, community-based support services, emergency intervention mechanisms, and continuity of care for women requiring further assessment and treatment. Further, the measure strengthens the capacity of healthcare providers and frontline workers through competency-based training and continuing education on maternal mental health detection, intervention, referral, and stigma-sensitive care. It promotes workplace and educational support systems, community awareness programs, and the responsible use of tele-mental health services to expand access, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. By recognizing maternal mental health as an essential component of women’s health, family well-being, and public health, this bill seeks to build a healthcare system that supports mothers not only in surviving pregnancy and childbirth but also in achieving mental, emotional, and social well-being throughout the postpartum period. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10884
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING MOBILE REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH CLINICS FOR UNDERSERVED AND GEOGRAPHICALLY ISOLATED COMMUNITIES, PROVIDING ACCESS TO ESSENTIAL WOMEN’S HEALTH SERVICES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the right to health of every Filipino and directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that shall make essential goods, health services, and other social services available to all. Despite existing efforts to improve healthcare delivery, many women, particularly those living in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs), rural communities, island barangays, Indigenous Peoples' communities, and disaster- or conflict-affected areas, continue to experience barriers in accessing timely, affordable, and quality reproductive, maternal, and preventive healthcare services. Limited healthcare facilities, geographic distance, inadequate transportation, socioeconomic challenges, and shortages in health personnel often delay access to essential services and contribute to preventable maternal and reproductive health complications. These challenges highlight the need for innovative and community- 1 based healthcare delivery mechanisms that can bring critical services closer to women and families who need them most. Thus, this bill seeks to establish the Mobile Reproductive Health Clinic Program under the Department of Health (DOH) to provide accessible, equitable, and quality reproductive, maternal, preventive, and women's healthcare services through mobile healthcare units deployed to underserved and hard-to-reach communities. By bringing healthcare services directly to communities, the measure aims to reduce disparities in health access, promote early detection and prevention of reproductive and maternal health conditions, and strengthen continuity of care through coordinated referrals with Rural Health Units, hospitals, and other appropriate healthcare facilities. The proposed Mobile Reproductive Health Clinics shall provide essential services such as prenatal and postnatal care, maternal health monitoring, reproductive health counseling and education, family planning information consistent with existing laws, breast and cervical health screening, nutrition counseling, preventive health services, mental health support, and referral assistance. Through this measure, the State shall strengthen primary healthcare delivery and improve access to essential women's health services. This represents a proactive investment in equitable healthcare delivery and advances the State’s commitment to ensuring that no woman is deprived of necessary health services because of geographic, economic, or social barriers. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 10885
title: AN ACT MANDATING A SMOKE-FREE AND VAPE-FREE ENVIRONMENT IN ALL PUBLIC AND WORKPLACES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9211 AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11900, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State has a constitutional duty to protect and promote the people’s right to health and to instill health consciousness among them. Consistent with this mandate, as well as with the country’s obligations under the World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, there is a need to strengthen the legal framework for creating genuinely smoke-free and vape-free public spaces and workplaces. The proposed “Smoke-Free and Vape-Free Environment Act” seeks to establish a clear and comprehensive national policy prohibiting smoking and vaping in public places, public conveyances, and workplaces, while strengthening the protection afforded to children, workers, commuters, students, patients, and the general public from exposure to tobacco smoke and vape emissions. It expands and clarifies the definitions of public places, public conveyances, smoking, vaping, workplaces, and other relevant terms to reflect the realities of modern transportation, 1 employment, commerce, education, and public life. The measure likewise recognizes that protection from exposure must extend beyond enclosed establishments to appropriate outdoor areas where people commonly gather, particularly schools, playgrounds, health facilities, transportation terminals, markets, parks, walkways, and other places frequented by the public. At the same time, the measure provides a carefully regulated framework for designated smoking and vaping areas in places where such areas may legally be established. Protection of public health remains the governing principle while providing clear and enforceable standards for establishments that choose to maintain designated areas. Further, this bill requires provinces, cities, and municipalities to establish Smoke-Free and Vape-Free Task Forces that will coordinate enforcement, monitoring, education, and community-level implementation.
