label: HB 10996
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 150-B AND 288-A OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE AND CREATING A NEW SECTION, 150-C, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen public health measures against diet-related diseases while generating sustainable funding for critical national health and nutrition initiatives. The primary policy objective of this legislation is to curb the rising prevalence of lifestyle illnesses, such as diabetes and obesity, by using fiscal policy to encourage healthier consumer choices and incentivize manufacturers to reformulate their products with lower sugar content. To achieve this health deterrent, the measure updates tax rates on sweetened beverages, establishing higher rates for drinks containing high fructose corn syrup to disincentivize its widespread industrial use. The policy scope is also broadened to encompass commercial sweetened milk and coffee products, ensuring a comprehensive framework across the beverage market. At the same time, the bill safeguards essential public nutrition by strictly exempting staple items such as plain unsweetened milk, infant formula, and standard unflavored coffee products. Beyond deterrence, a core outcome of this legislation is establishing a dedicated legal mechanism for statutory revenue earmarking. The bill guarantees that revenues collected are funneled directly into essential public services. To address rooted health disparities, forty percent of revenues are ring-fenced specifically for local government support, focusing on targeted nutrition programs for pregnant mothers and children in their first five years of life, alongside vital water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure. Finally, the bill incorporates an annual tax indexation mechanism so that the health deterrent maintains its real value over time without being eroded by economic changes. Coupled with expanded legislative oversight to strictly track the distribution and use of funds at the local level, the ultimate outcome of this measure is a self-sustaining cycle where taxes collected from sugary beverage consumption are directly transformed into long-term investments in maternal care, child nutrition, and accessible healthcare for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10997
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM FOR GRADUATE STUDIES IN GUIDANCE AND COUNSELING, STRENGTHENING THE GUIDANCE AND COUNSELING WORKFORCE OF THE COUNTRY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SEC. 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “National Guidance and Counseling Scholarship Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education and to the highest attainable standard of mental health, and to maintain a system of scholarship grants available to deserving students. Toward this end, the State shall build a sufficient, competent, and equitably distributed corps of Registered Guidance Counselors by financing graduate education in Guidance and Counseling, directing that investment to underserved regions, and securing a period of public service in return. SEC. 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: (a) Program refers to the Scholarship Program established under Section 4 of this Act; (b) Registered Guidance Counselor (RGC) refers to a person duly registered and licensed under Republic Act No. 9258, otherwise known as the “Guidance and Counseling Act of 2004”;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Programme for International Student Assessment recorded the Philippines as having the highest incidence of bullying among all participating countries in 2018, with 65% of Filipino learners reporting bullying at least a few times a month; in 2022, roughly 43% of girls and 53% of boys still reported repeated monthly incidents, against OECD averages of about 20% and 21%.1 DepEd itself has declared bullying a national concern rather than a school-level problem.2 Meanwhile, the National Center for Mental Health registered 7,189 suicide-related hotline calls from January to September 2025 mostly from individuals aged 18 to 30.3 These are the ordinary, daily conditions that a functioning guidance service exists to meet. Yet Filipino learners are in the middle of a mental health crisis that our schools are not staffed to answer. In the hearing of the Committee on Appropriations on 3 September 2025, the Department of Education (DepEd) confirmed that the country had only 4,069 licensed guidance counselors as against the more than 50,000 required to meet the recommended global ratio of one counselor for every 250 students.4 Roughly 79% of DepEd guidance counselor positions (4,460 positions) remain unfilled, with several regions posting vacancy rates above 80% and with single counselors covering multiple campuses.5 Higher education fares no better: data of the Philippine Guidance and Counseling Association (PGCA) show an 80% shortfall in higher education institutions (HEIs), where only 1,029 counselors serve against an ideal requirement of 5,315.6 1 EDCOM II, “High incidence of bullying in PH public schools alarming,” 13 June 2024, citing OECD, PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 results. 2 “Angara convenes the largest executive committee to combat bullying,” Department of Education, 15 April 2025. 3 “Mental health crisis hotline receives 7,189 suicide-related calls,” The Philippine Star, 2 November 2025, reporting National Center for Mental Health data for January to September 2025. 4 Statement of DepEd Secretary Juan Edgardo Angara before the House Committee on Appropriations, 3 September 2025, as reported in “Angara: Guidance counselor shortage worsens amid bullying surge in PH schools.” 5 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reform (2026–2035), Final Report, Priority 10: Home and School Environment, Issue No. 3, p. 198. 6 Philippine Guidance and Counseling Association survey data, as cited in Villarin et al., “The State of Guidance Counseling in Philippine Education,” International Multidisciplinary Journal of Research for Innovation, Sustainability, and Excellence (IMJRISE), Vol. 1, Issue No. 5 (2024). The deficiency is not one of demand but of supply. Since 2008, only a little over 3,000 individuals have passed the licensure examination for guidance counselors.7 Against approximately 4,286 counselors needed and only about 339 graduates of master's programs in Guidance and Counseling produced each year, there are roughly seventeen (17) vacant posts for every graduate, and the system would require twelve (12) to fourteen (14) years to close the existing gap even on the heroic assumptions of zero attrition and zero enrollment growth.8 The bottleneck is the graduate degree itself: Republic Act No. 9258 requires both a master's degree and licensure,9 yet the cost of that degree is borne almost entirely by the individual, while entry-level compensation begins at Salary Grade 11 (PhP 31,705.00) and rises only to PhP 36,125.00 at Salary Grade 13 for the same qualification.10 This bill institutionalizes that investment as a permanent national program. A scholarship alone will not solve a problem this large, and this bill does not pretend otherwise. It does, however, address the single constraint that no amount of plantilla creation, campus security hardware, or emergency deployment can overcome: there are simply not enough licensed professionals to hire. Metal detectors screen for weapons; only a counselor can screen for despair. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 10998
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL VETERANS BURIAL ASSURANCE PROGRAM THROUGH THE ACQUISITION OF PERPETUAL INTERMENT RIGHTS IN ACCREDITED MEMORIAL PARKS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6948, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XVI, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State “shall provide immediate and adequate care, benefits, and other forms of assistance to war veterans and veterans of military campaigns, their surviving spouses and orphans,” and directs that “[f]unds shall be provided therefor.”1 That obligation does not end at the veteran's death. A dignified place of interment is the last benefit the Republic can confer on those who bore its arms, and at present the Republic confers it unevenly. The Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City remains the principal national resting place for Filipino military veterans. It is also, for most of them, unreachable. Republic Act No. 6948, as amended, furnishes a burial flag and burial assistance now fixed at Twenty Thousand Pesos (PhP 20,000.00).2 That sum defrays funeral expenses. It does not purchase a burial lot, which in most provinces now costs several times that amount, and it does not secure perpetual care. The result is a benefit structure that pays for the rites but not for the ground. This bill takes the other road. Rather than build, the State buys, acquiring through competitive public procurement and in consolidated volume perpetual interment rights in memorial parks that already exist, that are already developed, and that are already subject to regulation and contractual perpetual care obligations. The economic case is not that the arrangement is free. It is that a single, fixed, present payment extinguishes an open-ended future liability: the cost of upkeep is prepaid into a perpetual care fund held in escrow, the land is never bought, no civil works are undertaken, and a plot becomes available to a grieving family in days rather than in budget cycles. The proponent reports a developed lot in Nueva Vizcaya, inclusive of perpetual care, 1 CONST. (1987), art. XVI, sec. 7. 2 Rep. Act No. 6948 (1990), secs. 19–20, as amended by Rep. Act No. 7696 (1994), sec. 6, and Rep. Act No. 10649 (2014), which increased burial assistance from PhP 10,000.00 to PhP 20,000.00. at approximately PhP 89,000.00.3 Bulk acquisition should improve on that figure; the bill requires that any such advantage be captured through competitive bidding under the New Government Procurement Act rather than assumed.4 Three safeguards distinguish this measure from a simple purchase order, and the Committee's attention is respectfully invited to them. First, a memorial lot in this jurisdiction is ordinarily conveyed not as titled land but as a right of interment under contract.5 A statute that assumed the Republic would receive a certificate of title for each plot would fail in the registry. The bill therefore secures the State's interest as a perpetual, irrevocable, and registered encumbrance annotated on the certificate of title of the memorial park itself, so that the veteran's resting place survives the sale, foreclosure, or insolvency of the developer. Second, perpetual care funds must be held in escrow with a government financial institution and pass automatically to a successor administrator upon default, rather than remaining an unsecured promise. Third, every plot is inalienable, exempt from execution, and traceable in a national registry, and its commercial resale is penalized. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11000
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE MINDANAO FUNCTIONAL LITERACY AND HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM IN SUPPORT OF THE MINDANAO AGENDA 2023–2028, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, particularly the 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS), reveal that while basic literacy remains high, functional literacy in the Philippines stands at only about 70.8%, leaving a significant portion of the population unable to effectively comprehend and apply information in daily life. This challenge is more pronounced in Mindanao, particularly in disadvantaged and conflict- affected regions, where educational access, poverty, and historical inequalities continue to constrain human capital development. The Mindanao Agenda 2023–2028, spearheaded by the Mindanao Development Authority, identifies human capital development, inclusive growth, and peacebuilding as central pillars to sustain Mindanao’s economic gains and long-term stability. However, functional illiteracy remains a structural barrier to achieving these objectives. The 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS) revealed that all Mindanao regions posted functional literacy rates lower than the national average functional literacy rate of 70.8%, with Zamboanga Peninsula (59.3%), Northern Mindanao (70.0%), Davao Region (66.7%), SOCCSKSARGEN (65.8%), Caraga (63.1%), and BARMM (64.7%) reflecting the percentage of the population aged 10 to 64 years who can read, write, compute, and comprehend. Functional illiteracy undermines workforce readiness, weakens productivity, limits civic participation, and constrains the successful reintegration of conflict-affected populations. Without targeted intervention, it threatens to erode the gains envisioned under the Mindanao Agenda. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Mindanao-wide Functional Literacy and Human Capital Development Program, anchored on the strategic priorities of the Mindanao Agenda 2023– 2028, integrating education, workforce development, digital inclusion, and community-based learning systems. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11001
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 15, 19, 30, AND 31 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12001, otherwise known as the "Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act" (RPVARA), was enacted to effectively establish a uniform, transparent, and equitable real property valuation system across the Philippines. This law centralizes valuation standards and implements a definitive framework for adopting the Schedule of Market Values (SMV). By doing so, it decisively eliminates arbitrary property assessments, strengthens local revenue generation, and guarantees a predictable environment for real property transactions. However, implementation since its passage has revealed structural gaps in specific procedural timelines, administrative coordination, and local governance adaptability. This amendatory bill addresses these practical hurdles by strengthening BLGF oversight, establishing clear fallback mechanisms for SMV approval, refining tax relief parameters, and providing a realistic transition period for capacity- constrained LGUs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11002
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING CLIMATE LITERACY IN THE BASIC EDUCATION CURRICULUM, MANDATING TEACHER TRAINING THEREFOR, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines consistently ranks among the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. As an archipelagic nation situated along the Pacific Typhoon Belt, the country bears the brunt of increasingly severe tropical cyclones, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and catastrophic flooding. While structural investments in climate adaptation and disaster risk management are critical, long-term resilience requires a fundamental shift in mindset—a transformation that must begin in the classroom. Section 16, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that the State shall "protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature." Furthermore, Paragraph 2, Section 3, Article XIV dictates that educational institutions shall inculcate patriotism and nationalism, foster love of humanity, and teach the rights and duties of citizenship. While existing subjects in the K to 12 basic education curriculum incorporate environmental concepts in general science, climate change education remains fragmented, abstract, and unevenly integrated. Youth today are not merely passive victims of environmental degradation; they are pivotal agents of community resilience, innovation, and climate action. To prepare Filipino youth for the reality of climate disruption, climate literacy must be institutionalized as a distinct, age-appropriate, and practical subject across elementary and secondary levels. True climate literacy extends beyond fundamental climate science—it encompasses ecological ethics, community disaster preparedness, local ecosystem conservation, renewable energy, and climate justice. This proposed measure seeks to mandate the Department of Education (DepEd), in coordination with the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), to institutionalize a comprehensive Climate Literacy Subject in the basic education curriculum. In light of the urgent need to build a climate-resilient citizenry from the ground up, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11003
title: AN ACT RESTRUCTURING THE MOTOR VEHICLE USER’S CHARGE, PROVIDING FOR A MOTOR VEHICLE ROAD USER’S TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8794, ENTITLED “AN ACT IMPOSING A MOTOR VEHICLE USER’S CHARGE ON OWNERS OF ALL TYPES OF MOTOR VEHICLES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to replace the Motor Vehicle User’s Charge (MVUC) established under Republic Act (RA) No. 8794 entitled “An Act Imposing a Motor Vehicle User’s Charge on Owners of All Types of Motor Vehicles and For Other Purposes”, as amended, and replace it with a Motor Vehicle Road User’s Tax (MVRUT). It aims to direct a portion of additional revenues toward public transportation and road safety. Since the enactment of RA No. 8794 in 2000, the number of motor vehicles has continued to increase and placed greater pressure on an already congested road network. Construction, maintenance, and rehabilitation costs have likewise increased, yet still the country continues to face persistent challenges in public transportation and road safety. Motor vehicles also vary in type, weight, capacity, use, and their impact on public roads likewise differs. Despite this, the existing rates do not provide a sufficiently responsive basis for determining the cost of road use. The proposed measure introduces a revised tax structure based on vehicle classification and gross vehicle weight, and shall cover registered private and government motor vehicles. It shall also provide a reduced rate for for-hire vehicles in recognition of their role in public transportation and commercial activity. It likewise recognizes that improving the country’s transportation system requires more than maintaining roads. Fifty percent (50%) of the incremental revenues will be directed to public utility vehicle modernization, programs for the prevention of road deaths, and assistance to road accident victims. This ensures that the additional tax placed on vehicle owners benefits not only them, but also the millions of Filipinos who depend on the country’s roads everyday. A road user tax should reflect the realities of road use today and contribute to addressing the transportation challenges that come with it. The modernization of the existing tax system for motor vehicle users provides a manageable transition and makes the country’s roads more sustainable, its public transportation more efficient and reliable, and its communities safer. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11004
title: AN ACT GRANTING RETIREMENT, HEALTH CARE AND MORTUARY BENEFITS TO PROFESSIONAL FILIPINO ATHLETES WHO WIN CHAMPIONSHIP TITLES IN INTERNATIONAL PROFESSIONAL SPORTS COMPETITIONS OR OTHER EQUALLY PRESTIGIOUS INTERNATIONAL GAMES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant retirement, health care, and death benefits to professional Filipino athletes who win championship titles in international professional sports competitions or other equally prestigious international sporting events. Professional Filipino athletes bring honor and international recognition to the Philippines through exceptional athletic achievement. However, many world champions face financial insecurity, limited access to health care, and inadequate social protection after retirement due to the absence of a dedicated welfare system. While Republic Act No. 10699, otherwise known as the “National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act,” provides incentives for amateur athletes, there is no comparable legal framework recognizing the long-term welfare needs of professional athletes who likewise achieve distinction for the country. This measure provides lifetime retirement pensions, PhilHealth coverage, hospitalization assistance, death benefits, and a Professional Filipino Athletes Welfare Development Trust Fund. It likewise authorizes the Games and Amusement Board to administer the program and ensure its long-term sustainability. The proposed measure recognizes the invaluable contributions of professional Filipino athletes and affirms the State’s commitment to safeguarding their welfare beyond their competitive careers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11005
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSTALLATION OF SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS IN ALL PUBLIC SCHOOLS, ESTABLISHING THE SUSTAINABLE SCHOOLS PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a Sustainable Schools Program which mandates the installation of solar energy systems in all public elementary and secondary schools. It promotes the use of renewable energy to improve learning environments, strengthen climate resilience, and reduce electricity costs in public schools. Many public schools continue to experience inadequate ventilation and rising indoor temperatures due to extreme heat, which adversely affect student health, concentration, and learning outcomes. At the same time, electricity costs consume a significant portion of school operating expenses, while schools in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas continue to face unreliable or limited access to electricity. The transition to renewable energy presents an opportunity to address these challenges while supporting the country’s clean energy and climate commitments. This measure institutionalizes a nationwide solarization program for public schools. It prioritizes schools with the highest heat indices, off-grid locations, and high student populations. The bill also establishes phased energy capacity targets, provides for maintenance funding and technical training, promotes net-metering for grid-connected schools, and ensures that procurement follows life-cycle cost and energy efficiency standards. These measures are intended to improve energy security, lower operating costs, and provide a more conducive environment for teaching and learning. Investing in renewable energy for public schools is an investment in both education and sustainable development. This bill promotes quality education while advancing energy security, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11006
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INCLUSION OF A PERSONAL FINANCIAL LITERACY COURSE IN THE TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING CURRICULUM OF TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY TRAINING CENTERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to include a Personal Financial Literacy Course (PFLC) as a mandatory component of the Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET) curriculum in all public and private Technical-Vocational Institutions (TVIs) and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) training centers. It recognizes that preparing Filipinos for employment and entrepreneurship requires not only technical competence but also the ability to manage income and make sound financial decisions. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas recognizes financial capability as essential to meaningful financial inclusion, since access to financial services do not by itself enable individuals to make informed financial decisions1. While TVET equips learners with industry-relevant skills for employment and livelihood, it does not uniformly provide structured instruction on personal financial management. Republic Act (RA) No. 10922, otherwise known as the “Economic and Financial Literacy Act”, and RA No. 10679, otherwise known as the “Youth Entrepreneurship Act”, promote financial education but do not specifically require a dedicated financial literacy course across TVET programs. The proposed measure requires the PFLC as a stand-alone course for all TVET learners, regardless of their chosen program or qualification. The course will cover essential personal finance concepts, which includes but are not limited to budgeting, saving, debt management, investment, insurance, retirement, planning, credit, consumer protection, and digital financial services. It shall also introduce learners to the Philippine financial system and cybersecurity risks in digital transactions. The curriculum shall be periodically reviewed to remain responsive to developments in financial products, technology, and national financial inclusion priorities. Financial literacy empowers individuals long before wealth is accumulated. For many technical-vocational graduates, their first paycheck is the beginning of a family’s opportunity to move forward. Technical skills may open the door to 1 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. (n.d.). Financial Inclusion. Accessed from: https://www.bsp.gov.ph/SitePages/InclusiveFinance/InclusiveFinance.aspx. Accessed on July 20, 2026. employment, but financial knowledge helps ensure that the fruits of that work are not lost to avoidable debt, fraud, or poor financial decisions. This measure recognizes that preparing Filipinos for decent work also means preparing them to achieve lasting financial stability and economic independence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11007
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK ON THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the development, deployment, and use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Philippines. It adopts a risk-proportionate approach that sets standards for transparency, human oversight, accountability, and safety according to the potential impact of AI systems. Artificial intelligence has rapidly become an essential component of public administration, commerce, finance, education, healthcare, media, and critical infrastructure. In 2025, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)1 reported that while the Philippines has legal frameworks on privacy and cybersecurity, it still lacks an AI-specific regulatory regime addressing transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, deepfakes, and other emerging risks associated with advanced AI systems. label: HB 11008
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DISABILITY SUPPORT FUND FOR THE EMPOWERMENT, FULL PARTICIPATION, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IN SOCIETY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide regular financial assistance and strengthen disability support services for indigent persons with disabilities (PWDs). It establishes a Disability Support Fund that augments the rights and benefits guaranteed under Republic Act (RA) No. 7277, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Disabled Persons”, as amended by RA No. 9442 and RA No. 10754. PWDs incur out-of-pocket expenses for rehabilitation, maintenance medicines, and other health-related needs. Inaccessible facilities and limited support services drive up these costs, pushing indigent PWDs and their families deeper into poverty and exclusion. Existing discounts, privileges, and social protection programs do not sufficiently cover these recurring expenses. This measure institutionalizes the Disability Support Fund that shall provide an Individual Support Allowance initially set at Two thousand pesos (Php 2,000.00) to qualified indigent PWDs and support disability services managed by local government units. It also mandates the development of a Disability and Needs Assessment System and an integrated disability data management system to ensure that assistance reaches eligible beneficiaries efficiently and transparently. A nation demonstrates its strength not by how it serves the most privileged, but by how it protects those who face the greatest barriers every single day. For many PWDs, every journey to school, every trip to work, every medical consultation, and every attempt to live independently comes with costs that others never have to bear. Without meaningful government support, these barriers become lifelong obstacles that deny opportunities, dignity, and equal participation. This measure recognizes that genuine inclusion demands more than legal recognition, it requires sustained public investment that empowers persons with disabilities to live with dignity, independence, and hope. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11009
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES AND SOLO PARENTS FROM GOVERNMENT FEES AND CHARGES IN THE ISSUANCE OF BASIC DOCUMENTARY REQUIREMENTS FOR EMPLOYMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to exempt persons with disabilities (PWDs) and solo parents from government fees and charges for the issuance of basic documentary requirements for employment. It aims to eliminate financial barriers that may prevent qualified jobseekers from securing gainful work. The Philippine Statistics Authority’s 2025 Labor Force Survey1 recorded more than fifty-two (52) million individuals in the labor force, with more than two (2) million unemployed. When applying for jobs, applicants are often required to secure clearances and certificates, like barangay or police clearances, medical certificates, and academic and other government-issued records. Although individually modest, the hefty accumulative cost of these pre-employment requirements can burden PWDs and solo parents who may find themselves having to prioritize expenses related to the everyday sustenance of their families. The bill therefore waives government fees and charges for essential pre-employment documents issued by national government agencies and local government units (LGU). Qualified beneficiaries may avail themselves of the exemption upon presentation of the appropriate identification issued or recognized by the concerned LGU. Employment should be determined through a person’s competence, determination, and potential, not merely by their ability to pay for documentary requirements before getting their first paycheck. This measure promotes equal opportunities and strengthens the economic participation of PWDs and solo parents without lowering employment standards. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. (2025, July 8). Accessed in July 5, 2026. label: HB 11010
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE PENALTIES FOR AND BANNING THOSE CONVICTED OF ANIMAL CRUELTY FROM OWNING ANIMALS, STRENGTHENING ANIMAL WELFARE PROTECTION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF 1988, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to impose higher penalties for acts of animal cruelty, maltreatment, and neglect; permanently prohibit persons convicted of violations under Republic Act (RA) No. 8485, otherwise known as the “Animal Welfare Act of 1998”, as amended, from owning animals; and establish a National Animal Offender Registry under the Department of Agriculture. In February 2025, public outrage followed the discovery of a dead dog inside a government-run dog pound in Masbate, prompting renewed calls for stronger accountability and animal welfare protections1. In March 2025, the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) likewise called for stronger enforcement following the fatal stabbing of a dog in Subic, Zambales. These incidents shows the challenges in reporting and prosecuting animal cruelty cases, particularly due to weak enforcement and limited public awareness of legal remedies2. Highly publicized cases of animal cruelty shared on social media have further stressed the need for stronger safeguards. “Tiktok”, a dog from Negros Occidental, was shot multiple times with arrows, while “Axle”, an American Bully from Mountain Province, was brutally beaten and killed after allegedly urinating on the perpetrator3. These cases show the continuing need to strengthen the country’s legal framework on animal welfare and ensure that such acts of cruelty are met with penalties commensurate with their severity. While RA No. 8485, as amended, prescribes criminal penalties for acts of animal cruelty, its existing safeguards remain limited in preventing convicted offenders from gaining access to animals in the 1 Barcelonia, W. Accessed from: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/940789/animal-cruelty-paws-tips/story/. Accessed in July 6, 2026. 3 Serquiña, M. (2025, December 18). Justice pursued: Rap filed for dog’s death in Mountain Province. GMA News Online. Accessed from: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/regions/970080/charges-dog-death-mountain-province/story . Accessed in July 6, 2026. future. The proposed measure increases the penalties for animal cruelty to ensure that the punishment reflects the gravity of the offense and strengthens its deterrent effect. It also permanently prohibits convicted offenders from owning animals and establishes a National Animal Offender Registry to enable law enforcement agencies, regulatory authorities, animal shelters, breeders, rescue organizations, and other authorized stakeholders to verify a person’s history of animal welfare violations. A nation’s compassion is measured not only by how it treats its people, but also by the mercy it extends to those without a voice. Animals depend entirely on human conscience for their protection, and when the law allows convicted abusers to regain access to them without meaningful safeguards, innocent lives remain vulnerable to repeated cruelty. As stewards of the environment and of creatures that cannot protect themselves, we have a duty to ensure that cruelty has no place in a civilized society. Advocating for the welfare of animals is not merely an act of kindness, but is a reflection of our collective commitment to justice and humanity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11011
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PUBLIC VETERINARY CLINIC IN EVERY CITY AND MUNICIPALITY IN THE COUNTRY, PROVIDING FOR THEIR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Public Veterinary Clinic in every city and municipality in the country. It aims to provide preventive, diagnostic, curative, and emergency animal health services, strengthen disease surveillance and response, promote responsible pet ownership, support livestock and poultry raisers, and advance animal welfare as an essential component of public health and food security. Despite the passage of Republic Act (RA) No. 8485, otherwise known as the “Animal Welfare Act of 1988”, as amended; and RA No. 9482, otherwise known as the “Anti-Rabies Act of 2007”, access to veterinary services remains uneven across the country. Many municipalities still lack permanent veterinary offices, adequate facilities, and sufficient veterinary personnel, leaving pet owners, farmers, and livestock raisers with limited access to essential animal health services. The Department of Health reported two hundred and sixty (260) human rabies cases from January to September 2025, with ninety-five percent (95%) of infections involving animals that were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status1. Likewise, veterinary experts have emphasized that many municipalities continue to operate without permanent veterinarians, making sustained vaccination campaigns, disease surveillance, and animal health planning difficult to implement effectively2. The proposed measure establishes fully operational public veterinary clinics in every city and municipality to expand vaccination and sterilization programs, improve disease surveillance and emergency response, enhance animal rescue and welfare services, provide technical assistance to livestock and poultry producers, and institutionalize accessible veterinary care as a regular local government service. It also reinforces local preparedness against zoonotic diseases while promoting healthier communities and protecting agricultural productivity. 1 Montemayor, M. (2025, September 29). DOH pushes for responsible pet ownership as rabies cases in PH hit 260. Philippine News Agency. Accessed from: https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1259841. Accessed on July 6, 2026. 2 Varcas, M. (2026, March 5). Experts push for municipal veterinary offices bill to curb rabies cases. Philippine Star-Business World. Accessed from: https://bworldonline.com/health/2026/03/05/734549/. Accessed on July 6, 2026. Animals enrich families, sustain livelihoods, and contribute to the nation’s food security, yet countless Filipinos continue to struggle to obtain even the most basic veterinary care because these services remain unavailable or financially out of reach in many communities. Every missed vaccination, untreated illness, or delayed response to disease increases the risk to both animal and human lives and places greater economic burdens on households and local governments. Establishing public veterinary clinics throughout the country transforms animal healthcare into an essential public service that protects families, strengthens rural economies, safeguards the nation’s food supply, and promotes a more compassionate and healthier society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11012
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING PROVINCIAL SOIL LABORATORY FACILITIES IN ALL PROVINCES OF THE PHILIPPINES, STRENGTHENING SOIL HEALTH MANAGEMENT AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish at least one (1) Provincial Soil Laboratory Facility in every province of the Philippines under the Department of Agriculture (DA), through the Bureau of Soils and Water Management (BSWM). It aims to provide accessible, reliable, and comprehensive soil testing, analysis, and technical advisory services for farmers and local government units. The agricultural sector continues to grapple with declining soil fertility, inefficient fertilizer application, increasing production costs, and the growing impacts of climate change. Although the BSWM currently provides laboratory services, access remains limited, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged provinces. Many farmers rely on generalized fertilizer recommendations or basic field-based Soil Test Kits that cannot adequately determine nutrient deficiencies, soil organic matter, salinity, contamination, and other critical indicators necessary for precision agriculture. The DA1 launched the country’s first Mobile Soil Laboratory in December 2024 to bring advanced soil testing closer to farming communities, acknowledging that access to science-based soil analysis remains a challenge. The DA-BSWM’s National Soil Health Program identifies accessible and accurate soil testing as a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture and productivity. Additionally, the 2024 Status of the World’s Soils2 reported that thirty-three percent (33%) of the global soils are already moderately to highly degraded, threatening food production and environmental sustainability. These realities highlight the urgent need to establish permanent provincial laboratories capable of providing comprehensive diagnostics to support informed fertilizer use, higher yields, and long-term food security. 1 DA-AFID. (2024, December 10). DA Unveils Mobile Soil Lab. Department of Agriculture. Accessed from: https://www.da.gov.ph/gallery/da-unveils-mobile-soil-lab-december-6-2024/. Accessed on July 5, 2026. 2 Smith, P. et al., 2024. Status of the World’s Soils. Annual Review Environment and Resources. 49:73-104. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-environ-030323-075629 This proposed measure ensures these facilities conduct macro- and micronutrient analysis, soil organic matter assessment, soil texture and structure evaluation, salinity and contamination testing, and other diagnostic procedures beyond conventional test kits. It integrates laboratory-generated data into fertilizer assistance programs, agricultural extension services, and provincial development planning through a mandatory Site-Specific Nutrient Management framework. The bill also ensures affordable access to soil testing, prioritizes smallholder farmers, promotes partnerships with state universities and research institutions, and establishes a nationwide soil health monitoring system that will enable evidence-based policymaking. Farmers have long carried the responsibility of feeding millions despite facing declining soil quality and escalating production costs. Every harvest lost to poor soil management weakens rural livelihoods, drives food prices upward, and threatens national food security. Investing in provincial soil laboratories is an investment in every farming family and Filipino household. Providing farmers with accurate soil information empowers them to make better decisions, improve productivity, reduce unnecessary expenses, and preserve the country’s most valuable agricultural resource for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11013
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ALTERNATIVE CLASSROOM LEARNING EXPERIENCE PROGRAM TO ALL SECONDARY AND TERTIARY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS THROUGHOUT THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience (ACLE) Program in all public and private secondary and tertiary educational institutions throughout the Philippines. It complements formal classroom instruction through student-led academic, civic, and experiential learning activities that cultivate critical thinking, democratic participation, leadership, and social responsibility. The country continues to confront a learning crisis that extends beyond academic performance, but also to the development of critical thinking, civic engagement, and leadership among learners. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II)1 described the state of Philippine education as a matter of “national survival” and emphasized that ninety one percent (91%) of Filipino ten-year-old learners are unable to read and understand age-appropriate texts, while persistent weaknesses in analytical reasoning, communication, and problem-solving continue to undermine the country’s human capital. The report further stressed that learning recovery cannot rely solely on traditional classroom instruction and called for transformative reforms that develop learners’ higher-order thinking, collaboration, and real-world competencies. Likewise, the Department of Education’s Quality Basic Education Development Plan (Q-BEDP) 2025–20352 recognizes that improving education quality requires learner-centered, experiential, and innovative approaches that prepare students for rapid technological change, artificial intelligence, and the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Internationally, UNICEF Philippines3 continues to warn that the country’s learning crisis threatens its demographic dividend, noting 1 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). (2025,January). Fixing the Foundations: A Matter of National Survival (Year Two Report). Accessed from: https://edcom2.gov.ph/media/2025/01/EDCOM-2-Year-2-Report-Fixing-the-Foundations-2025.pdf. Accessed on July 4, 2026. 2 Department of Education. (2025). Quality Basic Education Development Plan (Q-BEDP) 2025–2035. 2025. Accessed from: https://planipolis.iiep.unesco.org/en/2025/quality-basic-education-development-plan-2025-2035. Accessed on July 4, 2026. 3 Piojo, L. M. (2024, Updated2025). Education: The Learning Crisis. UNICEF Philippines. Accessed from: https://www.unicef.org/philippines/education. Accessed on July 4, 2026. that without quality and inclusive education, the Philippines risks producing a generation that is inadequately prepared for employment, civic participation, and sustainable national development. Despite these realities, opportunities for structured, student-led academic discussions, community immersion, interdisciplinary learning, and civic engagement remain largely dependent on the initiatives of individual schools rather than on a consistent national policy. This measure institutionalizes the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience (ACLE) Program as a mandatory activity to be conducted at least once every semester or academic term in all secondary and tertiary educational institutions. It empowers student councils and student governments to organize educational discussions, policy fora, workshops, community integration activities, lectures, symposia, fieldwork, film screenings, and other experiential learning initiatives with the support of school administrations. It transforms these activities into an integral component of the educational experience, guaranteeing that learners develop not only academic competence but also leadership, civic consciousness, social awareness, innovation, and the capacity to engage constructively with diverse ideas and contemporary national issues. The bill reinforces the policy objectives of Republic Act (RA) No. 9155, otherwise known as the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001”; RA No. 7722, otherwise known as the “Higher Education Act of 1994”; RA No. 8292, otherwise known as the “Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997”; and RA No. 9500, otherwise known as the “University of the Philippines Charter of 2008”, all of which uphold quality education, academic freedom, institutional autonomy, and the holistic development of Filipino learners. Education must do more than produce graduates who can pass examinations; it must nurture citizens who can question, innovate, lead, and serve. Every learner deserves opportunities to experience education beyond the confines of textbooks and classrooms, where ideas are challenged, perspectives are broadened, and meaningful engagement with society begins. As the nation strives to recover from years of learning loss while preparing its youth for an increasingly complex and interconnected world, investing in programs that cultivate critical thinkers and responsible leaders has become an urgent national imperative. Institutionalizing the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience Program will help ensure that Filipino students are not merely equipped to earn a diploma, but are empowered to shape communities, strengthen democratic institutions, and lead the country's future with competence, integrity, and purpose. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. title: AN ACT PROVIDING A LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR TRANSACTIONS AND OTHER LEGALLY RELEVANT ACTS PERFORMED THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGENTS, ESTABLISHING A VOLUNTARY DIGITAL AUTHORITY CREDENTIAL FRAMEWORK, PRESERVING ACCOUNTABILITY AND GOOD-FAITH RELIANCE, PROTECTING LAWFUL DIGITAL ASSET OWNERSHIP, SELF-CUSTODY, PEER-TO- PEER AND OPEN-SOURCE TECHNOLOGIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from a technology that merely generates recommendations or content into one capable of acting on behalf of people and businesses. AI agents can increasingly negotiate terms, communicate with counterparties, execute electronic documents, initiate payments, and interact with automated systems without requiring a human to approve every individual step. Philippine law already recognizes electronic transactions and automated information systems. The next policy challenge is to provide greater legal certainty when increasingly autonomous AI agents perform legally consequential acts: when should an act be attributed to the person who authorized the agent, when may a third party reasonably rely upon that authority, and how should accountability be preserved without granting legal personhood to software? This measure adopts an enabling rather than prohibitory approach. It recognizes AI agents as technological instruments through which natural and juridical persons may act, while ensuring that an identifiable Principal remains accountable. It establishes a primarily voluntary Digital Authority Credential framework so that persons and businesses that need greater certainty may make delegated authority verifiable to counterparties. Mandatory registration is reserved for narrowly designated high-risk autonomous transactions where existing regulation is inadequate. The measure is also founded on technological neutrality. AI agents may interact with conventional payment systems, application programming interfaces, blockchain networks, smart contracts, digital assets, self-custodial wallets, and future technologies, subject to laws independently applicable to the person or transaction. The Act does not create a new license for digital assets, does not require the registration of wallets or blockchain addresses, does not require disclosure of private keys or seed phrases, and does not prohibit lawful self- custody or peer-to-peer transactions. The bill likewise protects open-source and non-custodial innovation by providing that developers and infrastructure participants are not treated as Principals or financial intermediaries merely because they publish or maintain software without controlling users' assets or transactions. The objective is simple: to give Filipinos and Philippine businesses a clear legal framework for using AI agents to transact, while preserving accountability, consumer and third- party protection, privacy, cybersecurity, innovation, competition, and technological freedom. 1 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL CONTINUOUS VEGETABLE PLANTING INTENTIONS SURVEY AND MODERNIZING AGRICULTURAL STATISTICAL FORECASTING THROUGH REAL-TIME DATA AND GEOSPATIAL TECHNOLOGIES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide timely and forward-looking information on vegetable production, supply, demand, and market conditions. It aims to strengthen production planning and enable the government and agricultural stakeholders to identify emerging imbalances and respond before these translate into significant losses for farmers and disruptions in the market. In April 2026, cabbage farmers in Atok, Benguet reportedly received as little as Four pesos (Php 4.00) to Eight pesos (Php 8.00) per kilogram, while some opted not to harvest as prices fell below production and harvesting costs1. At the La Trinidad Vegetable Trading Post, adequate supply coincided with weaker demand, fewer buyers, and high transport costs, leaving some produce unsold2. Farmers and traders subsequently sought temporary floor prices for selected vegetables after cabbage prices fell to about Five pesos (Php 5.00) per kilogram against production costs of approximately Twenty pesos (Php 20.00) per kilogram3. These show the need for reliable information on what farmers intend to plant, where production will occur, and when harvests are expected, so that potential supply and market imbalances can be identified earlier. The proposed measure institutionalizes the National Vegetable Planting Intentions Survey under the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), which shall regularly collect information on intended crops, planting areas, locations, production schedules, expected output, and intended markets. Planting-intentions data will be integrated with production and administrative records, market and demand indicators, weather and climate information, and geospatial data. Digital reporting platforms, Geographic Information Systems, remote sensing, and statistical and econometric models may be used to generate geographically disaggregated forecasts and assess planting intentions against actual planting, harvested area, production, and market outcomes. For vegetable farmers, timely information can mean the difference between a profitable harvest and a crop that is left to rot. When vegetables are sold below production cost or abandoned in the fields, farmers lose not only their expected income but also the capital, labor, and months of work invested in every planting season. These losses also affect consumers, traders, transporters, and the broader agricultural economy. The State should not wait for farmgate prices to collapse, trading posts to be filled with unsold produce, or crops to spoil before responding. Farmers deserve a government that can see emerging risks, act ahead of market disruptions, and use public resources where they can have the greatest impact. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural assets. Stretching from Cagayan in the north to Quezon in the south, it forms a vast interconnected landscape of forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems. Its ecological functions extend far beyond the mountain range itself, providing essential services that sustain communities, agriculture, water systems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic activities in both upland and downstream areas. The Sierra Madre likewise serves as a critical natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, storm surges, drought, and other climate-related hazards. Its forests, watersheds, wetlands, riparian areas, ecological corridors, and coastal ecosystems regulate water flows, store and sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and contribute to the resilience of communities and critical infrastructure. The protection and restoration of the Sierra Madre are therefore not merely matters of environmental conservation, but matters of national development, public safety, water security, climate resilience, and national security. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre remains vulnerable to continuing degradation arising from illegal logging, destructive extraction, incompatible land conversion, habitat fragmentation, biodiversity loss, and other activities that undermine ecological integrity. Existing governmental mandates and management arrangements, while important, operate through different agencies, jurisdictions, plans, and regulatory systems. Such fragmentation makes it difficult to manage the Sierra Madre as one 1 interconnected ecological system and to consistently account for impacts that cross administrative boundaries. This proposed measure seeks to address this institutional and ecological gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA) as a government-owned or -controlled corporation with an original charter, attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination and administrative supervision. The Authority is envisioned as the lead policy, planning, coordinating, and regulatory body for range-wide ecological governance, while preserving the lawful mandates of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, Protected Area Management Boards, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, and other competent institutions. At the center of the proposed framework is the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, geospatially explicit, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. The measure adopts a landscape-scale and ridge-to-reef approach to conservation. Rather than treating forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems as isolated units, the proposed framework recognizes their ecological and hydrological interdependence. It provides for the identification and protection of ecological corridors, riparian buffers, critical habitats, key biodiversity areas, and other connectivity systems necessary to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The bill further advances a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy. Government interventions addressing flooding, landslides, erosion, watershed degradation, water insecurity, coastal hazards, and climate risks will be required to consider the feasibility of nature-based, green, or green-gray solutions before relying solely on conventional infrastructure. The proposed approach recognizes natural ecosystems as functional infrastructure capable of providing long-term disaster-risk reduction, water-security, and climate-adaptation benefits. Recognizing that conservation cannot be sustained without viable communities and economic incentives, the proposed measure promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples, upland communities, and lawful tenure holders to participate in conservation and restoration activities and benefit from verified ecological outcomes. A significant innovation of the measure is the establishment of a Sierra Madre Nature Credit System. The system is intended to create a transparent and independently verified mechanism through which measurable protection, restoration, biodiversity, watershed, water-security, and climate-resilience outcomes may be recognized and financed. Covered enterprises that materially depend upon Sierra Madre ecosystem services may be required to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby 2 helping align economic activity with the ecological services upon which such activity depends. The system expressly does not authorize prohibited activities or substitute for environmental, tenure, protected-area, or Indigenous Peoples safeguards. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, certain environmental charges, penalties and restoration recoveries when legally assignable, grants and technical assistance, and other lawful sources. The Fund is limited to the Authority’s statutory public-good and market-governance functions and is subject to government accounting, procurement, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. label: HB 11018
title: AN ACT CREATING THE BICOL RIVER BASIN MANAGEMENT OFFICE (BRBMO), DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bicol River Basin is one of the most significant river systems in the Philippines, serving as a vital source of water for agriculture, domestic use, fisheries, and ecological sustainability in the Bicol Region. It plays a critical role in supporting food security, livelihoods, and regional economic development. However, the basin continues to face persistent and complex challenges, including recurrent flooding, watershed degradation, sedimentation, climate change impacts, and fragmented governance mechanisms. Despite the existence of various national and local initiatives, the management of the Bicol River Basin remains institutionally fragmented, with multiple agencies exercising overlapping mandates over water resources, irrigation, flood control, environmental protection, and land use. This has resulted in inefficiencies, lack of coordination, and suboptimal outcomes in addressing both environmental and socio-economic concerns. The Constitution mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology (Article II, Section 16), and to ensure the rational utilization and conservation of natural resources. In line with this, there is a compelling need to adopt an integrated river basin management (IRBM) approach, which recognizes the interdependence of land, water, ecosystems, and human communities within a river basin. While prior executive issuances, such as Presidential Decree No. 926 and Executive Order No. 359, have established project-level and programmatic mechanisms for the Bicol River Basin, these measures remain limited in scope, continuity, and institutional authority. Moreover, existing structures under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), including the River Basin Control Office, primarily provide policy direction at the national level and are not designed to function as dedicated, basin-specific coordinating bodies with sustained operational capacity. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps through the creation of the Bicol River Basin Management Office (BRBMO), which shall serve as a central coordinating and integrative body for all programs, projects, and policies affecting the Bicol River Basin. The BRBMO is designed not to duplicate or supplant existing agencies, but to harmonize their efforts, facilitate inter-agency collaboration, and ensure a coherent and science-based approach to river basin management. Consistent with the principle of local autonomy under the Local Government Code of 1991, the proposed Office shall work in close coordination with local government units, ensuring that local development plans are aligned with basin-wide strategies while respecting the powers and functions of LGUs. Furthermore, the measure institutionalizes multi-stakeholder participation, recognizing that sustainable river basin management requires the active involvement of communities, farmers, fisherfolk, indigenous peoples, civil society, and the private sector. By establishing a dedicated institutional mechanism anchored on integrated, participatory, and science-driven management, this bill aims to enhance the resilience, sustainability, and productivity of the Bicol River Basin, thereby contributing to national priorities on environmental protection, disaster risk reduction, food security, and inclusive development. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11019
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CHARACTER EDUCATION IN THE PHILIPPINE BASIC EDUCATION SYSTEM THROUGH A HOLISTIC AND VALUES-BASED APPROACH INSPIRED BY INTERNATIONAL BEST PRACTICES, INCLUDING JAPAN’S EDUCATIONAL MODEL, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strength of a nation lies not only in the intelligence of its people, but in their character, discipline, and sense of responsibility to others. In recent years, concerns have been raised regarding declining discipline, lack of civic consciousness, and weakening social responsibility among the youth. While the Philippine education system has made significant strides in expanding access and improving academic outcomes, there remains a pressing need to reinforce character formation as a central pillar of education. Japan’s educational system offers a compelling model in this regard. It is globally recognized not only for academic excellence but for its deep-rooted emphasis on discipline, respect, responsibility, and collective accountability. Students are taught early on the value of hard work, cleanliness, cooperation, and respect for others, not merely through classroom instruction, but through daily school practices and community engagement. This proposed measure seeks to adapt these best practices to the Philippine context, strengthening the existing K to 12 curriculum by institutionalizing a more structured, experiential, and community-based approach to character education. It aims to produce learners who are not only academically competent but also morally grounded, socially responsible, and committed to nation-building. The bill is firmly anchored on Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates the State to promote quality education and develop moral character. It complements existing laws such as Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013 by reinforcing the holistic development of learners. Importantly, this measure respects academic freedom, cultural diversity, and inclusivity, ensuring that character education remains secular, values- based, and responsive to the needs of Filipino communities. At a time when the nation faces complex social and economic challenges, it is imperative to invest not only in knowledge, but in the values and character of future generations. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11020
title: AN ACT REQUIRING ALL SHIPPING LINES OPERATING IN THE PHILIPPINES TO ADOPT ELECTRONIC TICKETING (E-TICKETING) AND CASHLESS PAYMENT SYSTEMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The maritime transport sector remains a critical backbone of inter-island connectivity in the Philippines, particularly in regions such as Bicol where mobility, trade, tourism, and access to essential services rely heavily on domestic shipping. Despite its importance, many shipping operations in the country continue to rely on manual ticketing systems and cash-based transactions, which are prone to inefficiencies, long queues, revenue leakages, and limited transparency. The continued reliance on manual and cash-based systems also poses challenges to passenger convenience, financial inclusion, and public safety, especially in the context of increasing demand for contactless and technology- driven services. Moreover, the absence of standardized digital systems limits the ability of government agencies to maintain accurate passenger manifests, monitor compliance, and implement data-driven policies in the maritime sector. The proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by requiring all domestic shipping lines and maritime passenger carriers to adopt electronic ticketing (e-ticketing) systems and cashless payment options. This initiative is aligned with the State policy to promote the development of information and communications technology, digital innovation, and efficient delivery of public services, consistent with Article II of the 1987 Constitution. This measure complements existing laws such as the E-Commerce Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8792), which recognizes the legal validity of electronic transactions, and the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173), which ensures the protection of personal data in digital systems. It likewise aligns with the national government’s thrust toward digital transformation and financial inclusion, as supported by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and the Department of Information and Communications Technology. Importantly, the bill does not eliminate cash transactions entirely but instead requires the availability of cashless alternatives, thereby ensuring inclusivity for passengers in areas with limited digital access while gradually transitioning the sector toward modernization. The measure also strengthens inter-agency coordination by designating the Department of Transportation, the Maritime Industry Authority, the Philippine Ports Authority, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Department of Information and Communications Technology as implementing agencies. This ensures that existing mandates are respected and harmonized, thereby avoiding duplication of functions and potential conflicts in authority. For the Bicol Region, the adoption of e-ticketing and cashless systems is expected to significantly improve port efficiency, passenger experience, tourism flow, and regional economic activity, while enhancing transparency and accountability in maritime operations. By institutionalizing digital ticketing and payment systems in the maritime sector, this bill aims to promote a modern, efficient, and inclusive transportation system that is consistent with national development goals and the evolving needs of the Filipino people. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11021
title: AN ACT ADOPTING A NATIONAL FLOOD CONTROL BENCHMARK BASED ON INTERNATIONAL BEST PRACTICES, INCLUDING JAPAN’S FLOOD MANAGEMENT STANDARDS, STRENGTHENING INTEGRATED RIVER BASIN MANAGEMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Flooding remains one of the most persistent and destructive natural hazards in the Philippines, causing significant loss of life, displacement of communities, and damage to infrastructure and the economy. The increasing intensity of rainfall due to climate change, combined with rapid urbanization and environmental degradation, has further heightened the country’s vulnerability to flooding. Despite substantial investments in flood control infrastructure, many existing systems remain fragmented, reactive, and insufficiently coordinated, often focusing on isolated structural interventions rather than comprehensive, basin-wide solutions. Japan is widely recognized as a global leader in flood management, having developed highly advanced systems that integrate engineering excellence, river basin management, land use planning, early warning systems, and community preparedness.1 Its approach is characterized by a multi-layered flood control strategy, combining structural and non-structural measures and grounded in long-term planning and scientific data. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a National Flood Control Benchmark Framework, drawing from Japan’s proven practices while adapting them to Philippine conditions. The objective is not merely to replicate foreign models, but to establish a unified, science-based standard for flood control across the country, ensuring consistency, efficiency, and resilience. 1 Tsukasa Nakamura, Deloitte, “How Japan is turning climate and ﬂood risk into economic growth through infrastructure innovations,” World Economic Forum, 10 August 2026, available at: https://www.weforum.org/stories/climate-action/japan-climate-ﬂood-resilience-infrastructure/ The measure is anchored on the State’s constitutional duty to protect the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology (Article II, Section 16) and to promote the general welfare. It also complements existing laws such as the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 and the Climate Change Act of 2009, by strengthening the integration of infrastructure, environmental management, and disaster preparedness. Importantly, the bill respects the mandates of existing agencies and the autonomy of local government units, positioning the national framework as a coordinating and standard-setting mechanism rather than a centralizing authority. By adopting international best practices and institutionalizing integrated flood control standards, this measure aims to enhance the country’s capacity to prevent, mitigate, and respond to flooding, ultimately safeguarding lives, protecting property, and promoting sustainable development. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11022
title: AN ACT ENSURING GENDER-RESPONSIVENESS IN NATIONALITY LAWS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE COMMONWEALTH ACT NO. 473, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE REVISED NATURALIZATION LAW, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9139, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ADMINISTRATIVE NATURALIZATION LAW
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution enshrines the role of women in nation-building and the responsibility of the State to ensure the fundamental equality of women and men before the law (Article II, Section 14). Republic Act No. 9710, otherwise known as the Magna Carta of Women, and the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (UN CEDAW), of which the Philippines is a State Party, underscores the equal rights of men and women to acquire, change, or retain their nationality (Section 19; Article 9, respectively). Further, both emphasize that neither marriage to an alien nor change of nationality by the husband during marriage shall automatically change the nationality of the wife, render her stateless, or force upon her the nationality of the husband (Section 19(g); Article 9). Despite these frameworks, the Philippines has been identified as one of fifty (50) States that continue to have distinctions in terms of conferral and acquisition/retainment of citizenship1. These are embodied in the country’s 1 Reference: https://equalnationalityrights.org/the-issue/the-problem Page 1 of 14 naturalization laws which are governed by Commonwealth Act No. 473, otherwise known as the Revised Naturalization Law, and Republic Act 9139 No. or the Administrative Naturalization Law. Article 15 of the Revised Naturalization Law denies a married woman the right to choose her nationality following the naturalization of her husband. Furthermore, Section 12 of the Administrative Naturalization Law prevents married women that have been granted Philippine citizenship through naturalization, from conferring her nationality to her husband. Not only do these provisions violate the principles and commitments of the Philippines under international2 and national laws, but it also inhibits inclusive sustainable development as citizenship serves as the gateway to access other rights and services3. Hence, this bill seeks to (1) harmonize existing laws4, (2) amend the current Administrative and Judicial Naturalization Laws, especially, the automatic conferment of derivative naturalization in Section 15 of Commonwealth Act No. 473, and the differential effect of naturalization on non-national spouses as indicated in Sections 11, 12, and 13 of Republic Act No. 9139, and (3) ensure safeguards to prevent statelessness in line with the General Recommendation No. 32 of the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women5 and the recently ratified 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. This proposed measure is also in line with efforts to remove gender discrimination in nationality laws under Action Point 3 of the National Action Plan to End Statelessness by 2024. It contributes to the fulfillment of the Philippines’ pledge to enhance its “policy, legal, and operational framework” during the 2011 Ministerial Inter-Governmental Event on Refugees and Stateless Persons6 and 2019 High-Level Segment on Statelessness7. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 The right to nationality is also enshrined in several international and regional human rights instruments. The list of which could be found in pages 26-28 of 2020 Guidelines on Statelessness on Loss and Deprivation of Nationality under Articles 5-9 of the 1961 Convention. 3 Reference: https://equalnationalityrights.org/the-issue/the-problem 4 Harmonization of naturalization laws with the Republic Act 9710 and the UN CEDAW would also contribute to the fulfillment of the recommendation of the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination of Women in its Concluding Observations on the Combined 7th and 8th Reports of the Philippines. 5 Specifically, paragraph 63 (b, e, i) of the General Recommendation No. 32 of the Gender-related Dimensions of Refugee Status, Asylum, Nationality and Statelessness of Women. 6 Information on the 2011 Ministerial Inter-Governmental Event on Refugees and Stateless Persons as well as the pledges manifested by the Philippines can be accessed through: https://www.unhcr.org/4ff55a319.pdf 7 Pledges manifested by the Philippines during the 2019 High-Level Segment on Statelessness can be accessed through: https://www.unhcr.org/ibelong/results-of-the-high-level-segment-on-statelessness/ Page 2 of 14 REP.
