label: HB 11023
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FIFTEEN THOUSAND PESOS (PHP 15,000) ACROSS THE BOARD INCREASE IN THE BASIC MONTHLY SALARY OF TEACHERS AND EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC BASIC EDUCATION AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is the foundation of a strong, progressive, and inclusive nation. At the heart of our public education system are the teachers and employees who dedicate their knowledge, skills, time, and energy to shaping the future of our children and strengthening the human capital of our country. Every day, public school teachers and education personnel perform responsibilities that go far beyond the traditional boundaries of their jobs. Teachers prepare lessons, assess learners, provide individualized support, address learning gaps, manage classrooms, and respond to the diverse needs of students. Non- teaching personnel, meanwhile, provide essential administrative, technical, and support services that ensure the continuous and effective delivery of basic education. Despite the vital nature of their work, many public school teachers and employees continue to face increasing financial pressures brought about by the rising cost of food, transportation, housing, utilities, healthcare, and other basic necessities. The demands of the profession have likewise continued to grow, with education personnel being called upon to perform increasingly complex responsibilities in an evolving educational environment. The State recognizes the invaluable contribution of teachers and education personnel to national development. The 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall assign the highest budgetary priority to education and shall ensure that teaching will attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration and other means of job satisfaction and fulfillment. Providing adequate and competitive compensation is not merely an issue of employee welfare. It is an investment in the quality and stability of our public education system. Fair and meaningful increases in salaries can help improve the economic well- being of education personnel, strengthen employee morale, promote retention, and encourage qualified and competent individuals to remain in or enter the public education service. In recognition of their indispensable contribution to the Filipino people, this measure seeks to grant an across-the-board increase of Fifteen Thousand Pesos (₱15,000.00) in the basic monthly salary of teachers and employees in public basic education. To ensure fiscal sustainability and facilitate the orderly implementation of the measure, the proposed increase shall be implemented in three tranches: ₱6,000.00 in the first year, ₱5,000.00 in the second year, and ₱4,000.00 in the third year. The proposed salary increase shall be granted in addition to existing salary adjustments under applicable salary standardization laws and shall not prejudice any succeeding salary increases that may be granted to government employees pursuant to law. The measure further recognizes that the welfare of teachers and education personnel is directly connected to the quality of education that our children receive. By providing them with better compensation and stronger economic security, the government can help create a more motivated, committed, and resilient public education workforce capable of responding to the changing needs of Filipino learners. Our teachers and education personnel are not merely government employees. They are builders of communities, shapers of minds, and partners in nation-building. Their work creates opportunities, transforms lives, and lays the foundation for the country's future. It is therefore imperative that the State provide them with compensation commensurate with the importance of their work and the responsibilities they carry. This measure seeks to reaffirm our commitment to the men and women who serve at the frontlines of public education and to ensure that their dedication and sacrifices are met with meaningful support from the government. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11024
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING STANDARDS FOR RELATED LEARNING EXPERIENCES (RLE) IN NURSING EDUCATION, PROHIBITING THE COLLECTION OF RLE FEES FROM NURSING STUDENTS IN STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES (SUCs) AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES (LUCs), AND PROVIDING FUNDING SUPPORT THROUGH THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION (CHED)
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) Memorandum Order No. 14, Series of 2009, students of the Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) program are mandated to complete at least 46 units or 2,346 hours of Related Learning Experiences (RLE), which may be extended until expected competencies are satisfactorily achieved. RLE are integral to nursing education as teaching-learning opportunities designed to develop the competencies of nursing students utilizing the nursing process in varying health situations. Through RLE, Filipino nursing students are provided with hands-on clinical training and essential exposure to real-world healthcare settings. However, despite the existence of Republic Act No. 10931, otherwise known as the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act (UAQTE), that provides for free tuition and institutional fees in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) and Local Universities and Colleges (LUCs) and Tertiary Education Subsidies (TES) in private higher education institutions (HEIs), RLE impose substantial financial burdens on nursing students through various fees, including affiliation charges, hospital training fees, transportation expenses, and allowances for clinical instructors. These RLE fees and related expenses, which are mostly shouldered by the nursing students themselves, range from P20,000 to P80,000 per year,1 thus creating significant barriers and placing underprivileged nursing students at a disadvantage. 1 Bonzo, L.T. (26 May 2026). CHED rolls out financial aid for 19,000 healthcare students. GMA News. Retrieved from https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/989023/ched-rolls-out-financial- aid-for-19-000-healthcare-students/story/. 1 In recognition of the noble contribution and significant role of nurses to the country’s healthcare sector, and in fulfilling the State’s mandate to make quality education accessible to all citizens, this bill seeks to institutionalize the non-collection of RLE fees from students in SUCs and LUCs. Under this bill, all RLE-related expenses shall be considered part of the tuition or institutional costs charged to the government through the Unified Student Financial Assistance System for Tertiary Education (UniFAST). As such, this bill mandates that all SUCs and LUCs offering nursing programs submit projected RLE expenses to CHED for funding through the UniFAST or other designated CHED mechanisms. For nursing students enrolled in accredited private HEIs, this bill also expands eligibility for the TES program to cover RLE fees. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Walfredo “Arman” Dimaguila, Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Antolin Oreta III, and Javier Benitez in the House of Representatives, and Senator Bam Aquino in the Senate. This bill fully adopts Senator Bam Aquino’s Senate Bill No. 123. In view of the foregoing, early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 11025
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING JOB PLACEMENT OFFICES IN ALL PUBLIC SENIOR HIGH SCHOOLS, STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND CREATING A NATIONAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCIL AND LOCAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCILS TO ADDRESS JOBS- SKILLS MISMATCH AND PROMOTE DECENT EMPLOYMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution provides for the State’s commitment to promoting full employment and a rising standard of living. This is further affirmed by Article XIII, Section 3 which declares the State’s mandate to promote full employment and equality of employment of all. Additionally, Article XIV, Section 2(1) provides that, “[t]he State shall [e]stablish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” In recent years, the State has taken significant steps towards ensuring equal access to quality education at all levels, including tertiary education, through the enactment of landmark legislation such as Republic Act No. 10931, or the “Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education (UAQTE) Act,” and the continuous filings of, and deliberations on amendatory measures to strengthen existing laws. However, despite these efforts, unemployment and underemployment remain persistent problems facing Filipino graduates after completing their senior high school or college education. According to CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis, the June 2025 Labor Force Survey by the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) showed a 2.6% increase in the number of unemployed college graduates from 35.6% in December 2024.1 1 Cariaso, B. (15 August 2025). ‘Rising number of unemployed grads troubling.’ PhilStar. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/08/15/2465562/rising-number-unemployed-grads- troubling. 1 Additionally, “even when job opportunities exist, there is a persistent mismatch between available jobs and graduates’ skills.”2 In the January 2025 nationwide job fairs held by DOLE, only 3,364 out of 25,876 job seekers were hired and the majority were placed in “low-skilled roles that do not require a college degree.”3 Based on a recent study, an estimated 40% of Filipinos face educational-employment mismatches, where over 1 out of 3 Filipinos have an educational attainment way beyond their job requirements.4 This job mismatch problem underscores allocative inefficiency, given the greater public investment in education, and more importantly, the “wage penalties” that millions of Filipino workers suffer instead of reaping the full benefits that tertiary education promised. This bill seeks to establish Job Placement Offices (JPOs) in all public senior high schools, state universities and colleges (SUCs), and local universities and colleges (LUCs) to provide greater access for students transitioning from education to employment. A Tripartite National Industry-Academe Council (NIAC) shall be created to strengthen collaboration and coordination between the government, education, and industry sectors. Local Industry-Academe Councils (LIACs) shall be institutionalized in every province and highly urbanized city to guide local institutions and the JPOs. The Philippine Labor Market Information System (PhilLMIS) shall be established within the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to harmonize labor market data and guide policy. Lastly, the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF) shall be reinforced as the national reference for classifying qualifications and formalizes the Philippine Skills Framework (PSF) as the tool for defining job-specific competencies. In strengthening the linkages between the government, education, and industry sectors, providing greater access to career guidance for students transitioning from education to employment, and establishing a system of harmonizing labor market data, qualifications, and competencies, this bill does not merely intend to create new instrumentalities, but to establish the steps in bridging the current education- employment gap. This is essential for the Filipino people, especially the youth, to attain an educational system where every Filipino has an opportunity to fully use their skills to maximize their income and professional potential. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Lordan Suan, Walfredo Dimaguila, Mark Violago, Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Antolin Oreta, Ferdinand Martin Romualdez, Yedda Romualdez, Andrew Julian Romualdez, Jude Acidre, Ramon Jolo Revilla, Javier Benitez, Christopherson Yap, and Eric Yap, and Senators Bam Aquino and Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan. This bill adopts provisions from Senator Aquino’s and Pangilinan’s bills. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. 2 Ibid. 3 Ibid. 4 Melchor, M. (11 March 2024). label: HB 11026
title: AN ACT FURTHER STRENGTHENING THE INCENTIVES FOR PRIVATE SECTOR PARTICIPATION IN PUBLIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8525, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ADOPT-A- SCHOOL ACT OF 1998”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that “[t]he State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Almost three (3) decades ago, Republic Act No. 8525, otherwise known as the “Adopt-a-School Act of 1998,” was enacted as a step towards achieving accessible quality education by facilitating the participation of the private sector in the country’s education sector. Under the law, tax incentives are given to private entities supporting public schools. However, recent data reflect the need for the law to be amended to better respond to current challenges, such as bureaucratic red tape and administrative complexity that prevent private entities from receiving their mandated tax incentives.1 Amidst the education crisis, exacerbated by inadequate learning facilities and classroom shortages, limited digital connectivity, and insufficient teaching resources, Filipino children and students increasingly struggle with access to quality education.2 These gaps accumulate and become barriers hindering the Filipino youth from enjoying their freedoms and rights to education, to self-development and self- actualization, and to social mobility. This bill amends Republic Act No. 8525 to allow private sector donors to support a wider range of educational programs, including early childhood care, technical- 1 Second Congressional Commission on Education (2025). Fixing the Foundations: A matter of national survival, EDCOM II year two report. Congress of the Philippines. 2 Cariaso, B. (28 May 2025). Classroom shortage still at 165,000 – DepEd. The Philippine Star. https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/05/28/2446283/classroom-shortage-still-165000-deped. 1 vocational education and training (TVET), and alternative-learning system (ALS). The bill also restructures the tax incentives to include clear and enhanced deductions, payroll tax credits for employing senior high school graduates, and exemptions for imported donations. This bill recognizes that addressing the education crisis requires not only sustained government investment and action, but also participation from the private sector, communities, and civil society. label: HB 11031
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CLASSIFICATION OF DISTRICT OFFICE OF THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) IN LUCENA, QUEZON FROM CLASS "C"TO CLASS "A" DISTRICT OFFICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Land Transportation Ofice (LTO) District Office in Lucena City serves as the primary transportation regulatory and enforcement hub for Lucena City and the entire Second District of Quezon Province. However, operating under a restrictive Class "C" designation has created severe operational bottlenecks, resulting in long client waiting times due to an insufficient personnel complement, limited physical space, and inadequate IT workstations. LTO Lucena's actual workload and financial performance have far outgrown its current Class "C" classification. Under LTO Memorandum Circular No. 2020-2200, office reclassifications are evaluated based on annual transaction volume weighted at seventy percent and total revenue collection weighted at thirty percent. From CY 2023 to CY 2025, LTO Lucena handled an average of 114,794.67 total transactions annually, surpassing the 111,001 national threshold required for a maximum transaction score. Over the same three-year period, the office generated an average annual revenue ofP160,467,548.06, wellabove the P67.77 Million benchmark needed for a maximum revenue score. Official evaluation data from LTO Region IV-A confirms that LTO Lucena fully qualifies for classification as a Class "A" District Office. Upgrading its status wil formally expand its permanent staffing, improve its facility and IT capacity, shorten turnaround times, andstrengthen road safety and enforcement across the province. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sOught. label: HB 11035
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 33 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990," TO EXPAND THE COVERAGE OF BACCALAUREATE DEGREES ELIGIBLE FOR LATERAL ENTRY IN THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 33 of Republic Act No. 6975, or the “Department of the Interior and Local Government Act of 1990,” provides for the Lateral Entry Program of the Philippine National Police (PNP), allowing qualified professionals with specialized skills and expertise to enter the police service as commissioned officers. Since the law was enacted in 1990, however, the nature of crime and policing has significantly changed. The PNP now faces increasingly complex challenges, including cybercrime, financial fraud, digital threats, disaster response, and issues involving mental health and community safety. These challenges require a wider range of professional expertise beyond those specifically identified in the existing law. While Section 33 recognizes professions such as medicine, law, engineering, nursing, dentistry, optometry, chaplaincy, and criminology, it does not adequately cover emerging fields that are now essential to modern policing. These include Cybersecurity, Information Technology, Data Science, Accountancy, Finance, Psychology, Behavioral Sciences, Public Administration, and Disaster Risk Management, among others. This bill seeks to amend Section 33 of R.A. 6975 by expanding the qualifications for lateral entry and giving the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM), in coordination with the PNP, the flexibility to recognize additional baccalaureate and postgraduate degrees based on the evolving needs of the police organization. By opening the PNP to a broader pool of qualified professionals, the measure will strengthen the organization's capacity to respond to emerging threats, improve police operations, and provide more effective and specialized public safety services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. label: HB 11036
title: AN ACT MANDATING LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS TO USE BODY-WORN CAMERAS DURING LAW ENFORCEMENT OPERATIONS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article III, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, while Section 2 secures the fundamental right of the people against unreasonable searches and seizures. In recent years, public demand for greater transparency, accountability, and protection of human rights during police and law enforcement operations has escalated significantly. Although the Supreme Court, through A.M. No. 21-06-08-SC, requires the use of body-worn cameras (BWCs) during the execution of search and arrest warrants, no comprehensive law yet mandates their use in all law enforcement operations, including buy-bust operations, checkpoints, and warrantless arrests. This bill seeks to institutionalize the mandatory use of BWCs and authorized recording devices during police and field operations to promote transparency, accountability, and protection for both civilians and law enforcement officers. It also provides penalties for deliberate non-use, tampering, or unauthorized disclosure of recordings, while ensuring data privacy and due process and providing funding for equipment, training, and implementation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. label: HB 11037
title: AN ACT CONFERRING UPON THE CADETS OF THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY THE STATUS OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES, GRANTING SALARIES, BENEFITS, AND PRIVILEGES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine National Police Academy (PNPA) serves as the country's premier institution for educating and training future public safety leaders. Its cadets undergo intensive academic, military, and police training in preparation for their future service in the Philippine National Police (PNP), Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP), and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP). Despite the demanding nature of their training and the discipline expected of them, PNPA cadets currently do not enjoy the same status and benefits as cadets of the Philippine Military Academy (PMA). Their allowances and benefits remain limited and inconsistent, even though they are under full-time government supervision and are being prepared for careers in public service. This bill seeks to recognize PNPA cadets as government employees during their training. This recognition will entitle them to appropriate salaries and government benefits, including medical and disability coverage, life insurance, and other protections provided by law. Beyond providing financial security, this measure recognizes the commitment, sacrifices, and service of PNPA cadets and helps ease the financial burden on their families. It also promotes fairness by bringing their benefits closer to those enjoyed by cadets of other government service academies. By giving PNPA cadets the support and recognition they deserve, the State invests in the welfare and professional development of the men and women who will one day lead our country's police, fire, and jail services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE MARITIME INDUSTRY AUTHORITY SATELLITE OFFICE IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SOGOD, PROVINCE OF SOUTHERN LEYTE, INTO AN EXTENSION OFFICE AND TRANSFERRING ITS LOCATION TO THE MUNICIPALITY OF LILOAN, PROVINCE OF SOUTHERN LEYTE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Second Legislative District of Southern Leyte consists of coastal municipalities that have a long history of ishing, maritime trade, and participation in the country’s Overseas Employment Program. It is known as the “Gateway to Mindanao,” since both Liloan Ferry Terminal and San Ricardo Port provide passenger and cargo transport to Lipata, Surigao City. The easing of domestic and international travel restrictions has increased inter-island transport and maritime activity. This development has underscored the need to bring government maritime services closer to the public, vessel owners and operators, maritime education and training institutions, and Filipino seafarers. The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) is the government agency responsible for the regulation, promotion, and development of the Philippine maritime industry. Its functions include the registration and licensing of vessels and the implementation of applicable laws, rules, and standards relating to maritime safety, maritime education and training, and the certi ication of seafarers. MARINA’s regulatory powers and functions have been strengthened by existing law, including the transfer to MARINA of powers relating to the issuance, validation, veri ication, correction, revocation, or 1|Page cancellation of certi icates and other documentary evidence required of seafarers under the applicable provisions of Republic Act No. 10635. At present, MARINA maintains an extension of ice in Maasin City and a satellite of ice in the Municipality of Sogod, Province of Southern Leyte. This bill seeks to convert the Sogod satellite of ice into an extension of ice and transfer its location to the Municipality of Liloan. Liloan is strategically located within the Second Legislative District of Southern Leyte. It is home to the Liloan Ferry Terminal, which connects the Luzon-Visayas segment of the Pan-Philippine Highway with Mindanao. It is also in proximity to the Port of San Ricardo and the Port of Sogod and is accessible to the municipalities of Silago, Hinunangan, Hinundayan, Anahawan, San Juan, and Saint Bernard. The transfer and conversion of the of ice will improve access to vessel registration, licensing, inspection, maritime safety, seafarer certi ication, and related MARINA services. It will also enable the Authority to more effectively monitor maritime transport operations and maritime education and training activities within its area of responsibility. The measure is consistent with the policy of strengthening MARINA’s regional and local presence. Similar legislation has converted MARINA satellite of ices into extension of ices in Maasin City, Southern Leyte, and Calbayog City, Samar. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. title: AN ACT TO FURTHER DEVELOP CAPABILITY AND ESTABLISH EXPEDITIOUS TRANSFORMATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENSE AND ITS BUREAUS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A comprehensive national defense plan that addresses both conventional and non- conventional threats to national security in the present and the future goes beyond merely modernizing our military capabilities; it necessitates the modi ication of antiquated policies, starting with the Commonwealth Act No. 1, the National Defense Act of 1935. Crafted in an era when the Philippines was still under American control and protection, our ninety-year-old primary law on national defense is now obsolete and needs a major overhaul to keep up with the times. This proposal will modernize national security-related policies, principles, and concepts while institutionalizing reforms to the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the entire Department of National Defense which are introduced via executive or administrative iat. Key features of this measure include the: (1) Addition of the Secretary of Defense in the Chain of Command; the provision of maximum tenure for rank of icers; 1|Page (2) Establishment of the Warrant Of icers – highly technical experts, including combat leaders and trainers; (3) Provision of free legal assistance to military personnel charged with service- related offenses; (4) Establishment of the Government Arsenal tasked with the manufacture and/or supply of arms and ammunition to the Armed Forces and law enforcement; (5) Organization of the National Defense College into the National Defense University; (6) Integration of the Technical and Administrative Services and the Women’s Auxiliary Corps in the Component Services. With the growing geopolitical tension near our borders, the time to revisit our National Defense Act is now. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many people struggling with substance use, the hardest part of recovery is not only overcoming addiction but also overcoming the judgment of others. Negative labels and stereotypes can lead to discrimination, shame, and rejection, making it harder for recovering individuals to seek help and rebuild their lives. While accountability remains important, recovery should also give people a chance to change. A person who has completed rehabilitation should not be de ined forever by his or her past. Recovery does not end after rehabilitation. For many recovering individuals, the next challenge is inding a job, earning a living, and becoming productive and independent members of society. Without skills, livelihood opportunities, and support, they may struggle to rebuild their lives and become vulnerable to returning to harmful circumstances. The State must therefore provide them with a real opportunity to start again. This measure seeks to institutionalize Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET) and livelihood programs speci ically for rehabilitated drug dependents. These programs will help them gain practical skills, improve their chances of inding decent employment, and pursue small businesses or other livelihood opportunities. By 1|Page investing in their skills and self-reliance, we give recovering individuals not only a second chance, but also the means to make that second chance last. A similar measure was iled during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. label: HB 11041
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING AND EXPANDING THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT GOVERNMENT INTERNSHIP PROGRAM, PROVIDING INTERNSHIP OPPORTUNITIES IN NATIONAL GOVERNMENT AGENCIES, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND OTHER GOVERNMENT INSTRUMENTALITIES, GRANTING A STIPEND TIED TO THE PREVAILING REGIONAL MINIMUM WAGE, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The lack of work experience remains one of the biggest barriers faced by Filipinos seeking employment. While the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Government Internship Program (GIP) gives people a chance to gain skills and practical experience, its regular age requirement of 18 to 30 years old leaves many capable Filipinos behind. Not everyone gets their irst opportunity while they are young. For many, the need for a irst job comes later in life. This measure seeks to expand the GIP to Filipinos aged 18 years old and above who have no substantial prior work experience. This recognizes that irst-time jobseekers are not limited to young people. Adults who have never had stable employment, displaced workers, persons returning to the workforce, and older Filipinos who still want to work deserve a fair chance to learn, gain con idence, and become employable. The bill keeps the internship temporary and focused on training and skills development. It does not create a permanent position in government, guarantee employment, or allow interns to replace regular government employees. Instead, it gives participants meaningful exposure to actual workplaces in national government 1|Page agencies, local government units, and other government instrumentalities, while helping them develop skills that can open doors to future employment. To make the opportunity meaningful and accessible, interns shall receive a daily stipend equivalent to the highest prevailing regional minimum wage in their region of assignment. The measure also provides for government-funded accident insurance, proper supervision and training, fair and transparent selection, protection from discrimination and abuse, and employment facilitation after the internship. These safeguards ensure that interns are not merely given work but are given a genuine opportunity to grow. Every Filipino who wants to work deserves a chance to prove what they can do, regardless of when that opportunity comes in their life. Age should not be a barrier for a quali ied person who is willing to learn, work, and build a better future. By expanding the GIP, the government can give more Filipinos the experience, skills, and con idence they need to enter the workforce. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11042
title: AN ACT PROTECTING THE RIGHTS OF INTERNALLY DISPLACED PERSONS AND PENALIZING THE ACTS OF ARBITRARY INTERNAL DISPLACEMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has long faced disasters and armed con licts that force families to leave their homes and communities. Behind every evacuation is a family that has lost its home, livelihood, and sense of security. From Typhoon Yolanda to the Marawi Siege, millions of Filipinos have experienced the pain and uncertainty of being displaced. Yet, despite these recurring crises, our country still lacks a comprehensive law that clearly protects the rights of internally displaced persons (IDPs). Displacement does not end when people are brought to evacuation centers or temporary shelters. Many IDPs continue to struggle with access to safe housing, food, clean water, healthcare, education, livelihood, and other basic needs. Local governments and irst responders also face dif iculties in coordinating assistance and protecting the rights of displaced families. There is therefore an urgent need for a clear and uni ied framework that tells government what to do and, more importantly, reminds us of what displaced Filipinos are entitled to. This measure, which was previously iled during the 19th Congress, recognizes the rights and unique needs of IDPs, especially women, children, older persons, and other vulnerable groups. It strengthens coordination among national agencies, local governments, and other organizations, while ensuring access to adequate shelter, healthcare, education, livelihood, and other essential services. It also promotes durable solutions, including safe and voluntary return, relocation when necessary, 1|Page and meaningful reintegration into communities. Most importantly, it seeks to prevent arbitrary displacement and hold accountable those who unlawfully force people from their homes. As climate change, natural disasters, and armed con licts continue to threaten communities, displacement may become an even greater challenge in the years ahead. The government must be prepared not only to respond to emergencies, but also to protect the dignity, safety, and future of every displaced Filipino. No family should be left without protection simply because they were forced to lee their home. The immediate passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought to build a safer, more compassionate, and more resilient Philippines. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11043
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL-LIVELIHOOD CURRICULUM IN SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL, INSTITUTIONALIZING INDUSTRY-RESPONSIVE TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine economy needs workers who have not only academic knowledge, but also practical and industry-recognized skills. The Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) track in senior high school was created to help students prepare for work, entrepreneurship, or further education. However, outdated equipment, limited access to quali ied trainers, and weak links with industries can prevent students from gaining the skills employers need. We must make sure that every TVL student is given a real chance to succeed after graduation. This measure strengthens the TVL track by bringing government, schools, local governments, and industries together. It creates a TVL Coordinating Council to ensure that training remains relevant to actual jobs and industry needs, while improving access to competency assessment and certi ication. DepEd will continue to oversee the academic curriculum, while TESDA will remain responsible for technical skills, assessment, and certi ication. DOLE and DTI will help connect schools and learners with labor-market information, employers, work immersion, and entrepreneurship opportunities. The bill also encourages stronger partnerships with industries through work immersion, mentoring, teacher and trainer exposure, equipment support, job fairs, 1|Page and employment facilitation. These partnerships will help students learn skills that are actually used in the workplace, while ensuring that work-based learning is safe, supervised, educational, and free from exploitation. It also promotes support for quali ied donations and existing tax incentives allowed under the National Internal Revenue Code, helping schools gain access to needed resources without creating new tax exemptions. Education should open doors, not leave young Filipinos wondering what comes next after graduation. A strong TVL program can give students practical skills, con idence, and a pathway to decent and productive work even without a college degree. By making TVL more accessible, industry-responsive, and trusted by employers, we invest not only in our students but also in the future workforce and economy of the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11044
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PARTICIPATION OF THE YOUTH SECTOR IN ALL DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT COUNCILS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2010
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to harness their power and ensure the participation and entry of the youth sector, especially those who are no longer members of the Sangguniang Kabataan, in the country’s disaster risk reduction and management system. Considering the country’s vulnerability to natural disasters, especially with the impacts of climate change, it is important that all sectors, especially the majority of the population who are at the prime of their lives and technologically aware, are reminded and legally mandated to participate in and play an important role in disaster risk reduction. Speci ically, the bill mandates the inclusion of the Chairperson of the National Youth Commission as member of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC). Individuals and Youth organizations are likewise mandated to be included in all organizational levels of the disaster risk reduction and management system, in order to afford them a venue to participate and engage with government of icials and community leaders in formulating, planning and programming activities. 1|Page In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. label: HB 11049
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Guidance and Counseling Act of 2004 (RA 9258) was passed more than two decades ago, but until now, the need for guidance counselors still remains a problem in schools. In a feature article from 2018,1 the story of a “guidance teacher” was shown where a licensed teacher had to practice guidance and counseling due to the lack of registered guidance counselors in the public school system. This and many similar incidents happening in the country shows that it is almost impossible for the State to enforce RA 9258 at present and in the near future because the number of registered guidance counselors fall too short compared with the number of institutions and schools which are supposed to retain their services. While we are thankful for the teachers who are willingly undertaking to do this task, it is imperative that we do something to actually address the problem and not rely on band-aid solutions. We need to attract and retain guidance counselors. We need to make sure that students will see the profession of guidance and counseling as lucrative and fulfilling so that more will be encouraged to undertake the rigorous studies and training to become registered guidance counselors. We need to make sure that the young generation will have qualified persons who can help them in times of emotional distress so we can prevent incidents of dropping out from school, bullying, self-harm, and even death. Thus, this representation drafted the Magna Carta for Public Counselors and their Practice in response to the growing need for better access to counseling and psychological aid. It is our bounden duty to ensure that the youth are safe, secure, and holistically healthy, and we can only help them by making sure that the resources and people that they need are within 1 Lack of registered guidance counselors forces schools to keep unlicensed ones (Part 1), https://news.abs- cbn.com/focus/01/14/18/lack-of-registered-guidance-counselors-forces-schools-to-keep-unlicensed-ones- part-1, retrieved on February 19, 2020. their reach. As the sad events in the past months have shown us2, prioritizing counselors in schools is not only imperative, but necessary. Hence, this bill seeks to improve the current entry level salary for guidance counselors in order to attract more applicants to move into public service, and to create an enhanced guidance and counseling program, through the aid of concerned government agencies and organizations, that will target the needs of school children and teenagers. It is hoped that through this legislative policy, the state of guidance and counseling practice in the Philippines will improve not for us, but for our children. ALFRED C. label: HB 11050
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL METEOROLOGY SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall give priority to education and science and technology to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.1 The Constitution also states that science and technology are essential for national development and progress.2 Furthermore, the Constitution also provides that the State shall establish and maintain a system of scholarship grants, student loan programs, subsidies, and other incentives which shall be available to deserving students in both public and private schools, especially to the underprivileged.3 The country is visited by an average of twenty (20) typhoons annually. Typhoons naturally have destructive capabilities as a result of the strong winds they generate, the intense rainfall they bring, and the major floodings that they can produce. The effects range from structural damages both to man-made and natural structures in the surroundings as well as economic impacts on human life and livelihood. Especially now, as the globe grapples with the undeniable effects of climate change, the poly-crisis it brings, and its awe-inspiring negative impact on ways- of-life, livelihoods, safety, and societal peace overall, the country must increase its capacity to mitigate such negative effects by training professionals in the meteorological sciences. In order to mitigate the consequences brought by typhoons, it is important that government will continue to strengthen its weather forecasting and 1 1987 CONST., Art. II, Sec. 17. 2 1987 CONST., Art. XIV, Sec. 10. 3 1987 CONST., Art. XIV, Sec. 2 (3). monitoring efforts. To this end, it is imperative that the government ensure a capable and competent human resource trained in the field of meteorology and its allied sciences. In light of the foregoing, this bill proposes establishing a National Meteorology Scholarship Program to encourage the youth to pursue and gain expertise in the field of Meteorology. These deserving students who will benefit from the proposed scholarship program will be great assets to the country in the government's efforts in providing information to the public and organizations during typhoons, protecting life and property during weather disturbances, reducing weather-related economic losses, and promoting national safety and prosperity. Based on the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11051
title: AN ACT TO ESTABLISH FAIR AND INCLUSIVE CREDIT REPORTING MECHANISMS TO ENSURE EQUITABLE CREDIT ACCESS TO THE MOST VULNERABLE SECTORS OF SOCIETY AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to affordable and formal credit remains out of reach for millions of Filipinos, particularly those without an established credit history, such as informal sector workers, farmers, fisherfolk, and micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Financial institutions play a central role in closing this gap, and the growing availability of alternative and digital transaction data presents new opportunities to responsibly assess the creditworthiness of previously underserved borrowers. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has itself recognized the value of alternative data, such as mobile, utility, and online transaction data, in painting a more complete picture of a borrower’s creditworthiness, allowing more individuals and businesses, especially those with thin or no credit files, to be assessed for credit. Realizing this potential, however, requires that credit scoring models built on such data remain accurate, fair, and free from undue bias against the very sectors they are meant to serve. Given BSP’s immediate action in ensuring liquidity in the economy through decreased lending rates and reserve requirement during the COVID-19 Pandemic, the pressure is on for banks to operationalize such measures post- pandemic and continue to normalize such practice. While the intention of the government is to provide support, banks would need to immediately scale their operations to manage worsening credit positions of existing borrowers and accommodate possible increase in new credit due to lowered interest rates.1 The lack of alternatives and exclusionary mechanisms of financial credit scoring systems have led many FIlipinos to resort to more expensive, poorly- supervised, and potentially illegal lending operations that impose abusive 1 https://www.pwc.com/ph/en/business-unusual/banks-approach-to-covid-19.html interest rates and practice predatory lending activities, to the detriment of many disadvantaged and underprivileged sectors of the society. The lack of alternatives and exclusionary mechanisms of financial credit scoring systems have led many FIlipinos to resort to more expensive, poorly- supervised, and potentially illegal lending operations that impose abusive interest rates and practice predatory lending activities, to the detriment of many disadvantaged and underprivileged sectors of the society. This bill seeks to encourage the development of non-traditional approaches to credit scoring, with the aim of including more sectors of the society that have been excluded under more conventional and traditional approaches. With a fairer and more inclusive approach to credit scoring, more members of the agriculture sector, MSMEs, informal sector, and other vulnerable groups will be able to access more affordable credit that proactively enables them to engage in more productive economic activities. This Act specifically mandates a credit inclusiveness study to determine whether conventional credit scoring techniques exclude specific segments and sectors of the society; grants the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) clear regulatory oversight of credit scoring methods; requires a regular review of credit scoring models to assess their inclusivity; and allows the BSP to prohibit credit scoring models that are deemed to be unduly exclusionary. Finally, this bill responds to the continuing need to translate financial system liquidity into credit in the real economy, particularly for sectors that remain underserved by conventional credit scoring systems. Through this, more Filipinos will be able to engage in productive economic activity that will help sustain and broaden the country’s economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11052
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES AT THE LEVEL OF THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution makes it the State’s responsibility to “protect and promote the right to health of the people” and to “instill health consciousness among them. Acting upon this, in 2018, Republic Act No 11036 (“Mental Health Act”) was passed, which, in Section 3 thereof, bound the State to the following objectives: SECTION 3. Objectives. — The objectives of this Act are as follows: (a) Strengthen effective leadership and governance for mental health by, among others, formulating, developing, and implementing national policies, strategies, programs, and regulations relating to mental health; (b) Develop and establish a comprehensive, integrated, effective, and efficient national mental health care system responsive to the psychiatric, neurologic, and psychosocial needs of the Filipino people; (c) Protect the rights and freedoms of persons with psychiatric, neurologic, and psychosocial health needs; (d) Strengthen information systems, evidence and research for mental health; (e) Integrate mental health care in the basic health services; and (f) Integrate strategies promoting mental health in educational institutions, the workplace, and in communities. It is in furtherance of these policies and commitments that this Bill is proposed. This Bill aims to put into place barangay mental health workers and city/municipal mental health professionals. The barangay mental health workers, in particular, shall (1) maintain close contact with those most in need of mental health services and (2) take charge of building community awareness of, thereby boosting the accessibility of, the government’s mental health services. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11053
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE VALUE-ADDED TAX EXEMPTION FOR PRESCRIBED DRUGS AND MEDICINES FOR MENTAL HEALTH CONDITIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 109 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution provides as a policy that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.1 This policy covers all aspects of health vital to every Filipino’s well-being. The importance of mental health has received increasing recognition in recent years, and in line with the state policy abovementioned, Congress passed Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as “Mental Health Act” in 2018. To fully realize the essence of the Mental Health Act, and in recognition of the fact that Republic Act No. 11534, otherwise known as the “CREATE Act,” has already exempted the sale or importation of prescription drugs and medicines for mental illness from value-added tax (VAT) effective January 1, 2021 under Secion 109 (1)(AA)(ii) of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), this bill seeks to strengthen and clarify the scope of the said exemption by alighing coverage with the broader definition of “mental health condition” under the Mental Health Act. Absent a sufficiently broad and unamibigious definition, prescribed medicies for anxiety, depression, and other conditions recognized under the Mental Health Act risk being excluded from the existing VAT exemption if the term “mental illness” is narrowly construed. VAT is a tax on consumption levied on the sale, barter, exchange or lease of goods and services.2 It is an indirect tax which is often shifted or passed on to the buyer of the goods or services. In cases 1 1987 CONST., art. II, sec. 15. 2 Bureau of Internal Revenue. Value-Added Tax. of mental health conditions, it is the patient who will bear the burden of the value-added tax. This bill aims to remove this burden and makes prescribed mental health medicines more accessible to those who need it. After all, mental health conditions affect both the rich and the poor, and the poor are less capable of addressing this concern due to financial constraints. In light of these circumstances, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11054
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A BASIC EDUCATION SCHOOLS SAFETY FRAMEWORK TO ENSURE THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF STUDENTS AND SCHOOL WORKERS ALIKE, PROVIDING FOR FUNDING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strings of violent incidents that occurred in schools at various times and points in the country have rocked consciousness and have instilled unnecessary anxiety amongst students, parents, guardians, and school personnel alike. Violent school incidents that we used to hear from foreign news updates and which seemed to be light years away from us suddenly became real and chilling. With the advent and proliferation of various cyber-technological applications that promote or foster unhealthy fanaticism and individualism, violence, self-harm, hate and other extreme expressions of emotions, some unknowing and misguided young Filipino students have fallen victims of their own unguarded psyche, leaving in their path a trail of snuffed out lives, physiological damages, moral injuries, and destruction to properties in institutions that are supposed to be zones of peace and development and havens of learnings and education. There is a need for the government to immediately intervene in order to prevent the violent scenarios of recent from turning into common scenes. Gun violence, extreme physical harm, destruction of properties, and campus threats cannot be accepted as an ordinary part of Philippine school life. Moreover, while the Department of Education has launched a nationwide school safety campaign, the nationalization of basic education has thrust support to education services such as security personnel, equipment, and infrastructure into the already overly burdened coffers of the local government unit. The MOOE of schools may be used for this purpose, but schools prioritize allocating their meager MOOE allotment for school and office supplies, and similar expenditures. Thus, given the mandate of the Department of Education “to protect and promote the right of every Filipino to quality, equitable, culture-based, and complete basic education, which includes creating an enabling and supportive learning environment where learners are protected and secured from any form of harm, abuse, and violence within and under its jurisdiction,” there is a need for Congress to pass a law that institutionalize basic education schools safety framework to ensure the safety and well-being of students and school workers alike and to providing for funding. Schools need permanent funding to upgrade physical defenses and to hire security personnel. If the government wishes not to witness another violent incident in schools such as those that happened in Zamboanga City and Tacloban, then it must provide for mechanisms to prevent the same from happening. In view of the foregoing premises, approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ESMAEL G. label: HB 11058
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The school is supposed to be one of the safest places in a child's life—a place where learners acquire knowledge, develop character, build friendships, and prepare for their future. Yet recent events demonstrate that Filipino schools are facing increasingly complex threats to the safety and well-being of learners, teachers, and other school personnel. The need for a comprehensive and institutionalized school safety framework has become especially urgent following a series of violent incidents in and around Philippine schools. On June 22, 2026, a shooting occurred inside San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, resulting in the deaths of three students and injuries to several others. The Commission on Human Rights confirmed the deaths of the three students and noted that the incident involved minors aged 14 and 15. Subsequent police reports indicated that the attack had allegedly been planned for more than a month. The incident prompted heightened security measures in Tacloban schools, including stricter entry protocols and bag inspections. The gravity of the incident was underscored by the fact that the alleged perpetrators were themselves minors. This demonstrates that school violence cannot be addressed solely through guards, gates, and post-incident police investigations. There is a need for early identification of risks, effective reporting mechanisms, mental health and psychosocial support, learner formation, violence prevention, proper referral systems, and coordinated intervention among schools, families, communities, and government agencies. Barely two months later, on August 18, 2026, another deadly school shooting occurred at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School in Zamboanga City. According to the Department of the Interior and Local Government, a Grade 9 student entered the school carrying a pistol and a rifle, fired at another student, and subsequently took his own life. A Grade 10 student was killed, while other students were reportedly injured. The incident was reportedly livestreamed, raising additional concerns regarding the intersection of school violence, firearms, social media, and the digital environment in which young people increasingly live. These incidents are not isolated. Reports have also documented other forms of violence occurring within or in connection with schools. In 2025, a student in Nueva Ecija was reportedly shot by her former boyfriend inside a school, while in Lanao del Sur, a teacher was shot and killed inside a school after a student reportedly received a failing grade. In 2023, a medical technology student in Tuguegarao City was reportedly beaten and shot by a classmate at a university parking area. Even prior to the Tacloban tragedy, the Department of the Interior and Local Government noted two separate stabbing incidents involving students in schools in Cavite, emphasizing the need to strengthen school safety, early intervention, and community-based violence prevention. Taken together, these incidents reveal that threats to school safety are not limited to one particular type of violence. They may involve firearms, knives and other weapons, bullying, interpersonal conflicts, abuse, harassment, mental health concerns, online influence, cyberbullying, and other emerging threats. The increasing use of digital platforms further complicates the situation, as harmful content and incidents of violence can spread rapidly among young people. Recent national efforts to strengthen online child-safety measures likewise reflect growing concerns about the digital environment surrounding Filipino children and adolescents. The response to school violence must therefore go beyond reacting after an incident has already occurred. At present, various laws, policies, and programs already address particular aspects of learner protection, anti-bullying, mental health, disaster preparedness, child protection, and school security. However, these mechanisms must operate as part of a coordinated and comprehensive system. Schools need clear standards on prevention, risk assessment, reporting, emergency response, case management, referral, recovery, digital safety, infrastructure, security, and the protection and well- being of school personnel. This proposed measure seeks to establish such a system through a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework and require every school to develop and regularly update a School Safety Plan and School Safety Handbook appropriate to its circumstances and risk profile. The proposed measure also recognizes that school safety is not merely a security issue. A truly safe school must address the physical, mental, emotional, psychosocial, and digital well-being of learners and school personnel. It must provide mechanisms for early intervention before conflicts escalate into violence. It must ensure that learners have safe avenues to report bullying, threats, abuse, harassment, and other concerns. It must provide appropriate mental health and psychosocial support to those affected by violence and trauma. It must likewise establish clear coordination among school officials, parents, local government units, law enforcement, health and social welfare agencies, and other stakeholders. The bill further provides for appropriate school safety personnel, security and protective measures, emergency and life-safety equipment, visitor management, risk assessment, emergency drills, digital safety policies, learner well-being programs, incident reporting, case management, referral systems, recovery and reintegration programs, and protection and support for school personnel. Importantly, the measure adopts a prevention-oriented approach. The objective is not simply to make schools more difficult to enter or to increase security after a tragedy. label: HB 11059
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10742, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN REFORM ACT OF 2015,” AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11768, PROVIDING FOR THE APPOINTMENT OF SANGGUNIANG KABATAAN MEMBERS TO FILL PERMANENT VACANCIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) is an important institution for ensuring the participation of the youth in local governance. Through the SK, young Filipinos are given the opportunity to represent their fellow youth and participate in the formulation and implementation of programs and policies in their communities. However, vacancies in the Sangguniang Kabataan continue to occur for various reasons. These include positions that remain unfilled after elections, as well as vacancies arising from resignation, death, removal from office, permanent incapacity, failure to qualify, and other circumstances recognized by law. Under Republic Act No. 10742, as amended by Republic Act No. 11768, vacancies in the SK membership are generally filled through a special Katipunan ng Kabataan assembly and election. The number of unfilled positions after the 2023 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections demonstrates that the issue is not merely theoretical. Following the 2023 elections, 692 SK positions nationwide remained vacant because there were no candidates for those positions—139 SK Chairperson positions and 553 SK Member positions. The Commission on Elections subsequently had to provide rules for the conduct of special elections to address these vacancies. More importantly, vacancies do not occur only immediately after an election. During the term of office, an SK position may become vacant because of resignation, death, permanent incapacity, removal from office, failure to qualify, or other circumstances. These vacancies can leave an SK with fewer members than required and may affect its ability to meet quorum, deliberate on matters, and effectively implement programs for the youth. The existing requirement of a special election or special Katipunan ng Kabataan assembly may also result in delays in filling a vacant position. Conducting a separate electoral process for a single vacant seat requires coordination, administrative preparation, and resources, while the vacant position may remain unfilled during the process. This measure therefore proposes a simpler and more efficient mechanism for filling permanent vacancies in the membership of the Sangguniang Kabataan. Instead of conducting a special election for every vacancy, the remaining members of the Sangguniang Kabataan shall recommend a qualified member of the Katipunan ng Kabataan to fill the vacant position. The recommendation shall be submitted through a duly approved SK Resolution to the concerned City or Municipal Mayor, who shall make the appointment. This proposed mechanism is similar to the general approach under the Local Government Code in filling permanent vacancies in local sanggunian, while still preserving the participation of the youth sector in identifying the person who will represent them. The proposed appointment shall be limited to the unexpired portion of the term, and the appointee must possess all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications prescribed by law. The measure also provides a definite period for the SK to submit its recommendation to ensure that vacancies will not remain unfilled for an extended period. The objective of this measure is simple: to ensure that every Sangguniang Kabataan remains complete, functional, and capable of serving the youth of the barangay. By replacing the requirement of a special election with a timely appointment upon the recommendation of the SK Council and approval of the concerned Mayor, this measure will reduce administrative delays, avoid unnecessary electoral expenses, and ensure continuity in youth representation and governance. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 11061
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE FREIGHT SERVICES IN THE TRANSPORTATION OF RELIEF GOODS TO CALAMITY-STRICKEN AREAS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the countries most vulnerable to natural hazards. According to the World Risk Index, the Philippines has consistently ranked among the countries with the highest disaster risk in the world. The 2024 World Risk Index ranked the Philippines first among 193 countries, underscoring the country's continuing exposure to typhoons, floods, earthquakes, landslides, and other hazards. The frequency and scale of disasters place a significant burden on government and humanitarian organizations. The Office of Civil Defense (OCD) and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) regularly report millions of Filipinos affected by major typhoons and other disasters each year. In these situations, the timely delivery of food, water, medicines, and other essential supplies is critical. Yet transportation and freight costs remain a practical obstacle, particularly in geographically isolated and severely affected communities. Resources that should go directly to relief operations are instead spent on transporting donated goods. This measure seeks to provide free freight services for relief goods intended for calamity-stricken areas, subject to proper government coordination and verification. By reducing or eliminating transportation costs, the measure will enable government agencies, local government units, humanitarian organizations, and legitimate donors to deliver more assistance, faster, to families affected by disasters. In times of calamity, relief should not be delayed because of freight costs. Every available resource must be directed toward saving lives, protecting communities, and helping affected families recover. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 During a disaster, every minute matters and every household should be seen, heard, and accounted for. Yet recent weather-related tragedies continue to expose gaps in communication between households and the government, particularly in knowing who needs help, where they are, and whether assistance has reached them. 27 In times of disaster, a single phone call can mean the difference between life and death. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Every remittance sent home by an overseas Filipino worker carries more than money. It carries the sacrifice of a parent working far from home, a spouse enduring years of physical separation, and a son or daughter working abroad so that their family can live a little better. 25 For many Filipino families, these remittances pay for food, rent, schooling, health care, and other basic needs. Every peso sent home has been earned through hard work and personal sacrifice. 29 That is why every peso should reach the family it was meant for. Excessive remittance fees, unfavorable exchange rates, and other charges can slowly eat away at the money that OFWs worked so hard to send. For families who carefully stretch every remittance to cover their daily needs, even a small deduction can matter. 34 This proposed measure seeks to protect OFW remittances by reducing the burden of remittance fees, requiring greater transparency in exchange rates, and preventing the unauthorized taking or misuse of remitted funds. It also promotes financial education to help OFWs and their families manage their earnings and build a more secure future. 39 Our OFWs endure distance, loneliness, and hardship so that their families can have better lives. The least we can do is make sure that the fruits of their sacrifice are not unnecessarily diminished before they reach the people they worked so hard to provide for. 43 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 45 46 47 REP. label: HB 11066
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE AUTOMATIC PENSION ESCALATION MECHANISM FOR RETIREMENT, DISABILITY, DEATH, AND SURVIVOR PENSIONERS OF THE SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM (SSS), PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Retirement should provide security and dignity to those who have spent their productive years contributing to the Social Security System (SSS). Yet, the purchasing power of pensions can gradually decline as the cost of food, healthcare, utilities, and other basic necessities increases. Without a predictable mechanism for periodic adjustment, pensioners may find it increasingly difficult to meet their daily needs. The SSS has recognized the need to improve pension adequacy through its pension reform initiatives, including increases for retirement, disability, death, and survivor pensioners. These measures demonstrate the importance of providing pensioners with meaningful and predictable adjustments while taking into account the long-term sustainability of the Social Security Fund. This measure seeks to institutionalize an automatic pension escalation mechanism so that pension increases will no longer depend solely on periodic administrative action or discretionary adjustments. Under the proposed measure, retirement and disability pensioners shall receive an annual increase of ten percent (10%) or the official annual average inflation rate, whichever is higher, while death and survivor pensioners shall receive an annual increase of five percent (5%) or the official annual average inflation rate, whichever is higher. The adjustment shall be applied to the pension in effect immediately prior to the adjustment and shall be compounded annually. The ten percent (10%) and five percent (5%) rates are intended not merely to offset inflation but also to improve pension adequacy and provide a predictable minimum annual enhancement to pension income The proposed mechanism provides pensioners with a predictable minimum increase while protecting the purchasing power of their pensions against higher inflation. At the same time, the measure does not diminish any existing pension benefit or increase granted under existing law. Recognizing the importance of maintaining the long-term viability of the SSS, the measure requires an annual actuarial valuation and review of the Social Security Fund. The review will assess the financial impact of the pension escalation and consider contribution collections, investment income, membership growth, demographic trends, reserves, and other factors affecting the Fund. It will also provide Congress and the Department of Finance with timely information necessary to ensure the continued sustainability of the pension system. The measure further provides for a periodic Congressional review every five (5) years, allowing Congress to assess the adequacy of pension benefits in light of prevailing economic and demographic conditions while ensuring the long-term sustainability of the Social Security Fund. Through this measure, pensioners are provided with a fair, predictable, and inflation-responsive mechanism for maintaining the value of their pensions, while preserving the financial integrity of the SSS. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11067
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND WEAPON PREVENTION PROGRAM, MANDATING THE COLLABORATIVE IMPLEMENTATION OF PREVENTIVE MEASURES BY THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND BARANGAYS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The safety and security of learners, teachers, and school personnel are essential to the delivery of quality education. Schools must remain safe and secure environments where children can learn, develop, and participate in school activities free from the threat of firearms, weapons, violence, and other preventable dangers. The increasing complexity of school security concerns calls for a comprehensive and preventive approach. While existing laws, regulations, and Department of Education policies provide important safeguards, there is a need to institutionalize a coordinated framework that brings together schools, families, local government units, barangays, law enforcement agencies, and social welfare institutions. This measure, to be known as the “S.A.F.E. (Secure and Firearm-Free Education) Schools Act,” seeks to establish such a framework. It recognizes that school safety cannot depend solely on security personnel or law enforcement after an incident has occurred. Prevention, early identification of threats, responsible reporting, appropriate intervention, and secure school environments must form part of a unified school safety system. The bill directs the Department of Education to establish national standards for school access control, security risk assessments, an Anonymous Digital Tip Line, behavioral threat assessment, conflict resolution, peace education, and de-escalation training. It likewise requires public and private basic education institutions to adopt appropriate access- control procedures, reasonable security inspections, parental engagement, incident reporting, and environmental safety measures. The measure further strengthens the participation of local government units and barangays by providing for appropriate support for school security infrastructure, community coordination, school-zone safety, and preventive patrols. These measures are intended to complement, and not replace, the responsibilities of national government agencies and school authorities. Recognizing that children require a distinct and protective approach, the bill expressly provides that interventions involving minors shall be undertaken in accordance with Republic Act No. 9344, otherwise known as the “Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006,” and other applicable child- protection laws and regulations. The objective is not merely to punish misconduct, but to prevent violence while ensuring that children are afforded appropriate intervention, rehabilitation, counseling, and family support. The bill also promotes safe and responsible reporting of weapons and threats through confidential or anonymous mechanisms and encourages schools to establish controlled procedures for the voluntary surrender of prohibited items. These measures are intended to provide students with a safe avenue to prevent dangerous incidents before they occur, without diminishing accountability under existing laws. At the same time, the proposed framework recognizes the importance of privacy, dignity, due process, and the protection of personal information. Security measures must therefore be implemented in a manner that is reasonable, non-discriminatory, child-sensitive, and consistent with existing laws on data privacy and the rights and welfare of children. Ultimately, the S.A.F.E. Schools Act seeks to institutionalize a whole- of-community approach to school safety. By combining prevention, physical security, early intervention, responsible reporting, community participation, and child-sensitive measures, this Act aims to ensure that every school in the country remains a secure and supportive environment conducive to learning. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L.
