label: HB 11068
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DISABILITY SUPPORT ALLOWANCE PROGRAM AS A SOCIAL PROTECTION AND SUPPORT MEASURE TO PROMOTE THE INDEPENDENT LIVING, EMPOWERMENT, EQUAL PARTICIPATION, AND FULL INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IN SOCIETY, PROVIDING FOR A REGULAR DISABILITY SUPPORT ALLOWANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to full and effective participation in society. Beyond the challenges arising from their impairments, many persons with disabilities incur additional costs for transportation, personal assistance, medicines, rehabilitation, assistive devices and technologies, education, communication, and other disability-related needs. These additional costs can increase household expenses, limit opportunities for education and employment, and contribute to poverty, exclusion, and inequality. While existing laws and social protection programs provide important benefits and assistance to persons with disabilities, these measures do not always adequately address the recurring extra costs associated with disability. There is therefore a need for a targeted and disability-responsive social protection measure that directly assists persons with disabilities in meeting such costs and supports their independent living, economic security, and full participation in society. This measure seeks to establish a National Disability Support Allowance Program (DSAP) that will provide a regular Disability Support Allowance of at least Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) per month to eligible persons with disabilities. The allowance shall be periodically reviewed and adjusted to preserve its purchasing power and shall complement, rather than replace or diminish, existing benefits and privileges granted under other laws. The proposed measure adopts a phased implementation to ensure that the Program can be progressively expanded in accordance with available resources and administrative capacity. The initial phase prioritizes children with disabilities and adults with significant disabilities, followed by persons with moderate disabilities and, ultimately, other eligible persons with disabilities who incur disability-related extra costs. Eligibility shall be determined through a Disability and Needs Assessment System (DNAS) that takes into account functional limitations, support requirements, disability-related extra costs, and barriers to participation. The measure further seeks to improve coordination and data management among relevant government agencies through a Disability Management Information System (DMIS), while ensuring compliance with applicable data privacy and information security laws. The measure also strengthens accessibility in the application and payment of benefits, establishes a clear appeal and grievance mechanism, provides safeguards against fraudulent registration and misuse of benefits, and requires regular monitoring and periodic evaluation of the Program. This bill is filed as the House counterpart measure to Senate Bill No. 2386, which seeks to establish a National Disability Support Allowance Program for persons with disabilities. While maintaining the core objectives and framework of the Senate measure, this proposed House version further clarifies the coverage and phased implementation, strengthens eligibility and assessment procedures, protects existing benefits, improves payment and appeal mechanisms, reinforces data privacy safeguards, and promotes greater accountability and transparency in implementation. The enactment of this measure will strengthen the country's social protection framework for persons with disabilities and affirm the State's commitment to ensuring that disability-related costs do not become a barrier to dignity, independence, equal participation, and full inclusion in society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11069
title: AN ACT EXPANDING PHILHEALTH COVERAGE TO INCLUDE BENEFIT PACKAGE FOR ALL MENTAL HEALTH DISORDERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed bill addresses a critical gap in the Philippine healthcare system by treating mental health care not as an expensive luxury, but as a fundamental human right. While existing legislation recognizes the importance of mental well-being, the prohibitive costs of psychiatric evaluation, psychological services, neurological services, and long-term treatment prevent millions of Filipinos from seeking essential care. By explicitly mandating the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) to develop and implement a comprehensive benefit package within one year of its effectivity, this bill removes the financial barriers that have historically marginalized individuals with mental health conditions. This measure requires coverage for all mental health disorders, extending specific protections to minors, and incorporating emergency interventions, continuing care, and evidence-based services alongside the World Health Organization’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP). Furthermore, this bill strengthens the legal and financial frameworks necessary to sustain nationwide mental healthcare. It aligns national policy with international human rights standards and with Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” while explicitly recognizing individuals with mental health conditions under the protections of the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons (RA 7277) to curb systemic stigma and discrimination. Rather than creating a new budgetary burden, the Act utilizes PhilHealth’s existing revenue structure, funding the package through a combination of direct contributor premiums and government subsidies for indirect contributors. PhilHealth shall undertake the necessary actuarial and financial assessment to ensure that the benefit package is sustainable and appropriately integrated into its existing benefit structure. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11070
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face the challenges of high electricity costs, grid congestion, energy security, and the need to accelerate the adoption of renewable energy and energy storage technologies. Behind-the-meter electricity generation and energy storage systems, including rooftop solar photovoltaic systems and battery energy storage systems, enable households, businesses, and other electricity end-users to generate and store electricity primarily for their own consumption. These systems can reduce dependence on electricity supplied through the distribution system, improve energy resilience, and contribute to the reduction of system losses and peak demand. Existing regulatory and administrative requirements, however, may unnecessarily increase the cost and delay the installation of such systems, particularly where the system is designed and equipped to prevent the export of electricity to the distribution system. This Act seeks to remove unnecessary regulatory and administrative barriers while preserving legitimate electrical, structural, fire, environmental, and public safety requirements. It distinguishes between behind-the-meter systems that are incapable of exporting electricity and systems capable of exporting electricity to the distribution system, subjecting the latter to appropriate interconnection requirements. Accordingly, this measure promotes consumer choice, encourages private investment in distributed energy resources, strengthens energy security, and facilitates the wider adoption of renewable energy and energy storage technologies. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11071
title: AN ACT REINFORCING, PROTECTING, AND MANAGING THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION’S OWNERSHIP OF LOTS OCCUPIED BY PUBLIC SCHOOLS, PROVIDING FOR THE SUMMARY TITLING OF ALL REAL PROPERTIES USED AS PUBLIC SCHOOL SITES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Many public schools occupy lands that remain untitled, are covered only by incomplete records, or are still registered under previous jurisdictions. These unresolved property issues hinder the construction and improvement of school facilities and expose public investments to ownership disputes. The problem is widespread. As of May 2026, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) reported that only 7,075 public schools, or sixteen percent (16%), had sites titled in the name of the Department of Education (DepEd). Titling was ongoing for 7,373 schools, while 32,424 schools, or sixty-nine percent (69%), remained untitled. Of the untitled schools, 6,045 were already experiencing congestion.1 This bill creates a unified and expedited process for identifying, acquiring, titling, and managing lands used for public education. It also strengthens coordination among concerned government agencies while safeguarding due process, just compensation, environmental protection, and 1 According to the report of EDCOM II. the rights of affected landowners and communities. The land on which learning takes place should be as secure as the right to education it serves. Resolving the legal status of public school sites will protect government investments, remove obstacles to urgently needed infrastructure, and preserve these properties for the benefit of present and future generations of Filipino learners. Securing public school sites will protect government resources and provide schools with a stable foundation for their continued development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. MIRO S. label: HB 11072
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE PURPOSES AND APPLICATION OF THE SPECIAL EDUCATION FUND (SEF), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 100 AND 272 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Teachers should be able to devote their time and energy to teaching. Yet EDCOM II found that teachers were burdened with more than fifty ancillary and administrative tasks, while nearly half worked over fifty hours a week.1 This excessive workload takes valuable time away from lesson preparation, classroom instruction, assessment, and direct learner support. At the same time, access to the Special Education Fund (SEF) remains deeply unequal. EDCOM II reported a 68-fold resource gap between first- and sixth-class local government units, as well as a 394-fold difference in SEF resources per learner. In Makati, the SEF amounted to ₱25,587 per learner, compared with only ₱65 per learner in Guihulngan. Despite these disparities and the urgent needs of schools, ₱16.3 billion in SEF remained unutilized in 2022.2 This bill therefore expands the lawful uses of the SEF to allow schools to hire administrative and other non-teaching personnel and provide more responsive support to learners. label: HB 11073
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE “LARO’T SAYA SA PARKE” PROGRAM, PROMOTING WEEKEND COMMUNITY SPORTS AND RECREATIONAL ACTIVITIES IN PUBLIC PARKS, STRENGTHENING SPORTS DEVELOPMENT AMONG YOUTH AND COMMUNITIES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports and recreational activities are essential components of youth development, physical health, mental well-being, and nation-building. They foster discipline, teamwork, resilience, and social cohesion among individuals and communities. Despite the constitutional mandate recognizing the role of sports in fostering self-reliance and national development, access to safe and organized recreational spaces remains limited in many communities. Public parks, which are intended as communal spaces for recreation and social engagement, are often underutilized or lack structured programs that encourage active participation in sports and physical activities. 1 This bill seeks to institutionalize the “Laro’t Saya sa Parke (LSP)” Program, that was created under the Memorandum Circular No. 49 issued by the Office of the Presidential, as a national initiative that promotes organized sports and recreational activities in public parks during weekends. It aims to encourage active lifestyles, strengthen community engagement, and provide accessible sports opportunities for children, youth, and families. By leveraging public parks as inclusive spaces for recreation and sports development, this measure seeks to address sedentary lifestyles, promote mental and physical well-being, and cultivate a culture of sportsmanship and community participation among Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11074
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL EARLY-CAREER MENTORSHIP PROGRAM, ESTABLISHING THE EARLY CAREER MENTORSHIP ACCESSIBILITY FRAMEWORK, PROMOTING ONLINE AND INSTITUTION-BASED MENTORSHIP PLATFORMS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The transition from education to employment remains one of the most critical yet underserved stages in the development of Filipino youth. Many graduates and early-career professionals face significant barriers in accessing guidance, professional networks, and industry exposure necessary for successful career entry. While various government agencies, educational institutions, and private organizations implement mentorship initiatives, these programs remain fragmented, unevenly distributed, and largely inaccessible to youth outside urban centers or elite academic institutions. There is currently no unified national framework that ensures equitable, structured, and measurable access to early-career mentorship opportunities. This bill seeks to institutionalize the Early Career Mentorship Accessibility Act by establishing a national framework that integrates mentorship programs across government agencies, educational institutions, and private sector partners. It shall 1 promote the use of digital platforms to ensure accessibility, scalability, and inclusivity, particularly for geographically isolated, disadvantaged, and underrepresented youth. By formalizing mentorship pathways, standardizing program implementation, and strengthening public-private collaboration, this measure aims to bridge the gap between education and employment, enhance youth employability, and support the development of a competent, competitive, and future-ready Filipino workforce. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11075
title: AN ACT MANDATING FREE COLLEGE ENTRANCE EXAMINATIONS IN STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, PROHIBITING DISCRIMINATION BASED ON INABILITY TO PAY TESTING FEES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to higher education begins with access to college admission. However, for many Filipino students, especially those from low-income households, entrance examination fees remain a significant barrier to opportunity. While RA No. 12006 otherwise known as the ‘Free College Entrance Examinations Act’ has provided relief by mandating private higher education institutions to waive entrance examination fees for qualified students, its coverage remains limited. The law applies only to private institutions and imposes eligibility conditions, thereby excluding many deserving students who may not meet specific academic or income thresholds. Moreover, there is currently no uniform national policy mandating all State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) and Local Universities and Colleges (LUCs) to provide free entrance examinations, nor is there an explicit prohibition against exclusion due to inability to pay testing fees. 1 This bill seeks to institutionalize a universal, rights-based approach by mandating all SUCs and LUCs to provide free entrance examinations to all applicants, regardless of socioeconomic status, and to prohibit any form of exclusion or discrimination based on inability to pay. By removing financial barriers at the point of entry, the State ensures that access to higher education is determined by merit and potential, not by financial capacity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11076
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CREDIT ACCESS FOR SMALL FARMERS AND FISHERFOLK, MANDATING FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS TO ALLOCATE A PORTION OF THEIR LOAN PORTFOLIOS FOR AGRI- FISHERY BORROWERS, ESTABLISHING AN AGRI CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture and fisheries remain vital sectors of the Philippine economy, sustaining millions of livelihoods and ensuring food security. However, small farmers and fisherfolk continue to face significant barriers in accessing affordable credit, including high interest rates, stringent collateral requirements, and limited financial inclusion. Despite existing policies such as the Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act (Republic Act No. 8435) and the Agri-Agra Reform Credit Act of 2009 (Republic Act No. 10000), access to financing for small-scale producers remains inadequate. Many financial institutions continue to fall short of meaningful support, and compliance mechanisms have not fully addressed the structural constraints faced by the sector. 1 To address these gaps, this bill mandates financial institutions to allocate a portion of their loan portfolio specifically for agri-fishery borrowers, ensures affordable interest rates, removes collateral barriers through a government-backed guarantee mechanism, and strengthens institutional support for inclusive agricultural financing. By establishing an Agri Credit Guarantee Fund and promoting accessible, low-interest, and collateral-free loans, this measure seeks to empower small farmers and fisherfolk, increase productivity, reduce rural poverty, and enhance national food security. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11077
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH CORPS, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL VOLUNTEER PROGRAM FOR TRAINED YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH ADVOCATES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to confront a worsening mental health crisis notwithstanding advances in public discourse and the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” which established the country’s landmark policy framework on mental health. Despite its passage, significant gaps in implementation and service delivery persist nearly a decade thereafter. In 2023, the mental health experts characterized the situation as ‘a rising epidemic’, a condition that remains evident to date, as reflected in the increasing volume of crisis calls reported by the National Center for Mental Health (NCMH)1. This growing demand is further exacerbated by a shortage of mental health professionals which constraint attainment of access to timely, adequate and quality care. The urgency of addressing the country’s deteriorating mental health landscape 1 ABS-CBN (October 2025). NCMH Crisis Hotline receives more call; causes point to depression. https://www.abs- cbn.com/news/health-science/2025/10/28/ncmh-crisis-hotline-receives-more-calls-causes-point-to-depression-1947 1 has likewise been recognized in the present Congress, as manifested in inquiries initiated under Senate Resolution No. 992. Similarly, the 1987 Philippine Constitution, under Article II, Section 13, recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building. Notwithstanding the growing call for mental health-responsive communities and collective action, the potential of the youth remains underutilized due to fragmented and uncoordinated platforms for engagement. In 2021, UNICEF reported that young people increasingly seek mental health information and demonstrate a heightened willingness to participate in mental health discussions, as well as peer support programs and mechanisms3. Globally, there has likewise been a notable rise in youth engagement in mental health advocacy, peer counseling, and volunteer-driven initiatives4. Thus an urgent need to complement professional services with trained peer support systems that can provide immediate psychosocial assistance and facilitate early intervention at the primary care service level. Empowering the youth as mental health advocates not only expands access to care but also reduces stigma and promotes a culture of help-seeking behavior to expand. This bill seeks to establish a Youth Mental Health Corps, a national volunteer program composed of trained youth advocates equipped with skills in psychosocial first aid, suicide prevention, peer counseling, and crisis listening. By mobilizing the youth as frontliners of mental health support in schools, communities, and disaster settings, the State strengthens its commitment to safeguarding the mental well-being of every Filipino and uphold mental health as a fundamental human right In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 Senate of the Philippines (October 2025). label: HB 11078
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL BARANGAY HEALTH EQUITY INDEX, MANDATING THE DEVELOPMENT OF A HEALTH EQUITY SCORECARD FOR EVERY BARANGAY TO IDENTIFY DISPARITIES AND GUIDE TARGETED INTERVENTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes health as a fundamental right of every Filipino and mandates the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. In the current health landscape, landmark to this obligation is the enactment of Republic Act No. 11223, or otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act” which further institutionalizes a system that guarantees equitable access to quality and affordable health care for all Filipinos1. Despite these commitments, significant health disparities persist across communities, particularly at the barangay level. Many barangays continue to experience unequal access to health services due to variations in socioeconomic conditions, geographic isolation, infrastructure gaps, 1 LawPhil. Republic Act No. 11223. https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2019/ra_11223_2019.html 1 and uneven distribution of health personnel and resources. These disparities contribute to differences in health outcomes such as maternal and child mortality, disease burden, nutrition status, and access to preventive services2. However, current national and local planning mechanisms often lack a standardized, granular tool that systematically measures and compares these inequalities across barangays. This proposed measure seeks to address this gap through the establishment of a Barangay Health Equity Index (BHEI) and a corresponding Barangay Health Equity Scorecard for every barangay in the country. The BHEI will serve as a composite, data-driven index that measures key indicators of health status, disease burden, access to services, and the social determinants of health. Meanwhile, the Scorecard will function as an annual performance and monitoring tool that identifies priority health gaps, vulnerabilities, and necessary interventions at the barangay level. By institutionalizing a standardized equity-based measurement system, this measure will enable the government to adopt more evidence-driven health planning, targeted interventions, and responsive resource allocation. The BHEI and Scorecard will guide national agencies and local government units (LGUs) in prioritizing communities with the greatest health needs, strengthening primary care networks, improving service delivery, and ensuring that health investments are directed where they are most needed. Moreover, the proposed system will promote transparency and accountability in local health governance. The public availability of barangay-level health scorecards will empower communities to participate in monitoring health outcomes and encourage stronger coordination among the Department of Health, LGUs, and other relevant stakeholders. Ultimately, the establishment of a Barangay Health Equity Index will provide the national government and local governments with a powerful policy instrument to systematically identify and reduce health inequities across the country. Through better data, more strategic planning, and targeted public health action, this measure aims to strengthen the implementation of Universal Health Care and ensure that no community is left behind in the pursuit of health equity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 Paredes, K.P.P. label: HB 11079
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE PRODUCTIVE UTILIZATION OF IDLE LANDS THROUGH TAX REFORMS, INCENTIVES FOR AGRICULTURAL USE, AND PARTNERSHIPS WITH FARMERS AND COOPERATIVES, AMENDING PERTINENT PROVISIONS OF THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land is one of the most vital resources of the Philippines. Yet vast tracts of land across the country remain idle, underutilized, or deliberately held for speculative purposes. According to data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the total farm area in the country was estimated at around 7.27 million hectares based on the 2012 Census of Agriculture and Fisheries, highlighting the vast land resources available for agricultural production1. Despite the country’s vast agricultural potential, a significant portion of cultivable land remains idle or underutilized due to various constraints such as absentee landownership, financial limitations, lack of labor, or insufficient technical support2. Idle lands worsen food insecurity, deny local governments potential revenues, and contribute to inequitable land ownership. 1 Philippine Statistic Authority. Technical Notes on the Census of Agriculture and Fisheries (CAF). 2 Lebrilla, M. 2016. Idle Land Tax: Implementation Issues and Challenges. Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department. 1 The Constitution recognizes the duty of the State to promote the equitable distribution and productive use of land to advance national development. While the Republic Act No. 7160 or otherwise known as “Local Government Code of 1991” already authorizes local governments to impose taxes on idle lands, the existing framework has proven insufficient to deter speculative landholding or prolonged neglect of cultivable land. At the same time, many landowners are unable to cultivate their lands due to financial limitations, lack of labor, or absence from rural areas. However, these lands could be productively utilized by tenant farmers, agrarian reform beneficiaries, and agricultural cooperatives if appropriate institutional mechanisms and incentives were established. This measure therefore adopts a balanced and integrated approach to idle land reform. First, it strengthens idle land taxation to discourage land hoarding and speculative holding. Second, it introduces tax incentives and relief measures for landowners who voluntarily allow farmers, agrarian reform beneficiaries, or agricultural cooperatives to cultivate idle lands through formal utilization agreements. Third, it establishes a policy framework to facilitate land matching, support agricultural production, and ensure that idle lands contribute to national food security. The bill also provides for the allocation of revenues generated from idle land taxation to support agricultural modernization programs of the Department of Agriculture and land reform support services of the Department of Agrarian Reform. These resources will help farmers gain access to credit, farm inputs, and technical assistance necessary to ensure the productivity of newly utilized lands. By transforming idle lands into productive agricultural assets, the State can increase domestic food production, expand opportunities for small farmers, stimulate rural economies, and promote equitable and sustainable land use. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CHILD-CENTERED, FAMILY-BASED, AND REINTEGRATIVE VISITATION AND CARE STANDARDS IN ALL BAHAY PAG-ASA FACILITIES, ESTABLISHING A HOLISTIC SUPPORT SYSTEM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State affirms its constitutional duty to uphold the best interests of the child, particularly for children in conflict with the law (CICL), who require protection, rehabilitation, and meaningful reintegration into society. Under Republic Act No. 9344, Bahay Pag-asa facilities were established as child-caring institutions that provide temporary residential care and intervention services. These facilities are central to the country’s juvenile justice and welfare system and are intended to operationalize a child-centered and restorative approach to justice. Over the years, the Philippines has seen significant progress in reducing juvenile delinquency. Data from the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Council indicate that cases involving CICL declined from 26,850 in 2017 to 4,383 in 2024, reflecting the effectiveness of diversion and rehabilitation programs. However, recent trends suggest potential increases in cases, highlighting the need to strengthen existing mechanisms and prevent regression. Despite these gains, persistent gaps in Bahay 1 Pag-asa operations continue to undermine the delivery of holistic and rights-based care. Among the most critical gaps is the absence of a standardized, enforceable framework on child-sensitive visitation and reintegration practices. While family contact is widely recognized as essential to a child’s emotional well-being and successful reintegration, current practices across facilities remain inconsistent and, in some cases, unregulated. Visitation is often conducted without proper risk assessment, structured supervision, or meaningful child participation. Inadequate documentation and lack of post-visit psychosocial support further weaken the system. These deficiencies expose children to risks of retraumatization, coercion, manipulation, and continued exposure to harmful environments—factors that may ultimately undermine rehabilitation and increase the likelihood of recidivism. Compounding these issues are infrastructure and service delivery challenges faced by Bahay Pag-asa facilities nationwide. With approximately 118 operational centers, many experience overcrowding, limited resources, and insufficient facilities for safe and child-friendly visitation. Moreover, the shortage of trained personnel to manage visitation and reintegration processes constrains the ability of institutions to implement child-sensitive interventions effectively. International standards, including the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, emphasize that children deprived of liberty have the right to maintain contact with their families in a manner consistent with their well-being and best interests. Such contact must be facilitated within a safe, structured, and child- sensitive environment, with appropriate safeguards and professional oversight. The absence of a national framework places the implementation of these standards at risk of inconsistency across local government units. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a Child-Centered Reintegration and Visitation Standards Framework in all Bahay Pag- asa facilities. It mandates the development of individualized visitation and reintegration plans, grounded in social case studies and psychological assessments, and subject to regular review. It establishes risk-based visitor screening and accreditation, ensuring that only individuals who do not pose harm to the child are granted access. The measure also defines levels of visitation—including supervised, therapeutic, and virtual modalities—tailored to the needs and circumstances of each child. 2 Crucially, the bill ensures that children are recognized as active rights-holders by requiring their participation and assent in visitation decisions, while safeguarding them from forced or distressing interactions. It mandates the provision of safe, child- friendly visitation spaces, as well as strict prohibitions against abuse, coercion, and other harmful conduct during visits. To strengthen accountability, the measure requires comprehensive documentation, monitoring, and post-visitation assessment, enabling timely intervention and continuous improvement of care. Furthermore, the bill integrates visitation within a broader child-centered reintegration strategy, recognizing that meaningful family engagement, when properly managed, can significantly improve emotional recovery, strengthen support systems, and reduce reoffending. By embedding visitation within a structured and trauma-informed framework, the State ensures that family contact becomes a tool for healing rather than a source of harm. Ultimately, this measure reinforces the principle that children in conflict with the law are not merely subjects of legal processes but individuals in need of care, guidance, and opportunity. By establishing clear, enforceable standards for visitation and reintegration, the State strengthens its commitment to restorative justice and the long-term well-being of every child. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11081
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL ADULT IMMUNIZATION PROGRAM PROVIDING FREE VACCINES AGAINST INFLUENZA, PNEUMOCOCCAL DISEASE, AND HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS (HPV), ADOPTING A LIFE-COURSE IMMUNIZATION STRATEGY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Vaccination is one of the most cost-effective and impactful public health interventions for preventing disease, reducing healthcare expenditures, and saving lives. While the Philippines has made significant progress in childhood immunization, adult immunization remains fragmented and limited in scope, leaving millions of Filipinos vulnerable to vaccine-preventable diseases. Seasonal influenza continues to contribute to substantial morbidity and productivity loss, particularly among the elderly and individuals with underlying health conditions. Pneumonia remains a leading cause of mortality nationwide, disproportionately affecting senior citizens and immunocompromised individuals. Meanwhile, Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is a major cause of cervical cancer and 1 other HPV-related diseases, which continue to impose a significant burden on the healthcare system. Despite the availability of safe and effective vaccines, access remains inequitable due to financial barriers, limited government coverage, and persistent vaccine hesitancy. A life-course approach to immunization—extending protection beyond childhood—is essential to achieving universal health care and strengthening preventive health systems. This measure seeks to institutionalize a National Adult Immunization Program that ensures free and equitable access to priority vaccines, beginning with high-risk populations and progressively expanding coverage. It integrates national and local health systems, strengthens vaccine supply chains, addresses demand-side barriers, and ensures accountability through robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11082
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL ORGAN TRANSPLANT REGISTRY, PROVIDING FINANCIAL AND MEDICAL SUPPORT FOR INDIGENT ORGAN TRANSPLANT RECIPIENT, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Organ transplantation remains one of the most critical life-saving medical interventions for patients suffering from end-stage organ failure. While the Philippines has long recognized the importance of organ donation through Republic Act No. 7170, otherwise known as the ‘Organ Donation Act of 1991’, gaps persist in the implementation of a centralized, transparent, and efficient system for organ allocation and transplant coordination. The absence of an integrated national registry, coupled with the high cost of transplantation and post-operative care, continues to limit access—especially for indigent patients. Thousands of Filipinos suffer from chronic kidney disease, liver failure, and other organ-related conditions that could be treated through transplantation. Despite advancements in medical science, many patients are unable to receive timely and adequate care due to financial constraints and fragmented information systems for organ donation and recipient matching. 1 At present, the absence of a comprehensive national transplant registry hampers the efficient allocation of donated organs, resulting in delays, inequities, and preventable loss of life. Moreover, indigent patients often face insurmountable financial barriers, including costs related to surgery, hospitalization, post-operative care, and lifelong immunosuppressive therapy. This measure seeks to establish a National Organ Transplant Registry that integrates donor and recipient data, ensures equitable allocation of organs based on medical need and ethical standards, and strengthens government oversight. It likewise institutionalizes financial and medical support mechanisms for indigent patients, thereby promoting equitable access to transplantation services. In strengthening existing laws and addressing systemic gaps, this bill aims to save lives, uphold human dignity, and advance universal health care in the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11083
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A VARSITY SPORTS AND PARA-SPORTS PROGRAM IN ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS, STRENGTHENING INCLUSIVITY IN BASIC EDUCATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 19 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence for the development of a healthy and alert citizenry. It further mandates all educational institutions to undertake regular sports activities in cooperation with athletic clubs and other sectors. Consistent with this mandate, Republic Act No. 9155, otherwise known as the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001,” recognizes school sports and physical fitness as integral components of the basic education curriculum. Likewise, Republic Act No. 5708, otherwise known as the “Schools Physical Education and Sports Development Act of 1969,” underscores the importance of providing opportunities for the athletic development of children and youth. Complementarily, Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Disabled Persons,” as amended, affirms the State’s duty to promote the rehabilitation, self-development, and full participation of persons with disabilities in society, including through sports and physical development programs. Despite these policy directives, opportunities for systematic and sustained athletic and para-athletic development at the basic education level remain limited. While competitions such as the Palarong Pambansa and other school-based meets provide exposure, they do not fully address the need for continuous training, early talent identification, accessibility support, and structured development pathways for young athletes and para-athletes. Many student-athletes and student-para-athletes lack access to organized varsity sports and para-sports programs, competent coaching, adaptive training systems, accessible facilities, adequate equipment, and regular competition at the elementary and secondary levels. This results in missed opportunities to nurture athletic potential at an early stage, which is critical in building a strong pipeline of athletes and para-athletes for higher-level competition, including collegiate, national, and international tournaments. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize varsity sports and para- sports programs in public and private elementary and secondary schools by encouraging the organization of varsity teams, strengthening coaching systems, and improving access to facilities, training, competitions, and adaptive sports support systems. It also establishes mechanisms for athlete and para-athlete identification, performance profiling, and the creation of a national registry of student-athletes and student-para-athletes to support long-term athletic development. The bill likewise promotes collaboration among schools, local communities, local government units, and national sports institutions, including the Philippine Sports Commission, National Sports Associations, the Philippine Olympic Committee, and the Philippine Paralympic Committee, to ensure that training programs align with national, international, and adaptive sports standards. It further recognizes disparities in institutional resources and establishes mechanisms for inter-school clustering and resource-sharing to expand opportunities for learners from underserved and marginalized communities. Ultimately, this measure aims to expand the base of Filipino student- athletes and student-para-athletes, strengthen grassroots sports and para-sports development, and enhance the country’s competitiveness in international sporting events. By institutionalizing varsity sports and para-sports programs in basic education, the State invests in the development of disciplined, healthy, resilient, and high-performing youth, while promoting inclusivity and equal opportunities in sports participation. 2 Similar bills have been filed since the 17th Congress and were primarily referred to the Committee on Basic Education and Culture. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11084
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING FOOD SECURITY COLD STORAGE FACILITIES IN EVERY PROVINCE OF THE COUNTRY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 5, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to support agriculture through appropriate technology, research, and adequate financial, production, and marketing services. In line with this policy, the State must establish mechanisms that preserve perishable agricultural goods, reduce post-harvest losses, and ensure a stable and sufficient food supply for the population. Food security remains a fundamental national concern, closely linked to economic stability, public welfare, and national resilience. As an agricultural country, the Philippines continues to face persistent challenges in ensuring a stable and sufficient food supply, particularly in the context of post-harvest losses, price volatility, and inefficiencies in the distribution of perishable goods. A major contributor to these challenges is the lack of adequate cold storage infrastructure nationwide. Perishable agricultural products, such as fruits, vegetables, fish, and meat, are highly vulnerable to spoilage due to insufficient storage and handling facilities. The limited availability of accessible and strategically located cold storage facilities results in significant post-harvest losses, reducing farmers’ incomes and contributing to supply constraints and price volatility that ultimately burden consumers. Access to existing cold chain systems also remains uneven, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas and in provinces with high agricultural production. As a result, many farmers, fisherfolk, and small-scale food processors are compelled to sell their produce immediately at lower prices or risk spoilage, weakening the agricultural value chain and undermining overall food security. This proposed measure seeks to address these challenges by establishing food security cold storage facilities in every province. By ensuring the availability of temperature-controlled storage infrastructure, the State aims to reduce post- harvest losses, extend the shelf life of perishable goods, and enable more efficient distribution and market timing of agricultural products. The measure further promotes accessibility by requiring strategic placement of facilities and prioritizing underserved and high-producing areas through a phased implementation approach. It also designates the Department of Agriculture as the lead implementing agency and mandates coordination with local government units to ensure the effective establishment, operation, and maintenance of the facilities. Ultimately, the establishment of food security cold storage facilities is expected to strengthen the agricultural value chain, improve farmers’ incomes, stabilize food prices, and enhance the country’s capacity to respond to supply disruptions. By investing in critical post-harvest infrastructure, the State affirms its commitment to achieving long-term food security and building a more resilient and efficient food system. Measures seeking the establishment of cold storage facilities have been filed as early as the 8th Congress, although most were limited to specific local government units. Recognizing their growing importance, similar nationwide measures were also filed during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. label: HB 11085
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF THE OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State values the dignity of every human person and guarantees full respect for human rights. Consistent with this mandate, the State must ensure that out-of-school youth are not left behind in the country’s education, employment, and social protection systems. Out-of-school youth face intersecting barriers that limit their full participation in society. Many are unable to complete formal education due to poverty, family responsibilities, early pregnancy, lack of access to schools, displacement, abuse, disability, conflict with the law, or other difficult circumstances. Without adequate intervention, they are placed at greater risk of unemployment, exploitation, violence, trafficking, and long-term poverty. While existing programs such as the Alternative Learning System, technical-vocational education, livelihood assistance, youth development programs, and social welfare services provide important support, these interventions remain dispersed across different agencies and local government units. There is a need for a comprehensive rights-based framework that will clearly define the rights of out-of-school youth, harmonize government programs, and ensure coordinated delivery of education, employment, health, social protection, and reintegration services. This bill seeks to provide a Magna Carta for Out-of-School Youth by recognizing, protecting, and promoting their rights and by mandating government agencies to provide targeted assistance and support. It strengthens access to formal, non-formal, informal, and technical-vocational education; promotes decent work and livelihood opportunities; ensures health, psychosocial, and social welfare interventions; and provides special protection for those in especially difficult circumstances. The measure further mandates the creation of an updated database and profiling system for out-of-school youth, strengthens the role of the National Youth Commission, local government units, Sangguniang Kabataan, Local Youth Development Councils, and concerned agencies, and encourages partnership with the private sector and non-government organizations. Through these mechanisms, programs for out-of-school youth may be better coordinated, monitored, and made more responsive to their actual needs. Ultimately, this measure recognizes out-of-school youth not as liabilities, but as rights-holders and partners in nation-building. By providing them with meaningful access to education, skills training, employment, social services, and protection, the State invests in their potential and strengthens inclusive national development. This measure has been filed since the 16th Congress. During the 19th Congress, it was approved on the third and final reading. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11086
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT WORKERS, STRENGTHENING THEIR WELFARE, LABOR PROTECTION, AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 18, Article II of the 1987 Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Section 3, Article XIII further guarantees the rights of all workers to just and humane conditions of work, security of tenure, and a living wage, and promotes full employment and equality of employment opportunities. Complementarily, Section 5, Article XIII directs the State to provide support to agriculture through appropriate technology and research, and adequate financial, production, marketing, and other support services. These provisions underscore the State’s duty not only to strengthen the agricultural sector but also to protect and develop the workforce that sustains it. Agricultural development workers, who include agriculturists, engineers, technicians, extension workers, and support personnel, serve as the backbone of agricultural productivity, extension services, and rural transformation. While farmers and fisherfolk remain at the forefront of food production, agricultural development workers play an equally critical role in sustaining and strengthening the sector by providing the technical expertise, research support, extension services, and institutional capacity necessary for modern, efficient, and climate- resilient agriculture. They are indispensable in translating policies into practice, supporting communities on the ground, and ensuring that agricultural programs are effectively implemented across the country. Despite their indispensable role, agricultural development workers continue to face structural challenges, including inadequate compensation, limited career advancement opportunities, unsafe working conditions, and inconsistent labor protection across institutions and local government units. The devolution of agricultural services under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the “Local Government Code of 1991,” has resulted in uneven capacity and disparities in the delivery of agricultural services across local government units. This situation has been further shaped by the landmark ruling in Mandanas v. Ochoa,1 which expanded the fiscal resources of local governments by increasing their share in national taxes. While this development enhances the capacity of LGUs to deliver devolved services, it likewise underscores the need to strengthen institutional systems, standardize staffing, and ensure adequate protection and professionalization of agricultural development workers at the local level. While Republic Act No. 12215, otherwise known as the “Philippine Agriculturists Act,” and other professional laws regulate licensure and professional standards, there remains a significant policy gap in addressing the employment conditions, welfare, labor rights, and occupational safety of agricultural development workers across the public and private sectors. This proposed Magna Carta seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a comprehensive framework that ensures just compensation, wage protection, security of tenure, safe and humane working conditions, and occupational safety and health protection, while strengthening the professionalization of agricultural services, particularly at the local government level. The measure further integrates labor standards, human resource development mechanisms, and inter-agency coordination, recognizing that the effectiveness of agricultural programs depends not only on policy and funding but also on the competence, protection, and motivation of the workforce. Ultimately, this bill aims to strengthen the foundation of agricultural development by investing in the people who drive it. By protecting and 1 Mandanas v. Executive Secretary (G.R. Similar bills have been filed since the 10th Congress, but have remained pending with the Committee on Agriculture and Food. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11087
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF MUNICIPAL SMALL- SCALE AND SUBSISTENCE FISHERFOLK, STRENGTHENING THEIR RIGHTS, PROTECTION, AND ACCESS TO SUPPORT SERVICES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 7, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution guarantees the protection of the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore. It further mandates the State to provide support through appropriate technology and research, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other services; to protect, develop, and conserve such resources; to safeguard offshore fishing grounds against foreign intrusion; and, to ensure that fishworkers receive a just share from their labor in the utilization of marine and fishing resources. Complementing this mandate, Section 5, Article XIII of the Constitution directs the State to provide support to agriculture and fisheries, while Section 16, Article II guarantees the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology, and Section 18, Article II affirms the State’s duty to protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Taken together, these provisions establish the State’s obligation not only to secure the dignity, welfare, and economic resilience of fisherfolk, but also to ensure the sustainability of fisheries resources. Municipal small-scale and subsistence fisherfolk remain among the most economically vulnerable sectors in the country, despite their indispensable role in ensuring food security, sustaining coastal communities, and supporting local economies. Their contributions extend beyond food production, as they also serve as frontline stewards of marine and coastal ecosystems. However, structural challenges continue to limit their full participation in economic growth and development. While Republic Act No. 8550, otherwise known as the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, as amended, recognizes their preferential rights in municipal waters and provides the legal framework for fisheries management, many fisherfolk continue to face persistent and overlapping challenges. These include limited access to markets, inadequate post-harvest and cold storage facilities, exposure to exploitative trading practices, vulnerability to climate change and natural disasters, and increasing operational costs, particularly due to fuel price fluctuations. Existing government interventions, such as fuel subsidy programs, credit and insurance facilities, and livelihood assistance, have provided some relief. However, these initiatives remain fragmented, unevenly implemented, and often insufficient to address the long-term and systemic needs of the sector. Moreover, the growing role of digital technologies in governance and market systems highlights the need to improve the fisherfolk’s access to information, services, and economic opportunities through more integrated and accessible platforms. This proposed Magna Carta seeks to address these gaps by establishing a comprehensive and integrated policy framework for municipal small-scale and subsistence fisherfolk. It consolidates and reinforces their rights, strengthens access to fisheries support services, promotes fair and equitable market participation, and institutionalizes social protection mechanisms, particularly during emergencies such as natural disasters, fuel price shocks, and other disruptions affecting fisheries operations. The measure further promotes the adoption and use of digital systems to enhance access to government services, improve data-driven policy implementation, and ensure more efficient delivery of programs. It also strengthens inter-agency coordination and the targeting of beneficiaries through the integration of existing registry systems. By reinforcing existing laws and addressing implementation gaps, this measure aims to uplift the welfare of fisherfolk, enhance their resilience to economic and environmental shocks, and ensure the sustainable use of marine 2 resources. Ultimately, it contributes to long-term food security, inclusive economic growth, and the protection of coastal and marine ecosystems. Similar measures have been filed since the 8th Congress but have remained pending with the Committee on Agriculture and Food, underscoring the continuing need for a comprehensive and responsive policy framework for the sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11088
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE PUBLIC ACCESS TO INTERNATIONAL AND MAJOR LOCAL SPORTING EVENTS INVOLVING FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES THROUGH STATE-RUN BROADCAST AND DIGITAL PLATFORMS, PROMOTING MEDIA PARTNERSHIPS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the vital role of sports in fostering national unity, pride, and identity. Filipino athletes and para-athletes who compete in international and local sporting events serve as symbols of discipline, perseverance, and excellence, inspiring millions of Filipinos across the country. Pursuant to Section 19, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence for developing a healthy and alert citizenry. Complementarily, Section 24, Article II mandates the State to recognize the vital role of communication and information in nation- building. Ensuring accessible platforms for the dissemination of sports content aligns with this constitutional directive by enabling broader public engagement in national events. Despite widespread public interest, access to coverage of international competitions such as the Olympic Games, Asian Games, Southeast Asian Games, and Asian Beach Games remains limited, as broadcast rights are often held by private entities and made available primarily through subscription-based platforms. This restricts the ability of a significant portion of the Filipino public to readily watch and support national athletes and para-athletes in real time, resulting in limited lawful and accessible viewing opportunities and reducing broader public engagement in national sporting events. More critically, coverage of major local sporting events remains even more limited and, in many instances, inaccessible. Competitions that serve as training grounds, qualifiers, and talent-identification platforms for future national representatives are rarely televised or livestreamed, resulting in limited public awareness and engagement. This lack of visibility weakens the pipeline of support for emerging athletes and undermines efforts to build a sustained and inclusive sports culture. At the same time, media consumption patterns in the Philippines have increasingly shifted toward digital and mobile-based platforms, with a substantial number of Filipinos accessing audiovisual content through freely accessible online applications and social media platforms. Leveraging these technologies presents a strategic opportunity for the State to democratize access to sports content and ensure that Filipino representation in sporting events, whether at the elite, grassroots, or developmental level, becomes more visible and accessible to the public. In anticipation of the Philippines’ participation in the upcoming Southeast Asian Games, there is a timely need to ensure that Filipinos are able to follow and support their athletes and para-athletes through accessible and inclusive platforms. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by providing for free public access to sporting events involving Filipino athletes and para-athletes in both international and major local competitions through state-run television and official digital platforms, while respecting existing broadcast rights. It further promotes partnerships with media entities to expand coverage, improve reach, and ensure sustainability. 2 By making sporting events involving Filipino athletes and para-athletes more accessible to the public, the State affirms its commitment to inclusive recognition, sustained public engagement, and the continued development of Philippine sports. This measure seeks not only to expand access to sports content, but also to strengthen national pride, encourage broader support for Filipino athletes and para-athletes, and foster a culture that values participation, representation, discipline, and excellence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11089
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE MENTAL HEALTH AND PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT SYSTEM FOR FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES, PROMOTING SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SPORTS ENVIRONMENTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the importance of promoting the mental health and well-being of Filipino athletes and para-athletes as an integral component of sports development. Athletes at all levels, from grassroots and school-based participants to elite national representatives, face unique psychological pressures arising from training demands, performance expectations, injuries, and even career uncertainties. These challenges, if left unaddressed, may adversely affect not only the athletic performance but also the long-term personal development of the athletes. Pursuant to Section 19, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions. Complementarily, Section 15, Article II provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people, including mental health, while Section 13, Article II recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation- building. While existing laws such as Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” establish a general framework for mental health services, and Republic Act No. 12080, otherwise known as the “Basic Education Mental Health and Well-Being Promotion Act,” institutionalizes mental health programs in basic education, there remains a gap in the delivery of specialized and accessible mental health services tailored to the unique needs of athletes. Moreover, Republic Act No. 10699, otherwise known as the “National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act,” provides health-related benefits for national athletes but does not sufficiently address the systematic provision of mental health and psychosocial support within sports systems. At present, mental health services in sports remain fragmented, unevenly accessible, and often reactive rather than preventive. Grassroots and school-based athletes, in particular, have limited access to structured mental health support, despite being at a critical stage of development. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a comprehensive mental health and psychosocial support system for athletes and para-athletes across all levels of participation. It provides for increased access to mental health services, integration of mental health mechanisms in sports programs, capacity-building for stakeholders, and strengthened inter-agency coordination, while ensuring confidentiality and data privacy. By prioritizing mental health as a core component of athlete development, the State affirms its commitment to fostering resilience, sustaining performance, and promoting the overall well-being of Filipino athletes and para-athletes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11090
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DIGITAL SPORTS ARCHIVE FOR THE SYSTEMATIC COLLECTION, PRESERVATION, AND PUBLIC DISSEMINATION OF SPORTS RECORDS AND DATA INVOLVING FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the importance of preserving and promoting the achievements of Filipino athletes and para-athletes as part of the nation’s cultural, historical, and sporting heritage. Sporting events, whether at the international or local level, document the journey, performance, and progress of athletes and serve as valuable resources for public engagement, education, and future development. Pursuant to Section 15, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall conserve, promote, and popularize the nation’s historical and cultural heritage and resources. Complementarily, Section 24, Article II recognizes the vital role of communication and information in nation-building, underscoring the need for accessible platforms for the dissemination and preservation of information. Despite the increasing participation of Filipino athletes and para-athletes in both international and local competitions, there is currently no centralized and accessible repository of sports records, game footage, athlete profiles, and related data. Existing materials are often fragmented across various platforms, inconsistently documented, or entirely unavailable to the public. This results in the loss of valuable historical records and limits opportunities for analysis, recognition, and sustained engagement. Moreover, the absence of a unified digital archive, supported by standardized records management and archival practices, hinders the ability of coaches, researchers, policymakers, and aspiring athletes to access reliable data for performance analysis, training development, and evidence-based decision- making. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Digital Sports Archive that will serve as a centralized, publicly accessible platform for the systematic collection, preservation, and dissemination of Philippine sports data and audiovisual materials, in coordination with relevant agencies, including the National Archives of the Philippines, to ensure proper records management and long-term preservation. By institutionalizing a digital archive, the State affirms its commitment to preserving the nation’s sporting heritage, promoting transparency and accessibility, and strengthening the overall sports ecosystem. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11108
title: AN ACT DISQUALIFYING RELATIVES OF PUBLIC OFFICIALS WITHIN THE FOURTH CIVIL DEGREE OF CONSANGUINITY OR AFFINITY FROM PARTICIPATING IN GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Delicadeza is a Spanish word which means “delicateness, fineness or tact, or showing regard for the feelings of others, or sensitive in action or operation.” However, in Filipino culture, it is the character of holding oneself into a higher moral and ethical standard which is a burden of a public office. For the longest time in Philippine politics, delicadeza is no longer the standard. Rather, it is considered as a nuisance, an unwanted word word shall be kept out of the spotlight. Delicadeza should not only extend to public officials but also to their relatives. The past couple of months highlighted the outrageous luxury that these contractors possess. If they are so comfortable at public flaunting their wealth, then they must also be held accountable over how they made these luxuries. They shall be held into the same moral and ethical standards which public officials are being held to account. Under Section 79 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, no person shall be appointed in the career service of the local government if he or she is related to the appointing authority within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity. The proposed bill barring relatives within the 4th civil degree in from participating in government contracts is consistent with the policy against nepotism already recognized under Local Government Code. If the existing law prohibits an appointing authority from favoring a relative within the fourth civil degree in public employment, then there is a similar, if not stronger, reason to prohibit public officials from participating in, approving, recommending, or awarding government contracts where the contractor, supplier, beneficial owner, incorporator, officer, or controlling stockholder is related to them within the same prohibited degree. No longer shall relatives of public officials make money out of government contract. This bill seeks to disqualify them from making money out of the hard-earned tax money of Filipinos. label: HB 11109
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROVISION OF EXCLUSIVE PARKING SPACE FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES AND PENALIZING THE UNAUTHORIZED USE THEREOF, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ACCESSIBILITY LAW
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes persons with disabilities and their remarkable contributions to our development as a nation. In line with this, the country has enacted Batas Pambansa (B.P.) Blg. 344, otherwise known as the “Accessibility Law” in 1983. This piece of legislation has initially facilitated the inclusion of persons with disabilities into the mainstream of Philippine society. However, after almost 40 years of its enactment, it has been observed that the Accessibility Law does not fully cater to the accessibility needs of persons with disabilities. For one, B.P. 344 does not provide for sanctions for the unauthorized use and obstruction of parking spaces reserved for persons with disabilities. As such, these parking spaces are frequently used by persons without disabilities, thereby preventing persons with disabilities from being able to access essential services. Similarly, Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, simply states, in Section 25 thereof, that the State “shall ensure the attainment of a barrier-free environment for disabled persons in accordance with the Accessibility Law.” With the absence of clear penalties for the unauthorized use and obstruction of such designated spaces, persons with disabilities are further robbed of opportunities and spaces that ought to be for them. Thus, there remains a need to improve our existing laws for the welfare of Filipino persons with disabilities. This bill seeks to address this limitation of the Accessibility Law by mandating the provision of exclusive parking for persons with disabilities, defining the prohibited acts, and providing the penalties in cases of violation. It is the hope of this measure to strengthen the Accessibility Law and complement existing laws that protect and uphold the rights of persons with disabilities to attain an inclusive and barrier-free environment In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11110
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE EDUCATION TO SENIOR CITIZENS AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The role of senior citizens in the Filipino family and in nation-building is valuable and is recognized by the State, with laws such as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2003 and 2010 among others. Similarly, quality education for all is fervently valued by the State as well. Sec. 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall promote the “right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all,” calling for the establishment of a “complete, adequate and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” This bill seeks to affirm our recognition of the invaluable contributions of senior citizens and support those who have yet to gain access to education or are interested in continuing their academic journey. It is the hope of this measure to support the dreams of every Filipino, regardless of age, for quality education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11111
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE PRIVILEGES FOR SENIOR CITIZENS TO INCLUDE FREE PARKING IN ALL ESTABLISHMENTS AND EXEMPTION FROM THE NUMBER CODING SCHEME, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9994, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE EXPANDED SENIOR CITIZENS ACT OF 2010
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9994, or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, defines ‘senior citizens’ as individuals aged 60 years old and above. Senior citizens make up 10.2 percent of the total population, or 11.2 million Filipinos, as of the latest census of the Philippine Statistics Authority in 2024. The Philippine government recognizes the role of the elderly in nation- building and their continued contributions to society and development. As such, legislation that encourages mobility, growth, and protection for our dear elderly is of importance. In line with the State’s policy to promote the welfare of senior citizens, this legislation seeks to create opportunities for their continued participation in social and economic life, while ensuring that their rights and well-being are protected. It reflects the government’s continuing commitment to reduce the burdens faced by senior citizens and to support their meaningful contribution to national development. This bill seeks to provide additional benefits and privileges to the Filipino elderly. This proposed legislation exempts them from paying parking fees in all establishments and from the Unified Vehicular Volume Reduction Program or the number coding scheme implemented by the Government. Through this initiative, we are providing our senior citizens simple economic benefits that would reward their great contributions to our country’s development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11112
title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE CENTER FOR DISEASE CONTROL AND PREVENTION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) has taken most of the world by surprise, infecting more than five million persons and taking the lives of at least three hundred thousand persons worldwide. It has become a pandemic that threatens countries without strong public health care systems and facilities for control and prevention of communicable and infectious diseases. Our lack of institutional capacity to implement comprehensive public health management programs, especially in public health protection, shows the harsh reality that our country needs to modernize and upgrade our public health systems to decisively address the risks of communicable diseases. From sudden cases of polio-related diseases, to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related infections, to tuberculosis and dengue outbreaks, there is a need for an institution to focus and create scientifically accurate and research- backed solutions to combat infectious and emerging diseases. While the Department of Health has been effective to some degree in the delivery of health services amid the pandemic, we must strengthen its absorptive capacity and framework in dealing with difficult communicable diseases. This bill seeks to establish a Philippine National Center for Disease Control and Prevention, which shall serve as the principal health protection agency of the Philippines aimed at preventing, protecting, and managing the spread of communicable and infectious diseases and other health emergencies in the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D.
