label: HB 11113
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PANDEMIC AND OTHER PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS PLAN AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The COVID-19 pandemic remains one of the most significant public health crises in recent history. Although the World Health Organization ended the Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May 2023, COVID- 19 continues to circulate globally, with WHO reporting over 779 million confirmed cases and more than seven million confirmed deaths as of mid- 2026, and the global risk still assessed as moderate1. The pandemic exposed gaps in health systems worldwide, especially in countries with limited infrastructure, workforce, and emergency coordination capacity. It also underscored the need for stronger preparedness mechanisms that can respond quickly to future outbreaks while preserving essential health services and minimizing social and economic disruption.2 To reduce the impact of future pandemics and similar public health emergencies, there is a need to strengthen the country’s emergency preparedness architecture. This includes improving the capacity of health care facilities and workers, ensuring coordinated action among national and local authorities, and grounding policy responses in scientific evidence and real-time risk assessment.3 1 COVID-19 Dashboard. World Health Organization (2024) 2 Investing in Pandemic Preparedness for Resilient and Sustainable Health Systems.World Health Organization (2026) 3 Committee Meeting on Health Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and Response. World Health Organization (2026) This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive framework for responding to pandemics and other public health emergencies by creating a Pandemic Emergency Council and a National Emergency Preparedness Plan. It aims to promote resilient health systems, strengthen public health response capacity, and ensure that the Philippines is better equipped to prevent, detect, and respond to future crises. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11115
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL DAM SAFETY PROGRAM, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL DAM SAFETY AUTHORITY, PENALIZING VIOLATIONS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Dams are critical infrastructure that support water supply, irrigation, flood control, and power generation, but their operation also carries significant risks to communities located downstream, particularly during typhoons, extreme rainfall, earthquakes, and other hazards, making dam safety an essential component of national disaster risk reduction and public safety. The need for a dedicated and comprehensive national framework is underscored by the country’s multi-hazard environment. A recent national study on dam safety drawing on the assessments of 348 qualified National Irrigation Administration engineers noted that Philippine dams face limitations in monitoring capacity.1 At the same time, the urgency of strengthening such systems is heightened by climate variability and changing water conditions: in May 2026, the Climate Change Commission reported that major Luzon dams had recorded declining water levels amid prolonged dry conditions and high heat indices, with Angat Dam, Metro Manila’s primary water source, falling to 177.41 meters from its 210-meter normal water level.2 These changing conditions 1 Department of Science and Technology–National Research Council of the Philippines (DOST- NRCP), Multi-Criterion Evaluation of Dam Safety Using Analytic Hierarchy Process: A Case Study of Philippine Dams. 2 Climate Change Commission, reported by the Philippine Information Agency, “CCC: Local Climate Change Action Plans key to water security amid declining dam levels,” May 22, 2026. demonstrate that dam safety must address not only structural integrity but also the management of water levels, extreme weather, operational decisions, and timely communication with communities. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) already operates a Flood Forecasting and Warning System for Dam Operation covering five major dams in Luzon: Angat, Pantabangan, Magat, Binga, and Ambuklao. This system uses real-time rainfall and water-level monitoring, forecasting, warning dissemination, and inter- agency information sharing to help ensure safe reservoir operations and warn downstream communities of impending water releases.3 Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, already recognizes the importance of national risk mapping, monitoring, and comprehensive early warning and emergency alert systems, including the provision of timely information to national and local emergency organizations and the general public.4 This proposed measure builds upon that policy by establishing a dedicated National Dam Safety Authority tasked with coordinating the management and operation of dams, developing a comprehensive National Dam Safety Plan, ensuring safe construction and maintenance, and strengthening early warning, consultation, and public information mechanisms. The bill likewise requires consultation and disclosure of relevant dam information during calamities, typhoons, and other disasters, recognizing that a warning is effective only when communities receive timely, understandable, and actionable information. By institutionalizing a unified dam safety program and clearly assigning responsibility for prevention, monitoring, emergency coordination, and public disclosure, the measure seeks to shift the country from a reactive approach to dam-related emergencies toward one based on prevention, preparedness, accountability, and protection of human life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11116
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR SOLO PARENTS PROGRAM (FASPP) OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SOCIAL WELFARE AND DEVELOPMENT (DSWD) AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Solo parents carry the responsibility of raising and providing for their children without the full and regular support of another parent, making access to reliable social protection particularly important for families with limited resources. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) estimates that there are approximately 14 million solo parents in the Philippines, and the agency recognizes solo parents as a sector requiring social protection and government assistance under the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act, or Republic Act No. 11861.1 The scale of this sector underscores the need for government programs that not only recognize solo parents' rights in law but also provide practical assistance when families face immediate financial difficulty. The need for responsive assistance is particularly evident among low- income households facing rising costs of basic necessities. In June 2026, food inflation among the bottom 30% of income households reached 8.2 percent, while the cost of housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels increased by 8.7 percent and transport costs increased by 15.6 percent year-on-year.2 These 1 Department of Social Welfare and Development, Provision of Assistance to Solo Parents, citing National Statistics Office data on approximately 14 million solo parents and discussing the implementation of Republic Act No. 11861, the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act. 2 Philippine Statistics Authority, Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index for the Bottom 30% Income Households (2018=100): June 2026. pressures are especially significant for solo parents, who must stretch a single household income across food, utilities, transportation, health care, education, and other expenses for themselves and their dependents. The DSWD's experience with its Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program likewise demonstrates the continuing demand for government safety-net assistance: more than 8.2 million Filipinos in crisis received assistance from AICS from January to November 2025, exceeding the program's target for the year.3 While existing government programs provide important support, there is a need to institutionalize a dedicated and predictable mechanism through which qualified solo parents can receive assistance for essential needs. The proposed Financial Assistance for Solo Parents Program (FASPP) Act responds to this need by establishing a statutory framework for assistance that may cover food, medical expenses, education, livelihood, and cash relief, while allowing complementary assistance through LGUs in the form of rice assistance. The Bill also provides safeguards through eligibility requirements, social-worker assessment, documentary requirements, and penalties for fraudulent or improper claims, while ensuring that assistance may complement support from LGUs, other government agencies, and non-government organizations. By institutionalizing the FASPP and providing for its continuing appropriation, the measure seeks to make government assistance more accessible, coordinated, and responsive to the actual needs of solo parents and their dependents. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11117
title: AN ACT PROVIDING CASH ASSISTANCE TO KASAMBAHAY PARENTS, INCLUDING OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKER (OFW) HOUSEHOLD SERVICE WORKERS, WITH THE OPTION TO CONVERT SUCH ASSISTANCE INTO SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM (SSS) CONTRIBUTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sa araw-araw, milyon-milyong mga Pilipino ang nililisan ang kanilang tahanan bago magbukang-liwayway, iniiwan ang kanilang pamilya at kadalasan maging ang ating bansa upang mamasukan at mag-alaga ng hindi nila anak at ng ibang pamilya. Likas na mapagmahal ang mga Pilipino. Madali nating makapalagayan ng loob ang mga taong nakasasalamuha natin, lalo na kung palagi natin silang kapiling. Ngunit masakit para sa isang magulang na higit na maalagaan ang mga anak na hindi niya kadugo kaysa sa sarili niyang anak. Filipino kasambahay prepare another family’s meals, comfort another family’s children when they cry, and stay awake when someone else’s child is sick, while their own children wait for them, often under the care of a grandmother, an older sibling, or a neighbor, for months or even years at a time. This is the quiet burden carried by the Filipino kasambahay: those who give the best of their care to households that are not their own, often at the cost of the time and presence they wish they could give their own children. Based on a recent joint survey of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), there are approximately 1.4 million kasambahay in the Philippines1. Of this number, the majority are on a live-out arrangement, leaving their own households each day to care for another family's home and children. The same survey found that 83 per cent of kasambahay have no social security coverage at all, leaving them and their families exposed in the event of illness, disability, or 1 https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/dole-and-psa-survey-1-4-million-kasambahays-in-the-country- 72-on-live-out-arrangement-2/ old age, on top of the earnings they have spent by being away from their own children for most of the day2. For those who leave the country to work as domestic helpers, the burden is even heavier. The PSA reported that the number of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) rose to 2.19 million in 2024, from 2.16 million in 2023, with women comprising 57.2 per cent, or 1.25 million, of this workforce3. Approximately four (4) out of every ten (10) OFWs are in elementary occupations, which include domestic and household work. Moreover, Filipina household service workers are heavily concentrated in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, and Hong Kong4. Estimates from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) place domestic workers at 20 to 30 per cent of all OFWs deployed each year. These figures demonstrate that household service work is one of the most common forms of overseas employment for Filipino women. Hindi lamang ito basta mga numero… sa likod ng bawat datos na ito ay ang mga anak na naiiwan ng kanilang mga magulang na naghahanapbuhay. Researchers estimate that at least 1.5 million Filipino children are growing up with one or both parents working overseas. A study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific linked prolonged parental separation to loneliness, emotional strain, and health and developmental concerns among left-behind children, even as the remittances sent by their parents help support their education5. This is the irony this bill seeks to address: the very people entrusted with the care of other people's children often cannot afford the time, presence, or financial security to properly care for their own. Albeit existing laws such as Republic Act (RA) No. 10361, otherwise known as “Batas Kasambahay Act” and RA No. 8042, as amended by RA No. 10022 or the “Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act”, protect the kasambahay as a worker, there remains no law that directly assists them in their role as parents. The Kasambahay Parents Support Act aims to fill this gap. It provides monthly cash assistance to Kasambahay Parents, whether locally employed or deployed overseas, for the benefit of their qualified children left at home. This measure also addresses the concern that 83 per cent of kasambahay currently have no social security coverage. 2 https://dole.gov.ph/news/dole-psa-1-4m-hsws-72-on-liveout/ 3 philstar.com/business/2025/12/19/2495253/ofws-rise-219-million-2024-psa 4 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1758590/sws-survey-says-7-of-filipino-households-have- an-ofw 5 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9391573/ 1 The bill gives beneficiaries the option to apply the cash assistance toward their Social Security System (SSS) contributions, thereby enabling them to build long-term social protection for themselves and their families. Kasambahay devote their care, patience, and time to families that are not their own. It is only just that the State, in turn, help them care for the families waiting for them at home. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. Filipino kasambahay prepare another family’s meals, comfort another family’s children when they cry, and stay awake when someone else’s child is sick, while their own children wait for them, often under the care of a grandmother, an older sibling, or a neighbor, for months or even years at a time. label: HB 11130
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR AN AUTOMATIC TOLL RELIEF MECHANISM DURING MAJOR TOLL FACILITY DISRUPTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Toll facilities are established to ensure the safe, efficient, and reliable movement of motorists and vehicles. However, natural disasters, accidents, fires, landslides, infrastructure failures, and other emergencies may substantially disrupt their normal operation, resulting in prolonged delays, severe congestion, and significant hardship to motorists and passengers. The recent flooding along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX), particularly in the Tulaoc area and San Simon, Pampanga, underscores the need for a clear and predictable mechanism to address such disruptions. The flooding rendered portions of the expressway impassable, severely restricted traffic flow, and resulted in motorists being stranded for extended periods. The incident also demonstrated the difficulties faced by passengers who may require food, water, sanitation, medical attention, or other forms of assistance while trapped in prolonged traffic. In response to the situation, government authorities directed the provision of assistance to affected motorists and subsequently implemented toll-free passage along the San Fernando–Pulilan stretch of NLEX. The Department of Transportation and Toll Regulatory Board has also directed the NLEX Corporation to provide toll relief to assist motorists affected by the flooding and resulting traffic congestion, with the measure remaining in effect until normal conditions return, including the provision of food and drinking water and the setup of portable toilets for stranded motorists. While such measures provide necessary relief, the circumstances also highlight the need for a standing mechanism that does not rely solely on ad hoc decisions after a major disruption has already occurred. Motorists should not have to wait for separate directives before knowing whether they are entitled to toll relief when objectively verifiable conditions have substantially impaired their use of a toll facility. This measure therefore seeks to establish an Automatic Toll Relief Mechanism that will provide appropriate temporary suspension, waiver, reduction, credit, refund, or other adjustment of toll fees when defined conditions constituting a major toll facility disruption are met. The mechanism will provide uniform standards for determining when toll relief shall commence, the extent of relief to be provided, and when regular toll collection may resume. It likewise recognizes that the effects of major disruptions extend beyond traffic congestion and toll charges. Motorists and passengers may be exposed to prolonged periods of confinement, limited access to food, water, sanitation, medical assistance, and safe areas. Accordingly, toll operators shall be required to provide appropriate roadside and emergency assistance, facilitate access to safe locations when practicable, and give priority response to senior citizens, persons with disabilities, children, pregnant women, persons requiring medical attention, and others requiring immediate assistance. It also promotes timely and adequate public information during major disruptions so that motorists can make informed decisions regarding their routes and travel. Clear information on affected areas, available routes, emergency assistance, and applicable toll relief can help prevent motorists from entering severely affected portions of a toll facility and further aggravating congestion. The recent experience in San Simon, Pampanga demonstrates that major toll facility disruptions can occur with little warning and can affect thousands of motorists and passengers. Establishing an automatic and uniform mechanism before the next emergency will enable the government and toll operators to respond more efficiently, provide appropriate relief, and better protect the public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RODOLFO “OMPONG” M. label: HB 11131
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE UNDERPRIVILEGED AND HOMELESS FROM THE, REQUIRED PAYMENT OF SUPERSEDEAS BOND TO PERFECT AN APPEAL IN RELATION TO EJECTMENT CASES FILED AGAINST THEM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7279 OR THE "URBAN DEVELOPMENT HOUSING ACT OF 1992"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE More than three decades after the enactment of Republic Act (R.A.) No. 7279, or the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992, housing insecurity remains one of the pressing issues that the government seeks to address and end. Related to this, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) reported that 238,747 informal settler families, of whom only 57,134, or 23.93 percent, had been relocated as of August 2025, leaving more than 181,000 identified families still awaiting resettlement.1 The vulnerability of these families is aggravated when housing disputes and cases are filed before the courts. In May 2025, for instance, residents of a Tondo community resisted the implementation of a court-ordered demolition, with affected families expressing that they had nowhere else to go. The dispute had already undergone approximately four years of litigation before the final demolition order was issued.2 Similar disputes underscore the realities for indigent families that ejectment cases are not simply a question of possession but determines whether a family continues to have a roof over its head. Under Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, judgments against defendants in ejectment cases are immediately executory. To stay or put on hold the execution pending appeal, the defendant must, among others, file a sufficient supersedeas bond and continue making the required deposits for the use and occupation of the property. 1 INQUIRER.net (2025, August 15). 57,134 informal settler families relocated from Manila Bay — DILG. Accessed last 11 August 2026 from: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2096123/57134-informal-settler-families-relocated-from-manila-bay-dilg 2 Locus, S. (2025, May 26). Tension grips demolition in Tondo residential area. Accessed last 11 August from:https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/metro/947366/tension-grips-demolition-in-tondo-residential-area/story/ 1 The Supreme Court has consistently held that failure to comply with these requirements may result in the immediate execution of the judgment. For underprivileged and homeless citizens, however, the very financial incapacity that places them at risk of homelessness may also prevent them from securing the temporary protection necessary to meaningfully pursue their appeal. This measure seeks to amend Section 28 of R.A. No. 7279 by clarifying the treatment of court-ordered eviction and demolition and by exempting qualified underprivileged and homeless citizens from the supersedeas bond requirement, subject to appropriate proof of indigency. It does not extinguish the property rights of lawful owners, nor does it prevent courts from ultimately enforcing valid judgments. Rather, it ensures that the ability to seek appellate relief and temporarily stay displacement will not depend solely on one's ability to pay. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure, which is a counterpart measure of Senate Bill no. 70, is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 11132
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE JUDICIAL HAZARD COMPENSATION FOR ALL MEMBERS OF THE JUDICIARY IN THE FIRST AND SECOND-LEVEL COURTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strength of our democratic institutions rests upon the bedrock of a judiciary that is not only competent but, more importantly, insulated from the chilling effects of external pressures, physical threats, and other occupational hazards. Under Section 1, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, judicial power is vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law. To ensure the effective exercise of this power, the 1987 Constitution provides several safeguards to maintain the independence of the members of the Bench. Section 3, Article VIII also guarantees the fiscal autonomy of the Judiciary, ensuring that appropriations may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year, and shall be automatically and regularly released. Furthermore, Section 10, Article VIII protects the stability of the Bench by mandating that the salary of the Chief Justice and the Associate Justices of the Supreme Court, and of judges of lower courts, shall be fixed by law and shall not be decreased during their incumbency in office. In light of these constitutional protections, the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA) adopted by the Supreme Court of the Philippines was implemented to ensure that judicial independence is upheld as a precondition to the rule of law. The CJCA demands that judges stay resolute and fearless of threats, as Canon I of the CJCA requires that a judge must pursue their actions independently, resisting and rejecting any form of undue influence, intimidation, or pressure from whatever source. Despite the Herculean efforts of the members of the Bench, the grim reality on the ground presents a bleak outlook for achieving these ideals. In recent decades, the Philippine legal community, and the judges in particular, have faced an unprecedented surge in violence, with at least 61 lawyers, judges, and prosecutors having been killed since 2016. From 2004 to 2021, public reports indicate that only seven (7) cases have resulted in charges filed in court. As of 2022, documented attacks on legal professionals reached 271. These targeted assaults have continued into 2025 and 2026. Such violence constitutes a direct assault on the judiciary and threatens to diminish the public’s trust in the administration of justice. Tragically, the physical and psychological threats are not confined to the courtroom. Judges frequently risk their lives in transit to remote court stations, navigating land, air, and sea to serve as Acting Presiding Judges in areas lacking permanent appointees. For these magistrates, the journey itself is as hazardous as the high-stakes cases they adjudicate. In fact, there were noted incidents of death by accidents while judges were in transit, an ominous fact staring the members of the Bench in the face. Moreover, it is worth emphasizing that the adoption of Republic Act No. 11576, or the Act expanding the jurisdiction of first-level courts, has significantly increased the workload of first-level court judges, who are now tasked with adjudicating the heavier, more complex civil cases once reserved for second-level courts. The shift in the jurisdictional threshold, however, has not created a distinction in safety. Current threat assessments reveal that judges in both first and second-level courts face the same level of professional risks and physical threats. Accordingly, while their legal duties are differentiated, the danger to their personal security remains a shared and equally urgent reality across both tiers. Complementing the preventive approach of Republic Act No. 11691, or the “Judiciary Marshals Act,” a monumental step toward securing the physical safety of the Bench, with a measure that aims both to recognize the devotion to duty of magistrates and to augment their financial resources for security, is vital to maintaining the judiciary as a public institution and a workplace. The persistent threat of retaliation, the necessity of living under constant surveillance, and the hazards inherent in the judicial robe remain occupational risks that even the Judiciary Marshals Act itself recognizes by granting hazard compensation to the Marshals themselves. If such compensation is mandated for those sworn to protect, it is only fair and just that it be equally mandated for the judges who are the primary targets of those very threats. This would effectively place judges on a similar footing with public health workers,1 public social workers,2 and scientists (and science and technology personnel),3 among others, whose indispensable presence on the ground define the fulfilment of the service-oriented purposes of their organizations. Finally, this bill provides a long-overdue legislative response to the Supreme Court’s call for protection. By instituting tax-exempt hazard compensation, the State recognizes that while the judge is responsible for upholding ethical and legal standards, the State is accountable for safeguarding the judge’s physical and economic security. 1 Republic Act No. 7305 2 Republic Act No. 9433 3 Republic Act No. 8439 In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11133
title: AN ACT AMENDING THE PROBATION LAW INCREASING THE AMOUNT OF FINE FROM ONE THOUSAND PESOS (P1,000.00) TO FORTY THOUSAND PESOS (P40,000.00) IN VIEW OF THE PASSAGE OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10951
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Probation Law was enacted to afford convicted persons the opportunity for rehabilitation outside the confines of penal institutions, taking into consideration the nature and gravity of the offense committed. It is founded on the recognition that qualified offenders may be better reformed to become productive members of society if given the chance for reintegration rather than immediate incarceration. While the law principally seeks to promote the welfare and protection of society through the reformation of offenders, it likewise extends humanitarian consideration to deserving individuals by giving them the opportunity to avoid the harmful effects and social stigma of imprisonment. To preserve the integrity of the probation system and harmonize probation with the recognized ends of criminal justice, limitations are set on those who may avail themselves of alternative judicial relief by identifying disqualified offenders and offenses. However, with the enactment of Republic Act No. 10951, entitled “An Act Adjusting the Amount or the Value of Property and Damage on Which a Penalty is Based, and the Fines Imposed Under the Revised Penal Code,” the fines imposed for several offenses were substantially increased. As a consequence, certain offenses that were previously probationable effectively became excluded from the coverage of the Probation Law, thereby narrowing its application and depriving some accused persons of a remedy previously available to them under existing law. It bears stressing that the law favors interpretations and enactments that are beneficial to the accused. Rights and benefits already granted by law, and to which an accused has become entitled, should not be withdrawn absent a clear and compelling justification. Our legal system provides safeguards to uphold this principle. Section 22, Article III of the 1987 Constitution prohibits the passage of ex post facto laws, including laws that deprive an accused person of lawful protections or benefits already available at the time of the commission of the offense. Accordingly, this bill seeks to address the unintended consequences brought about by the enactment of Republic Act No. 10951 by restoring and clarifying the availability of probation in appropriate cases. In doing so, it upholds the rehabilitative and restorative objectives of the Probation Law, remains faithful to the constitutional policy of according favorable treatment to the accused where warranted, and reinforces the State’s commitment to justice tempered with compassion and social reintegration. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND L. label: HB 11134
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE COVERAGE OF QUALIFIED BENEFICIARIES UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9946, TO INCLUDE OTHER QUALIFIED DEPENDENTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The passage of Republic Act No. 910, as amended by Republic Act No. 9946, otherwise known as “An Act Granting Additional Retirement, Survivorship, and Other Benefits to Members of the Judiciary,” has long been recognized as a significant measure acknowledging the invaluable contributions of judges and justices to the administration of justice. By granting retirement, survivorship, and related benefits, the law not only provides financial security to members of the Judiciary and their families, but also reinforces judicial independence by ensuring that judges and justices are accorded proper protection even after their service. These benefits likewise encourage competent and distinguished members of the Bar to join the Judiciary despite the financial sacrifices and opportunity costs associated with leaving private practice. However, the present provisions of the law on survivorship benefits require reconsideration and expansion in light of evolving family structures and the realities faced by members of the Judiciary today. At present, the law primarily limits survivorship benefits to the surviving legitimate spouse and heirs or those who are entitled to succeed in the estate of the deceased Judge or Justice under the law on succession. Such limitation fails to account for situations where a judge or justice, although unmarried at the time of death, leaves behind dependents who relied upon them for support and who would otherwise qualify as their lawful heirs. In modern society, the concept of “heirs” and “dependents” has become more nuanced and should not be confined to a restrictive interpretation. The law must recognize that members of the Judiciary may have other qualified dependents, who remain financially and emotionally dependent upon them regardless of marital status. Extending survivorship benefits to these dependents promotes fairness and ensures that judges and justices who are differently situated in life are not unjustly excluded from the full protection intended by the law. Such an expansion is neither novel nor unprecedented. Section 1 of Republic Act No. 11643, otherwise known as “An Act Granting Survivorship Benefits to the Surviving Legitimate Spouse and Dependent Children of a Deceased Retired Member of the National Prosecution Service,” adopts a broader and more inclusive definition of dependents. Under the said law, dependents include legitimate, illegitimate, or legally adopted children who are chiefly dependent upon the deceased member of the National Prosecution Service, provided they are unmarried, not gainfully employed, and not more than twenty-one (21) years of age, or regardless of age if incapable of self-support due to mental or physical incapacity. Under similar considerations, this Bill seeks to expand the coverage of heirs and dependents entitled to survivorship benefits under Republic Act No. 910, as amended, in order to reflect the present realities faced by members of the Judiciary and their families. By doing so, the proposed measure strengthens the State’s continuing recognition of the sacrifices and service rendered by judges and justices, while ensuring equal and compassionate treatment regardless of their civil status or family circumstances. In view of the foregoing, , the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND L. label: HB 11135
title: AN ACT DECLARING SEPTEMBER 3 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL NONWORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF IRIGA, PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR, IN COMMEMORATION OF ITS CHARTER DAY ANNIVERSARY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The City of Iriga traces its roots to the Spanish colonial period, when it was established as a pueblo and later developed into a municipality that became a center of commerce, culture, education, and governance in the Rinconada District of Camarines Sur. With the enactment of Republic Act No. 5261 on June 15, 1968, the Municipality of Iriga was converted into a component city, granting it greater autonomy and strengthening its capacity for local governance and development. On September 3, 1968, the formal inauguration of the City of Iriga was held, marking a defining milestone in the history and identity of the Irigueño people. Since then, September 3 has been observed as an important occasion to commemorate Iriga's cityhood, celebrate its heritage, and recognize its continuing progress. The annual Charter Day provides an opportunity to honor the contributions of past and present generations while fostering civic pride, community unity, cultural appreciation, tourism, and economic development. Several cities across the country have similarly been granted special non- working holidays through national legislation to commemorate their charter anniversaries and cityhood. Consistent with this practice, declaring September 3 as a Special Non-Working Holiday in the City of Iriga would allow its residents to meaningfully participate in civic, historical, cultural, educational, religious, and community activities celebrating its cityhood and development. Recognizing Iriga's cityhood likewise affirms its distinct identity and acknowledges the significant contributions of the Irigueño people to the social, cultural, and economic life of Camarines Sur and the Bicol Region. 1 In view of the foregoing, it is fitting and proper to declare September 3 of every year as a Special Non-Working Holiday in the City of Iriga. The measure will provide the people of Iriga with an opportunity to celebrate their shared history and heritage, strengthen community solidarity, and honor the city's continuing growth and development. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 11136
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN INTEGRATED SCHOOL IN CIUDAD KAUNLARAN, BARANGAY MOLINO 2, CITY OF BACOOR, PROVINCE OF CAVITE TO BE KNOWN AS THE CIUDAD KAUNLARAN INTEGRATED SCHOOL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish an integrated school in Ciudad Kaunlaran, Barangay Molino 2, City of Bacoor, Province of Cavite to be known as Ciudad Kaunlaran Integrated School. Ciudad Kaunlaran is an in-city vertical socialized housing project of the National Housing Authority (NHA) located in Molino 2, City of Bacoor, Cavite built on 52,718 square meters of land. It has a total of 1,860 units allocated for informal settler families (ISFs) residing along the coastal barangays of Bacoor Bay, subject of Manila Bay continuing mandamus of the Supreme Court. The CKIS will be responsible for educating the school-aged children from the 1,860 families in Ciudad Kaunlaran, which is in compliance to Section 21 of Republic Act No. 7279 or the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992 which required the provision of basic services. As an integrated school, CKIS will offer complete basic education from Kindergarten to Grade 12 with a unified instructional program as defined under DepEd Order No. 40, series of 2014 ad Republic Act No. 10533 or the K to 12 Law. label: HB 11137
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL REGULATORY FRAMEWORK FOR THE DEVELOPMENT, DEPLOYMENT, AND USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REGULATORY AUTHORITY AND THE NATIONAL AI MULTI-STAKEHOLDER ADVISORY COUNCIL, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved from the margins of Philippine economic and civic life to its center. Independent industry research cited in recent House deliberations found that more than nine in ten surveyed Philippine organizations have already adopted AI in some form, with more than half using generative AI tools for over a year. AI already assists in hiring and firing decisions, credit and loan approvals, medical triage, classroom instruction, government frontline services, and the content millions of Filipinos see on their screens every day. This proliferation of AI across the economy and daily life can no longer be treated as a future concern to be legislated once the technology matures. It is a present reality, and a national regulatory framework must be set in place now, before gaps in oversight translate into irreversible harm to workers, consumers, and vulnerable groups. Despite this reality, the Philippines has no single law that defines or regulates AI as such. Existing statutes like the Data Privacy Act of 2012, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, and the recently enacted E-Governance Act each cover only a slice of the problem, while the executive branch's National AI Strategy for the Philippines (NAIS-PH), approved in May 2025, and the Department of Science and Technology's National Artificial Intelligence Center for Research and Innovation (NAICRI), activated in February 2026, provide policy direction and research infrastructure but carry no binding regulatory force on their own. Congress has not been silent on this gap. Both chambers of the 19th and 20th Congresses have seen a steady stream of measures responding to different facets of AI governance. The Department of Information and Communications Technology has consistently urged that AI regulation be "principle-based and flexible" and calibrated to actual risk, cautioning that heavy-handed rules could stifle innovation and discourage the investment the country needs to remain competitive; industry and startup groups have echoed concerns that blanket registration or documentation requirements could be disproportionately burdensome for micro, small, and medium enterprises. At the same time, labor advocates pointing to the Department of Labor and Employment's own acknowledgment that Filipino workers are already losing jobs to automation have pressed for enforceable protections: advance notice before AI-driven displacement, access to retraining, and an assurance that no worker will be dismissed by an algorithm alone. Civil society and academic voices behind the AI Bill of Rights language found in earlier bills have emphasized transparency, protection from discriminatory profiling, a right to human review of consequential decisions, and safeguards for children and other vulnerable groups. Data privacy regulators and legal commentators, for their part, have stressed that any new AI framework must remain harmonized with, rather than duplicate or contradict, the Data Privacy Act of 2012. Community concerns have also emerged around the energy and water footprint of the AI data centers now concentrating around Metro Manila and Cebu. This bill seeks to reconcile these positions in a single, risk-based, and workable framework. It does not impose uniform, one-size-fits-all obligations on every AI system regardless of its actual risk profile. Instead it: (i) affirms a Bill of Rights in Artificial Intelligence covering notice, explanation, human review, data control, and protection from discrimination; (ii) creates the National Artificial Intelligence Regulatory Authority (NAIRA) under the Department of Information and Communications Technology, supported by a National AI Multi-Stakeholder Advisory Council representing government, labor, industry, academe, and civil society; (iii) classifies AI systems by risk prohibiting unacceptable uses outright, subjecting only high-risk systems to registration and pre-deployment review, requiring basic transparency for limited-risk systems, and leaving minimal-risk innovation largely unencumbered; (iv) guarantees that no Filipino worker may be dismissed, demoted, or have compensation reduced on the sole basis of an automated decision, and requires at least sixty (60) days' advance notice and access to retraining before AI-driven displacement; (v) establishes a regulatory sandbox to keep the door open for startups, researchers, and MSMEs; and (vi) provides proportionate administrative, civil, and criminal remedies for violations. Innovation and regulation are not opposing goals. A clear, predictable, and appropriately calibrated legal framework is the foundation on which sustained public trust and, with it, sustained AI adoption and investment will be built. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly requested. REP. ALEXANDER T. label: HB 11138
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PERPETUAL EXISTENCE OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION (PITC), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 2 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1071, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED CHARTER OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine International Trading Corporation (PITC) was created through Presidential Decree No. 252, and its charter was subsequently revised by Presidential Decree No. 1071, otherwise known as the “Revised Charter of the Philippine International Trading Corporation.” Under Section 2 of Presidential Decree No. 1071, the Corporation is authorized to exist for a period of fifty (50) years, with its present corporate term set to expire on 25 January 2027. For several decades, PITC has served as a government corporate vehicle in pursuing the State’s objectives in international trade. Consistent with its charter, the Corporation has undertaken trade-related activities and provided services intended to facilitate international trade, promote Philippine products and enterprises, and support the Government in its foreign procurement and marketing activities. As the expiration of PITC’s corporate term approaches, there is a need to ensure the continuity of its juridical personality, operations, and existing commitments. The expiration of its corporate term without an appropriate legislative measure may create uncertainty regarding the Corporation’s authority to continue performing its lawful functions, administering its assets and liabilities, honoring its contractual commitments, and undertaking transactions necessary for the fulfillment of its mandate. The proposed measure seeks to address this concern by providing for the continued corporate existence of PITC, while ensuring that such continued existence remains subject to appropriate government oversight and accountability. The measure provides for the perpetual term of existence of the Corporation, unless otherwise provided by law, while recognizing the authority of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or -Controlled Corporations (GCG) to evaluate the Corporation in accordance with Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. The proposed framework recognizes that the continued existence of a government- owned or -controlled corporation must be accompanied by mechanisms for periodic assessment of its relevance, efficiency, financial viability, performance, and consistency with national development policies and priorities. Accordingly, the GCG may conduct periodic performance evaluation and oversight of PITC, taking into account, among others, its financial performance, operational efficiency, governance and risk management systems, delivery of services, and contribution to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. The measure further recognizes that perpetual corporate existence does not exempt PITC from continuing government evaluation, oversight, and accountability. The Corporation shall remain subject to the evaluation, monitoring, and other appropriate actions authorized under Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Where warranted by such evaluation and consistent with applicable law, the appropriate government authorities may undertake or recommend such lawful measures as may be necessary to ensure that the Corporation remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. The grant of perpetual existence is not intended to constitute a determination that the Corporation shall operate indefinitely regardless of its continued relevance, performance, or economic viability. Rather, PITC shall remain subject to the performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight mechanisms applicable to government-owned or -controlled corporations under Republic Act No. 10149 and other applicable laws. At the same time, the proposed measure does not seek to expand the substantive powers and functions of PITC under Presidential Decree No. 1071. Rather, it seeks to ensure the continuity of the Corporation’s juridical personality and operations while strengthening accountability and providing for continuing evaluation by the appropriate government authorities. The proposed perpetual corporate term will also eliminate the need for periodic legislative action solely for the purpose of extending the Corporation’s corporate existence, while preserving the authority of Congress to amend, repeal, or otherwise modify the Corporation’s charter or corporate existence through subsequent legislation. This approach provides greater institutional stability and continuity while maintaining the necessary safeguards to ensure that PITC remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. Perpetual corporate existence does not preclude the State from undertaking performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight of the Corporation's relevance, performance, efficiency, and financial viability, nor does it prevent the appropriate government authorities from recommending or undertaking such lawful measures as may be warranted by the results of such evaluation. The continued corporate existence of PITC is therefore intended to prevent disruption in its legal existence and operations and to ensure the orderly continuity of its contracts, obligations, assets, liabilities, and other lawful commitments. It will likewise enable the Corporation to continue performing its existing mandate and contributing, within the scope of its charter, to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. ROY M. label: HB 11140
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL-BASED SPORTS DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS AND VARSITY TEAMS IN BASIC EDUCATION, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR STUDENT-ATHLETES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to promote physical education, sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, and requires educational institutions to undertake regular sports activities. Republic Act No. 5708, or the Schools Physical Education and Sports Development Act of 1969, likewise provides for an integrated physical education and sports development program in schools. Consistent with these mandates, the Department of Education has adopted policies supporting the organization of junior and senior varsity teams and the gradual expansion of school sports programs. Despite these existing frameworks, implementation remains uneven. Many schools, particularly those that are small, geographically isolated, or economically disadvantaged, continue to face limitations in qualified coaches, facilities, equipment, training opportunities, competition, and medical and safety support. Some schools also lack the resources to maintain independent varsity teams or participate regularly in organized competitions. This measure seeks to strengthen and institutionalize school-based sports development by establishing a clear and sustainable framework for varsity teams in elementary and secondary schools. Its implementation shall be phased and responsive to the resources, facilities, student population, and sports interests of each school or school cluster. The proposed Act shall provide standards for the identification and development of student-athletes, training and recognition of coaches, provision of equipment, organization of training and competitions, maintenance of athlete records, and coordination among schools, local government units, the Philippine Sports Commission, national sports associations, and other stakeholders. It shall also promote equitable access to sports, including traditional and indigenous games, while protecting the health, safety, academic welfare, and rights of student-athletes. School sports contribute not only to athlete development but also to the physical, social, and personal growth of learners by fostering fitness, discipline, teamwork, leadership, resilience, and mental well-being. A properly supported varsity system can provide a structured pathway for grassroots talent development while ensuring that sports opportunities are accessible, safe, and inclusive. The measure therefore seeks to complement and strengthen existing constitutional, legislative, and DepEd policies by providing statutory support for the sustainable and equitable implementation of school sports programs throughout the country. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11141
title: AN ACT INCORPORATING SCAM PREVENTION EDUCATION IN THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL CURRICULA, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Over the years, fraudsters and scammers have become more dangerous and have proliferated even in the digital space, especially during the pandemic. Various scams and economic fraud have threatened not only wealthy businesses but also individual citizens. Those who do not have access to education or enough information on their existing modus operandi are vulnerable to these crimes. The continued expansion of digital services in the Philippines has been accompanied by persistent cyber-enabled fraud, phishing, identity theft, and other online scams. Enforcement activities and advisories from the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, the Department of Information and Communications Technology, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and telecommunications providers demonstrate the continuing need for stronger prevention, reporting, investigation, and victim-support mechanisms. Globe Telecom, for example, reported blocking 71 million spam and phishing messages and deactivating 5,670 confirmed spam and phishing numbers in 2021, illustrating the scale of fraudulent communications directed at mobile users. Children and adolescents are likewise increasingly exposed to online risks through smartphones, social-media platforms, online games, messaging applications, digital-payment services, and e-learning platforms. Their limited experience in recognizing phishing, impersonation, fraudulent offers, and improper requests for personal information may make them particularly vulnerable to scams and identity theft. There is therefore a need to strengthen digital-safety education and preventive measures for school- aged children, while promoting cooperation among schools, families, government agencies, telecommunications providers, financial institutions, and online platforms to protect minors and assist victims of cyber-enabled offenses. While scams typically target adults, the recent increased exposure and access of school-aged children to the internet have also made them prey to fraudulent schemes. The growing threat of fraud in society not only stresses the need to protect young people from scams. It also points to the alarming fact that students are exposed to the dangers these fraudsters create. It is therefore vital for schools to promote anti-scam awareness throughout society as well as equip students with the knowledge so that they can report cases once they encounter an incident of potential fraud or scam. This bill seeks the protection of students against fraud through the integration of scam prevention education in the school curriculum of senior high schools. It is the hope of this measure to empower the next generation of Filipinos with the critical thinking skills to be able to protect themselves and their families from exploitative scammers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11142
title: AN ACT CREATING THE HEALTH EMERGENCY AUXILIARY REINFORCEMENT TEAM UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure seeks to establish the Health Emergency Auxiliary Reinforcement Team (HEART) under the Department of Health as a pool of trained and qualified health professionals, allied health workers, students, retirees, and other volunteers who may be mobilized to assist government health facilities during disasters, disease outbreaks, pandemics, and other public health emergencies. The proposed HEART complements, rather than replaces, the regular health workforce by providing surge capacity whenever existing personnel become insufficient. The proposal is firmly anchored on the Constitution, which mandates the State to protect and promote the people's right to health and adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development.1 It likewise supports the objectives of Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, which recognizes the importance of strengthening the health workforce as an essential building block of an effective healthcare system.2 Furthermore, the bill aligns with Republic Act No. 11332 by enhancing the government's capacity to respond 1 1987 Philippine Constitution, Article II, Section 15, and Article XIII, Section 11. 2 Republic Act No. 11223 (Universal Health Care Act), particularly provisions on strengthening the National Health Workforce Support System and the National Health Workforce Registry. to notifiable diseases and public health events of national and international concern.3 Beyond domestic law, the measure advances the Philippines' commitment under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), which calls on States to strengthen health systems and improve preparedness for health risks and emergencies.4 By institutionalizing a trained reserve force and establishing clear mechanisms for recruitment, training, mobilization, protection, and coordination, the bill ensures that the country is better prepared to respond swiftly and effectively to future health crises while fostering the Filipino spirit of Bayanihan through organized public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11144
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE REVITALIZATION AND ADVANCEMENT OF ORIGINAL FILIPINO MUSIC AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino musicians and artists are world-class. Our country has produced countless artists to sing and perform abroad. Our kababayans have dominated the stage overseas, and we have seen the likes of Lea Salonga, Arnel Pineda, Apl.De.Ap., and Freddie Aguilar, whose song “Anak” became an international hit and was translated into 26 languages. It is undeniable that the Philippines is teeming with top-notch talent. However, many radio and television stations allot more of their airtime to foreign music rather than their local counterparts. Presently, Executive Order No. 225, which was issued on 25 July 1987, mandates all radio stations to “broadcast a minimum of four (4) original Filipino musical compositions in every clock hour of a program with a musical format.” However, the said law lacks strength as it merely imposes a fine in the amount of Php100.00 per violation. This bill seeks to mandate all radio stations and TV stations devoted to broadcasting music within the country to allot a sizeable amount of airtime for Original Pilipino Music or OPM. Through this, we are providing our OPM artists a wider platform, giving them the opportunity to showcase and offer their gifts to their countrymen and eventually, the world. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11145
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE SALARY SCALES OR LEVELS OF PUBLIC DENTISTS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Dental health experts often say that the mouth is the gateway to our overall health. Taking care of our dental health can protect our bodies from a variety of health problems. However, the public’s awareness of the importance of dental health care and services remains low, in part due to the scarcity of dentists working in the public sector. The country’s dentists-to-patients ratio is currently at 1:53,000, and only very few licensed dentists intend to work in the government due to its meager salary and benefits compared to private dental practitioners. To encourage more dentists to render public service in government and mainstream the importance of dental health care and services, this bill seeks to upgrade the salary grades of all public dentists in recognition of their essential role in maintaining and promoting the oral health of the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11146
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE INCENTIVIZED SOLID WASTE REDEMPTION AND RECOVERY SYSTEMS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, provides for an ecological solid waste management program and a framework that creates necessary institutional mechanisms and incentives, declaring certain acts prohibited and providing penalties therefor. Under the law, local government units (LGUs) are also mandated to be primarily responsible for the implementation and enforcement of the provisions of the Solid Waste Management Act within their respective jurisdictions. However, rewards and incentives have limitations and must be innovated to adapt to the needs of the “new normal”. The social and economic climate brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic has presented challenges to food security and environmental protection. The multitude of consumption in the pandemic has increased solid waste production, thus bringing up the need to properly organize solid waste management and segregation at the level of the household. In its efforts to aid its citizens economically amid the pandemic while also promoting efforts to save the environment, the Quezon City government has launched a point system program on waste management entitled the “Trash to Cashback” Program. Under the “Trash to Cashback” Program, residents can trade their recyclable materials for environmental points which can be exchanged for basic commodities such as rice, eggs, vegetables, and other essential grocery items. This bill seeks to institutionalize innovative efforts to incentivize solid waste management and recycling through the exchange or rewarding of basic commodities such as rice, eggs, vegetables, canned goods, basic household consumer items, other essential grocery items, or even cash. This legislation further provides that the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the Department of Agriculture (DA), and the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) shall determine the reasonable and compliance-inducing exchange values for graduated weights or volumes of solid waste provided. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COHERENT FRAMEWORK BY ALIGNING THE QUALITY ASSURANCE SYSTEMS OF THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION, THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, AND THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT WITH LABOR MARKET NEEDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as a fundamental instrument of national development and directs the State to establish and maintain an educational system that is responsive to the needs of the people and society. In an increasingly technology-driven and rapidly changing economy, this responsibility extends beyond expanding access to education. It also requires ensuring that the knowledge, skills, and competencies acquired by Filipinos remain relevant to the changing demands of work and enable them to obtain productive, decent, and sustainable livelihoods. The Philippines has made significant gains in educational access and attainment. Nevertheless, persistent unemployment, underemployment, skills shortages, and education-to-employment mismatches continue to challenge the country's human capital development. These conditions suggest that the issue is not simply whether Filipinos have access to education, but whether education and training are sufficiently connected to labor-market opportunities and the evolving requirements of the economy. Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) underscore the continuing challenge. In January 2026, the unemployment rate stood at 5.8 percent, equivalent to approximately 2.96 million unemployed Filipinos. In May 2026, approximately 2.50 million Filipinos remained unemployed, while the underemployment rate stood at 12.2 percent. These figures demonstrate that the challenge extends beyond creating jobs; it also involves improving the quality of employment and ensuring that workers are able to find jobs that appropriately utilize their skills and provide opportunities for advancement.1. 2 The concern is particularly significant as the Philippine economy undergoes technological and structural transformation. The World Bank's Philippines Country Growth and Jobs Report 2025 identified skills scarcity as one of the constraints affecting technology adoption and productivity among Philippine firms. It emphasized the need to address skills mismatches and strengthen human capital to support the creation of better and more productive jobs.3 Earlier World Bank research likewise found that Philippine employers experienced difficulty finding workers with the technical and socioemotional competencies required in the workplace, including communication, interpersonal skills, work ethic, adaptability, and other capabilities necessary for effective https://psa.gov.ph/content/number-unemployed-persons-january-2026-increased-296-million-filipinos-aged-15- years-and 2 https://psa.gov.ph/content/underemployment-rate-declined-122-percent-may-2026 3 https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/philippines/publication/philippines-growth-and-jobs-report-2025 participation in changing work environments.4 These findings demonstrate that employability cannot be measured solely by the possession of a degree, diploma, or technical certificate. Workers increasingly require a combination of technical, cognitive, interpersonal, and adaptive competencies that can be continuously developed throughout their careers. The education-employment mismatch has also been recognized by Philippine stakeholders. The Philippine Business for Education has consistently called attention to the gap between the competencies developed through education and the requirements of employers and has supported initiatives involving stronger industry participation and skills-based approaches to workforce development. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies has likewise identified skills mismatch as an issue affecting Philippine economic growth and the efficient utilization of human capital.5 The challenge, therefore, is not necessarily the absence of programs or institutions. Rather, it is the need for stronger coherence among the country's education, technical-vocational training, labor-market information, and employment systems. A stronger education-to-employment framework can help ensure that labor-market information is meaningfully considered in curriculum development, program review, quality assurance, skills training, career guidance, and workforce planning. Reliable information concerning occupational demand, skills shortages, vacancies, wages, emerging occupations, and regional labor-market conditions can enable educational and training institutions to make better-informed decisions while allowing government to identify areas requiring intervention. However, should not reduce education to a short-term response to employer vacancies. Educational institutions serve broader purposes, including intellectual development, professional formation, research, citizenship, creativity, and lifelong learning. Accordingly, labor-market information should be treated as an important source of evidence for continuous improvement, not as the sole or mechanical determinant of academic decisions. Academic freedom, institutional autonomy, diverse educational missions, and learner choice must remain protected. The transition from education to employment likewise requires greater attention. Possession of a qualification does not automatically guarantee successful entry into the workforce. Students and graduates may encounter barriers involving insufficient workplace experience, limited access to career information and professional networks, geographic constraints, or differences between classroom instruction and actual workplace requirements. Strengthening work-integrated learning, apprenticeships, internships, enterprise-based training, career guidance, job placement, and recognition of prior learning can help address these barriers. The proposed Comprehensive Education-to-Employment Alignment Act seeks to respond to these challenges by strengthening coherence among the existing education, training, and labor- market systems. label: HB 11181
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE INTERNATIONALIZATION CAPACITY OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, ESTABLISHING A HIGHER EDUCATION, CREATING AN INTERNATIONALIZATION SUPPORT FUND, PROVIDING FOR INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION ON EDUCATION EXPORT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has strong potential to become a competitive destination for international higher education. Its widespread use of English, cultural diversity, and relatively affordable tuition make its higher education sector attractive to foreign students and academic partners. Yet, despite these advantages, the country remains a modest participant in global academic mobility. Foreign student enrollment increased from 14,132 in 2017 to 22,247 in 2022, but still trails behind neighboring countries such as Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This gap reflects persistent institutional barriers, including complex regulatory processes, limited opportunities for foreign faculty, inadequate funding, weak international partnerships, and insufficient campus facilities. While existing laws, including Republic Act No. 7722 and Republic Act No. 11448, provide a foundation for higher education development and transnational education, they do not establish a comprehensive and sustained national strategy for internationalization. This measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a National Internationalization Framework for Higher Education, supported by institutional internationalization plans and an Internationalization Support Fund. The framework will support student and faculty mobility, international research partnerships, joint academic programs, and Internationalization at Home, allowing students to gain global competencies even without studying abroad.The measure also strengthens coordination among CHED, the Department of Trade and Industry, and the Department of Foreign Affairs to promote Philippine higher education internationally. Internationalization should not be pursued solely as a means of competing with other countries. It should strengthen the quality of Philippine higher education, expand opportunities for Filipino learners, and connect institutions across the country to the global academic community. Through a coordinated and inclusive national policy, the Philippines can move from having the potential to internationalize to actually becoming an active participant in global higher education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11183
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE HIGHER PARTNERSHIP FRAMEWORK, CREATING THE HIGHER EDUCATION-INDUSTRY COORDINATION COUNCIL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFORE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face a persistent mismatch between higher education outcomes and the needs of the labor market. Many college graduates remain underemployed or work in positions that do not require a college degree, while employers continue to report difficulty finding workers with the skills needed in key sectors. This reflects a deeper disconnect between what higher education produces and what the economy demands. One major cause is the fragmentation of labor market information. Relevant data are collected separately by government agencies, making it difficult for higher education institutions (HEIs), policymakers, training providers, and employers to work from a common and updated understanding of emerging skills needs. At the same time, partnerships between HEIs and industry remain largely informal and inconsistent, limiting opportunities to align curricula, internships, research, and training with actual workforce demand. This measure therefore a Higher Education-Industry Partnership Framework to establish sustained cooperation between HEIs and industry stakeholders. The bill creates a Higher Education-Industry Coordination Council to consolidate labor market and skills information and produce a National Skills Gap Inventory and an Annual National Skills and Labor Market Intelligence Report. It also establishes Regional Industry-Higher Education Advisory Boards to ensure that regional industries, local employment conditions, and the needs of state universities and colleges are reflected in higher education planning. By connecting education planning with reliable labor market intelligence and meaningful industry participation, this measure seeks to ensure that Filipino graduates are equipped not only with degrees, but with competencies relevant to the changing needs of the economy. It provides a more coordinated and responsive approach to reducing skills gaps, improving graduate employability, and strengthening the contribution of higher education to national and regional development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11184
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RECOGNITION, QUALITY ASSURANCE, STACKABILITY, AND PORTABILITY OF MICROCREDENTIALS AND SHORT COURSES, STRENGTHENING WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT, PROVIDING FLEXIBLE LEARNING PATHWAYS AND PROTECTIONS FOR LEARNERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face a growing mismatch between the skills possessed by its workforce and those required by a rapidly changing economy. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), in its Year Two Report, found that skills mismatches persist across all levels of education. Around one-third of employed Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) graduates are working in positions that do not fully utilize their qualifications, while senior high school graduates record the highest unemployment rate among educational cohorts. Moreover, from 2021 to 2022, approximately 35% of the labor force was engaged in the informal sector, many of whom have limited access to portable and recognized credentials that can be readily accepted by employers, educational institutions, and government programs. Despite these challenges, the country still lacks a unified legal framework governing microcredentials and short courses. The Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF), established under Executive Order No. 83 in 2012 and institutionalized through Republic Act No. 10968 in 2018, was intended to provide a national system for recognizing and building upon qualifications acquired through various learning pathways. However, EDCOM II reported that little substantial progress has been made in implementing the PQF since its establishment. The National Coordinating Council became nonfunctional in 2017 due to staffing and funding limitations, while the framework continued to lack a permanent secretariat, coordinated financing, and a comprehensive strategic plan at the time of the Year Two Report. As a result, skills and competencies gained through short courses, workplace-based training, and other forms of non-formal learning remain difficult to recognize, accumulate toward higher qualifications, or transfer across employers and educational institutions. EDCOM II likewise identified the lack of a clear national framework for the equivalency and recognition of non-formal and informal learning as a major barrier to lifelong learning and workforce development. Workers who acquire new skills through industry training, online learning platforms, or community-based learning programs often have no reliable mechanism through which these competencies can be converted into academic credit or formal certification. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by formally integrating microcredentials and short courses into the Philippine education and training system and aligning them with the PQF. It establishes minimum quality standards and requires the accreditation of qualified providers by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Department of Education (DepEd). It also provides for the creation of a Digital Credential Registry to facilitate the verification, portability, and interoperability of credentials. The proposed measure further safeguards learner rights, provides protections for employed individuals pursuing additional education or training, and institutionalizes access to Recognition of Prior Learning. An Inter-Agency Coordination Committee composed of CHED, TESDA, DepEd, and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) will be established to harmonize national standards. Its work will be complemented by an Industry Advisory Council and mechanisms for scholarships, training vouchers, and employer tax incentives. Through these reforms, the measure seeks to establish a unified and coherent national system for flexible learning that recognizes diverse forms of education and training and enables Filipinos to acquire, build upon, and carry their skills throughout their education and careers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A.
