label: HB 11217
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine education system stands at a critical juncture. Despite significant investments and continuing efforts by the government, persistent challenges in learning outcomes, teacher development, workforce preparation, access, and the transition of learners across different levels of education continue to affect the country’s capacity to develop a highly capable and productive citizenry. These challenges are complex and interconnected, requiring not only reforms within individual agencies but also stronger and more sustained coordination across the entire education and workforce development system. At present, education and workforce development concerns are addressed by several government institutions, each with distinct mandates, programs, priorities, and resources. While such specialization is necessary, the absence of a permanent, high-level mechanism that can consistently bring these efforts together may result in fragmented policies, overlapping initiatives, gaps in implementation, and difficulties in sustaining reforms. Changes in administration may likewise affect the continuity of priorities and programs, making it more difficult to pursue long- term reforms whose benefits may only become evident over many years. The passage of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) Act is therefore necessary to establish a durable institutional mechanism for coordination, policy coherence, and accountability in the education and workforce development sector. The proposed measure recognizes that improving education outcomes cannot be achieved through isolated interventions. It requires a whole-of-government approach in which agencies work toward common goals, share information, align resources, and collectively address problems that extend across basic education, higher education, technical and vocational education, employment, science and technology, and national development planning. The proposed Council is intended to strengthen the continuity and coherence of education reforms by providing a permanent platform for collaboration at the highest levels of government. This is particularly important in addressing the learning crisis and ensuring that reforms are not dependent solely on the priorities or organizational arrangements of a particular administration. Institutionalizing coordination can help ensure that important reforms are sustained, evaluated, improved, and carried forward over time. The measure is likewise important because education outcomes are closely connected with the country’s economic and workforce needs. Students must be equipped not only with foundational knowledge but also with skills relevant to a changing labor market. Stronger coordination between education institutions and agencies responsible for employment, economic planning, science and technology, and public resources can help bridge the gap between what the education system provides and what society and the economy require. Equally important is the need for greater accountability in the implementation of education reforms. A coordinated national mechanism can provide clearer lines of responsibility, strengthen monitoring of outcomes, and promote evidence-based decision-making. It can also facilitate the use of reliable and integrated information in determining priorities and allocating public resources, thereby helping ensure that government investments in education produce meaningful and measurable results. The proposed legislation also complements ongoing efforts to improve the Philippine education system, including reform initiatives arising from the work of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). Rather than allowing recommendations and reforms to remain isolated within individual institutions, there is a need for an institutional structure capable of translating national priorities into coordinated and sustained government action. Ultimately, education is a long-term national investment. The quality of today’s education system will shape the country’s workforce, productivity, competitiveness, social mobility, and capacity for inclusive development in the years ahead. Addressing the country’s education challenges therefore requires more than additional programs; it requires stronger institutional coordination and a sustained commitment to common national objectives. The passage of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) Act will provide the government with a permanent framework through which education and workforce development reforms can be coordinated, sustained, and held accountable. By strengthening the unity of purpose among government institutions, the measure seeks to ensure that education remains a consistent and enduring national priority, regardless of changes in administration. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11218
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING PERMANENT SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICER POSITIONS IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE, PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND SECURITY PROGRAM FOR SCHOOLS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE No learner’s right to education should be curtailed by a lack of security, yet Philippine public schools continue to send children into classrooms that the Department of Education (DepEd) itself admits it cannot adequately protect. This bill seeks to establish a Comprehensive School Safety and Security Program covering all public and private basic education institutions. It creates permanent civil service plantilla positions for School Security Officers (SSOs) in every public school, mandates a dedicated Emergency Hotline System with prioritized routing to the Philippine National Police (PNP) and local medical services, directs DepEd to fund metal detectors, CCTV systems, and fortified perimeter fencing, and institutes mandatory safety training for teachers and learners. Over the past year, campus violence in the Philippines has escalated from isolated incidents into a recurring national concern. A gun attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City in June 2026 left three (3) students dead and twenty (20) others wounded, barely two (2) months before a second fatal shooting struck the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School campus.1 Investigations on these tragedies have likewise flagged a string of earlier firearm-related incidents, including a student who accidentally shot himself after bringing a gun to school and another who fired a .45-caliber pistol inside a Batangas classroom, alongside stabbing incidents recorded within the same weeks.2 These episodes show that Philippine schools now face threats that existing child protection issuances were never designed to repel. Underlying these tragedies is a chronic shortage of trained security personnel. DepEd currently fields only around two thousand two hundred (2,200) permanent 1 Chi, C. (2026, August 21). DepEd sets nationwide school safety drill for campus threats on August 25. Philstar. Accessed via https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/08/21/2550825/deped-sets-nationwide-school-safety -drill-campus-threats-august-25. Accessed on 27 August 2026. 2 Sinaking, E. P., & Bacon, P. (2026, June 29). DepEd to roll out school safety measures after deadly Tacloban shooting. Business World. Accessed via https://bworldonline.com/the-nation/2026/06/29/760007/deped-to-roll-out- school-safety-measures-after-deadly-tacloban-shooting. Accessed on 27 August 2026. security guard positions across more than forty-eight thousand (48,000) public schools nationwide—roughly one (1) guard for every twenty (20) campuses—after a prior rationalization program stripped away most security plantilla items.3 DepEd has admitted that several campuses, particularly those enrolling more than a thousand learners, need more than a single guard, and that the department must request fresh funding from the Department of Budget and Management year after year rather than rely on a standing legal mandate. Without permanent, civil-service-protected SSO positions fixed in law, school security remains contingent on administrative discretion and annual budget negotiations instead of a guaranteed minimum standard. Beyond firearms, the PNP Women and Children Protection Center recorded one thousand, two hundred seventy-five (1,275) school-related incidents involving children in conflict with the law from 2022 to 2025, highlighting that violence, bullying, and other safety concerns extend beyond isolated shootings. While DepEd has responded through a nationwide School Safety Campaign, bag inspections, and proposed 2027 funding for guards, counselors, CCTV systems, fences, and metal detectors, these measures remain subject to administrative changes and budget priorities. This bill institutionalizes such safeguards by establishing permanent staffing, equipment, emergency hotline, and compliance requirements, ensuring that learner safety remains protected regardless of changes in administration or funding priorities. Parents send their children to school trusting that classrooms will nurture them, not endanger them. Every week without a permanent, funded, and legally mandated school safety framework is a week in which the State falls short of its constitutional promise of safe and accessible quality education. This Representation therefore pushes to accord this measure its immediate approval, so that no Filipino family has to bury a child because protection arrived too late. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JEFFREY SORIANO 3 Chi, C. (2026, June 30). DepEd has only 2,200 security guards for 48,000 public schools. label: HB 11219
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REHABILITATION AND SUPERVISION OF CHILDREN EXEMPT FROM CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY WHO COMMIT SERIOUS CRIMES, ESTABLISHING REGIONAL REHABILITATION CENTERS FOR YOUTH, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006”, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A child exempt from criminal responsibility who commits a serious crime deserves secure, government-run rehabilitation rather than confinement in an overcrowded facility that local governments were never funded to build. This bill amends Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630, otherwise known as the “Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006,” to strengthen the rehabilitation and supervision of children exempt from criminal responsibility who commit serious crimes. It establishes a Regional Rehabilitation Center for Youth (RRCY) in every region of the country, to be established, funded, administered, and operated directly by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD). After nearly a decade of decline, cases involving children in conflict with the law have begun climbing again: reported cases reached 5,698 by June 2025 alone, already surpassing the total recorded for the whole of 2024.1 The June 2026 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City exposed how unprepared the existing system is to respond. Tacloban, a highly urbanized city required by law to operate a Bahay Pag-asa, has none, thereby forcing authorities to place the accused minors in a regional youth facility in Tanauan, Leyte, while the nearest Bahay Pag-asa, in Biliran, was already operating beyond capacity.2 Nationwide, only 30 of 83 provinces and 28 of 33 highly urbanized cities have established a Bahay Pag-asa despite the mandate under Republic Act No. 10630, and only 28 of the existing facilities have secured DSWD accreditation more than a decade after that law took effect.2 Even where facilities exist, oversight has repeatedly fallen short. The Commission on Human Rights has documented congestion, understaffing, and subhumane conditions in several Bahay Pag-asa facilities nationwide, along with 1 Baclig, C. E. (2026, April 16). After decade of gains, juvenile offenses show signs of reversing. Inquirer. Retrieved from https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2213322/after-decade-of-gains-juvenile-offenses-show- signs-of-reversing. Accessed on 1 September 2026. 2 Ronquillo, A. & Mateo, J. (2026, July 6). Lack of facilities shows gaps in juvenile justice system. The Philippine Star. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/06/2540119/lack- facilities-shows-gaps-juvenile-justice-system. Accessed on 1 September 2026. allegations of abuse and mistreatment of the children placed in their care.4 Because these facilities remain locally built, funded, and managed, their quality varies sharply from one local government unit to the next, and children who commit the most serious offenses are sometimes held in the same under-resourced spaces as those facing minor infractions, without the specialized, secure treatment their cases demand.3 The national government has recognized the shortfall. The DSWD reports only about 118 operational Bahay Pag-asa facilities nationwide and has begun piloting five regional facilities with a ₱275-million allocation under the 2026 General Appropriations Act.4 This national pilot effort, however necessary, remains discretionary and incremental, built one region at a time on whatever budget survives yearly deliberation, rather than a guaranteed, nationwide network fixed in law. This bill transfers the establishment, funding, staffing, and operation of rehabilitation centers for the most serious child offenders from underfunded LGUs to the DSWD directly, mandates at least one Regional Rehabilitation Center for Youth in every region, and requires a dedicated, secure Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center within each one, so that a child’s access to proper rehabilitation no longer depends on which province or city happens to have built a facility. A justice system that exempts a child from criminal liability but offers no adequate place to rehabilitate him fails that child, fails his victims, and fails the communities awaiting his safe return. Every year this gap persists is another year in which accused children are warehoused in congested, understaffed facilities never designed for their needs, and in which victims and their families are left without the structured accountability the law promises. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JEFFREY SORIANO 3 Commission on Human Rights (2026, April 7). CHR calls for urgent action to improve conditions in Bahay Pag-asa Facilities. Commission on Human Rights. Retrieved from https://chr.gov.ph/chr-calls- for-urgent-action-to-improve-conditions-in-bahay-pag-asa-facilities. Accessed on 1 September 2026. 4 Department of Social Welfare and Development (2026, January 12). DSWD to pilot 5 Bahay Pag-Asa for rehab or children in conflict with the law. Department of Social Welfare and Development. Retrieved from https://www.dswd.gov.ph/dswd-to-pilot-5-bahay-pag-asa-for-rehab-of-children-in-conflict -with-the-law. Accessed on 1 September 2026. label: HB 11220
title: AN ACT DECLARING QUEZON CITY AS THE “FILM AND TELEVISION ARTS CAPITAL OF THE PHILIPPINES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Quezon City has already earned international recognition as the heart of Philippine cinema and television, and it is time national law caught up with what the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the industry, and generations of Filipino filmmakers have long known to be true. This bill declares Quezon City as the “Film and Television Arts Capital of the Philippines” in recognition of its status as home to the country’s largest film and television production companies and institutions. It directs the Department of Tourism (DOT), in consultation with the Quezon City government, to incorporate this official designation into its national tourism programs, and further directs the DOT to develop, together with the Quezon City government and local film and television institutions, tourism events and destinations that showcase the country’s film and television history and heritage. Quezon City is already the undisputed center of Philippine broadcast and film production. It hosts an estimated sixty to sixty-five percent (60-65%) of the country’s television transmission facilities and forty percent (40%) of its post-production capacity, anchored by the headquarters of GMA Network in Diliman, the ABS-CBN Complex nearby, and the Araneta City studios in Cubao that host forty-five percent (45%) of Metro Manila’s major concert and live event productions.1 This industry weight has already drawn international recognition: in October 2025, Quezon City became one of the first cities in Southeast Asia to be designated a UNESCO Creative City of Film, a title tracing back through the golden era of Sampaguita Pictures and the legacies of Lino Brocka, Dolphy, Nora Aunor, and Fernando Poe Jr.2 1 Quezon City Government. The Quezon City government has already moved to institutionalize this identity at the local level. In May 2025, the city established the Quezon City Screen Commission through a City Council ordinance, tasked with harmonizing film-related policies, streamlining permits through a dedicated Film Permits Office, and coordinating training and industry programs down to the barangay level.3 Building on its UNESCO designation, the Commission is now developing the QC Screen Academy, the Global Producers Exchange, and the Southeast Asia Film Summit to further cement the city’s role as a regional hub for film production and worker welfare. What remains missing is the corresponding recognition and support at the national level: without a law declaring Quezon City’s status and directing national tourism agencies to build around it, these local gains remain vulnerable to being under-promoted nationally and unsupported by the country’s tourism infrastructure. The scale of what is at stake is considerable. Quezon City’s media and creative production sector is estimated at forty-two and a half (42.5) billion and growing at six point two percent (6.2%) annually, generating thousands of jobs in production, post-production, and animation, with the city’s universities producing roughly fifteen thousand (15,000) communication and film graduates every year.4 A formal national declaration, implemented with a DOT-led tourism program built around the city’s film and television heritage, would not only affirm an identity Quezon City has already earned locally and internationally, but would also open new avenues for tourism revenue, structured industry promotion, and pride of place for the workers, artists, and institutions that have sustained the country’s film and television industry for generations. label: HB 11221
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING COMPREHENSIVE POLICIES TO PREVENT AND ADDRESS ACTS OF BULLYING, HARASSMENT, AND OTHER FORMS OF VIOLENCE IN THE WORKPLACE, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE No worker should have to endure daily humiliation, intimidation, or exclusion simply to keep a paycheck. This bill institutes comprehensive policies to prevent and address workplace bullying, harassment, and other forms of violence. It covers physical, verbal, psychological, social, cyber, and gender-based bullying, as well as abuse of authority and management by threat or intimidation. It requires all government and private offices to adopt written anti-bullying policies and report compliance to the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) or the Civil Service Commission (CSC), as applicable. A nationwide poll by the Lloyd’s Register Foundation and Gallup found that twenty-two percent (22%) of Filipino women and eighteen percent (18%) of men have experienced violence or harassment at work, with psychological harassment the most commonly reported form and sixty percent (60%) of victims saying it happened three (3) or more times.1 Yet, a majority of victims never report the abuse: forty-seven percent (47%) of women and sixty percent (60%) of men who experienced it stayed silent, largely out of fear of repercussions, or the belief that nothing would come of speaking up.1 This silence poses no surprise given how thin the country’s legal protections remain outside of the school setting. The Philippines currently has no standalone law against workplace bullying. Republic Act (RA) No. 10627, otherwise known as the “Anti-Bullying Act”, applies only to schools, leaving working adults to rely on a patchwork of statutes never designed to address bullying directly, including RA No. 11058, otherwise known as the “Occupational Safety and Health Standards Act”, RA No. 11313, otherwise known as the “Safe Spaces Act”, RA No. 7877, otherwise known as the “Anti-Sexual Harassment Act”, and general Labor Code due process rules, none of which squarely 1 Philstar. (2023, January 31). Around a Fifth of Filipino Employees Have Experienced Workplace Harassment — Poll. Philstar.com. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2023/01/31 /2241812/around-fifth-filipino-employees-have-experienced-workplace-harassment-poll. Accessed on 7 September 2026. define or penalize workplace bullying as such. This problem persists even after the Philippines ratified International Labour Organization Convention No. 190 in February 2024, becoming the first country in Asia to commit to eliminating violence and harassment in the world of work.2 In the absence of a unified statute, employers are left to assemble their own policies from overlapping and sometimes inconsistent frameworks, with no clear, government-wide standard for investigation timelines, reporting channels, or penalties.3 This bill creates a single and enforceable statute, defining workplace bullying in all its forms and applying uniformly across government and private establishments. It fixes concrete investigation timelines, in place of the vague standards that currently leave complainants uncertain of when their case will be resolved, and extends coverage to remote work and third parties such as clients and vendors, consistent with how modern workplaces actually operate. It also introduces a graduated schedule of administrative fines, rather than leaving penalties entirely to future rules, and expressly harmonizes this Act with the Safe Spaces Act, the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Act, and the Mental Health Act, so that victims of gender-based or sexual misconduct continue to receive the specific protections those laws provide, without being caught between overlapping and potentially conflicting processes. A worker who is bullied into silence loses more than comfort at work. They lose their health, productivity, and often their zest for life. This Representation therefore urges the immediate approval of this measure, so that Filipino workers finally have a clear, enforceable law that treats their dignity at work as a right, not a privilege left to the goodwill of their employer. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JEFFREY SORIANO 2 International Labour Organization. (2024, February 22). label: HB 11222
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF BARANGAY DRUGSTORES, TO BE CALLED AS “BOTIKA NG BARANGAY”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A barangay drugstore that runs out of medicine or funding is failing to serve its community. This bill institutionalizes the Department of Health’s (DOH) Botika ng Barangay (BNB) program, directing the establishment of barangay drugstores in every barangay within a three-year period, with priority given to economically depressed and underserved communities. More than two decades after it was first established under DOH Administrative Order No. 70, the BNB program remains hampered by the very problems the bill seeks to resolve. A government review found that while the number of BNBs expanded rapidly, not all of them received sufficient financial and management support to remain sustainable. This prompted the DOH to institute a moratorium on further BNB expansion until problems in restocking and financing could be addressed.1 Field research in Cebu Province similarly found that the top complaints among BNB clients were the availability of stocks, inconsistent operating hours, and limited variety of medicines sold, even as households that did have reliable access to a BNB saved significantly on health-related expenses compared to commercial drugstore prices.2 Part of the problem is that the program’s funding and supply mechanisms have relied on a patchwork of administrative issuances rather than a permanent statutory framework. DOH Administrative Order No. 70 provided the original licensing framework in 2002, DOH Administrative Order No. 64 in 2003 tapped Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office funds and Philippine International Trading Corporation procurement support to sustain BNB operations, and DOH 1 Picazo, O. F. (2012, September 12). Review of the Cheaper Medicines Program of the Philippines: Botika ng Barangay, Botika ng Bayan, P100 Treatment Pack, and the Role of PITC Pharma, Inc. in Government Drug Procurement. Discussion Paper Series No. 2012-13. Philippine Institute for Development Studies. doi.org/10.62986/dp2012.13. 2 Palompon, D. R., et. al. (2010, December 2). Community Drugstore (Botika ng Barangay): Its Contribution to Family Living Standards. Liceo Journal of Higher Education Research (Vol. 6 No. 2 (ISSN: 2094-1064). doi.org/10.7828/ljher.v6i2.69. Administrative Order No. 159 in October 2022 introduced financial assistance mechanisms through accredited Pharmaceutical Distribution Networks. These measures have kept the program alive, but each remains an executive issuance that can be revised or discontinued at any time, leaving BNBs without the guaranteed, continuous funding a program of this scale requires. This bill mandates the DOH to establish a standardized inventory monitoring and quarterly replenishment system to prevent the stockouts that have long undermined community confidence in the BNB program. It creates a revolving fund from BNB medicine sales, directs local government units to draw on their share of national taxes under the Mandanas-Garcia ruling and the Special Health Fund under the Universal Health Care Act, and allows continued access to Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office assistance. It further sets minimum operating-hour standards and provides for a Botika ng Barangay Aide honorarium, and adds an explicit appropriations clause so that funding for the program is guaranteed year after year rather than left to chance. A Botika ng Barangay that families cannot rely on to be open, stocked, or staffed defeats the very purpose for which it was built. It must be a dependable source of affordable medicine for the Filipino families who need it most. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 11223
title: AN ACT OFFICIALLY CREATING BARANGAY SANTA CRUZ IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF TAMPAKAN, PROVINCE OF SOUTH COTABATO, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This Bill seeks the official statutory creation and recognition of Barangay Santa Cruz in the Municipality of Tampakan, Province of South Cotabato, so that it may receive its lawful share in the National Tax Allotment, formerly referred to as the Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA). Similar measures were filed in previous Congresses. Barangay Santa Cruz came into existence through Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 122, Series of 2001, and succeeding Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution Nos. 13 and 170, both Series of 2001. Its creation was subsequently ratified in a plebiscite conducted by the Commission on Elections on 30 June 2003. Since its creation, Barangay Santa Cruz has functioned as a regular local government unit, serving its constituents, electing its officials, implementing public service projects and programs, and administering its assets and facilities. Because Barangay Santa Cruz was created by a local government unit after the effectivity of the Local Government Code of 1991 and was not created by statute, its financial requirements have historically been borne by the local government units concerned pursuant to the final proviso of Section 285 of Republic Act No. 7160. Its official recognition by Congress will allow Barangay Santa Cruz to receive its just share of national revenues and strengthen its ability to finance essential services and development programs. Fiscal autonomy at the barangay level translates directly into better and more responsive services for the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. ________________________________ FERDINAND L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure seeks the statutory recognition and creation of Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo in the Municipality of Tupi, Province of South Cotabato, and to ensure that it is entitled to its lawful share in the National Tax Allotment, formerly referred to as the Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA). Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo was created pursuant to Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 158, Series of 2023, which enacted Provincial Ordinance No. 14, Series of 2023. Its creation was ratified in a plebiscite conducted by the Commission on Elections on 13 July 2024. Section 285 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, provides that the financial requirements of barangays created by local government units after the effectivity of the Code shall be the responsibility of the local government unit concerned. Statutory recognition is therefore necessary to place Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo on the same fiscal footing as other barangays and to enable it to receive its corresponding share from national taxes. Barangays are the basic political units through which essential public services are delivered directly to communities. Providing Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo with a regular and predictable share in national revenues will strengthen its capacity to finance basic services, local development programs, public infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and other responsibilities entrusted to barangay governments. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. ________________________________________ FERDINAND L. label: HB 11227
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF PATIENTS AGAINST HOSPITAL DETENTION ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES AND PROVIDING STIFFER PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT 9439 TITLED “AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DETENTION OF PATIENTS IN HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL CLINICS ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way, you will fulfill the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2 “Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do so.” – Proverbs 3:27 Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution explicitly establishes that the protection and promotion of health, and access to health care is fundamentally a human right, to wit: “[T]he State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.” In the same vein, Article III, Section 20 stipulates that "[N]o person shall be imprisoned for debt or non-payment of a poll tax.” These key Constitutional provisions are the guiding principles on the enactment of Republic Act No. 9439, otherwise known as the Anti-Hospital Detention Law, which prohibits the unlawful detention of patients on account of unpaid medical obligations. However, gaps in the coverage and enforcement mechanisms of the law continue to leave patients and their families vulnerable, particularly those who are financially incapacitated and those confronted with the release of medical documents, personal belongings, or the remains of a deceased loved one. This measure seeks to strengthen the protections under Republic Act No. 9439 by expressly covering hospitals, medical clinics, and other similar healthcare facilities, and by prohibiting the detention not only of patients but also of their relatives, representatives, caregivers, and, in appropriate cases, newborn children. It further provides a clearer definition of detention to include acts that effectively prevent discharge or release, such as withholding documents necessary for discharge, benefit claims, or interment, refusing the medically appropriate removal of medical devices, withholding personal belongings, or refusing to release the remains of a deceased patient on account of unpaid obligations. The bill also establishes safeguards for patients who are financially incapable of settling their obligations. While allowing the execution of secured promissory notes 1 where appropriate, it provides alternative mechanisms such as guarantees from government agencies and assignments of benefits or proceeds. Indigent patients endorsed through the hospital's medical social services may be exempted from the requirement of a promissory note upon submission of an appropriate guarantee from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) or the Department of Health (DOH). These mechanisms seek to balance the legitimate financial interests of healthcare facilities with the patient's right to timely discharge and access to essential documents and benefits. Recognizing that vulnerable patients may require assistance beyond the immediate prohibition against detention, the measure mandates DOH to facilitate access to government medical assistance programs and establish a grievance and redress mechanism for unlawful detention. It likewise requires healthcare facilities to adopt standard discharge protocols, provide transparency in healthcare costs and billing, prominently post patients' rights, and refer indigent or financially incapacitated patients to medical social service offices. These provisions strengthen accountability and ensure that the prohibition against hospital detention is translated into an accessible and enforceable patient protection system. To ensure meaningful enforcement, the bill imposes higher penalties when unlawful detention is committed pursuant to an established institutional policy or management instruction. Repeated violations under such policy may likewise result in the revocation of the health facility's license to operate. The measure further provides a tax deduction for certain unpaid balances guaranteed to facilitate the discharge of financially incapacitated patients, thereby helping mitigate the financial burden on healthcare facilities while preserving the patient's right to timely release. By amending and strengthening Republic Act No. 9439, this measure seeks to ensure that financial hardship does not become a barrier to a patient's liberty, dignity, or access to necessary medical and legal documents. It establishes clearer responsibilities for healthcare institutions and government agencies while providing practical mechanisms for the recovery or settlement of legitimate medical obligations without resorting to the detention of patients or their families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 11231
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE UNIVERSITY OF ANTIQUE, EXPANDING ITS CURRICULAR OFFERINGS AND THE COMPOSITION OF THE GOVERNING BOARD, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The University of Antique (UA), established under Republic Act No. 9746, has long served as a principal institution of higher learning in the Province of Antique and a key contributor to human resource development, research, extension services, and socio-economic progress in Western Visayas. As the demands of higher education continue to evolve, there is a need to strengthen the University’s institutional framework and expand its capacity to respond to emerging academic, technological, and development priorities. This bill seeks to revise the Charter of the University of Antique by broadening its academic mandate, strengthening its governance and administrative structures, enhancing institutional autonomy, and improving access to quality higher education throughout the province. The measure expands the University’s curricular offerings to include undergraduate and graduate programs, advanced professional and technical instruction, and training in fields such as law, medicine, nursing, maritime education, engineering, information and communications technology, and other disciplines responsive to the needs of Antique and Western Visayas. It likewise strengthens UA’s functions in research, extension, innovation, technology transfer, and entrepreneurship. The bill also strengthens UA as a multi-campus state university. It recognizes its existing regular campuses in Sibalom, Tibiao, and Hamtic; converts the extension campuses in Caluya and Libertad into regular campuses; and mandates the creation of new regular campuses in Bugasong, Tobias Fornier, and San Remigio. It further authorizes the establishment of additional 1 branches or extension campuses as may be necessary to improve access to quality education and advance the University’s research and academic capabilities. Taken together, these reforms will provide the University of Antique with a stronger and more responsive institutional framework to deliver accessible, relevant, and globally competitive higher education, while further advancing research, innovation, public service, and sustainable regional development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. FELIMON M. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the "Magna Carta of Public Solid Waste Management Workers Act." SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is hereby declared the policy of the State to recognize the indispensable role of public solid waste management workers in safeguarding public health, protecting the environment, promoting ecological balance, and ensuring the effective implementation of ecological solid waste management programs. The State shall protect and promote the rights and welfare of public solid waste management workers by ensuring humane working conditions, just and equitable compensation, occupational safety and health, adequate social protection, opportunities for training and capacity development, and protection against discrimination, harassment, exploitation, and unsafe working conditions. Towards this end, the State shall adopt measures that enhance their dignity, improve their quality of life, and strengthen the delivery of public solid waste management services. SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: a. Public Solid Waste Management Workers refer to all personnel employed by national government, local government units (LGUs), government owned
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public solid waste management workers perform one of the most essential yet often overlooked public services. Every day, they collect, transport, process, and dispose of solid waste, ensuring the cleanliness of communities, protecting public health, and safeguarding the environment. Their work is indispensable to the effective implementation of ecological solid waste management programs and the promotion of sustainable urban and rural development. Despite the hazardous nature of their duties, public solid waste management workers continue to face numerous challenges, including prolonged exposure to harmful substances, infectious waste, toxic chemicals, extreme weather conditions, and occupational accidents. Many of them also endure inadequate compensation, limited access to healthcare and insurance, and the absence of comprehensive legal framework that recognizes and protects their rights and welfare. While existing laws, such as Republic Act No. 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, provide the policy framework for solid waste management, they do not comprehensively address the employment conditions, occupational safety, benefits, and professional development of the workers who carry out these vital functions. It is therefore imperative to establish a Magna Carta that institutionalize their rights, promote their welfare, ensure safe and humane working conditions, and recognize their invaluable contribution to society. This proposed measure seeks to provide public solid waste management workers with just compensation, hazard pay, appropriate personal protective equipment, health benefits, opportunities for training and capacity development, and protection against discrimination and unjust labor practices, among others. It likewise mandates the adoption of occupational safety standards and appropriates the necessary funds to ensure the effective implementation of these benefits. By recognizing the dignity of their profession and investing in their welfare, the State affirms its commitment to protecting workers who perform vital environmental and public health services while strengthening the country’s solid waste management system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 11233
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA FOR PUBLIC DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKERS, INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PUBLIC DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKFORCE CREATING THE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKERS SUPPORT FUND, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 12 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10121, the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, built a system. It did not build the workforce that the system runs on. Section 12 of that law requires every province, city, and municipality to establish a Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office headed by a DRRM Officer and assisted by three staff for administration and training, research and planning, and operations and warning. Where the offices exist, a large share of the people staffing them hold job order or contract of service engagements, renewed every six months, without security of tenure, without leave credits, without insurance, and without any legal claim to the hazard pay that the danger of their work plainly warrants. This is the workforce that clears the road before the convoy, that reads the rain gauge at two in the morning, that carries the body bags, and that signs the damage assessment on which every peso of relief depends. Several measures on this subject are pending before this Chamber, and this bill seeks to expand from all of them. It departs from them in three respects. First, on hazard pay. The pending measures set the hazard allowance at a rate "not exceeding twenty-five percent (25%)" of daily basic salary. The provision they are modeled on, Section 21 of Republic Act No. 7305, the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers, reads "at least twenty-five percent (25%)." A ceiling has been substituted for a floor, and under a ceiling a local government unit that grants one percent is fully compliant. This bill restores the floor and adds a fifteen-day release deadline, so that an earned benefit does not become a receivable. Second, on who pays. The pending measures charge the cost to local funds "subject to Personal Service Limitations pursuant to Section 325 of Republic Act No. 7160." For the fourth to sixth class local government units where DRRM staffing is thinnest and hazard exposure highest, that proviso is a legal bar on compliance: the unit cannot grant the benefit without breaching the Local Government Code. This bill excludes risk-related DRRM benefits from the personal services limitation and creates a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Workers Support Fund so that the poorest municipalities are not asked to fund a national mandate out of a budget they do not have. It likewise bars the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund from being converted into a payroll account, so that the workers are not funded by defunding the preparedness work they are hired to do. Third, on integrity. No pending measure protects a DRRM worker who refuses to sign a false damage assessment, refuses to certify a project that does not exist, or reports the misuse of disaster funds. The events of the past year have made the cost of that omission plain. A DRRM officer's signature is a control on public money, and a control is worth nothing if the person exercising it can be removed for exercising it. This bill protects that refusal and makes retaliation for it a punishable act. Beyond these, it amends Section 12 of Republic Act No. 10121 to require that the positions the law has demanded since 2010 are actually created, funded, and filled, on a deadline and against hazard-weighted staffing standards. It creates no new profession, no new board, and no new bureaucracy. It fills positions that existing law already requires, pays for exposure that already occurs, and protects people who are already doing the work. A Magna Carta for our DRRM workers is long overdue. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. title: AN ACT GRANTING AN AMNESTY ON UNPAID INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES IMPOSED BY THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT FOR TAXABLE YEAR 2026 AND PRIOR YEARS WITH RESPECT TO ESTATE TAX, OTHER INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES, AND TAX ON DELINQUENCIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino families, workers, entrepreneurs, and businesses are presently confronting an unusually difficult economic environment. The continuing effects of elevated prices, higher energy and transportation costs, disruptions in international trade and fuel markets, and slower economic growth have placed considerable pressure on household finances and business activity. Headline inflation remained elevated at 6.2 percent in July 2026, while economic growth slowed to 2.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026. These conditions are felt not merely in economic statistics, but in the everyday cost of food, electricity, transportation, housing, education, and the operation of small and medium enterprises. Government policy must therefore strike a careful balance. Revenue must continue to be raised for essential public services and national development, but taxation should not become an obstacle to the recovery and continued economic participation of otherwise productive citizens and enterprises. This policy direction was expressly articulated by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. during his 2026 State of the Nation Address. Recognizing the burden borne not only by low-income families but also by workers, the middle class, and small businesses, the President called upon Congress to pursue tax relief measures that promote economic growth, generate revenue, and advance equity. More particularly, 1 the President expressly called for an amnesty covering unpaid taxes, including income tax, estate tax, donor's tax, value-added tax, and the penalties attached thereto. This bill is modeled upon previous tax amnesty laws, but updated with additional safeguards against fraud and abuse in order to better attain the policy objectives of the current administration. Among the concerns raised were the following: the continued restrictions imposed by bank secrecy laws in cases of suspected fraud, the absence of an adequate framework for the automatic exchange of tax information, and insufficient mechanisms to verify the truthfulness of declarations of assets and net worth. Certain provisions involving the previous attempts for different versions of Estate Tax Amnesty were likewise changed. In particular, the issue over allowing several successive unsettled estates to be discharged through a single tax computation based only upon the last decedent, notwithstanding that estate tax attaches at each taxable transfer. Additionally, provisions regarding conclusive presumption of correctness, originally granted to Estate Tax Amnesty Returns, has been balanced with a safeguard in order to prevent a situation wherein the Government is deprived of a reasonable opportunity to verify ownership, valuation, succession, and other material information. Congress subsequently enacted Republic Act Nos. 11569 and 11956, progressively extending and simplifying the Estate Tax Amnesty. These amendments recognized that an effective amnesty must be accessible to ordinary taxpayers. They allowed easier filing, reduced documentary barriers, separated payment of estate taxes from the later process of transferring property, and permitted installment payments. This bill builds upon all of these legislative developments. First, it expands the coverage of the Estate Tax Amnesty to estates of decedents who died on or before December 31, 2026, and grants taxpayers two (2) years from the effectivity of the implementing rules and regulations within which to avail themselves of the program. Second, it reinstates the General Tax Amnesty originally contemplated under Republic Act No. 11213 and updates its coverage to taxable year 2026 and all prior years. Taxpayers are likewise granted two (2) years from the effectivity of the implementing rules and regulations within which to avail themselves of the amnesty. To encourage taxpayers to come forward promptly, the bill preserves the principle of the original early-availment incentive. A taxpayer who avails during the first six months receives a twenty percent reduction in the amnesty tax; those availing during the succeeding six months receive a fifteen percent reduction; those availing during the third six-month period receive a ten percent reduction; and those availing during the final six months may still obtain the amnesty but without an additional reduction. 2 Third, the bill directly addresses the objections that prevented the General Tax Amnesty from taking effect in 2019. Tax Amnesty Returns and declarations of assets and net worth will no longer become conclusively and immediately unassailable upon filing. Instead, honest taxpayers will enjoy a prima facie presumption of correctness, while the Bureau of Internal Revenue is afforded a three-year period within which to conduct ordinary verification. After this period, the amnesty becomes final and irrevocable, subject to the taxpayer’s continuing liability for the full payment of the correct tax due if the declarations are subsequently determined to contain an inaccuracy affecting the tax due. Fraud, willful concealment, or material misrepresentation receives no protection and may additionally give rise to revocation, civil penalties, and criminal liability even if discovered beyond the three-year verification period. Where the amnesty itself was obtained through fraud, willful concealment, or material misrepresentation, the special protection of the amnesty may be revoked. Consistent with the long-established principle under the National Internal Revenue Code applicable to fraudulent returns, the Government is given ten (10) years from the discovery of the fraud within which to pursue the appropriate action. This distinction is essential. The bill forgives tax violations committed during the periods covered by the amnesty; otherwise there would be no amnesty at all. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 A stronger Philippine economy begins with Filipinos who have the knowledge and opportunity to build businesses. 24 Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are undeniably the backbone of the Philippine economy. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) 2023 List of Establishments, MSMEs account for 99.6 percent of all business establishments and 67.0 percent of total employment in the country. They also contribute an estimated 25 percent of total export revenue and 40 percent of the country's GDP. 30 These figures only show that when Filipino entrepreneurs succeed, the Philippine economy grows with them. 33 However, starting and sustaining a business remains a challenge for many Filipinos. Access to proper training, business knowledge, technology, mentoring, financing, and markets remains uneven, while government programs for entrepreneurship are spread across different agencies and institutions. The market is here, and the audience is very much alive. 39 Hence, there is a need for a dedicated institution that brings these efforts together and makes entrepreneurship education more accessible and practical. 42 The proposed measure which establishes the Philippine Entrepreneurs Academy seeks to address this need by establishing a national institution dedicated to entrepreneurship education, training, research, and industry development. This will offer degree programs, technical-vocational courses, short-term training, and research while working with TESDA, DTI, DOST, the private sector, and other stakeholders. 48 The Academy will bridge the gap between learning how to start a business and actually building one. Through industry partnerships and practical training fit for the selected industry, it will equip aspiring and current entrepreneurs with the exact skills needed to establish, sustain, and grow their businesses. 5 By helping more Filipinos turn ideas into sustainable and profitable enterprises, the Academy can help create businesses that last, jobs that remain, and communities that grow. 9 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 11 12 13 REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 A bamboo pole sold cheaply at the farm gate can become furniture, a construction material, a household product, or an export commodity. 25 The Department of Science and Technology estimates that the Philippines has approximately 39,000 to 53,000 hectares of bamboo stands. Yet these resources remain largely scattered across backyards, forests, and even private properties, with relatively few established as commercial plantations. At the same time, DOST- PCAARRD has recognized that existing bamboo resources have struggled to meet the industry's demand for quality and quantity of raw materials. 32 This is a missed economic opportunity. 34 In 2023, Philippine bamboo production was reported at approximately 1.8 million poles, while recorded exports stood at around 2,000 kilograms. These figures might be commendable but somehow, it reveals a striking gap between the country's natural resource base and its ability to convert bamboo into a globally competitive industry. 39 The problem, therefore, is not the absence of bamboo’s economic potential. Despite the country's substantial bamboo resources, farmers and entrepreneurs continue to face barriers in plantation development, access to technology and financing, processing, and market access. 44 Without addressing these gaps, much of the economic value of bamboo will remain unrealized. Hence, this proposed measure seeks to transform bamboo from an underutilized natural resource into a sustainable engine of rural livelihood, domestic manufacturing, employment, and economic growth. 4 The proposed measure seeks to establish a national framework for the development of the Philippine bamboo industry. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When a building fails, the consequences are measured not only in pesos, but in lives. 23 In June 2026, a building collapse in Angeles City, Pampanga resulted in a government investigation that found violations of occupational safety and health standards and led to more than ₱11.7 million in liabilities and administrative fines. label: HB 11243
title: AN ACT FURTHER AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY,” AS AMENDED, TO PROVIDE FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities should not be required to repeatedly renew their identification cards when their disabilities are permanent and irreversible. The periodic renewal of PWD identification cards creates unnecessary inconvenience, administrative burdens, and expenses for persons who are already living with permanent conditions. This measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 7277, as amended, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Persons with Disability,” by providing for the lifetime validity of PWD identification cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities. Under the proposed measure, permanent disability shall be medically certified and appropriately verified, while the PWD identification card shall remain valid for the lifetime of the cardholder. Replacement shall remain available in cases of loss, damage, change in material information, or when the card becomes unusable, without requiring automatic re-certification of the permanent disability. The measure likewise provides that existing PWD identification cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities shall be deemed lifetime-valid, subject to the applicable rules on replacement and verification. By eliminating unnecessary periodic renewal while maintaining appropriate verification and registration safeguards, this measure seeks to make government services more accessible, efficient, and responsive to the needs of persons with permanent disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE HOUSING PROGRAM FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS, PROVIDING FOR GOVERNMENT- BUILT HOUSING, SUBSIDIZED HOUSING FINANCING, RENT- TO-OWN AND OTHER HOUSING ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS, CREATING A PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS' HOUSING FUND, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public school teachers play a vital role in educating the Filipino youth and advancing national development. Many teachers, however, continue to face difficulties in securing decent, safe, affordable, and accessible housing, particularly those assigned to remote, underserved, and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. This measure seeks to establish a Public School Teachers’ Housing Program that will provide qualified teachers with access to government-built and near-site housing, subsidized housing loans, rent-to-own arrangements, down-payment and rental assistance, housing construction financing, and other appropriate housing assistance. The bill also creates a Public School Teachers’ Housing Fund and a Public School Teachers’ Housing Program Council to ensure coordinated implementation, sustainable financing, transparent beneficiary selection, and proper monitoring of the Program. By providing teachers with affordable and secure housing, the State can strengthen their economic security and welfare while helping ensure that they remain able to serve effectively in schools and communities throughout the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11245
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE PASS-THROUGH AND RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential commodity that directly affects the daily lives of Filipino households, businesses, and industries. Ensuring that electricity rates remain fair, reasonable, and affordable is therefore a vital concern of the State. Under the existing framework, system losses incurred in the distribution of electricity may be reflected in the rates charged to consumers. These losses may result from technical inefficiencies, inadequate infrastructure, pilferage, and other conditions within the distribution system. Consumers, however, have no control over the operation, maintenance, efficiency, or security of the distribution system and should not be made to bear the cost of such losses. This measure seeks to prohibit distribution utilities and electric cooperatives from passing on or recovering system loss charges from electricity consumers, directly or indirectly. It likewise directs the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), in coordination with the Department of Energy (DOE) and other stakeholders concerned, to establish the necessary mechanisms to implement the prohibition and ensure that such charges are excluded from consumer billing. The measure aims to strengthen consumer protection, promote accountability and efficiency among distribution utilities, and ensure that consumers pay only for the electricity they actually consume. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11246
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THREATENING, HARASSING, COERCIVE, AND ABUSIVE DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES BY ONLINE LENDING APPLICATIONS, DIGITAL CREDIT PROVIDERS, FINANCING COMPANIES, LENDING COMPANIES, AND OTHER SIMILAR ENTITIES, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of digital financial services has expanded access to loans and credit facilities, but has likewise given rise to abusive debt collection practices through text messages, social media, mobile applications, and other digital platforms. Reports of threats, intimidation, public shaming, unauthorized disclosure of personal information, and coercive communications have caused serious harm to the dignity, privacy, and security of borrowers. While existing laws and regulations provide remedies against certain unlawful collection practices, there remains a need for a clear and comprehensive framework specifically addressing threatening, harassing, coercive, and abusive debt collection conducted through digital and electronic means. This measure seeks to establish fair and lawful standards for digital debt collection, prohibit specified abusive practices, protect borrowers from harassment and misuse of personal information, strengthen compliance and regulatory oversight, and provide appropriate administrative, civil, and criminal remedies, without prejudice to liabilities and penalties under other applicable laws. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11247
title: AN ACT PROVIDING INCENTIVES AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR THE MODERNIZATION OF PUBLIC UTILITY JEEPNEYS AND TRICYCLES, ENSURING THE PROTECTION OF DRIVERS AND SMALL TRANSPORT OPERATORS DURING THE TRANSITION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The continuing modernization of public transportation is necessary to provide the riding public with a safer, more reliable, accessible, and efficient transport system. The transition, however, also presents significant financial and livelihood challenges to small public utility jeepney and tricycle operators and drivers who may not have the resources to immediately comply with modernization requirements. This measure seeks to ensure that modernization is inclusive and does not unnecessarily displace small transport operators and drivers. It provides a special low- interest financing window, with an interest rate not exceeding four percent (4%) per annum and a repayment period of at least seven (7) years, together with reasonable transition assistance for qualified small transport operators. It likewise provides a minimum five-year transition period for small transport operators owning three (3) units or fewer and protects them from being compelled to consolidate with corporate operators solely to participate in the modernization program or access assistance under the Act. To protect affected drivers, the measure provides for priority consideration for employment in modernized fleets, free retraining through TESDA, and transitional livelihood assistance for up to three (3) months, subject to eligibility requirements and availability of appropriations. Through these measures, the bill seeks to make public transport modernization a just, gradual, and inclusive transition—modernizing the system while protecting the livelihood of those who have long provided this essential public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11248
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES OF STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mental health is an integral component of overall health and well-being and has become an increasingly pressing concern among young people, particularly students in higher education. College and university students face academic, financial, social, and personal pressures during a stage of life when mental health conditions may first emerge or become more pronounced. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that one in seven persons aged ten (10) to nineteen (19) years experiences a mental disorder, with depression and anxiety among the leading causes of illness in this age group. Suicide is likewise the third leading cause of death globally among persons aged fifteen (15) to twenty-nine (29) years, an age group that includes a significant portion of the college and university population. In the Philippines, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported a suicide mortality rate of 2.7 deaths per 100,000 population in 2024. At the same time, access to mental health services remains limited. The Department of Health’s National Objectives for Health 2023–2028 reports only seventy- five (75) mental health facilities nationwide and three hundred sixty-two (362) Mental Health Management and Assistance Program (MH-MAP) access sites, which the government seeks to expand to five hundred fifteen (515). The WHO Mental Health Atlas 2024 Country Profile for the Philippines further reflects gaps in available human resources, reporting only 3.9 mental health workers per 100,000 population, including 0.2 psychiatrists and 0.3 psychologists per 100,000 population. The same profile also reported no functioning school-based mental health program under WHO reporting criteria, underscoring the need to strengthen accessible mental health services in educational settings. This need is particularly relevant to State Universities and Colleges (SUCs). Data from the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) show that, as of June 26, 2025, there were one hundred thirteen (113) SUC main campuses and four hundred forty-two (442) satellite campuses nationwide. Their broad reach places SUCs in a strategic position to provide mental health promotion, early intervention, counseling, crisis response, and referral services to students, faculty, and personnel. Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” established the national policy for the promotion and protection of mental health and the delivery of integrated mental health services. Consistent with this policy and the Philippine Council for Mental Health Strategic Framework 2024– 2028, there is a need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for mental health services within SUCs. Thus, this bill seeks to institutionalize Mental Health Offices in SUC campuses and ensure the hiring, training, deployment, and professional development of qualified mental health personnel. Through accessible campus-based services, appropriate referral mechanisms, suicide prevention programs, and timely crisis intervention, SUCs can better support the mental health and well-being of their academic communities. During the 19th Congress, a similar measure, which this representation co-authored, was approved on Third Reading by the House of Representatives. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TOBIAS “TOBY” M. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 12 The right to travel is a fundamental liberty guaranteed by the Constitution. Article III, Section 6 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the right to travel shall not be impaired except in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health, as may be provided by law. 16 The issuance of a Philippine passport facilitates the exercise of this constitutional right by enabling Filipino citizens to travel internationally for lawful purposes, including employment, education, business, family reunification, and tourism. Under the New Philippine Passport Act (2024), the State shall protect the people’s constitutional right to travel, prescribe only minimum requirements, and ensure expeditious action on applications for and the issuance of passports and other travel documents.1 23 Further, the DFA may provide mobile passport services and consular outreach missions to Filipinos in areas outside its offices to make passport services accessible.2 This is particularly relevant given the continuing volume of Filipinos travelling abroad. 27 According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) 2025 Philippine Statistical Yearbook, there were 3,890,671 outbound Philippine residents in 2023 and 6,853,204 in 2024, representing a 76.14 percent increase.3 In addition, the DFA reported that it issued 2,615,953 passports in 2024. label: HB 11252
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE SAFE SPORTS CENTER, INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL ATHLETE SAFEGUARDING SYSTEM, PREVENTING AND ADDRESSING ABUSE, HARASSMENT, EXPLOITATION, NEGLECT, RETALIATION, UNSAFE PRACTICES, AND SERIOUS SAFETY FAILURES IN SPORTS, PRESCRIBING THE DUTIES OF COVERED ENTITIES, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR GRASSROOTS SPORTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On June 8, 2026, Ateneo de Manila University men’s basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili died by drowning during a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora. The Philippine Sports Commission subsequently formed a multi- stakeholder panel, while the National Bureau of Investigation and the Philippine National Police initiated separate investigative action. As these investigations remain pending, this measure makes no finding regarding fault, negligence, or liability. The tragedy presents a broader legislative concern: the responsibility of a sports organization does not end when formal training or competition ends. Camps, retreats, travel, billeting, swimming, recreation, and team-building activities conducted under institutional authority remain part of the sporting environment. These activities require proper risk assessment, competent supervision, emergency action plans, medical readiness, communication protocols, and clear accountability. Drowning remains a major public-health concern. The World Health Organization reported that more than 300,000 people died from drowning worldwide in 2021. Children and young people accounted for fifty-seven percent of these deaths, while approximately ninety-two percent occurred in low- and middle-income countries. More than half of global drowning deaths occurred in the Western Pacific and South- East Asia regions. The Constitution recognizes sports as an instrument of national development. Article II, Section 17 directs the State to give priority to sports, while Article XIV, Section 19 directs the State to promote physical education and sports programs to foster self-discipline, teamwork, excellence, and the development of a healthy and alert citizenry. These constitutional purposes cannot be achieved when athletes are exposed to abuse, harassment, exploitation, retaliation, unsafe training practices, inadequate supervision, preventable hazards, or deficient emergency response. Athletic excellence and athlete safety are not competing objectives. Safety is a necessary condition for sustainable participation and responsible sports development. Republic Act No. 6847 created the Philippine Sports Commission as the policy- making and coordinating body for amateur sports development. Philippine sports, however, is administered through a dispersed structure involving the PSC, National Sports Associations, schools, local governments, leagues, clubs, coaches, volunteers, and private organizers. This structure permits valuable autonomy but may also produce different safeguarding standards, reporting mechanisms, investigative procedures, and emergency protocols among organizations. Existing laws already address particular forms of abuse and misconduct. Republic Act No. 7610 protects children against abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, and discrimination. Republic Act No. 11313 penalizes gender-based sexual harassment in workplaces, educational institutions, training institutions, public spaces, and online settings. The Anti-Hazing Act, Anti-Bullying Act, Mental Health Act, criminal laws, civil laws, and child-protection statutes likewise provide applicable rights and remedies. These laws do not yet create a unified sports-specific system for safeguarding education, risk assessment, emergency action planning, background screening, confidential reporting, interim protective measures, independent investigation, and recognition of sports-related sanctions across organizations. The proposed Philippine Safe Sports Act addresses this institutional gap by creating the Philippine Safe Sports Center. The Center shall establish a National Safe Sports Code, receive and investigate serious safeguarding complaints, issue minimum safety standards, conduct education and certification, maintain appropriate records of sanctioned persons, and coordinate with law-enforcement and child-protection agencies. The bill covers not only sexual, physical, psychological, and emotional abuse, but also serious safety failures and unsafe practices. Covered entities must prepare written risk assessments and emergency action plans for training, competitions, camps, travel, billeting, team-building, swimming, open-water activities, and other high-risk undertakings. Independent investigation is necessary where a sports organization may otherwise be required to investigate its own coaches, officials, employees, or programs. Independence protects athletes, complainants, witnesses, respondents, and the integrity of the institution itself. At the same time, the bill preserves the proper autonomy of sports organizations. Team selection, playing time, technical coaching decisions, competition results, and ordinary game-related discipline remain with the appropriate sports bodies unless an identifiable safeguarding violation is involved. The measure incorporates due-process safeguards. Respondents are entitled to notice, an opportunity to be heard, access to relevant evidence subject to confidentiality rules, representation, and appeal. Provisional measures may be imposed when necessary to protect athletes or witnesses, but they do not constitute a final finding of liability. The United States Center for SafeSport illustrates both the need for an independent safeguarding institution and the importance of adequate resources and clear procedures. The Center reported receiving nearly 8,100 reports in 2024 and more than 32,000 reports since its establishment. Reports increased by more than 2,780 percent from 2017, demonstrating the substantial administrative demands placed on a national sports-safeguarding system. The proposed Philippine system therefore requires precise jurisdiction, reasonable case timelines, periodic review of provisional measures, confidentiality protections, an appeals process, phased implementation, and proportionate compliance requirements for schools, National Sports Associations, local leagues, barangay teams, and grassroots organizations. label: HB 11253
title: AN ACT PROMOTING URBAN FLOOD RESILIENCE AND RAINWATER HARVESTING THROUGH THE ADOPTION OF A NATIONAL URBAN DRAINAGE AND RUNOFF MANAGEMENT CODE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Urban flooding has become one of the most pressing public safety, economic, and environmental concerns in the Philippines. Typhoons, monsoon rains, and localized thunderstorms regularly overwhelm drainage systems, causing property damage, business disruptions, displacement of families, and loss of life. In Metro Manila alone, flood-related incidents cause an estimated ₱5 billion in annual economic losses. The situation is aggravated by rapid urbanization, which has replaced natural ground cover with impermeable surfaces such as concrete and asphalt. These changes increase surface runoff while reducing natural infiltration, overwhelming outdated drainage networks—many of which were designed for rainfall patterns that no longer reflect current climate conditions. Improper solid waste disposal further clogs waterways, reducing flow capacity. Current legal provisions addressing drainage and water management are scattered across various statutes, such as the Local Government Code, the Water Code of the Philippines, and certain environmental regulations. However, there is no single, binding national standard for urban runoff management that integrates both flood mitigation and water conservation. The proposed Urban Flood Resilience and Rainwater Harvesting Act seeks to fill this gap by mandating the creation of a National Urban Drainage and Runoff Management Code, to be developed by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in coordination with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD), and other agencies. The measure requires the installation of on-site detention and retention systems, permeable paving, and rainwater catchment facilities in all new developments above a certain threshold, while promoting retrofitting in older districts. Rainwater harvesting will serve the dual purpose of reducing peak runoff and conserving water for non-potable uses such as irrigation, fire suppression, cooling, and cleaning. Through uniform technical standards, strict compliance timelines for LGUs, and capacity-building programs, this measure will provide a clear national framework to address urban flooding while also promoting water sustainability. Incentives will be available for LGUs and private developers that go beyond compliance through innovative, climate-resilient solutions. By passing this bill, Congress will directly address urban flood risks, protect lives and livelihoods, and help achieve the country’s climate adaptation and sustainable development goals. In view of the urgent need to institutionalize a coherent and enforceable framework for stormwater and rainwater management in urban areas nationwide, the swift passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
