label: HB 11254
title: AN ACT DECLARING IT A POLICY OF THE STATE TO PROVIDE UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO RELIABLE, AFFORDABLE, AND ENVIRONMENTALLY SUSTAINABLE ELECTRICITY, ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE PROGRAM FOR THE SOLAR ELECTRIFICATION OF BARANGAYS THAT REMAIN OFF-GRID, PROVIDING A PACKAGE OF FISCAL AND NON-FISCAL INCENTIVES TO ENCOURAGE THE ACTIVE PARTICIPATION OF THE PRIVATE SECTOR, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Energy insecurity in the Philippines is no longer a distant or abstract risk—it is a present and pressing reality that directly affects the daily lives of millions of Filipinos. While significant progress has been made in electrification, a number of barangays, particularly those in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, remain without access to reliable and affordable electricity. For these communities, development is not merely delayed—it is effectively denied. The urgency of this measure is further magnified by recent economic conditions. The country remains heavily dependent on imported petroleum, exposing it to global price volatility. The recent surge in international oil prices, driven by geopolitical tensions, has resulted in consecutive increases in domestic fuel prices. At the same time, the depreciation of the Philippine peso has amplified the cost of imported fuel, compounding the burden on power generation, transportation, and basic goods. These factors are now feeding directly into inflation, eroding purchasing power and placing additional strain on Filipino households. Nowhere is this more acutely felt than in off-grid communities. In these areas, electricity is often generated using diesel, making power costs highly sensitive to fuel price movements and currency fluctuations. As global oil prices rise and the peso weakens, electricity becomes more expensive, less reliable, and increasingly inaccessible. This creates a cycle of disadvantage—where the most vulnerable communities pay the highest price for the least reliable service. This proposed measure responds to this urgent reality by advancing a decisive and forward-looking solution: the accelerated electrification of off-grid barangays through solar energy. Solar power offers a stable, indigenous, and sustainable alternative to imported fuel. It insulates communities from global oil shocks, reduces long-term electricity costs, and provides a reliable foundation for economic activity, education, healthcare, and local enterprise. Through the establishment of a comprehensive Solar Barangay Electrification Program, this bill sets a clear national target of achieving full electrification of all off- grid barangays within ten (10) years. It recognizes that government alone cannot carry this burden and therefore mobilizes private sector participation through well-structured incentives, streamlined processes, and viable public-private partnership models. In doing so, it unlocks capital, innovation, and efficiency at a scale necessary to meet this national objective. This measure is not merely about electrification—it is about equity. It is about ensuring that no Filipino is left behind simply because of geography. It is about transforming energy from a barrier into a bridge for development. And most importantly, it is about asserting that in the face of rising global uncertainty, the Philippines must invest in solutions that are resilient, sustainable, and within our control. In a time when fuel prices are volatile, the peso is under pressure, and inflation threatens the stability of every household, the shift toward renewable, decentralized energy is not optional — it is imperative. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11255
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING MOTORCYCLES AS PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLES, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LAND TRANSPORTATION AND TRAFFIC CODE,” AS AMENDED, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991,” AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 4136 does not currently recognize two-wheeled motorcycles as public utility vehicles (PUVs). The Local Government Code authorizes cities and municipalities to regulate tricycles under Sections 447(3)(vi) and 458(3)(vi), but it is silent on motorcycles-for-hire. The result is a regulatory gap: motorcycles are the country’s most accessible two-wheeled mode for short trips and first/last-mile connectivity, yet their carriage of passengers remains governed only by scattered issuances, local ordinances, and a time-bound pilot program. This bill closes that gap by expressly classifying motorcycles-for-hire as PUVs in the Land Transportation and Traffic Code and by aligning LGU franchising powers under the Local Government Code. It is a counterpart measure to Senator Imee R. Marcos’ Senate Bill No. 751. Urban congestion underscores the need for safe, regulated two-wheel public transport. The 2024 TomTom Traffic Index places Davao City, Manila, and Caloocan among the world’s slowest city centers, with average travel times per 10 kilometers of about 32:59, 32:10, and 30:44, respectively, and Davao ranked in the global top ten for worst traffic in 2024. These figures reflect substantial annual hours lost in rush hour for commuters in all three Philippine cities, based on TomTom’s floating-car-data methodology. Policy and regulatory context also point to the need for a clear statute. Republic Act No. 4136 (Land Transportation and Traffic Code) pre-dates platform-mediated transport and contains no category for motorcycles-for-hire; conversely, Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code) explicitly empowers sanggunians to regulate and franchise tricycles but does not address motorcycles-for-hire. The counterpart bill amends Section 3 and Section 7 of RA 4136 to define and classify “motorcycle-for- hire,” and aligns Sections 447(3)(vi) and 458(3)(vi) of RA 7160 so LGUs can franchise motorcycles-for-hire operating strictly within their jurisdictions, subject to LTFRB guidelines. The measure also harmonizes with established safety law. It preserves the helmet mandate and standards under the Motorcycle Helmet Act (RA 10054) and directs LTO to enforce roadworthiness through type-specific inspections, permitted accessories, and speed-limiting/monitoring devices. It further declares motorcycles- for-hire to be common carriers for purposes of Civil Code diligence and liability—an approach consistent with jurisprudence that defines common carriers by the nature of the transport business rather than by vehicle type. Finally, the bill provides institutional clarity between national and local regulation. LTFRB remains the public service franchising authority for route and service standards, while LGUs can set place-specific operating rules (e.g., terminals, lanes, parking) within their territory, consistent with DPWH right-of-way and traffic management standards. This is responsive to the transition from the Department of Transportation’s motorcycle-taxi pilot to a permanent legal framework, following official statements in 2025 acknowledging the 2024 end of the pilot and the urgency of legislation that protects commuters and livelihoods alike. By codifying a national standard for motorcycles-for-hire — including classifications, licensing, insurance, safety equipment, roadworthiness, and clear LGU coordination — Congress will replace ad-hoc, uneven regulation with a uniform, rights- and safety-based framework that matches how Filipinos actually move through their cities. The measure is straightforward: legal recognition in RA 4136, aligned LGU powers in RA 7160, explicit safety and insurance requirements, and Civil Code-based accountability. In a country where city-center trips routinely take half an hour or more per 10 kilometers, lawful, well-regulated motorcycles-for-hire are not a loophole; they are part of the solution. This is a counterpart bill of the Senate Bill No. 751 filed by Sen. Imee Marcos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11256
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DIRECT OR INDIRECT RECOVERY FROM WATER CONSUMERS OF COSTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO NON-REVENUE WATER, REQUIRING WATER SERVICE PROVIDERS TO REDUCE AND PUBLICLY DISCLOSE WATER LOSSES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 63 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 198, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is indispensable to life, health, sanitation, commerce, and the daily functioning of every Filipino household. How water is measured and billed is therefore not a mere matter of utility accounting; it is a question of consumer protection and responsible stewardship of a vital natural resource. The scale of the need is stark. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority's preliminary 2024 Annual Poverty Indicators Survey, only 53.1 percent of Filipino families had access to safely managed drinking water service. When water is this scarce and this essential, not a single drop lost to leaks, faulty meters, or mismanagement should be quietly charged to the very families struggling to obtain it. Yet that is precisely what happens. Non-revenue water—the gap between water entering a system and water actually billed—captures both real losses from leaking pipes, reservoirs, and connections, and apparent losses from inaccurate meters, unauthorized use, and billing errors. Authorized public uses such as firefighting and disaster relief are treated separately when properly documented. The Philippine Water Supply and Sanitation Master Plan 2019–2030 records the National Water Resources Board's mandate that non-revenue water should not exceed 25.0 percent. That ceiling exists precisely because water loss is a manageable operating condition — not an unlimited cost to be dumped onto consumers. This measure is the water counterpart to the reform now sweeping the power sector. Just as Congress and the Executive move to stop electric utilities from passing their system losses to consumers by amending Republic Act No. 7832, this bill stops water providers from passing their water losses down the line. The principle is identical across both utilities: the burden of losses belongs to those who control the infrastructure, not to the households at the end of the pipe. The Fair Water Billing Act is the companion measure to system-loss reform in electricity — one Congress, two utilities, a single standard of fairness. The Constitution supplies a firm foundation. Article II, Sections 15 and 16 direct the State to protect the rights to health and to a balanced and healthful ecology. Article XII, Section 2 vests ownership and full control of the nation's waters in the State. Presidential Decree No. 198 authorizes water districts to set cost-recovering rates, but nowhere establishes the nationwide, progressively declining framework this bill provides. Executive Order No. 22 (2023) recognized the sector's fragmentation and created the Water Resources Management Office to harmonize it. The gap this bill fills is therefore real and unaddressed by existing law. The Fair Water Billing Act delivers these principal reforms: 1. Consumers do not pay for inefficiency. During the transition, Sec. 5 bars recovery of non-revenue-water costs exceeding the efficiency benchmark. Even costs within it are recoverable only after audit, public hearing, and specific regulatory findings. 2. The benchmark must keep falling. Sec. 6 caps the initial benchmark at 25 percent of system input (or any lower binding benchmark) and drives it to zero by the end of the fifth year after the implementing rules take effect. 3. The transition is temporary, not a permanent allowance. On expiration, all recovery of non-revenue-water costs is prohibited. 4. The rule covers the whole sector. Sec. 3 reaches water districts, LGU waterworks, MWSS and its concessionaires, private utilities, cooperatives, community and subdivision systems, bulk suppliers, and operators under concessions, joint ventures, and similar arrangements. 5. Hidden recovery is barred. Secs. 7, 9, and 10 prevent prohibited costs from being buried in base rates, fixed charges, tariff adjustments, bulk- water contracts, affiliate transactions, management fees, or renamed billing lines. 6. Loss-reducing investment stays recoverable—under safeguards. Sec. 7 permits prudent pipeline rehabilitation, leak detection, district metering, pressure management, and meter replacement where necessary, cost-effective, transparently procured, independently verified, and protected against double recovery. 7. Consumers gain enforceable rights. Annual performance scorecards, disclosure of beneficial ownership and related-party transactions, public hearings, independent audits, refunds with legal interest, personal accountability for knowing violations, and whistleblower protection. The bill accounts for real differences among providers. A one-time extension of not more than two years may be granted only to a qualified financially distressed public, cooperative, community, or nonprofit provider, and only upon public hearing, an independently audited rehabilitation plan, definite targets, quarterly reporting, and a finding that its distress arose from neither fraud, gross negligence, fund diversion, prohibited related-party dealings, nor willful neglect. A Water Loss Reduction and Modernization Program further assists qualified public and community systems, with assistance walled off from dividends, bonuses, management fees, refunds, and any cost traceable to fraud or gross negligence. The principle is simple and fair: Ang tubig na hindi umabot sa gripo ay hindi dapat umabot sa bayarin. Responsibility must rest with those who control the pipelines, meters, reservoirs, billing systems, and investment decisions. By pairing a defined transition, declining benchmarks, public scrutiny, and eventual zero recovery, the Fair Water Billing Act protects consumers while preserving lawful and prudent utility operations — completing, on the water side, the same promise of fairness now being written into the nation's power bills. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11257
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS PENSION FUND TO PROVIDE PENSION TO OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The constitutional foundation is clear: the State affirms labor as a primary social and economic force and shall protect workers and promote their welfare. A permanent OFW pension responds to a measurable need in a sector that sustains national income and household consumption. Official statistics show the scale and persistence of overseas employment: the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) estimates 2.16 million OFWs worked abroad from April to September 2023, up 9.8 percent from 2022. This is not an abstract constituency but a large, continuing labor cohort whose earnings drive remittance flows and anchor macroeconomic stability. Remittances remain a pillar of external accounts. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas reports bank-coursed cash remittances reached US$34.49 billion in 2024, three percent higher than 2023, with monthly inflows approaching US$3.0 billion by August 2025. The reliability of these inflows is precisely why social protection for the workers who generate them merits statutory support. Institutional readiness also exists. The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), created under Republic Act No. 11641, is mandated to protect OFWs throughout the migration cycle, including reintegration. Assigning the DMW to design, administer, and regulate the OFW pension mechanism aligns with its legal mandate and consolidates accountability in a single implementing agency with sector expertise, existing field networks, and regulatory reach. The policy substance of this measure is straightforward and implementable. First, it establishes an OFW Pension Fund and a DMW-administered pension plan that guarantees not less than ₱5,000 per month to eligible retirees, separate from SSS or GSIS benefits, thereby avoiding overlap and preserving the integrity of existing social insurance systems. Second, it defines clear eligibility grounded in verifiable employment history and registration records, minimizing administrative discretion and enabling credible targeting. Third, it mandates inter-agency coordination among DMW, DOF, OWWA, POEA’s successor offices, and DFA to ensure sound fund governance, accurate data matching, and international servicing through posts and welfare offices. These features mirror institutional arrangements already used for OFW services and can be implemented with existing registries and remittance data, reducing transaction costs and leakage risk. The economic and social rationale is compelling: One, the OFW population skews toward occupations with physical strain and irregular income continuity; a predictable pension offsets late-life income volatility and reduces old-age poverty risk in households historically sustained by remittances. Two, remittance-dependent localities benefit when returning workers have stable purchasing power, supporting local enterprise and mitigating negative demand shocks. Three, the program codifies the State’s recognition of a group whose foreign earnings cushion the current account and stabilize consumption during domestic downturns, strengthening social cohesion and trust in public institutions. Each of these impacts is anchored in the documented size of the OFW workforce and the volume and stability of remittance inflows cited above. This bill is a counterpart measure to Senate Bill No. 252, “OFW Pension Act of 2025,” filed by Sen. Erwin Tulfo, which seeks to establish a dedicated pension fund for Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) to provide a minimum monthly pension upon retirement. In view of the magnitude of the sector, the proven role of remittances in the economy, and the DMW’s statutory mandate to protect and reintegrate OFWs, the immediate passage of this counterpart measure is respectfully sought. label: HB 11258
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR THE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs) THROUGH E‑COMMERCE AND RESPONSIBLE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro, small, and medium enterprises constitute 99.63 percent of the Philippines’ 1.24 million business establishments and generate 6.35 million jobs—roughly two-thirds of total employment nationwide. Yet only 15,998 of these firms were actively transacting online in 2023, a fraction of the sector’s potential market reach. This participation gap persists even as the digital economy contributed ₱2.25 trillion, or about 8.5 percent of gross domestic product, in 2024. Household connectivity barriers are receding: the Women and ICT Development Index survey recorded a surge in home internet access from 17.7 percent in 2019 to 76.9 percent in 2022, confirming that physical access is no longer the primary hurdle to online commerce. Instead, MSMEs cite cost, skills shortages, logistics frictions, and mounting cyber-risks. Fortinet’s 2024 threat-landscape report found that six in ten Philippine companies experienced a three-fold increase in cyber-attacks in 2023. At the same time, the Philippines climbed nine places to 56th out of 188 economies in Oxford Insights’ 2024 Government AI Readiness Index, evidence of growing institutional capacity to deploy artificial intelligence responsibly. Harnessing these twin trends — rapid connectivity gains and improving AI readiness — demands a coherent policy response that lowers the cost of digital entry, embeds cybersecurity, and accelerates skills formation for the country’s smallest firms. The MSME E-Commerce Support Act delivers that response. First, it creates a Digital and AI Transformation Grant that defrays the costs of web storefronts, AI-enabled marketing tools, smart-logistics interfaces, and mandatory data-protection safeguards. Second, it mandates a nationwide capacity-building programme — jointly implemented by DTI, DICT, TESDA, and CHED — to upskill entrepreneurs and employees in e-commerce operations, AI fundamentals, and cybersecurity compliance. Third, it institutionalises a logistics-access scheme that links MSMEs to affordable warehousing and last-mile delivery services, especially in underserved regions. Fourth, it establishes voluntary AI sandboxes where firms can pilot emerging technologies under regulatory guidance from the DICT and National Privacy Commission. Fifth, the bill directs the MSME Development Council to publish open-data dashboards tracking digital-adoption rates, sales growth, and risk-reduction outcomes, ensuring transparency and evidence-based course correction. The measure aligns squarely with Article XII, Section 1 of the Constitution, which obliges the State to promote industrialization and full employment. By lowering the threshold for digital participation, the bill empowers the sector that already provides the majority of jobs to reach new domestic and export markets, strengthens consumer protection through mandatory cybersecurity upgrades, and positions Philippine enterprises to capitalize on responsible artificial-intelligence tools. Enactment will not only modernize commerce but also deepen economic resilience and broaden the tax base—benefits that accrue to workers, consumers, and the national treasury alike. Passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought. label: HB 11259
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE WIDESPREAD USE OF SOLAR POWER AMONG FILIPINOS, PROVIDING INCENTIVES FOR SOLAR ENERGY ADOPTION, ESTABLISHING THE SOLAR POWER ACCESS PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, as an archipelago situated in the tropical Pacific, is among the most solar-rich countries in the world, receiving an average solar irradiance of approximately 4.5 to 5.5 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day. Despite this immense natural endowment, solar energy remains significantly underutilized, with millions of Filipinos — particularly those in rural, remote, and island communities — still lacking access to reliable and affordable electricity. According to the Department of Energy, the Philippines' total installed solar capacity stands at approximately 3,600 megawatts, a fraction of the country's enormous solar potential estimated at over 150,000 megawatts. The Philippine Development Plan and the National Renewable Energy Program have set ambitious targets for renewable energy, yet the pace of solar adoption — especially at the household and community levels — remains far too slow to meet these goals. The high upfront cost of solar power systems remains the single greatest barrier to adoption for ordinary Filipino families. A basic residential rooftop solar installation costs between Php 150,000 to Php 400,000 — far beyond the reach of most households, particularly the estimated 22 million Filipinos living below the poverty line. Compounding this is the lack of accessible financing options, insufficient consumer protection, and the absence of a comprehensive national framework targeting solar adoption among ordinary citizens. Meanwhile, the country continues to suffer from high electricity rates, among the highest in Southeast Asia, which disproportionately burden low-income families and undermine the competitiveness of Filipino businesses. Frequent power outages, dependence on imported fossil fuels, and the devastating impacts of climate change — to which the Philippines is acutely vulnerable as one of the world's most disaster- prone nations — underscore the urgency of accelerating the transition to solar energy. The enactment of Republic Act No. 9513 or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008 and subsequent Net Metering Rules were significant milestones. However, these laws have largely benefited middle- and upper-income consumers and businesses, leaving behind the very Filipinos who stand to gain the most from cheaper, cleaner electricity. There is presently no dedicated law that comprehensively addresses the barriers to solar adoption for low-income households, geographically isolated communities, and small enterprises. In response to this urgent need, this bill — the Solar Power Access and Adoption Act of the Philippines or the SolarPH Act — seeks to establish a comprehensive legal and institutional framework for the widespread adoption of solar energy among all Filipinos. Specifically, the bill aims to: First, establish the Solar Power Access Program (SolarPH Program) — a government-led initiative that will provide subsidized and affordable solar power systems to low-income households, fund community solar installations in public schools and health centers, and ensure the full electrification of geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs) through off-grid solar solutions; Second, provide a robust package of fiscal incentives — including a 25% income tax credit, VAT exemptions, customs duty exemptions, and low-interest concessional loans — to make solar power genuinely affordable for ordinary Filipino households and small businesses; Third, strengthen and expand the Net Metering Program to enable more Filipino solar prosumers to sell excess electricity back to the grid, transforming households from passive consumers into active participants in the energy market; Fourth, mandate local government units to play an active role in promoting solar energy adoption within their jurisdictions, streamlining permitting processes, and funding community solar projects; Fifth, promote the development of a local solar industry through domestic manufacturing incentives, a TESDA certification program for solar technicians, and government-funded research and development; and Sixth, establish strong consumer protection mechanisms, including mandatory product standards, warranty requirements, and a licensing system for solar installers, to safeguard Filipino consumers. The Philippines cannot afford to delay its solar transition. Every year without comprehensive solar policy is a year of continued dependence on expensive imported oil, continued exposure to fuel price volatility, continued carbon emissions, and continued energy poverty for millions of our countrymen. The sun shines generously on every Philippine island — this bill ensures that its light and warmth reach every Filipino home. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11260
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO PUBLIC ATTORNEYS EXPOSED TO HAZARDOUS SITUATIONS AND PERFORMING HAZARDOUS DUTIES RELATED TO THEIR OFFICIAL FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Republic Act No. 9406, the Public Attorney’s Office (PAO) is mandated to independently provide legal representation, assistance, and counseling to indigent persons in criminal, civil, labor, administrative, and other quasi-judicial cases. In the performance of this mandate, public attorneys are often required to handle cases involving serious and violent offenses and to represent persons who may be associated with dangerous criminal organizations, drug syndicates, or armed groups. They may likewise be assigned to remote, isolated, or conflict-affected areas, where they are exposed to threats of violence, retaliation, infectious diseases, and other substantial risks arising from the nature and circumstances of their duties. Republic Act No. 9406 and its Implementing Rules and Regulations provide for special allowances funded from a Special Trust Fund consisting principally of success fees collected after successful litigation. Those special allowances, however, are distinct from hazard pay because they are not specifically tied to the actual performance of dangerous assignments or exposure to hazardous conditions. The proposed measure seeks to grant a monthly hazard pay of Five Thousand Pesos ((₱5,000.00) to public attorneys who, by reason of the nature, location, or circumstances of their assignments, are exposed to substantial risks to their safety, health, or security. The measure recognizes that the hazards faced by public attorneys are not merely incidental to the practice of law but may arise 1 directly from their duty to provide legal assistance to indigent persons, particularly in criminal and other high-risk cases. In view of the foregoing, the passage of the bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11261
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO PUBLIC PROSECUTORS EXPOSED TO HAZARDOUS SITUATIONS AND PERFORMING HAZARDOUS DUTIES RELATED TO ASSIGNED CASES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public prosecutors are the State’s principal litigators. They are responsible for enforcing the law, protecting the public, and ensuring that justice is served. In the discharge of their duties, they handle sensitive and high-risk cases involving drug syndicates, terrorist groups, organized crime, corrupt officials, and other dangerous criminal elements. The nature of their work exposes prosecutors to threats, harassment, intimidation, and violence, with some even losing their lives in the line of duty. Records from 2013 to 2024 show that at least 14 prosecutors have been killed in connection with their official duties. These incidents demonstrate the serious risks associated with prosecutorial work and the need for the State to provide adequate protection and support to those who perform these vital functions. Despite the risks inherent in their work, public prosecutors do not currently receive hazard pay or a similar risk allowance under existing laws. This is in contrast to other frontline government workers, such as health personnel, disaster responders, and law enforcement officers, who are granted additional compensation for performing hazardous duties. Extending a similar benefit to public prosecutors is a recognition of the risks they face in the performance of their official functions. This measure seeks to address this disparity by granting a monthly hazard pay of Five Thousand Pesos (₱5,000.00) to qualified public prosecutors who are involved in the investigation or prosecution of cases involving crimes against national security, illegal drugs, graft and corruption, money laundering, terrorism, and other analogous offenses. The hazard pay shall be granted in 1 addition to their basic salary and other existing allowances and shall not be subject to reduction or diminution. This measure recognizes the hazardous nature of prosecutorial work and the personal risks undertaken by public prosecutors in the pursuit of justice. It seeks to provide appropriate compensation for such risks and affirm the State’s support for those who uphold the rule of law. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11262
title: AN ACT CREATING FIVE (5) ADDITIONAL BRANCHES OF THE REGIONAL TRIAL COURT IN THE CITY OF CEBU, PROVINCE OF CEBU, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 129, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUDICIARY REORGANIZATION ACT OF 1980”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cebu City is the most populous highly urbanized city in Central Visayas. It serves as a principal center for commerce, education, health care, and government services in the region and consequently receives a substantial volume of litigation arising from its dense population and extensive economic activity. The existing Regional Trial Court (RTC) branches in Cebu City are required to handle a broad range of cases, including criminal prosecutions, civil actions, commercial disputes, special proceedings, and other matters assigned by law. Evidently, the increasing volume of cases place significant burden on the existing courts, judges, and court personnel. When judicial dockets become congested, hearings may be scheduled farther apart, resulting in delays in the resolution of cases and litigants incurring additional expenses in pursuing or defending their claims. The creation of additional RTC branches will allow for a more equitable distribution of cases, improved calendar management, and closer attention to the requirements of each docket. It will also help promote the constitutional guarantee of a speedy disposition of cases and enhance public access to justice. Thus, enactment of this measure will help reduce docket congestion, improve the timely disposition of cases, lower the costs of litigation, and strengthen the delivery of judicial services in Cebu City. 1 It is therefore earnestly urged that this bill be given favorable consideration and immediate approval. label: HB 11265
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING CHILDREN BELOW TWELVE (12) YEARS OF AGE FROM CREATING OR MAINTAINING PERSONAL SOCIAL-MEDIA ACCOUNTS, PROVIDING FOR CHILD-SAFETY MECHANISMS, PLATFORM ACCOUNTABILITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.” — Psalm 127:3 (KJV) “The State shall defend the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation and other conditions prejudicial to their development.” — Article XV, Section 3(2), 1987 Constitution The Holy Writ warns of a generation that “curseth their father,” is “pure in their own eyes,” has “lofty” eyes, and whose words are like “swords” and “knives” that harm the poor and needy (Proverbs 30:11–14, KJV). In today’s digital age, social media can amplify and normalize the disrespect, self-righteousness, pride, cruelty, and harmful behavior described in these passages. Young children, whose judgment and character are still developing, are particularly vulnerable to absorbing, imitating, or becoming victims of such influences. The State must therefore establish reasonable safeguards to protect them from premature exposure to online environment they may not yet be equipped to navigate safely and responsibly. Against this moral and constitutional backdrop, children increasingly encounter digital technologies at home and through social-media services. While digital technologies may provide communication and access to information, social- media platforms may also expose young children to grooming, luring, online sexual abuse or exploitation, cyberbullying, harmful content, privacy violations, fraudulent schemes, excessive screen use, and manipulative design. Page 1 of 14 Young children below twelve (12) years of age require heightened protection because of their developing capacity to assess risks, understand privacy consequences, identify manipulation, and protect themselves from online abuse and exploitation. This bill therefore prohibits children below twelve (12) years of age from creating, registering, operating, or maintaining personal social-media accounts, but does not prohibit them from accessing the internet generally, viewing publicly available lawful content, or using an account controlled by a parent, guardian, government agency, or institution for a lawful non-personal purpose. Under the bill, covered platforms are mandated to take reasonable and proportionate measures to prevent children below twelve (12) years of age from creating or maintaining personal social-media accounts. They shall apply child-safety safeguards, provide child-friendly reporting mechanisms, restrict unlawful and seriously harmful content, and refrain from using age-assurance information for targeted advertising or behavioral profiling. The bill likewise requires privacy-preserving age assurance and prohibits the routine collection of government-issued identification documents and biometric information. It also requires covered platforms to maintain child-safety programs, designate responsible officers, establish reporting and appeals mechanisms, and cooperate with competent government authorities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. label: HB 11266
title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD COMMISSION AS AN INDEPENDENT PERSONNEL GOVERNANCE AND OVERSIGHT BODY FOR THE PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FOR ITS HARMONIZATION WITH THE REVISED PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD LAW, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9993, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD LAW OF 2009," APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 16 Article II, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution declares that civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military. Article XVI, Section 6 thereof mandates the State to establish and maintain one police force, national in scope and civilian in character, to be administered and controlled by a national police commission. Both provisions proceed from a common constitutional premise: that an armed and uniformed service of the Republic must remain accountable to an institutional authority beyond its own chain of command. 23 The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), notwithstanding its character as an armed and uniformed service, has never been accorded such an institutional mechanism. 26 Originally constituted as a major unit of the Philippine Navy under Republic Act No. 5173 in 1967, transferred to the then Department of Transportation and Communications in 1998, and subsequently established as an armed and uniformed service under Republic Act No. 9993 in 2010, the PCG has expanded from a force of approximately three thousand (3,000) personnel into one of the largest maritime law enforcement agencies in the region. It now comprises tens of thousands of officers and non-officers, maintains a fleet of ocean-going vessels and aircraft, and performs a frontline role in the assertion of the country's sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the West Philippine Sea. Its personnel bear arms, exercise powers of arrest, search, and seizure, board and detain vessels, and operate in contested waters where the decision of a single officer may carry consequences of national significance. 37 The institutional governance of the PCG, however, has not kept pace with the growth of its organization and mandate. Under existing law, the command of the service and the administration of its personnel are vested in a single office. The Commandant directs operations and, at the same time, determines matters of promotion, assignment to major commands, and discipline. Unlike the Philippine National Police, whose administration and control are vested in the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) under Republic Act No. 6975, as amended by Republic Act No. 8551, the PCG has no specialized statutory body that reviews these matters independently of the chain of command. 46 This deficiency is most pronounced at the highest ranks. Under Article VII, Section 16 of the Constitution, as construed by the Supreme Court in Manalo v. Sistoza (G.R. No. 107369, 11 August 1999), only officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain require confirmation by the Commission on Appointments. Flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines are thus subject to legislative scrutiny, while senior officers of the Philippine National Police are subject to the screening and endorsement of the NAPOLCOM. Flag officers of the PCG are subject to neither. No professional body evaluates their qualifications prior to appointment, nor reviews the exercise of their authority thereafter. 6 This measure is introduced while Congress undertakes a comprehensive revision of the statutory framework of the PCG. On 11 August 2026, the Senate approved on third and final reading Senate Bill No. 2116, or the proposed Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law, which reorganizes the PCG into functional, support, and technical commands, prescribes clearer rules on ranks, appointments, and promotions, and strengthens internal accountability through a Coast Guard Internal Affairs Service. In the House of Representatives, the Committee on Transportation is deliberating on a Substitute Bill to House Bills Nos. 426, 1120, 3390, 4693, 4758, 5127, 5131, 5471, 5552, 5758, 6104, 6173, 6244, 6386, 8027, and 9204, which seeks to strengthen the PCG through policy and organizational reforms. 16 Mindful of these parallel efforts, this bill is crafted to complement, and not to duplicate, the Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law. It does not establish a separate organizational, personnel, promotion, disciplinary, or career-management system. It contains an express harmonization clause and rule of construction; it requires that professional standards and career progression criteria conform to the functional organization adopted under the Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law; it relies upon the Internal Affairs Service for investigation and fact-finding, in lieu of creating a competing investigative body; and it limits any transfer of functions to those expressly vested in the Commission by law. 25 Neither does this bill place the Commission within, or above, the chain of command of the PCG. The Commission is constituted as an independent personnel governance and oversight body, not as an administrative superior of the Commandant, and is expressly denied any authority over the operations, budget, finances, procurement, and assets of the service. Its powers are confined to those enumerated by law, namely: the promulgation of governance standards and the review of compliance therewith; the validation of the promotion of senior officers; the validation of the assignment of flag officers to major unit commands; the professional screening of nominees for Commandant for the consideration of the President; and the exercise of appellate and review authority in administrative disciplinary cases. 35 The distinction between command and governance is deliberate. Command, being the direction of personnel, vessels, aircraft, and resources in the accomplishment of the mission, is vested in, and shall remain with, the Commandant. The PCG shall continue to administer its personnel system, including recruitment, training, assignment, career management, and personnel records, while the Commission shall safeguard the integrity of that system. The Commandant recommends; the Commission independently validates; and the President appoints or promotes where so required by the Constitution or by law. In no instance may the Commission substitute its own choice for the recommendatio

label: HB 11273
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL EYE HEALTH PROGRAM FOR SENIOR CITIZENS WITH FUNCTIONAL VISUAL IMPAIRMENTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide accessible and comprehensive eye care services for senior citizens with functional visual impairments. It establishes a National Eye Health Program for Senior Citizens which aims to improve early detection, treatment, rehabilitation, and vision support services to help older Filipinos maintain their independence and quality of life. Visual impairment is one of the leading causes of disability among older persons and is often caused by preventable or treatable conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration. According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people worldwide have a vision impairment, and over one (1) billion cases could have been prevented or have yet to be addressed.1 In the Philippines, the growing senior citizen population underscores the need to strengthen accessible eye care services to prevent avoidable blindness and vision loss.2 Despite existing public health programs, many elderly Filipinos continue to experience barriers to eye care due to financial constraints, limited access to specialists, and inadequate community-based vision services. This measure addresses these gaps by institutionalizing a dedicated national program under the Department of Health to deliver essential eye services and improve the functional capacity and overall well-being of older persons. Protecting the eyesight of senior citizens enables them to remain active, productive, and independent members of society while reducing preventable disability and improving their quality of life. Establishing a comprehensive 1 World Health Organization. (2026, February 10). Blindness and vision impairment. Accessed via https://www. who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/blindness-and-visual-impairment. Accessed on 6 July 2026. 2 Cruz, G.T. (2025), ‘The Shifting Demographics of the Philippines: Towards and Ageing Society', in Cruz, G.T., C.J.P. Cruz, and Y.Saito (eds.), Ageing and Health in the Philippines: Wave 2. Jakarta, Indonesia: Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia. national eye health program is a timely investment in healthy aging and dignified elderly care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11274
title: AN ACT TO PROHIBIT SECONDARY AND HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS FROM CONDUCTING MANDATORY IMMERSIONS, INTERNSHIP PROGRAMS, OR ON-THE-JOB TRAINING PROGRAMS OUTSIDE THE PROVINCE WHERE THE CAMPUS IS LOCATED OR ABROAD, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to prohibit secondary schools and higher education institutions from requiring students to complete work immersion, internship, or on-the-job training (OJT) programs abroad or outside the province where the institution is located as a mandatory requirement for graduation. It ensures that participation in such programs remains voluntary and subject to the informed consent of students and their parents or guardians. Experiential learning programs play a vital role in preparing students for the workforce. However, when these programs are conducted outside the student's home province or abroad and are made compulsory, they often impose significant financial burdens on students and their families. Transportation, accommodation, meals, and other incidental expenses can become prohibitive, particularly for learners from low-income households, forcing some students to incur debt, delay completion of their academic requirements, or forego educational opportunities altogether. Education shall be accessible to all, and existing laws recognize the duty of the State to remove barriers that prevent students from completing their education. This measure ensures that educational institutions cannot compel students to participate in costly off-site immersion or internship programs as a condition for graduation. At the same time, it preserves opportunities for students who voluntarily wish to participate in such programs and strengthens accountability through mandatory reporting and regulatory oversight. No student should be denied the opportunity to graduate simply because they cannot afford the additional expenses associated with mandatory out-of-province or overseas training. This measure upholds fairness, protects the right to accessible education, and ensures that experiential learning remains an opportunity rather than a financial obstacle. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11275
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE), a body under the Office of the President, which shall harmonize policies, plans, and investments across the Philippine education sector. It shall strengthen coordination among the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and other key agencies to ensure that education reforms are aligned with national development priorities and labor market demands. The Philippine education system continues to face fragmented governance, resulting in weak coordination and policy consistencies. The Second Congressional Commission on Education pointed out that the historical “trifocalization” of the Philippine education system, which split DepEd, CHED, and TESDA has led to fragmented planning and a lack of accountability. This resulting absence of a central coordinating mechanism has contributed to persistent learning gaps, skills mismatch, and inefficiencies in education planning and resource allocation.1 This measure establishes the NCCE as the government’s principal coordinating body for education and workforce development. It integrates aligning curricula with labor market needs, strengthening data-driven policymaking national education policies and aligns curricula with labor market needs. Education is the cornerstone of national development. Ensuring effective coordination across all levels of the education sector is indispensable to producing globally competitive, highly skilled, and future-ready Filipinos. This 1 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). (2026). Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reform (2026-2035), EDCOM II Final Report. Second Congressional Commission on Education. measure will help build a more responsive, efficient, and resilient education system capable of meeting the country's long-term development goals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11276
title: AN ACT CREATING A SUSTAINABLE FISCAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE PENSION SYSTEM OF THE MILITARY AND UNIFORMED PERSONNEL, PROVIDING MECHANISMS FOR THE DISPOSITION OF GOVERNMENT ASSETS FOR THE PURPOSE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a sustainable and fiscally responsible pension system for Military and Uniformed Personnel (MUP). It creates a comprehensive funding framework, institutionalizes dedicated trust funds, and safeguards the welfare of both current and future personnel. The country’s military and uniformed personnel perform indispensable roles in defending national sovereignty, maintaining peace and order, enforcing the law, responding to disasters, and ensuring public safety. In recognition of the unique risks and sacrifices inherent in their profession, the State has long provided retirement and pension benefits that serve as a vital form of social protection. However, the current pension system has become increasingly vulnerable to fiscal pressures due to its non-contributory structure, automatic indexation, rising life expectancy, and the growing number of retirees. These factors have significantly increased the financial burden on the National Government, raising concerns over the long-term sustainability of pension obligations. The measure introduces a contributory pension scheme for new entrants while preserving the vested rights of existing personnel. It likewise strengthens fiscal risk management, harmonizes retirement and disability benefits, provides assistance to indigent pensioners, and institutionalizes mechanisms that ensure transparency, accountability, and actuarial soundness in the administration of pension funds. This vital piece of legislation promotes a pension system that is equitable, sustainable, and responsive to future generations. It strengthens public confidence that those who dedicate their lives to protecting the nation will continue to receive secure retirement benefits without compromising the country's long-term financial stability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11277
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL AFFORDABLE STUDENT LOAN PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a National Affordable Student Loan Program, which offers a sustainable, low-interest student financing system for Filipino learners. It provides affordable education loans with a fixed interest rate, flexible repayment terms, and borrower protection mechanisms to complement existing government scholarship and financial assistance programs. While the government has expanded access to free tertiary education through Republic Act No. 10931, otherwise known as the “Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act”, many Filipino students continue to struggle with expenses that remain beyond the coverage of free tuition, including books, transportation, accommodation, digital learning tools, internship costs, review classes, and other education-related expenses. These financial burdens continue to prevent many students, particularly those from low-income families, from completing their education or pursuing graduate and professional studies. This measure institutionalizes the National Affordable Student Loan Program administered by government financial institutions, providing accessible financing at a fixed two percent (2%) annual interest rate. It likewise introduces a reasonable grace period, collateral-free borrowing, borrower protection measures, and transparent lending standards to ensure that financial assistance remains affordable, sustainable, and responsive to the needs of Filipino learners. Investing in education is an investment in the country's future. In making educational financing more accessible and equitable, the State continues to empower more Filipinos to acquire knowledge and skills that will strengthen the nation's workforce, improve social mobility, and promote inclusive economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11278
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE ACCESS OF UNQUALIFIED INDIVIDUALS TO ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to restrict the purchase, sale, possession, and provision of alcoholic beverages to persons below twenty-one (21) years of age and other individuals who, because of a physical or mental disability or condition, are unable to adequately protect themselves from abuse or exploitation. It also holds adults and establishments accountable for selling and providing alcohol to these individuals. The World Health Organization1, has identified alcohol as a psychoactive and dependence-producing substance associated with more than two hundred (200) diseases, injuries, and health conditions. Starting to drink at an early age may also increase the risk of developing harmful drinking habits later in life. Preventing access to alcohol among young people is therefore an important measure to protect their health and well-being. The Philippines currently does not have a law which prohibits underage access to alcoholic beverages, and that sets the guidelines for enforcing such prohibition. As a result, protection and enforcement may vary across communities. This proposed measure clearly defines the prohibited acts, allocates responsibilities among establishments, parents, local government units, and government agencies in enforcing the law. It also recognizes that young and vulnerable individuals should receive guidance rather than be subjected immediately to criminal penalties, therefore adopting interventions that emphasize rehabilitation over punishment for young offenders. The consequences of underage drinking extend far beyond a single act of alcohol consumption. Early exposure to alcohol can disrupt a young person’s education, impair physical and mental development, and increase the risk of 1 World Health Organization. (2024, June 28). Alcohol. Accessed from: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/alcohol. Accessed on July 26, 2026. behaviors that place both the individual and the community in harm’s way. Enacting this legislation shall strengthen the country’s commitment to safeguarding children and other vulnerable individuals while laying the foundation for healthier families, safer communities, and a more productive future. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11279
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE PAYMENT OF REVIEW FEES FOR BOARD AND BAR EXAMINATIONS FOR QUALIFIED INDIGENTS ON THEIR FIRST TAKE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to exempt qualified indigent Filipino graduates from paying review fees for their first board or bar examination. It helps remove what may prevent academically qualified graduates from obtaining the review preparation necessary to ace the exams. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (2026)1, eight hundred and eighty-one (881) out of one thousand six hundred eleven (1,611) cities and municipalities recorded poverty incidence levels of twenty percent (20%) or lower in 2023, while seven hundred and twenty two (722) localities continued to register poverty incidence above twenty percent (20%), including areas classified under higher poverty levels. Fresh graduates invest for review courses and examination materials after completing their degrees. For indigent graduates from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, these costs may delay their first attempt at the board or bar examination, thus limiting professional opportunities that their education would otherwise provide. The proposed measure provides assistance to indigent graduates who are first-time license exam takers who have demonstrated academic excellence. It shall cover review courses and related preparatory materials for board and bar examinations. Expanding opportunities for qualified indigent graduates to obtain professional licenses strengthens the country’s human capital and allows more Filipinos to contribute their knowledge and expertise to national development. Behind every aspiring professional is a family that invests years of sacrifice, perseverance, and hope toward achieving a better future. This represents a 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. label: HB 11280
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE OWNERSHIP AND OPERATION OF DRONES BY PRIVATE PERSONS AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to regulate the ownership and use of drones by private individuals. It authorizes the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) to regulate drone registration and operation and addresses public safety concerns arising from the increasing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). While the CAAP has adopted regulations governing drone registration, certification, and flight limitations, these remain administrative in nature and do not cover private ownership, accountability of registered owners, and enforcement of violations. The institutionalization of such regulations is necessary to provide a more stable and enforceable basis for regulating private drone ownership and use. The proposed measure requires all privately owned drones to register with the CAAP and subjects commercial operations to a permit-to-operate requirement. It also provides CAAP with authority to establish no-drone zones, prescribe operational standards, and impose measures responsive to developments in drone technology. It likewise provides penalties for violations of safety regulations and imposes responsibility for damage, injury, or loss which shall result from its negligent, reckless, or unlawful operation. Drones have become valuable tools in various industries and activities, but their increasing accessibility requires corresponding safeguards to protect public safety and individual rights. A single irresponsible operation can compromise airspace security and infringe upon personal privacy. The establishment of clear rules for drone ownership and use shall build public confidence in the safe adoption of emerging technologies. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11281
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL-BASED MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES FOR THE YOUTH, PROVIDING FOR THE DEPLOYMENT OF MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS AND STRENGTHENING EARLY INTERVENTION MECHANISMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to improve the delivery of mental health services for the Filipino youth in basic education institutions, secondary schools, and State Universities and Colleges (SUCs). It mandates the deployment of at least one (1) licensed mental health professional in each institution and strengthens early intervention efforts for the students. Mental health disorders among children and adolescents have become a growing public health concern, with excessive screentime seen as a contributing factor to it. It has also exposed young people to addictive platform designs, which adversely affects their mental health, and impedes their emotional development and academic performance1. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act”, access to mental health services in schools remains limited, and many educational institutions lack adequate personnel and structured intervention programs. This bill offers annual mental health screening, counseling services, and teacher training on mental health and psychosocial support. It likewise mandates the deployment of licensed mental health professionals, establishes an annual Digital Detox Week, and requires the publication of a national report on youth mental health and digital behavior. These steps are taken to strengthen prevention, facilitate early intervention, and improve coordination among the education, health, and digital governance sectors. Promoting the mental health and digital wellbeing of Filipino learners is essential to improving educational outcomes and developing a healthy, resilient, and productive generation. Institutionalizing these interventions will enable the government to provide sustained and evidence-based support to young Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 World Health Organization (2x026). Mental health of adolescents. World Health Organization. label: HB 11282
title: AN ACT PENALIZING THE ACT OF WAGE THEFT, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE ARTICLES 87 AND 116 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to amend Articles 87 and 116 of Presidential Decree No. 442, otherwise known as the “Labor Code of the Philippines”, and penalize the act of wage theft. It expands the prohibition against the unlawful withholding of wages and employment benefits, and imposes criminal and administrative penalties on employers who violate workers’ rights. Incidents of unpaid wages, underpayment, delayed compensation, non-payment of overtime pay, and withholding of employment benefits continue to undermine labor standards and workers’ right to just compensation. It affects low-income workers who rely on timely payment of wages to meet their daily needs, and that of the daily sustenance of their families. This bill expands existing prohibitions to cover unpaid wages, overtime pay, bonuses, tips, reimbursements, and other legally due benefits. It likewise penalizes discriminatory practices in the allocation of overtime work, imposes criminal liability on responsible employers and corporate officers, and authorizes the suspension or cancellation of business permits for repeated violations. These shall strengthen workers’ rights while promoting compliance with labor standards. The payment of lawful wages is not merely a contractual obligation but a matter of social justice. Legislation must uphold the dignity of labor and ensure that every worker receives the compensation rightfully earned. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11283
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS IN THE PREPARATION AND AUTHORIZATION PROCESS OF THE ANNUAL NATIONAL BUDGET, PROVIDING EFFECTIVE MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize the participation of civil society organizations (CSOs) in the preparation and authorization of the annual national budget. It establishes mechanisms for accreditation, consultation, and access to budget information. Meaningful public participation is a fundamental component of transparent, accountable, and responsive governance. While citizen participation in local governance exists, providing for its institutionalization ensures the systematic involvement of CSOs throughout the national budget process. This promotes transparency, enhances public trust in government institutions, and improves the allocation of public resources. This bill requires national government agencies and government-owned or -controlled corporations to adopt participatory mechanisms, grants accredited CSOs access to key budget documents and deliberations, and institutionalizes structured engagement during budget preparation and congressional authorization. It likewise promotes transparency by requiring the timely disclosure of budget information and safeguards the integrity of CSO participation through accreditation and conflict-of-interest provisions. The proposed measure reinforces the constitutional principles of transparency, accountability, and public participation in governance. Further, it ensures that the national budget more accurately reflects the needs and priorities of the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11284
title: AN ACT MAINSTREAMING CLIMATE ACTION ACROSS NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE A CLIMATE FINANCE UNIT UNDER THE CLIMATE CHANGE COMMISSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Climate Finance Unit (CFU) under the Climate Change Commission. This institutionalizes a comprehensive national climate finance framework and enhances access to multilateral climate financing mechanisms and public-private partnerships. The Philippines remains among the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Increasingly frequent and severe typhoons, floods, droughts, sea level rise, and extreme heat continue to threaten lives, livelihoods, infrastructure, food security, and economic development. While the country has adopted key climate policies, access to and coordination of climate finance remain fragmented across government agencies and local government units, limiting the timely implementation of climate adaptation and mitigation initiatives. The proposed measure likewise integrates climate finance into national and local development planning, promotes innovative financing instruments, and strengthens monitoring and reporting systems to ensure that public investments generate measurable climate resilience and sustainable development outcomes. Establishing a centralized climate finance mechanism shall improve resource mobilization, strengthen fiscal accountability, and accelerate the implementation of climate-resilient programs nationwide. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11285
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR AN ADVANCED NURSING EDUCATION PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9173, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE NURSING ACT OF 2002”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a more comprehensive nursing education framework that formally recognizes both basic and advanced nursing education programs. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9173, otherwise known as the “Philippine Nursing Act of 2002”, and integrates master’s and doctoral degree pathways into the nursing education system. It enhances faculty qualification standards and aligns the preparation of Filipino nurses with the evolving demands of healthcare delivery and higher education. The Philippine healthcare system continues to face increasing demand for highly trained nursing professionals capable of assuming advanced clinical, research, academic, and leadership roles. According to the World Health Organization1, nurses constitute the largest segment of the global health workforce. Yet, many countries continue to experience shortages of highly skilled nursing professionals capable of delivering specialized care and strengthening health systems. Nursing students are presented with limited opportunities for structured career progression and constrains the country’s capacity to expand nursing research, improve evidence-based practice, and strengthen healthcare leadership. The proposed measure establishes a legal framework for advanced nursing programs that cultivate expertise in clinical practice, research, health policy, leadership, and nursing education, while raising qualification standards for faculty engaged in graduate instruction. It likewise institutionalizes community-oriented learning and research that respond to the healthcare needs of underserved and vulnerable populations. These reforms require legislative action because they redefine the structure of nursing education under Republic Act No. 9173 and establish enduring national standards that cannot be achieved through administrative issuances alone. Filipino nurses have long carried the country’s reputation for excellence in 1 World Health Organization. (2025). State of the world's nursing 2025: Investing in education, jobs, leadership and service delivery. World Health Organization. Accessed from: https://www.who.int/publications/b/78362. Accessed on July 25, 2026. healthcare through their competence and dedication to patients both locally and around the world. Providing them with opportunities for advanced professional education will develop a new generation of nurse leaders, researchers, educators, and healthcare innovators who can strengthen patient care, contribute to evidence-based health policies, and respond effectively to emerging public health challenges. More importantly, the measure creates pathways for highly skilled nurses to further their careers within the country, allowing their expertise and experience to directly benefit Filipino communities, particularly those who remain underserved. Supporting advanced nursing education is therefore not only an investment in the nursing profession but also a commitment to building a stronger, more resilient, and more responsive healthcare system for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11286
title: AN ACT DEFINING GOOD CONDUCT AND PROVIDING CONDITIONS FOR THE GRANT OF GOOD CONDUCT TIME ALLOWANCE, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE ARTICLE 97 OF ACT NO. 3815, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REVISED PENAL CODE”, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10592
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish clear and objective conditions for the grant of Good Conduct Time Allowance (GCTA). It further amends Article 97 of Act No. 3815, otherwise known as the “Revised Penal Code”, as amended by Republic Act (RA) No. 10592, to strengthen the administration of sentence credits while preserving GCTA as an incentive for genuine rehabilitation. RA 10592 recognizes good conduct as a basis for reducing the period of imprisonment and encourages persons deprived of liberty to reform while serving their sentences. However, the lack of uniform standards to determine whether an inmate has earned sentence credits often lead to inconsistent assessments, which undermines the confidence in the fair and accountable administration of the GCTA. The proposed measure establishes the standard for determining good conduct based on an inmate’s demonstrated conduct and participation in rehabilitation, productive activities, restorative efforts, and institutional discipline. It recognizes that sentence reduction must be administered with due regard to the gravity of the offense, public safety, and the interests of victims and their families. Thus, it retains the GCTA for offenders who demonstrate meaningful compliance toward rehabilitation; and excludes persons convicted of heinous crimes. A credible correctional system must encourage reform without weakening accountability. This vital piece of legislation shall ensure that sentence credits are granted on the basis of demonstrable conduct rather than inconsistent standards. It therefore reinforces the integrity of the correctional system, recognizes genuine rehabilitation, and protects public confidence in the administration of criminal justice. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11287
title: AN ACT CREATING FLIGHT STANDARDS INSPECTORATE CENTERS UNDER THE CIVIL AVIATION AUTHORITY OF THE PHILIPPINES IN VISAYAS AND IN MINDANAO, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9497, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CIVIL AVIATION AUTHORITY ACT OF 2008”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish at least one (1) Flight Standards Inspectorate Centers (FSIC) each in Visayas and Mindanao under the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP). It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9497, otherwise known as the “Civil Aviation Authority Act of 2008”, and strengthens CAAP’s capacity to implement and enforce civil aviation safety standards. CAAP is mandated to regulate, supervise, and oversee civil aviation activities in the country. The concentration of a single FSIC in just one (1) region constrains the timely conduct of surveillance, certification, licensing, and other regulatory processes in distant areas. Thus, establishing additional FSICs shall provide extension services for these functions in Visayas and Mindanao. The proposed measure establishes FSICs which shall abide by International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices. They shall also certify commercial air transport and general aviation operators, approve training and maintenance organizations, and issue airmen licenses to qualified applicants within Visayas and Mindanao. This improves regulatory accessibility, strengthens monitoring capability, and allows the CAAP to deliver aviation safety services more efficiently. For an archipelagic nation where distance and geography often determine access to services and opportunities, the State must continue to improve the capacity of its aviation institutions to deliver timely and effective regulatory oversight. This vital piece of legislation brings aviation safety functions closer to the people and industries that depend on them. It strengthens the foundation of public trust in air transportation, supports balanced regional development, and safeguards the continued growth of Philippine civil aviation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11288
title: AN ACT CREATING ADDITIONAL DIVISIONS IN THE COURT OF APPEALS, INCREASING THE NUMBER OF COURT OF APPEALS JUSTICES FROM SIXTY-NINE (69) TO SEVENTY-EIGHT (78), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 129, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUDICIARY REORGANIZATION ACT OF 1980”, AS AMENDED, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to increase the number of Associate Justices from sixty-nine (69) to seventy-eight (78). It amends Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, otherwise known as the “Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980”, and improves the accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness of the justice system. According to the Supreme Court of the Philippines (2024)1, the judiciary continues to experience substantial appellate caseloads that require sustained institutional strengthening to preserve the constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases. The concentration of appellate divisions in Metro Manila also imposes additional logistical burdens on litigants, lawyers, witnesses, and government agencies coming from far-flung regions. This often results in higher litigation costs and delays in the administration of justice. This proposed measure decentralizes appellate services in the country and establishes permanent regional stations in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Every unresolved appeal represents individuals, families, businesses, and communities waiting for justice to take its course. Delayed appellate review prolongs uncertainty and burdens those who seek the protection of the law. Strengthening the Court of Appeals through expanded judicial capacity and broader regional accessibility shall bring the administration of justice closer to the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 Supreme Court of the Philippines. (2024). 2024 Supreme Court Annual Report. According to the Supreme Court of the Philippines (2024)1, the judiciary continues to experience substantial appellate caseloads that require sustained institutional strengthening to preserve the constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases. label: HB 11289
title: AN ACT TO INCLUDE OTHER BACCALAUREATE DEGREES TO THE LATERAL ENTRY PROGRAM FOR LINE AND TECHNICAL OFFICERS, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE SECTION 33 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the lateral entry program of the Philippine National Police (PNP). It amends Section 33 of Republic Act (RA) No. 6975, otherwise known as the “Department of the Interior and Local Government Act of 1990”, and expands the professional qualifications eligible for appointment to line and technical services, and establishes appropriate entry ranks. RA No. 6975 only identifies certain professions for lateral entry into the PNP technical services despite the growing operational requirements of a modern police organization. This bill includes professionals in fields such as physical and sports therapy, psychology, nutrition and dietetics, and other technical professions. It also recognizes qualified PNP personnel and creates a more structured pathway for career advancement and organizational development. A modern police organization requires more than traditional law enforcement capabilities. It demands specialized knowledge and diverse expertise to effectively respond to emerging threats and increasingly complex public safety concerns. A broader and more clearly defined lateral entry system shall enable the PNP to draw from a wider pool of qualified professionals. This shall maximize the expertise of its existing personnel and strengthens its capacity to provide an avenue for professional development within the service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G.
