label: HB 11290
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR INCENTIVES TO MEMBERS OF THE LEGAL PROFESSION ENGAGED IN THE DEFENSE OF THE RIGHTS OF INDIGENT INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8371, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES’ RIGHTS ACTS OF 1997”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to ensure that Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) have immediate access to legal assistance. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997, and provides tax incentives to lawyers who render pro bono legal services to ICC/IPs. Although RA No. 8371 recognizes and protects the rights of ICCs/IPs, other members of these communities do not have immediate access to legal representation when the situation calls for it. Mainly due to poverty, geographic isolation, and the complexity of legal proceedings involving ancestral domains, it prevents them from effectively asserting and protecting their rights guaranteed under the Philippine constitution. This bill empowers the National Commission on Indigenous People (NCIP) to appoint counsels de oficio for indigent ICC/IPs with pending cases. It also encourages lawyers to provide pro bono services through tax incentives. The call for justice for one of the country’s most vulnerable sectors is of utmost importance and thus shall be prioritized. This measure reinforces the State’s constitutional duty to recognize, protect, and promote the rights of indigenous people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11291
title: AN ACT RESTORING THE REGULATORY AND STABILIZATION FUNCTIONS OF THE NATIONAL FOOD AUTHORITY, STRENGTHENING DIRECT FARMER SUBSIDIES, AND ENSURING THE ACTIVE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY AND PEOPLE’S ORGANIZATIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8178, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “AGRICULTURAL TARIFFICATION ACT”, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to restore the National Food Authority’s (NFA) authority to perform market regulation and price stabilization functions. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 8178, otherwise known as the “Agricultural Tariffication Act”, and authorizes the NFA to procure palay directly from local farmers at competitive support prices and regulate rice warehouses and grain business operators to deter hoarding, price manipulation, and the circulation of smuggled rice. Agriculture remains a vital pillar of the Philippine economy, yet Filipino rice farmers continue to face depressed farmgate prices, rising production costs, and increasing competition from imported rice. While RA No. 11203, otherwise known as the “Rice Tariffication Law”, liberalized rice importation to stabilize consumer prices, its implementation has also diminished the regulatory functions of the NFA. Consequently, many small-scale farmers remain vulnerable to market volatility, while consumers continue to experience fluctuations in rice prices. The bill expands direct input subsidies under the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund, supports crop insurance and community-based post-harvest facilities, and ensures the meaningful participation of farmers’ organizations and civil society organizations in the formulation of rice industry policies. It further authorizes the Department of Agriculture to suspend the issuance of rice import clearances during peak harvest periods, following mandatory consultation with farmer representatives, to prevent the artificial depression of farmgate prices. Restoring the NFA’s regulatory mandate and expanding direct support to farmers shall contribute to a more resilient, competitive, and sustainable rice industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11294
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS, PROFESSIONALIZING AND STRENGTHENING THE BARANGAY HEALTH WORKFORCE, PROVIDING FOR THEIR REGULAR EMPLOYMENT, JUST COMPENSATION, BENEFITS, RIGHTS, AND SECURITY OF TENURE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay health workers (BHWs) are the first and often the most accessible link between Filipino families and the public health system. They assist in maternal and child care, immunization, disease prevention and surveillance, health education, patient navigation, community mobilization, and the maintenance of local health information. Their work is indispensable to a primary care-led health system and to the effective implementation of universal health care. Yet many BHWs continue to serve under uncertain volunteer arrangements, receive widely varying honoraria, and remain vulnerable to displacement whenever local political leadership changes. This situation undervalues essential community health work, much of which is performed by women, and weakens continuity of care at the barangay level. This measure combines professionalization with a comprehensive framework for the rights, welfare, development, and organization of BHWs. It provides for standardized registration and competency certification, continuing education, a national information 1 system, progressive creation of regular plantilla positions, a minimum Salary Grade 1 entry level for employed BHWs, security of tenure, minimum benefits for volunteer BHWs during the transition, and national assistance to local governments with limited fiscal capacity. The bill also protects BHWs against discrimination and political interference, recognizes their right to organize and participate in health policy discussions, and establishes clear grievance and appeal mechanisms. By investing in the people who sustain health care at the community level, the State strengthens both the dignity of BHWs and the reliability of public health services for every family. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11295
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS OF CHILDREN, PROVIDING ENABLING MECHANISMS FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION, MONITORING, ENFORCEMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES [ Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Title. This Act shall be known as the “Protection of Environmental Rights of Children Act.” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State: (a) To recognize, uphold, and protect the inherent dignity and worth of children and their fundamental right to a clean, healthy, safe, and sustainable environment; (b) To ensure that children’s rights are taken into account in environmental decision- making processes at all times and in all State instrumentalities, including situational analysis, environmental planning, implementation of interventions, and evaluation of impacts; (c) To implement programs, projects, and activities that promote sustainable development and environmental stewardship aligned with the environmental rights and well-being of children; (d) To hold relevant government instrumentalities, corporations, and citizens accountable for actions and decisions that adversely affect children’s environmental rights;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature. Children, however, experience environmental harm in a distinct, disproportionate, and often irreversible manner due to their physical, mental, and developmental vulnerabilities. Environmental degradation, climate change, pollution, unsafe water, hazardous living conditions, and disasters directly impair children’s rights to life, survival, development, health, education, and dignity. These harms also undermine the ability of future generations to enjoy a safe and sustainable environment. The Philippines is a State Party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), which obliges States to ensure the best interests of the child, the right to survival and development, non-discrimination, and the right of children to be heard in matters affecting them. Recent international standards further recognize the right of the child to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment as essential to the full enjoyment of all other rights. This measure seeks to operationalize these commitments by recognizing the environmental rights of children as enforceable legal rights, consistent with the proposed Protection of Environmental Rights of Children Act. It defines the substantive and procedural environmental rights of children, clarifies the obligations of State and non- State actors, institutionalizes child participation, strengthens child protection in environmental emergencies, and establishes accountability mechanisms with aggravated penalties when violations affect children. 1 By adopting a child-centered, rights-based, and intergenerational approach to environmental governance, this bill ensures that environmental protection becomes an instrument for safeguarding the present and future of Filipino children. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11296
title: AN ACT PROMOTING “SARILING KURYENTE” BY RECOGNIZING AND EMPOWERING HOUSEHOLDS, COMMUNITIES, FARMS, ENTERPRISES, ECONOMIC-ZONE LOCATORS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND OTHER END-USERS TO GENERATE, STORE, AND USE ELECTRICITY FROM RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES PRIMARILY FOR SELF-CONSUMPTION; ESTABLISHING SIMPLIFIED PERMITTING, INTERCONNECTION, NET-METERING, FINANCING, WORKFORCE-DEVELOPMENT, CONSUMER-PROTECTION, AND GRID- INTEGRATION MECHANISMS; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face high and volatile electricity costs. Households, farms, businesses, industries, and local communities remain exposed to imported-fuel price shocks, supply disruptions, natural disasters, and constraints in centralized power systems. Renewable energy technologies—particularly rooftop and on-site solar, battery storage, micro-hydro, biomass, and small wind systems—now allow electricity consumers to produce a substantial part of their own requirements. Yet many willing end-users are still discouraged by fragmented permits, uncertain interconnection rules, duplicative product requirements, limited financing, and delay in the approval and installation of net-metering facilities. Republic Act No. 9513, or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008, established net metering and other mechanisms for renewable energy development. Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, likewise recognizes the need for reliable, secure, and affordable electricity. The next step is to make distributed renewable energy practical and accessible not only for households and small businesses, but also for farms, cooperatives, communities, large enterprises, and economic-zone locators that seek to generate electricity primarily for their own use. This bill establishes a coherent national framework for “Sariling Kuryente.” It recognizes the right of qualified end-users to install and operate renewable energy systems for self- consumption, while preserving legitimate requirements for electrical safety, structural integrity, environmental protection, and grid reliability. The measure replaces an obsolete one-size-fits-all capacity approach with a connected-load framework: up to two hundred percent (200%) of verified connected load for systems without qualifying storage, and up to four hundred percent (400%) for systems with adequate energy storage, subject to technical standards. 1 The measure also provides a fairer net-metering design. Electricity exported within a billing period offsets an equivalent amount of electricity imported on a one-kilowatt-hour-to-one- kilowatt-hour basis. Exports beyond the consumer’s imports are credited at the applicable blended generation charge. Clear billing, carryover, and limited transfer rules are required, while the Energy Regulatory Commission retains authority to prevent double recovery and protect non- participating consumers. Permitting is simplified through a nationally uniform Unified Solar Permit, a single checklist, consolidated notices of deficiency, time-bound action, and a review pathway when a local office fails to act. The bill recognizes accredited domestic and international product certifications, discourages duplicative testing, establishes stronger post-market surveillance and warranty enforcement, and directs the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority to build a certified renewable-energy workforce. These safeguards are intended to expand deployment without tolerating unsafe equipment or unqualified installers. The bill further clarifies ownership of renewable energy certificates, creates financing windows subject to applicable fiduciary and public-finance laws, supports solarization of public facilities, and directs distribution utilities and system operators to plan for progressively higher renewable-energy hosting capacity. Ordinary network upgrades needed to meet approved hosting- capacity obligations are treated as utility system investments subject to ERC review, while purely applicant-specific facilities are governed by transparent and uniform cost-allocation rules. Distribution utilities may not use unsupported claims of grid saturation to defeat an application. Finally, the measure strengthens accountability. It prohibits unjustified delay, discriminatory requirements, unauthorized charges, falsified records, deceptive sales practices, and interference with lawful renewable-energy systems. Affected consumers may claim compensation for demonstrable loss of use caused by delay beyond prescribed periods, subject to fair exceptions and procedures. An inter-agency coordinating council, assisted by consumer, industry, labor, and technical representatives, will address implementation problems and report to Congress. By allowing Filipinos to produce more of the electricity they use, the State can lower exposure to volatile power prices, improve resilience, encourage domestic investment, create skilled green jobs, and reduce pressure on the national grid. Sariling Kuryente is therefore both a consumer-protection measure and a practical national energy-security strategy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11298
title: AN ACT REGULATING ADVERTISEMENTS ON GAMBLING-RELATED ACTIVITIES, PROVIDING LIMITATIONS AND SAFEGUARDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Gambling has become increasingly accessible and visible to the public due to the rapid expansion of digital platforms, online gaming services, social media, and other forms of electronic communication. While gambling activities may be subject to existing laws and regulations, the manner and extent to which gambling-related activities are advertised and promoted present emerging concerns that warrant appropriate legislative action. In the Philippines, gambling has long been part of the country's entertainment landscape. However, the rapid growth of online gambling, coupled with the widespread use of smartphones, social media, streaming services, and other digital platforms, has transformed the way gambling is promoted and accessed. Gambling-related advertisements can now reach Filipinos directly and repeatedly through the digital content they consume, including content viewed by minors. The increasing prevalence of gambling advertisements may contribute to the normalization of gambling as an ordinary form of entertainment or, more concerningly, as a means of earning money or addressing financial difficulties. This is particularly troubling for Filipino families and individuals who may be financially vulnerable and more susceptible to advertisements portraying gambling as a quick or easy path to financial gain. The use of celebrities, athletes, influencers, content creators, and other public personalities in gambling promotions may further enhance the appeal and perceived legitimacy of gambling, particularly among younger audiences. Similarly, gambling promotions integrated into sporting events, entertainment programs, social media content, and other popular forms of media can substantially increase public exposure to gambling-related messages. Of particular concern are advertisements that downplay the risks of gambling or create misleading impressions regarding the likelihood of winning. Representations that gambling can provide a reliable source of income, achieve financial security, or solve financial problems may encourage irresponsible gambling. Promotional offers, bonuses, and rewards may likewise be misleading when material terms and risks are not clearly disclosed. The State therefore has a legitimate interest in ensuring that gambling-related advertisements are truthful, transparent, and responsibly presented, while protecting minors and vulnerable persons from exploitative or deceptive marketing practices. Regulation of gambling advertising does not seek to prohibit lawful gambling activities, but to ensure that their promotion is consistent with consumer protection and the public welfare. This measure seeks to establish clear and comprehensive standards for gambling-related advertising and promotion in both traditional and digital media. It covers advertisements, sponsorships, endorsements, influencer and affiliate marketing, branded content, and other analogous commercial communications. It likewise provides for appropriate age-assurance measures, responsible gambling messages, restrictions on advertising directed toward minors, and safeguards against misleading claims concerning winnings, financial returns, bonuses, and promotional offers. The bill further promotes a whole-of-society approach to responsible gambling by providing for continuing public awareness and education on the risks of excessive, compulsive, and irresponsible gambling and on available counseling, treatment, rehabilitation, and support services. Ultimately, this measure seeks to foster a safer and more responsible advertising environment in the Philippines, balancing legitimate commercial interests with the State's responsibility to protect Filipino consumers, families, minors, and other vulnerable persons from harmful, deceptive, and irresponsible gambling promotion. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERNESTO “ERNIX” M. DIONISIO, JR. label: HB 11300
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PHILIPPINE SPORTS COMMISSION TO RECOGNIZE E- SPORTS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Video games as an industry and an activity have progressed alongside our society’s technological capabilities. From classic pixel games such as Pong and Tetris, to today’s triple A (AAA) titles such as the franchises of Resident Evil and Assassin’s Creed. The quality of today’s video games has indeed come a long way. Parallel to our technological progress is the number of people who play these games. With computers more accessible than ever, a large number of individuals across age brackets have turned to video games as one form of recreational activity, and in some instances, into full-time, professional, and culturally- relevant professions. Recently, the term E-Sports has been ingrained into the mainstream consciousness. What was seen as merely a recreation became a global phenomenon with the advent of games such as League of Legends, DOTA 2, Overwatch, and the like. For these games, several global tournaments are now held annually, with viewerships reaching millions, and pot sizes running into the millions of US Dollars. Indeed, the E-Sports scene had grown so large and prevalent that prize pools for events such as The International reach upwards of millions and millions of pesos, when converted. The rise of competitive video games has also caught on with major sporting events. In fact, the Southeast Asian Games now features video game titles as medal events. In a globally competitive sport that tests reflexes, spatial awareness, and technological access, amongst others, Filipinos must not fall behind. Philippine teams show the potential to go up the rankings in the worldwide E-Sports scene. That is why the State should offer its support towards this up-and-coming sporting events so we can proudly show the world just what the Filipino is capable of. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11301
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE INDISCRIMINATE DISPOSAL OF ELECTRONIC WASTE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With the onset and rapid development of technology, it follows that e-waste have also been increasing. E-waste are widely understood as various forms of electric and electronic equipment that have ceased to be of value to their users or no longer satisfy their original purpose.1 Electronic waste (e-waste) products have exhausted their utility value through either redundancy, replacement, or breakage and include both “white goods” such as refrigerators, washing machines, and microwaves and “brown goods” such as televisions, radios, computers, and cell phones. Every year, companies are releasing new electronic equipment which results into the ever-increasing waste. Given that the information and technology revolution has exponentially increased the use of new electronic equipment, it has also produced growing volumes of obsolete products; e-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams. Although e-waste contains complex combinations of highly toxic substances that pose a danger to health and the environment, many of the products also contain recoverable precious materials, making it a different kind of waste compared with traditional municipal waste. According to the WHO, e-waste constitutes one of the fastest form of solid waste streams in the world.2 This is a heavier burden in developing countries, such as ours, where informal and hazardous setups for the extraction and sale of metals are common. This leads to improper handling which may greatly affect human health of our people. In addition, manufacturing, reprocessing, and disposal of these products. The emission of fumes, gases, and particulate matter into the air, the discharge 1 World Health Organization. Available at: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/electronic-waste- (e-waste) 2 Ibid. of liquid waste into water and drainage systems, and the disposal of hazardous wastes contribute to environmental degradation. Thus, it is necessary that the disposal of e-waste be regulated. It is then for these reasons that this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11302
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE MULTI-HAZARD EARLY WARNING NETWORK, MANDATING A COMMON ALERTING STANDARD, PRESCRIBING AUTOMATIC AND LOCALIZED RULES ON THE SUSPENSION OF CLASSES AND WORK, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10639, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Amidst a changing climate and worsening natural disasters, early warning may sometimes spell the difference between safety, disaster, and even death. In the Philippines’ case, where typhoons after typhoons batter communities and send local economies to a halt, a warning system that advises early and in logical anticipation of impending disruption may allow for proper reaction in the part of citizens, institutions, schools, and the private sector, among others. Additionally, the poly-crises we are facing due to climate change and global warming, present a complex tapestry of natural disruptions that have found our disaster-response lacking. We are always playing catch-up. And we are still stuck with post-disaster action rather than pre-disaster preparedness. The poly-crises comes in multiple forms. It can be drought in one area, torrential rain in another. It can also be haze in some parts of the country, and unhealthy temperatures in others. What we need now, is to revamp and modernize our disaster warning systems so that we can plan, mitigate damage and loss, ease the burden of adaptation put on the individual, and overall, help with how the individual Filipino deals with a changing environment. Ours is an archipelago that is varied, storied, rich, and diverse. All the more reason to prepare and preserve our islands through more rigorous systems, innovative approaches, and maximizing the institutions that already exist. It is high time to consolidate and deliver early warning systems. It is high time we adapt before it is too late. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11303
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE OPERATION OF PRIVATELY-OWNED PARKING SPACES AND FACILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Republic Act No. 3262 or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, it is a declared policy of the State “to protect the interests of the consumer, promote his general welfare and to establish standards of conduct for business and industry.” To achieve the foregoing policy, the State endeavors to enact measures for the “protection against deceptive, unfair and unconscionable sales acts and practices. In line with the abovementioned policy and its commitment to enact the necessary measures, the State, through this Bill, will be able to properly regulate the operators of parking spaces and facilities which have been functioning without any form of regulation or standards of operation. As part of the various measures to be proposed, this Bill aims to impose a standardized grace period wherein vehicle users shall be under no obligation to pay for parking provided that they remain within the period prescribed. This particular measure effectively renders illegal the unconscionable practice of imposing a flat rate which is payable upon entry. Furthermore, this Bill aims to impose a standardized ceiling rate for all operators of parking spaces and facilities in order to control the imposition of unreasonably high and exorbitant fees. It must be noted that these measures are not proposed to dissuade the operators of parking spaces and facilities. These measures are imposed primarily under an ethical consideration in favor of the users or customers of the parking spaces and facilities. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11304
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SYSTEM OF NATIVE FLOWER PARKS, CREATING FOR THIS PURPOSE THE NATIONAL NATIVE FLOWER PARKS COUNCIL AND THE NATIVE FLOWER PARKS DEVELOPMENT FUND, PROMOTING THE CONSERVATION, PROPAGATION, AND PUBLIC APPRECIATION OF PHILIPPINE NATIVE AND ENDEMIC FLOWERING PLANTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every Filipino child knows the sampaguita. We string it into garlands. We give it to our mothers, to our teachers, and to the Santo Niño. We call it our national flower. Here is something most of us were never told: the sampaguita did not originally come from the Philippines. It was brought in from across the sea. Meanwhile, in our own forests and mountains, there are multiple species of jasmine that grow nowhere else in the world, and only few are aware of their names. Our country is home to more than nine thousand two hundred fifty (9,250) native plants.1 At least one out of every three is found only here, and nowhere else on Earth. Of our one thousand (1,000) orchid species, roughly seven out of ten grow only in these islands.2 By any honest measure, we are one of the most flower-rich countries on the planet. And yet most are not aware of this wonderous flora diversity. Our children grow up admiring the tulips of Holland, the cherry blossoms of Japan, and the lavender fields of France, places far from the realities and ecosystems of our own islands, while the waling-waling, the tayabak, and the Rafflesia bloom quietly in our own provinces, unvisited, unphotographed, and underappreciated. Recently, the Senate passed a measure declaring the waling-waling our national orchid.3 The harder truth is that the waling-waling is vanishing from the wild. We are naming our flowers faster than we are saving them. A title on 1 Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund, “Philippines – Species,” available at: https://www.cepf.net/our-work/biodiversity-hotspots/philippines/species 2 Henrylito D. Tacio, “Philippines' national orchid waling-waling faces extinction, conservation efforts urged,” Manila Bulletin, 06 July 2026, available at: https://mb.com.ph/2026/07/06/philippines-national-orchid-waling-waling-faces-extinction- conservation-efforts-urged 3 Ibid. paper does not water a plant. And where are these flowers? Not in Manila. They are in the Cordillera and in Apayao. In Samar and Palawan. In Davao, Bukidnon, and the Zamboanga Peninsula. They are in the provinces, in the same towns our people leave because there is no work, in the same barangays that wait longest for a road, in the same provinces handed the smallest sliver of our tourism money. The wealth is already there. It has been there for millions of years. The probinsya has been sitting on a treasure while being told it has nothing. This bill establishes a national system of Native Flower Parks, at least one in every region of the country, built in partnership with our local government units, people's organizations, the academe, and our indigenous communities. The Flower Parks will become pride you can touch. Pride you can smell. Pride that you can show off. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11312
title: AN ACT GRANTING PHILIPPINE CITIZENSHIP TO DAVID LORAN SISSON
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant Philippine citizenship to Mr. David Loran Sisson, an American national who has spent most of his life in the Philippines and has established deep and enduring ties to the country and the Filipino people. Mr. Sisson was born on September 24, 1991 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, United States of America. At the age of four, he moved with his family to General Santos City, Philippines, where his parents served as missionaries. He and his three siblings grew up in General Santos City and became immersed in Filipino culture and community life. In May 1998, his father established a church in General Santos City as part of the family's missionary work. From modest beginnings, their ministry expanded to reach thousands of children through weekly classes and developed various programs serving children, young people, persons with disabilities, widows, pastors, and members of the community. Their activities likewise included values formation programs involving police trainees and personnel, youth camps, pastors' conferences, a television ministry, a Bible institute, and a four-year Bible college. Having grown up in the Philippines, Mr. Sisson learned to communicate in Cebuano and Tagalog and developed strong personal and cultural ties with Filipinos. He pursued his college education at West Coast Baptist College in California from 2011 to 2015 and thereafter returned to a life closely connected with the Philippines. In 2015, Mr. Sisson became a full-time personal assistant to Filipino boxing champion and former Senator Manny Pacquiao. In 2016, he married Ruthie Alonzo Sisson, whose family is of Filipino descent, and the couple thereafter made the Philippines their home. They now have three children. For nearly three decades, Mr. Sisson's life has been closely intertwined with the Philippines. He spent his formative years in General Santos City, has participated in religious and community activities serving Filipinos, has established his family here, and has chosen the Philippines as the country where he intends to permanently reside and raise his children. His desire to become a Filipino citizen is therefore not merely incidental to his residence in the country, but is consistent with his longstanding attachment to the Philippines, his integration into Filipino society, and his commitment to continue living in and serving the country he considers his home. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. label: HB 11313
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RULES ON SYSTEM LOSS CAP OF ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832 AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE At every stage of the electric system—from generation power plants to substations of distribution utilities (DUs) up to household outlets—there are bound to be energy losses. System losses are inherent when electricity is transported from one place to another due to several reasons such as heat, noise, pilferage, and technical losses. The only way to zero-out system loss in the power system is to turn the power off. In a Senate Committee on Energy hearing conducted last 2017, a number of DUs presented simulations if reduction of technical losses to 5% will be required from them. Using 2017 financial parameters, Angeles Electric Corp. will need to spend P892 million, Cagayan Electric Power and Light Company will be needing P1.84 billion, and Meralco would have to spend P65.53 billion. Repeated simulations showed that the costs that the utilities will incur in investing on infrastructure will significantly outweigh any possible decrease in the system loss charge. Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) is a pass on charge to the consumers, hence it will eventually lead to electricity rate increases to customers. Since it is scientifically and technically impossible to eliminate system losses completely, governments and electric regulators around the world allow electric DUs to recover minimal system loss rates as part of their regulated charges. In the Philippines, the Congress enacted the Anti-Electricity Pilferage Act of 1994, which set an initial cap on losses that was gradually reduced over time. In 2017, the ERC issued a resolution further reducing the cap to its present level of 5.50 percent for private DUs and 12 to 8.25 percent for electric cooperatives. Recognizing the urgent need to mitigate the rapid increase of electricity rates while also taking into account the viability of distribution operations, this bill seeks to regulate and reduce system losses by institutionalizing a set of rules on the allowable systems loss cap of electric distribution utilities. As such, this measure is ultimately aimed at enhancing the efficiency and competitiveness of DUs in their delivery of electric service to the public. More importantly, this bill is envisioned to cushion the impact of electricity bill spikes to Filipino consumers as well as inflation and impending surges in fuel costs and other commodities. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly and sincerely sought. REP. SERGIO C. DAGOOC APEC Party-List REP. PRESLEY C. title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE RISE RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to create the Philippine Rise Resource Development Authority as the lead agency responsible for the management, protection, study, and development of the Philippine Rise. It ensures that the State effectively exercises its sovereign rights over the area and manages its resources in accordance with national interests and principles of sustainable development. Formerly known as Benham Rise and renamed under Executive Order No. 25, series of 2017, the Philippine Rise is a vast undersea plateau within the Philippines’ Exclusive Economic Zone and continental shelf. It includes the area recognized as part of the Philippines’ extended continental shelf under the recommendations of the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS). Its natural resources, scientific value, and strategic location create opportunities for research, fisheries, energy, maritime connectivity, investment, and tourism. This bill provides a development framework for the Philippine Rise that shall guide the coordination, implementation, and monitoring of programs, projects, and activities in the area. It shall facilitate public and private investments, provide technical and planning assistance, and recommend policies that support the sustainable and long-term development of the Philippine Rise. The measure strengthens the State’s capacity to assert and protect its rights over the Philippine Rise and to ensure that its resources serve the Filipino people. It recognizes the Philippine Rise not merely as an area of economic and scientific potential, but as a national asset whose protection, responsible development, and preservation are matters of enduring national interest. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11315
title: AN ACT CREATING PERMANENT SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICER POSITIONS IN ALL PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE AND ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND SECURITY PROGRAM FOR ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to create permanent School Security Officer (SSO) positions in all public schools, and establish a comprehensive school safety and security program for all public and private basic education institutions nationwide. The right to quality education cannot be fully realized when learners and school personnel remain exposed to preventable threats within school premises and during school-related activities. Schools must first and foremost maintain an environment that protects its community from physical, psychological, digital, and other hazards that may compromise their safety and well-being. The bill creates permanent SSO plantilla positions under the Department of Education (DepEd). This ensures that school security in all public schools is supported by a stable workforce rather than relying solely on contractual or outsourced personnel. Private schools shall likewise comply with applicable safety and security requirements, with compliance as one of the conditions to renew their license and permits. Through these, this measure establishes a baseline of protection while allowing security measures to respond to the emerging risks and threats. School safety must not depend on whether or not a tragedy has already occurred. Every learner deserves to enter a school knowing that measures are in place to protect them, and every parent deserves the assurance that the institution entrusted with their child’s education is prepared to keep them safe. The State must act before lives are lost, not only after. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11316
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING WORKPLACE BULLYING, HARASSMENT, AND OTHER FORMS OF VIOLENCE, PROVIDING FOR ITS PREVENTION, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to prohibit workplace bullying, harassment, and other forms of violence. It provides for its prevention, reporting, investigation, and resolution in both the public and private sectors. Workplace bullying may manifest in physical, verbal, psychological, social, digital, or financial forms. Repeated humiliation, intimidation, threats, malicious conduct, exclusion, and abuse of authority can cause physical, psychological, and emotional harm and cultivate negative workplace dynamics. Such conduct may also impair professional relationships, disrupt the performance of duties, and undermine a workplace culture founded on respect, fairness, and accountability. The bill establishes uniform standards for workplaces in the public and private sectors and defines workplace bullying to cover physical, verbal, psychological, social, digital, and authority-based conduct. It requires employers and heads of offices to adopt written anti-bullying policies, establish accessible and confidential reporting mechanisms, act promptly on complaints, and ensure impartial investigations with due process. It likewise requires the protection of complainants, witnesses, and persons who report or assist in an investigation from retaliation. Every worker deserves to perform his or her duties in an environment free from bullying, intimidation, humiliation, and abuse. Workplace dignity should be protected as a matter of law, not left to the discretion or goodwill of certain employers or offices. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11317
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING DRUGSTORES IN EVERY BARANGAY IN THE COUNTRY, TO BE CALLED AS “BOTIKA NG BARANGAY”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to create a Botika ng Barangay (BNB) in every barangay in the country and make essential medicines more accessible and affordable to Filipino families. It directs the Department of Health (DOH) to implement a nationwide establishment program within three (3) years, with priority to economically depressed and underserved communities. The DOH’s BNB program has brought affordable medicine closer to communities, but the continuing need to strengthen access to essential medicine calls for its institutionalization. A nationwide program of this scale requires a framework that shall ensure its continued implementation beyond administrative issuances. This measure establishes operational standards to make BNBs responsive to community needs. Each BNBs shall carry medicines included in the core list of the Philippine National Drug Formulatory and shall be managed by a trained BNB Aide. It further requires the establishment of a standardized inventory monitoring and replenishment system, with medicine supplies replenished at least once every quarter to prevent prolonged stockouts. A Botika ng Barangay must be a dependable community source of essential medicines, particularly for families who have limited access to commercial drugstores. Ensuring that every barangay has a reliable source of affordable medicines shall strengthen the State’s commitment to bringing essential health services closer to every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11318
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE ISSUANCE OF INJUNCTIONS AND TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDERS AGAINST WAGE ORDERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE ARTICLE 126 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to prohibit the issuance of injunctions and temporary restraining orders against the issuance, publication, implementation, or enforcement, or effectivity of Wage Orders. It amends Article 126, entitled “Prohibition against injunction” of Presidential Decree No. 442, otherwise known as the “Labor Code of the Philippines” to ensure that wage adjustments duly determined under the law are implemented without judicial restraint. Republic Act No. 6727, otherwise known as the “Wage Rationalization Act”, authorizes the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards (RTWPBs), under the supervision of the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC), to determine and adjust minimum wage rates based on prevailing economic and labor conditions through public hearings and tripartite consultations. Some parties, however, may seek temporary restraining orders or injunctions from regular courts to prevent the implementation of Wage Orders. The implementation of Wage Order No. NCR-27 on July 2026, which granted an Eighty-five pesos (Php 85.00) increase in the daily minimum wage of private-sector workers in the National Capital Region, was suspended following the issuance of a temporary restraining order by the Regional Trial Court of Pasig City in connection with a petition for declaratory relief filed by two private companies. Such judicial intervention can prevent a duly promulgated wage adjustment from taking effect even after the competent wage-setting bodies have completed the process prescribed by law. The bill expressly prohibits any court, tribunal, or other entity from issuing a preliminary or permanent injunction or temporary restraining order against the issuance, publication, implementation, enforcement, or effectivity of any Wage Order or resolution issued by the NWPC or the RTWPBs. It thereby protects the integrity of the statutory wage-setting mechanism and prevents duly determined wage adjustments from being rendered ineffective through judicial restraint. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11319
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REHABILITATION AND SUPERVISION OF CHILDREN EXEMPT FROM CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY WHO COMMIT SERIOUS CRIMES, ESTABLISHING REGIONAL REHABILITATION CENTERS FOR YOUTH, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006”, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Regional Rehabilitation Center for Youth (RRCY) in every region of the country, under the direction of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), with an Intensive Juvenile Intervention and Support Center in each RRCY. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9344, otherwise known as the “Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006”, as amended by RA No. 10630, to strengthen the rehabilitation and supervision of children exempt from criminal responsibility who commit serious crimes. Despite the enactment of RA No. 9344, as amended, the increasing number of cases involving children in conflict with the law provides an opportunity to strengthen the existing rehabilitation system. The current framework places significant responsibility on local government units (LGUs) for the establishment and operation of Bahay Pag-Asa facilities which results in uneven capacity to provide secure and specialized care. The bill transfers the primary responsibility for specialized residential rehabilitation to the DSWD, and strengthens the protection and assistance afforded to victims and their families. It likewise preserves the right of victims to recover restitution, indemnity, damages, and other civil remedies notwithstanding the child’s exemption from criminal liability. The protection of children and the protection of society are not competing obligations. A just juvenile justice system gives children a genuine opportunity to change while giving victims, families, and communities the assurance that serious offenses will be met with meaningful intervention and appropriate action. This measure gives the State the capacity to fulfill both responsibilities, because rehabilitation must be a system capable of protecting lives, restoring families, and giving children the chance to return to society as better and more responsible individuals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11320
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE NATIONAL AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES EXTENSION SYSTEM TO ACCELERATE AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT, CREATING THE BUREAU OF AGRICULTURAL EXTENSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The agriculture and fisheries sector remains fundamental to the Philippine economy and to the country's food security. Yet despite the sector's importance, farmers and fisherfolk continue to face persistent challenges in productivity, technology adoption, market access, climate resilience, and access to timely and appropriate technical assistance. The latest data of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) show both the importance of the sector and the continuing need to strengthen the systems that support our agricultural producers. In 2025, the value of production in Philippine agriculture and fisheries reached approximately P1.79 trillion at constant 2018 prices. Agriculture, forestry, and fishing likewise grew by 3.1 percent in 2025 and accounted for 7.9 percent of the country's GDP. However, growth in the sector remains uneven. The PSA reported that in 2025, the value of livestock production declined by 2.3 percent, while fisheries production declined by 0.3 percent in value. The volume of crop production also registered a decline in the fourth quarter of 2025, with palay production down by 5.2 percent during the period. The PSA's latest 2025 Official Poverty Statistics estimate that 9.7 percent of Filipinos, or approximately 11.08 million people, were living below the national poverty threshold in 2025. While national poverty has declined, poverty reduction must continue to reach the communities whose livelihoods depend heavily on agriculture and fisheries. At the same time, the government already recognizes the importance of agricultural extension as a means of transferring knowledge, technology, skills, and innovations from government institutions, researchers, and other stakeholders directly to farmers and fisherfolk. The Agricultural Training Institute continues to conduct capacity-building programs for agricultural extension workers and has been strengthening digital planning, monitoring, and evaluation of the agriculture and fisheries extension system. In 2026, ATI undertook initiatives to strengthen the competencies of agricultural extension resource persons and improve the use of its extension planning and monitoring system. Despite these efforts, there remains a need for a stronger, more coherent, adequately funded, and professionalized national extension system. The proposed measure therefore seeks to strengthen the national agriculture and fisheries extension system by transforming and strengthening the Agricultural Training Institute into a Bureau of Agricultural Extension (BAE) that will serve as the national apex organization for a unified and efficient extension system. The measure provides for a national Agricultural Extension Development Roadmap covering ten (10) years, stronger coordination among the Department of Agriculture, Commission on Higher Education, state universities and colleges, local government units, national government agencies, farmers and fisherfolk organizations, civil society, and the private sector, and a more systematic delivery of education, training, technology transfer, farm and business advisory services, and other extension interventions. It likewise seeks to professionalize agricultural extension work by establishing a dedicated plantilla of personnel, providing opportunities for training and scholarships, developing career paths, strengthening qualification standards, and providing appropriate incentives and benefits to agricultural and fisheries extension workers. Particularly important is the provision requiring a minimum of three (3) agricultural and fisheries extension workers in every municipality, while giving existing LGU extension workers the opportunity to join the national system without diminution of their existing benefits. The proposed institutionalization of the Bureau of Agricultural Extension is therefore not simply an administrative reorganization. It is a strategic investment in the people who produce the country's food. A strong agricultural sector requires not only seeds, machinery, irrigation, credit, infrastructure, and markets. It also requires people on the ground who can bring knowledge and technology to farmers and fisherfolk, understand their problems, connect them with institutions and markets, and help them adapt to changing economic, technological, and climatic conditions. By strengthening the national agricultural and fisheries extension system, this measure seeks to ensure that government assistance reaches farmers and fisherfolk more effectively, that public investments in agriculture generate greater impact, and that Filipino agricultural producers are equipped with the knowledge, skills, and support necessary to become more productive, competitive, resilient, and economically secure. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 11321
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR MULTI-FAITH PRAYER AND QUIET ROOMS IN PUBLIC OFFICES AND PUBLIC-FACING ESTABLISHMENTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a diverse nation composed of people belonging to different religions, denominations, and belief systems. The Constitution protects the freedom of religion and guarantees the free exercise thereof. Despite this constitutional protection, many Filipinos who are away from their homes, places of worship, or communities may have limited access to an appropriate and peaceful space for prayer, reflection, meditation, or quiet contemplation while transacting business or accessing services in public offices and other public places. This measure seeks to promote inclusivity and respect for religious diversity by providing for the establishment or designation of Multi-Faith Prayer and Quiet Rooms (MFPQRs) in government offices and encouraging their establishment in public-facing establishments. The proposed MFPQRs are intended to be neutral spaces that may be used by persons of different faiths, as well as individuals who simply need a quiet place for reflection. The measure does not promote or favor any particular religion. Rather, it seeks to provide reasonable accommodation while upholding the constitutional principles of religious freedom, non-discrimination, and inclusivity. The measure also provides practical standards for these facilities, including cleanliness, adequate lighting and ventilation, appropriate flooring, signage, flexible spaces, and, when practicable, an accessible ablution area. It recognizes, however, that the availability of space and resources may vary among government offices and establishments. For local governments, the bill provides that the voluntary establishment and maintenance of MFPQRs may be recognized as a non-obligatory indicator under the Seal of Good Local Governance. It also allows MFPQR-related projects to be considered among eligible projects under the Local Government Support Fund, subject to existing budgetary rules. Ultimately, this measure seeks to promote a more respectful, inclusive, and accommodating public environment where every Filipino, regardless of faith or belief, may have a safe and peaceful space for prayer, reflection, or quiet contemplation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 In 2025, 74% of Filipino adults were able to correctly answer at least half of six basic financial literacy questions, an improvement from 69 percent in 2021. However, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas noted that while understanding of risk and diversification is relatively strong, knowledge of interest rates, particularly compound interest, continues to lag. These findings show that progress in financial literacy does not mean that financial education is no longer needed. There remain important areas of personal finance that workers need to better understand in order to make informed decisions about their income, savings, debt, investments, and financial security. 31 This proposed measure now seeks to address this gap by requiring employers to provide a Personal Finance Education Program for their workers and employees. The employer is placed at the center of this measure because the workplace provides a practical and reliable avenue for reaching workers. Requiring financial education to be provided through the workplace therefore allows the State to reach a broad segment of the working population without requiring workers to seek out financial education on their own time or expense. 38 A regular paycheck does not automatically lead to financial security. For many Filipino workers, the challenge is not only earning enough, but knowing how to manage what they earn, prepare for emergencies, deal with debt, protect their income, and plan for the future. 42 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 44 45 46 REP. Declaration of Policy. – The State recognizes the vital role of the private sector in nation-building and shall 5 encourage its active participation in fostering sustainable economic 6 development and environment protection in the Philippines. 34 Towards this end, the government shall mobilize its various agencies, in coordination with nongovernment and people's organizations, to work hand-in-hand for the integration, promotion, and strengthening of corporate social responsibility in all business organizations. 39 SEC. 3. Corporate Social Responsibility. - All business organizations established and operating under Philippine laws, whether domestic or foreign, are hereby encouraged to observe corporate social responsibility in the operation of their businesses in the country. 44 As used in this Act, corporate social responsibility (CSR) refers to the commitment of business to contribute on a voluntary basis to sustainable economic development I working with relevant stakeholders to improve their lives in ways that are good for business, sustainable development agenda and society at large. CSR- related activities shall include the following: 50 (a) Charitable programs and projects; (b) Scientific research; (c) Youth and sports development;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Businesses have the resources to make a significant difference in the communities that sustain them. Corporate Social Responsibility allows businesses to use those resources not only for growth, but also to support education, health, environmental protection, disaster relief, poverty alleviation, community development or any other charitable purposes they prefer. 27 Existing laws already provide tax deductions and other incentives for donations and charitable activities that serve the public. While these measures encourage businesses to contribute to society, there is also a need to give corporations greater flexibility in allocating their resources to better plan these activities. 32 Under existing law, stock corporations are generally prohibited from retaining surplus profits in excess of one hundred percent (100%) of their paid in capital stock, subject to the lawful provided exceptions. This proposed measure seeks to recognize Corporate Social Responsibility as an additional legitimate purpose for which surplus profits may be retained, provided that the CSR projects or programs are duly approved by the board of directors. 39 By giving corporations greater leeway to retain and devote a portion of their profits to CSR, the measure seeks to encourage businesses to undertake programs that create lasting benefits for their employees, communities, and the environment. 43 The measure does not compel businesses to give away their profits. Rather, it gives corporations that are willing to do more the flexibility to use their resources for purposes that extend beyond the interests of their shareholders and contribute to the welfare of the communities in which they operate. 48 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. label: HB 11324
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING FOOD WASTE REDUCTION AND PREVENTION EDUCATION IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, PROMOTING RESPONSIBLE FOOD CONSUMPTION AMONG LEARNERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Food waste remains a pressing challenge in the Philippines, with substantial quantities of edible food discarded daily despite the continued prevalence of food insecurity and hunger. Many Filipino students likewise attend classes with inadequate nutrition, adversely affecting their learning, school participation, and overall development. Addressing food waste not only promotes food security but also supports better educational outcomes for learners. Schools play a vital role in shaping lifelong values and habits. Integrating food waste reduction and prevention into the basic education system will enable learners to appreciate the value of food, practice responsible consumption, and understand the link between food waste, nutrition, environmental sustainability, and climate change. Equipping teachers with the necessary knowledge and instructional resources will further ensure that these principles are effectively integrated into classroom instruction and school activities. This measure seeks to institutionalize food waste reduction and prevention education in all public and private basic education institutions through curriculum integration, teacher capacity-building, and school-based initiatives that promote responsible food management. By fostering a culture of responsible consumption among learners, this bill advances the State's commitment to quality education, food security, environmental protection, and sustainable development. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. NINA FRANCESCA P. title: AN ACT RECLASSIFYING AND CONVERTING PARCELS OF TIMBERLAND WITH A TOTAL AREA OF SEVENTY-SIX THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED NINETY-FIVE SQUARE METERS LOCATED IN POBLACION, BACACAY, ALBAY INTO ALIENABLE AND DISPOSABLE LANDS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land is highly valued not only because it is the people’s shared heritage, but also because it is an essential factor of production. Land is a witness to the struggles, dreams and aspirations of those who labor hard on it as well as those who unconscionably live off some poor tillers’ backs. Consistent with the constitutionally upheld principle that the use of property bears a social function, the use and ownership of lands are subject to reasonable restrictions by the State in order to promote distributive justice and optimized production. It is in the aforementioned context that this bill seeks to reclassify and convert parcels of timberland in Poblacion, Bacacay, Albay into alienable and disposable lands. The proposed disposable timberland covers a total of seventy-six thousand one hundred ninety-five (76,195) square meters which is a portion of the three hundred fifty-five thousand nine hundred forty-three (355,943) square meters timberland fringing the coastal areas of Bacacay. The area recommended for alienation and disposition had been thoroughly subjected to evaluation by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). The Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) initially expressed reservations against the reclassification as the identified assessed areas are prone to natural hazards like rain-induced landslides and floods. Further assessment, however, reconsidered that the 76,195 square meters portion of the current timberland is a built-up area, already inhabited and developed with concrete structures. Thus, reclassification and conversion will enhance the integration into the local government unit’s development plan of: 1) sustainable land use, 2) human settlements, 3) food production, 4) environmental protection, 5) infrastructure requirements, and 6) disaster risk reduction. Additionally, the legitimization of economic enterprises established in the unconverted timberland would increase the LGU’s revenues. To allay the apprehensions relative to susceptibility to hazards, the bill provides for health and safety and environmental safeguards that include: 1) declaring areas within the high hazard zones not suitable for commercial, industrial, residential and institutional development, and for evacuation centers; 2) construction of appropriate high integrity flood control mitigation structures, and 3) strict implementation of the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act (R.A. 9003). In view of the foregoing, approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CIELO KRISEL B. label: HB 11330
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is not merely a geographic feature; it is the ecological backbone of Luzon and the country’s primary natural shield against increasingly devastating tropical cyclones. As the widest remaining tropical rainforest in the region, its ecosystems store carbon, sustain endemic biodiversity, and regulate critical climate and water flows. Despite its irreplaceable role in national survival, water security, and disaster resilience, the Sierra Madre remains under severe threat from illegal logging, destructive mining, wildlife trafficking, and unchecked land conversion. Current conservation efforts are severely hampered by fragmented governance and misaligned economic incentives. Existing decision systems permit extractive and conventional development to generate immediate financial returns, while transferring the heavy ecological costs—such as flooding, landslides, and water insecurity—directly to the public. Furthermore, the institutions, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities acting as long-term stewards of the landscape do not receive reliable support proportionate to the essential ecosystem services they maintain. This bill seeks to correct this systemic imbalance by enacting the “Sierra Madre Mountain Range Protection, Conservation, and Sustainable Development Act”. It establishes the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA), an attached agency under the Office of the President, tasked to spearhead a 25-year comprehensive Sierra Madre Master Plan. This measure shifts the paradigm toward an integrated, ridge-to-reef, landscape-scale approach, establishing binding ecological limits and no-go areas across the entire mountain range. Crucially, the measure introduces a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy for climate and disaster risk investments. It pioneers the Sierra Madre Nature Credit System, which requires Covered Enterprises—businesses that financially benefit from or materially depend on the mountain's ecosystem services—to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby mobilizing private capital directly to the lawful rights holders and communities protecting the area. To deter environmental crimes, the bill institutionalizes the Sierra Madre Environmental Enforcement System (SMEES) and creates a specialized Anti- Illegal Logging Task Force and Forest Protection Corps, supported by satellite and geospatial monitoring technologies. It also mandates strict accountability, requiring those who cause environmental damage to fully restore affected ecosystems independently of other existing penalties. All these interventions are designed to interface seamlessly with existing laws, strictly safeguarding the rights of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) to their ancestral domains and customary governance. Protecting the Sierra Madre is an urgent matter of national security and intergenerational equity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11336
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000,” TO RECOGNIZE WASTE THERMAL TREATMENT AS AN ENVIRONMENTALLY SOUND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT OPTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000,” established a comprehensive framework for the proper management of solid wastes, emphasizing source reduction, reuse, segregation, recycling, composting, resource recovery, and the proper treatment and disposal of residual wastes. However, more than two decades after its enactment, the country continues to face serious solid waste management challenges. Increasing waste generation, limited waste diversion and recovery capacity, and inadequate treatment and final disposal facilities continue to place pressure on local governments and communities. Recent incidents underscore the urgency of strengthening the country’s solid waste management system. In January and February 2026, major trash slides occurred at sanitary landfills in different parts of the country, resulting in loss of lives and persons reported missing. These incidents prompted the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to undertake a nationwide review of operating sanitary landfills. More recently, on August 11, 2026, tons of garbage were reported to have clogged the water channel linking Parañaque and Pasay, underscoring the continuing challenge of keeping critical waterways and drainage systems free from solid waste. These incidents, although different in nature, highlight the need for a more comprehensive solid waste management system that addresses not only waste generation and diversion, but also the safe and proper treatment and final disposal of residual wastes. This proposed measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 9003 to expressly recognize Waste Thermal Treatment as an environmentally sound option for the treatment of residual solid wastes, subject to strict environmental, health and safety safeguards and compliance with applicable laws, rules and regulations. It defines Waste Thermal Treatment and Waste Thermal Treatment Facility and establishes a regulatory framework for their establishment and operation. The measure does not intend to make thermal treatment a substitute for waste prevention, segregation, recycling, composting, or other waste diversion measures. Rather, it provides an additional treatment option for residual wastes remaining after feasible source reduction, reuse, segregation, recycling, composting, and other waste diversion and recovery measures. Waste Thermal Treatment Facilities shall not be used to undermine or replace mandatory waste diversion programs under Republic Act No. 9003. To ensure safe and environmentally sound operations, the measure requires compliance with applicable emission and environmental quality standards, proper waste characterization and feedstock management, the use of appropriate and environmentally sound technology, continuous monitoring and reporting, and proper management and final disposal of ash and other residues. The necessary environmental permits and authorizations must also be secured before a facility may operate. The establishment of Waste Thermal Treatment Facilities shall not be mandatory for every province, city, or municipality. Such facilities may be established or utilized only where warranted by the applicable local solid waste management plan, waste characterization, technical and economic feasibility, environmental safeguards, and availability of appropriate feedstock. The measure likewise directs the DENR, in consultation with concerned agencies, local government units, and other stakeholders, to establish detailed technical and environmental standards for their operation. The proposed amendments seek to strengthen, and not weaken, the ecological solid waste management framework established under Republic Act No. 9003. By providing a properly regulated treatment option for residual wastes that cannot feasibly be diverted, the measure seeks to complement existing waste diversion programs, reduce pressure on limited treatment and final disposal capacity, and enable local governments to manage residual wastes more safely, efficiently, and sustainably. For the Filipino people, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11337
title: AN ACT FURTHER AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000,” AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11898, BY MANDATING E-COMMERCE PLATFORMS AND DIGITAL MARKETPLACES TO COMPLY WITH EXTENDED PRODUCER RESPONSIBILITY FOR PLASTIC PACKAGING WASTE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The exponential rise of the digital economy has transformed retail and consumer behavior across the Philippines. While e-commerce platforms and digital marketplaces have provided unparalleled convenience and expanded market access for thousands of businesses, this shift has also resulted in a dramatic surge in single-use plastic waste. Daily parcel deliveries generate vast amounts of secondary and tertiary packaging materials such as bubble wrap, plastic mailers, courier pouches, and adhesive tape. The use of such secondary and tertiary packaging materials created a severe burden on local solid waste management systems and marine ecosystems. In 2022, Republic Act No. 11898 amended Republic Act No. 9003 (the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000”) by institutionalizing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). This framework mandates large product producers to recover and manage their post-consumer plastic footprint. However, a critical regulatory gap persists regarding online retail logistics: the majority of e-commerce parcel packaging bypasses the EPR regime because individual micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) sellers do not qualify as "obliged enterprises," leaving the platform-facilitated plastic footprint largely unaccounted for. This bill seeks to address that loophole by extending EPR obligations to large-scale operators of e-commerce platforms and digital marketplaces. Specifically, this measure proposes to: a) explicitly define platform operators as product producers responsible for the aggregate plastic packaging generated through their networks; b) establish criteria for "obliged enterprises" in the e-commerce sector based on total assets, revenue, and logistics infrastructure (e.g., fulfillment centers, sorting hubs, and warehouses; and c) mandate a centralized digital tracking mechanism requiring platforms to monitor, account for, and compute the total platform-facilitated plastic footprint generated by transactions and third-party merchant deliveries. By requiring digital marketplace giants to take full institutional responsibility for the plastic waste generated through their ecosystems, this bill ensures a level playing field, supports circular economy initiatives, and protects our environment from mounting packaging waste. Further, the mechanisms that will be created in this proposed legislation will ensure that the endeavours to minimize plastic waste will come from all fronts, making a more wholistic effort to protect the environment. For the Filipino people, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
