label: HB 11382
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO WORKERS IN CRITICAL INDUSTRIES DURING A STATE OF CALAMITY OR EMERGENCY OR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY 24 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 27 Section 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Hazard Pay for Workers in Critical Industries Act.” 30 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — The State shall promote the protection of all workers and ensure their health and safety during a state of calamity or emergency or public health emergency concern. Towards this end, workers in critical industries shall be provided with additional benefit for the duration of these events, taking into account the nature of their functions and exposure to various hazards by reason of their functions.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When calamity strikes, most people are told to stay home for safety. There are, however, workers who cannot simply “stay home”. While communities seek safety, these workers continue to report for duty, keep hospitals operating, deliver food and medicine, maintain essential utilities, transport people and goods, and ensure that vital services continue. 27 These workers face greater risks to their health and safety precisely when their services are most needed. Their families also bear the worry and uncertainty of having a loved one leave home to serve others during dangerous conditions. 31 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to grant hazard pay equivalent to at least twenty five percent (25%) of the worker's daily basic salary to qualified workers in critical industries who actually render service during a state of calamity, emergency, or public health emergency. The State must, in turn, recognize the sacrifice of those who continue to serve the public in these trying times. Those who keep our communities running in times of calamity and emergency should not be left without additional protection and compensation. Their service is essential, and so is their safety. 39 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 41 42 43 REP. JERNIE JETT V. label: HB 11383
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR MANDATORY INSURANCE COVERAGE, BENEFITS AND HAZARD PAY FOR JOURNALISTS, EMPLOYEES OF MEDIA ENTITIES ON FIELD ASSIGNMENTS AND FREELANCE JOURNALISTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 Section 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the "Journalists Protection Act of 2026.” 32 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policies and Objectives. - The State recognizes the invaluable role of the free press in the protection and promotion of democracy, good citizenship, civic mindedness, and good governance. Towards this end, the State shall provide the necessary support to ensure that the journalists are properly compensated and insured as they practice their profession.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Journalists go where the story takes them, even when that means entering places where others are trying to escape. In conflict areas, disaster zones, and other dangerous surroundings, they risk their safety and their lives simply to bring the truth to the public. 26 Behind every journalist who goes into harm's way is a family waiting for their safe return. When injury, disability, or death occurs, the consequences are not borne by the journalist alone, but also by the loved ones who depend on them. 30 This proposed measure seeks to provide mandatory insurance coverage and hazard pay for journalists, field assigned media employees, and qualified freelance journalists exposed to dangerous conditions in the performance of their work. Their duty to inform the public should not come at the cost of leaving them and their families without adequate protection. 36 Those who risk their lives so that the public may know what is happening deserve the assurance that, when the worst happens, they and their families will not be left without support. 40 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 42 43 44 REP. title: AN ACT CREATING A TRIPARTITE COUNCIL TO ADDRESS UNEMPLOYMENT, UNDEREMPLOYMENT, AND THE JOB-SKILLS MISMATCH PROBLEM IN THE COUNTRY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 SECTION 1. Declaration of Policy. – It is declared the policy of the State to promote the sustained development of a skilled citizenry and maintain a reservoir of national talents consisting of Filipino scientists, entrepreneurs, professionals, managers, high-level technical manpower, and skilled workers and craftsmen in all fields. Skills development can reduce unemployment and underemployment, increase productivity, and improve the standards of living. 35 To this end, the State shall ensure the relevance and adequacy of academic courses in the higher education curriculum and training programs offered in technical-vocational institutions in relation to the needs and requirements of the business and industry sectors and the over-all human resource requirement of the country pursuant to its economic development goals. 41 SEC. 2. Creation of a Tripartite Council. – There is hereby established a Tripartite Council, hereinafter referred to as the Council, that shall formulate policies and programs to address the job-skills mismatch in the country. It shall be a coordinating body among the government, academe and industry sectors to primarily monitor economic trends in the global and domestic markets, including those pertaining to business and commerce and the local labor market, and to generate information relative to employment, unemployment, underemployment, and job-skills mismatch. The Council shall be made up of representatives from the government, academe, and industry. 51 The government representatives shall be composed of the following: a Commissioner of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED); a Deputy Director-
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 The country already has government agencies responsible for education, technical training, employment, and industry. However, these efforts are handled separately. There is no single body that specifically specializes in regularly bringing government, academe, and industries together to monitor changes in the labor market, identify the skills employers need, and determine whether the courses and training being offered are keeping pace with those needs. 29 Without this coordination, gaps can remain between what students are taught and what the labor market requires. 32 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to create a Tripartite Council composed of representatives from government, academe, and industry. The Council will regularly gather information on employment, unemployment, underemployment, and skills requirements, review existing academic and technical training programs, and recommend policies and programs based on the actual needs of the labor market. 38 Formal education and hands-on training should keep pace with the jobs available, and the skills of Filipino workers should keep pace with the needs of the industries that employ them. 42 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 44 45 46 REP. Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Bagong Paluwagan ng Bayan Act”. 34 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policies. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to pursue a program that emboldens the people to achieve financial autonomy through capacity building and self- financing activities. The Filipino people shall be encouraged to come together and undertake self-financing activities to inspire them to cultivate a culture of entrepreneurship, meet their basic needs, improve their financial resources, and promote income security. 41 In this regard, the State shall place great importance on facilitating easy and efficient access to necessary funds and credits, which are crucial elements in realizing the people's aspirations towards financial stability and self-reliance. 45 To achieve this end, the paluwagan, a traditional community fund pooling system for savings and investments, shall be formalized and strengthened for the protection and benefit of the people. Through this system, the people shall have access to affordable credit and financial assistance, and shall be empowered to engage in entrepreneurial activities and other forms of self-sustenance. 51 SEC. 3. Definitions. – As used in this Act: (a) Community Paluwagan refers to a small group of persons with residence or employment in a defined community, created in accordance with the
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 Every payday, Ana sets aside ₱500 for her paluwagan. She does this faithfully because she hopes that when her turn comes, the money will be enough to pay her child’s school expenses. She trusts the person keeping the contributions because the group is made up of people from her own community. 27 But when the time comes to collect her share, she learns that the money is no longer there. The person who managed the contributions has disappeared, leaving Ana and the other members with little protection and no clear way to recover their savings. 31 This is the risk faced by many Filipinos who rely on informal paluwagan arrangements. While paluwagan can help people save and access money for their needs, the absence of a clear legal framework and government supervision as well as intervention, when appropriate, can leave members vulnerable to fraud, misuse of funds, and poor financial management. 37 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to establish rules for the organization and operation of community paluwagan, provide supervision and safeguards for members' contributions, and give registered groups access to affordable credit, insurance, financial education, and entrepreneurship programs to make better use of the contributions without affecting liquidity. 43 For families who save what little they can, every contribution matters. Their trust and hard-earned money deserve protection. 46 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 48 49 50 REP. JERNIE JETT V. title: AN ACT PRESERVING THE INDIGENOUS GAMES OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 23 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 26 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Philippine Indigenous Games Preservation Act.” 29 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – Article II, Section 22 of the Constitution provides that the State shall recognize and promote the rights of indigenous cultural communities within the framework of national unity and development. Furthermore, Article 31.1 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples enjoins all State signatories to take effective measures to recognize and protect the exercise of the indigenous peoples’ rights which include the maintenance, control, and development of their cultural heritage, traditional knowledge and expression, oral traditions, literatures, designs, sports, and traditional games. 39 Pursuant to the aforesaid mandates, it is incumbent upon the State to lay down specific policy directives to promote the interest of our indigenous peoples, preserve the intangible cultural heritage as living heritage and help people connect with their historical roots. The State shall take the necessary steps to preserve the indigenous peoples’ games which serve as the best avenue for their self- expression, and for promoting peace, harmony, goodwill, and camaraderie among them. 47 SEC. 3. Indigenous Games. – The term “indigenous games” refer to the traditional sports and games distinctly connected and rooted in the traditions, customs, and practices, and reflect the rich cultural heritage of the different indigenous cultural communities or indigenous peoples, handed down from generation to generation such as bunong braso, ginnuyudan, hilahang lubid, kadang-kadang, karera sa sako, luksong-tinik, patintero, syato, unggoy-unggoyan. These include
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 The State has a responsibility to ensure that this heritage is not lost to modernization and changing ways of life. When an indigenous game disappears, a part of the culture and knowledge carried by generations may disappear with it. 26 Preserving these games therefore means preserving our cultural diversity, strengthening the identity of indigenous communities, and ensuring that future generations remain connected to their roots and the story behind it. 30 This proposed measure now seeks to preserve and promote indigenous games through regular competitions, educational activities, documentation, research, and continued community participation, in consultation with the indigenous peoples to whom these traditions belong. Cultural heritage is not only something to be remembered. It is something that must be kept alive. 36 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 38 39 40 REP. label: HB 11388
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE SAFE STORAGE AND SECURE CUSTODY OF FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10591, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “COMPREHENSIVE FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION REGULATION ACT,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10591, the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act, governs who may own a firearm in this country. It says almost nothing about what an owner must do with that firearm for the remaining hours of the day. Section 9 of the Act disposes of the entire question of safekeeping in a single sentence: that “a vault or a container secured by lock and key or other security measures” is an acceptable requirement. It fixes no standard for that container, imposes no continuing duty of custody, and attaches no consequence whatsoever to an owner or an accountable custodian whose carelessness places a deadly weapon within the reach of a child, a person in crisis, or a criminal. A locked drawer and a bank-grade safe are, under present law, legally indistinguishable. That silence has a body count. On June 22, 2026, two minors aged fifteen and fourteen opened fire at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, killing three students and injuring twenty others, fifteen of them by gunfire. The weapons were a Glock 17 pistol that was the service firearm of a Philippine National Police officer related to one of the assailants, and a .38-caliber revolver registered to a private security agency in Cebu City but kept in the home of a former security guard. On August 18, 2026, a minor killed two students and wounded nine others at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School, livestreaming the attack; the firearm was issued by the Bureau of Customs to his father. Between these events, authorities intercepted a fourteen-year-old at Lut-od National High School in Pinamungajan, Cebu, carrying a revolver said to belong to his grandfather. On September 18, 2026, a Grade 9 student opened fire at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, killing and wounding fellow students before taking his own life. These four incidents share a pattern that this Congress should find intolerable. In no case was the firearm a loose or black-market weapon. Every one of them was a firearm the State itself had licensed, registered, or issued — and in three of the four, the firearm had been placed in the custody of a public officer or a security professional. This is the gap the present measure closes, and it closes it at the point where the evidence says the failure actually occurs. This measure addresses the narrower and more tractable problem to which the last four tragedies point: the licensed, registered, and government-issued firearm that was lawfully acquired and then left within reach of a child. That firearm is already in the State’s records. Its custodian is already known. The only thing missing is a duty and a consequence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTONINO B. label: HB 11393
title: AN ACT ENHANCING CLIMATE RESILIENCE IN AGRICULTURE TO ADVERSE CLIMATE EVENTS BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE USE OF CROP CLIMATE CALENDARS, EQUIPPING FARMERS FOR CLIMATE- SENSITIVE DECISION-MAKING, AND PROVIDING ACCESS TO LOCALIZED WEATHER AND CLIMATE INFORMATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is highly vulnerable to climate-related hazards that threaten agricultural production, rural livelihoods, and food security. From 2012 to 2022, adverse weather and climate events caused average annual damages of approximately ₱44 billion to the country’s agriculture sector. Agriculture accounted for about 60 percent of total disaster-related property damage, making it the sector most affected by extreme climate events. 1 The continuing vulnerability of the sector is further demonstrated by data from the Department of Agriculture showing that agricultural production losses reached approximately ₱57.78 billion in 2024. These losses were attributed to El Niño, tropical cyclones, pests and diseases, volcanic activity, and other weather-related events. They affected approximately 1.4 million farmers and fisherfolk, damaged an estimated 993,823 hectares of agricultural land, and resulted in the loss of approximately 2.18 million metric tons of agricultural production.2 The increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events— including droughts, typhoons, floods, excessive rainfall, and prolonged periods of extreme heat—have caused substantial damage to crops, livestock, fisheries, agricultural infrastructure, and farm livelihoods. These events 1 Galang, Ivory Myka R., and Roehlano M. Briones. Culprit and Victim: Scenarios for Philippine Agriculture amidst Climate Change. PIDS Discussion Paper Series No. 2024-36, Philippine Institute for Development Studies, December 20, 2024. https://doi.org/10.62986/dp2024.36 2 Rappler. “Agri Losses Due to Calamities Hit P57.8 Billion in 2024.” Rappler, January 29, 2025. https://www.rappler.com/philippines/agriculture-losses-record-2024-due-calamities/ disrupt planting and harvesting schedules, reduce productivity, increase production costs, and threaten the stability of the country’s food supply. Climate change further intensifies these risks. Farmers, particularly smallholder farmers and those dependent on rain-fed agriculture, often make critical production decisions without timely, accessible, and location-specific information on weather and climate conditions. Without appropriate guidance on the timing of land preparation, planting, crop management, harvesting, and other farm activities, farmers may be exposed to avoidable losses. There is, therefore, an urgent need to strengthen the country’s institutional capacity for climate-resilient agriculture. The use of crop climate calendars can help align agricultural activities with local climate conditions, seasonal weather patterns, and projected climate risks. When combined with localized weather forecasts, climate advisories, early-warning systems, and appropriate technical assistance, these tools can enable farmers to make better-informed and climate-sensitive decisions. This measure recognizes that farmers must be at the center of the country’s climate adaptation and disaster-risk-reduction efforts. It seeks to institutionalize the development, updating, dissemination, and use of crop climate calendars for major crops and production areas; provide farmers with accessible and understandable weather and climate information; strengthen coordination among relevant government agencies, local government units, academic institutions, research organizations, and civil society organizations; and equip farmers with the knowledge and tools necessary to adjust their production practices in response to changing climate conditions. By promoting timely and localized decision-making, the proposed measure will help reduce production losses, improve agricultural planning, strengthen food security, and protect the livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolk. It will also support the adoption of climate-smart and science-based agricultural practices while ensuring that national climate-resilience initiatives respond to the actual conditions and needs of local farming communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11394
title: AN ACT CREATING A SYSTEM OF PARTNERSHIP BETWEEN LOCAL GOVERNMENTS AND CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS THROUGH THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A PEOPLE’S COUNCIL IN EVERY LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT, PRESCRIBING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Democratic governance is strengthened when citizens are given meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions that directly affect their communities. Civil society organizations—including people’s organizations, non- government organizations, labor groups, community organizations, professional associations, foundations, and other organized citizens—provide valuable knowledge, experience, and perspectives that can help the government identify local needs and develop more responsive policies. The proposed measure recognizes CSOs as partners in local governance and seeks to create a formal system through which their participation can become more consistent, organized, and effective. It defines CSOs and people’s organizations and establishes a registration system for qualified organizations operating within cities and municipalities. The bill proposes the establishment of a Local People’s Council in every local government unit, composed of accredited CSOs, to provide an institutional mechanism for citizen participation in local governance. Registered CSOs would be able to participate in joint undertakings with local governments involving basic services, capacity-building, livelihood, economic, environmental, cultural, and good-governance projects. The measure also provides for a convention of accredited CSOs to facilitate the organization of the Local People’s Council and requires the local Sanggunian to recognize the Council upon compliance with the prescribed requirements. The proposed People’s Councils are intended to give organized citizens a substantive role in the formulation and implementation of local policies and programs. Upon recognition, the Councils may elect or appoint representatives to LGU boards, councils, committees, task forces, and other special bodies; observe and participate in government deliberations; vote where authorized; evaluate government projects and activities; and propose legislation. The bill likewise provides for representation at the provincial level, thereby creating a mechanism through which community-level concerns can be elevated into broader local policy discussions.1 This framework builds upon Article XIII, Section 15 of the Constitution, which recognizes the role of independent and autonomous people’s organizations in enabling citizens to pursue and protect their legitimate and collective interests and aspirations through peaceful and lawful means. Meaningful participation, however, requires both institutional channels and practical means for citizens to communicate with the government. The bill therefore directs LGUs to provide the necessary facilities for the participation of People’s Councils, requires funding for CSO capacity-building and Council operations, and establishes information boards and suggestion boxes in accessible public places, with LGUs required to respond to suggestions within fifteen working days. By institutionalizing these mechanisms, the measure seeks to transform citizen participation from an occasional exercise into a continuing partnership between communities and local governments, promoting greater transparency, responsiveness, accountability, and public ownership of local development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11395
title: AN ACT TO INSTITUTIONALIZE AND ENCOURAGE PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN AGRICULTURE VILLAGE FARM MANAGEMENT (AVFM) ENTERPRISES AND SMALLHOLD FARMERS AND FISHERFOLKS IN ORDER TO HASTEN THE DOUBLING OF RURAL HOUSEHOLD INCOMES THROUGH THEIR ADOPTION OF BETTER PRODUCTION, PROCESSING, MARKETING, LOGISTICS AND FINANCING TECHNOLOGIES, AND BY ESTABLISHING ECONOMIES OF SCALE THROUGH SYNCHRONIZED COMMUNITY AGRICULTURE AND CONSOLIDATION OF PRODUCTION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State provides that it shall empower the agriculture and fisheries sectors to develop and sustain themselves by promoting industrialization and full employment based on sound agricultural development and agrarian reform and through market-oriented policies in agricultural production. For decades, the Government has introduced and implemented many affirmative action and support programs to help the Filipino farmers. Billion pesos in taxpayers' money have been spent on a wide array of programs and projects with the intent of boosting Philippine agriculture from its low levels of productivity. Most of the agriculture support programs have centered on government agencies providing not only the policy guidance and technology choices but also the personnel and extension workers, resources and inputs, credit and funding. Despite all the government initiatives and assistance in the agricultural sector, for most small-hold farmers, innovation and technology adoption have not advanced successfully. The country’s overall annual agricultural output reportedly shrank due to the decline in fisheries, livestock and crop production1. This Act seeks to adopt and encourage a new approach and direction in the development of the country’s rural sector with the objective of doubling our farmers’ incomes by capitalizing on the resources and technical expertise of professional agriculturists. It seeks to promote productivity-enhancing partnerships between small-hold farmers and the proposed Agriculture Village Farm Management (AVFM) enterprises formed by professional agriculturists and private sector investors. By linking the production and the marketing side of agriculture, this bill hopes to address the long-standing gaps of fragmented efforts of the State to alleviate the overall agricultural status of the country. If properly enacted, the bill should serve as a pillar for Filipino farmers in improving not only their income but also in ensuring sustainable agricultural and environmental practices, and most importantly in ensuring food security for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS Fifth District, Quezon City 1 Business World. label: HB 11401
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE COMPREHENSIVE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM ABUSE, NEGLECT, AND EXPLOITATION AND PROMOTION OF THEIR OVERALL HEALTH AND WELFARE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Ang kabataan ang pag-asa ng bayan.” This has been a line that has been used repeatedly to the point of cliché. However, it rings true then and it still rings true today. The youth will be the next nation builders of the Philippines. It is then necessary to realize that policies we will make today will ultimately affect them significantly in the future. Unfortunately, it is also a reality that their sector has been and is currently one of those marginalized and exploited. Their youth is sometimes seen as an instrument and opportunity for abuse. At least 17,600 cases of child abuse were reported in 2023 alone, with many such cases violating Republic Act No. 7610 or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation, and Discrimination.1 If we are going to believe in the potential that the youth has, it is equally important that they be protected from all kinds of abuse. The next generation is, and will still be, worth fighting for. It is for these reasons, and to strengthen the R.A. 7610, that further robust protection is given to children and the youth. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11402
title: AN ACT SETTING MINIMUM STANDARDS FOR THE OPERATION OF INTERNET CAFES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is an understatement when one says that technology has impacted our lives. Breakthroughs in communications technology, computing, and entertainment have significantly improved our lives and has enabled many individuals to pursue aspirations that were never thought of to be possible. As technology became faster, smaller, and cheaper more people have come into contact with it. With the rise of the internet and technology, internet cafes also sprouted one after the other. These internet cafes became community hubs in which this groundbreaking technology is made more accessible to the general populace. It is not far off to say that internet cafes are of vital importance in the daily lives of the people. Thus, it is the duty of the State to enact standards and regulations to see to it that these community hubs continue to perform their stated functions for the general populace in a safe and orderly manner; and to ensure that these facilities are used responsibly towards meaningful ends. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11403
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10870 OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE CREDIT CARD INDUSTRY REGULATION LAW
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Due to the advancement of technology, it cannot be denied that the use of credit cards has become indispensable in making consumer credit readily available to all Filipinos. It allowed Filipinos to transact conveniently without the need to shell out cash, plan purchases, and subsequently avail of advantageous rates in their purchases. With this growth in credit card use, some Filipinos have been taken advantaged by malicious and nefarious groups by noting their credit card information and details and have used these cards for their own gain. Fraudsters can get hold of one’s personal information in many ways, from hacking retailers to buying one’s data on the dark web, a shady corner of the internet that’s not accessible via search engines like Google. Or criminals can trick one into handing over your information through online scams. This is why we need to introduce more measures to protect consumers who are availing these credit card services. While there are laws currently in place that already aim to protect the consumers, the growing number of people being victimized despite these measures shows the need to introduce further programs and practices that will allow the public to trust the banking system and the convenience of using credit cards. It is for these foregoing premises that approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11404
title: AN ACT TO PROTECT FILIPINOS FROM THE HARMFUL EFFECTS OF TRANS- FATTY ACIDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) killed 43 million people in 2021, equivalent to 75% of all non-pandemic-related deaths globally.1 In the Philippines, NCDs account for 68% of all deaths and is the number one cause of mortality and morbidity in the country.2 One in every three Filipinos is likely to die before the age of 70 from one of the four major NCDs: cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), cancer, diabetes, or chronic respiratory diseases. CVDs, particularly coronary heart disease (CHD), account for nearly half of the world’s NCD related deaths. 2021 data shows that over 700,00 deaths in the country were due to NCDs,3 and is still trending upwards and may account more larger and larger share of premature deaths.4 High intake of trans-fatty acids (TFA) increases the risk of death from any cause by 34% and CHD mortality and morbidity by as much as 23% and 28%, respectively. Every year, more than half a million deaths are attributed to TFA globally. Dubbed as the “tobacco of nutrition,” TFA has no health benefits and is completely replaceable with no difference in taste or cost of food. Thus, the WHO published the REPLACE Technical Action Package as a road map towards a trans-fat free world. Denmark, Argentina, Thailand and Singapore have introduced policies to limit TFA consumption by banning partially hydrogenated oils (PHOs), the major source of TFA, and/or limiting TFA content in food. Countries that regulated TFA 1 Noncommunicable Diseases, World Health Organization, 25 September 2025, available at: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/noncommunicable-diseases 2 Health Philippines Alliance, available at: https://phealthalliance.ph/ncds-tracker/ 3 Ibid 4 Dexter Cabalza, “WHO: Premature death risk due to NCDs in PH among highest in region,” Inquirer, 18 October 2024, available at: https://globalnation.inquirer.net/252790/risk-of- premature-deaths-in-ph-due-to-ncds-among-highest-in-western-pacific-region have seen a significant decline in CHD deaths. Denmark’s regulation limiting TFA content to 2g per 100g of fat in food products contributed to a 75% reduction in CHD- related deaths. In Argentina, an estimated 301 to 1,517 cardiac deaths every year were averted by eliminating industrially-produced TFA, saving the government as much as USD 87 million in healthcare costs annually. The FDA Circular No.2021-028-A effectively banned TFA and is geared towards eliminating industrially-produced Trans-Fatty Acids (TFA) in the Philippines food supply chain.5 This Act aims to once and for all forbit TFA in the Philippine food supply chain. The importance of addressing the problem of CHDs and CVDs as a whole has never been more pronounced than now, as we recover from the pandemic early this decade, and pose to tackle emerging health risks as both the food industry and Filipino diet evolve. Now more than ever, the need for preventative health care and healthy lifestyle promotion must be realized in line with the vision of universal health care. According to the WHO, TFA elimination is considered as one of the simplest and most straightforward public health interventions to reduce the risk of CVDs and improve nutritional quality of diets. As more countries regulate TFA, countries without regulations become vulnerable to dumping of TFA-rich imported food. Together, let us protect all Filipinos from the harmful effects of TFA and promote healthy hearts for all. It is for these foregoing reasons that the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11405
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE PERSONNEL ECONOMIC RELIEF ALLOWANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In light of the consistently high inflation rate along with increases in various tax rates, the insufficient amount of the Personnel Economic Relief Allowance (PERA) of public school teachers has now become an alarming issue. In addition to the insufficiency, public school teachers, through the latest Salary Standardization Law (SSL) updates, only saw superficial grants vis-à-vis those granted to our uniformed personnel. As such, it has become necessary to grant the much-deserved increase in the benefits given to our public school teachers. Considering that the lowest salary grade available to teachers (i.e. Salary Grade 11 for Teacher I), after the first tranche of increase through the latest SSL falls far below the approximate living wage for a family of five, it is appropriate to increase the PERA of public school teachers by an amount which would, at the very least, initially cover for the said discrepancy. Hence, it is proposed in this Bill that the PERA granted to public school teachers must be increased to at least P8,000, an amount which would, at the onset, substantially cover the disproportion between the current monthly wage of public school teachers and the approximated living wage in the Philippines for a family of five. The State, through this increase, will be able to demonstrate its full commitment in enhancing and uplifting the living and working conditions of its employees, particularly those in the field of education. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11406
title: AN ACT PROVIDING TAX RELIEF IN AREAS UNDER A STATE OF CALAMITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Natural and human-induced calamities repeatedly inflict heavy loss of life, property damage, and prolonged disruption of basic services and local economies. In their wake, families and enterprises face severe cash flow stress from lost income and destroyed assets, even as tax obligations remain due and enforceable. This mismatch slows recovery and delays the return of normal economic activity. This measure establishes a predictable system of tax relief in areas placed under a state of calamity. It authorizes time-bound and clearly defined interventions that ease immediate burdens while preserving government revenues in the medium term, namely: 1. Extension of deadlines for filing returns and paying national taxes; 2. Suspension of penalties, surcharges, and interest during the relief period; 3. Deferment or partial waiver of tax obligations when warranted by the extent of damage and loss; 4. Suspension of the assessment and collection of real property taxes in affected localities for one fiscal year, with payments to resume afterward in staggered installments. To support private relief and rehabilitation efforts, the bill also grants an automatic exemption from donor’s tax for donations intended for calamity victims, subject to a ceiling that not more than ten percent of the donated amount may be used for administrative expenses. The policy goal is simple and practical: give disaster-stricken communities immediate fiscal breathing room so they can rebuild livelihoods, restore services, and restart local commerce, while setting clear rules for the resumption of obligations once minimal stability returns. By institutionalizing timely and targeted tax relief, the State affirms its duty to advance social justice, protect vulnerable sectors, and strengthen economic resiliency through partnership with local governments and the private sector. In view of the foregoing, the early passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. JAIME EDUARDO MARC D. label: HB 11407
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE AUTHORIZED BED CAPACITY OF THE CONGRESSMAN ENRIQUE "HENRY" M. COJUANGCO MEMORIAL DISTRICT HOSPITAL IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF MONCADA, PROVINCE OF TARLAC, FROM SEVENTEEN (17) TO ONE HUNDRED (100) BEDS, UPGRADING ITS FACILITIES, SERVICES, AND MANPOWER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Congressman Enrique "Henry" M. Cojuangco Memorial District Hospital (CEHMCDH) located in San Julian, Moncada, Tarlac, serves as a vital healthcare lifeline for its primary catchment areas spanning five (5) municipalities in Tarlac (Moncada, Paniqui, Anao, Pura, and San Manuel) and two (2) municipalities in Nueva Ecija (Cuyapo and Nampicuan), serving hundreds of thousands of residents. Since assuming office, the hospital administration of CEHMCDH has observed a steady and critical surge in its Bed Occupancy Rate (BOR) over the past several years. From 71.09% in 2022, the BOR rose sharply to 95.83% in 2023 and reached 176.87% in 2024. Currently, for the calendar year, the bed occupancy rate is an alarming 238%, forcing the hospital to use hallways as temporary areas to accommodate patients. Furthermore, the current nurse-to-patient ratio and overall manpower are severely stretched, structurally ill-suited to its meager authorized bed capacity of 17 beds. With the massive influx of patients and the expanding health demands of the community, the existing 17-bed capacity is grossly inadequate to deliver efficient, effective, and quality medical care. Upgrading the authorized bed capacity to one hundred (100) beds, alongside the corresponding enhancement of its facilities, medical equipment, and professional workforce, is an urgent necessity to bridge these healthcare gaps and ease the burden on both patients and healthcare providers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. JAIME EDUARDO MARC D. label: HB 11412
title: AN ACT IMPOSING EXCISE TAXES ON HIGH-SODIUM AND HIGH-SUGAR FOOD AND SWEETENED BEVERAGES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 150-B AND 288-A, CREATING A NEW SECTION 150-C, OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A healthy population is indispensable to national productivity and inclusive growth. The excessive intake of sodium and added sugars are dietary risk factors that drive the country’s most burdensome noncommunicable diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, all of which further contribute to chronic kidney disease (“CKD”). Diabetes and hypertension has been recognized as the two leading drivers of CKD, which was reported to contribute 50.62% and 23.26% to CKD worldwide, respectively.1 The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has found that approximately one- third of adults with diabetes have CKD, while approximately one-fifth of adults with hypertension have CKD.2 Diabetes and hypertension are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Since the cardiovascular system and kidneys are deeply interconnected, when one of these systems develops problems, it can lead to problems in the other. A UK Biobank study showed that about 5.6% of people with cardiovascular disease developed CKD within 10 years.3 1 Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Hepatitis C Work Group, "KDIGO 2018 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Prevention, Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Hepatitis C in Chronic Kidney Disease," Kidney International, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2018.03.018. 2 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "Risk Factors for Chronic Kidney Disease," U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, May 15, 2024, https://www.cdc.gov/kidney-disease/risk-factors/index.html. 3 Sophie Claudel et al., "Abstract 40: Risk of Incident Chronic Kidney Disease Among Subtypes of Prevalent and Incident Cardiovascular Disease: UK Biobank”, March 24, 2026, accessed at https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/cir.153.suppl_1.40. 1 Fiscal measures can reduce consumption of products that contain excessive levels of nutrients of concern while giving manufacturers a direct incentive to reformulate. A well- designed excise tax should therefore be objective, measurable, administratively workable, and structured so that a product can avoid or reduce the tax when its sodium or added-sugar content is lowered. This bill adopts that approach. For sweetened beverages already covered by Section 150-B of the National Internal Revenue Code, the bill retains the existing excise-tax framework but shifts calorically sweetened beverages toward sugar-concentration tiers. This aligns the tax more closely with the public- health objective by imposing a higher tax on beverages with more added sugar while preserving the existing treatment of beverages that use non-caloric sweeteners. Products already taxed under Section 150-B are not again taxed for sugar under the new Section 150-C. For prepackaged processed foods, it uses uniform nutrient concentrations per one hundred (100) grams and applies tiered specific excise taxes per kilogram of product. The use of a uniform one-hundred-gram basis avoids manipulation through artificially small serving sizes and creates a clear reformulation target. The tax is based on the highest applicable nutrient tier so that a single product is not subjected to cumulative sodium and sugar excises under the same section. Fresh and unprocessed basic foods, food prepared and sold for immediate consumption on-site, infant formula, and food for special medical purposes are excluded. The bill does not exempt particular high-sodium processed products merely because they are inexpensive. Instead, every manufacturer is given the same path to lower tax liability: reduce the sodium or added- sugar content below the statutory threshold. The measure also provides for inflation indexation of specific tax rates, objective rules for determining nutrient content, manufacturer and importer declarations subject to verification, a reasonable transition period for reformulation and compliance, and periodic review by Congress based on revenue, health, consumer, and industry effects. The revenues from the new food excise are dedicated to Universal Health Care, medical assistance and health facilities, and nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions. In this manner, the tax both discourages excessive consumption and helps finance the public health programs needed to address the diseases associated with unhealthy diets. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. _____________________________________ REP. HENRY “INDY” F. OAMINAL JR. label: HB 11413
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6770, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "OMBUDSMAN ACT OF 1989", GRANTING ANTI-CORRUPTION LAW ENFORCEMENT POWER TO THE OFFICE OF THE OMBUDSMAN
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 12, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution declares the Ombudsman and his Deputies as protectors of the people and directs them to act promptly on complaints against public officials and employees of the government. This constitutional mandate is further operationalized under Republic Act No. 6770, otherwise known as the “Ombudsman Act of 1989,” which vests the Office of the Ombudsman with broad powers to investigate and act upon acts or omissions of public officers and employees. The effective discharge of this mandate requires not only investigative and prosecutorial authority, but also an institutional capability to secure evidence, protect witnesses, enforce lawful orders, and undertake necessary law enforcement operations. Strengthening these capabilities will enable the Office of the Ombudsman to respond more effectively to acts of corruption, abuse, inefficiency, and other forms of misconduct in government. For this purpose, this measure seeks to establish an Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Service within the Office of the Ombudsman, to be known as the Ombudsman Marshal Service. The proposed Service is intended to provide the Office with a dedicated law enforcement arm capable of conducting proactive inspections, inquiries, investigations, arrests, detention, searches, seizures, and other lawful measures necessary for the effective implementation of the Ombudsman’s mandate. The bill likewise provides for the appropriate organization of the Office of the Ombudsman, including the Office of the Special Prosecutor and the Ombudsman Marshal Service, and defines their respective roles and authority under the supervision and control of the Ombudsman. It further provides for the necessary rank, salary, benefits, retirement privileges, staffing, and operational support for personnel performing these functions. Recognizing the importance of protecting witnesses, whistleblowers, detainees under investigation, and other persons placed in the custody of the proposed Service, the measure likewise provides for adequate facilities and appropriate safeguards. It also ensures that the implementation of the Service is supported by regular appropriations of the Office of the Ombudsman, with such augmentation as may be necessary for the sustained performance of its mandate. By strengthening the enforcement and institutional mechanisms available to the Office of the Ombudsman, this measure seeks to ensure that investigations are conducted effectively, lawful orders are carried out, evidence is secured, and cases involving corruption and other irregularities in government are pursued with greater efficiency and consistency. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 11419
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE TECHNICAL, VOCATIONAL AND LIVELIHOOD CURRICULUM FOR THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 Section 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “TVL Curriculum Act.” 30 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. The right to education shall be promoted with the end goal of producing graduates who are prepared to become civically active and economically productive members of society.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 After graduating from senior high school under the Technical, Vocational and Livelihood (TVL) track, a young Filipino applies for a job as an automotive technician. He has learned the fundamentals in school and has a senior high school diploma in hand. During the application, however, he is asked for a National Certificate and specific competencies required by the employer. He realizes that although he completed the TVL track, he does not have all the certifications and skills that the industry expects. 28 This situation reflects a gap that the TVL curriculum must address. For many students, choosing the technical and vocational education track is a deliberate choice to gain practical skills that can help them find work to support themselves and their families after graduation. They place their hopes in the skills they learn in school, trusting that these skills will open the door to a decent livelihood. Their education should therefore be closely connected to the realities of the workplace, giving them recognized certifications that employers value and significantly consider in employing them. 36 This proposed measure seeks to make sure that TVL graduates leave school with skills and National Certificates that can help them find work. They should not have to discover after graduation that the skills they learned are not enough for the job they want. 40 By bringing schools and industries closer together, and by specifically addressing what employers want, the measure seeks to give TVL graduates a fair chance to be hired, earn decent wages, and build a better life for themselves and their families. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 REP. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE SPECIAL PROGRAM IN CREATIVE ARTS FOR JUNIOR AND SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 24 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 27 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Special Program in the Creative Arts Act”. 30 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – The State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Moreover, the government is committed to fulfill its constitutional mandate to foster the preservation, enrichment, and dynamic evolution of a Filipino national culture based on the principle of unity in diversity in a climate of free artistic and intellectual expression and to place arts, design and other intellectual creative creation under the patronage of the State. 38 To this end, the State shall promote creative arts education, encourage arts programs, support national art competitions, and strengthen education for the development of creative industries. The State shall provide adequate training for students with artistic abilities, with the end in view of producing world-class artists with firm academic foundation and strong patriotic ideals. 44 SEC. 3. Objective. – The Special Program in the Creative Arts (SPCA) is hereby strengthened to provide a continuing source of artists of excellence and leaders in the preservation and promotion of culture, arts, and the creative industry in the Philippines. Admitted students shall be trained under a special curriculum oriented in the fields of architecture and allied arts, cinema, dance, dramatic arts, literary arts, music, visual arts, design, digital fabrication and new media, along with financial literacy, entrepreneurship skills, and basic knowledge on intellectual property rights, with the end in view of providing quality education to students while giving way to opportunities for a sustainable profession.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 A young Filipino student discovers that she has a gift for music. Another finds joy in painting, while another dreams of becoming a filmmaker, dancer, writer, or designer. They have the talent and the passion, but for many of them, the path to building a career from it is uncertain, if not expensive. Without proper training, guidance, and opportunities, many young artists eventually set aside their dreams and choose a different path simply because they don’t know where to start or where to better fluorish their talents. 29 Now, this proposed measure seeks to strengthen the Special Program in the Creative Arts by giving students specialized training in their chosen fields, access to experienced artists who can mentor them, and information on scholarships, college programs, and employment opportunities. Unlike similar existing programs, students will also learn how to manage their finances, start and manage a creative business, and protect their work through basic knowledge of intellectual property rights. Through these opportunities, students can graduate with stronger artistic skills, and a clearer path toward further education or a sustainable career in the arts. 37 The measure also seeks to strengthen the support given to SPCA schools by encouraging partnerships with the private sector and providing appropriate tax incentives for donations and the importation of equipment and materials needed for the training of students. 41 A young Filipino should not have to give up a talent simply because there is no clear sustainable path to pursue it. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 48 REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Republic Act No. 10912, or the Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016, recognizes the importance of continuing education for Filipino professionals. However, while CPD remains largely a requirement for maintaining professional credentials, it is without a clear system connecting CPD credits to career advancement, specialization, or higher qualifications. Access to CPD programs may also be difficult when training is costly, unavailable, or burdensome. 28 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to make CPD more meaningful by linking it with career progression and specialization, allowing professionals to earn and transfer credits toward recognized qualifications, while requiring government agencies and private employers to provide or support accessible and affordable CPD programs. 33 Continuing professional development should not simply be a requirement to maintain a license. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE CLIMATE DUE DILIGENCE, TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY OF THE STATE, ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE GREENHOUSE GAS INVENTORY AND ACCOUNTING SYSTEM AND THE CLIMATE ADVISORY COUNCIL, PROVIDING FOR THE PREPARATION, PUBLICATION AND REVIEW OF NATIONAL CLIMATE COMMITMENTS AND PLANS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice delivered its Advisory Opinion on the Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, rendered upon the request of the General Assembly. The Court held that the obligations of States in this field arise not only from the climate treaties but from customary international law; that limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius is the primary temperature goal of the Paris Agreement; that a State must exercise stringent due diligence and employ all means at its disposal, according to its capabilities and national circumstances, to prevent significant harm to the climate system; that the discretion of a State in preparing its nationally determined contribution is limited, and that such contribution must be capable of making an adequate contribution to the temperature goal and must reflect the highest possible ambition; that a State may incur responsibility where it fails to regulate the emissions of private actors within its jurisdiction; that climate effects, including downstream emissions, must be assessed in environmental impact assessment; and that the efforts of a State in this field may not be presented as entirely voluntary and exempt from scrutiny. The Court likewise affirmed that the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities is a core guiding principle, that the standard of conduct required is measured against the capabilities and circumstances of each State, and that breach of the obligations identified engages the ordinary consequences of State responsibility, including cessation, guarantees of non- repetition and full reparation. The year before, in its Advisory Opinion of 21 May 2024, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions constitute pollution of the marine environment within the meaning of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that States Parties owe a stringent obligation of due diligence to prevent, reduce and control it. The Philippines is an archipelagic State and a Party to that Convention. Under Section 2, Article II of the Constitution, the Philippines adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land. The customary obligations articulated by the Court are therefore already part of Philippine law. What is absent is the domestic machinery through which they are performed, recorded and made answerable. Republic Act No. 9729, as amended by Republic Act No. 10174, establishes a planning framework and a Commission, but it was enacted before the Paris Agreement and contains no duty to prepare a nationally determined contribution, no duty to maintain a greenhouse gas inventory, no duty to reconcile the national energy and development plans with the climate commitments the country has made, and no duty to report to Congress on whether those commitments are being met. The consequence is that the most consequential climate decisions of the State rest upon executive issuances that may be withdrawn without notice. The national greenhouse gas inventory system exists by Executive Order No. 174, series of 2014. The nationally determined contribution exists only as a submission to a treaty body. The National Adaptation Plan 2023-2050 has no statutory foundation at all. Climate change expenditure tagging rests upon a joint memorandum circular. A framework of this importance cannot rest upon instruments of this fragility. This bill supplies the machinery. It is important to state at the outset what it does not do. It does not establish a national emissions cap. It does not set a net-zero date. It does not create carbon budgets, and it does not convert the conditional component of the Philippine nationally determined contribution into a domestic legal obligation. Those omissions are deliberate and are matters of national interest, not of timidity. The Philippines accounts for less than one-half of one percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Our nationally determined contribution is expressly structured so that the greater part of our ambition is conditional upon the finance, technology and capacity-building that the instruments of the climate regime require developed country Parties to provide. That structure is the country’s position and its leverage. A statute which silently converted the conditional component into a domestic duty would surrender, for nothing, the very distinction upon which our claim to support rests, and would sit uneasily with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities which the Court has now affirmed. Section 7 of this Act therefore preserves the distinction expressly: the unconditional component is a duty of the State enforceable under this Act, and the conditional component is and remains contingent upon the means of implementation being actually provided. What the bill does establish is the conduct that the Court has held to be obligatory, and the record by which that conduct may be judged. It places the national greenhouse gas inventory on a statutory footing, with independent verification, mandatory submission of data by sectoral agencies and by large emitting establishments, and a particular requirement that the land use, land-use change and forestry account state its uncertainties, this being the account upon which our present contribution most heavily relies. It imposes a duty to prepare, publish and submit a nationally determined contribution and, for the first time, a long- term low greenhouse gas emission development strategy, which the Philippines has never adopted. It gives the National Adaptation Plan a statutory basis, adaptation having been recognized by the Court as a legal obligation and not a matter of policy preference alone. label: HB 11425
title: AN ACT REQUIRING CLIMATE AND DISASTER RISK SCREENING OF RESILIENCE PROJECTS, INSTITUTIONALIZING CLIMATE AND RESILIENCE EXPENDITURE TAGGING AND DISCLOSURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines does not lack laws on climate change and disaster risk reduction. It lacks any law that requires the money appropriated for climate and disaster resilience to actually reduce risk. Republic Act No. 9729, as amended by Republic Act No. 10174, establishes a planning framework. Republic Act No. 10121 establishes a disaster management system. Neither imposes on any agency or local government a duty to achieve a resilience outcome with the funds it receives, and neither provides a remedy when the funds are spent on works that do not reduce the hazard they were appropriated to address. The consequences of that gap are now a matter of public record. Flood control appropriations rose from roughly Seventy-Nine Billion Pesos (P79,000,000,000.00) in 2016 to more than Two Hundred Billion Pesos (P200,000,000,000.00) annually by 2021, without any corresponding change in how projects are selected, sited, disclosed or audited. What followed were ghost projects, substandard works, and structures built where they could not reduce risk or which displaced flooding onto communities downstream. Hazard information is not the missing element. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, modernized under Republic Act No. 10692, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority and the Mines and Geosciences Bureau produce the data. What is missing is any legal duty to consult it before a resilience project is designed, sited, funded, procured or built. A flood control structure may today be designed for historical rainfall, sited in a hazard zone, and built where it worsens flooding downstream, without any law being broken. This measure supplies the missing duty, and does so in the narrowest way that will work. It requires every resilience project to undergo climate and disaster risk screening and to obtain a Resilience Screening Certificate. The certificate states the hazard the project is meant to address, the hazard conditions projected over the design life of the project, the alternatives considered, the expected reduction in risk, and the effect of the project upon adjacent, upstream and downstream communities. The certificate is issued by a Resilience Screening Technical Panel composed of the agencies that already hold the hazard data, and not by the agency that proposes to build the project. An implementing agency cannot be permitted to certify to itself that its own project is well-sited and adequate to the hazard; that is the precise failure this measure is directed against. The Panel may issue the certificate, deny it, or issue it subject to conditions, and its action is appealable. The head of the implementing agency remains personally accountable for the truth and completeness of the application and for implementing the project in accordance with the certificate issued. The bill is deliberately modest in where it applies pressure. It contains no provision addressed to the contents of the National Expenditure Program or of the General Appropriations Act. Screening is required of the implementing agency as part of project development, before a project enters its pipeline and before detailed engineering design is commissioned. The certificate then operates as a condition precedent to the release of funds, to procurement and to award, all of which are matters of budget execution. Appropriations for items that remain uncertified are declared not to constitute savings, so that the requirement cannot be evaded by realignment. The bill creates no new department, bureau or office. The screening panel is composed of agencies that already exist and already produce the data on which it will act. The bill further institutionalizes in statute the climate and resilience expenditure tagging that has until now rested only upon a joint memorandum circular, requires an annual Climate and Resilience Budget Statement showing the certification status of every resilience item, mandates publication in machine- readable form within a fixed period, and requires the geotagging, as-built documentation and public marking of every resilience project. Compliance is secured by the nullity of any release or award made without a certificate, by the personal liability of the officers responsible, by the audit powers the Commission on Audit already possesses, by the right of any citizen to sue, and by the penalties provided in this Act. The question of a permanent body to conduct technical and engineering audits of public infrastructure is a substantial one, and it is reserved for separate legislation so that it may receive the deliberation it deserves without delaying the requirement established here. The right to a balanced and healthful ecology under Section 16, Article II of the Constitution, and the mandate that public office is a public trust under Section 1, Article XI, are not vindicated by appropriating larger sums for resilience. They are vindicated by ensuring that what is appropriated is spent on the right projects, at the right cost, at the right quality, by the right people, and delivered on time. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. label: HB 11426
title: AN ACT MANDATING COASTAL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES TO PROVIDE FREE EMERGENCY COMMUNICATION AND SAFETY GEAR TO MUNICIPAL FISHERFOLK, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL MARITIME SAFETY NETWORK, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Municipal fisherfolk constitute a vital productive force in the national economy, anchoring rural livelihoods and national food security while facing severe structural vulnerabilities, maritime risks, and a persistent lack of basic safety infrastructure within municipal waters. While the 1987 Constitution explicitly mandates the State to protect marginal fishers and advance social justice, small-scale producers remain exposed to sudden weather shifts, engine failures, and collision hazards without direct access to emergency response networks monitored by maritime authorities. The “Fisherfolk Safety at Sea Act” translates this constitutional obligation into a concrete operational framework by mandating coastal local government units to equip registered municipal fisherfolk with free waterproof two-way emergency radios, life vests, and emergency SOS distress beacons. Designed to respect the operational independence and daily realities of small-scale fishing without imposing restrictive bureaucracy, the bill mandates permanent equipment custody under Property Acknowledgement Receipts, eliminates burdensome clearance fees, guarantees automatic qualification through the Municipal Fisherfolk Registry, and secures direct funding through local disaster risk reduction resources supported by civil society collaboration. By strengthening local search-and-rescue capabilities and safeguarding the working conditions of small producers at sea, this measure advances a practical, rights-based policy that protects both the lives and the economic viability of our coastal communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A REAL-TIME MECHANISM FOR THE MONITORING OF FUEL PRICE MOVEMENTS AND THE AUTOMATIC GRANT OF EMERGENCY FUEL SUBSIDIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL FUEL PRICE VIGILANCE AND RAPID SUBSIDY COUNCIL, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE AHENSYA NG GABAY AT ALERTO SA PETROLYO OR AGAP UNDER THE OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Fuel price volatility constitutes one of the most immediate and disruptive economic shocks besetting the ordinary Filipino household. Every fluctuation in global crude oil benchmarks, or every depreciation of the peso vis-à-vis the United States dollar, is almost invariably and swiftly transmitted to pump prices, thereby imposing an undue burden upon public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers, tillers of the soil, fisherfolk, and low-income families who possess no adequate buffer against abrupt increases in the cost of living. Under the prevailing regulatory framework, the response of government to fuel price hikes remains largely reactive, ad hoc, and bereft of institutional permanence. While the Department of Energy (DOE) regularly monitors and publishes weekly pump prices, the grant of fuel subsidies — when extended at all — is customarily the product of piecemeal legislation or executive issuance, the formulation, funding, and implementation of which consume weeks, if not months. By the time relief is finally extended, the gravest impact of the price shock shall have already been absorbed by the sectors least equipped to bear it. It is in this regard that this Act serves as remedy to this deficiency. The proposed measure establishes the National Fuel Price Vigilance and Rapid Subsidy Council, otherwise known as the Ahensya ng Gabay at Alerto sa Petrolyo, or AGAP, under the Office of the President, and vests the same with the continuing mandate to monitor, in real time, domestic and international fuel price movements, and, upon the breach of a clearly defined price-hike threshold, to cause the automatic and immediate release of targeted fuel subsidies, without necessity of a new law or executive issuance for each such occurrence and in view of a prompt assistance to the country’s most vulnerable sectors during such tremors, which has become frequent these days. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 11428
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The recent school shootings in Tacloban City, Zamboanga City, and Banga, South Cotabato, have resulted in the loss of young lives and injuries to learners. These incidents have brought renewed urgency to the duty to protect children while they are in school. They also underscore the need for schools nationwide to be prepared to identify threats, respond promptly to emergencies, and support affected learners and personnel. School safety requires more than a response to an incident after it occurs. Schools must have clear preventive measures, accessible reporting channels, trained personnel, emergency protocols, and reliable referral systems. Learners and school personnel affected by violence must also receive appropriate care and assistance in returning safely to school. This bill seeks to institutionalize a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework for all public and private basic education institutions. It requires each school to adopt a School Safety Plan suited to its circumstances and establishes standards for learner protection, violence prevention, physical and digital safety, mental health support, incident response, and recovery. It further strengthens coordination among the Department of Education, other government agencies, local government units, families, and communities. The State has a duty to ensure that schools remain places where learners can pursue their education without fear and where school personnel can discharge their responsibilities in safety. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 11435
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly mandates that the State "shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." Furthermore, Article II, Section 13 underscores that the State "recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation- building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being." Implicit in these constitutional mandates is the obligation of the State to maintain learning environments where students, educators, and school workers can exercise their constitutional right to education free from physical harm, fear, and violence. However, our educational institutions—long revered as safe sanctuaries for learning and development—are increasingly being shattered by an unprecedented surge of violence. In recent months, a terrifying pattern of physical attacks, knife stabbings, and deadly shootings inside and immediately around school premises across the country has laid bare severe gaps in campus security, child protection, and early intervention mechanisms:  June 16, 2026 (General Trias, Cavite): A Grade 8 student armed with a kitchen knife entered a Grade 5 classroom at Bethel Academy and attacked seven young pupils without provocation, leaving two needing emergency surgery.  June 19, 2026 (Cavite City): A Senior High School student was repeatedly stabbed in the arm and back during a violent altercation inside Cavite National High School.  June 22, 2026 (Tacloban City): Two minors armed with firearms opened fire at San Jose National High School, killing three students and injuring 20 others.  June 23, 2026 (San Carlos City, Negros Occidental): A 17-year-old Grade 10 student was stabbed outside Julio Ledesma National High School due to a personal grudge.  July 1, 2026 (Zamboanga City & Bacolod City): Stabbing incidents erupted involving students at Cabaluay National High School in Zamboanga and near Sum- ag National High School in Bacolod.  July 31, 2026 (Las Piñas City): A 13-year-old Grade 9 student was fatally stabbed in the chest by a 14-year-old classmate right outside a classroom during recess at Las Piñas National High School.  August 18, 2026 (Zamboanga City): A tragic shooting incident inside the Junior High School premises of Ateneo de Zamboanga University left two dead.  September 18, 2026 (Banga, South Cotabato): A horrific campus shooting at Banga National High School claimed 3 lives and wounded 8 others. Between June and September 2026 alone, at least eight major violent incidents involving bladed weapons and firearms have resulted in 9 fatalities and over 40 injuries among learners. This alarming wave of campus violence—compounded by bullying, mental health crises, and the exposure of vulnerable youth to online radicalization and extremism— demands an immediate, structured, and comprehensive legislative intervention. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Comprehensive School Safety Framework. By adopting a whole-of-society and all-hazards approach, the measure strengthens institutional response mechanisms across prevention, preparedness, and recovery. Furthermore, it mandates seamless coordination among the Department of Education (DepEd), local government units (LGUs), law enforcement agencies, and community stakeholders to enforce strict access controls, mental health support, and child protection policies. In light of the constitutional duty to safeguard the youth and preserve the right to a secure, quality education, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 63 64 65 HON. label: HB 11436
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES PERSONNEL EXPOSED TO OCCUPATIONAL HAZARDS IN THE PERFORMANCE OF THEIR DUTIES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local government environment and natural resources personnel serve at the frontlines of environmental protection, conservation, solid waste management, pollution control, forest and watershed protection, environmental enforcement, and other environmental programs of local government units. The nature of their work regularly exposes some of these personnel to occupational hazards, including extreme weather, contaminated waste, polluted environments, dangerous terrain, poisonous plants, venomous animals, and other conditions that may endanger their health and safety. Recognizing these risks, the Philippine League of Local Environment and Natural Resources Officers, Inc. (PLLENRO-SOC), South Cotabato Chapter, through Resolution No. 01, Series of 2026, approved on July 26, 2026, requested the Representatives of the Province of South Cotabato to sponsor legislation granting hazard pay to qualified environmental workers regularly exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their official duties. While existing government compensation rules provide hazard duty pay under particular circumstances, there is a need for a specific statutory benefit for local environmental personnel who are actually exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their duties. This measure therefore seeks to recognize the risks borne by local environmental personnel by granting hazard pay when they are actually exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their official duties. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. __________________________________ FERDINAND L.
