label: HB 11437
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 19 The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the country’s most important natural sources. Stretching for more than 500 kilometers, it runs north-to-south along the entire eastern coast of Luzon, from Cagayan down to Quezon province.1 It is home to diverse wildlife, rivers, and a critical sanctuary for thousands of unique species. It is relevant not only to those areas near this mountain range, but also to the entirety of Luzon. 25 Perhaps the Sierra Madre's most well-known role is its function as a natural barrier and the country’s first line of defense against destructive tropical cyclones coming from the Pacific Ocean.2 As storms approach, the mountain range helps slow down and weaken their winds before they reach inland areas. This natural shield helps reduce the destructive effects of typhoons, protecting lives, infrastructure, ecosystems, and livelihoods. It also helps regulate water that supports communities and agricultural areas across the region.3 32 However, the “Backbone of Luzon” is in urgent need of protection. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre continues to face severe environmental degradation. Every year, the mountain range reportedly loses roughly 9,000 hectares of forest cover due to human activities, including illegal logging, agricultural expansion, mining, and other forms of 1 Climate Change Commission. (2024). Sierra Madre: Mountain range for resilience. Available at https://climate.gov.ph/news/934 2 Ibid. 3 Department of Environment and Natural Resources. (2026). DENR assists House committee in aerial inspection for proposed Sierra Madre Authority. Available at https://calabarzon.denr.gov.ph/news-events/denr-assists-house- committee-in-aerial-inspection-for-proposed-sierra-madre-authority/ 1 development.4 When the Sierra Madre loses its forest cover, its ability to absorb rainfall, regulate water flow, and reduce the impact of strong winds is also diminished. As forest degradation continues, communities in Central Luzon and Metro Manila may face greater risks of flooding and landslides. This proposed measure therefore seeks to establish the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA), which will lead the formulation and implementation of a comprehensive and long-term plan for the conservation, protection, and sustainable development of the Sierra Madre Mountain Range. It will also coordinate the efforts of concerned national government agencies and local government units to ensure a unified and sustained approach to the protection and development of the mountain range. The bill also proposes the creation of the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. This measure also promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples to participate in conservation and restoration activities. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, environmental charges, and grants and technical assistance. The Fund is limited to the SMMRA’s statutory functions and is subject to government accounting, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. The measure also strengthens accountability by establishing ecological standards, monitoring systems, environmental liability mechanisms, and stronger prohibitions against destructive activities. It prohibits, among others, unauthorized land conversion, destructive extractive activities, introduction of invasive species, unauthorized commencement of covered works, and the use of false compliance documents. The proposed legislation therefore seeks to move Sierra Madre governance from fragmented management toward an integrated, science-based, and investment-oriented system. It recognizes that protecting the Sierra Madre is an investment in the country’s overall well-being, which include food and water security, biodiversity, climate resilience, and disaster-risk reduction. 36 4 Sierra Madre losing 9,000 hectares of forest cover each year — Haribon. label: HB 11438
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING FOOD WASTE REDUCTION AND PREVENTION EDUCATION IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, PROMOTING RESPONSIBLE FOOD CONSUMPTION AMONG LEARNERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Food waste is a major socio-economic and environmental issue that impacts national food security, economic efficiency, and environmental sustainability. According to estimates from the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) Philippines and the Department of Agriculture, thousands of tons of edible food are wasted daily in the country, even as millions of Filipino families experience involuntary hunger and nutritional deficits. While supply chain inefficiencies and retail practices contribute significantly to food loss, consumer behavior—particularly wasteful consumption patterns—plays a critical role in generating preventable food waste. Establishing lifelong habits of mindful consumption, respect for food resources, and awareness of nutritional value must begin at an early age. Schools serve as the primary institutional setting for shaping the values, social consciousness, and daily behaviors of young citizens. By integrating comprehensive, age-appropriate food waste reduction, zero-waste principles, and responsible consumption education into the basic education curriculum, the State can foster a culture of sustainability among future generations. This bill seeks to institutionalize food waste reduction and prevention education across all public and private basic education institutions in the Philippines. It mandates the Department of Education (DepEd), in coordination with relevant agencies, to incorporate practical food management skills, zero-waste concepts, and agricultural literacy into existing curricular frameworks. Furthermore, it encourages schools to establish zero-waste canteen management guidelines, composting initiatives, and school garden programs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11439
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DISPLAY OF NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION ON THE MENUS AND MENU BOARDS OF FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution guarantees the protection and promotion of the right to health of the people and the instillment of health consciousness among them (Article II, Section 15). The Philippines has faced a rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and obesity. According to data from the Department of Health (DOH) and the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI), lifestyle-related conditions account for a significant portion of mortality in the country. A contributing factor to this trend is the shift in dietary habits, marked by an increased consumption of food prepared outside the home, which often contains high levels of sodium, saturated fats, added sugars, and total calories. While consumers are increasingly conscious of their health choices, they are often hindered by a lack of accessible and clear information regarding the nutritional value of the food they purchase in chain restaurants, fast-food outlets, and other commercial food establishments. Providing point-of-decision nutritional information empowers individuals to make informed, healthy dietary choices for themselves and their families. Similar policies implemented in other jurisdictions have encouraged food service operators to reformulate recipes to offer healthier alternatives, thereby fostering a culture of health responsibility across the food industry. This bill seeks to mandate standard food service establishments with five (5) or more branches to prominently display total calorie counts and core nutritional values on their menus, menu boards, and drive-thru displays. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11440
title: AN ACT MANDATING AND INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A PEOPLE'S COUNCIL IN EVERY CITY AND MUNICIPALITY IN THE PHILIPPINES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING MECHANISMS FOR CITIZEN PARTICIPATION IN LOCAL GOVERNANCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 16, Article XIII of the 1987 Philippine Constitution guarantees the right of the people and their organizations to effective and reasonable participation at all levels of social, political, and economic decision-making. Furthermore, Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, directs local government units (LGUs) to promote the establishment and operation of people's and non-governmental organizations to become active partners in the pursuit of local autonomy. Despite these constitutional and statutory mandates, civil society participation in many local government units remains consultative, informal, or merely symbolic. Citizens and sectoral organizations often lack a formal, institutionalized mechanism to directly participate in policy formulation, budget deliberation, program monitoring, and local governance. This bill seeks to mandate and institutionalize the establishment of a People's Council in every city and municipality across the Philippines. Inspired by successful local participatory models, such as the Naga City People's Council, this measure empowers accredited civil society organizations (CSOs), non- governmental organizations (NGOs), and sectoral groups to sit in local special bodies, attend legislative sessions, propose local measures, and participate directly in local decision-making processes. By providing a structured framework for civil society engagement, this legislation aims to deepen local democracy, ensure transparency, foster accountability, and guarantee that public policies genuinely reflect the needs of the community. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11441
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ELEMENTARY AND HIGH SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE, CREATING THE POSITIONS OF SCHOOL MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mental health is a fundamental component of overall well-being, directly influencing a child’s capacity to learn, build healthy relationships, and navigate life’s challenges. In recent years, the urgency of addressing mental health issues among Filipino youth has escalated significantly. Rates of anxiety, depression, and self-harm among primary and secondary school students have reached alarming levels, further exacerbated by modern social pressures, economic difficulties, and the aftermath of global disruptions. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the "Philippine Mental Health Act," and Republic Act No. 11206, or the "Career Guidance and Counseling Act," a severe gap remains in the actual delivery of mental health services within the basic education system. Currently, the public school system faces a catastrophic shortage of registered guidance counselors (RGCs), primarily due to low salary grades and non-competitive compensation structures. Consequently, thousands of elementary and high schools across the country operate without a single mental health professional on site. This bill seeks to address these critical vulnerabilities by establishing a comprehensive Mental Health Program in all public and private elementary and high schools nationwide and creating a dedicated mental health personnel positions with competitive compensation packages (adjusting salary grades for Guidance Counselors and creating Mental Health Associate positions) to recruit and retain qualified professionals. Prioritizing the mental health of our learners is an urgent social imperative. By building a resilient, supportive, and accessible mental health infrastructure within our schools, we safeguard the future of our nation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11442
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL CHILD RIGHTS AND RULE OF LAW EDUCATION PROGRAM, STRENGTHENING THE IMPLEMENTATION OF GOOD MANNERS AND RIGHT CONDUCT AND VALUES EDUCATION UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11476, PROVIDING FOR THEIR HARMONIZED INTEGRATION IN EDUCATIONAL AND YOUTH DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the vital role of our youth in nation-building and directs the State to promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. It likewise mandates the right of children to assistance and to special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. As a result, the Republic has enacted an extensive body of laws protecting children and learners from violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation, trafficking, bullying, discrimination, child marriage, online sexual abuse or exploitation, child sexual abuse or exploitation materials, and other threats to their safety and development. These include Republic Act No. 7610, as amended; Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630; Republic Act Nos. 10173, 11476, 11510, 11596, 11650, 11930, 12080, and 12199; and other child-protection, education, mental- health, disability, and data-privacy laws. These laws provide important substantive protections. Yet a legal right cannot fully protect a child who does not know, in an age-appropriate manner, that such right exists, how to recognize a situation requiring protection, whom to approach, and how to obtain lawful assistance. Child protection must therefore include not only response and enforcement, but also prevention through practical, inclusive, and developmentally appropriate education. Children need not be of legal age to understand their rights, recognize danger, seek assistance, respect the rights of others, and appreciate the responsibilities of citizenship. Legal literacy enables children and young people to understand the protections available to them, recognize situations requiring assistance, use lawful reporting and referral mechanisms, and appreciate the responsibilities that accompany the exercise of rights. This measure draws, among other sources, upon the policy proposal advanced by Atty. Robie P. Quiño in the legal research paper entitled “Not of Legal Age, but of Legal Mind.” It is likewise anchored on Articles 29 and 42 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the 1 Child, which relate education to respect for human rights and require the principles and provisions of the Convention to be made widely known to adults and children alike. Republic Act No. 11476 already institutionalizes Good Manners and Right Conduct (GMRC) as a separate subject from Grades 1 to 6, integrates GMRC into kindergarten learning activities, and establishes Values Education for the higher grade levels. Its full promise, however, depends upon faithful classroom implementation, trained teachers, adequate and relevant learning resources, meaningful character-building activities, school-family-community partnership, and continuing review of actual learner outcomes. This measure therefore strengthens, rather than duplicates or displaces, the GMRC and Values Education framework. It integrates age-appropriate child-rights and rule-of-law competencies with the formation of human dignity, respect, honesty, self-discipline, responsibility, peaceful conflict resolution, obedience to law, and concern for others, while preserving the separate-subject requirements and time allotments mandated under Republic Act No. 11476. The proposed National Child Rights and Rule-of-Law Education Program does not create an additional stand-alone academic subject where existing curricula and learning areas can adequately deliver the required competencies. Instead, it establishes a national framework through which existing education, child-protection, GMRC, values-education, mental-health, digital- safety, juvenile-justice, alternative-learning, technical-vocational, higher-education, and youth- development programs may be mapped, harmonized, strengthened, and connected. This integration shall not diminish the teaching of GMRC and Values Education as separate subjects where required by Republic Act No. 11476. The Program is age-progressive. For young children, it emphasizes dignity, personal safety, respectful relationships, personal boundaries, trusted adults, safe and unsafe situations, and help- seeking. For older learners, it progressively introduces children’s rights and responsibilities, digital citizenship, privacy, crime prevention, due process, restorative justice, civic participation, the functions of public institutions, and lawful mechanisms for obtaining protection and assistance. The measure also protects learners from retraumatization, compelled disclosure, stigma, retaliation, and misuse of personal information. Teachers and other education personnel are trained to recognize concerns, secure immediate safety, comply with applicable reporting duties, and make appropriate referrals, but they are not converted into investigators, forensic interviewers, social workers, counselors, prosecutors, or lawyers. Nothing in the measure creates a new criminal offense, increases criminal liability, or lowers the minimum age of criminal responsibility. The bill further provides measurable implementation standards, accessible and legally accurate learning resources, local referral directories, inter-agency coordination within existing mandates, phased implementation, administrative accountability through existing lawful mechanisms, monitoring, periodic review, and reporting to Congress. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11443
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE SEAL OF GOOD LOCAL GOVERNANCE BY REQUIRING DISTINCT, MEASURABLE, INCLUSIVE, AND OUTCOME-BASED LOCAL SPORTS DEVELOPMENT INDICATOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 7(E) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11292, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “SEAL OF GOOD LOCAL GOVERNANCE ACT OF 2019,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence and to develop a healthy and alert citizenry. Local government units, as the public institutions closest to their communities, are uniquely positioned to translate this policy into sustained and accessible opportunities for participation in sports and physical activity. Republic Act No. 11292, otherwise known as the “Seal of Good Local Governance Act of 2019,” already recognizes the fostering of sports development under Programs for Sustainable Education. It likewise empowers the Council of Good Local Governance to develop and revise outcome-based performance indicators while taking into account that local government units are not similarly situated. The law, however, does not expressly require at least one distinct and measurable sports-development indicator among the statutory examples under this assessment area. This measure closes that limited gap. It requires a durable, outcome-based indicator covering both school-based and community-based sports programs undertaken or supported by the local government unit, whether through the Local School Board, local sports development council, local youth development office, barangays, or other lawful local bodies. It directs the assessment to consider program continuity, participation, inclusion, qualified coaching, safe and accessible facilities, athlete health and welfare, safeguarding, sustained local support, and measurable community benefits. The measure deliberately avoids reducing good local governance to infrastructure spending, isolated tournaments, or medal counts. Verified competitive achievements may support an assessment, but they should demonstrate the results of a functioning local sports-development system rather than serve as the sole or controlling measure. Standards must also remain proportionate to the category, population, geography, fiscal capacity, and other circumstances of each province, city, or municipality. To integrate the reform into the existing SGLG system, the Council and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) are directed to revise the existing implementing rules, performance indicators, assessment tools, and technical notes in coordination with the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) and after consultation with the leagues of local government units, local sports development councils, organizations representing persons with disabilities, and recognized sports, athlete-welfare, and safeguarding stakeholders. By making local sports development mandatory, measurable, inclusive, and durable across assessment cycles, this measure will encourage local governments to build healthier communities, widen access to sports, protect athlete welfare, and invest consistently in grassroots development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICHARD I. label: HB 11446
title: AN ACT GRANTING EDUCATIONAL ASSISTANCE TO THE CHILDREN AND DEPENDENTS OF FARMERS AND FISHERFOLKS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our farmers and ﬁsherfolk remain to be among those with the highest poverty incidence in the country. It is unfortunate that despite their sacriﬁce and hard work, they struggle to meet the basic needs of their families. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the ﬁsherfolk sector recorded a poverty incidence of 27.4%, while farmers recorded a poverty incidence at 27%. Their livelihoods are highly susceptible to the adverse eﬀects of climate change, natural disasters, and ﬂuctuating market prices. In the face of these hardships, education serves as the great equalizer and the most sustainable pathway out of poverty. Under Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, ensuring it is accessible to all. It is our moral and social obligation to make true of this commitment to our agricultural workers. Through extending targeted educational assistance to their children and dependents, we ensure that the youth are not deprived of a brighter future simply due to ﬁnancial constraints. To this end, this bill seeks to provide a comprehensive educational assistance, speciﬁcally for the children and dependents of farmers and ﬁsherfolk. The proposed measure will cover all all the necessary expenses for primary, secondary and tertiary education, which includes tuition fees, miscellaneous fees, learning materials, board and lodging, transportation expenses, clothing allowance, and other similar expenses. By covering these miscellaneous expenses, our farmers and ﬁsherfolk will not be forced to make a diﬃcult choice between ﬁnancing the next harvest and sending their children to school. In addition, the bill proposes to establish a special fund to sustain this government assistance. Through this dedicated fund, we can guarantee the program’s continuity and wider reach across the country. This, in turn, will empower the next generation of our agricultural sector to break free from the vicious cycle of poverty. Let us honor the blood, sweat, and tears of our agricultural workers by giving their sons and daughters the ﬁghting chance they deserve. Through this measure, we are saying investing in a brighter and more digniﬁed future for the families who feed our entire nation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11447
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING MICRO AND SMALL ENTERPRISES FROM THE IMPOSITION OF MINIMUM CORPORATE INCOME TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 27 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local entrepreneurs, particularly micro and small enterprises, remain the backbone of the Philippine economy as they are estimated to form 99.5% of the businesses in the country. Considering the successive crises that the Philippine economy has suffered, it is undeniable that the livelihood of these micro and small enterprises was adversely affected. It is also undeniable that these businesses are responsible for employing millions of Filipino workers. The Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) recently warned that escalating fuel prices place the heaviest burden on micro and small enterprises, as they operate on notoriously thin margins. Maintaining a punitive tax on gross revenue forces small businesses to pay taxes out of their capital rather than their profits. Currently, the National Internal Revenue Code provides for the imposition of the 2% Minimum Corporate Income Tax (MCIT) on the gross income of Domestic Corporations. Without any distinction on the size of the corporation, this necessarily includes those corporations categorized as micro and/or small enterprises. Under current regulations, this means vulnerable enterprises are forced to pay income tax based on gross revenues, even when operating at a loss. When the 1987 Constitution speaks of equitable taxation, it pertains to the fairness of a tax levy in consideration of the totality of the circumstances of the concerned taxpayers. Applying a blanket MCIT goes against this principle by ignoring a small business’s actual ability to pay, most especially during times of high inflation and external shocks. This bill seeks to provide relief to Micro and Small enterprises by exempting them from the imposition of the 2% Minimum Corporate Income Tax. By doing so, we are giving them a direct relief which also translates to indirect economic benefits. Shielding these vulnerable businesses allows them to preserve local jobs, hire new workers, and confidently reinvest capital to stabilize their operations. This proposed exemption creates a win-win scenario for both the public and private sectors. In this manner, businesses are given the breathing room they need to survive periods of loss or unprofitability, while the government builds and cultivates a stronger, more resilient tax base that promises to yield higher regular corporate income taxes once these enterprises grow and become profitable. We should stop taxing the mere survival of our smallest businesses and start investing in the prosperity of our entire nation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11448
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION AGAINST BULLYING IN SCHOOLS, DEFINING AND PENALIZING THE CRIME OF BULLYING
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10627 or the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013 was the glimmer of hope for countless learners suﬀering in silence. Yet, the sad and painful reality is that the law has not served as a suﬃcient deterrent against bullies, nor has it oﬀered a strong shield for the victims. We can no longer stay complacent while our children are subjected to all sorts of acts or words that instill fear, humiliation, and life-threatening harm in spaces meant to be safe for learning and growth. The undeniable need to fortify our laws and impose penalties has never been clearer. According to the updated 2022 report of the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA), 1 out of 3 Filipino students reported being bullied in schools. Just recently, there was an 8-year-old student in Davao City who died from a traumatic brain injury after being mercilessly struck by a classmate, 1 and two 16-year-old students in Zamboanga City who were stabbed during a violent altercation fueled by bullying.2 The Department of Education (DepEd) has aWempted to stem the tide through internal administrative frameworks. Under DepEd Order No. 55, s. 2013, the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) for the Anti-Bullying Act required schools to form Child Protection CommiWees and adopt local intervention programs. Acknowledging the escalating severity of school violence, DepEd recently issued DepEd Order No. 006, s. 2026, or the Guidelines on Ensuring a Safe and Motivating 1 Kristoﬀer Lou Ataylar, Rojean Grace G. Patumbon, and David Ezra M. Francisquete, "Alleged Bullied Child Dies of Brain Injury," SunStar, July 24, 2026, hNps://www.sunstar.com.ph/davao/alleged-bullied-child-dies-of-brain-injury. 2 Leah D. Agonoy, "2 Students Wounded in Zamboanga City School Stabbing Incident," INQUIRER.net, July 1, 2026, hNps://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2256219/2-students-wounded-in-zamboanga-city-school-stabbing-incident. Learning Environment (ESMLE). This urgent policy enforces a progressive disciplinary framework where high-risk bullying oﬀenses can result in preventive suspension, non-readmission, permanent exclusion, and immediate turnover to law enforcement. However, administrative department orders alone are not enough to dismantle this systemic issue. While DepEd policies outline vital procedures for intervention and school-level discipline, the statutory law itself must evolve to mandate harsher penalties and broader institutional accountability. To address the gap, this bill seeks to strengthen the protection aﬀorded to the learners by clearly deﬁning what constitutes “bullying” and outline corresponding penalties for such acts. This aims to aﬀord protection to all the student population, particularly those who are disproportionately targeted, including students suﬀering from mental and/or physical disabilities, members of the LGBTQ Community, and all other vulnerable individuals who suﬀer silently in the hands of bullies. We should aim to create a society where bullying does not exist. Only when this culture of intimidation stops can we expect our students to thrive and excel, and our communities to remain peaceful. Thus, the swift passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11449
title: AN ACT FURTHER EXTENDING THE ESTATE TAX AMNESTY UNTIL JUNE 30, 2028, THEREBY AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11213, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE When an individual dies and leaves behind assets or properties, there arises an obligation to se4le the corresponding estate tax, among other tax implications. This process undoubtedly burdens the grieving families both emotionally and ﬁnancially. Without the se4lement of the estate and the payment of the estate tax, the property of the deceased become dormant, encumbered by legal impediment that hinder the heirs from developing and/or transferring them. The Estate Tax Amnesty by the government provides an opportunity for the family members or heirs to se4le the obligations a4ached to the decedent assets. This grants them the liberty to ﬁnally decide how to utilize the properties left behind by their loved ones, free from the paralyzing burden of compounded penalties and surcharges. This bill seeks to extend the Estate Tax Amnesty until June 30, 2028. It also proposes to expand the coverage of the amnesty to include the estates of those decedents who died on or before May 31, 2024. Through this, we are aﬀording this privilege to more Filipinos. Further, this bill will serve as a strategic economic measure. It will signiﬁcantly improve overall tax collection despite the waiver of penalties that would have been otherwise imposed on the estates. Families who were previously deterred from se4ling their obligations out of fear of exorbitant ﬁnes and penalties will now be encouraged to ﬁnally se4le the estates of their decedents and pay the estate tax. Through the removal of legal impediments a4ached to unse4led estates, families are empowered to legally act on the assets they stand to inherit, whether to transfer, sell, or develop their inheritance. This, in turn, will maximize the use of idle assets and boost productivity as dormant "dead capital" is brought back into the active market, broadly stimulating the Philippine economy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11451
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE USE AND MAINTENANCE OF SIDEWALKS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the policy of the State to safeguard life, health, property, and public welfare, consistent with the principles of environmental management and control. However, the Philippine streets and sidewalks are still among the world’s most dangerous for pedestrians.1 Our sidewalks remain to be unpassable due to poor conditions and obstructions at the expense of our citizens. Reports show that motorcycles and jeepneys passing through the sidewalks has been a common practice in some areas in the country. In one instance, this has led to a student acquiring phobia in an accident with a motorcycle while crossing the sidewalk.2 Unfortunately, this is just one of the pervasive cases caused by sidewalk obstruction. Illegally parked vehicles, store extension, signages, construction of pens or cages of animals among others, also pose threat to the welfare of our citizens. The Department of Transportation even observed the danger of the current state of our sidewalks, thus, the need to remove obstructions to give importance to our pedestrians.3 Efforts have been made to curb this prevalent dilemma through issuances of DILG Memorandum Circulars 019-121, 2020-027, 2020-145, and 2022-085. However, despite these national directives in place, proper implementation to clear out our sidewalks remains to be a challenge. Mobility is public service. label: HB 11452
title: AN ACT EXPANDING FRONTLINE SERVICE HOURS INCLUDING WEEKEND COVERAGE FOR VOICE AND NON-VOICE INQUIRIES AND IN-PERSON TRANSACTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, both private employees and government offices essentially follow the same weekday work schedule. This presents a fundamental difficulty for working Filipinos who must process official transactions during business hours such as license applications, loan and benefits facilitation, or payment of taxes and fees. They are often left with an impossible choice: postpone essential transactions, use their vacation leaves or absent themselves from work at the cost of their daily wage. This burden falls heaviest upon our daily wage earners and frontline workers. Through the years, technology has been integrated into government services to assist citizens who cannot personally visit government offices. Various agencies such as the Social Security Service (SSS), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), and Home Development Mutual Fund (PAG-IBIG) have adopted digital solutions, including mobile applications, chat support services, and online portals. However, these advancements remain insufficient. Certain transactions inherently demand face-to-face processing and personal review, particularly those involving frontline services that require physical presence, identity verification, or the submission of original documents. This bill seeks to institutionalize accessible government service. Frontline services shall operate on extended working hours, including Saturdays or even Sundays if deemed necessary, with 24/7 availability for digital platforms, hotline, inquiries, appointments, and document submissions. By mandating extended operating hours across all covered agencies, we ensure that Filipinos can complete essential matters including urgent and emergency transactions without sacrificing their time and wages. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 11455
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10029, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY ACT OF 2009”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 Section 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the "Philippine Psychology Professionalization Act". ARTICLE Il STATEMENT OF POLICY SEC. 2. Statement of Policy. The State recognizes that psychologists have an important role in nation-building and development. It also acknowledges the diverse specializations of psychologists and the distinct functions specific to the varied specializations, including those that do not involve the professional practice of psychology or the delivery of psychological services. It further acknowledges the need to protect the public by preventing unqualified individuals from engaging in psychological practice or offering psychological services. Hence, it shall nurture competent, upright, and diligent registered professional psychologists whose standards of practice and service shall be excellent and globally competitive through the administration of inviolable, effective, and credible licensure examinations and the imposition and promotion of regulatory measures, programs, and activities that enhance their professional growth and well-being.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When a Filipino seeks psychological help, the person should be able to find a professional who is properly trained for the kind of help that is needed. This need becomes more pressing in light of the limited number of mental health professionals in the country. The World Health Organization's Mental Health Atlas 2024 reports only 0.3 psychologists per 100,000 population, or approximately 3 psychologists for every 1,000,000 Filipinos. 28 With so few professionals available, it becomes even more important that the psychology profession is properly structured and that available professionals are able to perform the functions for which they are trained. 32 Republic Act No. 10029, or the Philippine Psychology Act of 2009, established the regulation of psychologists and psychometricians. Now, this proposed measure seeks to update this framework by replacing the psychometrician classification with the Registered Psychology Associate, giving it a broader and clearly defined scope of practice, while reserving specialized clinical assessment and intervention for Registered Psychologists. 39 The proposed measure also recognizes that psychology professionals should have a rightful place in the institutions where their services are needed. It mandates the creation of plantilla positions for Registered Psychologists and Registered Psychology Associates in local government units, hospitals, educational institutions, and workplaces, with appropriate job descriptions, ranks, and salary grades that reflect the training, responsibilities, and value of their work. 46 A stronger psychology profession means better protection for the people who need help and better support for those who provide it. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. JERNIE JETT V. label: HB 11457
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE COMPULSORY AGE OF RETIREMENT FOR OFFICERS AND NON-OFFICERS OF THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY (BJMP) FROM FIFTY-SIX (56) YEARS OLD TO FIFTY SEVEN (57) YEARS OLD, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990," AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), along with the Philippine National Police and the Bureau of Fire Protection, was created through the promulgation of Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the “Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Act of 1990.” Subsequently, some provisions of the said law were amended by Republic Act No. 9263, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology Professionalization Act of 2004.” With over thirty-five (35) years and twenty-two (22) years since these laws were passed, respectively, the BJMP has grown its personnel to a total of around twenty-six thousand (26,000). This annual increase is in response to the ever-increasing need for manpower to assist in the safekeeping and rehabilitation of persons deprived of liberty. Through its relevant programs, the Jail Bureau aims to reduce decreasing recidivism and ultimately provide an orderly, safe, and peaceful society for the general public. Given this number, there is a clear need to ensure continuity of leadership in the BJMP by raising the retirement age from fifty-six (56) to fifty-seven (57) years old. While this is only a one-year adjustment, it can help retain experienced senior officers and make better use of their leadership, expertise, and institutional knowledge. It also gives them more time to guide and mentor younger officers and personnel. At fifty-six (56), many jail officers remain physically fit, mentally sharp, and fully capable of performing their duties. Allowing them to serve for one more year will help the Bureau retain capable leaders and strengthen the continuity of its operations. 1 Likewise, the proposed age adjustment brings the BJMP in line with reforms affecting other uniformed personnel. This includes the Armed Forces of the Philippines under Republic Act No. 11939, as well as pending Senate and House measures seeking a similar adjustment for the Philippine National Police. The passage of this bill would therefore promote consistency in retirement policies across uniformed services and recognize the BJMP’s continuing role in public service. Raising the retirement age by one year will also support the fiscal sustainability of the government’s pension system. Extending the service of qualified personnel allows the State to defer pension obligations while continuing to benefit from the skills and experience of trained officers. This provides a practical balance between retaining capable personnel and managing long-term public expenditures. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully and fervently sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11458
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RANK CLASSIFICATION AND ORGANIZATION OF KEY POSITIONS IN THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION (BFP) AND THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY (BJMP), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9263, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION AND BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT OF 2004", AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9592
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the DILG Act of 1990, laid the foundation for a more organized public safety and peace and order system in the Philippines. Among the agencies established under the law are the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) and the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP)---agencies which have particularly important responsibilities in highly urbanized and densely populated cities. In communities where large numbers of people live and work within limited spaces, the risk of fires, emergencies, overcrowding, and other public safety concerns is greater. Hence, the effective performance of their respective mandates directly contributes to public safety, security, and the maintenance of peace and order. Given the increasingly complex demands placed upon these agencies, there is a need to strengthen their organizational structures and professional standards. In 2018, Republic Act No. 11200 was enacted to update the rank classifications of the BFP and BJMP. These reforms were intended to establish clearer lines of authority and responsibility, improve organizational efficiency, and address ambiguities in the existing rank structure. However, organizational reforms must be complemented by measures that strengthen the qualifications and capabilities of those entrusted with leadership and supervisory responsibilities. For this reason, this proposed measure seeks to prescribe higher educational qualifications for certain positions in the BFP and BJMP. Higher educational standards are expected to enhance the capacity of personnel to manage their 1 responsibilities, exercise sound judgment, and effectively lead uniformed personnel in the performance of their duties. The proposed measure recognizes that the BFP and BJMP are essential components of the country's public safety and peace and order framework. Strengthening their leadership and professional standards is particularly important in densely populated urban areas, where the demands on these agencies are greater and where effective coordination, supervision, and decision-making can have a direct impact on the safety and welfare of the public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully and fervently sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11459
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines now has the highest residential electricity rates in Southeast Asia, surpassing Singapore.1 As of June 2026, the average residential electricity rate was at an average of P12.43 per kilowatt hour.2 With volatile global conditions affecting fuel prices and supply, Filipino households may have to pay even more for electricity.3 Faced with these issues, Filipinos are turning to alternative sources of energy, particularly solar power. A Pulse Asia survey showed that 93% of Filipinos believe that affordable rooftop solar panels are necessary due to the rising demand and prices of electricity.4 There is also strong public support for policies that make renewable energy more accessible, thereby lowering consumers’ electricity expenses.5 In fact, rooftop installations of solar panels have nearly doubled in the country since early 2025.6 However, our current laws and regulatory framework has yet to fully adapt to the increasing ability of ordinary consumers to generate and store electricity for their own use. Republic Act No. 9136, or the “Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001,” was enacted at a time when electricity generation was largely undertaken by power generation companies operating large-scale facilities and selling electricity to the grid. Since then, advances in technology have made small-scale electricity generation more accessible to households and end-users. 1 Lelis, Brix. (2026). DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA. Philstar. Available at https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea. 2 Id. 3 Id. 4 Arayata, Ma. Cristina. (2026). Survey: Most Filipinos want affordable solar power. Philippine News Agency. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1278589. 5 Id. 6 High bills, cheap panels drive a Philippine solar surge. (2026). Inquirer.net. Available at https://globalnation.inquirer.net/333757/high-bills-cheap-panels-drive-a-philippine-solar-surge. 1 This measure therefore seeks to promote the installation of behind-the-meter electricity generation and storage, to help Filipinos reduce their electricity expenses and improve the country’s overall energy security. Behind-the-meter refers to energy systems installed on the consumer’s side of the utility meter, including solar panels, home batteries, heat pumps, and EV chargers.7 This is distinguished from front-of-meter systems which are located on the utility side for large-scale generation and storage and supply to the power grid.8 This proposed bill aims to reflect this distinction in regulation. As such, end-users who generate and store electricity for their own use should not be subjected to the same regulatory requirements imposed upon generation companies and commercial power producers. Further, systems using equipment certified under standards recognized by the Energy Regulatory Commission to prevent electricity from flowing into the distribution grid would no longer need a certificate of compliance or prior ERC authorization. Finally, the Department of Energy is tasked to promote the widespread adoption of behind-the-meter electricity generation and energy storage systems and to coordinate the removal of national and local administrative barriers to their installation. With this measure, we hope to ease the burden on ordinary Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11460
title: AN ACT REQUIRING DISASTER-RELATED INFORMATION TO BE STATED IN ACCESSIBLE LANGUAGE TO ENSURE PUBLIC UNDERSTANDING THEREOF TO PROTECT PUBLIC HEALTH AND SAFETY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Disasters demand immediate action. When typhoons, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other natural disasters strike, people must be able to quickly understand warnings, evacuation orders, safety instructions, and other information that may determine whether lives are saved or lost. Disaster preparedness, therefore, is not only about having plans and resources in place, but also about ensuring that critical information reaches people in a form they can readily understand and act upon. This is particularly important in the Philippines, one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world,1 and home to more than 175 living languages.2 While Filipino and English are our official languages, many Filipinos continue to use their regional languages and dialects in their homes and communities. Examples are Bicol, Samar, and Leyte, which are also communities that regularly face strong typhoons. In an emergency, a warning that is difficult to understand can mean the difference between taking immediate action and losing valuable time. As such, there have been some efforts to make disaster-related information more tailored to its intended recipients. For example, in Batanes, residents receive localized disaster information in Ivatan alongside national weather bulletins and government advisories.3 These experiences show that the language used to deliver a warning can be just as 1 Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft / IFHV (2025): WorldRiskReport 2025. Berlin: Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft. 2 Philippines: Ethnologue. Ethnologue (Free All). (n.d.). https://www.ethnologue.com/country/PH/ 3 Abuso, G. (2024). Living with Typhoons: Lessons from the Ivatans of Batanes, Philippines. https://th.boell.org/en/2024/11/18/living-ivatans-philippines 1 important as the warning itself, recognizing the simple reality that people are more likely to understand and act on warnings when they are delivered in a language familiar to them. Therefore, this bill mandates national government agencies, as well as local government units (LGUs), to make disaster- and emergency-related announcements, advisories, warnings, issuances, and other relevant information clear and easy to understand. Furthermore, it requires the translation of these information into Filipino and appropriate regional languages and dialects. In a country as diverse and disaster-prone as the Philippines, disaster preparedness must reflect the different realities of its communities. Ensuring that emergency information is available in languages that people understand is essential so that warnings can be heard, understood, and acted upon. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROPER INSTALLATION, MAINTENANCE, MANAGEMENT, AND REMOVAL OF DANGLING AND NON-OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD UTILITY WIRES AND CABLES BY ALL ENTITIES AUTHORIZED TO INSTALL OR MAINTAIN AERIAL UTILITY CABLES, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The fast-paced expansion of telecommunications, high-speed internet, cable service, and electric distribution networks has significantly driven the Philippines’ modernization and economic growth.1 However, this expansion heavily burdened major metropolitan areas because of dangling, sagging, and abandoned overhead wires, widely known as “spaghetti wires”. In 2023, one of the most prominent structural failures linked to “spaghetti wires” happened near the historic Binondo Church in Manila, where four consecutive electric poles collapsed simultaneously due to the weight of thousands of unmaintained communication lines.2 The incident left three people injured and several vehicles damaged. The continued accumulation of these overhead wires has created a dangerous and often neglected problem along public roads and in residential areas. These messy cables are more than just a form of visual pollution, but a critical threat to public safety as well.3 Dangling live wires may cause electrocution, sparks, and devastating structural fires, particularly in densely populated communities. Furthermore, around two million kilos of unutilized and unusable wires have been removed in Manila, highlighting how utility companies often abandon dead and non- 1 Dela Cruz, R. (2026). PH connectivity agenda gets boost with telco sector’s $2.2-B capex. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1283081 2 Philippine Daily Inquirer. (2023). Eyes on heavy cables after Binondo pylons’ collapse. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1812393/eyes-on-heavy-cables-after-binondo-pylons-collapse 3 Garcia, P. (2024). MMC to discuss moves vs 'spaghetti wires'. Available at https://mb.com.ph/2024/5/27/mmc-to-discuss-moves-vs-spaghetti-wires-1 1 operational cables instead of removing them before installing new ones.4 As a result, utility poles are left structurally overloaded, leaving them highly vulnerable to snapping or falling during typhoons. Currently, the country lacks a strict legal framework that clearly holds public utility entities accountable for the proper maintenance and removal of their infrastructure. The regulation of these wires and similar hazards are left to the local government units. Without clear responsibilities and enforceable standards however, the “spaghetti wires” will continue to accumulate, posing risks to both public safety and existing infrastructure. This proposed bill seeks to address this long-standing urban hazard by establishing clear standards for the installation, maintenance, identification, and removal of cables, while ensuring that utility companies will be held accountable for keeping their infrastructure safe and orderly. label: HB 11462
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE ELECTRONIC WASTE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM, MANDATING EXTENDED PRODUCER RESPONSIBILITY, PROVIDING INFRASTRUCTURE AND INCENTIVES FOR E- WASTE RECYCLING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes that every Filipino has the right to health and to a balanced and healthful ecology. Specifically Section 15, Article II directs the State to protect and promote the right to health, while Section 16 mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology. This constitutional responsibility takes on particular importance as the Philippines becomes increasingly dependent on electronic devices and digital technologies. The growth of electronics, however, also means a growing stream of discarded computers, mobile phones, appliances, batteries, spare parts and other electronic products. In 2022 alone, the Philippines generated approximately 537,000 tonnes of e-waste, equivalent to 4.7 kilograms per capita.1 But the problem appears more urgent when viewed from a global perspective. Reports from the Global E-waste Monitor 2024 show that a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste were generated globally in 2022, representing an 82 percent increase from our generation in 2010.2 Without intervention, the volume is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030. The scale is difficult to ignore: the 62 million tonnes generated in 2022 would fill an estimated 1.55 million 40-ton trucks, which are enough to form a bumper-to-bumper line around the Earth’s equator.3 Despite these, the Philippines has yet to enact a comprehensive law governing e- waste. Apart from environmental consequences, this gap also presents a pressing public health concern. Electronic products may contain lead, mercury, and other hazardous substances. When discarded, dismantled, or burned without appropriate safeguards, 1 Sumaria, M. G. C., & Sumaria, R. (2025). Waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) management and policy frameworks in the Philippines: A mini review. Annals of Tropical Research, 47(1), 17-33. 2 Balde CP, Kuehr R, Yamamoto T, McDonald R, D’Angelo E, Althaf S et al. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024. Bonn, Geneva: International Telecommunication Union, United Nations Institute for Training and Resources; 2024 (https://ewastemonitor.info/). 3 Id. 1 these substances can contaminate air, soil, water, and surrounding communities. The World Health Organization has identified associations between exposure to e-waste pollutants and adverse health outcomes, including impaired neurodevelopment, respiratory effects, adverse birth outcomes, and effects on the immune system.4 Children, adolescents, and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to such exposure, adversely affecting neonatal outcomes, neurodevelopment, learning and behaviour outcomes, and even causing reduced lung and respiratory function.5 Proper e-waste management therefore goes beyond environmental preservation. Rather, it is an urgent preventive public health measure and an investment in the health of the next generation. Existing environmental laws provide important foundations, but their scopes still leave a gap: Republic Act No. 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 primarily governs municipal solid waste, Republic Act No. 6969 or the Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act of 1990 addresses toxic substances and hazardous wastes largely in industrial and chemical contexts, while Republic Act No. 11898 or the Extended Producer Responsibility Act of 2022 established extended producer responsibility for plastic packaging but excludes electronics. The proposed National Electronic Waste Management Act fills that gap by providing rules specifically responsive to the distinct environmental and health risks and recovery potential of e-waste. Specifically, it creates a national framework for the proper segregation, collection, transport, storage, reuse, recycling, and disposal of e-waste; prohibits its mixed disposal with ordinary municipal waste; requires consumers and establishments to surrender e-waste through authorized collection and treatment channels; and assigns defined responsibilities to the DENR, DTI, LGUs, DOLE, TESDA, and other relevant agencies. The measure also recognizes that the government cannot address the e-waste problem alone. It institutionalizes Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) by requiring manufacturers, brand owners, and importers to establish or participate in systems for the recovery, recycling, or safe disposal of the electronic products they introduce into the Philippine market. Progressive recovery targets and Producer Responsibility Organizations provide a mechanism for producers to assume responsibility beyond the point of sale and encourage better product design, reuse, material recovery, and circularity. At the same time, the bill does not overlook the workers already engaged in informal recycling. It provides for their training, provision of appropriate safety equipment, accreditation, and integration into formal collection and recycling supply chains. Incentives for qualified enterprises and accredited facilities further support the development of a domestic e-waste recycling and resource-recovery industry. The proposed measure is, therefore, a whole-of-nation approach to a problem that will only grow with continued technological advancement. The national government will establish the standards and infrastructure; producers will share responsibility for the products they place in the market; LGUs and communities will participate in proper collection and segregation; and workers in the informal sector will be given a pathway toward safer and more formalized livelihoods. In doing so, the bill seeks to turn e-waste 4 World Health Organization, “Electronic waste (e-waste),” Fact Sheets, 1 October 2024, https://www.who.int/news- room/fact-sheets/detail/electronic-waste-(e-waste). 5 Id. 2 from a growing environmental and health liability into an opportunity for responsible innovation and a more circular economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought.

label: HB 11463
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE SALARY GRADE OF DENTISTS EMPLOYED IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A person’s overall health and well-being includes oral health. However, for many Filipino families, dental care is not a priority. Oftentimes, people just go to the dentist when the pain is no longer bearable. When a family’s financial resources are limited, it is understandable that they would rather spend on food, medicine, and other basic needs rather than preventive dental care. This is the reason why affordable and accessible dental services in public health facilities are vital to the country’s healthcare system. The state of oral health among Filipinos shows the need to prioritize dental services in the country. According to the DOH, in 2023, about 3 out of 10 Filipino children aged 5 years and older have decayed, missing, or filled teeth.1 Meanwhile, the Philippine Dental Association estimates that 7 out of 10 Filipinos have dental caries or tooth decay, and this number includes school-age children.2 Oral health problems, when left untreated, can cause pain and infection, and interfere with one’s daily life. Despite the importance of oral health, the country faces a shortage of dentists within the public health system. This year, the DOH reports that the current dentist-to- population ratio is at 1 to 53,000, which is below the ratio of 1 to 7,500 as recommended by the World Health Organization.3 To bridge this gap, the government must be able to attract and retain qualified dentists. 1 Oral Health of Young Filipino. The salaries for dentists must likewise be assessed against the opportunities available to them in private practice, where dentists have greater control over their professional fees and the volume of procedures performed. The adequacy of compensation is particularly important in ensuring that qualified dentists are encouraged to enter and remain in government service. When there are too few dentists serving in public health facilities, the burden of limited access to oral healthcare falls most heavily on communities that have fewer resources and fewer alternatives for obtaining dental services. Thus, addressing the shortage of public dentists is not only a matter of strengthening the public health workforce, but also of ensuring that underserved and low-income Filipinos have meaningful access to essential oral healthcare. With this measure, we hope to attract and retain qualified professionals in the public sector, and ultimately strengthen the government’s ability to deliver essential health services to the Filipino people. label: HB 11465
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 149 AND 150 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tax systems should be designed to promote a fair, progressive, and efficient system that requires those with greater capacity to contribute a proportionately greater share toward the financing of government programs and public services. The present tax structure, however, does not fully capture consumption expenditures associated with luxury and other non-essential goods. Expanding the coverage and increasing the rate of excise tax on such goods will help address this gap while discouraging conspicuous consumption and generating additional revenues for national development. The proposed measure aims to achieve greater tax progressivity and promote a more equitable distribution of wealth since luxury and high-value goods are generally purchased by consumers with greater disposable income and capacity to pay. By raising the cost of high-value discretionary purchases, the measure may discourage conspicuous consumption and redirect part of household resources toward savings, investment, or socially productive expenditure. This bill amends Section 149 of the NIRC of 1997, as amended, to put a limit to the current ceiling whilst introducing a new bracket above the current ceiling: automobiles priced over Four Million Pesos (P4,000,000.00) up to Eight Million Pesos (P8,000,000.00) will be taxed at fifty percent (50%), while automobiles priced beyond Eight Million Pesos (P8,000,000.00) will be taxed at seventy-five percent (75%). It likewise amends Section 150 of the Tax Code to raise the excise tax rate on non-essential goods from twenty percent (20%) to twenty-five percent (25%), to expressly bring yachts, jet skis, speedboats, sailboats, and motorboats, aircraft, planes, jets, and helicopters within the coverage of non-essential goods when acquired for pleasure, private use, or sport, and finally to remove perfumes and toilet waters from the coverage of the tax altogether. Crucially, this measure touches no one who cannot afford it. The tax treatment of ordinary passenger vehicles, motorcycles, and commercial vehicles such as trucks and cargo vans remains entirely untouched. Its entire burden falls on a narrow slice of transactions at the very top of the market. By removing perfumes and toilet waters from the coverage of Section 150, it also lifts an existing tax on everyday personal-care purchases that has never meaningfully reached the wealthy segment the tax was intended to target. In exchange, it is expected to generate additional, sorely needed revenue to help fund government priority programs, without asking anything more from the ordinary Filipino taxpayer. The increase in automobile tax alone translates to an estimated annual revenue of ₱3.91 billion. Strengthening the taxation of luxury consumption constitutes a practical means of enhancing the progressivity of the Philippine tax system. It enables the Government to tap revenue sources that are readily identifiable and administratively accessible, while ensuring that goods and assets used for essential, livelihood, public transportation, or productive purposes are not unduly burdened. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is urgently sought. ATTY. MIRO S. label: HB 11467
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural assets. Stretching from Cagayan in the north to Quezon in the south, it forms a vast interconnected landscape of forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems. Its ecological functions extend far beyond the mountain range itself, providing essential services that sustain communities, agriculture, water systems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic activities in both upland and downstream areas. The Sierra Madre likewise serves as a critical natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, storm surges, drought, and other climate- related hazards. Its forests, watersheds, wetlands, riparian areas, ecological corridors, and coastal ecosystems regulate water flows, store and sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and contribute to the resilience of communities and critical infrastructure. The protection and restoration of the Sierra Madre are therefore not merely matters of environmental conservation, but matters of national development, public safety, water security, climate resilience, and national security. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre remains vulnerable to continuing degradation arising from illegal logging, destructive extraction, incompatible land conversion, habitat fragmentation, biodiversity loss, and other activities that undermine ecological integrity. Existing governmental mandates and management arrangements, while important, operate through different agencies, jurisdictions, plans, and regulatory systems. Such fragmentation makes it difficult to manage the Sierra Madre as one interconnected ecological system and to consistently account for impacts that cross administrative boundaries. 1 This proposed measure seeks to address this institutional and ecological gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA) as a government-owned or -controlled corporation with an original charter, attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination and administrative supervision. The Authority is envisioned as the lead policy, planning, coordinating, and regulatory body for range-wide ecological governance, while preserving the lawful mandates of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, Protected Area Management Boards, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, and other competent institutions. At the center of the proposed framework is the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, geospatially explicit, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. The measure adopts a landscape-scale and ridge-to-reef approach to conservation. Rather than treating forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems as isolated units, the proposed framework recognizes their ecological and hydrological interdependence. It provides for the identification and protection of ecological corridors, riparian buffers, critical habitats, key biodiversity areas, and other connectivity systems necessary to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The bill further advances a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy. Government interventions addressing flooding, landslides, erosion, watershed degradation, water insecurity, coastal hazards, and climate risks will be required to consider the feasibility of nature-based, green, or green-gray solutions before relying solely on conventional infrastructure. The proposed approach recognizes natural ecosystems as functional infrastructure capable of providing long-term disaster-risk reduction, water-security, and climate- adaptation benefits. Recognizing that conservation cannot be sustained without viable communities and economic incentives, the proposed measure promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples, upland communities, and lawful tenure holders to participate in conservation and restoration activities and benefit from verified ecological outcomes. A significant innovation of the measure is the establishment of a Sierra Madre Nature Credit System. The system is intended to create a transparent and independently verified mechanism through which measurable protection, restoration, biodiversity, watershed, water-security, and climate-resilience outcomes may be recognized and financed. Covered enterprises that 2 materially depend upon Sierra Madre ecosystem services may be required to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby helping align economic activity with the ecological services upon which such activity depends. The system expressly does not authorize prohibited activities or substitute for environmental, tenure, protected-area, or Indigenous Peoples safeguards. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, certain environmental charges, penalties and restoration recoveries when legally assignable, grants and technical assistance, and other lawful sources. The Fund is limited to the Authority’s statutory public-good and market- governance functions and is subject to government accounting, procurement, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. label: HB 11468
title: AN ACT CREATING A DENTAL UNIT IN EVERY RURAL HEALTH UNIT AS PART OF THE PRIMARY HEALTH CARE APPROACH IN THE DELIVERY OF HEALTH SERVICES AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Oral health is an essential component of overall health and well-being. Access to basic dental services, however, remains a concern, particularly in rural and underserved communities where geographic, financial, and other barriers may limit access to regular dental care. The Rural Health Unit serves as an important primary health care facility within local communities. Integrating basic dental services into the Rural Health Unit will help bring preventive, promotive, and appropriate primary dental care closer to the people and facilitate the early detection and treatment of oral health conditions. This measure seeks to establish a Dental Unit in every Rural Health Unit, with at least one (1) public health dentist and one (1) trained dental aide, and to provide the Department of Health with the responsibility to establish appropriate standards, guidelines, and technical assistance for their operation. By strengthening dental services at the primary health care level, this Act will promote preventive oral health care, encourage early intervention, improve access to essential dental services, and strengthen the delivery of comprehensive primary health care in local communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11469
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH TO ESTABLISH A RESEARCH CENTER ON OBESITY PREVENTION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Corpulence or obesity has become significant public health concern in the Philippines. The 2023 National Nutrition Survey of the Department of Science and Technology–Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI) reported that 39.8% of Filipino adults aged 20 to 59 were classified as Obese I or II under the Asia-Pacific BMI classification. The survey also provides national data on anthropometry, blood pressure, blood glucose, lipid profiles, dietary intake, physical activity, and other factors relevant to nutrition and health. Despite the availability of national nutrition and health data, there remains a need for sustained and focused research on the prevention and management of overweight and obesity. Evidence on risk factors, effective interventions, treatment outcomes, costs, and the health and socioeconomic consequences associated with obesity can contribute to the development of effective and evidence-based public health policies and programs. This measure seeks to mandate the Department of Health to establish an Obesity Prevention Research Center that will conduct, support, coordinate, and promote research on overweight and obesity. The Center shall study their prevalence and determinants, evaluate preventive treatment interventions, assess their health and economic consequences, and generate evidence to guide the formulation and improvement of government policies and programs. The proposed Center shall also coordinate with existing government agencies, research institutions, academic institutions, local government units, and other stakeholders to maximize existing data and research resources and avoid unnecessary duplication of efforts. The collection and use of health information shall be undertaken in accordance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and applicable ethical standards for health research. Through a dedicated research mechanism, this measure seeks to strengthen the country's capacity to generate reliable evidence, evaluate interventions, and support informed strategies for the prevention and control of overweight and obesity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11470
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE MAINTENANCE MEDICATIONS, VITAMINS, AND MINERAL SUPPLEMENTS FOR SENIOR CITIZENS”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As the Filipino population ages, more senior citizens are living with chronic and age-related conditions that require continuous maintenance medications. The rising cost of medicines, vitamins, and other medically necessary supplements can place a significant financial burden on elderly Filipinos, particularly those who rely solely on pensions or have limited sources of income. While Republic Act No. 9994, otherwise known as the “Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010,” provides senior citizens with discounts and tax exemptions on medicines and other health-related goods, these benefits do not necessarily ensure that maintenance medications are available and affordable to all senior citizens. For many elderly Filipinos, even the remaining cost of regularly purchased medicines may constitute a substantial portion of their limited income. This measure seeks to establish a government program that will provide free maintenance medications and medically indicated vitamins and mineral supplements to qualified senior citizens, subject to an appropriate national formulary and prescription requirements. It also provides mechanisms for community-based access and delivery, particularly for the oldest- old, frail, homebound, and bedridden senior citizens. The measure further ensures coordination with the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation’s existing medication benefits, including the Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT), to complement existing programs and prevent duplication of benefits. By reducing the financial burden of essential medicines and promoting continuity of treatment, this measure seeks to improve medication adherence, prevent avoidable complications and hospitalizations, and promote healthier and more dignified aging among Filipino senior citizens. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L.
