label: HB 11471
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FRESH FILIPINO GRADUATES OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION AND TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND PROGRAMS WITH A ONE-TIME CASH GRANT OF FIVE THOUSAND PESOS (₱5,000.00)”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Entering the workforce after graduation is an important transition for young Filipinos, but it often comes with immediate expenses. Job applications, transportation, documentation, medical examinations, work attire, and other requirements can impose a financial burden at a time when many fresh graduates have yet to receive their first income from employment. For many young Filipinos, the lack of readily available funds can make the transition from education to employment more difficult. A modest and timely form of financial assistance can help bridge this gap and enable graduates to pursue employment opportunities without having to rely immediately on family members or incur debt for basic employment-related expenses. This measure seeks to provide qualified fresh Filipino graduates of duly recognized or authorized higher education institutions or duly registered technical-vocational programs in the Philippines with a one-time cash grant of Five Thousand Pesos (₱5,000.00). The proposed grant is not conditioned on unemployment or household income. Its purpose is to provide basic transition assistance to qualified graduates as they seek and commence employment. The measure likewise limits availment to one time per beneficiary and requires application within one year from graduation or completion of the program. The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is designated as the lead implementing agency, in coordination with the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) for the verification and processing of applications of graduates and completers of technical-vocational programs. The measure further provides for electronic verification of graduation records and safeguards against duplicate availment, while requiring compliance with existing data privacy laws. The amount necessary for implementation shall be provided through the annual General Appropriations Act. The enactment of this measure will provide practical and immediate assistance to young Filipinos as they take their first steps toward employment and productive participation in the economy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11472
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING PALLIATIVE AND HOSPICE CARE INTO THE PHILIPPINE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Palliative and hospice care are essential components of a compassionate and comprehensive health care system. Patients suffering from serious, life-threatening, life-limiting, chronic, or complex illnesses often experience significant pain and other physical, psychosocial, and emotional burdens that require care beyond the treatment of the underlying disease. While the Philippine health care system has made significant progress in expanding access to health services, access to organized and affordable palliative and hospice care remains uneven. Many patients and their families continue to face difficulties in obtaining appropriate pain and symptom management, home-based care, psychosocial support, continuity of care, and end-of-life services. This measure seeks to integrate palliative and hospice care into the Philippine health care system and the framework of Universal Health Care, ensuring that such services are available across hospitals, primary care facilities, communities, and appropriate home-based settings. The bill establishes standards for quality and accreditation, strengthens referral and continuity-of-care networks, promotes education and training of health professionals and volunteers, supports continuing research, and directs the development of appropriate PhilHealth benefit packages for inpatient, outpatient, and home-based services. It likewise facilitates support for indigent patients and recognizes the important role of family caregivers. Ultimately, this measure seeks to ensure that every Filipino facing serious or end-of-life illness may receive accessible, affordable, quality, and compassionate care that protects dignity, relieves suffering, and improves quality of life for both patients and their families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range (SMMR) makes up 40 percent of the forest cover in the Philippines. Its range starts at Cagayan in the north and extends to Quezon Province in the south of Luzon. The provinces that trail the SMMR also include Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Nueva Ecija, Aurora, Bulacan, Rizal, and Laguna. The forest cover spanning 540 kilometers is not just home to 3.5 million species but also a significant carbon-sequestering spot.1 The rich biodiversity of the SMMR has undoubtedly supplied the people with ecosystem services that benefited multi-generations of Filipinos. But the mountain range that Filipinos are fond of referring to as the first line of defense against disasters is hounded with illegal activities such as encroachment and deforestation. The indispensable contribution of this major ecological system is crucial to the life of all organisms that depend on it—human and non-humans alike. The conservation, protection, and sustainable management of the SMMR increases the chances of a better biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, water security, and disaster risk reduction of the systems that depend and are interconnected to the forest cover. In line with the constitutional mandate to uphold every Filipino’s right to a healthful ecology by protecting the largest tropical rainforest in Luzon, this bill seeks to establish the Sierra Madre Mountain Conservation and Development Authority. ______________________________ 1. Climate Change Commission. 2024. Through this agency, a Nature-based solutions and resilient-investment approach shall be operationalized to protect and enrich the mountain range of Sierra Madre. The agency shall create an ecosystem-scale governance framework that will harmonize and integrate mandates and function of national agencies and local government units. In this regard, passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. ROY M. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE IMPLEMENTATION, MANAGEMENT, AND UTILIZATION OF THE COCONUT FARMERS AND INDUSTRY TRUST FUND, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN SECTIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11524, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE COCONUT FARMERS AND INDUSTRY TRUST FUND ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Since its enactment in 2021, Republic Act No. 11524 or the Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund Act, has been regarded as the much-awaited hope for the coconut industry. With over 3.5 million coconut farmers in the Philippines and 14.5 million metric tons of coconuts produced in 2025, we are recognized as the second-largest coconut producer in the world. As such, it is imperative upon the government that we continue to improve and develop this industry. The Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund (CFITF) established pursuant to RA 11524, aims to boost the coconut industry through programs geared towards development and sustainability. However, coconut farmers have yet to experience the benefits of the programs under this law as much of the fund remains unused. President Marcos himself sought for the amendment of the law in order to facilitate faster utilization and disbursement of the funds and ensure effective and responsive programs for the industry. title: AN ACT TO PROMOTE THE DEVELOPMENT AND SUSTAINABILITY OF THE SEAWEED INDUSTRY IN THE PHILIPPINES, ENHANCING RESEARCH, SUPPORT, AND GLOBAL COMPETITIVENESS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a country rich in marine resources. With 1,065 seaweed species found in our waters, so far, only four are farmed. These are Eucheuma, Kappaphycus, Gracilaria, and Caulerpa1. The seaweed industry is one of the major contributors of our economy. In 20242, seaweed aquaculture accounted for an impressive 66% of overall fishery production and remains as one of the agriculture sector’s top export commodities. It sustains thousands of families in coastal communities and contributes significantly to national employment and aquaculture output. Beyond food, seaweed has diverse applications such as animal feed, fertilizer, cosmetic ingredient, and most recently, as raw material for bio-plastics 3 among others. However, the industry continues to face mounting challenges such as global warming, degradation, disease outbreaks like “ice-ice”, volatile market prices, and insufficient post-harvest infrastructure that significantly affect this industry. These challenges are no longer theoretical. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RECLASSIFICATION AND CONVERSION OF CERTAIN PARCELS OF FORESTLAND IN THE PROVINCE OF NUEVA VIZCAYA INTO ALIENABLE AND DISPOSABLE PUBLIC LANDS Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to conserve and protect the nation's forest lands as part of its patrimony, and, consistent with that duty, to determine by law the specific limits of such forest lands and to release from them only those areas which, by reason of long and actual human settlement, cultivation and use, no longer serve forest purposes. It is further the policy of the State to promote social justice and security of tenure for actual occupants and tillers of lands of the public domain, to respect the rights of indigenous cultural communities and indigenous peoples to their ancestral domains and ancestral lands, and to ensure that the reclassification of forestland does not impair watersheds, riverbanks, headwaters, or the ecological balance of the areas concerned. SECTION 2. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: (a) Alienable and disposable land refers to land of the public domain classified as agricultural land and declared available for alienation and disposition under Commonwealth Act No. 141, as amended, otherwise known as the Public Land Act; (b) Forestland refers to land of the public domain which has not been declared alienable and disposable, and which is subject to the system of land classification administered under Presidential Decree No. 705, as amended, otherwise known as the Revised Forestry Code of the Philippines; (c) Ancestral domain and ancestral land have the meanings assigned to them in Republic Act No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997; (d) Segregation survey refers to the ground survey conducted by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to delimit,
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 4, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution directs that the Congress shall, as soon as possible, determine by law the specific limits of forest lands and national parks, marking clearly their boundaries on the ground, and that thereafter such forest lands may not be diminished except by law. That mandate is not merely an allocation of power; it is the only door through which the situation this measure addresses can be resolved. In the Municipality of Kasibu, Province of Nueva Vizcaya, communities have for generations built their homes, planted their rice, banana and citrus, and raised their children on land that the State still carries on its maps as forest. The Department's own field assessment describes the covered areas as occupied by the community for residential, agricultural and agro-forest purposes, containing scattered residential houses occupied by farmers, with actual use recorded as agricultural, agroforest, rice field, banana and citrus plantations. They cannot obtain a title. They cannot pledge the land for a loan, pass it to their children with certainty, or be secure against displacement. The local government cannot assess the land for real property tax, so the municipality earns nothing from land it must nonetheless serve with roads, water and schools. For the Province as a whole, the Forest Management Bureau records that the conversion proposed here would reduce forest land by about six hundredths of one percent, leaving the provincial forest estate substantially intact. This bill reclassifies two (2) parcels of forestland in the Province of Nueva Vizcaya, described by metes and bounds as certified by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, into alienable and disposable public land, and opens them to disposition under the Public Land Act. It deliberately does three further things. It carries forward, as statutory exclusions, the protections of Section 16 of the Revised Forestry Code — the twenty-metre riverbank strips, the ridge tops and plateaus from which headwaters emanate, and the other areas needed for forest purposes — so that reclassification does not become deforestation. It excludes from coverage any land within an ancestral domain, ancestral land, Certificate of Page 1 of 9 Ancestral Domain Claim or Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title, and requires certification by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples before any segregation survey may proceed, in recognition that land held by indigenous cultural communities under native title has never been public land at all. And it requires that the boundaries between the reclassified land and the forestland that remains be marked on the ground with concrete monuments and maintained there, which is what Section 4, Article XII actually commands and what decades of paper-only classification have failed to deliver. Considering the potential economic, social and developmental benefits of the proposed measure, its immediate passage is respectfully and strongly recommended. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MINIMUM BASIC MONTHLY SALARY OF FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (P50,000.00) FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Tamang Sahod para sa Guro Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to assign the highest budgetary priority to education and to ensure that teaching attracts and retains its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration. SEC. 3. Coverage. – This Act shall cover all persons occupying teaching positions in public elementary and secondary schools, including those performing supervisory or administrative functions therein, as contemplated under Republic Act No. 4670, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Public School Teachers,” but excluding those in the professorial staff of state universities and colleges. As used herein, basic monthly salary refers to the compensation corresponding to the salary grade and step of the position, exclusive of allowances, bonuses, honoraria and other emoluments. SEC. 4. Minimum Basic Monthly Salary. – No public school teacher shall receive a basic monthly salary lower than Fifty Thousand Pesos (PhP 50,000.00), or the rate corresponding to the salary grade and step of the position under Republic Act No. 11466, otherwise known as the “Salary Standardization Law of 2019,” as amended, whichever is higher. SEC. 5. Preservation of Salary Differentials. – The Department of Budget and Management shall adjust the basic monthly salaries of public school teachers occupying positions higher than the entry-level teaching position so as to maintain the percentage differentials between successive salary grades and steps existing immediately prior to the effectivity of this
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 5(5), Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution commands that the State “shall assign the highest budgetary priority to education and ensure that teaching will attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration.”1 Of all the professions in the public service, teaching alone is singled out in the Constitution for a guarantee of adequate remuneration. That guarantee remains unfulfilled. A Teacher I presently earns Thirty Thousand Twenty-Four Pesos (PhP 30,024.00) monthly,2 below the family living wage of Thirty-Six Thousand Five Hundred Ten Pesos (PhP 36,510.00) estimated for a household of five.3 Some eight hundred three thousand two hundred seventy-two (803,272) personnel occupy Teacher I to Teacher III positions. While officials in Salary Grades 31 to 33 receive between Two Hundred Ninety-Three Thousand One Hundred Ninety-One Pesos (PhP 293,191.00) and Four Hundred Thirty-Eight Thousand Eight Hundred Forty-Four Pesos (PhP 438,844.00) monthly, teachers were granted increases of only 4.95% to 5.6%. Many take on part-time work or leave for posts abroad. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) DISTRICT OFFICE IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BAYOMBONG, PROVINCE OF NUEVA VIZCAYA, FROM CLASS “C” TO CLASS “A,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Land Transportation Office (LTO) District Office in the Municipality of Bayombong, Province of Nueva Vizcaya, is presently classified as a Class “C” district office. Situated in the provincial capital, it delivers the core services of the Office within its jurisdiction, including motor vehicle registration, the issuance of driver’s licenses and permits, and the enforcement of land transportation laws, rules and regulations, to the municipalities of Bayombong, Bagabag, Diadi, Villaverde, Solano, Quezon and Ambaguio. The sustained growth in motor vehicle registrations and licensing transactions within this area of responsibility has correspondingly increased the responsibilities and workload of the office. The present Class “C” classification no longer reflects the expanding functions and service demands of the office. Its existing organizational structure and resource allocation limit its capacity to efficiently serve the increasing number of clients while maintaining the quality of public service. Upgrading the Bayombong District Office to Class “A” will provide the appropriate organizational structure, additional personnel, and operational resources needed to effectively carry out its mandated functions. It will likewise enhance service efficiency, strengthen enforcement activities, and improve the delivery of LTO services to the communities within its jurisdiction. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA OF TRICYCLE DRIVERS AND OPERATORS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Magna Carta of Tricycle Drivers and Operators". SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to promote the welfare of workers in the tricycle sector, to secure for them access to social security and health insurance commensurate to their capacity to contribute, to protect them against deprivation of their livelihood without valid cause and due process, and to ensure that the regulation of tricycles-for-hire is uniform, predictable, and free from exaction. SECTION 3. Scope and Regulatory Authority. – This Act applies to operators of tricycles-for-hire, to the drivers they engage, and to the local government units and national agencies named herein. It does not apply to tricycles used exclusively for private purposes or to two-wheeled motorcycles however used. The grant, amendment, renewal, suspension, and cancellation of the MTOP and the designation of zones, routes, and terminals are exercised by the Sanggunian under Sections 447(a)(3)(vi) and 458(a)(3)(vi) of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, subject to guidelines issued by the Department of Transportation (DOTr). The registration of tricycles and the licensing of drivers remain with the LTO, and no LGU shall impose a requirement in the nature of either. SECTION 4. Operating Requirements. – No tricycle-for-hire shall operate on a national highway utilized by four-wheeled vehicles heavier than four (4) tons and on which the normal speed exceeds forty (40) kilometers per hour: Provided, That the Sanggunian may, by ordinance and with the approval of the DOTr, allow such operation where no other public transport services the route: Provided, further, That where allowed, the tricycle shall traverse only the outer right lane except when preparing to turn.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tricycles carry passengers where jeepneys and buses do not go, and their regulation is devolved to cities and municipalities.1 Devolution supplied no national floor: each sets its own requirements, fees, and processing periods, and that variation produces the exactions and brokered permits the sector reports. The gap in social protection is contribution capacity, not coverage. Self-employed persons are already compulsorily covered by the SSS, and every Filipino by the National Health Insurance Program.2 But a driver on an irregular daily income must remit PhP 1,250.00 a month to keep both current.3 This measure sets uniform operating requirements, caps the permit fee, requires a one-stop shop with a definite processing period, replaces impounding for documentary lapses with citations, and establishes a Tricycle Sector Registry. On that Registry it builds a Contribution Support Program paying half of a qualified beneficiary's contribution at the statutory floor, matched by the member and capped by the annual appropriation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. Representative Lone District of Nueva Vizcaya 1 Rep. label: HB 11481
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF LOCAL HOG RAISERS, ENSURING FARMGATE PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND FAIR TRADING PRACTICES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the “Local Hog Raisers Protection and Fair Pricing Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. It is the policy of the State to promote comprehensive rural development, to provide support to agriculture through adequate financial, production, marketing, and other support services, to promote the preferential use of locally produced goods, and to prohibit combinations in restraint of trade and unfair competition, consistent with Sections 1 and 5 of Article XIII, Sections 1, 6, 12, 13, and 19 of Article XII, and Section 21 of Article II of the Constitution. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to authorize the fixing of the purchase or selling price of any animal or animal product. SEC. 3. Coverage. This Act shall apply to farmgate transactions in swine throughout the country. SEC. 4. Livestock Transaction Reporting System. The Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) shall establish and maintain a Livestock Transaction Reporting System. Every buyer covered by the implementing rules shall report the date, location, volume, price, and terms of payment of each farmgate transaction, without disclosing the identity of the selling raiser without the raiser's written consent. Reported information shall be published only in aggregate form and shall not be used as the sole basis for any tax assessment or admitted in evidence against the reporting party, except in a proceeding for violation of this Act. SEC. 5. Reference Farmgate Price. The Department of Agriculture (DA), in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority, shall compute and publish weekly a reference farmgate price for hogs, at the national and regional levels, derived from data collected under Section 4. The reference price shall be published on official websites and disseminated to local agriculture offices and accredited raisers' associations, and shall be clearly identified as an administrative indicator distinct from official statistical series.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Backyard and small- hog raising provides livelihood and income to thousands of Filipino families, including many households in Nueva Vizcaya. Small-hold farms accounted for 70.0 percent of the country’s swine inventory as of 1 January 2023, underscoring their importance to the domestic pork supply and rural economy.1 Yet local hog raisers remain particularly vulnerable to low farmgate prices, rising production costs, weak bargaining power, and an increasingly complex livestock marketing chain. The Department of Agriculture has acknowledged that farmgate prices had fallen sharply without corresponding relief to consumers.2 Even the existing law provides significant resources for animal industry development, including repopulation, disease response, credit, and related support,3 the core market is still facing challenges as local producers remain largely unresolved. The measure is anchored on the constitutional policies promoting agricultural support, reduction of economic inequalities, preferential use of locally produced goods, and regulation of unfair competition.4 For these reasons, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11483
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY PROGRAM, STRENGTHENING DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS, AND PREVENTING SCHOOL VIOLENCE, ACTIVE ASSAILANT INCIDENTS, AND OTHER SAFETY AND SECURITY THREATS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools must always remain places of learning, formation, and safety. Recent successive incidents and threats involving bullying and cyberbullying, bomb scares, deadly weapons, online threats, and other acts of violence have haunted our places of learning and peace. They have also exposed the evolving risks faced by learners, teachers, and school personnel. In response, the Department of Education has strengthened its policies on weapons and bomb threats and introduced school safety audits, active-threat preparedness exercises, confidential reporting mechanisms, and mental-health interventions. Existing laws address particular aspects of school safety, including bullying, mental health, and disaster risk reduction. Nevertheless, there remains a need for a unified and permanent framework covering the prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery measures necessary to address both natural hazards and intentional acts of violence across educational institutions. This bill therefore establishes a National Comprehensive School Safety Program. It mandates school-specific safety and vulnerability assessments, emergency plans and drills, reasonable security infrastructure, weapons-control measures, violence-prevention and mental-health programs, confidential reporting and threat assessment mechanisms, inter-agency coordination, and post-incident recovery and continuity-of-learning measures. 1 Through this measure, school safety shall no longer depend on isolated or reactive interventions but shall become a coordinated, preventive, and adequately supported national responsibility. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 11484
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INTEGRATION OF SOLAR HOME SYSTEMS IN ALL SOCIALIZED HOUSING PROJECTS, ESTABLISHING A SOLAR HOME SYSTEM FINANCING PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The worsening housing gap in lower- and middle-income countries is largely attributed to rapid urbanization and population growth outpacing the housing supply (Lee and Singh, 2022). In 2018, the Philippine housing backlog reached 5.7 million units and absent any significant intervention, this housing backlog is projected to reach 22 million by 2040 (Padojinog and Yap, 2020). Furthermore, with 4.1 million individuals displaced due to government infrastructure projects in 2019 alone (Bermudez et al., 2020) and an estimated 3.7 million Informal Settler Families (ISFs) residing in hazard-prone areas (UN-Habitat, 2023), addressing the housing backlog remains a priority concern of the government. Despite ongoing government housing initiatives targeting the housing deficit, beneficiaries of socialized housing moved in to housing units without basic services such as electricity (Ebdane, 2024). Compounding this issue, plant outages and rising consumer electricity demand consistently triggered yellow and red alerts in the transmission grid, resulting in power interruptions and prompting several legislative inquiries (Baligad, 2024). While socialized housing programs are addressing the need for shelter, many resettlement communities remain unserved or underserved in terms of reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy access. The Philippines' reliance on imported fuel makes the country highly vulnerable to external energy shocks, contributing to rising food and energy costs (De Leon, 2026). Estimated electricity rates in the country are among the highest in Asia, ranking fourth overall (Dela Peña, 2026). These conditions expose Filipino households to high energy costs, unstable power supply, or limited access to grid electricity, with greater impact to households in resettlement sites, undermining the long-term livability and sustainability of housing interventions. Coupled with the increasing frequency and intensity of climate-related hazards, the vulnerability of traditional energy systems underscores the need for resilient, decentralized, and renewable energy solutions. Article XIII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to undertake a continuing program of urban land reform and housing which will make available at affordable cost decent housing and basic services to underprivileged and homeless citizens. Legislations, including Republic Act No. 9513 or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008, affirm the national policy to accelerate the utilization of renewable energy resources. However, despite existing policy frameworks, the integration of renewable energy systems, particularly solar home systems (SHS), into socialized housing developments remains largely dependent on project-level initiatives rather than a standardized national framework. This bill seeks to address the policy and implementation gap by mandating the integration of SHS in all socialized housing projects, whether on-grid, off-grid, or hybrid, and by establishing a dedicated financing mechanism to ensure its feasibility and affordability. By institutionalizing SHS as a standard component of housing design and delivery, this measure ensures that energy access is no longer treated as an auxiliary concern but as an essential element of housing adequacy. It likewise integrates the SHS Financing Program into housing amortization schemes with repayment terms of up to twenty-five (25) years, while employing a mix of subsidies, grants, and concessional financing to minimize the burden on beneficiary households. The financing structure is designed to ensure that total electricity-related expenditures remain comparable to, if not lower than, conventional grid-based electricity costs over time. The measure also establishes the technical standards, quality assurance mechanisms, and mandatory maintenance requirements to ensure system reliability and sustainability. It institutionalizes coordination among key agencies, including the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, Department of Energy, National Housing Authority, and Social Housing Finance Corporation, as well as Local Government Units, to ensure alignment in planning and execution. In addition, it provides for beneficiary orientation programs and a monitoring and evaluation system to track system performance, household energy savings, and broader socioeconomic and environmental impacts. Beyond ensuring energy adequacy, this measure promotes electricity security in socialized housing communities without adding strain to the national power grid. Additionally, where systems are grid-connected and eligible for net metering, these socialized housing communities may even contribute to the overall energy stability by serving as solar farms, supplying excess power back to the grid. The integration of solar energy systems in socialized housing represents a strategic shift toward building a climate-resilient, energy-secure, and sustainable communities, consistent with the State's commitment to inclusive development and environmental stewardship. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA ________ Baligad, J. (2024, May) Can't Take the Heat? label: HB 11485
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is one of the most powerful instruments for achieving inclusive and sustainable development. Access to quality higher education and technical- vocational training should not be limited by geographic location or economic circumstance. Students in geographically distant and underserved communities should likewise be given meaningful opportunities to pursue higher education and acquire the knowledge, skills, and competencies necessary to improve their lives and contribute to the development of their communities. Sultan Kudarat is a geographically expansive province with communities located at considerable distances from existing institutions of higher learning. For many students, particularly those coming from low-income families, the cost of transportation, board and lodging, and other expenses associated with studying outside their municipalities constitutes a significant barrier to obtaining a college education. Establishing campuses of the Sultan Kudarat State University (SKSU) in municipalities will substantially reduce these barriers and bring quality higher education closer to the people. This proposed measure seeks to establish campuses of the Sultan Kudarat State University (SKSU) in the Municipalities of Bagumbayan, Columbio, Esperanza, Lambayong, Lebak, President Quirino, Senator Ninoy Aquino, and SKSU-ACCESS in Tacurong City to expand access to affordable and quality higher education, technical-vocational training, research, extension services, and community development in these unserved municipalities. The proposed campuses shall primarily offer short-term, technical-vocational, undergraduate, and graduate programs consistent with their respective competencies, specializations, capabilities, and the standards prescribed by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED). Their programs shall be responsive to the human-resource requirements not only of the municipalities concerned but also of the Province of Sultan Kudarat and Region XII. The measure also further provides for the appointment or designation of Campus Director who shall be responsible for the effective administration and operation of the respective campuses, subject to the qualifications, standards, and guidelines prescribed by the University Board of Regents. It also requires compliance with the minimum requirements prescribed by CHED before the operation and program offerings of the campuses. The establishment of these provincial campuses is consistent with the constitutional policy of making quality education accessible to all and with the mandate of state universities and colleges to provide higher education, promote research and innovation, and extend their services to the communities they serve. More importantly, this measure will help ensure that the youth of Sultan Kudarat are given opportunities to obtain quality education without having to leave their respective municipalities merely to pursue their studies. It will also help develop a pool of competent professionals, skilled workers, researchers, entrepreneurs, teachers, and public servants who can contribute directly to the socioeconomic advancement of the Province of Sultan Kudarat and the SOCCSKSARGEN Region. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. » RUTH MANGUDADA AKALURAN Represent First District, Sultan Kudarat Representative Second District, Sultan Kudarat ONO KR WN = <e) PPAR HW WWWAHWWHWOW AN NNN NN NNN DND | |] B= Ba Bs a aa a a WBN HI OWA AN OO HhWNH HI TOA AN DOA RF WH H DHAWAN DOA WH =| OC Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Batasan Hills, Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS First Regular Session HOUSEBILL NO. 11485 Introduced by: REP. title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING BAMBOO AS A HIGH-VALUE AND INDUSTRIAL CROP, FURTHER STRENGTHENING THE HIGH-VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT ACT BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE NATIONAL HIGH- VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT AND BIOECONOMY PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7900, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “HIGH-VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT ACT OF 1995”” 22
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 24 Republic Act No. 7900, or the High-Value Crops Development Act of 1995, established the national framework for the production, processing, marketing and distribution of high-value crops. Three decades later, climate change, biotechnology, plant-variety innovation, stricter product standards, supply-chain disruptions and growing demand for renewable and bio-based materials require a more integrated, science-based, market-oriented and institutionally sustained approach. 31 This bill expressly includes bamboo as a high-value crop and recognizes it as a strategic industrial crop. Bamboo can provide food, fiber, biomass, engineered and construction materials, furniture, packaging, bioenergy, biochar, biomaterials, and other value-added products. Developed through appropriate agroforestry and multi- storey farming systems, it can diversify rural livelihoods and support climate, soil, water, and ecosystem objectives, subject to environmental, biodiversity, land-use, agrarian reform and ancestral-domain laws. 39 The measure establishes within the Department of Agriculture the Office of the Undersecretary for High-Value Crops Development, Innovation, and Bioeconomy. The Office shall provide policy guidelines on technology management and innovation, exercise direct oversight over the National High-Value Crops and Bioeconomy Development Program, and supervise the functional roles, mandates and performance of its component offices. The bill also proposes the creation of one (1) Assistant Secretary position to support the Undersecretary and lead the agricultural statistics and data science, knowledge management, market intelligence, geospatial services, monitoring, evaluation and results reporting. A National High-Value Crops Program Management Office will be created and headed by Director position to coordinate implementation, provide technical services, farming systems, bamboo and industrial- crop development, agribusiness, processing, standards, investment, and markets. 13 The bill further integrates research, innovation, biotechnology, genetic resources, plant-variety development, quality planting materials, climate-resilient production, integrated development areas, processing, enterprise development, financing, standards, trade, and agricultural bioeconomy applications. It strengthens the High-Value Crops Development Fund and permits the Department to propose an indicative initial program envelope of Fifty Billion Pesos to support the five-year implementation of the act, subject to the regular budget process and without creating an automatic appropriation. 22 The proposed structure is designed as an integrating and coordinating mechanism. It preserves the statutory mandates of the Philippine Statistics Authority and other competent regulatory, research, standards, environmental, and local- government institutions, while requiring compliance with government-optimization, civil service, position-classification, budgeting, accounting and auditing laws. 28 In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. 30 31 JOSE MANUEL F. label: HB 11487
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION, CONSERVATION, AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT OF THE SIERRA MADRE MOUNTAIN RANGE, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE SIERRA MADRE MOUNTAIN RANGE AUTHORITY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural assets. Stretching from Cagayan in the north to Quezon in the south, it forms a vast interconnected landscape of forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems. Its ecological functions extend far beyond the mountain range itself, providing essential services that sustain communities, agriculture, water systems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic activities in both upland and downstream areas. The Sierra Madre likewise serves as a critical natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, storm surges, drought, and other climate-related hazards. Its forests, watersheds, wetlands, riparian areas, ecological corridors, and coastal ecosystems regulate water flows, store and sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and contribute to the resilience of communities and critical infrastructure. The protection and restoration of the Sierra Madre are therefore not merely matters of environmental conservation, but matters of national development, public safety, water security, climate resilience, and national security. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre remains vulnerable to continuing degradation arising from illegal logging, destructive extraction, incompatible land conversion, habitat fragmentation, biodiversity loss, and other activities that undermine ecological integrity. Existing governmental mandates and management arrangements, while important, operate through different agencies, jurisdictions, plans, and regulatory systems. Such fragmentation makes it difficult to manage the Sierra Madre as one interconnected ecological system and to consistently account for impacts that cross administrative boundaries. This proposed measure seeks to address this institutional and ecological gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA) as a government- owned or -controlled corporation with an original charter, attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination and administrative supervision. The Authority is envisioned as the lead policy, planning, coordinating, and regulatory body for range-wide ecological governance, while preserving the lawful mandates of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, Protected Area Management Boards, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, and other competent institutions. At the center of the proposed framework is the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, geospatially explicit, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. The measure adopts a landscape-scale and ridge-to-reef approach to conservation. Rather than treating forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems 1 as isolated units, the proposed framework recognizes their ecological and hydrological interdependence. It provides for the identification and protection of ecological corridors, riparian buffers, critical habitats, key biodiversity areas, and other connectivity systems necessary to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The bill further advances a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy. Government interventions addressing flooding, landslides, erosion, watershed degradation, water insecurity, coastal hazards, and climate risks will be required to consider the feasibility of nature-based, green, or green-gray solutions before relying solely on conventional infrastructure. The proposed approach recognizes natural ecosystems as functional infrastructure capable of providing long-term disaster-risk reduction, water-security, and climate-adaptation benefits. Recognizing that conservation cannot be sustained without viable communities and economic incentives, the proposed measure promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples, upland communities, and lawful tenure holders to participate in conservation and restoration activities and benefit from verified ecological outcomes. A significant innovation of the measure is the establishment of a Sierra Madre Nature Credit System. The system is intended to create a transparent and independently verified mechanism through which measurable protection, restoration, biodiversity, watershed, water- security, and climate-resilience outcomes may be recognized and financed. Covered enterprises that materially depend upon Sierra Madre ecosystem services may be required to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby helping align economic activity with the ecological services upon which such activity depends. The system expressly does not authorize prohibited activities or substitute for environmental, tenure, protected-area, or Indigenous Peoples safeguards. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, certain environmental charges, penalties and restoration recoveries when legally assignable, grants and technical assistance, and other lawful sources. The Fund is limited to the Authority’s statutory public-good and market-governance functions and is subject to government accounting, procurement, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. label: HB 11488
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE EXTENSION OF TERMS OF PROTECTION OF COPYRIGHT AND RELATED RIGHTS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 213 AND 215 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8293, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines, or Republic Act No. 8293, provides protection to authors, performers, producers of sound recordings, and broadcasting organizations for their creative works and contributions. The existing law provides specific periods of protection for copyright and related rights, which this measure seeks to strengthen in view of the continuing development of the creative and digital industries. This measure seeks to extend the period of copyright protection for works covered under Sections 172 and 173 of Republic Act No. 8293 from fifty (50) years to seventy-five (75) years. It likewise extends the protection for photographic works and audio-visual works to seventy-five (75) years. For performers and producers of sound recordings, the period of protection is similarly proposed to be extended from fifty (50) years to seventy-five (75) years. The protection granted to broadcasting organizations is also proposed to be increased from twenty (20) years to fifty (50) years. The extension of these terms will provide Filipino authors, performers, producers, and other rights holders with a longer period within which they may benefit from their creative works. For performers and producers, in particular, a longer period of protection will allow them to continue receiving economic benefits from works that may remain commercially valuable for many years after their creation or initial release. It will likewise provide rights holders greater opportunity to recover investments made in the creation, production, marketing, and distribution of creative works. By strengthening the period of protection granted to creative works and related rights, this measure seeks to provide greater incentives for the creation, dissemination, preservation, and continued commercial exploitation of Filipino works. It will likewise contribute to the development of the Philippine creative industry, encourage investment in creative works, and help ensure that Filipino creators and rights holders continue to benefit from their intellectual and artistic contributions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMOB.B.RODRIGUEZ, MAXIMO RODRIGUEZ,JR. JR. label: HB 11489
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE RECRUITMENT, HIRING, AND TRAINING OF SCHOOL-BASED LICENSED GUIDANCE COUNSELORS, PSYCHOLOGISTS, SCHOOL SOCIAL WORKERS AND MENTAL HEALTH PERSONNEL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The mental health and psychosocial well-being of students are essential to their ability to learn, develop, and participate meaningfully in school and community life. Schools are often among the first places where behavioral, emotional, social, and psychological difficulties among children and young people may be identified. This measure seeks to provide public elementary and secondary schools with additional personnel who can provide counseling, psychosocial support, early intervention, referral, and other appropriate services to students. It likewise recognizes the important role of teachers, school personnel, and parents in identifying concerns and supporting the overall well-being of students. By strengthening the availability of qualified professionals within schools, the proposed Act aims to address mental, emotional, behavioral, and psychosocial concerns at an earlier stage and help create a more supportive learning environment. The measure therefore provides for the recruitment and training of appropriate school-based personnel, establishes supervision and service guidelines, and provides the necessary funding through the annual General Appropriations Act. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 11490
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE RIGHTS OF PATIENTS AGAINST HOSPITAL DETENTION ON THE GROUND OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS AND MEDICAL EXPENSES AND PROVIDING STIFFER PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9439, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DETENTION OF PATIENTS IN HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL CLINICS ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Patients should not be deprived of their liberty, nor should their families be prevented from securing their release or obtaining necessary medical documents, solely because of their inability to immediately settle hospital bills and medical expenses. Republic Act No. 9439, otherwise known as the “Anti-Hospital Detention Law”, was enacted to protect patients from being detained in hospitals and medical clinics on account of unpaid hospital bills or medical expenses. Despite the protection provided by law, cases continue to arise where patients and their families experience difficulty securing discharge, obtaining medical documents, or claiming benefits. There is therefore a need to strengthen the safeguards provided under the law and ensure that its protections are effectively implemented. This measure seeks to expressly prohibit the detention of patients, their relatives, representatives, or caregivers, as well as the withholding of newborn children, solely on account of unpaid hospital bills, medical expenses, or professional fees. It likewise seeks to ensure the prompt release of the remains of deceased patients and the timely issuance of the necessary documents. The bill further provides reasonable mechanisms by which financially incapacitated patients may secure their unpaid obligations. The enactment of this measure will strengthen the protection of patients and their families, promote humane and dignified treatment in health facilities, and ensure that inability to immediately pay for medical treatment does not become a ground for unlawful detention or withholding of essential documents. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11491
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every learner has the right to study in an environment that is safe, healthy, inclusive, and supportive. Schools should not only provide quality education but also protect learners and school personnel from violence, abuse, bullying, discrimination, harassment, disasters, health emergencies, and other threats to their safety and well-being. The continuing prevalence of violence and bullying among children underscores the need to strengthen school safety measures. The 2015 National Baseline Study on Violence Against Children, conducted by the Council for the Welfare of Children and UNICEF, found that 65% of Filipino children and youth aged 13 to 24 experienced peer violence, while 64.2% experienced physical violence and 61.5% experienced psychological violence during childhood. More recently, the Department of Education reported 2,500 bullying cases in the National Capital Region during School Year 2024–2025, demonstrating that bullying and violence continue to pose significant concerns within the school environment. These circumstances show that school safety must go beyond physical security. It must also address the mental, emotional, psychosocial, and digital well-being of learners and school personnel. With the increasing use of digital technologies, schools must likewise be prepared to address cyberbullying, online abuse, cybersecurity risks, and other emerging threats. This measure seeks to institutionalize a Comprehensive School Safety Framework for public and private basic education institutions. It provides common standards for the prevention of risks, preparedness for emergencies, response to incidents, and recovery and support for affected members of the school community. Under the proposed measure, every school shall develop a School Safety Plan and maintain a School Safety Handbook containing appropriate procedures for emergency response, learner protection, reporting and referral, mental health and psychosocial support, digital safety, disaster preparedness, and off-campus activities. The bill also strengthens the roles of school personnel and promotes coordination among the Department of Education, Department of Health, Department of Social Welfare and Development, Department of the Interior and Local Government, Philippine National Police, local government units, and other concerned agencies and stakeholders. It further provides for appropriate safety infrastructure, risk assessments, emergency drills, disaster preparedness, and mechanisms for addressing bullying, abuse, violence, discrimination, and other threats. By establishing a unified and preventive approach to school safety, this measure seeks to ensure that schools are equipped not only to respond to incidents, but also to identify and prevent risks before they result in harm. Ultimately, a safe learning environment is essential to quality education. Protecting learners and school personnel from violence, hazards, and other threats will allow schools to better fulfill their fundamental role in developing healthy, capable, and resilient Filipino children and youth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11492
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE FILIPINO FAMILY AS THE FOUNDATION OF THE NATION, INSTITUTIONALIZING FAMILY-CENTERED GOVERNANCE, ESTABLISHING MECHANISMS FOR THE PROTECTION, DEVELOPMENT, AND WELL-BEING OF FILIPINO FAMILIES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation and commands the State to strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development. It further recognizes marriage as an inviolable social institution and the foundation of the family, protects the right of spouses to found a family according to their religious convictions and the demands of responsible parenthood, affirms the natural and primary right and duty of parents in the rearing of the youth, protects the rights of children, and equally protects the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception. These guarantees reflect a fundamental principle of a free and humane society: the dignity of the person is ordinarily first encountered, recognized, protected and developed within the family. The family is more than an aggregation of individuals receiving separate government services. It is a community of persons joined by enduring relationships of marriage, parenthood, filiation, kinship, responsibility, care and mutual support. It is where children first experience belonging and formation, where parents assume primary responsibility for their upbringing, where generations care for one another, and where citizens first learn responsibility, solidarity and participation in society. The rights of persons and the integrity of the family therefore reinforce one another. The State must protect every individual from violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect while, at the same time, respecting the legitimate autonomy of family life and supporting families in the discharge of responsibilities that properly belong to them. This balance requires the principle of subsidiarity. Public authorities should assist families when assistance is needed, coordinate with communities and civil society when these can effectively respond, and intervene directly when protection or the public welfare requires it. Government should strengthen legitimate family functions rather than unnecessarily displace them. This principle is especially important today. Filipino families face increasingly complex economic, social and cultural pressures. Household size continues to decline. Marriage is occurring later and less frequently. Fertility has fallen below replacement level. Millions of families experience prolonged separation because of overseas or internal migration. Parents confront growing demands involving work, caregiving, education, technology, mental health and child protection. Grandparents increasingly 2 perform caregiving responsibilities. Poor and vulnerable families frequently navigate several government agencies merely to address problems experienced simultaneously within one household. Government possesses numerous family-related statutes and programs, yet these interventions remain dispersed across institutions organized according to administrative mandates rather than around the family that experiences these conditions as one reality. This bill therefore establishes a permanent national system of family- centered governance. It creates the National Commission on the Filipino Family, supported by a National Advisory Council and a professional Secretariat, as the principal policy, coordinating, monitoring and standards-setting institution for family-centered governance. It establishes a National Filipino Family Development Framework, measurable family well-being indicators, proportionate Family Impact Assessments for major government measures, local family-service convergence, and mechanisms for accountability and periodic evaluation. The bill recognizes the family as a subject of legitimate interests and participation while fully respecting the constitutional and statutory rights of each family member. It preserves the Family Code and expressly avoids altering marriage, filiation, parental authority, support, succession, property relations and other matters of substantive family law by implication. The measure strengthens marriage preparation and voluntary accompaniment during the early years of married life; expands parenting and family-formation services; promotes responsible fatherhood and motherhood; strengthens family-school cooperation and parental participation in education; 3 integrates family support with maternal and child health and early childhood services; and reinforces protection of children and other vulnerable family members. It also recognizes that work and family life are inseparable dimensions of human development. Families require adequate income and conditions of employment that allow parents and carers to perform their responsibilities. The bill therefore integrates family economic security, work-family balance, caregiving, housing, nutrition and social protection into the national family- policy framework. Consistent with the Constitution, the measure affirms the inherent dignity of every human being and the equal protection of the life of the mother and the unborn from conception. It strengthens prenatal, maternal and early-childhood support, particularly during the first one thousand days of life, while preserving existing laws governing legal personality, health services and family relations. It further recognizes solidarity with the weakest as an essential responsibility of society. Poor families, children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, solo parents, families affected by migration, disaster or displacement, and persons threatened by violence, abuse or exploitation require particular attention. At the same time, solidarity must strengthen rather than create unnecessary dependence. Public assistance should, whenever reasonably possible, increase the capacity of families and communities to care for their members and participate fully in economic and civic life. label: HB 11493
title: AN ACT REGISTERING AND REGULATING SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proliferation of social media platforms has revolutionized the way Filipinos communicate, access information, and participate in public discourse. These platforms have become essential tools for education, business, governance, and social interaction. However, the rapid expansion and influence of social media have also brought challenges, including the spread of misinformation, hate speech, cyberbullying, privacy violations, and other harmful online behaviors that threaten public order and individual rights. The Social Media Platform Regulation Act of 2026 seeks to establish a comprehensive legal framework to regulate social media platforms operating in the Philippines. This legislation aims to balance the protection of freedom of expression and innovation with the need to ensure accountability, transparency, and the safety of users in the digital space. The key provisions of the bill include: ● The establishment of clear guidelines for the operation of social media platforms to prevent the dissemination of harmful content such as fake news, hate speech, and illegal activities; ● Requirements for transparency in content moderation policies and algorithms used by social media companies; ● Safeguards to protect user privacy and data security; ● Mechanisms for prompt and effective response to complaints and grievances from users; ● Promotion of digital literacy and responsible online behavior among Filipinos; ● Strengthening the cooperation between the government, social media platforms, and civil society to foster a safer and more accountable online environment. This bill seeks to address that gap by mandating the registration and regulation of social media platforms operating in the Philippines, especially those with a significant user base or content reach in the country. It aims to ensure that these platforms observe standards of transparency, cooperate with government agencies in identifying sources of fake news, and implement robust mechanisms to detect and take down harmful content without infringing on constitutionally protected freedoms. It also seeks to promote accountability and discourage the spread of false information by imposing heavy fines and criminal prosecution, ensuring that addressing national and global issues is not hindered by disinformation. By enacting this law, the State reaffirms its commitment to uphold the constitutional rights of every Filipino while adapting to the evolving challenges posed by digital technologies. It ensures that social media platforms contribute positively to nation-building, democracy, and social cohesion. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. label: HB 11494
title: AN ACT EXTENDING THE CORPORATE LIFE OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION (PITC) FOR ANOTHER TWENTY FIVE YEARS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 2 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1071, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED CHARTER OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine International Trading Corporation (PITC) was created through Presidential Decree No. 252, and its charter was subsequently revised by Presidential Decree No. 1071, otherwise known as the “Revised Charter of the Philippine International Trading Corporation.” Under Section 2 of Presidential Decree No. 1071, the Corporation is authorized to exist for a period of fifty (50) years, with its present corporate term set to expire on 25 January 2027. For several decades, PITC has served as a government corporate vehicle in pursuing the State’s objectives in international trade. Consistent with its charter, the Corporation has undertaken trade-related activities and provided services intended to facilitate international trade, promote Philippine products and enterprises, and support the Government in its foreign procurement and marketing activities. As the expiration of PITC’s corporate term approaches, there is a need to ensure the continuity of its juridical personality, operations, and existing commitments. The expiration of its corporate term without an appropriate legislative measure may create uncertainty regarding the Corporation’s authority to continue performing its lawful functions, administering its assets and liabilities, honoring its contractual commitments, and undertaking transactions necessary for the fulfillment of its mandate. The proposed measure seeks to address this concern by providing for the continued corporate existence of PITC, while ensuring that such continued existence remains subject to appropriate government oversight and accountability. The proposed framework recognizes that the continued existence of a government- owned or -controlled corporation must be accompanied by mechanisms for periodic assessment of its relevance, efficiency, financial viability, performance, and consistency with national development policies and priorities. Accordingly, the GCG may conduct periodic performance evaluation and oversight of PITC, taking into account, among others, its financial performance, operational efficiency, governance and risk management systems, delivery of services, and contribution to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. The measure further recognizes that perpetual corporate existence does not exempt PITC from continuing government evaluation, oversight, and accountability. The Corporation shall remain subject to the evaluation, monitoring, and other appropriate actions authorized under Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Where warranted by such evaluation and consistent with applicable law, the appropriate government authorities may undertake or recommend such lawful measures as may be necessary to ensure that the Corporation remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. The grant of perpetual existence is not intended to constitute a determination that the Corporation shall operate indefinitely regardless of its continued relevance, performance, or economic viability. Rather, PITC shall remain subject to the performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight mechanisms applicable to government-owned or -controlled corporations under Republic Act No. 10149 and other applicable laws. At the same time, the proposed measure does not seek to expand the substantive powers and functions of PITC under Presidential Decree No. 1071. Rather, it seeks to ensure the continuity of the Corporation’s juridical personality and operations while strengthening accountability and providing for continuing evaluation by the appropriate government authorities. The proposed perpetual corporate term will also eliminate the need for periodic legislative action solely for the purpose of extending the Corporation’s corporate existence, while preserving the authority of Congress to amend, repeal, or otherwise modify the Corporation’s charter or corporate existence through subsequent legislation. This approach provides greater institutional stability and continuity while maintaining the necessary safeguards to ensure that PITC remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. Perpetual corporate existence does not preclude the State from undertaking performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight of the Corporation's relevance, performance, efficiency, and financial viability, nor does it prevent the appropriate government authorities from recommending or undertaking such lawful measures as may be warranted by the results of such evaluation. The continued corporate existence of PITC is therefore intended to prevent disruption in its legal existence and operations and to ensure the orderly continuity of its contracts, obligations, assets, liabilities, and other lawful commitments. It will likewise enable the Corporation to continue performing its existing mandate and contributing, within the scope of its charter, to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. RODRIGUEZ, JR. label: HB 11495
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION AND WELFARE OF ANIMALS, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL COMMISSION ON ANIMAL WELFARE, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, AS AMENDED, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Animal Welfare Act of 1998 (Republic Act No. 8485), as amended in 2013, was a landmark in Philippine law — the first to impose criminal liability for acts of cruelty against animals. However, more than a decade of enforcement has proven that the law is no longer equal to the scale of the problem. Institutional authority over animal welfare remains fragmented, penalties are weak and undifferentiated, population management tools are absent, and accountability for government-run facilities is virtually nonexistent.1 Science has also advanced. International standards now recognize animals as sentient beings capable of suffering, fear, and positive emotional states. Animal welfare policy is now based on the Five Domains framework: nutrition, physical environment, health, behavioral expression, and mental state.2 Philippine law has not kept pace. The gap between law and reality is stark. Petcare in 2024, there are 13 million stray cats and dogs in the Philippines.3 Despite the fact that a majority of Philippine households have at least one pet in their domestic residence,4 animal welfare has received little priority in State policy and government programs. Worse, in 2020, the Care and Responsibility for Animals (CARA) Welfare Philippines, Inc. reported 3,000 cases of animal abuse, including beating, kicking, and mutilating.5 Hence, this Bill, which is an overhaul of the Animal Welfare Act of 1998. It anchors Philippine policy on the Five Domains of Animal Welfare and the Philippines’ international commitments, including the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species.6 It replaces a weak and scattered enforcement architecture with a single empowered agency, and it closes the legal loopholes that have allowed cruelty to go unpunished. See WHO/WSPA, Guidelines for Dog Population Management (1990). 9 The 3Rs Principle was articulated by W.M.S. Russell and R.L. Burch, The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (1959), and has since been adopted by the International Council for Laboratory (5) Overhaul the penalty structure with a graduated scale of up to three years’ imprisonment and a fine of Php 500,000.00 for causing the death of an animal, up to eighteen months and Php 80,000.00 for grave injury, and up to one year and Php 30,000.00 for lesser harm, with maximum penalties automatically applied in aggravated cases; (6) Comprehensively prohibit all forms of dog-meat trading, animal cruelty content, animal fighting, and animal poisoning as inherently cruel and exploitative practices, and provide penalties for violation thereof. (7) Provides for the integration of Animal Welfare Education in basic and higher education institutions. (8) Establish a presumption of neglect against the owner or occupant of premises where an animal is found neglected, and codify the right of good- faith rescuers to enter such premises under the doctrine of negotiorum gestio10 without criminal liability; In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11496
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ASSIGNMENT OF AN AGRICULTURAL TECHNICIAN IN EACH LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT AND ENHANCING THE OPERATIONAL CAPABILITIES OF THE TECHNICIANS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture used to be one of the Philippines’ strongest sectors in the economy. We prided ourselves with the ability of our farmers to compete in the global market. However, present times show a completely different picture. What used to be a robust agricultural sector now has given way to other sectors such as the services and manufacturing sector. From exporters of products such as rice, we now import rice to be able to feed our growing population. But the agricultural sector should not be left to decline, in fact it may present the solution to many of our economic woes. A boosted agricultural sector would help us with food security issues. If agriculture becomes economically viable, rural economies would undergo a drastic transformation. Farmers would no longer have to venture into cities to find work, thereby reducing rural-urban migration. This in turn would lead to decongested cities and reduce the pressure to create more and more jobs in urban environments. This is why we need to inculcate advancements made in agricultural technology with our farmers. While there exist programs that already seek to impart such knowledge directly to our farmers, its effects may be attained faster and in greater magnitude if there is an assigned an expert in agricultural technology that routinely aids and assesses each farmer’s yield and capabilities. It is for these foregoing premises that approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C.
