label: HB 11540
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REGULATORY POWERS OF THE NATIONAL FOOD AUTHORITY TO SUPPORT THE RICE INDUSTRY AND ENSURE CONSUMER PROTECTION THROUGH ADEQUATE SUPPLY AND STABLE PRICE OF RICE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8178, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “AGRICULTURAL TARIFFICATION ACT”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rice is a staple food of Filipino households and remains central to the country’s food security, agricultural economy, and household welfare. Republic Act No. 8178, as amended by Republic Act No. 11203, liberalized rice importation and shifted the National Food Authority (NFA) away from its previous regulatory and commercial functions toward maintaining an emergency rice buffer stock.1 While rice tariffication was intended to improve market efficiency and provide consumers access to competitively priced rice, subsequent experience has underscored the continuing need for effective government capacity to monitor the rice market, protect consumers from unreasonable price movements, and safeguard the interests of domestic rice producers. The proposed measure therefore seeks to strengthen the regulatory powers of the 1 Republic Act No. 8178, Agricultural Tariffication Act, § 2, as amended by Republic Act No. 11203, Rice Tariffication Law (2019), Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines. Department of Agriculture (DA), through the NFA, and improve the government’s ability to respond to supply disruptions and market abuses.2 The measure recognizes that food security requires more than simply ensuring the availability of imports. The proposed amendments strengthen the government’s ability to register and inspect grain warehouses and other facilities, collect and analyze market data, and respond to cornering, hoarding, profiteering, artificial scarcity, and unwarranted increases in rice prices.3 These powers are intended to give the government the tools necessary to identify and address conduct that can undermine the normal operation of the rice market and adversely affect consumers. The bill also provides for greater coordination among the DA, NFA, Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), Bureau of Customs (BOC), local government units, and law-enforcement agencies, recognizing that effective rice-market regulation requires timely information and coordinated enforcement. At the same time, the bill seeks to strengthen the role of the government in maintaining a reliable rice buffer stock and supporting domestic farmers. It requires the NFA to source its buffer stock primarily from local farmers, farmer cooperatives, and farmers’ associations, while allowing procurement in milled- rice form when necessary and providing an order of preference that gives priority to local agricultural institutions and facilities. The measure also establishes more flexible mechanisms for the disposition of buffer stocks, including sales through accredited retailers, government entities, KADIWA outlets, farmers and farmer cooperatives, and public auction, subject to requirements of transparency, competitiveness, accountability, and public monitoring. These provisions are designed both to improve stock management and to ensure that government procurement can provide a dependable market for local farmers while preventing the unnecessary aging and wastage of public rice stocks. Finally, the measure seeks to provide farmers with greater protection against excessively low palay prices while balancing this objective with consumer welfare. It authorizes the DA to establish reasonable and flexible floor prices for palay at the national, regional, and provincial levels, taking into account production costs, prevailing market prices, reasonable farmer margins, and the welfare of both farmers and consumers. This approach recognizes that a resilient rice industry must protect both ends of the food-supply chain: consumers must 2 Republic Act No. 11203, An Act Liberalizing the Importation, Exportation and Trading of Rice, Lifting for the Purpose the Quantitative Import Restriction on Rice, and for Other Purposes, §§ 2, 5 and 6 (2019), Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines. 3 Republic Act No. 8178, as amended, § 5 have access to adequate and reasonably priced rice, while farmers must receive prices that make rice production economically sustainable. By restoring stronger regulatory capacity, improving buffer-stock management, strengthening enforcement against market abuses, and providing mechanisms for more reasonable farmgate prices, the proposed RICE Act seeks to build a rice sector that is more secure, responsive, and capable of serving the long-term interests of Filipino consumers and farmers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11541
title: AN ACT GRANTING FULL TAX BENEFITS TO GOVERNMENT PURCHASES DURING A STATE OF CALAMITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines remains among the countries most exposed and vulnerable to natural and climate-related hazards. Its location along the Pacific Ring of Fire, archipelagic geography, extensive coastline, and exposure to tropical cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, droughts, and other extreme-weather events make the country particularly susceptible to recurrent disasters. In the 2025 World Risk Index, the Philippines ranked first among 193 countries, with a “very high” disaster-risk score of 46.56, underscoring the continuing urgency of strengthening the country’s disaster preparedness, response, and recovery systems. The country’s experience with the COVID-19 pandemic further demonstrated that large-scale public emergencies may arise not only from natural hazards but also from public-health threats. The pandemic disrupted livelihoods, overwhelmed health systems, and required the immediate mobilization of public resources for medicines, vaccines, personal protective equipment, testing supplies, food assistance, emergency shelters, and other essential goods and services. To address the perennial challenge of the country, the State has enacted Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010,” which institutionalized a comprehensive, all-hazards, and multi-sectoral approach to disaster risk reduction and management. Republic Act No. 10821, or the “Children’s Emergency Relief and Protection Act,” likewise requires special protection and emergency relief for children affected by disasters and other emergency situations. More recently, Republic Act No. 12009, or the “New Government Procurement Act,” authorizes negotiated procurement in emergency cases, including when there is imminent danger to life or property during a state of calamity, when time is of the essence due to natural or human-induced calamities, or when immediate action is necessary to prevent loss of life or property and restore essential public services. While this mechanism expedites government procurement, government agencies may still incur value-added tax, excise tax, customs duties, and other applicable taxes in the purchase or importation of urgently needed goods and services, thereby reducing the quantity of life-saving assistance that limited emergency funds can procure. This bill seeks to grant full tax benefits to qualified government purchases made during a duly declared state of calamity. By exempting such purchases from applicable taxes, duties, fees, and charges, the measure will enable the government to obtain more relief goods, medicines, medical equipment, emergency shelter materials, food, water, fuel, rescue equipment, and other critical supplies using the same appropriated funds. The proposed measure complements existing disaster-risk-reduction and emergency-procurement laws by strengthening the government’s fiscal capacity to respond immediately and effectively to calamities. It ensures that public resources are directed principally toward the urgent needs of disaster-affected individuals, families, and communities, while promoting accessible, equitable, and timely delivery of emergency assistance and essential public services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11542
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SCIENCE HIGH SCHOOL IN BARANGAY SALVACION, CITY OF IRIGA, PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR, TO BE KNOWN AS THE IRIGA CITY NATIONAL SCIENCE HIGH SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1, of the 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Further, Section 10 states that science and technology are essential for national development and progress. Pursuant to this constitutional mandate, the Iriga City Science High School was granted authority by the Department of Education to offer Junior High School specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) beginning School Year 2024– 2025. Since then, the school has demonstrated academic excellence and has earned recognition through its outstanding performances in national and international academic competitions. This bill seeks to provide the school with a statutory basis for its continued operation and development. It likewise seeks to strengthen the school's institutional mandate and facilitate its access to appropriate national government support, thereby ensuring the continuity and sustainability of the quality science-oriented education it provides. Various stakeholders, including the Local School Board of the City of Iriga, concerned local government officials, and the DepEd Region V, have expressed their support for this measure. The establishment of the Iriga City National Science High School will expand access to specialized science and STEM education for academically capable learners in the district and neighboring municipalities, particularly those who may not have the financial means to pursue similar programs outside the Rinconada area. In the long run, it will contribute to the development of a pool of future scientists, engineers, and other professionals in Rinconada by providing learners with a specialized educational environment that nurtures their aptitude in STEM. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MIGUEL LUIS R. label: HB 11543
title: AN ACT CREATING PERMANENT SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICER POSITIONS IN ALL PUBLIC ELEMENTARY AND HIGH SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE AND ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND SECURITY PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 13 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Furthermore, Article XV, Section 3 guarantees the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. Schools are meant to be safe havens where young learners acquire knowledge, foster friendships, and build the foundation for their futures. However, public schools across the Philippines face growing vulnerabilities to security threats, unauthorized intrusions, theft of government equipment, vandalism, and physical violence. Elementary and high school students, owing to their tender age, are particularly vulnerable and require proactive protection. At present, many public schools lack dedicated, regular security personnel due to budgetary constraints or reliance on short-term contractual hiring and voluntary community assistance. This leaves basic educational facilities unprotected, placing both students and educators at risk. This bill seeks to address this critical gap by creating permanent, regular position titles for School Security Officers (SSOs) across all public schools nationwide. By establishing plantilla positions under the Department of Education (DepEd), the government ensures professionalized, well- trained, and stable security coverage in our basic education system. Additionally, this legislation mandates a Comprehensive School Safety and Security Program applicable to both public and private elementary schools. This program includes physical security enhancements, compulsory emergency drills, mandatory visitor screening protocols, anti-bullying initiatives, and close coordination with local law enforcement and disaster risk management units. In view of the paramount importance of safeguarding our children and ensuring a conducive learning environment, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11544
title: AN ACT REQUIRING MAJOR SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS AND DIGITAL CONTENT NETWORKS TO SECURE A CONGRESSIONAL FRANCHISE TO OPERATE IN THE PHILIPPINES, PROVIDING FOR REGULATORY COMPLIANCE, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Digital social media platforms have evolved far beyond basic communication networks; they are now the primary infrastructure for public discourse, commerce, news dissemination, and social interaction in the Philippines. As of recent estimates, over 90 million Filipinos—roughly 78 percent of the national population—utilize social media networks such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and X daily. Despite generating billions of pesos in advertising revenues from local businesses and content creators, major foreign technology conglomerates operate within Philippine digital borders without a physical corporate footprint, local regulatory oversight, or proper operational accountability. This lack of local jurisdiction creates significant public policy challenges. Platform operators frequently fail to act swiftly on takedown requests involving dangerous content, online scams, cyberbullying, hate speech, deepfakes, and illegal acts targeting Filipino minors. Further, these operators generate massive revenue streams locally while evading equivalent domestic corporate taxes, regulatory fees, and compliance burdens imposed on traditional broadcast and telecommunication entities. Under Commonwealth Act No. 146 (the Public Service Act), as amended, entities operating services of significant public consequence must be subject to state regulation to safeguard the public welfare. Just as traditional television, radio, and telecommunications networks require legislative franchises to access public airwaves and infrastructure, social media platforms operating at scale utilize public digital space and national telecommunications networks to reach citizens. This bill mandates that major social media platforms and digital content networks reaching a defined active user threshold must secure a Congressional Franchise to operate legally within the Republic of the Philippines. This requirement ensures that multinational technology companies establish a registered physical office, appoint local corporate officers subject to Philippine jurisdiction, comply with strict content safety protocols, and contribute fairly to the nation's tax base. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11545
title: AN ACT PROMOTING GREENING, FORESTLAND REHABILITATION, AND PROTECTION AT THE BARANGAY LEVEL, SPURRING LOCAL CLIMATE CHANGE ACTION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is recognized as one of the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Severe weather events, accelerated deforestation, watershed degradation, and loss of biodiversity threaten rural livelihoods, compromise food and water security, and trigger catastrophic disasters like flash floods and landslides. While national environmental frameworks such as the Revised Forestry Code (P.D. 705), the Climate Change Act of 2009 (R.A. 9729), and the National Greening Program (NGP) exist, their implementation often lacks localized, community-anchored execution and sustainable follow-through. The Barangay is the primary planning and implementing unit of government policies, plans, programs, projects, and activities in the community. It stands at the frontline of disaster risk reduction and environmental management. However, many barangays lack both explicit mandates and dedicated, localized financial support to sustain forestland rehabilitation, seedling propagation, and continuous protection activities within their territorial jurisdictions. This bill seeks to institutionalize community-driven climate action by mandating a nationwide Community-Based Greening and Forest Rehabilitation Program at the barangay level. Specifically, this measure mandates every barangay with degraded forestlands to establish community nurseries, initiate localized reforestation, and conduct regular maintenance and protection activities. By decentralizing reforestation and empowering local communities as primary stewards of their natural environment, we build climate-resilient barangays and safeguard our ecosystems for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11546
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL FACILITIES FROM IMPOSING ROOM, BOARD, AND DAILY ADMINISTRATIVE CHARGES ON PATIENTS CLEARED FOR DISCHARGE BUT REMAIN CONFINED DUE TO ADMINISTRATIVE REASONS BEYOND THEIR CONTROL, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution explicitly guarantees the right of the people to health and mandates the State to make essential goods, health, and other social services available to all at an affordable cost. However, a recurring issue in healthcare facilities across the country involves patients who, despite having been medically cleared for discharge, remain confined due to administrative delays and institutional processes beyond their control. These administrative delays include, but are not limited to, protracted discharge clearance workflows, delayed medical coding and billing preparation, unverified health insurance or PhilHealth coverage claims, delayed processing of government financial assistance (such as Malasakit Centers or DSWD medical aid), and system or software downtime. Under current practices, patients are frequently billed for extra days of room stay, nursing services, and administrative room fees accrued during these forced waiting periods. It is inherently unjust to financially penalize patients and their families for delays caused solely by institutional inefficiency, system failures, or third-party administrative processing. This bill seeks to address this injustice by prohibiting hospitals and medical facilities from imposing any room, board, nursing, or daily administrative charges on medically cleared patients whose physical discharge is delayed solely due to administrative reasons beyond their control. By enacting this measure, healthcare institutions will be incentivized to streamline their discharge protocols, ensuring fair treatment for patients while protecting families from unconscionable medical expenses. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11547
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DIGITALIZATION OF STUDENT ACADEMIC RECORDS IN ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DIGITAL STUDENT RECORDS SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Over twenty-three million students are enrolled in basic education, from elementary to senior high schools, in the Philippines‘. This translates to vast amounts of academic and learner information across thousands of schools nationwide. Yet, many schools, particularly public schools, rely on paper-based records, resulting in significant administrative work for teachers and school personnel in the preparation, filing, retrieval, verification, and transfer of student records. Given the delays and additional administrative work associated with these processes, there is a need to maximize the use of technology in the education system. The digitalization of academic records presents an opportunity to modernize and streamline these processes. As we reduce the administrative workload of school personnel, we also provide students more time to focus on learning. This measure seeks to modernize the management of academic records through the establishment of a National Digital Student Records System (NDSRS). Through this system, the government can reduce administrative burdens, improve the efficiency and accuracy of record management, and facilitate the timely retrieval and transfer of learner information. 1 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/19697 1 7/sy-2024-2025-sees-over-23-million -enrollees-in-elementary- high-school This proposed measure likewise recognizes the importance of interoperability across the broader basic education sector. While the digitalization of records in public elementary and secondary schools shall be mandated, private basic education institutions shall be allowed to voluntarily participate in the NDSRS. Their inclusion can promote greater continuity and efficiency in the movement and verification of learner records across public and private educational institutions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ETH T. label: HB 11548
title: AN ACT GRANTING UNRECOGNIZED ILLEGITIMATE CHILDREN THE RIGHT TO HAVE AND USE A MIDDLE NAME AND SURNAME
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant unrecognized illegitimate children the right to have and use a middle name and the surname of either parent. Article 176 of the Family Code of the Philippines originally provided that illegitimate children shall use the surname of their mother and be under her sole parental authority. However, on February 24, 2004, Republic Act No. 9255 was enacted amending the said article to allow the illegitimate children, upon recognition by the father, to use the father’s surname. As a result, the recognized illegitimate child may now use the surname of the mother as middle name and the father’s surname as the last name. However, illegitimate children whose parentage has not been formally acknowledged or recognized may be deprived of the opportunity to have and use a middle name. The absence of a middle name often serves as a visible marker of illegitimacy, which unfortunately perpetuates social stigma, invites discrimination, and undermines the inherent dignity of the child. This proposed measure allows an illegitimate child whose father has not acknowledged or recognized the child to use the mother’s middle name as the child’s middle name, followed by the mother’s surname. The mother may exercise this right by executing a Sworn Affidavit formally manifesting her choice of naming convention, subject to existing laws, civil registry rules, and the best interests of the child. Conversely, in cases where the mother has not acknowledged or recognized the child, the father may likewise exercise such right through a Sworn Affidavit, allowing the child to use the father’s middle name as the child’s middle name, followed by the father’s surname. The requirement of a Sworn Affidavit provides a formal mechanism through which the mother or father may manifest their choice of naming convention on behalf of the child. This mechanism is intended to provide the civil registry authorities with a clear documentary basis for the registration or annotation of the child’s middle name and surname, while ensuring that such exercise remains subject to existing laws, civil registry rules, and the best interests of the child. This approach is analogous in principle to the legal mechanism under Republic Act No. 9255, wherein an illegitimate father may execute the appropriate affidavit to allow the child to use his surname. In the same spirit, the mother should likewise be permitted to formally establish the child’s middie name and surname through a Sworn Affidavit, particularly in cases where the father has not acknowledged or recognized the child. The Supreme Court explained in re: Petition for Change of Name of Julian Lin Carulasan Wang, G.R. No. 159966, 30 March 2005, middle names identify maternal lineage and help distinguish individuals who may share the same given and family names. The absence or restriction of a middle name, therefore, has direct consequences on a child’s recognized identity, lineage, and dignity. This proposed measure ensures that unrecognized illegitimate children are legally acknowledged and given equal protection under the law. By allowing the use of the mother’s middle name or the father’s middle name as the child’s middle name, the proposed measure affirms the child’s right to identity, familial heritage, and legal recognition, thereby mitigating stigma and reinforcing the dignity of every child. More importantly, the measure is pro-poor and promotes equal access to justice. It provides a practical and accessible means for children to obtain legal recognition without requiring families, particularly those who lack financial means, to undergo costly and protracted court proceedings merely to secure a right that should be available to them by law. By removing this financial and procedural barrier, the measure ensures that legal recognition is not a privilege available only to those who can afford litigation, but a right accessible to every child regardless of economic status. In this way, the proposed measure advances not only the child’s right to identity and family affiliation, but also the State’s fundamental commitment to equality, social justice, and the protection of the dignity and welfare of every child. In view of the foregoing, an immediate apprgval is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEVELOPMENTAL-BEHAVIORAL PEDIATRICS FELLOWSHIP SPONSORSHIP PROGRAM, PROVIDING GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR PEDIATRICIANS PURSUING SUBSPECIALTY TRAINING IN DEVELOPMENTAL-BEHAVIORAL PEDIATRICS, REQUIRING RETURN SERVICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE One in every five children, or roughly fifteen to twenty percent of the world’s population is neurodivergent. This encompasses conditions like Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), ADHD, dyslexia, and dyspraxia, among others. In the Philippines, the population of neurodivergent is_ still undetermined due to underreporting, misdiagnosis, and limited screening. Nevertheless, albeit fragmented, available local health data and advocacy suggest that ASD affects 1 in every 100, which translates to 1.2 million Filipinos; ADHD affects up to 80% of adolescents; and specific learning disabilities such as dyslexia affect about 10% of the population. It remains a challenge for children and families to seek proper assessment and care for neurodivergent individuals due to the limited pool of developmental pediatricians in the country. Nationwide, there are only about 80-100 actively practicing developmental and behavioral pediatricians, fifty percent of whom are concentrated in Metro Manila, while others are spread mostly across major cities like Cebu and Davao!. Aside from the high cost of professional fees, parents find it hard to secure consultation schedules from developmental and behavioral pediatricians - that is, if they find one nearby. To bridge this gap and encourage more Filipino pediatricians to take the path of becoming a full-fledged developmental and_ behavioral pediatrician, this bill establishes the Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics t httos://onlinelibrary. wiley.com/doi/10.1111/pc.16055 Fellowship Sponsorship (DPFS) Program. This program shall provide financial and institutional support to qualified pediatricians pursuing accredited fellowship training in Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, with the aim of increasing the number of specialists serving neurodivergent Filipino children. Through this, early detection and intervention for neurodivergent children is more plausible, providing the public with more accessible, affordable, and responsive health care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KE TH T. label: HB 11550
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE WELFARE, SOCIAL PROTECTION, TRAINING, AND OTHER SUPPORT MECHANISMS FOR CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES (PWDs), AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE There are over 2.5 million Filipinos living with disabilities. While the country has programs and projects for PWDs, that is not enough to fully care for PWDs. They would need assistive care in their homes and their daily activities. Across the country, parents, spouses, siblings, relatives, and other family members devote countless hours each day to providing physical assistance, medical care, rehabilitation, supervision, and advocacy for their loved ones with disabilities. Their work is indispensable, yet it remains largely unpaid, unrecognized, and unsupported. While Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, affirms the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities, there remains no comprehensive law that recognizes and supports the equally vital role of their caregivers. Many caregivers are compelled to reduce their working hours, forego employment opportunities, or leave the workforce altogether to provide full-time care. Consequently, they experience financial hardship, physical exhaustion, emotional stress, social isolation, and increased vulnerability to mental health concerns. Amidst these, caregivers provide unpaid work 24 hours a day, seven days a week. While initiatives such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development's Therapy for Fee (TheraFee) Project, which provided cash-for- work assistance to family and community care workers who support persons with disabilities, represent a significant step forward, there remains a need for a comprehensive and sustainable framework that addresses the broader needs of caregivers of persons with disabilities. Financial assistance alone is not sufficient. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive support system for caregivers of persons with disabilities. It provides qualified primary caregivers with a monthly caregiver assistance allowance, free skills training and certification, access to livelihood and employment support, mental health and wellness services, respite care, and priority consideration in appropriate government programs. Empowering caregivers is likewise an investment in persons with disabilities. When caregivers are adequately supported, they are better equipped to provide consistent and quality care, facilitate rehabilitation and development, promote independence, and help persons with disabilities participate more fully in society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KE TH T. label: HB 11551
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A TEXTBOOK ASSISTANCE VOUCHER PROGRAM FOR STUDENTS ENROLLED IN PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education remains one of the most effective means of promoting social mobility, strengthening human capital, and ensuring national development. While the State recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions in the delivery of quality basic education, many Filipino families continue to struggle with the increasing cost of educational materials, particularly textbooks and learning resources. Although tuition and miscellaneous expenses are often the primary focus of educational assistance programs, the recurring cost of textbooks and instructional materials imposes a significant financial burden on parents and guardians, especially those belonging to low-income and middle-income households. In many cases, students rely on outdated, borrowed, or insufficient learning materials, adversely affecting learning outcomes and academic performance. This measure seeks to establish a Textbook Assistance Voucher Program that will provide qualified students enrolled in private elementary and secondary schools with targeted financial support for the acquisition of textbooks, workbooks, and other Department of Education-approved learning materials. The proposed voucher mechanism aims to promote equitable access to educational resources while supporting parental choice and the continued participation of private schools in the national education system. 1 The bill likewise ensures accountability and transparency through accreditation standards, digital tracking systems, and coordination with private schools, publishers, and authorized educational suppliers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11552
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE, INTEGRATED, AND SUSTAINABLE REINTEGRATION PROGRAM FOR OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) is an integral part of Filipino society and a significant contributor to our nation’s development. Yet, after years of working abroad and being separated from their families, many OFWs face another challenge upon returning home: rebuilding their livelihoods and reintegrating into their communities. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive, integrated, and sustainable reintegration program for OFWs covering the entire migration cycle—from pre-departure, to on-site support, and upon return. It adopts a whole-of-government approach to provide returning OFWs with access to employment, entrepreneurship, education and skills development, financial literacy, psychosocial support, and other social protection services. The measure likewise seeks to strengthen coordination among government agencies and private sector partners, improve job matching and skills recognition, and ensure that undocumented OFWs are not excluded from reintegration assistance. It recognizes that effective reintegration requires not only financial assistance, but sustained support that enables OFWs to achieve economic self-sufficiency, social stability, and psychosocial well-being upon their return. 1 We owe it to our OFWs and their families to ensure that, when they return home, they are provided meaningful opportunities to rebuild their lives and contribute once again to the country’s development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11553
title: AN ACT LOWERING THE OPTIONAL RETIREMENT AGE OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES FROM SIXTY (60) YEARS TO FIFTY-SIX (56) YEARS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 13-A OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Principle 3 of the 1991 United Nations Principles for Older Persons recognizes the right of older persons to participate in determining when and at what pace they withdraw from the labor force. Consistent with this principle, this measure seeks to lower the optional retirement age of government employees from sixty (60) years to fifty-six (56) years. Lowering the optional retirement age will allow government employees to enjoy their retirement benefits after years of dedicated public service and pursue other opportunities where their skills and experience may continue to contribute to the economy. At the same time, vacancies created by retirement will open opportunities for younger workers, bringing fresh skills and greater familiarity with emerging technologies into government service. This measure seeks to promote a more dynamic and responsive public service while expanding employment opportunities and supporting the financial independence of retiring government employees. Hence, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11554
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RIGHTS OF INFORMAL AMBULANT VENDORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every day, informal ambulant vendors earn a living by selling food, goods, and other products, or by offering services, in streets, parks, terminals, and other public spaces. They are part of the daily life of our communities and contribute to our local economies. Yet, despite their important role, many of them remain outside the reach of government programs and social protection because they are not formally registered or recognized by the local government units where they operate. Being part of the informal economy should not mean being invisible to government. Informal ambulant vendors face unique challenges. They often have no permanent place of business, limited access to social protection, and little security in their livelihood. At the same time, their operations must also be balanced with the legitimate concerns of consumers, communities, and local governments, particularly on public safety, sanitation, traffic, and the proper use of public spaces. This bill seeks to address these concerns by recognizing informal ambulant vendors as legitimate participants in our local economy and by providing a clear and simplified framework for their registration and protection. 1 The proposed Magna Carta of Informal Ambulant Vendors seeks to protect and promote their rights to just and humane working conditions, social protection, access to justice, and workplace security. It likewise provides for a simplified registration process at the local level so that informal ambulant vendors can be properly identified and connected to government programs and services without being burdened by complicated procedures and unnecessary fees. By formalizing the informal ambulant vending sector, this measure seeks to ensure that these workers are no longer overlooked, but are instead recognized as part of our communities and included in the social protection and economic opportunities that government provides. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11556
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the right to housing is a recognized fundamental human right ensuring that every person has access to a safe, secure, and affordable place to live. Adequate shelter means much more than just a roof and four walls. In keeping with international law, Article XIII, Section 9 of the Philippine Constitution mandates the State to undertake a continuing program of urban land reform and housing for the underprivileged and homeless in line with the policy of the State to promote a just and dynamic social order as enshrined in Section 9, Article II of our fundamental law. Despite the government's continuing efforts, however, millions of Filipinos remain without affordable, adequate, and secure shelter. This predicament is particularly significant among low-income families, informal settlers, and other vulnerable sectors who are unable to acquire or sustain homeownership due to the high cost of land, construction, and financing for housing. This bill seeks to establish a national policy providing qualified beneficiaries with free access to government-owned housing through usufruct. Under this arrangement, beneficiaries are granted the right to use and enjoy a government housing property for a specific period without transferring ownership of the property to the beneficiary. This approach allows the government to make productive use of its housing assets while providing qualified families with decent shelter. This bill proposes to accord underprivileged and homeless Filipino citizens who do not own any real property anywhere in the country. It shall also be extended to government employees under the auspices of Local Government units (LGUs) and other government agencies provided that the beneficiary does not own any real property within the territorial jurisdiction of the LGU where the employee is assigned or employed. This provision may help government institutions attract and retain personnel, particularly those assigned to areas where housing costs are beyond their means. To ensure that government housing resources remain available to future beneficiaries, the grant of usufruct shall not constitute a transfer of ownership and shall be subject to reasonable conditions on occupancy, maintenance, use, and termination. Beneficiaries are expected to use the property as their principal residence and to comply with the terms of the usufruct agreement. These safeguards will promote responsible stewardship of public housing assets and protect government property from unauthorized sale, transfer, or commercial use. The proposed policy is also intended to complement, rather than replace, existing national and local government housing programs. By introducing usufruct as an additional mechanism for providing secure housing, the government can expand access to shelter while maximizing the use of available public land and housing properties. It may likewise provide LGUs and government agencies with greater flexibility in addressing the housing needs of vulnerable communities and their qualified personnel. The urgency of this measure is underscored by the country's continuing housing deficit. Government estimates indicate that, without sustained intervention, the national housing backlog could reach approximately 22 million units by 2040. Addressing this gap requires not only the construction of additional housing units but also innovative approaches that make existing government resources more accessible to families who need them most. Free housing through usufruct offers a practical means of advancing the constitutional right to decent shelter while preserving public ownership of government housing assets. It places the State's existing land and housing resources at the service of Filipino families who have no adequate home of their own, while ensuring that these resources remain available for public benefit over the long term. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11557
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CLASSIFICATION OF TABACO DISTRICT OFFICE OF THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) IN TABACO CITY, PROVINCE OF ALBAY FROM CLASS “D” TO CLASS “B” DISTRICT OFFICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Province of Albay, where the world famous Mayon Volcano majestically sits, is the second most populous province in the Bicol region. The total population of the province stands at 1,379,398 distributed across 277,127 households (PSA Population Census 2024). Albay is accessible to tourists and other travelers via land, air or sea. A developing road network connects tourist destinations to urban centers and the countryside through public utility vehicles, i.e., buses, jeepneys, tricycles, padyaks (pedicabs) and privately owned motorcycles, cars and other conveyances. Expectedly, the rising vehicle density greatly contributes to traffic congestion – one of the critically urgent challenges to land transportation management. Albay is divided into three (3) Congressional Districts composed of fifteen (15) municipalities and three (3) cities. One of these three is Tabaco City, which together with the five (5) municipalities of Bacacay, Malilipot, Malinao, Sto. Domingo and Tiwi constitute the First District covering a population of approximately 433,349 (PSA Population Census 2024). The Land Transportation Office (LTO) Tabaco District Office hobbled by a meager workforce of only eight (8) plantilla positions as it is under the Class “D” category, provides the necessary major services. These include Licensing, Registration, Adjudication and Law Enforcement to a fast-growing population of road users. Despite human resource constraint, the LTO Tabaco District Office, although not without difficulty, has exhibited a commendable operational performance particularly for the period 2021-2025. An evidence-based analysis of the LTO Tabaco District Office’s overall performance for this five- year period reveals robust accomplishments in the delivery of the following services: • Motor Vehicle (MV) Registration: A total of 417,890 MV transactions were handled over the five-year period with an annual average of 83,578 transactions. Transactions increased significantly from 2021 to 1 2023, then declined in 2024 with a slight increase in 2025. This reduction may be attributed to the 2023 LTO policy extending the validity of initial registration for motorcycles to three (3) years, thereby decreasing the volume of annual renewal transactions in the succeeding years. • License and Permits: The office processed a total of 176,277 transactions, with an annual average of 35,255. The number of licenses and permits handled steadily rose from 2021 to 2024, before declining in 2025. The decrease may be partly due to the long- standing effect of the 10-year validity of driver’s licenses, which reduces the frequency of renewal activities, although overall figures remain higher compared to earlier years. • Apprehension Cases: A total of 4,367 apprehension cases were recorded over the five-year period, with an average of 873 cases per year. Cases gradually declined from 2021 to 2023, reflecting improved compliance with land transportation regulations. In 2024, apprehensions rose due to intensified enforcement operations; however, in 2025, the number decreased as motorists continued to adhere to traffic rules, demonstrating the positive impact of sustained enforcement and compliance efforts. • Revenue collection: The LTO Tabaco District Office generated a total revenue of P307,381,319.74, with an average annual collection of approximately P61.48 million. Despite the decline in some transaction volumes, revenue collection consistently increased from 2021 to 2023 and remained steady at a high level in 2024 and 2025, demonstrating sustained financial performance and efficiency in revenue-generating services. (Records of the Operations Division, LTO V) Needless to stress, the upgrade of the LTO Tabaco District Office from Class “D” to Class “B” is imperative. Hence, this proposed measure that seeks to implement the upgrade hopefully forthwith. The recommended upgrade shall necessarily increase the plantilla positions of the LTO Tabaco District Office to twenty (20), thereby creating an additional twelve (12) positions to its current eight (8) personnel complement. The change in classification and the consequent accompanying addition of personnel will indubitably benefit the patrons and clients from Tabaco City and nearby municipalities primarily through enhanced services and expedited transactions. These timely and much-needed reforms will trigger and promote higher revenue collection which in turn is expected to further expand and optimize provision of transport and allied public welfare services. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CIELO KRISEL B. title: AN ACT INCREASING THE BED CAPACITY OF THE DRUG ABUSE TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION CENTER IN THE CITY OF LAS PINAS FROM ITS CURRENT CAPACITY TO ONE THOUSAND (1000) BEDS, UPGRADING ITS FACILITIES AND PROFESSIONAL HEALTHCARE SERVICES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost. The highly urbanized City of Las Pifias has seen continuous population growth and urban density, which brings a corresponding surge in demand for public health and social protection services, particularly in substance abuse treatment, mental health support, and community rehabilitation. While local health initiatives and outpatient drug treatment facilities exist in the city, the current physical capacity, medical infrastructure, and specialized personnel remain insufficient to meet the volume of individuals seeking residential rehabilitation and long-term recovery support. This measure seeks to expand and modernize the existing drug treatment and rehabilitation infrastructure in the City of Las Pifias by converting the existing locai facility into a high-capacity center named the Las Pifias City Drug Treatment and Rehabilitation Center. The bill explicitly mandates an increase in bed capacity to at least one thousand (1,000) beds, upgrades existing clinical, psychiatric, and vocational facilities to guarantee that the government provides adequate support to the city’s health sector. By enhancing the facility's bed capacity and integrating comprehensive medical, psychological, and vocational services, this Act ensures that residents of Las Pifias and neighboring localities in southern Metro Manila receive accessible, humane, and evidence-based rehabilitation without being displaced from their support systems. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK ANTHONY G. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE LOCAL HOUSING LAND BANK SYSTEM, MANDATING THE SUITABILITY ASSESSMENT AND PRIORITY RESERVATION OF TAX-DELINQUENT REAL PROPERTIES FOR SOCIALIZED HOUSING, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 264 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to undertake, in cooperation with the public sector, a continuing program of urban land reform and housing that will make available affordable and decent housing and basic services to underprivileged and homeless citizens. Yet in many highly urbanized cities, one of the greatest obstacles to providing affordable housing is not merely the cost of construction, but the extreme scarcity and high market cost of available land. At the same time, local government units periodically acquire real properties as a consequence of unpaid real property taxes. Under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, real properties may, after compliance with the required notice, levy, and public auction procedures, be acquired by the local government when there is no qualified bidder or when the highest bid is insufficient to satisfy the taxes and related charges due. The law likewise preserves the property owner's statutory right of redemption before ownership finally vests in the local government unit. Once ownership has lawfully and finally vested in the local government, however, existing law generally allows the property to be subsequently disposed of through public auction. This measure seeks to introduce a more socially productive alternative. Before an LGU-owned property acquired through tax delinquency proceedings is resold, the property should first be evaluated to determine whether it can be utilized for socialized or public housing. Properties that are safe, accessible, appropriately located, and economically feasible for housing development may be placed in a Local Housing Land Bank rather than immediately returned to the private real estate market. This policy complements Republic Act No. 7279, otherwise known as the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992, which recognizes land banking as a mode of acquiring land for socialized housing and accords priority to government-owned, abandoned, and idle lands. The proposed Local Housing Land Bank will provide LGUs with an VX YS Zz additional mechanism to address their housing requirements, particularly in highly urbanized areas where land prices frequently make in-city relocation difficult. The measure expressly protects property owners. Mere tax delinquency shall never be sufficient to place privately owned property in the Local Housing Land Bank. No property may be included until all procedures required by law have been completed and the owner's statutory right of redemption has fully expired. The measure further promotes in-city and on-site development whenever practicable so that families receiving government housing are not unnecessarily displaced far from their employment, schools, health facilities, transportation, and established communities. Housing should not merely provide a roof over a family's head. It should provide security of tenure while keeping families connected to their livelihoods and communities. label: HB 11564
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAM FOR THE PREVENTION, EARLY DETECTION, DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT, AND MANAGEMENT OF SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS (SLE), PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR PERSONS LIVING WITH LUPUS AND THEIR FAMILIES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Lupus is a serious and lifelong illness that affects many Filipinos, yet it remains poorly understood by the general public. Its symptoms can differ from one person to another and may resemble those of other illnesses. As a result, some patients spend considerable time and resources seeking medical attention before their condition is properly identified. For an ordinary Filipino family, this delay has real consequences. Repeated consultations, laboratory tests, medicines, and continuing treatment can become a significant financial burden. More importantly, when the disease is not detected and properly managed early, the patient's condition may worsen and affect his or her ability to study, work, earn a living, and care for a family. Government intervention should therefore focus on a simple objective: help Filipinos recognize lupus earlier and make proper care more accessible and affordable. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive national program for lupus under the Department of Health. It provides for greater public awareness, early detection and proper referral, training of health workers, improved access to appropriate treatment and medicines, patient and family support, and the collection of reliable information necessary for government planning and research. The measure also recognizes that detecting an illness is only the beginning. A person diagnosed with lupus may require continuing care and regular monitoring. Thus, the bill directs the 1 Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) to provide appropriate coverage for lupus screening and early detection and to develop and periodically review an appropriate benefit package for medically necessary diagnostic procedures, laboratory monitoring, treatment, and other health services for persons living with lupus. Access to proper care should likewise not depend on where a Filipino lives or how much a family earns. The bill therefore strengthens the referral system among primary care facilities, government hospitals, specialists, and other health facilities, while giving particular attention to indigent and financially incapacitated patients and those living in underserved communities. No Filipino suffering from lupus should have to endure years of uncertainty before receiving proper care, nor should a family be left to face the financial and emotional burden of the disease on its own. Through greater awareness, earlier detection, accessible treatment, and continuing support, government can help persons living with lupus lead healthier and more productive lives. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. R. label: HB 11565
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, DEVELOPMENT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR THEIR FAMILIES AND CAREGIVERS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipinos with autism and their families face challenges that extend far beyond obtaining a diagnosis. Many families struggle to find affordable assessment, therapy, education, health services, and other forms of support. These difficulties become even greater for families with limited financial resources or those who do not have ready access to specialists and appropriate facilities. For parents and caregivers, raising and supporting a person with autism can be a lifelong responsibility. During childhood, families must navigate health care, education, therapy. and social services. As the child grows older, new concerns arise, including further education, skills development, employment, independent living, and continued care and support. Government assistance should therefore not end with diagnosis or childhood intervention. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive National Plan of Action for the Care, Support. and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder. It brings together the programs and responsibilities of government agencies involved in health, education, social welfare, employment, skills development, and local government services so that persons with autism and their families can receive more coordinated support. The measure promotes early identification and appropriate intervention, accessible health and rehabilitation services, inclusive education, skills development and employment opportunities, support for parents and caregivers, and greater public awareness and acceptance. It likewise 1 strengthens referral systems so that families can more easily determine where and how to obtain appropriate government services. More importantly, the measure recognizes that persons with autism have different needs at different stages of their lives. Government programs must therefore provide continuity of support from childhood and education to adulthood, employment, community participation, and, when necessary, continuing care. Persons with autism are members of our families and communities who deserve the same opportunities to learn, work, participate, and live with dignity. A more inclusive society requires not only awareness and acceptance, but also accessible services and concrete opportunities that allow every Filipino to reach his or her potential. title: AN ACT DECLARING AUGUST 25 OF EVERY YEAR AS ILOILO CITY CHARTER DAY AND DECLARING THE SAME AS A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF ILOILO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The City of Iloilo is one of the oldest and most historically significant urban centers in the Philippines and has played an important role in the political, economic, cultural, and social development of the country. The legal foundation for the establishment and organization of the City of Iloilo is found in Commonwealth Act No. 57, otherwise known as the Charter of the City of Iloilo, as subsequently amended by Commonwealth Act No. 158 and other amendatory laws. Commonwealth Act No. 158, approved on November 9, 1936, amended the Charter and provided for the organization and administration of the City of Iloilo. The inauguration of the city was originally scheduled by the President for July 16, 1937. On January 23, 1937, President Manuel L. Quezon issued Proclamation No. 133, entitled “Setting Aside July 16, 1937, as a Day for the Inauguration of the City of Iloilo, and Declaring It a Special Public Holiday for the Province of Iloilo.” The inauguration date was subsequently changed. On August 20, 1937, President Quezon issued Proclamation No. 172, expressly amending Proclamation No. 133 and setting aside August 25, 1937 as the day for the inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The same proclamation declared August 25, 1937 a special public holiday for the Province of Iloilo. Project - Proclamations Series of Thus, August 25, 1937 represents the date officially designated by the national government for the formal inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The date consequently acquired historical significance as the city's Charter Day. The establishment of the City of Iloilo was likewise part of the transformation of several historic communities into a unified urban political jurisdiction. The Charter was subsequently amended to further define the territorial jurisdiction of the city. Among these later developments, Commonwealth Act No. 604, approved on August 22, 1940, provided for the inclusion of the territory of the municipality of Jaro into the City of Iloilo. The national government has, on various occasions, continued to recognize August 25 as a significant date for the City of Iloilo through presidential proclamations declaring the date a special non-working day in the city. A permanent declaration by Congress will ensure that the historical significance of August 25 is recognized every year and will provide the people of Iloilo City with an opportunity to commemorate the city's beginnings, celebrate its heritage, and reflect upon its continuing contribution to the development of Western Visayas and the Philippines. 48 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 50 51 52 53 54 HON. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE SAFETY AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE SUPPORT PROGRAM, REQUIRING MANUFACTURERS, ASSEMBLERS, IMPORTERS AND, WHERE APPLICABLE, DISTRIBUTORS OF ELECTRIC VEHICLES TO PROVIDE THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION WITH ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE RESPONSE SAFETY EQUIPMENT FOR EVERY TEN (10) COVERED ELECTRIC VEHICLES INTRODUCED INTO THE PHILIPPINE MARKET, STRENGTHENING FIREFIGHTER TRAINING AND INDUSTRY COOPERATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Republic Act No. 11697, otherwise known as the “Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act” (EVIDA), established the national policy for the development and adoption of electric vehicles in the Philippines. 19 As electric mobility expands, the emergency-response capability of government must develop alongside it. 22 Electric vehicles equipped with rechargeable traction batteries present emergency-response considerations different from those encountered in conventional vehicle fires. Battery thermal runaway may involve extreme heat, hazardous gases, prolonged incident management, and the possibility of reignition even after visible flames have been controlled. 27 Republic Act No. 9514, otherwise known as the “Revised Fire Code of the Philippines of 2008”, mandates the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) to prevent and suppress destructive fires and enforce appropriate fire-safety standards. 31 Republic Act No. 11589, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection Modernization Act”, further strengthens the capabilities of the BFP through the acquisition of modern fire suppression, rescue, hazardous-materials, specialized equipment, training, research and other resources necessary for effective emergency response. 36 There is therefore a need to ensure that the continuing growth of the electric vehicle industry is accompanied by a corresponding strengthening of the capability of the BFP to respond to electric vehicle fires and battery-related emergencies. 40 This measure establishes a statutory public-safety responsibility requiring manufacturers, assemblers, importers and, where applicable, distributors that first introduce covered electric vehicles into the Philippine market to provide the BFP with one (1) approved Electric Vehicle Fire Response Safety Set (EVFRSS) for every ten (10) covered electric vehicles introduced into the Philippine market. 46 Each EVFRSS shall include an appropriate BFP-approved Electric Vehicle Fire Containment Device (EVFCD) and such complementary equipment as may be required by the BFP. 50 The measure adopts technology-neutral terminology and does not mandate any particular brand, design or proprietary product. Technical requirements shall be determined and periodically reviewed by the BFP, in coordination with concerned government agencies, based on prevailing fire science, applicable safety standards and technological developments. 56 The measure likewise provides safeguards against double counting, establishes reporting and accountability mechanisms, requires proper government inventory and accounting of equipment received, mandates technical cooperation and firefighter training, and provides administrative due process. 61 As the number of electric vehicles on Philippine roads increases, the country’s capacity to safely respond to electric vehicle emergencies must increase with it. 64 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 66 67 68 69 70 HON. label: HB 11569
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH (DOH) TO SET AND APPROVE THE BED CAPACITY AND SERVICE CAPABILITY OF ALL DOH HOSPITALS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people (Article II, Section 15) and to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that makes essential health services available to all at affordable cost (Article XIII, Section 11). Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, builds on this mandate by requiring a responsive network of public health facilities guided by a national facility development plan. Hospitals under the Department of Health (DOH) form the backbone of this public network, particularly for patients who cannot afford private care. Yet the authorized bed capacity and service capability of most DOH hospitals are fixed by statute, so any increase or change, however urgent, must pass through the full legislative process. As a result, Congress each term considers numerous local bills seeking to raise the bed capacity of individual hospitals. The process takes time, and in the interim hospitals operate beyond their authorized capacity, patients are placed in hallways and shared beds, and the plantilla positions, budget, and equipment that should accompany expansion lag behind actual demand. This bill proposes a more responsive arrangement. It authorizes the DOH, through an administrative issuance, to adjust and approve the bed capacities and corresponding service capabilities of hospitals under its supervision and control. Such decisions must be grounded on objective considerations, namely each hospital’s development plan, catchment population, burden of disease, available human resources, and health care provider networks, together with other standards the DOH may set. The DOH is directed to continue updating and implementing the Philippine Health Facility Development Plan (PHFDP) to 1 guide the modernization of government health facilities, and to include in its programs the funding requirements for each approved adjustment. Importantly, the measure preserves the constitutional power of the purse. Funding for bed capacity adjustments remains subject to the regular budget process and must be included in the annual General Appropriations Act. The DOH is likewise required to submit an annual report to the Committee on Health of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Health and Demography of the Senate on hospitals with approved bed capacities and the corresponding funding requirements, ensuring that Congress retains effective oversight. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1508, entitled “An Act Authorizing the Department of Health (DOH) to Set and Approve the Bed Capacity and Service Capability of All DOH Hospitals,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. For communities such as Marikina and its neighboring localities, which rely on DOH hospitals like the Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center, the ability of the health system to expand capacity promptly where the need is greatest is not an administrative detail but a matter of timely and dignified care. Rationalizing how DOH hospital capacity is set will allow resources to follow patients, rather than wait for a separate law for every hospital. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11570
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and to give priority to the needs of, among others, the disabled and children (Article XIII, Section 11). It further mandates the establishment of a special agency for persons with disability for their rehabilitation, self-development, and self- reliance, and their integration into the mainstream of society (Article XIII, Section 13). The Philippines, as a State Party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, has likewise committed to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disability. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects how a person communicates, interacts with others, and experiences the world. Advocacy groups such as the Autism Society Philippines have long estimated that more than a million Filipinos may be on the autism spectrum, yet the country still lacks a dedicated national framework to guide how government responds to their needs. Families commonly face late or costly diagnosis, a shortage of developmental specialists outside major urban centers, expensive and hard-to-access therapies, limited inclusive learning environments, and few pathways to meaningful work once formal schooling ends. Existing laws provide important but general protections. Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, as amended, sets out the rights and privileges of persons with disability; Republic Act No. 11228 provides for mandatory PhilHealth coverage of all persons with disability; and Republic Act No. 11650 institutes a policy of inclusion and services for learners with disabilities. None of these, however, establishes a single, coordinated plan that ties together screening, intervention, education, employment, and social protection specifically for persons with ASD across the life course. This bill seeks to close that gap. It mandates the formulation of a National Plan of Action for Autism Spectrum Disorder, to be led by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) through existing inter-agency mechanisms and in consultation with local government units, civil society, autism self-advocates, and parents’ groups. It assigns clear responsibilities: the Department of Health for integrating ASD screening, referral, and diagnostic protocols into primary and maternal and child health care; the Department of Health and PhilHealth for the progressive availability of evidence-based interventions in 1 public facilities; the Department of Education, the Commission on Higher Education, and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority for inclusive education and transition pathways; the Department of Labor and Employment and the Civil Service Commission for equal and supported employment; and the Department of Social Welfare and Development and local government units for social protection and community-based support. The bill also declares discrimination against persons with ASD unlawful, requires sustained public awareness campaigns, and provides for funding through the General Appropriations Act. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1822, entitled “An Act Instituting a National Plan of Action for the Care, Support and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Appropriating Funds Therefor,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. Local government units are often the first point of contact for families of children with ASD, whether through barangay health centers, child development programs, or local social welfare offices. A national plan that equips and connects these frontline services with national agencies will allow every Filipino with ASD, wherever he or she lives, to receive timely support and to take part in community life with dignity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11571
title: AN ACT EXPANDING DEPOSIT INSURANCE COVERAGE AND STRENGTHENING THE INDEPENDENCE, MANDATES, AUTHORITIES AND FINANCIAL CAPABILITY OF THE PHILIPPINE DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 3591, AS AMENDED, AND OTHER RELATED LAWS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC) was created under Republic Act No. 3591 in 1963 to insure bank deposits and help maintain a sound and stable financial system. Since then, its Charter has been amended only twice in over sixty years — through Republic Act No. 9302 in 2004 and Republic Act No. 9576 in 2009 — even as the Philippine financial system has grown substantially more complex, more digital, and more interconnected with non-bank deposit-taking channels. This bill seeks to enact the Responsive Deposit Insurance Act (ReDI) to modernize and strengthen the country’s deposit insurance framework. It expands deposit insurance coverage beyond traditional banks to include other deposit-taking institutions, subject to appropriate regulatory safeguards, thereby extending protection to a broader segment of the depositing public. The measure also empowers the PDIC to adopt a more responsive insurance system by allowing periodic adjustments in deposit insurance coverage based on economic conditions, implementing risk-based premium assessments, and enhancing its capacity to monitor and manage risks to the Deposit Insurance Fund. It further institutionalizes mechanisms to address systemic risks and ensure the sustainability of the deposit insurance system. To improve operational efficiency and financial resilience, the bill strengthens the PDIC’s fiscal and administrative autonomy, enhances its governance structure, expands its investment and resolution authorities, and authorizes the creation of a subsidiary to manage and dispose of assets acquired from closed banks. These reforms are intended to maximize asset recovery, reduce resolution costs, and improve the Corporation’s overall effectiveness. Ultimately, this measure aligns the Philippines’ deposit insurance regime with evolving financial sector realities and international best practices. By enhancing depositor protection, strengthening financial safety nets, and promoting confidence in the financial system, the proposed legislation will contribute to a more stable, resilient, and inclusive financial sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought REP. MARCELINO “MARCY” R.
