label: HB 11572
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE FILIPINO FAMILY MAINSTREAMING FRAMEWORK, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR THE FILIPINO FAMILY (NCFF), MANDATING FAMILY IMPACT ASSESSMENTS IN PUBLIC POLICYMAKING AND GOVERNANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution gives the Filipino family a place of special constitutional protection. Article II, Section 12 recognizes the sanctity of family life and directs the State to protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. Article XV further recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation and mandates the State to strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development. This constitutional command is now confronted by measurable social and demographic realities. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that registered marriages decreased from 414,213 in 2023 to 371,825 in 2024, while the crude marriage rate declined from 3.7 to 3.3 marriages per thousand population. The 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey reported a total fertility rate of 1.7 children per woman aged 15 to 49 for the three-year period preceding the survey, down from 1.9 in 2022 and below the replacement fertility level of 2.1 children per woman. PSA likewise recorded 1,358,989 registered live births in 2024, 6.2 percent fewer than the 1,448,522 registered in 2023. Of the 2024 registered live births, 808,965, or 59.5 percent, were non-marital births. This last figure does not, by itself, establish poor family functioning; rather, it underscores the range of family circumstances in which government must support children, parents, and caregivers. These demographic figures describe changing patterns of marriage, fertility, and childbearing; they do not, standing alone, measure family functioning or parental care. The case for family mainstreaming rests on the fact that child welfare and family resilience are shaped across multiple policy domains. A child’s welfare is affected by health, education, housing, labor, digital safety, local government capacity, and household economic resilience. A parent’s ability to raise and protect a child is likewise affected by employment conditions, childcare support, public safety, social protection, transport systems, housing affordability, and access to reliable services. The condition of the Filipino family is therefore a governance issue that cuts across agencies and sectors. The risks facing Filipino children further demonstrate the need for a coordinated family policy framework. UNICEF Philippines, citing the 2022 Disrupting Harm study conducted by UNICEF Office of Research, INTERPOL, and ECPAT International, reported that two in ten, or around two million, internet-using children aged 12 to 17 in the Philippines had experienced online sexual abuse and exploitation in the preceding year, while fewer than three percent reported such incidents to authorities. This study- based estimate highlights the need for stronger coordination among family support, child protection, law enforcement, education, digital safety, and community-based intervention systems. The proposed Filipino Family Mainstreaming Act responds to these realities by making family well-being a deliberate and measurable consideration in governance. It does not create a new large bureaucracy. Instead, it establishes the National Commission for the Filipino Family (NCFF), attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination, with the Department of Social Welfare and Development serving as Secretariat. It requires agencies to designate existing senior officials as Family Mainstreaming Focal Points, thereby avoiding unnecessary creation of new plantilla positions. It also integrates family mainstreaming into existing planning, budgeting, monitoring, and performance systems. The measure also introduces Family Impact Assessments (FIAs) as a policy discipline. Under Section 11, an FIA is mandatory for covered Executive department and agency measures, including nationally significant executive issuances, development plans, regulations, and major government programs reasonably expected to have substantial effects on Filipino families. For proposed legislation, however, the NCFF is directed to develop and make available an FIA methodology and technical assistance which either House of Congress, its committees, or legislative offices may use in accordance with their respective rules. FIAs are not another permit or clearance; they are intended to help decision-makers assess effects on child welfare, parental responsibilities, caregiving, household resilience, work- family balance, vulnerable family sectors, implementation costs, measurable outcomes, and less adverse policy alternatives. The proposal also addresses a recurring weakness of social legislation: the absence of measurable outcomes. It directs the National Commission for the Filipino Family, in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority and concerned agencies, to adopt National Family Well-being Indicators covering child development, educational participation and completion, family economic resilience, health and nutrition, housing conditions, caregiving, child protection, violence affecting family members, and work-life balance. These indicators will allow Congress, the Executive, local governments, researchers, and the public to evaluate family policy on the basis of evidence and measurable results. The bill also contains targeted obligations intended to give practical effect to the mainstreaming framework. In basic education, it requires advance curriculum transparency for defined Sensitive Topics, parental opt-out procedures, and specified parental consent and notification rules. In government procurement, it disqualifies natural or juridical entities with final administrative, civil, or judicial convictions for violations of specified laws protecting life, women, children, and family welfare, consistent with Republic Act No. 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act. label: HB 11573
title: AN ACT DECLARING OCTOBER 5 OF EVERY YEAR AS NATIONAL TEACHERS’ DAY, A NON-WORKING HOLIDAY FOR ALL TEACHERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our teachers play a big role in shaping our children into a responsible citizens and preparing the next generation to lead and contribute in the development of our country. The global celebration of "World Teachers' Day" during the month of October is dedicated to honoring the important role of teachers in transforming education. More importantly, it raises awareness about the systemic support they need to fully realize their potential as educators. Recent headlines in the Philippines have heavily underscored this need. While Republic Act No. 10743 already legally recognizes the ﬁfth day of October as National Teachers' Day, it currently designates it only as a special working holiday. Teachers cannot fully receive the appreciation of their students and communities if they are still required to report for their regular school responsibilities. Therefore, this bill seeks to declare October 5 of each year as a non-working holiday exclusively for all our teachers. This bill seeks to declare the ﬁfth day of October each year as the National Teachers’ Day, which will be a non-working holiday for all our teachers. Let us give our teachers the genuine recognition they truly deserve. They have tirelessness and selﬂessly dedicated their time and talents to imparting valuable lessons and even life skills to our children. They are indeed the unsung heroes of our society as that are often easily taken for granted. Giving them a dedicated, non-working day of rest is a small but meaningful token of gratitude. After all, it is the least we can do to honor the very people who spend their lives building the foundation of our country's future. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11574
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON THE PAYMENT OF LOANS, MORTGAGES, AND OTHER CREDIT OBLIGATIONS DURING A DECLARED STATE OF CALAMITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is frequently affected by typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, pandemics, and other natural or human-induced hazards. These calamities may result in the loss of lives and property, displacement of families, interruption of livelihoods, and temporary closure of businesses. For many individuals and households, the resulting loss of income significantly affects their ability to meet existing loan and credit obligations. During a declared state of calamity, affected borrowers may be compelled to prioritize food, shelter, medical needs, relocation, and the repair or reconstruction of damaged property. Requiring the immediate payment of loans during this period may further aggravate their financial hardship and expose them to penalties, additional interest, collection efforts, and possible legal action. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, recognizes the need for a comprehensive and coordinated system of disaster prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. Consistent with this policy, the State must adopt measures that protect affected communities and enable them to recover without being placed under additional and avoidable financial distress. mi ” * This bill seeks to establish a temporary moratorium on the payment and enforcement of loan and other credit obligations of natural persons residing in areas under a declared state of calamity. The proposed moratorium shall apply for a period not exceeding one hundred twenty (120) days from the declaration of the state of calamity, or until the declaration is lifted, whichever occurs earlier. The measure does not condone or extinguish the borrower’s obligation. Instead, it temporarily defers payment and allows the accumulated liability to be settled through not less than six (6) equal monthly installments without penalties or interest arising from the deferment. Borrowers who are able and willing to continue making payments may voluntarily do so during the moratorium period. By providing temporary financial relief during calamities, this measure will help affected individuals and families preserve their limited resources for essential needs, prevent the further deterioration of household finances, and support their recovery and rehabilitation. It will also promote fairness and social protection while preserving the underlying creditor-borrower relationship. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAE “pM” D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed measure seeks to strengthen campus security in educational institutions through the installation of Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) systems in strategic areas and the adoption of Campus Security Plans. Schools must provide safe and secure environments for students, teachers, non-teaching personnel, and visitors. label: HB 11576
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MORATORIUM ON RENTAL PAYMENT AND EVICTION DURING DISASTERS AND OTHER EMERGENCIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is highly vulnerable to natural hazards and other emergencies that may result in the loss of livelihoods, interruption of economic activities, damage to homes, and displacement of families. For low-income households, informal workers, and other vulnerable sectors, these disruptions may immediately affect their ability to pay rent and maintain stable housing. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, establishes a comprehensive framework for disaster prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. However, existing laws, including Republic Act No. 9653, or the Rent Control Act of 2009, do not provide a uniform and automatic mechanism for temporarily protecting tenants from rental enforcement and eviction during declared disasters and emergencies. This bill seeks to establish a time-bound moratorium on the enforcement of rental payments and eviction proceedings involving covered residential units during a declared state of calamity or emergency, including a reasonable period after its termination. The measure does not condone the cancellation of rental obligations; rather, it provides temporary relief by allowing deferred payments to be settled through a reasonable installment arrangement without penalties or interest arising from the covered period. mi = DATE October 5, 2026 Subject to appropriate rules and eligibility requirements, similar relief may be extended to qualified micro, small, and medium enterprises affected by the closure or interruption of business operations. The bill likewise preserves safeguards for lessors and property owners by allowing mutually agreed payment arrangements and recognizing exceptions involving criminal acts or conduct that threatens life, safety, or property. By providing temporary housing and rental-payment security during disasters and emergencies, this measure will help prevent displacement, protect vulnerable households, support affected enterprises, and strengthen the country’s disaster risk reduction and management framework. Jac view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRIC Cc “pM” D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is frequently affected by typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other calamities that may damage homes, disrupt livelihoods, reduce household income, and interrupt access to essential services. During such emergencies, affected families may find it difficult to pay electricity, water, telecommunications, and other utility charges while attending to their basic needs and recovery. Access to these services is essential to public health, safety, communication, disaster response, and community recovery. label: HB 11578
title: AN ACT REGULATING AND MODERNIZING THE PRACTICE OF OPTOMETRY, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8050, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "REVISED OPTOMETRY LAW OF 1995"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act (RA) No. 8050, otherwise known as the "Revised Optometry Law of 1995," has served as the principal legal framework governing the regulation and practice of optometry in the Philippines for more than three decades. Since its enactment, significant advances in eye care, diagnostic technology, clinical education, pharmaceutical science, digital health, and healthcare delivery have transformed the practice of optometry both locally and internationally. These developments underscore the need to modernize the law to ensure that Filipino optometrists are equipped to meet the evolving eye health needs of the public while maintaining the highest standards of professional competence, ethics, and patient safety. The proposed measure seeks to comprehensively update RA 8050 by strengthening the legal and regulatory framework governing the profession. It expands the clinical scope of optometric practice to reflect current standards of evidence-based eye care; enhances educational, licensure, and continuing professional development requirements; reinforces professional accountability and public protection; and recognizes the appropriate integration of technological innovations into the delivery of optometric services. Consistent with the State's policy under Section 15, Article II of the 1987 Constitution to protect and promote the right to health of the people, and in support of RA 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act,” this measure recognizes optometry as an integral component of the country's primary health care system. It likewise promotes greater access to quality eye care services, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, through the responsible use of digital health technologies and tele-optometry, subject to appropriate safeguards prescribed by law. The bill also strengthens professional education and competency by updating academic standards for the Doctor of Optometry program, reinforcing clinical training requirements, and introducing mechanisms to ensure that applicants for licensure possess the practical knowledge and clinical skills necessary for safe and effective professional practice. It likewise enhances the authority of the Professional Regulatory Board of Optometry to promote continuing competence, ethical practice, transparency, and effective regulation of the profession. Recognizing the rapid advancement of diagnostic technologies and pharmaceutical developments in eye care, the proposed measure provides a legal framework for the regulated use of authorized diagnostic pharmaceutical agents and other emerging technologies by duly qualified optometrists, subject to the supervision of the Professional Regulation Commission, the Department of Health, the Food and Drug Administration, and other appropriate government agencies. The bill likewise strengthens safeguards against the unauthorized practice of optometry, unlawful corporate interference with professional judgment, and other practices detrimental to public welfare. Furthermore, this measure harmonizes RA 8050 with existing national policies embodied in RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act of 2012), RA 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), RA 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012), and other applicable laws governing public health, digital governance, and professional regulation. By integrating these legal frameworks, the measure promotes innovation while ensuring accountability, patient confidentiality, cybersecurity, and responsible professional practice. Ultimately, this proposed legislation seeks not merely to update an existing law but to establish a modern, responsive, and internationally competitive legal framework that will enable the optometry profession to contribute more effectively to the promotion of public health, prevention of avoidable blindness and visual impairment, advancement of clinical excellence, and realization of universal access to quality eye care services for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICIA C. label: HB 11580
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ALLOWANCES OF BARANGAY OFFICIALS, GRANTING HONORARIA AND OTHER BENEFITS TO THE BARANGAY WORKERS, GRANTING A LUMP SUMP RETIREMENT PAY, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay oﬃcials and members serve as the primary frontliners of our government. They are the ﬁrst responders in times of crisis, the primary implementers of national and local policies, and the closest and immediate representatives of the government at the grassroots level. Despite their round-the-clock duties and heavy responsibilities, they do not receive a regular salary per se, but are instead compensated merely through honoraria and allowances. Currently, the Local Government Code of 1991 mandates a minimum honorarium of only One Thousand Pesos (P1,000.00) per month for the Punong Barangay, and Six Hundred Pesos (P600.00) for the Sangguniang Barangay members, Barangay Treasurer, and Barangay Secretary. While local ordinances may increase these ﬁgures, many lower-income barangays are unable to provide living wages to their oﬃcials. In view of the continuous rising cost of living and the severe economic challenges that we all face today, these statutory minimums set over three decades ago are no longer just or realistic. This bill seeks to amend Section 393 of Republic Act No. 7160, or the Local Government Code of 1991, to provide the long-overdue ﬁnancial upgrade for our barangay oﬃcials. This measure proposes to increase the minimum honoraria to Ten Thousand Pesos (P10,000.00) for the Punong Barangay, Eight Thousand Pesos (P8,000.00) for the Sangguniang Barangay members, Treasurer, and Secretary, and Five Thousand Pesos (P5,000.00) for Barangay Tanods and members of the Lupon ng Tagapamayapa. Further, it increases their Christmas bonus to Five Thousand Pesos (P5,000.00) and grants a lump sum retirement gratuity pay for their dedicated years of service. Through this, we empower our barangay oﬃcials to serve their constituents with greater eﬃciency, dignity, and dedication. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11581
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR COMPASSIONATE EARLY RELEASE TO QUALIFIED PERSONS DEPRIVED OF LIBERTY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE ‘In health, there is freedom. Health is the first of all liberties,” said Swiss philosopher Henri Frédéric Amiel. It is a woeful reality for some persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) that they are shackled not only by their being offenders serving sentence or as detainees awaiting trial for an offense they may not have at all committed, but also doubly restrained by severe health condition. This bill seeks to legislate Compassionate Early Release (CER) to afford PDLs with life-limiting illness, significant functional impairment, complex medical care needs that cannot be effectively addressed by the penitentiary or correctional institution particularly the elderly, women and juveniles a chance to return to their family and community and live productive and meaningful lives or spend their remaining days with dignity in the company of their loved ones. CER is imperative as it is a measure of compassion consistent not only with the constitutionally declared policy on the value of dignity and full respect for human rights but also with the Universal Health Care Act that seeks to improve access to appropriate, affordable and quality health care services for every Filipino. The law does not discriminate against institutionalized populations including PDLs who are more vulnerable to health service deprivation due to inherent security and legal barriers. No hapless Filipino rendered helpless by severe health and medical status deserves to languish in jail. Significantly as well is the fact that CER would contribute to solving the critical problem of congestion in jails and correctional institutions. Overcrowding has long hounded the country’s penitentiary system. The average congestion rate of all correctional facilities stands at 321% of the facilities’ capacity or more than three (3) times their budgeted capacity. There is only one (1) correctional officer to twenty-four (24) PDLs in the Bureau of Corrections. The already meagre health care budget is further constrained by the huge number of PDLs. Congestion necessarily restricts mobility and productivity which negatively impacts the mental health and overall well-being of PDLs. The dire situation likewise escalates the infection risk for communicable diseases and heightens the risk of exacerbation of disease for those with non-communicable diseases due to the poor living conditions and lack of access to regular health care. This multiplies mortality or morbidity of PDLs that can be thirty (30) times higher than that of the non-PDL population. Verily, decongesting places of deprivation of liberty through CER is beneficial to both the released PDLs and those who remain in the penal or correctional facility. Reducing the inordinately large number of PDLs would help government cut costs on food, water, health and medical care and allied services, and expend the freed funds to improve the living condition of the PDLs left behind. Highlighting the value of CER, former Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla posits that the mechanism “...reaffims our commitment to justice, human dignity and rehabilitation...” Mr. Remulla’s message brings to light the distinction between CER and medical parole. The two processes, although both mostly based on health and medical grounds, are not identical. The proposed CER which is heavily anchored on human rights and dignity, is based solely on the PDLs current health and medical condition as well as the corresponding prognosis regardless of the status of serving sentence or length of detention or deprivation of liberty. Whereas parole is the conditional release of a PDL before the full completion of a sentence on the undertaking of good behavior or non- commission of a crime after the release. In the case of a PDL on CER, they are unlikely to return to lawbreaking as they have been effectively or fully rehabilitated or too ill to have the capacity or energy to reoffend. The proposed law underscores appropriate, holistic, and inclusive rehabilitation of PDLs as it is guided by studies’ findings that inmates who undergo rehabilitation programs are less likely to recommit crimes and go back to prison compared to those who do not participate in the program. Congress should not temporize in actualizing deliverance of deserving PDLs through CER. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ~~ Sua [I~ ISEL B. LAGMAN LEILA M. DE LIMA - KAKA J. label: HB 11582
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL MICROPLASTICS RESEARCH PROGRAM, PROMOTING RESEARCH ON THE PRESENCE OF MICROPLASTICS IN THE HUMAN BODY, FOOD, DRINKING WATER, AND THE ENVIRONMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. Likewise, Article XIII, Section 12 mandates the State to undertake appropriate health manpower development and research responsive to the country's health needs and problems. In recent years, microplastics have emerged as one of the most critical public health concerns in the world due to the worldwide increase in consumption of plastic-based products. Scientific research conducted in different countries have detected the presence of these microplastics in food packaging material, salt, drinking water, contaminated seafood, agricultural products, and even infiltrating our bodies, such as in our blood, lungs, placentas, breast milk, and even brain tissue. While research is still ongoing, evidence suggests that prolonged exposure to these microplastics may have implications for human health, including inflammation, endocrine disruption, reproductive health concerns, and the potential to act as carriers of pathogens and toxins, among others. |? The Philippines, being one of the world's largest users and contributors of plastic waste leakage into the marine environment’, faces heightened risks of human exposure to microplastics through food, water, and air. Despite this, there remains very limited local scientific research on microplastic prevalence in tissues and organs. The precise entry points of microplastics are unknown, and their possible health consequences are yet unclear in the Philippine context. Due to this research gap, government agencies currently lack sufficient data to formulate specific evidence-based policies. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Microplastics Research Program to coordinate scientific studies on microplastics in the environment, food systems, drinking water, and the human body. It does not impose regulatory burdens on any sector. Rather, it is solely a research initiative anchored on the principle that effective policy must first be grounded on sound science. By investing in research today, the government can better protect public health, strengthen environmental management, and ensure that future decisions concerning plastic pollution are informed by credible and locally generated evidence. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CRISPI “PING” D. label: HB 11583
title: AN ACT REDUCING THE FINANCIAL BURDEN OF MANDATORY CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL EDUCATION, TRAINING, CERTIFICATION, AND PERIODIC COMPETENCY REQUIREMENTS UPON FILIPINO PROFESSIONALS AND WORKERS, PROVIDING FOR A FIFTY PERCENT (50%) DISCOUNT ON QUALIFIED MANDATORY TRAINING FEES, ESTABLISHING SUBSIDIES AND OTHER FORMS OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE, PROVIDING ADDITIONAL PROTECTION FOR QUALIFIED GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Professional competence is not static. Physicians and nurses must remain abreast of developments affecting patient care. Engineers, architects, accountants, teachers, and other regulated professionals must continuously update their knowledge and skills. Filipino seafarers undergo recurrent training and certification to maintain competencies demanded by domestic regulation and international maritime standards. Many other occupations likewise require periodic training as a condition for continued employment or professional practice. These requirements serve legitimate and important public purposes. The State is justified in requiring persons engaged in professions and occupations affecting public health, safety, welfare, and national development to maintain appropriate standards of competence. Yet mandatory training carries a corresponding economic consequence. When the State makes completion of a particular course, training program, continuing professional development activity, competency assessment, or certification a prerequisite for the continued exercise of one's profession or livelihood, the professional or worker effectively has no option but to incur the corresponding expense. For many Filipino workers and professionals, the burden is cumulative. Training fees may be accompanied by transportation, accommodation, meals, lost working days, certification expenses, examination fees, renewal fees, and other incidental costs. The financial burden is particularly significant for entry-level professionals, government employees, healthcare workers, seafarers between contracts, and workers supporting their families. Republic Act No. 10912, or the Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016, recognizes the importance of continuously improving the competence of Filipino professionals. The objective of continuing professional development is unquestionably important. The accessibility and affordability of compliance must, however, form an equally important component of the State's professional development policy. Congress has already recognized this principle in the maritime sector. Republic Act No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, expressly declares that seafarers shall have access to educational advancement and training at reasonable and affordable costs. The law further authorizes the regulation of fees charged by accredited maritime training institutions for mandatory training required under the STCW Convention. There is compelling reason to extend the underlying principle to other similarly situated Filipino professionals and workers. The Constitution provides ample basis for such legislative intervention. Article II, Section 9 directs the State to promote a just and dynamic social order and free the people from poverty through policies providing adequate social services, promoting full employment, a rising standard of living, and improved quality of life. Article II, Section 18 affirms labor as a primary social economic force and directs the State to protect workers and promote their welfare. Article XII, Section 6 further declares that the use of property bears a social function, that all economic agents shall contribute to the common good, and that private economic enterprise remains subject to the duty of the State to promote distributive justice and intervene when the common good so demands. Article XIII, Section 1 commands Congress to give the highest priority to measures that protect and enhance human dignity and reduce social and economic inequalities. Article XIII, Section 3 likewise commands the State to afford full protection to labor, local and overseas. The proposed measure is also consistent with established principles concerning the police power of the State. In Carlos Superdrug Corporation v. Department of Social Welfare and Development, the Supreme Court sustained legislation requiring private establishments to provide statutory discounts as a legitimate exercise of police power. The Court recognized that the State, in advancing the welfare of a class requiring legislative assistance, may validly require private establishments to participate in carrying out a public welfare program. This doctrine was subsequently reiterated in Manila Memorial Park, Inc. v. Secretary of Social Welfare and Development and subsequent cases involving statutory discounts. These decisions recognize the broad authority of Congress to regulate economic activity in furtherance of the general welfare, while preserving the constitutional limitation that regulation must not become arbitrary, oppressive, or confiscatory. This bill takes these constitutional considerations into account. It does not simply compel training institutions to absorb the entire cost of a public program. It provides a tax mechanism for discounts granted, authorizes subsidies and fiscal assistance, directs regulators to establish reasonable fee frameworks, and requires government to progressively expand affordable public and online training alternatives. The classification of lower-salaried government employees for additional assistance is likewise founded upon substantial distinctions directly related to the purpose of the measure. The Supreme Court has consistently held that equal protection does not prohibit reasonable classification. A classification is constitutionally permissible when it: (1) rests upon substantial distinctions; (2) is germane to the purpose of the law; (3) is not confined to existing conditions; and (4) applies equally to all members of the class. Lower-salaried government employees required to personally finance continuing professional requirements occupy a materially different economic position from employees possessing greater capacity to absorb recurrent professional expenses. label: HB 11584
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOL IN BARANGAY MATALAPITAP, MUNICIPALITY OF PANIQUI, PROVINCE OF TARLAC TO BE KNOWN AS MATALAPITAP PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a public elementary school in Barangay Matalapitap, Municipality of Paniqui, Province of Tarlac. As provided in Resolution No. 093-s2026 of the Sangguniang Bayan of the Municipality of Paniqui, statistics show that the local government of Paniqui, Tarlac is experiencing a steady increase in population - leading to a rise in the number of school-aged children and students within Barangay Matalapitap, Municipality of Paniqui, Province of Tarlac. Moreover, the nearest existing public elementary school in the same municipality is located approximately one (1) kilometer away from Barangay Matalapitap which exposes the students of tender age to safety hazards as they travel to the existing public elementary school. Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Furthermore, paragraph 2, Section 2 of the same article mandates the State to “Establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” Establishing and constructing a dedicated public school within Barangay Matalapitap will significantly alleviate classroom congestion in neighboring schools, reduce the financial burden on local families, and ensure a safer and more conducive learning environment for the youth of the Province of Tarlac. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. JAIME EDUARDO MARC D. label: HB 11585
title: AN ACT GRANTING CHILD CARE LEAVE TO PARENTS, LEGAL GUARDIANS, AND PERSONS LAWFULLY ENTRUSTED WITH THE CARE OF A CHILD, PROVIDING FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution recognizes the family's role in nation-building. Article XV, Section 1 expressly provides that “The State recognizes the family as the foundation of the nation.” It further declares that the State shall strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution and shall equally protect the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception. The Constitution likewise recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and guarantees their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Article II, Section 12 further mandates the State to protect the sanctity of family life and to protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. Article XV, Sections 2 and 3 likewise recognize parents' rights and responsibilities in rearing children and direct the State to defend children's right to assistance, including proper care and protection from neglect. abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. The Constitution also recognizes, under Article XIII, Section 3, the right of workers to humane working conditions and directs the State to afford full protection to labor. These constitutional guarantees reveal that safeguarding the family, nurturing children, and upholding the dignity of workers are not isolated duties. They are crafted together as shared responsibilities of the State. The latest available Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) Labor Force Survey as of September 2026 is for June 2026. It reports 53.25 million Filipinos aged 15 and over in the labor force, of whom 50.66 million were employed. The labor force participation rate was 65.1%, while unemployment stood at 4.9%. Current laws offer vital protections and leave benefits for workers and families, such as maternity, paternity, solo-parent, and service incentive leaves. This measure does not seek to replace or lessen these safeguards. Instead, it aims to complement them by addressing sitations that existing leave options may not fully cover. For many first-time parents, caring for a child can feel daunting, especially without experience, guidance, or enough external support. Parents, guardians, and caregivers may algo face tough situations but cannot easily seek help due to work demands. In these moments, even a short period of protected leave can open the door to meeting a child's essential needs, reaching out for help, talking with teachers or professionals, or simply being there when a child needs utmost care, comfort, and guidance. Even more urgently, some children suffer quietly, facing fear, neglect, confusion, or distress without understanding what is happening or how to seek help. Their struggles often go unnoticed when the adults meant to care for them cannot be present due to work commitments. The State must therefore recognize that child care is more than attending to illness or emergencies. It includes listening, guiding, observing, teaching, accompanying, protecting, and understanding a child's behavioral, emotional, developmental, educational, and psychesocial needs. This measure is likewise consistent with the broader principle of responsible parenthood recognized in existing Philippine legislation. Republic Act No. 10354, or the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act of 2012, recognizes responsible parenthood and provides for access to information and services concerning responsible parenthood and reproductive health. This proposed measure complements that framework by addressing the continuing responsibility of parents and caregivers to provide care, guidance, protection, and support after a child is born. The State must nurture the family from the home up. If the family forms the bedrock of society, then safeguarding its protection and strength is ensuring the nation's very foundation. We must guard that the basic unit of our society receives the care, dignity, protection, and support it deserves. This measure therefore seeks not merely to provide another workplace benefit, but to bring the Constitution's recognition of the family and its promise to children and workers to life. It acknowledges that presence is a powerful form of care, and that timely support from a pagent or caregiver can keep a child's struggles from growing into greater challenges. Statutory and contractual leave benefits. It therefore strengthens, rather than displaces, the protections already established by law. With this measure, the State affirms that whenever a child needs care, guidance, protection, or simply a listening ear, the person responsible for that child's well-being should have a real chance to be present. Passing this measure will help fortify families, support first-time parents and caregivers, aid those facing hardships, shield children who might otherwise suffer quietly, and fulfill the Constitution's call to protect families, champion children's welfare, and promote humane working conditions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11586
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PRE-MARRIAGE RESPONSIBLE PARENTHOOD PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE SECTION 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10354, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “RESPONSIBLE PARENTHOOD AND REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH ACT OF 2012,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the family as the foundation of the nation and directs the State to protect and strengthen it. Consistent with this policy, Republic Act No. 10354, otherwise known as the “Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act of 2012,” already requires applicants for a marriage license to receive instruction on responsible parenthood, family planning, breastfeeding, and infant nutrition as a condition for the issuance of a Certificate of Compliance. However, while Section 15 of Republic Act No. 10354 provides an important foundation for pre-marriage education, it does not prescribe a comprehensive and standardized curriculum on child development, child behavior, positive parenting, positive discipline, responsive caregiving, and child protection. Since the enactment of Republic Act No. 10354, Republic Act No. 11148, or the “Kalusugan at Nutrisyon ng Mag-Nanay Act,” has further recognized the importance of positive parenting, responsive caregiving, parent- or caregiver-child interaction, and early childhood development. Philippine policy has therefore evolved, but the pre-marriage education requirements under Section 15 have not been correspondingly expanded. This measure aims to enrich, not replace, Section 15 of Republic Aet No. 10354 by weaving these vital competencies into the current pre-marriage orientation and counseling program. It introduces a unified, evidence-based Pre-Marriage Responsible Parenthood and Family Preparation Course that explores child development, behavior, emotional regulation, positive discipline, parent-child communication, child protection, and responsible parenthood. The measure is educational and preventive. It does not create a parental-fitness test or authorize the government to determine an individual's moral, psychological, religious, economic, or parental suitability for marriage. Completion of the Course, rather than a determination of fitness, shall constitute compliance. By reinforcing an established legal framework and harmonizing it with evolving Philippine policies on positive parenting and child development, this measure aspires to equip future spouses for the challenges of family life and champion the protection, well-being, and flourishing of Filipino children. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11587
title: AN ACT CREATING THE ZAMBOANGA CITY INNOVATION HUB, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Innovation fuels economic growth, sparks technological breakthroughs, creates jobs, and paves the way for sustainable progress. When ideas, research, technology, and entrepreneurship come together, innovation empowers communities and industries to tackle new challenges, boost productivity, and unlock fresh opportunities for prosperity. The Zamboanga Peninsula boasts a vibrant and expanding economy, a wealth of talented people, and immense promise for research, entrepreneurship, and technological progress. Blessed with abundant raw materials, rich agricultural and marine resources, and unique local products, the region stands poised to add value, drive innovation, and compete on both national and global stages. By harnessing these assets through innovation, local ideas and products can become high- value goods, cutting-edge technologies, and thriving enterprises. Zamboanga City, especially its First Legislative District, stands ready to become the home of a vibrant innovation hub—a dynamic meeting ground for innovators, researchers, entrepreneurs, industries, government agencies, academic institutions, and all who share a vision for progress. Consistent with and in furtherance of Republic Act No. 11293, otherwise known as the “Philippine Innovation Act,” this measure seeks to establish the Zamboanga City Innovation Hub (ZCIH) as the main innovation hub serving Zamboanga City and the entire Zamboanga Peninsula. The Hub shall serve as a center for research, innovation, entrepreneurship, technology development, incubation, prototyping, and commercialization, while providing technical, institutional, and business support to innovators, startups, researchers, students, and micro, small, and medium enterprises. Creating the ZCIH will help bring the national innovation agenda to life by energizing the region’s innovation ecosystem, championing research and technology, elevating the value and competitiveness of local resources, nurturing technology-driven enterprises, and opening doors to inclusive and sustainable growth across the Zamboanga Peninsula. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly soughit. title: AN ACT CREATING THE ZAMBOANGA CITY HIGH SCHOOL FOR THE ARTS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipinos shine for their creativity, ingenuity, and resourcefulness, qualities that pulse through our music, dance, literature, theater, visual arts, crafts, and architecture. Art is the heartbeat of our history and cultural identity. Through art, generations have kept traditions alive, shared stories, voiced dreams, and handed down our vibrant heritage to those who come after. The 1987 Constitution recognizes the importance of both education and the arts. Article II, Section 17 provides that the State shall give priority to education, science and technology, arts, culture, and sports. Article XIV, Section 1 further mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education and to make such education accessible to all. The Constitution likewise calls for the preservation and enrichment of Filipino culture and equal access to cultural opportunities through the educational system. Yet, despite these mandates, countless young Filipinos with remarkable artistic gifts remain without access to the specialized instruction, facilities, and opportunities they need to flourish. Just as scholars and athletes thrive with guidance and training, artists deserve a nurturing environment where their talents can vibrantly blossom. This proposal seeks to establish the Zamboanga City School for the Arts, a specialized public secondary school for students with exceptional aptitude and potential in Arts and Design. The School shall provide quality general education alongside specialized training in various artistic disciplines, in accordance with the standards and programs of the Department of Education. Zamboanga City stands ready and eager to become the first in Region IX to host a high school devoted to the arts. With its vibrant tapestry of traditions, languages, music, dance, literature, crafts, and countless cultural expressions, the City is poised to become a beacon for arts education in the Zamboanga Peninsula. The School will not only safeguard Mindanao’s multitude of traditions but also empower young artists to explore, adopt. and invent new forms of cfeative expression. The School aims to welcome not only the youth of Zamboanga City but also gifted students from every corner of the Zamboanga Peninsula. With fair and inclusive admission standards, those with artistic promise can pursue specialized arts education, no matter their background or means. The School will offer inspiring studios, rehearsal and performance spaces, state-of-the-art facilities, technology, and resources essential for vibrant arts education. It may also forge partnerships with government agencies, local communities, cultural institutions, artists, universities, and other organizations to enrich its programs. This institution is a bold investment in the Region [X's cultural future. [ts graduates will emerge as artists, educators, cultural advocates, designers, and creative professionals who will safeguard and enrich their communities’ heritage while shaping the evolving tapestry of Philippine culture. The young artists who will walk the halls of the Zamboanga City School for the Arts are destined to become guardians of our cultural legacy. By providing them with education, resources, and opportunities, the State can help Filipino creativity, talent, and traditions thrive for generations yet to come. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SUPPORT FOR SEAWEED AND CARRAGEENAN SCIENCE AND INNOVATION, PROMOTING SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT AND COMPETITIVENESS, PROVIDING FOR CENTERS OF EXCELLENCE, CREATING THE SEAWEED AND CARRAGEENAN FUNDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines ranks among the world's major seaweed producers, and the industry provides livelihoods and incomes for thousands of coastal families, farmers, fisherfolk, processors, traders, and other stakeholders. Beyond its economic significance, seaweed is a primafy raw material for carrageenan and is used in diverse food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, agricultural, cosmetic, and industrial applications. Despite considerable potential, the Philippine seaweed and carrageenan sectors continue to encounter challenges related to productivity, climate change, disease management, post-harvest losses, technology adoption, product quality, value addition, research and development, and access to both domestic and international markets. A coordinated, science-based approach is required to strengthen the seaweed and carrageenan value chain in the Philippines. The proposed measure aims to establish a National Seaweed and Carrageenan Scienee and Innovation Program under the leadership of the Department of Science and Technology. This Program will provide a comprehensive framework for research, technology development, innovation, technology transfer, extension services, commercialization, and market development. A key provision of the bill is the establishment or designation of Centers of Excellence, which will serve as regional hubs for research and development, technology demonsffation, product development, training, testing, technology transfer, and collaboration among government, academia, industry, farmers, fisherfolk, and communities. The bill also establishes Seaweed and Carrageenan Funds to provide sustained fimancial support for research and innovation, technology development, training, technology transfer, commercialization, product development, and market promotion. Recognizing that scientific discoveries and technologies have limited impact unless effectively disseminated, the measure provides for strengthened technology transfer and extension services. These services will enable farmers, fisherfolk, processors, cooperatives, and enterprises to access and adopt appropriate technologies that can increase productivity, improve quality, reduce losses, enhance sustainability, and increase income. The bill further advances market development initiatives to strengthen the position of Philippine seaweed and carrageenan products in both domestic and international markets. Support in product development, certification, branding, standards compliance, trade promotion, and export development will enable Philippine producers and enterprises to compete more effeetively in the global marketplace. An Inter-Agency Committee on Seaweed and Carrageenan Science and Innovation will be established to ensure coordination among government agencies and stakeholders, and to prevent duplication of programs and resources. This measure will strengthen the scientific and technological foundations of the seaweed and carrageenan industries, while promoting environmental sustainability, inclusive development, innovation, and global competitiveness. The passage of this measure is expected to result in higher productivity and inéomes, stronger rural and coastal economies, increased value addition, expanded markets, amd the development of a more sustainable and globally competitive Philippine seaweed and carrageenan industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The mango is one of the Philippines' most important fruit crops and is recognized by law as a high-value crop under Republic Act No. 7900, otherwise known as the "High-Value Crops Development Act of 1995." The law recognizes mango as one of the country's high-value fruit crops and provides a framework to strengthen production, processing, marketing, distribution, research, training, and financing for high-value crops. Despite the mango industry’s vital role, a wealth of untapped potential remains to boost productivity, strengthen climate resilience, improve postharvest practices, innovate processifg and product development, and expand market reach and global competitiveness. The Department of Science and Technology’s latest profile highlights mango as the national fruit and underscofes the urgent need for strategic research, technology advancement, knowledge sharing, capacity building, and robust policy support to propel the industry forward. Zamboanga City stands out among the country’s mango-producing regions for its rich yet often overlooked mango resources and remarkable genetic diversity. The city’s mangoes, among the most underrated in the Philippines, offer a delightful local variety with a unique blend of sweetness and tang, a small seed, delicate skin, and an irresistible aroma. Grown across several barangays, this mango is a hidden agricultural gem, brimming with promise for scientific exploration, varietal discovery, propagation, innovative product development, branding, and commercial success. Beyond its prized mango varieties, Zamboanga City and the greater Zamboanga Pemiinsula are also home to the indigenous baluno (Mangifera caesia Jack), a unique mango-family fruit native to Mindanao and its neighboring regions. Recognized in scientific and forestry literature, the baluno tree thrives in these areas, bearing edible fruit that ripens into a sweet and delightful treat. The true value of these local and indigenous mango treasures goes far beyond their eurrent commercial output. Their rich genetics, distinctive flavors and aromas, adaptability to local environments, deep cultural roots, and exciting possibilities for food innovation and value-added products make them deserving of dedicated research, conservation, propagation, and thoughtful commercialization. The Philippine mango industry boasts a robust production base. According to the Philippine Mango Industry Roadmap, the Zamboanga Peninsula ranks among the nation’s key mango-producing regions, and local agricultural data show that Zamboanga City dedicates considerable land and resources to thriving mango cultivation. This proposed measure aims to launch the Philippine Mango Science, Innovation, and Sustainable Development Program, creating a unified platform for research, innoyation, conservation, production, processing, value enhancement, technology transfer, capacity building, market expansion, and export promotion. The proposed Act shall complement and strengthen existing national policies and programs, particularly: 1. Republic Act No. 7900, or the "High-Value Crops Development Act of 1995," which recognizes mango as a high-value crop and provides for financing, prodiiction, processing, marketing, research, experimental stations, seed farms, and farmer training. 2. Republic Act No. 7844, or the "Export Development Act of 1994," declares export development a national strategy and establishes mechanisms for export promotion, research and development, technical assistance, quality standards, market development, and strengthening the Export Development Council. 3. Republic Act No. 10848, which further provided for the implementation of the Agricultural Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (ACEF) and authorized support for agricultural productivity, production and postharvest machinery and equipment, processing facilities, agricultural research and development, and programs a to enhance the competitiveness of farmers and agricultural sectors in domestic and international markets. This measure complements, not replicates, existing laws. It will establish a targeted policy framework that unites government agencies, research and academic institutions, farmers’ groups, cooperatives, local governments, and private-sector partners in building a science-driven, globally competitive Philippine mango industry. Specifically, the bill champions research into mango genetics, varietal discovery and profiling, propagation, climate resilience, integrated pest and disease control, sustainable cultivation, advanced postharvest technologies, food safety, innovative processing and packaging, product development, and market intelligence, and responsible development of locally important mango varieties and indigenous mango-family resources, including the Zamboanga City local mango varieties and baluno, while ensuring that commercialization does not compromise biodiversity, ecological sustainability, or the rights and interests of local farming and indigenous communities. Passing this measure will empower farmers, spark agricultural innovation, boost rural enterprises, safeguard precious plant genetics, create jobs, open new doors for food processing and agribusiness, and drive the nation’s sustainable agricultural and export growth. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine sardine industry stands at the crossroads of fisheries, agriculture, food manufacturing, and coastal economic growth. It nourishes millions of Filipinos and supports the livelihoods of fisherfolk, workers, manufacturers, processors, transporters, distributors, tfaders, and a vibrant spectrum of enterprises, from micro to large-scale. At the heart of the industry lies the City of Zamboanga, celebrated as the “Sardines Capital of the Philippines.” Here, a thriving hub of sardine-related activities pulses with energy, from fishing and fish landing to warehousing, processing, canning, packaging, transportation, and distribution. Across Zamboanga’s coastal barangays, communities are woven into the fabric of the sardine industry. These neighborhoods host and support a network of facilities for storage, warehousing, canning, processing, packaging, logistics, and more. The sardine industry is aot just a fisheries pursuit, but a dynamic coastal industrial ecosystem that generates jobs and economic vitality throughout the city and neighboring areas. depend solely on increasing the quantity of sardines harvested or processed. The Philippines must move toward a science-driven, innoyation- led, higher-value sardine economy. The fundamental principle of this measure is straightforward: we must harness precise science and bold innovation to unlock greater economic value from every sustainably sourced sardine. By embracing scientific research, accurate stock assessments, cutting-edge fisheries technology, smarter post-harvest handling, modern processing, automation, artificial intelligence, energy-saving manufacturing, innovative packaging, creative product development, by-product utilization, digital traceability, and sharper market intelligence, the industry can boost productivity while trimming waste and unnecessary costs. These advancements translate directly into economic gains. When science and innovation empower enterprises to create more value from the same or fewer resources, profit margins rise. These stronger, more sustainable margins unlock new opportunities to reinvest in machinery, research, workforce training, business growth, new products, and untapped markets. Innovation increases productivity and value addition. Higher productivity and value addition improve profitability. Higher profitability encourages reinvestment and expansion. Expansion creates more jobs. Greater production of higher-value goods expands domestic economic activity and exports. Increased domestic economic activity and exports contribute to Philippine GDP growth. This measure sees science and innovation not just as research costs, but as powerful tools for job creation, investment growth, enterprise profitability, export expansion, and a stronger national economy. The proposed Support for Sardine Science and Innovation Program will offer a unified framework to realize these goals. It will champion research and development, fisheries s¢ience, technology transfer, modernized processing, sustainable packaging, energy efficiency, high-value product creation, digitalization, workforce training, export growth, and the commercialization of new ideas. Particular emphasis shall be placed on value addition. Instead of relying primarily on increasing fishing volume, the industry shall be encouraged to generate greater economié value from sustainably harvested resources through improved processing, premium products, innovative packaging, better quality, new food products, sardine-based ingredients, utilization of by-products, and access to higher-value markets. This strategy empowers Philippine enterprises to compete not just on price and volume, but on quality, technology, innovation, sustainability, reliability, and true value. The measure also honors the vital role of Zamboanga City. Its thriving sardine industry, coastal communities, processing plants, canneries, warehouses, packaging operations, skilled workforce, and allied enterprises form a solid foundation for building a national Sardine Science and Innovation Center. By boosting Zamboanga’s capacity for research, technology, processing innovation, skills training, export promotion, and investment, the city can shine as a model for science-driven fisheries industrialization, inspiring and supporting other sardine-producing regions acr@ss the Philippines. At its core, sustainability remains essential. Scientific innovation should never be a license for overexploiting marine resources. Instead, science must guide the nation in setting sustainable fishing levels, then harness technology, productivity, efficiency, and value addition to maximize economic returns within those boundaries. The long-term profitability of the sardine industry depends upon the continued availability of healthy sardine stocks and productive marine ecosystems. The proposed legislation aims to build an economic model where sustainability and profitability go hand in hand, each strengthening the other. With better science, the country gains a clearer understanding of its resources. With innovation, it processes them more efficiently. With value addition, it earns more from sustainable production. With higher profits, enterprises grow and create jobs. With rising exports and economic activity, the industry makes a stronger mark on Philippine GDP. It is to generate greater economic value, more jobs, stronger Filipino enterprises, inéreased investments, expanded exports, and a deeper contribution to the Philippine economy, all while safeguarding sardine resources for generations to come. Passing this measure will lay the groundwork to transform the Philippine sardine ; into a science-based, innovation-driven powerhouse that is globally competitive, creates jobs, and drives economic growth. label: HB 11592
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SUPPORT FOR SPANNER, RED FROG, OR CURACHA CRAB SCIENCE AND INNOVATION, PROMOTING ITS SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT, COMPETITIVENESS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Curacha, scientifically identified as Ranina ranina (Linnaeus, 1758), is internationally referred to as the spanner crab or red frog crab and locally as Curacha or Kuracha. This species, belonging to the family Raninidae, is recognized as an important edible and commercially valuable crab. Philippine scientific and fisheries literature identify the species as particularly abundant and economically significant in the coastal waters of southwestern Mindanao, including Zamboanga and the Sulu area. Curacha represents more than a seafood delicacy; it is a vital marine resource that supports the livelihoods of fisherfolk and coastal communities and contributes to the food cultufe and culinary identity of Zamboanga and neighboring areas. Scientific studies have documented its economic significance and the presence of both domestic and international markets for the species. Ranina ranina has a broad Indo-Pacific distribution and is commercially harvested in several countries. The species is particularly recognized in international seafood markets, including those in Australia and East Asia. Large specimens command significant value in live seafood markets, demonstrating the commercial potential of the species when supported by effective fisheries management, production systems, quality standards, and market infrastructure. The primary challenge for the Philippines is not solely to increase the volume of Curacha harvested from the sea. Rather, it is to develop the science and technology necessary to sustainably provide a stable, adequate, high-quality, and traceable supply of Curacha while safeguarding the resource that supports coastal communities. Science and innovation form the foundation for achieving this objective. Research on reproductive biology, population dynamics, genetics, nutrition, disease management, habitat, hatchery production, nursery systems, aquaculture, stock enhancement, responsible harvésting, post-harvest handling, processing, and value addition can enable the country to transition from reliance on unpredictable wild harvests to a more sustainable and knowledge-based Curacha industry. Studies on the reproductive biology of Ranina ranina in southwestern Mindana@ have already generated important scientific information regarding reproductive activity, egg-bearing females, maturity, and fecundity. These findings demonstrate that a robust and sustained scientific program can provide the information required for responsible management and the future development of production technologies. This proposed measure establishes the National Curacha Science and Innovation Program, designating the Department of Science and Technology as the lead agency. It also provides for Centers for Excellence, a Curacha Innovation Fund, technology transfer and extension sefvices, market development, and an inter-agency mechanism. The proposed Curacha Innovation Fund will support research institutions, universities, fisherfolk organizations, cooperatives, entrepreneurs, startups, processors, and other qualified stakeholders in developing technologies to enhanee the sustainability and competitiveness of the Curacha industry. The proposed Centers for Excellence, particularly in Zamboanga City, Sulu, and other strategic locations, will serve as research and innovation hubs where scientists, fisherfolk, industry, and government collaborate to develop practical solutions. These centers will build upon existing scientific capacity in Western Mindanao and the Sulu area, where research on Ranina ranina has already been conducted. The measure also recognizes that production alone is insufficient. The country must consistently deliver safe, high-quality, properly handled, traceable, and competitively priced products to both domestic and international consumers. Therefore, market development, branding, product development, food safety, export readiness, cold-chain infrastructure, and international market compliance are integral components of the proposed program. The ultimate objective is to establish a sustainable Curacha value chain, encompassing scientific research, resource management, production, harvesting, post-harvest handling, processing, technology transfer, market development, and exportation. This comprehensive approach aims to benefit fisherfolk, coastal communities, researchers, entrepreneurs, consumers, and the Philippine economy. Investing in science and innovation today will help ensure that Curacha remains an abundant and sustainable resource in the future. More importantly, the country can develop the capacity to adequately and sustainably produce Curacha for a growing domestic and international market, transforming a treasured seafood resource of Zamboanga and Sulu into a competitive Philippine marine product while safeguarding the ecosystems and communities that support it. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AND INSTITUTIONALIZING A TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY TRAINING CENTER WITHIN THE ZAMBOANGA CITY SPECIAL ECONOMIC ZONE AND FREEPORT, TO BE KNOWN AS THE ZAMBOANGA CITY TESDA TRAINING CENTER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Technical education and skills development are essential to building a productive, adaptable, and competitive workforce. Through relevant and accessible technical-vogational education and training, Filipino workers and jobseekers can acquire competencies that improve their employability, productivity, livelihood opportunities, and capacity for entrepreneurship. Republic Act No. 7796, otherwise known as the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994,” established the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) and mandated it to develop and implement technical education and skills development programs responsive to the requirements of the Philippine economy and the labor market. The Zamboanga City Special Economic Zone and Freeport, or ZAMBOECOZONE, was established pursuant to Republic Act No. 7903, otherwise known as the “Zamboanga City Special Economic Zone Act of 1995.” The law established the Zamboanga City Special Economic Zone Authority to manage and operate the economic zone and envisioned the ZAMBOECOZONE as an agro-industrial, commercial, financial, investment, and tourist center and free port capable of attracting investments, generating employment, and promoting the economic and social development of Zamboanga City and surrounding areas. As the ZAMBOECOZONE continues to grow, demand for a workforce equipped with the right skills to support its thriving enterprises also grows. To meet the needs of industries, investors, and employers within the Freeport, technical-vocational education and skills training must align closely with real-world manpower requirements. Establishing a TESDA training facility within the heart of the ZAMBOECOZONE brings skills development directly to the doorsteps of workers, jobseekers, businesses, and local communities. This proposed measure paves the way for the Zamboanga City TESDA Training Center to take root within the ZAMBOECOZONE, forging a strong and lasting connection Between TESDA’s mission and the Freeport’s economic ambitions. The Center will become a hub for technical-vocational education, offering training, competency assessment, reskilling, upskilling, retraining, entrepreneurship support, and services designed to empower the local workforée. Placing the Center within the ZAMBOECOZONE is a strategic move that allows TESDA to collaborate closely with enterprises and industry leaders to pinpoint the exact skills and qualifications employers seek. The Center can open doors to apprenticeships, enterprise-based training, work-based learning, industry immersion, trainer development, employment referrals, and other partnerships that help bridge the gap between training and real employment. The proposed legislation also considers the existing cooperation between TESDA and the ZAMBOECOZONE Authority. In September 2026, the ZAMBOECOZONE Authority reported establishing a TESDA Provincial Training Center within its First Industrial Park in Sitio San Ramon, Barangay Talisayan. The facility is located in the Left Wing, Lower Ground Floor of the ZAMBOECOZONE Administration Building, while the Authority continues to complete its establishment. The Authority also reported that a 25-year Deed of Usufruct signed with TESDA on May 9, 2024 covers an 8,805.326-square-meter lot within the First Industrial Park for the development of a Provincial Training Center. Zamboanga Ecozone The existing cooperation provides a practical foundation. This ongoing partnership lays a solid groundwork for the proposed legislation. Instead of creating a separate facility, the measure aims to institutionalize, expand, and sustain the TESDA training center within the ZAMBOECOZONE. By integrating existing agreements, facilities, personnel, programs, and resources, the Center can maximize the impact and efficiency of government efforts. label: HB 11594
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE ZAMBOANGA CULTURAL CENTER FOR INDIGENOUS PEOPLES IN THE CITY OF ZAMBOANGA, PROVIDING FOR ITS FUNCTIONS, GOVERNANCE, PROGRAMS AND SERVICES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines thrives with a vibrant tapestry of Indigenous Cultural Communities and Peoples, whose unique traditions, languages, wisdom, arts, histories, and institutions form the very heart of the nation's cultural heritage. The Constitution recognizes the rights of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples within the framework of national unity and development. Republic Act No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997, further recognizes and protects the rights of Indigenous Peoples to preserve and develop their cultures, traditions, and institutions and created the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples as the primary government agency responsible for protecting and promoting their rights and well-being. EeLibrary+1 Zamboanga City stands out as a beacon of cultural significance, home to a rich mgsaic of Indigenous Peoples and communities whose heritage shapes the vibrant identity of both the city and Western Mindanao. Recognizing this need, the City Government of Zamboanga acted in 2020 by emacting Ordinance No. 547, which established the Zamboanga Cultural Complex for Indigenous Peoples and other major cultures, with dedicated funding. This commitment was further strengthened with the passage of Ordinance No. 661 in 2024. This proposed measure aims to secure national government support and establish a lasting institutional foundation for a dedicated cultural center in Zamboanga City. The proposed Zamboanga Cultural Center for Indigenous Peoples shall serve as a venue for cultural education, exhibitions, research, documentation, preservation, performances, traditional arts, conimunity activities, and intergenerational transmission of indigenous knowledge systems and practi¢es. The Center shall not replace existing cultural institutions. Instead, it shall complement the programs of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, the National Museum of the Philippines, the National Library of the Philippines, the National Archives of the Philippines, and the City Government of Zamboanga. More importantly, the proposed Center shall ensure that Indigenous Peoples themselves have a meaningful role in determining how their cultures are documented, presented, taught, preserved, and transmitted. This is consistent with the principles of cultural integrity, self- determination, and participation embodied in Republic Act No. 8371. The creation of the Center will offer Zamboanga City and Western Mindanao a |asting public institution devoted to Indigenous cultural heritage, opening doors to education, research, cultural expression, community engagement, and mindful cultural tourism. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11595
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to upgrade the Batangas Provincial Medical Center into a Tertiary Level III General Hospital under the control, supervision, and management of the Department of Health. The proposed upgrade will enable the hospital to better respond to the medical needs of Batangueños and lessen the need for patients to seek higher-level care in hospitals located farther from their communities. A strong public healthcare system depends on hospitals that are capable of meeting the actual needs of the communities they serve. As demand for medical services increases, local health institutions must also be strengthened so that patients can receive appropriate and timely care without having to travel far from their homes. Improving hospital capacity is therefore an important step toward making quality healthcare more accessible, especially for families who rely heavily on public medical facilities. For years the Batangas Provincial Medical Center in the Municipality of Tuy has served as an important healthcare facility for residents of the municipality and nearby communities in Batangas. The continuing growth in demand for medical care further emphasizes the need for the institution to expand its comprehensive and specialized services. Strengthening the functions of this hospital will contribute to a more accessible and responsive healthcare system in the Province of Batangas and help ensure that patients receive appropriate care when they need it most. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Ryan S.
