label: HB 11636
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE POSSESSION AND OPERATION OF UNMANNED SYSTEMS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Unmanned systems, commonly known as drones, have become increasingly accessible and are now widely used for recreational, commercial, agricultural, scientific, media, disaster response, and government purposes. Their continued development has contributed to innovation, improved efficiency, and economic development across various sectors. The proliferation of unmanned systems, however, has also raised concerns relating to public safety, national security, privacy, aviation safety, and the protection of critical infrastructure. Unauthorized operations near airports, military installations, government facilities, densely populated areas, and public events demonstrate the need for a clear and comprehensive legal framework governing the registration, possession, operation, and accountability of unmanned systems. At present, regulations issued by the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) principally govern unmanned aircraft operations. There remains a need for legislation establishing a broader and coordinated framework covering unmanned systems operating in the air, on land, and in maritime environments, while recognizing the respective mandates of concerned government agencies. This proposed measure seeks to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the possession and operation of unmanned systems. It provides for appropriate registration and licensing requirements, operational standards, prohibited acts, privacy safeguards, enforcement mechanisms, and penalties, while recognizing legitimate uses of unmanned systems for commercial, educational, research, agricultural, humanitarian, disaster response, and other lawful purposes. The measure likewise establishes an inter-agency mechanism to promote coordination among concerned government agencies and to ensure that regulation keeps pace with technological developments. It recognizes the need to balance public safety and national security with innovation, research, economic activity, and the responsible development of the unmanned systems industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11637
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE STRATEGIC BITCOIN RESERVE OF THE PHILIPPINES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve for the Republic of the Philippines as a proactive measure to safeguard national economic sovereignty and diversify our foreign reserves away from excessive dependence on the US Dollar. The Philippines faces a structural dilemma rooted in its heavy reliance on the US Dollar. More than 80 percent of our international trade settlements, overseas Filipino worker (OFW) remittances (which contribute roughly 9- 10 percent of GDP annually), and foreign exchange reserves are denominated in USD. While the dollar has historically served as the global reserve currency, the United States’ monetary and fiscal policies have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to print money out of thin air through successive rounds of quantitative easing, massive deficit spending, and unchecked expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet. This practice has fueled persistent global inflation, eroded the real purchasing power of the dollar, and exported monetary instability to dollar-dependent economies like ours. Every time the US prints trillions to finance its domestic priorities, the value of our hard-earned dollar reserves declines in real terms. This translates into higher costs for imported fuel, food, and raw materials, reduced purchasing power for OFW families, and diminished returns on the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) reserve holdings. The Philippines is essentially subsidizing American fiscal profligacy while bearing the inflationary consequences without any say in US policy decisions. Bitcoin, by contrast, is the only major asset with a verifiably fixed supply of 21 million coins — a monetary policy enforced by unbreakable code Page 1 of 4 rather than political discretion. Its decentralized nature removes any single government’s ability to debase it. Establishing a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve will allow the Philippines to hedge against dollar depreciation, capture long-term appreciation potential, and position the country as a forward-looking digital-economy leader in Southeast Asia. The proposed reserve will be managed transparently by the BSP under strict custodial, security, and reporting standards. Initial funding will come from a modest reallocation of BSP profits and future appropriations, ensuring no immediate burden on the national budget. This is not speculation; it is strategic national insurance against the known risks of fiat-currency dependency. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly requested. label: HB 11638
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of social media has fundamentally changed the way children communicate, learn, obtain information, and interact with others. While social media platforms provide valuable opportunities for education, expression, creativity, and social connection, children are increasingly exposed to online risks, including cyberbullying, exploitation, grooming, harmful or age-inappropriate content, privacy violations, excessive and compulsive use, manipulation through algorithms, and artificially generated or altered content. Children, by reason of their age and evolving capacities, require a level of protection that is different from that afforded to adults in the digital environment. The State has the responsibility to promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, emotional, and social well-being of children and to ensure that their best interests remain paramount in all actions concerning them. For this reason, there is a need to establish a clear and comprehensive age-based regulatory framework for children's access to social media. This measure recognizes that children of different ages possess different levels of maturity, understanding, and capacity to identify and respond to online risks. Accordingly, the proposed Act adopts three distinct levels of protection. Beyond restriction and enforcement, the bill promotes digital literacy and responsible digital engagement among children, parents, guardians, and educators. It seeks to equip children with the knowledge and skills necessary to critically evaluate online information, recognize algorithmic influence, protect personal information, report harmful conduct, manage screen time, and engage responsibly in digital spaces. It likewise encourages local government units to provide community-based recreational, educational, cultural, civic, and device-free activities that support children's healthy development. Ultimately, this measure seeks to strike a careful balance between protecting children from the risks of the digital environment and respecting their rights to privacy, access to information, education, communication, and freedom of expression consistent with their age and evolving capacities. It does not seek to prevent children from participating in the digital world; rather, it seeks to ensure that such participation takes place in an environment that is safer, more responsible, age-appropriate, and respectful of their rights. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11639
title: AN ACT DECLARING JULY 16 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CARRASCAL, PROVINCE OF SURIGAO DEL SUR, IN CELEBRATION OF ITS ANNUAL TOWN FIESTA AND THE PAHINUNGOD FESTIVAL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Carrascal, Province of Surigao del Sur, celebrates its annual town fiesta in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, with the Pahinungod Festival serving as a distinctive cultural and religious celebration of the municipality. The Provincial Government of Surigao del Sur identifies the Pahinungod Festival as a major event of Carrascal, with festival activities traditionally held in July and centered on devotion, community participation, cultural expression, and thanksgiving. Declaring July 16 of every year a special non-working holiday in Carrascal will enable residents, visitors, workers, and families to participate meaningfully in the celebration and will help preserve and strengthen the municipality's cultural and religious heritage. This measure likewise recognizes the responsibility of the Local Government Unit of Carrascal to plan and support the orderly conduct of the Pahinungod Festival. For this purpose, the Municipality may appropriate funds in its annual budget, or utilize available and legally authorized local appropriations, subject to existing budgeting, accounting, auditing, procurement, and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. The celebration is a cultural and tourism event that showcases the municipality's natural resources, particularly its white sand beaches, while bringing together the local government, national government agencies, schools, community organizations, and other sectors of the local community. The declaration of June 24 as a special non-working holiday will provide residents, visitors, workers, students, and the various sectors of the community sufficient opportunity to participate in the festivities and will promote the preservation of the municipality's cultural identity, traditions, and tourism potential. This measure likewise recognizes the important role of the Local Government Unit of Cagwait in organizing and supporting the Kaliguan Festival. label: HB 11641
title: AN ACT DECLARING JANUARY 20 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CAGWAIT, PROVINCE OF SURIGAO DEL SUR, IN COMMEMORATION OF ITS FOUNDING ANNIVERSARY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Cagwait, Province of Surigao del Sur, was created into an independent municipality on January 20, 1953 by virtue of Executive Order No. 559, Series of 1953, issued by then President Elpidio Quirino, organizing a portion of the Municipality of Tago, Province of Surigao, into a new independent municipality named Cagwait. January 20 is annually observed by the Municipality of Cagwait as its Foundation Day, or “Adlaw Nan Cagwait,” which commemorates its establishment and highlights the municipality's historical significance while strengthening the people's sense of identity, pride, and belongingness. Declaring January 20 of every year as a special non-working holiday in Cagwait will provide the residents, government personnel, schools, businesses, and other sectors of the community an opportunity to participate fully in the activities commemorating the municipality's founding anniversary. This measure seeks to institutionalize the annual observance of the founding anniversary of Cagwait and recognize its importance to the cultural and historical life of the municipality. in view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11643
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE PRIVILEGES OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY TO INCLUDE FREE PARKING IN ALL ESTABLISHMENTS AND EXEMPTION FROM THE NUMBER CODING SCHEME, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 32 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bible reminds us in Proverbs 31:8–9: "Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute. Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy." This is a call to stand beside those whom society too often leaves behind, so that persons with disabilities may live with dignity, independence, and equal opportunity to take part in the life of the nation. The 2020 Census of Population and Housing found that about 8.47 million Filipinos aged five and over have difficulty in at least one functional domain, which the PSA reported as 8.7 percent of the household population. Among them, 1,895,026 have difficulty walking or climbing steps. For these Filipinos, the distance from the parking space to the door is only part of the journey. Over 135,000 have severe difficulty walking, and over 288,000 have moderate difficulty.1 For many persons with physical disabilities, walking to a destination or using available public transportation may not be feasible, making travel by private vehicle a necessity. Accessibility therefore extends beyond the distance from a parking space to the door: it also depends on whether they can afford the journey itself. Every trip may require careful planning, and even modest parking fees can add to the financial burden of reaching medical appointments, workplaces, and other essential destinations. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority (2020). Functional Difficulty in the Philippines: For Household Population Five Years Old and Over (2020 Census of Population and Housing) Retrieved from: https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/population-and-housing/node/168274 on October 5, 2026 Batas Pambansa Blg. 344 recognizes the right of persons with disabilities to access physically accessible parking facilities. However, the provision of a reserved parking space offers limited benefit when parking fees impose an additional financial burden on households already managing the costs of medicines, therapy, and assistive devices. Similarly, such accessibility measures lose their practical value when vehicle-number schemes compel persons with disabilities to postpone or cancel medical appointments, work obligations, or family engagements. These circumstances should not be regarded as mere inconveniences. Rather, they constitute recurring barriers that, over time, can significantly restrict a person’s mobility, independence, and ability to participate fully in community life. Some local governments have chosen to act. Taguig City maintains a dedicated PWD Affairs Office, provides free rehabilitation and therapy services, and delivers assistive devices to people's homes.2 Pasig City exempts vehicles carrying PWDs from its number-coding scheme3, and Marilao exempts PWDs from parking fees in business establishments and similar places.4 Their example demonstrates that genuine inclusion extends beyond the recognition of rights on paper. It requires ensuring that essential services and support are accessible, affordable, and within reach of those who need them most. The proposed "Free Parking and Coding Exemption for Persons with Disability Act" carries this compassion into national policy. It seeks to: 1. Grant free parking in commercial establishments and government facilities that charge parking fees; and 2. Exempt vehicles carrying or driven by a person with disability from the Unified Vehicular Volume Reduction Program, or number coding scheme. No Filipino should have to choose between a necessary trip and the cost or restriction that comes with it. By removing these barriers, the State affirms that persons with disabilities have an equal right to move freely, to work, to heal, to worship, and to be with their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the early approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. BOCOBO 2 City of Taguig Website (n.d.). Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Public Higher Education Faculty Salary Upgrading and Progression Act." SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to attract and retain competent faculty in public higher education through competitive pay and a fair, merit-based, regular, and adequately funded system of advancement in rank, while respecting institutional academic freedom. SECTION 3. Coverage. – This Act shall apply to all faculty members holding permanent plantilla positions in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs): Provided, That the University of the Philippines and Mindanao State University Systems shall retain their own promotion systems: Provided, further, That a local university or college may adopt this system by ordinance, subject to Section 325 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the "Local Government Code of 1991." SECTION 4. Upgrading of Faculty Salary Grades. – The salary grades of faculty positions in SUCs are hereby upgraded, as follows: Faculty Rank Sub-Rank Present SG Upgraded SG I 12 14 Instructor II 13 15 III 14 16 I 15 17 Assistant Professor II 16 18 III 17 19 IV 18 20 Associate Professor I 19 21 II 20 22
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our Constitution requires that teaching "attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration."1 For faculty in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs), higher pay comes mainly through reclassification, from Instructor I (SG 12, PhP 33,947 monthly) to College/University Professor (SG 30, PhP 210,718).2 Since 1998 this system has rested only on executive circulars, now DBM-CHED Joint Circular No. 3, s. 2022, as enhanced by Joint Circular No. 01, s. 2026.3 No law requires cycles to be held, limits processing time, or funds to adjust benefit amounts to account for normative cost of teaching, inflation, changing educational cost, regional variations and other considerations., which each SUC must now certify from its own resources.4 Work done from August 2023 reaches the DBM only by June 2027.5 No institution can demand academic excellence while offering systemic precarity. In placing this mandate squarely on national funding, the State affirms that investing in legal educators is indispensable to the administration of justice. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE “TULAY SA HANAPBUHAY PROGRAM”, PROVIDING FRESH FILIPINO GRADUATES OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION AND TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND PROGRAMS WITH A ONE-TIME CASH GRANT OF FIVE THOUSAND PESOS (PHP 5,000.00) TO SUPPORT THEIR TRANSITION FROM SCHOOL TO WORK, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Tulay sa Hanapbuhay Act." SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to promote the welfare of the youth and equality of employment opportunities for all. Toward this end, the State shall ease the transition of young Filipinos from education to employment by defraying the initial costs of seeking work, with preference for the poor and marginalized when resources are limited. SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: (a) Fresh Filipino Graduate refers to a Filipino citizen who has completed a bachelor's or associate degree program in a higher education institution recognized by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), or a program registered with the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) leading to a National Certificate or its equivalent; (b) Combined Annual Gross Family Income refers to the total gross income of the applicant's parents or legal guardians in the preceding year or, for a self-supporting applicant, the applicant's own gross income; and (c) Special Equity Group refers to Indigenous Peoples under Republic Act No. 8371; persons with disabilities under Republic Act No. 7277, as amended; solo parents and their dependents under Republic Act No. 8972, as
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and commits the State to full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all.1 Before their first paycheck, they must pay for applications, fares, medical examinations, and work attire, costs that existing fee waivers do not cover 2 and that can cut a job search short.3 In July 2026, the youth employment rate fell to 81.4 percent.4 This bill extends to every fresh Filipino graduate a one-time transition grant of Five Thousand Pesos (PhP 5,000.00), claimable within one (1) year from graduation. The Commission on Higher Education leads its implementation, with the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority serving technical-vocational completers. Should funds fall short, the poorest and most marginalized graduates are served first, every region receives its fair share, and public funds are shielded from fraud and political use. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. Representative Lone District of Nueva Vizcaya 1 Art. II, Sec. 13; Art. label: HB 11648
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NCR POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE THROUGH THE INTEGRATION OF THE TESDA TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTIONS (TTIs) IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION INTO A UNIFIED POLYTECHNIC SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The NCR Polytechnic Institute Act establishes a modern, unified polytechnic system in the National Capital Region to strengthen Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) as a strategic driver of national competitiveness, industrial transformation, innovation, and inclusive growth. Operating under the supervision of TESDA NCR, the measure integrates and transforms the TESDA NCR Regional Training Center (NCR RTC) and six (6) District Training Centers into a single institutional framework. This consolidation rationalizes existing TESDA technology institutions into an integrated polytechnic system to achieve stronger governance, operational efficiency, enhanced institutional performance, and academic excellence across the region. As the lead regional institution for higher-level and technology-driven TVET, the Institute is mandated to deliver Technical Diploma programs and specialized workforce courses designed in accordance with the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF). The academic framework promotes lifelong learning through stackable microcredentials, flexible learning pathways, and articulation agreements with higher education institutions to enable credit recognition and ladderization toward related bachelor's degree programs. Furthermore, the legislation establishes Regional TVET Innovation Centers to serve as regional hubs for applied research, technology demonstration, prototyping, entrepreneurship, and emerging technology training. Governance is structured around a centralized "One System" framework featuring One Governing Board, One Executive Management System, One Support Services System, and One Academic Delivery System. The multi- sectoral Governing Board includes representatives from TESDA, DOST, DOLE, DTI, LGUs, industry sectors, employers, workers, educational institutions, civil society, and students. Crucially, the legislation safeguards existing workforce rights by transferring all assets, personnel, and records without impairing the positions, rights, or security of tenure of faculty and staff. Initial implementation will be funded through current TESDA appropriations, with subsequent operations supported by the annual General Appropriations Act and local government contributions. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 11650
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SAFEGUARDS IN THE APPROPRIATION, RELEASE, UTILIZATION, REPORTING, AND AUDIT OF CONFIDENTIAL FUNDS OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the “Local Government Confidential Funds Accountability Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State to uphold local autonomy while ensuring fiscal responsibility, transparency, and accountability in the use of public funds. The State recognizes that certain legitimate peace and order and public safety activities may require confidentiality. However, confidentiality shall be the exception and shall be justified only by operational necessity. It shall not exempt any expenditure of public funds from lawful appropriation, accounting, audit, and appropriate government oversight. Accordingly, confidential funds shall be resorted to only when the intended public purpose cannot reasonably and effectively be accomplished through regular appropriations and ordinary government procedures without compromising a lawful confidential activity. SEC. 3. Coverage. This Act shall apply to confidential funds appropriated by provinces, cities, and municipalities for lawful peace and order and public safety purposes.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Confidential funds serve a legitimate purpose where peace and order operations require secrecy. Yet the same secrecy that protects sensitive operations also makes these funds particularly vulnerable to abuse and misuse, with fewer opportunities for public scrutiny. For this reason, confidential funds must be treated as an exception justified by actual necessity, rather than as an ordinary component of local government spending. The experience of local government units exhibits that the amount spent in confidential funds does not necessarily determine the quality of peace and order. Davao City reported ₱530 million in confidential expenses in 2023, after spending ₱460 million annually from 2019 to 2022. Cagayan de Oro City allocated ₱200 million in 2023 and ₱250 million in 2024, while Cavite Province proposed ₱193.5 million for confidential expenses in 2024, following approximately ₱183 million in 2023. By contrast, in 2024, eight Metro Manila cities— Las Piñas, Navotas, Makati, Pasig, Taguig, Mandaluyong, Malabon and Valenzuela—reported no confidential-fund expenditures at all. Quezon City LGU likewise reduced its confidential funds from ₱100 million in 2023 to ₱75 million in 2024, even as its index crimes declined from 2,359 to 1,958 over the same period. Other LGUs have likewise chosen to rely less on confidential spending. Naga City announced the total removal of confidential funds from its budget, while the LGU of Capas, Tarlac chose to forego its ₱8-million confidential fund for 2026, with the amount instead intended for programs benefiting senior citizens and public school students. This measure seeks to institutionalize safeguards requiring LGU confidential funds to be supported by necessity, proportionate to legitimate peace and order requirements, and subject to audit, reporting, and safeguards against misuse. This is not intended to diminish or unduly restrict confidential funds where genuinely necessary. Rather, it seeks to ensure that such funds are used only when justified by actual peace and order requirements and subject to transparency and accountability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. ADRIAN MICHAEL A. title: AN ACT GRANTING THE ORIENTAL MINDORO- ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. (QRMECO) A FRANCHISE TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE CITY OF CALAPAN AND MUNICIPALITIES OF BACO, BANSUD, BONGABONG, BULALACAO, GLORIA, MANSALAY, NAUJAN, PINAMALAYAN, POLA, PUERTO GALERA, ROXAS, SAN TEODORO, SOCORRO, AND VICTORIA IN THE PROVINCE OF ORIENTAL MINDORO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Oriental Mindoro Electric Cooperative, Inc. (ORMECO) plays a critical role in the electrification, economic development and public welfare of the Province of Oriental Mindoro. As a distribution utility operating within a defined franchise area, it is imbued with public interest consistent with Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution, which requires that public utilities operate under a legislative franchise subject to regulation by the State. This proposed measure grants ORMECO a franchise to construct, install, establish, operate, own, manage and maintain a distribution system for the conveyance of electric power to end- users within the City of Calapan and the municipalities comprising the Province of Oriental Mindoro. The bill aligns the operations of the Grantee with the regulatory framework established under Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA), ensuring continued oversight by the Energy Regulatory Commission, and with Republic Act No. 10531, strengthening the supervisory role of the National Electrification Administration. Recognizing the State policy to accelerate the exploration and development of renewable energy resources, the measure incorporates provisions consistent with Republic Act No. 9513. It mandates facilitation of renewable energy integration, compliance with Renewable Portfolio Standards, and implementation of net-metering mechanisms to enable households and private end-users to generate electricity from renewable sources and supply excess power to the distribution system under lawful and regulated conditions. To safeguard the independence of the cooperative and prevent undue political influence over a public utility, the bill includes a governance provision prohibiting members of the Board of Directors and the General Manager from having a relationship by consanguinity or affinity up to the third civil degree with incumbent elective officials within the franchise area. This measure promotes institutional integrity, policy independence, and public trust in the management of an essential public service. The bill likewise strengthens consumer protection, ensures transparency in rate-setting, preserves regulatory jurisdiction, provides procedural due process in franchise revocation, and harmonizes the franchise with existing statutory framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure ig earnestly sought. AN C. label: HB 11652
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ADMINISTRATIVE CANCELLATION OF BIRTH CERTIFICATES REGISTERED THROUGH FRAUDULENT MEANS BY FOREIGN NATIONALS, CREATING A SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CANCELLATION OF BIRTH CERTIFICATES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Civil registry documents, particularly Certificates of Live Birth, are fundamental because it serves as the primary legal proof of an individual’s name, parentage, date of birth, and citizenship. However, the integrity of the Philippine civil registry is currently threatened by foreign nationals exploiting the system through the fraudulent registration of births, with an estimated 50,000 spurious records currently suspected in the database of the Philippine Statistic Office (PSA) (Cruz, 2026). Because birth certificates are the foundational document establishing citizenship, these fraudulent registrations grant illicit access to exclusive national rights, privileges, and government services reserved to legitimate citizens. The core of this systemic failure is the absence of an administrative remedy to address such fraudulent entries resulting in protracted proceedings thereby the continued existence of spurious records in official databases. With some government officials allegedly involved in this scheme (Casilao, 2026), a comprehensive, immediate, and effective intervention is imperative. The 1987 Constitution mandates the government to serve and protect the people, promote general welfare, and maintain honesty and integrity in public service. Likewise, the State remains the ultimate authority over matters of citizenship. Inherent to these Constitutional principles is the duty of the State to preserve the sanctity and reliability of its civil registry, particularly documents establishing birth and citizenship. This measure seeks to directly address these civil registry gaps by establishing an administrative mechanism for the cancellation of birth certificates fraudulently obtained by foreign nationals. Central to this proposed measure is the creation of a Special Committee on Cancellation of Birth Certificates, composed of representatives from key agencies authorized to resolve such matters with finality. This introduces a streamlined procedure that ensures due process while preventing undue delay. The proposed measure, which was previously introduced during the 19 th Congress, strengthens accountability by authorizing the Special Committee to recommend the institution of appropriate criminal, civil, administrative, and deportation proceedings against foreign nationals and any individuals, whether private or public officers, who participated in or facilitated the fraudulent registration. Through this bill, erroneous records are corrected while deterring future abuses of our civil registry system. Additionally, this version of the bill recognizes evidentiary realities by providing that the absence of any primary and secondary civil registry records, duly certified by local civil registrars after diligent and exhaustive search, shall constitute prima facie evidence of fraudulent registration. In such cases, this bill allows for the expeditious cancellation of the birth certificate by the Special Committee. Finally, the enactment of this measure affirms the State’s commitment to uphold the integrity of its legal identity systems, protect the rights and privileges of lawful citizens, and reinforce public trust and confidence in government records and procedures. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA 2nd District of Cavite AGIMAT Partylist REP. label: HB 11653
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF COMPOSTING FACILITIES IN ALL BARANGAYS, PROMOTING RESIDENTIAL COMPOSTING, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Global waste generated in 2022 reached 2.56 billion tons, an amount originally projected for 2030. Without intervention, global waste is estimated to grow by fifty percent (50%) by 2050, or a total of 3.86 billion tons (Cook et al., 2026). Driven by urbanization, population growth, and rising consumption patterns, the Philippines ranked 27th globally in municipal solid waste production, at 15 million tons annually (Dela Peña, 2025). The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) reported that 52 to 58 percent of the country’s waste is biodegradable. With proper segregation, biodegradable waste is recovered and composted, diverting usable trash away from our dumpsites (Teves, 2021). Without segregation, a significant portion of biodegradable waste is disposed of in landfills or open dumpsites, contributing to environmental degradation, methane emissions, and public health risks. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000,” full compliance at the local level remains uneven and inconsistent, particularly in the segregation and processing of organic waste. A major gap in the solid waste management system is the limited support mechanisms for solid waste disposal, recycling, and recovery, including technologies, facilities, and systems at the barangay level (Rebullida & Taguibao, 2020). While Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs) are mandated under existing law, many lack the capacity, coverage, and functionality for composting, resulting in the continued disposal of organic waste in landfills (Andaya, 2025). Decomposing biodegradable waste in landfills generates methane, a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming and climate change. Conversely, composting transforms organic waste into soil amendments that support agriculture, landscaping, and ecological restoration. In recognition of this challenge, grounded on Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution guaranteeing “the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature,” there is a need to strengthen the implementation of ecological solid waste management by shifting toward localized, decentralized, and resource-oriented approaches. This includes empowering barangays as primary units of implementation, institutionalizing composting infrastructure, and promoting household and community participation in organic waste diversion. To address these gaps, this bill seeks to amend the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 by providing for the establishment, operationalization, and integration of Barangay Composting Facilities (BCFs) within existing solid waste management systems. By requiring all barangays to develop composting capacity, the measure ensures that biodegradable waste is processed at or near the source, thereby reducing dependence on landfills. Further, this measure strengthens community-level participation by institutionalizing the Residential Composting Support Desk (RCSD) in every barangay. The RCSD is designed to provide material and technical assistance to households, homeowners’ associations (HOAs), and condominium corporations, including the distribution of composting starter kits, training programs, and access to scaled composting equipment for larger residential developments. This approach lowers the barriers to entry for composting and promotes sustained behavioral change at the household level. To ensure coverage, subdivisions and condominium projects are required to divert organic waste either through on-site composting facilities or by utilizing their barangay’s BCF. Registered participants retain the right to the finished compost they produce, including personal use, public greening programs, agricultural use, and community distribution, with provisions allowing surplus compost to be sold commercially or directly to the government. This mechanism transforms organic waste from a disposal burden into an economic opportunity and environmental resource. Furthermore, while the Barangays are primarily responsible in organic waste diversion, this bill mobilizes key national agencies, including the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Science and Technology (DOST), Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD), and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), to ensure coordinated implementation, technical standard- setting, and regulatory oversight. Ultimately, this measure advances a circular approach to solid waste management by institutionalizing composting as a core component of environmental governance. By reducing landfill dependence, lowering greenhouse gas emissions, promoting resource recovery, and strengthening community participation, the bill contributes to building sustainable, climate-resilient, and environmentally responsible communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA, MSLG, DM (hc) REP. RAMON JOLO REVILLA III REP. BRYAN B. label: HB 11654
title: AN ACT PREVENTING AND PENALIZING FOREIGN INTERFERENCE IN THE PHILIPPINES, STRENGTHENING MECHANISMS TO DETECT AND COUNTER FOREIGN INTERFERENCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Foreign interference in domestic and governmental processes has emerged as a significant and evolving threat to democratic states, including the Philippines. Global trends reveal how foreign actors utilized coordinated disinformation campaigns during elections, covert funding of political groups, and cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure to influence public opinion and policy outcomes. The European Commission, through its Action Plan Against Disinformation, documented the exploitation of online platforms to manipulate democratic discourse by polarizing communities and inciting antagonism in the society. 1 The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) warns that information threats can cause real- world harm, directly endangering national security.2 Similarly, the Koffi Annan Foundation observed that new digital platforms and internet culture contributed to the scale, nature, and reach of foreign interference operations. 3 In the Philippine context, the absence of a comprehensive and unified legal framework specifically addressing foreign interference leaves critical gaps, as existing laws on espionage, cybercrime, and election offenses remain fragmented and insufficient to address the full scope of these modern threats. This measure is anchored on the constitutional principle of national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national interest, while guaranteeing the protection of civil liberties under the Bill of Rights. It complements existing statutes such as the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001 and the Anti-Wiretapping Law, the Foreign Agents Act of 1979, which promotes transparency in foreign-linked political activities. 1 European Commission. Retrieved from h7ps://www.koﬁannanfounda=on.org/news/foreign- interference-in-elections-how-to-deﬁne-it/ The proposed Foreign Interference Prevention Act establishes a comprehensive framework by clearly defining and penalizing foreign interference, including disinformation, covert influence operations, and support to foreign intelligence services; requiring the registration of foreign agents engaged in political or advocacy activities; addressing digital threats through access blocking; enabling financial investigation; strengthening inter-agency coordination; while explicitly safeguarding civil liberties, ensuring that speech, journalistic, and academic freedoms are respected and protected. The enactment of this measure is expected to strengthen national sovereignty and security by deterring foreign interference, protect the integrity of our election and democratic processes, enhance transparency and accountability in foreign- linked activities, improve the State’s capacity to respond to hybrid and cyber threats, and align the Philippines with international standards in countering foreign interference. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA 2nd District of Cavite AGIMAT Partylist REP. label: HB 11655
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL NUTRITION COMMISSION, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 491, ENTITLED “CREATING A NATIONAL NUTRITION COUNCIL AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has an obligation to protect and promote the right to nutrition and adequate food under relevant domestic and international laws: 1987 Philippine Constitution; Universal Declaration of Human Rights; International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights; Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women; Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In line with this, several offices of government have taken on the task of directly or indirectly protecting and promoting the right to nutrition and adequate food, namely: The National Nutrition Council, created through Presidential Decree (PD) No. 491, s. 1974; National Food Authority, established through PD No. 4, s. 1972; Anti-Hunger Task Force, created through Executive Order (EO) No. 616, s. 2007; Inter-Agency Task Force on Hunger, established through EO No. 101, s. 2020; Presidential Assistant for Food Security and Agricultural Modernization under the Office of the President, established through Memorandum Order No. 70, s. 2014; Food and Nutrition Research Institute, which is one of the research and development institutes of the Department of Science and Technology; and, Department of Agriculture, specifically through its Food Staples Sufficiency Program. While the government has committed to AmBisyon Natin 2040, which promises a strongly rooted, comfortable, and secure life for every Filipino, where “no one is poor, no one is ever hungry,” undernutrition and malnutrition remain as perennial problems besetting the country. In fact, the Philippines missed its Millennium Development Goal of lowering the undernutrition and malnutrition rate to 15% by 2015, and the problem appears to be getting worse. The World Bank reports 1 that as of 2019, one in every three Filipino children younger than five years old suffer from stunting, resulting in the country being ranked fifth among countries in the East Asia and Pacific Region with the highest number of stunted children. The effect of COVID 19 on the economy has made hunger, undernutrition and malnutrition even worse in the country. The Social Weather Stations reported an alarming 31% of families experiencing hunger, and 9% suffering severe hunger in September 2020, seven months after the enforcement community quarantine—in both cases, the highest levels recorded in more than 20 years. In this regard, this Bill seeks to create a National Nutrition Commission to serve as the overarching agency responsible for establishing a unified policy direction and a comprehensive approach towards food accessibility and security, improved nutrition and overall health development of the Filipino people. This shall replace the existing National Nutrition Council, as well as streamline the nutrition functions rendered by other offices of government. Furthermore, nutrition programs at sub-national levels shall be guaranteed with manpower complement, as a way of improving nutrition performance. Immediate passage of this bill is hereby earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. label: HB 11656
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING TRADITIONAL AND COMPLEMENTARY MEDICINE INTO THE NATIONAL HEALTH CARE SYSTEM, REORGANIZING THE PHILIPPINE INSTITUTE OF TRADITIONAL AND ALTERNATIVE HEALTH CARE (PITAHC), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8423, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TRADITIONAL AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE ACT OF 1997,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine health care system continues to face persistent challenges in ensuring accessible, affordable, and culturally responsive health services for all Filipinos. Despite advances in modern medicine, a significant portion of the population continues to rely on traditional and complementary medicine as part of their health care practices. Globally, the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that 88% of the population adopts traditional medicine for preventive, curative, or rehabilitative purposes (Agoot, 2023). In the Philippines, 43% of adult Filipinos have sought complementary and alternative medicine, particularly the services of manghihilot or bone setter and partera and albularyo or herbalist (Ladia, et al., 2018). These figures highlight the continuing relevance and demand for traditional and complementary health modalities. Republic Act No. 8423, otherwise known as the “Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act of 1997,” was enacted to promote and advocate the use of traditional and alternative health care. However, nearly three decades since its passage, significant gaps remain in terms of regulatory capacity, integration into the broader health system, and alignment with current health frameworks such as the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act. With growing preference on herbal formulations over synthetic medicine underscores the necessity to introduce regulation of herbal medicines to ensure quality, safety, and efficacy (Sachan, Vishnoi, & Kumar, 2016). The lack of standardized regulation and clinical validation mechanisms for traditional and complementary medicine may results in inconsistent quality, safety concerns, and limited integration into formal health systems. Moreover, under the Global Survey on Traditional Medicine conducted by the WHO, member States are assisted to research, integrate, and regulate traditional medicine in their national health systems (Zhao & Terry, 2023). This bill seeks to address gaps in the traditional and complementary medicine in the country by reorganizing the Philippine Institute of Traditional and Alternative Health Care (PITAHC) into the Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine Administration (TRACIMA), strengthening its mandate as the lead policy, regulatory, and research body. To achieve these objectives, TRACIMA shall be responsible to conduct research and development, validation, integration, regulation, consumer protection, and protection of indigenous knowledge systems of traditional and complementary health care practices. Through this measure, TRACIMA can establish the minimum standard of health care based on validated medical data. Finally, the bill strengthens inter-agency coordination and health technology assessment (HTA) mechanisms to ensure that only safe, effective, and cost-efficient practices are adopted within the national health system allowing coverage and inclusion in the health packages of the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) under the UHC. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought to modernize the country’s approach to traditional and complementary medicine, ensure public safety, and fully harness its potential as a complementary pillar of a responsive and inclusive health care system. label: HB 11658
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ACADEMIC AND INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITIES OF THE CAMIGUIN POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE, EXPANDING ITS CURRICULAR OFFERINGS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7923, ENTITLED “AN ACT CONVERTING THE CENTRAL MINDANAO UNIVERSITY CAMPUS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CATARMAN, THE MINDANAO POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE CAMPUS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF MAMBAJAO, AND THE CAMIGUIN SCHOOL OF ARTS AND TRADES, ALL IN THE PROVINCE OF CAMIGUIN, INTO A STATE COLLEGE TO BE KNOWN AS THE CAMIGUIN POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7923, approved in 1995, consolidated three public postsecondary institutions in Camiguin into the Camiguin Polytechnic State College and gave the College a mandate centered on the educational and development conditions prevailing at that time. More than three decades later, CPSC serves a substantially changed province and higher-education environment. New professions, technologies, regulatory standards, modes of instruction, research needs, and workforce requirements have emerged, while the College has developed academic institutes, programs, extension activities, and institutional responsibilities that were not contemplated in detail by the original charter. CPSC remains the principal public higher-education institution based in the island province. Its present offerings provide important pathways in teacher education, engineering and computer studies, industrial technology, agriculture, business and public administration, tourism, marine biology, and graduate education. These programs have enabled generations of students to obtain an affordable public education close to their families. The statutory authority of the College, however, has not kept pace with the breadth of present and anticipated demand. Many qualified students seek programs that CPSC does not presently offer, particularly in nursing and allied health sciences, medicine and public health, emerging technologies, specialized engineering, environmental and marine-resource management, and other fields required by the province and the region. When a needed program is unavailable locally, a student may be compelled to leave Camiguin, assume additional transportation and living expenses, postpone higher education, or pursue a course that does not match the student’s aptitude or intended profession. These burdens fall most heavily on low-income families and may prevent the province from developing and retaining the professionals it needs. The proposed amendment is therefore not a conversion of CPSC into a university and does not alter the composition of its Board of Trustees. It strengthens the existing State College by modernizing its academic mandate and authorizing it to retain its current programs and, when justified, establish additional technical-vocational, undergraduate, graduate, postgraduate, professional, continuing-education, and flexible-learning programs within its competence and areas of specialization. The authority to offer additional programs is not automatic or unlimited. A program may open only after demonstrated local or regional need, inclusion in the institutional development plan, availability of funds, recommendation through the appropriate academic process, and full 1 compliance with the policies, standards, and requirements of the Commission on Higher Education, the Professional Regulation Commission, and other competent authorities. Programs requiring licensure, laboratories, clinical training, internships, affiliations, accreditation, or specialized facilities may not admit students until the necessary faculty, curriculum, facilities, equipment, learning resources, and regulatory authority are in place. Academic authority must be matched by institutional capacity. The bill accordingly provides a legal basis for the phased construction, repair, renovation, upgrading, and maintenance of classrooms, laboratories, simulation and clinical-training facilities, workshops, libraries, research and innovation centers, digital systems, student-support facilities, accessibility features, safety systems, and disaster-resilient infrastructure. It also supports the acquisition and maintenance of books, databases, software, medical and laboratory equipment, instructional technologies, and other learning resources. Implementation will follow institutional priorities and available appropriations and will remain subject to procurement, property, budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws. The measure also recognizes that facilities alone cannot sustain quality education. CPSC must be able to maintain a sufficient complement of qualified faculty members, researchers, specialists, librarians, laboratory and clinical personnel, information-technology personnel, student-support personnel, and administrative personnel. The College must likewise support graduate study, professional certification, licensure, clinical or industry exposure, research training, and other forms of faculty and personnel development. These investments are essential to regulatory compliance, program accreditation, instructional quality, research, extension, and student welfare. To support orderly implementation, the bill requires an updated institutional development plan, phased program development, and coordination with CHED, the Department of Budget and Management, and other concerned agencies. It modernizes selected powers and procedures of the Board, facilitates institutional partnerships and lawful resource sharing, and updates the appropriations provision so that additional academic programs, facilities, equipment, plantilla requirements, faculty development, research, scholarships, student support, accreditation, and regulatory compliance may be properly considered in the annual national budget. Amending the charter will enable CPSC to respond to student aspirations and the human- resource requirements of Camiguin and Northern Mindanao without compromising academic quality or fiscal responsibility. It will give the College the legal and institutional framework to expand carefully, accommodate more qualified students as capacity permits, and deliver programs supported by the personnel, facilities, equipment, and public funding necessary for their success. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JURDIN JESUS M. label: HB 11659
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE ANGAT - SAN RAFAEL ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF ANGAT, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the Angat - San Rafael Road, located in the Municipality of Angat, Province of Bulacan, into a national road. The Angat - San Rafael Road spans approximately 11.85 kilometers. It serves as a crucial arterial route connecting the municipalities of Angat and San Rafael, facilitating the movement of people, agricultural produce, commercial goods, and public services across eastern Bulacan. Due to increasing traffic volume and the growing economic activities in the region, the local government unit faces significant financial constraints in maintaining, expanding, and upgrading this road to meet safety and structural standards. Converting this local road into a national road will transfer its repair, maintenance, and future improvement under the jurisdiction and funding of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This development will enhance regional connectivity, lower transportation costs, ensure public safety, and bolster economic growth not only for the Municipality of Angat but for the entire Province of Bulacan. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11660
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE NEW BAGBAGUIN BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan serves as a major industrial, commercial, and agricultural hub in Central Luzon. Due to its strategic location and proximity to Metro Manila, the municipality experiences high volumes of daily vehicular traffic, ranging from light passenger vehicles to heavy cargo trucks transporting agricultural and manufactured goods. To alleviate severe traffic congestion along major thoroughfares, particularly within the urban center and major arterial roads, the local government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) undertook the construction and development of the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road. Stretching approximately two (2) kilometers, this bypass road provides a critical alternative route, diverting heavy traffic away from congested residential and commercial centers, reducing travel time, and improving overall logistical efficiency in the province. While the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road serves a vital regional function in supporting interstate trade and transport, its maintenance, repair, and future improvement currently rest on local government funds. Given the heavy volume and high axle loads of commercial traffic utilizing this bypass, local funding constraints hamper continuous, optimal maintenance and necessary upgrades. Converting the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road into a National Road will transfer its administration, maintenance, and further development under the responsibility of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This will guarantee standard quality maintenance, enhance road safety, and ensure long-term sustainability to keep up with regional economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11661
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE CITYLAND – PEREZ ROAD IN BARANGAY PULONG BUHANGIN, MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria, Bulacan, has undergone rapid urbanization and commercial expansion over recent years, driven by its strategic location and growing population. Barangay Pulong Buhangin, one of the largest and most populous barangays in the municipality, serves as a major hub for residential communities, educational institutions, commercial establishments, and local trade. Connecting to primary transportation arteries, the Cityland – Perez Road in Barangay Pulong Buhangin spans approximately 3.78 kilometers. It plays a crucial role in facilitating the daily movement of commuters, agricultural goods, and commercial transport within Santa Maria and neighboring municipalities in Bulacan. However, the continuous increase in traffic volume, heavy vehicle loads, and local economic development have placed a heavy financial and operational strain on the local government’s road maintenance capacity. Classifying this key thoroughfare as a local road limits the resources available for necessary repairs, drainage improvements, and safety upgrades. Converting the Cityland – Perez Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and improvement responsibilities to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift will ensure the upgrading of the road to national engineering standards to handle high traffic density and heavy freight safely. In view of the foregoing benefits to the community and the region, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11662
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE MEYCAUAYAN-SANTA MARIA BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Meycauayan-Santa Maria Bypass Road, stretching approximately 4.53 kilometers within the Municipality of Santa Maria, Province of Bulacan, serves as a vital transportation artery connecting key municipalities in eastern Bulacan to major thoroughfares, including the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX). As the Municipality of Santa Maria and surrounding areas continue to experience rapid economic growth, industrial expansion, and population increases, local traffic congestion has intensified. The bypass road was constructed to relieve traffic along inner municipal roads, facilitate the seamless movement of goods and agricultural products, and improve travel time for commuter and commercial traffic across the province. However, the maintenance, repair, and upgrade requirements of a heavy-traffic arterial road pose a continuous financial burden on the local government unit (LGU). Converting the Meycauayan-Santa Maria Bypass Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and future improvements under the supervision and funding of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift ensures that the road complies with national safety standards, receives dedicated annual budget allocations, and continues to sustain regional economic growth without overburdening local municipal funds. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11663
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE NORZAGARAY–SAN JOSE ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF NORZAGARAY, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the Norzagaray–San Jose Road, located in the Municipality of Norzagaray, Province of Bulacan, into a national road under the jurisdiction and supervision of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). Spanning approximately 11.46 kilometers, the Norzagaray–San Jose Road serves as a vital arterial route within Bulacan. It facilitates the movement of people, agricultural produce, industrial supplies, and essential goods between local communities and neighboring commercial centers. Norzagaray is host to vital national infrastructure, including major water reservoirs and quarrying/cement manufacturing hubs, making its road network integral not only to municipal commerce but to regional trade and economic activity. Despite its strategic importance, the continuous maintenance and upgrade of this 11.46-kilometer stretch place a significant financial burden on the local government unit (LGU) of Norzagaray. Municipal funding limitations often restrict the LGU's capacity to undertake comprehensive road widenings, structural reinforcements, and routine rehabilitation necessary to support heavy vehicular traffic and adverse weather conditions. Converting the Norzagaray–San Jose Road into a national road will transfer its control, maintenance, and improvement to the DPWH. This ensures regular budget allocation under the General Appropriations Act (GAA), bringing the road up to national standards, enhancing road safety, and boosting regional socio- economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11664
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE SANTA MARIA - PANDI BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan is a rapidly growing urban and commercial hub in Central Luzon. Its strategic location serves as a primary gateway connecting neighboring municipalities to the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) and major economic centers. Due to continuous industrialization and population growth, local traffic density has increased significantly. The Santa Maria - Pandi Bypass Road, spanning approximately three (3) kilometers within the territorial jurisdiction of Santa Maria, was constructed to alleviate heavy traffic congestion along the town center and facilitate smoother transit between Santa Maria and the Municipality of Pandi. Despite its vital function as an arterial bypass, the maintenance, repair, and operational upkeep of the Santa Maria - Pandi Bypass Road currently burden the local government unit (LGU) funds. Converting this local road into a national road will transfer its supervision and maintenance to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift ensures continuous funding for infrastructure maintenance, improvement, and safety upgrades under the National Expenditure Program (NEP). Furthermore, integrating this bypass road into the national road network will enhance regional connectivity, lower transportation costs for agricultural and commercial goods, boost local economic activity, and support public safety and disaster response mobility. In view of the foregoing considerations, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11666
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE SANTA MARIA RIVER SIDE ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan is a rapidly expanding suburban and commercial hub in Central Luzon. Serving as a crucial gateway between Metro Manila and inner Bulacan municipalities, its road networks experience an increasingly heavy volume of daily vehicular traffic, ranging from private vehicles to commercial trucks carrying agricultural goods. The Santa Maria River Side Road, which spans a length of 2.18 kilometers within the municipality, serves as a critical bypass and feeder road that helps decongest primary arterial roads, facilitates faster local transportation, and connects surrounding barangays to vital economic centers, public markets, and schools. However, due to its current status as a municipal road, maintenance and repair are funded solely through the limited local government budget. Given the high traffic density and environmental exposure along the river basin, the road requires continuous structural upgrades, concrete re-paving, adequate drainage infrastructure, and regular safety enhancements that exceed the financial capacity of the local government unit. Converting the Santa Maria River Side Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and future improvement responsibilities to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This transition will ensure a higher standard of road quality, enhanced safety features, and sustained national infrastructure funding In view of the foregoing urgent considerations, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11676
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to declare as unlawful the making and dissemination of hoax threats of mass violence, false active shooter reports, and related malicious pranks in academic institutions and public spaces, and to provide penalties therefor. The Constitution recognizes the vital role of youth in nation-building and explicitly charges the State with protecting their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Crucial to this duty is ensuring that educational institutions remain safe, secure, and conducive environments for learning. In recent years, schools, universities, malls, transport terminals. and other public spaces across the country have repeatedly been disrupted by hoax reports of mass shootings, bombings, and other acts of violence. These false alarms -— whether spread through social media, text messages, phone calls, or word of mouth — force the evacuation of buildings, the deployment of law enforcement and school personnel, and the diversion of scarce security resources, all in response to a threat that does not exist. While Presidential Decree No. 1727, otherwise known as the "Anti-Bomb Joke Law.” already penalizes the malicious dissemination of false bomb threats, existing law does not squarely address hoax threats involving firearms, active shooter scenarios, and other forms of mass violence that do not involve explosives. This gap has allowed perpetrators — often students or minors acting as a "prank" — to escape appropriate liability, or has forced prosecutors to stretch other penal provisions, such as unjust vexation or the alarms and scandals provisions of the Revised Penal Code, that were never designed for threats of this scale and impact. This bill seeks to close that gap by specifically criminalizing hoax threats of mass violence and false active shooter reports, whether made in academic institutions or in other public spaces. The bill defines the prohibited acts, fixes penalties calibrated to be consistent with, and not in conflict with, the penalties already imposed under other special penal laws of similar nature. It also provides for graduated, current, and proportionate penalties depending on the gravity of the disruption caused and the offender's age. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill 1s earnestly sought. label: HB 11677
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE REVISED RANK CLASSIFICATION AND SALARY-GRADE STRUCTURE OF THE UNIFORMED PERSONNEL OF THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION AND THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE, REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9263, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION AND BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT OF 2004,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9263, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology Professionalization Act of 2004,” was enacted to professionalize the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) and the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), strengthen their organizational structures, and promote the professional development and welfare of their personnel. 1 More than two decades after its enactment, however, the operational responsibilities, organizational requirements, and manpower needs of both agencies have substantially evolved, warranting a reassessment of their existing rank classification and compensation structure. The growing demands placed upon the BFP and BJMP underscore the need for adequate manpower and a rank structure commensurate with the responsibilities of their personnel. In July 2026, the BJMP added 2,226 newly appointed jail officers, bringing its reported workforce to 28,963 personnel, as the Bureau continues efforts to address its manpower requirements and move toward a target workforce of 46,984.2 Meanwhile, the BFP has reported 39,289 1 Republic Act No. 9263, “Bureau of Fire Protection and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology Professionalization Act of 2004,” March 10, 2004. 2 Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), “2,226 New Jail Officers Take Oath Nationwide,” Philippine Information Agency, July 17, 2026, https://pia.gov.ph/press-release/2226-new-jail-officers- take-oath-nationwide/. authorized positions for uniformed personnel, of which 37,105 are filled, leaving a substantial number of positions to be filled. 3 These manpower requirements must be considered alongside the increasingly complex functions performed by both agencies. The BFP is responsible not only for fire suppression but also for fire prevention, investigation, emergency response, rescue, and disaster-risk reduction, while the BJMP is tasked with the safe and humane custody, management, and rehabilitation of persons deprived of liberty (PDLs). The adequacy of personnel and the effectiveness of their command structures are therefore essential to public safety. The urgency of strengthening BFP manpower is further demonstrated by the reported increase in fire incidents. During the first quarter of 2026, the BFP recorded 4,092 fire incidents, a 28% increase from the 3,184 incidents recorded during the same period in the previous year. Despite the increase in incidents, reported fire-related fatalities and property damage declined during the period.4 The continuing volume and complexity of emergency incidents demonstrate the need for sufficient personnel who are properly trained, organized, and compensated according to the demands of their functions. The measure seeks to establish a clear and uniform rank and salary structure for BFP and BJMP personnel, from Fire/Jail Officer to Fire/Jail General. Salaries will reflect the duties and responsibilities of each rank and will be reasonably aligned with other uniformed services. Promotions and reclassifications will remain based on merit and existing qualification and plantilla requirements. During the transition, incumbent personnel shall retain their existing rank, appointment status, tenure, and basic pay. No personnel shall be demoted, separated, or deprived of security of tenure solely because of the new rank classification. The BFP and BJMP, in coordination with the DILG, DBM, and CSC, shall develop a transition plan to guide the orderly implementation of the new system. The reform will help build a more professional and motivated BFP and BJMP workforce. Fair ranks and appropriate compensation will improve morale and support career growth. It will also help retain qualified personnel and strengthen their ability to perform their duties. By investing in these essential uniformed services, the State can better protect communities and ensure public safety. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. MA.
