label: HB 11742
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF LETTER CARRIERS, COURIERS, MESSENGERS, AND DELIVERY WORKERS, PROVIDING FOR THEIR SAFETY, WELFARE, AND PROTECTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Letter carriers, couriers, messengers, delivery workers, and other workers engaged in the movement and delivery of letters, documents, parcels, goods, and other lawful articles perform essential functions in sustaining commerce, communication, government transactions, and the country's logistics and delivery systems. Yet, despite the essential nature of their work, they are routinely exposed to traffic accidents, extreme weather, fatigue, robbery, theft, cargo-related risks, unsafe working conditions, and other occupational hazards. The growth of app-based and platform-enabled delivery services, as well as the increasing participation of logistics companies and logistics service providers in delivery and fulfillment operations, has further changed the nature of this work. Many workers now perform substantially similar delivery and messenger functions under different employment or contractual arrangements, including through contractors, subcontractors, fleet operators, and digital platforms. These arrangements should not result in the denial of basic safety, welfare, and protection to workers performing essential delivery and logistics functions. This measure therefore seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for the safety, welfare, and protection of letter carriers, couriers, messengers, delivery workers, platform-based delivery workers, in-house messengers, logistics workers, and similarly situated workers. The proposed “Kartero Law of 2026” seeks to provide covered workers with appropriate occupational safety and health measures, safety training, protective equipment, access to social protection and insurance, protection against unfair deductions and unreasonable financial liability, safeguards in the handling of cash and cargo, protection against robbery and fraud, reasonable access to delivery facilities, and appropriate mechanisms for addressing adverse actions and workplace concerns. The measure likewise recognizes the realities of modern platform-based work by promoting transparency in task assignment, compensation, incentives, ratings, suspension and deactivation policies, and other automated systems that materially affect a worker's ability to earn a livelihood. At the same time, it respects existing laws and jurisprudence governing employment and contractual relationships and does not, by itself, determine the employment status of any covered worker. Recognizing the growing role of logistics companies and logistics service providers, the bill expressly includes workers engaged or deployed by such entities, including those performing delivery, courier, messengerial, sorting, handling, dispatch, fulfillment, distribution, fleet, and related functions. It likewise prevents employers, principals, contractors, subcontractors, logistics service providers, platform operators, and other intermediaries from shifting regulatory obligations to individual workers or using contracting arrangements to circumvent the protections granted by the measure. The bill does not seek to deregulate the logistics or transportation sectors. In particular, it preserves the existing jurisdiction of the appropriate government agencies over transportation and logistics activities that are independently subject to regulation. It merely clarifies that the performance of delivery, courier, messengerial, parcel, last-mile delivery, fulfillment, dispatch, or related logistics activities does not, by itself, constitute passenger transportation requiring an LTFRB franchise or Certificate of Public Convenience. Existing requirements applicable to truck-for-hire, freight or cargo transportation for hire, passenger transportation, and other regulated transportation services remain unaffected. Finally, the measure seeks to strengthen coordination among the Department of Labor and Employment, Department of Information and Communications Technology, Department of Transportation and its attached agencies, Philippine Postal Corporation, local government units, and other concerned agencies, while ensuring that its provisions are harmonized with existing labor, occupational safety and health, transportation, social protection, data privacy, and other applicable laws. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11743
title: AN ACT STANDARDIZING TRAFFIC APPREHENSION PROCEDURES, INSTITUTIONALIZING THE TRAFFIC ADJUDICATION UNIT, PRESCRIBING RULES FOR CITATION PURPOSES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Traffic enforcement is important for keeping roads safe and orderly. However, One of the growing concerns among motorists is the proliferation of improper traffic apprehensions. Some traffic enforcers may be pressured by ticket quotas or incentive systems to issue a certain number of citations. This can lead to unfair or baseless apprehensions of drivers who have not broken any law. Being wrongly apprehended can cause drivers financial loss, stress, and inconvenience. Although drivers can challenge an improper ticket, many do not because the process is often slow, complicated, and time-consuming. Daily wage earners, public utility vehicle drivers, and employees may lose income or miss work just to contest a ticket. Because of this, some drivers choose to pay the fine even when they are innocent. This bill seeks to protect drivers by compensating those who are wrongfully apprehended for the time, inconvenience, and expenses they incur. It also imposes administrative penalties on traffic personnel who make improper apprehensions. The bill further prohibits traffic ticket quotas and incentive systems. By removing these pressures, traffic enforcers can focus on enforcing the law fairly and providing penalty thereof. Overall, the bill aims to make traffic enforcement fairer, more transparent, and more accountable. It seeks to protect drivers from unjust penalties while ensuring that traffic personnel follow the law and prioritize public safety. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. RAMON RODRIGO L. label: HB 11744
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE COVERAGE OF THE SOCIAL PENSION PROGRAM BY GRANTING SOCIAL PENSION TO ALL SENIOR CITIZENS AGED 65 YEARS OLD AND ABOVE, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9257, REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9994, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11916, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Filipino family has long been regarded as the first source of care and support for its elderly members. This duty is expressly recognized in Section 4, Article XV, of the 1987 Constitution: “The family has the duty to care for its elderly members but the State may also do so through just programs of social security.” The Constitution likewise directs the State to make essential health and social services available at affordable cost, with priority given to the elderly, among other vulnerable sectors (Article XIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution). Congress has acted on these constitutional commitments through Republic Act No. 7432, as amended by Republic Act Nos. 9257, 9994, and 11916. These laws established and expanded various benefits and forms of government assistance for senior citizens. In particular, Republic Act No. 9994 institutionalized the Social Pension Program for indigent senior citizens, while Republic Act No. 11916 subsequently increased the monthly social pension to One Thousand Pesos (Php 1,000.00). The existing program, however, remains principally directed toward indigent senior citizens. This measure seeks to take a further step in strengthening social protection for the country's aging population by extending a monthly social pension to all senior citizens who are sixty-five (65) years old and above, regardless of their economic status. It likewise maintains assistance for indigent senior citizens aged sixty (60) to sixty-four (64), who may face financial hardship even before reaching the age covered by the proposed universal benefit. The proposed social pension is intended to serve as a modest and continuing source of support for ordinary expenses, particularly food, medicine, and other medical and subsistence needs. The amount provided under this measure is not intended to replace employment income, retirement benefits, or pensions received under existing systems such as the Social Security System or Government Service Insurance System. Rather, it is conceived as a basic form of social protection that may supplement whatever resources a senior citizen may already have. Ultimately, this measure recognizes that the protection of older Filipinos should not depend solely on whether they have been classified as indigent. Reaching old age is a stage of life in which many citizens experience increased medical expenses, reduced earning capacity, and greater dependence on family or other forms of assistance. A universal social pension for senior citizens aged sixty-five (65) years and above provides a straightforward form of government support while preserving additional assistance for younger senior citizens who are already experiencing serious economic vulnerability. The State has a continuing responsibility to ensure that its senior citizens are able to live their later years with dignity and a reasonable measure of financial security. By expanding the social pension, this measure seeks to make that responsibility more responsive to the realities faced by an aging Filipino population. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. MARLYN L. label: HB 11746
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COLLEGE OF MEDICINE IN THE PANGASINAN STATE UNIVERSITY (PSU) IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF STA. MARIA, PROVINCE OF PANGASINAN, TO BE KNOWN AS THE “PANGASINAN STATE UNIVERSITY COLLEGE OF MEDICINE”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as a fundamental concern of the State. Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides: “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” In higher education, the Constitution expressly guarantees academic freedom and recognizes the right of every citizen to choose a profession or course of study, subject to fair, reasonable, and equitable admission and academic requirements. Article XIV, Section 5(3) of the 1987 Constitution provides: “Every citizen has a right to select a profession or course of study, subject to fair, reasonable and equitable admission and academic requirements.” These constitutional policies are particularly significant in the field of medical education. The availability of qualified physicians is inseparable from the State’s responsibility to provide accessible and responsive health services, especially in communities where geography, economic circumstances, and the limited availability of medical professionals may affect access to care. Eastern Pangasinan, specifically the Sixth (6 th) District of Pangasinan, presents a compelling setting for the development of a government medical school. The province is geographically situated at the eastern portion of the country, and its communities include areas where distance and transportation may affect access to higher education and health services. A medical school located within the province would allow qualified students from the Sixth (6th) District of Pangasinan and nearby communities to pursue medical education closer to their homes while developing physicians who are familiar with the health conditions and needs of the communities they are expected to serve. By bringing medical education to the Sixth (6th) District of Pangasinan, the State can widen the pool of students who have the opportunity to become physicians while strengthening the connection between medical training, community health, research, and public service. The establishment of the Pangasinan State University College of Medicine is ultimately an investment in both education and public health. It will provide another pathway for qualified Filipinos to enter the medical profession, create opportunities for students from Pangasinan and neighboring areas, and contribute to the development of physicians who may serve communities where the need for health professionals remains significant. Moreover, it is also in line with the goal of the establishment of Pangasinan State University (PSU) under Presidential Decree No. 1497, Series of 1978, to “provide better service in professional and technical training in the arts, sciences, humanities, and technology and in the conduct of scientific research and technological studies[.]” For these reasons, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11747
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 36 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8491, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "FLAG AND HERALDIC CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES", TO PROVIDE FOR THE OFFICIAL LYRICS OF THE NATIONAL ANTHEM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The National Anthem is more than a song performed at the opening of government programs, school ceremonies, and other public gatherings. It is one of the symbols through which the Filipino people express their shared history, identity, and continuing commitment to the nation. For this reason, its words and manner of rendition are matters properly governed by law. The 1987 Constitution recognizes the authority of Congress to adopt, by law, a national anthem that reflects and symbolizes the ideals, history, and traditions of the Filipino people. Section 2, Article XVI, of the 1987 Constitution provides that:“The Congress may, by law, adopt a new name for the country, a national anthem, or a national seal, which shall all be truly reflective and symbolic of the ideals, history, and traditions of the people. Such law shall take effect only upon its ratification by the people in a national referendum.” Pursuant to this constitutional authority, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 8491, otherwise known as the “Flag and Heraldic Code of the Philippines.” The law in its Section 2 declares that reverence and respect shall at all times be accorded to the national flag, the anthem, and other national symbols: “Reverence and respect shall at all times be accorded the flag, the anthem, and other national symbols which embody the national ideals and traditions and which express the principles of sovereignty and national solidarity. [x x x]” Section 36 of Republic Act No. 8491 provides: “The National Anthem shall always be sung in the national language within or without the country. The following shall be the lyrics of the National Anthem: Bayang magiliw, Perlas ng Silanganan Alab ng puso, Sa Dibdib mo'y buhay. Lupang Hinirang, Duyan ka ng magiting, Sa manlulupig, Di ka pasisiil. Sa dagat at bundok, Sa simoy at sa langit mong bughaw, May dilag ang tula, At awit sa paglayang minamahal. Ang kislap ng watawat mo'y Tagumpay na nagniningning, Ang bituin at araw niya, Kailan pa ma'y di magdidilim, Lupa ng araw ng luwalhati't pagsinta, Buhay ay langit sa piling mo, Aming ligaya na pag may mang-aapi, Ang mamatay ng dahil sa iyo.” Section 36 of Republic Act No. 8491 has served as the statutory reference for the Filipino lyrics of Lupang Hinirang for more than two decades. Its importance extends beyond the wording printed in the law. The present measure seeks to make a limited amendment to Section 36 by adopting the forms “’Di” and “’Pag” in the corresponding portions of the lyrics to make it more accurate since “’Di” came from the root word “Hindi” and “’Pag” came from the root word “Kapag.” The proposed amendment does not introduce a new national anthem, change its melody, or alter its message. It likewise leaves untouched the provisions of Republic Act No. 8491 governing the manner in which the National Anthem is rendered and the respect accorded to it during public gatherings. The measure is intended to provide a clear and uniform statutory text for the words that Filipinos are required to sing as the National Anthem. The proposed amendment aims at precision in the statutory text while preserving the National Anthem that generations of Filipinos have known. It does not diminish the historical character of Lupang Hinirang. Rather, it affirms that its words, as prescribed by law, should be stated with the same care and consistency expected of any other national symbol established by statute. At a time when national identity is expressed not only within our borders but also by Filipinos living, studying, working, and representing the country abroad, maintaining a clear and uniform statutory formulation of the National Anthem is a modest but meaningful exercise of legislative responsibility. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. MARLYN L. label: HB 11748
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING IN THE SECOND DISTRICT OF ZAMBOANGA CITY, THE ZAMBOANGA CITY STATE UNIVERSITY FOR MARINE SCIENCES AND TECHNOLOGY (ZCSUMST), A SPECIALIZED INSTITUTION OF HIGHER LEARNING FOR BLUE ECONOMY, FISHERIES, AND MARITIME INNOVATION, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS, MANDATE, RESEARCH, TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER, AND INDUSTRY LINKAGES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Zamboanga City and the Zamboanga Peninsula occupy a strategic position at the confluence of the Sulu and Celebes Seas, one of the world’s richest marine corridors. The region is recognized as the Sardine Capital of the Philippines and serves as a major hub for tuna processing, seaweed production, and shipbuilding. These industries sustain thousands of Filipino families and contribute significantly to the nation’s blue economy. Yet, despite its abundant resources, the region remains constrained by limited research capacity, inadequate technology transfer, and the absence of a world-class academic and industrial ecosystem to fully harness its maritime potential. The Philippines faces a critical human capital challenge. According to the World Bank Human Capital Index, Filipino children born today are projected to achieve only 52% of their potential productivity as future workers due to gaps in health and education investments (HCI score: 0.516). Similarly, the country’s Human Development Index (HDI) stands at 0.720, below the global average of 0.744, while the Zamboanga Peninsula lags further behind with an HDI of 0.674, among the lowest in Mindanao. These figures underscore systemic disparities in education and skills development. The urgency is amplified by findings from the 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS): while 93.1% of Filipinos aged 10–64 are basically literate, only 70.8% are functionally literate, meaning nearly 3 in 10 Filipinos struggle with comprehension—a gap most severe in regions with high poverty, including Zamboanga Peninsula. This learning crisis limits workforce readiness and perpetuates socio-economic vulnerability. Against this backdrop, the establishment of the Zamboanga City State University for Marine Sciences and Technology (ZCSUMST) is not merely a regional initiative, it is a national imperative. This specialized, autonomous, and research-intensive state university will serve as the premier hub for fisheries science, aquaculture innovation, shipbuilding technology, and blue economy development, integrating science, enterprise, and policy across the entire marine value chain. The University will host centers of excellence for sardine and tuna repopulation, marine biosciences, seaweed bioproducts, shipbuilding and maritime engineering, and climate and water systems. It will institutionalize a Blue Economy Innovation and Business Hub, a Smart Campus Framework, and a Climate Resilience Observatory to align education and research with sustainable coastal development. To attract investment and global partnerships, the measure provides fiscal incentives, including a 15-year income tax holiday for BOI or PEZA-registered enterprises engaged in R&D, hatchery, or shipbuilding operations within the University, followed by a preferential 5% tax rate, consistent with the CREATE Act. It also introduces the Fisherfolk Equivalency Program, granting academic credits for traditional maritime skills, thereby empowering fisherfolk and maritime workers to access higher education. The proposed University aligns with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028, the ASEAN Blue Economy Framework, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goals 2 (Zero Hunger), 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), 13 (Climate Action), and 14 (Life Below Water). It is not a mere campus conversion but the creation of a world-class institution that fuses science, industry, culture, and sustainability for the long-term prosperity of the Zamboanga Peninsula and the nation. Given the region’s strategic maritime position, its economic potential, and the pressing need to address human capital and literacy gaps, the immediate passage of this Act is earnestly sought to transform Zamboanga into a global center for marine sciences and innovation. label: HB 11749
title: AN ACT MANDATING FOOD MANUFACTURERS TO PROMINENTLY DISPLAY WARNING LABELS ON PREPACKAGED FOOD PRODUCTS CONTAINING HIGH LEVELS OF SUGAR, SODIUM, CALORIES, OR FAT, AND PROVIDING FOR RELATED PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A healthy nation begins with an informed citizenry, and an informed citizenry begins with knowing what is on its plate. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), heart diseases remain the leading cause of death in the Philippines, accounting for approximately 21.2% of registered deaths, followed by neoplasms at 9.9%, cerebrovascular diseases at 9.6%, pneumonia at 8.0%, and diabetes at 5.7%!. While these conditions arise from multiple and complex causes, unhealthy dietary patterns are among the significant and preventable risk factors associated with many of them. Their continued prevalence highlights the need for policies that go beyond treating illness and instead strengthen prevention, promote healthier food choices, and empower Filipinos to make informed decisions about their health. Diets high in sugar, sodium, saturated fat, and calories are associated with various health risks, particularly when consumed excessively and regularly. According to the Department of Science and Technology (DOST), Filipinos consume more than twice the : https://psa.gov.ph/content/2026-causes-death-philippines-provisional-31 -july-2026 recommended limit of sodium and high amounts of sugar from processed foods, while the country continues to face widespread micronutrient deficiencies. These concerns are compounded by the consumption of ready-made and highly processed products commonly found in groceries and other retail establishments, including instant noodles, processed meats, salted eggs, and other processed or preserved foods. This reflects the country's dual nutritional challenge: inadequate intake of essential micronutrients alongside excessive consumption of nutrients associated with diet-related diseases. Addressing this problem requires not only promoting healthier diets but also ensuring that consumers can readily identify the nutritional risks of the products they purchase. The 1987 Constitution provides a clear foundation for such measures. Article II, Section 15 declares that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. Article XIII, Section 11 directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development, while Article XIII, Section 12 provides for an effective food and drug regulatory system responsive to the country's health needs. Existing legislation likewise provides consumer safeguards. Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, requires manufacturers to provide appropriate information about their products, including their contents and ingredients. However, disclosure alone may not ensure that consumers recognize excessive levels of sugar, sodium, fat, or calories. Consumers may have to examine detailed nutrition facts, interpret serving sizes, and compare nutrient quantities before determining the nutritional risks of a product. Information that is technically available may therefore remain difficult to interpret at the point of purchase. Hence, this measure seeks to strengthen existing food-labeling and consumer- protection policies by requiring manufacturers of prepackaged food products to display prominent warning labels on products containing excessive levels of sugar, sodium, calories, saturated fat, and other food components that may pose health risks when consumed excessively, based on scientifically established thresholds and standards to be determined by the appropriate regulatory authorities. The measure does not prohibit consumers from purchasing or consuming these products. Instead, it enables them to make informed choices by providing an immediate indication of products that exceed established nutritional thresholds. In doing so, the measure advances consumer protection while supporting the constitutional mandate to instill health consciousness among Filipinos. The potential of this approach is demonstrated by Chile, which implemented nutrient warning labels as part of a broader strategy addressing unhealthy food consumption. During Phase 2 of its implementation, researchers found reductions in household purchases of products subject to the warning-label regulations”. While the Philippine context differs from Chile in terms of dietary practices, markets, and socioeconomic conditions, the study provides relevant evidence that front-of-package warnings can form part of a public-health strategy and encourage healthier purchasing decisions. Ultimately, addressing the country's burden of heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and other diet-related noncommunicable diseases require a comprehensive preventive approach. Healthcare must not begin only when a person enters a hospital; it must also begin with the choices made before illness develops. This measure complements existing nutrition programs, healthcare services, food regulations, and consumer-protection laws by giving Filipinos a simpler way to recognize potential nutritional risks in the products they purchase. By making excessive levels of sugar, sodium, calories, saturated fat, and other regulated nutrients immediately visible, the measure seeks to promote health consciousness, strengthen consumer protection, encourage responsible food manufacturing, and contribute to disease prevention. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. AUDREY KAY T. label: HB 11750
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools are meant to be safe spaces where children can learn, develop, and thrive. However, the growing threats of bullying, violence, abuse, mental health concerns, cyberbullying, and other emerging digital risks, compounded by natural disasters and security- related incidents, underscore the urgent need for a comprehensive and coordinated approach to school safety. While existing laws and policies provide safeguards against specific threats, there remains a need to institutionalize an integrated framework that addresses the physical, mental, emotional, psychosocial, and digital safety and well-being of learners and school personnel. School safety must go beyond responding to incidents and instead emphasize prevention, preparedness, timely intervention, and recovery. This proposed Comprehensive School Safety Act seeks to establish a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework covering all public and private basic education institutions. It mandates the adoption of School Safety Plans, appropriate security and emergency preparedness measures, strengthened anti-bullying and child protection mechanisms, mental health and psychosocial support services, responsible technology use, and effective incident reporting, response, and recovery systems. Q om 7) The measure likewise strengthens coordination among schools, parents, local government units, and relevant national government agencies, while ensuring that school personnel are adequately equipped, trained, and supported in carrying out their responsibilities. Ultimately, this bill recognizes that the right to education must necessarily include the right to learn in an environment free from fear, violence, abuse, and harm. By institutionalizing a proactive, inclusive, and responsive school safety system, we can better protect our learners, empower our educators, and foster school communities where every child is safe, supported, and given the opportunity to reach their full potential. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. AUDREY KAY T. label: HB 11751
title: AN ACT DECLARING TRANSNATIONAL DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATIONS AS TERRORIST ORGANIZATIONS, DEFINING AND PENALIZING NARCO-TERRORISM, STRENGTHENING INTERNATIONAL LAW ENFORCEMENT COOPERATION AGAINST ILLEGAL DRUG SYNDICATES, AND AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11479, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS "THE ANTI-TERRORISM ACT OF 2020," AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9165, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS "THE COMPREHENSIVE DANGEROUS DRUGS ACT OF 2002," AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Illegal drug syndicates that operate across borders are no longer mere criminal enterprises. They finance violence, corrupt public institutions, and undermine national security. This bill treats these transnational organizations for what they are: threats to the security of the State. Recent law enforcement operations involving massive cross-border drug shipments originating from international hubs and destined for the Philippines demonstrate the evolving sophistication of transnational narco-trafficking. Investigations into these operations frequently reveal complex networks involving local logistics, air transport, and foreign supply chains. When illicit transactions are intercepted prior to reaching Philippine territory, legal action within domestic jurisdiction is often limited to conspiracy charges. To effectively combat these cartels and enable seamless international cooperation, there is a compelling need to classify major transnational drug syndicates as terrorist organizations. Under existing anti-terrorism statutes, designation and enforcement measures are strictly tied to acts motivated by political, religious, or ideological objectives. Because organized drug cartels operate primarily for financial gain and profit, the Anti-Terrorism Council lacks the statutory authority under current law to designate them as terrorist entities. Without an explicit legislative mandate, executive agencies cannot apply critical enforcement tools, such as asset freezing, court-authorized surveillance, and extraterritorial jurisdiction, against commercial narco-trafficking networks. Existing drug laws also focus primarily on acts committed within domestic borders, leaving financing, procurement, and logistics organized abroad difficult to prosecute prior to the physical arrival of illicit cargo. Classifying transnational drug trafficking organizations as terrorist entities bridges these legal gaps, grants the Council the necessary statutory authority regardless of motive, and aligns domestic requests for intelligence sharing, asset freezing, and extradition with international anti-terrorism standards. This bill formally defines a transnational drug trafficking organization (TDTO), authorizes the Anti-Terrorism Council to designate such entities upon a finding of probable cause, and requires judicial proscription by the Court of Appeals. It establishes the offense of narco-terrorism, penalizes material support, financing, and membership, and grants domestic courts jurisdiction over acts committed abroad when illicit drugs are intended for local distribution. Furthermore, public officers or law enforcement personnel found aiding or abetting these organizations shall suffer maximum statutory penalties and perpetual disqualification from public service. . To ensure constitutional integrity, the bill incorporates essential safeguards. Designation rests solely on an independent finding of probable cause by the Council, formal delisting procedures are made available, and mandatory notification to human rights authorities is required upon any arrest. Transnational drug cartels operate without regard to national borders. Our legal framework must be equipped with the necessary extraterritorial reach and statutory tools to suppress them. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK ANTHONY G. label: HB 11752
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SPECIAL INSURANCE AND INDEMNITY COVERAGE FOR FILIPINO FISHERFOLK AND FISHING VESSELS AGAINST LOSS OR DAMAGE ARISING FROM FOREIGN MARITIME INTERFERENCE WITHIN PHILIPPINE MARITIME ZONES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For generations, Filipino fisherfolk have depended on our seas for their livelihood. For many Palaweño fisherfolk, the West Philippine Sea is not an abstract question of maps, boundaries, or foreign policy. It is where they work, where they fish, and where they provide for their families. Yet going out to sea has become increasingly difficult and dangerous. Filipino fisherfolk continue to face water cannoning, blocking, dangerous maneuvers, and other forms of interference by foreign vessels in the West Philippine Sea. In October 2026, Philippine authorities also encountered unauthorized foreign fishing vessels in the Kalayaan Island Group, including a Chinese fishing vessel and smaller boats found fishing without authorization within the territorial sea of Lawak Island, Palawan. Behind every damaged fishing boat or destroyed net is a fisherfolk who may not be able to return to sea the next day. For families who depend on the day's catch, the loss of a boat, engine, fishing gear, or catch already obtained can mean losing their source of income. In more serious encounters, it is not only their livelihood that is at risk, but their safety and their lives. Government programs already provide livelihood, fisheries, and insurance assistance to fisherfolk. The Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation (PCIC), in particular, provides insurance protection for fisherfolk and certain fishing assets. However, existing insurance policies may exclude losses arising from invasion, acts of foreign enemies, hostilities, or similar events. A fisherfolk may therefore have insurance and still find that damage caused by foreign maritime interference is not covered. This bill seeks to address that gap. It directs the PCIC to develop special insurance and indemnity coverage for qualified Filipino fisherfolk and fishing vessels operating within Philippine maritime zones. Rather than create another government agency or a separate compensation fund, the measure builds on the government's existing insurance system. The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) will assist in verifying incidents, while the PCIC will administer the coverage and process claims. The coverage is intended for actual and verifiable losses, including damage to fishing boats, engines, gear and equipment, loss of catch already obtained, and reasonable rescue and recovery expenses. Projected catch, expected profits, and other speculative losses are not covered. Our fisherfolk should not have to bear these losses alone. They go to sea to work, not to become casualties of a maritime dispute. If they suffer actual damage while lawfully earning a living in Philippine waters, there should be a clear mechanism to help them recover and return to sea. As the Philippines continues to assert and defend its rights in the West Philippine Sea, we must also stand behind the Filipino fisherfolk who exercise those rights through their everyday livelihood. Protecting our waters must also mean protecting the people who depend on them. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11753
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PRESIDENT RAMON MAGSAYSAY STATE UNIVERSITY, RECOGNIZING AND INTEGRATING ITS SATELLITE CAMPUSES IN THE MUNICIPALITIES OF SANTA CRUZ, MASINLOC, BOTOLAN, AND CASTILLEJOS, ALL IN THE PROVINCE OF ZAMBALES, PROVIDING FOR THE COMPOSITION AND POWERS OF ITS GOVERNING BOARD, PRESCRIBING ITS CURRICULAR OFFERINGS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the vital role of education in nation-building and mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels. State universities and colleges give concrete expression to this mandate by bringing affordable and responsive higher education closer to communities, particularly to students whose circumstances would otherwise limit their access to tertiary education. President Ramon Magsaysay State University (PRMSU) has long served as a principal center of higher learning, research, innovation, and extension in the Province of Zambales and Central Luzon. Since its establishment and subsequent conversion and renaming under Republic Act Nos. 8498 and 11015, the University has expanded its reach and academic responsibilities in response to the changing educational, economic, and development needs of the Province, the region, and the country. Notwithstanding this growth, the University’s existing charter no longer fully reflects the scope of its present operations. In particular, the PRMSU campuses in the Municipalities of Santa Cruz, Masinloc, Botolan, and Castillejos require express statutory recognition and integration to place them on a firm institutional footing and ensure their sustained development. Formal recognition will enable these campuses to receive appropriate funding, infrastructure, faculty and non-teaching personnel, and other resources necessary to deliver quality instruction, research, extension, and community services. This bill therefore seeks to strengthen and modernize the charter of PRMSU by recognizing the satellite campuses in Santa Cruz, Masinloc, Botolan, and Castillejos as constituent campuses of the University, while affirming the continued operation of its existing campuses in Iba, San Marcelino, and Candelaria. It likewise broadens the University’s curricular mandate to include emerging and high-impact fields such as artificial intelligence, information and communications technology, maritime education, medicine and health-related programs, law and legal management, the creative industries, and peace and security studies, subject to the standards of the Commission on Higher Education and the capabilities of the University. 2 The measure also updates the composition, powers, and duties of the Board of Regents; strengthens participatory, transparent, and accountable governance; and clarifies the roles of the University President, the Administrative Council, and the Academic Council. It further safeguards academic freedom and institutional autonomy, promotes equitable access through scholarships and affirmative action programs, and provides for the orderly transfer and administration of the assets, liabilities, personnel, and lands of the University and its campuses. By providing a unified and responsive charter, this measure will allow PRMSU to plan and develop as one University system, allocate resources more equitably among its campuses, and offer programs aligned with local and national development priorities. It will also strengthen the University’s capacity to produce competent professionals, undertake relevant research, support industry and local government, and create opportunities for learners throughout Zambales and neighboring communities. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. ACIDRE DORIS E. label: HB 11754
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A MONTHLY CASH ASSISTANCE FOR BEDRIDDEN INDIVIDUALS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 76 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 79 SECTION 1. Short Title. 81 This Act shall be known as the "Bedridden Individuals Cash Assistance Act." 83 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. 85 It is the policy of the State to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services, promote full employment, a rising standard of living, and an improved quality of life for all. The State further recognizes its obligation to protect and provide special support to vulnerable sectors, including persons with severe medical impairments and disabilities, ensuring their right to health, purchasing power stability, and human dignity. 92 SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. 94 For purposes of this Act, the following terms shall mean: 96 a. Bedridden Individual — refers to any Filipino citizen who is continuously confined to bed or chair due to a permanent or long-term severe physical disability, chronic terminal illness, advanced age, neurological impairment, or injury that completely prevents them from performing primary activities of daily living (ADLs) without full assistance from a caregiver. 102 b. Authorized Representative — refers to a primary caregiver, legal guardian, or immediate family member within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity designated by or on behalf of the bedridden individual to apply for and receive the cash assistance. 107 c. Consumer Price Index (CPI) — refers to the indicator generated by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) that measures the average changes in the retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services usually purchased by households. 111 d. C/MSWDO — refers to the City or Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office. 114 SECTION 4. Cash Assistance Benefit, Inflation Adjustment, and Non-Exclusion. 116 a. Base Benefit: Every qualified bedridden individual shall be entitled to receive a direct cash assistance in the initial base amount of Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) per month. The cash benefit shall be disbursed on a monthly or quarterly basis directly to the beneficiary or through their designated Authorized Representative.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Bedridden individuals—whether due to severe illness, advanced age, neurological disorders, or major physical disabilities—face profound vulnerabilities. Beyond the emotional and physical toll on both the individuals and their families, the financial burden of caring for a bedridden family member is immense. Daily expenses for specialized medical supplies, adult diapers, catheter care, bedsore management, prescription medication, and home-based caregiving place extreme strain on low- to middle-income households. 22 While current social welfare legislation provides general subsidies to indigent senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs), these existing social safety nets were not designed to cover the extraordinary and continuous cost of full home-based care for bedridden individuals. 26 This bill establishes a direct base financial subsidy of Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) per month to qualified bedridden individuals across the country. Crucially, this measure explicitly provides that this subsidy shall be over and above any benefit, social pension, or assistance granted under existing laws for Senior Citizens and PWDs, ensuring that receiving this support will not reduce or disqualify a beneficiary from other statutory benefits. Furthermore, to safeguard the purchasing power of this support against economic fluctuations and rising costs, the bill mandates an automatic annual inflation adjustment based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI) published by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). 35 In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 37 38 39 HON. label: HB 11755
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE WESTERN VISAYAS REGIONAL FOOD HUB IN ILOILO CITY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING AN IMPLEMENTING FRAMEWORK, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 77 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 80 SECTION 1. Short Title. 82 This Act shall be known as the "Western Visayas Regional Food Hub Act." 84 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. 86 It is hereby declared the policy of the State to promote agricultural productivity, ensure regional food security, increase the income of agricultural workers, and modernize the post-harvest supply chain. To achieve these ends, the State shall establish state-of-the-art regional food hubs that integrate cold-chain infrastructure, modern logistics, trading platforms, quality control, and direct producer-to-market channels. 92 SECTION 3. Creation and Establishment of the Regional Food Hub. 94 There is hereby established a modern agro-industrial and logistical complex to be known as the Western Visayas Regional Food Hub (WVRFH), located in a strategically designated area within Iloilo City. 98 The WVRFH shall serve as the central aggregation, processing, cold storage, warehousing, testing, and wholesale trade terminal for agricultural, aquatic, livestock, and processed food products sourced from across Region VI. 102 SECTION 4. Objectives and Functions of the WVRFH. 104 The WVRFH shall fulfill the following core objectives and operational functions: 106 1. Aggregation & Logistics: Provide a centralized hub for small farmers, fisherfolk, agri- cooperatives, and commercial producers to aggregate produce efficiently. 109 2. Cold-Chain & Post-Harvest Preservation: Equip the hub with cold storage units, blast freezers, ambient warehouses, and modern packing facilities to minimize post-harvest losses. 112 3. Market Access & Price Stabilization: Facilitate direct trading between agricultural producers and institutional buyers, exporters, retail networks, and commercial establishments, minimizing multi-tiered middleman markups. 116 4. Quality Control & Standard Compliance: Establish testing and inspection facilities in coordination with the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI), Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to enforce food safety and quality standards.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Western Visayas (Region VI) serves as one of the primary agricultural and food baskets of the Philippines, producing substantial yields of rice, sugar, seafood, livestock, poultry, and high-value crops across its six provinces—Aklan, Antique, Capiz, Guimaras, Iloilo, and Negros Occidental. However, the region faces recurring challenges in post-harvest handling, supply chain inefficiencies, market volatility, and inadequate cold-chain logistics, which result in substantial post-harvest losses and depressed incomes for small farmers and fisherfolk. 22 Iloilo City, strategically positioned as the economic, administrative, and logistical hub of Region VI, possesses the necessary infrastructure, port facilities, and inter-island connectivity to host a centralized agri-fishery distribution system. Establishing a modern Regional Food Hub in Iloilo City will consolidate agricultural produce from across Western Visayas, streamline farm-to-market trade, reduce reliance on unnecessary intermediaries, and ensure stable, affordable food supplies for consumers. 29 Furthermore, this initiative aligns with national programs led by the Department of Agriculture (DA) to deploy strategic mega food hubs and strengthen cold storage, processing, and distribution networks across key regions. 33 In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 35 36 37 HON. label: HB 11756
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING HAZARDOUS TRADITIONAL TRIALS BY ORDEAL AND DANGEROUS RITUALS, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR FACILITATORS, ORGANIZERS, AND PUBLIC OFFICIALS, AND AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE RELEVANT PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8371, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' RIGHTS ACT OF 1997" 139 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 142 SECTION 1. Short Title. 144 This Act shall be known as the "Protection Against Hazardous Customary Ordeals Act." 147 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. 149 It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the right to life, physical integrity, and safety of all persons. While the State recognizes and respects the traditional justice systems and customary laws of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) pursuant to Section 15 of Republic Act No. 8371, such practices must at all times adhere to national legal standards and human rights. No customary practice, agreement, or voluntary consent shall justify acts that subject human life or physical well-being to grave peril. 156 SECTION 3. Prohibited Acts. 158 It shall be unlawful for any person or group to organize, conduct, order, facilitate, or require participation in any trial by ordeal, hazardous ritual, or customary practice that poses a direct threat to physical safety, bodily integrity, or human life, including but not limited to underwater endurance tests, exposure to fire or hazardous substances, or physical tortures used as dispute resolution mechanisms. 164 SECTION 4. Criminal Liability of Facilitators, Organizers, and Community Leaders. 166 Any elder, leader, spiritual guide, organizer, or individual who facilitates, directs, encourages, or conducts any traditional trial by ordeal, hazardous ritual, or practice involving physical danger or harm shall be held criminally liable as follows: 170 171 a. Resulting in Death or Serious Physical Injuries: The penalty of arresto mayor in its maximum period to prisión correccional in its medium period. 174 b. Resulting in Less Serious Physical Injuries: The penalty of arresto mayor in its minimum and medium periods. 177 c. Resulting in Slight Physical Injuries: The penalty of arresto menor in its maximum period. 180
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly commits the State to recognize, promote, and protect the rights of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) within the framework of national unity and development. This constitutional guarantee was given statutory form through Republic Act No. 8371, or the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 (IPRA), particularly Section 15, which recognizes the right of ICCs/IPs to use their customary laws, traditional justice systems, and conflict resolution mechanisms. 22 However, Section 15 of RA 8371 sets a clear and non-negotiable legal boundary: customary practices and dispute resolution mechanisms must always be compatible with the national legal system and internationally recognized human rights. 26 While customary law plays a vital role in community cohesion and dispute settlement, recent tragic events highlight how hazardous trials by ordeal and dangerous traditional rituals place human lives at grave risk. 30 A tragic illustration of this legislative gap occurred in Alabel, Sarangani Province. Two indigenous farmers belonging to the Tagakaulo community—holding a long-standing land dispute that failed to reach a settlement at the barangay level—agreed to undergo a traditional trial by ordeal known as "Sulif" to resolve land ownership. 35 Under the Sulif ritual, disputing parties remain submerged underwater in a river, with the individual remaining under longer declared the innocent or rightful party. Conducted at the Glamang River in Alabel, the ritual resulted in catastrophic loss of life: both farmers experienced severe breathing distress after remaining underwater for approximately 12 minutes. Both men subsequently drowned—one declared dead on arrival at the Sarangani Provincial Hospital, and the other dying shortly thereafter. 42 This heartbreaking incident in Sarangani underscores the urgent necessity of clear legislation: 44 45 1. Human Rights and Bodily Integrity Precede Customary Ordeals: No customary law, tribal agreement, voluntary consent, or community ritual can override the fundamental constitutional rights to life, safety, and bodily integrity. 49 2. Accountability for Facilitators and Authorities: Elders, leaders, spiritual guides, organizers, or public officers who facilitate, direct, encourage, or tolerate rituals involving physical danger, hazardous ordeals, or harm shall be held criminally and administratively liable if such acts result in injury or death. 54 3. Harmonization with RA 8371: It reinforces that while customary dispute resolution remains protected under Section 15 of IPRA, any practice causing physical injury or loss of life falls outside the legal protections of customary law and is subject to full prosecution under penal law. 59 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 61 62 63 64 HON. label: HB 11757
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A STANDARD NUMERICAL DATE FORMAT IN ALL OFFICIAL AND LEGAL DOCUMENTS IN THE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Standardization is the process of establishing a framework to be observed and adopted by involved parties to promote regularity, uniformity, and compatibility. This bill seeks to standardize the written format of a date when represented in numerical characters. Establishing a universal standard numerical date format will promote efficiency and accuracy in day-to-day transactions. It will also prevent misrepresentation, ambiguity, and confusion in written official and legal documents. This bill proposes to adopt the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 8601 international standard on date representation, which is a number sequence in decreasing units of time: year, month, and day (YYYY- MM-DD). This format is now being observed by several countries in the world. This unambiguous calendar-and-clock standard is intentionally adapted by the ISO and features the added benefit of being understood by machines following the ISO Standard, further streamlining tech-based encoding and transacting. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution commands the State to give priority to science and technology! and to pursue the industrialization and full employment of the nation.? Electronics already account for 58.81 percent of our total exports, worth USD 49.64 billion in 2025.8 Yet for all the chips that pass through Filipino hands, the country captures only a modest share of their value. Most of our work remains in assembly and testing, while the design, fabrication, and advanced packaging that command the highest returns are done elsewhere. Our critical minerals leave our shores as raw ore, only to return in finished products made by other nations. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DAVAO CENTRAL STATE POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE, INTEGRATING THE TESDA REGIONAL TRAINING CENTER - KOREA-PHILIPPINES VOCATIONAL TRAINING CENTER (RTC- KPVTC) DAVAO, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - DAVAO, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - DAVAO DEL SUR, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - MALITA, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - DAVAO DEL NORTE, CITY TRAINING CENTER - IGACOS, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - DAVAO DE ORO, PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - DAVAO ORIENTAL, AND PROVINCIAL TRAINING CENTER - SIMTRAC, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FOR ITS ADMINISTRATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET) serves as an essential backbone in transforming Filipino workforce into a competitive, future-ready, and skills-based economy. The optimization of TVET will ensure that our workforce remains highly responsive to the ever-changing and rapid evolution of industry demands. As the Davao Region continues to accelerate as a premier economic and industrial hub in Mindanao, elevating the existing TVET infrastructure is critical to sustaining its rapid growth in manufacturing, agriculture, and eco-tourism To address this, this bill seeks to establish the Davao Central State Polytechnic Institute by consolidating and rationalizing nine (9) TESDA Technology Institutions (TTIs) across the Davao Region under the leadership of the TESDA Regional Training Center - Korea-Philippines Vocational Training Center (RTC-KPVTC) Davao as its main campus and cluster convenor. This proposed measure directly responds to Memorandum RO-XI No. 07-1583 s. 2026 issued by the TESDA Region XI Regional Office. It is aligned with the national education reform framework, including the key recommendations of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), the National Technical Education and Skills Development Plan (NTESDP) 2023-2028, the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF) Act (R.A. 10968), and the Philippine Development Plan. Currently, individual training centers face persistent operational constraints, fragmented resource allocation, and restricted credit-transfer pathways into higher education. Transforming these isolated centers into a unified, multi-campus State Polytechnic System elevates TVET delivery from basic skill certifications (NC I to IV) to advanced three-year diploma programs, applied research, technology incubation, and Industry 4.0 technical competencies. Adopting a strategic "Hub-and-Spoke" model, RTC-KPVTC Davao will serve as the central hub and Regional Technology Innovation Center (RTIC) for higher-level technical education. Simultaneously, constituent campuses in Davao City (Mintal), Davao del Sur, Davao del Norte, Davao de Oro, Davao Oriental, Malita, IGACOS, and SIMTRAC will capitalize on specialized domain strengths—spanning industrial automation, smart agriculture, eco-tourism, logistics, heavy equipment, and marine technologies. Further, the bill grants necessary fiscal autonomy through a Special Trust Fund and mandates ladderized diploma-to-degree pathways, ensuring long-term financial sustainability and seamless academic progression for students. Ultimately, the Davao Central State Polytechnic Institute will serve as a vital engine for industrial productivity, MSME competitiveness, and inclusive economic growth throughout Mindanao. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A substantial component of the government staﬃng operates under temporary engagements or arrangements. As per the latest data from the Civil Service Commission’s Inventory of Government Human Resources (IGHRS)1 as of June 30, 2026, there are 1,038,284 Job Order (JO), Contract of Service (COS), and Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) [JO/COS/MOA] workers, and 178,850 Casual and Contractual employees across the country. JO/COS/MOA workers account for 31.51% and Casual and Contractual employees accounts 5.43% of the total workforce. It is a fact that there is strict legal limitation regarding their employment status. Speciﬁcally, there is a lack of an employer-employee relationship based on the Civil Service Commission, Commission on Audit, and Department of Budget and Management Joint Circular No. 1, s. 2025. However, it is undeniable that they play an important role in supporting government programs, projects, administrative functions, and frontline services. The government must ensure that while they are actively serving under their respective contracts, they still enjoy essential ﬁnancial safety nets. To address this, this bill seeks to provide beneﬁts to JO, COS, Casual and Contractual workers serving in the government. This measure lists beneﬁts which include: 13th-month Pay, HMO coverage, Mid-year Bonus, Performance-based Bonus, Sick Leave, PhilHealth Coverage, and Pag-IBIG Membership. 1 Civil Service Commission, "Approved IGHR Report as of June 30, 2026," Civil Service Commission Republic of the Philippines, June 30, 2026, hCps://csc.gov.ph/phocadownload/userupload/irmo/ighr/2026/Approved%20IGHR%20Report%20as%20of%2 0June%2030%202026.pdf. The enactment of this bill will provide these dedicated workers with a strong sense of ﬁnancial security and employment beneﬁts, alongside standard bonuses and mandatory social protections. By institutionalizing these safety nets, the government leads by example in eﬀectively upholding labor dignity, giving the genuine recognition to the hard work of JO, COS, Casual, and Contractual workers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11761
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF SENIOR CITIZENS NURSING HOMES IN ALL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Everyone will get old; it is inevitable. When we reach that age, we are hopeful that we can spend it surrounded by our family. However, the sad reality is that this is not an absolute fact that applies to every Filipino. There are heartbreaking stories of elderly Filipinos abandoned by their children, left homeless on the streets, or struggling to get by in charitable institutions due to the inability of their families to provide the supportive care that they need. While our culture reveres the elderly, the State must step in when traditional family support structures fail, break down, or simply lack the financial capacity to provide adequate medical and daily care. This bill seeks to establish and maintain a Senior Citizens Nursing Home in every city and municipality. This is crucial for elderly individuals who are abandoned, neglected, homeless, or whose families cannot meet or provide for their special needs. A key feature of these Senior Citizens Nursing Homes is the provision of continuous, specialized care 24 hours a day, seven days a week. These facilities will include Residential Care Services (RCS) that offer long-term or temporary multi-disciplinary care. This ensures that Senior Citizens, those who require support with daily activities due to specific health, medical, or cognitive needs, receive the specialized attention they require when they have no surviving significant others to care for them. Our lolas and lolos have dedicated their youth, strength, and love to raising our families and building our communities. It is now our collective duty as a nation to give back to them. By providing a safe haven, proper medical attention, and a roof over their heads, we can ensure that they receive the compassion, dignity, and care that they truly deserve as they safely and comfortably enjoy the sunset of their lives. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11762
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MAGNA CARTA FOR BARANGAY TANODS, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS BARANGAY PUBLIC SAFETY OFFICERS (BPSO), BARANGAY POLICE OFFICERS (BPO), OR BARANGAY PEACEKEEPING AND SECURITY OFFICERS, PROVIDING FOR THEIR RIGHTS, BENEFITS, PROFESSIONALIZATION, WELFARE, MODERNIZATION, AND CAREER DEVELOPMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay Tanods serve as our unsung heroes in the grassroots. They play a vital role as frontliners in maintaining peace and order and ensuring public safety in our communities. Despite their crucial role, they are still considered as volunteer with honoraria and allowances rather than fixed monthly wages with benefits. Article II, Section 5 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution declares that the maintenance of peace and order, the protection of life, liberty, and property, and the promotion of the general welfare are essential for the enjoyment by all the people of the blessings of democracy. The Barangay Tanods are the direct realization of this constitutional mandate at the grassroots level. While the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Memorandum Circular No. 2024-086, otherwise known as the "Omnibus Policy on the Administration and Strengthening Capacities of Barangay Tanods as Agents of Peace and Development," provides a foundational framework for their duties, organization, and basic incentives, the reality is that these volunteers remain undercompensated and highly vulnerable. Their current benefits vary and are heavily dependent on the limited financial capacities of their respective barangays, creating a glaring disparity in the welfare of these dedicated peacekeepers. This bill seeks to address the disparity through the creation of a Magna Carta for Barangay Tanod. This measure will recognize their vital contributions and extend the commensurate benefits, privileges, and protections they rightfully deserve at a national scale. Under the Magna Carta, Barangay Tanods will be assured that their services will be met with tangible support. It is outlined that they will receive additional benefits such as Hazard Pay of no less than One thousand pesos (P1,000.00) per month, comprehensive insurance coverage through PhilHealth, SSS or GSIS, and Pag-IBIG, and a retirement gratuity equivalent to one year of honoraria and allowances for those who have served at least fifteen (15) years. To further professionalize their role, this bill also seeks to establish a National Barangay Tanod Training Program to cover peacekeeping, first aid, disaster risk reduction, and human rights. Lastly, it also seeks to create a Barangay Tanod Welfare Fund to provide medical and hospitalization assistance, as well as death and disability benefits for their families. The enactment of Magna Carta is not merely a matter of administrative policy, but a profound moral imperative. By institutionalizing the dignity, safety, and livelihood of our barangay frontliners, we ultimately strengthen the very foundation of our nation's peace, security, and resilience. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11765
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA FOR DIGNIFIED COMMUTING, CREATING THE NATIONAL OFFICE OF COMMUTER AFFAIRS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mobility is fundamental to the exercise of many constitutional rights and the availment of a number of economic and social opportunities. Every day, millions of Filipinos rely on public transportation to access employment, education, healthcare, and other essential services. Yet for many commuters, what should be a routine journey has become a daily struggle marked by overcrowding, long waiting times, unreliable services, unsafe infrastructure, and rising transportation costs. The country's public transportation system remains inadequate to meet the growing demands of an expanding urban population1. While public utility vehicles continue to serve as the primary mode of transport for the majority of Filipinos, years of underinvestment, fragmented planning, and inadequate transport infrastructure have resulted in persistent congestion and declining service quality2. Studies and commuter surveys consistently show that traffic congestion, delays, and overcrowding impose significant economic, physical, and emotional costs on commuters, adversely affecting productivity, work-life balance, and overall quality of life.3 1 Culla, Lex. (29 July 2025). Wasted hours, crowded lines: How the PUV shortage wastes commuters’ time. Retrieved from: https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/07/29/2459611/wasted-hours-crowded- lines-how-puv-shortage-wastes-commuters-time 2 Council for People’s Development and Governance. (04 June 2025). Commuting in Metro Manila: A daily struggle rooted in Inequality. Retrieved from: https://cpdg.ph/commuting-in-metro-manila-a-daily- struggle-rooted-in-inequality/ 3 Agile Data Solutions Inc. (21 November 2025). Commuting in the Philippines: A Daily Struggle That Shapes How Filipinos Live and Work. Retrieved from: 1 The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 itself recognizes the inadequacy of the country's public transportation system and the need to improve mobility by expanding efficient, accessible, and sustainable transport networks 4. These challenges are further aggravated by transport systems that have historically prioritized private motor vehicles over public transportation, pedestrians, cyclists, and other active modes of mobility5. Although various laws govern transportation, road safety, accessibility, and environmental protection, there remains no single measure that establishes commuter welfare as a primary consideration in transport planning, infrastructure development, and public service delivery. This bill seeks to fill this legislative gap by enacting the Magna Carta for Commuters. It institutionalizes a comprehensive Bill of Rights for Commuters, guarantees access to adequate and affordable public transportation, promotes safe and accessible mobility infrastructure, including suitable facilities for persons with disabilities, prioritizes pedestrians, cyclists, and public transport users in the allocation of public road space, strengthens road safety measures, ensures access to timely transportation information, provides compensation during service disruptions, and guarantees meaningful public participation in transportation policymaking. The bill also establishes National and Local Offices of Commuter Affairs to promote commuter welfare, coordinate mobility policies, assist the riding public, and ensure accountability. It further requires comprehensive Public Transportation Services and Infrastructure Plans aligned with the mobility needs of Filipinos. By placing commuters at the center of transportation governance, this measure seeks to transform mobility from a daily burden into a reliable public service that promotes economic productivity, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and human dignity. It affirms that transportation is not merely about moving vehicles, but about enabling people to participate in society safely and efficiently and fully exercise their rights. label: HB 11767
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE MARKETING OF PREPACKAGED FOOD PRODUCTS CONTAINING EXCESSIVE AMOUNTS OF NUTRIENTS OF CONCERN, REQUIRING FRONT-OF-PACKAGE WARNING LABELS, PROTECTING CHILDREN FROM THE MARKETING OF SUCH PRODUCTS, PROVIDING FOR IMPLEMENTATION AND ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: ARTICLE I. GENERAL PROVISIONS SECTION 1. Short title. This Act shall be known as the “Healthy Food Marketing Environment Act”. SECTION 2. Declaration of policy. It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the right to health of all Filipinos, and instill health consciousness among them. It is likewise the policy of the State to protect and promote the right of every child to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health and to defend their right to proper care and nutrition, which includes the right to healthy environments. The State therefore recognizes die need to enable all Filipinos to make informed food choices and avoid food and beverages that are harmful to one’s health in line with its policy to protect consumers from trade malpractices and substandard or hazardous food products. The State also recognizes the urgent need to protect children from obesogenic food environments that promote the sale and marketing of unhealthy food and beverages, such as foods high in saturated and trans fat, sodium, and sugar. SECTION 3. Objective. This Act aims to: a. Guide the population in making informed food purchases and discourage Filipinos— especially children— from consuming food containing energy, fat, sodium, and sugar in excess of the prescribed maximum thresholds; and b. Minimize the power of and reduce the exposure of children to, marketing of food and beverages containing energy, fat, sodium and sugar in excess of the prescribed maximum thresholds.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State has the constitutional duty to protect and promote the right to health and to instill health consciousness among the people (Section 15, Article II, of the 1987 Constitution). Section 12, Article XIII, of the 1987 Constitution further provides that “[t]he State shall establish and maintain an effective food and drug regulatory system which shall develop the country's capability to undertake scientific and technological innovations, and make them available to all.” Existing legislation likewise recognizes the State’s authority and responsibility to regulate food information, labeling, and marketing. The Consumer Act of the Philippines declares: “The State shall ensure safe and good quality of food, drugs, cosmetics and devices, and regulate their production, sale, distribution and advertisement to protect the health of the consumer” (Article 20). The same law requires compulsory labeling and fair packaging: “The State shall enforce compulsory labeling, and fair packaging to enable the consumer to obtain accurate information as to the nature, quality and quantity of the contents of consumer products and to facilitate his comparison of the value of such products” (Article 74). The Food Safety Act of 2013 adopts a corresponding policy of maintaining a food-safety system that protects consumers and promotes informed choices. It provides that consumer protection shall be directed toward “[p]revention of adulteration, misbranding, fraudulent practices and other practices which mislead the consumer” and “[p]revention of misrepresentation in the labelling and false advertising in the presentation of food” (Section 8). Food choices are made every day, but they are not always made with complete or easily understood information. A consumer may hold a packaged food product and find a long list of ingredients, a nutrition facts panel, and several statements describing what the product contains or what it supposedly does for one’s health. Yet, the information that matters most to a consumer deciding what to buy may not be the information that is easiest to see. The proposed measure addresses the manner in which consumers, particularly children and their parents, receive and encounter information about foods that are high in nutrients associated with diet-related noncommunicable diseases. The issue is not the mere existence of processed or packaged food. Nor is the measure intended to prohibit Filipinos from purchasing or consuming such products. Rather, it seeks to make important information more visible at the point when a purchasing decision is being made, while establishing reasonable safeguards against marketing practices that take particular advantage of children’s developing capacity to understand commercial messages. The problem extends beyond the label itself. Children encounter food marketing in television, online platforms, retail establishments, public spaces, sporting activities, and other environments where commercial messages can become part of their ordinary surroundings. The proposed legislation therefore adopts two complementary approaches. First, it requires a clear front-of-package warning when a prepackaged food product exceeds scientifically determined thresholds for specified nutrients of concern. Instead of requiring a consumer to interpret a detailed nutrition panel before understanding the basic nutritional concern associated with a product, the warning is intended to communicate that information immediately and plainly Second, the measure addresses the marketing of products covered by the warning-label requirement. Children are not simply smaller consumers. Their ability to recognize and critically evaluate advertising is still developing, making them particularly susceptible to marketing techniques involving cartoon characters, celebrities, games, toys, competitions, fantasy themes, promotional bundles, and similar appeals. The bill consequently limits child- directed marketing of food products that exceed the prescribed nutrient thresholds and restricts such marketing in settings where children are particularly likely to encounter it. The State cannot and should not make every food decision for every Filipino. Families and individuals will continue to make their own choices. Government’s role, however, includes ensuring that those choices are made in an environment where essential information is visible, understandable, and not obscured by misleading claims or marketing practices directed at children. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARLYN L.
