label: HB 11768
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE MODERNIZATION AND REORGANIZATION OF THE BUREAU OF IMMIGRATION BY DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, FURTHER PROFESSIONALIZING ITS ORGANIZATION, UPGRADING THE COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS OF ITS OFFICIALS AND EMPLOYEES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every day, foreign nationals arrive in the Philippines for tourism, business, education, employment, family reunification, diplomatic and official purposes, humanitarian reasons, and other lawful activities. This is why, the State must be able to identify persons who pose risks to national security and public safety, prevent irregular entry and stay, enforce immigration laws, and ensure that those ordered removed from the country are properly dealt with under law. Under Section 31, Chapter 10, Title III of the Administrative Code of 1987: “The Bureau of Immigration is principally responsible for the administration and enforcement of immigration, citizenship and alien admission and registration laws in accordance with the provisions of the Philippine Immigration Act of 1940, as amended (C.A. No. 613, as amended). [x x x].” These responsibilities have become more complex as migration, technology, transnational crime, human trafficking, terrorism, and cross-border economic activities have developed. Yet the principal statute governing immigration remains Commonwealth Act No. 613, or the Philippine Immigration Act of 1940. The law has served as the foundation of Philippine immigration administration for decades, but its institutional framework was designed for circumstances vastly different from those confronting the country today. There is therefore a need to modernize not only the rules governing the entry, stay, and departure of foreign nationals, but also the institution charged with administering those rules. This bill seeks to establish a more comprehensive statutory framework for the Bureau of Immigration by defining its powers and functions, strengthening its organizational structure, professionalizing its personnel, improving its systems and facilities, and providing a more appropriate framework for the compensation and career development of its officials and employees. One of the principal reforms under this bill is the clearer delineation of the powers and responsibilities of the Bureau and its principal officers. The creation of a Board of Commissioners, together with defined appellate and procedural mechanisms, is intended to provide a more coherent institutional framework for the exercise of the Bureau’s regulatory and quasi-judicial functions. The proposed Boards of Special Inquiry will likewise provide a more structured venue for the initial evaluation and disposition of immigration cases before 2 matters requiring final action are elevated to the proper authority. The bill also seeks to strengthen the Bureau’s professional character. Immigration officers perform functions that directly affect a person’s ability to enter, remain in, or leave the Philippines. They are therefore entrusted with significant governmental authority. Such authority must be matched by appropriate qualification standards, training, career development, supervision, and accountability. Particular attention is also given to information and communications technology. The bill directs the Bureau to develop electronic systems for admission, visa transactions, citizenship-related transactions, alien registration, submissions, notices, and other immigration services. This is consistent with the State’s broader policy of recognizing electronic transactions and improving the delivery of government services through digital means. Such systems, however, must operate within the requirements of applicable laws on data privacy, information security, records management, and government accountability. The bill also seeks to strengthen border control beyond traditional international airports and seaports by providing for Border Control Checkpoints where necessary. This recognizes the changing nature of travel and the need for coordinated controls at appropriate points of entry and exit. Another important component of the measure is the professional and financial sustainability of the Bureau. Immigration personnel are expected to perform duties that may require round-the-clock operations, specialized knowledge, exposure to security risks, and significant responsibility in the exercise of governmental authority. The bill therefore provides for the upgrading and reclassification of positions, career development, night shift differential subject to applicable law, and overtime compensation for actual work rendered in accordance with existing rules. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARLYN L. label: HB 11769
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REGULATORY CAPACITY OF THE FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION OVER ADVANCED LIFE SCIENCE HEALTH PRODUCTS, CREATING THE CENTER FOR LIFE SCIENCES REGULATION AND RESEARCH AND THE POSITION OF DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL FOR LIFE SCIENCES, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 3720, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “FOODS, DRUGS AND DEVICES, AND COSMETICS ACT,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cell and gene therapies, stem-cell-based and tissue-engineered products, medicines made through biotechnology (such as recombinant proteins, monoclonal antibodies, and therapeutic peptides), and new vaccine technologies such as mRNA and viral-vector vaccines are changing how many diseases are treated and prevented. Many of these products are made from living cells or genetic material, and some keep acting in the body for years after a single dose. Regulating them well requires specialized scientific review, close oversight of how they are made, and long-term monitoring of the patients who receive them. These products raise questions that conventional drug review was not designed to answer: how to confirm that a living-cell product is what it claims to be, that it is pure and potent, that every batch is made the same way, and that patients stay safe over many years. At the same time, the public needs protection from unproven “stem cell” and similar treatments that are promoted without adequate evidence. Both concerns call for specialized scientific and regulatory expertise within the Philippine Food and Drug Administration. Under Republic Act No. 3720 (the Foods, Drugs and Devices, and Cosmetics Act), as amended by Executive Order No. 175 (1987) and Republic Act No. 9711 otherwise known as the “Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Act of 2009,” the FDA has four (4) product-based Centers and is headed by a Director-General assisted by two (2) Deputy Directors-General. Veterinary medicines, vaccines, and biologicals all fall under the Center for Drug Regulation and Research (CDRR). Given the rapid growth and scientific complexity of these products, this bill creates a fifth Center, the Center for Life Sciences Regulation and Research (CLSRR), and the position of Deputy Director-General for Life Sciences. Conventional vaccines, as well as plasma-derived and other traditional biologicals, will stay with the CDRR unless the FDA assigns them to the new Center under published criteria. Veterinary medicines will remain with the CDRR. This measure gives the FDA clear legal authority for risk-proportionate review of these products, reliance on the work of trusted foreign regulators, independent scientific advice, long-term safety monitoring, specialist staffing, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. It provides for a phased transition so that existing registrations and pending applications are not disrupted. It does not expand FDA jurisdiction over academic research laboratories, and it does not change the existing oversight of biosafety, research ethics, health facilities, or professional practice. In view of the vital role of regulatory modernization in safeguarding public health and fostering innovation in the life sciences, the immediate approval of this bill is respectfully requested. label: HB 11770
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE STANDARD AND MAXIMUM CLASS SIZES IN PUBLIC BASIC EDUCATION SCHOOLS, PROVIDING FOR THEIR PHASED ATTAINMENT, AND INSTITUTIONALIZING THE LARGE CLASS ALLOWANCE FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Corollary to this mandate is the responsibility of the State to ensure that the learning environment in schools and classrooms is conducive for learning. In May 2026, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) heard from junior high school students in Manila whose regular classes hold about sixty (60) learners, and whose school starts classes as early as 5:30 in the morning to accommodate them.1 An article from The Asia Foundation reported that studies show that overcrowded classrooms not only make it difficult for learners to concentrate on their lessons, but also limit the amount of time teachers can spend on improving their teaching methods. Teachers in congested classrooms are also generally over-stretched and are more likely to suffer from burnout.2 EDCOM 2 likewise found that overcrowded classrooms fuel bullying, disruption, and absenteeism.3 The scale of the problem is documented. The Department of Education (DepEd) placed the classroom backlog at more than 144,000 as of January 2026.4 Figures released in October 2026 show that 68,147 additional classrooms are needed to decongest 4,492 schools with more than fifty (50) learners per classroom, and 52,871 more to end double and triple shifting in 1 Andrea Gregorio, “Smaller classrooms, more learning, says Edcom 2,” Philippine Daily Inquirer, 1 June 2026, available at: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2237477/smaller- classrooms-more-learning-says-edcom-2 2 N. Jones, “School Congestion in the Philippines: A Breakthrough Solution,” The Asia Foundation, 5 April 2017, available at: https://asiafoundation.org/2017/04/05/school- congestion-philippines-breakthrough-solution/ 3 Ibid. 4 “DepEd, DPWH team up to address 144,000 classroom shortage nationwide,” Manila Bulletin, 16 April 2026, available at: https://mb.com.ph/2026/04/16/backlog-no-more- deped-dpwh-team-up-to-address-144000-classroom-shortage-nationwide 1,889 schools.5 Congestion is most severe in the National Capital Region, CALABARZON, the Davao Region, and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.6 Yet no law sets how many learners a single teacher may be made to handle. The Magna Carta for Public School Teachers, enacted in 1966, limits teaching hours but is silent on class size. Without a legal yardstick, there is no fixed measure against which classroom construction and teacher hiring can be planned, funded, and held to account. The problem on school congestion is multi-faceted and requires various solutions on different fronts. In 2026, the national budget gave the DepEd a record one trillion fifteen billion pesos (PHP 1.015 trillion), including sixty-five billion pesos (PHP 65 billion) for new classrooms,7 and the DepEd targets the hiring of 32,916 new teachers in 2026.8 This bill seeks to standardize the number of learners in a class to serve as the guidepost in formulating plans and strategy for the country's education sector. It sets a standard of thirty- five (35) learners and a maximum of fifty (50), to be attained within five (5) school years under a National Classroom and Teacher Complement Plan that puts the most congested schools and the poorest municipalities first. It also guarantees that no learner will be turned away because a class is full. This bill also seeks to compensate public school teachers who handle large classes through Large Class Allowance that increases with every learner above the standard, while the government simultaneously addresses other aspects of the school congestion problem. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11771
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A LIBINGAN NG MGA BAYANI EXTENSION IN NORTHERN LUZON AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Libingan ng mga Bayani (LNMB) in Fort Bonifacio, Taguig City, serves as the final resting place for the nation’s military personnel, veterans, national heroes, and martyrs. It is a hallowed ground that symbolizes the Republic’s eternal gratitude for the sacrifices made by these extraordinary men and women in defense of freedom and democracy. However, the geographical location of the LNMB in Metro Manila poses a significant logistical and financial burden for the families of heroes and veterans residing in the northern provinces of the country. Many descendants and surviving spouses from Regions I, II, and the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR) are unable to pay their respects or visit their departed loved ones due to the prohibitive cost and time required to travel to the capital. To truly honor their memory, the State must ensure that the families of our fallen heroes have accessible means to visit and commemorate them. This bill proposes the establishment of the Libingan ng mga Bayani - Northern Luzon Extension to be situated within a suitable military reservation in the northern part of the country. This extension will serve as a regional pantheon for deceased veterans, military personnel, and recognized heroes from Northern Luzon, granting them the dignified burial they deserve closer to their ancestral homes. By bringing this sacred institution closer to the provinces, we not only alleviate the burden on grieving families but also create a regional monument that will inspire local communities and future generations with the values of patriotism and selfless service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11772
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE INTERNMENT OF QUALIFIED FILIPINO SPORTS HEROES AT THE LIBINGAN NG MGA BAYANI AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under existing Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) regulations and Department of National Defense (DND) directives, the Libingan ng mga Bayani (LNMB) serves as the primary resting place reserved for individuals who rendered exemplary service to the nation. This includes former Presidents, military personnel, Medal for Valor awardees, statesmen, and National Artists or National Scientists. However, current regulations do not explicitly extend eligibility for interment at the Libingan ng mga Bayani to Filipino sports heroes—athletes and sports icons whose extraordinary accomplishments on the global stage have brought immense honor, international prestige, and national pride to the Republic of the Philippines. Sports heroes represent the finest traits of the Filipino spirit: perseverance, discipline, patriotism, and unity. From pioneer champions to modern Olympic gold medalists, World Champions, and international Hall of Famers, these individuals have elevated the nation's standing globally, united millions of Filipinos across generations, and inspired youth toward civic excellence and healthy living. This bill seeks to formally accord Filipino sports heroes the honor of burial at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in recognition of their legendary contributions to Philippine society and international sports history. By establishing clear eligibility criteria—such as winning Olympic medals, securing official World Championship titles, or receiving prestigious national orders for sports achievement—this measure ensures that our national sports icons are permanently commemorated alongside the nation's honored statesmen and patriots. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11773
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE LEGAL ASSISTANCE TO ANY OFFICERS OR ENLISTED PERSONNEL OF THE ARMED FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES AND THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE ON ANY CHARGE BEFORE THE PROSECUTOR’S OFFICE, COURT OR ANY COMPETENT BODY ARISING FROM AN INCIDENT OR INCIDENTS RELATED TO THE PERFORMANCE OF OFFICIAL DUTY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The members of our Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and Philippine National Police (PNP), have the highest duty of safeguarding the people’s freedom, preserving lives and properties, and protecting the constitutional rights of every citizen. In the recent years, many uniformed officers have been involved in various administrative and criminal cases in their line of duty. In 2019, the PNP reported a total of more than six thousand cases against uniformed personnel. As defenders of people’s freedom, it is important that, while performing their duties, our military and police are also protected in their own rights. When and if faced with cases that require legal representation, they should also be allowed access to legal assistance from the government. By ensuring that our uniformed personnel can afford the cost of litigation, the State also protects the very sector that protects the citizens and is adequately safeguarded. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11774
title: AN ACT MANDATING LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS TO ALLOCATE ONE PERCENT (1%) OF THEIR NATIONAL TAX ALLOTMENT (NTA) FOR PROGRAMS AND PROJECTS FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AND 1% OF NTA FOR PROGRAMS AND PROJECTS FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The National Government directs all local government units to allocate at least one percent (1%) of their Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA) to programs, projects, and activities (PPAs) proportionately divided among senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs). While there are some LGUs in the country that have already begun implementing the 1% allocation for the senior and PWD sectors, many LGUs have not yet established this ruling for their allocation, possibly due to limited resources. With the increase of financial resources in every local government unit brought about by the Mandanas-Garcia Ruling of the Supreme Court in 2018 (and confirmed in 2019), which increases the share of national government tax revenue transferred to local governments, LGUs are now capable of institutionalizing the increase in allocation for the sectors of senior citizens and persons with disabilities. Under the Mandanas-Garcia Ruling, the National Tax Allotment (NTA), formerly the Internal Revenue Allotment, of local government units reached PhP1.035 trillion in 2025, an 18.73-percent increase from PhP871.4 billion in 2024. Recognizing the role of senior citizens and persons with disabilities in developing a strong Filipino nation, this bill mandates LGUs to earmark 1% of their IRA shares for the PPAs for the elderly and another separate 1% for the persons with disabilities. These PPAs shall include medical and dental services, fitness and wellness, social services, livelihood and employment, legal assistance, and recreation. Through this, the State will be able to provide sufficient monetary support for the PPAs that shall address the necessities of millions of senior citizens and persons with disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR NURSES' APPRECIATION THROUGH RAISED SALARIES (NARS) BY UPGRADING THE MINIMUM SALARY GRADE LEVEL OF ALL PUBLIC NURSES FROM SALARY GRADE 15 TO 16 IN ALL PUBLIC HOSPITALS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT INSTITUTIONS, AND INCREASING THE SALARY RATE OF ALL PRIVATE NURSES IN ALL PRIVATE HOSPITALS AND HEALTH INSTITUTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the largest migrant-sending countries in the world and among the world’s largest suppliers of nurses. Over the years, Filipino nurses have continuously migrated in search of greener pastures overseas, while those who remain in the country often opt to bring their services to other relatively lucrative sectors which do not involve the practice of their profession. Republic Act No. 9173, otherwise known as the Philippine Nursing Act of 2002, established Salary Grade 15 as the minimum base pay for nurses in public health institutions. However, in light of rising living costs and the increasing demands of the nursing profession, there is a need to further improve their compensation by upgrading the minimum salary grade to Salary Grade 16. The country's continuing nursing workforce challenges underscore the urgency of this measure. According to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), the Philippines needs an additional 196,000 nurses to meet its healthcare workforce requirements. Meanwhile, a 2023 Department of Health survey revealed that 48.3 percent of surveyed healthcare workers had considered leaving their respective facilities, highlighting concerns over compensation, working conditions, and professional opportunities. The proposed measure seeks to upgrade the minimum salary grade of nurses in public hospitals and other government institutions from Salary Grade 15 to Salary Grade 16, while providing for increased salary rates for nurses employed in private hospitals and healthcare institutions. Through more competitive and equitable compensation, the measure aims to recognize the contributions of nurses, strengthen workforce retention, and encourage more nursing professionals to serve in the country. Investing in the welfare of nurses is an investment in the strength and sustainability of the Philippine healthcare system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11776
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE SCIENCE FOR PEOPLE AND COMPETITIVENESS PROGRAM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The country has made considerable efforts to prepare for the Fourth Industrial Revolution and strengthen its science, technology, and innovation capabilities. However, investment in research and development (R&D) remains significantly below international benchmarks and regional levels. According to the Department of Science and Technology's Compendium of Science and Technology Statistics, the country's gross expenditure on R&D reached only ₱41.96 billion in 2022, equivalent to approximately 0.19 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). This remains substantially below the one percent (1%) R&D expenditure target under the Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028. The country's limited investment in R&D underscores the need to strengthen research capabilities, expand scientific infrastructure, develop a competitive research workforce, and accelerate the development and commercialization of homegrown technologies. R&D, however, is only one component of a broader driver of national development—science, technology, and innovation. Without substantially increased investment in these areas, the Philippines risks falling further behind in productivity, industrial competitiveness, digital transformation, and its capacity to harness the opportunities of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. To quote US Navy Vice Admiral Herbert A. Browne (Ret.) in Armed Forces Communications and Electronics Association (AFCEA)’s1 SIGNAL 1 AFCEA is a member-based, non-profit association for professionals that provides highly sought after Newsletter, “(T)here is a significant difference between science and technology versus research and development, and government funding should be delineated along these lines. Science and technology involve pushing the outside of the technology envelope to generate breakthroughs in engineering disciplines or even in basic science itself. Research and development is focused more on generating an end product that may owe its origins to proven science and technology. With these definitions in mind, in these times of scarce resources, it is better to concentrate funds for government work on science and technology.” 2 The Department of Science and Technology (DOST) endeavors to significantly accelerate Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) in the country through a massive increase in investments in S&T, HRD, and R&D over a 5-year period. We must support DOST’s efforts. While the passage of this important legislation will further boost science and technology research necessary for the competitiveness of Philippine products and services, it is critical that our people –particularly farmers, fisherfolk, domestic entrepreneurs, and the local science community – will be the primary beneficiaries of all the knowledge and information generated by these initiatives. This bill therefore ensures not just the availability of funds but likewise promotes a “Science for People and Competitiveness Program.” The Science for People and Competitiveness Program (SPCP) Act consists of four (4) components: Program Expansion in 7 areas, New Programs in 6 areas, the Grand Plan for S&T Human Resource Development, and the Accelerated R&D Program for the Capacity Building of Research and Development Institutions and Industrial Competitiveness. The proposed measure also requires a substantial five-year budget to support its various R&D initiatives. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11777
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE CATCHING, SALE, PURCHASE, POSSESSION, TRANSPORTATION, IMPORTATION, AND EXPORTATION OF ALL SHARKS, RAYS, AND CHIMAERAS AND ANY PART THEREOF IN THE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sharks, rays, and chimaeras are among the most ecologically important and vulnerable groups of marine animals. Collectively known as chondrichthyans, these species generally grow slowly, mature late, and produce relatively few young. These biological characteristics make their populations particularly vulnerable to overfishing and slow to recover once depleted.1 Globally, the conservation situation has become increasingly serious: a major assessment found that oceanic shark and ray populations declined by approximately 71 percent between 1970 and 2018, while 77 percent of assessed oceanic species qualified as threatened with extinction.2 The Philippines, as an archipelagic State with extensive marine resources, has a particular interest in ensuring the long-term conservation and sustainable use of these species. Existing Philippine legislation already recognizes the need to conserve aquatic resources and maintain ecological balance. The Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998 declares a policy of rational and sustainable management and conservation of fisheries and aquatic resources,3 while the Wildlife 1 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Sharks: International Plan of Action for Conservation and Management of Sharks. 2 Pacoureau, N., Rigby, C. L., Kyne, P. M., et al. (2021). Half a century of global decline in oceanic sharks and rays. Nature, 589, 567–571. 3 Republic Act No. 8550. (1998). The Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998. Resources Conservation and Protection Act recognizes the State's responsibility to conserve wildlife and their habitats and regulate the collection and trade of wildlife.4 However, sharks and their relatives present distinctive management challenges because many species are migratory, are caught incidentally in fisheries, and are traded in multiple forms, including whole animals, meat, fins, cartilage, oils, and other derivatives. The proposed measure responds to these concerns by establishing a regulatory system covering the catching, sale, purchase, possession, transportation, importation, and exportation of sharks, rays, chimaeras, and their derivatives. The bill expressly provides for science-based non-detriment findings, improved bycatch reporting and release, identification of threatened species, establishment of critical habitats and shark sanctuaries, catch ceilings and closed seasons, and traceability throughout the supply chain. Importantly, the proposed Act does not rely solely on prohibitions. It recognizes the need to balance conservation with the legitimate interests of fisherfolk by directing government agencies to provide appropriate technology, research, credit, marketing assistance, and supplementary livelihood opportunities. It also seeks to strengthen enforcement through traceability, labeling, inter-agency cooperation, information and education campaigns, and meaningful penalties for destructive practices such as finning, illegal trade, habitat disturbance, and the unauthorized possession or movement of sharks and their derivatives. The proposed legislation therefore provides a focused policy framework for conserving sharks, rays, and chimaeras while promoting sustainable fisheries, protecting marine ecosystems, supporting fishing communities, and ensuring that the utilization and trade of these resources remain consistent with their biological capacity to recover. Its enactment would strengthen the Philippines' existing fisheries and wildlife conservation framework and provide a more coordinated, science-based approach to the protection of these increasingly threatened marine species. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. VARGAS Fifth District of Quezon City 4 Republic Act No. 9147. (2001). label: HB 11778
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE LIBMANAN CAVES PROTECTED LANDSCAPE IN THE PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR AS A PROTECTED AREA UNDER THE CATEGORY OF PROTECTED LANDSCAPE, PROVIDING FOR ITS MANAGEMENT AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State shall protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.” Republic Act No. 7586, otherwise known as the “National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act of 1992,” provides the framework for protecting the country’s most ecologically significant areas. Among its initial components is the Libmanan Caves National Park (LCNP) in Libmanan, Camarines Sur, a 19.4-hectare game refuge and bird sanctuary proclaimed as a national park on February 6, 1934, under Presidential Proclamation No. 654.1 To date, the LCNP is the only proclaimed protected area for caves in the Bicol Region.2 The park is a forest-over-limestone landscape with ten caves and three rock shelters.3 It is home to 138 species of flora and 136 species of fauna, including two newly described tarantula species.4 Five caves adjacent to the protected area boundary and twenty-two caves within the proposed expansion area have also been identified.5 1 Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) Sipocot. (2022). Protected Area Suitability Assessment (PASA) of Libmanan Caves National Park, with Initial PA Plan, Public Notification, Public Consultation, and Public Hearing. Sipocot, Camarines Sur. 2 Ibid. 3 Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Office (PENRO) Camarines Sur. (2026). Protected Area Briefer: Libmanan Caves National Park. 4 Ibid. 5 Ibid. 1 Despite its unique biophysical characteristics, the LCNP remains under pressure. Farming, grazing, poaching, firewood gathering, and tree cutting continue in and around it,6 and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) itself cites the need for immediate legislation, additional personnel, and a site development plan.7 Legislation is therefore necessary to secure the protection of the park and the caves around it. Recognizing these concerns, the DENR conducted assessments in 2018 and 2022 and, after public consultations and the endorsement of the Protected Area Management Board (PAMB), recommended establishing the park and its surroundings as a protected landscape covering 274.5776 hectares.8 This bill seeks to establish the Libmanan Caves Protected Landscape under the NIPAS by expanding the protected area, defining its boundaries, authorizing the designation of buffer zones, and requiring a management plan. Furthermore, it vests the management of the protected area in a PAMB, with a Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) headed by a Protected Area Superintendent (PASu), and creates a trust fund to finance its projects and activities. By doing so, this bill seeks to safeguard an important site of ecotourism and biodiversity in the country and reaffirm the State’s commitment to building a sustainable future for Filipinos through a harmonious coexistence with nature. In the 20th Congress, a similar bill was filed by Representative Terry Ridon. This bill was filed upon the request of the PAMO of the Libmanan Caves National Park. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 11779
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE EDUCATION IMPLEMENTATION SUPPORT FUND FOR BASIC EDUCATION, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Department of Education (DepEd), through DepEd Order No. 003, s. 2026, or the Foundational Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Basic Education, has established a national framework for the safe, responsible, and meaningful use of artificial intelligence in basic education. The Order provides guidance on the appropriate use of AI while emphasizing human oversight, learner protection, data privacy, academic integrity, and the responsible adoption of AI technologies in schools. The effective implementation of these policies, however, requires adequate and equitable resources. Schools differ significantly in their access to trained teachers, digital learning resources, devices, connectivity, technical assistance, and other infrastructure necessary to support the responsible use of AI. Without sustained support, schools with limited resources may face greater difficulty in implementing the standards and safeguards established under DepEd Order No. 003, s. 2026. This measure therefore seeks to establish a National Artificial Intelligence Education Support Fund to provide the financial and technical resources necessary to support the implementation of DepEd's existing and subsequent policies on artificial intelligence in basic education. The Fund shall support teacher training and professional development, curriculum-aligned learning resources, necessary digital infrastructure and connectivity, technical assistance, data privacy and cybersecurity measures, and targeted assistance to schools with limited resources and technical capacity. The proposed measure does not seek to replace or duplicate the substantive policies of DepEd Order No. 003, s. 2026. Rather, it provides a statutory and sustainable funding mechanism to help DepEd translate these policies into effective and equitable school-level implementation, consistent with school readiness, available resources, and applicable laws and regulations. By providing dedicated and targeted support, the measure seeks to ensure that the benefits of responsible AI use in education are not limited to schools and communities that already possess greater technological resources. It aims to strengthen teacher capacity, improve access to appropriate educational resources and technology, and enable schools to adopt AI-related initiatives in a safe, responsible, and sustainable manner. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11781
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS (CSOs) IN THE PREPARATION AND AUTHORIZATION PROCESS OF THE ANNUAL NATIONAL BUDGET, PROVIDING EFFECTIVE MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Transparency is the foundation of any democracy. The national budget, which is the most critical legislation Congress passes each year, must reflect the genuine needs of the Filipino people. While the 1987 Constitution guarantees public participation in decision-making, citizen involvement in the budget process remains limited, leaving taxpayer-funded allocations vulnerable to misalignment and controversies. Building on initial Senate transparency initiatives, which include dedicated civil society consultations and an online budget portal, this bill institutionalizes Civil Society Organization (CSO) engagement across all budget stages: from agency preparation to congressional approval. Specifically, it establishes an accreditation framework granting CSOs access to budget documents, allowing them to submit alternative proposals and serve as resource persons, mandates a dedicated congressional hearing day for their input, and opens deliberations, including the bicameral conference committee, to public scrutiny through accessible records and recordings. Public funds belong to the people; therefore, citizen participation must be substantive rather than symbolic. In view of these considerations, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 11782
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PARTICIPATORY GRASSROOTS BUDGETING, STRENGTHENING (CSOs), EMPOWERING CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS, INSTITUTIONALIZING A BOTTOM-UP BUDGETING MECHANISM IN DEVELOPMENT PLANNING AND BUDGETING, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 23, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State shall encourage non-governmental, community-based, or sectoral organizations that promote the welfare of the nation. Furthermore, Section 16, Article XIII mandates that the right of the people and their organizations to effective and reasonable participation at all levels of social, political, and economic decision-making shall not be abridged, and the State shall facilitate the establishment of adequate consultation mechanisms. A study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) found that evaluations of early participatory budgeting initiatives must guide our laws today. The study highlighted bottlenecks that hinder effective community consultation and the lack of formal integration between community action plans and local investment frameworks. 1 Moreover, the persistent corruption scandals and irregularities that have destroyed public infrastructure and public funds over the past years mean that funds meant for classrooms, hospitals, and basic public services vanished into questionable contracts while ordinary families continue to struggle with basic needs. This is what happens when public funds are allocated through ambiguous, top-down channels without direct public oversight; they become highly susceptible to misuse and diversion. 1 PIDS Policy Notes ISSN 1656-5266 (December 2014). https://pidswebs.pids.gov.ph/CDN/PUBLICATIONS/pidspn1423.pdf This bill seeks to institutionalize a permanent bottom-up budgeting mechanism in local and national development planning. The primary goal of this bill is to promote inclusive development by ensuring that government funds are allocated to projects that directly address the needs and priorities of local communities. By empowering Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) to actively participate in project formulation, budget prioritization, and transparent third-party monitoring, public governance becomes more transparent, responsive, and aligned with grassroots needs. label: HB 11784
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ACCREDITATION OF ALL PET CREMATORIUMS OPERATING IN MUNICIPALITIES AND CITIES IN THE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On October 31, 2026, Bacoor City Government ordered the closure of Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in connection with allegations that the remains of twenty-six (26) dogs and three (3) cats, which were supposed to be cremated by the establishment, were instead in a vacant lot in San Jose Del Monte Bulacan. Pets are not just domesticated animals, they become part of the family and are beloved by their owners. They also provide emotional support to their owners, and it is just right that they should be accorded proper burial or cremation services once they pass away. The reported dumping of the remains of these pets in Bulacan may constitute violations of applicable sanitation, environmental, animal-welfare, and local ordinances. Presidential Decree No.856, otherwise known as the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines, provides for the protection of public health and proper management of matters that may constitute nuisances or sources of danger to public health. Republic Act No. 8485, otherwise known as the Animal Welfare Act of 1998, as amended by Republic Act No. 10631, already provides for the supervision and regulation of facilities utilized for the breeding, maintaining, keeping, treating, or training of animals, including household pets. Existing regulations likewise require covered facilities to register with the Department of Agriculture – Bureau of Animal Industry (DA-BAI) before operation, and local government units are directed to require proof of such registration before issuing or renewing business permits. However, there is a need for a specific and uniform regulatory framework for pet crematoriums, particularly with respect to inspection, operational capability, equipment, documentation, chain of custody, proof of cremation, and proper disposal or release of animal remains. Hence, this proposed legislation aims to hold responsible the owners and operators of pet crematoriums for the improper or indiscriminate handling of animal remains and shall mandate the accreditation of such establishments by the DA-BAI before commencing or continuing operations. It likewise requires local government units to verify accreditation before issuing or renewing business permits, without dispensing with other requirements under sanitation, environmental, fire-safety, building, zoning, animal-welfare, and related laws. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 11785
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A REGULATORY FRAMEWORK FOR THE PROTECTION, HANDLING, CREMATION, BURIAL, AND OTHER AFTER-LIFE CARE SERVICES FOR COMPANION ANIMALS, PROVIDING FOR THE REGISTRATION AND LICENSING OF SERVICE PROVIDERS, PRESCRIBING STANDARDS AND SAFEGUARDS, AND IMPOSING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many Filipino families. companion animals are more than pets. They are valued companions and members of the household. The bond formed with them does not end when they die, Pet owners who entrust the remains of their companion animals to after-life care service providers do so with the expectation that these will be treated with dignity, respect. and professionalism. The growing demand for pet cremation, burial. and other after-life care services has given rise to businesses and establishments offering to collect. transport, handle. store. cremate, bury. and otherwise dispose of deceased companion animals. These services address an important need among pet owners. However, the Provision of such services also carries significant responsibilities, particularly because the remains entrusted to these establishments are often irreplaceable and hold considerable emotional significance for the owners. Recent reports of the alleged improper handling and disposal of companion animal remains in Bulacan have brought attention to the need for stronger regulation and accountability in this sector. Such reports raise serious concerns not only about the treatment of deceased animals, but also about the protection of pet owners who entrust their animals’ remains to service providers in good faith. They underscore the need for clear standards. effective oversight, and appropriate mechanisms to ensure that these services are carried out lawfully, safely, and with due regard for the dignity of the animals and the rights of their owners. At present, there is a need for a comprehensive and coordinated regulatory framework specifically addressing after-life care services for companion animals. The collection. transportation. identification. handling. temporary storage, cremation, burial, and final disposition of animal remains involve considerations relating to animal welfare, consumer protection, environmental protection. sanitation, and public health. Without clear and uniform standards governing these activities, gaps in regulation, monitoring, and enforcement may expose pet Owners to deceptive practices. improper handling, unauthorized disposal, and other violations. This proposed measure seeks to address these concerns by establishing a regulatory framework for after-life care services for companion animals. It mandates the registration and licensing of service providers, prescribes minimum standards for their facilities. equipment, personnel, and operations, and establishes safeguards for the proper identification. handling, transportation, storage, cremation. burial, and final disposition of animal remains. The measure likewise requires proper documentation and chain-of-custody procedures to ensure that animal remains can be identified and accounted for from the time they are received until their final disposition or release to the owner. It requires meaningful disclosure and informed written consent, particularly with respect to individual and communal cremation, so that pet owners are fully informed of the services they avail themselves of and the manner in which their animals' remains will be handled. Recognizing that after-life care services also have implications for the environment, sanitation, and public health, the proposed measure provides for compliance with applicable environmental, sanitation. and public-health requirements. It further establishes the respective roles of national government agencies and local government units in setting standards. licensing. inspecting, monitoring, and enforcing compliance. Appropriate administrative and criminal liabilities are likewise provided to ensure accountability for violations. Ultimately. this measure recognizes that the responsibility to protect companion animals should not end upon their death. Animals whose remains are entrusted to after-life care service providers deserve dignified treatment, while their owners deserve the assurance that the trust they have placed in these establishments will not be abused. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BRIAN BOE. PhD. label: HB 11786
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL CARE TO ENCOURAGE COOPERATION, ACCOUNTABILITY AND RESEARCH FOR THE EDUCATION AND SUPPORT TO PERSONS WITH AUTISM AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism spectrum disorder is a developmental condition that may affect communication, social interaction, behavior, and sensory processing in different ways. Persons with autism have diverse abilities and support requirements, and their needs may change as they progress from early childhood to school age, adolescence, and adulthood. Access to timely assessment, appropriate educational support, healthcare, and family guidance can help improve participation and quality of life. A comprehensive national framework can help address fragmentation among education, health, and social welfare services. It can encourage cooperation among agencies, strengthen professional training, improve access to evidence-based support, and support research that informs national policy. The legislation should also ensure that programs respect the rights and preferences of persons with autism and do not treat a diagnosis as a basis for discrimination or exclusion. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately one in every 100 individuals is on the autism spectrum. Applied to the Philippine population, this translates to an estimated 1.13 million Filipinos with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). However, government records show that only 98,245 individuals with ASD were registered in the country's identification card registry from 2021 to 2025. This substantial disparity suggests that many persons with autism remain unidentified or undiagnosed and are consequently not reflected in official records. These figures underscore the need to strengthen early identification, diagnostic services, intervention programs, and sustained support for persons with autism and their families through a comprehensive and coordinated national framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11787
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR DISABLED PERSONS”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, persons with disabilities (PWDs) represent at least 12% of the adult population. According to the Department of Health and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons With Disabilities, PWDs include those who have long-term physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairments which, in interaction with various barriers, may hinder their full and effective participation in society.1 The State’s commitment to removing barriers and assisting persons with disabilities in their reintegration to mainstream society is enshrined in Republic Act No. 7277 or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons. However, presently, PWDs are required to renew their IDs every three (3) years for the re-evaluation of their entitlement to the benefits pertaining to their status as a person with disability. This additional bureaucracy creates unwanted hurdles, especially for persons with total permanent disability. A permanent disability is a mental or physical illness or a condition that affects a major life function over the long term. A permanent disability could 1 https://doh.gov.ph/persons-with-disabilities be as severe as the loss of an eye or as moderate as a broken leg leaving the inability to walk on grossly uneven surfaces. After dialogues and consultations with advocates, this Representation echoes the sentiments that the amendment of the relevant provisions of Republic Act No. 7277, as amended, so as to provide lifetime validity of PWD IDs, would be a welcome relief for PWDs with permanent disabilities such as pre-existing birth defects, permanent blindness or deafness, or loss of limb or body parts, sparing them the burden and inconvenience of renewing their PWD IDs every three years. This bill recognizes the important contributions of persons with disabilities and their well-deserved reintegration to society. Thus, this proposed legislation allows for the issuance of PWD cards with lifetime validity for persons with permanent disabilities, duly certified by the Municipal or City Health Office where the person with disability resides. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11788
title: AN ACT GOVERNING THE REGISTRATION OF SHIPS FOR INTERNATIONAL TRADE UNDER THE PHILIPPINE FLAG AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE International maritime transport is fundamental to the Philippine economy and to global commerce. The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) reports that more than 80 percent of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea, with the proportion generally higher for developing countries.1 The Philippines likewise has a substantial maritime labor force: according to the Maritime Industry Authority’s 2024 Statistical Report, 504,057 Filipino seafarers were deployed in 2024, following 578,626 in 2023 and 385,239 in 2022.2 The importance of the maritime industry in creating employment is not localized in any specific part of the country. For example, Quezon City is well- positioned to benefit from a strong maritime industry because it has an established base of maritime and engineering education that can supply skilled workers not only for international shipping but also for shipbuilding, ship repair, maintenance, and related maritime industries. As of May 2025, MARINA’s list of recognized Maritime Higher Education Institutions identifies two institutions in Quezon City offering Bachelor of Science in Marine Transportation (BSMT) and/or Bachelor of Science in Marine 1 United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Review of Maritime Transport 2 Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), 2024 MARINA Statistical Report Engineering (BSMarE).3 This maritime education base is complemented by a much broader engineering ecosystem in the city, with higher-education institutions offering fields directly relevant to shipbuilding and maritime industrial activity, including mechanical, electrical, electronics, civil, computer, industrial, environmental, and sanitary engineering. By attracting more vessels, shipowners, maritime enterprises, and potentially shipbuilding and repair investments to the Philippine registry, the proposed law can therefore create a larger local market for Quezon City’s maritime and engineering graduates, strengthen technical employment opportunities, and encourage the development of ancillary maritime businesses in the city. A stronger Philippine flag registry can therefore complement the country’s established pool of maritime professionals by encouraging more ships and maritime business activities to be placed under Philippine jurisdiction. Despite the country’s strong position as a source of maritime labor, the benefits associated with ship ownership, ship registration, management, financing, and related maritime services can be further developed. The proposed measure addresses this gap by creating a dedicated legal framework for ships engaged in international trade under the Philippine flag. It establishes a comprehensive Philippine Ship Registry under MARINA, provides for permanent, provisional, and temporary registration, and expressly permits the registration or reflagging of qualifying foreign-registered ships subject to ownership, safety, environmental, crew-welfare, insurance, and international-convention requirements. It also provides a framework for recognizing and recording ship mortgages, maritime liens, and encumbrances, thereby improving legal certainty for shipowners, financiers, charterers, and other maritime stakeholders. To make the Philippine registry commercially competitive while advancing national objectives, the bill proposes targeted fiscal and regulatory incentives. These include a seven-year income tax holiday, a five-percent special corporate income tax rate thereafter, an optional tonnage-tax regime, exemptions from specified import duties and taxes, VAT incentives, and personnel tax incentives for Philippine-registered ships engaged in international trade.4 Additional incentives are provided for ships employing Filipino officers and crew and for certified “Green Ships,” while government financial institutions are directed to develop financing programs for MARINA-accredited maritime enterprises. At the 3 Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), List of Maritime Higher Education Institutions Offering the BSMT and/or BSMarE Programs as of May 2025 4 same time, the bill retains strong safeguards: registered ships must comply with international standards on safety, security, environmental protection, and labor; ships are subject to inspection and surveys; and MARINA is empowered to suspend, cancel, or revoke registration for violations. The measure thus seeks to combine competitiveness with responsible flag- State regulation, allowing the Philippines to capture a greater share of the economic activity generated by international shipping while sustaining the country’s role as a major provider of qualified maritime personnel. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11789
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL WASTE REDUCTION AND SEGREGATION SYSTEM, PRESCRIBING UNIFORM STANDARDS FOR WASTE SEGREGATION, SEPARATE COLLECTION, AND WASTE ACCOUNTABILITY, AND PROVIDING INCENTIVES FOR WASTE REDUCTION AND PROPER SEGREGATION THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face significant challenges in reducing the volume of waste generated, and ensuring that waste is properly segregated before collection and disposal. Existing environmental Jaws have already established important policies and obligations concerning ecological solid waste management, producer responsibility, pollution prevention, and sustainable resource use. However, persistent problems remain in the actual implementation! of waste segregation and reduction at the household, establishment, community, collection, and local government levels. Contamination represents the most significant challenge in waste segregation systems. This occurs when inappropriate materials end up in recycling streams, rendering entire batches unusable. While waste segregation is to build a systematic process of sorting different types of waste materials based on their composition, poor system design undermines even well- intentioned efforts. Insufficient training leaves people guessing about proper sorting. Effective implementation across different environments, such as offices, schools, and public spaces, relies on clear visual labeling, convenient placement, and proper training to prevent user mistakes. Proper segregation delivers significant financial and environmental benefits by reducing waste processing fees, generating revenue from clean recyclables, and lowering overall carbon footprints. This measure seeks to establish a stand-alone national framework focused specifically on waste reduction, source segregation, separate collection, and accountability throughout the ordinary waste collection chain. It does not seek to replace or amend the existing ecological solid 1 yazawa. T.. Tablada. K. N.. Baring. K. M.. Alojipan. K. L.. & Watanabe, M. (2025). The bill also does not regulate matters properly belonging to a circular economy framework, or other economic mechanisms governing the life cycle of products and materials. Such matters shall remain governed by existing and subsequently enacted laws. Reducing waste at source, properly separating waste streams, preventing the re-mixing of segregated waste, and ensuring that waste reaches its proper destination are essential to reducing the amount of residual waste requiring final disposal. By establishing clear national standards while respecting the existing functions of national government agencies and local government units, this bill seeks to transform waste segregation from a largely fragmented practice into a measurable and accountable national system. in view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 7, Keith Micah “Atty. label: HB 11790
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF LOCAL HOG RAISERS, AND ENSURING FARMGATE PRICE TRANSPARENCY, FAIR TRADING PRACTICES, AND IMPORTATION SAFEGUARDS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Agriculture is the backbone of the Philippine economy and the essential foundation of national food security. The domestic swine industry, among the economy's vital subsectors, sustains millions of rural livelihoods, ranging from small and backyard raisers to commercial farm enterprises and allied agricultural businesses across the country. However, local hog raisers currently face a severe economic crisis that threatens their survival and the long-term stability of the national food supply. The Philippine livestock sector is severely impacted by continuously depressed farmgate prices alongside escalating production costs. Reports! indicate liveweight hog farmgate prices dropping to between PhP 120 and PhP 160 per kilogram in several regions, significantly below average production costs, inflicting cumulative daily losses on local raisers and forcing many small and backyard farmers to reduce production or exit the industry altogether. This bill seeks to establish transparent, market-driven mechanisms to safeguard local hog raisers without authorizing price fixing. Furthermore, the bill standardizes trading operations by mandating liveweight transactions using calibrated weighing instruments and mandatory transaction receipts stating recorded liveweights, agreed prices per kilogram, and payment terms. By promoting fair trading practices, curbing unfair trading practices, and enhancing market transparency, this bill seeks to protect the rights and welfare of local hog raisers, safeguards consumer welfare, and fosters a balanced, competitive, and self-reliant domestic swine industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Keith Micah “Atty. Mike” D.L. Tan Ath District, Quezon 7 uentes. A. (2026. October 9). title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE CLASSROOM-BUILDING ACCELERATION PROGRAM (CAP), AUTHORIZING LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS AND PRIVATE SECTOR ENTITIES TO UNDERTAKE CLASSROOM CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE None other than the 1987 Constitution mandates that “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Currently, our country is struggling with a staggering classroom shortage of more than 166,000 units.1 In our region alone, there is a shortage of 6,298 classrooms for a looming 1,295,463 K to 12 learners enrolled in the same according to DepEd Negros Island Region (NIR) data for school year 2025-2026.2 This shortage may even get worse by 2028 if this crisis will not be addressed considering a dual plight of an accumulating classroom backlog and deteriorating facilities of existing classroom inventory. Moreover, administrative data indicates that out of roughly 329,716 school buildings, approximately 122,518 have already exceeded the 25-year lifespan for standard classrooms. Within this aging inventory, 51,222 classrooms are projected to be dilapidated by 2028 once they reach 50 years of age,3 not to mention the catastrophic impact of disasters in our country and other contributing factors. A classroom shortage crisis is a profound learning crisis. Without safe and adequate classrooms in place, students’ academic performance and general growth are compromised for lack of a conducive learning environment. Regrettably, the country’s classroom backlog may take over 20 years to resolve.4 To 1 https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/25/2544543/deped-still-faces-backlog-166000-classrooms 2 https://mb.com.ph/2025/06/27/deped-negros-island-lacks-6298-classrooms-877-teachers 3 https://edcom2.gov.ph/edcom-ii-51000-classrooms-likely-to-be-condemned-by-2028/ 4 https://www.rappler.com/philippines/classroom-shortage-slow-construction-edcom-2-report/ address this shortage, the institutionalization of a diversified strategy is of utmost importance. A whole-of-government and whole-of-nation approach shall be adopted by enabling local government units (LGUs) and the private sector to actively participate in the construction of school buildings, in coordination with the Department of Education (DepEd), and supported by national government funding, private sector participation, and technical assistance. With the passage of this bill, a Classroom-Building Acceleration Program (CAP) will enable and authorize qualified LGUs and private sector entities to propose, plan, and access corresponding government funds for the implementation of classroom construction projects in public schools within their respective jurisdictions. This will empower local governments and private sector to deliver and raise quality education and improve learning outcomes in the country. In the best interest of the next generation, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. JANICE V. label: HB 11793
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The school environment is fundamental to the education, development, and well-being of every child. Schools must therefore be places where learners can study, participate, and develop free from violence, abuse, bullying, discrimination, harassment, exploitation, and other threats to their safety and well-being. Beyond physical protection, however, school safety extends to the mental, emotional, psychosocial, and digital well-being of learners and school personnel, including the capacity to prevent, prepare for, respond to, and recover from emergencies, disasters, and other natural or human-induced hazards (Reeves et al., 2011). Research has likewise associated feelings of being unsafe at school with adverse mental health outcomes, including depressive symptoms and suicidal behavior (Mori et al., 2021). Similarly, Lacoe (2016) found a negative relationship between feeling unsafe in the classroom and academic achievement among middle school students. The evolving nature of these risks further calls for a comprehensive approach. Digital technologies have created new forms of bullying, abuse, privacy violations, and cybersecurity risks, while natural hazards and other emergencies continue to threaten school operations and educational continuity. Digital safety identifies new concerns including exposure to harmful content, inappropriate contact, and unauthorized disclosure of personal information (Martin et al., 2022). Existing laws and policies provide important safeguards concerning child protection, anti-bullying, mental health, disaster risk reduction, safe spaces, and learner welfare. Nevertheless, limited public education funding resulting in highly congested schools have resulted in higher rates of campus violence (EDCOM 2 Communications, 2026). Policy gaps regarding emerging digital threats, particularly use of social media platforms by minors, continue to expose students to violent or radicalizing content (Cagayan et al., 2026). Further, the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) reported that exposure to violence at home is linked to adverse academic outcomes, underscoring that a child’s trauma follows them into the classroom (Herrin et al., 2024). These interconnected concerns highlight the need for an overarching framework that harmonizes these mechanisms and establishes clear standards and responsibilities for comprehensive school safety. This measure proposes to establish a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework and requires every school to develop a School Safety Plan and maintain a School Safety Handbook. It mandates the Department of Education (DepEd) to lead in the strengthening school safety governance, risk assessment, emergency preparedness, learner protection, digital safety, mental health and psychosocial support, reporting and referral, and monitoring. It likewise promotes coordinated action among government agencies, local governments, school personnel, parents, learners, and other stakeholders. This measure is consistent with the Philippines' commitments under Sustainable Development Goal 4 on Quality Education, particularly Target 4.a on safe, non-violent, inclusive, and effective learning environments, and Sustainable Development Goal 16, particularly Target 16.2 on protecting children from abuse, exploitation, and violence. It is likewise anchored on Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education and seeks to complement existing laws such as Republic Act (RA) No. 11053 or the Anti-Hazing Act of 2018, RA No. 10627 or the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013, and RA No. 12080 or the Basic Education Mental Health and Well-Being Promotion Act. Ultimately, the proposed measure recognizes that a child cannot be expected to learn where safety is uncertain. Every learner deserves an environment where protection is not merely a policy, but a continuing institutional responsibility. By establishing a comprehensive and coordinated school safety system, this measure ensures that our schools become places where children are taught in a secure and learner-friendly environment free from threats and given the opportunity to thrive and grow. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA 2nd District of Cavite Cagayan, A., Sarmiento B., & Basilio, K. (2026). label: HB 11794
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PROTECTION OF THE RIGHTS AND WELFARE OF DIGITAL PLATFORM AND GIG WORKERS, PROMOTING FAIR WORKING CONDITIONS, ENSURING TRANSPARENCY IN DIGITAL LABOR ARRANGEMENTS, AND PROVIDING MECHANISMS FOR SOCIAL PROTECTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The emergence of digital labor platforms has created new opportunities for Filipinos to earn a living through delivery services, transportation, online freelancing, virtual assistance, and other forms of platform-based work. While these arrangements provide flexibility and additional sources of income, they also expose workers to challenges concerning fair compensation, job security, social protection, and access to effective grievance mechanisms. Digital platform workers often have limited control over platform policies and automated systems that determine their compensation, work assignments, performance ratings, and continued access to employment opportunities. Account suspension, unexplained deductions, and changes in compensation may adversely affect their livelihood without adequate notice or opportunity to contest such decisions. This measure seeks to establish minimum standards for the protection of digital platform and gig workers by requiring transparency in compensation and platform policies, providing safeguards against arbitrary account deactivation, promoting access to social protection benefits, and ensuring fair treatment in platform-based work arrangements. It likewise recognizes the right of workers to organize and seek appropriate remedies while maintaining the distinction between employees and independent contractors under existing labor laws. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 11795
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL GOVERNMENT FLEET MODERNIZATION PROGRAM, PROVIDING FOR THE GRADUAL TRANSITION FROM FUEL- POWERED GOVERNMENT VEHICLES TO ELECTRIC VEHICLES, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The modernization of government vehicles is essential to the country's pursuit of environmental sustainability, energy security, and efficient public administration. Government agencies, local government units, and government-owned or controlled corporations continue to rely heavily on gasoline and diesel-powered vehicles, contributing to air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and recurring public expenditures on fuel. The country's dependence on petroleum exposes government operations to fluctuating oil prices, supply disruptions, and rising maintenance costs. Transitioning to electric vehicles (EVs) offers an opportunity to reduce these expenses, minimize carbon emissions, and promote energy efficiency while supporting the development of the local electric mobility industry. However, the transition requires adequate financing, charging infrastructure, technical support, and trained personnel. A systematic and phased approach is therefore necessary to ensure that modernization remains financially sustainable and does not disrupt government operations. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Government Fleet Electrification and Modernization Program, mandating government agencies and local government units to gradually replace conventional vehicles with electric vehicles. It further directs the Department of Energy (DOE), in coordination with other concerned agencies, to develop charging infrastructure, financing mechanisms, and technical standards to support the transition. By adopting this measure, the government can lead the country's shift toward cleaner transportation, reduce dependence on imported petroleum, and ensure more efficient utilization of public funds while advancing environmental protection and energy security. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 11796
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING LANGUAGE ACCESSIBILITY IN PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT SERVICES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8759, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10691, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT SERVICE OFFICE ACT OF 1999, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Finding a job is already a challenge for many Filipinos. For some, that challenge becomes even greater when job requirements, application procedures, and employment-related information are communicated in a language they do not fully understand. A qualified applicant may have the skills and willingness to work, yet still struggle to simply understand the qualifications for a vacancy, the documents needed to apply, or the steps required to access government employment assistance. Language should not become another obstacle for Filipinos who are simply seeking an opportunity to earn a decent living and provide for their families. Under Republic Act No. 8759, as amended by Republic Act No. 10691, otherwise known as the Public Employment Service Office Act of 1999, Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs) across the country provide essential services such as job matching, employment referrals, career guidance, pre-employment orientation, and labor market information. While many PESOs already communicate with jobseekers in Filipino or languages commonly spoken in their communities, there is no express and uniform statutory requirement to provide reasonable language assistance when a jobseeker encounters difficulty understanding essential employment information. This may place certain jobseekers, particularly those more comfortable communicating in their regional or indigenous languages, at a disadvantage in accessing available employment opportunities. This measure thus seeks to address this gap by making language assistance an express function of PESOs within the existing public employment service system. It does not seek to establish a separate employment program or duplicate the functions already performed by PESOs. Rather, it aims to strengthen the delivery of existing services by ensuring that jobseekers may request assistance in understanding job qualifications, application procedures, employment referrals, pre-employment orientation, and other essential employment information. The proposal likewise recognizes the different capacities and circumstances of local government units. It does not require PESOs to hire dedicated interpreters, maintain personnel proficient in every Philippine language, or impose additional translation obligations on private employers. Instead, PESOs may utilize existing personnel, coordinate with other government offices, access standardized language resources, or employ appropriate remote and technology- assisted means to provide reasonable assistance according to local needs and available resources. To support implementation, the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), in coordination with the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (KWF), the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), and other relevant agencies, shall develop or facilitate access to practical language resources for commonly delivered employment services. These resources are intended to help PESOs explain essential employment terms and procedures more clearly, without requiring the translation of every job posting, employment contract, or government document into multiple languages. For a Filipino looking for work, understanding a job opportunity should not depend on how well they speak English or another language unfamiliar to them. What matters is that they are able to understand the requirements, make informed decisions, and pursue employment opportunities for which they may be qualified. By making existing public employment services more accessible and responsive to the languages spoken by Filipino communities, this measure seeks to remove an avoidable barrier between jobseekers and the opportunities that can help improve their lives.
