label: HB 11797
title: AN ACT PROTECTING EMPLOYEES AGAINST UNFAIR EMPLOYMENT DECISIONS ARISING FROM AUTOMATED WORKPLACE MONITORING SYSTEMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Technology has changed the way Filipinos work. From offices and factories to businesses operating under remote and hybrid arrangements, employers increasingly use digital tools to monitor attendance, measure productivity, and evaluate employee performance. While these technologies can help businesses operate more efficiently, their growing use must not come at the expense of workers' rights and job security. For many employees, workplace monitoring is no longer limited to attendance records or direct supervision. Some companies use software that tracks computer activity, records keystrokes, captures screenshots, or generates automated productivity scores. While these systems may serve legitimate business purposes, they do not always reflect the full extent of an employee's work. The integration of Automated Workplace Monitoring Systems (AWMS) and algorithmic tools highlights the critical need to maintain clear professional boundaries, transparency, and personal privacy in the workplace. A worker may be marked inactive because of an unstable internet connection, a technical problem, or time spent performing tasks that monitoring software cannot properly measure. An automated report may indicate poor performance without considering the actual work completed or the circumstances surrounding it. When these reports become the basis for disciplinary action, reduced compensation, or dismissal, workers may find themselves defending their livelihood against information they cannot fully explain or question. No Filipino worker should risk losing a job simply because a computer system produces an unfavorable score. Technology may help employers assess performance, but decisions affecting a person's employment must still involve fairness, accountability, and human judgment. Existing laws, particularly Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012, already protect employees against improper collection and processing of personal information. Labor laws likewise provide safeguards against unlawful dismissal and other employment violations. However, the growing use of automated workplace monitoring raises a specific concern: how automated reports are verified and used in decisions affecting workers. This bill seeks to establish practical safeguards when automated monitoring records are used in employment decisions. It requires employers to inform workers when monitoring results may affect their employment, ensures that such records undergo meaningful human review, and gives affected employees a reasonable opportunity to question inaccurate findings. It likewise protects workers against retaliation for exercising these rights. The measure does not prohibit employers from using technology or exercising legitimate management prerogatives. Rather, it seeks to ensure that technological advancement is accompanied by fairness and accountability in the workplace. As workplaces become increasingly digital, the rights and livelihoods of Filipino workers must not be left behind. label: HB 11798
title: AN ACT FACILITATING THE PAYMENT AND MONITORING OF SOCIAL PROTECTION CONTRIBUTIONS OF FREELANCERS AND SELF-EMPLOYED WORKERS THROUGH AN INTEGRATED SOCIAL PROTECTION CONTRIBUTION SERVICE WITHIN THE GOVERNMENT'S EXISTING E-GOVERNANCE INFRASTRUCTURE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In recent years, the transformation of the Philippine labor market has given rise to a growing number of Filipinos earning a living through freelance work, online selling, delivery services, and other forms of self-employment. Unlike employees whose contributions are ordinarily deducted and remitted through their employers, these workers must personally keep track of how much to pay, when payments are due, and whether their contributions have been properly recorded. For a freelance graphic designer, an online seller, a delivery rider, or a self- employed professional, this often means navigating different government systems and completing separate transactions simply to maintain their social protection coverage. The Social Security System (SSS), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), and Home Development Mutual Fund (Pag-IBIG Fund) already provide various payment channels and online services. However, these systems generally operate separately, requiring workers to access different platforms, follow different procedures, and monitor their contributions across multiple accounts. For those balancing irregular income, multiple clients, or the daily demands of running a small business, these additional steps can become an unnecessary burden. Missed or delayed contributions may also affect their access to benefits, subject to the applicable rules of each agency. Social protection should not be more difficult to maintain simply because a Filipino earns a living outside a traditional employer-employee arrangement. This measure therefore seeks to establish an Integrated Social Protection Contribution Service within the government's existing eGovPH platform, or its successor, through which freelancers and self-employed workers may conveniently view their applicable contributions, obtain payment references, make consolidated payments, and monitor their payment status across SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG Fund. Consistent with Republic Act No. 12254, otherwise known as the E-Governance Act, the proposal seeks to bring together existing government contribution services through a common access point, rather than create another application, payment system, or government office. While the E-Governance Act already provides for the integration of government frontline services and digital payment systems, this measure specifically addresses the payment and monitoring of social protection contributions by workers who manage their own remittances. In particular, it seeks to enable these workers to pay contributions to multiple agencies through a single transaction, rather than requiring separate payment transactions for each agency. The measure builds on the existing digital infrastructure of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and the participating social protection agencies, while preserving their respective responsibilities over membership, contribution assessment, collection, and official records. Importantly, this bill does not impose new contributions, increase existing contribution rates, or change the benefits and eligibility requirements established under current social protection laws. These shall remain governed by Republic Act No. 11199, or the Social Security Act of 2018; Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act; Republic Act No. 9679, or the Home Development Mutual Fund Law of 2009; and other applicable laws and regulations. The proposal concerns the manner by which workers access, pay, and monitor their existing contributions, not the amount they are legally required to contribute. The measure also recognizes that not all workers have reliable internet access or are comfortable using digital platforms. Participation in the integrated service shall therefore be voluntary, and existing payment channels and assistance through government service offices shall remain available. Appropriate safeguards for data privacy, payment security, transaction verification, and correction of payment errors shall likewise be established to protect workers using the service. Workers must also be able to determine whether their payments have been successfully received and recorded, and know where to seek assistance when a payment fails or is not properly reflected in their contribution records. For Filipino workers who already shoulder the responsibility of finding clients, earning their income, and sustaining their livelihoods, keeping their social protection contributions up to date should not require navigating several separate government systems. They should be able to spend less time managing payment transactions and more time working, earning, and caring for their families. By making these transactions simpler and more accessible, this measure seeks to help freelancers and self-employed workers maintain their contributions and better protect themselves and their families against illness, loss of income, and other uncertainties. label: HB 11799
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING ACCOUNTABILITY FOR UNMET SCHOOL-BASED MENTAL HEALTH SERVICE NEEDS AND PERSISTENT SCHOOL COUNSELOR VACANCIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12080, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “BASIC EDUCATION MENTAL HEALTH AND WELL-BEING PROMOTION ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The shortage of qualified guidance counselors remains a serious challenge in Philippine basic education. For many learners,school is more than a place for learning. It is where they spend much of their formative years, build friendships, face challenges, and begin to understand themselves and the world around them. Yet behind the classrooms and school activities are young people who may be quietly struggling with anxiety, family problems, bullying, or other emotional difficulties. For some, seeking help from a trusted adult in school may be the first step toward getting the support they need. Unfortunately, not every school has a qualified guidance counselor available to provide that support. In August 2026, the Department of Education (DepEd) reported that fewer than 1,000 registered guidance counselors were serving more than 45,000 public schools nationwide.! In CALABARZON, an October 2025 report by the Philippine Information Agency documented approximately 50 licensed guidance counselors serving more than three million learners across some 6,000 schools, with some counselors assigned to multiple schools due to the shortage of qualified personnel.” These figures represent more than a shortage of government personnel. They reflect the difficulties faced by students who need professional guidance, parents who worry about their children's well-being, and teachers who are often among the first to notice when a learner is struggling. While teachers and school administrators do their best to provide assistance, they cannot be expected to take the place of qualified mental health professionals. Republic Act No. 12080, or the Basic Education Mental Health and Well-Being Promotion Act, is an important step toward addressing this problem. It established a framework for school- based mental health services, the deployment of qualified counseling personnel, and mechanisms for counseling assistance and referrals. However, as the government continues to fill the necessary positions, many schools must still contend with limited access to professional mental health services. The challenge, therefore, is not simply to create more positions or establish additional programs, but to ensure that the needs of students who remain underserved are not lost in the process. When referrals cannot be accommodated because qualified personnel are unavailable, or when schools continue to experience prolonged counselor vacancies, these gaps must be properly accounted for and reflected in government priorities. It further seeks to ensure that schools experiencing prolonged shortages receive appropriate priority, particularly where the number of affected learners and limited access to qualified professionals demonstrate a greater need for assistance. The proposed measure does not create another government office, program, or plantilla position, nor does it impose additional professional counseling responsibilities on teachers. Rather, it seeks to make existing mechanisms more responsive and accountable, particularly to students in underserved and geographically isolated communities where professional assistance may be difficult to access. No Filipino student should feel that seeking help is pointless simply because there is no guidance counselor available in their school. While addressing the nationwide shortage of qualified professionals will take time, recognizing and responding to the needs of those who remain without adequate support cannot wait. Every learner deserves to know that their well-being matters, and that their struggles will not be overlooked. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnesfly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Ube has long been part of Filipino food and culture. From traditional delicacies to modern desserts and other food products, it has become increasingly popular both in the Philippines and abroad. This growing demand presents an opportunity not only to strengthen the country's agricultural and food industries, but also to create more jobs and livelihoods for Filipino workers. Today, the Philippine ube industry continues to gain recognition both locally and internationally, opening new opportunities for economic growth and employment. According to the United Ube PH Federation, the global ube market was valued at approximately USDS95 million in 2025, while the Philippines accounted for only around USD3.06 million.! The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) also described ube as a “rising star” export commodity, particularly in markets such as the United States, Japan, and South Korea. Behind the growth of this industry are Filipino farmers, workers, and communities whose livelihoods depend on the opportunities it creates.” While existing government initiatives and legislative proposals seek to increase ube production, support farmers, develop processing facilities, and expand markets, equal attention must be given to the people who will work in these growing enterprises. Beyond farming and harvesting, the industry offers opportunities in food processing, manufacturing, packaging, quality assurance, storage, logistics, and other related activities. Yet without the necessary skills, training, and access to employment information, Filipino workers risk being left behind by the very industry growing around them. The government already implements programs supporting agricultural development, technical-vocational training, enterprise development, and employment facilitation. These include the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority's (TESDA) Agricultural Crops Production NC II, Food Processing NC II, and Agro-Entrepreneurship NC II; the DTI's ProoSPER Project; the Department of Agriculture's (DA) High-Value Crops Development Program; and the Department of Labor and Employment's (DOLE) Integrated Livelihood Program. What is needed is to ensure that these existing programs respond to the actual skills and employment needs of workers as the ube industry expands. This measure therefore seeks to integrate workforce development and employment considerations into existing government initiatives for the Philippine ube and ube-based products industry. It provides for the assessment of workforce requirements, alignment of training and certification programs with industry needs, and facilitation of employment opportunities for Filipino workers and jobseekers. label: HB 11801
title: AN ACT PROTECTING FILIPINO COFFEE FARMERS AGAINST UNFAIR BUYING PRACTICES, PROMOTING TRANSPARENCY AND FAIR DEALING IN COFFEE PURCHASE TRANSACTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Coffee cultivation represents both an integral part of Philippine cultural heritage and a vital source of livelihood for tens of thousands of farming households and rural upland communities across the country. From the heritage Liberica traditions of Batangas and Cavite, popularly celebrated as Barako, to the diverse commercial plantings of Robusta, Arabica, and Excelsa in Mindanao, Northern Luzon, and the Visayas, the domestic coffee sector holds immense economic promise. Growing local consumption, the rise of homegrown specialty coffee shops, and government initiatives under the Philippine Coffee Industry Roadmap reflect the continued growth and potential of the Philippine coffee industry. Yet while opportunities and profits expand across coffee processing, branding, and retailing, many smallholder coffee farmers continue to struggle to earn a fair and sustainable income from their harvests. The growing success of Philippine coffee must also be felt by the farmers whose hard work makes it possible. Despite the Philippines’ favorable climate and soil conditions for coffee cultivation, domestic production has struggled to keep pace with growing local demand in recent years. Although the Philippines produced 35,650 metric tonnes (MT) of coffee in 2025,' 11.5% higher than 2024 production, the Philippine Coffee Board, Incorporated estimates that the country’s annual demand sits at a minimum of 150,000 MT. This makes the Philippines highly dependent on imports, while worsening climate conditions further constrain production. While government initiatives have sought to improve coffee production, provide agricultural assistance, and expand market opportunities, greater attention must also be given to protecting farmers during the actual sale of their harvest. For small coffee farmers, selling their produce is not always a straightforward transaction. Some may have limited means to verify the weight or quality assessment of their coffee, understand deductions from the agreed price, or determine whether promised premiums have been properly paid. Without clear buying terms or written records, farmers may be unable to question discrepancies or establish the amount they should have received. These concerns are especially important for farmers who invest additional time and resources to improve the quality of their coffee in the hope of earning better prices. When such efforts do not translate into the compensation originally promised, it is not only their income that suffers, but also their ability to provide for their families and sustain their livelihoods. This bill seeks to protect Filipino coffee farmers by establishing basic standards of transparency and fairness in transactions with commercial buyers. It requires the disclosure of buying terms, allows farmers to witness the weighing of their produce, and ensures that they receive purchase records showing how their earnings were computed. It likewise prohibits 1 https: //philcoffeeboard.com/phi-coffee-production-may-fall-below-30000-mU/ deceptive buying practices, undisclosed deductions, and the fraudulent withholding of agreed quality-based premiums. The measure does not seek to dictate coffee prices or establish another government program. Rather, it seeks to ensure that farmers are properly informed, treated fairly, and paid according to the terms agreed upon. After months of working to produce a good harvest, no farmer should be left wondering whether they were paid what they rightfully earned. As we continue to strengthen the Philippine coffee industry, we must remember that its success should not be measured solely by how much coffee we produce or sell, but also by whether the farmers behind every harvest are able to earn a decent and dignified living. label: HB 11802
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SAFEGUARDS FOR PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLE DRIVERS AND CONDUCTORS DURING SAFETY-RELATED INTERRUPTIONS OF TRANSPORT OPERATIONS, PROVIDING FOR THE FAIR ACCOUNTING OF TRIP-RELATED FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public transportation is essential to the daily lives of millions of Filipinos. Every day, workers, students, and commuters rely on public utility vehicles (PUVs) to reach their workplaces, schools, and essential services. At the heart of this system are PUV drivers and conductors, whose livelihoods often depend on the completion of daily trips, passenger collections, and other operational requirements of public transportation services. For many transport workers, particularly those engaged under boundary, trip-based, commission-based, or similar arrangements, interruptions in transport operations may have immediate financial consequences. Such interruptions may arise from government-imposed transport safety restrictions, serious vehicle defects, or other objectively verifiable conditions that prevent the safe continuation of an assigned trip. Existing labor and occupational safety and health laws recognize the nghts of workers to safe working conditions, appropriate compensation, and protection against retaliation. These safeguards remain applicable to transport workers covered by such laws. Nevertheless, public transportation presents distinct operational circumstances. Drivers and conductors may be required to account for passenger collections, remit boundary amounts, or comply with trip-related financial arrangements even when assigned trips cannot be completed because of safety-related interruptions. The absence of a clear, transport-specific procedure for documenting these interruptions and accounting for their financial consequences may expose affected workers to disputed charges, unexplained collection adjustments, and disagreements over obligations arising from trips that could not lawfully or safely proceed. This measure seeks to address these concerns by establishing safeguards for public utility vehicle drivers and conductors during safety-related interruptions of transport operations. Under the proposed measure, transport operators shall recognize duly established safety-related interruptions, provide an accounting of affected trip-related financial obligations upon request, and refrain from imposing additional financial penalties solely because drivers or conductors complied with applicable safety restrictions. The measure likewise prohibits the recovery of unrealized trip collections from covered transport workers when such collections could not be generated because of a qualifying safety- related interruption. The proposed safeguards shall apply without prejudice to existing wage protections, occupational safety and health standards, and lawful contractual obligations. The bill does not establish a new mandatory paid leave entitlement, automatically cancel lawful boundary obligations, or require compensation for all periods of interrupted operations. Rather, it provides a practical mechanism for ensuring that the financial consequences of safety- related interruptions are documented, transparent, and not unfairly transferred to transport workers. By promoting accountability in the treatment of interrupted trips, the measure seeks to protect the livelihood of public transport workers while reinforcing compliance with lawful safety requirements and safeguarding the commuting public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11803
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING EMPLOYMENT ACCESS FOR JOBSEEKERS IN GEOGRAPHICALLY ISOLATED AND DISADVANTAGED AREAS THROUGH REMOTE RECRUITMENT FACILITATION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8759, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT SERVICE OFFICE ACT OF 1999"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Finding employment remains a challenge for Filipinos living in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDA). Limited transportation, unreliable internet connectivity, and the distance from major employment centers often make it difficult for jobseekers to pursue opportunities outside their communities. While online job platforms have made vacancies easier to find, attending interviews and completing recruitment assessments can still require considerable travel and expenses, particularly for young and first-time jobseekers. In Barangay Sagrada, Palawan, Joshua Alarcon, a young student featured in a 2026 account by Dualtech Training Center, reportedly walked nearly 1.5 kilometers each day just to find a mobile signal and check updates on his technical training application. Although his experience involved access to training, it reflects the difficulties that residents of remote communities face in pursuing opportunities that others can access more easily.! Republic Act No. 8759, or the Public Employment Service Office Act of 1999, as amended by Republic Act No. 10691, established Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs) to provide employment information, job matching, referrals, and other employment assistance services. While the law authorizes the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to develop additional employment assistance programs, it does not expressly recognize remote recruitment facilitation for jobseekers in GIDA communities as a PESO service or require specific service standards for its implementation. This bill seeks to address that gap by expressly including remote recruitment facilitation among the services provided through the PESO system and requiring DOLE to establish minimum service standards for its implementation. Where practicable, PESOs shall facilitate the participation of jobseekers in remote preliminary interviews, screening activities, and recruitment assessments, in coordination with willing employers and using available facilities and resources. The measure does not require employers to conduct recruitment activities remotely or establish a new government program or office. Rather, it seeks to make existing public employment services more accessible to communities where distance and connectivity remain significant barriers to employment. A qualified applicant should not lose the chance to pursue a job simply because of the distance between home and the nearest employment center. label: HB 11804
title: AN ACT GRANTING EMPLOYEES PROTECTED LEAVE TO ATTEND TO THE HOSPITALIZATION, TREATMENT, OR OTHER MEDICAL CARE OF IMMEDIATE FAMILY MEMBERS WITH SERIOUS MEDICAL CONDITIONS, PROHIBITING EMPLOYMENT-RELATED RETALIATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The family is a crucial cornerstone of society. For many Filipino workers, caring for their families does not end when they report for work. When a child falls seriously ill, a parent needs to undergo treatment, or a spouse is rushed to the hospital, being present for their loved ones becomes just as important as fulfilling their responsibilities at work. Yet, for employees who have exhausted their leave credits or have no available paid leave, attending to these family emergencies may mean risking their jobs and the very livelihood that supports their families. While existing labor laws provide for maternity, paternity, and solo-parent parental leave, these benefits address specific circumstances. There remains no general statutory entitlement to protected leave for employees who must accompany or assist an immediate family member during hospitalization, serious illness, or significant medical treatment. In the absence of such protection, workers may find themselves having to choose between being there for their loved ones when they are needed most and fulfilling their obligations to their employers. This bill seeks to address this gap by granting covered private-sector employees up to ten (10) working days of family medical care leave per calendar year when their presence or assistance is reasonably necessary due to a qualifying medical circumstance involving an immediate family member. More importantly, it seeks to ensure that employees who avail of such leave are protected against dismissal, disciplinary action, or other adverse employment consequences. Recognizing the operational and financial considerations of employers, particularly small businesses, the proposed measure does not impose an additional mandatory paid leave benefit. Employees may choose to use their available service incentive leave, vacation leave, or other applicable paid leave credits, while any remaining portion shall be unpaid. The bill likewise establishes reasonable notice and verification requirements to ensure that the leave is availed of for legitimate medical circumstances, without imposing unnecessary administrative burdens on employers. Family and livelihood are important areas of one’s life and attending to personal and professional responsibilities need not come into conflict. At its core, this measure recognizes a simple reality: workers are also parents, children, and spouses who have responsibilities beyond the workplace. No employee should have to fear losing their job simply because they need to accompany their loved ones undergoing serious medical treatment. Protecting workers in these circumstances is not only a matter of humane working conditions, but also of recognizing the importance of family in the lives of Filipino workers. When a child falls seriously ill, a parent needs to undergo treatment, or a spouse is rushed to the hospital, being present for their loved ones becomes just as important as fulfilling their responsibilities at work. Yet, for employees who have exhausted their leave credits or have no available paid leave, attending to these family emergencies may mean risking their jobs and the very livelihood that supports their families. label: HB 11805
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PHILIPPINE BLOOD CENTER (PBC), SUBNATIONAL, AND REGIONAL BLOOD CENTERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Blood is an essential component of the health care system. Every day, blood and blood products may be needed in the treatment of patients suffering from severe trauma, complications of childbirth, major surgery, cancer, and other serious illnesses, as well as in emergency and disaster situations. The availability of a safe and adequate blood supply is therefore an essential public health concern. A sustainable blood services system cannot depend solely on periodic blood donation campaigns or on the capacity of individual hospitals and institutions. It requires a coordinated national system capable of supporting blood collection and distribution while also developing the current local capacity to respond to the needs of their respective communities. This bill seeks to establish the statutory mandate of the Philippine Blood Center (PBC), Subnational, and Regional Blood Centers in order to rationalize and improve the provision of an adequate, safe, and accessible supply of blood and blood components, and to set the standards for scientific and professional operations of blood service facilities nationwide. Republic Act (RA) No. 7719, otherwise known as the "National Blood Services Act of 1994," established the framework for a national policy on voluntary blood donation. However, the rising incidence of medical emergencies, trauma cases, maternal mortality challenges, and complex hematologic conditions necessitates a re-engineered legal framework. There is an urgent need to institutionalize the Philippine Blood Center as the apex national reference and coordinating hub, strengthen subnational and regional blood 1 centers, actively engage private corporations, and empower Local Government Units (LGUs) to establish and maintain local blood service facilities. Section 4(d) of RA No. 7719 directs that blood centers be strategically established nationwide within a National Blood Transfusion Service Network spearheaded by the Department of Health (DOH). This Act operationalizes that statutory mandate through a multi-pronged approach anchored on existing health and tax laws: 1) Empowerment of Local Government Units (LGUs): Pursuant to the devolution of health services under Section 17 of RA No. 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991 and the revenue-capacity classifications under RA No. 11964 otherwise known as the Automatic Income Classification of Local Government Units Act, this bill mandates Provinces, Cities, and Municipalities to establish local blood service facilities. It also operationalizes Inter-LGU cooperation pursuant to Section 33 of RA No. 7160 and authorizes local blood funding through the Special Health Fund under Sections 19–21 of RA No. 11223 or the Universal Health Care Act. Not all local government units are equally situated. The bill therefore takes a graduated approach based on the political classification of LGUs the Local Government Code of 1991 and their income classification under RA No. 11964: a) Highly urbanized cities, independent component cities, and first- to third- class provinces shall establish and maintain at least one (1) DOH-licensed Hospital-Based Blood Center or Blood Bank capable of collection, component processing, and cross- matching blood center or hospital-based blood banks that can serve as referral points for nearby LGUs; b) Component cities, fourth- and fifth-class provinces, and first- to third-class municipalities shall establish and maintain a Blood Collection Unit (BCU) or Blood Station (BS) attached to their city or municipal health offices or local district hospitals; and c) Fourth- and fifth-class municipalities shall establish and maintain Blood Stations (BS) or partner with adjacent LGUs to form an Inter-LGU Blood Service Network. They may also enter into cooperative or clustering arrangements with their province or neighboring LGUs where an independent facility is not practicable. So that no local government unit is discouraged from taking part because of limited resources, the DOH shall give priority technical assistance, capacity-building, and, subject to available funds, financial support to lower-income LGUs. 2) Corporate and Private Sector Engagement: Consistent with the non-profit and non-remunerated voluntary donation principles of RA No. 7719 and corporate 2 social responsibility (CSR) frameworks under Republic Act No. 11232 (Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines), this bill incentivizes corporate participation through tax mechanisms. Contributions of cash, mobile vans, or testing equipment are granted 100% income tax deductions pursuant to Section 34(H) of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC) of 1997, as amended, and exempted from Donor's Tax under Section 101(A)(2) of the NIRC. Furthermore, duty-free importation of specialized medical equipment is provided pursuant to Section 800 of Republic Act No. 10863 (Customs Modernization and Tariff Act). The measures incorporated in this bill recognize the important role of local government units in ensuring access to health services. Local government units are in a good position to identify the blood requirements of their communities and to mobilize local resources. Accordingly, the bill seeks to empower provinces, cities, and municipalities to establish and maintain appropriate local blood service facilities, subject to the standards and regulations prescribed by the Department of Health. Moreover, it allows cooperation among local government units where the establishment of an independent facility may not be practicable. The private sector also has an important role in strengthening the country’s blood supply through organized workplace and community-based blood donation programs. Rather than being an individual effort, the measures under this bill establish mechanisms through which private corporations may participate in and support the national blood services program while preserving the principle that blood donation must remain voluntary and non-remunerat

label: HB 11806
title: AN ACT BANNING THE IMPORTATION, MANUFACTURE, PROCESSIN G, USE OR DISTRIBUTION IN COMMERCE OF ASBESTOS AND ASBESTOS-CONTAINING PRODUCTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The International Association for Research on Cancer classified asbestos as one of the highest cancer-hazard substances with no known safe level of exposure. Lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis are some fatal diseases attributed to exposure to this substance. Asbestos diseases have a latency period of 10 to 40 years. Asbestos is a danger to everyone because the fibers penetrate deep into the lungs when inhaled. Workers are exposed and their families are at risk because of asbestos brought home with clothes and protective equipment from work. Most exposed workers are those in shipbuilding, ship repair, ship breaking, boiler work, manufacturing of asbestos containing fibers and in building and construction construction workers, plumbers, insulators, carpenters, pipe fitters, electricians, auto workers, insulators and sheet metal workers among other workers. Workers' families are also at risk because of asbestos brought home with clothes and protective equipment from work. Asbestos poses danger not only to workers and their families but also to the public exposed to houses, buildings, workplaces and materials with asbestos. Despite its dangers, asbestos remains in use in the Philippines. More industrialized countries are banning the substance. Worldwide, 60 countries, including those in the European Union, have banned the use of asbestos, in whole or in part. In Asia-Pacific, South Korea, Japan and Australia have implemented a total asbestos ban. And if industrialized countries cannot 'control' the risks of asbestos, how are countries like the Philippines expected to do so? The most efficient way to manage the risks and prevent asbestos diseases is to ban the use of all types of asbestos and asbestos containing materials. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. D DE TOC. label: HB 11807
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mental health is an important part of the rights to health, human dignity, and social development. It supports individuals' personal well-being, family stability, productivity, and meaningful participation in society when they have access to timely, affordable, appropriate, and high-quality mental health services. As stated in Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution, the State must recognize the right to health and promote consciousness; this constitutional policy provides the basis for legislation that ensures access to mental health services and strengthens the national health care system. Meanwhile, Republic Act No. 11036, or the Mental Health Act, is a national policy framework that aims to promote mental health, provide care, and ensure individuals’ rights. Sections 15 and 16 of the same Act relate to the development of community-level mental health services and provide that the national government, through the Department of Health, should establish and operate community-based mental health care facilities. Section 18 addresses psychiatric, psychosocial, and neurological services in regional, provincial, and tertiary hospitals. Section 29 recognizes the role of the National Center for Mental Health (NCMH)as the principal training and research center within the Department of Health, and Sections 30, 37, and 38 specify the respective responsibilities of the Department of Health and the local government units with regard to the delivery and development of mental health services. Republic Act No. 11223, the Universal Health Care Act, also demonstrates the government's commitment to ensuring access to preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and other essential health services, including mental health services through an integrated health care system. Even with these legal obligations, access to specialist mental health services still depends on properly equipped facilities, qualified staff, necessary medicines, effective referral systems, and sustained funding. Therefore, the legislation should address this problem by strengthening the government's mental health capacity in far-flung and underserved areas. Zamboanga City is suitable for the proposed facility because it serves as an urban and service center for several communities in south-western Mindanao. The presence of a specialist facility there would provide the opportunity to improve access to psychiatric consultations, psychological assessment, emergency mental health evaluation, appropriate inpatient care, rehabilitation, community outreach, professional training, and research. The new Zamboanga City Center for Mental Health will act as a satellite specialist facility of the National Center for Mental Health and will be placed under the administrative control of the Department of Health. This arrangement will enable the center to make use of the National Center for Mental Health's institutional expertise, clinical standards, training facilities, and research capabilities while at the same time offering specialized services to a community which might otherwise have difficulty accessing such care. The Center must not limit itself to institutional treatment, rather, it should advocate for a comprehensive continuum of care that includes early identification, outpatient treatment, emergency assessment, appropriate referral, rehabilitation, family support, community-based interventions, and ongoing care after discharge. Through cooperation with local government authorities, hospitals, general practitioners, educational institutions, social welfare agencies, and community organisations, the Center will assist in improving mental health services in the area for which it is responsible. The measure also emphasizes the importance of protecting the rights and dignity of service users. It contains provisions relating to informed consent, confidentiality, data privacy, non-discrimination, appropriate complaint procedures, and measures designed to prevent involuntary treatment and restrictive interventions. Furthermore, it promotes recovery-oriented, least-restrictive care, in accordance with Republic Act No. 11036 and other pertinent laws. In order to secure a responsible implementation, the suggested legislation requires a thorough feasibility study and the preparation of an implementation plan. This plan should specify the location that will be used, the expected level of service demand, the necessary infrastructure, the staffing and equipment needed, the anticipated operational costs, the funding required, and the schedule for implementation. The Department of Health, via the National Center for Mental Health, will conduct the study in cooperation with the Department of Budget and Management, the Department of Public Works and Highways, the City Government of Zamboanga, the office of the First Legislative | istrict Representative, and other appropriate agencies. The measure also provides for coordination with the City Government of Zamboanga and other local government units through legal agreements, without automatically imposing any unfunded obligations on them. It also establishes a step-by- step implementation procedure that accounts for the need for adequate resources, qualified personnel, appropriate facilities, and the necessary licenses and authorizations before specialized services can start. The amount of funding required for the establishment of the Centre and for its continued operation should be suggested in the annual General Appropriations Act. on the basis of the feasibility study and the detailed project proposal. provided that it is approved by Congress and conforms to the existing laws relating to budgeting, procurement, accounting and auditing. The measure also includes the requirement for monitoring, evaluation and annual reporting in order to promote transparency, accountability, patient safety and the efficient use of public resources. label: HB 11808
title: AN ACT CREATING THE ZAMBOANGA PENINSULA HALAL INDUSTRY INNOVATION CENTER, PROVIDING FOR ITS ORGANIZATION, FUNCTIONS, AND FUNDING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The agricultural sector, food processing, manufacturing, research, entreprencurship, employment generation, and international trade in the Zamboanga Peninsula offer significant opportunities for the development of the halal industry. To realize these opportunities, coordinated technical assistance must be provided, access to shared service facilities ensured, business incubation and product innovation supported, compliance with reliable standards facilitated, and sustained assistance extended to enterprises secking to participate in domestic and international markets. Republic Act No. 10817, otherwise known as the “Philippine Halal Export Development and Promotion Act of 2016,” establishes the national policy and institutional framework for the development and promotion of the Philippine halal industry. It seeks to promote halal industries, improve export competitiveness, protect consumers, provide common service facilities, strengthen institutional capacity, develop human resources, and advance research, development, and extension services. Despite the existence of this national framework, enterprises in the Zamboanga Peninsula may continue to face challenges in accessing coordinated technical services, laboratory facilities, product development expertise, business incubation, standards- compliance assistance, and export-readiness support. These challenges underscore the need for a dedicated regional institution that can consolidate and facilitate access to the resources and services necessary for the growth of the halal industry. For this purpose, the proposed establishment of the Zamboanga Peninsula Halal Industry Innovation Center, hereinafter referred to as the “Center,” is envisioned as a regional institution dedicated to halal industry development, enterprise innovation, research coordination, technical assistance, business incubation, and market access facilitation. Its headquarters and principal office shall be established in Zamboanga City, which shall serve as its principal administrative, operational, and industry-development hub. The designation of Zamboanga City as the permanent headquarters will provide a stable institutional base for the Center to implement its programs, coordinate interagency initiatives, develop research partnerships, facilitate access to technical and laboratory services, support business incubation, and promote innovation and commercialization. Through appropriate partnerships, satellite offices, shared service facilities, mobile technical assistance units, and other outreach mechanisms, the Center may extend its services to stakeholders throughout the Zamboanga Peninsula and other eligible communities in Western Mindanao without altering the location of its designated headquarters. The Center shall be attached to the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) for policy coordination, administrative supervision, and program implementation. It shall work in cooperation with the Department of Agriculture, the Food and Drug Administration, the Department of Science and Technology, the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, the Department of Health, the Philippine Accreditation Bureau, the Bureau of Philippine Standards, the Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Standards, the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, the Commission on Higher Education, the Mindanao Development Authority, local government units, academic and research institutions, private-sector organizations, and other appropriate agencies. It shall coordinate with the Philippine Halal Export Development and Promotion Board and respect the statutory mandates and regulatory authority of all competent government agencies. The Center shall prioritize enterprise development. product innovation, halal certification assistance, regulatory-compliance preparation, research and laboratory access, human-resource development, technology transfer, and domestic and international market access. It shall provide targeted support to Muslim Filipino entrepreneurs, women-led enterprises, young entrepreneurs, cooperatives, farmers, fisherfolk, manufacturers, processors, and micro, small, and medium enterprises, with particular attention to underserved communities. The establishment of the Zamboanga Peninsula Halal Industry Innovation Center is intended to strengthen the competitiveness, inclusiveness, and sustainability of the halal industry; create employment and livelihood opportunities; encourage investment; advance research and innovation; improve access to appropriate facilities and technical services; and increase the participation of enterprises based in the Zamboanga Peninsula in the national and global halal economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11809
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2010,” TO INSTITUTIONALIZE A FIVE-YEAR ACTION PLAN FOR THE IDENTIFICATION, PREVENTION, PREPAREDNESS, AND RESPONSE TO FORESEEABLE DISASTERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines faces significant exposure to a broad spectrum of natural, biological, technological, and human-induced hazards. These include tropical cyclones, floods, storm surges, landslides, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, drought, extreme heat, epidemics, pandemics, and other threats that jeopardize lives, livelihoods, infrastructure, public services, and economic development. Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010,” established a comprehensive disaster risk reduction and management system and institutionalized the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan. The law likewise established the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) and vested it with functions relating to disaster risk assessment, planning, coordination, preparedness, response, recovery, and the implementation of disaster risk reduction and management policies and programs. Despite the presence of these mechanisms, further strengthening of disaster risk reduction and management is necessary. This can be achieved through a specific, time- bound, measurable, and continuously monitored action plan that addresses disasters and risks which can be reasonably anticipated using scientific evidence, historical data, hazard assessments, risk maps, climate projections, early warning systems, and other reliable sources. A lack of a sufficiently integrated, long-term operational mechanism may lead to fragmented preparedness activities, program duplication, gaps in inter-agency coordination, inadequate resource allocation, and delays in implementing preventive and anticipatory measures. This measure seeks to institutionalize a Five-Year Action Pian for the Identification, Prevention, Preparedness, and Response to Foreseeable Disasters as an integral and complementary component of the existing national disaster risk reduction and management framework. The proposed Five-Year Action Plan will operationalize national disaster risk reduction and management policies by establishing concrete and measurable programs, projects, activities, targets, timelines, responsibilities, and resource requirements. It will m 78) identify priority hazards and high-risk areas, strengthen early warning and anticipatory actions, enhance preparedness and response capabilities, protect critical infrastructure and essential services, and establish mechanisms for monitoring, evaluation, and public accountability. The proposed measure is not intended to replace the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan. Instead, it aims to provide a five-year operational mechanism to translate the objectives and strategies of the national framework into specific and measurable actions. The State maintains a continuing duty to protect life and property and to strengthen the capacity of national government agencies, local government units, communities, and other stakeholders to anticipate and manage disaster risks. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11810
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE ZAMBOANGA CITY MARITIME TECHNOLOGY AND OCEAN RESEARCH AGENCY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FOR ITS ORGANIZATION AND OPERATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Since the Philippines is an island country with abundant marine ecosystems and large coastal waters, it has come to realize how important maritime technology. ocean research, and coastal monitoring are for promoting national development. The seas and oceans of the country are a vital source of food, provide people with a means of livelihood, are used for transportation, contribute to scientific knowledge and offer economic opportunities. At the same time, the growing problems of marine pollution, coastal crosion, climate change, the decline in marine resources, and the demand for technological progress show how essential it is to improve the nation's scientific and institutional abilities in the fields of maritime research and innovation. Even though the maritime sector plays a significant part in the country's development, there is still a requirement to further strengthen a specific institutional framework which will promote and coordinate marine technology development, oceanographic research, coastal monitoring, and maritime innovation. Creating a specialized government agency would offer a more targeted and coordinated method of developing scientific solutions, progressing marine engineering, supporting research projects, and encouraging the sustainable use of the country's marine and coastal resources. We are therefore proposing the creation of the Zamboanga City Maritime Technology and Ocean Research Agency (ZCMTORA). The Agency will function as a national government body whose role it will be to promote and coordinate marine scientific research, to develop maritime technologies, to set up coastal monitoring systems, to support technology transfer, and to promote innovation in the maritime field. By means of research collaboration, scientific capacity-building, and the development of suitable marine research infrastructure, the Agency will aid in enhancing the country's capacity to meet emerging maritime challenges and to obtain the maximum benefits from its marine resources. Zamboanga City is also suggested as the main headquarters of the Agency in view of its strategic position in south-western Mindanao and its capacity to function as a centre for maritime research, marine technology development, and scientific cooperation. It is expected that setting up the Agency in the city will provide opportunities for research partnerships, technical education, local employment, and the development of maritime- related industries, as well as help promote marine science and technology in Mindanao and all over the Philippines. The Agency should also work together with the appropriate national government agencies, state universities and colleges, research institutions, local government bodies, and private-sector organizations in order to facilitate the exchange of scientific know ledge, prevent unnecessary duplication of current programs, and make sure that its maritime research activities align with the mandates of existing institutions. Its programs must support coastal environmental protection, disaster risk reduction, sustainable fisheries, the conservation of marine biodiversity, and the responsible development of the blue economy. The measure also includes provision for the Agency's organizational structure, powers and functions, interagency coordination, the rules and regulations necessary for its implementation, and the initial appropriation required for its establishment and operation. It is suggested that Five Hundred Million Pesos (P500,000,000.00) be made available to assist with the Agency's establishment, research facilities, equipment, personnel, and priority programs, on condition that it receives congressional authorization and complies with the government's relevant budgetary and auditing requirements. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11811
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Occupational therapy and speech-language therapy are essential rehabilitation services that help individuals develop, regain, or maintain the functional, communication, and daily living skills necessary for independent and meaningful participation in society. For many indigent Filipino families, the cost of these services remains a significant barrier to obtaining appropriate and continuous treatment. Children with developmental delays, autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, and communication disorders may require sustained therapeutic interventions to support their development and participation in school and community life. Likewise, persons with disabilities and individuals recovering from stroke, traumatic brain injury, or other serious medical conditions may require occupational therapy or speech-language therapy to improve their functional independence and quality of life. Financial hardship and limited access to qualified professionals and rehabilitation facilities prevent many individuals from receiving the services they need. These barriers are particularly significant in underserved communities and areas where rehabilitation resources are limited. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Free Occupational and Speech- Language Therapy Program for Indigents, to be created, administered, and implemented by the Department of Health in all public hospitals nationwide. The proposed measure establishes two alternative means of determining indigency: inclusion in the latest applicable official Listahanan of the Department of Social Welfare and Development, or formal assessment and endorsement by the Local Social Welfare and Development Office of the beneficiary's city or municipality of residence. By recognizing local social welfare endorsements as an alternative basis for eligibility, the measure seeks to accommodate indigent individuals who may not appear in Listahanan but whose financial circumstances have been assessed and verified by the appropriate local social welfare office. The measure further requires public hospitals to establish appropriate service units or referral arrangements, provides for the development of qualified rehabilitation personnel, and requires coordination among national government agencies and local government units to ensure equitable access to services. Through this proposed legislation, the State shall take steps to remove financial barriers to essential rehabilitation services, promote functional independence and communication, support families and caregivers, and protect the dignity and well-being of indigent Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11812
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE AUTOMATIC GRANT OF CASH ASSISTANCE TO POOR AND NEAR-POOR HOUSEHOLDS DURING INFLATION OR PRICE SURGES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to the 1987 Constitution, the State shall promote a just and dynamic social order that frees the people from poverty through adequate social services and an improved quality of life. Republic Act No. 11310, or the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program Act, likewise institutionalizes cash assistance as a core tool of social protection for poor households. Rising prices hit the poorest families first and foremost. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), inflation for the bottom thirty percent (30%) of income households rose to nine nine point five percent (9.5%) in October 2026, its highest since early 2023, against a headline rate of seven point eight percent (7.8%). It has stayed at eight percent (8%) or higher every month since April 2026, while the same group saw prices fall a year earlier. Many of these families are not even counted as poor. According to the PSA, the 2025 poverty threshold for a family of five is only ₱14,634 a month, or about ₱96 per person a day for both food and non-food needs. The PSA itself has admitted that its food threshold is insufficient. Families earning slightly above this line receive no protection, even when price increases push them back into hardship. Notwithstanding the said irregular threshold, the law already recognizes automatic triggers. While Republic Act No. 12316 allows the President to suspend or reduce fuel excise taxes once Dubai crude reaches US$80 per barrel, no similar trigger exists for the prices that poor households actually pay. Hence, relief remains ad hoc, discretionary, and often late. The proposed measure seeks to close the said gap by mandating the automatic release of cash assistance to poor and near-poor households whenever inflation for the bottom thirty percent (30%) of income households reaches 6 percent nationally, or 8 percent in a region, for two consecutive months. The assistance ranges from ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 a month depending on the severity of inflation, and is released by the Department of Social Welfare and Development within thirty days of the PSA's certification, without need of further executive approval. The said bill also prohibits the use of the names and images of public officials on the assistance. 1 In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. label: HB 11813
title: AN ACT CREATING THE SOCCSKSARGEN POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION (SPITE), INTEGRATING THE TESDA TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTIONS IN REGION XII INTO A UNIFIED MULTI-CAMPUS POLYTECHNIC SYSTEM, DEFINING ITS POWERS, FUNCTIONS, GOVERNANCE, AND ADMINISTRATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Introduced by Representative SHIRLYN L. BAÑAS-NOGRALES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Section 2(2) thereof further directs the State to establish and maintain a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society. Likewise, Section 10 recognizes science and technology as essential for national development and requires the State to prioritize research and development, innovation, and technical education and training to foster productivity, self-reliance, and global competitiveness. The SOCCSKSARGEN Region (Region XII) has emerged as one of the country's major economic growth centers and among Mindanao's leading contributors to agriculture, fisheries, manufacturing, logistics, tourism, and agro-industrial exports. The region is recognized as the Tuna Capital of the Philippines and serves as a strategic hub for the tuna industry, aquaculture, rubber, banana, pineapple, coconut, coffee, and the rapidly expanding halal industry. It is likewise experiencing sustained growth in construction, renewable energy, digital services, information and communications technology, and advanced manufacturing. These developments have significantly increased the demand for highly skilled workers possessing competencies in Industry 4.0 technologies, digital transformation, automation, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, sustainable agriculture, logistics, entrepreneurship, and globally recognized technical qualifications. Despite the presence of several Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) Technology Institutions across Region XII, technical-vocational education and training remains fragmented. The existing institutions operate independently with separate administrative systems, planning mechanisms, and resource allocations. Such fragmentation has resulted in duplication of programs, inefficient utilization of resources, uneven institutional development, limited specialization, and inadequate industry integration. 1 Recent labor market analyses likewise indicate persistent shortages of skilled workers in priority sectors such as agriculture, fisheries, construction, tourism, healthcare, manufacturing, digital technologies, logistics, renewable energy, and emerging industries. Unless these structural deficiencies are addressed, Region XII risks losing opportunities for higher productivity, greater investments, and inclusive economic growth. This Bill seeks to establish the SOCCSKSARGEN Polytechnic Institute of Technical Education (SPITE) as a unified, multi-campus, industry-driven regional polytechnic institution under the supervision of TESDA. The proposed Institute shall consolidate existing TESDA Technology Institutions in Region XII into a single coordinated system governed by one administration, one development framework, and one strategic vision. SPITE shall serve as the premier institution for competency-based technical education, diploma programs, lifelong learning, applied research, technology innovation, entrepreneurship, and industry collaboration in SOCCSKSARGEN. It shall provide seamless educational pathways from National Certificates to diploma programs and other higher-level technical qualifications consistent with the Philippine Qualifications Framework. The Institute shall likewise establish specialized Centers of Innovation in sectors where Region XII possesses strategic advantages, including tuna processing, aquaculture, rubber technology, agri-processing, halal industry development, renewable energy, construction technologies, digital innovation, tourism, hospitality, and advanced manufacturing. Through strengthened partnerships with industries, local government units, higher education institutions, and international organizations, SPITE shall ensure that its programs remain responsive to present and future labor market requirements. Beyond strengthening technical education, the establishment of SPITE will contribute to regional industrialization, innovation, employment generation, poverty reduction, entrepreneurship, and inclusive economic development. It will enhance workforce competitiveness, promote lifelong learning, support technology transfer, and serve as a catalyst for sustainable growth not only in SOCCSKSARGEN but throughout Mindanao. The establishment of the SOCCSKSARGEN Polytechnic Institute of Technical Education is therefore a strategic investment in human capital development that advances the Constitutional mandate to provide quality, relevant, and accessible technical education responsive to the demands of national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. SHIRLYN L. title: AN ACT DECLARING DECEMBER 10 OF EVERY YEAR AS A LOCAL HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CARRASCAL, SURIGAO DEL SUR, IN CELEBRATION OF THE “ADLAW NAN CARRASCAL”.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Carrascal in the Province of Surigao del Sur commemorates its Charter Day every 10th of December, known as “Adlaw nan Carrascal.” This annual celebration marks a significant milestone in the municipality's history, recognizing its establishment as a distinct local government unit and honoring the generations of people of Carrascal whose dedication, contributions, and collective efforts have shaped the community into what it is today. The observance of Adlaw nan Carrascal provides an opportunity for the people of Carrascal to reflect on their municipality's historical roots, celebrate its accomplishments, and recognize the progress it has achieved through the years. More than a commemoration of its founding, the occasion strengthens the people’s sense of identity, civic pride, and solidarity, while reaffirming their shared commitment to the continued growth and development of their municipality. Declaring December 10 of every year a special non-working holiday in the Municipality of Carrascal will allow its residents, local government officials and employees, and other stakeholders to fully participate in the activities commemorating this important occasion. It will provide the community with an opportunity to honor its heritage, promote local traditions, and celebrate the achievements and aspirations of the municipality. label: HB 11815
title: AN ACT PROTECTING DIGITAL LIKENESS AND PERSONA RIGHTS BY CONFERRING ECONOMIC RIGHTS OVER AN INDIVIDUAL'S IMAGE, VOICE, AND LIKENESS, ESTABLISHING TECHNICAL FORENSIC AND REGULATORY CAPABILITIES, PROVIDING SAFE HARBORS AND EXEMPTIONS, AND IMPOSING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With the rapid emergence and proliferation of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, cloning vocal signatures, manipulating visual media, and synthesizing realistic deepfakes have become increasingly accessible. This technological leap has severely blurred the line between authentic human conduct and fabricated digital media, leaving individuals vulnerable to unauthorized digital exploitation. Beyond personal privacy, this capability poses acute threats to personal reputation, individual dignity, financial security, and public trust. When deployed without consent, synthetic media becomes a potent tool for online harassment, defamation, fraud, commercial exploitation, and targeted misinformation. Across the globe, governments are recognizing that legacy laws are no longer sufficient to combat algorithmic impersonation, prompting a massive wave of international legislative action. To cite examples, there is the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act enacted in 2024 which establishes strict transparency and disclosure requirements for synthetic media, enforcing mandatory machine-readable watermarking for generative AI outputs and clear, visible labeling for all deepfakes and AI-manipulated content, specifically stated in Article 50 of the Act. In Denmark, there is a pending bill which proposes a copyright law that would give citizens ownership of their face, voice, and body to fight against AI deepfakes. In the United States, the State of Tennessee pioneered direct identity safeguards through the Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act (ELVIS Act) enacted in 2024, protecting vocal and visual likenesses from AI cloning, while federal initiatives like the TAKE IT DOWN Act (An Act to Require Covered Platforms to Remove Nonconsensual Intimate Visual Deceptions, and for Other Purposes) passed by the U.S. Congress and signed into law in May 2025, it criminalizes the online publication of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII)—including AI-generated deepfake pornography—and mandates that online platforms remove such content within 48 hours. South Korea enacted its AI Basic Act and severe criminal amendments penalizing the distribution and possession of sexually explicit deepfakes, while Singapore enforces strict election and safety laws, such as the Elections Integrity of Online Advertising (Amendment) Act or (ELIONA), which targets deceptive digital media during election periods. While several statutory frameworks in the Philippines touch upon aspects of personal identity and digital misuse, none were structurally designed to address the unique complexities presented by generative AI and synthetic identity theft: • The Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386): Article 26 protects personal dignity and privacy, providing civil remedies against prying into private life and the unauthorized commercial exploitation of a person's name or portrait. However, its remedies are strictly retroactive and civil in nature, lacking rapid- response mechanics or preventive administrative recourse against real-time digital dissemination. • The Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 8293): Section 123(c) prevents the registration of trademarks containing the name, portrait, or signature of a living individual without written consent. Beyond trademark registration, however, traditional intellectual property law remains anchored to fixed original works, leaving a critical statutory gap regarding non- commercial deepfakes, synthetic voice replication, and personal digital persona rights. • The Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10175): Section 4(b)(3) penalizes computer-related identity theft involving the unauthorized acquisition or misuse of identifying data online. Yet, establishing computer-related identity theft requires proving traditional elements of fraud or economic deceit, which fails to capture non-fraudulent reputational damage, deepfake harassment, or non-consensual biometric simulation. • The Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173): While protecting personal data processing and empowering the National Privacy Commission to penalize unauthorized profiling, it treats personal image and voice primarily as informational data points rather than conferring an affirmative, standalone property right over one's synthesized digital persona. • The Safe Spaces Act (Republic Act No. 11313): Section 12 addresses gender- based online sexual harassment, penalizing non-consensual cyber-flashing and the unauthorized upload of intimate photos or videos. While vital, its scope is restricted to sexually explicit content and gender-based harassment, leaving non- intimate commercial deepfakes, unauthorized political impersonations, and general vocal/visual cloning unaddressed. To bridge these statutory divides, a specialized, sui generis legislative framework is necessary. Existing laws remain fragmented, reactive, and reliant on legal definitions tailored to pre-AI paradigms. Current statutes fail to hold online hosting services and social media platforms explicitly accountable under compulsory notice-and-takedown mandates with strict statutory deadlines. Furthermore, existing laws do not grant individuals an inherent, enforceable property right over their voice timbre, speech patterns, facial features, and digital likeness independent of a pre-existing copyrighted work. This measure — the "Digital Likeness and Persona Rights Act" — establishes a comprehensive, specialized legal regime tailored directly to the challenges of artificial intelligence. The bill explicitly vests in every individual an exclusive, personal economic right over the commercial exploitation and public dissemination of their own image, voice, and likeness, including any realistic digital imitation or deepfake thereof. By classifying this right as a sui generis intellectual property right that subsists independently of traditional copyright fixation

label: HB 11816
title: AN ACT PROMOTING ACCESS TO AFFORDABLE AND DECENT RENTAL HOUSING FOR POOR AND LOW-INCOME HOUSEHOLDS THROUGH THE PROVISION OF INCENTIVES FOR THE DEVELOPMENT, CONSTRUCTION, REHABILITATION, AND OPERATION OF QUALIFIED RENTAL HOUSING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to adequate, safe, and affordable housing is a fundamental human right enshrined in the Philippine Constitution. Yet, despite steady economic growth, a significant segment of the population—particularly poor and low-income households— continues to grapple with skyrocketing housing costs and a severe shortage of decent shelter. Rapid urbanization has exacerbated this crisis, forcing millions into informal settlements or substandard living conditions devoid of basic infrastructure and services. While government programs have historically prioritized homeownership, buying a home remains an unattainable dream for marginalized families whose daily struggles focus on basic survival. Recognizing rental housing as an essential component of a holistic national housing strategy is long overdue. For millions of urban poor and low- income citizens, a well-regulated, affordable, and decent rental housing market provides a realistic, flexible, and sustainable path to secure shelter. To bridge this monumental housing gap, the State must actively partner with the private sector. Private enterprise possesses the capital, efficiency, and scalability required to rapidly develop and manage residential housing units on a mass scale. However, developers are frequently deterred by high construction costs, stringent regulatory burdens, and narrow profit margins when targeting the low-income segment. This measure, the proposed "Affordable and Decent Rental Housing Incentives Act", seeks to unlock private sector investment by providing a robust, targeted package of fiscal and non-fiscal incentives. Specifically, the bill offers: • Value-Added Tax (VAT) exemptions on the lease of residential units dedicated to qualified tenants. • Applicable tax incentives under Republic Act No. 11534, otherwise known as the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises (CREATE) Act. • A 25% tax credit on gross rentals derived from qualified rental housing for a period of five years. • Preferential interest rates, flexible repayment arrangements, and risk-sharing mechanisms from government financial institutions. • Credits toward compliance with the Balanced Housing Development Program under Republic Act No. 7279. Furthermore, to ensure comprehensive social protection and long-term program integrity, this expanded measure incorporates critical safeguards: • Rent Control and Price Escalation Caps: Mandates joint DHSUD and DTI guidelines to cap annual rent increases, preventing sudden, unaffordable price spikes for vulnerable households. • Tenant Security of Tenure and Grievance Mechanisms: Protects qualified tenants from arbitrary eviction and establishes dedicated channels for resolving tenant-management disputes. • Green Building and Climate Resilience Standards: Requires compliance with Republic Act No. 10866 (Philippine Green Building Code) and disaster-resilient building standards to guarantee structural safety against extreme weather events. • LGU Streamlining and Support: Directs local government units to fast-track permits within a non-extendable period of thirty working days and encourages local tax relief for registered projects. • Congressional Oversight: Institutes biennial impact evaluation reports submitted by the DHSUD to Congress to measure unit output, fiscal sustainability, and beneficiary outcomes. By lowering the barriers to entry for developers and operators while embedding clear- cut tenant safeguards and green standards, this Act ensures that the private sector is strongly incentivized to build and maintain safe, dignified, and reasonably priced rental communities. In turn, strict monitoring by the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD) guarantees that these housing options remain strictly dedicated to underprivileged families throughout the mandated affordability period. Passing this legislation is a crucial step toward dismantling urban poverty and upholding the dignity of every Filipino worker and family through secure, resilient, and accessible housing. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. MARCELINO “MARCY” R.
