label: HB 11817
title: AN ACT PROVIDING EQUAL CASH INCENTIVES TO OLYMPIC AND PARALYMPIC MEDALISTS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 8 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10699, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "NATIONAL ATHLETES AND COACHES BENEFITS AND INCENTIVES ACT," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10699, othenrvise known as the "National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and lncentives Act," recognizes the contributions of Filipino athletes who bring honor and recognition to the country through their achievements in international sports competitions. Among its principal provisions is the grant of cash incentives to athletes who win gold, silver, and bronze medals in recognized international competitions. Despite this recognition and the honor that the Filipino athletes bring to our nation through their achievements, Section 8 of the law prescribes different cash incentives for medalists in the Olympic Games and the Paralympic Games, as well as in other corresponding internationalsporting competitions. Underthe existing statutory schedule, an Olympic gold medalist is entitled to Ten Million Pesos (F10,000,000.00), while a Paralympic gold medalist is entitled to Five Million Pesos (P5,000,000.00). Similar disparities apply to silver and bronze medalists and to athletes competing in the Asian Games and Asian Para Games, and the Southeast Asian Games and ASEAN Para Games. This distinction warrants legislative reconsideration. Olympic and Paralympic athletes alike undergo rigorous training, demonstrate exceptional discipline and athletic excellence, and compete at the highest levels of international sport while representing the Republic of the Philippines. Their respective competitions demand dedication, preparation, and performance worthy of national recognition. The State's obligation to promote sports development and protect the welfare of national athletes should be consistent with the principles of equality, inclusivity, and recognition of human dignity. This commitment necessarily includes ensuring that persons with disabilities are afforded equal treatment and equal opportunities to participate in sports, pursue athletic excellence, and receive recognition for their achievements. The achievement of a medal for the country should be accorded equal statutory recognition, regardless of whether it is earned in the Olympic Games or the Paralympic Games. Such recognition affirms that disability should not be a basis for diminished acknowledgment of an athlete's contribution to the nation. This proposed measure therefore seeks to amend Section I of Republic Act No. 10699 by equalizing the cash incentives granted to medalists in the Olympic and Paralympic Games, the Asian Games and Asian Para Games, and the Southeast Asian Games and ASEAN Para Games- By establishing equality in the statutory rewards for conesponding competitions, the measure seeks to ensure that all Filipino athletes who bring honor to the country receive equal recognition for comparable sporting achievements, regardless of their circumstances. ln view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. c MA. title: AN ACT REGULATING THE "FLOATING STATUS" OF EMPLOYEES IN THE FORMAL SECTOR TO PREVENT ABUSE, PROTECT SECURITY OF TENURE, AND PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AND CONTINUITY OF EMPLOYEE BENEFITS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES," AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution upholds the right of workers to security of tenure as a fundamental right and mandates the State to afford full protection to labor. At the same time, it recognizes the right of enterprises to reasonable returns on investments and to expansion and growth. These constitutional principles underscore the need to balance the protection of workers' rights with the legitimate business interests of employers. Notwithstanding, the status of employees whose work is dependent upon a client or principal of their employer remains one of the recurring difficulties that is inadequately addressed by our labor statutes and related executive issuances. For instance, if an employer loses a service contract or experiences a reduction in the client's requirements, the employees may be placed on floating status without wages while awaiting reassignment, potentially leaving them without a reliable source of income. The issue is particularly significant in industries where work assignments depend on contracts with third-party clients, including the private security and business process outsourcing industries. When a client contract expires, is terminated, or is reduced, affected employees may be placed on floating status without wages while awaiting reassignment. Although temporary suspension may be justified when work is genuinely unavailable, the absence of clear statutory standards creates a risk that the practice may be used to avoid the payment of wages and benefits or to circumvent security of tenure. While the Department of Labor and Employment has previously issued Department Order No. 150-16, or the Revised Guidelines Governing the Employment and-Working Conditions of Security Guards and Other Private Seci,iity personnel in the Private Security lndustry, a statutory framework is needed to establish consistent minimum protections--for employees across industries without diminishing the protections already afforded to private security personnel. The proposed measure therefore defines the circumstances under wftich floating status may be imposed, requires written notice and periodic review, places the burden on thl employer to establish the legitimacy of the placement, and prohibits the use of such status to evade labor standards or circumvent security of tenure. Recognizing that employees placed on floating status may be deprived of income while their employment remains in force, the proposeO legislation requires employers to provide financial assistance throughout the perioO of su-ctr status. These measures are intended to cushion the financial hardship employees may face while awaiting reassignmen_t or redeployment. The continuing fi'nancial obligation also provides employers with an incentive to promptly explore aiailable assignments rather than allow employees to remain on floating status indefinitely without iicome. To prevent floating status from becoming indefinite, the proposed measure retains the six-month limit and requires employers, before its expiraiion, to recall or reassign affected employees to suitable work or terminate their employment only on a lawful ground and in accordance with applicable legal requiremenis. iogether,ihese safeguards seek to protect emptoyees from undue financial hardship aid proionged uncertainty while accommodating the legitimate operational needs of enterpriJes, consistent with the constitutional guarantee of security of tenure and the State;s duty to protect labor. ln view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnesily sought. label: HB 11819
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE YEAR 2027 AS “NATIONAL GOLF TOURISM YEAR” IN THE ENTIRE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 19 of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, competitions, and related activities to foster self- discipline, teamwork, and excellence for the development of a healthy and alert citizenry. This constitutional policy recognizes sports not only as a driver of personal health and discipline, but also as a powerful vehicle for broader social and economic development. Consistent with this mandate, Republic Act No. 9593, or the Tourism Act of 2009, declares tourism an industry of national interest and importance, recognizing its critical role in generating investment, employment, foreign exchange, and inclusive national growth. It explicitly directs the Government to promote sustainable tourism, encourage private-sector participation, strengthen local tourism development, and position the Philippines as a premier, competitive global destination. This bill seeks to declare the year 2027 as the “National Golf Tourism Year” in the Philippines to promote golf as a key component of the country’s tourism strategy and to highlight the Philippines as a premier destination for sports, leisure, and high-value travel. This measure is both strategic and timely. While the Philippine tourism sector continues its steady recovery, international visitor arrivals and overall visitor spending require further diversification to reach and surpass pre-pandemic levels. Golf tourism presents a unique economic opportunity: golf travelers spend significantly more than average tourists, stay for longer durations, and create extended demand across accommodation, food and dining, transportation, retail, and local recreation services. The Philippines already possesses a rich, substantial foundation for golf tourism, boasting world-class courses across Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao. Importantly, the year 2027 carries profound historical significance for Philippine sports and heritage. The Iloilo Golf and Country Club in Santa Barbara, Iloilo—established in 1907 by British engineers associated with the Panay Railways—will celebrate its 120th anniversary in 2027. As the oldest golf course in the Philippines, its milestone provides a fitting, historic centerpiece to showcase the Ry oP) nation’s deep golfing heritage while connecting sports tourism directly with local history, culture, and regional hospitality. This national observance also builds upon demonstrated industry capabilities and prior congressional momentum. The Philippines successfully hosted the Asian Golf Tourism Convention in 2018, and the Department of Tourism launched the Philippine Golf Experience in 2025. Furthermore, this initiative aligns with earlier legislative actions, notably House Bill No. 7905 (substituting HB 5770) filed by former 2" District of lloilo Representative Michael B. Gorriceta in the 18 Congress, which was favorably recommended by the Committee on Tourism under Committee Report No. 567. The proposed 2027 observance consolidates these historical, administrative, and private-sector efforts under a single national platform. Rather than creating a new bureaucracy, the measure authorizes the Department of Tourism to lead the observance in voluntary collaboration with local government units, private golf clubs, and tourism stakeholders. By unifying the country’s golf courses, historical landmarks, local governments, and sports organizations under a shared national umbrella, the 2027 National Golf Tourism Year is expected to elevate the Philippines’ standing in global sports tourism and generate vibrant economic opportunities for host communities across the archipelago. label: HB 11820
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA BARBARA AS THE OFFICIAL CAPITAL OF THE PROVINCE OF ILOILO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution underscores the vital importance of a responsive and accountable local government structure anchored on local autonomy and decentralization. In this context, the designation of a provincial capital should consider not only historical heritage but also geographic accessibility, institutional capacity, existing infrastructure, economic potential and its ability to support the long-term development of the province. The Municipality of Santa Barbara, Province of Iloilo, presents a compelling basis for such designation. It holds a distinguished place in Philippine history as the Cradle of the Revolution in the Visayas. On November 17, 1898, it witnessed the historic Cry of Santa Barbara, where the Philippine flag was raised for the first time outside Luzon. It also served as the military headquarters of General Martin Teofilo B. Delgado, a revolutionary leader who later became the first civil governor of Iloilo. Designating Santa Barbara as the official provincial capital would provide lasting institutional recognition to this important chapter in Iloilo’s history and its contribution to the country’s struggle for independence. Beyond its historical significance, Santa Barbara possesses geographic and physical characteristics that support its role as a provincial administrative center. It is a first-class municipality comprising sixty (60) barangays and covering more than 13,000 hectares. Located approximately fifteen (15) kilometers from Hoilo City and near the Hoilo International Airport, it is connected by national and provincial road networks that link it with neighboring municipalities and other parts of the province. Its location provides a practical setting for strengthening access to provincial government services while complementing the existing functions of Iloilo City. Santa Barbara also has an established and diversified economic base anchored on agriculture, commerce, transportation and services. Its agricultural resources, growing commercial activity and strategic location provide opportunities for further development in agribusiness, manufacturing, tourism and other investments. Its development as a provincial center may likewise support a more balanced distribution of economic activity and infrastructure across Tloilo. Equally significant is Santa Barbara’s demonstrated institutional and public-service capacity. The municipality has an established network of health, education, disaster-response and other public facilities serving its sixty (60) barangays. Its local government has likewise demonstrated capacity in revenue administration and public-sector management, including recognition for its performance in real property tax collection and assessment. These existing capabilities provide a practical foundation for assuming a broader role in provincial administration. The municipality is also already becoming a site for provincial government infrastructure. The development of the Iloilo Government Center in Barangay Bolong Oeste, together with existing provincial government properties in Santa Barbara, provides a concrete foundation for strengthening government-related activities and inter-agency coordination. The ongoing development of this government center demonstrates that the municipality is not being proposed solely on the basis of future potential, but also on existing institutional and infrastructural foundations. By bringing together Santa Barbara’s historical significance, geographic accessibility, economic base, public-service infrastructure and demonstrated institutional capacity, this measure provides a practical foundation for recognizing the municipality as the official capital of Iloilo Province. It seeks to strengthen the province’s administrative and developmental framework while supporting a more balanced and sustainable distribution of government activity and economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KATHRYN JGYACE F. label: HB 11823
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL EYE HEALTH PROGRAM FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide comprehensive eye care services for senior citizens by establishing a National Eye Health Program for Senior Citizens and improving early detection, treatment, rehabilitation, and vision support services to enable the elderly to maintain their independence. As one of the leading causes of disability among older persons, visual impairment is often caused by preventable or treatable conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration. Worldwide, at least 2.2 billion people suffer from vision impairment, and of these, over one (1) billion cases could have been prevented or addressed early on. In the Philippines, the growing senior citizen population underscores the need to strengthen accessible eye care services to prevent avoidable blindness and vision loss due to financial constraints, limited access to specialists, and inadequate community-based vision services. This measure is designed to address these gaps by institutionalizing a dedicated national program under the Department of Health to address these critical concerns, provide essential eye services, and improve the functional capacity and overall well-being of older persons. By this measure, we hope to protect the eyesight of our senior citizens so they may remain productive and independent members of society while reducing preventable disability and improving their quality of life. A national eye health program is a worthwhile investment in geriatric medicine and dignified “« elderly care. SITTIE SHAH PLE” 1. label: HB 11824
title: AN ACT REPEALING BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 36, ENTITLED “AN ACT IMPOSING AN ENERGY TAX ON ELECTRIC POWER CONSUMPTION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Batas Pambansa Bilang 36, entitled “An Act imposing an Energy Tax on Electric Power Consumption”, was enacted in 1979, at a time when the country was confronted with economic difficulties, justifying the imposition of an energy tax. At present, the conditions that BP 36 tried to address no longer hold, given that electricity is now a necessity and a crucial component of people’s daily lives, which renders such additional imposition outdated and an unnecessary burden to every Filipino household. The continued collection of an additional energy tax increases the financial burden on families already struggling with rising prices and cost of living expenses, particularly on electricity, which includes generation, transmission, distribution, system losses, universal charges, and other government-imposed taxes and fees. This bill seeks to repeal Batas Pambansa Blg. 36 to ensure that taxes remain responsive to the reality and do not unnecessarily burden the public. Repealing this outdated tax shall help reduce electricity costs, provide meaningful relief to Filipino families, and allow households greater flexibility in managing their income for food, education, healthcare, and other necessities. 4 Lone District, Maguindanao det with Cotabato City Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City, Metro Manila 20 CONGRESS 2nd Regular Session HOUSE BILL NO. 1] 824 Introduced by Representative SITTIE SHAHARA “BAI DIMPLE” I. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to declare Mt. Minandar, located in Barangay Kusiong in the Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat, as an eco-tourism site. Rising about 450 meters above sea level, the summit overlooks the shores of illana Bay, offers breathtaking views of Cotabato City from afar, and overlooks nearby Timako Hill, attracting hikers for its beautiful coastal panoramas. A short trek from the nearby village as a starting point, the sunrise and sunset views at Mt. Minandar make it all worth the day trip for local hikers and nature lovers. Because of its potential to attract hiking enthusiasts and beginner mountaineers, Mt. Minandar can be a better alternative for landscape and nature photographers looking for new and exciting areas to discover. Declaring Mt. Minandar as an ecotourism site will result in its development and improvement as a tourist destination, and more importantly, contribute to the overall economic progress of the local community and Municipality of Datu Odin Sinsuat. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. PLE” |. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MULTI-PURPOSE FARM FOR THE BREEDING, SPAWNING, AND HATCHERY OF CATFISH, TILAPIA, MUDFISH, EEL, AND OTHER FRESHWATER FISHES IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF KABUNTALAN, PROVINCE OF MAGUINDANAO DEL NORTE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bilt seeks to establish a multi-purpose farm for the breeding, spawning, and hatchery of catfish, tilapia, mudfish, eel, and other freshwater fishes that are viable in mud ponds and concrete tanks in the Municipality of Kabuntalan, Province of Maguindanao de! Norte. The people of Kabuntalan generally rely on agriculture for their livelihood, particularly the cultivation of rice, corn, and assorted vegetables. As such, the supply of fish and other aquatic resources for their important dietary needs is far from ideal, resulting in their price becoming quite prohibitive for many of its people. The establishment of a multi-purpose fishery farm in the Municipality of Kabuntalan, Province of Maguindanao del Norte, therefore will greatly benefit its people, as this will address the demand for affordable fish; provide a stable source of fry or fingerlings and reliable technical expertise for the setting up, management, and operation of small-scale fish farms, empowering many of its residents and creating secondary income streams from aquaculture. label: HB 11828
title: AN ACT DECLARING BUBULUDTUA FALLS, LOCATED IN BARANGAY NABALAWAG, MUNICIPALITY OF BARIRA, PROVINCE OF MAGUINDANAO DEL NORTE, AN ECOTOURISM SITE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to declare Bubuludtua Falls, located in Barangay Nabalawag within the Municipality of Barira, as an eco-tourism site. This 200-foot waterfall was named after the term “Bubuludtua”, an Iranon word meaning “rainbow”; such a name describes the waterfall’s signature attraction: sunlight hitting the water spray, creating rainbow-like shimmers, making it a popular subject for loca! travel and landscape photography. It is one of the taller waterfalls in the region, surrounded by dense forests, cool mists, and a dramatic vertical drop, documented by local travelers since 2018, and is now included in commercial travel listings. The area is ideal for quiet, off-the-beaten-path adventures, hiking, trekking, camping, nature, wildlife, and bird photography. As one of the many tourism havens that has the potential to attract even international visitors, established nature and bird photography enthusiasts, and mountaineers, declaring Bubuludtua Falls an ecotourism site will result in its development and improvement as a tourist destination, and more importantly, the economic progress of the local community. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. E” i. label: HB 11831
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE GENDER AND DEVELOPMENT BUDGET BY ESTABLISHING OUTCOME-BASED ALLOCATION, ATTRIBUTION, MONITORING, AUDIT, AND ACCOUNTABILITY MECHANISMS, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9710, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA OF WOMEN”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9710, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta of Women,” established the Gender and Development (GAD) budget as a critical instrument for mainstreaming gender equality in government planning, programming, and resource allocation. It requires government agencies and instrumentalities to allocate at least five percent (5%) of their total budget appropriations for programs, activities, and projects (PAPs) that address gender issues and advance gender equality. The five percent (5%) requirement is an important statutory commitment. However, compliance with a financial threshold, by itself, cannot be the measure of whether government is effectively advancing gender equality. Public resources devoted to GAD must be directed toward identified gender issues, properly attributed, actually utilized, reach their intended beneficiaries, and produce measurable and verifiable results. Government audit findings demonstrate why this distinction is necessary. The Commission on Audit (COA), through its GAD Audit Performance Summary Reports, has documented recurring deficiencies in the implementation of the GAD budget. Among the common audit observations identified are the absence of GAD Plans and Budgets, GAD allocations below the required five percent (5%), underutilization of GAD funds, and partial implementation of approved GAD Plans and Budgets. COA has noted that some of these deficiencies have remained prevalent even in more recent audit periods. The COA’s consolidated reporting for Calendar Years 2019 to 2023 further underscores the continuing need to strengthen the implementation, monitoring, and accountability mechanisms governing GAD resources. These findings are significant because they demonstrate that the challenge is not limited to whether the required amount has been allocated. The more fundamental question is whether resources reported as GAD expenditures are genuinely responsive to identified gender issues and whether they are producing the results for which they were appropriated. COA’s existing audit framework itself recognizes the need to examine more than financial compliance. Its audit procedures include determining whether GAD programs, activities, and projects are correctly attributed to GAD and whether they have achieved their stated goals, objectives, targets, and performance indicators. Where implementation falls short, auditors are expected to determine the causes and recommend appropriate corrective measures. The audit framework likewise recognizes the need to address deficiencies through audit observations and, where warranted, notices and other appropriate audit actions. Despite these existing mechanisms, gaps remain in translating the five percent (5%) requirement into a consistent, measurable, and results-oriented system of public accountability. Paper compliance, unsupported or inappropriate attribution of expenditures, routine expenditures charged to GAD, underutilization of available funds, incomplete implementation, weak outcome measurement, and recurring audit observations can diminish the effectiveness of the GAD budget and weaken public confidence in the use of resources intended to advance gender equality. This measure therefore seeks to strengthen the statutory five percent (5%) GAD budget requirement under Republic Act No. 9710. It establishes a clearer connection between GAD allocations, identified gender issues, program objectives, measurable targets, performance indicators, actual beneficiaries, and verifiable outcomes. The bill introduces an outcome-based framework under which every GAD program, activity, and project must demonstrate a clear relationship between the gender issue being addressed, the resources allocated, the intervention undertaken, and the results achieved. It seeks to ensure that the amount attributed to GAD corresponds to the actual gender-responsive component of the program or activity and is supported by appropriate documentation and a defensible basis for attribution. The measure further strengthens the preparation, review, certification, monitoring, and reporting of GAD Plans and Budgets and GAD Accomplishment Reports. It establishes more consistent standards for budget attribution and requires agencies to maintain adequate documentation and outcome information that can be subjected to audit and verification. The bill also strengthens coordination between the Philippine Commission on Women (PCW), the Commission on Audit (COA), the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and other concerned oversight and implementing agencies. The framework is intended to harmonize planning, budgeting, implementation, monitoring, and audit so that the five percent (5%) requirement is not treated as an isolated budgeting exercise but as part of a continuing cycle of gender analysis, resource allocation, implementation, measurement, audit, and corrective action. Public transparency is likewise strengthened by requiring the systematic reporting of GAD allocations, utilization, attribution, implementation status, audit observations, corrective actions, and measurable results. Annual reporting to Congress will provide a basis for legislative oversight and allow policymakers to determine whether public resources devoted to GAD are addressing persistent gender gaps and producing meaningful improvements. Accountability mechanisms are likewise provided for improper attribution, unsupported GAD expenditures, misuse or diversion of GAD resources, failure to implement approved GAD programs without sufficient justification, and persistent noncompliance with statutory requirements. These mechanisms are intended not merely to penalize deficiencies, but to promote correction, institutional learning, and continuous improvement in the implementation of gender-responsive programs. label: HB 11832
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE NATIONAL COMMISSION ON THE FILIPINO FAMILY, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FAMILY WELFARE AND DEVELOPMENT FRAMEWORK, PROVIDING FOR FAMILY-CENTERED POLICY COORDINATION, MONITORING, AND ACCOUNTABILITY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Filipino family is the foundation of Philippine society and a vital institution in the development of a strong, productive, and resilient nation. The Constitution recognizes the sanctity of family life and the family as the foundation of the nation. Yet, while government programs address health, education, employment, housing, social protection, child welfare, senior citizens, disability, migration, and other concerns affecting families, these interventions are often implemented separately, making it difficult to see the family as a whole and to determine whether government action is actually improving family welfare. The National Committee on the Filipino Family (NCFF), created through Executive Order No. 241, series of 1995, and strengthened and renamed under Executive Order No. 238, series of 2003, was established to promote coordination and a national approach to family welfare. After more than two decades, however, the changing needs of Filipino families call for a stronger and more permanent institutional mechanism capable of providing policy leadership, coordinating existing programs, identifying gaps and duplication, generating evidence, and holding government efforts to measurable outcomes. This measure therefore transforms the existing NCFF into the National Commission on Filipino Family (NCFF), a permanent statutory institution that will serve as the country's principal policy and coordination body on family welfare and development. It does not create a parallel bureaucracy or take over the mandates of existing agencies. Instead, it brings together their efforts within a coherent national framework while respecting their respective legal and technical responsibilities. The proposed Commission will establish a National Family Welfare and Development Framework and Plan, develop measurable family welfare indicators, conduct Family Impact Assessments of major government interventions, monitor implementation, and submit an annual State of the Filipino Family Report to the President and Congress. It will also promote recognition of care work, strengthen family resilience, facilitate family participation in policymaking, and identify gaps and duplication in existing programs. The measure recognizes that family welfare is not the responsibility of one agency alone. It requires coordinated action across government and meaningful participation by families and other stakeholders. By transforming the existing NCFF into a permanent National Commission, this Act provides the institutional structure needed to make family welfare a measurable, coordinated, and sustained component of national development. label: HB 11833
title: AN ACT PROMOTING FOOD SECURITY AND COMMUNITY NUTRITION THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF THE GULAYAN SA BARANGAY AT PAARALAN PROGRAM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Household food insecurity remains a pressing and persistent challenge in the Philippines. According to the 2023 DOST-FNRI National Nutrition Survey, an alarming 31.4% of Filipino households were classified as moderately to severely food insecure, with rural areas experiencing a higher incidence at 35.3% compared to urban households at 27.8%. These figures underscore that food vulnerability is deeply tied to constraints in household-level food access and heavy exposure to sudden global or domestic price and supply shocks. To address this structural vulnerability, the State is mandated by the fundamental law to step forward. Section 15, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly declares that "The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them." Furthermore, Section 9 of the same Article mandates that the State shall promote a just and dynamic social order that will guarantee the enjoyment of health, economic security, and an improved quality of life for all. True human development and national progress cannot be attained when a significant portion of our population suffers from chronic hunger and nutritional deficiencies. In response to this, grassroots initiatives have proven that local food production serves as an immediate, practical, and scalable intervention. Existing practices demonstrate massive public uptake: the Department of Education (DepEd) shows that the Gulayan sa Paaralan Program has covered a significant number of schools nationwide, while numerous households have engaged in community fruit and vegetable planting through initiatives like the Department of the Interior and Local Government's (DILG) Halinat Magtanim ng Prutas at Gulay (HAPAG) sa Barangay program. However, relying solely on administrative campaigns leaves these vital nutrition efforts vulnerable to shifting political priorities and uneven local implementation. A stable, statutory framework is urgently required to institutionalize these practices permanently. “SEN RECEIVED 2 DATE OS NOY 2026 This bill seeks to institutionalize the "Gulayan sa Barangay at Paaralan Program" as a permanent, regular program of the national government. By mandating every barangay and encouraging public schools with available vacant spaces to establish community farming areas and food gardens, this measure transforms localized gardening into a robust national strategy for food security, community nutrition, and self-reliance. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 7) te D. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING EMPATHY EDUCATION AND SOCIAL-EMOTIONAL DEVELOPMENT IN BASIC EDUCATION, INSTITUTIONALIZING FOR THE PURPOSE SCHOOL-BASED PROGRAMS FOR COMPASSION, RESPECT AND POSITIVE RELATIONSHIPS, AND PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR TEACHERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as an essential instrument in the development of the Filipino learner and directs the State to promote and protect the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels. It likewise recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and the responsibility of the State to foster the development of the Filipino child as a responsible, compassionate, and productive member of society. Education, however, is not limited to the transmission of academic knowledge. A child who can read, compute, analyze, and memorize but cannot recognize the feelings of others, manage conflict, respect differences, listen with understanding, or respond appropriately to another person's needs remains incompletely prepared for life in a family, a school, a workplace, and a democratic society. Empathy is therefore not merely a desirable personal trait. It is a learnable and developable capacity that supports respectfu! relationships, responsible decision-making, peaceful conflict resolution, inclusion, and a positive schoo} climate. It helps children understand experiences different from their own and respond to others with appropriate concern while maintaining respect for boundaries, dignity, and individual differences. The urgency of developing these capacities has become even more evident amid growing concerns over the mental health and emotional well-being of Filipino children and adolescents. No less than Education Secretary Sonny Angara publicly called attention to what he described as a “mental! health epidemic” among the Filipino youth and urged the education sector to understand its roots and take positive steps to address it. He emphasized the need for educators to look beyond academic performance, recognize the personal circumstances and struggles of learners, and strengthen meaningful connections between teachers and students.! This concern comes at a time when schools are increasingly confronted with issues involving learner isolation, emotional distress, interpersonal conflict, bullying, harmful online influences, and_ difficulties in forming healthy relationships. DepEd has likewise emphasized the importance of closer attention to learners' well-being and is strengthening efforts involving parents, Child Protection Committees, guidance personnel, and other school and community partners. The present situation demonstrates that academic achievement alone cannot fully address the needs of today's learners. A comprehensive education must also help children understand and manage their emotions, recognize the emotions and experiences of others, communicate respectfully, resolve disagreements constructively, establish healthy relationships, seek help when needed, and respond appropriately to the needs of people around them. Empathy education therefore has an important preventive and developmental role. It can help create school environments in which learners feel seen, heard, respected, and connected, while giving them practical skills for dealing with differences, conflict, emotional challenges, and relationships. These competencies are particularly important during childhood and adolescence, when social relationships, identity, emotional development, and exposure to new influences are rapidly evolving. This measure does not seek to replace mental health services, professional psychological interventions, guidance and counseling, or other specialized support. Rather, it complements these services by strengthening the social and emotional foundations that can contribute to learner well-being and positive school environments. Where learners require professional assessment, treatment, psychological first aid, or other specialized intervention, existing referral mechanisms and qualified professionals shall continue to perform those functions. The Philippine education system already recognizes the importance of these competencies. The Department of Education expressly includes socio- emotional and values development among the developmental domains, including the ability to relate well with others, appreciate cultural diversity, and demonstrate concern for oneself and others. Existing learning materials likewise address the recognition and expression of one’s emotions, understanding the emotions of others, appreciation of differences, and interaction with others as members of the school 1DepEd flags ‘mental health epidemic’ among youth (https://bworldonline.com/the- nation/2026/09/22/780501/deped-flags-menta!-health-epidemic-among- youth/?fbclid =IwY2xjawUgGZ1wZG9IMBWV4dG4DYWVtAjJEWAGJyaWORMTIVVmEOQKShQ 1BOoWHR2bXRzcnRiBmFEwcF9pZBAyMjIWMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEeLA8V40fcDfTMomKwlx EXTJgJySbRi0zy-JwgXA30t9GjipyDVAxPj4468ras_aem eZ2iEL782JvOplIVVG2BRmQ) Accessed on 23 September 2026 and community. The Good Manners and Right Conduct and Values Education framework further incorporates social and emotional learning, experiential learning, role-playing, collaborative learning, conflict resolution, healthy relationships, and other approaches that develop interpersonal and character competencies. label: HB 11835
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING BLUE AND GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE FOR CLIMATE-RESILIENT AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT, INTEGRATING NATURE-BASED SOLUTIONS AND WATER-SENSITIVE DESIGN INTO INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEVELOPMENT PLANNING, AND PROVIDING FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS AND IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISMS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines faces a fundamental reality: natural hazards cannot be prevented, but their impacts can be reduced through better planning, stronger infrastructure, and reduced vulnerability. The WorldRiskReport 2026 ranks the Philippines first in the WorldRiskIndex, underscoring the country's exceptionally high exposure to natural hazards and significant societal vulnerability. The WorldRiskReport 2025, meanwhile, provides a more detailed analysis of flood risk in the Philippines and highlights the importance of land use, infrastructure, natural retention areas, wetlands, mangroves, and floodplains in reducing flood risk. These findings reinforce a principle already embodied in the 1987 Constitution, which directs the State to protect and advance the people's right to a balanced and healthful ecology and to protect and promote the right to health. They are likewise consistent with the State's existing commitments under Republic Act No. 9729, or the Climate Change Act of 2009, which requires climate change to be integrated into government policies, plans, programs, and development decisions, and recognizes the need to build national and local resilience to climate-related disasters. Similarly, Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, requires a holistic, comprehensive, integrated, and proactive approach to reducing disaster risks and addressing the root causes of vulnerability. Republic Act No. 10174, which established the People’s Survival Fund, further provides a long-term financing mechanism for climate change adaptation, including activities involving water resources, infrastructure, and natural ecosystems. Yet these mandates must be translated more deliberately into the way infrastructure is planned and built. Blue and green infrastructure offers that bridge. Wetlands, mangroves, riparian buffers, urban forests, parks, permeable surfaces, rain gardens, bioswales, natural drainage systems, and other nature-based solutions can retain and slow water, reduce runoff, mitigate heat, protect ecosystems, and complement conventional drainage and flood-control infrastructure. The proposed “Blue and Green Resilient Infrastructure Development and Governance Act” or BRIDGE Act therefore institutionalizes blue and green infrastructure as a national approach to climate-resilient and sustainable development, integrating nature-based solutions and water-sensitive design into infrastructure and development planning and establishing national standards and implementation mechanisms suited to the diverse conditions of Philippine communities. The bill seeks to bridge conventional infrastructure with nature-based solutions, infrastructure planning with ecological planning, and present development needs with long-term climate and disaster resilience. It does not seek to replace conventional infrastructure. Rather, it seeks to bridge engineered and natural systems so that roads, drainage and flood-control structures, public spaces, buildings, waterways, and ecological assets work together to reduce risk and strengthen resilience. For a country highly exposed to storms, floods, and other natural hazards, resilience cannot begin when disaster strikes. It must begin in the way we plan, design, and build. This measure gives concrete expression to the constitutional mandate for a balanced and healthful ecology and complements the country's existing climate-change and disaster-risk reduction laws by making resilience and ecological protection integral considerations in infrastructure development. title: AN ACT PROMOTING SUSTAINABLE AND INCLUSIVE TRANSPORTATION AND MOBILITY, STRENGTHENING PUBLIC AND ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEMS, AND PROVIDING FOR INTEGRATED AND EFFICIENT MOBILITY OPTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Heto na naman sa EDSA kahabaan But I'm riding on I keep riding hard Kita nang siksikan ba‘t mo pa pinagpilitan But I'm riding on I keep riding hard (from Edsa song by Pablo) Mobility is not merely about moving vehicles. It is about enabling people to reach their work, schools, hospitals, markets, and communities safely, affordably, and efficiently. For millions of Filipinos, however, daily mobility remains defined by long travel times, traffic congestion, inadequate public transportation, unsafe or disconnected sidewalks, limited bicycle facilities, and transport systems that too often prioritize vehicles over people. The consequences go beyond inconvenience: congestion consumes productive time, transport costs burden household incomes, air pollution affects public health, and poor mobility limits access to economic and social opportunities. The country therefore needs to move beyond a transportation policy centered primarily on expanding road capacity and toward a mobility system that provides practical, safe, and accessible alternatives to private motor vehicles. This measure promotes walking, cycling, public transportation, water- based transportation, bus rapid transit, intermodal connectivity, and other sustainable modes as integral components of the country’s transportation system. It provides for safer walkways and bicycle networks, improved public transportation standards, travel demand management, bicycle parking, integrated mobility facilities, and national and local sustainable transportation plans. The bill recognizes that sustainable transportation cannot be achieved through isolated projects. Mobility must be planned as a connected system, RECEIVED coordinated with land use, public services, economic activity, environmental objectives, and the actual needs of communities. It therefore promotes maintenance, climate resilience, local government capacity building, and the responsible use of public and private financing. Ultimately, this measure seeks to ensure that Filipinos have real, safe, convenient, affordable, and accessible choices. When public transportation is reliable, walking is safe, cycling is practical, and different modes are properly connected, sustainable transportation becomes a viable choice rather than a sacrifice. A people-centered mobility system can help reduce congestion, improve air quality, promote physical activity, ease transportation burdens, expand access to jobs and essential services, and strengthen community resilience. Transportation infrastructure should bring people closer to opportunity— not keep them trapped in traffic. Every Filipino deserves to move safely, efficiently, affordably, and with dignity. label: HB 11837
title: AN ACT ENHANCING TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE THROUGH THE PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE MONITORING SYSTEM (PIMS) AND MANDATORY TIMELAPSE DOCUMENTATION FOR ALL PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public infrastructure consumes billions of pesos in public funds and leaves a permanent footprint on the lives of Filipinos. Every road, bridge, school building, flood control structure, water facility, port, airport, and other public work represents a public investment that must deliver what was promised, when it was promised, and at the quality for which the government paid. Yet accountability in infrastructure cannot depend solely on what appears in contracts, accomplishment reports, inspection certificates, or financial records. There must also be reliable evidence of what actually happened at the project site. This is the accountability gap that this measure seeks to address. The government should not have to rely exclusively on periodic reports to know whether a project is progressing as scheduled. Citizens should not have to wait unti! a project is completed—or until an audit is conducted—to discover that a project was delayed, substantially deviated from its approved plan, or failed to deliver the expected physical output. Modern technology makes it possible to close this gap. Hence, this bill establishes the Public Infrastructure Monitoring System (PIMS), a government digital platform that will provide continuous, verifiable, and accessible documentation of covered public infrastructure projects. It requires contractors to maintain and submit timelapse documentation and project implementation data, while requiring implementing agencies to establish project baselines, disclose planned and actual accomplishments, document material changes, and make project information accessible through public dashboards. More importantly, the measure connects information with accountability. PIMS will enable government and the public to compare what was planned with what was actually accomplished; identify delays and material variances; preserve a chronological record of project implementation; generate compliance alerts; facilitate risk-based verification; and provide reliable electronic records for auditing, investigation, and other lawful government proceedings. This is not simply a transparency measure. It is a_ preventive accountability mechanism. The objective is to identify problems while they can still be corrected—not only after public funds have already been spent and the opportunity for corrective action has passed. By making project implementation more visible and verifiable, the measure seeks to strengthen existing procurement, engineering, financial management, and auditing safeguards and make it more difficult for irregularities to remain hidden behind paper reports. At the same time, the bill recognizes that technology must not become another source of bureaucracy or unnecessary expense. It therefore requires interoperability with existing government systems, technology-neutral standards, cybersecurity and data protection safeguards, risk-based monitoring, and mechanisms for emergencies and connectivity failures. It likewise preserves the constitutional and statutory mandates of the Commission on Audit and other oversight institutions. Public money deserves public accountability. A government that can digitally track financial transactions, procurements, and other government activities should likewise be capable of showing the public the physical progress of the infrastructure it finances. The PIMS seeks to make that principle operational: what government funds, government should be able to monitor; what government builds, the public should be able to see; and what government reports, authorized oversight bodies should be able to verify. Through this measure, transparency is transformed from a passive disclosure requirement into an active system of monitoring, verification, early warning, and accountability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. - reas lk 8 trees Kababaihan Kabalikatan para sa Kapakanan at Kaunlaran ng Bayan (4K) Party-list Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City ® TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session House BiLLNo. _11837 Introduced by: Kababaihan Kabalikatan para sa Kapakanan at Kaunlaran ng Bayan (4K) Party-list Representative Iris Marie D. label: HB 11838
title: AN ACT DECLARING A ONE-TIME AMNESTY ON ALL UNPAID INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES IMPOSED BY THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT FOR TAXABLE YEAR 2024 AND PRIOR YEARS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2018, Republic Act No. 10963, otherwise known as the “Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Act,” was enacted as a landmark measure to reform the country’s tax system and make it more equitable, efficient, and responsive to the needs of a growing economy. To complement these reforms, Republic Act No. 11213, otherwise known as the “Tax Amnesty Act,” was signed into law on February 14, 2019. The law sought to serve a two-fold purpose: first, to provide taxpayers with an opportunity for a fresh start by allowing them to settle outstanding tax liabilities under more reasonable terms; and second, to strengthen tax administration and revenue collection by broadening the tax base and encouraging taxpayers to fulfill their obligations to the State. The Tax Amnesty Act, however, did not fully accomplish its intended scope. The President vetoed the provisions granting general amnesty for all unpaid internal revenue taxes, citing the absence of sufficient safeguards and mechanisms to prevent tax evasion and protect the integrity of the tax system. The veto underscored a fundamental principle: while the State may extend opportunities for taxpayers to settle their obligations, tax amnesty must never become an avenue for concealing wealth, evading lawful taxes, or undermining the fairness and integrity of tax administration. The need to strengthen the country’s tax system was further recognized with the enactment in 2024 of Republic Act No. 11976, otherwise known as the “Ease of Paying Taxes (EOPT) Act.” The law seeks to modernize and streamline tax administration, make compliance more efficient and convenient, and ultimately foster greater voluntary compliance among taxpayers. By simplifying processes and improving the administration of tax obligations, the EOPT Act recognizes that a fair and effective tax system must not only enforce compliance but must also make compliance clear, accessible, and achievable. Complementing these reforms, Republic Act No. 12066, otherwise known as the “CREATE MORE Act,” was enacted to further improve the country’s investment and tax environment. Among the rationales for its enactment was the need to clarify inconsistencies between Republic Act No. 11534, otherwise known as the “Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises (CREATE) Act,” and its implementing rules and regulations— inconsistencies that resulted in the imposition of penalties upon Registered Business Enterprises that, in certain instances, were affected by or relied upon conflicting or unclear requirements. These successive reforms reflect the continuing effort of the State to build a tax system founded upon fairness, efficiency, clarity, accountability, and voluntary compliance. Yet reforms in tax policy and administration must be accompanied by measures that allow taxpayers to correct past noncompliance and re-enter the tax system without carrying indefinitely the burdens of penalties and interest arising from past tax liabilities. It is in this context that the General Tax Amnesty Act of 2026 is hereby proposed. The measure seeks to complement the reforms introduced by the EOPT Act and support the objectives of the CREATE MORE Act by encouraging taxpayers to voluntarily comply with their tax obligations. It provides a reasonable opportunity for taxpayers to settle unpaid taxes by granting relief from the penalties and interest that have accumulated on such obligations, thereby removing barriers that may otherwise discourage taxpayers from coming forward and regularizing their tax affairs. The proposed general tax amnesty, however, is not intended to be a blanket forgiveness of tax obligations without accountability. The measure incorporates safeguards designed to address precisely the concerns that previously prevented the enactment of a general tax amnesty. It seeks to strike a careful balance between extending a genuine opportunity for taxpayers to make a fresh start and protecting the integrity of the tax system against abuse. Accordingly, the bill incorporates measures relating to the lifting of bank secrecy under appropriate circumstances, the automatic exchange of information, and the imposition of penalties for untruthful declarations of net worth or total assets. These safeguards are intended to strengthen the capacity of the government to detect concealment, discourage tax evasion, and ensure that the benefits of the amnesty are extended only within a framework of transparency and accountability. The enhanced general tax amnesty program envisioned under this measure therefore seeks to achieve a principled balance: to give taxpayers a meaningful opportunity to settle their obligations and begin anew, while ensuring that such opportunity does not come at the expense of the integrity, fairness, and credibility of the tax system. A tax amnesty, properly designed, should not weaken the State’s capacity to collect revenues. Rather, it should serve as a bridge toward greater voluntary compliance, a broader and more transparent tax base, and a more efficient system of tax administration. By pairing meaningful relief with stronger safeguards against evasion and concealment, this measure seeks to transform the opportunity for a clean slate into a renewed commitment to compliance. In this manner, the proposed General Tax Amnesty Act of 2025 complements the continuing modernization of the Philippine tax system and advances the broader objective of building a culture in which taxpayers can comply with their obligations with greater certainty, fairness, and confidence, while the government exercises its taxing power with transparency, integrity, and accountability. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. - IRIS MA D. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING, INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE STRATEGY FOR PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Beyond frequent earthquakes and voicanic eruptions, an average of 20 typhoons make landfall every year in the Philippines; this leads to significant losses and damages to properties. The government as an institution is certainly not immune to losses and damages in public infrastructures. Public asset insurance serves as a vital "last line of defense" for disaster resilience. Between 2013 and 2017, the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) paid P3.7 billion in claims for government property damages, including P1.3 billion indemnified for Typhoon Yolanda alone—highlighting both the role and necessity of expanding disaster risk financing to cover total asset exposure.* While Republic Act No. 10121 (The Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010) successfully shifted the country’s disaster policy from reactive disaster response to proactive risk reduction and preparedness, a significant structural gap remains: the absence of a multi-layered, pre-arranged financial protection system for state-owned physical assets.’ To bridge this gap, this measure seeks to create a Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council that will, among others, develop a framework to ensure streamlined, seamless, responsive, and timely financing for disaster-related repair, reconstruction, mitigation, and rehabilitation of government-owned infrastructure assets through both insurance and non-insurance financing mechanisms. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. rc IRIS MARIE D. label: HB 11840
title: AN ACT PROMOTING BUSINESS CONTINUITY AND ENTERPRISE RESILIENCE THROUGH THE STRENGTHENING OF MICROINSURANCE MUTUAL BENEFIT ASSOCIATIONS AND THE EXPANSION OF WNON-LIFE MICROINSURANCE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For millions of Filipino microentrepreneurs, a small business is more than a source of income—it is the foundation of a family’s livelihood. A sari-sari store, a small eatery, a home-based enterprise, a tricycle, a fishing boat, a set of livelihood tools, or a farmer’s crop inventory may represent years of savings, sacrifice, and hard work. These productive assets allow families to earn, provide for their needs, employ others, serve their communities, and build a more secure future. Yet the very livelihood that sustains a family can be placed at risk by a single unexpected event. A typhoon can destroy crops or business inventory. A flood can damage equipment and facilities. A fire can wipe out a small store in a matter of hours. A disease outbreak, accident, livestock loss, or other emergency can deprive a family of its ability to earn. Sudden disruptions in supply, markets, or other economic conditions can likewise interrupt business operations and erode already limited working capital. For a large enterprise, such losses may be absorbed through financial reserves, diversified assets, or conventional insurance. For a microenterprise, however, the same loss can mean the loss of the family’s principal source of income. Without adequate protection, recovery may require borrowing, selling productive assets, reducing household necessities, or abandoning the enterprise altogether. What took years to build can be lost in a single event—and rebuilding can push a family deeper into debt. This is why supporting our microentrepreneurs must go beyond helping them start a business. We must also help them protect what they have built, keep their enterprises operating, and recover when unexpected shocks occur. Enterprise development must therefore include not only access to capital, markets, skills, and technology, but also practical and affordable mechanisms for managing the risks that can threaten a livelihood. The bill seeks to address this gap by promoting greater access to appropriate non-life microinsurance and other risk-protection mechanisms for microentrepreneurs. It recognizes that risk protection should be understandable, affordable, accessible, and responsive to the actual circumstances of micro and small enterprises and the communities they serve. To achieve this, the bill strengthens the role of the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), particularly through its Negosyo Centers and other appropriate enterprise-support mechanisms, in providing information on available risk-protection options and facilitating referrals to appropriate organizations and providers. The measure enables Negosyo Centers to serve as accessible points of information and referral so that microentrepreneurs are better equipped to make informed decisions about protecting their livelihoods. The bill likewise recognizes Microinsurance Mutual Benefit Associations (Mi-MBAs) as important partners in promoting business continuity, enterprise resilience, and livelihood protection. By strengthening their sustainability, governance, operational capacity, and ability to provide appropriate microinsurance and other risk-protection products and services, the measure seeks to ensure that these community-based institutions are better positioned to serve the people who depend upon them. The measure also promotes stronger coordination among government agencies, microfinance and enterprise-support institutions, local stakeholders, and risk-protection providers. Through greater awareness, appropriate product development, digital and accessible delivery mechanisms, and_ stronger consumer and member protection, the bill seeks to make risk protection a more practical component of enterprise development rather than a resource available only to those who can afford conventional insurance. Ultimately, a resilient microenterprise is a more secure livelihood, and a protected livelihood gives a family a better chance to recover without losing everything it has worked to build. By helping microentrepreneurs understand and access appropriate risk protection, and by strengthening the institutions that provide and facilitate such protection, this measure seeks to reduce the economic consequences of unexpected shocks, support faster recovery, and help ensure that temporary setbacks do not become permanent losses of livelihood. In protecting the productive assets of our microentrepreneurs, we are not merely protecting businesses. We are protecting incomes, families, communities, and the opportunity for ordinary Filipinos to build a better future through their own work and enterprise. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. nf enced Wasbres Kababaihan Kabalikatan para sa Kapakanan at Kaunlaran ng Bayan (4K) Party-iist Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session HOUSE BILL NO. 11849 Introduced by: Kababaihan Kabalikatan para sa Kapakanan at Kauntaran ng Bayan (4K) Party-list Representative Iris Marie D.
